lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise causal argument with one obvious gap: the lozenge's effect must explain the recoveries rather than the illness resolving on its own.
lr.stimulus: Pediatrician: Every child in our clinic who received the new antiviral lozenge recovered from the sore throat within four days. So the lozenge must be effective at curing this type of sore throat.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the pediatrician's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The children would not have recovered within four days without taking the lozenge.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No other antiviral treatment cures sore throats more quickly than the lozenge does.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The lozenge has been tested in clinics other than the pediatrician's.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sore throats of this type are caused by a virus rather than by bacteria.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every child who took the lozenge followed the dosing instructions exactly.

explanations.correct: The argument credits the lozenge for the recoveries. If the children would have recovered anyway in the same timeframe, the lozenge did nothing. Negating A destroys the inference.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument claims the lozenge works, not that it is the fastest available treatment.
explanations.C: Out of scope — external replication is not a link in the pediatrician's reasoning.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — the argument is about whether the lozenge cures these sore throats, not about their underlying cause.
explanations.E: Defender disguised as strengthener — compliance would bolster the argument, but the pediatrician observed recoveries regardless of strict adherence.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise ethical argument with one clear gap linking the premise's category (promise under duress) to the conclusion's category (contract under threat).
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: A promise made under duress is not morally binding. Thus, the contract Mara signed while being threatened by her employer imposes no moral obligation on her.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mara's employer will face legal consequences for threatening her.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A contract signed under threatening conditions counts as a promise made under duress.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No contract is ever morally binding if one party benefits more than the other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mara intended to break the contract from the moment she signed it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Contracts and promises differ in the legal obligations they create.

explanations.correct: The premise speaks of promises under duress; the conclusion is about a contract signed under threat. Without the bridge that such a contract qualifies as a promise made under duress, the premise does not reach the conclusion.
explanations.A: Out of scope — the argument is about moral obligation, not legal consequences for the employer.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — introduces a sweeping rule about benefit that the argument does not need.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — Mara's intent is irrelevant to whether the contract binds her morally.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the ethicist's claim concerns moral, not legal, force.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward economic analogy argument with one evident gap — conditions responsible for the cited town's outcome must carry over.
lr.stimulus: Economist: When the neighboring town of Parrish raised its minimum wage last year, overall consumer spending in Parrish rose within six months. If our town raises its minimum wage by a similar amount, consumer spending here will also rise within six months.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the economist's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Parrish's minimum-wage increase was the largest in the region that year.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumer spending is the most important indicator of a town's economic health.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No economic conditions unique to Parrish were responsible for the rise in spending there.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every business in our town supports raising the minimum wage.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Our town has a larger population than Parrish does.

explanations.correct: The analogy needs the Parrish result to transfer. If something peculiar to Parrish caused the rise there, the inference to our town collapses. Negating C destroys the argument.
explanations.A: Out of scope — magnitude rank does not connect Parrish's outcome to ours.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument does not claim spending is the most important indicator, only that it will rise.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — business support is not a link in the economist's causal chain.
explanations.E: Reversed direction — if anything, the argument would prefer similarity of size, not a size difference.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise legal argument with one obvious gap linking a statutory category to the specific case at issue.
lr.stimulus: Attorney: The statute prohibits any commercial use of the public fountain. My client used the fountain as the backdrop for a paid photography shoot. Therefore, my client violated the statute.
lr.questionStem: The attorney's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: using the fountain as a backdrop for a paid photography shoot is a commercial use of the fountain

choices.label: B
choices.text: the statute has been enforced against other photographers in the past

choices.label: C
choices.text: the client was aware of the statute at the time of the photo shoot

choices.label: D
choices.text: no public official granted the client permission to use the fountain

choices.label: E
choices.text: the fountain is the only public landmark covered by the statute

explanations.correct: The statute prohibits commercial use; the conclusion asserts a violation. Unless the photo shoot counts as commercial use, the premise cannot reach the conclusion. Negating A breaks the argument.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Out of scope — past enforcement patterns are not part of the reasoning.
explanations.C: Shift in subject — the argument turns on what the client did, not on what the client knew.
explanations.D: Defender disguised as strengthener — permission would rebut the charge, but the argument does not need to rule it out to connect its premise to its conclusion.
explanations.E: Out of scope — coverage of other landmarks is irrelevant to whether this use violated the statute.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise causal inference with one obvious chronological alternative that must be ruled out.
lr.stimulus: Ecologist: Populations of the spotted salamander have declined sharply in ponds where a certain pesticide has been detected. So the pesticide must be responsible for the decline of the spotted salamander in those ponds.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the ecologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The pesticide was present in these ponds before the salamander populations began to decline.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The pesticide is more harmful to salamanders than to any other amphibian.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Salamander populations have not declined in any pond where the pesticide is absent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The pesticide will eventually cause the salamander to become extinct.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulators intend to ban the pesticide in response to the ecologist's findings.

explanations.correct: For the pesticide to be responsible, it must have been present before the decline, not after. Negate A — the pesticide arrived after the decline — and it cannot be the cause.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument only claims the pesticide is responsible in these ponds, not that it is uniquely harmful.
explanations.C: Too strong — the argument does not need declines to happen exclusively in pesticide ponds; other causes elsewhere are allowed.
explanations.D: Out of scope — extinction projections are not part of the inference.
explanations.E: Out of scope — regulatory response is unrelated to whether the pesticide caused the observed decline.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise inference from a test result to a product property, with one evident gap about what the test actually measures.
lr.stimulus: Reviewer: The new laptop ran every benchmark program we tried without slowing down once. So this laptop is powerful enough for any task our readers are likely to perform.
lr.questionStem: The reviewer's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The benchmark programs collectively demand at least as much of the laptop as any task the readers are likely to perform.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The laptop is priced within the range most readers can afford.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No other laptop on the market outperformed this one on the benchmarks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Benchmark programs have improved significantly over the past decade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most readers have previously owned a laptop from the same manufacturer.

explanations.correct: The conclusion extrapolates from benchmarks to real-world tasks. Without the assumption that the benchmarks are at least as demanding as those tasks, the benchmark success tells us nothing about readers' tasks.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Out of scope — price is not linked to the laptop's power.
explanations.C: Too strong — the conclusion is about sufficiency for readers' tasks, not about ranking among competitors.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — trend data on benchmarks is not used by the argument.
explanations.E: Out of scope — prior ownership has no bearing on the laptop's capability.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise dating inference with one obvious gap: the inscription and the tablet must be contemporaneous.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: The inscription on this stone tablet is written in Old Phrygian, and every known Old Phrygian inscription dates from between the 8th and 4th centuries BCE. Therefore, this tablet dates from between the 8th and 4th centuries BCE.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the linguist's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No language other than Old Phrygian used a writing system that resembled the one on the tablet.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The inscription was not added to the tablet long after the tablet itself was made.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most Old Phrygian inscriptions are found on stone rather than on other materials.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tablet was discovered in a region where Old Phrygian was spoken.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Old Phrygian is closely related to the language now called Modern Phrygian.

explanations.correct: The inscription's date only dates the tablet if the two were made at the same time. Negate B — the inscription was added much later — and the tablet itself could be far older or younger than the inscription.
explanations.A: Defender disguised as strengthener — misidentification would undermine the argument, but the stimulus already stipulates the inscription is in Old Phrygian.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Out of scope — typical material of Old Phrygian inscriptions is irrelevant to this tablet's date.
explanations.D: Out of scope — where the tablet was found is not a link in the dating inference.
explanations.E: Shift in subject — a relationship to a modern language has no bearing on the dating of Old Phrygian inscriptions.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise historical inference with one obvious gap about what the document actually reports.
lr.stimulus: Historian: A letter written by General Halpern on June 3, 1794, describes his troops marching through the town of Valcour that morning. Therefore, Halpern's troops were in Valcour on June 3, 1794.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Halpern's letter accurately describes where his troops were on the day it was written.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Halpern personally marched alongside his troops as they passed through Valcour.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No other general's troops were in Valcour on June 3, 1794.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Halpern wrote letters describing his troops' movements on most days of the campaign.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The town of Valcour was strategically important to both sides in the conflict.

explanations.correct: The argument treats the letter as a reliable report. If the letter misstates where the troops were that morning, the conclusion does not follow. Negating A destroys the inference.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Shift in subject — Halpern's personal location is not what the conclusion claims.
explanations.C: Out of scope — the argument does not require Halpern's troops to be the only ones present.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the historian needs one accurate letter, not a pattern of letter-writing.
explanations.E: Out of scope — strategic importance has nothing to do with where the troops actually were.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise policy argument with one clear gap between program goal and program adoption.
lr.stimulus: City planner: Residents have said repeatedly that their top priority is reducing traffic congestion downtown. The proposed congestion-pricing plan would reduce traffic congestion downtown. Therefore, the city should adopt the congestion-pricing plan.
lr.questionStem: The city planner's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The city should adopt any plan that advances residents' top priority.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Congestion pricing has successfully reduced traffic in every city that has tried it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Residents would be willing to pay significantly higher fees to drive downtown.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The plan would reduce congestion more effectively than any alternative the city is considering.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The planner was hired specifically to address downtown traffic congestion.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from a plan that advances residents' top priority to the conclusion that the city should adopt it. Without a principle connecting those two, the premises do not support the conclusion. Negating A blocks the inference.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument does not require universal success, only that this plan will reduce congestion.
explanations.C: Out of scope — willingness to pay is not invoked in the reasoning.
explanations.D: Too strong — the planner claims the plan should be adopted, not that it is the best available option.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the planner's hiring is not a link in the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise attribution argument with one obvious gap linking stylistic features to authorship.
lr.stimulus: Art historian: The brushwork on this newly examined landscape displays all the distinctive features of Vermeer's known paintings. So this landscape was painted by Vermeer.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the art historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No painter other than Vermeer produces brushwork displaying all the distinctive features of Vermeer's known paintings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vermeer painted more landscapes than any other subject during his career.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The landscape was found in a location where Vermeer is known to have worked.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The canvas and pigments used in the landscape are consistent with those available in Vermeer's lifetime.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Art historians can identify any painting's creator on the basis of brushwork alone.

explanations.correct: The argument infers Vermeer's authorship from brushwork features. If another painter could produce the same distinctive features, the inference fails. Negating A destroys the argument.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Out of scope — the frequency of Vermeer's landscapes does not help link this painting's brushwork to him.
explanations.C: Defender disguised as strengthener — location would bolster attribution, but the stylistic argument does not depend on it.
explanations.D: Defender disguised as strengthener — material consistency would support the attribution, but it is not what the brushwork inference turns on.
explanations.E: Too strong — the argument claims this painting is a Vermeer, not that brushwork alone identifies every painting.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise argument with one obvious gap. The argument infers illness from symptom without considering alternative causes.
lr.stimulus: Physician: All patients who came to my clinic with persistent cough were treated with antibiotics. Every one of them recovered within two weeks. Therefore, the antibiotics must have caused the recovery.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the physician's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibiotics are the only available treatment for persistent cough.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The patients' recovery would not have occurred without the antibiotic treatment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Persistent cough is a serious condition that requires medical intervention.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two weeks is the typical time frame for recovery from any illness treated with antibiotics.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The patients followed the physician's treatment instructions exactly.

explanations.correct: The argument assumes that without antibiotics, recovery would not have happened. If negated—the patients could have recovered without treatment—the conclusion that antibiotics caused the recovery falls apart.
explanations.A: Too strong; the argument needs only that this treatment worked, not that it's the only option.
explanations.C: Irrelevant to whether antibiotics caused the recovery.
explanations.D: Timeline support is not required; the argument just needs the causal link.
explanations.E: Patient compliance is not part of the causal claim being made.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple one-premise argument with gap between observation and conclusion about categorization.
lr.stimulus: Economist: The stock market rose sharply after the new tax policy was announced. Therefore, investors believe the new policy is good for the economy.
lr.questionStem: The economist's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: A rising stock market is always a reliable indicator of economic health.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The rise in the stock market was caused by investor belief in the policy's positive effects.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The new tax policy will actually improve the economy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Investors always behave rationally when trading stocks.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No other factors besides the tax policy announcement caused the stock market to rise.

explanations.correct: The argument links the market rise to investor belief about the policy. Negate B: if the rise was not caused by belief in the policy, the inference collapses. B is necessary.
explanations.A: Too broad; the argument is about what investors believe, not general reliability.
explanations.C: The argument is about investor belief, not actual economic outcomes.
explanations.D: Rationality is not required; investors could believe for any reason.
explanations.E: Out of scope—the argument is about the link between policy and belief, not about competing causes.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Direct single-premise argument with transparent gap between observation and categorical claim.
lr.stimulus: Literary critic: Every novel by Martinez that I have read is beautifully written. Therefore, all of Martinez's novels are beautifully written.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Martinez has written more novels than the critic has read.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The critic's personal taste in literature is shared by most readers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The novels the critic has read are representative of Martinez's entire body of work.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Beauty in writing is an objective quality that can be measured.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The critic is more knowledgeable about literature than other critics.

explanations.correct: To infer all novels from some novels, the read sample must be representative. Negate C: the read novels are not representative—then the conclusion doesn't follow. C is necessary.
explanations.A: Confirms the gap but is not itself the assumption bridging it.
explanations.B: Reader agreement is irrelevant to whether all of Martinez's novels are beautiful.
explanations.D: Objectivity of beauty is not required for the inference.
explanations.E: The critic's standing relative to others is out of scope.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise argument drawing a causal conclusion from mere correlation.
lr.stimulus: Nutritionist: People who eat more leafy green vegetables have lower rates of heart disease. Therefore, eating leafy greens prevents heart disease.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in developed nations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People who eat leafy greens do not differ from others in ways that independently reduce heart disease risk.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leafy green vegetables contain more nutrients than any other type of vegetable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A diet of only leafy greens would prevent heart disease entirely.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The correlation between leafy greens and lower heart disease has been observed in all populations.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from correlation to causation. B assumes no confounding variables (e.g., leafy-green eaters exercise more). Negate B: they do differ in independent ways—then the greens may not be the cause. B is necessary.
explanations.A: Prevalence of heart disease is not relevant to the causal claim.
explanations.C: Nutrient density relative to other vegetables is irrelevant.
explanations.D: Too strong; the argument needs only that greens help, not that they're sufficient.
explanations.E: Universal correlation is not required; the argument concerns a general causal relationship.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple argument with transparent gap between two premises and conclusion about attribution.
lr.stimulus: Detective: The theft occurred while the store was closed. The only employee with a key is Rosa. Therefore, Rosa committed the theft.
lr.questionStem: The detective's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rosa was in the store when the theft occurred.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Theft is a more serious crime than other offenses Rosa might have committed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No one other than Rosa could have had access to the store.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rosa had a motive to steal from the store.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The store's security system was not functioning at the time of the theft.

explanations.correct: For access to imply culpability, no one else could have accessed the store. Negate C: others could have accessed it—then access doesn't point to Rosa. C is necessary.
explanations.A: Presence during the theft is confirmed by C without being explicitly stated.
explanations.B: Crime severity is irrelevant to identifying the perpetrator.
explanations.D: Motive is not part of the access-based reasoning.
explanations.E: Security status is out of scope; the argument is about key access.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward inference from one premise to conclusion, with a single implicit assumption.
lr.stimulus: Engineer: The bridge's steel cables have not been inspected in ten years. Therefore, the bridge is unsafe and must be closed.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Steel cables that have not been inspected for ten years are likely to have developed defects.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The bridge was safe when the cables were last inspected ten years ago.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Regular inspection of steel cables can prevent all bridge failures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No bridge with uninspected cables has ever remained safe for long.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bridge closures are the only effective way to prevent accidents.

explanations.correct: The argument links lack of inspection to unsafety. This requires assuming that uninspected cables are likely defective. Negate A: old cables could be fine—then the inference to unsafety fails. A is necessary.
explanations.B: Historical safety status is not what the argument depends on.
explanations.C: Prevention of all failures is too strong; the argument needs only that inspection matters.
explanations.D: Absolutist claim not required; the argument needs only that uninspected cables pose risk.
explanations.E: Whether closure is the only remedy is irrelevant to whether the bridge is unsafe.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Basic argument with one premise and a conclusion that requires bridging a simple conceptual gap.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Children who grow up hearing two languages learn to read earlier than children exposed to only one language. Thus, bilingualism helps children develop reading skills.
lr.questionStem: The linguist's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: Learning two languages is more difficult than learning one language.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Early reading ability is causally linked to later academic success.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The early reading advantage of bilingual children is due to their bilingual exposure, not other factors.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bilingual parents are more attentive to their children's education than monolingual parents.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reading is more important than other language skills in child development.

explanations.correct: The argument infers causation from a correlation between bilingualism and early reading. C rules out confounds (educated parents, socioeconomic factors). Negate C: the advantage comes from other factors—then bilingualism doesn't help. C is necessary.
explanations.A: Difficulty level is irrelevant to whether bilingualism helps.
explanations.B: Later outcomes are not part of the argument's reasoning.
explanations.D: Parental attentiveness is a potential confound, but the argument doesn't explicitly address it.
explanations.E: Relative importance of reading vs. other skills is out of scope.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise inference with an obvious and testable gap via negation.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Ancient Rome's collapse was caused by barbarian invasions. Rome had no standing armies large enough to repel them. Therefore, Rome was doomed once the invasions began.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Barbarian invasions were unexpected by Roman leadership.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rome could not have successfully defended itself against the invasions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Barbarian invasions were the primary cause of Rome's decline in other ancient civilizations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Military technology favored the barbarians over the Romans.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rome had previously repelled invasions using the same military forces.

explanations.correct: The argument claims inadequate armies meant doom. This assumes the armies could not have succeeded. Negate B: Rome could have defended—then insufficient army size doesn't doom the state. B is necessary.
explanations.A: Expectation is irrelevant to capability.
explanations.C: Other civilizations' experiences are out of scope.
explanations.D: Technology advantage is one possible reason but not a necessary assumption.
explanations.E: Past success is not required; previous repulsion doesn't determine future capability.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward argument with one evident gap between evidence and categorical conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientist: Wetlands in the region have been drained to build housing developments. Species that depend on wetlands are now disappearing. Therefore, the loss of wetlands is causing the species decline.
lr.questionStem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Housing developments are built with no concern for environmental impact.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The species' disappearance is not caused by hunting, pollution, or other factors unrelated to wetland loss.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Wetlands are more important to species survival than any other type of habitat.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All species in the region depend on wetlands for their survival.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Housing developments cause more habitat loss than any other human activity.

explanations.correct: The argument infers causation from temporal and ecological correlation. B assumes no confounding causes. Negate B: other factors cause the decline—then wetland loss isn't the cause. B is necessary.
explanations.A: Developer intent is irrelevant to the causal claim.
explanations.C: Relative importance is not required; wetlands need only be relevant.
explanations.D: All species need not depend on wetlands; the argument concerns species that do.
explanations.E: Comparative impact of development vs. other activities is out of scope.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple inference from policy implementation to expected outcome, with a clear causal assumption.
lr.stimulus: Policy advisor: The city implemented a curfew for teenagers. Youth crime has since decreased by 20 percent. Therefore, the curfew reduced youth crime.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 20 percent decrease in youth crime is significant enough to warrant the curfew policy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Youth crime would not have decreased by 20 percent without the curfew.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Curfews are more effective at reducing crime than other police interventions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The decrease in youth crime affected all demographic groups equally.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Police enforcement of the curfew was consistent throughout the city.

explanations.correct: To attribute the crime decrease to the curfew, the argument must assume the decrease wouldn't have happened otherwise. Negate B: crime would have fallen anyway—then the curfew didn't cause the decrease. B is necessary.
explanations.A: Significance is a separate evaluative question, not a causal assumption.
explanations.C: Relative effectiveness vs. alternatives is out of scope.
explanations.D: Equal demographic impact is not required for the causal inference.
explanations.E: Consistency of enforcement affects strength but not the causal logic itself.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise argument with one obvious gap. The doctor concludes the medication works because patients recovered, but assumes they would not have recovered without it.
lr.stimulus: Cardiologist: All patients with heart arrhythmia who took the new medication recovered within two weeks. We can therefore conclude that the medication is effective.
lr.questionStem: The cardiologist's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: patients with heart arrhythmia cannot recover on their own

choices.label: B
choices.text: the new medication is less expensive than existing treatments

choices.label: C
choices.text: heart arrhythmia is the most common cardiac condition

choices.label: D
choices.text: two weeks is a reasonable amount of time for recovery

choices.label: E
choices.text: all medications have some side effects

explanations.correct: The argument depends on the recovery being due to the medication. If patients could have recovered without it, then recovery alone does not prove effectiveness. So the argument must assume that recovery would not have occurred naturally.
explanations.A: Correct. Negating this (patients *could* recover on their own) undercuts the causal claim.
explanations.B: Cost is irrelevant to efficacy; this is out of scope.
explanations.C: Prevalence of the condition has no bearing on whether the medication works.
explanations.D: The reasonableness of the timeframe is not required for the efficacy claim.
explanations.E: The existence of side effects elsewhere does not affect this argument's validity.

lr.difficultyReason: Direct logical gap: the speaker concludes a policy will lower emissions but assumes the policy actually creates the stated incentive.
lr.stimulus: Environmental economist: The government's new carbon tax will lower industrial emissions because it makes polluting more expensive, and companies respond to financial incentives.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the carbon tax will not harm low-income workers

choices.label: B
choices.text: companies will view the carbon tax as a genuine financial disincentive to pollute

choices.label: C
choices.text: industrial pollution is the leading cause of climate change

choices.label: D
choices.text: no other country has ever implemented a carbon tax

choices.label: E
choices.text: the government has consulted with environmental scientists

explanations.correct: The economist's reasoning is: tax → financial disincentive → companies respond → lower emissions. This chain assumes companies will actually perceive and act on the tax as a disincentive. If they don't view it that way, the mechanism breaks.
explanations.A: Distributional fairness is a separate policy question; the efficacy of the tax does not depend on it.
explanations.B: Correct. Without this assumption, companies might ignore or discount the tax.
explanations.C: The argument is about reducing industrial emissions, not ranking climate causes.
explanations.D: Other countries' policies do not affect whether this tax works.
explanations.E: Consultation with scientists is not required for the tax to achieve its economic effect.

lr.difficultyReason: One clear gap: the speaker infers quality from a single observable fact and assumes that fact reliably indicates quality.
lr.stimulus: Art dealer: The newly discovered painting bears the artist's signature and was found in her estate. Therefore, it is an authentic work by her.
lr.questionStem: The art dealer's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the artist never signed paintings that were not her own work

choices.label: B
choices.text: paintings found in an artist's estate are always valuable

choices.label: C
choices.text: the artist lived during the twentieth century

choices.label: D
choices.text: forgeries of the artist's work are rare in the market

choices.label: E
choices.text: the artist kept all her completed paintings in her estate

explanations.correct: The dealer uses signature + estate location as proof of authenticity. This only works if a genuine signature is not found on forgeries or unsigned works. Negating A (the artist *did* sign non-authentic works) would destroy the inference.
explanations.A: Correct. Without this, the signature proves nothing about authenticity.
explanations.B: Value is independent of whether the argument for authenticity succeeds.
explanations.C: The artist's era does not affect the validity of the signature-based inference.
explanations.D: Rarity of forgeries is not required; even one forgery with her signature would be enough to break the argument.
explanations.E: Whether she kept all paintings is irrelevant to whether this one is authentic.

lr.difficultyReason: Clear causal gap: the speaker attributes a result to a specific cause but must assume that cause is the only operative factor.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Speakers of Language X struggle to distinguish the sounds /l/ and /r/. This is because Language X has no separate phonemes for these sounds. Therefore, language structure determines perception.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Language X is more difficult to learn than English

choices.label: B
choices.text: the inability to distinguish /l/ and /r/ is not due to factors other than phonemic structure

choices.label: C
choices.text: all languages that lack a phonemic distinction are equally difficult

choices.label: D
choices.text: speakers of Language X never hear /l/ and /r/ distinguished in their environment

choices.label: E
choices.text: perception of sounds cannot be improved through training

explanations.correct: The argument infers that language structure (lack of phoneme distinction) causes the perceptual difficulty. This inference requires that no other cause—such as exposure, age of acquisition, or individual hearing variation—accounts for the difficulty.
explanations.A: Overall language difficulty is broader than this specific sound-perception claim.
explanations.B: Correct. If other factors caused the difficulty, structure wouldn't be the determining cause.
explanations.C: Relative difficulty across languages is not required for the causal claim.
explanations.D: Speakers of Language X may hear these sounds outside their language and still fail to distinguish them natively.
explanations.E: Whether training can improve perception later does not affect the current causal attribution.

lr.difficultyReason: Single gap: the speaker uses absence of evidence as evidence of absence, assuming the absence is reliable.
lr.stimulus: Historian: No documents from the medieval period mention a royal decree abolishing trade guilds. Therefore, no such decree was ever issued.
lr.questionStem: The historian's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: medieval trade guilds were not very powerful

choices.label: B
choices.text: if such a decree had been issued, it would have been documented

choices.label: C
choices.text: most medieval documents have been preserved

choices.label: D
choices.text: trade guilds existed throughout the entire medieval period

choices.label: E
choices.text: the monarch had the authority to issue such a decree

explanations.correct: The argument treats the absence of documentary evidence as proof the decree never happened. This only holds if a real decree *would* have been documented. Negating B (the decree might not have been documented) lets the decree exist undocumented, so the argument collapses.
explanations.A: Guild power does not determine whether a decree would be documented.
explanations.B: Correct. Without this, the absence of documents proves nothing.
explanations.C: The assumption is narrower: only that a royal decree (if issued) would be documented, not all documents.
explanations.D: Whether guilds persisted is separate from whether a decree abolishing them occurred.
explanations.E: Formal authority to issue a decree is not required to argue whether it was issued.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward causal inference with one necessary link: the speaker assumes that a measured property reflects what they claim.
lr.stimulus: Psychologist: The study measured cortisol levels in participants before and after meditation. Cortisol levels dropped significantly. We can conclude that meditation reduces stress.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the psychologist's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: cortisol is the only hormone affected by meditation

choices.label: B
choices.text: elevated cortisol levels are a reliable indicator of stress

choices.label: C
choices.text: participants in the study had never meditated before

choices.label: D
choices.text: meditation is more effective than prescription anxiolytics

choices.label: E
choices.text: cortisol levels should be measured in the morning

explanations.correct: The psychologist infers stress reduction from a drop in cortisol. This inference assumes that cortisol drop reflects stress reduction—i.e., that elevated cortisol indicates stress. Without this, a cortisol drop could be meaningless to the stress claim.
explanations.A: Other hormones need not be affected; only cortisol's relationship to stress matters.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument chains cortisol-drop to stress-reduction via this link.
explanations.C: Prior meditation history does not affect the current meditation→cortisol drop inference.
explanations.D: Comparative effectiveness versus other treatments is outside the argument's scope.
explanations.E: Measurement timing is not required for the causal claim itself.

lr.difficultyReason: One clear assumption: the speaker uses a definition or category membership to make an inference and assumes that category assignment is correct.
lr.stimulus: Legal scholar: The contract specifies that disputes will be resolved by arbitration. Therefore, the parties cannot bring a lawsuit in court.
lr.questionStem: The scholar's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the parties did not intend to preserve their right to litigate

choices.label: B
choices.text: courts will enforce an arbitration clause by refusing to hear the case

choices.label: C
choices.text: the contract was signed by both parties simultaneously

choices.label: D
choices.text: arbitration is cheaper than litigation

choices.label: E
choices.text: there are no exceptions to the arbitration clause

explanations.correct: The argument infers that an arbitration clause bars court proceedings. This assumes courts will actually enforce the clause by dismissing lawsuits. Without this enforcement assumption, the clause could be unenforceable or ignored.
explanations.A: Intent is subsumed in the clause itself; the argument does not turn on what the parties internally intended.
explanations.B: Correct. The clause's existence alone does not bar litigation unless courts enforce it.
explanations.C: Timing of signing does not affect the clause's meaning or enforceability.
explanations.D: Cost considerations do not determine legal effect.
explanations.E: The argument does not require that the clause is absolute; even limited enforceability would support the conclusion that court suits are barred in most cases.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple inference linking two observable facts; assumes the link is not coincidental.
lr.stimulus: Technology analyst: After the company released version 3.0 of its software, user complaints about lag dropped by 50 percent. Therefore, version 3.0 fixed the lag problem.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: users did not stop using the software after the update

choices.label: B
choices.text: the drop in lag complaints was caused by the release of version 3.0, not by an unrelated change

choices.label: C
choices.text: version 2.0 had more features than version 3.0

choices.label: D
choices.text: the company hired more customer service representatives after the update

choices.label: E
choices.text: users prefer version 3.0 to all previous versions

explanations.correct: The analyst infers causation from temporal sequence: update → complaint drop. This requires that the drop was caused by the update, not by coincidence or some other intervening event (e.g., users switching to a different app, change in reporting platform). Negating B (the drop was due to something else) breaks the causal inference.
explanations.A: User retention is not directly required; the argument concerns complaint reduction.
explanations.B: Correct. Without this, the timing is merely coincidental.
explanations.C: Feature parity between versions does not affect the lag-fix inference.
explanations.D: Customer service staffing does not explain a technical lag fix.
explanations.E: User preference ranking is separate from whether the lag problem was fixed.

lr.difficultyReason: One clear gap: the speaker categorizes something and assumes the category membership has a stated implication.
lr.stimulus: Ethics instructor: All cases of deception that harm others are morally wrong. This business practice is a case of deception that harms consumers. Therefore, this business practice is morally wrong.
lr.questionStem: The instructor's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the business knew the practice would harm consumers

choices.label: B
choices.text: consumers are more vulnerable than other groups

choices.label: C
choices.text: there are no other moral considerations that override the wrongness

choices.label: D
choices.text: the practice does indeed harm consumers

choices.label: E
choices.text: businesses are held to a higher ethical standard than individuals

explanations.correct: The instructor uses categorical logic: if it's deception-that-harms, then it's morally wrong. The conclusion requires that the premise is true—i.e., that the practice actually does harm consumers. If it doesn't harm them, the major premise doesn't apply.
explanations.A: Intent (knowledge) is not required; only that harm actually occurs.
explanations.B: Vulnerability ranking is irrelevant to the moral-wrongness categorization.
explanations.C: The argument does not address competing moral considerations; necessity doesn't extend to it.
explanations.D: Correct. Without this factual premise, the deception doesn't fall under the 'harms-others' category.
explanations.E: Standard of care for businesses vs. individuals is not part of the logical structure.

lr.difficultyReason: Direct causal inference: the speaker links two phenomena and assumes one did not occur without the other.
lr.stimulus: Nutritionist: The study tracked two identical groups of office workers over six months. Group A was given access to a standing desk, while Group B continued using traditional chairs. Group A reported significantly less back pain. Therefore, standing desks reduce back pain.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the nutritionist's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: standing desks are not more expensive than traditional desks

choices.label: B
choices.text: back pain in Group B was not caused by other workplace factors unrelated to desk type

choices.label: C
choices.text: the two groups had no prior differences in back pain history

choices.label: D
choices.text: standing desks are used by most office workers today

choices.label: E
choices.text: sitting in a chair is the primary cause of all back pain

explanations.correct: The argument compares two groups and attributes the difference in back pain outcomes to the desk type. For this comparison to be valid, the groups must have been equivalent at the start. If Group A already had less back pain history, the desk type is not the cause of the observed difference.
explanations.A: Cost does not affect the causal efficacy of the desks.
explanations.B: Other workplace factors in Group B are addressed by the group comparison structure; the assumption concerns initial equivalence, not confounds within groups.
explanations.C: Correct. A controlled experiment (identical groups) requires identical starting conditions.
explanations.D: Current usage rates do not affect the causal inference from the study.
explanations.E: The argument claims desks reduce pain, not that sitting causes all back pain.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise argument with one clear gap. The claim that increased advertising caused sales growth assumes no other factor (seasonal demand, competitor exit, price change) explains the sales increase.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Our company increased its advertising spending by 40% last quarter, and sales revenue rose by 35% during that same period. Therefore, the increased advertising directly caused the rise in sales.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No other factor besides increased advertising contributed to the rise in sales revenue.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The company's competitors did not increase their advertising spending during the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The advertisements reached a large percentage of the target market.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sales revenue had been declining in previous quarters.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The 35% rise in sales was larger than anticipated.

explanations.correct: The argument infers causation from a temporal correlation: ad spending increased, then sales increased. For this inference to hold, the economist must assume that no other factor—seasonal uptick, price reduction, competitor failure, new product feature—explains the sales rise. Negate A: if other factors did contribute, the argument collapses.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Competitor behavior is irrelevant; the argument cares only whether ad spending caused *this* company's sales rise, not whether competitors also advertised.
explanations.C: The percentage of the target market reached is not invoked as evidence in the argument.
explanations.D: Previous quarters' performance is not required; the argument works whether sales were declining, stable, or rising before.
explanations.E: Whether the rise met expectations is irrelevant to the causal claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward single-premise inference. A doctor concludes a patient's symptoms are psychosomatic; the gap is that medical tests ruled out physical causes, which the argument must assume to make the conclusion valid.
lr.stimulus: Physician: Patient M has complained of chronic fatigue and body aches for two months. I have conducted a thorough physical examination and found no signs of infection, inflammation, or organ dysfunction. Therefore, the patient's symptoms are likely psychosomatic in origin.
lr.questionStem: The physician's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: Psychosomatic symptoms are more common than physically caused symptoms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The patient is not consciously fabricating symptoms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A thorough physical examination can rule out all major physical causes of fatigue and body aches.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients who are skeptical of psychiatric treatment are likely to have psychosomatic symptoms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The patient's symptoms will resolve without pharmaceutical intervention.

explanations.correct: The physician's reasoning is: no physical causes found → symptoms are psychosomatic. This inference depends on the assumption that a thorough exam can actually rule out physical causes. Without C, there could be undetected physical conditions (rare diseases, subclinical infection, etc.), and the conclusion would be unsupported. Negate C: if the exam missed physical causes, the inference fails.
explanations.A: The prevalence of psychosomatic versus physical symptoms is irrelevant to diagnosing this patient.
explanations.B: Conscious fabrication (malingering) and psychosomatic symptoms are different; the argument doesn't invoke malingering.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Patient attitudes toward psychiatry are not mentioned or required.
explanations.E: Prognosis without drugs is not necessary for the diagnosis.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-sentence argument with an obvious gap. Historian infers a manuscript's date from its subject matter; assumes that the subject (medieval warfare tactics) was not written about before or after the claimed period.
lr.stimulus: Historian: This manuscript describes medieval warfare tactics and strategies in great detail. Medieval warfare was most prevalent in Europe between the 10th and 15th centuries. Therefore, this manuscript was likely written during the medieval period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No one has written about medieval warfare tactics since the medieval period ended.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The manuscript's author was a European military officer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Medieval warfare was more prevalent in Europe than in other parts of the world.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The physical condition of the manuscript indicates its age.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Medieval warfare tactics are not used in modern military practice.

explanations.correct: The argument infers date from subject matter: medieval-warfare content → medieval-period origin. This assumes that detailed descriptions of medieval tactics were not written outside the medieval period. If modern scholars wrote such detailed descriptions (A negated), the content alone cannot date the manuscript to the medieval period. Negate A and the argument fails.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The author's identity and profession are not invoked in the argument.
explanations.C: Geographic prevalence is mentioned but not required for the dating inference.
explanations.D: Physical condition is explicitly not mentioned as evidence.
explanations.E: Modern military use of medieval tactics is not discussed and not necessary for the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple conditional argument. If students don't study, they fail; student failed → student didn't study. The gap is that failure has no other cause.
lr.stimulus: Teacher: Students who do not study for the final exam will fail the exam. Student X failed the exam. Therefore, Student X did not study for the exam.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most students who fail the final exam do not study.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Studying is the only factor that determines exam performance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The only reason a student would fail the exam is failure to study.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Student X had the opportunity to study before the exam.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The final exam is more difficult than previous exams.

explanations.correct: The argument reasons: not studying → failure. Then, failure → not studying (illicit reverse). This backward step requires assuming no other cause of failure exists. If a student could fail due to illness, test anxiety, or learning disability even while studying (C negated), the failure doesn't prove non-study. Negate C and the inference breaks.
explanations.A: Statistical frequency is irrelevant to whether this specific student studied.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument only needs studying to be *a* cause, not *the only* determinant.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Opportunity is not mentioned and not required for the logical form.
explanations.E: Difficulty level is not invoked in the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward inference from a single observation. Lawyer concludes a law is effective because crime decreased after enactment; assumes the crime decrease was caused by the law, not by other factors.
lr.stimulus: Legal analyst: The new anti-fraud law was enacted three years ago, and since then, reported instances of fraud in the financial sector have declined by 50%. Therefore, the new law has been highly effective in reducing fraud.
lr.questionStem: The analyst's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The decline in reported fraud was primarily caused by the new law rather than by other factors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fraud prevention was the primary goal of the legislature in enacting the law.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The financial sector did not experience unusually high fraud rates before the law was enacted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All fraud in the financial sector is now reported to authorities.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The law will continue to be effective in reducing fraud in the future.

explanations.correct: The argument observes temporal correlation (law enacted → fraud declined) and infers causation (law caused decline). This requires assuming the law, not other causes (improved auditing technology, market downturn reducing fraud opportunities, increased enforcement resources), drove the decline. Negate A: if other factors caused the decline, the law's effectiveness is unsupported.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Legislative intent is not relevant to whether the law actually reduced fraud.
explanations.C: Baseline fraud rates before the law do not determine whether the law was effective after enactment.
explanations.D: Reporting completeness affects measurement but is not necessary for the causal inference.
explanations.E: Future effectiveness is not required for claiming present effectiveness.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple environmental argument. Wildlife biologist observes a species thriving and concludes its habitat is healthy; assumes habitat health is the cause of thriving population, not vice versa or independent variables.
lr.stimulus: Wildlife biologist: The river ecosystem is home to a diverse population of native fish species that have increased in number over the past five years. This growth demonstrates that the river's ecosystem is healthy.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A healthy river ecosystem can only support native fish species.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The increase in fish population did not cause the ecosystem's health but rather resulted from it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fish populations are more reliable indicators of ecosystem health than water quality measurements.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The river did not experience any harmful pollution events in the past five years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Diverse populations of native fish require unpolluted water to survive.

explanations.correct: The argument reasons: thriving fish population → healthy ecosystem. This assumes health is the cause of thriving populations, not the reverse (a thriving population creating its own conditions) or mutual dependence. If population increase somehow caused ecosystem health rather than vice versa (B negated), the inference would be backwards. Negate B and the causal direction collapses.
explanations.A: The argument doesn't claim exclusive relationship; other organisms can coexist.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The argument doesn't compare fish to other indicators; it uses fish as evidence.
explanations.D: Absence of pollution is a separate claim; the argument relies on the causal link between health and population, not pollution history.
explanations.E: Too strong — the argument only needs a plausible connection, not an absolute requirement.

lr.difficultyReason: One-premise argument about linguistic change. Speaker concludes a language evolves because it has been spoken for centuries; assumes stability or slow change is not the default outcome of long language use.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: English has been spoken continuously for over a thousand years and has evolved significantly in vocabulary, pronunciation, and grammar. Therefore, languages naturally evolve over time.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: English is representative of all spoken languages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A language spoken for a thousand years is more likely to evolve than one spoken for a shorter period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Languages do not remain static over long periods of continuous use.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Evolution in pronunciation is a more significant change than evolution in vocabulary.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The speakers of English have always valued linguistic innovation.

explanations.correct: The argument observes that English evolved over a millennium and concludes languages naturally evolve. This assumes that evolution is not merely coincidental but that languages inherently change with time. Negate C: if languages can remain static over centuries, then English's evolution would not support the claim that evolution is natural. C fills the gap by asserting that change, not stasis, is typical.
explanations.A: The argument claims languages naturally evolve (plural); it doesn't require English to be representative of all.
explanations.B: The argument doesn't compare durations; it observes evolution occurred over a long period.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The relative significance of different types of change is not invoked.
explanations.E: Speaker attitudes toward innovation are not mentioned in the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise argument about ethics. Ethicist concludes an action is wrong because it violates a principle; assumes the principle is valid or applicable, not that violations are always acceptable.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Promising to help a friend and then failing to do so violates the principle of keeping one's commitments. Therefore, it is wrong to break a promise to a friend.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: All promises made to friends are equally important.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Violating the principle of keeping one's commitments is morally wrong.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Friends are more deserving of commitments than strangers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No one has ever broken a promise to a friend without regret.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Keeping promises is more important than any other moral principle.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'violates a principle' to 'therefore wrong.' This requires assuming that violating the principle is indeed morally wrong—i.e., the principle itself has moral force. Without B, the violation would be a mere fact without moral weight. Negate B: if violating commitments were not morally wrong, then the argument's conclusion wouldn't follow.
explanations.A: The argument doesn't rank promise importance; it applies uniformly.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The argument applies to friends without comparing them to others.
explanations.D: Psychological reactions to promise-breaking are irrelevant to moral status.
explanations.E: Too strong — the argument needs the principle to be morally relevant, not necessarily supreme.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-premise medical argument. The gap is a hidden equivalence between the experimental marker (inflammation) and the clinical outcome (arthritis), and a reference-class trap is available. Negating the correct answer severs the marker-to-disease bridge.
lr.stimulus: Researcher: Patients who took the experimental compound Relvanix for six months showed significantly lower levels of joint inflammation than a comparable group who took a placebo. Since elevated joint inflammation is a precursor to osteoarthritis in older adults, we conclude that Relvanix will reduce the incidence of osteoarthritis among older adults who take it.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the researcher's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Relvanix produces no side effects more serious than the osteoarthritis it is intended to prevent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reducing joint inflammation through means other than Relvanix would also lower the incidence of osteoarthritis.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The reduction in joint inflammation produced by Relvanix is sufficient to decrease the rate at which osteoarthritis develops.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most older adults who develop osteoarthritis have previously exhibited elevated joint inflammation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No medication currently on the market reduces joint inflammation as effectively as Relvanix does.

explanations.correct: The argument leaps from 'Relvanix lowers inflammation' to 'Relvanix prevents osteoarthritis.' Inflammation being a precursor does not guarantee that any reduction in it is large enough to change disease rates. Negate C — the reduction is not sufficient — and the conclusion about osteoarthritis incidence falls apart.
explanations.A: Out of scope — side effects are not a link in the inflammation-to-arthritis inference.
explanations.B: Shift in subject — the argument concerns Relvanix specifically, not alternative means of reducing inflammation.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Reversed direction — the argument needs inflammation reduction to prevent arthritis, not that arthritis patients had inflammation.
explanations.E: Too strong and off-point — relative efficacy against other drugs is not required for the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Economic argument relies on a conditional about consumer behavior. The necessary assumption rules out a specific alternative explanation (stockpiling) that would otherwise undermine the causal claim.
lr.stimulus: Economist: In the month after the city imposed a new tax on sugary drinks, sales of those drinks within city limits dropped by nearly 30 percent. Clearly, the tax has succeeded in discouraging residents from consuming sugary drinks.
lr.questionStem: The economist's argument depends on the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: residents did not stockpile significant quantities of sugary drinks before the tax took effect

choices.label: B
choices.text: the tax revenue collected will be used to fund public health programs

choices.label: C
choices.text: sugary drinks are the leading cause of preventable illness in the city

choices.label: D
choices.text: no other city has imposed a comparable tax on sugary drinks

choices.label: E
choices.text: the tax applies equally to all sugary drinks sold in the city

explanations.correct: The argument infers reduced consumption from reduced post-tax sales. If residents had stockpiled before the tax took effect, post-tax sales would drop even though total consumption was unchanged. Negate A and the sales drop no longer shows discouraged consumption.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Out of scope — how revenue is used has no bearing on whether the tax discouraged consumption.
explanations.C: Shift in subject — the conclusion is about this tax's effect, not about the overall health importance of sugary drinks.
explanations.D: Irrelevant comparison — other cities' taxes are not a link in the inference.
explanations.E: Out of scope — uniform application is not required for the sales drop to reflect reduced consumption.

lr.difficultyReason: Historical argument with a chronological subtlety: the coin's presence at the site only dates the settlement if the coin arrived during occupation rather than later. Several close-cousin distractors.
lr.stimulus: Archaeologist: A silver coin minted between 180 and 160 B.C.E. was unearthed last summer in a soil layer at the Helvetian hill settlement. This strongly suggests that the settlement was inhabited during the second century B.C.E.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the archaeologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Coins from this mint circulated widely throughout the region during the second century B.C.E.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No other artifacts at the settlement have been dated to earlier than the second century B.C.E.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The coin was not deposited in that soil layer long after the settlement was abandoned.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most inhabitants of the settlement would have handled silver coins at some point in their lives.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The coin was minted within a few years of reaching the settlement.

explanations.correct: The argument dates occupation from the coin's presence. If the coin was dropped at the site centuries after the settlement was abandoned (by a later traveler, a burial, soil disturbance), the coin tells us nothing about when the site was inhabited. Negate C and the inference collapses.
explanations.A: Too strong — wide circulation is not required for a single coin to reach the site during occupation.
explanations.B: Out of scope — other artifacts' dates are not a link in this particular inference.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — whether most inhabitants handled coins is irrelevant to dating the settlement from this coin.
explanations.E: Too strong — the coin could have reached the site decades after minting and still fall within the occupation period.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental argument pivots on a reference-class assumption: the studied wetlands must be representative of the ones the policy would protect. Strong distractors invoke related scope.
lr.stimulus: Environmental analyst: Wetlands in the Bayou Tertre region that have been fenced off from cattle over the past decade have regenerated native grasses at three times the rate of unfenced wetlands. Therefore, a statewide policy that fences cattle out of wetlands would significantly accelerate native-grass regeneration across the state.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wetlands outside the Bayou Tertre region do not differ from those within it in ways that would prevent fencing from having the same effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cattle are the most significant threat to native grasses in the state's wetlands.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No native grasses will regenerate in wetlands that remain accessible to cattle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cost of fencing cattle out of wetlands statewide will not exceed the ecological benefits.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ranchers in the Bayou Tertre region were legally required to fence their cattle out of wetlands.

explanations.correct: The argument generalizes from Bayou Tertre to the whole state. If wetlands elsewhere differ in ways that defeat the fencing effect (different grass species, different soil, other dominant pressures), the generalization fails. Negate A and the conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument needs only that fencing helps, not that cattle are the single leading threat.
explanations.C: Too strong — the conclusion requires acceleration, not that unfenced wetlands regenerate nothing.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — cost-benefit is not part of the regeneration-rate inference.
explanations.E: Out of scope — what motivated the Bayou Tertre fencing is not a link in the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal-reasoning argument with a hidden conditional: the conclusion that the ordinance is void requires not only a conflict but that state law prevail over municipal law in this area. The defender-style assumption is easy to overlook.
lr.stimulus: Legal analyst: The city's new ordinance forbids short-term rentals of residential property for fewer than thirty days. But state law grants property owners the right to rent their homes for any length of time they choose. Consequently, the city's ordinance is unenforceable.
lr.questionStem: The analyst's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most homeowners in the city would prefer to rent their property for fewer than thirty days.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The state legislature has the exclusive authority to regulate all real-estate transactions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When a municipal ordinance conflicts with state law on this subject, state law prevails.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city had no legitimate reason to restrict short-term rentals.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts have previously struck down similar short-term rental ordinances in other cities.

explanations.correct: The argument assumes the conflict between the ordinance and state law resolves in favor of state law — otherwise the ordinance remains enforceable despite the conflict. Negate C and the conclusion no longer follows.
explanations.A: Out of scope — homeowner preferences are not a link in the enforceability inference.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument needs state law to prevail on this subject, not exclusive state authority over all real-estate matters.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — whether the city's reasons are legitimate is irrelevant to legal enforceability against state law.
explanations.E: Out of scope — what other courts have done is not cited as a premise in this argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology argument relies on a hidden bridge between a security metric (password strength) and the conclusion (reduced breaches). The assumption must rule out the main alternative cause of breaches.
lr.stimulus: Technology consultant: Last year our firm rolled out a password manager that generated long, randomized passwords for every employee account. Since then, the number of successful breaches of employee accounts has dropped by more than half. The password manager has clearly been the key to improving our security.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the consultant's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every employee at the firm uses the password manager for each of their accounts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No other change made during the past year was largely responsible for the drop in successful breaches.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Randomized passwords are harder to crack than any passwords employees would have chosen themselves.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Successful breaches of employee accounts had been increasing before the password manager was introduced.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The password manager's randomized passwords cannot be recovered even by the manager's developer.

explanations.correct: The argument credits the password manager for the drop in breaches. If some other change (new firewall, staff training, phishing filter) was largely responsible, the causal claim fails. Negate B and the conclusion loses its support.
explanations.A: Too strong — the argument needs the manager to drive the drop, not universal adoption.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — the conclusion needs the manager to have contributed to the drop, not that its passwords are uncrackable-relative-to-every-alternative.
explanations.D: Out of scope — a pre-existing trend is not required by the argument.
explanations.E: Out of scope — developer access is not a link in the causal claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistic argument hinges on a subtle equivalence between a writing system's age and the language's age. Several distractors mimic the correct answer's scope.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Inscriptions written in the Turvanic script have been recovered from sites dated to at least 3,200 years ago. Because the Turvanic script was used exclusively to record the Turvanic language, we conclude that the Turvanic language was spoken at least 3,200 years ago.
lr.questionStem: The linguist's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the Turvanic script was not developed significantly earlier than it began to be used for inscriptions

choices.label: B
choices.text: the inscriptions were produced by people who were native speakers of the Turvanic language

choices.label: C
choices.text: any language used for inscriptions at a site must have been spoken at that site

choices.label: D
choices.text: the Turvanic script was the only script in use in the region 3,200 years ago

choices.label: E
choices.text: the Turvanic language was not used exclusively for ceremonial purposes at the time of the inscriptions

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that the language was spoken, based on an inscribed script. But a script can be used to record a language that was not actually spoken by the inscribers (a liturgical or imported language, as with Latin in medieval Europe). The bridge needed is that the script was being used to record a spoken language at the time. Negate B — the inscribers did not speak Turvanic — and the conclusion that Turvanic was spoken 3,200 years ago loses support.
explanations.A: Shift in subject — the conclusion is about the language, not about when the script was invented.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — the argument needs only that someone spoke Turvanic, not that every inscribed language was locally spoken.
explanations.D: Out of scope — other scripts' presence doesn't affect the Turvanic inference.
explanations.E: Reversed direction — this rules out ceremonial-only use, which is close, but the argument actually needs the stronger claim that speakers produced the inscriptions; E alone permits a script without any living speakers using it.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts/aesthetics argument contains a category-bridge: a 'mastery of perspective' attribution requires ruling out that the work is a later copy. Sharp negation test.
lr.stimulus: Art historian: The recently discovered panel depicting a market square uses precise single-point perspective of a kind not developed until the 1420s. The panel is signed by Pietro di Marco, who died in 1398. Since works signed by Pietro are almost never forged, we may conclude that Pietro anticipated single-point perspective by more than two decades.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The panel was not painted by a later artist and signed with Pietro's name for commercial reasons.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pietro di Marco was the most accomplished painter of his generation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No other painter working before 1420 made use of single-point perspective.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The perspective techniques developed in the 1420s were based on Pietro's work.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The market square depicted on the panel was a familiar subject for painters of Pietro's era.

explanations.correct: The argument infers Pietro's authorship from the signature, then credits Pietro with anticipating perspective. If a later artist painted the panel and appended Pietro's signature (even without a forgery's typical intent to deceive collectors), Pietro didn't anticipate anything. Negate A and the conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Out of scope — Pietro's overall standing isn't a link in the inference.
