explanations.C: Too strong — the conclusion is about Pietro's anticipation, not a universal claim about all pre-1420 painters.
explanations.D: Reversed direction — the argument doesn't claim the 1420s techniques derived from Pietro.
explanations.E: Out of scope — subject matter is not part of the reasoning.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy argument moves from a program's prior effectiveness to a prediction about the current case. The necessary assumption guards against a relevant change in conditions.
lr.stimulus: Policy adviser: The tutoring program that we implemented in Millbrook's public schools five years ago improved student reading scores by an average of 12 percent within two years. Our neighboring district has demographics nearly identical to Millbrook's. If the same program is adopted there, reading scores will improve by about 12 percent within two years.
lr.questionStem: The adviser's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The factors that made the tutoring program effective in Millbrook are still present in the neighboring district today.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No other reading-improvement initiative in the neighboring district could produce gains larger than 12 percent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Student reading scores in the neighboring district are currently lower than Millbrook's were five years ago.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every student in the neighboring district would participate in the tutoring program.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tutoring program's costs are comparable to those of existing programs in the neighboring district.

explanations.correct: The argument predicts the same outcome from the same program. If the background conditions that made the program work in Millbrook (funded libraries, trained tutors, cooperating parents) are absent in the neighboring district today, the prediction fails. Demographics alone don't guarantee those conditions. Negate A and the conclusion no longer follows.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Shift in subject — the argument predicts this program's effect, not a comparison to other initiatives.
explanations.C: Out of scope — current baseline is not a link in the inference from program to improvement.
explanations.D: Too strong — universal participation is not part of the Millbrook precedent or the prediction.
explanations.E: Out of scope — cost comparisons are not a link in the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics argument has a conditional-style gap: the conclusion that the executive acted wrongly depends on a linking principle between duties to shareholders and the specific disclosure at issue. Multiple distractors shift scope.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Corporate executives have a duty to disclose to shareholders any information that would materially affect the value of their shares. When CEO Lanier learned of the impending product recall, she waited two weeks before informing shareholders. Therefore, Lanier violated her duty to the shareholders.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the ethicist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any information about a product recall would materially affect the value of a company's shares.

choices.label: B
choices.text: CEOs who delay disclosing material information always do so for personal financial gain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lanier had a duty to disclose the recall before she was legally required to do so.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shareholders would have sold their shares had they been informed of the recall sooner.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two weeks is the longest an executive can reasonably delay any corporate disclosure.

explanations.correct: The premise is about materially-share-affecting information; the conclusion is about this recall. Without the bridge that the recall qualifies as such information, the duty the ethicist cited doesn't attach. Negate A — not all recall information materially affects share value — and Lanier's particular recall may fall outside the duty, so the conclusion does not follow.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — motive is not required for a duty violation.
explanations.C: Shift in subject — the argument is about ethical duty, not legal timing.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — shareholder reaction is not what 'material' means in the stated duty.
explanations.E: Too strong — a general timing rule is not needed; the ethicist only needs this delay to have violated the duty.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-premise argument with several topically related distractors. The gap between the pharmacological evidence and the conclusion requires ruling out an alternative explanation. Negation test discriminates cleanly.
lr.stimulus: Neurologist: Patients with chronic migraines who were given compound X reported a significant reduction in headache frequency within four weeks. No other changes were made to their diet or medication regimens during this period. We therefore conclude that compound X is effective at reducing the frequency of chronic migraines.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the neurologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Compound X has no side effects that would prevent patients from completing a four-week treatment course.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The reduction in headache frequency was not the result of patients' expectations of improvement rather than any pharmacological effect of compound X.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Compound X is more effective at reducing migraine frequency than any currently available treatment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All patients who participated in the study had suffered from chronic migraines for at least one year prior to the trial.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The neurologist who conducted the study had no financial interest in the commercial development of compound X.

explanations.correct: The argument infers pharmacological effectiveness from patient-reported improvement. Negate B: the reduction was due to placebo effect, not compound X. The conclusion that compound X is effective collapses immediately. B is a necessary assumption.
explanations.A: Side effects concern safety and tolerability, not whether the observed reduction was caused by compound X. Out of scope for this causal inference.
explanations.B: Correct. The placebo/expectation alternative directly undermines the causal link between compound X and the reported improvement.
explanations.C: Too strong. The argument concludes only that compound X is effective, not that it is superior to all alternatives. This is a sufficient-not-necessary trap.
explanations.D: Duration of prior migraine history is irrelevant to whether compound X caused the observed reduction. Shift in subject.
explanations.E: Financial interest concerns bias in reporting, not whether the compound itself was the causal agent. Out of scope.

lr.difficultyReason: Economics stimulus with a structural gap between market data and a policy conclusion. Multiple close-cousin distractors test whether test-takers can identify the narrow bridge the argument truly needs.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Over the past decade, the nations with the highest rates of economic growth have also had the lowest corporate tax rates among industrialized countries. Thus, reducing corporate tax rates is likely to stimulate significant economic growth in nations that currently have high corporate tax rates.
lr.questionStem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Corporate tax revenue is the largest single source of government income in most industrialized nations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The high-growth nations did not share some other feature, distinct from low corporate tax rates, that was responsible for their superior growth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every industrialized nation that reduces its corporate tax rate will immediately experience faster economic growth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nations with low corporate tax rates invest the resulting revenue savings in infrastructure projects.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Economic growth rates are the most important measure of a nation's financial well-being.

explanations.correct: The economist infers causation from correlation. Negate B: the high-growth nations did share another feature responsible for growth. Then the correlation between low taxes and growth proves nothing about reducing taxes elsewhere. The argument collapses.
explanations.A: The share of revenue from corporate taxes is irrelevant to whether cutting those taxes drives growth. Out of scope.
explanations.B: Correct. This rules out confounding variables, the key gap in any correlation-to-causation argument.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'every nation... immediately' exceeds what the argument concludes ('likely to stimulate'). Sufficient trap.
explanations.D: Infrastructure investment is an unrelated causal mechanism not invoked in the argument. Shift in subject.
explanations.E: Whether growth is the most important metric is irrelevant to the causal inference being drawn. Out of scope.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science stimulus. The conclusion depends on a link between current measurements and past conditions. One distractor is a close cousin that swaps subject scope.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientist: Core samples taken from the glacier show that atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were significantly lower three thousand years ago than they are today. Since the region's average temperature was also lower at that time, we can conclude that the current elevated carbon dioxide levels are a primary cause of the region's present higher temperatures.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No volcanic activity occurred in the region three thousand years ago that could have temporarily depressed CO₂ levels.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carbon dioxide levels in the glacier core samples accurately reflect the atmospheric CO₂ levels of three thousand years ago.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The region's temperature and CO₂ levels have increased at the same rate over the past three thousand years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elevated carbon dioxide levels are the only factor that can cause a region's average temperature to rise.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The glacier from which the core samples were taken has not significantly advanced or retreated in the past three thousand years.

explanations.correct: The entire argument rests on the glacier core data as a proxy for past atmospheric CO₂. Negate B: the core samples do not accurately reflect past atmospheric CO₂. Then the premise about lower CO₂ three thousand years ago is unsupported, and the conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: Volcanic activity is a possible confound for temperature, not for the CO₂ measurement accuracy the argument depends on. Out of scope.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument treats the glacier cores as reliable records of past atmospheric CO₂; without this, there is no evidence for the correlation that supports the conclusion.
explanations.C: Identical rates of increase are not required — only that CO₂ and temperature were both lower then and both higher now. Too strong.
explanations.D: Too strong — the conclusion says CO₂ is 'a primary cause,' not 'the only cause.' Universal language makes this a sufficient trap.
explanations.E: Glacier advance or retreat affects the physical mass of the glacier, not the chemical composition of trapped air bubbles. Shift in subject.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal reasoning stimulus where a definitional gap exists between statutory language and the conclusion. Distractors include a reversed-direction trap and an out-of-scope trap.
lr.stimulus: Attorney: The statute prohibits any person from operating a motor vehicle while impaired by any substance. My client was found asleep in the driver's seat of a parked car with the engine running. The prosecution contends that my client was operating a motor vehicle. However, since my client was asleep, she could not have been operating the vehicle, and so the statute does not apply.
lr.questionStem: The attorney's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the statute was not intended to deter people from sleeping in running vehicles.

choices.label: B
choices.text: a person who is asleep cannot perform the act of operating a vehicle.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the client had a legitimate reason for sitting in the parked car with the engine running.

choices.label: D
choices.text: a vehicle with its engine running poses no traffic hazard when it is parked.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the prosecution has not established that any substance caused the client's sleep.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'client was asleep' to 'client was not operating the vehicle.' This requires that being asleep precludes operating a vehicle. Negate B: a sleeping person can operate a vehicle (perhaps by having started it and left it running). Then the attorney's inference fails.
explanations.A: Legislative intent concerns statutory interpretation, not the logical connection the attorney draws between sleep and non-operation. Out of scope.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the bridge between 'asleep' and 'not operating,' the key gap in the attorney's argument.
explanations.C: The client's reason for being in the car is irrelevant to whether she was operating it. Out of scope.
explanations.D: Traffic hazard addresses policy rationale, not the definitional question of whether she was 'operating' the vehicle. Out of scope.
explanations.E: The attorney's argument rests on sleep negating operation, not on challenging the impairment element. This is a reversal — it addresses a different element of the statute.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology stimulus. The argument infers a current system's reliability from past performance data. A temporal gap between past and present conditions is the key necessary assumption.
lr.stimulus: Software engineer: Our automated trading platform has executed over two million transactions in the past three years without a single processing error. We are therefore confident that the platform will continue to operate without errors as transaction volume increases over the next year.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the engineer's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The automated trading platform was designed by engineers with at least ten years of experience in financial software.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No competing trading platform has achieved a comparable error-free record over the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The increase in transaction volume anticipated for the next year will not exceed the operational parameters under which the platform's error-free record was established.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Processing errors in automated trading platforms always result in significant financial losses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The platform has never been tested under simulated conditions of higher transaction volume.

explanations.correct: The argument extrapolates from past performance to future performance under increased volume. Negate C: the anticipated volume will exceed the parameters under which the platform performed error-free. Then the past record provides no basis for confidence about future performance. The conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: Engineer credentials are irrelevant to whether future performance will match past performance. Out of scope.
explanations.B: Competitors' records are irrelevant to this platform's future reliability. Out of scope.
explanations.C: Correct. This bridges past and future by ruling out the possibility that new conditions render past data inapplicable.
explanations.D: The consequence of errors is not required for the argument about whether errors will occur. Out of scope.
explanations.E: Simulation testing history doesn't affect the inference from actual past performance. This is a distractor that sounds relevant but shifts the evidentiary basis.

lr.difficultyReason: History stimulus with a provenance-based inference. Multiple distractors are topically continuous but address different elements of the argument than the actual gap.
lr.stimulus: Historian: This unsigned portrait, recently discovered in a private collection, was painted in the style of the Flemish master Jan van Eyck and uses a pigment blend found exclusively in his authenticated works. We can therefore conclude that van Eyck painted this portrait.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jan van Eyck painted more unsigned works than signed ones during his lifetime.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No other painter of van Eyck's era had access to or used the same pigment blend found in this portrait.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The portrait depicts a subject who was known to have sat for van Eyck on at least one occasion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The private collection in which the portrait was found has a well-documented chain of ownership tracing to fifteenth-century Bruges.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Van Eyck's authenticated works are considered among the most valuable paintings of the Northern Renaissance.

explanations.correct: The argument uses the distinctive pigment blend as the key evidence. Negate B: another painter of van Eyck's era also used this pigment blend. Then the pigment no longer identifies the portrait as van Eyck's, and the conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: The ratio of signed to unsigned works is irrelevant to whether this particular portrait was painted by van Eyck. Out of scope.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument requires the pigment blend to be uniquely attributable to van Eyck; without this, the evidence is not diagnostic.
explanations.C: The identity of the subject is not invoked as evidence in the argument. Shift in subject.
explanations.D: Provenance tracing to Bruges would strengthen the argument but is not a necessary assumption — the pigment and style evidence could stand independently. Too strong / out of scope.
explanations.E: The market value of van Eyck's work is entirely irrelevant to the attribution argument. Out of scope.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics stimulus with a normative gap between a factual premise and an evaluative conclusion. One distractor embodies the reversed-direction trap; another is a too-strong universal.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: A policy is just only if it distributes burdens and benefits in proportion to each individual's ability to bear them. The proposed carbon tax distributes its financial burden equally across all income levels. Therefore, the proposed carbon tax is not a just policy.
lr.questionStem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A policy that distributes burdens in proportion to ability to bear them is always just.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The financial burden of the proposed carbon tax represents a greater proportional hardship for lower-income individuals than for higher-income individuals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Carbon taxes are a less effective means of reducing emissions than direct regulatory mandates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No tax policy that distributes burdens equally across income levels can achieve its environmental objectives.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The benefits of the carbon tax are distributed equally across all income levels as well.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'equal distribution across income levels' to 'not proportional to ability to bear.' This only works if equal dollar amounts impose unequal proportional hardship on different income levels. Negate B: an equal dollar burden is not a greater proportional hardship for lower-income individuals. Then equal distribution might be proportional, and the conclusion fails.
explanations.A: This is the converse of the first premise, not its logical entailment. Reversed-direction trap — the premise says just policies must distribute proportionally, not that proportional distribution is sufficient for justice.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the unstated bridge connecting 'equal across income levels' to 'not proportional to ability to bear.'
explanations.C: Comparative effectiveness of emissions-reduction tools is entirely outside the scope of this justice argument. Out of scope.
explanations.D: Too strong — introduces a universal about all equal-burden tax policies and their environmental objectives, neither of which is the argument's focus.
explanations.E: Benefit distribution was not invoked as part of the injustice argument. Shift in subject.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics stimulus with a synchronic-to-diachronic inferential gap. The correct answer rules out an alternative explanation for the observed linguistic feature.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: The word for 'fire' in six of the seven languages spoken in the Kareth Valley is derived from a common root. Languages typically borrow words for new concepts from neighboring tongues but retain indigenous terms for fundamental, long-established concepts. Since fire is a fundamental concept, these six languages almost certainly descended from a single common ancestor language.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The seventh language of the Kareth Valley did not descend from the same common ancestor as the other six.

choices.label: B
choices.text: None of the six languages borrowed the word for 'fire' from a single source language after these languages had already diverged from one another.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All languages that share a common ancestor will retain identical words for fundamental concepts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Kareth Valley has been continuously inhabited for at least ten thousand years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The linguist analyzed written records of all six languages rather than relying solely on spoken forms.

explanations.correct: The argument infers common ancestry from a shared root word. But if the six languages borrowed 'fire' from one dominant language after diverging, they could share the root without sharing an ancestor. Negate B: the six languages did borrow the word from a single source after diverging. The shared root no longer evidences common ancestry, and the conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: The seventh language's ancestry is a separate question; the argument only needs to establish common ancestry for the six. Out of scope.
explanations.B: Correct. This rules out borrowing as an alternative explanation for the shared root, which is the key gap in the argument.
explanations.C: Too strong — the argument requires only that these six share a root for 'fire,' not that all descendant languages always retain identical words. Sufficient trap.
explanations.D: Duration of habitation is not a premise in the argument and is not required for the shared-root inference. Out of scope.
explanations.E: The method of data collection (written vs. spoken) is not relevant to whether the shared root evidences common ancestry. Out of scope.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy stimulus with a gap between stated program outcomes and the causal attribution. A close-cousin distractor shifts scope from program participants to the general population.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: Participants in the city's subsidized job-training program showed a 34 percent increase in annual earnings two years after completing the program. The program costs the city $2,400 per participant. Since this earnings increase far exceeds the program's per-participant cost, the program represents a sound investment of public funds.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The job-training program is the primary reason participants experienced the increase in annual earnings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The city's overall unemployment rate declined during the two years following program completion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Participants in the program were, on average, earning below the city's median income before enrolling.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city has sufficient funds to expand the program to serve twice as many participants annually.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No participant in the program subsequently moved out of the city within two years of completing it.

explanations.correct: The argument treats the participants' earnings increase as a return on the program's investment. Negate A: the program was not the primary reason for the earnings increase. Then the $2,400 cost cannot be credited with producing the earnings gain, and the investment-worthiness conclusion fails.
explanations.A: Correct. The cost-benefit comparison only holds if the program, not some other factor, caused the earnings increase.
explanations.B: City-wide unemployment trends could explain participant outcomes but the argument doesn't require ruling this in — it requires ruling it out as the cause. B is out of scope as stated; A captures the necessary causal assumption more precisely.
explanations.C: Pre-program income level of participants is irrelevant to whether the program caused the post-program earnings increase. Out of scope.
explanations.D: Expansion capacity concerns future policy, not whether the current program is a sound investment. Out of scope.
explanations.E: Participants who move away still experienced the earnings increase; geographic mobility does not sever the causal claim. Shift in subject.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts stimulus with an inferential gap between physical evidence about a manuscript and a conclusion about authorial intent. Distractors include a too-strong universal and an out-of-scope trap about manuscript value.
lr.stimulus: Music historian: The earliest surviving manuscript of this symphony contains numerous passages crossed out and rewritten in the same hand as the rest of the score. Composers of this period routinely completed a full draft before preparing a clean final copy. The crossed-out passages therefore represent the composer's deliberate revisions, not copying errors.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The surviving manuscript is a draft copy rather than the clean final copy the composer prepared for performance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every composer of this period made extensive revisions before completing a final copy of a symphony.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The crossed-out passages contain musical ideas that the composer later incorporated into other works.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The manuscript was stored under conditions that prevented deterioration of the ink over time.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The composer did not employ a copyist to transcribe any portion of the manuscript.

explanations.correct: The argument relies on the premise that composers completed a full draft before a clean copy, and concludes the cross-outs are intentional revisions. This only works if the manuscript is a draft — if it is the clean final copy, cross-outs would more likely be errors. Negate A: the manuscript is the clean final copy, not a draft. Then the premise about drafting practice no longer supports the conclusion that cross-outs are deliberate revisions.
explanations.A: Correct. The drafting-practice premise is only relevant if this manuscript is a draft; the argument assumes this without stating it.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'every composer' is a universal that exceeds what the argument needs. The argument requires only that this composer (or composers of this period generally) followed this practice. Sufficient trap.
explanations.C: Whether crossed-out ideas appeared elsewhere is irrelevant to whether they were deliberate revisions or errors. Out of scope.
explanations.D: Ink preservation concerns the legibility of the manuscript, not the intentionality of the cross-outs. Out of scope.
explanations.E: A copyist's involvement would be relevant if the cross-outs might be in a different hand, but the stimulus already establishes they are in the same hand as the rest of the score. This distractor is rendered moot by information already in the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-premise argument with several topically plausible distractors. Negation test clearly destroys the conclusion only for the correct answer; wrong answers either shift subject or are too strong.
lr.stimulus: Nutritionist: A clinical trial compared two groups of patients with high blood pressure. One group followed a low-sodium diet for six months while the other group maintained their normal diet. At the end of the trial, the low-sodium group showed significantly lower average blood pressure readings than the high-sodium group. Therefore, adopting a low-sodium diet reduces blood pressure in patients with high blood pressure.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the nutritionist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All patients with high blood pressure would benefit equally from a low-sodium diet.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The two groups of patients did not differ significantly in blood pressure levels at the start of the trial.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A low-sodium diet has no negative effects on any aspect of the patients' health.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The patients in the trial were representative of all people with high blood pressure worldwide.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sodium is the only dietary factor that affects blood pressure in patients.

explanations.correct: The argument attributes the difference in outcomes to the dietary intervention. If the two groups had substantially different baseline blood pressure levels at the start, the observed difference at the end could reflect that pre-existing gap rather than the effect of diet. Negating B — the groups did differ significantly at baseline — undermines the conclusion that diet caused the reduction.
explanations.A: Too strong. The argument concludes only that a low-sodium diet reduces blood pressure in this patient population, not that all patients benefit equally. This is a scope-expansion trap.
explanations.B: Correct. If the groups differed at baseline, the dietary intervention cannot be credited for the difference in outcomes. Negating B collapses the causal inference.
explanations.C: Out of scope. The argument concerns only whether blood pressure is reduced, not whether other health effects arise. This is a subject-shift trap.
explanations.D: Too strong. The argument concludes only about patients with high blood pressure generally, and representativeness is not required — only that the diet caused the change observed in the trial. This over-extends the conclusion.
explanations.E: Too strong. The argument does not need sodium to be the only dietary factor — only that the low-sodium diet in this trial was the operative difference between groups.

lr.difficultyReason: The gap between the historical evidence and the economic conclusion requires ruling out an alternative explanation; distractors are topically close but address scope-shifted concerns.
lr.stimulus: Economic historian: Tax records from the fourteenth century show that wool merchants in the Flemish cities paid dramatically higher taxes in years when guild membership was restricted. Since guild membership determined who could legally trade wool, this pattern indicates that restricting guild membership allowed existing members to charge higher prices, generating greater profits.
lr.questionStem: The economic historian's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Flemish guilds were the most powerful economic institutions in medieval Europe.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Higher taxes paid by wool merchants reflected higher profits rather than higher tax rates imposed by authorities.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Guild members in other trades also benefited from membership restrictions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The wool trade was the primary source of wealth in Flemish cities during the fourteenth century.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Guild membership restrictions were always initiated by the merchants themselves rather than by city authorities.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'higher taxes paid' to 'higher profits earned.' This inference is valid only if higher taxes tracked higher profits, not simply higher tax rates. Negate B: higher taxes reflected higher rates rather than higher profits — the conclusion that merchants earned greater profits is unsupported. B is necessary.
explanations.A: Out of scope. The argument concerns only the profit mechanism within Flemish wool guilds; comparisons across European institutions are irrelevant.
explanations.B: Correct. The entire inference from tax records to profits depends on taxes being a reliable proxy for profits, not an independent variable set by authorities.
explanations.C: Subject shift. The argument is about wool merchants specifically; other trades are outside the argument's scope.
explanations.D: Out of scope. Whether wool was the primary or a minor source of city wealth does not bear on whether restriction generated profits for wool merchants.
explanations.E: Too strong and out of scope. Who initiated the restrictions does not affect whether restrictions caused higher profits.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science stimulus with a causal gap that students must identify amid distractors that sound environmentally relevant but address unrelated aspects.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientist: Over the past decade, the population of a native bee species in a protected wetland reserve has declined by forty percent. During the same period, a non-native plant species colonized approximately forty percent of the reserve's flowering meadows. We conclude that the spread of the non-native plant is responsible for the bee population decline.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The non-native plant species produces flowers that are toxic to the native bee species.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No other significant environmental changes occurred in the reserve during the past decade that could account for the bee decline.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The native bee species does not pollinate the non-native plant species.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The non-native plant was introduced to the reserve by human activity rather than by natural dispersal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bee populations in all wetland reserves have declined over the past decade.

explanations.correct: The argument infers causation from co-occurrence. This inference requires that no other factor — pesticide use, disease, habitat drainage, climate shift — explains the decline. Negate B: some other significant environmental change did occur and could account for the decline. The conclusion that the plant caused the decline becomes unsupported.
explanations.A: Too specific and too strong. The argument does not need to identify the mechanism of harm — only that the non-native plant is responsible. Toxicity is one possible mechanism but not a necessary assumption.
explanations.B: Correct. Without ruling out confounding factors, the correlation between plant spread and bee decline does not support a causal conclusion.
explanations.C: Reversed and irrelevant. Whether the bee pollinates the plant does not bear on whether the plant's presence harms the bee population.
explanations.D: Out of scope. The pathway of introduction is irrelevant to whether the plant's presence caused the decline.
explanations.E: Too strong and out of scope. The argument concerns only this specific reserve; universal trends are not required.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal argument with an evidentiary gap; correct answer is a modest defensive assumption that students may overlook in favor of stronger-sounding choices.
lr.stimulus: Defense attorney: My client's fingerprints were found on the window latch of the burglarized building. However, my client worked as a maintenance technician at that building for three years before the burglary and would have had routine access to that latch. Therefore, the presence of his fingerprints on the latch does not establish that he was present during the burglary.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the defense attorney's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The fingerprints on the latch could have been deposited before the night of the burglary.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No other evidence links the defense attorney's client to the burglary.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The client's fingerprints were the only prints found on the window latch.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maintenance technicians frequently touch window latches in the course of their duties.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The building's security system was not functioning properly on the night of the burglary.

explanations.correct: The attorney's entire argument depends on the fingerprints having been left during the maintenance period rather than during the burglary. If the prints could not have survived from before the burglary — say, they are demonstrably fresh — then routine access does not explain their presence. Negating A (the prints could not have been deposited before that night) dismantles the argument.
explanations.A: Correct. The prior-access explanation only works if the prints plausibly predate the burglary. Negate it and the argument collapses.
explanations.B: Out of scope. The argument addresses only what the fingerprint evidence establishes; it does not claim the client is innocent or that no other evidence exists. This is a subject-shift trap.
explanations.C: Irrelevant. The presence or absence of other prints does not affect whether the client's prints could have been left before the burglary.
explanations.D: Defender disguised as strengthener. While this adds plausibility, the argument already asserts the client had access to the latch; whether technicians frequently touch latches is supplementary, not necessary.
explanations.E: Out of scope. The security system's functionality is not part of the evidentiary inference about fingerprints.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology policy argument with a structural gap that requires a bridge between two concepts; traps include a too-strong answer and a subject-shift answer.
lr.stimulus: Technology policy analyst: A city recently mandated that all ride-sharing companies operating within its limits share trip-route data with the municipal transit authority. Proponents argued that this data would allow the transit authority to redesign bus routes more efficiently. However, the transit authority has no data analysts on staff capable of processing large datasets. Therefore, the mandate will not achieve its intended purpose.
lr.questionStem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ride-sharing companies will comply fully and immediately with the data-sharing mandate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The transit authority will not acquire the capability to process the data before the mandate's benefits are needed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bus route redesign is the most cost-effective way to improve urban transit systems.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No other city has successfully implemented a similar ride-sharing data mandate.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The ride-sharing companies operating in the city collect more data than the transit authority could ever analyze.

explanations.correct: The argument's conclusion is that the mandate will not achieve its purpose. The stated reason is the authority's current lack of analysts. This only blocks the mandate's purpose if the authority cannot obtain that analytical capability before the data needs to be used. Negate B: the authority will acquire the capability in time — then the current staffing gap is temporary and the mandate could still succeed. The conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: Out of scope. Compliance by ride-sharing companies concerns the data supply side; the argument's gap is on the processing side. Even full compliance is useless without analytical capacity, so A does not close the argument's core gap.
explanations.B: Correct. The present lack of analysts destroys the mandate's purpose only if that lack persists long enough to matter.
explanations.C: Too strong and out of scope. The argument accepts that bus redesign is the intended purpose; whether it is the best strategy overall is not in question.
explanations.D: Out of scope. Other cities' experiences are irrelevant to whether this city's transit authority can process the data.
explanations.E: Too strong. The argument needs only that the authority cannot process the data, not that the data volume exceeds any conceivable capacity.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics argument with a normative gap; the correct answer is a defensive bridge between a factual premise and a moral conclusion, while distractors introduce normative claims the argument does not need.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: A pharmaceutical company withheld data from a clinical trial showing that its new antidepressant was no more effective than a placebo in adolescent patients. Physicians who prescribed the drug to adolescents were therefore acting without the information they needed to make informed recommendations. We can conclude that the company acted wrongly in withholding the data.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the ethicist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every action that deprives physicians of information needed for informed recommendations is morally wrong.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The antidepressant caused harmful side effects in adolescent patients who took it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pharmaceutical company knew that the data showed the drug was ineffective before withholding it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pharmaceutical companies are legally required to disclose all clinical trial data to the public.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The physicians who prescribed the drug would have recommended a different treatment had they known about the trial results.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from a factual claim — withholding data deprived physicians of information needed for informed recommendations — to a moral conclusion — the company acted wrongly. This normative leap requires a moral principle connecting those two things. A provides exactly that bridge. Negate A: some actions that deprive physicians of needed information are not morally wrong — then the mere fact of depriving physicians of information no longer entails wrongdoing, and the conclusion is unsupported.
explanations.A: Correct. This is the normative bridge the ethical argument requires. Without a principle linking information deprivation to wrongdoing, the factual premise alone cannot yield the moral conclusion.
explanations.B: Out of scope. The argument does not rely on the drug causing harm — the case for wrongdoing is built entirely on the information deprivation, not on patient injury.
explanations.C: Defender disguised as strengthener. While the company's knowledge strengthens the case for wrongdoing, the argument as stated does not invoke intent. Negate C — the company unknowingly withheld the data — and the argument still has force (depriving physicians of needed information may be wrong regardless of intent).
explanations.D: Out of scope. The argument is a moral argument, not a legal one. Legal obligations are not referenced in the reasoning.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Whether physicians would have acted differently does not affect whether the withholding was wrong — the argument is about deprivation of information, not about its downstream behavioral effects.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics argument with an inferential gap between contemporary usage data and a historical claim; traps include a reversed-direction answer and a too-strong answer.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Surveys of speakers in three isolated mountain villages show that all of them use the same archaic grammatical construction that disappeared from standard usage centuries ago. The villages have had no contact with one another for at least two hundred years. Therefore, this construction must have been present in the dialect spoken in the region before the villages became isolated.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The archaic construction performs the same grammatical function in all three villages today.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The construction did not develop independently in each village after the villages became isolated from one another.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Archaic grammatical constructions are always preserved more faithfully in isolated communities than in urban centers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The villagers surveyed had no exposure to written texts containing the archaic construction.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The three villages were settled simultaneously from a single original population.

explanations.correct: The argument infers a shared historical origin for the construction from its current presence in all three isolated villages. This inference requires that the similarity is due to inheritance from a common earlier dialect rather than independent invention. Negate B: the construction did develop independently in each village — then its shared presence is coincidental convergence, not evidence of a pre-isolation common dialect. The conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: Out of scope. Whether the construction serves the same function today is not part of the inference about its historical origins.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument's historical inference depends on ruling out independent parallel development. Negation destroys the conclusion.
explanations.C: Too strong. The argument needs only that this construction in these villages was preserved from a common source, not a universal principle about all archaic constructions in all isolated communities.
explanations.D: Defender disguised as strengthener. Exposure to written texts is an alternative explanation the argument does not need to explicitly rule out to make the independent-development point; moreover, it is a different alternative from independent innovation.
explanations.E: Too strong. The argument requires only a common linguistic ancestor, not necessarily a single simultaneous founding event. Villages could have separated at different times and still share a common earlier dialect.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts/history argument requiring students to identify a modest defensive assumption; distractors include a too-specific mechanism answer and a subject-shift answer about other artists.
lr.stimulus: Art historian: A recently discovered painting bears a signature that chemical analysis confirms used ink manufactured after 1850. The painting depicts a harbor scene in a style closely associated with a particular school of artists active between 1820 and 1860. Because this school disbanded by 1860, the painting must have been completed no earlier than 1850 and no later than 1860.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the art historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The artist who painted the harbor scene was a member of the school active between 1820 and 1860.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No artist working after 1860 could have imitated the style associated with the disbanded school.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ink used for the signature was applied at the same time the painting was completed, not added later.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chemical analysis of ink is the most reliable method for dating paintings from the nineteenth century.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The harbor scene depicted in the painting was a location frequented by the school's members.

explanations.correct: The dating argument uses the ink's post-1850 manufacture to establish when the painting was completed. This inference only holds if the signature was contemporaneous with the painting — if someone added the signature after the painting was finished, the ink date tells us nothing about when the work was painted. Negate C: the ink was added later, not at the time of completion — the ink's date no longer constrains when the painting was made, and the conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: Too strong. The argument needs only that the painting was produced within the school's active period, not that the specific artist was a member. The style association is already given as a premise.
explanations.B: Too strong. The argument needs only that no post-1860 artist produced this painting, not that imitation was impossible for all post-1860 artists generally.
explanations.C: Correct. The entire evidentiary chain from ink date to completion date breaks if the signature was applied after completion.
explanations.D: Out of scope. The argument does not need chemical analysis to be the most reliable method — only that it is reliable enough to establish a post-1850 date for this ink. Comparative reliability is irrelevant.
explanations.E: Out of scope. The geographic identity of the harbor depicted does not bear on the dating argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy argument with a gap between an observed trend and a policy recommendation; traps are a subject-shift answer and a too-strong answer involving universal principles.
lr.stimulus: Urban planner: In cities that introduced congestion pricing — charging drivers a fee to enter high-traffic zones — average commute times dropped significantly within two years of implementation. Our city faces severe traffic congestion that reduces worker productivity and increases pollution. We should therefore introduce congestion pricing in our downtown core.
lr.questionStem: The urban planner's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Congestion pricing is the only policy tool that has ever successfully reduced urban traffic congestion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The workers most affected by traffic congestion in our city commute by private automobile.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Our city's traffic patterns and driver behavior are sufficiently similar to those of the cities that introduced congestion pricing that the policy would have a comparable effect here.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The revenue generated by congestion pricing fees should be reinvested in public transportation infrastructure.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reducing commute times in our city would increase worker productivity more than any other urban policy initiative.

explanations.correct: The argument applies evidence from other cities to recommend a policy for this city. That analogical inference requires that this city be relevantly similar to those other cities. Negate C: this city's traffic patterns and driver behavior are not sufficiently similar to those of the cities that implemented congestion pricing — then the success observed elsewhere provides no basis for predicting success here. The recommendation becomes ungrounded.
explanations.A: Too strong. The planner needs only that congestion pricing would work here, not that no other policy has ever worked. Ruling out all alternatives is not required by the argument.
explanations.B: Out of scope. The argument does not hinge on the transportation mode of affected workers; it is about whether congestion pricing reduces congestion and thus improves productivity and pollution.
explanations.C: Correct. The analogical inference from other cities to this city requires relevant similarity. Negation undercuts the basis for the recommendation.
explanations.D: Out of scope. How revenues are used is not part of the argument's reasoning; the conclusion concerns only whether to introduce the policy.
explanations.E: Too strong. The planner recommends congestion pricing as beneficial, not as superior to every alternative policy.

lr.difficultyReason: History argument about an archaeological inference; the gap concerns whether the physical evidence was produced by the inferred activity, with traps targeting subject-shift and too-strong errors.
lr.stimulus: Archaeologist: Excavations at a Bronze Age settlement revealed a large central structure whose floor was covered with a thick layer of ash and charred grain. Storage vessels for grain were found along the walls, and the settlement shows no evidence of attack or violent destruction. We conclude that the structure served as a communal granary in which a fire accidentally destroyed the stored grain supply.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the archaeologist's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bronze Age settlements always designated a single central structure for communal food storage.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The ash and charred grain were not deposited in the structure as part of a deliberate ritual burning rather than an accidental fire.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The settlement's inhabitants did not trade grain with neighboring settlements.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The storage vessels found along the walls were used exclusively for grain rather than for other foodstuffs.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The central structure was the largest building in the settlement.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes the fire was accidental based on the absence of evidence of attack. But a deliberate ritual burning of grain — a practice attested in various ancient cultures — would produce exactly the same physical evidence: ash, charred grain, storage vessels, no signs of violence. Negate B: the burning was deliberate and ritual — then the ash and charred grain no longer support the conclusion that an accidental fire destroyed the grain supply, and the argument fails.
explanations.A: Too strong and out of scope. The argument concerns only this specific structure at this settlement. A universal claim about all Bronze Age settlements is not required.
explanations.B: Correct. Ritual burning is an alternative explanation for the physical evidence that the argument implicitly rules out. Negating B introduces that alternative and undermines the conclusion.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Whether the inhabitants traded grain does not affect what happened inside the central structure or whether the fire was accidental.
explanations.D: Out of scope. The identity of what was stored in the vessels (grain vs. other food) is not central to the argument about whether the fire was accidental; the charred grain on the floor already establishes grain was present.
explanations.E: Out of scope. The building's relative size within the settlement does not bear on the inference that the fire was accidental rather than intentional.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-premise argument with several topically plausible distractors. The necessary assumption bridges the causal claim to the conclusion; negation test eliminates a specific alternative explanation.
lr.stimulus: Cardiologist: In a recent clinical study, patients who ate a Mediterranean diet for one year showed significantly lower levels of arterial inflammation than they had at the study's start. Because arterial inflammation is a primary driver of heart disease, we can conclude that the Mediterranean diet reduces patients' risk of developing heart disease.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the cardiologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Mediterranean diet is the most effective dietary intervention for preventing heart disease.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The reduction in arterial inflammation observed in the study was not caused by some other change in participants' behavior during the study period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All patients who adopt the Mediterranean diet will experience a reduction in arterial inflammation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Arterial inflammation is the only cause of heart disease.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The patients in the study had not previously attempted any other dietary interventions.

explanations.correct: The cardiologist attributes the reduction in arterial inflammation to the Mediterranean diet. If the reduction was actually caused by something else — say, increased exercise or stress reduction — then the diet gets undeserved credit and the conclusion collapses. Negating B destroys the argument, making it necessary.
explanations.A: Too strong — the argument only claims the diet reduces risk, not that it is the best intervention. This is a 'sufficient not necessary' trap.
explanations.B: Correct. Negating B (the reduction was caused by something else) dismantles the causal attribution that the entire conclusion rests on.
explanations.C: Too strong — a universal claim about all patients exceeds what the argument needs. The argument only draws from the study group.
explanations.D: Too strong — the argument depends on inflammation being a 'primary driver,' not the only cause. This overstates the premise.
explanations.E: Prior dietary history is out of scope; the argument concerns what caused the observed change, not patients' history before enrollment.

lr.difficultyReason: Economic argument with a subtle gap between market behavior and a normative conclusion; two distractors are close topical cousins of the correct answer.
lr.stimulus: Economist: When a government subsidizes a domestic industry, the artificially lowered prices that result drive foreign competitors out of the market. Once foreign competitors are eliminated, the subsidized domestic industry no longer faces competitive pressure to innovate. Therefore, industrial subsidies ultimately harm consumers in the subsidizing country.
lr.questionStem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Foreign competitors always produce higher-quality goods than domestic industries receiving subsidies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Governments that subsidize industries always intend to eliminate foreign competition.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A lack of competitive pressure to innovate results in outcomes that are worse for consumers than the original competitive market.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Industrial subsidies never produce any short-term benefits for domestic consumers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Domestic industries receiving subsidies eventually request additional government support.

explanations.correct: The argument's chain ends with 'no competitive pressure to innovate' and concludes 'consumers are harmed.' That leap requires that reduced innovation actually worsens consumer welfare. Negate C — reduced innovation pressure does NOT worsen consumer outcomes — and the conclusion evaporates.
explanations.A: Too strong and out of scope; the argument says nothing about quality comparisons between foreign and domestic goods.
explanations.B: Government intent is not part of the argument's reasoning chain; only the effect of subsidies matters.
explanations.C: Correct. This bridges the final premise (no innovation pressure) to the conclusion (harm to consumers).
explanations.D: Too strong — ruling out all short-term benefits exceeds what is needed. The argument concerns the ultimate, long-run outcome.
explanations.E: Whether industries seek additional subsidies is out of scope; it plays no role in the stated reasoning.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal argument with a conditional structure; two distractors exploit reversed-direction and too-strong traps.
lr.stimulus: Defense attorney: The prosecution's case rests entirely on the testimony of a single eyewitness who identified my client at the scene. However, cognitive psychologists have established that eyewitness identifications made under conditions of low lighting are frequently unreliable. The incident in question occurred in a dimly lit alley. Therefore, the jury should not convict my client solely on the basis of this identification.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eyewitness testimony is never sufficient to establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The lighting conditions in the alley were poor enough to render eyewitness identification unreliable in this instance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The eyewitness had no prior acquaintance with the defendant that would have aided recognition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The prosecution has no other evidence linking the defendant to the crime.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cognitive psychologists have studied the specific alley in which the incident occurred.

explanations.correct: The general principle that low-light identifications are unreliable only applies if the alley's lighting was actually low enough to trigger that unreliability. Negate B — the lighting was not poor enough to render identification unreliable here — and the psychological research no longer applies to this case, collapsing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Too strong — this blanket claim goes far beyond what the argument requires. The argument only concerns this specific identification under low-light conditions.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument applies a general principle to this case, which requires assuming the case falls within the principle's scope.
explanations.C: Prior acquaintance is an interesting alternative-explanation defeater, but the argument doesn't invoke recognition mechanisms beyond the lighting point. This is out of scope.
explanations.D: The attorney explicitly says the prosecution's case 'rests entirely' on the eyewitness, so this is already stated in the stimulus, not an assumption.
explanations.E: Specific study of this alley is far stronger than necessary and implausible as an assumed premise; the general psychological research is what the argument invokes.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science argument; the gap is between a measurement and what it is taken to represent. Two distractors are plausible defenders of the conclusion but address the wrong link.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientist: Core samples from a glacier in the Andes show elevated concentrations of black carbon — a byproduct of fossil fuel combustion — beginning in layers deposited approximately 150 years ago. Because glaciers accumulate layers of ice annually, we can use these samples to date the onset of large-scale industrialization in the region to roughly 150 years ago.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the scientist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Black carbon from fossil fuel combustion cannot be transported by wind from distant industrial regions to the Andean glacier.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The glacier has not undergone any significant melting or compression that would have disrupted the chronological ordering of its layers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Large-scale industrialization requires the combustion of fossil fuels.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No other substance besides black carbon can be used to date industrialization in glacial core samples.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The region surrounding the glacier was completely uninhabited before industrialization began.

explanations.correct: The argument uses the depth of the black-carbon layer to date the onset of industrialization, which requires that the layers be in their original chronological order. If the glacier melted and refroze or was compressed, the layer sequence could be distorted, making the 150-year date meaningless. Negating B destroys the dating methodology.
explanations.A: If black carbon came from distant sources rather than local industry, the conclusion about when local industrialization began would be undermined — but the argument assumes the black carbon marks local industrial onset, not that it couldn't have come from afar. This is a plausible strengthener but not a gap the argument itself bridges; the scientist implicitly uses local deposition. However, A addresses a different link (local vs. distant source) that could also be necessary. On close inspection, B is more directly necessary to the annual-layer dating method explicitly invoked.
explanations.B: Correct. The dating method relies on annual-layer accumulation; disruption of that sequence severs the chronological inference entirely.
explanations.C: While plausible, this reverses the direction the argument needs. The argument goes from black carbon to industrialization, not from industrialization to fossil fuels. It's a premise restatement trap.
explanations.D: Too strong — the argument doesn't require that black carbon be the only marker, only that it be a reliable one in this case.
explanations.E: Prior habitation is out of scope; small-scale pre-industrial activity is not what 'large-scale industrialization' refers to, and the argument doesn't need the region to have been uninhabited.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology policy argument; the necessary assumption is a modest defensive claim ruling out an alternative mechanism. Distractors include a too-strong version and a scope-drift trap.
lr.stimulus: Technology policy analyst: Several major social media platforms recently modified their content-ranking algorithms to reduce the spread of health misinformation. Following these modifications, surveys showed a marked decrease in users' belief in common health myths. We can therefore conclude that algorithm modifications are an effective tool for reducing health misinformation belief.
lr.questionStem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Social media platforms are the primary source through which people encounter health misinformation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The decrease in belief in health myths was not due to a concurrent public health campaign unrelated to the algorithm changes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Algorithm modifications are the only effective means of combating health misinformation online.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Users of these platforms were aware that the algorithms had been modified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The surveys measuring health myth belief were conducted by independent researchers with no affiliation to the platforms.

explanations.correct: The argument credits algorithm modifications for the drop in misinformation belief. If an independent public health campaign coincidentally ran at the same time and caused the drop, the algorithm changes get unwarranted credit. Negate B — the decrease was due to such a campaign — and the causal conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: Too strong — even if social media is not the primary source, algorithm changes could still be an effective tool for those who do encounter misinformation there.
explanations.B: Correct. This rules out the most obvious confounding alternative, which the causal argument requires.
explanations.C: Too strong — claiming algorithm changes are the only effective means goes far beyond the argument's modest conclusion that they are an effective tool.
explanations.D: User awareness of the algorithm change is not part of the causal mechanism the argument invokes; reduced exposure to misinformation, not user cognizance of the change, drives the effect.
explanations.E: Survey methodology and researcher independence are not part of the argument's inferential chain; this is an out-of-scope trap.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics argument with a subtle gap between historical evidence and a linguistic conclusion; includes a reversed-direction trap and a subject-shift trap.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Ancient inscriptions recently unearthed in the Indus Valley contain symbols that also appear in writing systems used by populations in Mesopotamia during the same period. Because shared symbols between writing systems typically indicate either cultural contact or a common ancestor script, these inscriptions suggest that Indus Valley and Mesopotamian civilizations were not linguistically isolated from one another.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Indus Valley and Mesopotamian writing systems descended from a single common ancestor script.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The shared symbols were not introduced into one of the writing systems long after the period when both civilizations flourished.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All symbols that appear in multiple ancient writing systems reflect cultural contact between those civilizations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The inscriptions discovered are representative of the full range of writing used in the Indus Valley during that period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Linguists have fully deciphered both the Indus Valley and Mesopotamian writing systems.

explanations.correct: The argument dates the contact or common ancestry to the same period when both civilizations existed. If the shared symbols were added to one script much later — after the relevant period — then they would not serve as evidence of contemporaneous contact or a shared ancestor. Negating B collapses the temporal basis for the conclusion.
explanations.A: This picks one of two explanations (common ancestor vs. cultural contact) that the linguist leaves open. The argument does not require a common ancestor specifically — cultural contact is equally acceptable to it.
explanations.B: Correct. The temporal integrity of the symbol overlap is essential; symbols introduced after the period would not support the claim about these two civilizations' relationship.
explanations.C: Too strong — this universal claim eliminates the possibility of coincidence or independent invention, going beyond what the argument needs.
explanations.D: The representativeness of the sample is out of scope; the argument is about what shared symbols indicate, not whether more symbols exist.
explanations.E: Full decipherment is not required to observe that the same symbols appear in both systems; this is an irrelevant standard.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics argument with a normative conclusion; the gap concerns whether a factual premise is morally relevant in the way the argument requires. Includes a too-strong trap and a scope-drift trap.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Individuals who voluntarily accept positions of public trust — such as elected officials or corporate executives — implicitly consent to greater scrutiny of their professional conduct than private citizens receive. Because journalists who investigate and report on the professional misconduct of such figures are merely fulfilling the public's legitimate interest in accountability, such journalism cannot constitute an unjustifiable invasion of privacy.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Public figures have no reasonable expectation of privacy with respect to any aspect of their lives.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The professional conduct of public figures is among the matters to which their implicit consent to scrutiny extends.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Journalism that serves the public interest is always ethically justified, regardless of its methods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elected officials accept more public scrutiny than corporate executives do.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most privacy violations involving public figures are committed by journalists rather than by private individuals.

explanations.correct: The argument relies on the public figure's implicit consent to scrutiny to justify the journalism. But that consent must cover professional conduct specifically — which is what is being investigated. Negate B — their consent does not extend to professional conduct — and the ethical justification evaporates even if they accepted some scrutiny.
explanations.A: Too strong — the argument concerns professional conduct only, not 'any aspect of their lives.' This overstates the necessary assumption.
explanations.B: Correct. The scope of implicit consent must include the specific subject matter being investigated for the justification to work.
explanations.C: Too strong — this would justify any journalistic method, which goes far beyond the argument's reasoning about consent and professional conduct.
explanations.D: The comparison between elected officials and executives is not part of the argument's inferential chain; this is a subject-shift distractor.
explanations.E: Who typically commits privacy violations is out of scope; the argument concerns whether this journalism is unjustifiable, not statistical frequency.

lr.difficultyReason: History argument that requires connecting a behavioral explanation to an artifact's function; includes a shift-in-subject trap and a reversed-direction trap.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Court records from a sixteenth-century Italian city show that the same families who commissioned the most elaborate private chapels were also those most frequently cited for tax evasion. Historians have shown that elaborate chapel commissions in this period were used by wealthy families to publicly demonstrate piety and thereby enhance their social standing. Therefore, these families' chapel commissions were most likely motivated by a desire to offset the reputational damage caused by their tax evasion.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tax evasion in sixteenth-century Italy was considered a serious moral failing by the general public.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The families cited for tax evasion were aware that their evasion had damaged their public reputations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No sixteenth-century Italian family commissioned an elaborate chapel without having engaged in tax evasion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The elaborate chapels commissioned by these families were completed before the tax evasion citations were recorded.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Chapel commissions were the only means available to wealthy Italian families for restoring damaged reputations.

explanations.correct: The argument's chain requires that tax evasion caused reputational damage that the families then sought to repair. For tax evasion to damage reputation, it must have been viewed negatively by the public. Negate A — tax evasion was not considered a moral failing — and there is no reputational damage to offset, dismantling the motivation the historian attributes.
explanations.A: Correct. Reputational harm from tax evasion is the trigger for the compensatory behavior; without public moral condemnation, no such harm exists.
explanations.B: While awareness is relevant, the argument does not require that families consciously recognized the damage — only that the damage existed and could be offset. The historian attributes motivation based on the correlation, not on documented self-awareness.
explanations.C: Too strong — this universal claim would make chapel-commissioning exclusive to tax evaders, which the argument doesn't need.
explanations.D: This reverses the chronology the argument implies; if chapels came before citations, they couldn't have been motivated by reputational damage from those citations. This is actually a negation of a necessary assumption — but note the argument says 'offset damage,' implying chapels came after. D as stated (chapels completed before citations) would actually undermine the argument, so it is not an assumption the argument makes.
explanations.E: Too strong — the argument doesn't require chapels to be the only means of repairing reputation.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy argument about urban planning; the necessary assumption is a modest defensive claim that rules out a disqualifying alternative. Distractors include scope-drift and too-strong variants.
lr.stimulus: Urban planner: Cities that have replaced surface parking lots in their downtown cores with mixed-use developments have seen marked increases in pedestrian traffic and retail sales in surrounding blocks. Because increased pedestrian traffic and retail sales are the primary indicators of a vibrant downtown, these cities demonstrate that eliminating surface parking is an effective strategy for revitalizing downtown areas.
lr.questionStem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cities that replaced surface parking lots did not simultaneously undertake other major downtown revitalization initiatives that could account for the increases in pedestrian traffic and retail sales.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eliminating surface parking is the single most cost-effective revitalization strategy available to city planners.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pedestrian traffic and retail sales are better indicators of downtown vitality than any other available measures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every city that eliminates surface parking in its downtown core will experience increased pedestrian traffic.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The residents displaced by the removal of parking lots did not subsequently avoid the downtown area.

explanations.correct: The argument attributes the increases in pedestrian traffic and retail sales to the elimination of surface parking. If those cities also launched transit expansions, public events programs, or other revitalization efforts simultaneously, those could explain the increases instead. Negating A destroys the causal attribution that grounds the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Confounding simultaneous initiatives must be ruled out for the parking-elimination-to-revitalization causal chain to hold.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument only claims eliminating parking is an effective strategy, not the most cost-effective or the single best one.
explanations.C: The argument stipulates pedestrian traffic and retail sales as 'primary indicators' in a premise; this choice merely restates that premise rather than filling a gap.
explanations.D: Too strong — the argument draws from observed cases; a universal claim about every city exceeds what is needed.
explanations.E: While resident parking loss could theoretically reduce downtown visits, this is a speculative alternative mechanism not central to the argument's stated inferential chain; A addresses the more structurally critical confound.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts criticism argument where the gap involves connecting an interpretive method to a conclusion about artistic intent; includes a subject-shift trap and a too-strong trap.
lr.stimulus: Art critic: The preparatory sketches for a celebrated Baroque painting show that the artist originally depicted the central figure with an open, beseeching hand gesture.
