explanations.E: The location of authenticated works is irrelevant to the attribution argument. Out of scope.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental policy argument with a conditional chain. The argument has two premises leading to a resource conclusion. Distractors include a too-strong trap and a reversed-direction trap. The correct answer provides a necessary link in the causal chain.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientist: The region's primary aquifer is recharged almost entirely by snowmelt from the surrounding mountain range. Climate projections indicate that annual snowpack in those mountains will decline by 40 percent over the next 50 years. Therefore, communities that depend on the aquifer for their water supply will face serious water shortages within that period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the scientist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The communities dependent on the aquifer will not develop alternative water sources that compensate for the reduced recharge.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A 40 percent decline in snowpack will cause a proportionally equal decline in aquifer recharge.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The climate projections cited by the scientist have been verified by at least three independent research institutions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The affected communities currently extract water from the aquifer at or near its maximum sustainable yield.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No new precipitation patterns will emerge in the mountain range that could offset the projected snowpack decline.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that communities will face shortages. Even if the aquifer is significantly reduced, communities could avoid shortages by securing alternative water sources. Negating A — the communities do develop adequate alternative sources — means reduced aquifer recharge does not translate into shortages, collapsing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. The argument must assume that the communities will not compensate for the decline through alternative sources, otherwise the shortage conclusion does not follow from reduced recharge alone.
explanations.B: Too strong and overly precise. The argument needs only that a 40% snowpack decline will cause a significant reduction in recharge sufficient to produce shortages — not a perfectly proportional decline. The exact proportionality is not required.
explanations.C: The number of institutions that verified the projections is irrelevant to whether the conclusion follows from those projections. This is an out-of-scope epistemic condition.
explanations.D: Reversed-direction trap. Even if communities are extracting well below maximum sustainable yield, a large enough reduction in recharge could still create shortages. Whether current extraction is near maximum yield is not a required bridge.
explanations.E: Too strong. The argument need not rule out every possible offsetting weather change — only that the net effect of the projected snowpack decline will be a meaningful reduction in aquifer recharge. This answer over-extends the required assumption.

lr.difficultyReason: Medical argument with a hidden reference-class shift: the trial measured a surrogate biomarker in one population, but the conclusion generalizes to a clinical outcome in a broader, older population. Tempting distractors include a too-strong universal, a shift-in-subject about alternative mechanisms, and a reversed-direction trap. Negation test requires re-identifying what the researchers actually measured.
lr.stimulus: Cardiologist: In our six-week trial, adults aged 40 to 55 who took the drug Noviran had, on average, measurably lower resting blood pressure than those who took a placebo. Since sustained high blood pressure is a leading cause of stroke in older adults, physicians should prescribe Noviran to their patients over 70 to reduce those patients' risk of stroke.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the cardiologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any intervention that lowers blood pressure in middle-aged adults will lower blood pressure by a comparable margin in adults over 70.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Noviran has no side effects in older adults that outweigh its benefits for stroke prevention.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Noviran's effect on blood pressure in middle-aged adults is not attributable solely to mechanisms that cease to operate in adults over 70.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most adults over 70 who suffer strokes have had elevated blood pressure for an extended period before the stroke.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No drug currently prescribed to adults over 70 lowers blood pressure more effectively than Noviran.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'Noviran lowered blood pressure in 40-to-55-year-olds' to 'Noviran will reduce stroke risk in people over 70.' That requires the drug still to lower blood pressure in the older group. Negate C: the mechanism by which Noviran lowers blood pressure in middle-aged adults ceases to operate in people over 70. Then the trial data no longer supports any stroke-risk claim about over-70s, and the conclusion collapses. C is therefore necessary — stated defensively, ruling out the specific alternative that the drug simply doesn't work in the target population.
explanations.A: Too strong and shifted. The argument doesn't need 'any intervention' to work comparably — only Noviran. A universal claim about all blood-pressure-lowering interventions is not required.
explanations.B: Out of scope. Side-effect balance is a separate prudential question, not a link in the inflammation-to-stroke inference. Negating B (there are worse side effects) would make prescribing imprudent but would not undermine the reasoning from trial data to stroke-risk reduction.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Reversed direction. The argument needs lowering blood pressure to reduce stroke risk, not that stroke patients previously had high blood pressure. Negating D leaves the argument intact.
explanations.E: Out of scope and too strong. Relative efficacy against other drugs is not what the conclusion depends on; Noviran could be second-best and the stroke-reduction claim could still hold.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science stimulus with a counterfactual trap. The recovery of the fish population after the pollution-control policy is being credited to the policy itself; the necessary assumption rules out a non-policy explanation (prior natural rebound already underway). Close-cousin distractors include a too-strong comparison claim and an out-of-scope observation about other species.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientist: Five years after Lake Halberg's watershed council imposed strict limits on agricultural runoff, the lake's yellow perch population, which had declined for decades, had rebounded to near its historical average. The council's chair credits the limits with the recovery. Since nothing else changed about the lake's management in that period, the chair's explanation is almost certainly correct.
lr.questionStem: The scientist's argument depends on the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: runoff limits of comparable strictness have produced measurable fish recoveries in other lakes with similar pollution profiles

choices.label: B
choices.text: the yellow perch population would not have rebounded to near its historical average during those five years had the runoff limits not been imposed

choices.label: C
choices.text: agricultural runoff was the single largest source of pollution in Lake Halberg prior to the limits

choices.label: D
choices.text: no other species in Lake Halberg declined during the five years following the imposition of the limits

choices.label: E
choices.text: the watershed council enforced the runoff limits consistently throughout the entire five-year period

explanations.correct: To credit the limits with the recovery, the scientist must assume the recovery would not have happened without them. Negate B: the perch would have rebounded to near the historical average over those five years even without the limits (for example, a long-delayed natural cycle). Then the post-policy recovery is not evidence that the policy caused it, and the chair's explanation is undercut. B is thus the indispensable counterfactual bridge.
explanations.A: Shift in subject and too strong. Other lakes' responses are not a premise of the argument; the conclusion is about Lake Halberg specifically. Negating A leaves this lake's situation unchanged.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong. The limits could have caused the recovery even if runoff was not the single largest pollution source — only that limiting it made the difference. Negating C does not destroy the argument.
explanations.D: Out of scope. Other species' trajectories are not a link in the reasoning about perch recovery.
explanations.E: Tempting but not strictly necessary. Even inconsistent enforcement could have produced the rebound if sufficient overall; the argument needs only that the limits (however enforced) made the difference, not that enforcement was consistent throughout.

lr.difficultyReason: Economic argument with a comparative-claim subtlety. The conclusion says Brindale has a lower cost of living than Coverdale, but the evidence is that Brindale residents spend less on housing and groceries. The necessary assumption is that the non-measured categories do not make up the difference — a defensive assumption easily overlooked in favor of more aggressive-sounding distractors.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Residents of Brindale spend, on average, a smaller share of their income on housing and groceries than residents of Coverdale do. Since housing and groceries are among the largest household expenses in both cities, the overall cost of living in Brindale must be lower than that in Coverdale.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Residents of Brindale do not spend a sufficiently larger share of their income on expenses other than housing and groceries to offset the difference in housing and grocery spending.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Housing and groceries together account for more than half of an average household's spending in both Brindale and Coverdale.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Residents of Brindale earn, on average, the same income as residents of Coverdale.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any city in which housing and groceries consume a smaller share of income than in Coverdale has a lower overall cost of living than Coverdale.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Brindale's housing and grocery prices are lower in absolute terms than those in Coverdale.

explanations.correct: The conclusion compares overall cost of living. The premises compare only housing and groceries. Negate A: Brindale residents spend enough more on other categories to offset the housing-and-grocery savings. Then overall cost of living in Brindale is not lower, and the conclusion fails. A is necessary — a classic defensive, gap-closing assumption.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Close cousin but not required. The argument needs only that the offset not erase the difference, not any specific threshold share. The argument could hold even if housing plus groceries were less than half of total spending.
explanations.C: Shift in subject. The comparison is of shares of income, not absolute income. Equal income is not needed for the share-based inference to yield a cost-of-living conclusion.
explanations.D: Too strong. This is a general principle that would prove the conclusion rather than merely enabling it; necessary assumptions are narrower. It is a sufficient-assumption, not necessary-assumption, answer.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. The premises are about share of income, not absolute prices. Negating E (absolute prices are equal or higher in Brindale) does not block the argument, which works off share-of-income data.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal argument with a statistical-inference gap. The prosecutor infers from a matching DNA profile that the defendant was present; the necessary assumption constrains the reference class — specifically, that the profile is not shared by a substantial number of other people who could plausibly have been at the scene. Distractors include a reversed-direction assumption and a too-strong uniqueness claim.
lr.stimulus: Prosecutor: DNA extracted from a hair found at the crime scene matches the defendant's genetic profile on all thirteen markers tested. Profiles matching on all thirteen markers are extremely rare in the general population. We should therefore conclude that the hair came from the defendant, placing him at the scene.
lr.questionStem: The prosecutor's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the hair could not have been transferred to the scene by someone other than the person it came from

choices.label: B
choices.text: the thirteen markers tested are the markers least likely to coincide by chance in unrelated individuals

choices.label: C
choices.text: the population from which potential contributors to the hair would plausibly be drawn is not substantially enriched in people sharing the defendant's thirteen-marker profile

choices.label: D
choices.text: the defendant has no identical twin living within the city where the crime occurred

choices.label: E
choices.text: the matching profile alone constitutes sufficient evidence to convict the defendant of the crime

explanations.correct: The argument hinges on the rarity of a thirteen-marker match in the general population. But what matters is rarity in the reference class of people who could plausibly have contributed the hair. Negate C: that reference class is substantially enriched in matching profiles (for example, because the defendant's close relatives live nearby and were frequent visitors). Then the match is no longer strong evidence that the hair is the defendant's, and the conclusion collapses. C fills the reference-class gap.
explanations.A: Out of scope for this conclusion. The conclusion is that the hair came from the defendant, placing him at the scene; secondary transfer is a separate issue from source identification.
explanations.B: Too strong. The argument doesn't need the thirteen markers to be the best possible choice, only that a match on them be rare enough in the relevant population.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Close cousin, but narrower than necessary. The problem of enriched reference-class matches is broader than identical twins; ruling out only twins leaves other enrichment sources (close relatives, an isolated subpopulation) unaddressed.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. Whether the match suffices for conviction is a legal-standard question, not a premise of the source-identification inference.

lr.difficultyReason: History stimulus with a chronology-dependent gap. The historian dates a trade network from merchandise found in a shipwreck, but the conclusion requires that the ship sank while the merchandise was in active trade, not long after. Distractors include a too-strong claim about trade routes and a reversed-direction temporal claim.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Amphorae bearing stamps that were used only by vintners in the port city of Rhodion between 140 and 110 B.C.E. have been recovered from a shipwreck off the coast of Sicily. The amphorae still contained residues of Rhodian wine when found. We conclude that a commercial wine trade connecting Rhodion to western Mediterranean markets was active during the second half of the second century B.C.E.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rhodian vintners did not export wine to western Mediterranean markets at any time before 140 B.C.E.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The ship carrying the amphorae sank no more than a few decades after the amphorae were filled.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The stamps used by Rhodian vintners after 110 B.C.E. differed from those used during 140 to 110 B.C.E.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No stamped Rhodian amphorae from the period in question have been recovered from sites outside the western Mediterranean.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rhodian wine was the most valuable cargo commonly shipped to western Mediterranean ports during the period in question.

explanations.correct: The dating premise is the stamps' production window, 140 to 110 B.C.E. To conclude that the wine trade was active in that window, the historian must assume the shipwreck occurred close to that window rather than long afterward. Negate B: the ship sank two centuries later, perhaps while transporting antique-filled amphorae for some unrelated purpose. Then the wreck's existence does not establish an active second-century trade, and the conclusion falls apart. B is the necessary chronological bridge — parallel to the lake-sediment bones case.
explanations.A: Shift in subject. The conclusion concerns whether the trade was active in 140 to 110 B.C.E., not whether it was uniquely active then. Earlier trade is compatible with the conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Close cousin, but not required. Even if later stamps were identical, the stamps recovered could still plausibly be from the 140 to 110 B.C.E. window. The argument can work without ruling out later identical stamps, provided B holds.
explanations.D: Too strong and out of scope. Whether other amphorae surface elsewhere is independent of whether this wreck establishes the trade.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Relative cargo value is not a premise of the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology stimulus with a hidden reference-class issue: benchmark tests on a processor were run under controlled lab conditions, but the conclusion generalizes to everyday performance. The necessary assumption rules out the alternative that the lab conditions favored the tested chip in ways not replicated in typical use. Distractors include a shift-in-subject comparison and a too-strong universal.
lr.stimulus: Technology reviewer: In our laboratory benchmarks, the Aster X7 processor completed standard computational tasks, on average, 18 percent faster than the leading competitor's chip. Because these benchmarks are the accepted industry standard for gauging processor speed, consumers should expect the Aster X7 to handle their everyday computing needs noticeably more quickly than the competitor's chip handles them.
lr.questionStem: The reviewer's argument depends on the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the Aster X7 is priced competitively with the leading competitor's chip

choices.label: B
choices.text: the conditions under which the laboratory benchmarks were run did not give the Aster X7 an advantage that is absent in typical everyday computing use

choices.label: C
choices.text: no other processor currently sold to consumers performs better on the industry-standard benchmarks than the Aster X7

choices.label: D
choices.text: every task that consumers commonly perform on a personal computer is included in the industry-standard benchmark suite

choices.label: E
choices.text: consumers typically choose processors on the basis of laboratory benchmark performance rather than on the basis of other considerations

explanations.correct: The argument extrapolates from controlled benchmarks to everyday performance. That extrapolation requires that the benchmark setup not have favored the Aster X7 in ways absent from normal use (for example, thermal management tuned to the benchmarks, or minimal background processes). Negate B: the lab conditions did favor the Aster X7 in ways absent from everyday use. Then the 18-percent advantage would not transfer to consumer settings, and the conclusion falls apart.
explanations.A: Out of scope. Pricing is irrelevant to whether the processor handles tasks more quickly; the conclusion is about speed, not value.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong and shifted. The conclusion compares the Aster X7 to 'the leading competitor's chip,' not to all other processors. Negating C does not block the argument.
explanations.D: Too strong. The argument needs only that benchmark performance reasonably predict everyday performance, not that every common task appear in the suite. Negating D (some tasks are missing) does not destroy the argument provided the suite is reasonably representative.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. The conclusion is a prediction about what consumers should expect, not about how consumers in fact choose. Consumer purchasing criteria are orthogonal to the speed claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics stimulus with a scope-narrowing gap. The corpus shows a vocabulary contraction, but the conclusion generalizes to speakers' actual vocabulary knowledge. The necessary assumption rules out the possibility that the corpus is unrepresentative of general usage. Trap answers include a too-strong universal and a reversed-direction claim about written versus spoken language.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: A study of text messages sent by teenagers over the past twenty years finds that the average number of distinct English words appearing in a year's worth of messages has declined by roughly 15 percent. We conclude that the working vocabulary of the average English-speaking teenager has contracted correspondingly over the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contraction in the number of distinct words appearing in teenagers' text messages does not primarily reflect shifts in what teenagers choose to write about in messages rather than in what words they know.

choices.label: B
choices.text: English-speaking teenagers today send, on average, approximately the same number of text messages per year as teenagers did twenty years ago.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every word known by a teenager has some probability of appearing in a year's worth of that teenager's text messages.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Teenagers whose working vocabularies contract are also the teenagers whose text messages contain the fewest distinct words.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The vocabularies used by teenagers in text messages are a larger subset of their overall vocabularies than are the vocabularies they use in spoken conversation.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from corpus evidence (distinct words in messages) to a claim about working vocabulary. If the contraction reflects a narrowing of message topics rather than a narrowing of known words, then the corpus is not a valid proxy for working vocabulary. Negate A — the contraction does primarily reflect topic shift — and the conclusion collapses. A is the narrow, defensively phrased bridge required.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Close cousin, but not strictly necessary. Even if teenagers send fewer or more messages today, the distinct-word count per year could still track vocabulary. The argument can survive a moderate change in message volume.
explanations.C: Too strong. The argument doesn't need every word to have some chance of appearing — only that the sample be representative enough for the comparison.
explanations.D: Reversed direction. This states how vocabulary contraction correlates with corpus data, not what the argument requires to move from corpus data to vocabulary.
explanations.E: Out of scope. The argument is about text-message corpora, not a comparison between written and spoken vocabularies. Negating E does not break the inference.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics stimulus with a counterfactual gap. The ethicist concludes the sanctions policy was morally justified on the grounds that it achieved its stated aim. The necessary assumption is that the aim could not have been achieved by an alternative with less serious harm. Tempting wrong answers include a too-strong impossibility claim and a shift-in-subject about general sanctions theory.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: The economic sanctions imposed by nation A on nation B succeeded in compelling nation B's government to abandon its program of forced labor. The sanctions also caused meaningful hardship for many civilians in nation B who had no role in the program. Nevertheless, because the sanctions accomplished their stated aim, imposing them was morally justified.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the ethicist's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No alternative measure available to nation A would have compelled nation B's government to abandon the forced-labor program while causing less hardship to uninvolved civilians.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Economic sanctions are, in general, morally justified whenever they succeed in achieving their stated aim.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The hardship caused to uninvolved civilians in nation B was not foreseeable by nation A at the time the sanctions were imposed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nation B's government would not have abandoned the forced-labor program in the absence of the sanctions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The forced-labor program caused harm to nation B's civilians at least as severe as the hardship imposed by the sanctions.

explanations.correct: The ethicist must bridge 'sanctions achieved the aim' to 'sanctions were justified' given that they harmed civilians. A policy with avoidable collateral harm is hard to call justified if a less harmful alternative would have worked. Negate A: an alternative was available that would have succeeded with less civilian hardship. Then the sanctions' collateral harm was avoidable, and their justification evaporates. A is the necessary assumption.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — a universal principle about sanctions. Necessary assumptions are narrow; the argument needs only this case, not a general rule. This is a sufficient-assumption trap.
explanations.C: Close cousin, but not required. Foreseeability affects blame but not whether these sanctions were justified given the alternatives available. The argument can be defended even if the hardship was foreseeable, so long as A holds.
explanations.D: Tempting as a counterfactual but concerns effectiveness, which is already granted. The sanctions are stipulated to have succeeded; the argument does not additionally need that the program would have continued otherwise.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. A comparison of severity between forced labor and sanctions hardship is not a link in the argument as stated; the argument rests on the achievement of the aim plus justification. Negating E does not block A's reasoning.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy argument with a statistical-inference subtlety. The analyst infers that the tutoring program raised test scores from a year-over-year jump at participating schools; the necessary assumption rules out a confounding change that coincided with the program. Distractors include a too-strong claim about causation in general and a shift-in-subject about non-participating schools.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: After the state launched its after-school tutoring initiative, participating schools saw standardized math scores rise by an average of 9 percent in a single year — a jump far larger than any observed in the preceding decade. Since the initiative is the most salient change at these schools over that time, the initiative must be responsible for the jump.
lr.questionStem: The analyst's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: no factor other than the tutoring initiative that could plausibly have produced the jump in math scores changed at the participating schools during that year

choices.label: B
choices.text: the tutoring initiative increased math scores at every individual school that participated in it

choices.label: C
choices.text: schools that did not participate in the tutoring initiative did not see any comparable jump in math scores during the same year

choices.label: D
choices.text: standardized math scores are a reliable indicator of students' overall academic achievement

choices.label: E
choices.text: the tutoring initiative will continue to raise math scores in subsequent years if funding is maintained

explanations.correct: The argument infers causation from a coincident change, reasoning that the initiative is 'the most salient change.' That inference holds only if no other plausible cause changed too. Negate A: another plausible cause (for example, a simultaneous curriculum overhaul) did change at those schools. Then the initiative is not uniquely positioned to explain the jump, and the conclusion fails. A is the necessary alternative-cause-ruled-out assumption.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong. The conclusion concerns average improvement, not school-by-school uniformity. Some participating schools could have seen no gain while the average still rose.
explanations.C: Close cousin. It would strengthen the argument, but it is not required: the initiative could still be responsible for the participating-school jump even if other forces independently produced a comparable jump elsewhere. Necessary-assumption answers do not usually require this kind of comparison across populations.
explanations.D: Shift in subject. The conclusion is about the score jump, not about overall academic achievement. Score reliability for broader claims is not a premise here.
explanations.E: Out of scope. The conclusion is about what happened, not about what will happen in later years.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts argument with a comparative-claim gap. The critic concludes a novelist is the greatest of her generation based on literary-prize tallies over a period, but the conclusion requires that the prizes track greatness and that the comparison population is her generation. Tempting wrong answers include a reversed-direction claim and a too-strong universal about prize-giving.
lr.stimulus: Literary critic: Over the past two decades, Mira Adelaide has received more major international literary prizes than any other novelist writing in English during that period. These prizes are awarded by expert panels specifically to recognize the highest literary achievement. We can therefore conclude that Adelaide is the greatest English-language novelist of her generation.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the critic's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A novelist who writes in a language other than English cannot belong to Adelaide's generation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The major international literary prizes awarded over the past two decades tracked literary achievement at least as reliably among English-language novelists of Adelaide's generation as among those of other generations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adelaide's generation of English-language novelists is represented among the novelists who received major international literary prizes over the past two decades.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No novelist writing in English over the past two decades who did not receive as many major international prizes as Adelaide achieved as much as she did in literary terms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The expert panels awarding the major international literary prizes over the past two decades consisted of members drawn from diverse national and cultural backgrounds.

explanations.correct: The argument needs the prize-tally lead to translate into a greatness lead over Adelaide's generation. Negate D: some other English-language novelist of the past two decades, with fewer prizes, in fact achieved more in literary terms than Adelaide. Then Adelaide is not the greatest of her generation, and the conclusion fails. D is the necessary defensive bridge — phrased as 'no one uncredited surpassed her.'
explanations.A: Shift in subject and too strong. The conclusion concerns English-language novelists, but restricting Adelaide's generation to English speakers is not required by the argument; it would alter the conclusion's scope rather than support it.
explanations.B: Close cousin but inverted. The argument does not need a cross-generational reliability comparison; it needs only that within Adelaide's generation, the prizes track greatness well enough for her tally lead to correspond to a greatness lead — which is what D establishes.
explanations.C: Necessary-sounding but vacuous: Adelaide herself is an English-language novelist of her generation who received prizes, so representation is guaranteed by the stimulus. C adds nothing the argument needs.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Panel diversity is not a link in the argument; the stimulus already asserts that the panels are expert and award for literary achievement.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument turns on a subtle temporal gap: the clinical improvement must be attributable to the drug and not to a concurrent change in patient behavior. The necessary assumption rules out a specific alternative causal pathway, and several distractors are defensible-sounding strengtheners rather than true gap-fillers.
lr.stimulus: Neurologist: Patients in our trial who took the new compound daily for eight weeks showed a statistically significant reduction in migraine frequency. No other pharmacological treatment was administered during this period. We therefore conclude that the compound itself was responsible for the reduction in migraines.
lr.questionStem: The neurologist's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The compound has no significant side effects in the patient population studied.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The patients in the trial did not make lifestyle changes during the eight-week period that could have independently reduced their migraines.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The compound would produce the same results in patients outside the trial population.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All participants completed the full eight-week course of treatment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Migraine frequency in the trial patients was higher than average before the trial began.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'no other pharmacological treatment' to 'the compound caused the reduction.' But this only holds if non-pharmacological factors — lifestyle changes, stress reduction, dietary shifts — were also absent. Negate B: the patients did make lifestyle changes that could have reduced migraines. The conclusion that the compound caused the reduction collapses entirely.
explanations.A: Side effects are irrelevant to whether the compound caused the reduction in migraines. This is an out-of-scope choice — it concerns safety, not causal attribution.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument rules out other pharmacological treatments but leaves open non-pharmacological explanations. B closes that gap; its negation destroys the causal conclusion.
explanations.C: Generalizability to populations outside the trial is not required for the conclusion, which concerns only the trial patients. This is a scope-shift trap.
explanations.D: Completion rates might affect the strength of the data but are not required for the causal inference; even partial completion would not automatically point to lifestyle changes as the cause.
explanations.E: Baseline migraine frequency relative to population averages has no bearing on whether the compound caused the observed reduction within the trial.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument contains a conditional chain embedded in a policy context. The necessary assumption concerns whether the mechanism the policy relies on was actually operative before the policy change — a chronological subtlety that makes the negation test non-obvious.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Since the city lowered its marginal income tax rate three years ago, annual tax revenues have actually increased. Critics who predicted a revenue shortfall were wrong. This shows that reducing the tax rate caused higher economic activity, which in turn generated more total revenue.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The city's population did not increase substantially during the three years following the tax cut.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The critics who predicted a revenue shortfall based their predictions solely on static revenue models.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The increase in tax revenues was not primarily due to factors unrelated to the tax rate reduction, such as national economic growth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Other cities that have cut tax rates have also experienced revenue increases.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The city did not simultaneously reduce its spending on public services during the same period.

explanations.correct: The argument attributes rising revenue to the tax cut via increased economic activity. But if national economic growth — independent of the rate change — drove the increase, the causal chain breaks. Negate C: the revenue increase was primarily due to factors unrelated to the rate reduction. The conclusion that the tax cut caused the increase is unsupported.
explanations.A: Population growth could itself be a confound, but the argument's chain specifically requires ruling out non-rate-related economic factors; population change is a narrower and less central alternative than C.
explanations.B: Whether critics used static models concerns the quality of their predictions, not the causal chain the economist asserts. This is out of scope.
explanations.C: Correct. The economist infers causation from correlation. The argument requires that no external confound explains the revenue increase; C negation destroys the causal conclusion.
explanations.D: Evidence from other cities would strengthen the argument but is not required — the argument concerns only this city. This is a sufficient-not-necessary trap.
explanations.E: Spending levels are not part of the causal mechanism described (tax rate → activity → revenue), so they are irrelevant to the argument's gap.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses a linguistic artifact (a word's etymology) to draw a conclusion about ancient cultural practice. The assumption bridges the gap between what the word's form implies and what it must have actually referred to — a subtle evidential link that the negation test exposes only on careful re-reading.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: The Proto-Indo-European root word reconstructed as *welg- is the source of both the Latin word for 'moist' and the Sanskrit word for 'rain.' Both daughter languages preserve the root in contexts exclusively associated with water. We can therefore conclude that speakers of Proto-Indo-European used *welg- to refer to naturally occurring water sources in their environment.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the linguist's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Proto-Indo-European speakers lived in a region with plentiful rainfall and surface water.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The water-related meanings in the daughter languages were not independently acquired after the languages diverged from Proto-Indo-European.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No other Proto-Indo-European root word was also associated with water.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Linguists can reconstruct Proto-Indo-European vocabulary with complete accuracy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Latin and Sanskrit words derived from *welg- are among the oldest attested words in those languages.

explanations.correct: The argument infers *welg-'s original meaning from its meaning in daughter languages. This works only if those meanings were inherited, not developed independently. Negate B: the water-related meanings were independently acquired after divergence. Then the shared water associations tell us nothing about the proto-language word's meaning, and the conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: The argument concerns the word's meaning, not the ecology of the speakers' homeland. This is an out-of-scope strengthener.
explanations.B: Correct. The entire inference from daughter-language meanings back to proto-language meaning requires that those meanings were inherited, not convergently developed.
explanations.C: The existence of other water-related roots is irrelevant; the argument is about what *welg- meant, not whether it was the only such word. This is a shift-in-scope trap.
explanations.D: 'Complete accuracy' is too strong a requirement — the argument needs only that the reconstruction is reliable enough to support a meaning inference, but more importantly, reconstruction accuracy is not the gap in this argument at all.
explanations.E: The age of attestation in daughter languages has no bearing on whether the shared meanings were inherited versus independently developed.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument draws an ethical conclusion from a legal precedent, requiring an assumption about the relationship between legal and moral obligations. The trap choices are morally resonant but either too strong or subtly reversed in direction.
lr.stimulus: Legal scholar: Courts in this jurisdiction have consistently held that parties to a contract are obligated to disclose information that would be material to the other party's decision to enter the contract. Since the defendant knew that the bridge inspection report was materially relevant to the buyer's decision, the defendant had an obligation to disclose it. The defendant therefore acted wrongly in withholding the report.
lr.questionStem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The buyer would have refused to enter the contract had the report been disclosed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failing to fulfill a legal obligation in this jurisdiction constitutes acting wrongly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The defendant was aware of the court decisions establishing the disclosure obligation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All material information relevant to a contract must always be disclosed regardless of cost.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The bridge inspection report accurately reflected the structural condition of the bridge.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'the defendant had a legal obligation to disclose' to 'the defendant acted wrongly.' This requires a bridge between legal obligation and moral wrongness. Negate B: failing to fulfill a legal obligation here does not constitute acting wrongly. The conclusion that the defendant 'acted wrongly' is then unsupported, even if the legal violation is established.
explanations.A: The buyer's counterfactual response would strengthen the argument about harm, but the conclusion is about wrongful action, not about the outcome. The argument does not require the buyer to have behaved differently.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument's conclusion is ethical ('acted wrongly'), but its premises are legal. The bridge between the two domains is precisely what B provides; its negation severs the conclusion from the premises.
explanations.C: Awareness of case law is not required for the obligation to exist or for the action to be wrong — ignorance of the law is not a defense here, and the argument doesn't invoke knowledge of the rule as a premise.
explanations.D: This is too strong — 'regardless of cost' introduces a universal claim the argument does not need. The argument requires only that this disclosure was obligatory, not a universal principle.
explanations.E: The accuracy of the report bears on how harmful the withholding was, not on whether withholding a materially relevant report was legally required and ethically wrong.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument relies on the absence of a species from a fossil record to date the species' extinction. The necessary assumption concerns the completeness of the record for the relevant period — a methodological point that requires careful attention to what the evidence could or could not show.
lr.stimulus: Paleontologist: Fossils of the large marine reptile Xanthosaurus have been recovered from sedimentary deposits dating from 180 to 145 million years ago, but none have been found in deposits laid down after that period. The fossil record for the relevant marine environments is otherwise rich and well-preserved for the subsequent 20 million years. Xanthosaurus therefore became extinct approximately 145 million years ago.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the paleontologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Xanthosaurus was the apex predator of its marine environment during its existence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The absence of Xanthosaurus fossils from later deposits is not due to the animal's having migrated to environments that are poorly preserved in the fossil record.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No marine reptile species that appeared after 145 million years ago was closely related to Xanthosaurus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The sedimentary deposits containing Xanthosaurus fossils have been thoroughly excavated.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Xanthosaurus fossils are as durable as those of other large marine reptiles found in the same deposits.

explanations.correct: The argument infers extinction from absence in the fossil record, and attempts to shore this up by noting that the record is otherwise rich for those later environments. But this only rules out fossilization gaps in environments that were already well-preserved. If Xanthosaurus migrated to a poorly-preserved environment, absence from the well-preserved record proves nothing. Negate B: the absence is due to migration to poorly-preserved environments. The extinction conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: Apex predator status is entirely outside the scope of the extinction-dating inference.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument uses the richness of the post-145-million-year record to validate the absence as genuine. But this only works if the animal didn't move to an area where fossilization would be unlikely. Negation destroys the evidential basis for the conclusion.
explanations.C: Phylogenetic relationships to later species are irrelevant to when Xanthosaurus itself went extinct.
explanations.D: Thorough excavation concerns how many fossils we've found in known deposits, but the argument already grants that none have been found after 145 mya — completeness of excavation of the known fossils is not the gap.
explanations.E: Fossil durability affects preservation rates across the same environment, but the argument specifically notes the record is rich; durability differences between species would only matter if we expected to find Xanthosaurus but didn't due to fragility.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument attributes a historical outcome to a specific policy decision, but the necessary assumption is that the policy change was implemented as enacted — a procedural gap that is easy to overlook because readers naturally assume enacted policies are carried out.
lr.stimulus: Historian: In 1847, the colonial administration enacted a policy requiring all grain merchants to register their stores with a central authority. Records show that famines became far less frequent in the region during the two decades following 1847. The registration policy must therefore have contributed to reducing famines by enabling authorities to identify and redistribute grain surpluses.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the historian's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The colonial administration was motivated primarily by humanitarian concerns when enacting the policy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Grain merchants in the region complied with the registration requirement to a sufficient extent that authorities could track surplus stores.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No other administrative reforms were enacted by the colonial government during the same two-decade period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Famines in the region before 1847 were caused exclusively by uneven distribution of grain rather than by crop failures.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The colonial administration's records from the period after 1847 accurately reflect the true frequency of famines.

explanations.correct: The causal mechanism the historian proposes is: registration → visibility of surpluses → redistribution → fewer famines. This chain requires that the registration policy was actually used — i.e., that merchants registered to a degree that made tracking possible. Negate B: merchants did not comply sufficiently for authorities to track surpluses. The entire redistributive mechanism breaks down, and the policy cannot have reduced famines in the way described.
explanations.A: The administration's motivations are irrelevant to whether the policy had the stated effect. This is an out-of-scope trap.
explanations.B: Correct. The mechanism requires compliance; without it, the policy is nominal and cannot have enabled redistribution.
explanations.C: Too strong — other concurrent reforms would provide alternative explanations, but the argument doesn't need to be the only explanation, merely a contributing one. Also, the question of other reforms concerns alternative causation rather than a gap in the mechanism described.
explanations.D: 'Exclusively' is too strong; the argument only needs grain redistribution to have been able to reduce famine, not that all past famines were purely distributional.
explanations.E: Record accuracy is a meta-evidential concern and is not a gap within the causal chain the argument constructs.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument moves from a statistical pattern in software adoption to a conclusion about user preference, but the necessary assumption concerns whether the statistical pattern reflects genuine choice rather than constrained options — a subtle distinction that distractors obscure with plausible tech-policy framing.
lr.stimulus: Technology analyst: A survey of enterprise software deployments shows that open-source database systems now account for 58 percent of all new installations, up from 31 percent five years ago. Since enterprises choose software based on their operational needs, this shift demonstrates that open-source databases have become better suited to enterprise operational requirements than proprietary alternatives.
lr.questionStem: The technology analyst's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Open-source databases will continue to gain market share over the next five years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The enterprises surveyed represent a cross-section of industries rather than a single sector.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The increased adoption of open-source databases was not driven primarily by cost constraints that made proprietary alternatives unaffordable rather than by operational fit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Open-source database systems have more features than proprietary systems available five years ago.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The enterprises that adopted open-source databases did not later revert to proprietary systems.

explanations.correct: The argument assumes that the choice reflects operational suitability because enterprises choose based on operational needs. But if enterprises adopted open-source databases mainly because budget cuts made proprietary software unaffordable, the shift reflects cost constraints, not superior operational fit. Negate C: the increase was driven primarily by cost constraints. The conclusion that open-source systems became better suited to operational requirements is then unsupported.
explanations.A: Future market share trends are outside the scope of an argument about why the past shift occurred. This is a scope-drift trap.
explanations.B: Industry diversity in the survey sample would affect generalizability, but the argument's conclusion is not about all industries — it concerns the demonstrated shift. Survey composition is not the argument's gap.
explanations.C: Correct. The key premise is that enterprises choose based on operational needs; if a non-operational factor (cost) drove the switch, the operational-fit conclusion doesn't follow.
explanations.D: Having more features is a specific way of being better suited operationally, but the argument concludes only that open-source became better suited — not necessarily through feature count. Also, this would make the answer sufficient rather than necessary.
explanations.E: Subsequent reversion would affect long-term conclusions but is not required for the argument's inference about why the shift occurred in the first place.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument draws a conclusion about the intended audience of a Renaissance painting from the physical location of a detail within the composition. The necessary assumption concerns viewing conditions — a subtle perceptual link that most readers take for granted, making the negation test unexpectedly decisive.
lr.stimulus: Art historian: In a 1523 altarpiece, the painter concealed a self-portrait in the lower-left corner of the composition, rendered at a scale requiring close inspection to identify. The altarpiece was installed above the high altar of a private chapel accessible only to the patron's household. The self-portrait was therefore intended to be seen by the patron, not by a general congregation.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the art historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The painter was personally acquainted with the patron before accepting the commission.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Paintings installed above altars in the sixteenth century were generally intended to be viewed from a distance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The patron's household members regularly approached the altarpiece closely enough to view its details at the scale at which the self-portrait was rendered.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The painter did not include any other hidden figures elsewhere in the altarpiece.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The patron commissioned the altarpiece specifically because of the painter's reputation for including self-portraits.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes the self-portrait was intended for the patron based on (1) restricted access — only the household could enter, and (2) small scale — requiring close inspection. But restricted access to a space does not guarantee that viewers approached the work closely. If household members never came near enough to see details at that scale, the self-portrait was effectively invisible to everyone. Negate C: household members did not regularly approach closely enough. The argument that the patron was the intended audience collapses.
explanations.A: Prior acquaintance is not required for the viewing-access argument; the argument depends on physical access to the chapel and the scale of the detail, not on the relationship between artist and patron.
explanations.B: General conventions about altarpiece viewing would undercut the argument rather than support it, and in any case conventions elsewhere have no bearing on what was possible in this specific private chapel.
explanations.C: Correct. The chain requires that restricted access implies the patron could see the detail — but that only holds if those with access actually viewed the work at close range.
explanations.D: Other hidden figures would complicate interpretation of the artist's intent but are not required for the conclusion that this self-portrait was aimed at the patron. This is an out-of-scope trap.
explanations.E: The patron's motivation for the commission has no bearing on whether the viewing conditions existed for the self-portrait to be seen.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses a proposed environmental regulation's failure to pass as evidence of legislative priorities, but the necessary assumption concerns whether the vote accurately reflects preferences rather than procedural obstacles — a conditional subtlety that makes most distractors seem relevant.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: The legislature recently voted down a bill that would have imposed strict emissions limits on agricultural operations. Since legislators vote in accordance with their constituents' preferences, the defeat of the bill shows that the public in this jurisdiction does not prioritize reducing agricultural emissions over protecting farm revenues.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The bill's sponsors did not make procedural errors that caused the bill to fail independent of legislators' views on its merits.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Agricultural emissions are a significant contributor to air quality problems in the jurisdiction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Legislators in this jurisdiction are more responsive to rural constituents than to urban constituents.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The public in this jurisdiction is aware of the scientific evidence linking agricultural operations to emissions problems.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No similar emissions-limiting legislation will be introduced in the next legislative session.

explanations.correct: The analyst's reasoning is: legislators vote per constituent preferences → bill failed → public prefers farm revenue over emissions control. But this requires the vote to reflect legislative preferences about the bill's merits. If the bill failed due to a procedural technicality (a missed deadline, a quorum failure, a committee error), the vote tells us nothing about legislators' — or constituents' — substantive views. Negate A: the bill did fail due to procedural errors independent of legislators' views. The inference about public priorities collapses.
explanations.A: Correct. The argument requires that the vote outcome tracks legislators' views on the merits, which is only true if non-merit procedural factors didn't determine the outcome.
explanations.B: Whether agricultural emissions are actually significant is an out-of-scope scientific question; the argument concerns what the vote reveals about preferences, not whether the bill addressed a real problem.
explanations.C: Urban vs. rural responsiveness is a plausible concern but not required — the argument only needs that legislators track constituents' preferences generally, not that they do so differentially by geography.
explanations.D: Public awareness of scientific evidence is not a link in the argument's chain; the argument infers preferences from a vote, not from what the public knows.
explanations.E: Future legislative sessions are entirely outside the scope of an argument about what a past vote reveals about current public priorities.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument moves from a philosophical claim about moral desert to a specific normative conclusion about punishment, bridging desert theory with institutional practice. The necessary assumption is a modest defensive claim that is easily confused with two stronger distractor answers that prove too much.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Punishment is justified only when the person being punished deserves to suffer for what they have done. A person deserves to suffer only if they acted freely and with full knowledge of the wrongness of their act. Since individuals who commit crimes under severe psychological compulsion do not act freely, they do not deserve punishment.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Severe psychological compulsion always completely eliminates an individual's freedom of action.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No consideration other than desert could ever justify imposing suffering on an individual who has committed a crime.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Individuals who act under psychological compulsion are not morally responsible for any of their actions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The legal system should not punish individuals who do not deserve punishment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An individual who lacks full knowledge of the wrongness of an act is not acting freely in the relevant sense.

explanations.correct: The ethicist's conclusion is that compelled individuals 'do not deserve punishment,' meaning punishment of them is not justified. The first premise states punishment is justified only when deserved. The argument then establishes that compelled actors don't deserve it. But the conclusion requires that justified punishment is tied exclusively to desert — that no alternative ground (deterrence, incapacitation, public safety) could justify punishing someone who doesn't deserve it. Negate B: some consideration other than desert could justify imposing suffering on a compelled offender. Then the first premise ('only when deserved') would be violated, but more importantly, the argument's conclusion that punishment is not justified would be undermined by that alternative ground.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'always completely eliminates' goes beyond what the argument needs. The argument only requires that severe compulsion eliminates freedom in the specific cases at issue; a universal claim is not required and makes this a sufficient-not-necessary trap.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument's first premise defines justified punishment as requiring desert. The conclusion that compelled actors don't deserve punishment entails they can't justifiably be punished — but only if desert is the sole ground for justified punishment. Negating B opens an alternative justificatory route and undermines the conclusion.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'any of their actions' introduces a universal that the argument doesn't need. The argument concerns punishment for specific crimes, not global moral responsibility.
explanations.D: This adds an institutional prescription (what the legal system should do) that the argument doesn't assert; the ethicist's conclusion is about justification in principle, not about what legal institutions must do. This is a scope-shift trap.
explanations.E: The argument treats freedom and knowledge as two independent conditions for desert. Whether lack of knowledge affects freedom is an internal conceptual question the argument doesn't require — the premises list them as separate conjuncts.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument hinges on a subtle temporal gap: the policy was enacted before the data shift, but the necessary assumption concerns whether a confounding variable—not the policy—explains the improvement. Negation test requires close re-reading of the causal chain.
lr.stimulus: City health official: After the municipal water-fluoridation program was expanded three years ago, the rate of tooth decay among children in this city fell by 22 percent. No other city-wide dental health initiative was launched during that period. Therefore, the expansion of the fluoridation program was responsible for the decline in tooth decay.
lr.questionStem: The health official's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The fluoridation program is the most cost-effective dental health intervention available to the city.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The rate of tooth decay among adults in the city did not decline over the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No factor other than the expanded fluoridation program accounts for the observed decline in tooth decay among children.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fluoridated water reduces tooth decay in children more effectively than fluoridated toothpaste does.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The children whose tooth decay rates were measured were the same children throughout the three-year period.

explanations.correct: The official infers causation from correlation, ruling out only other city-wide initiatives. But dietary changes, improved school dental programs, or demographic shifts could explain the decline. Negate C—some other factor does account for the decline—and the fluoridation program is no longer the established cause. The conclusion collapses, so C is necessary.
explanations.A: Cost-effectiveness is irrelevant to whether the program caused the observed decline. Out of scope.
explanations.B: Adult decay rates are not part of the reasoning about children's decay. Shift in subject trap.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The comparison to toothpaste is never invoked in the argument; this introduces an external comparison not required for the causal conclusion.
explanations.E: The argument is about population-level rates, not the same individual children; whether the same cohort was tracked does not determine whether the program caused the decline.

lr.difficultyReason: The chronological subtlety—whether the inscription was added at the time of composition or later—is easy to miss on a first read. The necessary assumption concerns the provenance of the manuscript evidence, not the content of the inscription itself.
lr.stimulus: Historian: A manuscript discovered in a Florentine archive bears an inscription attributing it to a scribe who died in 1423. The manuscript's parchment has been dated by chemical analysis to between 1400 and 1440. Scholars have therefore concluded that the manuscript was produced during the scribe's lifetime.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the scholars' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The scribe named in the inscription produced other manuscripts that survive to this day.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The inscription attributing the manuscript to the scribe was not added to the parchment after the scribe's death.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chemical dating of parchment is the most reliable method of establishing a manuscript's age.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No manuscripts produced in Florence before 1400 have survived into the present day.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Florentine archive acquired the manuscript before any alterations could be made to it.

explanations.correct: The argument uses the inscription as evidence that the scribe produced the manuscript. But if the inscription was added after the scribe's death—say, as a false attribution—the parchment date merely tells us when the parchment was made, not who wrote on it. Negate B: the inscription was added after the scribe's death. Then the conclusion that the manuscript was produced during his lifetime is unsupported. B is necessary.
explanations.A: The existence of other manuscripts by the scribe is irrelevant to whether this particular manuscript was produced during his lifetime.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The argument doesn't require chemical dating to be the most reliable method—only that the dating result here is accurate enough to draw the conclusion. Too strong/comparative trap.
explanations.D: The survival of pre-1400 manuscripts is wholly unrelated to dating this manuscript.
explanations.E: Archive acquisition history is out of scope; alterations before archive entry are what matter, and the argument doesn't invoke the archive's custodial record.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument involves a conditional inference about software security. The necessary assumption is a narrow defender—ruling out a specific alternative pathway for the breach—rather than a broad causal claim. Distractors are carefully calibrated to sound like gap-fillers without passing the negation test.
lr.stimulus: Security analyst: Access to the company's proprietary database requires both a valid employee credential and a device registered on the internal network. The breach that occurred last month exposed customer records stored in that database. Since none of the company's registered devices were reported stolen or missing at the time of the breach, the attacker must have used a stolen employee credential to gain access.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the security analyst's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The company's internal network monitoring system was functioning properly at the time of the breach.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The attacker did not gain access to the database by exploiting a software vulnerability that bypassed the credential and device requirements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Employee credentials are more frequently stolen than registered devices are reported missing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The company had not recently expanded the list of employees authorized to access the proprietary database.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The customer records exposed in the breach were the most sensitive data stored in the database.

explanations.correct: The analyst reasons that because no registered device was stolen, the attacker must have used a stolen credential. But this assumes the two-factor access requirements were the only way in. If the attacker bypassed both requirements through a software vulnerability, then neither a stolen device nor a stolen credential was needed. Negate B—the attacker did exploit such a vulnerability—and the conclusion evaporates. B is necessary.
explanations.A: Whether monitoring was functioning affects detection, not the mechanism of access. The argument is about how access was gained, not whether it was observed.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: A comparative frequency claim is irrelevant to this specific breach; it would strengthen the argument at best but is not required for the conclusion.
explanations.D: Whether the authorized-user list expanded is out of scope; the argument concerns how the attacker got in, not who was legitimately authorized.
explanations.E: The sensitivity of the exposed records is irrelevant to how the breach was accomplished.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument turns on a subtle sufficiency-of-evidence gap: ancient pollen deposits are used to date agricultural activity, but the necessary assumption concerns whether the pollen arrived via human cultivation rather than natural dispersal. Students often pick a too-strong distractor about all agriculture in the region.
lr.stimulus: Archaeobotanist: Core samples taken from a peat bog in northern Europe contain cereal pollen deposits dating to approximately 4,800 years ago. Because cereal grasses are not native to this region and do not disperse their pollen over long distances, the presence of this pollen indicates that people were cultivating cereal crops near the bog at that time.
lr.questionStem: The archaeobotanist's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: no other archaeological sites in the region show evidence of agriculture predating 4,800 years ago.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the cereal pollen found in the bog was not transported there by traders passing through the region.

choices.label: C
choices.text: peat bogs are the most reliable repositories of ancient pollen deposits in northern Europe.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the people cultivating cereal crops near the bog 4,800 years ago were permanent settlers rather than nomadic farmers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: cereal grasses had not been introduced to the region earlier than 4,800 years ago by migratory birds.

explanations.correct: The argument's key premise is that cereal pollen doesn't disperse over long distances, so its presence implies local cultivation. But if traders carrying cereal grain passed through and deposited pollen—e.g., from stored grain—the pollen could be present without local cultivation. Negate B: the pollen was transported by traders. Then local cultivation is no longer established. The argument requires B.
explanations.A: Earlier sites elsewhere are irrelevant to whether this pollen indicates local cultivation 4,800 years ago; out of scope.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Peat bogs being the most reliable repository is a comparative claim not required for the conclusion; the argument uses this bog's data, not a claim about bogs generally.
explanations.D: Whether the farmers were nomadic or permanent is out of scope; the conclusion is only that people were cultivating crops nearby, not about their lifestyle.
explanations.E: Migratory birds could introduce live plants but not pollen deposits in the relevant sense; moreover, this would not undermine the premise that the pollen doesn't travel long distances on its own.

lr.difficultyReason: The economic argument contains a conditional chain with a hidden assumption about market structure. The necessary assumption is a narrow defender ruling out a specific mechanism that would sever the causal link. Trap choices mimic the correct form but address different links in the chain.
lr.stimulus: Economist: When the central bank raises the benchmark interest rate, commercial banks typically increase the rates they charge on consumer loans. Higher consumer loan rates reduce household borrowing. Reduced borrowing, in turn, leads to decreased consumer spending. Therefore, the central bank's recent rate increase will likely slow overall economic growth.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consumer spending constitutes a sufficiently large share of the economy that a reduction in it would slow overall economic growth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The central bank raises the benchmark interest rate only when inflation is above its target level.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Commercial banks earn higher profits when the benchmark interest rate is elevated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Household borrowing is the primary driver of consumer spending in the economy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The central bank did not simultaneously implement other policies that would stimulate economic growth.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from decreased consumer spending to slowed overall economic growth. This step requires that consumer spending be a large enough component of the economy to affect overall growth. Negate A: consumer spending does not constitute a sufficiently large share—then reduced consumer spending would not slow overall growth, and the conclusion fails. A is necessary.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The reason the bank raises rates is irrelevant to whether the rate increase, once made, will slow growth through the described mechanism.
explanations.C: Bank profits are out of scope; the argument is about the effect on consumers and growth, not bank revenues.
explanations.D: Too strong—the argument requires only that reduced borrowing leads to decreased spending (as stated), not that borrowing is the primary driver of all consumer spending.
explanations.E: Simultaneous stimulative policies would undermine the conclusion, but the argument does not need to rule this out to establish the described causal chain; this is a strengthener, not a necessary assumption.

lr.difficultyReason: The legal argument involves an evidentiary inference about intent. The necessary assumption rules out an alternative interpretation of a document—a subtle defender rather than a broad causal claim. Several traps address the legal standard rather than the logical gap.
lr.stimulus: Attorney: The defendant signed a contract containing a clause that explicitly prohibited subletting the leased property. The defendant later sublet the property to a third party. My client, the property owner, is therefore entitled to damages, since the defendant cannot claim ignorance of the prohibition—the clause was clearly stated in the document the defendant signed.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the attorney's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The defendant understood the legal consequences of subletting at the time the contract was signed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Signing a contract constitutes sufficient evidence that the signer has read and understood its contents.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The property owner suffered measurable financial harm as a result of the subletting.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The no-subletting clause is enforceable under the jurisdiction's contract law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The defendant did not sublet the property under a reasonable belief that the property owner had given oral permission to do so.

explanations.correct: The attorney's argument that the defendant cannot claim ignorance rests on the fact that the clause was in the signed document. This only defeats an ignorance defense if signing is taken as evidence of having read and understood the document. Negate B: signing does not constitute such evidence—then the defendant could still plausibly claim ignorance, and the attorney's specific rebuttal of that defense collapses. B is necessary.
explanations.A: Understanding legal consequences is a different matter from knowing about the prohibition; the argument is about awareness of the clause, not its legal ramifications.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The argument is about the defendant's knowledge and the contractual prohibition, not about whether damages are quantifiable; financial harm may be legally required but is not the logical gap the argument bridges.
explanations.D: Enforceability is a legal background condition, but the attorney's specific argument is about the ignorance defense—the logical gap is about notice, not enforceability per se.
explanations.E: Oral permission is a different defense not addressed in the argument; ruling it out would strengthen the case but is not required for the argument as stated.

lr.difficultyReason: A linguistics argument about language change contains a subtle gap between synchronic evidence (current dialect features) and a diachronic conclusion (contact in the past). The necessary assumption concerns whether the shared feature originated in contact rather than independent development.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: The dialect spoken in the coastal villages of this island shares seventeen phonological features with a dialect spoken in a region 400 kilometers away on the mainland. The probability of two dialects independently developing even a handful of such features is negligibly small. Therefore, the ancestors of the coastal villagers must have had sustained contact with speakers of the mainland dialect.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The coastal villagers are currently aware of the linguistic similarities between their dialect and the mainland dialect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The seventeen shared phonological features were not all inherited from a common ancestral language spoken by both populations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phonological features are more reliable indicators of language contact than grammatical features are.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The coastal villagers' ancestors traveled to the mainland more frequently than mainland speakers traveled to the island.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The island's coastal villages were established before the mainland dialect developed its distinctive phonological features.
