explanations.correct: The argument attributes the shared features to contact between the two populations. But shared features inherited from a common ancestor language would explain the similarities without any direct contact. Negate B: the features were all inherited from a common ancestral language—then the conclusion that the ancestors had sustained contact is unsupported. B is the necessary assumption.
explanations.A: Current awareness of the speakers is irrelevant to historical contact; out of scope.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: A comparative reliability claim about feature types is not required; the argument uses phonological features and does not need to establish their superiority over other types.
explanations.D: The direction of travel is irrelevant to whether contact occurred at all; this is too specific and not required for the conclusion.
explanations.E: The chronological relationship between the villages and the mainland dialect's development is not part of the argument's reasoning chain.

lr.difficultyReason: The medical argument uses a clinical trial result to draw a conclusion about mechanism. The necessary assumption is a narrow bridge ruling out an alternative mechanism (placebo effect) rather than confirming the drug's efficacy broadly. Students often choose a too-strong distractor about all patients.
lr.stimulus: Clinical researcher: In our double-blind trial, patients who received the experimental compound showed a 40 percent reduction in inflammatory markers compared to those who received the placebo. Because the trial was double-blind, neither the patients nor the administering physicians knew who received the compound. We can therefore conclude that the compound itself, not patients' expectations of improvement, produced the reduction in inflammatory markers.
lr.questionStem: The researcher's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inflammatory markers are the most accurate available measure of the condition the compound is intended to treat.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The double-blind design prevented patients' expectations from differentially influencing inflammatory marker levels in the treatment group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All patients who received the compound experienced at least some reduction in inflammatory markers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The placebo used in the trial was chemically inert and had no therapeutic properties of its own.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients who received the placebo did not experience any reduction in inflammatory markers.

explanations.correct: The researcher concludes that the compound—not patient expectations—caused the reduction. This relies on the double-blind design having successfully equalized expectations across both groups. If, despite the blinding, patients in the treatment group somehow formed stronger expectations of improvement (inflating the treatment effect), then patient expectation could still be responsible. Negate B: the double-blind design did not prevent differential expectation effects—then the conclusion that the compound itself caused the reduction is unsupported. B is necessary.
explanations.A: Whether inflammatory markers are the best measure is irrelevant to the causal attribution between the compound and those markers.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong—the argument is about the group average, not that every single patient responded; requiring all patients to benefit is not part of the reasoning.
explanations.D: The placebo's inertness affects the interpretation of the control group's result but is not the logical gap the researcher's specific conclusion (compound vs. expectations) bridges.
explanations.E: Too strong—placebo patients could show some reduction and the conclusion would still hold, as long as the treatment group's greater reduction is attributed to the compound.

lr.difficultyReason: An ethics argument about moral responsibility contains a hidden scope condition: the necessary assumption limits the principle invoked so that it doesn't overreach. The negation test requires identifying which limiting condition the argument silently depends on.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: A person is morally responsible for an outcome only if that person could reasonably have foreseen it. The engineers who designed the bridge followed all applicable safety codes and had no access to the geological data that would have revealed the unusual soil conditions contributing to the collapse. Therefore, the engineers bear no moral responsibility for the bridge's collapse.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the ethicist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The safety codes the engineers followed were adequate for most soil conditions likely to be encountered in bridge construction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Moral responsibility for an engineering failure cannot be distributed among multiple parties simultaneously.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The engineers could not reasonably have foreseen the bridge's collapse given the information available to them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The geological survey that would have revealed the unusual soil conditions was not required by the applicable safety codes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No one who contributed to the bridge's design had access to the relevant geological data.

explanations.correct: The ethicist's principle is: moral responsibility requires reasonable foreseeability of the outcome. The conclusion is that the engineers bear no moral responsibility. To get there, the argument must establish that the engineers could not reasonably have foreseen the collapse. The premise says they followed codes and lacked the geological data, but the argument needs the further step that this means the collapse was not reasonably foreseeable. Negate C: the engineers could reasonably have foreseen the collapse—then even granting the principle, the engineers may bear moral responsibility. C is necessary.
explanations.A: Whether the codes were adequate for most conditions is background information, not the logical link needed to apply the principle to these engineers.
explanations.B: The argument is about these engineers specifically; whether responsibility can be shared is not required for the conclusion that they bear none.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Whether a geological survey was required is relevant to culpability under professional standards, not to the ethicist's specific foreseeability principle.
explanations.E: Too strong—even if some contributors had data, the argument concerns the specific engineers; but more importantly, the gap is about foreseeability, not about who had data.

lr.difficultyReason: An arts-criticism argument uses provenance evidence to attribute a painting. The necessary assumption is a temporal defender—ruling out that the stylistic features were acquired after the artist's death through restoration—mirroring the lake-sediment anchor's chronological subtlety. Distractors address attribution criteria without targeting the temporal gap.
lr.stimulus: Art historian: This unsigned painting depicts a scene and employs a color palette virtually identical to those in three works securely attributed to the seventeenth-century painter Vermeer. Dendrochronological analysis of the oak panel on which it is painted dates the panel to between 1650 and 1670—precisely Vermeer's most productive period. The painting must therefore be an authentic work by Vermeer.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the art historian's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vermeer painted more works on oak panels than on canvas during the period from 1650 to 1670.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No other seventeenth-century painter used a color palette and compositional approach identical to Vermeer's.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The stylistic features linking this painting to Vermeer's known works were not added by a later restorer who painted over an earlier composition on the panel.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dendrochronological analysis of oak panels is accurate to within a margin of twenty years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vermeer signed the majority of the paintings he produced during his most productive period.

explanations.correct: The argument uses stylistic similarity plus panel dating to conclude Vermeer painted this work. The panel dates to Vermeer's era, but the stylistic features connecting it to Vermeer could have been applied by a later restorer who repainted an older panel in Vermeer's style. Negate C: the stylistic features were added by a later restorer—then the similarity to Vermeer's work does not establish that Vermeer was the artist, and the conclusion collapses. C is necessary.
explanations.A: Whether Vermeer preferred oak to canvas is irrelevant; the argument uses the dating, not a preference claim, to support the attribution.
explanations.B: Too strong—the argument requires that the combination of features points to Vermeer specifically, but ruling out every other seventeenth-century painter entirely is not the narrow assumption required; the argument could succeed even if a few others had similar styles.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The argument already uses a twenty-year date range, so the accuracy of the method within that range is a background premise, not the logical gap; moreover, even some imprecision wouldn't undermine the conclusion as long as the panel dates to roughly Vermeer's era.
explanations.E: The painting being unsigned is noted, not used as counter-evidence; whether Vermeer habitually signed works does not bridge the evidentiary gap the argument relies on.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument hinges on a subtle conditional gap: the antibiotic's effect is inferred from a drop in infection rates, but only if the drop coincided with the antibiotic's introduction rather than some prior trend. Negation test requires careful tracking of timing.
lr.stimulus: Hospital administrator: Since we introduced the new broad-spectrum antibiotic in our intensive care unit six months ago, the rate of post-surgical infections has dropped by forty percent. No other changes to surgical protocols or staffing were implemented during that period. We therefore conclude that the antibiotic is responsible for the reduction in infections.
lr.questionStem: The administrator's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Broad-spectrum antibiotics are more effective than narrow-spectrum antibiotics in intensive care settings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The rate of post-surgical infections had not already been declining before the antibiotic was introduced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No patients in the intensive care unit were allergic to the new antibiotic.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The antibiotic was administered to every patient who underwent surgery during the six-month period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Post-surgical infection rates at other hospitals did not decline during the same period.

explanations.correct: Negate B: the infection rate had already been declining before the antibiotic was introduced. Then the observed forty-percent drop could simply be the continuation of a preexisting trend, and attributing the reduction to the antibiotic is unsupported. The argument collapses, confirming B is necessary.
explanations.A: The argument is about this specific antibiotic's effect in this unit, not a comparative claim about antibiotic types. This is out of scope.
explanations.B: Correct. A preexisting downward trend is the most natural alternative explanation the argument must rule out; negating B destroys the causal conclusion.
explanations.C: Allergic reactions are not part of the causal chain the administrator invokes; whether some patients were allergic does not undermine the infection-rate inference.
explanations.D: Too strong — the argument does not require universal administration, only that the antibiotic caused the observed aggregate drop. Partial administration could still drive a significant reduction.
explanations.E: Trends at other hospitals are irrelevant to this unit's causal inference; the argument is restricted to this ICU's data.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument involves a legal inference about authorship intent that depends on a chronological assumption about when a clause was drafted relative to a dispute. The needed assumption is defensive and easily missed amid topically plausible distractors.
lr.stimulus: Attorney: The contract between Delmar Industries and its supplier includes a force majeure clause exempting Delmar from liability for delivery failures caused by events beyond its control. The clause was written before any dispute between the parties arose. We can therefore conclude that the clause was not inserted to protect Delmar from the particular supplier dispute that is now in litigation.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the attorney's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Force majeure clauses are standard in contracts between manufacturers and their suppliers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Delmar Industries did not anticipate the specific dispute when the clause was drafted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The supplier was aware of the force majeure clause before signing the contract.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A clause written before a dispute arose cannot have been inserted to address that specific dispute.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Delmar Industries has prevailed in prior litigation involving similar contractual clauses.

explanations.correct: The attorney moves from 'written before the dispute' to 'not inserted to protect against this dispute.' That inference only holds if pre-dispute drafting rules out the clause being tailored for this dispute. Negate D — a pre-dispute clause could have been inserted to address a specific anticipated dispute — and the conclusion evaporates.
explanations.A: Whether force majeure clauses are standard is irrelevant to the argument about this clause's purpose.
explanations.B: This is too strong and is actually the conclusion repackaged. The argument does not require proving Delmar lacked foresight; it relies only on the timing of drafting.
explanations.C: The supplier's awareness is out of scope; the argument concerns the clause's purpose, not the supplier's knowledge.
explanations.D: Correct. This is the bridging principle the attorney's reasoning requires and is confirmed by negation.
explanations.E: Prior litigation outcomes are irrelevant to the question of this clause's drafting intent.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument conflates two different senses of 'value' in an economic context, requiring a careful assumption that bridges market price to intrinsic productive value. Distractors exploit the ambiguity skillfully.
lr.stimulus: Economist: The market price of a commodity reflects the collective judgment of buyers and sellers about that commodity's value. Since the market price of skilled labor in the technology sector has risen sharply over the past decade, it follows that the productive contribution of technology workers has increased substantially over that period.
lr.questionStem: The economist's argument relies on the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the supply of skilled technology workers has remained constant over the past decade.

choices.label: B
choices.text: market prices for labor accurately reflect the actual productive contributions of workers, not merely shifts in supply and demand for their skills.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the technology sector has grown faster than any other sector of the economy over the past decade.

choices.label: D
choices.text: wages in all sectors rise when the market price of skilled labor in one sector rises.

choices.label: E
choices.text: workers in the technology sector are more productive than workers in other sectors.

explanations.correct: The economist moves from 'market price has risen' to 'productive contribution has increased.' This inference only holds if rising market prices track productive contribution rather than mere scarcity or fashion. Negate B — if market prices can rise due to supply shortages without any increase in individual productive contribution — and the conclusion is unsupported.
explanations.A: Constant supply is one reason prices might rise, but the argument does not depend on supply being constant; it depends on price tracking productivity.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument requires that market price be a reliable proxy for productive contribution, not just for negotiating leverage or scarcity.
explanations.C: Sector-level growth comparisons are not part of the argument; the conclusion concerns workers' productive contribution, not the sector's overall size.
explanations.D: Cross-sector wage effects are out of scope; the argument is confined to technology-sector workers.
explanations.E: Comparative productivity across sectors is irrelevant; the argument concerns the change in technology workers' contribution over time, not their rank relative to other sectors.

lr.difficultyReason: The environmental science argument rests on a dating inference that requires the sample to have been sealed from contamination at a specific time. The necessary assumption involves the integrity of the evidentiary record — a subtle chronological condition.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientist: Core samples taken from the glacier contain a distinct layer of ash that matches the chemical signature of the Toba supervolcano eruption. Ice layers above this ash horizon contain atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations lower than those in layers below it. Therefore, the Toba eruption caused a reduction in atmospheric CO₂ levels.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Toba supervolcano was the largest volcanic eruption in the past two million years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Atmospheric CO₂ concentrations can be accurately measured from gases trapped in glacier ice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The CO₂ measurements in the ice layers above the ash horizon were not affected by gas migration through the ice after the layers were formed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No other volcanic eruption occurred in the region within one thousand years of the Toba eruption.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The glacier from which the core samples were taken did not melt partially between the time of the eruption and the time of sampling.

explanations.correct: The argument uses CO₂ readings from layers above the ash as evidence of post-eruption conditions. If gas migrated through the ice after the layers formed, the readings might reflect later atmospheric conditions rather than the post-Toba environment. Negate C — gas migration did affect those measurements — and the CO₂ data no longer reliably represents post-eruption conditions, destroying the conclusion.
explanations.A: The eruption's relative magnitude is irrelevant to the causal inference drawn from the ice-core data.
explanations.B: The accuracy of the measurement method is assumed at a general level, but this distractor is too broad — the argument's specific vulnerability is whether the measurements in those particular layers were contaminated, not whether the method works in general.
explanations.C: Correct. The evidentiary integrity of the post-eruption layers is the precise gap the argument must bridge.
explanations.D: Other eruptions in the region would be a potential confound, but the argument does not depend on their absence — it could still hold even if other eruptions occurred, as long as the Toba eruption caused the drop. This is a strengthener, not a necessary assumption.
explanations.E: Partial melting of the glacier would affect layer positions but is not the specific inferential gap the argument relies on; the ash-matching process already presupposes usable stratigraphy.

lr.difficultyReason: The ethics argument moves from a premise about moral obligations to a conclusion about institutional policy, requiring an assumption that bridges individual duty and collective mandate. Distractors exploit plausible but non-necessary ethical principles.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Individuals have a moral obligation to avoid actions that foreseeably harm others. A corporation is, in legal terms, a collective of individuals acting in concert. Therefore, a corporation has a moral obligation to avoid policies that foreseeably harm the public.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Corporations are capable of experiencing moral responsibility in the same way that individual persons are.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The moral obligations that apply to individuals acting alone also apply to those same individuals when acting collectively through a corporation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every policy adopted by a corporation will foreseeably harm at least some members of the public.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Legal definitions of corporate personhood are adequate guides to the moral status of corporations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Individuals within a corporation cannot be held personally liable for harms caused by corporate policy.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'individuals have moral obligations' to 'corporations (collections of individuals) have moral obligations.' This step only works if the obligations of individuals don't evaporate when those individuals act collectively. Negate B — collective action dissolves individual moral obligations — and the premise about individual duty cannot ground a conclusion about corporate duty.
explanations.A: Too strong. The argument does not require corporations to experience moral responsibility subjectively; it only requires that the same obligations transfer. Whether corporations 'experience' anything is a separate metaphysical question.
explanations.B: Correct. The bridging principle that individual obligations persist in collective action is precisely what the argument requires.
explanations.C: This reverses the logic; the argument discusses foreseeably harmful policies, not that all policies harm. This overclaims beyond the argument's scope.
explanations.D: The argument invokes legal personhood only as a definitional premise about what a corporation is, not as a moral guide. Whether legal definitions are adequate is beside the point.
explanations.E: Personal liability of individual employees is out of scope; the argument is about corporate obligation, not about shielding individuals from liability.

lr.difficultyReason: The linguistics argument relies on inferring original word meaning from current usage patterns, with a hidden assumption about whether current usage reflects historical continuity. The necessary assumption is defensive and easy to overlook amid distractors about linguistic methodology.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: In all five of the earliest surviving manuscripts of this medieval text, the word rendered in modern translations as 'justice' appears in contexts describing the return of property to rightful owners. Contemporary translators have concluded that in this text, the word primarily meant 'restoration.' However, in later manuscripts of the same tradition, the word appears in contexts involving punishment of wrongdoers. The original meaning must therefore have shifted over time.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The later manuscripts were copied from the earlier manuscripts without modification to the contexts in which the word appears.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The scribes who produced the later manuscripts were aware of the word's usage in the earlier manuscripts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The later manuscripts belong to the same linguistic tradition as the earlier manuscripts rather than being independent compositions in which the word carried a different meaning from the outset.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Words in medieval texts rarely shifted meaning over periods of less than two centuries.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Modern translators have access to all surviving manuscripts of the medieval tradition in question.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that the word's meaning 'shifted over time' — implying a single continuous tradition with a changing meaning. If the later manuscripts are independent compositions that always used the word to mean punishment, there is no shift, just two separate usages. Negate C — the later manuscripts are independent — and the conclusion of meaning-shift is destroyed.
explanations.A: Verbatim copying is not required; the argument concerns contextual usage differences, not textual fidelity. Even altered copies can show semantic drift.
explanations.B: Scribal awareness is out of scope; the semantic inference depends on the tradition's continuity, not on what scribes knew.
explanations.C: Correct. The shift-over-time conclusion requires that both sets of manuscripts belong to a single continuous tradition.
explanations.D: A general claim about the pace of medieval semantic change is irrelevant; the argument does not depend on any timeline of how fast meanings shift.
explanations.E: Completeness of the manuscript record is not invoked in the argument; the argument proceeds from the manuscripts cited, not from a claim of exhaustiveness.

lr.difficultyReason: The technology argument involves an inference from adoption rates to user preference, requiring the argument to rule out an alternative explanation — cost barriers — as the driver of adoption. The necessary assumption is a 'defender' that blocks an alternative, making it easy to mistake for a mere strengthener.
lr.stimulus: Technology analyst: Among consumers who purchased a new smartphone last year, those who chose a device with the new high-resolution display format outnumbered those who chose a standard-resolution device by a margin of three to one. Clearly, most consumers prefer the new high-resolution format.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High-resolution display technology produces images that are objectively superior to those produced by standard-resolution technology.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The consumers surveyed had previously owned a standard-resolution device before purchasing the high-resolution one.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Standard-resolution devices were not significantly more expensive than high-resolution devices at the time of purchase.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The proportion of high-resolution devices sold was not primarily determined by manufacturers' decisions to discontinue standard-resolution models.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Consumer preferences for display technology do not change significantly from one year to the next.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that consumers prefer high-resolution displays because they bought them at higher rates. This only holds if the purchase rate reflects genuine preference rather than the fact that manufacturers eliminated the alternative. Negate D — manufacturers did discontinue standard-resolution models — and the purchase data no longer shows preference; consumers simply had no choice. The conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: Objective image quality is out of scope; the argument is about consumer preference as revealed by purchasing behavior, not about inherent technical merit.
explanations.B: Prior ownership history is irrelevant to the inference from current purchase rates to current preferences.
explanations.C: This reversal of cost direction is a trap. If standard-resolution devices were more expensive, it would explain away high-resolution purchases even more, not support the preference claim. But the key alternative the argument must rule out is that high-resolution was the only option — which is what D addresses.
explanations.D: Correct. The argument requires that the purchase pattern reflects preference, which means the alternative (no standard-resolution options available) must be ruled out.
explanations.E: Year-to-year stability of preferences is not needed; the argument makes a claim about preferences at the time of purchase, not about how they change.

lr.difficultyReason: The history argument depends on an inference from physical evidence to a social practice, with a necessary assumption about what the physical evidence could have been caused by. The chronological subtlety — when the evidence was produced — is the key gap.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Excavations at the site of the ancient city of Marveth uncovered a large plaza paved with fired brick, surrounded by the remains of administrative buildings. The plaza bears no evidence of domestic structures or food storage facilities. Archaeologists have noted that the plaza's central axis aligns precisely with the midsummer sunrise. We therefore conclude that the plaza served a ceremonial rather than a commercial function.
lr.questionStem: The historian's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ancient cities in the same region as Marveth consistently used solar alignment to designate ceremonial spaces.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The absence of domestic structures and food storage facilities from a space is sufficient evidence that it was not used commercially.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The solar alignment of the plaza's central axis was intentional rather than coincidental.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marveth's inhabitants engaged in ceremonial practices that required large open-air spaces.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The administrative buildings surrounding the plaza were constructed at the same time as the plaza itself.

explanations.correct: The argument uses the solar alignment as evidence of ceremonial function. If the alignment is coincidental — the plaza happened to face that direction for practical or topographical reasons — the alignment provides no evidence of ceremony. Negate C: the alignment was coincidental. Then one of the argument's two key evidentiary pillars collapses, leaving only the absence of domestic structures, which is insufficient on its own to establish a ceremonial function over, say, a military one.
explanations.A: Regional comparisons are out of scope; the argument relies on the specific evidence at Marveth, not on a general pattern.
explanations.B: Too strong. The argument does not require that absent domestic structures are sufficient for a commercial-use denial; it uses them as one of two supporting factors. This overstates what the argument needs.
explanations.C: Correct. An unintentional alignment carries no inferential weight for ceremonial purpose; the argument requires it to be deliberate.
explanations.D: This nearly restates the conclusion and is too strong; the argument does not need to establish that Marveth's people had such practices beforehand — that is what the argument concludes.
explanations.E: Contemporaneous construction of the surrounding buildings would strengthen the argument but is not necessary for the solar-alignment-plus-absence inference to function.

lr.difficultyReason: The policy argument requires a necessary assumption about the mechanism by which a proposed measure would achieve its stated goal — specifically, that the mechanism was not already at work before the measure. Students tend to pick a distractor that is relevant but merely strengthens rather than fills the logical gap.
lr.stimulus: City planner: Our proposal to require new residential developments to include ten percent affordable housing units has been criticized on the grounds that it will reduce the overall number of new units built, since developers will find some projects less profitable. But our modeling shows that the number of affordable units created under the proposal will exceed the number of affordable units that would be created without it. The proposal therefore advances the city's goal of increasing affordable housing stock.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the planner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Developers who find projects unprofitable under the proposal will not relocate their investment to other cities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The city's goal of increasing affordable housing stock is more important than its goal of increasing the overall housing supply.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increasing the number of affordable units created is sufficient to advance the goal of increasing affordable housing stock.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The modeling used to project unit creation accurately reflects how developers will respond to the proposal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No other policy currently in effect will independently produce more affordable housing units than the proposal would.

explanations.correct: The planner infers that creating more affordable units advances the goal of increasing affordable housing stock. This step is not trivial: if affordable units are simultaneously being demolished or converted to market-rate housing at a faster rate, creating more units might not increase the stock. Negate C — creating more units does not suffice to increase stock — and the conclusion that the goal is advanced collapses.
explanations.A: Developer relocation is a potential concern but is not the inferential gap the argument relies on; the argument already concedes some projects may not be built.
explanations.B: The argument does not weigh competing city goals; it is solely about whether the proposal advances the affordable-housing goal. This is out of scope.
explanations.C: Correct. The planner equates 'more units created' with 'advancing the stock goal,' which requires that unit creation is sufficient for stock increase.
explanations.D: Model accuracy is relevant to the premise's credibility but is not the logical gap the argument depends on; the argument is about whether the modeled outcome — if true — advances the goal.
explanations.E: Other policies' independent effects are not part of the argument; the comparison is between the proposal and no proposal, not between the proposal and alternative policies.

lr.difficultyReason: The arts argument involves an inference from an artist's public statements about intent to a claim about the meaning of the work, requiring an assumption about the relationship between stated intent and actual artistic meaning. Distractors introduce plausible art-critical principles that are close but either too strong or reversed.
lr.stimulus: Art critic: The painter Selene Varga has stated in interviews that her large-format canvases depicting empty industrial spaces are meant to evoke the melancholy of labor displaced by automation. Several of Varga's most prominent canvases show machines standing idle in otherwise bare factory floors. We can therefore conclude that the melancholy of displaced labor is a genuine component of the meaning of these works.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the art critic's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The visual elements in Varga's canvases would evoke melancholy in viewers who were unaware of her stated intentions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An artist's publicly stated intentions about a work's meaning are relevant to what that work actually means.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The melancholy depicted in Varga's work is aesthetically superior to other emotional registers explored in contemporary painting.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All large-format paintings of industrial spaces are intended to comment on economic displacement.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Varga's canvases have been exhibited in contexts where viewers would associate idle machinery with labor displacement.

explanations.correct: The critic moves from Varga's stated intention to a claim about the work's actual meaning. This inference is only valid if stated authorial intent is a legitimate input to meaning. Negate B — an artist's publicly stated intentions are entirely irrelevant to meaning — and the critic's premise (Varga said X) cannot support the conclusion (X is part of the work's meaning). The argument collapses.
explanations.A: Viewer response independent of stated intention is a separate theory of meaning; the argument rests on the artist's stated intent, not on independent viewer response. This is out of scope.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument requires that stated intent be relevant to meaning; otherwise the premise about Varga's interviews is evidentiary dead weight.
explanations.C: Comparative aesthetic value is entirely out of scope; the argument makes no comparative evaluative claim.
explanations.D: Too strong and a shift in subject — the argument concerns Varga's specific canvases and her specific intentions, not a general claim about all industrial-space paintings.
explanations.E: Exhibition context might affect viewer interpretation, but the argument's inferential chain runs from the artist's statement to meaning, not from exhibition context to viewer association.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument hinges on a conditional timing subtlety: the drug's effectiveness is inferred from remission rates, but only if the remission was not already underway before treatment began. Students must recognize that the conclusion depends on when remission started, not merely that it occurred.
lr.stimulus: Oncologist: In our trial, patients with stage II melanoma who received the new immunotherapy drug showed a remission rate of 74 percent over six months, compared with 31 percent for patients receiving the standard treatment. Critics argue that the trial was too short to draw conclusions. However, the six-month window fully captures the period during which stage II melanoma characteristically either progresses or resolves. Therefore, the immunotherapy drug is significantly more effective than the standard treatment.
lr.questionStem: The oncologist's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the patients in both trial groups had melanoma of equivalent severity at the time treatment began.

choices.label: B
choices.text: none of the patients in the immunotherapy group had begun experiencing spontaneous remission before the trial started.

choices.label: C
choices.text: stage II melanoma is more dangerous than stage I melanoma.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the standard treatment has not improved in efficacy over the past decade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: immunotherapy drugs work through mechanisms that differ from those of standard treatments.

explanations.correct: The argument compares remission rates between the two groups to conclude the drug is more effective. This comparison is meaningful only if the groups started in equivalent condition. Negate A — the immunotherapy group had milder melanoma — and the higher remission rate is explained by disease severity, not the drug, collapsing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Negating this destroys the comparison: if the immunotherapy group had less severe melanoma, the higher remission rate reflects patient selection, not drug efficacy.
explanations.B: Too strong and out of scope for the argument's actual gap. The argument compares group outcomes, not individual pre-trial trajectories. Even if some patients had early spontaneous remission, equivalent group composition (answer A) would still validate the comparison.
explanations.C: Irrelevant. The relative danger of stages is not a link in the inference from remission-rate comparison to drug superiority.
explanations.D: Shift in subject. The argument compares the new drug to the current standard treatment; historical improvement in the standard treatment is not part of the inference.
explanations.E: Out of scope. The mechanism of action is not invoked anywhere in the argument; only outcomes are compared.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument contains a conditional subtlety about legal intent: the conclusion that a contract clause is unenforceable rests on ambiguity, but only if that ambiguity was not itself deliberately introduced by the party now seeking enforcement. Students must trace the gap between 'ambiguous' and 'unenforceable' carefully.
lr.stimulus: Attorney: The liquidated-damages clause in this contract specifies 'reasonable compensation' without defining that term. Under settled contract law, a clause is unenforceable when its key term is so vague that a court cannot determine what the parties agreed to. Since 'reasonable compensation' provides no objective measure, a court cannot determine what the parties agreed to. Therefore, the liquidated-damages clause is unenforceable.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the attorney's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The parties to the contract are both represented by legal counsel.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Courts have previously declined to enforce clauses containing the phrase 'reasonable compensation.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: The vagueness of 'reasonable compensation' cannot be resolved by reference to industry-standard definitions or other contract provisions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Liquidated-damages clauses are generally disfavored in contract law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The party seeking enforcement drafted the clause containing the ambiguous term.

explanations.correct: The attorney's argument moves from 'reasonable compensation is vague' to 'a court cannot determine what the parties agreed to.' This works only if the vagueness cannot be resolved by context — industry standards, other clauses, or extrinsic evidence. Negate C: the vagueness can be resolved elsewhere in the contract. Then the court can determine what was agreed, and the unenforceability conclusion fails.
explanations.A: Out of scope. Legal representation of the parties is not a link in the unenforceability inference.
explanations.B: This is a strengthener about precedent, not a necessary gap-filler. The argument appeals to the general rule, not to prior specific cases.
explanations.C: Correct. Negating this destroys the premise that the court cannot determine what was agreed, undercutting the unenforceability conclusion.
explanations.D: Too strong and reversed. General disfavor of liquidated-damages clauses isn't required — only this specific clause's vagueness drives the argument.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. Who drafted the clause is a separate legal doctrine (contra proferentem) that the argument does not invoke.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument infers a causal direction from a correlation in an economic context, and the necessary assumption rules out a specific alternative causal explanation. The chronological detail — wage increases preceded productivity gains — is the key evidentiary link, but it holds only if measurement timing was not reversed.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Data from 47 manufacturing firms show that average wages rose in the first quarter, and productivity per worker increased in the second quarter of the same year. Because the wage increases uniformly preceded the productivity gains, the wage increases most plausibly caused the productivity gains, rather than the reverse.
lr.questionStem: The economist's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Firms that raised wages in the first quarter did not also reduce their workforces during that period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The productivity gains in the second quarter were not the result of capital investments made before the wage increases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 47 manufacturing firms are representative of the broader economy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Higher wages always motivate workers to increase productivity.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Productivity data were collected using the same methodology in both quarters.

explanations.correct: The argument infers that wage increases caused productivity gains because wages rose first. This inference collapses if an earlier, independent cause (capital investment predating the wage hike) actually drove the productivity gains. Negate B: the gains were caused by prior capital investments. Then the temporal sequence no longer establishes wages as the cause, and the conclusion fails.
explanations.A: Workforce reductions could affect per-worker productivity, but the argument is about causal direction between wages and productivity, not about headcount. This is a partial strengthener, not a necessary gap-filler.
explanations.B: Correct. Negating this introduces a prior common cause that severs the wage-to-productivity causal link the argument asserts.
explanations.C: The argument is restricted to the 47 firms; representativeness would matter for generalization but is not a link in the causal inference.
explanations.D: Too strong — 'always' exceeds what the argument needs. The argument claims only that wage increases caused productivity gains in this data set.
explanations.E: Methodological consistency is relevant to data reliability, but consistent methodology was not a premise the argument relied upon to establish causal direction.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses a linguistic-change inference with a subtle chronological gap: the presence of loanwords in a language is taken as evidence of contact between populations at a specific time. The necessary assumption concerns whether the loanwords entered before or after that period — a distinction easily missed.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Scholars have long debated when the Vethric and Ossulan peoples first came into sustained contact. The Vethric language contains seventeen words borrowed from Ossulan that refer specifically to maritime trade practices. Since vocabulary items relating to novel activities are typically adopted at first exposure, these loanwords indicate that Vethric speakers first encountered Ossulan maritime culture no later than the period when those trade practices were introduced.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the linguist's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Vethric people had no maritime trade practices of their own before encountering the Ossulan people.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The seventeen loanwords were not borrowed into Vethric through an intermediary language rather than direct contact.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The loanwords were incorporated into the Vethric language during the period when the relevant Ossulan trade practices were current, not after those practices had already ceased.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ossulan is a more linguistically complex language than Vethric.

choices.label: E
choices.text: All loanwords in a language reflect direct cultural contact between the borrowing and lending populations.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that the loanwords date the contact to 'no later than when the trade practices were introduced.' This requires that the borrowing happened while those practices were still active — not centuries later, from historical texts or secondary contact. Negate C: the words were borrowed after the practices had ceased. Then the loanwords no longer date the contact to the period of active trade, and the conclusion about timing fails.
explanations.A: Whether Vethric speakers had prior maritime experience is irrelevant to the timing inference; the argument is about when they encountered Ossulan maritime vocabulary, not whether they were maritime novices.
explanations.B: Intermediary borrowing is a real-world concern, but the argument's conclusion is about timing of first contact, not the mechanism of borrowing. Eliminating intermediaries would strengthen the argument but is not required by its stated logic.
explanations.C: Correct. Negating this severs the link between the presence of the loanwords and the timing of contact.
explanations.D: Comparative linguistic complexity is out of scope; no premise invokes it.
explanations.E: Too strong — the argument does not claim all loanwords reflect direct contact, only these seventeen, and its logic does not depend on a universal rule about all loanwords.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument moves from a policy outcome to a policy cause, but the necessary assumption rules out an alternative explanation for the outcome that the argument's author treats as already excluded. The gap is subtle because the alternative cause operates through a mechanism the stimulus implicitly acknowledges.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: After the city adopted its mandatory composting ordinance, landfill tonnage from residential sources dropped by 22 percent over two years. Opponents had predicted that residents would simply shift organic waste to illegal dumping sites. Municipal waste-management inspectors, however, found no increase in reports of illegal dumping during that period. The ordinance therefore succeeded in reducing the total amount of residential waste produced.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mandatory composting ordinances are more effective than voluntary recycling programs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drop in landfill tonnage was not caused primarily by a concurrent decline in the residential population.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Waste-management inspectors reported all illegal dumping incidents that occurred during the two-year period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Composting converts organic waste into substances that have no environmental impact.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The city's commercial waste also decreased during the two-year period.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that the ordinance reduced total waste produced. This holds only if the landfill-tonnage drop reflects reduced waste generation, not some other cause. A declining residential population would produce less waste regardless of any ordinance. Negate B: the drop was caused mainly by population decline. Then the ordinance gets credit it doesn't deserve, and the conclusion fails.
explanations.A: The argument does not compare ordinance types; this is out of scope.
explanations.B: Correct. Negating this provides an alternative explanation for the tonnage drop that does not involve the ordinance reducing waste production.
explanations.C: This concerns inspector reliability, which would matter if the illegal-dumping premise were central to the conclusion. But the conclusion is about total waste reduction, not about illegal dumping — so inspector thoroughness is a side issue, not a required assumption.
explanations.D: Environmental impact of composted material is irrelevant to whether total residential waste was reduced.
explanations.E: The argument is explicitly about residential waste; commercial waste trends are out of scope.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument rests on an analogy between two historical periods to establish an ethical claim, and the necessary assumption is that the relevant moral circumstances are genuinely comparable — a subtle gap that looks like a simple analogy but requires careful negation to expose.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Historians agree that nineteenth-century physicians who performed experimental surgeries without patient consent acted wrongly, even though consent was not legally required at the time. By parallel reasoning, pharmaceutical companies today that conduct trials in low-income countries under consent protocols weaker than those required domestically act wrongly, even though those weaker protocols satisfy local law.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pharmaceutical companies are subject to the same ethical standards as individual physicians.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The participants in the overseas trials have less access to alternative medical care than the nineteenth-century surgery patients had.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The moral wrongness of an action is not fully determined by whether it complies with applicable local law.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Informed consent is the most important requirement in research ethics.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Low-income countries should adopt domestic consent standards rather than maintaining their own protocols.

explanations.correct: The argument's entire structure depends on the premise that legal compliance does not exhaust moral permissibility — it says nineteenth-century surgeons acted wrongly despite legal permission, and concludes that modern pharmaceutical companies act wrongly despite legal compliance. Negate C: moral wrongness is fully determined by local legal compliance. Then the historical premise collapses (surgeons were lawful, therefore not wrong) and the conclusion about pharmaceutical companies fails.
explanations.A: Too strong. The argument draws a structural analogy between historical individual physicians and modern corporations, but it does not require that the two are subject to identical standards.
explanations.B: Comparative access to care for trial participants is not a link in the argument's analogical reasoning.
explanations.C: Correct. Negating this destroys the shared moral logic of both the historical premise and the contemporary conclusion.
explanations.D: Too strong. The argument invokes consent but does not claim consent is the single most important research-ethics requirement.
explanations.E: A policy recommendation about legal reform is out of scope; the argument is about ethical evaluation, not regulatory prescription.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument infers species presence at a historical site from artifact composition, but the inference holds only if the material was locally sourced — a conditional provenance assumption that is easily overlooked and requires re-reading to locate.
lr.stimulus: Archaeologist: Excavations at the Bronze Age site of Durrath revealed that 40 percent of the bone refuse consists of aurochs bones, a species known to require vast unfragmented forest habitat. Settlements of this period typically consumed only locally hunted game. We can therefore conclude that extensive old-growth forest existed in the Durrath region during the Bronze Age.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the archaeologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aurochs were the most nutritionally valuable game animal available to Bronze Age inhabitants of the Durrath region.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The aurochs bones found at Durrath were not brought to the site through long-distance trade rather than local hunting.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No other Bronze Age sites in the region show a comparable proportion of aurochs bones.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aurochs populations were not larger during the Bronze Age than in later historical periods.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Durrath inhabitants did not supplement their diet with domesticated animals.

explanations.correct: The argument infers that old-growth forest existed locally because local game was eaten and aurochs bones were found. The key premise is that consumption was of locally hunted game. If the aurochs bones arrived through trade from a distant forested region, the presence of those bones no longer implies local forest. Negate B: the bones were brought through long-distance trade. Then local hunting of aurochs is not established, and the inference to local old-growth forest fails.
explanations.A: Nutritional value of aurochs is not part of the argument; the inference runs from bone presence to habitat inference, not through dietary preference.
explanations.B: Correct. Negating this severs the link between bone presence at Durrath and local environmental conditions.
explanations.C: Comparative frequency at other sites is irrelevant to the local-forest inference from this single site.
explanations.D: Historical changes in aurochs population size do not affect the habitat-requirement logic on which the argument depends.
explanations.E: Domesticated animal consumption is out of scope; the argument uses the proportion of aurochs bones in refuse, not the absence of other food sources.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument infers a conservation conclusion from satellite data, but the necessary assumption is that the measurement technology captures the relevant variable accurately — a methodological gap that superficially resembles a scope issue but is actually structural to the evidence chain.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientist: Satellite imagery analyzed over a fifteen-year period shows that the canopy cover in the Valendi watershed has increased by 18 percent. Canopy cover is the most reliable indicator of overall forest ecosystem health. Conservationists had argued that unchecked logging in the watershed was causing irreversible ecosystem degradation. The imagery therefore demonstrates that the watershed's ecosystem has not been irreversibly degraded.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The logging that occurred in the Valendi watershed was conducted using sustainable harvesting methods.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The satellite imagery accurately measures canopy cover rather than other reflective surface features such as invasive shrub growth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Canopy cover in the Valendi watershed had declined before the fifteen-year measurement period began.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Conservationists' concerns about the watershed were not based on factors other than canopy cover.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The government agencies responsible for the watershed enforced logging restrictions during the fifteen-year period.

explanations.correct: The argument's entire evidential chain runs: satellite data shows increased canopy cover → canopy cover indicates ecosystem health → therefore no irreversible degradation. This chain depends on the satellite data actually measuring canopy cover (native tree growth), not a visually similar phenomenon like invasive shrub proliferation. Negate B: the imagery does not accurately measure canopy cover. Then the increase in satellite readings does not establish an increase in real canopy cover, and the health inference collapses.
explanations.A: The sustainability of logging methods is not a link in the argument; the argument proceeds from observed canopy increase to ecosystem health, not from logging practices.
explanations.B: Correct. Negating this undermines the evidentiary basis for the canopy-cover increase that drives the conclusion.
explanations.C: Whether cover declined earlier is irrelevant; the argument needs current canopy increase to indicate current ecosystem health, not a recovery narrative.
explanations.D: Too strong. Even if conservationists had additional concerns, the argument only addresses what the satellite data shows about canopy cover — a specific indicator the argument itself defines as the most reliable. The argument doesn't require that conservationists based their concerns solely on canopy cover.
explanations.E: Enforcement history is out of scope; the argument proceeds from observational data, not from causal explanation.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument attributes a change in consumer behavior to a technology feature, but the necessary assumption rules out a prior confounding condition. The gap is subtle because the confound operates through the same behavioral pathway the argument describes, making it easy to mistake for a strengthener.
lr.stimulus: Technology analyst: After a major streaming platform introduced its auto-play feature — which automatically begins the next episode without user action — average per-session viewing time increased by 34 percent. Critics claim the increase reflects subscribers' pent-up demand for new content that coincidentally became available at the same time. However, per-session viewing time increased equally among subscribers who had already exhausted available new content and those who had not. Therefore, the auto-play feature itself caused the increase in per-session viewing time.
lr.questionStem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Subscribers who had exhausted available new content were not disproportionately likely to cancel their subscriptions after auto-play was introduced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The streaming platform did not also introduce other interface changes simultaneously with the auto-play feature.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Subscribers who had access to new content watched that content more attentively than subscribers who had exhausted it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Auto-play features work primarily by reducing the friction of choosing what to watch next.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Streaming platforms in general benefit from features that increase per-session viewing time.

explanations.correct: The argument rules out new-content availability as the cause by showing that viewing time rose equally in both subscriber groups. But this only isolates auto-play as the cause if no other change was introduced simultaneously. If another interface change (e.g., a new recommendation algorithm) was also deployed at the same time, that change — not auto-play — could explain the uniform increase across both groups. Negate B: the platform introduced other changes simultaneously. Then the uniform increase no longer isolates auto-play as the cause, and the conclusion fails.
explanations.A: Subscriber attrition is irrelevant to the causal inference about viewing time among remaining subscribers.
explanations.B: Correct. Negating this reintroduces a confounding simultaneous change that the argument's design failed to control for.
explanations.C: Attentiveness is not a variable in the argument; the argument concerns session duration, not engagement quality.
explanations.D: The mechanism by which auto-play operates is not required by the causal conclusion; the argument needs only that auto-play caused the change, not how.
explanations.E: Industry-wide benefit claims are out of scope; the argument is about causal attribution for one platform's data.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses the commercial failure of an artwork as evidence for a claim about the prevailing critical standards of a period, but only if commercial reception was not independent of those critical standards. The assumption is defensive and concerns the relationship between two evaluative frameworks the argument treats as linked.
lr.stimulus: Art historian: The sculptor Maren Voss completed her most ambitious series in 1923, during a period when critics universally praised geometric abstraction. The series, however, sold poorly and received almost no critical attention. Since commercial success in that milieu closely tracked critical recognition, the series' commercial failure indicates that it did not conform to the critical standards that dominated contemporary art discourse.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the art historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Maren Voss was not already well known to collectors before completing the 1923 series.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The 1923 series was exhibited in venues where it could have received critical attention.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Geometric abstraction remained the dominant critical standard throughout the 1920s.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The poor sales of the series were not caused by economic conditions unrelated to critical reception.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Voss herself considered the 1923 series to be her most important work.

explanations.correct: The argument's chain is: commercial failure → (because commercial success tracked critical recognition) → lack of critical recognition → did not conform to critical standards. This chain requires that the commercial failure actually reflected critical reception, not some independent economic cause (e.g., an economic recession, a war, distribution failures). Negate D: poor sales were caused by unrelated economic conditions. Then the commercial failure no longer signals critical rejection, and the conclusion about critical standards fails.
explanations.A: Prior collector familiarity could affect expectations but is not a link in the argument's inference from commercial failure to critical non-conformity.
explanations.B: Exhibition access is a plausible concern, but the argument infers from commercial failure, not from the absence of critical review opportunities; the argument's chain runs through the commercial-tracks-critical premise.
explanations.C: Whether geometric abstraction persisted throughout the decade is out of scope; the argument only concerns the period when the series was completed.
explanations.D: Correct. Negating this severs the link between poor sales and critical rejection that the argument's chain depends upon.
explanations.E: The artist's self-assessment is entirely out of scope for an argument about critical reception and commercial sales.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument contains a conditional/temporal subtlety: the conclusion depends on the ink composition being fixed at the time of manufacture, not altered afterward. The necessary assumption concerns *when* the chemical signature was established, not whether the document is forged. Negation test requires careful re-reading of the inferential chain. Several distractors are topically close and sound plausible on first reading.
lr.stimulus: Art historian: A letter purportedly written by the painter Vermeer in 1668 has been offered for sale at auction. Forensic analysts recently determined that the iron-gall ink used in the letter contains a ratio of sulfate ions to ferrous ions that matches the ratio found in ink manufactured in the Dutch Republic during the 1660s. Because no forger working after Vermeer's death could have replicated that precise ratio using materials available in later centuries, the letter must be authentic.
lr.questionStem: The art historian's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Iron-gall inks produced in different regions of seventeenth-century Europe all shared identical sulfate-to-ferrous-ion ratios.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sulfate-to-ferrous-ion ratio in the letter's ink has not been significantly altered by chemical processes occurring after the letter was written.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vermeer personally mixed the ink he used for his correspondence rather than purchasing it from a commercial supplier.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Forensic analysis of ink composition is the most reliable method currently available for authenticating historical documents.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No authentic letters written by Vermeer have previously been identified and sold at auction.

explanations.correct: The argument's entire evidentiary chain runs from 'the ink now has ratio R' to 'the ink was manufactured in the 1660s.' That inference holds only if the ratio measured today is the same ratio the ink had when originally applied — i.e., that post-composition chemical change has not distorted it. Negate B: the ratio *has* been significantly altered by later chemical processes. Then the current measurement no longer reflects the original ink signature, and the conclusion that the letter is authentic collapses. B is therefore necessary.
explanations.A: This is a scope-shift trap. The argument needs only that this letter's ink ratio matches 1660s Dutch Republic ink — not that all European regions shared identical ratios. Even if other regions differed, the specific match cited still supports authenticity. Negating A does not damage the argument.
explanations.B: Correct. See explanation above.
explanations.C: Whether Vermeer mixed his own ink or bought it commercially is irrelevant to whether the ratio characteristic of 1660s Dutch manufacture is present. The argument depends on the ratio being a marker of period and place, not of personal production method. This is an out-of-scope distractor.
explanations.D: This is a 'too strong / sufficient' trap phrased as a comparative superlative. The argument needs only that this forensic test provides valid evidence of manufacture date — not that it is the *most reliable* method available. Negating D (i.e., some other method is more reliable) leaves the argument intact.
explanations.E: Prior auction sales of Vermeer letters have no bearing on whether this particular letter is authentic. This answer is topically continuous with the stimulus but entirely disconnected from the inferential gap the argument must bridge — a classic out-of-scope distractor.

lr.difficultyReason: One-step conditional gap. Stimulus places Dr. Aronson in a named category; conclusion moves her to a second category; the correct answer supplies the missing universal link between the two categories.
lr.stimulus: Every physician at Brighton Clinic is certified in emergency medicine. Dr. Aronson practices at Brighton Clinic. So Dr. Aronson is qualified to staff the county trauma ward.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anyone certified in emergency medicine is qualified to staff the county trauma ward.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some physicians qualified to staff the county trauma ward are certified in emergency medicine.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No physician who lacks certification in emergency medicine practices at Brighton Clinic.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Anyone qualified to staff the county trauma ward is certified in emergency medicine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most physicians at Brighton Clinic have staffed a trauma ward at some point in their careers.

explanations.correct: The premises establish that Dr. Aronson is certified in emergency medicine. To force the conclusion that she is qualified to staff the trauma ward, we need every emergency-certified physician to be so qualified. (A) supplies exactly that universal bridge.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too weak. 'Some' qualified staffers being certified does not put Dr. Aronson in the qualified group.
explanations.C: This restates the first premise in contrapositive form. It tells us who can practice at Brighton, not who is trauma-ward qualified.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional. This says qualified → certified, but the argument needs certified → qualified.
explanations.E: 'Most' does not guarantee Dr. Aronson is among them, and past staffing is not the same as present qualification.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-step gap between 'breaks a promise' and 'acts wrongly.' The correct answer is a universal ethical principle that closes the gap directly.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Councilor Marsh pledged during her campaign to vote against the stadium subsidy, but last week she voted in favor of it. In doing so, she broke a promise she had made to her constituents. Therefore, Councilor Marsh acted wrongly.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anyone who breaks a promise made to constituents acts wrongly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A councilor who votes for a stadium subsidy acts wrongly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most promises made during political campaigns ought to be kept.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Anyone who acts wrongly has broken a promise.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No councilor who keeps her campaign promises acts wrongly.

explanations.correct: The premise establishes that Marsh broke a promise to her constituents. To force the conclusion that she acted wrongly, the argument needs the universal 'breaking such a promise → acting wrongly.' (A) is that conditional.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The stimulus never claims that voting for the subsidy is itself wrong — only that breaking the promise is the wrong act.
explanations.C: 'Most' is too weak to force a conclusion about Marsh's particular promise.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional: wrong → promise-breaking, rather than promise-breaking → wrong.
explanations.E: Tells us only what follows when promises are kept; Marsh did not keep hers, so this yields no conclusion about her conduct.

lr.difficultyReason: Direct one-concept gap. Premise identifies a firm as a monopolist; conclusion attributes a consequence (raises prices above competitive levels). Correct answer is the universal linking the two.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Northgate Utilities is the sole provider of natural gas in this region and therefore operates as a monopolist. It follows that Northgate charges prices above the level that a competitive market would produce.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every monopolist charges prices above the level that a competitive market would produce.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any firm that charges prices above competitive levels is a monopolist.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monopolists tend to charge higher prices than firms facing competitors.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A firm that is the sole provider of a service in a region faces no meaningful substitutes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some monopolists charge prices above the level that a competitive market would produce.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'Northgate is a monopolist' to 'Northgate charges above competitive prices.' Forcing that inference requires every monopolist to charge above competitive prices. (A) supplies the universal link.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional. This guarantees only that above-competitive firms are monopolists, not that Northgate prices above the competitive level.
explanations.C: 'Tend to' falls short of certainty. Sufficient assumptions demand all, not a tendency.
explanations.D: Explains why Northgate counts as a monopolist but says nothing about its pricing.
explanations.E: 'Some' leaves open that Northgate belongs to the monopolists who do not price above competitive levels.

lr.difficultyReason: One-step gap between 'contract signed under duress' and 'unenforceable.' The correct answer is the universal principle linking duress to unenforceability.
lr.stimulus: Attorney: The settlement agreement that Rollins signed was obtained under duress, for the opposing party threatened to publicize confidential medical records unless he signed. It follows that the settlement agreement cannot be enforced against Rollins.
lr.questionStem: The attorney's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No contract signed under duress can be enforced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any threat to publicize medical records constitutes duress.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some contracts signed under duress cannot be enforced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any contract that cannot be enforced was signed under duress.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rollins signed the settlement agreement only because of the threat.

explanations.correct: The premise places the contract in the category 'signed under duress,' and the conclusion places it in 'cannot be enforced.' A universal from the first category to the second forces the conclusion. (A) does that.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Supports that what happened counts as duress, but duress is already granted in the premise.
explanations.C: 'Some' leaves open that Rollins's contract is one of the enforceable duress-signed contracts.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional. The argument needs duress → unenforceable, not the reverse.
explanations.E: Fills in a causal detail but does not connect duress to unenforceability, which is the unbridged step.

lr.difficultyReason: Transparent one-step gap. Premise: the wetland is classified as an old-growth fen. Conclusion: it merits protection under the statute. The missing universal is the bridge.
lr.stimulus: Ecologist: The Alderbrook wetland has been formally classified as an old-growth fen by the state survey. Therefore, the Alderbrook wetland merits protection under the Wetlands Heritage Act.
lr.questionStem: The ecologist's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every old-growth fen merits protection under the Wetlands Heritage Act.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every wetland that merits protection under the Wetlands Heritage Act is an old-growth fen.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most old-growth fens in the state have been formally classified by the state survey.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No wetland can be classified as an old-growth fen unless it merits protection.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Wetlands Heritage Act protects wetlands that are rare or ecologically significant.

explanations.correct: The argument places Alderbrook in 'old-growth fen' and concludes it is in 'merits protection.' The universal 'every old-growth fen merits protection' is the missing link. (A) states precisely that.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional: meriting protection → old-growth fen. Does not put Alderbrook into the protected category.
explanations.C: Shifts the subject to classification practice; irrelevant to whether Alderbrook merits protection.
explanations.D: This would be a requirement for classification, not an entailment from classification to protection.
explanations.E: Too vague — 'rare or ecologically significant' is not stipulated of Alderbrook, and protection is not guaranteed by this general description.

lr.difficultyReason: Single transparent gap. Premise: the device uses end-to-end encryption. Conclusion: intercepted messages cannot be read by third parties. The universal that links the two is the needed assumption.
lr.stimulus: The new Larkspur messaging app uses end-to-end encryption for all communications between users. It follows that any message sent through Larkspur cannot be read by a third party who intercepts it in transit.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No message protected by end-to-end encryption can be read by a third party who intercepts it in transit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any message that cannot be read by a third party who intercepts it is protected by end-to-end encryption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most messaging apps that use end-to-end encryption also encrypt stored copies of messages.

choices.label: D
choices.text: End-to-end encryption prevents third parties from determining who sent a given message.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Messages sent through Larkspur are encrypted on the sender's device before transmission.
