The stimulus's general rules handle the rest. Choice A provides both elements in a single universally applicable bridge. With A, the chain is: out-of-court + offered to prove truth = hearsay (premise 1); hearsay + no exception = inadmissible (premise 2); inadmissible = should be excluded (implicit in legal practice). The conclusion that the defense attorney's argument is sound follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too broad — the stimulus itself carves out recognized exceptions for hearsay, and premise one only addresses statements offered for truth. This overgeneralization contradicts the stimulus's structure.
explanations.C: Reliability concerns about the bystander's vision are a different basis for exclusion (credibility) unrelated to the hearsay rule invoked in the stimulus. Subject-shift trap.
explanations.D: This reverses the relevant role: it is the judge, not the defense attorney, who excludes evidence; more importantly, it does not establish that this particular evidence is inadmissible in the first place.
explanations.E: This introduces a new condition (prejudice to the defendant) not mentioned in the stimulus's hearsay framework, and it narrows admissibility in a direction that doesn't close the gap about this specific statement.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology/computer science domain. Two-concept gap: stimulus links 'open-source code' to 'publicly auditable' and 'publicly auditable' to 'more secure'; conclusion is about a specific system. Reversed-conditional and too-weak traps.
lr.stimulus: Any software system whose source code is publicly auditable is more secure against undisclosed vulnerabilities than a system whose code is proprietary. The city's new traffic-management system relies entirely on open-source components, every line of whose code is available for public inspection. City officials who worry that the system is less secure than a comparable proprietary system are therefore mistaken.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any software system composed entirely of open-source components has source code that is publicly auditable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Software systems used by municipal governments are more frequently targeted by malicious actors than privately operated systems.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A software system is more secure against undisclosed vulnerabilities only if its developers actively respond to publicly reported flaws.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most open-source software projects receive more external security audits than proprietary systems of comparable complexity.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any system that is more secure against undisclosed vulnerabilities relies on open-source components.

explanations.correct: The stimulus states: publicly auditable → more secure (premise 1). The traffic-management system uses open-source components with all code available for public inspection. The conclusion says the system IS more secure. The gap is that 'open-source with code available for public inspection' has not been formally equated to 'publicly auditable.' Choice A closes this: any system composed entirely of open-source components IS publicly auditable. With A, the chain is: open-source system (A) → publicly auditable → more secure (premise 1). The conclusion follows.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The frequency of attacks on municipal systems is irrelevant to whether this system is more or less secure than a comparable proprietary one. This is an extraneous comparative claim.
explanations.C: This introduces an additional necessary condition (active developer response) that would actually undermine the conclusion rather than support it, since the stimulus's conditional does not include this caveat.
explanations.D: 'Most' is too weak — sufficient-assumption answers must force certainty. Even if most open-source projects get more audits, this does not guarantee this system is more secure.
explanations.E: Reversed conditional trap. The stimulus says publicly auditable → more secure; this choice reverses to more secure → open-source. This does not license the inference that the open-source system is more secure.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics domain. Two-concept gap: stimulus links 'language with no native speakers' to 'extinct language' and concludes about a specific language (Dalmatian). Reversed-conditional, subject-shift, and too-weak traps present.
lr.stimulus: A language that has no remaining native speakers is, by the standard definition used in comparative linguistics, an extinct language. Scholars of Romance languages have documented that Dalmatian, a language once spoken along the eastern Adriatic coast, has had no native speakers since the death of its last known fluent speaker in 1898. It follows that Dalmatian is an extinct language.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dalmatian is classified within the Romance language family by comparative linguists.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No language that has ever had native speakers can be fully reconstructed from written records alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The standard definition used in comparative linguistics applies to Dalmatian.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any language classified as extinct by comparative linguists had no native speakers for at least a century before being so classified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most languages that lose their native speakers are eventually replaced by a dominant regional language.

explanations.correct: The stimulus's first premise invokes 'the standard definition used in comparative linguistics' to define extinct language. The conclusion applies this definition to Dalmatian. The gap is whether that standard definition actually applies to Dalmatian — perhaps Dalmatian is excluded from the definition's scope for some reason. Choice C closes this gap directly: the standard definition DOES apply to Dalmatian. With C, the chain is complete and the conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: That Dalmatian is in the Romance family is already implied by the stimulus; moreover, being a Romance language does not by itself determine whether the comparative-linguistics definition applies to it. Subject-shift trap.
explanations.B: Reconstructibility from written records is entirely irrelevant to the definition of extinction used in the argument. Extraneous concept.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Reversed-direction trap. This describes a condition for classification (extinct → no speakers for a century) rather than establishing that the no-speakers condition triggers extinction. It also introduces a time threshold not present in the stimulus.
explanations.E: 'Most' is too weak and speaks to language replacement, not to whether Dalmatian specifically qualifies as extinct under the stated definition.

lr.difficultyReason: History domain. Argument concludes a Roman general's campaign was unjustified; premises establish that unjustified campaigns are those launched without senatorial authorization and that this campaign lacked such authorization. Gap: student must link the specific general's campaign to the no-authorization premise. Partial-bridge and reversed-conditional traps.
lr.stimulus: In the late Roman Republic, any military campaign launched by a general without prior authorization from the Senate was, by Roman constitutional convention, an unjustified campaign. Julius Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon River in 49 BCE with his army was a military campaign launched without prior senatorial authorization. Historians who characterize that crossing as constitutionally justified are therefore in error.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Julius Caesar was aware that crossing the Rubicon without senatorial authorization violated Roman constitutional convention.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any campaign that is constitutionally unjustified in Roman terms was launched without prior senatorial authorization.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Roman constitutional convention during the late Republic was the appropriate standard by which to evaluate the justification of Caesar's crossing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No Roman general ever received retroactive senatorial authorization for a campaign already under way.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Caesar's political motivations for the crossing were self-serving rather than directed at the welfare of Rome.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes: no senatorial authorization → unjustified (under Roman constitutional convention). Caesar's crossing lacked authorization (premise 2). The conclusion is that historians who call it 'constitutionally justified' are in error. The gap: one could argue Roman constitutional convention is the wrong standard, or doesn't apply. Choice C closes this: Roman constitutional convention IS the appropriate standard for evaluating Caesar's crossing. With C, the argument is airtight — the conclusion that the crossing was unjustified, and that historians calling it justified are wrong, follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Caesar's awareness of the violation is irrelevant to whether the campaign was constitutionally unjustified. The argument is about objective constitutional status, not mens rea.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. The stimulus already establishes no authorization → unjustified. Choice B gives the converse: unjustified → no authorization. This does not license a new conclusion and is not what is needed.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Retroactive authorization is a novel concept not present in the stimulus's framework. Even if true, it does not close the gap about whether the convention applies to evaluate this crossing.
explanations.E: Caesar's motivations are irrelevant to the constitutional analysis; the argument relies solely on the authorization criterion, not intent.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy/public health domain. Two-step conditional chain: mandatory disclosure → informed consent preserved; informed consent preserved → policy is ethically permissible. Conclusion targets a specific pharmaceutical pricing policy. Too-weak and reversed-conditional traps present.
lr.stimulus: A pharmaceutical pricing policy is ethically permissible only if it preserves patients' informed consent regarding treatment options. Any policy that requires mandatory disclosure of all available therapeutic alternatives to patients preserves their informed consent. The federal government's proposed tiered-pricing policy for insulin includes a mandatory disclosure requirement covering all available therapeutic alternatives.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion that the proposed tiered-pricing policy is ethically permissible to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Preserving patients' informed consent is sufficient for a pharmaceutical pricing policy to be ethically permissible.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The proposed tiered-pricing policy will make insulin more affordable for most patients who currently cannot access it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any pharmaceutical pricing policy that is ethically permissible includes a mandatory disclosure requirement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Informed consent is preserved in most cases where patients receive some information about treatment alternatives.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Federal pharmaceutical policies are subject to ethical review only when they affect a broad population of patients.

explanations.correct: The stimulus gives: (1) ethically permissible → preserves informed consent (necessary condition only); (2) mandatory disclosure → preserves informed consent; (3) the policy has mandatory disclosure. From (2) and (3), the policy preserves informed consent. But (1) only says preserving informed consent is necessary, not sufficient for permissibility. The conclusion requires it to also be sufficient. Choice A supplies exactly this: preserving informed consent IS sufficient for permissibility. With A, the chain closes: policy has disclosure (3) → preserves informed consent (2) → ethically permissible (A).
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Affordability is an entirely separate ethical consideration not invoked in the stimulus's framework. This is an extraneous concept that does not close the logical gap.
explanations.C: Reversed conditional trap. The stimulus's premise says mandatory disclosure → preserves informed consent, and the question is about sufficiency for permissibility. Choice C asserts permissible → mandatory disclosure, the converse of what the argument needs.
explanations.D: 'Most cases' and 'some information' are both too weak; sufficient-assumption answers require universal force. This does not guarantee that this policy preserves informed consent.
explanations.E: The scope of ethical review applicability is irrelevant to whether this policy, once subject to ethical evaluation, is permissible.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts/aesthetics domain. Stimulus concludes a critic's negative review of a minimalist sculpture is unfounded; gap requires linking 'deliberately evoking discomfort' to 'aesthetic merit.' Reversed-conditional, subject-shift, and too-weak traps present.
lr.stimulus: Art critics sometimes dismiss works that deliberately evoke discomfort in the viewer as lacking aesthetic merit. This dismissal is unfounded whenever the discomfort is integral to the work's intended meaning. The sculptor Nadia Voss has stated that the visceral unease her installation 'Threshold' provokes is not incidental but is the precise vehicle through which the work communicates its meaning. The critic who recently dismissed 'Threshold' as lacking aesthetic merit was therefore unjustified.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any work in which deliberately evoked discomfort is integral to the work's intended meaning possesses aesthetic merit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Art critics who dismiss works as lacking aesthetic merit rarely engage with the artist's stated intentions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A critic is unjustified in dismissing a work as lacking aesthetic merit only when the work has received acclaim from other critics.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Works that possess aesthetic merit are those that deliberately evoke discomfort in the viewer.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The aesthetic merit of an installation is usually best assessed by examining the artist's own account of the work's purpose.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes: dismissal is unfounded when discomfort is integral to intended meaning (premise 1); Voss says the discomfort in 'Threshold' IS the vehicle of its meaning, i.e., integral to intended meaning (premise 2). The conclusion is that the critic's dismissal was unjustified. The gap: 'unfounded dismissal' needs to be connected to 'unjustified' dismissal. More precisely, we need that when discomfort is integral to meaning, the work HAS aesthetic merit — so that dismissing it as lacking merit is factually wrong, and therefore unjustified. Choice A closes this: any work where integral discomfort is present possesses aesthetic merit. With A, 'Threshold' has aesthetic merit, so the critic's claim that it lacks merit is wrong, making the dismissal unjustified.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Whether critics generally engage with artist statements is a sociological observation irrelevant to whether this dismissal was unjustified. Extraneous.
explanations.C: This introduces an external criterion (acclaim from other critics) not present in the stimulus's reasoning, and as a necessary condition for unjustified dismissal it would actually make the conclusion harder to draw.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. The stimulus's framework implies integral-discomfort → aesthetic merit; Choice D asserts aesthetic merit → deliberately evokes discomfort. This is the converse and does not force the conclusion.
explanations.E: 'Usually' is too weak to force the conclusion. Moreover, this speaks to assessment method rather than to whether 'Threshold' in fact possesses aesthetic merit.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-concept conditional gap: stimulus links 'board-certified' to 'eligible for hospital privileges' and 'eligible for hospital privileges' to 'covered by the malpractice policy,' but the conclusion jumps to coverage; students must identify the missing conditional chain link rather than a one-step bridge.
lr.stimulus: Only physicians who are board-certified are eligible for hospital privileges at Westbrook Medical Center. Every physician who is eligible for hospital privileges at Westbrook is covered under the center's group malpractice policy. Dr. Reyes is board-certified. Therefore, Dr. Reyes is covered under Westbrook's group malpractice policy.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every physician who is covered under Westbrook's group malpractice policy is board-certified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dr. Reyes is eligible for hospital privileges at Westbrook Medical Center.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some physicians who are board-certified are not covered under any malpractice policy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No physician is covered under Westbrook's group malpractice policy unless that physician practices internal medicine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Physicians who are not board-certified may still be covered under some malpractice policies.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes: board-certified → eligible for privileges → covered by policy. Dr. Reyes is board-certified, but the first conditional goes from 'only board-certified are eligible' — which means eligible → board-certified, not board-certified → eligible. Adding B (Dr. Reyes is eligible) directly bridges her into the second conditional, forcing the conclusion that she is covered. With B in place, the chain is complete and the conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: This reverses the second conditional (covered → board-certified instead of board-certified → covered). Reversed-conditional trap: it does not establish that board-certified physicians are covered.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: This weakens rather than closes the gap, suggesting board-certified physicians might lack coverage — the opposite of what is needed.
explanations.D: Introduces a new restriction (internal medicine) not present in the premises, which would actually undermine the conclusion rather than support it.
explanations.E: This addresses physicians who are NOT board-certified, which is irrelevant to Dr. Reyes, who is board-certified.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step conditional gap in an economics context. The stimulus introduces 'price controls' and 'market distortions,' then concludes about 'reduced investment.' Students must supply the link between distortions and investment — a non-obvious but not deeply nested bridge.
lr.stimulus: Economists agree that whenever a government imposes strict price controls on essential goods, those controls inevitably produce significant market distortions. The government of Caldoria has just imposed strict price controls on fuel. Consequently, investment in Caldoria's energy sector will decline.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Significant market distortions always lead to a decline in investment in the affected sector.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Investment in Caldoria's energy sector was already low before the price controls were imposed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Governments that impose price controls on essential goods usually do so for political rather than economic reasons.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some market distortions in the energy sector can eventually be corrected without reducing investment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fuel is not considered an essential good in some economic models.

explanations.correct: The premises establish: strict price controls → significant market distortions. The conclusion is: investment in Caldoria's energy sector will decline. Choice A supplies the missing universal conditional: significant market distortions → decline in investment. Combined with the premise chain, this forces the conclusion with logical necessity.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Prior investment levels are not the gap the argument needs to close; they are irrelevant to whether distortions cause decline.
explanations.C: The motivation behind imposing controls is irrelevant to whether investment will decline as a result.
explanations.D: This is a partial concession that actually weakens the link from distortions to declining investment rather than closing it.
explanations.E: Weakens the argument by questioning whether fuel qualifies as an essential good, rather than bridging the gap to the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in an environmental science context. The stimulus connects 'deforestation above threshold' to 'watershed instability' and needs a bridge to the conclusion about 'municipal water shortages.' Moderate distractor density with a reversed-conditional trap.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientists have established that when deforestation in a river basin exceeds forty percent of the forested area, the basin's watershed becomes unstable. The Korvenna River basin has now lost more than forty percent of its forested area to logging. The city of Aldenmoor, which draws all of its water from the Korvenna River, will therefore face a shortage of potable water.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cities that draw water from unstable watersheds always face shortages of potable water.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aldenmoor has never invested in water-purification infrastructure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some cities that face shortages of potable water are located near unstable watersheds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Watershed instability in the Korvenna basin is caused exclusively by logging.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unstable watersheds sometimes recover if deforestation is halted immediately.

explanations.correct: The premises yield: deforestation > 40% → watershed unstable; Korvenna basin has lost > 40% → Korvenna watershed is unstable; Aldenmoor draws all water from Korvenna. Choice A supplies the universal conditional needed: city draws from unstable watershed → faces potable water shortage. This closes the gap and forces the conclusion with necessity.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Purification infrastructure is a new concept not present in the premises; even with purification, the link from instability to shortage is not established.
explanations.C: Too weak — 'some cities' establishes only a partial correlation, not the universal link needed to force the conclusion.
explanations.D: The cause of the instability is not the gap; the gap is between instability and the shortage conclusion.
explanations.E: This is irrelevant to whether Aldenmoor will face a shortage now; potential recovery does not close the inferential gap.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in a law/policy context. The stimulus establishes a legislative rule about 'conflicts of interest' and 'recusal,' then concludes a specific official must recuse herself. Students must bridge the official's situation to the conflict-of-interest category.
lr.stimulus: Under the Harwick municipal code, any official who holds a financial interest in a company that is the subject of a pending regulatory decision must recuse herself from voting on that decision. Councilmember Draven holds stock in Meridian Logistics, and the council is currently deliberating a zoning variance that would directly affect Meridian Logistics. Therefore, Councilmember Draven must recuse herself from the vote.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Holding stock in a company constitutes holding a financial interest in that company.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Councilmember Draven was aware that Meridian Logistics had a pending regulatory matter before the council.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No official who recuses herself from a vote may later cast a vote on any related matter.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The zoning variance would benefit Meridian Logistics financially.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Officials who recuse themselves from votes on conflicts of interest are praised by ethics watchdog groups.

explanations.correct: The municipal code requires recusal for any official who 'holds a financial interest' in the company. The premises state Draven holds stock. Choice A bridges these: stock-holding = financial interest. With this assumption, Draven satisfies the code's condition and must recuse herself — the conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Awareness is not a condition stated in the municipal code; the code's recusal requirement does not depend on the official's knowledge.
explanations.C: This introduces a further restriction about future votes, which is irrelevant to whether Draven must recuse herself now.
explanations.D: Whether the variance would benefit Meridian financially is not what the code requires — it requires a financial interest in the company, not proof of directional benefit.
explanations.E: External praise from watchdog groups is irrelevant to the logical necessity of recusal under the municipal code.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in a technology context. The stimulus links 'unencrypted transmission' to 'interception risk' and 'interception risk' to 'data breach,' but the conclusion states the company is 'in violation of its security protocol.' The missing link between data breach risk and protocol violation must be supplied.
lr.stimulus: Tessatech's internal security protocol states that any data transmission carrying personal client information must be encrypted. An audit revealed that several of Tessatech's servers have been transmitting client data without encryption. Any unencrypted transmission of personal data creates a risk of unauthorized interception. Therefore, Tessatech is in violation of its own security protocol.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tessatech's security protocol was drafted by external cybersecurity consultants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Transmitting personal client information without encryption violates Tessatech's security protocol.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any company that faces a risk of unauthorized interception is liable under data-protection law.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Encrypted transmissions occasionally carry a risk of unauthorized interception as well.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tessatech's clients were informed that their data might be transmitted without encryption.

explanations.correct: The premises establish that (1) Tessatech's protocol requires encryption for client data, and (2) several servers transmitted client data without encryption. Choice B directly bridges these to the conclusion: transmitting personal client information without encryption = violating the protocol. With B, the conclusion follows necessarily from the audit finding.
explanations.A: Who drafted the protocol is irrelevant to whether transmitting unencrypted data violates it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Legal liability under data-protection law is a separate issue from whether Tessatech violated its own internal protocol.
explanations.D: Risks associated with encrypted transmissions do not bear on whether unencrypted transmissions violate the protocol.
explanations.E: Client notification does not determine whether Tessatech violated its own security protocol.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in a history/ethics context. The stimulus introduces a principle about 'collective punishment' and 'moral illegitimacy,' then applies it to a historical event; students must supply the link between the specific policy and the category of collective punishment.
lr.stimulus: Any policy that imposes suffering on individuals solely because of their membership in a group, rather than because of anything those individuals have done, is an instance of collective punishment and is therefore morally illegitimate. The internment policy carried out during the Second World War against Japanese-American citizens imposed suffering on those citizens solely because of their ethnic heritage. Therefore, that internment policy was morally illegitimate.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Policies that are morally illegitimate should always be repealed as quickly as possible.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ethnic heritage is a form of group membership.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Collective punishment is wrong only when it targets ethnic minorities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The internment policy was the result of widespread racial prejudice rather than genuine security concerns.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Morally illegitimate policies always cause greater suffering than the policies they replace.

explanations.correct: The general principle covers suffering imposed 'because of membership in a group.' The premise states the internment was based on 'ethnic heritage.' For the principle to apply, ethnic heritage must qualify as group membership. Choice B supplies exactly this bridge, forcing the conclusion with logical necessity.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.A: What should be done about morally illegitimate policies is outside the scope of the argument's conclusion, which is only about whether the policy was illegitimate.
explanations.C: This narrows the principle to ethnic minorities, which would actually weaken the generality of the argument rather than complete it.
explanations.D: The motivation behind the policy (prejudice vs. security) is not the gap; the gap is whether ethnic heritage constitutes group membership under the principle.
explanations.E: Comparative suffering is irrelevant to whether the policy qualifies as morally illegitimate under the stated principle.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-concept conditional gap in a linguistics context. The stimulus bridges 'phonemic inventory reduction' to 'language contact,' then concludes about dialect merger; students must supply the link between contact-driven inventory reduction and merger, resisting a reversed-conditional distractor.
lr.stimulus: Linguists have found that whenever two dialects of the same language come into sustained contact, each dialect's phonemic inventory tends to undergo reduction. Sociolinguists have documented that the northern and southern dialects of Varennic have been in sustained contact for the past three generations. Therefore, linguists should expect the northern and southern dialects of Varennic to eventually merge into a single dialect.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any two dialects whose phonemic inventories have undergone reduction due to sustained contact will eventually merge into a single dialect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dialects that merge into a single dialect always share identical phonemic inventories beforehand.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phonemic inventory reduction is the only linguistic change that results from sustained dialect contact.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some dialects that undergo phonemic inventory reduction do not merge with other dialects.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The northern dialect of Varennic has a larger phonemic inventory than the southern dialect.

explanations.correct: The premises establish: sustained contact → phonemic inventory reduction; northern and southern Varennic dialects have been in sustained contact → their inventories have undergone reduction. Choice A supplies the final conditional: phonemic inventory reduction due to sustained contact → eventual dialect merger. This completes the chain and forces the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: This is the reversed conditional (merged dialects had identical inventories), which runs backward and does not force the forward conclusion that reduction leads to merger.
explanations.C: Whether inventory reduction is the only change is irrelevant; the question is whether it leads to merger.
explanations.D: This actually undermines the conclusion by allowing that reduction does not guarantee merger — the opposite of what is needed.
explanations.E: The relative sizes of the phonemic inventories are irrelevant to whether the dialects will merge.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step gap in a policy/environmental science context. The stimulus links 'carbon tax' to 'emission reductions' and needs the bridge to 'treaty compliance.' Moderate distractor density including a too-weak answer and a partial-bridge trap.
lr.stimulus: The Nordenvaal climate treaty requires every signatory nation to reduce its industrial carbon emissions by at least fifteen percent within ten years. Economic analysts have demonstrated that a sufficiently high carbon tax is the only policy instrument that can guarantee a fifteen-percent reduction in industrial carbon emissions within a decade. Ruland, a signatory to the Nordenvaal treaty, has just enacted such a carbon tax. Ruland will therefore comply with the Nordenvaal treaty's emission-reduction requirement.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any nation that achieves at least a fifteen-percent reduction in industrial carbon emissions within ten years satisfies the Nordenvaal treaty's emission-reduction requirement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ruland's carbon tax is likely to reduce industrial emissions by more than fifteen percent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nations that comply with the Nordenvaal treaty tend to benefit economically in the long run.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Carbon taxes are the most popular policy instrument among Nordenvaal signatories.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some nations that enact carbon taxes do not achieve the required emission reductions.

explanations.correct: The premises establish that (1) the treaty requires a 15% reduction, (2) a sufficiently high carbon tax guarantees a 15% reduction, and (3) Ruland enacted such a tax. This means Ruland will achieve a 15% reduction. Choice A supplies the final bridge: achieving the 15% reduction = satisfying the treaty requirement. The conclusion then follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too weak: 'likely to reduce by more than fifteen percent' is probabilistic, not universal, and does not force the conclusion with logical necessity.
explanations.C: Long-term economic benefits are irrelevant to whether Ruland satisfies the treaty's emission requirement.
explanations.D: The popularity of carbon taxes among signatories does not bear on whether Ruland's enactment satisfies the treaty.
explanations.E: This undermines the argument by suggesting the carbon tax might not work, which is the opposite of what is needed.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in an arts context with a refutation structure. The stimulus cites a specific artist to refute a critical claim; students must supply the conditional that connects the artist's properties to the refutation, resisting a subject-shift trap.
lr.stimulus: Several art critics have argued that any painter who works exclusively in a nonrepresentational style cannot produce work that is emotionally accessible to general audiences. This claim is mistaken. Consider Vera Solano, a painter whose entire body of work is nonrepresentational and who has drawn overwhelmingly positive emotional responses from gallery visitors with no specialized training in art.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No painter who draws positive emotional responses from untrained gallery visitors works in a representational style.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any painter who produces work that draws positive emotional responses from untrained audiences produces work that is emotionally accessible to general audiences.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vera Solano is widely regarded as the most important nonrepresentational painter of her generation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Painters who work in both representational and nonrepresentational styles are more emotionally accessible than those who work in only one style.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The emotional accessibility of a painting is determined primarily by its color palette rather than its representational content.

explanations.correct: To refute the critics' claim, the argument needs to show that Solano — a nonrepresentational painter — produces emotionally accessible work. The premises show she gets positive emotional responses from untrained gallery visitors. Choice B bridges this to the critics' specific vocabulary: positive emotional responses from untrained audiences = emotional accessibility to general audiences. With B, the counterexample is complete and the critics' claim is definitively refuted.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.A: This is the reversed conditional — it says painters with positive responses don't work representationally, running backward from the needed direction.
explanations.C: Solano's reputation or standing among peers does not establish that her work is emotionally accessible to general audiences in the critics' sense.
explanations.D: This introduces a comparison between painters who use both styles, which is irrelevant to refuting the claim about exclusively nonrepresentational painters.
explanations.E: This principle-wrapping trap invokes color palette as a determining factor, but even if true, it does not force the conclusion that Solano's work is emotionally accessible in the required sense.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step gap in a medicine/ethics context. The stimulus links 'experimental treatment' to 'informed consent requirement' and needs a bridge to the conclusion about a specific clinical trial's status. Moderate distractor density with a partial-bridge trap and a too-weak trap.
lr.stimulus: Under medical ethics guidelines, any experimental treatment administered to human subjects without their informed consent constitutes a violation of patient autonomy. Researchers at Galloway Institute administered a novel drug compound to participants in a clinical trial. Several participants later reported that they had not been told the compound was experimental at the time they enrolled. Therefore, the Galloway Institute trial constitutes a violation of patient autonomy.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Participants who were not informed that a treatment is experimental have not given informed consent to that treatment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Violations of patient autonomy in clinical trials should result in the immediate suspension of the trial.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Galloway Institute researchers were aware that some participants had not been told the compound was experimental.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Informed consent procedures at the Galloway Institute are generally less rigorous than industry standards.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some participants in the Galloway trial may have consented to receive an experimental treatment under a different name.

explanations.correct: The ethics guideline states: experimental treatment + no informed consent → violation of patient autonomy. The premises establish the treatment was experimental and that several participants were not told it was experimental. Choice A supplies the definitional bridge: not being told the treatment is experimental = not giving informed consent. This closes the gap and forces the conclusion with logical necessity.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: What should happen after a violation is identified is irrelevant to whether the trial constitutes a violation in the first place.
explanations.C: The researchers' awareness (scienter) is not a condition in the ethics guideline; the guideline requires only that consent was absent, not that researchers knew it was absent.
explanations.D: Comparative rigor of consent procedures is a partial bridge at best — it suggests the institute may have failed to obtain consent but does not establish with necessity that the specific participants lacked informed consent.
explanations.E: This actually undermines the conclusion by suggesting some participants may have consented under different conditions, which is the opposite of what the argument needs.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step conditional chain in a medical context. The gap between 'approved for clinical use' and 'safe for patients' requires a bridging universal. One trap reverses the conditional; another weakens with 'generally.'
lr.stimulus: A new analgesic compound has completed all three phases of clinical trials without producing serious adverse events in any participant. The regulatory agency has therefore approved it for clinical use. Dr. Reyes concludes that the compound is safe for patients to use.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any compound approved for clinical use by the regulatory agency is safe for patients to use.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any compound safe for patients to use will be approved for clinical use by the regulatory agency.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most compounds that complete all three phases of clinical trials without serious adverse events are safe for patients.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No compound that produces serious adverse events in clinical trials should ever be approved for clinical use.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Compounds that are safe for patients to use rarely produce serious adverse events during clinical trials.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'approved for clinical use' to 'safe for patients.' The only link that forces the conclusion is a universal conditional: approved → safe. Choice A supplies exactly this link, making the conclusion logically necessary.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: This reverses the required conditional (safe → approved), leaving the gap between approval and safety unbridged.
explanations.C: 'Most' is too weak — it allows for exceptions and does not guarantee this compound is safe.
explanations.D: This concerns compounds that should not be approved, which is irrelevant to whether an approved compound is safe.
explanations.E: This runs the conditional in the wrong direction and uses 'rarely,' a hedge that cannot force any conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in economics: the argument jumps from 'reduces consumer spending' to 'slows GDP growth.' Students must supply the conditional bridge. A trap answer conflates cause and effect direction.
lr.stimulus: An economist argues that the recently enacted tariff on imported consumer electronics will reduce consumer spending on those goods. She therefore concludes that the tariff will slow overall GDP growth in the country.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tariffs on imported goods always produce trade deficits that reduce GDP growth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any policy that reduces consumer spending on a significant category of goods will slow overall GDP growth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Overall GDP growth tends to slow whenever consumer confidence declines.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Slowing GDP growth in a country will generally reduce consumer spending on imported goods.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most economists agree that tariffs on electronics are harmful to economic growth.

explanations.correct: The argument needs a bridge from 'reduces consumer spending on a significant goods category' to 'slows overall GDP growth.' Choice B is a universal conditional that closes this gap exactly, making the conclusion logically necessary.
explanations.A: Introduces trade deficits, a concept absent from the stimulus, and commits to a different causal mechanism than the one the economist uses.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: 'Consumer confidence' is not mentioned in the stimulus; this is a partial bridge using a different concept.
explanations.D: This reverses the causal direction — slow GDP → reduced spending — rather than reduced spending → slow GDP.
explanations.E: 'Most economists agree' is an appeal to authority, not a conditional link, and cannot force the conclusion logically.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step gap in environmental science. The argument moves from 'increased surface runoff' to 'degraded water quality in the reservoir.' Students must bridge these via a universal conditional. Trap choices use hedges or shift the subject to groundwater.
lr.stimulus: Deforestation along the Miren River watershed has substantially increased surface runoff into the river during rainfall events. Hydrologists therefore conclude that water quality in the downstream reservoir will degrade.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deforestation always reduces the biodiversity of the affected watershed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any substantial increase in surface runoff into a river will degrade water quality in any downstream reservoir fed by that river.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Water quality in most reservoirs tends to decline when upstream land use changes occur.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Degraded water quality in a reservoir will typically increase surface runoff in the surrounding watershed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Groundwater quality in areas affected by deforestation is generally lower than in forested areas.

explanations.correct: The argument needs a universal bridge from 'substantial increase in surface runoff' to 'degraded reservoir water quality.' Choice B supplies exactly this conditional, forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Biodiversity is irrelevant to the argument's conclusion about water quality.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: 'Most reservoirs' and 'tends to decline' are too weak — they allow for exceptions and do not guarantee degradation in this case.
explanations.D: This reverses the causal direction: degraded quality → increased runoff, the opposite of what the argument requires.
explanations.E: Groundwater is a different subject from the surface runoff and reservoir water quality at issue in the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in law. The argument moves from 'signed without legal counsel' to 'contract is unenforceable.' Students must supply the missing universal conditional. A reversed-conditional trap and a 'generally' hedge trap are present.
lr.stimulus: When Denholm signed the licensing agreement, he had not yet retained legal counsel and did not fully understand the indemnification clause. His attorney now argues that the contract is unenforceable against Denholm.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any contract signed by a party who did not fully understand a material clause is unenforceable against that party.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any contract that is unenforceable against a party was signed without full understanding of its material clauses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Contracts signed without legal counsel are generally considered unenforceable in most jurisdictions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An indemnification clause is always the most important clause in a licensing agreement.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No contract signed without legal counsel can be considered legally binding on either party.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes that Denholm did not fully understand the indemnification clause (a material clause) and concludes the contract is unenforceable. Choice A supplies the universal conditional — not understanding a material clause → unenforceable — that makes the conclusion logically necessary.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: This reverses the conditional: unenforceable → signed without understanding. It does not bridge from Denholm's lack of understanding to unenforceability.
explanations.C: 'Generally considered' and 'most jurisdictions' are too weak and do not guarantee unenforceability in Denholm's case.
explanations.D: Importance of the clause is irrelevant; the argument turns on comprehension, not significance.
explanations.E: The argument focuses on Denholm's failure to understand the clause, not on the absence of counsel per se; E also over-extends to both parties.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step gap in technology/policy. The argument moves from 'collects data without user consent' to 'violates users' privacy rights.' The correct answer supplies the universal bridge. A trap introduces a scope shift to 'personal data'; another trap uses 'usually.'
lr.stimulus: The fitness-tracking application automatically uploads users' location data to a third-party advertising network without obtaining explicit user consent. A consumer-rights group concludes that the application violates users' privacy rights.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any application that collects personal data without consent is likely to be used for commercial purposes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any application that transmits a user's data to a third party without the user's explicit consent violates that user's privacy rights.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Users whose privacy rights are violated usually had their data transmitted without consent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Location data is the most sensitive category of personal data that an application can collect.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Advertising networks that receive user data without consent often misuse that data.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes that user data is transmitted to a third party without consent and concludes that privacy rights are violated. Choice B is the universal conditional — transmits data without consent → violates privacy rights — that forces the conclusion.
explanations.A: Commercial purpose is a different concept from privacy violation; this choice does not bridge to the conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: This reverses the direction: violated rights → transmitted without consent. It does not force the conclusion from the given facts.
explanations.D: The relative sensitivity of location data is irrelevant; the argument turns on consent, not data type.
explanations.E: 'Often misuse' is too weak and concerns downstream harm rather than the violation of rights established by the transmission itself.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in linguistics. The argument moves from 'language lacks written records before 1500' to 'cannot be classified as a literary language.' Students must supply the universal conditional. A trap widens the scope incorrectly; another trap uses 'most.'
lr.stimulus: Linguists have confirmed that Vashiri, a language spoken in the northern highlands, has no written records predating the sixteenth century. A historian therefore argues that Vashiri cannot be classified as a literary language in the premodern period.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most languages spoken in the northern highlands lack written records from the premodern period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A language can be classified as a literary language in a given period only if it has written records from that period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a language has written records from a period, it will always be classified as a literary language for that period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No language spoken in the northern highlands has ever been classified as a literary language.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Languages that lack written records are generally less complex than those that have them.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that Vashiri cannot be a literary language in the premodern period because it lacks written records from that time. Choice B supplies the necessary conditional: literary language classification requires written records from the period. With this premise, the conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: 'Most languages' is too weak and discusses other languages, not the classification criterion for Vashiri.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: This runs the conditional in the permissive direction (records → literary) rather than the restrictive direction (no records → not literary) required to force the conclusion.
explanations.D: This overstates the case by ruling out all highland languages, and does not rest on the written-records criterion used in the argument.
explanations.E: Complexity is a different dimension from literary classification; this choice does not bridge to the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in ethics/policy. The argument moves from 'receiving payment for endorsement without disclosure' to 'acting deceptively toward consumers.' Correct answer supplies the universal bridge. Trap reverses direction; another trap shifts subject to advertisers.
lr.stimulus: A prominent nutrition blogger accepted payment from a supplement company to promote its products in posts but never disclosed this financial relationship to readers. An ethics board argues that the blogger acted deceptively toward consumers.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anyone who acts deceptively toward consumers has accepted payment without making the required disclosures.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Supplement companies that pay bloggers for promotion without requiring disclosure are themselves acting deceptively.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anyone who accepts payment to endorse a product and fails to disclose that arrangement to the audience is acting deceptively toward that audience.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deceptive endorsements usually involve financial relationships between content creators and the companies whose products they promote.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Readers of nutrition blogs generally assume that product endorsements are unpaid unless otherwise disclosed.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes that the blogger accepted payment and failed to disclose it, then concludes the blogger acted deceptively. Choice C is a universal conditional — paid undisclosed endorsement → deceptive act toward audience — that makes the conclusion logically necessary.
explanations.A: This reverses the required conditional: deceptive → undisclosed payment. It does not force the conclusion from the established facts.
explanations.B: The subject shifts to the supplement company, not the blogger whose conduct is under scrutiny.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: 'Usually involve' is too weak; it does not guarantee that this blogger's conduct was deceptive.
explanations.E: Reader assumptions make the deception more plausible but do not logically force the conclusion that the blogger acted deceptively.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step conditional chain in history. The argument moves from 'city lost its primary trade route' to 'city experienced economic decline.' Students must bridge these two concepts with a universal conditional. A trap introduces a temporal hedge; another trap shifts subject to regional economies.
lr.stimulus: Historical records indicate that the port city of Calentum lost access to its primary Mediterranean trade route in the third century CE after a series of silting events blocked its harbor. Scholars argue that Calentum therefore experienced economic decline during this period.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any city that loses access to its primary trade route will experience economic decline.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any city that experiences economic decline has previously lost access to an important trade route.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cities dependent on maritime trade routes often struggle economically when those routes are disrupted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Silting events in the third century CE affected the economies of most Mediterranean port cities.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Economic decline in regional trade networks usually follows from the loss of multiple major ports simultaneously.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from loss of primary trade route to economic decline. Choice A is a universal conditional — loses primary trade route → economic decline — that bridges the gap and forces the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: This reverses the conditional: economic decline → prior loss of trade route. It does not force economic decline from the loss of the route.
explanations.C: 'Often struggle' is too weak; it permits exceptions and does not guarantee decline for Calentum.
explanations.D: Other Mediterranean cities are irrelevant; the argument is specifically about Calentum and its primary route.
explanations.E: The argument concerns a single city losing one route, not the simultaneous loss of multiple ports across a region.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-concept gap in arts/criticism. The argument moves from 'the composer borrowed melodic material without attribution' to 'the symphony is not an original work.' Correct answer supplies universal bridge. Trap uses 'most'; another trap shifts subject to the publisher.
lr.stimulus: Musicologists have established that the finale of Brandt's Fifth Symphony incorporates several melodic passages drawn directly from unpublished folk songs collected by a regional ethnographer, without any acknowledgment of this source. A critic concludes that the symphony cannot be considered an original work.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No work that incorporates unattributed material drawn from another source can be considered an original work.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most symphonies that borrow from folk traditions are not considered original works by musicologists.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any work that cannot be considered original was composed by borrowing melodic material from unattributed sources.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Publishers who release works containing unattributed borrowed material are responsible for the lack of attribution.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Folk songs that were never published cannot be protected by intellectual property law.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes that Brandt's symphony incorporates unattributed borrowed material and concludes it is not original. Choice A supplies the universal conditional — unattributed borrowed material → not original — making the conclusion logically necessary.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: 'Most symphonies' and 'most musicologists' introduce a hedge and a scope shift; this cannot guarantee the conclusion about Brandt's specific symphony.
explanations.C: This reverses the conditional: not original → borrowed unattributed material. It does not force the originality conclusion from the established facts.
explanations.D: The publisher's responsibility is a different subject from whether the symphony itself is original.
explanations.E: Intellectual property law is irrelevant to the question of whether the work is original in the critical/artistic sense.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step gap in policy/public health. The argument moves from 'program reduces sedentary behavior' to 'program will reduce rates of type 2 diabetes.' Students must bridge these two concepts. Trap reverses direction; another trap uses 'tends to.'
lr.stimulus: A public health agency has introduced a community exercise program that has been shown to significantly reduce sedentary behavior among participants. The agency concludes that the program will reduce rates of type 2 diabetes in the community.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any intervention that reduces rates of type 2 diabetes must first reduce sedentary behavior among the target population.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any program that significantly reduces sedentary behavior in a community will reduce rates of type 2 diabetes in that community.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sedentary behavior tends to increase the likelihood of developing type 2 diabetes in most populations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Community exercise programs are the most cost-effective means of addressing type 2 diabetes rates.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rates of type 2 diabetes in a community are determined primarily by the level of physical activity among residents.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes that the program reduces sedentary behavior and concludes it will reduce type 2 diabetes rates. Choice B supplies the universal conditional — significantly reduces sedentary behavior → reduces type 2 diabetes rates — that closes the gap and forces the conclusion.
explanations.A: This reverses the conditional: reduces diabetes → must reduce sedentary behavior. It does not force the diabetes reduction conclusion from the established reduction in sedentary behavior.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: 'Tends to increase' and 'most populations' are too weak; they do not guarantee this program's effect on diabetes rates in this community.
explanations.D: Cost-effectiveness is irrelevant to whether the program will actually reduce diabetes rates.
explanations.E: 'Determined primarily by' does not establish a sufficient conditional relationship; other factors could override physical activity, so the conclusion does not follow necessarily.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-concept gap: stimulus links 'board-certified' to 'eligible for hospital privileges' and separately establishes that Dr. Renner is board-certified, but the conclusion is about hospital privileges. Student must supply the missing universal conditional. One reversed-conditional trap and one 'tends to' trap present.
lr.stimulus: Only physicians who are board-certified are eligible for hospital privileges at Crestview Medical Center. Dr. Renner has recently completed board certification in internal medicine. Therefore, Dr. Renner is eligible for hospital privileges at Crestview Medical Center.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any physician who is board-certified in internal medicine is a board-certified physician.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any physician who is eligible for hospital privileges at Crestview Medical Center is board-certified in internal medicine.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dr. Renner completed board certification more recently than most other physicians on staff at Crestview Medical Center.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most physicians who seek hospital privileges at Crestview Medical Center are board-certified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dr. Renner will apply for hospital privileges at Crestview Medical Center once the certification process is complete.

explanations.correct: The first premise says only board-certified physicians are eligible for hospital privileges. Dr. Renner is board-certified in internal medicine. The gap is whether board-certification in a specialty counts as being a 'board-certified physician' generally. Choice A supplies exactly that link — internal medicine board certification is a form of board certification — closing the chain and forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. This bridges the gap between 'board-certified in internal medicine' (what the premise says about Renner) and 'board-certified physician' (what the eligibility rule requires), making the conclusion logically necessary.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. This runs the eligibility condition backwards: eligible → board-certified in internal medicine, rather than board-certified → eligible. It doesn't help establish that Renner is eligible.
explanations.C: Irrelevant comparison. How recently Renner completed certification relative to others has no bearing on whether the eligibility condition is satisfied.
explanations.D: Too weak. 'Most physicians' does not force the conclusion about Dr. Renner specifically; Renner could be among the minority who are not certified under this reading.
explanations.E: Introduces an unrelated future action. Whether Renner will apply is not what the conclusion asserts; the conclusion is about eligibility, not intent.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step conditional chain in an economics context. Stimulus establishes that price controls reduce supply and concludes that a proposed rent-control ordinance will worsen housing shortages, but the link between reduced supply and worsened shortages requires an assumption about demand. One partial-bridge trap and one scope-shift trap present.
lr.stimulus: Economic research consistently shows that price controls on any commodity reduce the supply of that commodity over time. The city council is currently debating a rent-control ordinance that would cap residential rents citywide. If the ordinance passes, the city's housing shortage will only get worse.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rent-control ordinances have been shown to fail in every city that has adopted them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Residential rental housing is a commodity whose supply would be reduced by the proposed rent-control ordinance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The city council does not fully understand the economic consequences of the ordinance it is considering.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any reduction in the supply of residential rental housing in a city that already has a housing shortage will worsen that shortage.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cities that implement rent control tend to experience higher rates of housing deterioration than cities that do not.

explanations.correct: The argument needs two links: (1) rent control is a price control that reduces supply, and (2) a supply reduction worsens an existing shortage. Choice D provides the second, decisive link in universal form — any supply reduction in a city with an existing shortage worsens it — forcing the conclusion with logical necessity.
explanations.A: Overly broad historical claim. Past failures of rent control do not logically entail the conclusion about this specific city's housing shortage; the mechanism is not established.
explanations.B: Partial bridge. This supplies only the first link (rent control reduces housing supply) but does not connect reduced supply to a worsened shortage. The conclusion still does not follow.
explanations.C: Attacks the council's reasoning rather than supplying a missing logical link. The conclusion is about the housing shortage, not about the council's competence.
explanations.D: Correct. Combined with the premise that price controls reduce supply and the implied premise that the city already has a housing shortage, this universal conditional forces the conclusion.
explanations.E: Too weak and off-target. 'Tend to experience' is probabilistic, not universal, and housing deterioration is a different phenomenon from a worsening shortage.

lr.difficultyReason: Gap between an environmental premise about protected wetlands and a conclusion about a specific development project. Student must identify the universal conditional that ties the two concepts together. Reversed-conditional and 'most' traps present.
lr.stimulus: No development project may legally proceed if it would destroy protected wetlands. An environmental impact assessment has determined that the Hargrove Industrial Park expansion would drain and fill the Millbrook Marsh, which is a federally designated wetland. Clearly, the Hargrove expansion cannot legally proceed.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Draining and filling a wetland constitutes destroying that wetland.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any project that cannot legally proceed should be denied all government funding.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most development projects that threaten wetlands are ultimately halted by environmental regulators.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Millbrook Marsh has greater ecological value than most other wetlands in the region.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If a development project cannot legally proceed, it must have been found to destroy protected wetlands.

explanations.correct: The legal prohibition applies to projects that 'destroy' protected wetlands. The assessment says the expansion would 'drain and fill' Millbrook Marsh. The gap is whether draining and filling = destroying. Choice A supplies this definitional identity in universal form, forcing the conclusion that the expansion cannot legally proceed.
explanations.A: Correct. This bridges the language gap between 'destroy' (used in the legal prohibition) and 'drain and fill' (used in the environmental assessment), making the conclusion logically necessary.
explanations.B: Irrelevant extension. What should happen to projects that cannot legally proceed is outside the scope of the conclusion, which is only about whether the expansion can proceed.
explanations.C: Too weak. 'Most' projects does not force a conclusion about this specific project, and 'ultimately halted' is not the same as 'cannot legally proceed.'
explanations.D: Comparative ecological value is irrelevant to whether the legal prohibition applies; the prohibition covers all federally designated wetlands.
explanations.E: Reversed conditional trap. This says cannot legally proceed → found to destroy wetlands, the reverse of the rule needed. It doesn't help establish that the expansion falls under the prohibition.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics domain with a two-concept gap between 'causing harm' and 'acting wrongly.' Stimulus applies a general moral principle to a specific agent but leaves the bridging conditional unstated. Principle-wrapping trap and scope-shift trap are present.
lr.stimulus: Greta knowingly released a software update that she was aware would corrupt user data on older devices. Her company's legal team has confirmed that no law was violated. Some have therefore concluded that Greta did nothing wrong. This conclusion is mistaken.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Corporate employees are generally held to a higher standard of conduct than private individuals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anyone who knowingly causes harm to others acts wrongly, regardless of whether any law is violated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Software companies have a legal obligation to warn users before releasing updates that may affect older devices.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Actions that corrupt data are usually more harmful than other types of software errors.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The wrongness of an action is most decisively determined by the intentions of the person who performed it.

explanations.correct: The conclusion is that Greta acted wrongly despite no law being violated. The premises establish that she knowingly caused harm. Choice B provides the universal moral conditional — knowingly causing harm = acting wrongly, regardless of legality — which, combined with the established facts, forces the conclusion.
explanations.A: Scope shift. The argument is about whether Greta acted wrongly, not about differential standards for corporate vs. private actors. Even if true, this doesn't force the conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct. This universal conditional directly bridges 'Greta knowingly caused harm' (premise) and 'Greta acted wrongly' (conclusion), making the conclusion logically necessary.
explanations.C: Introduces a legal obligation that is irrelevant to the conclusion, which concerns moral wrongness, not legal duty. The legal team already confirmed no law was violated.
explanations.D: Too weak and comparative. 'Usually more harmful' does not force a conclusion about wrongness, and a comparative claim about harm types does not close the gap.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap. 'Most decisively determined by intentions' is an appealing principle but does not force the conclusion — it does not specify that Greta's intentions were wrong, and 'most decisive' is not the same as 'sufficient.'

lr.difficultyReason: Technology domain with a two-step gap: an algorithm is shown to use personal data without consent, and the conclusion is that the company violated its privacy policy. The bridging conditional relating unconsented data use to policy violation is missing. One partial-bridge trap and one reversed-conditional trap present.
lr.stimulus: Veridian Technologies' published privacy policy states that the company will never use a customer's personal data for purposes beyond those to which the customer has explicitly consented. An independent audit found that Veridian's recommendation algorithm routinely incorporates customers' location data to generate targeted advertisements, a use to which no customer had been asked to consent. Veridian has therefore violated its own privacy policy.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Generating targeted advertisements constitutes using personal data for a purpose beyond those to which customers have consented.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any company that violates its own privacy policy is subject to regulatory penalties under applicable consumer-protection law.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Location data is among the most sensitive categories of personal information that technology companies collect.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a company has violated its privacy policy, then it must have used customer data without consent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Veridian's customers were generally unaware that their location data was being collected at all.

explanations.correct: The privacy policy prohibits using data beyond consented purposes. The audit establishes that location data was used for targeted advertising without consent. The gap is whether targeted advertising counts as a 'purpose beyond those consented to.' Choice A supplies this definitional link in universal form, forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. This bridges the audit's finding (targeted ads using location data without consent) with the policy's language (uses beyond consented purposes), making the policy violation logically necessary.
explanations.B: Irrelevant extension. Regulatory consequences are outside the scope of the conclusion, which is only about whether a violation occurred, not what follows from it.
explanations.C: Comparative sensitivity of location data is irrelevant to whether the policy was violated; the policy applies to all personal data, not only the most sensitive.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. This says violation → unconsented use, the reverse of what is needed (unconsented use → violation). It presupposes the conclusion rather than supporting it.
explanations.E: Customer awareness of data collection is a separate issue from whether the company violated its policy by using data without consent for advertising.

lr.difficultyReason: Law domain. Argument moves from a statute's plain text to a conclusion about a specific case, but requires a bridging assumption about how the statute's terms apply to the facts. 'Tends to' trap and partial-bridge trap included.
lr.stimulus: Under the Fairview Zoning Code, any structure used primarily for commercial activity must obtain a commercial-use permit before construction begins. Thornton built a barn on his rural property without obtaining any permits. He now rents out the barn to a local artisan for use as a pottery studio, charging a monthly fee. Thornton's construction of the barn was in violation of the Fairview Zoning Code.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Thornton was aware of the Fairview Zoning Code's permit requirements before he began construction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A structure is used primarily for commercial activity if it is rented out for compensation, regardless of the nature of the tenant's work.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most rural property owners in Fairview who build barns eventually convert them to commercial uses.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The artisan who rents the barn generates significant revenue from the pottery produced there.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any violation of the Fairview Zoning Code is subject to fines and mandatory remediation.

explanations.correct: The zoning code requires a commercial-use permit for structures 'used primarily for commercial activity.' Thornton rents the barn for compensation. The gap is whether renting for compensation = using primarily for commercial activity. Choice B supplies that definitional bridge universally, making the violation logically necessary.
explanations.A: Thornton's awareness is legally relevant to intent, not to whether a violation occurred under a strict-liability zoning rule. The conclusion is about the fact of violation, not culpability.
explanations.B: Correct. This bridges 'rented out for a monthly fee' (premise) with 'used primarily for commercial activity' (statutory requirement), making the conclusion that Thornton violated the code logically necessary.
explanations.C: Too weak and probabilistic. That most rural owners eventually convert barns does not force a conclusion about Thornton's specific barn or the timing of its use.
explanations.D: The tenant's revenue is irrelevant. The statutory trigger is how the structure is used and whether compensation is charged, not the tenant's profitability.
