explanations.D: Too weak — 'usually' does not force that the museum must deaccession this particular canvas.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping distractor — talks about 'moral standing' and 'transparency,' not about deaccessioning obligations.

lr.difficultyReason: Five conditional answer choices with reversed-conditional and scope-shift traps. The stimulus requires identifying that a person who acts on incomplete data cannot be held negligent — a subtle conceptual link buried in medical terminology.
lr.stimulus: A physician who prescribes a medication without disclosing all known side effects to the patient is acting negligently. Dr. Chen prescribed a newly approved antiviral medication to a patient without disclosing several side effects that had appeared only in post-market surveillance reports published after the drug's approval. Some colleagues have argued that Dr. Chen acted negligently. This conclusion is unwarranted.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No physician can be expected to monitor post-market surveillance reports for every drug they prescribe.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A physician does not act negligently unless the side effects that were not disclosed were known to the physician at the time of the prescription.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Post-market surveillance reports are less reliable than data gathered during clinical trials.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any physician who discloses all side effects known at the time of prescription cannot be found negligent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Physicians who prescribe newly approved medications are generally held to a lower standard of disclosure than those who prescribe established drugs.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes Dr. Chen was not negligent. The only premise available is that the side effects appeared in post-market reports published after approval — implying Dr. Chen did not know them at time of prescription. Choice B supplies the conditional: not negligent unless side effects were known at time of prescription. With B, the chain is complete: the side effects were not known to Dr. Chen at the time → Dr. Chen does not meet the condition for negligence → conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: This weakens the expectation on physicians generally but does not close the logical gap between 'unknown side effects' and 'not negligent.' It introduces a frequency qualifier ('every drug') that doesn't force the conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Reliability of the reports is irrelevant — the issue is whether Dr. Chen knew the side effects, not the quality of the data source.
explanations.D: This is the reversed conditional trap. The stimulus's negligence standard is 'fails to disclose known side effects → negligent'; choice D affirms the contrapositive of a different, weaker claim and does not force the conclusion about Dr. Chen.
explanations.E: This introduces a comparative standard not mentioned in the stimulus and at best makes the conclusion more plausible rather than logically necessitated.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus involves a chain of economic terms with a scope shift between 'price-competitive' and 'profitable.' Reversed-conditional trap is prominent in choice D, and a too-weak trap appears in choice A.
lr.stimulus: An industry analyst argues that any domestic manufacturer that cannot compete on price with foreign rivals will eventually lose its market share entirely. Helios Manufacturing has introduced a new automated production line that reduces its per-unit cost below that of its primary foreign competitor. The analyst's prediction, as applied to Helios, is therefore mistaken.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most domestic manufacturers that reduce their per-unit costs are able to compete on price with foreign rivals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any domestic manufacturer whose per-unit cost falls below that of its primary foreign competitor can compete on price with that competitor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Helios Manufacturing's automated production line will not require costly maintenance that offsets its per-unit savings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any domestic manufacturer that retains its market share is one that can compete on price with foreign rivals.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Automated production lines are the most effective means by which domestic manufacturers can achieve price competitiveness.

explanations.correct: The conclusion is that the analyst's prediction does not apply to Helios. The prediction says: cannot compete on price → loses market share. To refute this for Helios, we need to show Helios CAN compete on price. The stimulus only tells us Helios's per-unit cost fell below its competitor's. Choice B supplies the missing link: per-unit cost below competitor's → can compete on price. This forces: Helios can compete on price → analyst's prediction does not apply → conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Too weak — 'most' does not guarantee that Helios is among those that can compete. A sufficient assumption needs universal or unambiguous coverage of the specific case.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: This addresses a future contingency and at best makes the cost reduction more durable; it does not logically bridge per-unit cost to price competitiveness.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. The analyst's claim is 'cannot compete → loses share'; the contrapositive is 'retains share → can compete.' Choice D states exactly this contrapositive but does nothing to establish that Helios retains its share or can compete — it merely restates a conditional that goes in the wrong direction for the argument.
explanations.E: Automation being the 'most effective' means is a comparative claim that does not force the conclusion about Helios specifically competing on price.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus involves an ethics argument about culpability with a subtle scope shift between 'foreseeable' and 'intended.' Five choices include a reversed conditional, a too-weak 'tends to' trap, and a principle-wrapping trap.
lr.stimulus: Under our legal tradition, a person is morally culpable for an outcome only if that person either intended the outcome or could reasonably have foreseen it. Corporate executives at Vantara Inc. restructured employee pension plans in a way that eliminated retirement benefits for workers hired before 1990. The executives claim they did not intend this result. Several ethicists have argued that the executives are nonetheless morally culpable. Those ethicists are correct.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any restructuring of pension plans by corporate executives tends to produce outcomes that affect pre-1990 employees disproportionately.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Corporate executives who restructure pension plans without consulting affected employees often fail to foresee the consequences of their actions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any corporate executive who restructures an employee pension plan could reasonably foresee how that restructuring would affect workers' benefits.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A person is morally culpable for an outcome only if a reasonable person in that position would have intended the same outcome.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The elimination of retirement benefits for a class of workers is a more serious moral harm than any financial benefit the corporation might gain.

explanations.correct: The conclusion is that the executives are morally culpable. They deny intent, but culpability requires either intent OR reasonable foreseeability. Choice C supplies the missing link: any corporate executive who restructures a pension plan could reasonably foresee the effects on benefits. With C, the executives satisfy the foreseeability prong → they are morally culpable → conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Too weak — 'tends to' does not establish that the executives specifically could reasonably foresee the outcome, which is what the culpability standard requires.
explanations.B: 'Often fail to foresee' cuts against culpability rather than supporting it, and 'often' is too weak regardless.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: This is a scope-shift and reversal trap: it substitutes 'intended' for 'would have intended' and eliminates the foreseeability prong entirely, which actually makes the culpability standard harder to meet rather than supplying the missing link.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap. The severity of the harm is irrelevant to the logical gap; the argument needs a link between the executives' actions and the conditions for culpability, not a moral ranking of outcomes.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science domain with a multi-step conditional chain. The scope shift is between 'releases carbon' and 'accelerates warming.' Partial-bridge and reversed-conditional traps are both present.
lr.stimulus: Any land-use practice that accelerates global warming should be prohibited by international treaty. Extensive research has established that draining coastal wetlands releases large quantities of carbon dioxide and methane into the atmosphere. Environmental advocates have therefore concluded that wetland drainage should be prohibited by international treaty.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any practice that should be prohibited by international treaty is one that releases large quantities of greenhouse gases.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No land-use practice that fails to release greenhouse gases accelerates global warming.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any land-use practice that releases large quantities of carbon dioxide and methane into the atmosphere accelerates global warming.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Draining coastal wetlands is among the land-use practices most frequently subject to international environmental agreements.

choices.label: E
choices.text: International treaties are the most effective mechanism for curtailing land-use practices that harm the environment.

explanations.correct: The argument needs two links: (1) releases large quantities of CO₂ and methane → accelerates global warming, and (2) accelerates global warming → should be prohibited. Link (2) is given in the stimulus. Choice C supplies link (1), completing the chain: wetland drainage releases large quantities of CO₂ and methane (given) → accelerates global warming (C) → should be prohibited by international treaty (given premise) → conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Reversed conditional trap. The given premise runs 'accelerates warming → should be prohibited.' Choice A states 'should be prohibited → releases greenhouse gases' — the reverse — which does not close the gap from 'releases gases' to 'should be prohibited.'
explanations.B: This addresses a negative condition (no gases → no warming) that is irrelevant; we already know wetland drainage does release gases, so this adds nothing to the chain.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Frequency of treaty coverage is irrelevant to whether wetland drainage should be prohibited; this is a partial-bridge trap.
explanations.E: A comparative claim about treaty effectiveness does not bridge the logical gap between releasing greenhouse gases and being prohibited.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology domain with a scope shift between 'open-source' and 'publicly auditable.' Trap choices include a plausible but too-weak probabilistic answer and a reversed conditional. Students must identify the precise missing conditional link.
lr.stimulus: Any encryption algorithm that is not publicly auditable cannot be trusted to protect sensitive government communications. The encryption algorithm embedded in the Argos secure messaging platform is proprietary and its source code has never been released to independent researchers. Therefore, the Argos platform should not be used for sensitive government communications.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most proprietary encryption algorithms contain vulnerabilities that have been exploited by adversarial state actors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any encryption algorithm whose source code has never been released to independent researchers is not publicly auditable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any encryption platform that should not be used for sensitive government communications is one whose source code has never been released.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No encryption algorithm that has been released to independent researchers can be trusted to protect sensitive government communications.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Proprietary encryption algorithms are less likely than open-source algorithms to be subjected to independent security audits.

explanations.correct: The argument needs to connect 'source code never released to independent researchers' to 'not publicly auditable.' The given premise states: not publicly auditable → cannot be trusted → should not be used. Choice B supplies: source code never released → not publicly auditable. Combined with the premises, the chain is complete and the conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Too weak — 'most' does not cover Argos specifically, and exploited vulnerabilities are not the same as being untrustworthy in the precise sense the argument requires.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Reversed conditional trap. The argument concludes 'should not be used → ···'; choice C states the reverse: 'should not be used → source code never released,' which tells us nothing about whether Argos falls into the prohibited category.
explanations.D: This is a scope-shift trap that addresses released algorithms, which are not the subject of the argument's conclusion about Argos.
explanations.E: Too weak — 'less likely' is probabilistic and cannot force a conclusion; it also shifts from 'not publicly auditable' to 'less likely to be audited.'

lr.difficultyReason: Law domain. The stimulus involves a statutory interpretation argument with a scope shift between 'willful' and 'knowing.' The reversed-conditional trap is embedded in choice A, and choice E wraps a principle that sounds strong but uses different vocabulary.
lr.stimulus: Under the Caldwell Act, a contractor is liable for damages only if the contractor willfully violated the terms of the contract. Pemberton Construction knowingly used substandard materials on the Harlow Bridge project, in direct contravention of the project's specifications. A trial court has ruled that Pemberton is liable for damages under the Caldwell Act. That ruling is correct.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any contractor who is liable for damages under the Caldwell Act is one who knowingly violated the terms of the contract.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any contractor who knowingly uses materials that contravene project specifications has willfully violated the terms of the contract.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No contractor who complies with project specifications can be found liable for damages under the Caldwell Act.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Caldwell Act was intended by its drafters to apply to contractors who use materials that endanger public safety.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Contractors who repeatedly violate project specifications should be held to a higher standard of willfulness than first-time offenders.

explanations.correct: The conclusion is that Pemberton is liable under the Caldwell Act. Liability requires willful violation (given). Pemberton is established to have knowingly used substandard materials. The gap is between 'knowingly' and 'willfully.' Choice B bridges this: knowingly using noncompliant materials = willfully violating the contract. With B, the chain is complete: Pemberton knowingly used substandard materials → Pemberton willfully violated the contract → Pemberton is liable → ruling is correct.
explanations.A: Reversed conditional trap. The Caldwell Act states 'willfully violated → liable'; choice A states 'liable → knowingly violated,' which is the reverse. This doesn't establish that Pemberton's knowing conduct satisfies the willfulness requirement.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: This addresses compliance (the negative case) and does not help establish liability for Pemberton, who already violated specifications.
explanations.D: Legislative intent is a tool of interpretation, not a logical bridge between 'knowingly' and 'willfully'; it introduces new subject matter (public safety) absent from the argument.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap. A comparative standard for repeated offenders is irrelevant to whether Pemberton's single instance of knowing noncompliance constitutes willfulness.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics domain. The argument involves a scope shift between 'borrowed lexical items' and 'linguistic borrowing sufficient to alter syntactic structure.' Five conditional choices with partial-bridge and reversed traps.
lr.stimulus: Linguists generally agree that a language undergoes structural change only when sustained contact with another language alters its syntactic patterns, not merely its vocabulary. Several scholars have argued that Medieval English underwent structural change due to contact with Norman French. Their argument relies entirely on evidence that Norman French contributed thousands of lexical borrowings to English. This evidence does not support the scholars' conclusion.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No language that borrows vocabulary from another language ever undergoes structural change as a result of that contact.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medieval English adopted more lexical borrowings from Latin than from Norman French.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lexical borrowing alone, without accompanying changes to syntactic patterns, does not constitute the kind of sustained contact that produces structural change in a language.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any language that undergoes structural change as a result of contact with another language must also borrow lexical items from that language.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The syntactic patterns of Medieval English were more resistant to external influence than those of contemporary English.

explanations.correct: The conclusion is that lexical borrowing evidence doesn't support the claim of structural change. The given principle is: structural change requires sustained contact that alters syntactic patterns (not merely vocabulary). Choice C makes explicit that lexical borrowing alone does not constitute the required contact. This forces the conclusion: the scholars' evidence (lexical borrowings) → does not demonstrate altered syntactic patterns → does not show the requisite sustained contact → does not support the structural change conclusion.
explanations.A: Too strong and introduces a different claim. The argument doesn't require that vocabulary borrowing never co-occurs with structural change — it only needs to show that lexical evidence alone doesn't prove structural change. Choice A overclaims and would be empirically problematic.
explanations.B: A comparative claim about Latin vs. French borrowings is irrelevant to the logical gap between lexical evidence and structural-change conclusions.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. The principle implies 'structural change → sustained syntactic contact'; choice D states 'structural change → lexical borrowing,' which is a different and weaker claim that does not address the sufficiency of lexical evidence.
explanations.E: Resistance of syntactic patterns is a historical claim that, even if true, does not logically connect the lexical evidence to the insufficiency of the scholars' conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: History domain. Multi-conditional chain with scope shift between 'military campaign' and 'politically motivated.' Reversed conditional is in choice D; too-weak trap in choice A; principle-wrapping trap in choice E.
lr.stimulus: Historical actions taken solely to consolidate a ruler's domestic political power are not genuine military campaigns; they are political theater. Contemporary chronicles record that Emperor Aldric III launched his invasion of the Varell provinces primarily to suppress dissent among his noble rivals at court. Critics who describe the Varell invasion as one of the great military campaigns of the medieval period are therefore mistaken.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most military historians distinguish between invasions motivated by territorial ambition and those motivated by domestic political considerations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any invasion launched primarily to suppress domestic political dissent is an action taken solely to consolidate a ruler's domestic political power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Emperor Aldric III had no genuine territorial or strategic ambitions in the Varell provinces at the time of the invasion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any action that constitutes political theater rather than a genuine military campaign was launched primarily to suppress domestic dissent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The greatness of a military campaign should be assessed by its strategic consequences rather than by the scale of forces involved.

explanations.correct: The conclusion is that describing the Varell invasion as a genuine military campaign is mistaken. The given principle: actions taken solely to consolidate domestic political power → not genuine military campaigns. The chronicles establish: Aldric launched the invasion primarily to suppress dissent among noble rivals. The gap is between 'primarily to suppress court dissent' and 'solely to consolidate domestic political power.' Choice B closes that gap: any invasion launched primarily to suppress domestic political dissent = action taken solely to consolidate domestic political power. The chain is complete and the conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Too weak — 'most historians' and their distinctions are neither universal nor directly applicable to the Varell invasion; this does not force the conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Even if Aldric had no territorial ambitions, this does not by itself establish that the invasion falls under the 'solely to consolidate political power' category without the bridge choice B provides. It is a partial bridge at best.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. The given principle runs: solely political → not genuine campaign. Choice D states: political theater → launched primarily to suppress dissent, which is the reverse direction and adds nothing to the argument.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap. Assessment criteria for greatness are irrelevant to the logical question of whether the invasion was a genuine military campaign at all.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy domain with a subtle scope shift between 'publicly funded' and 'subject to open-records requirements.' Five conditional choices with a reversed conditional, a too-weak probabilistic answer, and a partial-bridge trap.
lr.stimulus: Any institution that is subject to open-records requirements must disclose all communications pertaining to the use of public funds. The Dellwood Foundation accepted a substantial grant from the state government to fund its community health programs and has refused to disclose internal communications about how the grant money was allocated. Critics argue that Dellwood has violated open-records requirements. Their argument is well-founded.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Private foundations that accept state grants are more likely to misuse public funds than government agencies that administer those funds directly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any institution that discloses all communications about public fund use has complied with open-records requirements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any private foundation that accepts a state government grant thereby becomes subject to open-records requirements.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any institution that violates open-records requirements is one that has accepted public funding from a government source.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Open-records requirements were designed primarily to ensure that institutions managing public funds remain accountable to taxpayers.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that Dellwood violated open-records requirements. The given rule is: subject to open-records requirements → must disclose all communications about public funds. Dellwood accepted a state grant and refused to disclose. The gap is between 'accepted a state grant' and 'subject to open-records requirements.' Choice C supplies this exactly: any private foundation accepting a state grant → subject to open-records requirements. With C, the chain is: Dellwood accepted a state grant → subject to open-records requirements → must disclose → refused to disclose → violated requirements. The conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Too weak and probabilistic — 'more likely to misuse' does not establish that Dellwood is subject to open-records requirements or that it violated them.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. The given rule runs: subject to requirements → must disclose. Choice B states: discloses → complied, which is the compliant case and does nothing to establish that Dellwood, which refused to disclose, violated the requirements without first establishing Dellwood was subject to them.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. This states: violated open-records → accepted public funding. This is the converse of what is needed and does not help establish that Dellwood was subject to the requirements.
explanations.E: Legislative purpose is irrelevant to the logical gap; even if true, it does not close the chain between accepting a state grant and being subject to the requirements.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts domain mirroring the Peacock/Hacker paradigm: a critic's claim is refuted by a counterexample, and the correct answer must establish that the counterexample's property is incompatible with the critic's characterization. Reversed-conditional and principle-wrapping traps are prominent.
lr.stimulus: Several critics have asserted that any composer who relies exclusively on algorithmic procedures to generate musical material is incapable of genuine artistic expression. This claim is without merit. Consider Lena Voss and Dario Ferrante, two celebrated composers whose work is generated entirely through algorithmic processes and who are widely recognized in the concert world as artists of remarkable expressive depth and originality.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No composer who is widely recognized as an artist of expressive depth relies exclusively on algorithmic procedures.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any composer who is widely recognized as an artist of remarkable expressive depth and originality is capable of genuine artistic expression.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Algorithmic procedures can generate musical structures that are indistinguishable from those produced by non-algorithmic composition methods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any composer who is capable of genuine artistic expression will eventually abandon exclusive reliance on algorithmic procedures.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The originality of a musical work is determined primarily by the composer's conceptual intent rather than by the method used to generate its material.

explanations.correct: The argument refutes the critics by pointing to Voss and Ferrante as composers who use exclusively algorithmic procedures yet possess 'remarkable expressive depth and originality.' For this counterexample to defeat the claim that algorithmic composers are incapable of genuine artistic expression, we need: recognized expressive depth → capable of genuine artistic expression. Choice B supplies exactly this. Combined with the premise that Voss and Ferrante are recognized as artists of remarkable expressive depth, the chain is: Voss and Ferrante are recognized as having expressive depth and originality (given) → they are capable of genuine artistic expression (B) → the critics' claim that algorithmic composers are incapable is false → conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Reversed conditional and subject-shift trap. Choice A states: widely recognized expressive depth → not exclusively algorithmic. This directly contradicts the premises about Voss and Ferrante and would actually undermine the argument, not support it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: This addresses the output of algorithmic processes, not whether the composer is capable of genuine artistic expression — a scope shift that does not close the logical gap.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. Choice D implies capable of expression → eventually abandons algorithms, which is irrelevant to and inconsistent with the counterexample's force.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap, echoing Peacock choice (E). Even if conceptual intent is the primary determinant of originality, this does not entail that recognized expressive depth constitutes capability of genuine artistic expression — the precise link the argument requires.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus involves a two-step conditional chain in a medical context. The gap between 'immunosuppressed' and 'should not receive live vaccines' requires the student to bridge 'immunosuppressed' through 'cannot mount a safe immune response' to the conclusion. All five answer choices are in conditional form and multiple reversed conditionals are present as traps.
lr.stimulus: Any patient who cannot mount a safe immune response to a pathogen is at serious risk from live-attenuated vaccines. Dr. Vance's new patient, Teodora, is currently undergoing chemotherapy, which invariably renders patients immunosuppressed. Dr. Vance therefore concludes that Teodora should not receive any live-attenuated vaccine.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any patient who is at serious risk from live-attenuated vaccines should not receive them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any patient who should not receive live-attenuated vaccines is currently undergoing chemotherapy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immunosuppressed patients can sometimes mount a safe immune response if closely monitored by a physician.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No vaccine is entirely safe for patients who are undergoing chemotherapy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients who are at serious risk from a medical intervention should avoid that intervention only when safer alternatives exist.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes: (1) chemotherapy → immunosuppressed; (2) immunosuppressed → cannot mount safe immune response; (3) cannot mount safe immune response → at serious risk from live-attenuated vaccines. The conclusion is that Teodora should not receive live-attenuated vaccines. The only missing link is: at serious risk from live-attenuated vaccines → should not receive them. Choice A supplies exactly this universal conditional, closing the chain to force the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. This bridges 'at serious risk' to 'should not receive,' completing the logical chain to the conclusion.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. The conclusion requires moving from 'at serious risk' to 'should not receive,' not from 'should not receive' back to 'undergoing chemotherapy.'
explanations.C: This actually weakens the argument by suggesting immunosuppressed patients might sometimes be safe; it does not force the conclusion.
explanations.D: Too broad — the conclusion concerns live-attenuated vaccines specifically, not all vaccines. Even if true, it does not close the gap between risk and the prescriptive conclusion.
explanations.E: Too weak. The phrase 'only when safer alternatives exist' introduces a condition not present in the argument, making it insufficient to force the conclusion without additional premises.

lr.difficultyReason: An economics stimulus with a scope shift between 'price-setting power' and 'monopoly,' where the conclusion about regulatory intervention depends on a universal conditional that students must identify among five plausible-sounding answer choices. The reversed conditional and a 'tends to' trap are both present.
lr.stimulus: Regulators should intervene in any market where consumers are being harmed by a firm's unchecked price-setting power. The recent investigation of Darwick Pharmaceuticals revealed that the company holds an exclusive patent on a life-saving drug and has raised the drug's price by 400 percent over three years. Economists consulted in the investigation unanimously agreed that Darwick operates as a monopoly in this market. The agency should therefore intervene in this market.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any firm that operates as a monopoly tends to harm consumers through unchecked price-setting power.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any firm that operates as a monopoly in a market exercises unchecked price-setting power that harms consumers in that market.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Regulators should intervene in any market dominated by a pharmaceutical company that holds an exclusive patent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any market in which regulators should intervene is one in which a firm operates as a monopoly.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Price increases of more than 100 percent over three years are sufficient evidence that a firm has unchecked price-setting power.

explanations.correct: The argument needs: monopoly → unchecked price-setting power that harms consumers. Combined with the established premise that regulators should intervene wherever consumers are harmed by unchecked price-setting power, and the fact that Darwick is a monopoly, choice B closes the chain to force the conclusion.
explanations.A: Too weak. 'Tends to' is probabilistic and does not guarantee harm in Darwick's specific case; a sufficient assumption requires a universal that closes the gap with necessity.
explanations.B: Correct. This universal conditional bridges 'monopoly' to 'unchecked price-setting power that harms consumers,' completing the chain to the regulatory conclusion.
explanations.C: Partial bridge and scope shift. It addresses pharmaceutical patent-holders specifically, but the argument's first premise is about 'unchecked price-setting power,' not patents per se; this bypasses rather than closes the logical gap.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. The argument's first premise runs 'harm by unchecked power → should intervene,' not 'should intervene → monopoly.' Reversing it does not force the conclusion.
explanations.E: Partial bridge only. Even if the price increase proves unchecked power, the argument still needs 'unchecked power → consumer harm' to reach the conclusion; this choice does not supply that link.

lr.difficultyReason: An environmental science stimulus whose conclusion about a species losing protected status depends on bridging 'population recovered' to 'no longer endangered.' All five answer choices are conditionals; the reversed-conditional trap and a subject-shift trap (this species vs. all species) are both built in.
lr.stimulus: Under current environmental law, a species should be removed from the endangered list only if it is no longer endangered. Wildlife biologists monitoring the gray wolf population in the Northern Rockies have documented that the population has fully recovered to pre-decline levels and that the wolves are reproducing at a self-sustaining rate. Critics who argue that the gray wolf should remain on the endangered list are therefore mistaken.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any species whose population has fully recovered to pre-decline levels and is reproducing at a self-sustaining rate is no longer endangered.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any species that is no longer endangered has a population that has fully recovered to pre-decline levels.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Wildlife biologists are more reliable authorities on endangerment than critics who lack field data.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A species should be removed from the endangered list if environmental law permits its removal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The gray wolf population in the Northern Rockies is the only wolf population relevant to the species' overall endangered status.

explanations.correct: The argument needs: (fully recovered population + self-sustaining reproduction) → no longer endangered. Combined with the legal premise that a species should be removed from the list only if it is no longer endangered, choice A forces the conclusion that the critics are wrong to oppose removal.
explanations.A: Correct. This supplies the universal conditional linking the documented biological facts to the legal status of 'no longer endangered,' completing the chain.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. The argument needs recovery → not endangered, but B gives not endangered → recovery. This does not force the conclusion.
explanations.C: Appeals to authority rather than closing the logical gap. Even if biologists are more reliable, this does not establish that the wolves' documented recovery entails they are no longer endangered.
explanations.D: Circular and incomplete. Whether environmental law permits removal depends on whether the wolves are no longer endangered — the very point at issue — so this choice presupposes rather than establishes the conclusion.
explanations.E: Partial bridge. Even if the Northern Rockies population is the only relevant one, the argument still needs the documented facts to entail 'no longer endangered'; this choice does not supply that entailment.

lr.difficultyReason: A law stimulus where the conclusion about inadmissibility depends on a two-step chain. The scope shift between 'obtained without a warrant' and 'obtained in violation of the Fourth Amendment' is the primary gap, and a reversed conditional plus a 'tends to' trap are present among the answer choices.
lr.stimulus: Any evidence obtained in violation of the Fourth Amendment is inadmissible in a federal criminal proceeding. The arresting officers in the Kellerman case searched the defendant's vehicle without obtaining a warrant and without the defendant's consent. The defense has therefore correctly argued that the evidence recovered from that search is inadmissible.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any warrantless, nonconsensual vehicle search conducted by arresting officers constitutes a violation of the Fourth Amendment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any search that violates the Fourth Amendment was conducted without a warrant.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Evidence is inadmissible in federal proceedings whenever the defendant objects to its introduction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Warrantless searches tend to violate constitutional protections in most circumstances.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any evidence that is inadmissible in a federal criminal proceeding was obtained in violation of the Fourth Amendment.

explanations.correct: The argument needs: (no warrant + no consent → Fourth Amendment violation). The first premise already gives Fourth Amendment violation → inadmissible. Choice A supplies the missing link, so the chain becomes: no warrant + no consent → Fourth Amendment violation → inadmissible, forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. This universal conditional bridges the factual circumstances of the Kellerman search to a Fourth Amendment violation, completing the logical chain.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. The argument needs warrantless + nonconsensual → Fourth Amendment violation, not Fourth Amendment violation → warrantless. This runs the conditional backwards.
explanations.C: Introduces an entirely different basis for inadmissibility (defendant's objection) that is not present in the argument's premises, and does not close the stated logical gap.
explanations.D: Too weak. 'Tend to violate in most circumstances' is probabilistic and does not establish that this particular search violated the Fourth Amendment, which is required to force the conclusion.
explanations.E: Reversed conditional trap. The argument's first premise already states Fourth Amendment violation → inadmissible; choice E gives inadmissible → Fourth Amendment violation, which is the converse and does not force the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: A technology/ethics stimulus with a scope shift between 'collects user data without explicit consent' and 'violates user privacy,' where the conclusion about a software platform's ethical status depends on a universal principle. The partial bridge and principle-wrapping traps are both present.
lr.stimulus: Any technology platform that violates user privacy acts unethically. Forensic analysis of the Helios social media platform has confirmed that the platform's data-collection module records and transmits users' precise location data without ever presenting users with an explicit consent prompt. Helios therefore acts unethically.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any technology platform that collects and transmits data without explicit user consent violates user privacy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any technology platform that acts unethically collects user data without explicit consent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Collecting location data is more privacy-invasive than collecting other categories of personal data.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A technology platform acts unethically whenever it prioritizes data monetization over the interests of its users.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The transparency of a platform's data practices is the most important factor in determining whether that platform acts ethically.

explanations.correct: The argument needs: collects and transmits data without explicit consent → violates user privacy. Combined with the first premise (violates user privacy → acts unethically) and the fact about Helios, choice A closes the chain: Helios collects without consent → violates privacy → acts unethically.
explanations.A: Correct. This universal conditional bridges the forensic finding about Helios to a privacy violation, completing the chain to the ethical conclusion.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. The argument needs the direction 'no explicit consent → violates privacy,' not 'acts unethically → no explicit consent.'
explanations.C: Comparative claim about severity does not establish that any violation of privacy occurs, let alone that Helios acts unethically. This is a partial bridge that addresses degree rather than the logical gap.
explanations.D: Introduces 'data monetization' as a new concept not present in the premises. Even if true, it does not connect the established fact (no consent prompt) to the conclusion via the argument's existing chain.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap. 'Most important factor' language is too weak — it does not entail that Helios's specific practice constitutes unethical action; it merely gestures at a relevant consideration.

lr.difficultyReason: A linguistics stimulus where the conclusion about a language's creole status depends on bridging 'emerged from a pidgin spoken by a first generation' to 'is a creole.' Five conditional answer choices include subject-shift and reversed-conditional traps. The authentic LSAT voice requires use of named linguistic terms.
lr.stimulus: Linguists classify a language as a creole only if it emerged as the native language of a generation of speakers whose parents communicated in a pidgin. Scholars studying the Tok Pisin language of Papua New Guinea have established that the current generation of native Tok Pisin speakers are the children of a community that used an earlier pidgin form as its primary contact language. Several commentators who deny that Tok Pisin is a creole are therefore in error.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any language that emerged as the native language of speakers whose parents used a pidgin as their primary contact language is a creole.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any language that is a creole emerged as the native language of speakers whose parents used a pidgin.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tok Pisin is the only language spoken in Papua New Guinea that developed from a pidgin contact language.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Languages that develop from pidgins are more grammatically complex than the pidgins from which they derive.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A language's status as a creole is determined primarily by the social conditions under which it arose rather than by its grammatical features.

explanations.correct: The argument needs: (emerged as native language of speakers whose parents used a pidgin) → is a creole. The definitional premise states a creole is classified as such 'only if' it meets this condition, which gives creole → pidgin-origin, not the needed direction. Choice A supplies the converse universal, forcing the conclusion that Tok Pisin is a creole and thus that the commentators are wrong.
explanations.A: Correct. This supplies the missing direction of the conditional — pidgin-origin → creole — which, combined with the established facts about Tok Pisin, forces the conclusion.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. The classification premise already contains this direction (creole → pidgin-origin via 'only if'). Restating it does not bridge the gap; the argument needs pidgin-origin → creole.
explanations.C: Subject-shift trap. The uniqueness of Tok Pisin's development is irrelevant to the logical gap between the documented facts and its classification as a creole.
explanations.D: Grammatical complexity is a different dimension from classification status. This does not establish that Tok Pisin qualifies as a creole under the stated linguistic definition.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap. Even if social conditions are the primary determinant, this vague principle does not force the conclusion that Tok Pisin specifically qualifies as a creole given the established facts.

lr.difficultyReason: A history stimulus where the argument concludes a medieval manuscript was produced at a specific scriptorium. The gap requires bridging 'uses the Insular half-uncial script associated with Lindisfarne' to 'was produced at Lindisfarne,' and all five answer choices are conditionals, with subject-shift and too-weak traps prominent.
lr.stimulus: Historians attribute a manuscript's origin to a particular scriptorium only if the manuscript bears scribal features uniquely associated with that scriptorium. A newly examined manuscript, the Codex Arvensis, employs an Insular half-uncial script whose particular letterforms and ligatures have been identified by paleographers as uniquely associated with the Lindisfarne scriptorium. The Codex Arvensis must therefore have been produced at Lindisfarne.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any manuscript bearing scribal features uniquely associated with a particular scriptorium was produced at that scriptorium.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any manuscript produced at Lindisfarne employs an Insular half-uncial script with the letterforms and ligatures identified by paleographers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Historians are justified in attributing a manuscript's origin to a scriptorium whenever the manuscript's script is consistent with that scriptorium's known output.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paleographers are generally reliable in identifying scribal features uniquely associated with specific scriptoria.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Codex Arvensis is the only extant manuscript bearing the specific letterforms and ligatures identified as unique to Lindisfarne.

explanations.correct: The attribution premise gives: historian attribution → unique scribal features present. The argument needs to run in the productive direction: unique scribal features present → was produced there. Choice A supplies this universal conditional, so: Codex Arvensis has Lindisfarne-unique features → was produced at Lindisfarne.
explanations.A: Correct. This universal conditional bridges the paleographic finding to the production conclusion, completing the logical chain.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. The argument needs unique features → produced at Lindisfarne, but B gives produced at Lindisfarne → has those features, which is the converse and does not force the conclusion.
explanations.C: Too weak. 'Consistent with known output' is weaker than 'uniquely associated'; the argument's first premise already requires uniqueness, and consistency does not entail origin.
explanations.D: Appeals to the reliability of paleographers but does not establish the logical link between unique features and place of production. Even with reliable experts, the inference needs a conditional bridge.
explanations.E: Subject-shift trap. The uniqueness of the Codex Arvensis among extant manuscripts is irrelevant to whether its scribal features entail a Lindisfarne origin.

lr.difficultyReason: A policy stimulus about public funding where the conclusion that a program should be defunded depends on bridging 'failed to meet its stated outcome benchmarks' to 'no longer serves the public interest.' The too-weak trap ('often') and a scope-shift trap (one benchmark vs. all benchmarks) are built into the wrong answer choices.
lr.stimulus: Municipal programs that no longer serve the public interest should be defunded. An independent audit of the Riverside Youth Literacy Initiative found that the program has failed to meet every one of its stated outcome benchmarks for the past four consecutive fiscal years. The city council should therefore defund the Riverside Youth Literacy Initiative.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any municipal program that has failed to meet all of its stated outcome benchmarks for four consecutive fiscal years no longer serves the public interest.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any municipal program that no longer serves the public interest has failed to meet its stated outcome benchmarks.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Municipal programs that often fail to meet stated outcome benchmarks should be restructured before being considered for defunding.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Independent audits are the most reliable means of determining whether a municipal program serves the public interest.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A municipal program fails to serve the public interest whenever it is administered by officials who lack accountability to the city council.

explanations.correct: The argument needs: (failed all outcome benchmarks for four consecutive years) → no longer serves the public interest. Combined with the first premise (no longer serves public interest → should be defunded) and the audit finding, choice A closes the chain to force the defunding conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. This universal conditional bridges the audit finding to the public-interest standard, completing the chain to the policy conclusion.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. The argument needs failed benchmarks → no longer serves public interest, but B gives no longer serves public interest → failed benchmarks. This runs the conditional backwards.
explanations.C: Too weak and introduces restructuring as an alternative to defunding, which actually undermines the conclusion rather than forcing it.
explanations.D: Appeals to audit reliability but does not establish that benchmark failure entails loss of public interest. Even if audits are reliable, the logical gap between the findings and the public-interest standard remains open.
explanations.E: Introduces administrative accountability as a new and unrelated basis for the public-interest determination, which does not connect the benchmark-failure finding to the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: An arts/ethics stimulus modeled on the Peacock/Hacker paradigm. The argument refutes critics by producing counterexamples, and the conclusion depends on bridging a person's moral identity to their artworks' moral classification. The scope shift between 'artist's moral commitments' and 'work's moral character' is the key gap, and a principle-wrapping trap and reversed conditional are present.
lr.stimulus: Several critics have argued that any artwork produced with commercial intent is necessarily a morally compromised work. This claim is mistaken. The muralist Diego Rivera and the composer Dmitri Shostakovich both produced numerous works under explicit commercial or state commission, yet both artists are widely regarded as artists of profound moral integrity whose work gave voice to the oppressed.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No artist who works primarily in a tradition of political protest ever produces commercially commissioned work.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No artwork produced by an artist of profound moral integrity is a morally compromised work.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any artwork that gives voice to the oppressed is more morally valuable than commercially commissioned work that does not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any artist whose work is produced under commission has necessarily allowed commercial considerations to compromise that work's moral character.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The moral character of an artwork is determined primarily by the sincerity of the artist's intentions rather than by the circumstances of the work's commission.

explanations.correct: The argument's counterexample strategy is: Rivera and Shostakovich (1) produced works under commercial/state commission, yet (2) are artists of profound moral integrity. For these facts to refute the claim that commercially commissioned works are necessarily morally compromised, we need: profound moral integrity → works are not morally compromised. Choice B supplies exactly this universal negative conditional, forcing the refutation.
explanations.A: Subject-shift trap. The argument is about commercially commissioned work being morally compromised, not about artists in political-protest traditions. Rivera and Shostakovich are identified by their moral integrity, not their protest tradition.
explanations.B: Correct. This bridges 'profound moral integrity' (the established quality of Rivera and Shostakovich) to 'not morally compromised work,' exactly what is needed to refute the critics' claim using the counterexamples.
explanations.C: Comparative claim about moral value does not establish that Rivera's and Shostakovich's commercially commissioned works are not morally compromised; it merely ranks them, leaving the critics' claim potentially intact.
explanations.D: This actually supports the critics' position rather than refuting it, stating that commission necessarily compromises moral character — the opposite of what the conclusion requires.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap. 'Primarily determined by sincerity' is too weak; it does not entail that works by artists of moral integrity are not morally compromised, which is what the refutation requires.

lr.difficultyReason: An ethics/policy stimulus where the conclusion that a whistleblower acted permissibly requires bridging 'disclosed information to prevent serious harm' to 'violated no professional duty.' The gap involves a scope shift between 'harm prevention' and 'duty override,' and both a reversed conditional and a partial-bridge trap are embedded in the wrong answer choices.
lr.stimulus: A professional violates a duty of confidentiality impermissibly only if the disclosure serves no purpose beyond the professional's personal interest. Dr. Nadia Osei, a research scientist at a chemical firm, disclosed confidential proprietary data to federal regulators after discovering that her employer was concealing evidence that its flagship product causes acute neurological damage. Dr. Osei therefore did not act impermissibly.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any professional who discloses confidential information to prevent serious public harm acts in a purpose beyond personal interest.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any professional who acts in a purpose beyond personal interest does not violate a duty of confidentiality.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Disclosing confidential information to federal regulators is impermissible only when the disclosed information does not concern public health.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No professional who violates a duty of confidentiality acts permissibly, regardless of the circumstances of the disclosure.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Scientists who discover evidence of corporate concealment of safety data are obligated to report that evidence to the appropriate authorities.

explanations.correct: The argument's key premise states: impermissible violation of confidentiality → serves no purpose beyond personal interest (i.e., impermissible → purely personal). Contrapositive: serves purpose beyond personal → not impermissible. The argument establishes that Osei disclosed to prevent serious public harm. Choice A bridges this: preventing serious public harm → acting in a purpose beyond personal interest. Combined with the contrapositive of the first premise, the chain forces: Osei disclosed to prevent harm → beyond personal interest → not impermissible.
explanations.A: Correct. This supplies the link between 'disclosing to prevent serious public harm' (Osei's established motive) and 'acting beyond personal interest,' which activates the contrapositive of the first premise to force the conclusion.
explanations.B: Partial bridge trap. B states: beyond personal interest → does not violate confidentiality. But Osei did violate confidentiality — the issue is whether she did so impermissibly. This choice misstates the relevant conditional, conflating 'violating confidentiality' with 'violating it impermissibly.'
explanations.C: Reversed and partial. The stimulus's premise addresses what makes a confidentiality violation impermissible; choice C addresses when disclosure is impermissible on different grounds, and the phrase 'only when' introduces a condition that doesn't map onto the argument's logical structure.
explanations.D: This flatly contradicts the argument's first premise, which implies that some confidentiality violations are not impermissible. Adding D would make the argument incoherent rather than forcing its conclusion.
explanations.E: This establishes an affirmative obligation but does not close the logical gap between Osei's motive and the permissibility standard stated in the first premise.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument requires a two-concept conditional bridge: the conclusion that a particular drug trial result is inadmissible as evidence depends on connecting 'lack of independent replication' to 'inadmissibility,' but all five answer choices are in conditional form and three exploit the reversed-conditional or partial-bridge traps. Test-takers must distinguish the direction of the conditional and verify that the answer's subject terms match the conclusion's exactly.
lr.stimulus: A pharmaceutical company recently submitted results from a single internal trial as the primary evidence for a new drug's safety profile. Several independent researchers have noted that no external laboratory has yet replicated the trial's findings. A regulatory attorney argued that the submission is therefore inadmissible as primary safety evidence in the approval proceeding.
lr.questionStem: The regulatory attorney's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any trial whose findings have been replicated by an external laboratory is admissible as primary safety evidence in an approval proceeding.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No trial result that has not been replicated by an independent external laboratory is admissible as primary safety evidence in an approval proceeding.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pharmaceutical companies should never conduct safety trials without external oversight.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any evidence that is inadmissible in an approval proceeding is evidence whose findings have not been replicated by an external laboratory.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trial results submitted by the sponsoring company are admissible only if no independent researcher has raised concerns about them.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'no external lab has replicated the findings' to 'inadmissible as primary safety evidence.' For this to follow necessarily, we need the universal conditional: any unreplicated trial result is inadmissible. B provides exactly that link — it is the missing major premise that, combined with the factual premise about lack of replication, forces the conclusion.
explanations.A: Reversed conditional trap. A says replicated → admissible, but the argument needs unreplicated → inadmissible. Establishing the positive case does nothing to force the negative conclusion about this specific trial.
explanations.B: Correct. This supplies the universal negative conditional (not replicated → not admissible) that, together with the premise that no external lab has replicated the trial, entails the attorney's conclusion with logical necessity.
explanations.C: Shifts the subject to oversight procedures rather than admissibility of evidence. Even if true, this principle does not connect the absence of replication to inadmissibility in a proceeding.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. D says inadmissible → not replicated, which is the converse of what is needed. It tells us something about already-inadmissible evidence, not about what makes unreplicated evidence inadmissible.
explanations.E: Partial bridge and scope shift. E addresses researcher concerns, not the absence of replication specifically. A trial could be unreplicated with no one raising concerns, leaving the conclusion unsupported.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument contains a buried scope shift between 'showing economic growth' and 'benefiting the majority of citizens,' requiring a universal bridge that equates the two. All five answer choices use conditional or universal language; the reversed-conditional trap and a 'too-weak' trap (using 'often' and 'tends to') closely mimic the correct answer's surface form, making discrimination among choices genuinely difficult.
lr.stimulus: A government economist recently argued that a nation's official GDP figures, if they show consistent annual growth, demonstrate that the nation's economic policies are benefiting the majority of its citizens. Several development scholars have challenged this claim, pointing out that GDP growth can coexist with rising inequality. The economists' critics are correct.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Economic policies that benefit the majority of a nation's citizens always produce consistent annual GDP growth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any nation in which GDP grows consistently while inequality also rises is a nation whose economic policies are not benefiting the majority of its citizens.

choices.label: C
choices.text: GDP growth figures often fail to capture distributional effects and therefore tend to overstate broad-based prosperity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No statistical measure that can coexist with rising inequality is capable of demonstrating that a majority of citizens benefit from any policy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Development scholars are better positioned than government economists to evaluate the welfare effects of national economic policies.

explanations.correct: The argument's conclusion is that the critics of the economist are correct — i.e., that GDP growth does NOT demonstrate that policies benefit the majority when it can coexist with rising inequality. For this to follow necessarily, we need a principle that rules out any measure capable of coexisting with rising inequality as a valid demonstration of majority benefit. D supplies exactly that universal link: no measure that can coexist with rising inequality can demonstrate majority benefit. Combined with the premise that GDP growth can coexist with rising inequality, D forces the conclusion that GDP growth cannot demonstrate majority benefit, vindicating the critics.
explanations.A: Reversed conditional trap. A says benefit → GDP growth, but the argument needs to deny that GDP growth → benefit. Establishing the positive direction does not force the negative conclusion.
explanations.B: Partial bridge. B requires an additional premise that this particular nation actually has rising inequality concurrent with GDP growth. The stimulus does not assert that this nation currently has rising inequality — only that GDP growth can coexist with it in principle. B therefore does not force the conclusion with necessity.
explanations.C: 'Too weak' trap. 'Often' and 'tend to' are probabilistic qualifiers; they raise doubt about GDP as a reliable indicator but do not force the logical conclusion that GDP growth categorically cannot demonstrate majority benefit.
explanations.D: Correct. This universal negative conditional closes the gap between the co-existence premise and the conclusion about what GDP figures can and cannot demonstrate.
explanations.E: Shifts the subject to the relative credibility of economists versus scholars. Even if scholars are better evaluators, that does not force the logical conclusion that GDP growth fails as a demonstrative measure.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus involves a buried scope shift between 'using a dead language in liturgy' and 'alienating contemporary practitioners,' and all five answer choices are universally quantified conditionals, three of which implement the reversed-conditional, partial-bridge, or near-neighbor-subject traps described in the rubric. Test-takers must identify the precise directional conditional that bridges the argument's exact terms.
lr.stimulus: A historian of religion recently claimed that any religious institution that conducts its central liturgical rites exclusively in a language no longer spoken as a native tongue by any living community is necessarily alienating its contemporary practitioners. This claim has been disputed. Yet the critic who disputes it acknowledges that the institution in question conducts all of its central rites exclusively in Classical Latin, which has no living native-speaking community. The historian's claim, applied to this institution, must therefore be correct.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any religious institution that alienates its contemporary practitioners conducts its central liturgical rites in a language with no living native-speaking community.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No religious institution can maintain the loyalty of contemporary practitioners while conducting all central rites in a language that no living community speaks natively.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Classical Latin is a language that no living community speaks as a native tongue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Religious institutions that use dead languages in their rites do so primarily for reasons of tradition rather than accessibility.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any institution whose central practices are inaccessible to those it serves is failing in its primary social function.

explanations.correct: The historian's general claim is: if a religious institution conducts rites exclusively in a language with no living native speakers, it alienates contemporary practitioners. The institution conducts all its rites exclusively in Classical Latin. The conclusion is that this institution is alienating its practitioners. The only missing factual link is whether Classical Latin qualifies as 'a language no longer spoken as a native tongue by any living community.' C supplies exactly that premise, completing the modus ponens: general rule + C + acknowledged fact about the institution → conclusion follows with necessity.
explanations.A: Reversed conditional trap. A says alienates → dead language, but the argument needs dead language → alienates. This is the converse and does not force the conclusion.
explanations.B: Near-neighbor scope shift and redundancy trap. B partially restates the historian's general claim but uses 'cannot maintain loyalty' rather than 'alienates,' shifting the subject slightly. More importantly, the general claim is already stipulated as accepted in the stimulus; what is missing is the factual premise linking Classical Latin to the definition of a dead language. B does not supply that missing link.
explanations.C: Correct. The argument is a straightforward modus ponens once we confirm that Classical Latin has no living native-speaking community. C provides that confirmation, making the conclusion follow by logical necessity.
explanations.D: Principle-wrapping trap. D introduces the motivation for using dead languages (tradition vs. accessibility) — a consideration entirely absent from the argument's terms. Even if true, it does not connect to 'alienating practitioners' as a logical entailment.
explanations.E: Near-neighbor subject shift. E speaks of 'inaccessible central practices' and 'primary social function,' which are different concepts from 'conducting rites in a dead language' and 'alienating practitioners.' The answer introduces new vocabulary that does not map onto the argument's conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Five conditional answer choices, all superficially plausible. The gap involves a scope shift between 'a physician who accepts gifts' and 'a physician whose clinical judgment is compromised.' Reversed-conditional trap (D) and a too-weak trap (E) both tempt strongly.
lr.stimulus: Medical ethicists have argued that any physician who accepts gifts from pharmaceutical representatives is thereby allowing commercial interests to corrupt their clinical judgment. This conclusion is unwarranted. Dr. Renata Solís and Dr. Kwame Addo, both of whom have accepted such gifts on occasion, are widely recognized as physicians whose clinical recommendations reflect only the medical needs of their patients.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No physician whose clinical recommendations reflect only patient medical needs has allowed commercial interests to corrupt their clinical judgment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any physician who allows commercial interests to corrupt their clinical judgment will eventually accept gifts from pharmaceutical representatives.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No physician who accepts gifts from pharmaceutical representatives can be recognized as an expert in their field.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any physician whose clinical judgment is corrupted by commercial interests will accept gifts from pharmaceutical representatives.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Accepting gifts from pharmaceutical representatives tends to make physicians more susceptible to commercial influence over time.

explanations.correct: The counterexample works only if Solís and Addo, whose recommendations reflect only patient needs, have thereby NOT allowed commercial interests to corrupt their judgment. Choice A supplies exactly that link — recommendations reflecting only patient needs ↔ judgment not corrupted — making the conclusion that the ethicists' universal claim is false follow necessarily.
explanations.A: Correct. It bridges 'recommendations reflect only patient needs' (established by the premise) to 'judgment not corrupted' (what is needed to refute the ethicists), forcing the conclusion.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. This runs corruption → gift-acceptance, the opposite of what is needed. It does not let us infer anything about Solís and Addo's judgment from the fact that they accept gifts.
explanations.C: Introduces 'recognized as an expert,' a concept absent from both the premise about Solís/Addo (who are recognized for patient-centered recommendations, not expertise per se) and the conclusion. Irrelevant subject shift.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap identical in structure to B. Corrupted judgment → accepts gifts does not close the gap between accepting gifts and having corrupted judgment.
explanations.E: Too-weak trap. 'Tends to make more susceptible' is probabilistic and does not force the conclusion that the ethicists' categorical claim is false.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument involves nested conditionals in environmental law. The scope shifts subtly between 'listed as endangered' and 'legally protected habitat.' Multiple answer choices close one gap but leave another open, and the reversed-conditional trap is present in choice B.
lr.stimulus: Under the federal statute, any species listed as endangered must receive legally protected habitat. The marbled murrelet was listed as endangered three years ago. Environmental advocates therefore conclude that old-growth forests used by the marbled murrelet must now be legally protected. Critics contend that the forests are not legally protected because the listing was procedurally defective. But a court recently ruled that the listing was procedurally valid. The critics' objection has therefore been answered, and the forests must be legally protected.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Old-growth forests used by an endangered species are the only habitat that species requires for survival.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a habitat is legally protected, then the species depending on it must have been listed as endangered through valid procedures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A listing that is procedurally valid entitles the listed species to all protections mandated by the federal statute.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Courts are the sole authority competent to determine whether an endangered-species listing is procedurally valid.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Old-growth forests used by the marbled murrelet cannot be protected under any statute other than the federal endangered-species statute.

explanations.correct: The argument's chain is: listing is valid (per court) + valid listing → statutory protections → habitat protection. The gap is between 'the listing is procedurally valid' and 'the statutory protections therefore apply.' Choice C closes that gap: a procedurally valid listing activates all statutory mandates, including habitat protection, making the conclusion follow necessarily.
explanations.A: Introduces survival requirements, which are not part of the statute's mandate or the argument's logic. Irrelevant.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. Protection → valid listing runs backwards and does not help us conclude that valid listing → protection.
explanations.C: Correct. Bridges the court's procedural-validity ruling to the statutory mandate for habitat protection.
explanations.D: Court authority is already stipulated by the premise (the court ruled). Whether courts are the sole authority is irrelevant to whether the protection follows.
explanations.E: The argument depends on this statute's mandate, not on the absence of other statutes. Whether other statutes could protect the forest is beside the point.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument involves a historical claim about economic causation. The scope shift is between 'trade surplus' and 'currency appreciation.' Four answer choices are plausible strengtheners but only one forces the conclusion. The too-weak trap (E) uses 'often' and tempts strongly.
lr.stimulus: Historians have claimed that the Ming dynasty's trade surpluses with European merchants during the sixteenth century caused a significant appreciation of the Chinese currency. This is mistaken. The records of the imperial treasury show that during this same period the Ming court was melting down silver currency to fund military campaigns at a rate that exceeded all recorded silver inflows from foreign trade.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A currency cannot appreciate significantly unless the net supply of that currency in circulation is increasing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Military expenditures funded by currency destruction always produce economic instability in premodern states.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Trade surpluses with foreign merchants were the primary driver of silver inflows into Ming China.

choices.label: D
choices.text: European merchants consistently underreported the volume of silver they transferred to Ming China.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Melting down currency often reduces the money supply enough to offset gains from trade surpluses.

explanations.correct: The premises establish that silver was being destroyed faster than it arrived from trade, so the net currency supply was shrinking. Choice A states that significant appreciation requires a net increase in currency supply. Together, shrinking supply + (appreciation requires increasing supply) → no appreciation occurred, which refutes the historians' claim.
explanations.A: Correct. Links the premise about net currency destruction to the impossibility of the appreciation the historians assert.
explanations.B: Economic instability is a different outcome from currency appreciation. Irrelevant concept substitution.
explanations.C: Strengthens the premise but does not close the gap between net silver destruction and the impossibility of currency appreciation.
