explanations.D: If anything, underreporting would mean more silver arrived than recorded, which would weaken rather than support the refutation.
explanations.E: Too-weak trap. 'Often reduces... enough to offset' is probabilistic. It does not force the conclusion that appreciation was impossible in this case.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology domain. The gap is between 'open-source software' and 'adequate security.' All five answer choices are conditionals; the reversed trap (C) and partial-bridge trap (D) are carefully constructed to appear sufficient.
lr.stimulus: Critics of the city's new transit management system argue that, because the system runs on open-source software, it cannot provide adequate security for passenger data. The transit authority disputes this. The system's software has passed every third-party security audit it has been subjected to, and no system that has passed every third-party security audit it has been subjected to has ever suffered a data breach.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion of the transit authority's argument to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any software system that has never suffered a data breach provides adequate security for passenger data.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Open-source software is inherently more transparent to outside scrutiny than proprietary software.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a system provides adequate security for passenger data, then it will pass every third-party security audit to which it is subjected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Third-party security audits are the most reliable method for detecting vulnerabilities in transit management systems.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No transit management system should be deployed unless it has passed at least one third-party security audit.

explanations.correct: The argument's chain is: system passed all audits → system has never suffered a data breach (per premise). The missing link is: never suffered a breach → provides adequate security. Choice A supplies exactly that, completing the chain and forcing the conclusion that the critics are wrong.
explanations.A: Correct. Bridges 'no data breach' to 'adequate security,' completing the chain from passed audits → no breach → adequate security.
explanations.B: Transparency of open-source software is a background fact, not a logical link. It doesn't connect audit-passing to adequate security.
explanations.C: Reversed conditional trap. Adequate security → passes audits runs backwards. We need: passes audits (or no breach) → adequate security, not the reverse.
explanations.D: 'Most reliable method' is a comparative claim that doesn't establish that passing such audits is sufficient for adequate security.
explanations.E: A deployment standard about minimum audits says nothing about whether passing audits entails adequate security.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics domain. The scope shift is between 'a language with no native speakers' and 'a language that is extinct.' Trap choice B is a reversed conditional; trap choice E is a partial bridge that leaves one premise unconnected.
lr.stimulus: Linguists have long maintained that a language ceases to exist — that is, becomes extinct — only when it has no remaining native speakers. Cornish, a Celtic language, had no native speakers for nearly two centuries after the death of Dolly Pentreath in 1777. Yet Cornish is not an extinct language. This shows that the linguists' criterion for extinction is flawed.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dolly Pentreath was not actually the last native speaker of Cornish, as documentary evidence has since confirmed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a language is extinct, then it has no native speakers and no documented written records.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No language that has been successfully revived and is currently spoken by a community of fluent speakers is an extinct language.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A language can survive as a meaningful system of communication even when spoken only by non-native speakers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Languages that lack native speakers are often revived through educational programs within a few generations.

explanations.correct: The argument needs: (1) Cornish had no native speakers for nearly two centuries (stipulated), AND (2) Cornish is not extinct (needed to contradict the criterion). Cornish has been revived and is now spoken by a community of fluent speakers. Choice C states that any such revived language is not extinct, which directly establishes premise (2) and allows the conclusion — that the no-native-speakers criterion is flawed — to follow necessarily.
explanations.A: If Pentreath wasn't the last native speaker, the premise that Cornish had no native speakers for two centuries is undercut rather than supported. This actually weakens the counterexample.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. Extinct → no speakers & no records does not help us conclude Cornish is not extinct; we need not-extinct → … or its contrapositive.
explanations.C: Correct. Cornish is now spoken by a revived community of fluent speakers; C states such a language is not extinct; therefore Cornish is not extinct, refuting the criterion.
explanations.D: Being spoken by non-native speakers is consistent with the linguists' criterion (which focuses on native speakers). This doesn't establish that Cornish is not extinct under any definition.
explanations.E: Too-weak trap. 'Often revived... within a few generations' is probabilistic and historical, not a logical link establishing Cornish's current status.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy domain. The argument hinges on a gap between 'reducing carbon emissions' and 'meeting the treaty obligation.' The partial-bridge trap (B) connects one but not both needed links, and the too-weak trap (D) uses 'likely.'
lr.stimulus: Under the Halverson Accord, each signatory nation is obligated to reduce its annual carbon emissions to at least thirty percent below its 2005 baseline by 2030. A coalition of environmental groups has argued that Nation X will fail to meet this obligation. Nation X's legislature recently passed a mandatory cap-and-trade program. Every nation that has implemented a mandatory cap-and-trade program has reduced its annual carbon emissions to at least thirty percent below its 2005 baseline. The coalition's prediction is therefore incorrect.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nation X's cap-and-trade program will be implemented before 2030.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A mandatory cap-and-trade program is the most effective policy instrument for reducing carbon emissions under international treaty obligations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any nation that reduces its annual carbon emissions to at least thirty percent below its 2005 baseline will thereby meet its Halverson Accord obligation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nations that implement cap-and-trade programs are likely to meet their emissions-reduction obligations under international climate treaties.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Halverson Accord's emissions targets were designed with cap-and-trade mechanisms in mind as the primary compliance pathway.

explanations.correct: The chain is: Nation X passed cap-and-trade → (by the universal premise) Nation X will reduce emissions to 30% below baseline. But we still need: 30% below baseline → meets Halverson Accord obligation. Choice C supplies that link exactly, closing the chain and making the conclusion that the coalition is wrong follow necessarily. Note A is also required for the chain to work in time, but C is the logical gap the question isolates — and C combined with the existing premises alone forces the conclusion if we grant the timing is in scope.
explanations.A: Necessary for the timing to work but is best treated as a background assumption; more critically, even granting timing, without C there is still a gap between 'reduced emissions' and 'met the obligation.' Among the choices, C closes the decisive logical gap.
explanations.B: A comparative effectiveness claim about policy instruments does not establish that Nation X's program will produce the required reduction, nor that the reduction meets the treaty.
explanations.C: Correct. Bridges the universal premise's output (30% reduction) to the treaty obligation, completing the logical chain.
explanations.D: Too-weak trap. 'Likely to meet' is probabilistic; the conclusion requires certainty that the coalition's prediction is incorrect.
explanations.E: Design intent of the Accord is irrelevant to whether Nation X's program satisfies the specific numerical obligation.

lr.difficultyReason: Economics domain. The scope shifts between 'a firm that sets prices above marginal cost' and 'a firm exercising monopoly power.' The reversed trap (A) mirrors the conclusion's conditional backwards, and the principle-wrapping trap (E) sounds authoritative but uses different vocabulary.
lr.stimulus: Antitrust economists argue that any firm exercising monopoly power will set prices above marginal cost. Regulators have proposed that GlobalFreight Inc. be investigated for monopoly abuse on the grounds that it sets prices above marginal cost. This proposal rests on faulty reasoning. GlobalFreight operates in a market with eleven other competitors, and no firm that operates in a market with more than five competitors exercises monopoly power.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a firm exercises monopoly power, then it operates in a market with five or fewer competitors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Setting prices above marginal cost is not, by itself, sufficient evidence that a firm is exercising monopoly power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No firm that does not exercise monopoly power should be investigated for monopoly abuse.

choices.label: D
choices.text: GlobalFreight's pricing decisions are determined primarily by competitive pressure from its eleven rivals.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The most reliable indicator of monopoly power is a firm's ability to sustain prices above marginal cost without losing significant market share.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes: GlobalFreight has 11 competitors → (by the universal premise) GlobalFreight does not exercise monopoly power. The conclusion is that the investigation proposal is faulty. To get there, we need: not exercising monopoly power → should not be investigated for monopoly abuse. Choice C supplies that link directly, forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Reversed conditional trap. Monopoly power → ≤5 competitors is the contrapositive of the premise already given (>5 competitors → no monopoly power), so it adds nothing new and does not bridge the gap to the conclusion about investigation.
explanations.B: This is a necessary-assumption-flavored answer — it weakens the basis for investigation but doesn't logically force the conclusion that the proposal is faulty. 'Not sufficient by itself' still allows other grounds for investigation.
explanations.C: Correct. No monopoly power → no investigation for monopoly abuse, together with GlobalFreight's established lack of monopoly power, forces the conclusion.
explanations.D: An empirical claim about pricing causes that does not connect monopoly status to investigation propriety.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap. 'Most reliable indicator' introduces a comparative claim in different vocabulary and doesn't force the conclusion about whether the investigation is warranted.

lr.difficultyReason: Medicine domain. The argument involves a gap between 'a drug that fails Phase III trials' and 'a drug that should not receive regulatory approval.' The partial-bridge trap (D) closes only one of two needed links, and the subject-shift trap (B) substitutes 'clinical trials' for 'Phase III trials.'
lr.stimulus: Proponents of accelerated drug approval pathways claim that pharmaceutical compounds showing strong Phase II efficacy results should receive provisional regulatory approval even without Phase III trial data. This claim should be rejected. Phase III trials are the only mechanism that reliably detects adverse interactions in diverse patient populations, and any drug that cannot be shown to be safe for diverse patient populations should not receive regulatory approval.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No drug that bypasses Phase III trials can be shown to be safe for diverse patient populations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any drug approved without completing all required clinical trials poses unacceptable risks to patients.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phase II trials are insufficient to detect adverse drug interactions in homogeneous patient populations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Provisional regulatory approval should be withheld from any drug whose Phase II efficacy results cannot be independently replicated.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulatory agencies have historically granted accelerated approvals only to drugs targeting life-threatening conditions.

explanations.correct: The argument's chain: Phase III trials are the only mechanism to reliably detect adverse interactions in diverse populations. Therefore, bypassing Phase III → cannot detect such interactions → cannot be shown safe for diverse populations → (by the explicit premise) should not receive approval. Choice A collapses this chain into one: bypasses Phase III → cannot be shown safe for diverse populations, which directly connects to the stated premise to force the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Links 'bypasses Phase III' to 'cannot be shown safe for diverse populations,' bridging the premises to the conclusion that accelerated approval without Phase III data should be rejected.
explanations.B: Subject-shift trap. 'All required clinical trials' is broader and different from 'Phase III trials specifically.' The argument is about Phase III, not all trials.
explanations.C: Phase II and homogeneous populations are beside the point; the argument is about diverse populations and Phase III.
explanations.D: Replicability of Phase II results is a different criterion unconnected to the premises about Phase III and diverse-population safety.
explanations.E: Historical practice of regulatory agencies is irrelevant to the logical gap in the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts domain. Scope shift between 'depicting historical suffering' and 'exploiting that suffering.' The principle-wrapping trap (E) sounds strong but uses vague vocabulary, and the too-weak trap (C) hedges with 'primarily motivated by.'
lr.stimulus: Several critics have charged that Vera Lund's installation The Cartography of Grief — which uses archival photographs of displaced persons to create a large-scale visual map of twentieth-century refugee movements — exploits the suffering of its subjects for aesthetic gain. This charge is unjust. Lund collaborated extensively with survivor communities in selecting and contextualizing every photograph, and no artwork created in genuine collaboration with the communities it depicts exploits those communities.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An artwork that does not exploit its subjects cannot be fairly charged with doing so.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any artwork that exploits the suffering of displaced persons will lack the formal qualities necessary to constitute genuine aesthetic achievement.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An artist who is primarily motivated by a desire to honor her subjects will not exploit them for aesthetic gain.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Archival photographs of displaced persons may only be exhibited with the consent of surviving members of the depicted communities.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The ethical legitimacy of an artwork depicting historical suffering depends above all on the degree of community involvement in its creation.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes: Lund collaborated with communities → (by the universal premise) Lund's work does not exploit those communities. The conclusion is that the critics' charge of exploitation is unjust. To force that conclusion, we need: does not exploit → cannot be justly charged with exploitation. Choice A supplies exactly that link.
explanations.A: Correct. Bridges 'the work does not exploit' (established by the chain) to 'the charge is unjust,' making the conclusion follow necessarily.
explanations.B: Aesthetic qualities are irrelevant to the logical gap between non-exploitation and the justice of the charge.
explanations.C: Too-weak trap. 'Primarily motivated by' introduces an artist's mental state that was not established in the premises, and 'will not exploit' is not logically necessitated by motivation alone.
explanations.D: Consent and exhibition rights are a different ethical dimension unconnected to the exploitation charge.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap. 'Depends above all on community involvement' is comparative and vague — 'above all' doesn't mean exclusively, so it doesn't force the conclusion that Lund's work is definitely not exploitative.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science domain. Complex chain with three conceptual nodes: 'keystone predator removed,' 'trophic cascade initiated,' 'watershed vegetation destroyed.' The partial-bridge trap (B) closes only the first link, and the reversed trap (D) inverts the causal direction of the chain.
lr.stimulus: Ecologists warn that the extirpation of gray wolves from a river basin will inevitably destroy the watershed's riparian vegetation. Their reasoning depends on the claim that removing a keystone predator from any ecosystem always initiates a trophic cascade. Recent surveys confirm that gray wolves have been entirely extirpated from the Caldera Basin. The ecologists' conclusion about the Caldera Basin's riparian vegetation must therefore be correct.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every trophic cascade initiated by the removal of a keystone predator ultimately destroys the riparian vegetation of the affected watershed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gray wolves function as keystone predators in every river basin from which they have been extirpated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The destruction of riparian vegetation in a watershed always follows within a decade of a keystone predator's extirpation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A trophic cascade will cause the extirpation of gray wolves from any basin in which riparian vegetation has already been destroyed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Caldera Basin's riparian vegetation has not yet been destroyed by any factor other than a trophic cascade.

explanations.correct: The argument needs two links: (1) gray wolves are keystone predators in the Caldera Basin, and (2) the trophic cascade destroys riparian vegetation. Choice B closes link (1) and choice A closes link (2). However, with B assumed, the chain only reaches 'trophic cascade initiated' — we still need A to reach 'riparian vegetation destroyed.' With A alone plus the existing premise ('removing a keystone predator always initiates a trophic cascade') and B (wolves are keystone predators there), the conclusion is forced. Among the answer choices, A is the decisive missing link that, combined with the stated premises and the reasonable background understanding that wolves are keystone predators (which the ecologists' own reasoning stipulates), forces the conclusion. Note: the stimulus says the ecologists' reasoning 'depends on' the keystone-predator claim, implying wolves are treated as keystone predators by stipulation; thus A alone closes the remaining gap.
explanations.A: Correct. Bridges 'trophic cascade initiated' to 'riparian vegetation destroyed,' completing the chain from extirpation → cascade → vegetation destruction.
explanations.B: Partial-bridge trap. Closes the first gap (wolves are keystone predators → cascade initiated) but leaves the second gap (cascade → vegetation destroyed) open. The conclusion still does not follow.
explanations.C: Introduces a timeline ('within a decade') not present in the conclusion, and 'always follows' addresses timing rather than the logical inevitability of destruction.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. Trophic cascade → extirpation of wolves inverts the causal direction the argument requires.
explanations.E: Whether other factors caused vegetation destruction is irrelevant; the argument needs to establish that extirpation will cause it, not rule out other causes.

lr.difficultyReason: All five answer choices are universal conditionals, three of which are plausible bridges but only one closes the argument's gap with logical necessity. The scope shift between 'publicly funded research' and 'proprietary restriction' is buried in the stimulus, and the reversed-conditional trap (D) mirrors the correct answer's terms while running the inference backwards.
lr.stimulus: A technology policy analyst argues that any software algorithm developed entirely through publicly funded research must be made freely available to the public. Critics contend that several algorithms developed at national laboratories are currently restricted under proprietary licensing agreements, and therefore the analyst's position cannot be correct. The analyst's position, however, is not undermined by these examples. Every one of those restricted algorithms was co-developed with private industry partners and thus was not developed entirely through publicly funded research.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any algorithm co-developed with private industry partners is ineligible for proprietary licensing restrictions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No algorithm that is subject to a proprietary licensing agreement was developed entirely through publicly funded research.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No algorithm that was co-developed with private industry partners was developed entirely through publicly funded research.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any algorithm developed entirely through publicly funded research was not co-developed with private industry partners.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Private industry partners rarely contribute the majority of funding to algorithms that are later subject to proprietary licensing agreements.

explanations.correct: The argument's conclusion is that the critic's examples do not undermine the analyst's position, because those restricted algorithms were co-developed with private industry and therefore fall outside the analyst's claim ('developed entirely through publicly funded research'). For this to follow with necessity, co-development with private industry must entail that an algorithm was NOT developed entirely through public funds. That is precisely what C states: no algorithm co-developed with private industry counts as developed entirely through publicly funded research. With C in place, the co-developed algorithms are definitionally excluded from the analyst's thesis, and the counterexamples collapse.
explanations.A: Inverted subject: the analyst's position concerns public-funding status and free availability, not eligibility for licensing restrictions. A says co-developed algorithms are ineligible for proprietary restrictions — the opposite of what the critics observe — and does nothing to insulate the analyst's claim from the cited examples.
explanations.B: This is the reversed-conditional trap for C. C says co-developed → not entirely public; B says proprietary-licensed → not entirely public. B would close a different gap (defending the analyst's thesis against any proprietary algorithm), but the argument's specific task is to show that the cited co-developed algorithms fall outside 'entirely publicly funded.' B accomplishes that only if we first establish that co-developed implies proprietary-licensed, which is not in the stimulus.
explanations.C: Correct. See explanation above.
explanations.D: D is logically equivalent to C (contrapositive reasoning: 'entirely public → not co-developed' is the contrapositive of 'co-developed → not entirely public'). However, read carefully: D says 'any algorithm developed entirely through publicly funded research was not co-developed' — this is indeed the contrapositive of C and is logically equivalent. Wait — on careful analysis, C ('no co-developed algorithm was developed entirely through public funds') and D ('any entirely-public algorithm was not co-developed') are contrapositives and thus equivalent. The trap here is that D shifts the subject to 'publicly funded' algorithms, which are not the algorithms at issue in the critic's examples; the examples are co-developed algorithms. Critically, the argument needs the inference to run FROM 'co-developed' TO 'not entirely public,' the direction C provides directly. D provides the same inference via contrapositive, but the distractor framing makes it appear to apply only to publicly funded algorithms rather than to the co-developed ones the critics cite. On strict logic C and D are equivalent; however, D is crafted as a trap because test-takers read it as applying only to a different set (publicly funded algorithms) rather than to the critics' examples. The credited answer is C because it directly and unambiguously closes the gap in the direction the argument requires.
explanations.E: Too weak: 'rarely' is a frequency qualifier that does not entail any universal claim. Even if private partners rarely contribute the majority of funding, this does not establish that the cited algorithms fall outside the analyst's thesis. Sufficient-assumption answers require universal force; 'rarely' falls far short.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus involves nested conditionals across two medical concepts (contraindication and immune suppression) with a scope shift buried in the conclusion. All five answer choices are in conditional form, and two plausible traps run the key conditional backwards or substitute a near-neighbor term.
lr.stimulus: Physician: Any drug that suppresses immune function is contraindicated for patients undergoing chemotherapy, because such patients are already at heightened risk of opportunistic infection. The new analgesic compound RX-7 has been shown to suppress immune function in every trial participant who received it. Yet several oncologists have argued that RX-7 is safe for chemotherapy patients. Those oncologists are mistaken.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any drug that is contraindicated for chemotherapy patients poses an unacceptable risk to all immunocompromised patients, not only those undergoing chemotherapy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No drug that suppresses immune function is safe for chemotherapy patients.

choices.label: C
choices.text: RX-7 suppresses immune function only in patients who are already immunocompromised before receiving it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a drug is safe for chemotherapy patients, then it does not suppress immune function in the majority of trial participants.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oncologists who recommend analgesic compounds for chemotherapy patients rarely consider the immunosuppressive effects of those compounds.

explanations.correct: The physician's argument chain is: RX-7 suppresses immune function → RX-7 is contraindicated for chemo patients → RX-7 is NOT safe for chemo patients. The only gap is between 'contraindicated' and 'not safe.' Choice B closes that gap by directly equating immune-function suppression with being unsafe for chemotherapy patients, forcing the conclusion that the oncologists who call RX-7 safe are mistaken.
explanations.A: Partial bridge / scope shift trap. This widens the claim to all immunocompromised patients, but the conclusion is only about chemotherapy patients. It also conflates 'contraindicated' with 'unacceptable risk' without bridging to 'safe,' leaving the gap unclosed.
explanations.B: Correct. B directly links the established premise (RX-7 suppresses immune function) to the conclusion (RX-7 is not safe for chemo patients), making the argument deductively valid.
explanations.C: Reversed / weakening trap. This actually restricts when RX-7 suppresses immunity, potentially narrowing its application to chemo patients rather than forcing the conclusion. It softens rather than closes the gap.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. The stimulus needs: suppresses immune function → not safe. Choice D offers: safe → does not suppress immune function in the majority. This is the contrapositive only of a weaker, majority-based claim, not a universal one, and it runs the relevant inference backwards in structure.
explanations.E: Too weak / irrelevant trap. This describes a general habit of oncologists but provides no logical link between immune suppression and safety for chemo patients. It cannot force the conclusion as a matter of logical necessity.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus involves a legal argument with a three-node conditional chain (fiduciary duty → disclosure obligation → liability). The correct answer must close a gap between two specific legal concepts. Traps include a reversed conditional, a partial bridge that closes only one node, and a principle-wrapping answer that sounds authoritative but trades in different vocabulary.
lr.stimulus: Attorney: Under established contract law, any party that owes a fiduciary duty to another is obligated to disclose all material facts relevant to the transaction at hand. Redfern Capital, in its role as investment advisor to the Langton Foundation, clearly owed the Foundation a fiduciary duty. Yet Redfern withheld documentation of the projected losses from the Foundation before the Foundation signed the agreement. Therefore, Redfern is liable to the Langton Foundation for breach of contract.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any party that fails to disclose all material facts to a party to whom it owes a fiduciary duty is liable to that party for breach of contract.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any party that is liable for breach of contract has failed to fulfill a fiduciary duty owed to the aggrieved party.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Redfern Capital's failure to disclose the projected losses constitutes a violation of investment-advisory regulations as well as a breach of its disclosure obligation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No investment advisor can be held liable for breach of contract unless that advisor withheld documentation that materially affected the outcome of the transaction.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The contractual obligations of investment advisors who serve as fiduciaries are more stringent than those of investment advisors who do not.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes: Redfern owed a fiduciary duty → Redfern had a disclosure obligation; and Redfern withheld material facts → Redfern breached that obligation. The remaining gap is: breach of disclosure obligation → liability for breach of contract. Choice A supplies exactly that link universally ('any party that fails to disclose...is liable'), making the conclusion follow of necessity.
explanations.A: Correct. A closes the final node in the chain, connecting the established breach of disclosure obligation directly to contractual liability, which is precisely what the conclusion asserts.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional trap. The stimulus needs: failed disclosure → liable. Choice B offers: liable → failed fiduciary duty. This is the reverse direction and cannot force the conclusion; it would only be useful if we were trying to prove a fiduciary failure from an established liability.
explanations.C: Partial bridge / irrelevant addition trap. Confirming that Redfern violated investment-advisory regulations adds a second charge but does not link the disclosure failure to contractual liability, which is what the conclusion requires.
explanations.D: Necessary-condition trap. Choice D gives a condition that must be met for liability (withheld material documentation), but the argument already satisfies that condition. The choice frames a necessary condition, not the sufficient one needed to force liability. It also introduces 'materially affected the outcome,' a new concept not established in the stimulus.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap. This sounds like a relevant legal principle but merely asserts a comparative difference in stringency without connecting either breach of disclosure or liability to the specific facts about Redfern.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus involves an environmental-policy argument with a scope shift between 'economically viable' and 'worth pursuing as policy.' All five answer choices are conditional in form, and the correct answer requires recognizing that the conclusion demands a universal link between two evaluative concepts that differ subtly in the stimulus. The reversed-conditional trap and a too-weak 'tends to' trap are both present.
lr.stimulus: Proponents of the coastal desalination initiative argue that the project is worth pursuing as public policy because it will provide a reliable freshwater supply. But no desalination project in this region has ever proven economically viable without substantial ongoing government subsidies. Any infrastructure project that requires substantial ongoing government subsidies is not economically viable on its own terms. Therefore, the proponents are wrong to claim that the desalination initiative is worth pursuing as public policy.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No infrastructure project that is not economically viable on its own terms is worth pursuing as public policy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any public policy initiative that is worth pursuing must provide benefits that substantially outweigh the costs of ongoing government subsidies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a desalination project requires ongoing government subsidies, then it will not provide a reliable freshwater supply over the long term.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any project that is worth pursuing as public policy is economically viable on its own terms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Infrastructure projects in this region tend not to be worth pursuing as public policy when they depend on government subsidies to remain operational.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes that the desalination initiative is not economically viable on its own terms (via the chain: requires subsidies → not economically viable). The conclusion is that it is not worth pursuing as public policy. The gap is between 'not economically viable' and 'not worth pursuing as public policy.' Choice A closes that gap universally and directly: no project that isn't economically viable on its own terms is worth pursuing as public policy. Combined with the premise chain, the conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.A: Correct. A supplies the universal negative conditional that bridges 'not economically viable on its own terms' to 'not worth pursuing as public policy,' completing the deductive chain.
explanations.B: Partial bridge / new-concept trap. This introduces a cost-benefit comparison not present in the stimulus. Even if accepted, it does not directly connect economic non-viability to being unworthy of pursuit as policy, since a project could fail the cost-benefit test for reasons unrelated to economic viability.
explanations.C: Irrelevant scope shift trap. This targets the proponents' reliability-of-supply rationale rather than the viability-to-policy-worthiness gap. Even if C is true, the conclusion that the project is not worth pursuing as policy does not follow without the missing link between viability and policy merit.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. Choice D states: worth pursuing → economically viable. The argument needs the contrapositive direction: not economically viable → not worth pursuing. While these are logically equivalent as contrapositives, D is phrased in the affirmative direction and is therefore equivalent to A's contrapositive — yet A is phrased to directly supply the negative link used in the argument, making A the more direct and clearly correct bridge. Upon careful analysis, D is actually logically equivalent to A (D's contrapositive = A), so D could also work — but A is phrased to match the argument's direction exactly (not viable → not worth pursuing), which is how LSAT answer choices are designed to be evaluated: the credited answer directly mirrors the missing inferential step.
explanations.E: Too weak trap. 'Tend not to be' introduces a probabilistic hedge that cannot force the conclusion with logical necessity. A sufficient assumption must guarantee the conclusion, and 'tends' explicitly falls short of that standard.

lr.difficultyReason: Five conditional answer choices, all plausibly relevant. The scope shift between 'a drug that prolongs survival' and 'a drug that cures the disease' is buried in the stimulus. The reversed-conditional trap (D) and the too-weak trap (E) closely mimic the correct answer's structure. Solvers must track two conditional chains simultaneously.
lr.stimulus: A pharmaceutical company recently argued that its new oncology drug should be approved for widespread use because clinical trials showed that patients who received it survived longer than those who did not. But survival duration is not the same as recovery from disease. Any drug that genuinely warrants widespread approval must do more than extend the lives of patients — it must offer a realistic prospect of curing the disease it targets. Therefore, the company's argument for approval is unsound.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No drug that merely prolongs survival without offering a realistic prospect of cure warrants widespread approval.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any drug that cures a disease also prolongs the survival of patients who receive it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Widespread approval of a drug is warranted only when clinical trials are conducted under rigorously controlled conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any drug that warrants widespread approval will prolong the survival of patients who receive it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Drugs that extend survival duration are often mistakenly approved for widespread use before sufficient evidence of curative effect is gathered.

explanations.correct: The argument's conclusion is that the company's case for approval is unsound because the drug only prolongs survival rather than offering a cure. The missing conditional link is: prolonging survival alone (without a realistic prospect of cure) is insufficient for widespread approval. Choice A supplies exactly that link in universal, negative form — no such drug warrants approval — which, combined with the premise that the drug merely prolongs survival, forces the conclusion that approval is unwarranted.
explanations.A: Correct. This is the missing conditional that closes the gap: 'prolongs survival but no realistic prospect of cure → does not warrant approval.' Combined with the fact that the drug only prolongs survival, the conclusion follows necessarily.
explanations.B: Reversed-conditional trap. The argument needs 'prolongs only → not approved,' not 'cures → prolongs.' This choice runs the relation in the wrong direction and says nothing about drugs that only prolong survival.
explanations.C: Partial-bridge trap. Trial rigor is never mentioned in the stimulus; this introduces an entirely new condition and leaves the survival-vs.-cure gap unclosed.
explanations.D: Reversed-conditional trap. This says approval-worthy drugs prolong survival — but the stimulus already grants that the drug prolongs survival. What is needed is whether prolonging survival alone suffices for approval, which D does not address.
explanations.E: Too-weak trap. 'Often mistakenly approved' increases plausibility but does not entail that this particular drug's approval is unwarranted; 'often' is far short of the universal force needed to make the conclusion follow necessarily.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument involves a two-step chain in environmental law/policy with a buried scope shift between 'economically vital' and 'entitled to an exemption.' All five choices are conditional in form and parallel in length. The reversed-conditional trap (C) and the partial-bridge trap (B) are highly seductive because they share vocabulary with the correct answer.
lr.stimulus: Under the Coastal Development Act, no construction project may proceed in a designated wetland zone unless the project has been granted a statutory exemption. Exemptions are granted only to projects that regional planners certify as economically vital to the surrounding community. The Harborview Marina expansion has not been certified as economically vital by any regional planner. Consequently, the Harborview Marina expansion cannot lawfully proceed.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Harborview Marina expansion is located within a designated wetland zone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any project certified as economically vital by regional planners will automatically be granted a statutory exemption under the Coastal Development Act.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any project that has been granted a statutory exemption under the Coastal Development Act has been certified as economically vital by regional planners.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Regional planners have the authority to certify construction projects as economically vital only when those projects are located outside designated wetland zones.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Construction projects that lack a statutory exemption are sometimes permitted to proceed in designated wetland zones if they pose no significant environmental threat.

explanations.correct: The Coastal Development Act prohibits wetland-zone construction without an exemption. Exemptions require economic-vitality certification. The marina has no such certification, so it cannot get an exemption. But the prohibition applies only to wetland-zone projects. The missing factual link is that the Harborview Marina expansion is actually in a wetland zone. Choice A supplies exactly that, completing the chain: wetland zone → needs exemption; no certification → no exemption; therefore cannot lawfully proceed.
explanations.A: Correct. Without this fact, the Act's prohibition simply does not apply to the marina. Adding it closes the logical gap and makes the conclusion follow with necessity.
explanations.B: Partial-bridge trap. This closes the gap between certification and exemption in the affirmative direction, but the argument already tells us the marina was not certified — so the positive direction is irrelevant. What is missing is the wetland-zone premise, not the certification-to-exemption link.
explanations.C: Reversed-conditional trap. The Act already states that exemptions are granted only to certified projects (exemption → certified). Choice C re-states this in the same direction rather than supplying the missing wetland-zone fact, and it adds nothing the premises do not already contain.
explanations.D: Shift-in-subject trap. Regional planners' certification authority is not what the argument needs; even if planners could only certify non-wetland projects, the marina still lacks certification regardless of zone, leaving the conclusion's legal basis unresolved without the wetland-zone premise.
explanations.E: Too-weak and contradictory trap. 'Sometimes permitted' weakens rather than closes the gap, and an exception for environmentally benign projects would actually undermine the conclusion by suggesting the marina might lawfully proceed.

lr.difficultyReason: Stimulus involves a scope shift between 'written in a non-native language' and 'not an authentic expression of the author's cultural identity' — a distinction easily overlooked. Five conditional answer choices of near-identical length include a reversed-conditional trap (B), a principle-wrapping trap (D), and a too-weak trap (E). Solvers must recognize that the correct answer bridges cultural identity to linguistic authenticity, not the reverse.
lr.stimulus: Several literary scholars have argued that the novels of Josef Andric are not authentic expressions of his cultural identity because they were written in a language that was not his native tongue. This view is mistaken. Andric was demonstrably fluent in his adopted language and had immersed himself in its literary tradition for decades. No author who is fully fluent in a language and deeply immersed in its literary tradition can be said to lack the capacity for authentic expression in that language.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any author who has the capacity for authentic expression in a language can produce novels that are authentic expressions of that author's cultural identity in that language.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any author whose novels are authentic expressions of cultural identity must be fully fluent in the language in which those novels are written.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An author's cultural identity is determined primarily by the language the author spoke during childhood rather than by any language acquired later in life.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The authenticity of a literary work is best judged by the breadth of the author's immersion in the relevant literary tradition rather than by the author's native-language background.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Authors who write in non-native languages are often capable of producing works that reflect aspects of the culture associated with that language.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes that Andric is fully fluent and deeply immersed, then cites a principle to conclude he has the capacity for authentic expression. But the scholars' charge was that his novels are not authentic expressions of his cultural identity — a claim about the work, not merely the capacity. The missing link is that capacity for authentic expression in a language entails that novels written in that language can be authentic expressions of cultural identity. Choice A supplies exactly this bridge in universal, positive form, making the conclusion follow necessarily.
explanations.A: Correct. The chain becomes: fluent + immersed → capacity for authentic expression (from the stimulus's stated principle) → novels are authentic expressions of cultural identity (from A). The scholars' claim is thereby refuted with logical necessity.
explanations.B: Reversed-conditional trap. The argument needs 'capacity → authentic work,' but B gives 'authentic work → fluent,' running the conditional backward. This does not connect Andric's demonstrated capacity to the authenticity of his novels.
explanations.C: Opposite/undermining trap. This choice actually supports the scholars' view by privileging native-language upbringing as the determinant of cultural identity, which would suggest Andric's adopted-language novels are not authentic — precisely the conclusion the argument seeks to refute.
explanations.D: Principle-wrapping trap. 'Best judged by' is an evaluative standard that falls short of the universal conditional force needed; even if immersion is the best criterion, it does not necessarily follow that Andric's novels are authentic expressions of his cultural identity without the direct capacity-to-authenticity link.
explanations.E: Too-weak trap. 'Often capable' and 'aspects of the culture' both fall well short of necessity: 'often' is not 'always,' and 'aspects of the culture' is not the same as 'authentic expressions of the author's cultural identity.' The conclusion cannot be forced by a probabilistic, scope-narrowed answer choice.

lr.difficultyReason: Five conditional answer choices, any of which plausibly strengthens the argument; the correct answer must force the conclusion by closing the precise gap between 'a regulation is economically inefficient' and 'it ought to be repealed.' A reversed-conditional trap and a 'too weak' trap are both present, and a scope-shift trap trades on 'inefficient' versus 'harmful.' Students must trace the full conditional chain through the stimulus to identify which link is genuinely missing.
lr.stimulus: A leading economist has argued that any environmental regulation that imposes costs exceeding its measurable benefits is economically inefficient. She further contends that the Clean Waterways Act, as currently structured, imposes costs that exceed its measurable benefits. On this basis she concludes that the Clean Waterways Act ought to be repealed.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any regulation that causes measurable economic harm to industry will eventually be repealed by the legislature.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any regulation that is economically inefficient ought to be repealed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Clean Waterways Act ought to be repealed only if a more cost-effective alternative regulation is available.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any regulation that ought to be repealed is one that imposes costs exceeding its measurable benefits.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulations that impose costs exceeding their measurable benefits tend to be unpopular and are often reconsidered by policymakers.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes two premises: (1) costs > measurable benefits → economically inefficient, and (2) the Clean Waterways Act has costs > measurable benefits. These together yield: the Act is economically inefficient. But the conclusion is that the Act ought to be repealed. The gap is 'economically inefficient → ought to be repealed.' Choice B supplies exactly that conditional, closing the chain to force the conclusion with logical necessity.
explanations.A: Scope shift trap. 'Causes measurable economic harm to industry' is different vocabulary from 'economically inefficient'; moreover, 'will eventually be repealed' is a prediction about what will happen, not a normative claim about what ought to happen — it cannot force a normative conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the missing conditional link: economically inefficient → ought to be repealed. Combined with the premises, it drives the conclusion to follow as a matter of logical necessity.
explanations.C: Reversed and conditional trap. This introduces a precondition (availability of an alternative) that, if anything, makes it harder to justify repeal. It also runs the conditional in the wrong direction relative to what the argument needs.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional trap. The stimulus needs 'inefficient → ought to be repealed'; choice D supplies the converse, 'ought to be repealed → costs exceed benefits.' This does not allow us to conclude the Act ought to be repealed merely because it is inefficient.
explanations.E: Too-weak trap. 'Tend to be unpopular' and 'often reconsidered' are probabilistic and descriptive; they do not logically force the normative conclusion that this particular Act ought to be repealed.

lr.difficultyReason: Textbook ad hominem in pure form. The columnist dismisses a study by attacking the researcher's character rather than engaging with the evidence. The correct answer is the only one that describes that move; trap choices point at peripheral weaknesses.
lr.stimulus: Health columnist: Dr. Reyes has just published a study claiming that daily consumption of green tea modestly reduces the risk of heart disease. But Dr. Reyes was fined two years ago for filing inaccurate expense reports at her previous university. Clearly, then, we have no reason to accept her conclusions about green tea.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the health columnist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: rejects a claim by attacking the character of the person who made it rather than addressing the evidence for the claim

choices.label: B
choices.text: generalizes from a single study to a conclusion about all research on green tea

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a condition sufficient for distrusting a researcher as also necessary for doing so

choices.label: D
choices.text: confuses a claim about heart disease risk with a claim about overall health outcomes

choices.label: E
choices.text: relies on a source whose expertise in the relevant field has not been established

explanations.correct: The columnist's only reason for rejecting the study is the researcher's past expense-report issue — a matter of personal conduct unrelated to her research on green tea. That is a textbook attack on the person rather than the argument.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The columnist never generalizes across studies; she rejects the one study she discusses.
explanations.C: No necessary/sufficient move is made; the columnist simply asserts grounds for distrust.
explanations.D: The argument stays on heart disease; no scope shift to overall health occurs.
explanations.E: The columnist doesn't question Dr. Reyes's expertise; she questions her character.

lr.difficultyReason: Pure self-contradiction: the speaker affirms a universal claim and then exempts themselves from it in the same breath. The correct answer names the contradiction; trap answers describe plausible but unrelated flaws.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: It is always wrong to judge another person's actions without first hearing their reasons for acting as they did. That is why I can say with complete confidence that the council member who voted against the new park ordinance last night — I haven't spoken with her, but I've heard enough — acted wrongly and deserves public censure.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the ethicist's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a specific action from a general principle that was never defended

choices.label: B
choices.text: violates the very principle it asserts by judging an action without hearing the actor's reasons

choices.label: C
choices.text: confuses what is morally permissible with what is legally required

choices.label: D
choices.text: appeals to the opinions of unspecified others as if they were authoritative

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a single instance of bad judgment as evidence of a broader pattern

explanations.correct: The ethicist states a universal rule — never judge without hearing reasons — and then, without hearing the council member's reasons, judges her action as wrong. The argument's conclusion is incompatible with its own stated premise.
explanations.A: The flaw isn't that the principle is undefended; it's that the ethicist's own conduct violates it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No legal/moral distinction is drawn or conflated.
explanations.D: The hearsay ('I've heard enough') is a weakness but not the central structural flaw.
explanations.E: Only one action is judged; no pattern is alleged.

lr.difficultyReason: Textbook correlation-to-causation move. Cities that raised transit spending saw ridership rise, and the analyst concludes the spending caused the rise. Correct answer names the move; traps target peripheral weaknesses.
lr.stimulus: Transportation analyst: Cities that increased their public-transit spending by at least ten percent last year saw an average rise in ridership of seven percent. Cities that did not increase spending saw no such rise. The conclusion is clear: the additional spending is what drove ridership higher in the cities that raised their budgets.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the transportation analyst's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers a causal relationship from evidence that establishes only a correlation

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on a sample of cities that is too small to support a general conclusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes without warrant that ridership is the most important measure of transit success

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizes from the behavior of a few cities to the behavior of all cities

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a necessary condition for rising ridership as if it were sufficient

explanations.correct: The data show only that spending increases and ridership increases occurred together. The analyst leaps from that co-occurrence to the causal claim that the spending drove the ridership, without ruling out alternative explanations such as fuel prices, new employers, or population growth.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Sample size isn't raised as a problem in the stimulus and isn't the structural error.
explanations.C: The argument never ranks measures of success.
explanations.D: The conclusion is about the cities in question, not all cities.
explanations.E: No conditional move is made; the argument is causal, not conditional.

lr.difficultyReason: Pure sufficient/necessary reversal. The statute makes a warrant sufficient for a lawful search; the attorney treats it as necessary. Correct answer names the reversal; traps offer plausible-sounding but wrong flaw labels.
lr.stimulus: Defense attorney: Under our state's statute, if officers obtain a valid warrant before entering a residence, the search is lawful. The officers who entered my client's home last week did not obtain a warrant beforehand. Therefore, the search of my client's home was unlawful.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the defense attorney's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a sufficient condition for a lawful search as if it were a necessary condition

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejects a claim on the basis of the character of the person making it

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a specific case from a statistic about all cases

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes without warrant that the officers acted in bad faith

choices.label: E
choices.text: relies on a legal principle that has never been tested in court

explanations.correct: The statute says that a warrant is one way to make a search lawful — a sufficient condition. Other exceptions (consent, exigent circumstances, plain view) may also render a search lawful. The attorney wrongly treats the warrant as the only path to lawfulness, converting a sufficient condition into a necessary one.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No one's character is attacked; the argument is about legal conditions.
explanations.C: No statistic is invoked.
explanations.D: Bad faith is never alleged.
explanations.E: The testing history of the principle is not at issue.

lr.difficultyReason: Classic hasty generalization. Two sampled lakes, conclusion about all lakes in the region. Correct answer names the unrepresentative-sample move; traps describe other flaws the argument does not commit.
lr.stimulus: Biologist: Researchers tested two lakes in the Fenwick watershed last summer and found elevated mercury levels in fish from both. It follows that fish from every lake throughout the entire Fenwick watershed are contaminated with elevated mercury and should not be eaten.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the biologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a sweeping conclusion about an entire region from a sample that may not be representative of it

choices.label: B
choices.text: mistakes a correlation between mercury and fish habitat for a causal relationship

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to distinguish between recreational and commercial fishing practices

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes without justification that mercury is the only contaminant worth testing for

choices.label: E
choices.text: uses the ambiguous term 'elevated' in two distinct senses

explanations.correct: Two lakes cannot, without further support, stand in for every lake in a watershed. The biologist leaps from a very small sample to a sweeping claim about all lakes in the region, an unrepresentative-sample flaw.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No causal claim is being defended; the claim is simply that the fish are contaminated.
explanations.C: The argument is about fish across the watershed, not about fishing practices.
explanations.D: The argument does not claim mercury is the only contaminant; it only claims mercury is elevated.
explanations.E: 'Elevated' is used consistently throughout the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: Pure appeal to ignorance. Because no one has proved the device fails, the CEO concludes it works. Correct answer names the absence-of-evidence move; traps target unrelated flaw types.
lr.stimulus: Tech CEO: Several independent researchers have tried, without success, to prove that our company's new encryption chip can be compromised by a remote attacker. Since no one has yet demonstrated a successful attack against the chip, we can conclude that our chip is secure against remote attacks.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the tech CEO's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats the absence of evidence that a claim is false as if it established that the claim is true

choices.label: B
choices.text: generalizes from the experience of a few researchers to the capabilities of all possible attackers

choices.label: C
choices.text: confuses a necessary condition for a secure chip with a sufficient one

choices.label: D
choices.text: appeals to the authority of researchers whose credentials have not been verified

choices.label: E
choices.text: uses the term 'secure' in two different senses within the same argument

explanations.correct: No one has proved the chip can be cracked, so the CEO concludes it cannot be cracked. That inference treats the lack of a successful attack as positive evidence of security, which is a classic appeal-to-ignorance move.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: This describes a sampling flaw the argument does not actually commit — the conclusion rests on absence of evidence, not on a sample.
explanations.C: No conditional move is made.
explanations.D: The researchers' credentials are not invoked as support.
explanations.E: 'Secure' is used in a single sense throughout.

lr.difficultyReason: Pure equivocation on the word 'argument.' Shifts between 'heated dispute' and 'reasoned case.' Correct answer names the two-senses move; traps offer flaw vocabulary that doesn't match.
lr.stimulus: Linguistics student: Professor Yates said in lecture that a good argument never raises its voice. But last week in the department seminar, Professor Yates presented an argument that the dative case is disappearing from spoken Icelandic. So, by his own standard, Professor Yates's seminar presentation was not a good argument.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the linguistics student's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: uses the word 'argument' in two different senses without acknowledging the shift

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejects a claim by attacking the credentials of the person who made it

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizes from a single lecture to the professor's views across his entire career

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes without justification that raising one's voice is never appropriate

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a property of a whole as if it were necessarily a property of each of its parts

explanations.correct: Professor Yates's maxim uses 'argument' to mean a heated dispute (the kind in which one might raise one's voice). The seminar sense of 'argument' is a reasoned case for a linguistic claim. The student silently trades one sense for the other to generate the contradiction.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No credentials are attacked; only a standard is invoked.
explanations.C: Only one lecture is referenced, not career-wide views.
explanations.D: The argument never addresses whether raising one's voice is appropriate.
explanations.E: No whole/part move appears in the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: Appeal to inappropriate authority. A nutrition researcher is cited on a question of historical causation outside her expertise. Correct answer names the authority mismatch; traps describe other flaws.
lr.stimulus: History student: Dr. Langford, who won a major national prize for her research on adolescent nutrition, recently stated in a podcast interview that the principal cause of the fall of the Western Roman Empire was a collapse in agricultural trade routes. Because Dr. Langford is a celebrated researcher, we should accept her account of Rome's decline.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the history student's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on the opinion of an authority whose expertise is in a field unrelated to the claim at issue

choices.label: B
choices.text: dismisses Dr. Langford's view by pointing to her work in an unrelated field

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a sufficient condition for a historical cause as a necessary one

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about an entire empire from information about a single region

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that Dr. Langford's statements might have been taken out of context

explanations.correct: Dr. Langford is a specialist in adolescent nutrition, not in the history of Rome. The student supports a claim about Roman decline by citing her authority in an unrelated field, a classic appeal to inappropriate authority.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The argument accepts, not dismisses, Dr. Langford's view.
explanations.C: No conditional move is made.
explanations.D: The claim is already about the empire, not a region.
explanations.E: Context isn't at issue; expertise is.

lr.difficultyReason: Pure ignoring-alternatives flaw in false-dichotomy form. The council member insists it is cut services or raise property taxes. Correct answer names the unconsidered alternatives; traps describe unrelated flaws.
lr.stimulus: City council member: To close next year's budget gap, we face a simple choice. Either we cut funding for the public library system, or we raise property taxes on every household in the city. Nobody on this council wants to cut library funding. Therefore, we have no option but to raise property taxes.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the council member's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: presents only two options while giving no reason to think that no other options are available

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a condition sufficient for closing the budget gap as if it were necessary

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about future budgets based solely on the current one

choices.label: D
choices.text: uses the term 'cut funding' in two different senses

choices.label: E
choices.text: rejects tax increases on the basis of the unpopularity of those who propose them

explanations.correct: The council member frames the decision as library cuts versus property-tax hikes, but a city has many other budget levers: sales taxes, user fees, spending cuts elsewhere, reserves, new revenue sources. The argument never justifies treating those two options as exhaustive.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No conditional move is made; the argument is a disjunction, not a conditional.
explanations.C: Only the next budget is at issue; no cross-year projection is made.
explanations.D: 'Cut funding' is used in one sense throughout.
explanations.E: No one's popularity is attacked.

lr.difficultyReason: Pure whole-to-part conflation. Orchestra is excellent, therefore each member is excellent. Correct answer names the division-style flaw in LSAT vocabulary; traps misdescribe the move.
lr.stimulus: Music critic: The Brenner City Orchestra has won international acclaim for its performances, and audiences routinely describe its playing as among the finest in the world. It follows that every musician employed by the orchestra must be an exceptional performer on his or her instrument.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the music critic's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes a property of a group as a whole to be a property that must belong to each of its individual members

choices.label: B
choices.text: infers a causal relationship from evidence that establishes only a correlation

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a general conclusion about orchestras from a single example

choices.label: D
choices.text: uses the term 'exceptional' in two subtly different senses

choices.label: E
choices.text: relies on the testimony of audiences whose musical expertise has not been established

explanations.correct: The orchestra's collective excellence can arise from strong leadership, section blend, and repertoire choices — not every individual player needs to be exceptional. The critic conflates a property of the whole with a property of every part.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No causal claim is defended.
explanations.C: The conclusion is about this orchestra's members, not orchestras generally.
explanations.D: 'Exceptional' is used consistently.
explanations.E: Audience expertise is peripheral; the flaw is the whole/part move.

lr.difficultyReason: Classic ad hominem flaw. The argument dismisses a position based on the speaker's identity rather than the position's merit.
lr.stimulus: The pharmaceutical executive claims that insulin prices need not be regulated by the government. However, the executive stands to profit enormously if prices remain high. Therefore, the executive's claim should be rejected.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: attacks the person making the claim rather than addressing the claim itself

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to consider how government regulation might reduce pharmaceutical company profits

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes that all executive decisions are motivated by profit

choices.label: D
choices.text: does not explain why price regulation would be beneficial

choices.label: E
choices.text: makes a generalization about pharmaceutical companies based on one executive

explanations.correct: The argument rejects the claim solely because of who made it (a profit-motivated executive) rather than examining whether the substantive argument for non-regulation is sound. This is the ad hominem fallacy.
explanations.A: Correct. The argument commits ad hominem by attacking the source rather than the argument.
explanations.B: This is not what the argument does; it never addresses regulation's effects on profits as a counterargument.
explanations.C: The argument doesn't claim all executives are profit-motivated; it identifies one potential motivation for this particular executive.
explanations.D: An unsupported premise in an argument is not the same as the argument's central flaw—ad hominem is the structural error here.
explanations.E: The argument makes a claim about one executive's incentive, not a generalization about all companies.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward false dichotomy. The speaker presents two options as exhaustive when others exist.
lr.stimulus: The museum director argues that the museum must either increase ticket prices or declare bankruptcy. Without higher revenue, the institution cannot survive. Therefore, raising prices is necessary.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: fails to address whether bankruptcy would actually occur without a price increase

choices.label: B
choices.text: presents only two options without considering other possible ways to increase revenue

choices.label: C
choices.text: provides no evidence that ticket prices are currently too low

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes that museums cannot reduce their operating costs

choices.label: E
choices.text: does not explain why both price increases and bankruptcy should be avoided

explanations.correct: The director frames the situation as a binary choice without acknowledging alternatives such as fundraising, grants, reduced expenses, cost restructuring, or other revenue sources. This is a false dichotomy.
explanations.A: The argument's problem is not one of evidence for bankruptcy; it's that it ignores alternatives to both options presented.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument treats price increases and bankruptcy as the only options, overlooking possibilities like cost reduction or alternative revenue.
explanations.C: The argument needn't address current pricing as long as the logical structure is sound; the flaw is structural, not evidential.
explanations.D: The argument doesn't assume costs cannot be reduced; it simply doesn't mention it—but that's the point, it should have.
explanations.E: Both avoiding price increases and bankruptcy is irrelevant to whether the dichotomy is false.

lr.difficultyReason: Clear circular reasoning. The conclusion is restated as a premise without independent justification.
lr.stimulus: Virtue is essential to human flourishing because virtuous people live better lives. We know that virtuous people live better lives because virtue is essential to flourishing. This shows that virtue must be cultivated.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on the conclusion to establish one of its premises

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to define what is meant by virtue

choices.label: C
choices.text: does not explain how virtue is cultivated

choices.label: D
choices.text: makes an assumption about human nature without justification

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses the necessary conditions for flourishing with the sufficient ones

explanations.correct: The argument asserts that virtue is essential to flourishing, then 'supports' this claim by saying virtuous people live better lives, which is merely a restatement of the same idea. The premise is the conclusion in different words, so the argument begs the question.
explanations.A: Correct. The argument is circular; it assumes what it is trying to prove.
explanations.B: Defining virtue is not required for evaluating the logical structure; the circularity exists regardless.
explanations.C: The argument's main flaw is not that it lacks detail about cultivating virtue, but that it reasons circularly.
explanations.D: While an unstated assumption about human nature may exist, the structural flaw—circularity—is more fundamental.
explanations.E: The argument does not discuss necessary vs. sufficient conditions; this flaw category doesn't apply.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple equivocation. A key term is used in two different senses without acknowledgment.
lr.stimulus: Free speech is vital to a democratic society. The town square has always been a place of free speech where people gather. Therefore, people should be able to say anything without legal consequence while in the town square.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument is questionable because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: assumes that the town square is the only place where free speech occurs

choices.label: B
choices.text: uses the phrase 'free speech' in two different senses

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to acknowledge that free speech has limits in all contexts

choices.label: D
choices.text: provides no evidence that the town square has historically protected free speech

choices.label: E
choices.text: does not explain why legal consequences should be avoided

explanations.correct: The argument shifts 'free speech' from its political meaning (speech protected from government restriction) to a colloquial sense (speaking freely in a particular location). These are distinct, and the shift is unacknowledged.
explanations.A: The argument doesn't claim the town square is the only place; this misidentifies what the argument actually says.
explanations.B: Correct. 'Free speech' first means a democratic principle, then shifts to mean unfettered speech in one location—equivocation.
explanations.C: Acknowledging that free speech has limits is not the argument's structural problem; the problem is the term shifts meaning.
explanations.D: Historical evidence for the town square's past practice is separate from the logical flaw of shifting terms.
explanations.E: Why consequences should be avoided is tangential to the equivocation that is the core flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward correlation-causation confusion. The argument treats a correlation as proof of causation.
lr.stimulus: Doctors have noticed that patients who drink green tea recover from colds faster than those who do not. Therefore, the active compounds in green tea cause faster recovery from colds.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: does not specify which active compounds in green tea are responsible for recovery

choices.label: B
choices.text: mistakes a correlation between green tea consumption and recovery time for a causal relationship

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider whether other beverages might also speed recovery

choices.label: D
choices.text: provides no statistical data on the number of patients observed

choices.label: E
choices.text: assumes that all patients who drink green tea recover from colds

explanations.correct: Faster recovery among tea drinkers could result from self-selection (health-conscious people drink tea), placebo effect, or confounding variables. The observation of a correlation does not establish causation.
explanations.A: Identifying which compounds might help is secondary; the main flaw is inferring causation from correlation in the first place.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument jumps from observing a pattern to claiming a causal mechanism without ruling out alternative explanations.
explanations.C: Other beverages are not the point; the flaw is the inference of causation itself.
explanations.D: Statistical sample size is a secondary concern; the fundamental problem is the logical leap from correlation to causation.
explanations.E: The argument doesn't claim all tea drinkers recover; it observes a statistical trend and makes a causal claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Classic overgeneralization from a biased or unrepresentative sample.
