choices.label: E
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a specific family from a policy statement that applies only to applicants in general

explanations.correct: Demonstrating financial need is a necessary condition for qualifying — you must have it to qualify, but having it alone does not guarantee qualification. The analyst concludes that meeting this necessary condition is enough to secure qualification, confusing it with a sufficient condition.
explanations.A: The argument does not treat this as a mere correlation — it treats the condition as logically determinative. Correlation-causation is not the structural flaw here.
explanations.B: Correct. Financial need is necessary (required) but not sufficient (alone enough) for qualification. The argument treats meeting a necessary condition as guaranteeing the outcome.
explanations.C: Funding availability is a real-world concern but is outside the argument's logical structure — a 'plausible but absent' trap.
explanations.D: The argument concerns qualifying, not disqualifying. This choice reverses the direction of the conditional and misdescribes the argument.
explanations.E: The argument applies a general policy rule to a specific case — this is standard deductive application, not a flaw in itself.

lr.difficultyReason: Appeal to consequences / overgeneralization flaw in an ethics context. The argument rejects a moral principle because of undesirable implications rather than engaging with the principle's justification. A plausible scope-shift trap is included.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Some philosophers argue that we are morally obligated to give aid to anyone we can help at little cost to ourselves. But if we accepted this principle, we would be required to donate virtually all of our disposable income to famine relief and similar causes. Since this demand is clearly unreasonable, the principle that we must help those we can help at little cost to ourselves must be false.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: shifts from discussing obligations to individuals to drawing conclusions about obligations to societies

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejects a moral principle solely because accepting it would have demanding consequences, without showing the principle is unjustified

choices.label: C
choices.text: takes for granted that donating to famine relief is the only way to fulfill an obligation to help others at little cost

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about what is morally required from premises that describe only what is psychologically feasible

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to distinguish between moral obligations that are binding on all people and those that apply only to the wealthy

explanations.correct: The ethicist's argument is a 'tollensing the ponens' move: because the principle leads to demanding consequences, the principle must be false. But finding a conclusion demanding or uncomfortable does not show the supporting argument for the principle is flawed — the ethicist never engages the reasons offered in support of the principle itself.
explanations.A: The argument operates at the level of individual obligations throughout; no shift to societal obligations occurs. This misdescribes the argument's scope.
explanations.B: Correct. Rejecting a principle because its implications are demanding is an appeal to consequences, not a demonstration that the principle lacks justification.
explanations.C: The argument acknowledges that famine relief is one example of what the principle demands — it does not treat it as the only possible fulfillment. This misdescribes the argument.
explanations.D: The argument appeals to what is 'unreasonable,' which is a normative claim, not a psychological feasibility claim — this choice misidentifies the type of premise used.
explanations.E: The ethicist argues against the principle universally, not against any wealth-relative version — this introduces a distinction the argument does not make and is a 'plausible but absent' trap.

lr.difficultyReason: A standard correlation-causation flaw with two or three plausible mis-descriptions in the answer set. One trap choice names a genuine flaw type (false dichotomy) that does not match the actual move in the stimulus; another accurately describes a minor weakness rather than the central structural error.
lr.stimulus: Economist: A study of twelve major cities found that those with the highest rates of small-business formation also had the highest median household incomes. Clearly, encouraging the formation of small businesses is an effective strategy for raising household incomes in urban areas.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the economist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about all urban areas from evidence limited to a small number of major cities

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that a correlation between two trends establishes that one trend causes the other

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to specify the precise measures used to calculate rates of small-business formation

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats the absence of high household income as a sufficient reason to encourage small-business formation

choices.label: E
choices.text: presents only two possible explanations for high household incomes without considering any others

explanations.correct: The economist observes that high small-business formation rates and high median household incomes co-occur across cities, then concludes that encouraging small-business formation raises incomes. This move treats the correlation as proof of causation — a classic structural flaw. The direction of causation could be reversed (wealthier cities attract more entrepreneurs), or a third factor could explain both.
explanations.A: This is the unrepresentative-sample trap. While the sample of twelve cities is small, the argument's central error is not about sample size — it is about inferring a causal relationship from a correlation. This choice targets a peripheral weakness, not the main structural fault.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument moves directly from a correlation (cities with more small businesses also have higher incomes) to a causal policy recommendation (encourage small-business formation to raise incomes) without ruling out reverse causation or confounding factors.
explanations.C: This is the 'accurate but harmless' trap. Measurement details are unspecified, but vagueness about methodology does not constitute the central structural flaw; the argument fails because correlation is taken as causation, not because of definitional imprecision.
explanations.D: This misdescribes the argument. The economist never treats low income as sufficient grounds for any action; the conclusion is simply that the strategy is effective. This choice imposes a necessary/sufficient confusion that does not reflect the actual reasoning.
explanations.E: This is the false-dichotomy trap. The economist does not present two and only two explanations for high incomes; the argument does not engage in an either/or framing at all. This flaw type is absent from the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: Classic correlation-causation flaw with two plausible trap answers. Students must distinguish between 'ignores a third factor' and 'reverses cause and effect,' both of which are live distractors.
lr.stimulus: A hospital administrator noticed that patients who are visited frequently by family members tend to recover from surgery more quickly than those who receive few visits. The administrator concluded that family visits must speed up the surgical recovery process and recommended that the hospital expand visiting hours accordingly.
lr.questionStem: The administrator's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about all surgical patients based on the experience of only a small number of them

choices.label: B
choices.text: mistakes a correlation between two factors for a causal relationship between them

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider whether expanding visiting hours would be financially feasible for the hospital

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes that whatever benefits some patients must benefit all patients equally

choices.label: E
choices.text: takes for granted that the speed of recovery is the most important measure of surgical success

explanations.correct: The administrator observes that frequent visits and faster recovery co-occur and immediately infers that the visits cause the recovery. But the correlation could reflect a third factor — e.g., patients in better overall health both recover faster and attract more visitors — or could even run the other way. Inferring causation from correlation alone is the central structural flaw.
explanations.A: Nothing in the stimulus indicates the sample was small; the administrator's observation is presented as a general pattern. This is a plausible-but-absent flaw.
explanations.B: Correct. The stimulus moves directly from 'tend to co-occur' to 'must speed up,' which is an unwarranted causal inference from a correlation.
explanations.C: Financial feasibility concerns the recommendation's practicality, not the logical validity of the causal reasoning. This is an accurate-but-harmless observation.
explanations.D: The argument doesn't claim uniform benefit; it makes a general causal claim. This misdescribes the argument's structure.
explanations.E: Speed of recovery is the metric observed, but the argument doesn't assert it is the most important metric. This is a peripheral observation, not the structural flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: False dichotomy with a tempting trap answer that correctly identifies the flaw type but misdescribes its location in the argument. Students must verify which dichotomy the stimulus actually presents.
lr.stimulus: City Councilor: Our city's budget shortfall can be addressed in only one of two ways: we either raise property taxes or we lay off municipal employees. Since laying off employees would devastate essential services, it is clear that we must raise property taxes.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the councilor's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes for granted that raising property taxes will actually eliminate the budget shortfall

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that only two solutions to the budget shortfall are available

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider that laying off some employees might not devastate essential services

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about fiscal policy based on emotional considerations rather than economic analysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: takes for granted that property tax increases and employee layoffs are mutually exclusive responses

explanations.correct: The councilor asserts there are exactly two options without justifying why other approaches — spending cuts, new revenue streams, federal grants, debt restructuring — are unavailable. Presenting an artificially narrow set of options without defending their exhaustiveness is a false dichotomy.
explanations.A: Whether taxes will fully close the shortfall is a separate concern; the argument's flaw is in the prior step of restricting the options. This is accurate but peripheral.
explanations.B: Correct. The councilor states the choice is between only two options without ruling out alternatives, which is the defining false-dichotomy move.
explanations.C: Even partial layoffs might be harmful; but this addresses the severity of one horn, not the false restriction of the dilemma to two horns.
explanations.D: Nothing in the stimulus signals that the councilor is appealing to emotion rather than reasoning; 'devastate essential services' is presented as a factual consequence. This misdescribes the argument.
explanations.E: The argument doesn't assume they're mutually exclusive — it frames them as the only options. The issue is exhaustiveness, not exclusivity, mirroring the trap from the mayor anchor.

lr.difficultyReason: Necessary/sufficient confusion in an economics context. One trap answer describes the flaw in the reverse direction; another plausibly describes a different but related logical error.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Every thriving national economy has a stable currency. Clearly, then, if a country stabilizes its currency, its economy will thrive.
lr.questionStem: The economist's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on a sample of national economies that may not be representative of all economies

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a condition that is sufficient for economic prosperity as though it were merely necessary for it

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a condition that is necessary for economic prosperity as though it were sufficient for it

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to define what it means for an economy to be described as thriving

choices.label: E
choices.text: draws a conclusion about future economic conditions from evidence about past economic conditions

explanations.correct: The premise establishes that a stable currency is present in every thriving economy — making it a necessary condition (thriving → stable currency). The economist then concludes that having a stable currency guarantees a thriving economy, treating the necessary condition as if it were sufficient (stable currency → thriving). This is the classic necessary/sufficient confusion.
explanations.A: The stimulus presents a universal generalization ('every thriving economy'), not a sample-based inference. No sampling is involved.
explanations.B: This describes the flaw in reverse: the argument actually treats a necessary condition as sufficient, not a sufficient condition as necessary.
explanations.C: Correct. Stable currency is necessary (all thriving economies have it) but the economist concludes it is sufficient (having it produces thriving), which is unwarranted.
explanations.D: While 'thriving' could be vague, this is a peripheral concern and does not identify the structural logical error the argument commits.
explanations.E: The argument doesn't make a temporal claim about future versus past; it makes a conditional logical claim. This misdescribes the argument's structure.

lr.difficultyReason: Ad hominem flaw clearly present but paired with a tempting trap that describes a real weakness (unsupported premise about credibility) rather than the structural error.
lr.stimulus: Nutritionist: The senator's proposal to mandate nutrition labels on restaurant menus deserves no serious consideration. After all, the senator has accepted significant campaign contributions from the fast-food industry and therefore has a clear financial conflict of interest.
lr.questionStem: The nutritionist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: attacks the senator's character rather than addressing the merits of the proposal itself

choices.label: B
choices.text: assumes without justification that campaign contributions always influence a legislator's policy positions

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider that mandatory nutrition labeling might impose costs on restaurant owners

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a general conclusion about nutrition policy from a single case

choices.label: E
choices.text: presupposes that the nutritionist's own position is free of bias

explanations.correct: The nutritionist dismisses the proposal not by showing it is bad policy, but by pointing to the senator's financial ties. Whatever the senator's motives, the proposal's merits stand independently of who proposed it. This is an ad hominem (circumstantial) flaw.
explanations.A: Correct. The argument targets the senator's circumstances rather than engaging with whether mandatory nutrition labeling is a good or bad policy idea.
explanations.B: This identifies an unsupported premise in the argument (the link from contributions to influence), but the more fundamental structural flaw is that even if the senator is biased, the proposal could still be sound. B is a peripheral weakness, not the central error.
explanations.C: Restaurant costs are a separate policy consideration the argument never engages; this is accurate-but-harmless and doesn't identify the logical flaw.
explanations.D: No generalization across cases is made; the argument focuses on a single proposal. This misdescribes the argument.
explanations.E: The nutritionist's own bias is not raised in the stimulus; this imports an external consideration irrelevant to the stated reasoning.

lr.difficultyReason: Overgeneralization from a potentially unrepresentative sample. The trap answers include a plausible correlation-causation error and an accurate-but-harmless criticism about methodology.
lr.stimulus: A technology journalist surveyed software engineers at three large Silicon Valley firms and found that the majority preferred working remotely full-time. The journalist concluded that most software engineers in the country prefer remote work.
lr.questionStem: The journalist's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: mistakes a preference for remote work for a demonstrated ability to be productive while working remotely

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws a broad conclusion about software engineers generally from a sample that may not be representative of all software engineers

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider whether engineers at these firms were given a genuine choice about their work arrangements

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats the majority preference within each firm as equivalent to a majority preference across all firms

choices.label: E
choices.text: takes for granted that the conditions that apply in Silicon Valley apply equally in all technology sectors

explanations.correct: The journalist surveys engineers at three large Silicon Valley firms — a geographically concentrated, industry-specific sample — and generalizes to all software engineers nationwide. Engineers at smaller firms, in different regions, or in non-tech-hub cities may have very different preferences. Drawing a broad conclusion from this restricted sample is the flaw.
explanations.A: The argument is about preferences, not productivity. Introducing productivity confuses the conclusion's content. This is a plausible-but-absent flaw.
explanations.B: Correct. Three large Silicon Valley firms are not representative of the full population of software engineers across the country, making the generalization unwarranted.
explanations.C: Whether the choice was genuine is a concern about the survey's internal validity, but the primary structural flaw is the unrepresentative sample, not the quality of the choice offered.
explanations.D: The argument draws a national conclusion, not a cross-firm aggregation error specifically. This misdescribes the precise move the journalist makes.
explanations.E: This is a reformulation of the unrepresentativeness concern but is narrower and less precisely captures the flaw than B, which covers geographic and firm-size dimensions together.

lr.difficultyReason: Circular reasoning (question-begging) in an ethics context. The trap answer describes a real concern about the argument's premise but mistakes it for a different flaw type.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Euthanasia must be morally wrong because deliberately ending a person's life is always an immoral act. And we know that deliberately ending a person's life is always immoral because euthanasia — which is a form of deliberately ending a life — is morally wrong.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning above is questionable because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on a definition of euthanasia that is disputed by those who support the practice

choices.label: B
choices.text: uses the conclusion it is trying to establish as part of the support for that very conclusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider cases in which ending a life might prevent greater suffering

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a universal conclusion from a limited number of cases involving deliberate harm

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a moral intuition as though it were an established philosophical principle

explanations.correct: The ethicist argues that euthanasia is wrong because deliberately ending life is immoral, and then supports the claim that deliberately ending life is immoral by pointing to euthanasia being wrong. Each claim depends on the other, making the reasoning circular — the conclusion is embedded in the premises.
explanations.A: Whether euthanasia is contested is not relevant to the logical structure of the argument; the flaw is in how the premises relate to the conclusion, not in how the term is defined.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument is classically circular: euthanasia is wrong (conclusion) ← deliberately ending life is immoral (premise) ← euthanasia is wrong (conclusion reused as support).
explanations.C: This introduces a consequentialist consideration absent from the stimulus. While relevant to the broader debate, it does not identify the structural logical error in the argument as presented.
explanations.D: The argument doesn't enumerate cases; it makes a categorical claim. No sample-based inference occurs here.
explanations.E: Nothing in the stimulus suggests the claim is merely an intuition versus a principle; this description does not capture the circular structure.

lr.difficultyReason: Scope shift / equivocation on a key term ('significant') in a law context. One trap describes a real but peripheral weakness; another reverses the direction of the logical error.
lr.stimulus: Legal scholar: Any law that has a significant impact on commerce is subject to congressional oversight. The proposed environmental regulation would require companies to disclose their carbon emissions quarterly, which would certainly affect how companies allocate their reporting resources. Therefore, this regulation is subject to congressional oversight.
lr.questionStem: The legal scholar's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a condition sufficient to trigger congressional oversight as though it were the only such condition

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to consider that congressional oversight may itself be subject to legal challenge

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes without justification that affecting how companies allocate reporting resources constitutes a significant impact on commerce

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a specific regulation without examining the full text of the relevant statute

choices.label: E
choices.text: takes for granted that all environmental regulations have a significant impact on commerce

explanations.correct: The general rule requires a 'significant impact on commerce.' The scholar then points to an impact on 'reporting resources' — an administrative burden — and treats that as equivalent to a significant commercial impact without any justification for the equivalence. This is a scope shift: the term 'significant impact on commerce' in the premise is quietly replaced with a narrower, weaker effect in the application.
explanations.A: The argument doesn't claim that commercial impact is the only trigger for oversight; it simply applies that one trigger. This misdescribes the argument.
explanations.B: Whether oversight itself is legally challengeable is entirely external to the argument's logical structure. This is accurate-but-harmless.
explanations.C: Correct. The scholar slides from 'significant impact on commerce' to 'affects reporting resource allocation' without establishing that these are equivalent, which is the central gap.
explanations.D: Consulting statutory text is a legal practice concern, not a logical flaw. This is peripheral and does not describe the structural error.
explanations.E: The argument concerns only this specific regulation; it makes no general claim about all environmental regulations.

lr.difficultyReason: Reversed causation flaw in an environmental science context. The trap answers include a correlation-causation variant and a false dichotomy, requiring the student to identify the specific direction of the causal error.
lr.stimulus: Environmental researcher: In regions where the population of large predators has declined sharply, we observe significant increases in soil erosion. This demonstrates that the loss of large predators is causing the soil erosion in these regions.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it fails to consider the possibility that

choices.label: A
choices.text: soil erosion and predator population decline may both be caused by a third factor, such as habitat destruction

choices.label: B
choices.text: large predators may play no meaningful role in regulating the plant species that prevent erosion

choices.label: C
choices.text: the regions studied may not be representative of all regions experiencing predator decline

choices.label: D
choices.text: soil erosion rates may be influenced by seasonal weather patterns unrelated to predator populations

choices.label: E
choices.text: preventing soil erosion may require restoring predator populations to levels higher than those that previously existed

explanations.correct: The researcher observes that predator decline and soil erosion co-occur and concludes that one causes the other. But a third variable — such as large-scale habitat destruction — could independently reduce predator populations and destabilize the plant cover that prevents erosion. The researcher fails to rule out this common-cause explanation, making the causal inference unwarranted.
explanations.A: Correct. The existence of a common cause (habitat destruction, deforestation, drought) would explain the correlation without any direct causal link between predator decline and erosion.
explanations.B: This would challenge whether the proposed mechanism is plausible, but the flaw identified in the question stem is that the argument ignores alternative explanations for the observed correlation — not that the mechanism is biologically implausible.
explanations.C: Sample representativeness is a separate concern about generalizability, not about whether the causal inference from the observed data is valid.
explanations.D: Weather patterns could affect erosion rates, but this is a competing causal factor for erosion alone, not a common cause of both observed phenomena. It is a weaker version of the relevant flaw.
explanations.E: What level of predator restoration would be needed is a policy concern entirely outside the logical scope of the causal argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Division fallacy (what is true of the whole treated as true of each part) in a linguistics/history context. The trap answers include an overgeneralization and a false dichotomy, both plausible on quick reading.
lr.stimulus: Historian: The Roman Empire was extraordinarily successful at assimilating foreign cultures, incorporating diverse languages, religions, and customs into a cohesive imperial identity. Therefore, each Roman provincial administrator must have been skilled at managing cultural diversity.
lr.questionStem: The historian's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about an institution's policy from evidence about the attitudes of its individual members

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a characteristic true of a collective entity as necessarily true of each member of that entity

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider that Roman assimilation may have involved coercion rather than voluntary cultural exchange

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes that success in one domain of governance guarantees success in all domains

choices.label: E
choices.text: bases a historical conclusion on sources that may reflect imperial propaganda rather than objective fact

explanations.correct: The argument attributes a quality of the Roman Empire as a whole — skill at cultural assimilation — to each individual administrator within it. But a collective can achieve something through structural, systemic, or aggregate factors even when many individual members lack that quality. This is the division fallacy.
explanations.A: This describes the reverse of the actual move: the argument goes from collective to individual, not from individuals to institutional policy.
explanations.B: Correct. The historian infers from Rome's collective success at assimilation that each individual administrator must have been skilled — treating the group's property as necessarily a property of every member.
explanations.C: Whether assimilation was coercive is relevant to the empire's character but does not identify the structural logical flaw in the inference from collective to individual.
explanations.D: The argument stays within the domain of cultural management; it does not generalize across different domains of governance.
explanations.E: Source reliability is a historical methodology concern, not the logical flaw in the inference pattern itself.

lr.difficultyReason: Equivocation on a key term ('original') in an arts/aesthetics context. Trap answers include a scope-shift description that almost fits and a plausible-but-absent ad hominem.
lr.stimulus: Art critic: The works displayed in this gallery are truly original — no other artist has produced anything quite like them. And since original works are always more valuable than derivative ones, these works are clearly more valuable than anything else being sold at the art fair.
lr.questionStem: The art critic's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: uses the term 'original' in two different senses: first to mean stylistically unique and then to mean aesthetically superior in market value

choices.label: B
choices.text: assumes without evidence that the works displayed are the only original works at the art fair

choices.label: C
choices.text: takes for granted that aesthetic value and market value are equivalent measures of worth

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to consider that some derivative works may have sold for higher prices than original works in the past

choices.label: E
choices.text: bases its valuation on the critic's personal taste rather than on objective artistic standards

explanations.correct: The critic establishes that these works are original (no other artist has produced anything like them) and that original works are more valuable than derivative ones. But the conclusion — that these works are more valuable than anything else at the art fair — requires that nothing else at the art fair is original. The critic never establishes this, taking for granted that these are the only original works present.
explanations.A: The word 'original' is used consistently to mean 'stylistically unlike others' in both uses; the critic does not shift to a different meaning. This is the most tempting trap: it correctly identifies equivocation as a flaw type but mislocates it in this argument.
explanations.B: Correct. The general principle that original works beat derivative ones only lets the critic conclude these works are better than derivative works — not better than everything at the fair, unless everything else is derivative. That assumption is never supported.
explanations.C: The argument operates within a single domain of 'value' without conflating aesthetic and market value; this introduces a distinction absent from the stimulus.
explanations.D: Historical counterexamples would undermine the general premise, but the flaw identified here is in the argument's logical structure given its premises, not in whether those premises are empirically accurate.
explanations.E: Nothing in the stimulus indicates the critic's judgment is based on personal taste rather than on the stated criterion of originality. This is a plausible-but-absent ad hominem.

lr.difficultyReason: Classic correlation-causation flaw with two plausible trap answers. Students must verify the stimulus commits the causal inference rather than a sampling or scope error.
lr.stimulus: A study of urban neighborhoods found that areas with a higher density of coffee shops also had lower rates of violent crime. The city council should therefore encourage the opening of new coffee shops throughout the city, since coffee shops clearly reduce violent crime.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about all neighborhoods based on a sample drawn only from urban areas

choices.label: B
choices.text: mistakes a correlation between two phenomena for evidence that one phenomenon causes the other

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes without warrant that the city council has the authority to regulate business openings

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to consider whether the density of coffee shops varies by time of day

choices.label: E
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that reducing violent crime might itself cause neighborhoods to attract more coffee shops

explanations.correct: The argument observes a correlation — coffee shop density and lower crime rates co-occur — and infers that the coffee shops cause the lower crime. That is a textbook correlation-causation error; the evidence supports association, not causation.
explanations.A: The study is explicitly of urban neighborhoods, and the conclusion targets city neighborhoods, so the scope is consistent. No unrepresentative sample flaw is committed here.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument takes co-occurrence as proof of a causal direction, which is unwarranted by the correlational data alone.
explanations.C: The city council's authority is not at issue in the argument; this concern is extraneous to the reasoning.
explanations.D: Time-of-day variation is a peripheral detail that would not undermine the core logical structure even if addressed.
explanations.E: This is a tempting trap — reversed causation is a real flaw — but the argument doesn't address direction at all; it simply infers causation from correlation. (E) correctly names reversed causation but mis-locates it as the primary error. The structural fault is treating correlation as causation in the first place.

lr.difficultyReason: Necessary/sufficient swap with a plausible 'right flaw, reversed' trap. Students must distinguish which direction the swap runs.
lr.stimulus: To be admitted to the bar, a candidate must pass the bar examination. Marcus passed the bar examination last month. It follows that Marcus has been admitted to the bar.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a condition sufficient for bar admission as though it were merely necessary for it

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to establish that passing the bar examination is a reliable indicator of legal competence

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a condition necessary for bar admission as though it were sufficient for it

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about an individual from a general rule that applies only to groups

choices.label: E
choices.text: presumes without justification that the bar examination is the only requirement for practicing law

explanations.correct: Passing the bar exam is stated as a necessary condition for admission (you must pass to be admitted), but the argument concludes that because Marcus passed, he has been admitted. That treats the necessary condition as if it were sufficient — the classic necessary/sufficient swap.
explanations.A: This describes the opposite error: treating a sufficient condition as merely necessary. The bar exam is a necessary, not sufficient, condition, so this reverses the flaw.
explanations.B: Whether the exam measures competence is irrelevant to the logical structure of the argument about admission.
explanations.C: Correct. Passing is required for admission but does not by itself guarantee it; the argument assumes it does.
explanations.D: The rule applies to all individual candidates; no group-versus-individual confusion is present.
explanations.E: This is close to the correct flaw but frames it as an unstated assumption about law practice rather than identifying the logical error in the conditional reasoning.

lr.difficultyReason: Ad hominem / circumstantial flaw with one trap that correctly names the flaw category but misapplies it, and one that describes a real but minor weakness.
lr.stimulus: Dr. Pelham argues that the proposed pharmaceutical merger will harm consumer access to affordable medications. But Dr. Pelham is a paid consultant for one of the competitor firms that would benefit from blocking the merger. We should therefore disregard her analysis of the merger's effects.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning above is questionable because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: assumes that the pharmaceutical merger would necessarily reduce competition in the market

choices.label: B
choices.text: dismisses a claim by questioning the motives of the person making it rather than addressing the substance of the claim

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider whether the competitor firm that employs Dr. Pelham also opposes the merger

choices.label: D
choices.text: confuses a conflict of interest with proof that the claim in question is false

choices.label: E
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the merger's effects without consulting an independent economic analysis

explanations.correct: The argument attacks Dr. Pelham's financial interest rather than engaging with her analysis of the merger's effects. This is the circumstantial ad hominem flaw: impugning the person's motives as a basis for rejecting their argument.
explanations.A: The argument does not assume anything about the merger itself; it only dismisses Dr. Pelham's testimony. This flaw is absent from the stimulus.
explanations.B: Correct. Regardless of Dr. Pelham's financial ties, those ties do not show her analysis is wrong. The argument should address the evidence she presents.
explanations.C: Whether her employer also opposes the merger is a peripheral factual detail irrelevant to the logical flaw in dismissing her testimony.
explanations.D: This is a tempting trap — it correctly identifies that the conflict of interest is misused — but it frames the error as a confusion rather than the structural ad hominem move. (B) more precisely names the reasoning error as described in LSAT flaw vocabulary.
explanations.E: Calling for an independent analysis describes a remedy, not the flaw in the existing reasoning.

lr.difficultyReason: False dichotomy with a scope-shift trap. Students must see that the argument ignores intermediate options rather than making a statistical error.
lr.stimulus: Our city's public schools are failing students academically. The school board must choose between completely overhauling the current curriculum and abandoning public education altogether in favor of a voucher-based private school system. Since a complete curriculum overhaul would be prohibitively expensive, the school board should adopt the voucher system.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes for granted that academic failure in public schools is caused primarily by inadequate curriculum

choices.label: B
choices.text: presents only two options without justifying the claim that no other options exist

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes that what is true of the school board's budget is true of all individual schools

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to consider whether private schools would produce better academic outcomes than public schools

choices.label: E
choices.text: mistakes the expensiveness of one option for evidence that the other option is inexpensive

explanations.correct: The argument restricts the choice to two options — full overhaul or a voucher system — without showing these are the only possibilities. Targeted reforms, increased funding, teacher training programs, or hybrid models are all alternatives the argument ignores.
explanations.A: The argument mentions curriculum failure but does not explicitly attribute it to curriculum alone as a cause. More importantly, this is a peripheral premise issue rather than the central structural flaw.
explanations.B: Correct. This is a false-dichotomy flaw: the argument manufactures an exclusive binary choice without justification.
explanations.C: No part of the argument moves from the school board's budget to individual school budgets; this composition/division flaw is not present.
explanations.D: Whether private schools perform better is relevant but its absence is a weakness in supporting the conclusion, not the structural flaw in the reasoning that restricts options.
explanations.E: The argument never implies the voucher system is inexpensive; this mis-describes what the argument does.

lr.difficultyReason: Overgeneralization from unrepresentative sample with a plausible correlation-causation trap that students must rule out.
lr.stimulus: A technology company surveyed 200 of its own software engineers and found that 85 percent preferred working remotely to working in the office. The company's CEO concluded that the majority of workers in the technology sector as a whole prefer remote work.
lr.questionStem: The CEO's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: mistakes the employees' expressed preferences for evidence of what working arrangement produces the highest productivity

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws a general conclusion about an entire sector based on a sample that may not be representative of that sector

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes that remote work preferences remain stable over time

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats the absence of evidence that workers prefer office work as evidence that workers prefer remote work

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider whether the survey methodology adequately measured worker preferences

explanations.correct: The survey sampled only engineers at one company — a subset that may differ systematically from the broader technology sector, which includes workers in hardware, manufacturing, sales, and support roles. Generalizing from this narrow group to the whole sector commits the unrepresentative-sample flaw.
explanations.A: The argument is about preferences, not productivity; this describes a scope shift that the argument does not make.
explanations.B: Correct. The sample is drawn from a single company's software engineers, which may not represent the diversity of roles and workers across the entire technology sector.
explanations.C: Temporal stability of preferences is a minor background assumption not central to the structural flaw in the generalization.
explanations.D: The argument does not argue from an absence of evidence; it draws a positive conclusion from positive survey data.
explanations.E: Survey methodology concerns are peripheral; the flaw is not in how preferences were measured but in the scope of the generalization from the measured group.

lr.difficultyReason: Equivocation flaw on a key term used in two senses. Students must track the semantic shift rather than being drawn to a false-dichotomy or correlation trap.
lr.stimulus: Historian: The law must be blind. Any system of justice that is not blind inevitably favors the powerful over the powerless. Our current legal system, however, is clearly not blind — judges regularly distinguish between categories of defendants based on their circumstances. Therefore, our legal system inevitably favors the powerful over the powerless.
lr.questionStem: The historian's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: presents a conclusion about the entire legal system based on the behavior of some judges

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on an ambiguous term that is used in different senses in the premise and the conclusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes without evidence that powerful defendants are treated more favorably than powerless defendants

choices.label: D
choices.text: mistakes a feature of legal systems in general for a feature of the current legal system in particular

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider whether a legal system that distinguishes among defendants could still treat them fairly

explanations.correct: 'Blind' in the premise 'the law must be blind' means impartial or unbiased — not favoring the powerful. But the argument then takes 'not blind' to mean 'makes distinctions among defendants,' which is a different sense. The equivocation on 'blind' drives the invalid inference.
explanations.A: The argument generalizes from judges' behavior to the system, but this is not the primary structural flaw — the equivocation on 'blind' is what makes the reasoning invalid.
explanations.B: Correct. 'Blind' shifts from meaning 'impartial' (normative sense) to 'makes no distinctions' (descriptive sense). The two senses are conflated, making the inference invalid.
explanations.C: The argument infers that the system favors the powerful; it doesn't assume this without evidence — it derives it via the flawed equivocation. This choice misdescribes the structure.
explanations.D: The argument does not move from general to particular; it moves from a general principle to a conclusion about the current system. The flaw is equivocation, not a scope shift of this kind.
explanations.E: This correctly identifies a gap in the argument but describes a missing consideration rather than the logical flaw — the equivocation — that makes the inference invalid.

lr.difficultyReason: Circular reasoning flaw with a well-disguised trap that names an absent flaw (false dichotomy) and one that is plausible but describes a peripheral weakness.
lr.stimulus: Nutritionist: Organic produce is healthier than conventionally grown produce because food grown without synthetic pesticides is better for human consumption. And food grown without synthetic pesticides is better for human consumption because organic produce — which avoids synthetic pesticides — is inherently healthier.
lr.questionStem: The nutritionist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: assumes without justification that synthetic pesticides are the only difference between organic and conventional produce

choices.label: B
choices.text: bases its conclusion on a study that may not represent all types of produce

choices.label: C
choices.text: supports its conclusion by simply restating the conclusion in different words

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats a characteristic of some organic produce as a characteristic of all organic produce

choices.label: E
choices.text: presents only two options — organic or conventional — without considering intermediate alternatives

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'organic is healthier' to 'food without synthetic pesticides is better' and then back to 'organic is healthier because it avoids synthetic pesticides.' Both the premise and the conclusion express the same claim in rephrased terms; the argument is circular.
explanations.A: This concern about other differentiating factors would be relevant to a causal argument, but here the problem is circularity, not an omitted variable.
explanations.B: No study is cited in the argument; this choice fabricates a premise that isn't present.
explanations.C: Correct. The nutritionist's reasoning traces a loop: organic is healthier → avoiding pesticides is better → organic is healthier. This is textbook circular reasoning.
explanations.D: The argument makes no distinction between some and all organic produce; it speaks universally, so no composition error is committed.
explanations.E: The argument does not set up a dichotomous choice between organic and conventional — it simply asserts the superiority of organic. No false dichotomy is present.

lr.difficultyReason: Scope shift / composition flaw with a tempting correlation-causation trap. Students must notice the argument moves from individual to group level.
lr.stimulus: Each individual species in a coral reef ecosystem is highly adaptable to changing ocean temperatures. It follows that a coral reef ecosystem, considered as a whole, is highly adaptable to changing ocean temperatures.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: mistakes the fact that ocean temperatures are changing for evidence that coral reef ecosystems will not survive

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to consider whether the rate of temperature change affects the adaptability of individual species

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats what is true of each part of a whole as necessarily true of the whole itself

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about ocean ecosystems in general based on evidence drawn only from coral reefs

choices.label: E
choices.text: presumes without justification that adaptability to temperature change is the most important feature of an ecosystem

explanations.correct: Even if every individual species can adapt, the ecosystem as a whole might not be adaptable — species interact in complex webs; losing even one species can cascade and destabilize the whole system. The argument commits the composition fallacy: attributing a property of each part to the whole.
explanations.A: The argument never mentions whether reefs will survive; this introduces a conclusion the argument does not draw.
explanations.B: The rate of change is a peripheral consideration and its absence does not constitute the structural flaw in the reasoning.
explanations.C: Correct. This precisely names the composition fallacy: inferring a property of the whole from properties of its individual parts.
explanations.D: The argument does not generalize to all ocean ecosystems; it reasons only about the coral reef. No overgeneralization across ecosystems is committed.
explanations.E: Adaptability's relative importance is irrelevant to the logical move from parts to whole that constitutes the flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: Appeal to inappropriate authority / ignores counter-evidence flaw with a trap that correctly names ad hominem but misapplies it, and one that describes the conclusion rather than the reasoning error.
lr.stimulus: Art critic: The painting currently attributed to Vermeer cannot be authentic. Professor Holt, the world's foremost expert on seventeenth-century Dutch painting, has declared it a forgery. No one is more qualified than Holt to make such a determination, so the painting is definitively a forgery.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: attacks the credibility of those who believe the painting is authentic rather than addressing their reasons

choices.label: B
choices.text: concludes that the painting is a forgery without examining the painting itself

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats an expert's opinion as conclusive proof while failing to consider that even qualified experts can be mistaken

choices.label: D
choices.text: confuses the question of who is most qualified to assess a painting with the question of whether that assessment is correct

choices.label: E
choices.text: draws a conclusion about this painting based on characteristics of seventeenth-century Dutch paintings in general

explanations.correct: Being the most qualified expert does not make one's judgment infallible. The argument treats Holt's opinion as definitively settling the matter, ignoring the possibility that even the most qualified expert can err, especially in contested authentication cases.
explanations.A: The argument does not attack anyone who disagrees with Holt; it simply accepts his opinion. No ad hominem move is made.
explanations.B: The argument does not specify whether the critic examined the painting; this introduces a factual claim not supported or denied by the stimulus.
explanations.C: Correct. The argument moves from 'most qualified' to 'definitively correct,' which is unwarranted — expertise reduces error but does not eliminate it.
explanations.D: This is a tempting paraphrase of the flaw, but it misframes the error as a confusion about questions rather than identifying the unwarranted inference from expertise to certainty. (C) is more precisely correct.
explanations.E: The argument makes no claim about seventeenth-century Dutch paintings in general; it focuses exclusively on this painting's attribution.

lr.difficultyReason: Absence-of-evidence flaw with a plausible scope-shift trap. Students must recognize the argument treats a lack of findings as positive evidence of absence.
lr.stimulus: Archaeologist: No written records from the Harappan civilization have been successfully deciphered. This strongly suggests that the Harappan people did not use writing as a tool for administrative governance — if they had used writing for governance, we would certainly have found decipherable records of it by now.
lr.questionStem: The archaeologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about ancient administrative practices based on evidence drawn only from the Harappan civilization

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that the absence of deciphered records proves the absence of written governance, without ruling out that such records exist but remain undeciphered

choices.label: C
choices.text: mistakes a feature of some ancient civilizations for a feature of all ancient civilizations

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to provide an alternative explanation for how the Harappans administered their civilization

choices.label: E
choices.text: assumes that written governance is necessary for a civilization to achieve a high level of administrative complexity

explanations.correct: The archaeologist infers from 'no deciphered records' to 'no written governance.' But absence of decipherment is not absence of records — Harappan script remains undeciphered, meaning governance records could exist but simply not yet be understood. The argument treats failure to decode as evidence of nonexistence.
explanations.A: The argument draws no comparison to other civilizations; it makes no generalization beyond the Harappan case. No overgeneralization is present.
explanations.B: Correct. The flaw is treating the inability to decipher existing records as equivalent to the nonexistence of such records — a version of the absence-of-evidence fallacy.
explanations.C: The argument makes no claim about other civilizations; this flaw is not committed.
explanations.D: The archaeologist need not provide an alternative governance model; failing to do so is not a logical flaw in the negative conclusion being drawn.
explanations.E: The argument does not claim written governance is necessary for administrative complexity; it only claims the Harappans probably didn't use writing for governance. This flaw is not present in the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: Correlation-causation flaw in a medical context. One clear trap describes a related but absent flaw (unrepresentative sample); another reverses the causal direction plausibly.
lr.stimulus: A recent hospital study found that patients who received daily visits from family members recovered from surgery faster than patients who received no visits. The hospital administrator concluded that family visitation directly causes faster surgical recovery and recommended that the hospital revise its visitation policies to encourage more frequent family contact.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the administrator's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about all surgical patients based solely on a study conducted at one hospital

choices.label: B
choices.text: mistakes a correlation between two factors for a causal relationship between them

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes without justification that changing visitation policy will be embraced by hospital staff

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to consider that faster recovery might be caused by the same underlying factor that leads families to visit more

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a condition sufficient for faster recovery as though it were merely necessary for it

explanations.correct: The administrator observes that visitation and faster recovery co-occur and concludes that visitation causes recovery. This is the correlation-causation flaw: the data show an association, not a directional causal mechanism.
explanations.A: The stimulus does not restrict itself to one hospital in a way the argument exploits; the administrator's error is inferring causation, not generalizing from a small sample. This is a 'plausible but absent' trap.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument moves from 'patients who were visited recovered faster' (correlation) to 'visitation causes faster recovery' (causation) without ruling out confounds.
explanations.C: Staff acceptance is entirely outside the argument's scope; the administrator has not even addressed implementation. This is an 'accurate but harmless' trap.
explanations.D: This describes a specific version of the confound—a common cause—which is a subset of the correlation-causation flaw, not the structural label for the central error. Answer B names the flaw at the right level of abstraction.
explanations.E: The argument makes no claim about necessary or sufficient conditions; it simply infers causation from correlation. This is a 'wrong flaw type' trap.

lr.difficultyReason: False dichotomy in an economics/policy context. Two traps describe genuine weaknesses (unsupported premises) that are peripheral to the central structural error.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Our nation faces a choice between imposing strict carbon taxes and allowing our manufacturing sector to collapse under the weight of international competition. Since we cannot allow our manufacturing sector to collapse, we must impose strict carbon taxes.
lr.questionStem: The economist's argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: fails to establish that carbon taxes would be effective at reducing emissions

choices.label: B
choices.text: presents only two courses of action as available without justifying the exclusion of other options

choices.label: C
choices.text: takes for granted that the manufacturing sector's collapse would harm the broader economy

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws on economic data without acknowledging the limits of economic forecasting

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses a policy that is economically desirable with one that is politically feasible

explanations.correct: The economist frames the situation as a binary choice—carbon taxes or manufacturing collapse—without ruling out alternatives such as subsidies, regulatory reforms, or gradual transition policies. This is a false-dichotomy flaw.
explanations.A: Effectiveness of carbon taxes is a peripheral concern; the conclusion is that we must impose them, and the flaw is in how the options are framed, not in whether the chosen option works. This is a 'too charitable / peripheral weakness' trap.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument restricts the option space to two without justifying that no third path exists.
explanations.C: The harm from collapse is an assumed premise, but it is not the central structural flaw; the economist never claims to prove this. The false dichotomy is the primary error.
explanations.D: No economic data or forecasting methods are cited; this choice fabricates a feature of the argument. 'Plausible but absent' trap.
explanations.E: The argument never conflates desirability with feasibility; this flaw type is not committed here.

lr.difficultyReason: Necessary/sufficient confusion in a legal context. The trap choices include a reversed version of the flaw and a correlation-causation decoy.
lr.stimulus: Attorney: To be admissible as evidence, a document must be authenticated. This contract has been authenticated by two independent witnesses. Therefore, this contract is admissible as evidence.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning above is questionable because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a condition that is necessary for admissibility as though it were sufficient for admissibility

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a condition that is sufficient for admissibility as though it were necessary for admissibility

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes without support that the two witnesses authenticated the contract independently

choices.label: D
choices.text: mistakes a correlation between authentication and admissibility for a causal relationship

choices.label: E
choices.text: draws a conclusion about this specific contract from generalizations about contracts in general

explanations.correct: The attorney's premise is: to be admissible, a document must be authenticated (authentication is necessary). The conclusion treats authentication as sufficient—as though satisfying this one requirement guarantees admissibility. Other requirements (relevance, hearsay rules, etc.) may also apply.
explanations.A: Correct. Authentication is stated as a necessary condition ('must be authenticated'), but the attorney concludes it is sufficient ('has been authenticated, therefore admissible').
explanations.B: This is the reversed flaw: treating a sufficient condition as merely necessary. The stimulus does the opposite—necessary treated as sufficient. Classic 'right flaw, reversed' trap.
explanations.C: The independence of the witnesses is asserted by the stimulus; the argument does not need to prove it. This is a peripheral factual assumption, not the structural flaw.
explanations.D: The attorney makes no causal claim; admissibility is a legal standard, not a causal relationship. Wrong flaw type.
explanations.E: The attorney does apply a general rule to a specific case, but this is standard legal reasoning (applying a rule to facts), not a flaw. The structural error lies in the necessary/sufficient confusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Ad hominem / attacking the source in an environmental science context. One trap describes circular reasoning plausibly; another misidentifies the target of the attack.
lr.stimulus: Environmental advocate: We should disregard the consulting firm's report concluding that the proposed pipeline poses minimal ecological risk. The firm was hired and paid by the pipeline company itself, so the report's findings cannot be trusted.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: dismisses the report's conclusions solely on the basis of the source's potential bias rather than identifying errors in the report's reasoning or evidence

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that any study funded by an interested party must contain deliberate falsification

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a general conclusion about all environmental consulting firms from a single case

choices.label: D
choices.text: takes for granted that the pipeline company has a financial interest in a particular outcome

choices.label: E
choices.text: uses the conclusion that the report is untrustworthy as a premise in establishing the same conclusion

explanations.correct: The advocate dismisses the report entirely by pointing to who funded it, without engaging with the report's methodology, data, or reasoning. This is an ad hominem (or 'appeal to motive') flaw: the source's potential conflict of interest does not automatically invalidate the findings.
explanations.A: Correct. The advocate attacks the report's source rather than any flaw in the report itself.
explanations.B: The advocate says the report 'cannot be trusted,' which implies doubt, not necessarily deliberate falsification. This overstates what the argument actually claims—a 'misdescribes the argument' trap.
explanations.C: The argument is about one specific firm and one report; no generalization to all consulting firms is made. 'Plausible but absent' trap.
explanations.D: The pipeline company's financial interest in a favorable report is obvious and uncontroversial; the advocate does not need to argue for it. This describes a harmless premise, not the structural flaw.
explanations.E: The argument does not use the conclusion as a premise; it uses the funding relationship as a premise. This misidentifies circular reasoning where none exists.

lr.difficultyReason: Overgeneralization from unrepresentative sample in a technology context. Traps include a correlation-causation decoy and a scope-shift description that partially fits.
lr.stimulus: A technology journalist surveyed fifty software engineers at a single Silicon Valley startup and found that most preferred working remotely. The journalist concluded that software engineers in general strongly prefer remote work to working in an office.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the journalist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: mistakes a preference expressed by engineers for a claim about the objective quality of remote work

choices.label: B
choices.text: infers a causal connection between remote work availability and job satisfaction from a mere correlation

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a general conclusion about software engineers from a sample that may not be representative of that population

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to consider that some engineers' preference for remote work could change over time

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats the absence of evidence that engineers prefer office work as evidence that they do not prefer it

explanations.correct: The journalist's sample is fifty engineers at one startup in Silicon Valley—a narrow, geographically and culturally specific group. Drawing a conclusion about 'software engineers in general' from this sample commits an unrepresentative-sample flaw.
explanations.A: The journalist never moves from preference to objective quality; the conclusion is about preference throughout. 'Plausible but absent' trap.
explanations.B: No causal claim about job satisfaction is made; the argument is about preferences. Wrong flaw type.
explanations.C: Correct. The sample is drawn from one company in one location and may not reflect the preferences of software engineers broadly.
explanations.D: Changing preferences over time is a peripheral concern unrelated to the structural error of over-generalizing from a narrow sample. 'Too charitable / peripheral' trap.
explanations.E: The argument does not reason from absence of evidence; it reasons from positive survey data. This misidentifies the logical move being made.

lr.difficultyReason: Circular reasoning in an ethics context. Traps include an ad hominem decoy and a false dichotomy that doesn't fit.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Capital punishment is morally wrong because intentionally taking the life of any person is an immoral act, and capital punishment involves the intentional taking of a person's life.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: applies a general moral principle without establishing that the principle holds in cases where the state acts on behalf of society

choices.label: B
choices.text: takes for granted the very claim it is attempting to establish, since calling any killing 'immoral' presupposes capital punishment's wrongness

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider that some who oppose capital punishment do so on non-moral grounds

choices.label: D
choices.text: attacks those who support capital punishment rather than addressing the merits of their position

choices.label: E
choices.text: presents only two options—capital punishment or moral permissibility of all killing—without exploring intermediate positions

explanations.correct: The ethicist's key premise—'intentionally taking the life of any person is immoral'—is simply a restatement of the conclusion in more general terms. The argument assumes what it must prove: that capital punishment (a form of intentional killing) is immoral. This is circular reasoning.
explanations.A: The ethicist uses a general principle ('any person'), but the flaw is not in failing to address state action—it is in using a premise that presupposes the conclusion. This is a 'too charitable / peripheral' trap.
explanations.B: Correct. The premise that all intentional killing is immoral already contains the conclusion about capital punishment; the argument moves in a circle.
explanations.C: Non-moral grounds for opposing capital punishment are irrelevant to whether the ethicist's argument is structurally valid. 'Plausible but absent' trap.
explanations.D: No person is attacked in the stimulus; the argument is entirely about the act, not about proponents of capital punishment. Wrong flaw type.
explanations.E: The argument does not present a dichotomy between capital punishment and permissibility of all killing; this misreads the stimulus entirely.

lr.difficultyReason: Equivocation on a key term in a linguistics/policy context. The shift between two senses of 'language' is the flaw; traps include a scope-shift decoy and a false dichotomy description.
lr.stimulus: Language preservation advocate: Every language encodes a unique way of understanding the world. Therefore, when a government promotes a single official language, it destroys unique ways of understanding the world. We must oppose any government that promotes an official language.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the advocate's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: presumes without warrant that promoting an official language requires actively suppressing all other languages

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws a conclusion about what governments must not do from premises about what languages contain

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a condition that is sufficient to destroy linguistic diversity as though it were merely necessary

choices.label: D
choices.text: bases its conclusion on an appeal to the authority of linguistics researchers

choices.label: E
choices.text: presents only two options—promoting one official language or preserving all languages—ignoring multilingual official policies

explanations.correct: The advocate equivocates on 'promotes an official language.' Promoting one language (e.g., for government documents) does not necessarily destroy other languages—other languages can survive alongside an official one. The argument takes for granted that promotion equals suppression.
explanations.A: Correct. The leap from 'promotes an official language' to 'destroys unique ways of understanding the world' requires the hidden assumption that promotion entails suppression or elimination of other languages, which the argument does not justify.
explanations.B: Moving from descriptive premises about languages to normative conclusions about government conduct is a scope shift, but the more precise and central flaw is the unwarranted assumption that promotion equals destruction. B names a real weakness but at too abstract a level to capture the specific error.
explanations.C: No necessary/sufficient language appears in the stimulus; the argument does not discuss conditions in those terms. Wrong flaw type.
explanations.D: No authority is cited in the stimulus. 'Plausible but absent' trap.
explanations.E: The stimulus does not explicitly claim there are only two options; it moves from promotion to destruction without acknowledging a spectrum. The false-dichotomy label does not precisely capture the unwarranted assumption being made.

lr.difficultyReason: Scope shift from sample to population in a history context. Traps include a correlation-causation decoy and a necessary/sufficient description that sounds plausible.
lr.stimulus: Historian: The diaries and personal correspondence of nineteenth-century factory workers that have survived to the present day consistently describe dangerous working conditions and widespread dissatisfaction. We can therefore conclude that nineteenth-century factory workers were, in general, dissatisfied with their working conditions.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers that dangerous conditions caused dissatisfaction without ruling out other sources of worker discontent

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats evidence of dissatisfaction as sufficient to establish that working conditions were objectively dangerous

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a broad conclusion about nineteenth-century factory workers from records that may systematically exclude workers who were satisfied

choices.label: D
choices.text: mistakes a necessary condition for worker satisfaction for a sufficient condition

choices.label: E
choices.text: takes for granted that workers who kept diaries were representative of factory workers in terms of literacy and social class

explanations.correct: The historian relies on surviving diaries and correspondence—a sample that is likely skewed. Workers who were motivated to write (and whose writings survived) may disproportionately be those with grievances. Workers who were satisfied may have been less likely to write or less likely to have their writings preserved, making the sample unrepresentative.
explanations.A: The historian does not make a causal argument about what caused dissatisfaction; the conclusion is simply that dissatisfaction existed. Wrong flaw type.
explanations.B: The historian does not move from dissatisfaction to objective dangerousness; the conclusion is about dissatisfaction only. This inverts the direction of inference. 'Misdescribes the argument' trap.
explanations.C: Correct. The sample of surviving documents may systematically overrepresent dissatisfied workers, making the generalization to 'workers in general' unwarranted.
explanations.D: No necessary or sufficient condition language appears in the argument. Wrong flaw type.
explanations.E: While literacy and class are real concerns about the sample, choice C more precisely identifies the specific selection-bias problem: the sample excludes satisfied workers. E is a narrower version of the same worry but does not capture the full scope of the representativeness problem.

lr.difficultyReason: Reversed causation in an arts/economics context. The trap choices include a plausible false-dichotomy decoy and an unrepresentative-sample lure.
lr.stimulus: Arts administrator: Cities with thriving art museum attendance figures also tend to have strong local economies. Clearly, high museum attendance stimulates economic activity by drawing tourists, increasing spending, and elevating a city's cultural profile. Any city seeking economic growth should therefore invest heavily in its art museums.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the arts administrator's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about all cities from a sample that may not represent cities with different economic conditions

choices.label: B
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that a strong local economy is what enables high museum attendance rather than the reverse

choices.label: C
choices.text: presents only two options—investing in museums or accepting economic stagnation—without considering alternative growth strategies

choices.label: D
choices.text: takes for granted that tourists who visit museums spend money in ways that benefit local residents

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses the cultural value of art museums with their economic value

explanations.correct: The administrator observes a correlation between museum attendance and strong economies and infers that attendance causes economic strength. But the causal arrow may run in the opposite direction: wealthy cities can afford to invest in museums and residents have disposable income to attend them. This is the reversed-causation version of the correlation-causation flaw.
explanations.A: The administrator does not specify a sample of cities; the argument is about a general tendency. While sampling could be questioned, the central structural flaw is the causal inference. 'Plausible but absent' trap.
explanations.B: Correct. The administrator assumes the correlation runs causally from attendance to economic strength, overlooking that economic strength may cause high attendance.
explanations.C: The administrator's conclusion is a recommendation to invest in museums, but does not explicitly frame this as the only option. No clear either/or structure is presented. 'Plausible but absent' trap.
explanations.D: Tourist spending patterns are a peripheral empirical concern, not the structural flaw in the causal inference. 'Too charitable / peripheral' trap.
explanations.E: The argument is entirely about economic value; no conflation with cultural value occurs. 'Plausible but absent' trap.

lr.difficultyReason: Scope shift from individual to group (composition fallacy) in an environmental science context. Traps include a false dichotomy decoy and a necessary/sufficient description that sounds applicable.
lr.stimulus: Environmental consultant: Each of the individual farms in the Clearwater Valley uses only a small amount of pesticide—an amount that poses no measurable risk to local waterways. Therefore, the combined pesticide runoff from all the farms in Clearwater Valley poses no measurable risk to local waterways.
lr.questionStem: The consultant's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a level of pesticide use that is sufficient to avoid risk for one farm as necessary to avoid risk across all farms

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that local farmers are aware of the cumulative effects of their pesticide use

choices.label: C
choices.text: takes for granted that what is true of each part of a system is necessarily true of the system as a whole

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to consider that some farms in Clearwater Valley may use more pesticide than others

choices.label: E
choices.text: presents a choice between unrestricted pesticide use and complete elimination without acknowledging intermediate regulation

explanations.correct: The consultant infers that because each farm individually poses no risk, the collective runoff from all farms also poses no risk. This commits the composition fallacy: what is harmless in small individual amounts may be harmful when aggregated. The argument incorrectly transfers a property from parts to the whole.
explanations.A: The argument makes no claim about what is necessary or sufficient for risk avoidance across all farms; it simply transfers the individual property to the collective. Wrong flaw type.
explanations.B: Farmer awareness of cumulative effects is irrelevant to the logical structure of the consultant's inference. 'Plausible but absent' trap.
explanations.C: Correct. The consultant assumes that the harmlessness of each individual farm's pesticide use entails the harmlessness of all farms' combined runoff—a classic composition fallacy.
