explanations.D: Even if some farms use more than others, the core flaw is in reasoning from individual harmlessness to collective harmlessness. D identifies a peripheral empirical gap, not the central structural error.
explanations.E: No dichotomy between unrestricted use and complete elimination appears in the argument. 'Plausible but absent' trap.

lr.difficultyReason: A standard correlation-causation flaw with two plausible trap answers: one misdescribes the direction of the causal inference, and another names a real flaw type (unrepresentative sample) that is absent from this stimulus. Students must verify the actual move made.
lr.stimulus: A technology columnist recently reported that among the top-performing employees at a major software firm, nearly 80 percent use a standing desk. The columnist concluded that using a standing desk improves employee performance. Companies that want to boost productivity should therefore require all employees to switch to standing desks.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the columnist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about all employees from a study of only one company's workforce

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that a correlation between standing-desk use and high performance establishes that standing-desk use causes high performance

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider that standing desks may be harmful to the health of some employees

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats the absence of evidence that standing desks reduce performance as evidence that they improve it

choices.label: E
choices.text: mistakes a condition that is sufficient for high performance for one that is merely necessary for it

explanations.correct: The columnist observes that high performers tend to use standing desks and infers that using a standing desk causes improved performance. This is the classic correlation-causation flaw: the data show only an association, not a causal direction. High performers might choose standing desks for independent reasons, or a third factor could explain both.
explanations.A: This is a plausible unrepresentative-sample charge, but the stimulus does not draw a conclusion about all employees in general — it draws a causal conclusion about standing desks. The conclusion is causal, not a demographic generalization, so this misdescribes the actual error.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument infers a causal relationship (standing desks improve performance) from a correlational observation, without ruling out reverse causation or confounding variables.
explanations.C: This names a missing consideration, not a structural flaw in the reasoning. The argument could still be valid even if some employees experience discomfort; the core error is causal, not a failure to weigh side-effects.
explanations.D: The argument does not rely on an absence of evidence. It cites positive observational data. This describes a different flaw — argument from ignorance — that is not committed here.
explanations.E: The argument makes no conditional claim about necessary or sufficient conditions; it asserts a causal relationship. Invoking the necessary/sufficient distinction misdescribes the reasoning entirely.

lr.difficultyReason: A false-dichotomy flaw with a confident authority figure, comparable to the mayor/expressway anchor. Two trap answers describe real flaw types — circular reasoning and unrepresentative sample — that are absent from this stimulus, requiring careful verification.
lr.stimulus: Environmental policy director: Our city must choose between expanding the downtown light-rail network and investing in a fleet of electric buses. Expanding the light-rail network would require demolishing several historic buildings, which is unacceptable to the community. We must therefore invest in the electric bus fleet instead.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the policy director's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes for granted that community opposition to one option is sufficient reason to reject it entirely

choices.label: B
choices.text: bases its conclusion on the testimony of community members who may not be representative of the broader population

choices.label: C
choices.text: supports its conclusion by merely restating a premise in different words

choices.label: D
choices.text: presents two options as though they were the only ones available without establishing that no other alternatives exist

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider the long-term environmental impact of electric buses relative to light rail

explanations.correct: The policy director frames the choice as exclusively binary — light rail or electric buses — and eliminates light rail, concluding the buses must be chosen. But other alternatives (congestion pricing, hybrid transit systems, car-share programs, or a scaled light-rail plan that avoids historic buildings) are never ruled out. The dichotomy is asserted, not justified.
explanations.A: This is a plausible trap targeting the director's dismissal of light rail, but it misdescribes the flaw. The argument's structural error is not about the adequacy of community opposition as a reason; it is about the illegitimate restriction to only two options. Even if community opposition were deemed sufficient reason to reject light rail, the conclusion that buses must follow only holds if those are the only two choices.
explanations.B: No survey or testimony sample is cited in the stimulus. The policy director asserts community unacceptability as a fact, not a statistic from a poll. This flaw is simply absent.
explanations.C: Circular reasoning requires the conclusion to appear as a premise. The director's premises (community opposition, unacceptability) are distinct from the conclusion (invest in electric buses). No circularity is present.
explanations.D: Correct. The argument commits a false dichotomy by presenting light-rail expansion and electric buses as the only two options without justifying the exclusion of all other alternatives.
explanations.E: This names a missing consideration rather than a logical flaw in the structure of the argument. Even granting all the argument's premises, the structural error is the unjustified binary framing.

lr.difficultyReason: An overgeneralization from a potentially unrepresentative sample, set in a medical context. Trap answers include a reversed-causation charge that sounds plausible and a necessary/sufficient confusion that is entirely absent, requiring students to identify what the argument actually does.
lr.stimulus: A physician at an urban trauma center reviewed the cases of fifty patients who had been admitted following bicycle accidents. She found that none of the patients who sustained serious head injuries had been wearing a helmet at the time of the accident. She concluded that helmets effectively prevent serious head injuries in bicycle accidents and that all cyclists should wear them.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a condition necessary to prevent serious head injury as though it were sufficient to prevent any injury at all

choices.label: B
choices.text: infers that helmets cause cyclists to feel safer and therefore take greater risks

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a broad conclusion about helmet effectiveness from a sample that may not be representative of all bicycle accidents

choices.label: D
choices.text: mistakes the absence of helmets among injured patients for evidence that helmets always prevent serious injury

choices.label: E
choices.text: relies on the authority of a physician rather than on controlled experimental data

explanations.correct: The physician's sample consists exclusively of patients admitted to an urban trauma center following accidents severe enough to require hospitalization. This excludes cyclists who had accidents but were not admitted — including helmeted cyclists who may have sustained serious injuries but were treated elsewhere, or unhelmeted cyclists who escaped serious injury. The sample is drawn from a systematically skewed population, making any broad conclusion about helmet effectiveness unreliable.
explanations.A: The argument makes no conditional claim about necessary or sufficient conditions for injury prevention. The physician simply notes an association and draws a causal conclusion. The necessary/sufficient framework is not the operative logic here.
explanations.B: This describes a risk-compensation hypothesis — a real phenomenon sometimes raised in helmet debates — but the physician's argument makes no such inference. This is a plausible-but-absent flaw that does not reflect what the stimulus actually does.
explanations.C: Correct. The sample is limited to trauma-center admissions, which excludes a large class of relevant bicycle accidents. Drawing a general conclusion about helmet effectiveness from this skewed subset is an overgeneralization from an unrepresentative sample.
explanations.D: This is a tempting paraphrase, but it subtly misdescribes the flaw by suggesting the error is an argument from ignorance ('absence of X as evidence for Y'). The actual error is about sample composition, not about misreading an absence of evidence. The physician does not argue from the absence of helmeted injured patients — she argues from the presence of unhelmeted injured patients.
explanations.E: This describes an ad verecundiam concern, but the physician is not cited as an authority in lieu of evidence — she is the investigator who collected the data. Questioning her authority misdescribes where the reasoning goes wrong.

lr.difficultyReason: Classic correlation-causation flaw with two plausible trap answers: one describes a false dichotomy (absent from the argument) and one reverses the causal direction. Students must confirm the actual structural move.
lr.stimulus: A researcher studying elementary schools found that schools with larger libraries consistently had higher student test scores than schools with smaller libraries. The researcher concluded that increasing the size of a school's library will therefore raise its students' test scores.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about all schools based only on those schools that were studied

choices.label: B
choices.text: mistakes a correlation between two factors for a causal relationship between them

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes without warrant that test scores are the only meaningful measure of student achievement

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to consider that students who score higher on tests may cause their schools to acquire larger libraries

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a condition sufficient for raising test scores as if it were merely one of several contributing factors

explanations.correct: The researcher observes that larger libraries and higher scores go together, then concludes that enlarging a library will raise scores — treating the correlation as evidence of a causal direction. A third factor (school funding, for instance) could explain both. This is a textbook correlation-causation flaw.
explanations.A: The stimulus doesn't indicate the sample is unrepresentative or that the conclusion extends beyond studied schools. This trap describes overgeneralization, but the argument's conclusion is about what increasing library size will do, not a claim about an unstudied population.
explanations.B: Correct. The researcher observes that library size and test scores move together, then infers a causal mechanism — a classic unwarranted causal inference.
explanations.C: The argument never claims test scores are the only measure of achievement; this is an absent premise flaw, not one the argument actually commits.
explanations.D: This describes reversed causation — a tempting trap, but the argument's flaw is the unwarranted leap from correlation to any causal claim, not specifically the reversal of cause and effect.
explanations.E: The argument does not treat library size as sufficient; it treats it as causally responsible. This choice describes a necessary/sufficient confusion that is not present in the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: Necessary/sufficient swap in an ethics context. One trap answer names the right category but reverses the direction; another describes an ad hominem not present in the argument.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Any action that causes unnecessary suffering is morally wrong. Eating factory-farmed meat causes unnecessary suffering. Therefore, anyone who eats factory-farmed meat is acting immorally. Of course, those who act immorally cannot be trusted to make sound ethical judgments, so we should disregard the opinions of factory-farmed-meat eaters on any ethical question.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes for granted that causing unnecessary suffering is the only criterion for moral wrongness

choices.label: B
choices.text: dismisses the views of a group of people solely on the basis of a characteristic that is irrelevant to their reasoning ability

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the trustworthiness of all factory-farmed-meat eaters from premises that, at most, establish that some such eaters act immorally

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes without warrant that a single instance of acting immorally disqualifies a person from offering sound ethical judgments

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a condition that is sufficient for moral wrongness as though it were also necessary for moral wrongness

explanations.correct: The ethicist argues that because factory-farmed-meat eaters act immorally (in this instance), they cannot be trusted on any ethical question. This presumes without justification that a single immoral act is sufficient to disqualify all of a person's ethical reasoning — a leap the argument never supports.
explanations.A: The argument doesn't claim causing unnecessary suffering is the only criterion for wrongness; it uses it as a sufficient condition. This choice describes a flaw not actually committed.
explanations.B: This describes ad hominem circumstantial — dismissing views based on an irrelevant personal trait. But eating factory-farmed meat is not irrelevant per the argument's own premises; the argument treats it as evidence of immorality. The flaw is in what that immorality is supposed to establish.
explanations.C: The argument actually concludes about all factory-farmed-meat eaters, but the premises do establish that all of them (not just some) cause unnecessary suffering. The scope isn't the issue; the unwarranted inference about trustworthiness is.
explanations.D: Correct. The argument leaps from one instance of immoral behavior to a blanket disqualification from ethical judgment, a premise the argument never defends.
explanations.E: The argument treats causing unnecessary suffering as sufficient for wrongness — which it explicitly states — not as necessary. This choice describes the reverse of what the argument does.

lr.difficultyReason: False dichotomy in a policy context. One trap names an unrepresentative sample flaw; another describes an ad hominem — both absent from the argument. Students must verify the actual structural move.
lr.stimulus: City Councilmember: Our city must decide how to address its growing homelessness crisis. Either we construct a new large-scale emergency shelter facility, or we allow homelessness to continue unchecked. Since allowing homelessness to continue unchecked is clearly unacceptable, the council must approve the new shelter facility immediately.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the councilmember's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes for granted that the proposed shelter facility will successfully reduce homelessness

choices.label: B
choices.text: bases its conclusion on the testimony of a person with a vested interest in the outcome

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes without justification that the two options it presents are the only ones available

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about city policy from a sample of cases that may not be representative

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats the absence of evidence that the shelter will fail as evidence that it will succeed

explanations.correct: The councilmember presents only two options — build the shelter or allow homelessness to continue unchecked — without justifying that these exhaust the available choices. Alternatives such as outreach programs, housing vouchers, or zoning reform could also address the crisis. This is a false dichotomy.
explanations.A: This is a legitimate concern about the argument's unstated premise, but the central structural flaw is the false choice between two options — not whether the shelter will work.
explanations.B: There is no suggestion of improper personal interest; the councilmember speaks in a legislative capacity. This ad hominem trap does not match the argument.
explanations.C: Correct. The argument limits the options to exactly two without warrant, committing a false dichotomy.
explanations.D: No sample of cases is invoked; the argument is prescriptive, not inductive. This trap names a real flaw category that does not match what the argument actually does.
explanations.E: The argument makes no claim about evidence for or against the shelter's success; it simply says homelessness must be addressed. This absence-of-evidence pattern is not present.

lr.difficultyReason: Ad hominem / circumstantial attack in a law context. One trap describes a correlation-causation error; another names circular reasoning. Students must locate the actual structural error.
lr.stimulus: Defense attorney: The prosecution's expert witness testified that the defendant's financial records show clear signs of fraud. However, this expert has previously worked as a consultant for the prosecution on three other cases. Since the expert has a professional relationship with the prosecution, her testimony is biased and should be disregarded entirely.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning above is questionable because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers that a conclusion is false from the mere fact that someone with questionable motives has asserted it

choices.label: B
choices.text: mistakes the frequency with which an expert has testified for the prosecution for evidence that her analysis is incorrect

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws on evidence about a limited number of cases to reach a conclusion about all cases involving expert testimony

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes without justification that the testimony of any expert who has worked with the prosecution is inadmissible

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats the conclusion that the testimony is biased as itself establishing that the financial records do not show fraud

explanations.correct: The attorney challenges the content of the expert's testimony — that the records show fraud — by pointing to the expert's relationship with the prosecution. This is a circumstantial ad hominem: attacking the source rather than addressing the argument's substance. The testimony may be accurate regardless of the expert's professional history.
explanations.A: Correct. The attorney attacks the witness's motives rather than rebutting the financial analysis itself — a classic ad hominem move.
explanations.B: The attorney doesn't argue that frequency of testimony indicates the analysis is incorrect; the argument is about bias, not the number of cases. This misdescribes the move.
explanations.C: The three prior cases are cited to establish a professional relationship, not to generalize about all expert testimony. This overgeneralization trap is not the argument's flaw.
explanations.D: While this is a defensible concern, it describes a different gap — the leap to inadmissibility — rather than the core flaw of rejecting the testimony's content without addressing its substance.
explanations.E: This describes a scope-shift from 'testimony is biased' to 'records don't show fraud.' Although the argument does essentially do this, choice A more precisely identifies the structural error of attacking the messenger rather than the message.

lr.difficultyReason: Overgeneralization from an unrepresentative sample in an economics context. Traps include a false dichotomy and a correlation-causation confusion, both absent from the argument.
lr.stimulus: Financial analyst: I surveyed twenty of my colleagues who work in investment banking, and all twenty reported that they feel financially secure. Clearly, most working adults in this country feel financially secure about their economic futures.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: mistakes a claim about subjective feelings of security for a claim about objective financial conditions

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes without warrant that financial security and economic optimism are the same thing

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a general conclusion about working adults from a sample that is likely unrepresentative of that population

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats the absence of financial insecurity among survey respondents as the cause of positive economic outcomes

choices.label: E
choices.text: concludes that working adults must feel financially secure because there is no evidence that they do not

explanations.correct: The analyst surveys twenty colleagues in investment banking — a high-earning, specialized profession — and generalizes to 'most working adults.' Investment bankers are almost certainly not representative of the broader working adult population, making the generalization unwarranted.
explanations.A: The conclusion is also about feelings of security, not objective conditions. There is no gap between subjective and objective in the conclusion, so this misdescribes the argument.
explanations.B: The argument never mentions economic optimism; this introduces a concept absent from the stimulus.
explanations.C: Correct. The sample is drawn exclusively from investment bankers — a small, atypical professional group — and cannot support conclusions about working adults generally.
explanations.D: This describes a causal inference the argument never makes; there is no claim that financial security causes any outcome. This is a correlation-causation trap that does not fit.
explanations.E: The argument does not appeal to an absence of contrary evidence; it appeals to positive survey results. This inverts the actual structure of the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Equivocation on a key term in a technology context. One trap describes a false dichotomy; another names circular reasoning. Students must identify the shift in how a word is being used.
lr.stimulus: Software engineer: Our company's new algorithm is entirely transparent. Every step of its decision-making process can be examined by our engineering team. Therefore, consumers who use products powered by this algorithm can trust that it will treat them fairly.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: presumes without justification that fairness to consumers is the primary goal of any algorithm

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws on the concept of transparency in two different senses without acknowledging the shift

choices.label: C
choices.text: takes for granted that any process that engineers can examine is one that produces fair outcomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats the inability of consumers to detect unfair treatment as evidence that no unfair treatment occurs

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that the engineering team's access to the algorithm may be restricted in the future

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'engineers can examine every step' to 'consumers can trust it will treat them fairly.' Examinability by engineers does not entail fairness to consumers — these are entirely different properties. The argument takes for granted that technical inspectability guarantees fair outcomes, which does not follow.
explanations.A: The argument says nothing about whether fairness is the primary goal of algorithms generally. This introduces an absent premise.
explanations.B: While 'transparent' could equivocate between technical inspectability and ethical openness, the argument's deeper flaw is the unwarranted leap from inspectability to fairness — the equivocation alone doesn't explain why consumers should trust fair treatment. C is a more precise description of the structural error.
explanations.C: Correct. Examinability by engineers is the only basis offered for the claim of fairness to consumers, but the argument never justifies why inspectability implies fairness.
explanations.D: The argument never claims consumers cannot detect unfair treatment; it relies on the engineers' access, not consumer unawareness. This trap misdescribes the argument's structure.
explanations.E: Future restriction of access is an extraneous concern not relevant to the argument's current structural flaw. This is a 'plausible but absent' trap.

lr.difficultyReason: Circular reasoning in a history context. One trap names an ad hominem; another describes a false dichotomy. Students must identify that the conclusion is smuggled into a premise.
lr.stimulus: Historian: The Roman Empire declined primarily because its military became overextended. We know the military was overextended because the empire was unable to defend its borders effectively. And we know the borders were not defended effectively because the empire ultimately declined.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: fails to consider alternative explanations for the decline of the Roman Empire

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on a chain of reasoning in which each claim is used to support the next and the last is used to support the first

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the cause of a historical event based on a sample of cases from only one civilization

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats the decline of the Roman Empire as both the conclusion to be established and a premise used in establishing it

choices.label: E
choices.text: mistakes a necessary condition for the empire's decline for a sufficient condition

explanations.correct: The historian's reasoning is circular: the empire declined because the military was overextended, the military was overextended because borders weren't defended, and borders weren't defended because the empire declined. The conclusion — that the empire declined — appears as the final supporting evidence, making the argument circular.
explanations.A: Failure to consider alternatives is a real weakness, but it is not the central structural flaw. The flaw is that the argument is self-supporting in a circle, not merely incomplete.
explanations.B: This describes the circular structure accurately but less precisely than D. Choice B captures that the reasoning loops, but D specifically identifies that the conclusion itself functions as a premise — a more precise characterization of circular reasoning in this argument.
explanations.C: The historian is not generalizing from one civilization to all civilizations; the conclusion is about the Roman Empire specifically. Unrepresentative sample doesn't apply here.
explanations.D: Correct. The empire's decline is both what the argument is trying to explain and the evidence offered for one of the premises in the chain. The conclusion and a key premise are the same claim.
explanations.E: No necessary/sufficient distinction is made in the argument. This is a category trap — the right kind of logical terminology applied to the wrong argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Scope shift / part-to-whole flaw in an environmental science context. One trap describes reversed causation; another names a false dichotomy. Students must spot the composition error.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientist: Each of the individual components of this wetland ecosystem — the water, the soil, the plant species, and the animal populations — has been found to be in healthy condition. It is safe to conclude, therefore, that the wetland ecosystem as a whole is in a healthy and stable condition.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes for granted that the health of individual ecosystem components is caused by the overall stability of the ecosystem

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that conditions found to hold in one wetland ecosystem will hold in all wetland ecosystems

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats what is true of each part of a system as necessarily true of the system as a whole

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the current state of the ecosystem on the basis of studies that may be outdated

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that the ecosystem might be healthy without all of its components being individually healthy

explanations.correct: The argument infers that because each component is healthy, the whole system must be healthy. This is the fallacy of composition — the interactions among components, or systemic factors like nutrient cycles or invasive species dynamics, could render the whole unhealthy even if each part is individually fine.
explanations.A: The argument makes no causal inference from ecosystem stability to component health; it moves in the opposite direction. This trap describes reversed causation that the argument does not commit.
explanations.B: The argument draws no comparison to other wetlands. The conclusion is about this ecosystem only, so unrepresentative generalization is not the flaw.
explanations.C: Correct. The argument commits the fallacy of composition: healthy parts are used to infer a healthy whole, ignoring that interactions among parts can produce unhealthy system-level dynamics.
explanations.D: No indication of the studies' age is given, and this concern is peripheral to the argument's structural flaw. This is a 'too charitable / harmless' trap.
explanations.E: This describes the converse — a healthy whole without healthy parts — which would undermine the argument's premise, not its inference. The argument's flaw is the direction from parts to whole, not whole to parts.

lr.difficultyReason: Necessary/sufficient swap in a linguistics context. One trap describes the confusion in the correct direction; another reverses it. Students must determine which direction the swap runs.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: A language can survive across generations only if it is spoken by children as their primary language. Mandarin is spoken by hundreds of millions of children as their primary language. Therefore, Mandarin will certainly survive across generations.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a condition that is necessary for a language's survival as though it were sufficient to guarantee survival

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a condition that is sufficient for a language's survival as though it were merely necessary for survival

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the future of a language based on evidence about the number of its current speakers

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes without warrant that a language spoken by children as their primary language cannot be replaced by another language

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that some languages spoken by children as their primary language have nevertheless gone extinct

explanations.correct: The first premise establishes that children speaking a language as their primary language is necessary for survival (without it, the language cannot survive). The argument then treats satisfying this necessary condition as sufficient — because Mandarin meets this condition, survival is certain. Satisfying a necessary condition does not guarantee an outcome; other conditions may also be required.
explanations.A: Correct. Being spoken by children as a primary language is stated as a necessary condition for survival. The argument wrongly concludes that because Mandarin satisfies this necessary condition, its survival is guaranteed — treating necessity as sufficiency.
explanations.B: This reverses the direction of the confusion. The argument does not treat a sufficient condition as merely necessary; it treats a necessary condition as sufficient. This is the reversed-flaw trap.
explanations.C: The evidence about Mandarin's speakers is directly relevant to the necessary condition stated. The argument's flaw is in how it uses that evidence logically, not in using speaker numbers per se.
explanations.D: This is a paraphrase of the correct flaw in content terms rather than logical terms, but it is less precise than A because it focuses on replacement rather than the logical structure of necessary vs. sufficient conditions.
explanations.E: This describes a real-world counterexample concern but frames it as a failure to consider, which is weaker than identifying the structural logical error. It also conflates the observation with the structural flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: Reversed causation in an arts/policy context. Traps include an unrepresentative sample and a false dichotomy, both absent from the argument. Students must confirm the actual causal move.
lr.stimulus: Arts administrator: Cities that have invested heavily in public arts programs over the past decade have seen significant increases in tourism revenue. This proves that robust public arts funding drives economic growth in cities. Municipalities should therefore increase their arts budgets if they want to improve their economies.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: presents only two courses of action — increasing arts funding or accepting economic stagnation — without considering other approaches

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws a conclusion about all municipalities from evidence gathered only from cities that already invest in arts programs

choices.label: C
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that cities experiencing economic growth may simply have more resources available to invest in arts programs

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats an increase in tourism revenue as equivalent to overall economic growth without justification

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that arts programs in some cities may have been funded by tourism revenue rather than by city budgets

explanations.correct: The administrator observes that heavy arts investment correlates with increased tourism revenue and concludes that arts funding causes economic growth. But the causation could run in the opposite direction: economically thriving cities may have the surplus revenue to invest in arts programs. The correlation is consistent with either causal direction, and the argument does not rule out the reversed explanation.
explanations.A: The argument does not construct a two-option scenario; it is a causal argument, not a dilemma. This false dichotomy trap does not match the argument's structure.
explanations.B: The argument does only examine cities that invest in arts, which could be an unrepresentative sample concern — but the central flaw is causal, not about the representativeness of the sample. C more precisely names the structural error.
explanations.C: Correct. Economically prosperous cities have more discretionary funding, which could explain both higher arts investment and higher tourism revenue — reversing the proposed causal arrow.
explanations.D: This is a legitimate secondary concern about the scope of 'economic growth' vs. 'tourism revenue,' but it is peripheral to the main structural flaw, which is the unwarranted causal inference.
explanations.E: This describes a specific funding-source concern that is a variant of the reversed causation idea but frames it too narrowly (arts funded by tourism) and is not the most precise characterization of the argument's central error.

lr.difficultyReason: Standard correlation-causation flaw with two plausible trap answers: one misdescribes the direction of causation, the other names an absent flaw about sample size.
lr.stimulus: A recent survey found that patients who reported high levels of satisfaction with their physicians recovered from illness more quickly than those who reported low satisfaction. The hospital administrator concluded that improving patient satisfaction with physicians will therefore speed up patient recovery times across the board.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the hospital administrator's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about all patients from a survey that may have included only hospitalized patients

choices.label: B
choices.text: mistakes a correlation between two factors for a claim that one of those factors causes the other

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to specify the precise methods by which patient satisfaction could be improved

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes that physicians are the only relevant factor in determining patient recovery times

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a condition necessary for improved recovery as though it were sufficient to produce it

explanations.correct: The administrator observes that satisfaction and faster recovery co-occur and concludes that increasing satisfaction will cause faster recovery. But the correlation could run the other way (patients recovering quickly feel more satisfied) or both could result from a third factor (e.g., less severe illness). This is the classic correlation-causation flaw.
explanations.A: The stimulus says 'patients,' which is consistent with a hospital sample; the administrator's conclusion is also about patients in general, so the scope shift is plausible but not the primary structural error. More importantly, even a perfectly representative sample would not fix the causal inference problem.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument observes a correlation and treats it as establishing that improving satisfaction will produce faster recovery — a textbook mistaking of correlation for causation.
explanations.C: The absence of implementation detail is not a logical flaw in the inference being drawn; it is a practical gap, not a reasoning error.
explanations.D: The administrator's conclusion does not say satisfaction is the only factor; it says improving it will speed recovery. Claiming one cause matters does not presume it is the only cause.
explanations.E: No necessary/sufficient relationship is invoked anywhere in the stimulus; this choice imports a flaw type that is simply absent.

lr.difficultyReason: False dichotomy flaw with a strong trap that accurately describes a secondary weakness but not the central structural error. Student must distinguish the primary move from a peripheral one.
lr.stimulus: Environmental consultant: The proposed offshore drilling site either poses a negligible risk to marine ecosystems or it poses an unacceptable one. Our environmental impact assessment found no evidence of significant harm to the surrounding ecosystem in our test samples. Therefore, the site poses a negligible risk, and drilling should proceed.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the entire drilling site from test samples that may not represent conditions throughout the site

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats the absence of evidence of harm as conclusive evidence that no harm will occur

choices.label: C
choices.text: presents only two possible characterizations of risk without justifying that no intermediate level of risk exists

choices.label: D
choices.text: confuses a condition sufficient for proceeding with drilling with a condition necessary for it

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider the economic benefits that offshore drilling would provide to the surrounding region

explanations.correct: The consultant's argument rests on a binary: either negligible risk or unacceptable risk. But risk exists on a spectrum — a site could pose moderate, elevated, or manageable risk that is neither negligible nor unacceptable. The dichotomy is not justified, making this a false dilemma.
explanations.A: This describes an unrepresentative-sample flaw and is a genuine secondary weakness, which makes it a strong trap. However, the deeper structural error is the unjustified two-option framing: even a comprehensive sample cannot fix the logic if the only options offered are negligible vs. unacceptable.
explanations.B: The argument does rely on absence of evidence, which is a recognizable flaw, but the stimulus says the assessment 'found no evidence of significant harm' — this is used as the basis for choosing the first horn of the dilemma, not as a standalone proof. The false dichotomy is the more fundamental error.
explanations.C: Correct. The argument partitions risk into only two categories without warrant, then uses evidence to select one — a classic false dichotomy.
explanations.D: No necessary/sufficient relationship between conditions for drilling is invoked; this flaw type is absent from the stimulus.
explanations.E: Economic benefits are irrelevant to the logical structure of the argument about risk; raising them would not fix or expose the reasoning error.

lr.difficultyReason: Overgeneralization from an unrepresentative sample, with traps that misdescribe the argument as causal or as confusing necessary and sufficient conditions.
lr.stimulus: A linguistics professor surveyed students enrolled in upper-division language courses at a single research university and found that most of them had begun studying a second language before the age of ten. She concluded that early childhood language instruction is the most effective way to produce adult bilingualism.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning above is questionable because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers that early instruction causes adult bilingualism without ruling out the possibility that both result from a common factor such as family background

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that bilingualism is universally preferable to monolingualism

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats early childhood instruction as sufficient for adult bilingualism when it may only be necessary

choices.label: D
choices.text: bases a broad conclusion about the most effective method of producing bilingualism on a sample drawn from a narrow and potentially unrepresentative population

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to define precisely what counts as fluency in a second language

explanations.correct: The professor surveys only students already enrolled in upper-division language courses at one research university — a highly self-selected, academically motivated group that is not representative of adults generally. Drawing a universal conclusion about the most effective method from this sample is an overgeneralization from an unrepresentative sample.
explanations.A: This is a correlation-causation trap. The argument does leap from correlation to causal claim, but the more fundamental error is that the sample is too narrow to support any general conclusion about adult bilingualism, causal or otherwise. A also accurately describes a flaw in the argument, making it a tempting trap, but D better identifies the primary structural error.
explanations.B: The argument never evaluates whether bilingualism is preferable; it only claims to identify how to produce it. This preference claim is entirely absent.
explanations.C: The professor does not discuss sufficiency or necessity; she claims early instruction is the most effective method, not that it is necessary or sufficient. This flaw type is imported from outside the stimulus.
explanations.D: Correct. Upper-division language students at a single university are a narrow, self-selected group; they are not representative of the adult population at large, making any general conclusion about optimal instruction methods unwarranted.
explanations.E: Definitional vagueness is a peripheral concern here, not the structural error in the reasoning.

lr.difficultyReason: Necessary/sufficient swap flaw. The stimulus clearly confuses a condition necessary for success with one sufficient for it, but trap choices describe the reversal or import absent flaw types.
lr.stimulus: Career counselor: Every successful entrepreneur I have studied was willing to take substantial financial risks. It is clear, therefore, that if you want to become a successful entrepreneur, you should cultivate a willingness to take substantial financial risks.
lr.questionStem: The career counselor's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about what a person should do from premises that describe only what successful people have done

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a characteristic that may be necessary for entrepreneurial success as though it were sufficient to produce that success

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a characteristic sufficient for entrepreneurial success as though it were merely necessary for it

choices.label: D
choices.text: bases its conclusion on a sample of entrepreneurs that may be too small to be reliable

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that some people may be unwilling to tolerate financial risk regardless of career ambitions

explanations.correct: The counselor observes that all successful entrepreneurs shared a willingness to take risk — making risk-tolerance at most a necessary condition for their success. But the conclusion advises cultivating this trait as though doing so will produce success, treating it as sufficient. The flaw is precisely the necessary/sufficient swap.
explanations.A: This is an is-ought gap trap. The argument does move from descriptive data to a prescriptive recommendation, which is a genuine concern, but the central logical error is the necessary/sufficient confusion: even granting that we can move from 'is' to 'should,' the counselor is still treating a necessary trait as though it suffices.
explanations.B: Correct. Risk-tolerance is observed only in already-successful entrepreneurs, establishing it as necessary at most; advising people to cultivate it as if that will generate success treats it as sufficient.
explanations.C: This is the reversed flaw — it describes the opposite error (treating sufficient as necessary), which is not what the counselor does. A classic 'right flaw, wrong direction' trap.
explanations.D: Sample size could be a weakness, but the stimulus does not give us reason to think the sample is especially small; more importantly, the logical error would persist even with a very large sample.
explanations.E: Whether some people are unwilling to take risks is irrelevant to the logical structure of the argument's inference.

lr.difficultyReason: Ad hominem / circumstantial flaw. Stimulus dismisses an argument by attacking the arguer's interests rather than addressing the argument's merits. Traps include a plausible but absent appeal-to-authority error and a misdescription of the actual attack.
lr.stimulus: City councilmember: The urban planning firm's report recommends against rezoning the waterfront district for commercial development. But the firm was hired by a coalition of neighborhood associations that opposed the rezoning from the start. Given that the firm had every financial incentive to produce a report favorable to its clients, we should disregard the report's conclusions.
lr.questionStem: The flaw in the councilmember's reasoning is that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on the testimony of experts whose qualifications in urban planning have not been established

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that a report commissioned by one party cannot reach conclusions that are correct

choices.label: C
choices.text: attacks the coalition of neighborhood associations rather than addressing the substance of their position

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a firm's future behavior from evidence about the behavior of its past clients

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that commercial rezoning might reduce the quality of life for existing waterfront residents

explanations.correct: The councilmember dismisses the report solely because the firm had a financial incentive to produce client-favorable conclusions. But having an incentive to reach a conclusion does not mean the conclusion is wrong. The argument presumes that a financially motivated report cannot be correct — a classic ad hominem circumstantial fallacy.
explanations.A: The councilmember does not question the firm's qualifications; expertise is not mentioned. This imports a flaw that is entirely absent from the stimulus.
explanations.B: Correct. The councilmember's reasoning treats the firm's financial incentive as proof that the report's conclusions are wrong. But bias is not the same as error; the report could still be correct regardless of the firm's motivations.
explanations.C: The councilmember attacks the planning firm, not the neighborhood coalition. This choice misdescribes who is being attacked.
explanations.D: The argument does not draw conclusions about future behavior from past clients; this describes a flaw that is not present in the stimulus.
explanations.E: Quality of life for residents is a separate policy consideration irrelevant to the logical error in dismissing the report.

lr.difficultyReason: Equivocation flaw on the word 'original.' The argument uses the term in two senses. Traps include a correlation-causation misdescription and an absent unrepresentative-sample charge.
lr.stimulus: Art critic: A painting has aesthetic value only if it is original. The work currently on display at the Harmon Gallery is a faithful reproduction of a seventeenth-century Dutch masterpiece, not an original. Therefore, this reproduction has no aesthetic value.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the art critic's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: bases a sweeping conclusion about all reproductions on evidence drawn from a single example

choices.label: B
choices.text: mistakes the cause of a painting's reputation for the source of its aesthetic value

choices.label: C
choices.text: uses the word 'original' in two different senses without acknowledging the shift in meaning

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes without justification that aesthetic value is the only relevant criterion for evaluating a work of art

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a condition sufficient for aesthetic value as though it were necessary for it

explanations.correct: In the first premise, 'original' means creatively novel or artistically innovative — capturing the idea that derivative or copied work lacks intrinsic artistic merit. In the second premise, 'not an original' means the painting is not the historically first physical object (the seventeenth-century canvas). These are different senses: a reproduction could be 'original' in the creative sense even if it is not the first physical instance. The argument equivocates between them.
explanations.A: The critic's conclusion is about this specific reproduction, not all reproductions. The argument does not generalize across a sample; this trap misdescribes the scope of the conclusion.
explanations.B: The argument makes no causal claims about reputation; it proceeds deductively from a principle about originality. This imports a flaw type that is not present.
explanations.C: Correct. 'Original' shifts from meaning 'creatively novel' in the first premise to meaning 'the first physical instance' in the second, and the argument's validity depends on both uses meaning the same thing.
explanations.D: The critic is not claiming that aesthetic value is the only evaluative criterion; the argument is narrowly about whether this work has aesthetic value. This describes an absent concern.
explanations.E: The first premise states that originality is necessary for aesthetic value (only if original → has value). The critic does not treat this necessary condition as sufficient; the necessary/sufficient structure here is stated correctly and is not where the error lies.

lr.difficultyReason: Scope shift / composition flaw. The argument moves from a property true of individual policy components to a claim about the aggregate policy. Traps describe absent flaw types (false dichotomy, circular reasoning) that fit similar-sounding arguments.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: Each of the twelve provisions in the proposed tax reform bill has been shown in independent analyses to reduce the federal deficit when modeled in isolation. We can therefore be confident that enacting all twelve provisions together will produce a significant reduction in the federal deficit.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: presents only two possible outcomes for the tax reform bill without justifying that no other outcomes are possible

choices.label: B
choices.text: takes for granted the very conclusion it is trying to establish, namely that the bill will reduce the deficit

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes that because each component of a policy produces a particular effect individually, the policy as a whole will produce that same effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws on independent analyses without evaluating whether those analyses employed consistent methodologies

choices.label: E
choices.text: mistakes the claim that deficit reduction is likely for the stronger claim that it is certain

explanations.correct: The analyst shows each provision individually reduces the deficit, then concludes the combined policy will too. But provisions can interact: a tax cut in one provision might offset a revenue gain in another, or combined effects may produce unintended economic feedback. What is true of each part need not be true of the whole — a composition flaw.
explanations.A: The argument presents no dichotomy at all; it moves from component-level evidence to a whole-policy conclusion. A false dilemma is entirely absent from the stimulus.
explanations.B: The argument does not use the deficit-reduction conclusion as a premise; it derives it from the component analyses. Circular reasoning is not the flaw here.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the composition fallacy: inferring that a property of each part (deficit-reducing in isolation) must belong to the whole (all twelve enacted together).
explanations.D: Methodological consistency is a peripheral concern, not the structural error. Even if all analyses were methodologically identical, the composition problem would remain.
explanations.E: The analyst says 'confident' and 'significant reduction,' not certainty; moreover, the argument's core problem is not about hedging language but about the invalid inference from parts to whole.

lr.difficultyReason: A correlation-causation flaw in a medical context. Two plausible traps misdescribe the direction or nature of the error; students must verify the actual move in the stimulus against close-but-wrong answer choices.
lr.stimulus: Epidemiologist: A recent survey of hospital records found that patients who were visited frequently by family members recovered from surgery faster than those who were visited infrequently. Therefore, frequent family visits must accelerate post-surgical recovery. Hospitals should accordingly revise their visiting-hour policies to allow unlimited family access to recovering patients.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the epidemiologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about all patients from a sample limited to surgery patients

choices.label: B
choices.text: mistakes a correlation between two factors for a causal relationship between them

choices.label: C
choices.text: takes for granted that revising visiting-hour policies will be endorsed by hospital administrators

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to specify the precise frequency of visits that would qualify as "frequent"

choices.label: E
choices.text: presumes without warrant that faster recovery is always preferable to slower recovery

explanations.correct: The epidemiologist observes a correlation — frequent visits co-occur with faster recovery — and concludes that visits cause faster recovery. But the relationship could run the other way (patients recovering faster may be more alert and invite more visits), or a third factor (e.g., stronger social support networks) could explain both. Inferring causation from correlation alone is the central structural error.
explanations.A: The conclusion is explicitly about surgery patients, so the sample's restriction to surgery patients is not a mismatch. This is a 'plausible but absent' trap — it could apply to a different argument but doesn't bite here.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument moves directly from a co-occurrence pattern to a causal claim without ruling out reverse causation or confounding variables.
explanations.C: Administrator endorsement is not assumed by the argument's logic; the conclusion is a normative recommendation about policy, and the flaw lies earlier — in the causal inference. This is a 'too charitable / peripheral' trap.
explanations.D: Definitional vagueness about 'frequent' is a minor rhetorical weakness, not the structural error that undermines the causal conclusion. This is an 'accurate but harmless' trap.
explanations.E: The argument never questions whether faster recovery is desirable — it treats that as obvious background. The real flaw is the unwarranted causal step, not an assumption about desirability. This is a 'plausible but absent' trap.

lr.difficultyReason: A necessary/sufficient confusion flaw in an economics context. One trap describes the flaw in the correct category but reverses the direction; another is a plausible-but-absent generalization error. Students must carefully match the logical structure of the stimulus.
lr.stimulus: Financial advisor: Every highly successful entrepreneur I have studied possessed an extraordinary tolerance for risk. It is clear, then, that if someone hopes to become a highly successful entrepreneur, that person must cultivate a high tolerance for risk. I therefore advise all of my clients who aspire to entrepreneurial success to begin taking on riskier financial positions immediately.
lr.questionStem: The financial advisor's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: bases a universal conclusion on a sample that may not be representative of all entrepreneurs

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a characteristic that is sufficient for entrepreneurial success as though it were merely necessary for that success

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a characteristic shared by successful entrepreneurs as necessary for entrepreneurial success when it may be merely typical of such success

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to consider whether cultivating a tolerance for risk carries financial dangers for the advisor's clients

choices.label: E
choices.text: presumes without justification that the advisor's clients are capable of cultivating a higher tolerance for risk

explanations.correct: The advisor observes that every successful entrepreneur in the sample had a high risk tolerance, then concludes that risk tolerance is necessary (i.e., one must have it to succeed). But the evidence only establishes that risk tolerance is a common trait among a studied group — it does not show that success is impossible without it. The advisor mistakes a feature that accompanies success for one that is required for success.
explanations.A: While the sample may not be perfectly representative, the argument's core error is inferring necessity from observed co-occurrence, not overgeneralizing a frequency claim. This is a 'plausible but absent' trap — the sample issue is real but not the structural flaw being exploited.
explanations.B: This reverses the actual error. The advisor infers a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. The flaw described here ('sufficient treated as merely necessary') is the mirror image of what the stimulus commits. This is a 'right flaw, reversed' trap.
explanations.C: Correct. Every successful entrepreneur had risk tolerance → risk tolerance is necessary for success. But 'every S has P' does not establish 'P is necessary for S.' It only establishes that P accompanies S in the observed cases.
explanations.D: Possible dangers of the recommended action are a peripheral concern; the structural flaw in the causal-to-normative inference chain lies earlier. This is a 'too charitable / peripheral' trap.
explanations.E: Whether clients can cultivate risk tolerance is an unstated assumption, but it is not a logical flaw in the inferential move from observation to necessity. This is an 'accurate but harmless' trap.

lr.difficultyReason: A false dichotomy flaw in an environmental policy context. Two traps target real weaknesses in the argument (an unsupported premise, a scope gap) that are less central than the binary framing error; students must identify the structural flaw rather than peripheral concerns.
lr.stimulus: Environmental policy director: The new coastal development ordinance has been criticized on the grounds that it restricts economic growth. But either we enact strict development restrictions along our coastline, or we accept the permanent destruction of the region's marine ecosystems. Since no responsible government can accept permanent ecosystem destruction, the ordinance must stand as written.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: dismisses the economic criticism without providing evidence that the economic concerns are overstated

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes without warrant that permanent ecosystem destruction would have no economic consequences

choices.label: C
choices.text: presents only two possible courses of action without establishing that no other options exist

choices.label: D
choices.text: appeals to the authority of responsible governments rather than to evidence about ecological outcomes

choices.label: E
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the entire coastline from evidence about only selected marine ecosystems

explanations.correct: The director presents strict development restrictions and permanent ecosystem destruction as the only two possibilities, then eliminates one to conclude the other must be accepted. But intermediate or alternative options — partial restrictions, mitigation measures, zoning reforms, phased development — are never ruled out. The argument's validity depends entirely on the exhaustiveness of the two-option framing, which is simply assumed.
explanations.A: The argument does sidestep the economic criticism, but the more fundamental structural error is the false dichotomy that makes the conclusion appear to follow. Dismissing a counterargument without rebuttal is a weaker peripheral concern. This is a 'too charitable' trap.
explanations.B: Whether ecosystem destruction has economic consequences is relevant background but is not the logical move that makes the argument invalid. The dichotomy is already flawed before any economic comparison is made. This is a 'plausible but absent' trap.
explanations.C: Correct. The argument's structure is: A or B; not-B; therefore A. That is valid only if A and B are exhaustive alternatives — and the director provides no justification for that assumption.
explanations.D: The reference to 'responsible government' is used to eliminate one horn of the dilemma, not as an authority appeal meant to substitute for ecological evidence. The choice misdescribes the argumentative function of that premise. This is a 'misdescribes the argument' trap.
explanations.E: The stimulus makes no reference to selected ecosystems versus the whole coastline; this distinction is entirely fabricated. This is a 'plausible but absent' trap that invents a scope issue the argument never raises.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a classic correlation-causation flaw, but two trap answers plausibly misdescribe it — one names the right category reversed, and another names a flaw that fits a related argument but not this one. Students must verify the actual inferential move.
lr.stimulus: A technology researcher reports that among software engineers who regularly attend industry conferences, career advancement rates are significantly higher than among those who do not attend. The researcher concludes that attending industry conferences causes software engineers to advance more rapidly in their careers.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about all software engineers based on evidence drawn only from those who attend conferences

choices.label: B
choices.text: mistakes a correlation between conference attendance and career advancement for a causal relationship

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to specify what proportion of software engineers attend industry conferences

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes without warrant that career advancement is the primary goal of software engineers

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats the absence of conference attendance as sufficient evidence of slow career advancement

explanations.correct: The researcher observes that conference attendance and high advancement rates co-occur, then concludes that attendance causes advancement. But the correlation could run the other direction (already-advancing engineers are more likely to be sent to conferences), or both could share a common cause (e.g., employer investment in high-performers). Inferring causation from correlation alone is the central flaw.
explanations.A: Misdescribes the argument. The researcher does not draw a conclusion about all software engineers from a selective sample; the comparison explicitly involves both attendees and non-attendees. This is a 'plausible but absent' trap.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument moves from a statistical correlation directly to a causal claim without ruling out reverse causation or a common cause.
explanations.C: The proportion of attendees is irrelevant to the validity of the causal inference; this is an 'accurate but harmless' trap — the argument would be equally flawed regardless of the proportion.
explanations.D: The argument says nothing about the goals of software engineers; this flaw is entirely absent from the stimulus.
explanations.E: Reverses the flaw. The argument does not treat non-attendance as sufficient for slow advancement; it draws a positive causal claim about attendees, not a negative inference about non-attendees.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus contains a false dichotomy, but the trap choices include a misdescription of the actual options (labeling them non-exclusive when exhaustiveness is the real issue) and an irrelevant peripheral weakness, requiring careful verification against the stimulus.
lr.stimulus: Environmental policy advocate: The proposed coastal wetlands must either be placed under permanent federal protection or they will be destroyed by commercial development within a decade. Since destroying these wetlands would eliminate habitat for dozens of endangered species, we have no choice but to support permanent federal protection.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes for granted that protecting the wetlands would be sufficient to prevent the extinction of all endangered species in the region

choices.label: B
choices.text: appeals to the harmful consequences of one option in order to establish that a second, incompatible option is preferable

choices.label: C
choices.text: presents only two possible outcomes without establishing that no other options are available

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats the two options it considers as mutually exclusive when they could both be implemented simultaneously

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider whether the endangered species could survive in habitats other than the wetlands

explanations.correct: The advocate asserts that the choice is either permanent federal protection or destruction, but never establishes that these are the only possibilities. State-level protection, private conservation trusts, temporary moratoriums on development, or negotiated land purchases are alternatives left unconsidered. Presenting an unjustified two-option dilemma is a false dichotomy.
explanations.A: The conclusion is about supporting protection of the wetlands, not about preventing all extinctions region-wide. This is a 'too charitable / peripheral' trap — it identifies a possible overreach in implication but not the argument's central structural error.
explanations.B: This describes a legitimate argumentative move — pointing out that one option has bad consequences is a standard reason to prefer the alternative. It names something the argument does but is not a flaw in context.
explanations.C: Correct. The argument assumes a binary without demonstrating that the two options exhaust the space of possibilities.
explanations.D: The two options — federal protection vs. commercial development — are genuinely incompatible; the criticism that they could be implemented simultaneously is inapplicable. This is the 'right flaw, wrong direction' trap (confuses exhaustiveness with exclusivity).
explanations.E: Whether species could survive elsewhere is irrelevant to whether the dichotomy is justified; this is a plausible-but-absent trap that would apply to a different argument about species survival strategies.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus swaps a necessary condition for a sufficient one. Two trap answers are plausible: one names the flaw reversed, and another correctly identifies a real logical category but mislocates the direction of the error in this specific argument.
lr.stimulus: Legal scholar: A valid contract requires that both parties give genuine consent. The agreement between the two firms clearly involved genuine consent from both parties. Therefore, the agreement is certainly a valid contract.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning above is questionable because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a specific case from a principle that applies only to cases in general

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a condition that is necessary for an outcome as though it were sufficient to produce that outcome

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a condition that is sufficient for an outcome as though it were necessary to produce that outcome

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to consider that one of the parties may have had a stronger bargaining position than the other

choices.label: E
choices.text: assumes without justification that the legal scholar is qualified to evaluate the validity of contracts

explanations.correct: The legal scholar's premise establishes that genuine consent is a necessary condition for a valid contract (a contract requires consent). But the argument then concludes that because consent is present, the agreement is a valid contract — treating consent as if its presence alone were sufficient for validity. A valid contract likely requires additional conditions (consideration, legal capacity, lawful purpose, etc.) beyond consent alone.
explanations.A: The argument moves from a general principle to a specific case, which is standard deductive reasoning, not a flaw. No overgeneralization from a specific case to a general rule occurs here.
explanations.B: Correct. 'Requires consent' establishes consent as necessary; concluding the agreement is valid because consent exists treats consent as sufficient.
explanations.C: This states the flaw in reverse. If the scholar had treated consent as sufficient and concluded it was also necessary, that would fit choice C. Here, the move is from necessity to sufficiency, not the other way around.
explanations.D: Bargaining power is not relevant to the argument's logical structure; this is a peripheral real-world concern, not the structural flaw the argument commits.
explanations.E: An ad hominem or credential-based objection that has no basis in the stimulus; nothing in the argument makes the scholar's qualifications relevant to the logical error.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: the epidemiologist treats a percentage increase as if it were an increase in the absolute number of cases, and buries that move inside an appeal to her own credentials. Students who spot only the ad hominem framing or only the statistical slip miss the interaction.
lr.stimulus: Epidemiologist: As someone who has spent thirty years analyzing outbreak data, I can assure the council that the new pathogen poses a graver threat than the old one. The old pathogen's incidence rose by just 4 percent last year, whereas the new pathogen's incidence rose by 60 percent. Anyone who has not worked in the field, as I have, should hesitate to dispute these numbers.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the epidemiologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a comparison of rates of change as if it established a comparison of total case counts, while implying that the speaker's expertise insulates that inference from challenge

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that no other pathogens pose a comparable threat to public health

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers a causal relationship between the speaker's expertise and the accuracy of the data cited

choices.label: D
choices.text: relies on statistics drawn from a sample that is too small to support a general conclusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: assumes that what is true of the new pathogen's incidence must also be true of its mortality rate

explanations.correct: A percentage rise from a small base can still leave the new pathogen's total caseload far below the old one's; the argument slides from rate-of-change to absolute threat, and wards off objections by citing the speaker's experience rather than addressing the inference.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The argument compares only two pathogens; it does not need to rule out others.
explanations.C: The expertise claim is used to deflect disagreement, not to explain why the data are accurate.
explanations.D: Sample size is never characterized; this is a plausible-but-absent flaw.
explanations.E: Mortality is never mentioned; the conclusion is about threat, but the scope-shift at issue is rate-to-absolute, not incidence-to-mortality.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: an appeal to authority (the Nobel laureate) is used to license a scope shift from 'effective in clinical trials' to 'effective in routine practice.' Students who name only the appeal to authority or only the scope shift miss that the authority is doing the work of papering over the shift.
lr.stimulus: Pharmacologist: The new anticoagulant should be prescribed routinely to patients at risk of stroke. Dr. Reyes, a Nobel laureate in medicine, has publicly endorsed the drug, and controlled clinical trials have shown that it reduces clot formation more reliably than the current standard. Her endorsement, together with the trial data, settles the matter.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the pharmacologist's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: presumes that because controlled trial results imply routine effectiveness, a respected endorsement can substitute for evidence of such effectiveness

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to consider that Dr. Reyes's Nobel Prize was awarded in an unrelated field

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a necessary condition for prescribing the drug as a condition sufficient to do so

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizes from an unrepresentative sample of clinical trial participants

choices.label: E
choices.text: attacks Dr. Reyes's credentials rather than the substance of her endorsement

explanations.correct: Controlled-trial performance and routine-practice performance are different claims; the argument leans on the laureate's endorsement to bridge that gap instead of supplying evidence that trial results carry over. The endorsement and the scope shift work together.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The stimulus never indicates Reyes's field; assuming she is unqualified would be an unsupported gloss on the argument.
explanations.C: No conditional relationship is stated; this is an accurate description of a different, absent flaw.
explanations.D: Trial representativeness is never raised.
explanations.E: The argument defers to Reyes; it does not attack her.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: the ethicist equivocates on 'natural' (naturally occurring vs. morally natural) and uses that equivocation to collapse a descriptive-to-normative gap. Students who flag only the is/ought move or only the ambiguity miss that each enables the other.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Competition among members of a species is found in every biological environment we have studied; it is entirely natural. Whatever is natural in this sense is morally natural as well, since our moral intuitions themselves evolved under selection pressures. It follows that ruthless competition among humans in the marketplace is morally above reproach.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the ethicist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: exploits an ambiguity in the term 'natural' in order to move from a claim about what is widespread in nature to a claim about what is morally permissible

choices.label: B
choices.text: takes for granted that what is true of a species as a whole must be true of each of its members

choices.label: C
choices.text: relies on evidence drawn exclusively from non-human species

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes that moral intuitions cannot be subjected to further critical scrutiny

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses a claim about the origins of moral intuitions with a claim about their content

explanations.correct: The first premise uses 'natural' descriptively (occurring in nature); the second premise silently shifts 'natural' into a normative register ('morally natural'); the conclusion then treats the second sense as if it had been established by the first. The equivocation is what makes the is-to-ought leap look licensed.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No part-whole move is in play.
explanations.C: The argument draws on biology generally, including human evolution; the evidentiary scope isn't the issue.
explanations.D: The argument assumes intuitions are trustworthy, but that isn't the structural move at fault.
