explanations.E: Tempting — origins-vs-content is nearby — but the argument doesn't isolate 'origins' as its hook; the equivocation on 'natural' is the pivot.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: percentage-vs-absolute confusion hidden inside selection bias. The rise in 'share of claims' could reflect fewer good drivers being insured, not worsening driving. Students who name only the selection bias or only the percentage confusion miss the interaction.
lr.stimulus: Insurance analyst: Drivers under 25 now account for 42 percent of collision claims filed with our company, up from 34 percent five years ago. Over the same period, our company raised premiums for drivers over 50, prompting many of them to switch carriers. It is therefore clear that drivers under 25 have become considerably more dangerous on the road.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the insurance analyst's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers a change in the behavior of one group from a change in that group's share of a pool whose composition has itself been altered by the speaker's own company

choices.label: B
choices.text: generalizes from the claims experience of a single insurance company to that of the industry as a whole

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes that collision claims are a reliable proxy for collisions

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes without warrant that drivers over 50 are safer than drivers under 25

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a cause of an increase in premiums as if it were an effect of that increase

explanations.correct: When older drivers leave the pool, younger drivers' share of claims can rise even if their absolute claim rate is unchanged. The argument also ignores that its own company caused the compositional shift, so 'more dangerous' isn't warranted.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The scope of the conclusion is plausibly about this company's drivers; even on a broader reading, the central error is the compositional shift.
explanations.C: Plausible-but-absent; no claim-vs-collision distinction is raised.
explanations.D: The argument doesn't rank the groups' safety; it claims under-25s got worse.
explanations.E: No causal reversal is asserted.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: treats evidence about what the framers individually believed as evidence about what the Constitution as a ratified document means — a category error, combined with an appeal to the framers' authority. The trap answer describes ad hominem reversed.
lr.stimulus: Constitutional scholar: Several of the framers wrote privately that they viewed a standing peacetime army as a threat to liberty. Because the framers are the supreme interpretive authorities on the Constitution they drafted, the Constitution, properly read, prohibits the maintenance of such an army. Any judge who rules otherwise is simply ignoring what the document means.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the constitutional scholar's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats the private views of individual drafters as if they determined the meaning of a ratified legal text, and treats the drafters' authority as settling an interpretive question rather than bearing on it

choices.label: B
choices.text: attacks the character of judges who disagree rather than engaging their legal arguments

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes that a document's meaning can change over time without any formal amendment

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a universal conclusion from the views of only a few of the framers

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses what the framers hoped the Constitution would accomplish with what it in fact accomplished

explanations.correct: Private letters are a different object from a ratified text; the scholar collapses that distinction while elevating the framers from relevant authorities to decisive ones. Both moves are needed to reach the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Tempting, because the last sentence stings — but the argument targets judges' reasoning, not their character; ad hominem is the wrong label.
explanations.C: The argument implicitly denies meaning can shift; that denial is not the structural flaw.
explanations.D: The argument doesn't quantify how many framers held the view; weakening on 'only a few' would miss the category error.
explanations.E: Hopes-vs-accomplishments isn't the distinction being conflated.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: a necessary/sufficient confusion wrapped in an ad hominem. The columnist discredits opponents to distract from the logical slip between 'without clean water, no civilization' and 'clean water suffices for civilization.'
lr.stimulus: Columnist: Without access to clean water, no ancient civilization ever flourished. Critics who dismiss modern aid programs that focus on water infrastructure are either ignorant of history or indifferent to suffering. The lesson is plain: any region that receives clean water will become a flourishing society.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the columnist's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a condition whose absence precludes an outcome as if its presence were enough to produce the outcome, and deflects objections by impugning the motives of those who raise them

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to consider that ancient civilizations differed in important respects from modern societies

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes, without giving reasons, that clean water programs are the most cost-effective form of aid

choices.label: D
choices.text: confuses a claim about what has happened with a claim about what ought to happen

choices.label: E
choices.text: relies on evidence that is consistent with the denial of the conclusion it is meant to support

explanations.correct: 'Without X, never Y' makes X necessary for Y, not sufficient. The columnist upgrades necessity to sufficiency, and uses a character attack on critics to preempt scrutiny of the upgrade.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Plausible reading, but the flaw isn't ancient-modern disanalogy; even within ancient cases, necessity wouldn't yield sufficiency.
explanations.C: Cost-effectiveness isn't the conclusion.
explanations.D: No is/ought confusion; the conclusion is predictive.
explanations.E: Too vague; the conditional slip is the specific error.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: the consultant equivocates on 'efficient' (completes tasks quickly vs. delivers business value) and then generalizes from the fastest team to the organization. Students who pick the equivocation miss that generalization isn't at fault; students who pick the generalization miss the term shift.
lr.stimulus: Management consultant: Our internal analytics team is the most efficient group in the company: it closes assigned tickets faster than any other team. Because maximally efficient teams are precisely the ones whose practices generate the greatest business value, the firm should require every department to adopt the analytics team's practices wholesale.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the management consultant's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: uses 'efficient' in one sense to characterize the analytics team and in a different sense to connect efficiency with business value

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws a conclusion about every department from evidence about a single department that may not be representative of the others

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes that the analytics team's practices cannot be improved upon

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes that a correlation between speed and value establishes that speed causes value

choices.label: E
choices.text: takes for granted that practices effective within one organization will be effective within another

explanations.correct: The first premise measures efficiency by ticket-closing speed; the bridging premise implicitly treats 'efficient' as meaning 'value-generating.' Without the shift, the conclusion loses its support.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Tempting distractor, but representativeness isn't the issue — the consultant asserts a link between efficiency and value, so the trouble is the word 'efficient,' not sampling.
explanations.C: Improvability isn't claimed or denied.
explanations.D: Causation language doesn't appear; the link is conceptual (via the definition of 'efficient').
explanations.E: The argument is intra-firm, not cross-firm.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: absence-of-evidence inference folded into a scope shift between 'endangered in our surveys' and 'endangered globally.' Students who identify only the absence-of-evidence move miss that the scope shift does most of the damage.
lr.stimulus: Biologist: Our three-year survey of the central rainforest failed to locate a single specimen of the blue-throated tanager. The earlier belief that the species was endangered must therefore be mistaken: had it been endangered, some individuals would surely have appeared in our data. The species is plainly thriving in regions we did not survey.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the biologist's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers from a failure to detect a species in a limited area that the species must be flourishing in unsurveyed areas

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on survey methods that are not described in sufficient detail to be evaluated

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizes from a three-year period to a conclusion about the species' long-term status

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats the belief that the species is endangered as settled rather than as an assumption requiring support

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses being undetected with being extinct

explanations.correct: Not finding a rare species in one area can just mean the species is rare there (consistent with being endangered). The argument treats that absence as evidence of abundance and then leaps to regions it didn't study.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Methodological opacity isn't what the argument turns on.
explanations.C: Time horizon isn't the key move; the spatial leap is.
explanations.D: Reversed — the argument challenges the endangered-status belief, not assumes it.
explanations.E: Opposite of what the argument does: it concludes thriving, not extinction.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: percentage-vs-absolute confusion hidden in statistical language. Declines in 'share of listening time' don't entail declines in hours listened if the overall pie grew; the critic also slips from listening data to 'cultural significance.'
lr.stimulus: Critic: Streaming data show that classical music's share of total listening time fell from 8 percent to 5 percent over the last decade. Since listening is the primary measure of a genre's cultural significance, classical music is undeniably losing cultural significance, and arts foundations should redirect their support accordingly.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the critic's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a decline in a genre's proportion of listening time as establishing a decline in the genre's cultural significance, without ruling out that total listening hours devoted to the genre rose as the overall volume of listening grew

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that streaming data are representative of all forms of music consumption

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes that arts foundations have a duty to fund only genres whose listenership is growing

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizes from a ten-year window to a long-term trend

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses the cause of classical music's decline with its effect

explanations.correct: Share can fall while absolute hours rise if the streaming pie grows faster. The critic converts a relative statistic to a claim about absolute cultural significance without addressing that gap.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Plausible-but-absent — representativeness is a different flaw than the stats slip.
explanations.C: The argument doesn't assign foundations a duty; it draws a policy suggestion.
explanations.D: Time window isn't the pivot.
explanations.E: No cause/effect reversal is asserted.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: part-whole (composition) error wrapped in a category confusion. 'Idiomatic' is a property of sentences within a language; the speaker treats it as a property a whole language can have. Students who pick the composition move alone miss the category piece.
lr.stimulus: Linguistics professor: Every competent speaker of English occasionally produces sentences that are idiomatic — expressions whose meanings cannot be predicted from their parts. It follows that English, as a language, is fundamentally idiomatic, and therefore that any formal grammar that assigns meaning compositionally must fail to describe it.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the linguistics professor's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a property that can characterize particular sentences within a language as if it were a property that could characterize the language itself

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that competent speakers are reliable reporters of their own linguistic intuitions

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizes from a feature of English to a feature shared by all natural languages

choices.label: D
choices.text: takes for granted that formal grammars are intended to describe every sentence a speaker might produce

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses a sufficient condition for a formal grammar's success with a necessary condition for it

explanations.correct: 'Idiomatic' describes how some sentences behave; calling the language itself idiomatic conflates a sentence-level property with a language-level one — a composition/category slip. The jump to 'compositional grammars must fail' rides on that slip.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reliability of introspection isn't the structural problem.
explanations.C: The conclusion concerns English only, not all languages.
explanations.D: The argument doesn't hinge on the scope of what grammars aim to cover; it hinges on misapplying 'idiomatic.'
explanations.E: No necessary/sufficient inversion occurs around grammar's success conditions.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw involves a subtle scope shift from 'linked to' (correlation) to 'caused by' (causation), compounded by ignoring a third-variable explanation. Trap choices use abstract logical vocabulary that nearly fits but mis-describes the inferential move.
lr.stimulus: Epidemiologist: Several recent studies have linked high consumption of processed foods to elevated rates of cardiovascular disease. We can therefore conclude that processed foods directly cause cardiovascular disease. Accordingly, a policy requiring warning labels on processed food products would reduce the incidence of cardiovascular disease in the population.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the epidemiologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: presumes, without justification, that warning labels are the only effective means of reducing cardiovascular disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: mistakes a correlation between two phenomena for a direct causal relationship between them

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider that the studies cited may have examined unrepresentative samples of the population

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats a condition that is necessary to reduce cardiovascular disease as though it were sufficient to do so

choices.label: E
choices.text: draws a conclusion about individual behavior from statistical claims about populations

explanations.correct: The epidemiologist moves from 'linked to' (a statistical association) directly to 'directly cause,' without ruling out confounding variables or establishing a causal mechanism. This is the classic correlation-causation flaw.
explanations.A: The argument does not claim warning labels are the only means; it claims they would help. This misdescribes what the argument actually asserts.
explanations.B: Correct. The studies establish a correlation; the epidemiologist infers direct causation without warrant.
explanations.C: The argument does not hinge on sample representativeness — the flaw is in the inferential step from association to causation, not in the quality of the samples.
explanations.D: The argument makes no necessary/sufficient distinction regarding the warning-label policy; this is an accurate-but-absent trap.
explanations.E: The conclusion is a population-level policy recommendation, not a claim about individual behavior — this misdescribes the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is equivocation on the word 'free' — used in one sense (no cost) in the premise and in a different sense (at liberty) in the conclusion. This is subtle because the equivocation is embedded in natural language and both readings are plausible in isolation.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Any transaction in which both parties participate without coercion is, by definition, a free transaction. Markets, by design, permit participants to enter and exit without government compulsion. Therefore, all market transactions are free, which shows that any regulation of markets necessarily constrains freedom.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the economist's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on a premise that itself presupposes the truth of the conclusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats the absence of government compulsion as both necessary and sufficient for a transaction to be free

choices.label: C
choices.text: uses the word 'free' in one sense when establishing a definition and in a subtly different sense when drawing its conclusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to consider that some forms of market regulation do not involve government compulsion

choices.label: E
choices.text: draws a universal conclusion from a limited set of examples of market transactions

explanations.correct: 'Free transaction' is defined as 'without coercion' (a liberty sense), but the conclusion invokes 'freedom' in a broader normative or political sense. The argument slides between two meanings of the same word.
explanations.A: The premise ('transactions without coercion are free') is not obviously circular — it is a definitional claim, not one that presupposes the conclusion about regulation.
explanations.B: This describes a necessary/sufficient confusion, which is a real flaw type but is not what the argument commits; the problem is the semantic shift in 'free,' not the conditions for freedom.
explanations.C: Correct. The equivocation on 'free' is the structural error that makes the conclusion appear to follow when it does not.
explanations.D: Whether some regulations avoid compulsion is irrelevant to the equivocation flaw; this is a plausible-but-absent trap.
explanations.E: The argument proceeds by definition, not by generalizing from examples; this misdescribes the argumentative structure.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is a necessary/sufficient swap in a legal context, with answer choices using formal logical vocabulary. The 'right flaw, reversed' trap and a plausible-but-absent procedural trap make this particularly difficult.
lr.stimulus: Legal scholar: The constitutional right to a fair trial guarantees that no one may be convicted without sufficient evidence. In the Hartwell case, the evidence was clearly sufficient. We can therefore conclude that Hartwell received a fair trial.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the legal scholar's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a condition that is sufficient to violate the right to a fair trial as though it were necessary to do so

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that sufficiency of evidence is both necessary and sufficient for a fair trial, when the guarantee only establishes it as necessary

choices.label: C
choices.text: takes for granted that the standard of 'sufficient evidence' is uniformly applied across all jurisdictions

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers that because a condition required for a fair trial was met, a fair trial was therefore ensured

choices.label: E
choices.text: draws a conclusion about what the law requires from a premise about what it permits

explanations.correct: The constitutional guarantee establishes that sufficient evidence is necessary to convict fairly (no conviction without sufficient evidence). The scholar treats this necessary condition as sufficient — because evidence was sufficient, a fair trial is concluded. But many other conditions (impartial jury, proper procedure, etc.) are also required.
explanations.A: This reverses the flaw: it would describe someone arguing that because a fair trial wasn't violated in a certain way, it couldn't be violated at all. The scholar's error is about sufficiency, not about conditions for violation.
explanations.B: Partially correct in spirit but imprecise: the guarantee establishes sufficient evidence as necessary for conviction, not necessary for a 'fair trial' per se. Choice D captures the actual inferential error more cleanly.
explanations.C: The argument makes no claims about jurisdictional uniformity; this is a plausible-but-absent trap.
explanations.D: Correct. Sufficient evidence is a necessary condition for fair conviction; the scholar mistakenly treats satisfying this one condition as guaranteeing a fair trial overall.
explanations.E: The argument does not conflate what the law requires with what it permits; this misdescribes the logical structure.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is an overgeneralization from a potentially unrepresentative sample, but the trap choices include a plausible ad hominem and a reversed-causation distractor that are difficult to eliminate without careful attention to what the argument actually does.
lr.stimulus: Arts critic: I surveyed ten prominent contemporary novelists, all of whom said they found traditional plot structures constraining to genuine artistic expression. This shows that traditional plot structures are an obstacle to literary creativity, and critics who defend them simply do not understand what serious artistic work demands.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the arts critic's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: attacks the competence of critics who hold a different view rather than providing reasons to think that view is mistaken

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws a general conclusion about traditional plot structures from the opinions of a small, potentially unrepresentative group of writers

choices.label: C
choices.text: mistakes the cause of a writer's dissatisfaction for its effect on the quality of the literary work

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes that whatever prominent writers find constraining must, in fact, constrain all forms of artistic expression

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that some critics who defend traditional plot structures are themselves accomplished novelists

explanations.correct: Ten prominent novelists constitute a narrow, self-selected sample. The conclusion — that traditional plot structures are generally an obstacle to literary creativity — sweeps far beyond what this small group's opinions can establish.
explanations.A: The dismissal of critics is a secondary move; it is an ad hominem, but it is not the primary structural flaw that drives the conclusion. The central error is the generalization from the sample.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument generalizes from ten prominent (and therefore non-representative) novelists to a universal claim about creative writing.
explanations.C: The argument makes no causal claim about dissatisfaction producing lower-quality work; this misdescribes the argument's structure.
explanations.D: This is close but imprecise: the critic doesn't limit the conclusion to 'all forms of artistic expression' broadly — the conclusion is about literary creativity specifically. Choice B better names the sampling flaw.
explanations.E: Whether some critics are novelists is irrelevant to the generalization flaw; this is a plausible-but-absent distractor.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is circular reasoning in a policy context, disguised by the authority of a scientific framing. The circularity is subtle because the conclusion and the key premise use different vocabulary, requiring the test-taker to recognize that they express the same claim.
lr.stimulus: Environmental policy analyst: We know that the proposed emissions standard is the correct one because it was derived using the best available climate models. Those models are reliable precisely because they have been calibrated to produce outputs consistent with the proposed emissions standard.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning above is questionable because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: appeals to the authority of scientific models without examining whether those models are relevant to the policy question

choices.label: B
choices.text: conflates the accuracy of a predictive model with the desirability of the policy outcomes it projects

choices.label: C
choices.text: uses the correctness of the emissions standard to support the reliability of the models while simultaneously using the reliability of the models to support the correctness of the standard

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes that emissions standards derived from climate models are necessarily more reliable than those arrived at through legislative negotiation

choices.label: E
choices.text: draws a conclusion about what environmental policy should require from premises that describe only what current models predict

explanations.correct: The analyst argues: the standard is correct because the models are reliable; the models are reliable because they are calibrated to produce outputs consistent with the standard. This is a closed loop — each claim is used to justify the other, which is circular reasoning.
explanations.A: The argument does not question the models' relevance; it assumes their reliability. The flaw is circularity, not an irrelevant appeal to authority.
explanations.B: The argument does not conflate accuracy with desirability of outcomes; this misdescribes the inferential structure.
explanations.C: Correct. The mutual justification between the standard and the models constitutes a vicious circle.
explanations.D: The argument makes no comparison to legislative processes; this is a plausible-but-absent trap.
explanations.E: The shift from 'is' (what models predict) to 'ought' (policy) is a real logical gap in some arguments, but here the argument's conclusion is about correctness of a standard, not a normative ought — this misdescribes the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is a scope shift from individual-level claims to group-level conclusions (division/composition confusion). The trap choices include a near-miss necessary/sufficient distractor and a plausible-but-absent sampling error.
lr.stimulus: Technology executive: Every engineer on our software development team is highly skilled. Our team was responsible for building the platform. Therefore, the platform itself must be the product of highly skilled work, and any failures in the platform cannot be attributed to the skill level of the engineers involved.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes for granted that individual skill is both necessary and sufficient to produce a high-quality collective outcome

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to consider that engineers with different skill sets may have contributed unequally to the platform's failures

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes, without justification, that properties of each member of a group are thereby properties of the group's collective output

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the cause of the platform's failures without establishing that any failures have occurred

choices.label: E
choices.text: relies on the authority of the executive's professional position rather than on independent evidence

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'each engineer is highly skilled' (a property of individual members) to 'the platform is the product of highly skilled work' (a property of the collective output). Individual skill does not guarantee collective quality — coordination, process, and organizational factors intervene. This is a composition fallacy.
explanations.A: The necessary/sufficient framing is a tempting vocabulary match, but the argument does not actually structure its inference around a condition being necessary or sufficient; it assumes skill transfers from parts to whole.
explanations.B: Unequal contribution is irrelevant to the structural flaw; this is a plausible-but-absent trap.
explanations.C: Correct. The argument treats individual-level properties as automatically transferring to the group-level output — a composition error.
explanations.D: The argument does acknowledge the possibility of failures ('any failures') — this misdescribes the premise structure.
explanations.E: The argument does not invoke the executive's authority as a premise; this is an absent ad-hominem-style distractor.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is a false dichotomy presented in a historical argument, but unlike simpler false-dichotomy questions the two options are described with technical-sounding language and a third, obvious alternative must be inferred. The 'accurate but harmless' trap and a plausible correlation-causation trap add difficulty.
lr.stimulus: Historian: The decline of the Roman Empire was caused either by the military pressures of barbarian invasions or by internal economic deterioration. Since recent scholarship has largely discredited purely economic accounts of Roman decline, we must conclude that barbarian military pressure was the primary cause.
lr.questionStem: The historian's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: mistakes a temporal sequence — barbarian invasions preceding economic decline — for a causal relationship

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on scholarly consensus to establish a historical conclusion, when scholarly opinion is itself subject to revision

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes, without adequate justification, that exactly two mutually exclusive explanations exhaust the possible causes of the Roman Empire's decline

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats the refutation of one explanation as establishing, rather than merely supporting, an alternative explanation

choices.label: E
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the primary cause of a complex historical event from evidence pertaining only to secondary factors

explanations.correct: The historian restricts causes to two options (military pressure vs. economic deterioration) without establishing that these are exhaustive. Political instability, religious transformation, climate change, disease, and combined multi-factor accounts are all possibilities that the dichotomy ignores.
explanations.A: The argument does not rely on a temporal sequence; it sets up a logical disjunction. This misdescribes the argumentative move.
explanations.B: The historian's reliance on scholarly consensus is a minor weakness, but it is not the central structural flaw; this is an 'accurate but harmless' trap.
explanations.C: Correct. The disjunction is presented without justification that it is exhaustive, making it a false dichotomy.
explanations.D: This is partially right — ruling out one option does not definitively establish another when there are more than two options — but this description captures a symptom rather than the root flaw, which is the unjustified binary. C names the flaw more precisely.
explanations.E: The argument draws no distinction between primary and secondary factors; this misdescribes the premises.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw involves inferring the absence of evidence for a claim constitutes evidence against that claim — a subtle error in the logic of evidence. This is dressed in technical linguistic framing, and the trap choices include a plausible-but-absent sampling distractor and a reversed-causation option.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: No written records from before 3000 BCE contain grammatical structures resembling those of the proposed proto-language. This absence of evidence shows that the proto-language could not have existed prior to 3000 BCE and that linguists who claim otherwise are simply mistaken.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the linguist's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: generalizes about the grammatical structures of all ancient languages from a sample limited to surviving written records

choices.label: B
choices.text: attacks the credibility of opposing linguists rather than addressing the merits of their evidence

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats the absence of evidence for the proto-language's existence before 3000 BCE as sufficient evidence that it did not exist

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes that grammatical structures in written records are sufficient to determine the full range of spoken languages that existed

choices.label: E
choices.text: infers that because the proto-language did not exist before 3000 BCE, it could not have influenced languages that developed after that date

explanations.correct: The linguist moves from 'no written records show these structures' (absence of evidence) to 'the proto-language could not have existed' (evidence of absence). Written records may be incomplete, unrecovered, or may not reflect spoken language — the lack of evidence in records does not establish non-existence.
explanations.A: This is a plausible sampling concern, but the argument's flaw is more fundamental: even if the sample were representative, absence of evidence still would not constitute proof of non-existence.
explanations.B: Calling opposing linguists 'mistaken' follows from the conclusion rather than serving as its basis; this misdescribes the argumentative structure.
explanations.C: Correct. The absence of records containing the proto-language's features does not constitute positive evidence that the language never existed.
explanations.D: The argument does assume that written records are diagnostic, but the precise flaw is that it treats the absence within those records as proof of non-existence — D is more specific and accurate.
explanations.E: The argument draws no inference about subsequent linguistic influence; this is an absent distractor.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is a promotion-without-necessity-or-sufficiency error structurally identical to the LSAC democracy anchor, here transplanted to an ethics and social policy context. The trap includes a classic necessary/sufficient swap that sounds correct but mis-locates the error.
lr.stimulus: Social ethicist: Voluntary charitable giving does not advance social justice. Societies with high levels of charitable giving still exhibit profound economic inequality, and some of the most just societies on record have achieved equality through institutional means rather than private charity. Therefore, charitable giving has no role to play in creating a more just society.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the social ethicist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: confuses the conditions that are necessary for social justice with those that are sufficient to produce it

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the value of charitable giving from premises that concern only its effectiveness at reducing inequality

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes that because charitable giving has not historically produced just societies, it cannot contribute to justice in any society

choices.label: D
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that charitable giving promotes social justice even if it is neither necessary nor sufficient by itself to produce it

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a condition that is sufficient to undermine social justice as though it were the only obstacle to achieving it

explanations.correct: The ethicist shows that charitable giving is neither necessary (just societies achieved justice without it) nor sufficient (high-charity societies still have inequality) for social justice. But from this, one cannot conclude that charitable giving plays no role — it may still promote justice as a contributing factor without being independently decisive.
explanations.A: The argument does not confuse necessary and sufficient conditions; it establishes that charity is neither. The flaw is in drawing too strong a conclusion from that finding. This is the 'right flaw, reversed' trap.
explanations.B: The premises do concern effectiveness at reducing inequality, and the conclusion is about social justice broadly — there is a slight scope issue, but the central structural flaw is the leap from 'neither necessary nor sufficient' to 'no role at all,' which D captures.
explanations.C: This describes a hasty generalization from historical cases, which is a real but secondary concern. The primary flaw is the inference from 'not necessary or sufficient' to 'no role,' named precisely by D.
explanations.D: Correct. The ethicist overlooks that a factor can contribute to or promote an outcome without being independently necessary or sufficient — matching the LSAC-anchored flaw pattern.
explanations.E: The argument does not make any claim about a condition being sufficient to undermine justice; this misdescribes the argument's premises.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is an ad hominem combined with a scope shift: the arguer attacks the source of a policy proposal rather than its merits, then extends the dismissal beyond the person to the entire category of policy. Multiple trap answers address real but secondary weaknesses in the argument.
lr.stimulus: Policy advisor: The senator's proposal to restructure the tax code has been endorsed by the same lobbying group that funded her last three election campaigns. Since the proposal clearly serves the financial interests of that group, we have every reason to reject not only this proposal but the entire approach to tax reform it represents.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the policy advisor's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: fails to consider that a proposal can serve the interests of a lobbying group and still be sound policy

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that all proposals endorsed by lobbying groups are designed primarily to benefit those groups

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the merits of a tax reform approach from premises that only establish a conflict of interest regarding one specific proposal

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats the senator's motivation for introducing the proposal as evidence that the proposal's content is factually incorrect

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses the legal question of campaign finance ethics with the separate policy question of tax reform

explanations.correct: The advisor dismisses the proposal solely because it serves the interests of the funding lobbying group. But the origin or beneficiary of a proposal is independent of its policy merit. A tax reform could benefit a lobbying group and still be economically sound, equitable, or otherwise good policy. The advisor never engages with the substance.
explanations.A: Correct. The argument's central flaw is assuming that because a proposal serves a group's interests, it must be rejected on those grounds — without examining whether the proposal is meritorious. This is the genetic/ad hominem fallacy.
explanations.B: The advisor does not generalize to all lobbying-endorsed proposals; this overstates the argument's scope and misdescribes it.
explanations.C: This names a real scope-shift problem — the rejection is extended from the specific proposal to the entire reform approach — but it is a secondary flaw. The primary error is the ad hominem dismissal on which the scope shift is built.
explanations.D: The advisor questions the proposal's policy desirability, not its factual correctness; this misdescribes the conclusion.
explanations.E: The argument draws no distinction between legal and policy questions; this is a plausible-but-absent trap.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is a subtle scope shift — the argument moves from 'associated with' to 'caused by' while also smuggling in a reversal of the causal direction. Trap answer (A) names a real flaw type but locates the error incorrectly; (C) describes a flaw present in related arguments but not this one.
lr.stimulus: Epidemiologist: Communities with higher rates of green-space use consistently report lower rates of depression. Since increasing access to parks and green spaces reduces depression, city planners should prioritize green-space development over investments in mental health clinics.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the epidemiologist's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: fails to consider that depression rates may influence how much green space a city develops

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a correlation between green-space use and lower depression rates as sufficient to establish that green-space use reduces depression

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about all cities based on evidence drawn only from communities with high park access

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes without warrant that city planners have the authority to override mental health policy

choices.label: E
choices.text: assumes that two policy goals are mutually exclusive when both could be pursued simultaneously

explanations.correct: The epidemiologist moves from an observed correlation — communities with more green-space use have lower depression — to the causal conclusion that green-space use reduces depression. Correlation does not establish causation; this is the central structural error.
explanations.A: This names the reversed-causation possibility, which is a real concern for a causal claim but does not capture the primary flaw in the argument as stated — the argument never addresses directionality at all, so the core problem is treating correlation as causation, not reversing the direction. B is more precise.
explanations.C: The stimulus does not indicate the communities studied are restricted to high-access areas; this misdescribes the evidence base presented.
explanations.D: The argument makes no claim about authority; this is entirely absent from the stimulus.
explanations.E: Although the argument does recommend one option over another, the flaw is not a false dichotomy — the argument's structural error is the correlation-causation move that underlies the recommendation, not the comparison of options itself.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw involves a necessary/sufficient confusion embedded in a legal context with abstract vocabulary. The trap answer (D) describes a flaw that sounds structurally identical but reverses the direction of the error.
lr.stimulus: Legal scholar: A contract is enforceable only if both parties have provided consideration. The parties in this dispute have both provided consideration. It follows that their contract is enforceable.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the legal scholar's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on a legal standard that has been superseded by more recent case law

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a specific case from a principle that applies only to general categories of contracts

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a condition that is necessary for enforceability as though it were sufficient to guarantee it

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats a condition that is sufficient for enforceability as though it were necessary to establish it

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider whether both parties understood the terms of the consideration they provided

explanations.correct: The scholar's first sentence states that consideration is necessary for enforceability (enforceable ONLY IF consideration). The conclusion then treats consideration as sufficient — if they provided it, the contract is enforceable. This is the classic necessary-to-sufficient swap.
explanations.A: No information in the stimulus suggests the legal standard is outdated; this introduces content external to the argument.
explanations.B: The principle is applied to a specific case, but the argument doesn't limit the principle to general categories — this misdescribes the logical structure.
explanations.C: Correct. 'Only if' marks a necessary condition; the conclusion infers enforceability from its presence, treating it as sufficient.
explanations.D: This reverses the error. Treating a sufficient condition as necessary would mean concluding that because the contract is enforceable, consideration must have been given — the opposite of what the argument does.
explanations.E: Understanding of terms is a peripheral concern not implicated by the logical structure of the argument; this is a 'too charitable / minor weakness' trap.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is equivocation on the term 'competitive,' used first to mean 'economically efficient' and then to mean 'rivalrous with other firms.' The answer choices all use plausible abstract logical vocabulary, making it difficult to identify the equivocation.
lr.stimulus: Economist: A competitive market is one in which no single firm can dictate prices. Our analysis shows that the technology sector is highly competitive. Therefore, consumers in the technology sector are protected from price manipulation.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about consumer welfare from premises that concern only market structure

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on an ambiguous term, using it in one sense in the premises and a different sense in the conclusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats the absence of monopoly power as conclusive evidence that collusion cannot occur

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to consider that technology markets may behave differently from markets in other sectors

choices.label: E
choices.text: presumes that consumer protection from price manipulation is the primary goal of market competition

explanations.correct: The word 'competitive' is defined in the first sentence as meaning no single firm dictates prices. When the argument then says the tech sector is 'highly competitive,' it may be using that word in a colloquial sense (vibrant, fast-growing). The conclusion then re-applies the original definition's implication. This is equivocation.
explanations.A: While the argument does move from market structure to consumer welfare, this describes a scope shift rather than the equivocation that is the primary structural error. The connection is plausible given the definition provided, so the more precise flaw is the equivocation on 'competitive.'
explanations.C: The argument never discusses collusion; this introduces a concept not present in the stimulus.
explanations.D: Sector-specific differences are a peripheral concern; the argument's structural flaw is the equivocation, not an unsupported generalization across sectors.
explanations.E: The argument doesn't claim price-manipulation protection is the primary goal of competition; this misdescribes the conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is circular reasoning with an intermediate step that disguises the circularity. The correct answer must identify the circularity without simply restating the conclusion. Trap (B) describes a genuine weakness but is peripheral to the central structural error.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: We should trust the conclusions of moral intuition because those conclusions reflect deeply held human values. Deeply held human values are the foundation of any reliable ethical framework. And we know that moral intuitions reflect such values because we trust their conclusions.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning above is questionable because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: appeals to the authority of human values without defining what makes a value genuinely human

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to consider that moral intuitions vary significantly across cultures and historical periods

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes as a premise the very claim that the argument purports to establish

choices.label: D
choices.text: confuses the reliability of an ethical framework with its widespread acceptance among moral philosophers

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a property that is common to all ethical frameworks as if it were unique to frameworks based on moral intuition

explanations.correct: The argument's support for trusting moral intuition is that intuitions reflect deeply held values; but the sole support for that claim is that we trust moral intuition's conclusions. The conclusion ('we should trust moral intuition') is used, circularly, to support a premise needed to reach it.
explanations.A: The argument does invoke human values without defining them, but this is a peripheral weakness. The central structural error — circularity — is far more damaging and is what the question asks about.
explanations.B: Cultural variability is a real objection to moral intuitionism but is not a flaw in the argument's internal logical structure; it is an external objection the argument fails to address, making this a 'plausible but absent' trap.
explanations.C: Correct. The trustworthiness of moral intuition is both the conclusion and an implicit premise.
explanations.D: The argument never mentions moral philosophers or widespread acceptance; this misdescribes the content.
explanations.E: The argument makes no comparative claim about other ethical frameworks having or lacking the same property.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument commits an overgeneralization from an unrepresentative sample with a subtly disguised scope shift. The trap (A) names correlation-causation, which is tempting but not the primary error; the actual flaw is the unrepresentative sample leading to a sweeping policy conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: We surveyed residents of three coastal cities and found that a majority favor stricter carbon-emission regulations. Since most people support stronger environmental regulations, legislators across the country should enact them without delay.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the policy analyst's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: mistakes a widespread preference for regulation with evidence that such regulation would be effective

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws a broad conclusion about national public opinion from a survey of a potentially unrepresentative sample

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes that legislators are obligated to follow majority opinion on all policy matters

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to specify the precise level of carbon-emission reduction that would constitute 'stricter' regulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats the findings of one survey as more reliable than findings from multiple independent studies

explanations.correct: The analyst surveys only three coastal cities — a geographically and demographically skewed group — then generalizes to 'most people,' a claim about national public opinion. Coastal urban populations may have systematically different views on environmental regulation than inland or rural populations, making the sample unrepresentative.
explanations.A: The argument does not claim the regulations would be effective; it claims people support them. No effectiveness-to-causation move is made, so this misdescribes the argument.
explanations.B: Correct. The conclusion about what 'most people' support cannot be reliably derived from surveying only coastal city residents.
explanations.C: While the argument assumes legislators should act on public support, this is more of an unstated normative premise than the primary logical flaw, which is the unrepresentative sample.
explanations.D: Vagueness of the term 'stricter' is a peripheral concern that does not identify the structural error in the reasoning.
explanations.E: The argument does not compare its survey to other studies; this introduces a contrast not present in the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is a subtle promotion/necessary-sufficient confusion in an environmental science context, mirroring the difficulty of the democracy anchor. The correct answer requires recognizing that reducing a contributing factor doesn't eliminate an effect when that factor is neither necessary nor sufficient. Trap (C) inverts the error.
lr.stimulus: Environmental consultant: Nitrogen runoff from fertilizers is one factor that contributes to algal blooms in freshwater lakes. If we eliminate nitrogen runoff, we will eliminate algal blooms. Therefore, stricter fertilizer regulations are the key to restoring the health of our lakes.
lr.questionStem: The argument's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: fails to consider that fertilizer regulations may be economically harmful to the agricultural sector

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that eliminating one contributing factor is sufficient to eliminate an effect that may have multiple independent causes

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a condition that is sufficient to produce algal blooms as though it were merely one contributing factor among many

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about lake health in general from evidence that concerns only freshwater lakes

choices.label: E
choices.text: mistakes the goal of reducing algal blooms for the broader goal of restoring full ecological health

explanations.correct: The consultant acknowledges nitrogen runoff is 'one factor' — not the only factor — contributing to algal blooms. Yet the argument concludes that eliminating nitrogen runoff will eliminate algal blooms entirely. This presumes that a single contributing factor (which is neither necessary nor sufficient on its own) can, if removed, eliminate a multi-causal effect.
explanations.A: Economic harms to agriculture are not implicated by the logical structure of the argument; this is an external concern that does not identify the internal flaw.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument promotes one contributing factor to the status of a necessary cause, inferring that its elimination will eliminate the effect — overlooking that other causes could still produce the blooms.
explanations.C: This reverses the error. The consultant actually does the opposite — she starts by saying nitrogen runoff is one factor (correctly) but then treats its elimination as sufficient to eliminate blooms, not as if the factor were merely contributory.
explanations.D: The scope of 'freshwater lakes' versus 'lakes in general' is not relevant to the flaw; the argument concerns freshwater lakes throughout.
explanations.E: The argument equates eliminating algal blooms with restoring lake health, but this peripheral scope issue is not the primary logical flaw in the reasoning chain.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument commits an ad hominem combined with a subtle genetic fallacy in a technology context. The difficulty comes from distinguishing the genetic fallacy (correct) from the ad hominem (trap), since both involve attacking the source rather than the argument.
lr.stimulus: Technology critic: The software engineer who authored this widely cited report on social-media addiction has received substantial funding from a social-media company. We should therefore disregard the report's finding that moderate social-media use does not impair adolescent cognitive development.
lr.questionStem: The technology critic's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: attacks the character of the report's author rather than addressing the evidence and methods underlying the report's findings

choices.label: B
choices.text: assumes that financial relationships always compromise the integrity of scientific research

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider that the funding source may have had no influence on the report's methodology or conclusions

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a specific report based on generalizations about the behavior of funded researchers

choices.label: E
choices.text: dismisses a conclusion on the basis of the circumstances of its origin rather than on its logical or evidential merits

explanations.correct: The critic dismisses the report's finding solely because of who funded it, not because of any flaw in the evidence or methodology. This is the genetic fallacy: rejecting a claim because of the circumstances of its origin rather than its merits.
explanations.A: The critic attacks the funding source (a circumstance), not the author's character (personal traits). Ad hominem attacks character; the genetic fallacy attacks origin. The distinction matters — E is more precise.
explanations.B: While the critic's argument implies this assumption, identifying an assumed premise is not the same as identifying the flaw. The flaw is the inferential move from 'funded by X' to 'conclusion should be disregarded,' which E captures directly.
explanations.C: This correctly identifies a gap in the argument but frames it as a failure to consider a possibility rather than naming the structural flaw. E names the error more precisely.
explanations.D: The argument does not explicitly generalize about funded researchers; it makes a specific inference about this report. This misdescribes the structure.
explanations.E: Correct. The report is rejected because of where its funding came from, not because of any demonstrated error in its reasoning or evidence.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument involves a subtle composition fallacy — inferring a property of the whole from properties of its parts. The difficulty lies in distinguishing this from the closely related overgeneralization trap, and the answer choices use precise abstract terminology that requires careful matching to the actual error.
lr.stimulus: Art historian: Each individual brushstroke in Vermeer's paintings is remarkably precise and controlled. His canvases are therefore the product of a meticulous, unhurried creative process — one that must have been entirely free of spontaneity.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the art historian's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about all of Vermeer's works on the basis of a feature shared by only some of them

choices.label: B
choices.text: infers that because each component of a whole has a certain property, the whole process that produced it must have that property

choices.label: C
choices.text: mistakes a description of technical execution for a psychological claim about the artist's creative state

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes that precision in artistic output precludes the use of assistants or collaborators

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that meticulous technique in one medium does not indicate meticulous technique across all artistic media

explanations.correct: The argument attributes precision to each individual brushstroke (a property of parts) and then infers that the entire creative process was meticulous and free of spontaneity (a property of the whole). A process can involve spontaneous, exploratory stages that nevertheless produce precise final marks; the precision of parts does not guarantee the same character of the whole process. This is the composition fallacy.
explanations.A: The stimulus does not suggest that only some of Vermeer's paintings were examined; it speaks of his paintings generally. This misdescribes the evidence base.
explanations.B: Correct. The precision of individual brushstrokes (parts) is used to infer a property — methodical, non-spontaneous process — of the whole creative act, which is the composition fallacy.
explanations.C: While this identifies a real tension, it is a 'too charitable / minor weakness' description that does not name the structural flaw — the composition error is the more fundamental logical problem.
explanations.D: The use of assistants is not mentioned or implied in the stimulus; this is an external concern.
explanations.E: Cross-medium comparisons are absent from the argument; this introduces a scope not present in the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument commits a scope shift from historical evidence to a universal claim, combined with an absence-of-evidence inference. The correct answer requires recognizing both moves; trap (A) correctly identifies half the flaw but mislocates the direction of the error.
lr.stimulus: Historian: No written records from the early settlement period mention any form of organized resistance by the indigenous population. We can therefore conclude that the indigenous population accepted the settlers' presence without opposition.
lr.questionStem: The historian's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats the written record as a complete and unbiased account of events during the early settlement period

choices.label: B
choices.text: infers from the absence of recorded evidence for resistance the positive conclusion that no resistance occurred

choices.label: C
choices.text: conflates organized resistance with all possible forms of opposition to settlers

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to consider that indigenous populations may have had oral rather than written records

choices.label: E
choices.text: draws a conclusion about indigenous attitudes from evidence that concerns only settler behavior

explanations.correct: The historian moves from 'no written records mention resistance' (absence of evidence) to 'no resistance occurred' (evidence of absence). The absence of documentation does not establish the absence of the documented phenomenon — records may be incomplete, biased, or lost.
explanations.A: This correctly identifies an assumption the argument makes, but it describes a missing premise rather than naming the inferential flaw. B names the logical error more precisely: treating absence of evidence as positive evidence of absence.
explanations.B: Correct. The core flaw is the illicit inference from 'not recorded' to 'did not occur.'
explanations.C: The argument does limit its scope to 'organized resistance,' but this is a legitimate scope restriction, not a flaw — the conclusion also speaks only of 'opposition' broadly, so there is some conflation, but this is a peripheral issue relative to the absence-of-evidence error.
explanations.D: The existence of oral records is a specific consideration that could rebut the argument's premise, but identifying a possible counter-evidence source is not the same as naming the structural flaw in the inference.
explanations.E: The evidence concerns written records generally, not specifically settler behavior; this misdescribes the evidence.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument shifts the meaning of 'accessible' — first used to mean 'understandable to non-specialists' and then used to mean 'widely distributed and available' — in a way that makes the conclusion appear to follow when it does not. The equivocation is subtle because both senses are relevant to the topic of linguistic communication. Trap (D) names the correct flaw type but describes it in reverse.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Languages with simpler grammatical structures are more accessible to adult second-language learners. Mandarin Chinese, despite its tonal system, has a simpler grammatical structure than German. Therefore, Mandarin Chinese is more accessible to adult learners and should be made more widely available in public school curricula.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning above is questionable because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on a comparison of only two languages to draw a conclusion about language learning in general

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to consider that tonal systems may pose greater challenges to adult learners than grammatical complexity

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats grammatical simplicity as the sole determinant of a language's value for educational purposes

choices.label: D
choices.text: uses the term 'accessible' in two different senses, shifting from ease of acquisition to broad availability within a single argument

choices.label: E
choices.text: presumes that public schools are the most effective venue for second-language instruction

explanations.correct: In the first sentence, 'accessible' means 'learnable/understandable' — a cognitive property. In the conclusion, 'should be made more widely available' uses 'accessible' in the sense of physical or institutional availability. The argument slides from one sense to the other, making the conclusion appear to follow from the cognitive-ease premise when it does not.
explanations.A: The argument compares two languages to establish a ranking, not to generalize about all language learning. The conclusion concerns Mandarin specifically, so this misdescribes the scope of the inference.
explanations.B: This correctly identifies a gap — tonal difficulty is acknowledged but bracketed. It is a legitimate concern but describes a missing consideration rather than naming the structural equivocation that drives the flawed inference.
explanations.C: The argument uses grammatical simplicity as the basis for the comparison but does not claim it is the sole determinant of educational value; this overstates the argument's claim.
explanations.D: Correct. The equivocation on 'accessible' — cognitive ease in the premise, institutional availability in the conclusion — is the structural flaw that makes the conclusion appear supported when it is not.
explanations.E: The argument recommends that Mandarin be offered in public schools but does not compare public schools to other venues; this introduces a comparison absent from the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is a subtle equivocation on the word 'resistance' — used first in a physiological sense (immune tolerance) and then in a behavioral sense (refusal to comply). Answer choices use abstract logical vocabulary and two strong traps describe adjacent but inaccurate flaw types.
lr.stimulus: Epidemiologist: Overprescription of antibiotics has produced bacterial strains with genuine resistance to those drugs. Since resistance to authority is also increasing among hospital patients who refuse to follow prescribed treatment regimens, we should not be surprised that medical compliance is declining across the board. Both phenomena stem from the same cultural erosion of deference to expert judgment.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the epidemiologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a causal conclusion from evidence that establishes only a correlation between two trends

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a term that has a precise technical meaning in one context as though it carries the same meaning in a different context

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes without warrant that phenomena occurring simultaneously must share a common cause

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizes from a limited set of clinical observations to a conclusion about all medical contexts

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that the decline in medical compliance could be a cause rather than an effect of overprescription

explanations.correct: The epidemiologist uses 'resistance' in two entirely different senses: bacterial resistance is a biological property of microorganisms, while patient resistance is a behavioral disposition of people. By treating these as related instances of the same phenomenon, the argument equivocates — the surface similarity of the word does the logical work that evidence should do.
explanations.A: The argument does assert a causal claim (cultural erosion drives both), but the primary structural fault is not a correlation-causation confusion — no statistical correlation between two trends is even cited. The argument links the phenomena through linguistic overlap, not through observed co-variation. This is a plausible-but-absent trap.
explanations.C: This describes a simultaneity fallacy. The argument does not claim the two phenomena are simultaneous; it asserts a shared root cause. More importantly, the deeper error is that the two 'phenomena' are only superficially related — they share a word, not a nature. This choice misidentifies the locus of the flaw.
explanations.D: No clinical observations are cited. The argument proceeds by conceptual linkage, not by induction from a sample. This is a plausible-but-absent trap invoking the overgeneralization flaw type.
explanations.E: This is a reversed-causation trap. While reversed causation is a legitimate flaw type, the argument does not actually present a causal chain from overprescription to patient noncompliance; it posits cultural erosion as the common cause of both. This choice attacks a causal structure the argument does not have.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is a scope shift from 'no evidence has been found against X' to 'there is evidence that X is safe' — a subtle inversion of absence-of-evidence reasoning. The trap choices include a genuine necessary/sufficient confusion and a plausible-but-absent sample bias charge, both of which demand close reading of the stimulus.
lr.stimulus: Technology ethicist: Critics of autonomous vehicle software argue that the systems may harbor undiscovered biases in pedestrian-detection accuracy across demographic groups. However, extensive independent audits have failed to uncover any such bias. We therefore have good evidence that these systems treat all pedestrians equitably, and regulators should approve them for public deployment without further delay.
lr.questionStem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: mistakes the absence of evidence for a claim as constituting positive evidence against that claim

choices.label: B
choices.text: infers from the failure to detect a phenomenon that the phenomenon does not exist

choices.label: C
choices.text: takes a condition sufficient for regulatory approval to be necessary for it

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws on audits whose methodology may be biased in favor of the technology being evaluated

choices.label: E
choices.text: presumes that equitable pedestrian detection is the only consideration relevant to deployment approval

explanations.correct: The audits found no evidence of bias — but the argument converts this into positive evidence that no bias exists. Failure to detect is not the same as detection of absence. The audits may simply lack the sensitivity or scope to identify disparities that are nonetheless present. This is the classic 'absence of evidence is not evidence of absence' flaw.
explanations.A: This describes a subtly different error: treating no-evidence-for-X as evidence-against-X. The argument does not conclude the systems are biased against equitability claims; it concludes the systems are equitable. Choice A reverses the direction of the inference. This is a 'right flaw, reversed' trap.
explanations.C: The argument does not discuss what conditions are necessary or sufficient for regulatory approval in general. It simply recommends approval. No conditional structure is inverted. This is a plausible-but-absent necessary/sufficient trap.
explanations.D: This attacks the quality of the evidence rather than the logical structure of the inference. Even perfectly unbiased audits cannot support the conclusion that the argument draws — the flaw is structural, not evidentiary. This is a 'too charitable / peripheral weakness' trap.
explanations.E: The argument's conclusion is specifically about equitable treatment, not about all deployment considerations. The argument does not claim equitability is the only relevant factor; it simply does not address other factors. This is a plausible-but-absent trap.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is a necessary/sufficient confusion in an economic-policy context with abstract framing. The argument treats a factor shown to be sufficient (in historical cases) for economic recovery as though it is necessary, then concludes the absence of that factor dooms current policy. Two traps — a false dichotomy charge and a correlation-causation charge — are rendered plausible by surface features of the stimulus.
lr.stimulus: Economic historian: Every sustained recovery from a major recession in the past century has been accompanied by significant public infrastructure investment. It is therefore clear that without such investment, the current government's austerity program cannot produce a genuine economic recovery. The administration is simply ignoring the historical record.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning above is questionable because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a factor that has always accompanied past recoveries as though it must be present for any recovery to occur

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that historical patterns observed over a limited period will necessarily extend into the future

choices.label: C
choices.text: mistakes a correlation between infrastructure investment and recovery for a causal relationship

choices.label: D
choices.text: presents only two policy options — infrastructure investment and austerity — without considering alternatives

choices.label: E
choices.text: draws on historical cases that may differ from the current situation in economically relevant ways

explanations.correct: The historical record shows that infrastructure investment always accompanied recovery — establishing it as, at most, a factor present in every past sufficient condition for recovery. But the economist concludes that investment is necessary: that without it, recovery cannot occur. This treats a sufficient-condition accompaniment as a necessary condition, which is an unwarranted logical leap. Past co-occurrence does not establish that the factor is required.
explanations.B: This is a plausible-but-absent trap invoking a 'limited sample extrapolation' charge. The argument's flaw is not about the temporal scope of the historical data but about the logical relationship being inferred from that data. Even if the data covered every recession in history, the necessary/sufficient confusion would remain.
explanations.C: This is a tempting correlation-causation trap. The argument does seem to assume a causal role for infrastructure investment, but the specific structural error is more precise: even granting a causal role, the argument still illicitly converts sufficiency into necessity. Choice C names a related but less precise flaw.
explanations.D: The argument does not claim austerity and infrastructure investment are the only two possible policies. The conclusion is specifically that austerity without investment cannot produce recovery — not that those are the only options available. This is a false dichotomy charge that misdescribes the argument's actual structure.
explanations.E: This is a 'too charitable / peripheral weakness' trap. Disanalogous historical cases is a genuine generic objection to arguments from historical precedent, but it does not identify the central logical error — namely, inferring necessity from observed co-sufficiency.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is a subtle scope shift between 'reduces symptoms' and 'cures the disease.' Answer choices use abstract logical vocabulary and include a trap that correctly identifies a real but peripheral weakness, and another that reverses the causal direction.
lr.stimulus: Physician: A clinical trial showed that patients who took the new antihistamine reported a significant reduction in allergy symptoms compared to those who took a placebo. We can therefore conclude that the antihistamine eliminates the underlying allergic condition, not merely its outward manifestations.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the physician's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: bases its conclusion on a sample of patients that may not represent the broader population of allergy sufferers

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats evidence that a treatment reduces observable symptoms as sufficient to establish that it resolves the condition producing those symptoms

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider that patients who took the placebo may have had more severe allergic conditions than those in the treatment group

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes without warrant that all antihistamines operate through the same mechanism

choices.label: E
choices.text: mistakes a correlation between medication intake and symptom reduction for a causal relationship

explanations.correct: The physician infers from the fact that symptoms are reduced (an observable, surface-level outcome) that the underlying allergic condition itself is eliminated. This is a scope shift: the evidence supports only symptomatic relief, not a cure of the root condition.
explanations.A: Unrepresentative sample is a genuine flaw type, but the stimulus does not give any reason to doubt the sample's representativeness — the argument's central error is the leap from symptom reduction to cure, not sample quality.
explanations.B: Correct. The move from 'reduces symptoms' to 'eliminates the underlying condition' is unsupported; the evidence only establishes the former.
explanations.C: This describes a confound that could undermine the trial's internal validity, but it is a peripheral methodological worry, not the core structural flaw the physician commits in the conclusion.
explanations.D: The argument is about one specific antihistamine and makes no comparison to other antihistamines, so this flaw is simply absent from the stimulus.
explanations.E: A randomized controlled trial with a placebo group is specifically designed to establish causation; dismissing it as a mere correlation misreads the stimulus and names the wrong flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument equivocates on the word 'value' — shifting from economic value to moral or intrinsic value. The trap choices include a plausible necessary/sufficient swap and an accurate-but-harmless description.
lr.stimulus: Art critic: The auction price of a painting is determined entirely by what buyers are willing to pay for it, which in turn depends on the painting's perceived desirability. Since desirability is a matter of taste rather than objective fact, we must conclude that a painting has no genuine value — only a price.
lr.questionStem: The art critic's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats the conditions under which market price is set as sufficient to determine what makes something genuinely valuable

choices.label: B
