choices.text: appealing to an authority in order to settle a disputed empirical question

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two cases to show that they should be treated alike

choices.label: C
choices.text: offering a single instance as a counterexample to a universal claim

choices.label: D
choices.text: distinguishing between two senses of a key term used by an opposing side

choices.label: E
choices.text: inferring a general pattern from a representative sample of cases

explanations.correct: The commentators claim every widely prescribed drug went through large-scale trials first. The physician cites one drug that did not, which is exactly how a counterexample refutes a universal claim.
explanations.A: No authority is cited; the physician offers a factual case, not an expert opinion.
explanations.B: Only one case is discussed; no second case is compared to it.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No term is parsed into distinct senses.
explanations.E: The physician is refuting a generalization, not building one from a sample.

lr.difficultyReason: Single move: the ethicist draws an analogy between two cases. Only (B) describes that operation.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Many people believe that it is wrong to break a promise to a friend but perfectly acceptable to break a promise to a stranger. But a promise to a stranger, like a promise to a friend, creates an expectation in the person to whom the promise is made. Since breaking a promise to a friend is wrong because it violates such an expectation, breaking a promise to a stranger must be wrong for exactly the same reason.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's reasoning proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing empirical evidence to overturn a widely held moral belief

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two cases in order to argue that they should be judged alike

choices.label: C
choices.text: appealing to a definition in order to show that a commonly used term is misapplied

choices.label: D
choices.text: pointing out an internal contradiction in an opposing position

choices.label: E
choices.text: generalizing from a single instance to a broad moral principle

explanations.correct: The ethicist identifies a feature shared by both kinds of promises (creating an expectation) and uses the parallel to argue that the moral verdict must be the same. That is the structure of an argument by analogy.
explanations.A: No empirical evidence is introduced; the argument is conceptual.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No definition of any term is offered.
explanations.D: No contradiction within the opposing view is exposed.
explanations.E: The ethicist does not move from one instance to a broad principle; the principle about expectations is a premise, not a conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: One move: the economist applies a general principle to a specific case to predict an outcome. Only (D) names that operation.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Whenever a government imposes a price ceiling below the market-clearing price for a good, a shortage of that good inevitably develops. The proposed cap on rental prices in our city would set the legal maximum well below the current market rate. So we should expect a shortage of available rental units in our city to follow.
lr.questionStem: The economist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: appealing to a historical example in order to predict a future outcome

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejecting a policy proposal by identifying an unintended benefit

choices.label: C
choices.text: inferring a cause from an observed correlation between two variables

choices.label: D
choices.text: applying a general principle to a particular case in order to predict its consequences

choices.label: E
choices.text: distinguishing between short-term and long-term effects of a policy

explanations.correct: The first sentence states a general principle about price ceilings. The economist then shows that the proposed cap fits the description in that principle and concludes about this particular case.
explanations.A: No specific past episode is cited.
explanations.B: The argument predicts a negative effect (shortage), not a benefit.
explanations.C: No correlation is mentioned; the reasoning is principle-to-case, not statistical.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: No timeframe distinction is drawn.

lr.difficultyReason: One move: the attorney appeals to the testimony of a recognized expert to support a factual claim. Only (A) describes that technique.
lr.stimulus: Attorney: The opposing side claims that the fracture in the victim's wrist could have been caused by a simple fall, not by the defendant's grip. But Dr. Ayala, who has served as head of orthopedic trauma at the regional medical center for over twenty years, has testified that fractures of this precise pattern almost never result from falls and are nearly always the product of direct twisting force. So we should accept that the fracture was caused by a twisting grip rather than by a fall.
lr.questionStem: The attorney's reasoning proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing the testimony of a recognized expert to support a factual claim

choices.label: B
choices.text: offering a counterexample to a broad generalization advanced by opponents

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between the present case and a previously decided one

choices.label: D
choices.text: rejecting an opposing claim by showing that it rests on a contradiction

choices.label: E
choices.text: arguing from the absence of evidence to the truth of a positive claim

explanations.correct: The attorney's sole support for the conclusion is Dr. Ayala's credentials and testimony. That is a textbook appeal to expert authority.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No single case is cited against a universal claim; the argument relies on expert statements, not instances.
explanations.C: No previously decided case is introduced.
explanations.D: The opposing side's position is not shown to contradict itself.
explanations.E: The attorney relies on positive expert testimony, not on a gap in evidence.

lr.difficultyReason: One move: the ecologist offers an alternative explanation for an observed decline. Only (E) describes that operation.
lr.stimulus: Ecologist: Some researchers have argued that the recent decline in the population of native songbirds in our region must be due to increased pesticide use on nearby farms. But there is another possibility that deserves serious consideration: over the same period, the population of feral house cats in the region has more than doubled, and feral cats are well-documented predators of songbirds.
lr.questionStem: The ecologist responds to the researchers' argument by

choices.label: A
choices.text: offering an alternative explanation for the phenomenon the researchers have identified

choices.label: B
choices.text: denying that the phenomenon the researchers describe has actually occurred

choices.label: C
choices.text: pointing out that the researchers' evidence is drawn from an unrepresentative sample

choices.label: D
choices.text: showing that the researchers' conclusion contradicts another of their own claims

choices.label: E
choices.text: citing a counterexample that undermines the researchers' general principle

explanations.correct: The ecologist accepts that the songbird population has declined and that it needs explaining, but proposes cat predation as a rival cause to pesticide use. That is an alternative-explanation move.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The ecologist does not dispute the decline.
explanations.C: Sample representativeness is not challenged.
explanations.D: No contradiction within the researchers' position is identified.
explanations.E: The ecologist does not refute a universal claim with a single instance; the move is to supply a competing cause.

lr.difficultyReason: One move: the engineer distinguishes between two cases the critic has treated as equivalent. Only (C) names that technique.
lr.stimulus: Software engineer: Critics of our new messaging platform argue that because our earlier video-conferencing product suffered from frequent connection failures, the new platform will suffer from similar problems. But the earlier product relied on a centralized server architecture, whereas the new messaging platform uses a peer-to-peer architecture in which no single server's failure can disrupt communication. The critics' inference therefore does not go through.
lr.questionStem: The software engineer's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: rejecting a claim by showing that accepting it leads to absurd consequences

choices.label: B
choices.text: conceding a critic's premise while denying that the conclusion follows from it alone

choices.label: C
choices.text: distinguishing between two cases in order to show that a comparison between them is unwarranted

choices.label: D
choices.text: citing statistical evidence to undermine an anecdotal generalization

choices.label: E
choices.text: offering a definition that shows a key term has been misapplied

explanations.correct: The critics lump the two products together. The engineer's entire move is to identify a relevant difference in architecture that breaks the analogy the critics rely on.
explanations.A: No reductio-style absurdity is derived.
explanations.B: The engineer does not concede the critics' analogy; he rejects it outright by showing the cases differ.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No statistics are introduced.
explanations.E: No definitional move is made.

lr.difficultyReason: One clean move: the linguist appeals to a definition to argue that a term has been misapplied. Only (B) describes that technique.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Commentators in the popular press routinely describe the way young people use the word "literally" as a grammatical error. But a grammatical error is, by definition, a violation of the structural rules governing word order and inflection in a language. The pattern in question involves neither word order nor inflection; it is simply a shift in the meaning speakers attach to a particular word. So whatever else one may say about it, it is not a grammatical error.
lr.questionStem: The linguist's reasoning proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing empirical data about usage to refute a prescriptive claim

choices.label: B
choices.text: appealing to a definition in order to show that a term has been misapplied

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy to a parallel case in another language

choices.label: D
choices.text: identifying an unstated assumption in an opposing argument and rejecting it

choices.label: E
choices.text: generalizing from several instances to a rule about a broad class of cases

explanations.correct: The linguist offers a definition of "grammatical error" and then argues that the phenomenon the commentators describe does not fall under it. That is an appeal to definition to show misapplication of a term.
explanations.A: No usage data or statistics are invoked.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No second language or parallel case appears.
explanations.D: The linguist doesn't surface a hidden assumption; she relies on the meaning of a term.
explanations.E: The argument moves from a definition to a case, not from instances to a rule.

lr.difficultyReason: One move: the historian supports a general claim by generalizing from representative cases. Only (D) describes that operation.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Nearly every major technological transition in the past three centuries — the shift from water power to steam, from steam to electricity, and from electricity to electronics — was accompanied by a substantial, if temporary, rise in unemployment in the industries being displaced. Given this consistent pattern, it is reasonable to expect that major technological transitions in general will be accompanied by similar temporary unemployment.
lr.questionStem: The historian's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: distinguishing between short-term effects and long-term effects of a single trend

choices.label: B
choices.text: applying a general principle to a particular case in order to predict an outcome

choices.label: C
choices.text: rejecting an opposing explanation by offering a competing one

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizing from a series of cases that exhibit a common pattern

choices.label: E
choices.text: citing an authoritative source to support a contested empirical claim

explanations.correct: The historian lists several past technological transitions, notes that each shared a feature, and on that basis extends the pattern to technological transitions as a class.
explanations.A: No long-term effect is contrasted with a short-term one; the argument is about the general pattern.
explanations.B: The move runs the other direction: from cases to a general expectation, not from a principle to a case.
explanations.C: No opposing explanation is rejected.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: No authority is cited.

lr.difficultyReason: One clear move: the policy analyst rejects a proposal by showing that the principle behind it leads to an absurd consequence. Only (E) describes that technique.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: The council has proposed requiring background checks before anyone may buy any item that could conceivably be used to harm another person. But the principle behind this proposal — that we should screen purchasers of anything that could conceivably be used to cause harm — would equally require us to screen buyers of kitchen knives, garden shears, heavy hammers, and even rolls of duct tape. Clearly, then, the proposal cannot be accepted as it stands.
lr.questionStem: The policy analyst's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: offering a counterexample that falsifies a universal empirical claim

choices.label: B
choices.text: appealing to expert testimony to cast doubt on a legislative proposal

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between the proposal and a successful policy in another jurisdiction

choices.label: D
choices.text: distinguishing between two categories of items that the proposal fails to separate

choices.label: E
choices.text: rejecting a proposal by showing that the principle behind it has unacceptable consequences

explanations.correct: The analyst extracts the principle implicit in the proposal, shows that applying it consistently would require screening kitchen knives and duct tape, and treats that outcome as reason to reject the proposal. That is the structure of a reductio-style objection.
explanations.A: The claim being attacked is a policy recommendation, not a universal empirical claim.
explanations.B: No expert is cited.
explanations.C: No other jurisdiction's policy is introduced.
explanations.D: The analyst lumps items together to embarrass the proposal rather than distinguishing categories within it.
explanations.E: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: One move: the curator draws a conclusion about an individual work from a general claim about a class it belongs to. Only (A) describes that technique.
lr.stimulus: Curator: Every painting produced by the Delft workshop during the 1660s was executed on a panel of oak imported from the Baltic region. The small landscape that has just been donated to our museum was, as our own laboratory has confirmed, produced by the Delft workshop during the 1660s. So the panel on which it was painted must be Baltic oak.
lr.questionStem: The curator's reasoning proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: applying a generalization about a class of objects to a particular member of that class

choices.label: B
choices.text: inferring a general claim about a class of objects from information about one of its members

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two objects in order to argue that they share a feature

choices.label: D
choices.text: citing expert testimony to resolve a disagreement about a historical fact

choices.label: E
choices.text: rejecting a hypothesis about an object by appealing to a counterexample

explanations.correct: The curator starts from a general statement about every painting produced by the Delft workshop in the 1660s, identifies the donated painting as a member of that class, and concludes that it must have the property the generalization ascribes to the class.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The argument runs in the opposite direction — from a generalization to a particular case.
explanations.C: No second object is introduced for comparison.
explanations.D: The laboratory's confirmation establishes membership in the class but is not used to resolve a dispute about a historical fact.
explanations.E: No hypothesis is being refuted; the curator is establishing, not refuting, a claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-move argument using an analogy. The physician draws a parallel between two medical scenarios. Only one answer choice correctly names the analogical reasoning; other choices describe techniques the argument does not employ.
lr.stimulus: Physician: When a patient has a bacterial infection and we prescribe antibiotics, we expect the infection to clear within days. Similarly, when a patient develops an autoimmune condition, we should expect that targeted immunosuppressants will resolve the condition quickly. The logic is the same: a targeted intervention addresses the root cause.
lr.questionStem: The physician's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: argues from a sample of medical cases to a generalization about all patients

choices.label: B
choices.text: cites an authority in medicine to support a claim about treatment outcomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws an analogy between two medical scenarios to support a conclusion about one of them

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers that because one treatment works, a different treatment will work for another condition

choices.label: E
choices.text: bases a prediction on a statistical comparison of disease outcomes

explanations.correct: The physician compares the bacterial-infection case (where antibiotics work quickly) to the autoimmune-condition case and applies the same logic. That is analogical reasoning: drawing a parallel to support a claim about one case using evidence about another.
explanations.A: The argument does not move from several cases to a general rule about all patients; it compares two specific types of cases.
explanations.B: No medical authority is cited; the physician reasons about the logic of the interventions.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: This slightly mischaracterizes the analogy. The physician argues the treatments are similar in structure, not just that different treatments will work.
explanations.E: No statistical data about disease outcomes is presented.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-move argument applying a definition. The ethicist relies on a stated definition of 'theft' to classify an action. Only one answer describes this definitional application; others describe unrelated techniques.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Theft is the unauthorized taking of another's property with intent to deprive that person of it. An employee who takes office supplies home without permission is committing theft under this definition, regardless of the minimal value of the items.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: appealing to a definition to determine whether a particular action falls under a given category

choices.label: B
choices.text: citing a counterexample to show that a general rule does not always apply

choices.label: C
choices.text: reasoning from the harmlessness of an action to the conclusion that it is not unethical

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizing from one workplace norm to a universal principle

choices.label: E
choices.text: inferring the intent of an agent from the consequences of the agent's action

explanations.correct: The ethicist states a definition of theft and applies it to the case of office supplies, determining that the employee's action meets the definition's criteria. This is definitional application.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No counterexample is offered; the argument supports a position rather than attacking one.
explanations.C: The ethicist does not argue from harmlessness; instead, the minimal value is irrelevant to meeting the definition.
explanations.D: No workplace norm is generalized; the argument applies a stated definition.
explanations.E: The ethicist takes intent as a given element of the definition, not inferred from consequences.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-move argument using a counterexample to refute a universal claim. The linguist provides a single case that contradicts the claim. Only one answer correctly names the counterexample technique; others describe irrelevant moves.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Some have claimed that all languages must have a word for the color red. However, the Pirahã language of the Amazon basin famously has no single term for red; speakers instead use phrases that reference the brightness of fire or blood. This counterexample shows the claim is false.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following describes a technique of reasoning used in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: generalizes from a single linguistic example to a broad principle

choices.label: B
choices.text: cites a counterexample to a universal claim to show the claim is not always true

choices.label: C
choices.text: argues that a language is deficient because it lacks a common word

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers the structure of a language from the structure of its speakers' natural environment

choices.label: E
choices.text: appeals to the authority of linguistic experts to support a conclusion

explanations.correct: The linguist directly cites Pirahã as a case that violates the universal claim ('all languages must have a word for red'). This is textbook counterexample reasoning: one true instance that falsifies a universal statement.
explanations.A: The argument works in the opposite direction: it uses a specific example to refute a general claim, not to support one.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The linguist does not evaluate the Pirahã language as deficient; the existence of an alternative expression is the point.
explanations.D: No inference about language structure from environment is made.
explanations.E: No appeal to expert authority; the linguist reasons from a publicly acknowledged fact about Pirahã.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-move argument applying a general principle to a specific case. The economist states a principle about inflation and applies it to a particular economy. Only one answer correctly describes this application; others describe unrelated techniques.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Whenever a central bank rapidly increases the money supply without a corresponding increase in goods and services, inflation results. The Central Reserve increased the money supply by 8 percent last year while gross domestic product grew only 2 percent. Therefore, we should expect significant inflation in the coming months.
lr.questionStem: The economist's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: cites a historical precedent to predict a future economic outcome

choices.label: B
choices.text: applies a general economic principle to a particular situation to support a specific prediction

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers a causal relationship from a correlation between two economic variables

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizes from the economic policies of one nation to the policies of all nations

choices.label: E
choices.text: argues that rapid money supply growth will always cause inflation without exception

explanations.correct: The economist first states a general principle (rapid money-supply increases without corresponding output growth cause inflation), then applies it to a concrete case (the Central Reserve's recent actions), concluding inflation will result. That is principle-to-case application.
explanations.A: No historical precedent is cited; the argument uses a general principle.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The argument does not infer causation from observed correlation; it applies an already-established principle.
explanations.D: No generalization across nations is made; the principle applies universally but the application is to one specific case.
explanations.E: The principle allows for some exceptions in principle; the argument claims the condition is met in this case.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-move argument citing expert authority. The environmental scientist appeals to expert consensus to support a conclusion. Only one answer correctly names the appeal-to-authority technique; others describe unrelated moves.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientist: The overwhelming consensus among climate scientists worldwide is that anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions are driving rapid global warming. Given the expertise and rigor of the scientific consensus, we should adjust our environmental policies accordingly.
lr.questionStem: The scientist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: cites the consensus of expert opinion to support a claim about environmental policy

choices.label: B
choices.text: generalizes from climate patterns in one region to predictions about global climate

choices.label: C
choices.text: argues that a policy will succeed because it aligns with majority opinion

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers a causal mechanism from observations of statistical correlation

choices.label: E
choices.text: rejects a competing theory by showing it contradicts established scientific law

explanations.correct: The scientist explicitly cites the consensus view of climate experts as a basis for accepting the claim about anthropogenic warming and making policy recommendations. This is a direct appeal to expert authority.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No regional data or generalization to global climate is presented; the argument cites scientific consensus.
explanations.C: Majority opinion is not invoked; the argument appeals to expert consensus specifically.
explanations.D: No causal inference from correlation is drawn; the consensus is treated as authoritative.
explanations.E: No competing theory is explicitly rejected; the argument appeals to the positive consensus view.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-move argument drawing an analogy between a hypothetical case and a real policy. The policy analyst compares two governance structures. Only one answer correctly names analogical reasoning; others describe unrelated techniques.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: Allowing corporations to self-regulate environmental standards is like hiring a student to grade their own exam. In both cases, the evaluator has a direct incentive to report a favorable outcome, undermining the integrity of the assessment. Therefore, corporations cannot be trusted to enforce their own environmental standards.
lr.questionStem: The analyst's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: argues from a generalization about academic practices to a conclusion about corporate behavior

choices.label: B
choices.text: uses an analogy to suggest that a policy is flawed because a parallel situation is obviously problematic

choices.label: C
choices.text: cites empirical evidence that corporations have failed to regulate themselves

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers a causal mechanism that explains corporate noncompliance with standards

choices.label: E
choices.text: applies a principle about conflicts of interest to the specific case of corporate regulation

explanations.correct: The analyst draws a parallel between self-grading (clearly problematic) and self-regulation (the policy in question). The analogy illustrates why the policy is flawed: both involve conflicted evaluators with incentives to report favorably.
explanations.A: This is an analogy, not a generalization from academic practices to corporate behavior per se.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No empirical evidence of past corporate failures is cited.
explanations.D: The causal mechanism (incentive misalignment) is explained through the analogy, not inferred independently.
explanations.E: While a principle about conflicts of interest is implicit, the reasoning is fundamentally analogical, not principle-based.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-move argument using a counterexample. The historian provides a historical case that contradicts a claim about law. Only one answer correctly names the counterexample technique; others describe unrelated reasoning moves.
lr.stimulus: Historian: It is sometimes claimed that common law systems always protect individual rights more effectively than civil law systems. However, several civil law countries, including Portugal and Spain, have robust constitutional protections for individual freedoms. This shows the claim is too broad.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following describes a technique of reasoning used in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: generalizes from two civil law systems to a conclusion about all civil law systems

choices.label: B
choices.text: cites concrete historical examples to refute a universal claim about legal systems

choices.label: C
choices.text: argues that civil law is superior to common law based on a comparison of protections

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers that because two countries share a legal tradition, they have identical rights protections

choices.label: E
choices.text: applies a principle from constitutional theory to evaluate competing legal systems

explanations.correct: The historian provides concrete historical examples (Portugal and Spain) that contradict the universal claim that common law always protects rights more effectively. These are counterexamples: specific instances that show the claim is false.
explanations.A: While two examples are cited, the reasoning is not a generalization; it is a refutation of a universal claim using counterexamples.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The argument does not establish civil law superiority; it only shows the original claim is too broad.
explanations.D: No such inference is made; the examples are cited to refute a claim, not to compare countries within a tradition.
explanations.E: No abstract principle is applied; the argument relies on historical facts.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-move argument applying a definition to resolve a dispute. The lawyer uses a legal definition to classify a contract term. Only one answer correctly describes definitional application; others describe unrelated techniques.
lr.stimulus: Lawyer: A contract is unconscionable if one party had no meaningful choice and the terms unreasonably favor the other party. This employment contract requires workers to waive all legal claims in exchange for continued employment, and most workers have no realistic alternative employment. Therefore, the contract is unconscionable under the legal definition.
lr.questionStem: The lawyer's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: establishes a causal link between a contractual term and economic harm

choices.label: B
choices.text: applies a legal definition to determine whether a contract meets the criteria for a particular classification

choices.label: C
choices.text: cites precedent from prior cases to support a conclusion about the current contract

choices.label: D
choices.text: argues that the workers would have rejected the contract if they had been fully informed

choices.label: E
choices.text: infers the intent of the employer from the restrictive language of the contract

explanations.correct: The lawyer states the legal definition of unconscionability and applies it point by point to the contract: lack of meaningful choice (workers have no alternatives) and unreasonably favorable terms (broad waiver of legal claims). This is definitional application to determine classification.
explanations.A: The argument does not establish a causal mechanism; it applies a definition.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No case precedent is cited.
explanations.D: The argument does not counterfactually speculate about worker preferences; it applies a legal standard.
explanations.E: The employer's intent is not inferred; the definition focuses on the situation and terms, not intent.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-move argument using an analogy between two technological systems. The engineer draws a parallel to support a design claim. Only one answer correctly names analogical reasoning; others describe unrelated techniques.
lr.stimulus: Engineer: The redundancy in airplane engine design has proven invaluable for safety: if one engine fails, the aircraft can still reach its destination. Similarly, data storage systems with redundant backups protect against catastrophic loss. Therefore, critical software systems should be designed with redundant components.
lr.questionStem: The engineer's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: generalizes from the success of redundancy in aviation to the success of redundancy in all systems

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws an analogy between two systems with redundant design to support a recommendation for a third

choices.label: C
choices.text: cites statistical evidence that redundancy improves system reliability

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers that because two technologies are similar in one respect, they are similar in all respects

choices.label: E
choices.text: argues that redundant systems are always more expensive but worth the cost

explanations.correct: The engineer compares airplane engines (redundancy works for safety) and data storage (redundancy prevents loss) to support a conclusion about software systems. This is analogical reasoning: using parallel cases to support a recommendation.
explanations.A: The analogy is limited to two successful examples; it does not overgeneralize to all systems.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No statistical data is presented.
explanations.D: The argument identifies a specific parallel (redundancy benefit), not a claim of similarity in all respects.
explanations.E: Cost is not addressed; the argument focuses on the benefit of redundancy.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-move argument citing expert opinion. The music critic appeals to the judgment of experienced musicians. Only one answer correctly names the appeal-to-authority technique; others describe unrelated reasoning moves.
lr.stimulus: Music critic: Professional conductors and orchestral musicians consistently regard the symphonies of Mahler as among the most challenging to perform well. Given the expertise of these musicians, their assessment should inform our understanding of Mahler's compositional complexity. Therefore, Mahler's work demonstrates extraordinary technical mastery.
lr.questionStem: The critic's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: cites the judgment of experienced practitioners to support a claim about artistic achievement

choices.label: B
choices.text: generalizes from the difficulty of Mahler's work to a universal principle about musical complexity

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers that if musicians find a work difficult, the composer intended it to be difficult

choices.label: D
choices.text: argues that a work is great because performers struggle with it

choices.label: E
choices.text: draws an analogy between Mahler's symphonies and other challenging musical compositions

explanations.correct: The critic appeals to the consistent judgment of professional musicians (conductors and orchestral musicians) as evidence supporting the claim about Mahler's technical mastery. This is an appeal to expert authority.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The argument cites expert judgment, not a generalization from specific cases to a universal rule.
explanations.C: No inference about the composer's intentions is made.
explanations.D: The argument does not equate difficulty with greatness; it uses difficulty as evidence of mastery.
explanations.E: No analogy to other compositions is drawn; the argument cites expert consensus about Mahler alone.

lr.difficultyReason: One-move argument: the physician applies a general medical principle to a specific patient case. Only the correct answer describes this application; the others describe techniques the argument clearly does not employ.
lr.stimulus: Physician: Chronic inflammation is known to be a precursor to many serious diseases, including heart disease and diabetes. My patient has been suffering from chronic inflammation for over a year. Therefore, my patient is at elevated risk for developing serious disease.
lr.questionStem: The physician's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: generalizes from a single patient's medical history to a claim about all patients with inflammation

choices.label: B
choices.text: applies a general principle about a medical condition to a specific case involving that condition

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers that a patient's disease will progress based on the rate of progression in comparable cases

choices.label: D
choices.text: rejects a diagnosis by showing it is inconsistent with established medical evidence

choices.label: E
choices.text: predicts future symptoms based on past patterns of disease development

explanations.correct: The physician states a general principle (chronic inflammation precedes serious disease) and applies it directly to this specific patient. This is exactly what B describes.
explanations.A: The argument does not generalize from this one patient to all patients; it moves in the opposite direction—from a universal principle to a particular case.
explanations.C: The argument does not cite comparable cases or their rates of progression; it applies a known medical relationship.
explanations.D: The argument is not rejecting any diagnosis; it is assessing risk based on a known medical principle.
explanations.E: The argument does not predict specific future symptoms; it assesses risk level based on a general principle.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: One-move argument: the economist cites a counterexample to a universal economic claim. The correct answer plainly describes this move; the others mischaracterize the reasoning strategy.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Some people argue that market deregulation always leads to efficiency gains. However, the telecommunications industry was significantly deregulated in the 1990s, yet service quality in rural areas actually declined. This shows the universal claim cannot be correct.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following describes the technique of reasoning used in the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: cites a single counterexample to refute a universal claim

choices.label: B
choices.text: argues that a policy is ineffective by comparing outcomes in different regions

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrates that deregulation causes efficiency losses by analyzing market data

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizes from a historical case to predict outcomes in future deregulation efforts

choices.label: E
choices.text: appeals to expert opinion in order to challenge a popular belief about markets

explanations.correct: The economist cites the telecommunications deregulation case—where efficiency did not improve—as a counterexample to the claim that deregulation always produces efficiency gains. This directly falsifies the universal claim, which is what A describes.
explanations.B: The argument is not comparing different regions; it is using one historical case to challenge a universal principle.
explanations.C: The argument does not analyze market data systematically; it points to one outcome that contradicts the universal claim.
explanations.D: The argument uses a past case to reject a universal claim, not to predict future outcomes.
explanations.E: The argument does not appeal to expert authority; it cites a factual case.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: One-move argument: the environmental scientist draws an analogy between two ecosystems. The correct answer plainly describes this analogical move; the others describe different reasoning techniques not employed.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientist: In the Amazon rainforest, the loss of canopy cover led to soil degradation and a cascading collapse of the ecosystem. The boreal forests of Siberia have a similar structure and climate sensitivity. If canopy loss occurs in Siberia, we should expect comparable ecological damage.
lr.questionStem: The scientist's reasoning proceeds by which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two ecosystems to infer that a process in one will have similar effects in the other

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that all forest ecosystems are vulnerable to the same environmental stressors

choices.label: C
choices.text: predicting future ecological change based on the rate of change observed in the Amazon

choices.label: D
choices.text: inferring the cause of ecosystem collapse by comparing outcomes in two regions

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to the structural similarity of two systems to establish a causal law

explanations.correct: The scientist identifies key similarities between the Amazon and Siberian forests and uses the known outcome in the Amazon to predict an analogous outcome in Siberia. This is the definition of analogical reasoning, which A captures exactly.
explanations.B: The argument is about two specific ecosystems, not a universal claim about all forests.
explanations.C: The argument does not extrapolate a rate of change; it draws an analogy based on structural and climatic similarity.
explanations.D: The cause of collapse in the Amazon is already established (canopy loss); the argument uses this to predict effects in Siberia, not to infer causes.
explanations.E: The scientist is not establishing a universal causal law; she is drawing a specific analogy between two systems.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: One-move argument: the attorney appeals to a definition to establish a legal conclusion. The correct answer clearly describes this definitional move; other choices describe inference patterns the argument does not follow.
lr.stimulus: Attorney: Under the statute, a contract is enforceable only if both parties agreed to all material terms. In this dispute, the plaintiff and defendant never agreed on the price term, which is clearly material. Therefore, the contract cannot be enforceable.
lr.questionStem: The attorney's argument derives its conclusion by which one of the following methods?

choices.label: A
choices.text: applying a statutory definition of enforceability to the facts of the case

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that a contract will fail because prior agreements were not properly documented

choices.label: C
choices.text: inferring that the price term was material because the parties did not agree on it

choices.label: D
choices.text: reasoning from the absence of a written agreement to the conclusion that a contract never existed

choices.label: E
choices.text: establishing that a dispute arose due to disagreement over material contract terms

explanations.correct: The attorney cites the statutory definition (enforceability requires agreement on all material terms), identifies that a material term was not agreed upon, and applies the definition to conclude the contract is unenforceable. This is application of a definition to case facts, which A describes.
explanations.B: The argument is not about documentation; it is about the absence of agreement on a material term.
explanations.C: The attorney does not infer that the price is material because there was disagreement; she asserts that price is materially important and notes the parties did not agree on it.
explanations.D: The argument is about enforceability, not the existence of the contract.
explanations.E: The argument is not explaining why a dispute arose; it is determining the legal enforceability of a contract.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: One-move argument: the linguist cites linguistic research as an authority. The correct answer plainly names this appeal to authority; the others describe alternative reasoning moves not present in the stimulus.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Some claim that spoken language is inherently superior to written language. However, recent research in psycholinguistics demonstrates that written language activates different but equally sophisticated cognitive processes. This research undermines the claim that spoken language has any inherent superiority.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following describes a technique of reasoning used in the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: appeals to empirical research to challenge a claim about the relative merits of two language forms

choices.label: B
choices.text: argues that written language is more complex than spoken language by citing specific examples

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizes from research subjects to all speakers of a language

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers that cognitive sophistication is equally distributed across both language modalities

choices.label: E
choices.text: reasons that because the two language forms are different, they must be equally effective

explanations.correct: The linguist cites empirical research (a form of authority/evidence) showing that written language involves sophisticated cognitive processes, and uses this to undermine the claim that spoken language is inherently superior. This is an appeal to research to challenge a claim, exactly as A states.
explanations.B: The argument does not claim written language is more complex; it says both forms involve sophisticated processes.
explanations.C: The argument refers to research findings, not a generalization from specific subjects to an entire population.
explanations.D: The argument does not argue for equal distribution of sophistication; it only notes that both forms activate sophisticated processes.
explanations.E: The argument is not based on difference implying equivalence; it cites research evidence.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: One-move argument: the ethicist cites a counterexample to a universal ethical principle. The correct answer clearly describes this move; the others mischaracterize the reasoning structure or content.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Some philosophers claim that keeping promises is always a moral obligation with no exceptions. Yet consider a case where a promise was made under duress to a person who intends to cause serious harm. Keeping such a promise would enable that harm. Clearly, the universal claim about promises cannot be correct.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's argument proceeds by which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: showing that moral obligations sometimes conflict by constructing a hypothetical case

choices.label: B
choices.text: using a specific example to demonstrate that a universal moral principle admits of exceptions

choices.label: C
choices.text: arguing that promises made under duress should never be kept

choices.label: D
choices.text: appealing to the intuition that preventing harm is always more important than keeping promises

choices.label: E
choices.text: establishing that duress nullifies moral responsibility for any action

explanations.correct: The ethicist constructs a specific example (a promise made under duress to someone planning harm) and uses it to show that the universal claim 'keeping promises is always a moral obligation with no exceptions' cannot be correct. This exemplifies using a counterexample to show a universal principle has exceptions, which B describes.
explanations.A: The argument is not primarily about conflicts between obligations; it is about exceptions to one principle.
explanations.C: The ethicist does not conclude that such promises should never be kept; she only shows the universal rule has exceptions.
explanations.D: The ethicist does not appeal to an intuition; she constructs a logical counterexample.
explanations.E: The argument does not establish a rule about duress and moral responsibility in general; it shows one universal principle has exceptions.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-move argument: the historian first undermines a general claim with a counterexample, then advances an alternative explanation. The correct answer must capture both moves; traps describe only one.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Many scholars maintain that the printing press was the principal cause of the Reformation's rapid spread across Europe. But the Waldensian movement spread widely across the same regions three centuries earlier, entirely by hand-copied manuscripts and itinerant preachers. A better explanation for the Reformation's reach, then, is the dense network of lay preachers already connecting parishes long before any press was built.
lr.questionStem: The historian's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing a historical case that conflicts with a widely accepted explanation and then proposing a different explanation in its place

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that because two phenomena share a feature, they must share a cause

choices.label: C
choices.text: rejecting an explanation solely on the ground that its proponents have a vested interest in defending it

choices.label: D
choices.text: showing that an explanation is self-contradictory and therefore cannot be true

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to expert consensus in order to settle a disputed historical question

explanations.correct: The historian invokes the Waldensian movement as a counterexample that undercuts the printing-press explanation, then offers the preacher-network as an alternative. A captures both moves.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No shared-feature-to-shared-cause inference is made; the Waldensian case is used against an explanation, not to infer causal identity.
explanations.C: The historian never attacks the motives of the scholars, only their explanation.
explanations.D: The printing-press explanation is shown to be insufficient, not internally contradictory.
explanations.E: No expert consensus is cited; the historian pushes back against the prevailing view.

lr.difficultyReason: The physician both questions whether the reported data actually support a causal claim and offers a competing mechanism. Traps describe only the critique or only the alternative.
lr.stimulus:
Columnist: A recent study reports that adults who take a daily multivitamin have fewer colds per year than those who do not, and concludes that the multivitamin strengthens the immune response.
Physician: The study surveyed only people who already took multivitamins voluntarily. Such people also tend to exercise, sleep more regularly, and eat more fresh produce. The apparent benefit is more plausibly attributed to those habits than to the vitamin itself.
lr.questionStem: The physician responds to the columnist by

choices.label: A
choices.text: identifying a feature of the study's sample that undermines its causal conclusion and offering an alternative explanation for the reported correlation

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that the study's authors have falsified their data in order to promote a product

choices.label: C
choices.text: denying that any correlation between multivitamin use and cold frequency exists

choices.label: D
choices.text: showing that the columnist's conclusion rests on an ambiguous definition of 'immune response'

choices.label: E
choices.text: generalizing from personal clinical experience to reject a finding supported by quantitative research

explanations.correct: The physician points to a sampling problem (self-selection) that weakens the causal claim and then supplies a rival cause. Both moves are captured by A.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No accusation of fabrication is made.
explanations.C: The correlation itself is accepted; what is challenged is the causal reading.
explanations.D: No ambiguity in terminology is raised.
explanations.E: The physician cites patterns in the study population, not personal clinical anecdotes.

lr.difficultyReason: The ethicist uses a hypothetical variant to show that an opposing principle produces an unacceptable verdict, then endorses a rival principle. Traps isolate only the hypothetical or only the endorsement.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Some argue that any act done to produce a greater overall good is thereby justified. But suppose a surgeon could save five patients by harvesting the organs of one unwilling donor who walked into the clinic. Few would accept that the surgeon acts rightly. A more adequate principle, then, is that even acts that maximize good are impermissible when they treat a person merely as a resource.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: presenting a hypothetical case whose implications conflict with one principle and offering a revised principle that better accommodates them

choices.label: B
choices.text: defending a familiar moral principle by deducing it from more basic axioms

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between medical ethics and ordinary commercial transactions

choices.label: D
choices.text: citing statistical evidence about public attitudes toward organ donation

choices.label: E
choices.text: claiming that a principle is false because it is not universally followed

explanations.correct: The surgeon hypothetical functions as a counterexample to the maximizing-good principle; the ethicist then proposes a revised principle. A captures this combined maneuver.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: There is no deduction from more basic axioms; the argument is driven by a counterexample.
explanations.C: No analogy with commerce is drawn.
explanations.D: No statistics are invoked; the ethicist appeals to what 'few would accept,' not polling data.
explanations.E: The principle is rejected as producing wrong verdicts, not as being unfollowed in practice.

lr.difficultyReason: The economist both denies a causal inference drawn from a correlation and supplies a mechanism that fits the data equally well. Traps describe only the denial or only the alternative.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Commentators frequently claim that minimum-wage increases cause long-term unemployment among teenagers, pointing to the fact that teenage joblessness has risen in several states shortly after such increases. But teenage labor-force participation in those same states declined as school enrollment grew, which on its own would raise measured unemployment. The rise in joblessness is better explained by shifting educational patterns than by the wage policy.
lr.questionStem: The economist's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: challenges a causal claim about an observed trend by identifying a separate factor that would produce the same trend

choices.label: B
choices.text: concedes that a policy had the effects attributed to it, but argues that those effects were worth the cost

choices.label: C
choices.text: appeals to a general economic principle and applies it to a specific policy question

choices.label: D
choices.text: argues that because a policy has one beneficial effect, it must have no harmful effects

choices.label: E
choices.text: attacks a conclusion by questioning the credentials of those who proposed it

explanations.correct: The economist concedes the rise in joblessness but denies the causal link to minimum-wage policy by pointing to a confounding factor (enrollment-driven drops in participation) that would yield the same statistic. A captures this technique.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No concession about minimum-wage effects is made; the economist denies those effects.
explanations.C: No general principle is cited or applied; the argument works through a specific competing cause.
explanations.D: The economist does not argue that minimum-wage policy is wholly benign.
explanations.E: No ad hominem is offered.

lr.difficultyReason: The law professor first distinguishes two kinds of cases, then applies the distinction to defeat a proposed rule. Traps describe only the distinction or only the conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Law professor: It is sometimes said that judges should never rely on unpublished decisions. But a judge may rely on an unpublished decision either as binding precedent or merely as persuasive reasoning. When treated as binding, the decision controls outcomes other courts have never had a chance to scrutinize; when treated as persuasive, it is simply one more source of argument. So the blanket prohibition is unwarranted: only reliance of the first kind raises the concerns critics actually cite.
lr.questionStem: The law professor's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: drawing a distinction between two uses of a practice and arguing that the objection to the practice applies only to one of them

choices.label: B
choices.text: showing that a proposed rule would produce an outcome the critics themselves would condemn

choices.label: C
choices.text: rejecting a rule on the ground that it has never been adopted in any jurisdiction

choices.label: D
choices.text: identifying an ambiguity in a legal term and concluding that the term should be abandoned

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to an analogy between legal practice and scientific experimentation

explanations.correct: The professor separates 'binding' from 'persuasive' reliance, then argues the critics' worry applies only to the first, so a blanket ban is too broad. A captures both moves.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No reductio targeting critics is developed; the professor analyzes the critics' concern rather than turning it on them.
explanations.C: Adoption history is not cited.
explanations.D: The term 'unpublished decision' is not treated as ambiguous; two ways of relying on it are distinguished.
explanations.E: No analogy to science is made.

lr.difficultyReason: The ecologist concedes a premise of the opposing view but argues it does not support the recommended conclusion, and then proposes a different policy consistent with the same evidence.
lr.stimulus: Ecologist: Conservationists urge that, since the population of the spotted salamander has fallen sharply across the region, logging in the adjacent forest should be halted. It is true that the population has fallen. But the decline tracks almost perfectly with the loss of breeding pools well away from logging sites. Limiting logging would do little for the salamander; restoring those pools would do a great deal more.
lr.questionStem: The ecologist's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: accepts the factual claim on which an argument is based but denies that it supports the recommended policy, and advances a different policy better supported by the same evidence

choices.label: B
choices.text: disputes the reliability of data cited by an opponent and proposes collecting better data before any policy is set

choices.label: C
choices.text: argues that a proposed policy, though well-intentioned, would actually accelerate the problem it aims to solve

choices.label: D
choices.text: concludes that because two policies address the same problem, both should be implemented simultaneously

choices.label: E
choices.text: derives a general principle about species decline from a single local case

explanations.correct: The ecologist grants the decline but denies that logging restrictions are warranted by it, substituting pool restoration. A captures concede-then-redirect.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The population data are accepted, not impugned.
explanations.C: There is no claim that halting logging would worsen matters.
explanations.D: The argument rejects one policy in favor of another, not both.
explanations.E: No general principle about species decline is offered; the reasoning is specific to this case.

lr.difficultyReason: The engineer rejects an analogy as misleading and replaces it with a more apt one. Traps isolate one half of the move or invert the direction.
lr.stimulus: Engineer: Critics compare self-driving cars to commercial aircraft, claiming that, since aviation autopilot has had decades to mature, self-driving systems will require equally long timelines before they are safe. But aircraft operate in sparse, highly regulated airspace, while cars share crowded roads with unpredictable human drivers. A closer comparison is to industrial robotics, where machines learned to work safely alongside people only through extensive real-world co-operation, not merely through internal refinement.
lr.questionStem: The engineer's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: rejecting a comparison on the basis of a relevant dissimilarity and substituting a different comparison that the engineer regards as more apt

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that because two technologies share a feature, predictions about one apply to the other

choices.label: C
choices.text: claiming that critics of self-driving cars have a financial stake in delaying their deployment

choices.label: D
choices.text: using a mathematical model of risk to establish a precise timeline

choices.label: E
choices.text: conceding that self-driving cars are unsafe and arguing that they should be banned

explanations.correct: The engineer points out that aviation and driving environments differ in ways that break the analogy, then proposes industrial robotics as a better match. A captures the replace-analogy technique.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The argument denies that aviation and cars share the relevant features; it does not transfer predictions on that basis.
explanations.C: No ad hominem is made.
explanations.D: No quantitative model is introduced.
explanations.E: The engineer implies self-driving cars can become safe, not that they should be banned.

lr.difficultyReason: The linguist disputes a definition-based claim by producing a counterexample and then offers a refined criterion. Both moves must be captured; traps name only one.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Some grammarians define a 'pidgin' as any simplified language formed from contact between speakers of different tongues. On that definition, the contact variety used by sign-language interpreters would count as a pidgin, yet it plainly is not. What distinguishes a pidgin is not simplification but the lack of native speakers for whom it is a first language.
lr.questionStem: The linguist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: offering a case that a proposed definition wrongly classifies and then introducing a different criterion that avoids the misclassification

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that because a term is used loosely in everyday speech, it should not be defined at all

choices.label: C
choices.text: establishing a general claim about language change from a single example

choices.label: D
choices.text: showing that two definitions of a term are logically equivalent

choices.label: E
choices.text: conceding a definition but arguing that it applies to fewer cases than its proponents claim

explanations.correct: The interpreter example is offered as a misclassified case under the simplification-based definition; the linguist then supplies the native-speaker criterion. A captures both moves.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The argument does not say the term should go undefined; it offers a better definition.
explanations.C: No general claim about language change is drawn.
explanations.D: Two definitions are contrasted, not shown to be equivalent.
explanations.E: The original definition is rejected as wrong, not accepted with narrower scope.

lr.difficultyReason: The curator critiques a general aesthetic principle by showing a valued work would be excluded under it, then reformulates the principle. Traps describe only the reductio-like move or only the reformulation.
lr.stimulus: Curator: The dean argues that, because good art must reward close visual attention, the museum should collect only figurative painting. But the best works of mid-century color-field abstraction reward prolonged attention every bit as fully as figurative works, and excluding them would impoverish our collection. The dean's principle is sound in its emphasis on sustained attention, but it should be framed in terms of rewarding attention, not in terms of depicting recognizable subjects.
lr.questionStem: The curator's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: arguing that a proposed criterion would exclude works it ought to include, and then restating the criterion in a way that covers them

choices.label: B
choices.text: defending one school of painting by attacking the artistic credentials of another

choices.label: C
choices.text: showing that the dean's principle rests on a false historical claim about mid-century art

choices.label: D
choices.text: arguing that aesthetic principles cannot be formulated in general terms

choices.label: E
choices.text: deriving a new principle by combining two principles already accepted by the dean

explanations.correct: The curator shows that figurative-only collecting would wrongly exclude color-field works, then reframes the principle around sustained attention rather than recognizable subjects. A captures both moves.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The curator does not attack figurative painting's credentials; it argues for a broader inclusion.
explanations.C: No historical falsehood is alleged against the dean.
explanations.D: The curator offers a revised general principle, not a rejection of general principles.
explanations.E: Only one principle is in play, not a combination of two.

lr.difficultyReason: The analyst undermines a policy recommendation by showing its premise does not fit the relevant population, and then identifies a subgroup for which a different recommendation would follow.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: The mayor proposes free citywide transit on the ground that free transit in several small towns has increased ridership and cut car use. But those towns had little car traffic to begin with; residents walked or biked for most trips. In a dense city where most commuters already drive long distances, free transit is unlikely to pull drivers out of their cars. If the aim is reducing car use, congestion pricing in the downtown core, where driving is a real choice rather than a necessity, is a better lever.
lr.questionStem: The analyst's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: arguing that evidence supporting a proposal does not transfer to the relevant setting, and advocating a different measure targeted at conditions in that setting

choices.label: B
choices.text: conceding that free transit would reduce car use, but arguing that it would cost more than the city can afford

choices.label: C
choices.text: appealing to the preferences of a majority of residents to reject a mayoral proposal

choices.label: D
choices.text: assuming that because a policy has worked in one large city, it will work in any large city

choices.label: E
choices.text: arguing that a policy should be judged solely by whether it eliminates car use entirely

explanations.correct: The analyst argues that the small-town evidence fails to apply to a dense, car-dependent city, and then advocates congestion pricing in the relevant subsetting. A captures the transferability critique plus targeted alternative.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Cost is never mentioned; transferability of effects is the issue.
explanations.C: No appeal to majority preferences is made.
explanations.D: The analyst denies a generalization across settings rather than relying on one.
explanations.E: The analyst treats 'reducing car use' as the aim, not 'eliminating' it.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument makes two moves — establishing an opposing view, then refuting it by appeal to a general principle — requiring test-takers to track both steps and match them to an abstract description. Traps offer plausible partial descriptions.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Some analysts contend that raising the minimum wage always harms employment because businesses facing higher labor costs must reduce their workforce. But this reasoning overlooks a well-established economic principle: when workers earn more, consumer spending rises, which in turn increases demand for goods and services. Higher demand typically leads businesses to hire more workers, not fewer. Therefore, minimum wage increases do not necessarily harm employment.
lr.questionStem: The economist's argument proceeds by doing which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing statistical data to demonstrate that a widely held economic claim is factually incorrect

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejecting an opposing conclusion by identifying a causal chain that undermines the reasoning behind it

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two economic situations to show that a general principle applies to both

choices.label: D
choices.text: accepting the premises of an opposing argument while showing those premises lead to a different conclusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to the authority of established economists to discredit an alternative theory

explanations.correct: The economist acknowledges the opposing claim (higher labor costs → fewer workers) and then introduces a competing causal chain (higher wages → more spending → more demand → more hiring) that undermines that claim's conclusion. B captures both moves accurately.
explanations.A: No statistical data are cited; the economist relies on a general economic principle, not empirical figures.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No analogy between two situations is drawn; the economist reasons through a single causal sequence.
explanations.D: The economist does not accept the opposing premises; the argument challenges the reasoning itself by introducing an overlooked factor.
explanations.E: No named authority is invoked; the appeal is to a principle, not a person.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus involves a physician applying a general diagnostic principle to a specific case. Two trap answers are close — one describes induction, one describes analogy — requiring careful attention to direction of reasoning.
lr.stimulus: Physician: It is a well-established medical principle that any drug effective against a bacterial infection in vitro will also be effective in vivo, provided the drug can reach the infection site in sufficient concentrations. This patient's test results confirm that the proposed antibiotic is highly effective against the relevant bacteria in vitro, and imaging shows that the drug accumulates at the infection site. Therefore, this antibiotic should be effective for this patient's condition.
lr.questionStem: The physician's argument derives its conclusion by doing which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: inferring a general medical rule from observed outcomes across many individual patient cases

choices.label: B
choices.text: using an analogy between laboratory conditions and clinical conditions to predict treatment success

choices.label: C
choices.text: applying a general principle to a specific case whose features satisfy the principle's conditions

choices.label: D
choices.text: ruling out competing treatment options to establish that a single option must be correct

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to a correlation between in vitro results and patient outcomes to predict drug efficacy

explanations.correct: The physician starts with a general principle (in vitro effectiveness + sufficient concentration → in vivo effectiveness), confirms both conditions are met in this specific case, and concludes the treatment will be effective. This is textbook application of a general principle to a specific case.
explanations.A: This describes induction — moving from instances to a general rule. The physician moves the opposite direction: from rule to case.
explanations.B: No analogy is drawn between two separate situations; the physician applies a principle that directly governs both lab and clinical settings.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No elimination of alternatives occurs; the physician does not mention or rule out other treatments.
explanations.E: The physician does not appeal to a correlation; the general principle is treated as established, not inferred from co-occurrence data.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument rejects a universal claim by providing a counterexample. Trap answers paraphrase the content or misdescribe the move as an analogy or a causal argument, requiring test-takers to distinguish counterexample reasoning from other techniques.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Some scholars maintain that all major social revolutions are driven primarily by economic deprivation among the lower classes. However, the French Revolution of 1789 offers a clear challenge to this view. Many of the revolution's most influential leaders — including lawyers, merchants, and minor nobles — were not economically deprived; in fact, several were quite prosperous. Yet their participation was indispensable to the revolution's success. This shows that the claim about economic deprivation is too sweeping.
lr.questionStem: The historian's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: uses a specific historical case to argue that a universal claim about revolutions is not always correct

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws an analogy between the French Revolution and other revolutions to show they share a common cause

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers that economic prosperity, rather than deprivation, is the true cause of major social revolutions

choices.label: D
choices.text: argues that scholarly consensus about revolutions is unreliable because historians often overlook evidence

choices.label: E
choices.text: establishes a general principle about revolutions by generalizing from the case of the French Revolution

explanations.correct: The historian presents the French Revolution as a counterexample: a major social revolution whose key leaders were not economically deprived, which refutes the universal claim that all major revolutions are primarily driven by economic deprivation among the lower classes. A describes this move precisely.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No analogy between the French Revolution and other revolutions is drawn; the French Revolution is used as a counterexample, not a parallel case.
explanations.C: The historian does not argue that prosperity causes revolutions — only that the universal deprivation claim is too sweeping. This answer misidentifies the conclusion and overstates it.
explanations.D: The historian does not attack scholars' reliability in general; the argument stays focused on a specific claim and specific evidence against it.
explanations.E: The historian moves from a case to challenge a generalization, not to establish a new one — this describes the opposite direction of reasoning.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses elimination of alternatives. Two trap answers describe other common two-move patterns (analogy, causal chain) that could seem plausible without careful reading.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: There are only three ways a city government can address a budget shortfall: raise taxes, cut services, or increase municipal debt. Raising taxes is politically infeasible given the upcoming election cycle, and further increasing municipal debt would trigger a credit-rating downgrade that would cost more in the long run than the shortfall itself. Therefore, cutting services is the only viable option available to the city.
lr.questionStem: The policy analyst's argument proceeds by doing which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: applying an economic principle to show that one approach to a problem produces better outcomes than the others

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing an analogy between this city's situation and that of other municipalities that have faced similar shortfalls

choices.label: C
choices.text: eliminating all alternatives to a course of action in order to establish that course of action as the only viable option

choices.label: D
choices.text: citing expert consensus to demonstrate that a proposed policy is preferable to available alternatives

choices.label: E
choices.text: identifying a causal relationship between debt accumulation and credit-rating changes to predict long-term costs

explanations.correct: The analyst explicitly identifies all three possible options, then rules out two of them on specific grounds, leaving service cuts as the only remaining possibility. This is argument by elimination, precisely what C describes.
explanations.A: No economic principle is invoked; the analyst reasons through feasibility and consequences of each specific option.
explanations.B: No analogy to other municipalities is drawn; the argument concerns only this city's specific circumstances.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No expert or consensus is cited; the analyst's own reasoning eliminates the alternatives.
explanations.E: While the credit-rating consequence is mentioned, it functions as a reason to eliminate one option — not as the main technique of the argument, which is elimination of alternatives.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument draws an analogy between a case with known outcomes and an analogous case with unknown outcomes. The anchor sample uses the same technique; test-takers must track which case is the evidence base and which is the conclusion target.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientist: We have extensive data showing that introducing grey wolves into Yellowstone National Park dramatically increased biodiversity by reducing elk overgrazing, allowing riverbank vegetation to recover, and stabilizing stream channels. A similar elk overgrazing problem now threatens the Greater Cascade ecosystem, where no large predators remain. Although we cannot yet observe the outcome, reintroducing wolves there should produce comparable ecological benefits.
lr.questionStem: The environmental scientist's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers a causal relationship between predator populations and biodiversity from a single observed correlation

choices.label: B
choices.text: uses outcomes observed in one ecosystem to draw a conclusion about a comparably situated ecosystem

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizes from several well-documented cases to establish a universal ecological principle

choices.label: D
choices.text: appeals to scientific consensus about predator reintroduction to justify a specific conservation policy

choices.label: E
choices.text: rules out alternative explanations for Yellowstone's biodiversity increase before drawing a conclusion
