explanations.correct: The scientist has direct evidence about Yellowstone (the known case) and uses that evidence to draw a conclusion about the Cascade ecosystem (the analogous case where outcomes are not yet observable). This is reasoning by analogy from a case with known data to a comparable case without it — exactly what B describes.
explanations.A: The argument treats the Yellowstone outcome as established fact, not as a single correlation; moreover the reasoning is analogical, not simply causal inference from correlation.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Only one case (Yellowstone) is the evidence base; the argument does not generalize across several cases to establish a universal principle.
explanations.D: No scientific consensus or authority is cited; the argument relies on specific empirical data from one ecosystem.
explanations.E: No alternative explanations are considered or ruled out; the argument moves directly from the Yellowstone evidence to the Cascade prediction.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument appeals to a definitional criterion to settle a disputed classification. Trap answers describe empirical or causal reasoning that sounds related but misidentifies the logical move.
lr.stimulus: Legal scholar: Critics argue that the city's new surveillance ordinance does not constitute a 'search' under the Fourth Amendment because no physical intrusion occurs and no warrant is required for cameras placed on public streets. However, the Supreme Court has made clear that a 'search' is defined as any government action that violates a reasonable expectation of privacy. Citizens do have a reasonable expectation that their movements over extended periods will not be systematically recorded and analyzed. Therefore, the ordinance does constitute a search within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment.
lr.questionStem: The legal scholar's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws an analogy between the surveillance ordinance and previously litigated cases involving physical intrusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: applies an established definitional criterion to a disputed case to resolve a classification question

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers from the pattern of Supreme Court decisions that courts will rule against the surveillance ordinance

choices.label: D
choices.text: argues that because a practice is harmful to citizens, it should be treated as legally prohibited

choices.label: E
choices.text: accepts the critics' premises about physical intrusion while reaching the opposite conclusion

explanations.correct: The scholar invokes the Supreme Court's definition of 'search' (any government action violating a reasonable expectation of privacy), then shows the ordinance meets the definitional criteria. This is reasoning from a definition to a classification — precisely what B describes.
explanations.A: No analogy to prior litigated cases is drawn; the scholar uses a definition, not a comparison to a parallel case.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The scholar does not predict court outcomes; the argument concerns what the ordinance constitutes under the definition, not how courts will rule.
explanations.D: No harm-based reasoning appears; the argument turns on the legal definition of 'search,' not on whether the ordinance is harmful.
explanations.E: The scholar does not accept the critics' premises; the argument rejects the implied premise that physical intrusion is required for a 'search.'

lr.difficultyReason: The argument rejects a position by showing it leads to an absurd or self-undermining consequence. Trap answers describe the move as a counterexample or as an analogy, which are superficially close.
lr.stimulus: Philosopher: Some theorists hold that every belief a person has is the product of social conditioning and therefore no belief can be held rationally. But consider what this claim implies about itself: if every belief is a product of social conditioning, then the theorists' belief that no belief can be held rationally is itself a product of social conditioning — and therefore, by their own standard, cannot be held rationally. A position that undermines the rational basis of its own assertion cannot be coherently maintained.
lr.questionStem: The philosopher's argument proceeds by doing which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing empirical evidence showing that some beliefs are formed independently of social conditioning

choices.label: B
choices.text: showing that a position is false by demonstrating that it conflicts with a widely accepted ethical principle

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between the theorists' belief and ordinary beliefs to show they are subject to the same standard

choices.label: D
choices.text: arguing that a position cannot be coherently maintained because it undermines the rational grounds for asserting it

choices.label: E
choices.text: generalizing from several cases of socially conditioned beliefs to establish that all beliefs are rationally questionable

explanations.correct: The philosopher applies the theorists' own claim to itself: if all beliefs are products of social conditioning and therefore irrational, then that very claim is irrational by its own standard. The position is self-refuting. D describes this move — rejecting a view because it defeats its own rational basis — without importing content from the argument.
explanations.A: No empirical evidence about belief formation is cited; the argument is purely logical, turning the claim against itself.
explanations.B: No ethical principle is invoked; the refutation is based on logical self-reference, not ethics.
explanations.C: No analogy is drawn between two separate cases; the philosopher shows the claim applies to itself — this is self-referential critique, not analogy.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: The philosopher does not generalize from cases of socially conditioned beliefs; the move is to apply the universal claim reflexively to the claim itself.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses an intermediate generalization from sample to population, then applies the generalization to a new conclusion. Two trap answers are close — one describes the analogy pattern, one describes the principle-application pattern — requiring test-takers to identify the inductive move as the primary technique.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: In studying five unrelated language families — Indo-European, Sino-Tibetan, Afro-Asiatic, Austronesian, and Niger-Congo — researchers found that in each family, words denoting basic kinship relations (mother, father, sibling) are among the most stable elements of the lexicon, changing far more slowly than vocabulary for technology or commerce. Given the diversity of these language families and the independence of the data sets, it is reasonable to conclude that kinship terminology is cross-linguistically resistant to rapid lexical change.
lr.questionStem: The linguist's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: applies a universal linguistic law to each of the five language families to show that kinship terms are stable

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws an analogy between kinship terminology and technical vocabulary to establish a contrast in stability

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers a general cross-linguistic pattern from consistent findings across a diverse sample of language families

choices.label: D
choices.text: rules out alternative explanations for lexical stability in order to conclude that kinship relations are the cause

choices.label: E
choices.text: uses a definition of lexical stability to classify kinship terms as belonging to a particular category of vocabulary

explanations.correct: The linguist collects findings from five diverse, independent language families (the sample) and projects the observed pattern — kinship terms change slowly — onto languages in general (the population). This is inductive generalization from a varied sample, which C describes.
explanations.A: No pre-existing universal law is invoked; the argument builds toward a generalization rather than applying one already established.
explanations.B: The contrast with technical vocabulary is a premise that shows the pattern, not the reasoning method itself; no analogy between kinship and technical terms is the main move.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No alternative explanations are considered or eliminated; the argument moves directly from sample findings to a general conclusion.
explanations.E: No definitional criterion is applied; the argument is inductive, not classificatory.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument rejects an opposing view by showing it is inconsistent with a principle the opposing side itself accepts. Test-takers must distinguish this two-move technique from simple counterexample reasoning or causal argument, both of which appear as traps.
lr.stimulus: Technology ethicist: Advocates of unrestricted data collection by tech companies often appeal to the principle that individuals should be free to enter any voluntary agreement they choose. Yet these same advocates also support consumer protection laws that prohibit deceptive contract terms, on the grounds that meaningful consent requires adequate information. If meaningful consent requires adequate information, then users who agree to lengthy, opaque data-collection terms without understanding them have not given meaningful consent. Therefore, the advocates' own principle does not support unrestricted data collection when consent is uninformed.
lr.questionStem: The technology ethicist's argument proceeds by doing which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing empirical research showing that most users do not read data-collection agreements before accepting them

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing an analogy between data-collection agreements and other types of contracts to show they are equivalent

choices.label: C
choices.text: showing that an opposing position is inconsistent with a principle that the proponents of that position themselves endorse

choices.label: D
choices.text: arguing that unrestricted data collection causes demonstrable harm to users and should therefore be regulated

choices.label: E
choices.text: establishing a new ethical principle to replace the voluntariness principle invoked by data-collection advocates

explanations.correct: The ethicist accepts the advocates' own principle (voluntary agreement) and then shows that the advocates themselves acknowledge meaningful consent requires adequate information — a commitment that entails their principle does not support opaque data agreements. The opposing position is caught in an internal inconsistency. C describes this technique precisely.
explanations.A: No empirical research or survey data is cited; the argument is logical, turning the advocates' own commitments against their position.
explanations.B: No analogy between data agreements and other contracts is the argumentative move; the ethicist uses the advocates' accepted principle about deceptive terms, not a structural analogy.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No harm-based argument appears; the ethicist's challenge is about the logical coherence of the advocates' position, not about injury to users.
explanations.E: The ethicist does not propose a new principle; the argument relies on the existing principle the advocates already accept.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument rejects a causal explanation by introducing a case in which the supposed cause is present but the effect is absent, then proposes an alternative explanation. Two trap answers describe adjacent techniques (counterexample to a universal claim; elimination) that capture only one part of the move.
lr.stimulus: Art critic: Many commentators explain the decline in traditional portraiture during the late nineteenth century by pointing to the invention of photography — arguing that photography made painted portraits obsolete. But this explanation is inadequate. Photography was just as available in the United States as in France, yet traditional portraiture remained a prestigious and commercially thriving genre in France well into the twentieth century. The actual explanation lies in differences in cultural patronage: French academic institutions continued to commission and exhibit painted portraits at a level that American institutions did not.
lr.questionStem: The art critic's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: uses a case in which a proposed cause is present but the expected effect is absent to discredit that causal explanation, and offers an alternative explanation

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws an analogy between the American and French art markets to show that cultural institutions follow the same patterns in different countries

choices.label: C
choices.text: eliminates photography as a relevant factor in art history by showing that technological change rarely affects artistic traditions

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizes from the case of French portraiture to establish that photography never causes the decline of any artistic genre

choices.label: E
choices.text: appeals to art-historical consensus to show that the photography-based explanation has been widely rejected by scholars

explanations.correct: The critic points out that in France, photography was equally available (cause present) but portraiture did not decline (effect absent), which undermines the photography-as-cause explanation. The critic then offers cultural patronage as the real explanation. A captures both moves — discrediting the causal account via a disconfirming case and proposing an alternative.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The comparison between the U.S. and France is used to challenge a causal claim, not to show the two markets follow the same patterns — in fact the argument highlights their difference.
explanations.C: The critic does not claim photography is never relevant to art history, nor does the argument rely on a general claim about technology and tradition; it focuses on this specific causal explanation.
explanations.D: The critic does not generalize from France to establish a universal claim about photography and artistic genres; the argument is narrowly about the inadequacy of one explanation.
explanations.E: No scholarly consensus is cited; the argument rests on the France-vs.-U.S. comparison and the alternative patronage explanation.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument involves two moves — establishing a general principle about diagnostic accuracy, then applying it to reject an opposing position. Test-takers must distinguish the full two-step technique from answers that capture only one step or describe a different operation.
lr.stimulus: Physician: My colleague argues that imaging results alone are sufficient to diagnose a particular nerve disorder. But imaging can only detect structural abnormalities, and the disorder in question sometimes produces no structural changes whatsoever. Any diagnostic method that can fail to detect a condition even when that condition is fully present is not sufficient on its own. Therefore, my colleague's view cannot be correct.
lr.questionStem: The physician's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing experimental data to establish that a widely used diagnostic tool produces unreliable results

choices.label: B
choices.text: applying a general principle about diagnostic sufficiency to show that a specific claim is mistaken

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two different medical conditions to undermine a colleague's recommendation

choices.label: D
choices.text: inferring a causal relationship between a structural abnormality and a nerve disorder from observed correlations

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to expert consensus in order to cast doubt on an alternative diagnostic approach

explanations.correct: The physician states a general principle (a method that can miss a fully present condition is insufficient on its own), then applies it directly to imaging for this disorder, concluding that the colleague's claim fails. That is exactly applying a general principle to reject a specific claim.
explanations.A: No experimental data are cited; the physician argues from the nature of imaging and a stated principle. This answer invents evidence not in the argument.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No analogy between two conditions is drawn; the argument concerns one condition and one method. This is an 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.D: No correlation is observed and no causal inference is made; causation is never the subject. This is a content-over-technique trap.
explanations.E: No expert consensus is invoked; the physician relies on a principled definition, not authority. This is an extreme-verb / wrong-move trap.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument sets up a rival position and then defeats it by producing a counterexample. Students must track whether the argument is generalizing, analogizing, or counterexampling — three superficially similar moves — and select the one that correctly describes the structure.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Some scholars maintain that economic hardship is always the primary driver of revolutionary movements. Yet the French Revolution of 1789 erupted during a period of relative economic growth in several regions of France, with revolutionary ferment strongest among literate professionals who were not themselves impoverished. This case alone demonstrates that the scholars' universal claim cannot stand.
lr.questionStem: The historian's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: surveys a broad range of historical cases to support a statistical generalization about revolutions

choices.label: B
choices.text: appeals to an authority on revolutionary history to cast doubt on a competing interpretation

choices.label: C
choices.text: cites a specific historical instance as a counterexample to a universal claim

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws an analogy between the French Revolution and a contemporary political movement

choices.label: E
choices.text: infers that economic conditions are irrelevant to revolutionary movements based on a single case

explanations.correct: The historian identifies a universal claim (economic hardship is always the primary driver) and then produces the French Revolution as a case that violates it, which is precisely the move of citing a counterexample to a universal claim.
explanations.A: Only one case is used, not a broad survey. This is the mis-scaled trap — describing the argument as a generalization when it is a specific refutation.
explanations.B: No authority is cited; the historian relies on historical facts, not another scholar's endorsement.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No contemporary movement appears; the argument is confined to one historical episode.
explanations.E: The conclusion is that the universal claim fails, not that economics is wholly irrelevant — this overstates the argument's conclusion (extreme-verb trap).

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses an analogy between two economic situations — one with observable data and one without — mirroring the structure of the authentic anchor. Test-takers must recognize the analogical move and resist traps describing causal inference or statistical generalization.
lr.stimulus: Economist: We have detailed productivity data for the manufacturing sector following last year's regulatory overhaul, and those data show a marked decline in output per worker. We have no comparably direct data for the agricultural sector, which underwent the same overhaul at the same time. Given the structural similarities between the two sectors' labor arrangements, we can reasonably conclude that agricultural productivity per worker also declined.
lr.questionStem: The economist's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: uses data from one sector where measurement is possible to draw a conclusion about an analogous sector where direct measurement is unavailable

choices.label: B
choices.text: establishes a causal connection between regulatory policy and productivity by comparing outcomes across multiple industries

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers a general economic principle from observed trends in a single industry

choices.label: D
choices.text: predicts future productivity levels by extrapolating from historical baseline data

choices.label: E
choices.text: rejects a competing economic model by identifying an internal inconsistency in its assumptions

explanations.correct: The economist has direct productivity data for manufacturing, lacks direct data for agriculture, notes structural similarity, and infers the same outcome. This is exactly the pattern of using an observable case to draw a conclusion about an analogous unobservable case.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No causal connection is established; the argument infers an outcome by analogy, not by demonstrating causation. 'Establishes' is also an extreme verb the argument does not warrant.
explanations.C: The movement is in the opposite direction — from one sector to another, not from a sector to a general principle.
explanations.D: The conclusion concerns the same regulatory overhaul period, not a future event. This is the mis-temporal trap.
explanations.E: No competing model is identified or attacked; the argument is constructive, not adversarial.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument appeals to a definition to settle a disputed classification. Students must identify the definitional move rather than confusing it with an empirical or analogical argument, and must distinguish the correct answer from a trap that accurately describes only half of the reasoning.
lr.stimulus: Legal scholar: Critics argue that the new surveillance ordinance constitutes an unlawful search. However, an unlawful search, by legal definition, requires an intrusion into a space in which the subject has a reasonable expectation of privacy. The ordinance in question covers only activity conducted in publicly visible areas, where no such expectation exists. The critics' objection therefore fails on its own terms.
lr.questionStem: The legal scholar's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing precedent established by prior court decisions to override the critics' interpretation of the ordinance

choices.label: B
choices.text: appealing to the accepted definition of a legal concept to show that a particular case does not fall within it

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between the new ordinance and a prior surveillance law that courts have upheld

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrating that the critics' position leads to a conclusion that is inconsistent with their own stated values

choices.label: E
choices.text: surveying empirical evidence about privacy expectations to refute the critics' factual claim

explanations.correct: The scholar invokes the accepted legal definition of 'unlawful search' (requires intrusion into a space with a reasonable privacy expectation), then shows the ordinance targets only public spaces lacking that expectation — a definitional exclusion of the case from the category.
explanations.A: No court precedent is cited; the argument rests on a definitional standard, not judicial authority.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No prior law or analogous ordinance is introduced; the argument stays within the current ordinance and the definition.
explanations.D: The critics' values are not mentioned; the inconsistency alleged is between their objection and the legal definition, not their personal commitments. This is the 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.E: No empirical survey of privacy expectations is conducted; the claim that public spaces lack such expectations is treated as a definitional given.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument rejects an opposing position by deriving an absurd consequence from it. Test-takers must recognize reductio ad absurdum and distinguish it from counterexample reasoning and from causal-inference traps.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Some philosophers contend that an action is morally obligatory whenever it would produce a net increase in overall happiness. But if that were true, then a surgeon would be morally required to harvest the organs of one healthy patient to save five dying ones, since doing so would increase net happiness. Because virtually everyone recognizes that such an act would be deeply wrong, the proposed criterion cannot be correct.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: appeals to empirical research on human moral intuitions to establish a competing ethical theory

choices.label: B
choices.text: cites a generally recognized moral judgment to undermine a criterion that would entail a conflicting conclusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizes from a single thought experiment to a broad conclusion about the nature of moral obligation

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws an analogy between medical ethics and philosophical ethics to resolve a conceptual dispute

choices.label: E
choices.text: identifies a logical contradiction within the philosophical criterion by analyzing its internal assumptions

explanations.correct: The ethicist takes the opposing criterion, derives from it a consequence (organ harvesting is obligatory) that virtually everyone recognizes as morally wrong, and uses that widely accepted moral judgment to reject the criterion. This is citing a generally recognized judgment to undermine a criterion that entails a conflicting conclusion.
explanations.A: No empirical research is cited; the ethicist relies on a widely shared intuition, not a study. And no competing theory is established — only the rival criterion is rejected.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The argument rejects a criterion rather than building a generalization; the thought experiment is the vehicle of refutation, not the basis of a new general claim.
explanations.D: The argument does not compare two domains — medical ethics and philosophical ethics — as analogous fields; the medical scenario is a logical test case for one criterion.
explanations.E: The criterion is not internally contradictory; the problem is that it generates an externally unacceptable conclusion, not that its own assumptions conflict.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses elimination — ruling out all alternatives to establish the remaining option. Students must recognize this structure and not confuse it with analogy, authority appeal, or causal inference, all of which appear as tempting traps.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientist: The sharp decline in the local amphibian population must be attributable to the increase in ultraviolet radiation reaching the lake bottom. Habitat loss is not a factor, since the wetland area has actually expanded over the same period. Introduced predators have been ruled out by recent wildlife surveys. Disease has been excluded by comprehensive pathological testing. UV radiation is the only remaining candidate.
lr.questionStem: The environmental scientist's argument derives its conclusion by

choices.label: A
choices.text: drawing an analogy between the local lake ecosystem and a comparable ecosystem in which UV radiation caused a similar decline

choices.label: B
choices.text: citing the results of controlled laboratory experiments that demonstrate the harmful effects of UV radiation on amphibians

choices.label: C
choices.text: systematically eliminating alternative explanations to establish the only remaining candidate as the cause

choices.label: D
choices.text: identifying a correlation between UV radiation levels and amphibian population counts across multiple study sites

choices.label: E
choices.text: applying a general ecological principle about the sensitivity of amphibians to radiation to this particular case

explanations.correct: The scientist goes through habitat loss, predators, and disease one by one, dismissing each, and concludes that UV radiation must be the cause because it is all that remains. This is argument by elimination.
explanations.A: No comparable ecosystem is introduced; the argument stays within the local lake. This is the 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.B: No laboratory experiments are cited; the evidence cited concerns field surveys and pathological tests, not controlled lab work.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No cross-site correlation data are mentioned; the argument is purely eliminative, not correlational.
explanations.E: No general ecological principle about amphibian radiation sensitivity is stated; the argument proceeds by elimination, not by applying a stored principle.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument infers from a sample to a population. Students must recognize this inductive move and distinguish it from analogical reasoning, definitional appeal, and causal inference — all present as traps — while noticing that the 'partially true' trap describes one premise rather than the full reasoning move.
lr.stimulus: Sociologist: A recent longitudinal study tracked eight hundred randomly selected adults across fifteen cities over a ten-year period. Researchers found that, within this group, individuals who reported consistent daily exercise routines had significantly lower rates of clinical depression than those who did not. We can therefore conclude that, among adults generally, regular exercise is associated with reduced rates of clinical depression.
lr.questionStem: The sociologist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: establishing a causal mechanism by which exercise chemically reduces the neurological basis of depression

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing an analogy between the study participants and a different population whose mental health outcomes are already known

choices.label: C
choices.text: appealing to expert consensus among psychiatrists about the therapeutic benefits of physical activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: inferring a general population-level association from observed patterns in a representative sample

choices.label: E
choices.text: applying an established psychological principle to account for the depression rates observed in the study

explanations.correct: The sociologist observes a pattern in a sample (800 randomly selected adults) and extends that pattern to the general adult population. This is the classic sample-to-population inductive move.
explanations.A: No causal mechanism is identified; the conclusion explicitly uses 'associated with,' not 'causes.' Claiming a causal mechanism is established overstates what the argument does (extreme-verb trap).
explanations.B: No second population is introduced; the argument moves from the sample directly to the general adult population, not via analogy with another known group.
explanations.C: No expert consensus is invoked; the argument relies solely on the study's data.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: No pre-existing psychological principle is applied; the argument builds up from data rather than applying a stored principle downward.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument rejects a technological claim by showing it is inconsistent with a broadly accepted principle about how verification works. Students must distinguish this from counterexample reasoning, authority appeals, and causal arguments — all present as traps.
lr.stimulus: Software engineer: Proponents of this new encryption protocol claim it is unbreakable. Yet any claim that a system is unbreakable requires that every possible attack method has been considered and shown to fail. No finite team of engineers can enumerate every conceivable attack vector on a sufficiently complex system. Therefore, the claim that this protocol is unbreakable cannot be justified.
lr.questionStem: The software engineer's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: identifies a specific attack vector that the protocol's designers failed to consider, thereby disproving the protocol's security

choices.label: B
choices.text: appeals to a general epistemic principle about what is required for a claim of completeness to show that a specific security claim is unjustified

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws an analogy between the new encryption protocol and a prior protocol that was eventually compromised

choices.label: D
choices.text: surveys the opinions of cryptography experts to establish that the protocol has not been independently verified

choices.label: E
choices.text: infers from the complexity of the protocol that it is likely to contain undiscovered flaws

explanations.correct: The engineer states a general epistemic principle (claiming unbreakability requires showing every attack method fails), then applies it: since no team can enumerate all attack vectors, the claim cannot be justified. This is applying a general principle about what justification requires to show a specific claim falls short.
explanations.A: No specific attack vector is identified; the argument is about the impossibility of complete enumeration, not about a particular overlooked attack. This invents a move the argument does not make.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No prior protocol is mentioned; the argument is entirely about the logical requirements for the current claim.
explanations.D: No expert survey is cited; the engineer's objection is principled, not empirical.
explanations.E: The argument's conclusion is about justifiability of the claim, not about the likelihood of flaws — a subtle but important content-over-technique distinction.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument involves a linguist setting up a competing claim and then using a specific observable phenomenon to challenge it. The correct answer must capture both the adversarial setup and the evidential move; traps either drop the adversarial component or misdescribe the evidence as a generalization.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Some cognitive scientists assert that all human languages share a universal deep grammar encoded in our biology. However, recent fieldwork on Pirahã, a language spoken by an Amazonian community, has documented the absence of grammatical features — such as recursion — that these scientists consider universal and innate. If even one language lacks a supposedly universal feature, the universality claim is refuted.
lr.questionStem: The linguist's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: generalizes from patterns observed in a single language to a conclusion about the structure of all human languages

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws an analogy between Pirahã grammar and the grammatical systems of other Amazonian languages

choices.label: C
choices.text: uses a specific documented case to challenge a claim that a grammatical feature is universal to all human languages

choices.label: D
choices.text: appeals to the authority of fieldwork researchers to override the theoretical conclusions of cognitive scientists

choices.label: E
choices.text: argues that biological innateness cannot be the source of any grammatical feature because languages differ from one another

explanations.correct: The linguist identifies a universal claim (all languages share certain innate grammatical features) and uses Pirahã as a documented case lacking those features — a counterexample — to refute the universal claim. The answer accurately describes this as using a specific documented case to challenge a universality claim.
explanations.A: The argument moves in the opposite direction: from Pirahã as a case to the rejection of a universal claim, not from Pirahã to a new generalization about all languages. This is the mis-scaled trap.
explanations.B: No other Amazonian languages are introduced; Pirahã is used alone as a counterexample.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The argument does not pit researchers' authority against scientists' authority; it uses documented empirical findings as evidence, not as an appeal to credibility.
explanations.E: The conclusion is narrower — that this specific universality claim fails — not the sweeping claim that innateness can explain no grammatical feature.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument proceeds by drawing an analogy between two arts-funding situations — one with outcome data and one without — to support a conclusion about the second. Students must isolate the analogical structure and resist traps that describe causal inference, generalization, or definitional appeal.
lr.stimulus: Arts administrator: Last year, the city provided direct subsidies to twelve independent theater companies, and surveys showed that attendance at subsidized venues increased by thirty percent while overall attendance in the broader theater market stayed flat. This year, the city is considering identical subsidies for independent music ensembles. Because the market conditions and audience demographics for independent music are closely comparable to those for independent theater, we should expect a similar attendance boost for the music ensembles.
lr.questionStem: The arts administrator's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers a causal relationship between public subsidies and increased attendance by comparing subsidized and unsubsidized venues in the same market

choices.label: B
choices.text: applies a general economic principle about arts funding to predict outcomes in a specific municipal context

choices.label: C
choices.text: uses observed outcomes in one arts sector to draw a conclusion about expected outcomes in a comparable arts sector

choices.label: D
choices.text: surveys a broad range of arts subsidy programs to establish a statistical pattern linking funding to attendance growth

choices.label: E
choices.text: rejects the city's prior funding model by showing that the data from theater subsidies contradict its underlying assumptions

explanations.correct: The administrator has outcome data from one sector (theater), notes comparable conditions in another sector (music), and concludes the same outcome should be expected there. This is the analogical move of using results in one observable case to draw a conclusion about a comparable case.
explanations.A: While the argument does rely on the subsidy-attendance relationship, it does not establish causation — it infers by analogy that the same pattern will hold in a new sector. Saying it 'infers a causal relationship' misdescribes the reasoning move (content-over-technique trap).
explanations.B: No general economic principle is invoked; the administrator draws directly on the theater case without appealing to a stored principle.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Only one prior program (theater) is referenced, not a broad survey of many programs. This is the mis-scaled trap.
explanations.E: The administrator supports the subsidy model, not rejects it; the theater data are used constructively. This describes a different, adversarial argument.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument involves two moves: establishing an opposing view and then rejecting it by appeal to a general principle. Test-takers must identify both moves and their relationship. Trap choices capture only one move or misdescribe the logical operation.
lr.stimulus: Physician: Some colleagues argue that a patient's refusal of a recommended treatment should always be honored, regardless of the patient's mental state. But this position cannot be correct. We routinely and justifiably override decisions made by individuals who lack the cognitive capacity to evaluate consequences — for instance, when we prevent a severely delirious patient from removing a life-sustaining IV line. A refusal is only meaningful if the person refusing is capable of understanding what they are refusing.
lr.questionStem: The physician's argument proceeds by doing which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: appealing to statistical evidence about patient outcomes to refute a claim about ethical obligations

choices.label: B
choices.text: citing a counterexample to an absolute claim and then deriving a qualification from a general principle

choices.label: C
choices.text: identifying an ambiguity in an opposing position and arguing that one interpretation of it is unacceptable

choices.label: D
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two ethically distinct situations to establish a universal rule

choices.label: E
choices.text: conceding that a general principle is correct and then arguing that it does not apply to the case at hand

explanations.correct: The physician first cites the delirious patient case as a counterexample to the absolute claim that refusals must always be honored, then derives the qualification that a refusal is only meaningful when made by someone with cognitive capacity — a general principle that limits the original claim. Choice B captures both moves precisely.
explanations.A: No statistical evidence appears anywhere in the argument; this is a content-over-technique trap.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The physician does not locate an ambiguity in the opposing position; the attack is via counterexample and principle, not semantic analysis.
explanations.D: No analogy between two separate situations is drawn; the delirious patient is a counterexample, not an analogue.
explanations.E: The physician rejects the opposing position outright rather than conceding the general principle and carving out an exception.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses an analogy between a known case and an unknown case — mirroring the authentic anchor. Trap choices use causal, predictive, or generalization language that partially fits the domain but misidentifies the logical move.
lr.stimulus: Historian: We have no surviving written records from the early settlements of the Indus Valley civilization regarding their system of governance. However, archaeologists have found that their cities show a remarkably uniform layout — standardized street grids, consistent brick dimensions, and similarly positioned public buildings — across sites separated by hundreds of kilometers. The same degree of architectural uniformity in contemporary Bronze Age Mesopotamia is well documented as evidence of centralized political administration. We can therefore conclude that the Indus Valley settlements were also likely governed by some form of centralized authority.
lr.questionStem: The historian's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: generalizes from a representative sample of settlements to a conclusion about all ancient civilizations

choices.label: B
choices.text: predicts the likely future discovery of records by citing a parallel case in which records were preserved

choices.label: C
choices.text: uses a case in which direct documentary evidence is available to draw a conclusion about an analogous case in which such evidence is unavailable

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers that two civilizations shared a common origin because they display similar architectural features

choices.label: E
choices.text: applies a definition of centralized governance to determine whether a known political arrangement qualifies

explanations.correct: The historian has documentary evidence about Mesopotamia's centralized governance and no documentary evidence about the Indus Valley, then uses the architectural analogy between the two to infer centralized governance for the Indus Valley. This precisely matches choice C.
explanations.A: No generalization from a sample to all ancient civilizations is made; the argument concerns a specific inference about one civilization.
explanations.B: The historian draws no prediction about future discoveries; the conclusion is about the past governance structure.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The argument does not claim common origin; it infers a shared type of political organization from a shared architectural feature.
explanations.E: No definition of centralized governance is offered or applied; the argument reasons by analogy, not by definitional criteria.

lr.difficultyReason: The economist sets up a causal claim made by others and then rejects it by pointing to a case where the alleged cause is present but the alleged effect is absent. Test-takers must distinguish this counterexample move from a correlation-based inference or a principled rebuttal.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Many commentators claim that high corporate tax rates are the primary cause of sluggish domestic investment. Yet the Nordic economies maintain some of the highest corporate tax rates in the developed world and consistently record among the highest levels of domestic business investment. If high corporate taxes reliably suppressed investment, we would not observe this pattern. The commentators' causal claim is therefore unwarranted.
lr.questionStem: The economist's argument derives its conclusion by doing which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: applying a general economic principle to a specific national case to confirm a prediction

choices.label: B
choices.text: citing cases in which the proposed cause is present but the proposed effect is absent, thereby challenging the causal claim

choices.label: C
choices.text: inferring that two economic phenomena are correlated on the basis of data from a single country

choices.label: D
choices.text: arguing that because an alternative explanation exists, the original explanation must be false

choices.label: E
choices.text: accepting the causal relationship but arguing that other factors outweigh it in the cases cited

explanations.correct: The economist points to the Nordic economies where the purported cause (high corporate taxes) is present but the purported effect (low investment) is absent, making these cases counterexamples that undermine the causal claim. Choice B describes this move precisely.
explanations.A: The economist does not apply a principle to confirm a prediction; rather, observed data contradicts a causal hypothesis.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Multiple Nordic economies are cited; furthermore, the move is a counterexample to a causal claim, not a correlation inference.
explanations.D: No alternative explanation is offered; the economist simply shows the causal pattern fails, not that something else explains investment levels.
explanations.E: The economist does not accept the causal relationship; the argument explicitly rejects it as unwarranted.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses a reductio ad absurdum structure — deriving an unacceptable consequence from a competing position. Test-takers must recognize this move and distinguish it from a simple counterexample or an analogy.
lr.stimulus: Legal scholar: Some theorists maintain that a contract should be enforceable only if both parties explicitly negotiated every one of its terms. But if we accepted this standard, virtually no contract in commercial history would be enforceable, since parties routinely rely on implied terms and standard industry practice rather than spelling out every contingency. A standard that renders all commercial contracts void cannot be a sound basis for contract law.
lr.questionStem: The legal scholar's argument proceeds by doing which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: appealing to historical precedent to establish that a proposed standard has always been rejected

choices.label: B
choices.text: identifying a counterexample that proves the opposing position is self-contradictory

choices.label: C
choices.text: showing that the opposing position, if accepted, would produce a consequence that is itself unacceptable

choices.label: D
choices.text: arguing that the standard proposed by the theorists is vague and therefore inapplicable to real cases

choices.label: E
choices.text: deriving the correct standard for enforceability by eliminating all other proposed standards

explanations.correct: The legal scholar takes the opposing standard, extends it to its logical conclusion (virtually no contracts would be enforceable), and then argues that this consequence is unacceptable — a classic reductio move. Choice C captures this accurately.
explanations.A: The argument does not appeal to historical precedent showing past rejection; it derives an unacceptable consequence from the proposed standard.
explanations.B: The position is not shown to be self-contradictory; it is shown to produce an absurd practical outcome.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No charge of vagueness is made; the scholar accepts what the standard means and shows where it leads.
explanations.E: Only one alternative standard is addressed; no process of elimination across multiple standards occurs.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument applies a general principle to a specific case to reach a conclusion. Test-takers must identify this deductive move and distinguish it from inductive generalization, analogy, or causal reasoning — all of which appear as traps.
lr.stimulus: Environmental regulator: Any industrial process that releases byproducts directly into a shared waterway without treatment poses an unacceptable risk to downstream communities. The Caldwell Manufacturing facility discharges its cooling-water runoff untreated into the Merrow River, which supplies drinking water to three counties. Therefore, the Caldwell facility's discharge process poses an unacceptable risk to those communities.
lr.questionStem: The environmental regulator's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers a general standard of industrial safety from observed patterns of harm in several specific cases

choices.label: B
choices.text: uses evidence about the typical behavior of industrial facilities to predict the Caldwell facility's future conduct

choices.label: C
choices.text: applies a general principle to a specific case to derive a conclusion about that case

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws an analogy between the Caldwell facility and other facilities to argue that all pose equivalent risks

choices.label: E
choices.text: argues that because a risk is present, harm will necessarily occur

explanations.correct: The regulator states a general principle (untreated discharge into shared waterways is unacceptable), identifies the Caldwell facility as a case meeting the principle's conditions, and concludes that the principle applies to it. This is a straightforward application of a general principle to a specific case.
explanations.A: The general principle is asserted as a premise, not derived inductively from observed cases of harm.
explanations.B: No prediction about future conduct is made; the conclusion is about the current risk posed by the existing discharge process.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No analogy to other facilities is drawn; the argument concerns only the Caldwell facility.
explanations.E: The conclusion is about unacceptable risk, not about certainty of harm — the argument does not claim harm will necessarily occur.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument reasons from a definition to exclude a candidate case. Trap choices misattribute the move as an analogy, a causal inference, or a generalization — each of which superficially resembles the definitional reasoning here.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Critics claim that Esperanto should be classified as a natural language on the grounds that it has native speakers — children raised from birth by Esperanto-speaking parents. But a natural language, properly understood, is one that arose through spontaneous, unplanned processes within a community over generations, without the deliberate design of any individual. Esperanto was systematically constructed by Ludwig Lazarus Zamenhof in the 1880s. Whatever Esperanto is, it is not a natural language.
lr.questionStem: The linguist's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws on historical evidence to refute a claim about the contemporary status of Esperanto

choices.label: B
choices.text: argues that a proposed classification is incorrect by appealing to the defining criteria of the relevant category

choices.label: C
choices.text: uses the existence of native speakers of Esperanto to generalize about constructed languages broadly

choices.label: D
choices.text: accepts that Esperanto meets one criterion for natural language status while arguing a second criterion is more important

choices.label: E
choices.text: infers that because Zamenhof designed Esperanto, it cannot function effectively as a means of communication

explanations.correct: The linguist offers a definition of 'natural language' (spontaneous, unplanned, multigenerational community origin) and then shows Esperanto was deliberately designed by one person, thus failing the definitional criteria. This is a paradigm case of arguing against a classification by appeal to defining criteria.
explanations.A: While historical facts about Zamenhof are cited, the reasoning move is definitional, not a weighing of historical versus contemporary evidence.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The linguist draws no generalization about constructed languages broadly; the conclusion is specifically about Esperanto's classification.
explanations.D: The linguist does not accept that Esperanto meets any criterion for natural language status; the argument is that it fails the essential criterion.
explanations.E: No claim about communicative effectiveness is made; the argument is purely about classification.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument eliminates alternatives to establish a conclusion — a process-of-elimination move. Traps describe the argument as an analogy, a causal inference, or a principle application, each of which is plausible-sounding but misidentifies the logical structure.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: The decline in voter participation in Millbrook's local elections over the past decade must be attributable to the shift to mail-in ballots. We know that the socioeconomic composition of Millbrook's population has remained stable, so economic hardship cannot explain it. The local candidates themselves have also become more, not less, diverse and competitive over the same period, ruling out voter disengagement from the choices available. That leaves the procedural change to mail-in ballots as the only remaining explanation.
lr.questionStem: The policy analyst's argument proceeds by doing which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: applying a general principle about voter behavior to explain a specific electoral trend

choices.label: B
choices.text: using survey data from Millbrook residents to identify the cause of declining participation

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between Millbrook's experience and that of other municipalities that adopted mail-in ballots

choices.label: D
choices.text: ruling out alternative explanations for an observed phenomenon and concluding that one remaining explanation is correct

choices.label: E
choices.text: inferring that a correlation between mail-in ballots and low turnout proves a causal relationship

explanations.correct: The analyst systematically eliminates economic hardship and candidate disengagement as explanations, and then concludes that the mail-in ballot change must be the cause. This is a paradigm argument by elimination — process-of-elimination reasoning.
explanations.A: No general principle about voter behavior is stated or applied; the argument proceeds by elimination, not deduction from a principle.
explanations.B: No survey data are mentioned; the evidence concerns demographic stability and candidate diversity.
explanations.C: No analogy to other municipalities is drawn; the argument focuses solely on Millbrook's internal data.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: The argument does not merely assert a correlation; it eliminates rivals and then attributes the cause — the structure is eliminative, not simply correlational.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument infers a conclusion about a specific artwork's authenticity from an analogy with a case where authenticity was confirmed. Test-takers must recognize the two-step move and distinguish it from causal reasoning, generalization, or a definitional argument.
lr.stimulus: Art curator: We cannot directly carbon-date the pigments in the disputed Vermeer painting because the process would damage the work. However, we have confirmed through spectroscopic analysis that the chemical composition of the pigments is identical to those in three Vermeer paintings whose authenticity has been independently verified and whose pigment dates have been established. When similar spectroscopic matches were found in another disputed work last year, subsequent non-invasive thermoluminescence testing confirmed that work's authenticity. The disputed Vermeer is therefore likely authentic.
lr.questionStem: The curator's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers from the chemical composition of pigments that a specific artist must have produced the disputed work

choices.label: B
choices.text: uses a case in which corroborating tests were available to draw a conclusion about an analogous case in which such tests cannot be applied

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizes from three verified Vermeer paintings to a conclusion about all disputed Vermeer works

choices.label: D
choices.text: establishes the authenticity of the disputed painting by applying a universally accepted standard of art verification

choices.label: E
choices.text: argues that because the disputed painting resembles verified Vermeers stylistically, it was produced in the same period

explanations.correct: The curator has a case (the work tested last year) where spectroscopic matching was followed by confirming thermoluminescence results, and applies that precedent to the disputed Vermeer where direct carbon-dating (the corroborating test) is unavailable. This precisely mirrors the authentic anchor's structure: a case with direct evidence supports an analogous case without it.
explanations.A: The argument does not claim pigment composition alone identifies the artist; it uses the composition as corroborating evidence in an analogical inference.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No generalization to all disputed Vermeer works is made; the conclusion is about this specific disputed painting.
explanations.D: No universally accepted standard is invoked; the argument reasons by analogy to one prior case.
explanations.E: The argument does not appeal to stylistic resemblance or period dating; it relies on chemical composition and an analogous verification case.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument challenges an opposing view by appealing to an accepted moral principle that the opposing view violates. Test-takers must identify this two-step move (state opposing view, invoke principle to reject it) and distinguish it from a reductio, a counterexample, or a definitional argument.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Proponents of so-called enhancement genetic screening argue that parents should be free to select embryos based on traits like predicted athletic ability or musical aptitude, since parents are already permitted to provide children with music lessons and sports coaching. But the widely accepted principle of respect for persons holds that individuals must not be treated merely as objects to be shaped according to others' preferences. Selecting an embryo for traits that serve parental ambitions treats the future person as a means to parental ends, not as an end in themselves. The practice is therefore ethically impermissible.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: accepts the analogy between genetic screening and postnatal coaching and then argues the analogy supports a different conclusion than proponents claim

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejects a position by showing it is inconsistent with a widely accepted moral principle

choices.label: C
choices.text: cites empirical evidence about parental motives to undermine a claim about permissible enhancement practices

choices.label: D
choices.text: derives an absurd consequence from the opposing position and uses that consequence to reject the position

choices.label: E
choices.text: argues that genetic screening and postnatal coaching differ in a morally relevant way and uses that difference to reject the comparison

explanations.correct: The ethicist invokes the respected principle of treating persons as ends in themselves, shows that enhancement screening violates this principle by treating the future person as a means to parental ends, and concludes the practice is impermissible. This is a rejection of the opposing view via inconsistency with an accepted principle.
explanations.A: The ethicist does not accept the analogy; rather, the principal argument runs through the moral principle rather than through the coaching analogy at all.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No empirical evidence about parental motives is presented; the argument is purely normative, proceeding from a moral principle.
explanations.D: No absurd consequence is derived; the argument identifies a principled objection, not a reductio.
explanations.E: While the ethicist might implicitly be rejecting the analogy, the explicit reasoning move is the appeal to the principle of respect for persons — the difference between screening and coaching is established through the principle, not independently.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument reasons from a specific observed instance to a qualified general claim — an inductive move. Traps describe the argument as applying a principle, drawing an analogy, or eliminating alternatives, each of which is a plausible-sounding misdescription.
lr.stimulus: Technologist: Critics have claimed that artificial intelligence systems cannot exhibit genuine creative output because they merely recombine existing data rather than generating truly novel ideas. Yet consider the AI system that recently composed a symphony that professional musicians, in a blind evaluation, rated as indistinguishable from the work of a skilled human composer. If a system produces outputs that experts cannot distinguish from creative human work, there is at least some basis for attributing creative capacity to that system. The critics' blanket denial of creative capacity in AI systems is therefore too strong.
lr.questionStem: The technologist's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: applies a general principle about creativity to show that artificial intelligence systems satisfy its conditions

choices.label: B
choices.text: uses survey data about expert preferences to establish a causal connection between AI design and creative output

choices.label: C
choices.text: cites a specific instance that is inconsistent with a universal claim, thereby weakening that claim

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws an analogy between AI-generated music and human-composed music to show that they share a common origin

choices.label: E
choices.text: eliminates alternative explanations for expert assessments of AI output to conclude that AI systems are fully creative

explanations.correct: The technologist cites a specific AI system that produced expert-rated creative work — a case that is inconsistent with the universal claim that AI systems cannot exhibit genuine creative output — and uses this to argue the blanket denial is too strong. This is a counterexample weakening a universal claim.
explanations.A: The technologist does offer a functional criterion (outputs experts cannot distinguish from human work), but the reasoning move is counterexample-based, not deductive application of a prior principle to show conditions are met.
explanations.B: No survey data are mentioned; the blind evaluation is an expert assessment, and the argument draws no causal connection about AI design.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No analogy between AI music and human music is drawn to establish common origin; the argument is about expert indistinguishability as evidence of creative capacity.
explanations.E: No alternative explanations are eliminated; and the conclusion is the qualified claim that the blanket denial is too strong — not that AI is 'fully creative.'

lr.difficultyReason: The argument makes two moves: it cites an opposing view and then attacks it by invoking a general principle. Students must track both moves to identify the correct answer; traps describe only one move or mislabel the technique.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Some scholars argue that the decline of the Roman Empire was primarily caused by military overextension. But this explanation cannot be correct. Any empire whose administrative capacity grows proportionally with its territorial expansion will not collapse for military reasons alone. Rome's administrative infrastructure actually kept pace with its expansion for most of the imperial period — it was internal political fragmentation, not overextension, that eroded Roman cohesion.
lr.questionStem: The historian's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing statistical evidence to establish that military overextension was less severe than previous scholars believed

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejecting a proposed explanation by showing that the conditions required for that explanation to apply were not present

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between Rome's administrative system and those of other empires that did not collapse

choices.label: D
choices.text: establishing a general causal principle and then offering Rome as the primary evidence for that principle

choices.label: E
choices.text: conceding that military overextension played a role in Rome's decline while arguing that internal factors were more decisive

explanations.correct: The historian first states a general principle (an empire whose administration grows proportionally with expansion won't collapse from military overextension alone), then shows that Rome's administration did keep pace — meaning the condition required for the military-overextension explanation does not hold. This is precisely what B describes: rejecting an explanation by showing its required conditions were absent.
explanations.A: No statistical evidence is cited; the historian makes a structural argument about administrative capacity. This answer imports content not in the stimulus.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No analogy to other empires appears; the argument stays focused on Rome and an abstract principle. This is an 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.D: The principle is not derived from Rome — it is stated independently and then applied to Rome. D reverses the logical direction.
explanations.E: The historian does not concede that military overextension played any role; the argument rejects that explanation outright. 'Conceding' is an extreme-mischaracterization trap.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument sets up a symmetry between two cases and draws an inference from the one where evidence is available to the one where it is not. Traps either mislabel the move as causal or describe a generalization rather than an analogy.
lr.stimulus: Physician: We have extensive outcome data on patients who received the newer minimally invasive procedure for gallstone removal, and those outcomes were no better than outcomes for the traditional open surgery. We have no comparable outcome data yet for the newer procedure as applied to elderly patients with multiple comorbidities, because that population was excluded from early trials. Given the similarity of the underlying physiology, however, the newer procedure likely offers no advantage over open surgery for elderly patients either.
lr.questionStem: The physician's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers that two medical procedures are equally risky by showing that they share the same physiological mechanism

choices.label: B
choices.text: uses outcome data from a general population to derive a statistical generalization applicable to all surgical patients

choices.label: C
choices.text: uses a case in which direct evidence is available to draw a conclusion about an analogous case in which direct evidence is unavailable

choices.label: D
choices.text: rejects a proposed treatment protocol by showing that it contradicts well-established physiological principles

choices.label: E
choices.text: bases a prediction about future clinical outcomes on a controlled experimental study involving elderly patients

explanations.correct: The physician has direct outcome data for general patients (evidence available) and no direct data for elderly patients (evidence unavailable). The analogy between the two groups — grounded in similar physiology — bridges the gap. This is exactly what C describes, mirroring the structure of the authentic LSAC anchor question.
explanations.A: The argument is about comparative effectiveness, not comparative risk. 'Equally risky' misrepresents the conclusion, and 'same physiological mechanism' overstates the claim. This is a content-echoing trap.
explanations.B: The argument does not derive a statistical generalization applicable to all surgical patients — it draws a specific conclusion about elderly patients. 'All surgical patients' is an over-generalization trap.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No treatment protocol is rejected, and no contradiction with physiological principles is alleged. This describes a different type of argument entirely.
explanations.E: There is no controlled experimental study involving elderly patients — that is precisely what is lacking. This answer inverts the evidential situation described in the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument invokes a definition to settle an apparently empirical dispute. Students must recognize that the key move is definitional rather than evidential, causal, or analogical — traps dress up each of those alternatives plausibly.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Critics of free-trade agreements claim that such agreements harm workers by suppressing wages. But wages in industries exposed to import competition have, in several well-documented cases, actually risen in the years following trade liberalization. This shows that free-trade agreements do not harm workers in the relevant sense — because economic harm to workers, properly understood, means a reduction in real compensation, and no such reduction has occurred in these cases.
lr.questionStem: The economist's argument derives its conclusion by

choices.label: A
choices.text: appealing to a definition of economic harm to show that the critics' evidence does not establish the critics' conclusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: citing a counterexample to the universal claim that free-trade agreements always benefit workers

choices.label: C
choices.text: showing that the causal mechanism proposed by critics cannot produce the effect they allege

choices.label: D
choices.text: drawing an analogy between wage trends in trade-exposed industries and wage trends in protected industries

choices.label: E
choices.text: inferring from a sample of industries that free-trade agreements universally raise wages across all economic sectors

explanations.correct: The economist's key move is definitional: economic harm to workers means reduction in real compensation. Having established that definition, the economist notes wages rose, so no harm occurred in the defined sense. The critics' conclusion is undercut not by disputing their evidence but by showing the evidence doesn't satisfy the definition of 'harm.'
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The argument does not offer a counterexample to a claim that free trade always benefits workers — it defends free trade against critics. The direction of the argument is reversed. This is an 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.C: No causal mechanism is examined or refuted; the economist does not engage with why wages rose, only with whether the outcome counts as harm. This describes a causal-rebuttal argument not present here.
explanations.D: No analogy to protected industries appears in the stimulus. This introduces content absent from the argument.
explanations.E: The economist draws a specific conclusion about cases of trade liberalization, not a universal generalization about all sectors. 'Universally raises wages' is an extreme-verb trap.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument eliminates alternatives to arrive at its conclusion, a technique students often confuse with simple generalization or counterexample citation. Two traps each partially describe part of the argument without capturing the elimination structure.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientist: The sharp decline in the local honeybee population over the past decade must be attributable to pesticide exposure. It cannot be explained by habitat loss, because the wildflower meadows in the region have actually expanded during this period. It cannot be explained by disease, because pathogen surveys have found no novel pathogens in the hives. With the other leading explanations ruled out, pesticide exposure is the only remaining candidate.
lr.questionStem: The environmental scientist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: identifying a correlation between pesticide use and bee population decline and inferring that the correlation reflects a causal relationship

choices.label: B
choices.text: applying a general ecological principle to predict the consequences of pesticide exposure for pollinator populations

choices.label: C
choices.text: eliminating alternative explanations for a phenomenon in order to conclude that a particular explanation must be correct

choices.label: D
choices.text: citing experimental evidence that directly links pesticide compounds to the observed decline in bee populations

choices.label: E
choices.text: conceding that habitat loss and disease are contributing factors while arguing that pesticide exposure is the dominant cause

explanations.correct: The scientist does not present positive evidence for pesticide exposure; instead, the argument proceeds by ruling out habitat loss and disease and concluding that pesticide exposure must therefore be the explanation. This is argument by elimination — exactly what C describes.
explanations.A: No correlation between pesticide use and bee decline is stated in the stimulus; the argument never establishes that pesticide exposure actually occurred at elevated levels. This is a content-importing trap.
explanations.B: No general ecological principle is cited or applied. The argument is particular and eliminative, not principle-driven.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No experimental evidence is mentioned; the stimulus explicitly relies on ruling out alternatives rather than on direct positive evidence. 'Directly links' is an extreme-verb trap.
explanations.E: The scientist does not concede that habitat loss and disease are contributing factors — the argument explicitly rules them out. This is a mischaracterization trap that reverses the logical force of the premises.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument applies an abstract principle to a specific case, but the principle is embedded in a counterargument structure, making it easy to misidentify the main move. Traps either describe the counterargument alone or mislabel the move as an analogy.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Some argue that it is always permissible to break a promise when doing so would produce better overall consequences. But a legal contract that could be voided whenever a party believed doing so would yield better outcomes would provide no meaningful security to anyone who relied on it. The same is true of personal promises: a norm permitting promise-breaking whenever consequences favor it would undermine the very practice of promising, since no rational person would rely on a promise made under such a norm.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following describes a technique of reasoning used in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: drawing an analogy between legal contracts and personal promises to argue that the same standard of permissibility should govern both

choices.label: B
choices.text: citing an authority on contract law to establish that promise-breaking is impermissible under existing legal standards

choices.label: C
choices.text: rejecting a normative claim by showing that universally applying it would produce a result incompatible with the purpose the norm is meant to serve

choices.label: D
choices.text: offering a series of historical counterexamples to demonstrate that consequentialist ethics has never successfully guided promise-keeping behavior

choices.label: E
choices.text: conceding that consequences are morally relevant while arguing that they are not the only consideration in evaluating promises

explanations.correct: The ethicist's central move is a reductio-style rejection: if the norm 'break promises whenever consequences favor it' were universally applied, it would destroy the practice of promising itself — a result incompatible with the norm's own purpose. The legal-contract case is an illustration of this self-defeating quality, not the main technique. C captures the full move accurately.
explanations.A: The analogy to legal contracts is an illustrative device, not the main technique. The argument's conclusion is about promising in general, not about aligning legal and personal standards. Selecting A would be a 'partially true' trap — the analogy is present but is not the primary reasoning technique.
explanations.B: No legal authority is cited; the legal-contract example is used analogically, not as an appeal to authority. This describes a move the argument does not make.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No historical counterexamples are offered; the argument is abstract and hypothetical, not historical. This is an 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.E: The ethicist does not concede that consequences are morally relevant — the argument attacks the consequentialist norm directly. 'Conceding' misrepresents the rhetorical posture of the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-move argument with an embedded concession: the jurist grants a premise for the sake of argument, derives an unacceptable verdict from it, and then uses the contradiction to reject the premise. Traps describe only one or two of the moves, or invert the concession as a genuine endorsement.
lr.stimulus: Jurist: Defenders of mandatory minimum sentences contend that any policy which reduces average sentencing disparity across judges is thereby just. Grant, for the moment, that this standard is correct. It would then follow that a statute requiring every convicted defendant, regardless of offense, to receive the same five-year term would be a model of justice, since disparity would be eliminated entirely. But such a statute would plainly be monstrous. The defenders' standard must therefore be mistaken.
lr.questionStem: The jurist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
