choices.text: granting an opposing standard for the sake of argument, deriving a verdict from it that is manifestly unacceptable, and concluding on that basis that the standard is in error

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejecting an opposing standard by showing that its defenders are motivated by considerations other than justice

choices.label: C
choices.text: arguing that because a standard has been applied inconsistently, it must be replaced with a more precise formulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: drawing an analogy between sentencing disparity and other forms of legal inequality in order to support an opposing standard

choices.label: E
choices.text: establishing a standard of justice by eliminating each of the rival standards in turn

explanations.correct: The jurist concedes the disparity-reduction standard arguendo, derives the uniform-five-year consequence, labels that consequence monstrous, and treats the contradiction as grounds to reject the standard. A names all three moves in order.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The jurist never impugns defenders' motives; the argument is about entailments, not interests.
explanations.C: No claim is made that the standard has been inconsistently applied; it is rejected on entailment grounds.
explanations.D: No analogy to other forms of legal inequality is drawn, and the analogy would cut the wrong way.
explanations.E: Only one rival standard is in view, and no process of elimination across multiple candidates is run.

lr.difficultyReason: The economist draws an analogy, flags a disanalogy in the next breath, and proposes a refined principle grounded in that very disanalogy. Students must track all three beats; traps stop after the analogy or treat the disanalogy as a rejection of the original comparison rather than a refinement.
lr.stimulus: Economist: A central bank's inflation target is often compared to a thermostat setting: adjust the dial, and the temperature moves toward it. The comparison is a useful first pass, since expectations and interest-rate moves do anchor prices over the long run. But a thermostat works against a simple, passive medium, whereas prices are set by agents who anticipate the bank's own future moves. A more adequate rule, therefore, would direct the bank not simply to set a target but to commit credibly to a path of future policy, since only such a commitment can shape the expectations that a passive medium lacks.
lr.questionStem: The economist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two phenomena, noting a feature that limits the analogy's force, and proposing a refined principle grounded in the feature that marks the disanalogy

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejecting a familiar analogy outright on the ground that analogies cannot settle empirical questions

choices.label: C
choices.text: defending a controversial policy by showing that alternatives to it have failed when tried

choices.label: D
choices.text: inferring, from the fact that two systems share one feature, that they must share all of their important features

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to the consensus of central bankers to resolve a theoretical dispute about inflation targeting

explanations.correct: The thermostat analogy is affirmed as a useful first pass; the passive-medium disanalogy is then flagged; the refined rule (commit to a path, not just a target) is built on the expectations feature that is the very point of disanalogy.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The analogy is not rejected outright; it is refined. And no general claim about analogies is made.
explanations.C: No alternative policy is said to have failed when tried; the argument is conceptual.
explanations.D: The economist highlights a difference between the systems, not a shared-feature inference.
explanations.E: No appeal to consensus is made.

lr.difficultyReason: A dialogue in which the second speaker accepts a premise for argument's sake, extracts a further commitment that clashes with the first speaker's own practice, and uses the clash to undercut the first speaker's stance. Traps invert the role of the concession or describe only the final accusation.
lr.stimulus:
Critic: Any musical work whose score is not fixed note-for-note is an inferior composition, since genuine compositions must be reproducible exactly.
Composer: Grant that reproducibility is the measure of genuine composition. Then the great jazz standards, whose charts leave melodic and harmonic improvisation to the performer, would have to be dismissed as inferior; so would the improvised passages built into the cadenzas of Mozart's own concertos, which you otherwise praise as paradigms of composition. Your own judgments therefore cannot survive the standard you have just endorsed.
lr.questionStem: The composer responds to the critic by

choices.label: A
choices.text: provisionally accepting the critic's standard, drawing out consequences that conflict with judgments the critic elsewhere accepts, and concluding that the critic's position is untenable as it stands

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejecting the critic's standard by offering a single counterexample drawn from a genre the critic has no familiarity with

choices.label: C
choices.text: arguing that because the critic's standard is widely disputed among musicologists, it should not be accepted

choices.label: D
choices.text: claiming that the critic's standard presupposes a definition of 'composition' that the composer denies

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to the authority of Mozart in order to settle a question about the nature of improvisation

explanations.correct: The composer says 'grant that reproducibility is the measure,' follows out what that would entail (dismissing jazz standards and Mozart cadenzas), and points out that the critic's own praise for those works conflicts with the entailment.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The composer does not reject the standard by an unrelated counterexample; the force comes from the critic's own judgments, not from unfamiliar genres.
explanations.C: No claim about dispute among musicologists is made.
explanations.D: No ambiguity or redefinition of 'composition' is invoked; the standard is taken as given.
explanations.E: Mozart is cited as an example the critic already praises, not as an authority to settle a theoretical question.

lr.difficultyReason: The linguist identifies a regularity, acknowledges apparent exceptions, and reframes the regularity as a statistical tendency whose exceptions actually confirm the proposed mechanism. Traps describe the exception-handling as abandonment or as a shared-feature causal inference.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Across unrelated languages, words for close kin — 'mother,' 'father,' 'baby' — tend to contain the simplest consonants infants can produce. Some point to Georgian 'deda' for mother and 'mama' for father as evidence that the pattern is accidental. But those are precisely the sounds infants produce; the Georgian data show only that which simple consonant gets mapped to which parent varies, not that simple consonants fail to dominate. The regularity, then, is best understood not as a universal law but as a statistical tendency whose very 'exceptions' still fall inside its mechanism.
lr.questionStem: The linguist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: identifying a cross-linguistic regularity, addressing data that appear to contradict it, and reformulating the regularity in a way that the seeming counterevidence in fact supports

choices.label: B
choices.text: concluding that because two languages share a surface feature they must be genealogically related

choices.label: C
choices.text: rejecting a statistical tendency on the ground that it admits of exceptions

choices.label: D
choices.text: defending a universal law by dismissing apparent counterexamples as defective data

choices.label: E
choices.text: arguing that because infants cannot produce complex consonants, no language contains complex consonants in kin terms

explanations.correct: Regularity (simple consonants for kin terms) → apparent counterevidence (Georgian 'deda'/'mama') → reformulation (statistical tendency whose mechanism accommodates the Georgian mapping). A captures the three moves.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No claim of genealogical relatedness is made; the argument is typological, not historical.
explanations.C: The tendency is reformulated, not rejected; the linguist treats the Georgian case as inside the mechanism.
explanations.D: The linguist explicitly declines to treat the pattern as a universal law and does not dismiss the Georgian data as defective.
explanations.E: This overgeneralizes wildly; the linguist's claim is about kin terms, not all vocabulary.

lr.difficultyReason: Dialogue in which the respondent draws an analogy, acknowledges its limits, and proposes a refined policy grounded in the point of disanalogy. Traps collapse the argument to the analogy alone or describe only the policy recommendation.
lr.stimulus:
Minister: Critics argue that a carbon tax would be as intrusive on household budgets as a tax on bread.
Economist: The comparison illuminates one thing correctly — both taxes raise the sticker price of something households buy every week. But bread has no close substitute, while carbon-intensive energy does: households can shift to transit, insulation, or off-peak usage. A carbon tax's fairness therefore depends on a feature the bread analogy cannot reach: whether the revenue is rebated in ways that let households act on the substitutes the tax newly makes cheaper by comparison.
lr.questionStem: The economist responds to the minister by

choices.label: A
choices.text: accepting the limited force of a proposed analogy, identifying a feature on which the two cases diverge, and building a policy criterion around the feature that marks the divergence

choices.label: B
choices.text: dismissing an analogy as entirely without merit because the two items taxed are not physically similar

choices.label: C
choices.text: arguing that because carbon taxes have been endorsed by economists, the minister's critics must be mistaken

choices.label: D
choices.text: attempting to show that a carbon tax is not really a tax at all, on the ground that its revenues can be rebated

choices.label: E
choices.text: generalizing from the experience of a single jurisdiction to conclusions about carbon taxes in general

explanations.correct: The economist grants one thing the analogy gets right (sticker-price impact), names the substitution disanalogy, and builds the fairness criterion (rebate structure) on the substitution feature that the bread analogy lacks.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The analogy is partly credited, not dismissed wholesale; physical similarity is never the point.
explanations.C: No appeal to the endorsement of economists is made.
explanations.D: The economist never denies that a carbon tax is a tax; the rebate feature is invoked as a fairness condition, not a redefinition.
explanations.E: No single jurisdiction's experience is cited.

lr.difficultyReason: The biologist grants an inferential rule, applies it to a case where it yields an accepted verdict, and then applies the same rule to a disputed case to argue the verdict there must also hold. The three-move pattern (grant rule, test on easy case, extend to hard case) is dense; traps describe only the extension.
lr.stimulus: Biologist: Conservation policy rests, most agree, on the principle that when removing a species from an ecosystem leads to cascading collapse, that species is ecologically essential. On that principle, sea otters in North Pacific kelp forests are plainly essential: when they were hunted out, kelp beds collapsed as urchin populations exploded. The same reasoning, then, applies to beavers in continental river systems: wherever beavers have been eradicated, wetland habitat has dwindled and downstream flows have become erratic. Beavers, too, must be counted ecologically essential.
lr.questionStem: The biologist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: invoking a widely accepted principle, confirming its application in an uncontroversial case, and extending the same reasoning to a further case to establish a parallel conclusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that because two species share a habitat type, they must play the same ecological role

choices.label: C
choices.text: rejecting the principle that cascading collapse marks ecological essentiality, on the ground that the sea otter case is an outlier

choices.label: D
choices.text: defending a policy recommendation by appealing to the personal expertise of field biologists

choices.label: E
choices.text: arguing that since no ecosystem has remained unchanged after species loss, every species is ecologically essential

explanations.correct: Move 1: grant the cascading-collapse principle; Move 2: confirm it applies to sea otters; Move 3: extend the same application to beavers. A describes this three-step pattern.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Shared habitat type is not the basis of the inference; cascading collapse is.
explanations.C: The principle is invoked and applied, not rejected.
explanations.D: No appeal to personal expertise is made; the principle and its applications carry the argument.
explanations.E: The biologist's claim is about species whose removal triggers cascades, not about every species.

lr.difficultyReason: A dialogue in which the respondent accepts an empirical correlation, points out that it fits two rival causal structures equally well, and proposes a test designed to separate them. Traps ignore the middle move or describe the test as itself the conclusion.
lr.stimulus:
Researcher: Users of our messaging app who enable two-factor authentication report 30 percent fewer account compromises. Security advocates cite this as evidence that two-factor authentication reduces compromise rates.
Engineer: The correlation is real, but it is just as consistent with a different hypothesis: security-conscious users, who were already less likely to be compromised, are the ones most willing to turn the feature on. To choose between the two explanations, we should compare compromise rates for users who were randomly assigned to receive the feature by default versus those assigned to the opt-in flow; only that comparison isolates the feature itself from the kind of user who adopts it.
lr.questionStem: The engineer responds to the researcher by

choices.label: A
choices.text: granting the correlation at issue, noting that a rival causal hypothesis accounts for it equally well, and proposing a further comparison designed to discriminate between the two hypotheses

choices.label: B
choices.text: denying that the reported correlation exists in the underlying data at all

choices.label: C
choices.text: arguing that because security-conscious users are unrepresentative, no conclusions about messaging app security are possible

choices.label: D
choices.text: rejecting two-factor authentication on the ground that security advocates have a financial interest in promoting it

choices.label: E
choices.text: concluding that two-factor authentication does not reduce compromises, because self-selection is a known confounder

explanations.correct: The engineer accepts the correlation, names a selection-based rival hypothesis, and proposes a randomized-assignment comparison that would separate the two. The correct description names all three beats.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The correlation is explicitly granted.
explanations.C: No general skepticism about messaging-app conclusions is advanced.
explanations.D: No claim about advocates' financial interests is made.
explanations.E: The engineer does not conclude that two-factor authentication fails; a test is proposed, not a verdict.

lr.difficultyReason: The ethicist distinguishes two readings of a principle, shows that the strong reading collapses under a variant case, and endorses the weaker reading as the one that survives. Three moves (distinction, reductio, endorsement) that traps collapse into one.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: When we say a physician ought not deceive her patient, the claim might mean either that no deception is ever permissible or that deception is impermissible absent a compelling reason. Suppose a patient, delirious and momentarily convinced that a benign reflection is an intruder, asks whether anyone else is in the room; suppose too that a truthful 'no' would only deepen the terror, while a brief reassurance would allow sedation and recovery. Few would condemn the reassurance. The strong reading therefore fails the case, and the weaker reading — deception requires a compelling reason, which is present here — is the one that survives.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: distinguishing two readings of a principle, showing that the stronger reading is defeated by a test case, and endorsing the weaker reading because it accommodates that case

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that because physicians enjoy public trust, any deception by them is especially blameworthy

choices.label: C
choices.text: defending the claim that deception is never permissible by dismissing alleged counterexamples as fabricated

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizing from the ethicist's own clinical experience to a universal rule about patient communication

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to the fact that deception sometimes succeeds in order to show that it is sometimes required

explanations.correct: Two readings are distinguished; the strong reading is refuted by the delirium case; the weaker reading is endorsed because it accommodates the case. A describes all three moves in order.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Physician trust is never invoked; the argument is about which reading of the principle survives.
explanations.C: The strong reading is not defended — it is rejected. And the case is not dismissed.
explanations.D: No clinical experience is cited; the case is hypothetical.
explanations.E: The argument does not infer from success to requirement; it distinguishes two readings.

lr.difficultyReason: The historian acknowledges a correlation, argues that it fails to establish causation because of a confound, and proposes a narrower claim that the evidence does support. Three moves packed tightly; traps describe the reduction as outright rejection.
lr.stimulus: Historian: It is often said that the widespread adoption of mechanized looms caused the decline of the cottage textile industry in nineteenth-century England. The timing fits — looms spread as cottage weaving contracted. But railway construction spread on the same timetable, and rail access made long-distance grain markets, not mechanized textiles, the more immediate threat to cottage wages. The available evidence supports the weaker claim that mechanized looms contributed to the decline, not the stronger claim that they caused it.
lr.questionStem: The historian's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: conceding that a correlation holds between two phenomena, identifying a confounding development that undermines a causal reading, and retreating to a weaker claim that the evidence can bear

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that because two developments occurred on the same timetable, they must share a common cause

choices.label: C
choices.text: denying that mechanized looms had any effect on cottage textile wages

choices.label: D
choices.text: rejecting a causal claim solely on the ground that its defenders have failed to provide a plausible mechanism

choices.label: E
choices.text: arguing that since the railway was more consequential, the mechanized loom must have been wholly irrelevant to the cottage industry's decline

explanations.correct: Timing correlation is granted; the railway/grain-market confound is named; the claim is softened from 'caused' to 'contributed to.' All three beats are covered by A.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No shared-cause inference is drawn from shared timing.
explanations.C: The historian affirms looms contributed to the decline, not that their effect was zero.
explanations.D: The causal claim is not rejected for lack of mechanism; it is weakened because of the confound.
explanations.E: The argument ends with 'contributed to,' not with 'wholly irrelevant.'

lr.difficultyReason: Dialogue in which the respondent accepts a study's finding for argument's sake, derives a prediction that the data in fact fail to show, and concludes that the proposed mechanism cannot be what the original speaker claims. Three moves embedded in doctor's voice; traps invert the roles or attribute motives.
lr.stimulus:
Pharmacologist: A recent trial shows that patients given drug X experience 20 percent fewer migraine days per month than those given placebo. The authors infer that the drug suppresses the vascular mechanism they hypothesize to cause migraines.
Physician: Grant for the moment that the drug does suppress that vascular mechanism. If so, patients who experience migraines through that mechanism should respond robustly, while those whose migraines are known to arise from other mechanisms should not. But the trial reports a uniform effect across both subgroups. The finding is therefore not evidence for the mechanism the authors name; at most, it is evidence that the drug helps by some route the trial does not distinguish.
lr.questionStem: The physician responds to the pharmacologist by

choices.label: A
choices.text: accepting a proposed mechanism for the sake of argument, deriving a pattern the trial should have shown if the mechanism were operative, and concluding, because the pattern is absent, that the trial does not support the mechanism

choices.label: B
choices.text: denying that drug X reduces migraine days at all, on the ground that the trial's controls were inadequate

choices.label: C
choices.text: arguing that because the trial's authors stand to benefit from the drug's approval, their conclusions should be dismissed

choices.label: D
choices.text: inferring from the uniform effect across subgroups that drug X operates through the very vascular mechanism the authors describe

choices.label: E
choices.text: claiming that the trial is worthless because it used a placebo rather than an active comparator

explanations.correct: The physician grants the vascular mechanism arguendo, predicts differential subgroup response as a consequence, and notes that the uniform subgroup effect defeats the prediction — so the trial fails to support that mechanism.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The physician never denies the drug's overall effect.
explanations.C: No claim about authors' interests is made.
explanations.D: This reverses the physician's point; uniform subgroup effect is the reason the mechanism is not supported, not why it is.
explanations.E: The comparator design is never challenged; the issue is the mechanism inference.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument contains an intermediate conclusion, an embedded concession, and a final inference. Students must track three logical moves to identify the correct abstract description. Trap choices describe partial moves or reverse the direction of inference.
lr.stimulus: Physician: Some of my colleagues argue that a patient who has not responded to two successive antidepressant medications should automatically be considered treatment-resistant and switched to electroconvulsive therapy. I agree that non-response to two medications is a reliable indicator of treatment resistance in most patients. Nevertheless, there is a well-documented subgroup of patients who fail to respond to those medications solely because of undetected drug interactions caused by concurrent prescriptions. For such patients, treatment resistance is not the correct diagnosis. Therefore, automatic reclassification after two failed medications is unwarranted without first ruling out pharmacological interference.
lr.questionStem: The physician's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: accepting a general principle endorsed by an opposing view, then identifying a class of exceptions that prevents applying that principle universally

choices.label: B
choices.text: providing a counterexample to a statistical generalization and concluding that the generalization should be abandoned entirely

choices.label: C
choices.text: deriving an absurd consequence from a rival position in order to establish that the rival position is self-contradictory

choices.label: D
choices.text: inferring a causal relationship between drug interactions and treatment resistance from the correlation observed in a large clinical sample

choices.label: E
choices.text: citing the authority of clinical colleagues to support the claim that electroconvulsive therapy is the preferred second-line treatment

explanations.correct: The physician explicitly grants that non-response to two medications is a reliable indicator of treatment resistance — the general principle colleagues rely on — then carves out an exception subgroup (drug-interaction patients) to argue the principle cannot be applied automatically. This is precisely 'accepting the general principle but identifying exceptions that limit its universal application.'
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Partially true trap: the physician does identify an exception subgroup, but does not argue that the generalization should be abandoned entirely — the physician explicitly endorses the generalization as reliable in most cases.
explanations.C: No absurd consequence is derived; the physician never claims the colleagues' position is internally contradictory.
explanations.D: No clinical sample or correlation is cited; the drug-interaction subgroup is introduced as a documented category, not as the product of a new causal inference.
explanations.E: The physician disagrees with colleagues rather than appealing to their authority, and nowhere endorses ECT as the preferred treatment.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses an analogy between two domains (economics and ecology) as an intermediate step before reaching a policy conclusion. Answer choices differ in subtle ways — one correctly identifies the two-domain analogy while others misdescribe the direction of inference or the type of reasoning.
lr.stimulus: Economist: When a dominant firm in a market suddenly exits, smaller competitors rarely fill the void immediately; instead, productivity in the sector declines for years before recovery. Ecologists have documented a structurally identical pattern: when a keystone predator is removed from an ecosystem, subordinate species do not simply expand to occupy the vacated niche, and overall biodiversity declines sharply before a new equilibrium emerges. Given this parallel, economic policymakers who are considering breaking up a dominant technology firm should expect a prolonged period of reduced innovation, not the immediate competitive flourishing that proponents of the breakup predict.
lr.questionStem: The economist's argument derives its conclusion by

choices.label: A
choices.text: generalizing from a large number of economic cases to predict the outcome of a specific proposed policy

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing an analogy between a well-documented pattern in ecology and a structurally similar situation in economics to support a prediction about policy outcomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: appealing to an established economic principle to argue that a proposed action will have the opposite of its intended effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: using historical data about past regulatory interventions to predict that a proposed breakup will reduce innovation

choices.label: E
choices.text: rejecting the proponents' prediction by showing that it relies on a definition of competition that is too narrow

explanations.correct: The economist introduces ecological evidence about keystone predators, explicitly identifies it as structurally parallel to the economic situation, and uses that cross-domain analogy to forecast prolonged reduced innovation. Choice B captures this two-domain analogical inference precisely.
explanations.A: Partially true trap: the economist does cite economic cases, but the core logical move is the cross-domain analogy to ecology, not a generalization from many economic cases alone.
explanations.C: No established economic principle is invoked by name; the argument works through analogy, not a named principle. The 'opposite effect' language fits, but the mechanism described is wrong.
explanations.D: The evidence comes from ecology, not from historical data about past regulatory interventions — this is an accurate-sounding but content-displaced description.
explanations.E: No definitional dispute about 'competition' appears anywhere in the argument.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument eliminates alternatives to reach a conclusion by elimination, but also contains a concession. Students must distinguish the eliminative structure from the partially true trap describing it as a generalization from examples.
lr.stimulus: Historian: The rapid abandonment of the gold standard by industrialized nations in the 1930s is sometimes attributed to ideological shifts among economists, and sometimes to coordinated international political pressure. But detailed archival research has shown that economists of the era were deeply divided rather than ideologically unified, and that the relevant international negotiations had collapsed well before the abandonments occurred. The only remaining explanation that is consistent with the archival record is that individual governments abandoned the gold standard in direct response to domestic unemployment crises that made currency deflation politically untenable.
lr.questionStem: The historian's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing expert consensus among economic historians to establish that domestic unemployment was the decisive factor in abandoning the gold standard

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing an analogy between the political pressures of the 1930s and those of a more recent economic crisis to support the preferred explanation

choices.label: C
choices.text: eliminating competing explanations on the basis of archival evidence and inferring that the remaining explanation is correct

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizing from several specific national cases to conclude that domestic unemployment universally drives currency policy changes

choices.label: E
choices.text: accepting one of the two competing explanations as partially correct and incorporating it into a revised account

explanations.correct: The historian names two rival explanations, uses archival evidence to show each is inconsistent with the historical record, and then infers that the only remaining explanation must be correct. This is argument by elimination.
explanations.A: No expert consensus is cited; the historian actively notes that economists were divided, which is the opposite of consensus.
explanations.B: No analogy to a more recent crisis appears anywhere in the stimulus.
explanations.D: Mis-scaled trap: the historian infers a specific historical explanation, not a universal generalization about all currency policy changes.
explanations.E: The historian dismisses both competing explanations rather than accepting either as partially correct.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument applies an abstract legal principle to a concrete case, but the principle is stated in conditional form and the application involves a non-obvious intermediate step. Trap choices misidentify the direction of the inference or describe the argument as an analogy rather than a principle application.
lr.stimulus: Legal scholar: A contract is enforceable only if the party against whom enforcement is sought had a genuine opportunity to read and understand its terms before agreeing. Software end-user license agreements are typically presented in small print after payment has been made and the product has been downloaded. At that point, the user has no practical alternative to clicking 'agree,' because declining would require returning a product the user has already used. Accordingly, software license agreements of this type do not satisfy the condition for enforceability and should not be treated as binding contracts.
lr.questionStem: The legal scholar's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: uses an analogy between software license agreements and other adhesion contracts to argue that both should be treated as unenforceable

choices.label: B
choices.text: applies a general principle governing contract enforceability to a specific category of agreements and derives a conclusion about their legal status

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers a causal relationship between the timing of disclosure and consumer harm from survey data about user comprehension

choices.label: D
choices.text: rejects a rival legal standard by deriving a consequence from it that contradicts a widely accepted judicial precedent

choices.label: E
choices.text: establishes that software companies act in bad faith by demonstrating that license agreements are designed to prevent meaningful consent

explanations.correct: The scholar states a general principle (enforceability requires genuine opportunity to read and understand terms), argues that software EULAs as described fail to meet that condition, and concludes they are unenforceable. This is a straightforward principle-application-to-case structure.
explanations.A: No other category of adhesion contracts is mentioned; the argument works by applying a principle, not by drawing an analogy to a sister category.
explanations.C: No survey data or causal inference appears; the argument is purely a principled deduction.
explanations.D: No rival legal standard is named and no judicial precedent is cited; the scholar offers a direct principled argument.
explanations.E: Extreme-verb trap: the scholar nowhere attributes bad faith or intent to software companies; the argument is about structural features of the agreement, not corporate motive.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument cites a single verifiable counterexample to defeat a universal claim, but the counterexample is embedded in a longer setup that could mislead students into thinking the main move is a causal inference or a generalization. The partially-true trap accurately describes a secondary move.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Proponents of the critical-period hypothesis claim that any individual who does not acquire a first language before puberty will be permanently incapable of achieving full grammatical competence in any language. However, documented cases of late-language-acquisition individuals — such as those raised in extreme social isolation — show that some adults who had no language exposure before puberty do eventually acquire the grammar of a taught language to a level indistinguishable from that of native speakers, at least in controlled testing environments. This demonstrates that the critical-period hypothesis, in its strongest universal form, is false.
lr.questionStem: The linguist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: generalizing from documented cases of late language acquisition to conclude that critical periods do not exist for any aspect of language development

choices.label: B
choices.text: applying a principle about developmental windows in biology to argue that the critical-period hypothesis overstates the evidence

choices.label: C
choices.text: identifying a verifiable instance that contradicts a universal claim and concluding that the claim in its strongest form cannot be sustained

choices.label: D
choices.text: inferring from a correlation between social isolation and language delay that puberty itself is not the cause of permanent grammatical deficits

choices.label: E
choices.text: conceding that the critical-period hypothesis applies in most cases while arguing that its proponents have misidentified the relevant developmental mechanism

explanations.correct: The linguist explicitly targets the 'strongest universal form' of the hypothesis ('any individual… will be permanently incapable') and cites documented cases of late acquirers who achieved native-level competence. One genuine counterexample is logically sufficient to refute a universal claim, and that is exactly the move being made.
explanations.A: Mis-scaled trap: the linguist's conclusion is specifically about the universal form of the hypothesis, not a sweeping generalization that critical periods don't exist for any aspect of language at all.
explanations.B: No biological developmental-window principle is invoked; the argument stays within linguistics and uses a direct counterexample.
explanations.D: The argument does not pursue a causal analysis of puberty vs. social isolation as competing causal factors; it uses the cases as counterexamples, not as evidence for an alternative causal chain.
explanations.E: The linguist does not concede the hypothesis applies in most cases — the conclusion is that the universal form is false, not that it is mechanistically misdescribed.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses a reductio structure: it conditionally accepts a rival claim and shows it entails an empirically false consequence. Distinguishing a reductio from a direct counterexample is challenging; the partial-truth trap names the consequence without identifying the conditional structure.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientist: Proponents of large-scale iron fertilization of the oceans argue that seeding the surface ocean with iron will cause phytoplankton blooms large enough to sequester atmospheric carbon at a scale sufficient to meaningfully offset industrial emissions. If this were true, we would expect to observe sustained high-carbon organic matter sinking to deep-sea sediments in proportion to the bloom size in every large-scale fertilization trial conducted to date. Yet in every such trial, the expected carbon export to deep sediments has been negligible relative to the bloom size, with most carbon recycled in the surface layer. The proposed mechanism therefore does not operate as proponents describe.
lr.questionStem: The environmental scientist's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: argues that the rival claim, if true, would require an outcome that empirical trials have consistently failed to produce, and concludes that the claim is incorrect

choices.label: B
choices.text: cites a single anomalous trial result to cast doubt on the generalization that iron fertilization sequesters carbon

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws an analogy between deep-sea carbon cycling and terrestrial carbon storage to challenge the proposed sequestration mechanism

choices.label: D
choices.text: accepts the proponents' goal of carbon sequestration while rejecting their proposed method on grounds of economic inefficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: infers from the correlation between bloom size and surface-layer recycling that iron fertilization causes net increases in atmospheric carbon

explanations.correct: The scientist conditionally assumes the proponents' claim ('if this were true'), derives what would have to be observable (deep-sediment carbon export proportional to bloom size), notes that every trial fails to show this, and concludes the proposed mechanism is wrong. This is a conditional-derivation / reductio-style refutation.
explanations.B: Partially true trap: multiple trials are cited, not a single anomalous result; and the argument's structure is a reductio, not merely a counterexample citation.
explanations.C: No analogy to terrestrial carbon storage appears; the argument relies on trial data within oceanography alone.
explanations.D: Economic inefficiency is never mentioned; the argument is about whether the mechanism works as described, not about cost.
explanations.E: Extreme-verb trap with content distortion: the scientist does not infer that iron fertilization increases atmospheric carbon — the conclusion is only that the sequestration mechanism doesn't operate as claimed.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument first establishes an intermediate conclusion via a causal claim, then uses that intermediate conclusion as a premise in a further ethical inference. Students must recognize the two-step structure — empirical premise to intermediate conclusion, then intermediate conclusion to normative conclusion — and not select a choice that describes only the first or only the second step.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Architects who design buildings without adequate accessibility features are often said to be merely complying with client budgetary constraints. But the unavailability of physical access demonstrably excludes people with disabilities from civic participation — from voting locations, courtrooms, and public offices — that is legally guaranteed to them. Any professional practice that predictably produces outcomes in which legally guaranteed rights are systematically denied constitutes a form of complicity in rights violations. Therefore, architects who knowingly design inaccessible public buildings bear a form of professional moral responsibility for the exclusions that result.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: drawing an analogy between architectural decisions and legal decisions to argue that architects should be held to the same accountability standards as judges

choices.label: B
choices.text: first establishing empirically that inaccessible design produces rights-excluding outcomes, then applying a moral principle to those outcomes to derive a conclusion about professional responsibility

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizing from a series of individual architects' decisions to conclude that the profession as a whole endorses discriminatory design practices

choices.label: D
choices.text: rejecting the budget-constraint defense by demonstrating that it is internally inconsistent with professional codes of ethics

choices.label: E
choices.text: inferring that architects intend to exclude people with disabilities from the fact that they knowingly produce buildings that have that effect

explanations.correct: The ethicist first makes an empirical claim (inaccessible design excludes people with disabilities from legally guaranteed civic participation) and treats that as an established intermediate conclusion. The ethicist then invokes a moral principle (any practice that predictably produces rights violations is complicity) and applies it to derive the normative conclusion about architects' moral responsibility. Choice B captures this two-step empirical-then-normative structure.
explanations.A: No analogy between architects and judges is drawn; architects and courthouses appear, but courts are examples of excluded civic venues, not analogical comparators for architects' roles.
explanations.C: Mis-scaled trap: the conclusion is about individual architects who knowingly design inaccessibly, not a generalization about the profession's collective endorsement of discrimination.
explanations.D: The budget-constraint defense is acknowledged but not refuted by showing it is internally inconsistent; the ethicist simply bypasses it by grounding the conclusion in a separate principle.
explanations.E: Extreme-verb trap: the ethicist concludes responsibility, not intent. The argument explicitly works from predictable outcomes, not from inferred mental states.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses an appeal to definition as its core move, but the definition is stipulated mid-argument after an empirical description, making the logical structure harder to identify. Traps include a partially-true causal inference and a misdescribed generalization.
lr.stimulus: Technology critic: Supporters of algorithmic content curation claim that recommendation engines merely help users find content they would already prefer. But a preference, properly understood, is a disposition that exists prior to and independently of the choices presented to a person. When a recommendation engine systematically withholds entire categories of content from a user's feed, the user has no opportunity to form a preference regarding that content. What the algorithm produces, therefore, is not the satisfaction of pre-existing preferences but the creation of artificially constrained preference profiles — meaning that the claim that curation merely serves user preferences is false by definition.
lr.questionStem: The technology critic's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing empirical research showing that users exposed to algorithmically curated content report lower satisfaction than users who browse without algorithmic assistance

choices.label: B
choices.text: invoking a stipulated definition of 'preference' to show that what recommendation engines produce cannot qualify as the satisfaction of user preferences

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between algorithmic curation and traditional editorial decisions to argue that both manipulate audience preferences

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizing from the behavior of a few poorly designed recommendation engines to condemn all algorithmic curation

choices.label: E
choices.text: inferring from the correlation between content withholding and narrowed user interests that algorithms cause long-term preference decay

explanations.correct: The critic defines 'preference' as a disposition formed prior to and independently of presented choices, then argues that because recommendation engines prevent users from encountering content, no genuine preference regarding that content can form — so the engine cannot be 'satisfying preferences' in the defined sense. The phrase 'false by definition' signals this explicitly.
explanations.A: No empirical user-satisfaction research is cited anywhere in the argument.
explanations.C: No analogy to traditional editorial decisions appears; the argument is entirely internal to the analysis of algorithmic curation.
explanations.D: Mis-scaled trap: the critic does not limit the argument to 'a few poorly designed' engines — the structural point is meant to apply to recommendation engines generally insofar as they withhold categories of content.
explanations.E: Causal inference trap: the conclusion is about whether curation satisfies preferences by definition, not about a long-term causal effect on preference formation.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument establishes a conclusion about current policy by using evidence from a historical case as the direct basis for inference about an analogous present situation, but the analogical structure is obscured by the long historical setup and the embedded concession that the two situations differ in one respect. Students must identify which similarities drive the inference and whether the conceded difference defeats the analogy.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: Critics of the proposed urban density mandate point out that a similar mandatory densification policy introduced in a major European city in the 1970s led to increased traffic congestion that persisted for over a decade. Admittedly, that city had a less developed public transit infrastructure than the city targeted by the current proposal. However, the mechanism behind the congestion — an influx of new residents whose daily travel patterns had not yet adapted to the density — operates independently of the quality of existing transit, as transit adoption takes years regardless of system quality. The critics' caution is therefore well founded: the proposed mandate is likely to produce the same kind of prolonged congestion.
lr.questionStem: The policy analyst's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: accepts a disanalogy between a historical case and the current situation, argues that the disanalogy does not undermine the relevant parallel, and uses the historical case to support a prediction about the current policy

choices.label: B
choices.text: establishes a general causal law about urban densification and applies it to the current proposal to predict a specific negative outcome

choices.label: C
choices.text: dismisses the critics' concern by showing that the historical case they rely on is not sufficiently similar to the current situation

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers from a series of historical densification failures that mandatory density mandates are always counterproductive

choices.label: E
choices.text: uses a comparison of transit infrastructure quality across cities to argue that the current city is better prepared for densification than the historical case

explanations.correct: The analyst acknowledges the critics' disanalogy (the historical city had worse transit), but neutralizes it by arguing the congestion-causing mechanism operates independently of transit quality. Having neutralized the disanalogy, the analyst uses the historical case as an analogy to predict the same prolonged congestion. This is a three-move structure: acknowledge disanalogy → neutralize it → deploy the analogy.
explanations.B: No general causal law is formally established across multiple cases; the analyst works from a single historical parallel, not a law derived from many instances.
explanations.C: Direction-reversal trap: the analyst does the opposite — supports the critics' concern rather than dismissing it, and preserves the similarity rather than undermining it.
explanations.D: Mis-scaled trap: the conclusion is about this specific proposal, not a universal generalization that all mandatory density mandates are always counterproductive.
explanations.E: Content-reversal trap: the analyst concedes the historical city had worse transit (less developed), then argues that doesn't matter — never claims the current city is better prepared.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument combines a distinction between two senses of a term with an argument by elimination, then uses both moves together to reach a conclusion. Traps include answers describing only one of the two moves, and an extreme-verb answer falsely attributing a refutation of expert consensus.
lr.stimulus: Art critic: When people say that a work of art is 'difficult,' they sometimes mean that it requires specialized training to appreciate, and sometimes mean that it resists full comprehension even for trained experts. These are entirely different claims. Works that merely require training are difficult only in the way that advanced mathematics is difficult: the difficulty is contingent on education and disappears with sufficient exposure. Works that resist expert comprehension, by contrast, are difficult in a deeper sense. The compositions of a certain late modernist composer have been extensively studied by trained musicians for decades, and professional analyses remain genuinely divergent and inconclusive. The composer's work is therefore not merely educationally difficult but irreducibly so.
lr.questionStem: The art critic's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: drawing an analogy between musical difficulty and mathematical difficulty to conclude that both forms of difficulty are educationally contingent

choices.label: B
choices.text: surveying expert critical opinion on the composer's work to establish that the work has been misclassified by earlier critics

choices.label: C
choices.text: distinguishing two senses of a term, eliminating one sense as inapplicable, and concluding that the other sense correctly characterizes the case at hand

choices.label: D
choices.text: inferring from the divergence of expert analyses that the composer's work is of higher aesthetic quality than works that admit of consensus interpretation

choices.label: E
choices.text: refuting the consensus view among music scholars by demonstrating that their training is insufficient to resolve the work's fundamental ambiguities

explanations.correct: The critic opens by distinguishing two senses of 'difficult' (educationally contingent vs. irreducibly resistant to expert comprehension), then shows that the composer's work does not fit the first sense (since decades of expert study have not resolved it), and concludes it fits the second sense. The structure is: draw a distinction → eliminate one horn → apply the other.
explanations.A: Partially true trap: the analogy to mathematics is used to characterize the first sense of difficulty — the sense being eliminated — not to reach the conclusion. The math analogy is a subsidiary move, not the main technique.
explanations.B: No claim is made that earlier critics misclassified the work; the critic is drawing a distinction and applying it fresh, not correcting prior misclassification.
explanations.D: Extreme-verb trap with content distortion: the critic draws no conclusion about aesthetic quality or superiority; the argument is about the category of difficulty, not about evaluative ranking.
explanations.E: Extreme-verb trap: the critic does not refute a consensus view among scholars nor claim their training is insufficient. The divergence of expert opinion is cited as evidence that the difficulty is irreducible, not as a criticism of the experts.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument has an intermediate conclusion (the drug is effective against the virus in vitro) and an embedded concession (in vivo conditions differ), requiring the student to track two logical moves and match both to the abstract correct answer. Traps exploit partial accuracy.
lr.stimulus: Pharmacologist: A newly synthesized compound has demonstrated strong antiviral activity against influenza A in cell-culture studies. Granted, cell-culture results do not always translate to effective treatments in living organisms, since metabolic processes can neutralize a compound before it reaches target tissues. Nevertheless, every antiviral drug currently approved for clinical use first showed activity in cell-culture studies of this kind. We are therefore justified in regarding the new compound as a promising candidate for further clinical investigation.
lr.questionStem: The pharmacologist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing the uniformity of past successful cases to support an inference that an intermediate step is both necessary and sufficient for a final outcome

choices.label: B
choices.text: acknowledging a limitation of the evidence, then appealing to a pattern shared by all prior confirmed members of a category to support a qualified conclusion about a new candidate

choices.label: C
choices.text: dismissing a counterexample to a general principle by showing that the counterexample involves conditions not present in the case under consideration

choices.label: D
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two experimental methods to conclude that the results of one method are interchangeable with the results of the other

choices.label: E
choices.text: inferring that a compound will succeed in clinical trials by generalizing from the outcomes of a large sample of previously tested compounds

explanations.correct: The pharmacologist concedes that cell-culture results don't always translate (acknowledges a limitation), then uses the fact that all approved antivirals passed through this exact same step (a pattern shared by all prior confirmed members of the category) to conclude the new compound is a promising candidate (qualified conclusion). B captures both moves.
explanations.A: The argument does not claim that cell-culture activity is sufficient for clinical success — in fact it explicitly concedes it is not. 'Sufficient' is an extreme claim the pharmacologist explicitly avoids.
explanations.C: No counterexample is dismissed. The limitation of cell-culture studies is conceded, not refuted. This is the 'dismisses a counterexample' trap.
explanations.D: The argument does not claim the two methods produce interchangeable results; it explicitly notes their results can diverge. This is an extreme-verb / mis-description trap.
explanations.E: The conclusion is qualified ('promising candidate'), not that the compound will succeed. Also, the argument cites a universal pattern (all approved antivirals), not a large sample used for statistical generalization.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument involves applying a principle through a reductio-style move against an opposing claim, with an embedded analogy. Students must distinguish 'deriving an absurd consequence' from 'citing a counterexample,' and the correct answer uses dense formal vocabulary.
lr.stimulus: Legal theorist: Some scholars argue that contracts entered into under conditions of severe economic duress should be enforceable, on the grounds that both parties voluntarily agreed to the terms. But this reasoning proves too much. By the same logic, a person who agrees to hand over her wallet at gunpoint has 'voluntarily' transferred property, and that transfer should be legally binding. Since we clearly do not accept that conclusion, we must reject the premise that economic duress is compatible with the kind of voluntariness required for enforceable agreement.
lr.questionStem: The legal theorist's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: appeals to a general principle about contracts to show that a specific case of economic duress is not legally binding

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejects a position by constructing a parallel case whose conclusion is clearly unacceptable, then uses that unacceptability to impugn the original position's premise

choices.label: C
choices.text: cites empirical evidence about how courts have treated duress cases to undermine a theoretical claim about voluntary agreement

choices.label: D
choices.text: argues that because two situations share one relevant feature they must share all legally significant features

choices.label: E
choices.text: establishes a universal definition of voluntariness and then deduces from that definition which contracts are enforceable

explanations.correct: The theorist takes the scholars' logic, applies it to the gunpoint wallet case (a parallel case), shows the conclusion is clearly unacceptable, then uses that unacceptability to reject the premise that economic duress is compatible with voluntariness. This is a reductio-by-analogy move, precisely described by B.
explanations.A: The theorist does not appeal to a pre-established contract principle; the argument works by constructing the parallel case. This is the 'content over technique' trap.
explanations.C: No empirical data about court rulings is cited. This is the 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.D: The theorist does not claim the two situations share all legally significant features — only that the underlying logic of voluntariness applies equally. D overstates the move.
explanations.E: No universal definition of voluntariness is established in the argument. The conclusion about voluntariness is derived, not stated as a premise-definition.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses elimination of alternatives as its core move, embedded within a causal framing. Students must distinguish 'arguing by elimination' from 'inferring a cause from a correlation' and from 'generalizing from instances,' all of which are plausible-sounding traps.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientist: Coral reef systems in the northern survey zone have declined significantly over the past two decades. Three hypotheses have been advanced: elevated ocean temperatures, increased sediment runoff from adjacent agricultural land, and overfishing of herbivorous species that control algal growth. Temperature records show no anomalous warming in the northern zone during the relevant period. Sediment levels in the northern zone have remained stable throughout. We are therefore left with the conclusion that the removal of herbivorous fish populations is the most plausible explanation for the observed decline.
lr.questionStem: The environmental scientist's argument derives its conclusion by

choices.label: A
choices.text: inferring a causal relationship from a correlation between the decline of coral reefs and changes in fish populations across multiple reef systems

choices.label: B
choices.text: applying a general ecological principle about predator-prey balance to predict the consequences of removing herbivorous species

choices.label: C
choices.text: eliminating the other candidates from a previously enumerated set of competing explanations on the basis of evidence specific to the case

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizing from observed declines in a sample of reef systems to all reef systems in the northern survey zone

choices.label: E
choices.text: establishing that overfishing is both a necessary and a sufficient condition for coral reef decline in any marine environment

explanations.correct: The scientist explicitly lists three hypotheses, then eliminates temperature and sediment by citing evidence specific to the northern zone, leaving the overfishing hypothesis as the survivor. This is textbook argument by elimination from an enumerated set.
explanations.A: No correlation across multiple reef systems is presented. The evidence is confined to the northern zone, and the argument's structure is eliminative, not correlational. This is the 'mis-scaled' trap.
explanations.B: No general ecological principle about predator-prey balance is invoked. The argument reaches its conclusion by elimination, not by principle application.
explanations.D: The decline is stipulated as a known fact about the northern zone; the argument is about explaining that decline, not generalizing from a sample.
explanations.E: The conclusion is that overfishing is the 'most plausible explanation' — a qualified claim, not an assertion of necessity and sufficiency. 'Establishes' and 'necessary and sufficient' are both extreme-verb traps.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument contains an intermediate conclusion drawn from an analogy, then used as a premise to reach a normative conclusion. Students must track the two-step structure and the analogical bridge, and must avoid traps that describe only one step.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Scholars who argue that the Athenian assembly was a genuinely democratic institution often point to the fact that all male citizens could participate in debates. But participation in formal deliberation is not equivalent to meaningful political power; modern shareholders can speak at annual meetings without thereby exercising real control over corporate decisions. Since historians agree that shareholder meetings do not constitute democratic governance of corporations, we should equally conclude that the mere right to speak in the Athenian assembly did not, by itself, make Athens a democracy in any substantive sense.
lr.questionStem: The historian's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: challenging an accepted definition of democracy by offering an etymology that reveals a different original meaning

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing an analogy to a case whose conclusion is already accepted in order to derive a parallel conclusion about a disputed case

choices.label: C
choices.text: citing historical evidence that Athenian citizens in practice rarely exercised their formal right to speak in assembly debates

choices.label: D
choices.text: establishing a universal principle about political power and then deducing the conclusion as a special case of that principle

choices.label: E
choices.text: refuting the opposing scholars' conclusion by providing a direct counterexample drawn from Athenian historical records

explanations.correct: The historian constructs an analogy: shareholders can speak at meetings but don't control corporations (the already-accepted conclusion), just as Athenians could speak in assembly but didn't thereby hold meaningful power. The accepted verdict on shareholder meetings is imported to settle the disputed question about Athens. This is precisely B.
explanations.A: No etymology is offered. The argument does not appeal to the historical origin of the word 'democracy.' This is the 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.C: The argument makes no empirical claim about how often Athenian citizens actually spoke; it challenges the significance of the formal right, not its exercise rate. This is the 'content over technique' trap.
explanations.D: No universal principle is formally established. The claim that formal participation ≠ meaningful power serves as a bridging analogy, not a deductive universal. D overstates the logical structure.
explanations.E: The argument uses an analogy, not a direct counterexample from Athenian records. And the opposing scholars' conclusion is challenged, not refuted by empirical evidence.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses a definitional move to rebut a causal claim, embedding that rebuttal within a concession. Students must identify that the core technique is appealing to a definition to undermine a causal inference, rather than presenting counterevidence or a counterexample.
lr.stimulus: Economist: It is sometimes claimed that rising consumer debt levels cause recessions, because high debt burdens force households to reduce spending, thereby contracting aggregate demand. This causal story has intuitive appeal, but it conflates correlation with explanation. A recession, by definition, is a period of sustained decline in economic output. Household deleveraging — debt reduction — is itself a contraction of economic activity. So the supposed cause and the supposed effect are not independent phenomena; they are two descriptions of the same underlying process. One cannot coherently claim that a recession is caused by something that is constitutively part of that very recession.
lr.questionStem: The economist's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: offers statistical evidence that correlations between debt levels and recessions are weaker than previously assumed

choices.label: B
choices.text: appeals to the definition of the phenomenon under discussion to argue that a proposed cause and its supposed effect are not genuinely distinct

choices.label: C
choices.text: concedes the empirical accuracy of a causal claim while denying that the claim has any policy implications

choices.label: D
choices.text: identifies an exception to the general pattern of household deleveraging to show that the causal claim does not hold universally

choices.label: E
choices.text: argues by elimination that because debt-driven explanations of recession are implausible, an alternative explanation must be correct

explanations.correct: The economist invokes the definition of recession (sustained decline in output) and the definition of deleveraging (itself a contraction of activity) to show the two are constitutively the same process, making the causal relationship incoherent. This is a paradigm case of appealing to a definition to undermine a causal claim — exactly B.
explanations.A: No statistics are presented. The argument is purely conceptual-definitional. This is the 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.C: The economist does not concede empirical accuracy; rather, the argument denies the causal story is even coherent. The move is not about policy implications.
explanations.D: No exception is cited. The argument does not work by finding a case where deleveraging occurs without recession. This is the 'counterexample' trap.
explanations.E: No alternative explanation is offered or argued for. The argument's purpose is to undermine the proposed cause, not to eliminate alternatives and select a survivor.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument applies a general ethical principle to a specific case through a two-step inference, with an intermediate normative claim. Students must distinguish 'applies a principle to a case' from 'establishes a principle by generalization,' and must notice the intermediate step.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: We generally accept that a person who knowingly benefits from a harm inflicted on another bears some moral responsibility for that harm, even if the person did not directly cause it. Consider now the case of a consumer who purchases goods produced under conditions of forced labor in a distant country. The consumer benefits from the artificially suppressed prices that result from exploited workers. Given that the consumer knows that such conditions exist in the industries whose products they buy, it follows that the consumer bears some degree of moral responsibility for the harms those workers endure.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's argument derives its conclusion by

choices.label: A
choices.text: establishing a new moral principle about consumer behavior through induction from a series of analogous cases

choices.label: B
choices.text: showing that a consumer who purchases goods knowingly produced under forced labor is a counterexample to the claim that only direct perpetrators bear moral responsibility

choices.label: C
choices.text: applying an accepted general moral principle to a particular case to derive a conclusion about the moral status of that case

choices.label: D
choices.text: drawing an analogy between the economic relationship of consumers to producers and a legal relationship that carries established liability

choices.label: E
choices.text: arguing that because forced labor is widely condemned, any practice that supports it is equally subject to condemnation

explanations.correct: The ethicist begins with an accepted general principle (knowingly benefiting from harm = some moral responsibility), then identifies the specific case (consumer buying forced-labor goods) as satisfying the conditions of that principle, and draws the conclusion that the consumer bears some responsibility. This is a canonical application of a general principle to a specific case.
explanations.A: The principle is not established by induction in the argument — it is stated as a pre-existing, generally accepted premise. The direction is principle → case, not case → principle.
explanations.B: The consumer is not presented as a counterexample to anything; the argument uses the consumer as a new instance that falls under the general principle. No opposing claim about direct perpetrators is under attack.
explanations.D: No specific legal analogy is constructed. The argument operates through a moral principle, not by mapping an economic relationship to a legal liability framework.
explanations.E: The argument does not rely on widespread condemnation of forced labor as its logical engine. The move is from principle about knowing benefit to conclusion about this consumer.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses a two-stage move: a counterexample to an opposing universal generalization, followed by an intermediate conclusion that reframes the debate. Students must track both stages and avoid traps that capture only the counterexample move or only the reframing move.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: Proponents of mandatory minimum sentencing often claim that such sentences invariably reduce crime rates by incapacitating repeat offenders and deterring potential criminals. Yet jurisdictions that have repealed mandatory minimum statutes have not experienced increases in crime — in several cases, crime rates have actually declined. This is sufficient to show that mandatory minimums are not necessary to maintain public safety. The real question, then, is not whether mandatory minimums reduce crime, but whether the social costs they impose — including prison overcrowding and racial disparities in sentencing — are justified by any marginal crime-reduction benefits they may produce.
lr.questionStem: The policy analyst's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: cites instances that undermine a universal claim, uses that to establish an intermediate conclusion, and then shifts the framing of the debate to a cost-benefit question

choices.label: B
choices.text: establishes through a statistical survey that mandatory minimum sentences have failed to reduce crime in the majority of jurisdictions that have adopted them

choices.label: C
choices.text: argues by analogy that because sentencing policy in comparable jurisdictions did not increase crime, it will not do so in the jurisdiction under consideration

choices.label: D
choices.text: applies a general principle about the necessity of incarceration to conclude that mandatory minimums are an insufficient tool of crime prevention

choices.label: E
choices.text: concedes that mandatory minimum sentences reduce crime and argues instead that their social costs are an overriding moral objection to their use

explanations.correct: The analyst first cites cases of jurisdictions that repealed mandatory minimums without crime increases (undermining the universal claim that such sentences are necessary). This yields the intermediate conclusion that mandatory minimums are not necessary for public safety. Then the argument explicitly reframes the debate away from efficacy toward cost-benefit analysis. A captures all three moves accurately.
explanations.B: The argument does not present a statistical survey or claim that mandatory minimums have failed in most jurisdictions. The evidence is narrower: repeal jurisdictions didn't see crime increases. 'Majority of jurisdictions' overstates the evidence.
explanations.C: No analogy to a specific comparable jurisdiction is constructed. The argument's structure is counterexample + intermediate conclusion + reframing, not analogical inference.
explanations.D: No general principle about the necessity of incarceration is invoked. The argument's logical structure is counterexample-driven, not principle-application.
explanations.E: The analyst does not concede that mandatory minimums reduce crime; the intermediate conclusion is that they are not necessary, which is a stronger challenge to the proponents' claim than a mere cost concession.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses a structural move rarely tested: distinguishing a token from a type to rebut an opposing inference. Students must identify this type/token distinction as the core technique rather than confusing it with a counterexample move or a definitional appeal.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Some cognitive scientists claim that because all known human languages share certain structural features — such as the noun-verb distinction — these features must be innately specified in the human mind. But this inference is unwarranted. The fact that all observed instances of a phenomenon share a property does not show that the property is innately determined rather than the result of common environmental pressures. After all, every observed human language has developed in the context of communities that engage in reference and predication, and those communicative demands alone could account for the universality of noun-verb structure.
lr.questionStem: The linguist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: providing a direct counterexample — a human language that lacks the noun-verb distinction — to falsify the cognitive scientists' generalization

choices.label: B
choices.text: challenging the inference from universal co-occurrence to innateness by offering a competing explanation for the observed universality

choices.label: C
choices.text: applying a general principle about language acquisition to show that structural features must arise from experience rather than innate specification

choices.label: D
choices.text: arguing that the noun-verb distinction is not in fact universal across all human languages, undermining the empirical premise of the opposing view

choices.label: E
choices.text: drawing an analogy between linguistic universals and biological universals to conclude that universality is not evidence of genetic determination

explanations.correct: The linguist does not deny the universality of noun-verb structure, nor provide a counterexample. Instead, the argument attacks the inference from universality to innateness by offering an alternative explanation (common communicative demands), thereby showing the cognitive scientists' conclusion does not follow from the premise. B captures this precisely.
explanations.A: The linguist explicitly accepts the universality premise; no counterexample language is provided. This is the 'counterexample' trap — the argument challenges the inference, not the empirical claim.
explanations.C: No general principle about language acquisition is invoked. The competing explanation (communicative demands) is offered as a possibility, not derived from a principle.
explanations.D: The linguist does not dispute that noun-verb structure is universal — the argument concedes this and attacks the inference to innateness. D directly contradicts the argument's actual move.
explanations.E: No analogy to biological universals is constructed. The argument works by offering an alternative explanation, not by drawing a parallel to another domain.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses a nested structure: it identifies what a claim presupposes, shows the presupposition is false, and concludes the claim fails. Students must distinguish this 'undermining a presupposition' technique from a straightforward counterexample or refutation by contradiction.
lr.stimulus: Art critic: The view that digital photography has democratized fine-art photography rests on the assumption that access to professional-quality equipment is the primary barrier to producing art-quality images. But this assumption is false. The most significant barriers to producing art-quality work are not technological but perceptual and conceptual: knowing what to photograph, how to frame a subject, and how to use light expressively. These capacities are developed through sustained study and practice, not through access to equipment. Consequently, the claim that digital photography has democratized fine-art photography is not well supported.
lr.questionStem: The art critic's argument does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: surveys the history of fine-art photography to show that the most celebrated works were produced with minimal equipment, thereby undermining the view that equipment determines quality

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws an analogy between fine-art photography and other art forms to argue that perceptual skill is more important than technological access in all creative domains

choices.label: C
choices.text: identifies and rejects a presupposition of an opposing claim, and uses that rejection to conclude that the opposing claim is not adequately supported

choices.label: D
choices.text: concedes that digital photography has lowered equipment costs and then argues that this cost reduction is insufficient to constitute genuine democratization

choices.label: E
