choices.text: establishes through empirical evidence that practitioners who use digital equipment produce work of lower quality than those trained in traditional methods

explanations.correct: The critic identifies the assumption that equipment access is the primary barrier (a presupposition underlying the democratization claim), shows this assumption is false (the real barriers are perceptual and conceptual), and concludes the democratization claim is not well supported. C describes this 'undermine the presupposition, undermine the claim' structure precisely.
explanations.A: No historical survey is offered. The argument makes no reference to specific works or periods in photography history. This is the 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.B: No analogy to other art forms is constructed. The argument stays entirely within the domain of photography and makes no comparative claim about creative domains generally.
explanations.D: The critic does not concede that digital photography has lowered equipment costs — cost is never mentioned. The argument attacks the underlying assumption about what the barrier is, not the cost-reduction claim.
explanations.E: No empirical comparison between digital and traditional practitioners is presented. The argument is conceptual, not evidential in this sense.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses a scope-narrowing move: accepting a general claim but arguing it does not apply to the case at hand due to a distinguishing feature. Students must identify this 'distinguishing the case from the general rule' technique and avoid traps that describe the general rule as the argument's conclusion rather than its premise.
lr.stimulus: Technology policy researcher: Critics of open-source software in government systems argue that because open-source code is publicly readable, it exposes security vulnerabilities to potential attackers. This concern is legitimate as a general matter. However, the government systems in question use a security-through-obscurity model only for their outermost interfaces; the core cryptographic protocols rely on algorithms whose security is mathematically provable regardless of whether the underlying code is public. For these particular systems, then, the general concern about public readability simply does not apply.
lr.questionStem: The technology policy researcher's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: arguing that the critics' general concern about open-source security is empirically unfounded because no government system using open-source code has been successfully attacked

choices.label: B
choices.text: conceding the general validity of an opposing concern but identifying a feature of the specific case that renders the general concern inapplicable to it

choices.label: C
choices.text: applying a general principle about cryptographic security to conclude that open-source code is always more secure than proprietary code

choices.label: D
choices.text: drawing an analogy between government security systems and commercial cryptographic systems to establish that the critics' standard does not apply to either

choices.label: E
choices.text: refuting the critics' position by demonstrating that security-through-obscurity is an inherently flawed model in all software contexts

explanations.correct: The researcher explicitly concedes that the critics' concern is 'legitimate as a general matter,' then identifies a distinguishing feature of the specific systems (their core protocols rely on mathematically provable cryptography, not obscurity) that makes the general concern inapplicable to this case. B captures this two-step concede-then-distinguish structure precisely.
explanations.A: No empirical claim about absence of successful attacks on open-source government systems is made. The argument is structural-conceptual, distinguishing the case by reference to cryptographic architecture. This is the 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.C: The researcher does not conclude that open-source code is always more secure. The argument is narrowly about these particular systems, and no general superiority claim is made. 'Always' is an extreme-verb trap.
explanations.D: No analogy to commercial cryptographic systems is constructed. The argument works by distinguishing the case, not by drawing a parallel to another domain.
explanations.E: The researcher does not refute or claim that security-through-obscurity is always flawed — the argument explicitly concedes the general concern is legitimate. 'Refuting' and 'inherently flawed in all contexts' are both extreme-verb traps.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument contains an intermediate conclusion (the concession that placebo responses are real physiological events) embedded within a multi-step structure, before arriving at the main conclusion. Test-takers must track both the concession and the eliminative move to identify the correct technique. Several traps describe accurate partial moves or use extreme verbs.
lr.stimulus: Physician: Some skeptics argue that patients who improve after receiving placebos have not experienced genuine medical treatment, since placebos contain no active pharmacological agents. I grant that placebos lack such agents. Nevertheless, the physiological changes observed in placebo responders — reduced cortisol levels, altered neurotransmitter activity, measurable immune responses — are indistinguishable from those produced by pharmacologically active compounds. If what defines genuine treatment is the production of beneficial physiological change, then the skeptics' position cannot be sustained: the criterion they implicitly rely upon actually supports the opposite conclusion.
lr.questionStem: The physician's argument proceeds by doing which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: conceding a claim made by an opposing view, then arguing that the criterion implicit in that view, when applied consistently, undermines its own conclusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: citing statistical evidence about physiological outcomes to establish that a widely held medical consensus is factually mistaken

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two distinct medical treatments to suggest that the boundary between them is merely conventional

choices.label: D
choices.text: rejecting a definition by demonstrating that it leads to an internal contradiction when applied to standard cases

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to the authority of physiological research to refute the claim that placebo responses are psychologically rather than biologically mediated

explanations.correct: The physician first concedes the skeptics' factual point (placebos lack active pharmacological agents), then turns it against them: the criterion the skeptics implicitly use — beneficial physiological change as the mark of genuine treatment — is satisfied by placebos, so their own standard defeats their conclusion. This is the 'concede-then-turn' structure that A captures precisely.
explanations.A: Correct. The physician grants the factual concession and then shows the skeptics' implicit criterion generates the opposite verdict.
explanations.B: Partially true trap. The physician does mention physiological data, but the argument's main move is logical (turning the criterion against the skeptics), not statistical. This answer also uses the extreme verb 'establish' and misdescribes the target as a 'widely held medical consensus' rather than a specific skeptical position.
explanations.C: The argument does not draw an analogy between two treatments; it argues that one phenomenon meets the definitional criterion of another category. No 'merely conventional' language or analogical structure is employed.
explanations.D: The physician does not show that the skeptics' definition is internally contradictory. Rather, the physician shows it supports the wrong conclusion for the skeptics — a reductio of their position, not a demonstration of logical contradiction within the definition itself. This is a subtly mis-scaled description.
explanations.E: Content-over-technique trap. The physician never invokes authority, and the claim that placebo effects are 'biologically rather than psychologically mediated' is not the argument's conclusion — the conclusion is about whether placebos constitute genuine treatment.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument contains three logical moves: an eliminative step (ruling out two alternative explanations), an intermediate conclusion (the remaining explanation must be correct), and a general principle applied to generate the main conclusion. Test-takers must identify the eliminative structure as the primary technique rather than latching onto the principle-application, which is merely the final step. Traps exploit the multiple-move structure by describing only one step accurately.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Economists have long debated why real wages for urban laborers in fourteenth-century England rose sharply following the Black Death. Two explanations have been proposed: either guild regulations broke down, allowing previously suppressed wage competition to emerge, or the dramatic reduction in the labor supply forced employers to offer higher wages to attract workers. The historical record, however, shows that guild regulations remained firmly intact throughout this period — guild court records document vigorous enforcement well into the 1380s. Since only these two explanations have ever been offered, and since labor supply reduction is the sole remaining candidate, we must conclude that the labor supply shock drove the wage increases. This conclusion is significant: it demonstrates that demographic factors, not institutional arrangements, were the primary engine of preindustrial wage growth.
lr.questionStem: The historian's argument derives its conclusion by doing which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: eliminating all but one of the candidate explanations for a phenomenon by providing evidence that disconfirms the others, and then applying a general principle to extend that conclusion beyond the original case

choices.label: B
choices.text: inferring from a statistical pattern in historical records that a commonly accepted theory about preindustrial economics must be revised

choices.label: C
choices.text: appealing to a general principle about demographic change to establish that guild-based institutional explanations are inherently inadequate

choices.label: D
choices.text: using evidence from a specific historical case to argue that an accepted generalization holds without exception across preindustrial economies

choices.label: E
choices.text: establishing the cause of a phenomenon by demonstrating that the only available evidence is consistent with exactly one of two competing hypotheses

explanations.correct: The argument proceeds in two distinct stages. First, the historian uses guild court records to rule out the regulatory-breakdown explanation, leaving labor supply reduction as the sole candidate — this is argument by elimination. Second, having established that intermediate conclusion, the historian applies a broader principle (demographic factors, not institutional arrangements, drive preindustrial wages) to extend the finding from fourteenth-century England to preindustrial wage growth generally. Answer A accurately captures both the eliminative step and the principle-application extension.
explanations.A: Correct. The two-stage structure — elimination of alternatives followed by application of a general principle — is precisely what the argument does.
explanations.B: Partially true trap. The historian does consult historical records, but no statistical pattern is cited — only qualitative evidence about guild court enforcement. Moreover, the argument does not revise a 'commonly accepted theory'; it settles a debate between two proposed explanations.
explanations.C: Inverts the argument's structure. The historian does not begin with a general principle about demographics and then infer that guild explanations fail; rather, the historian uses specific evidence to eliminate the guild explanation and then derives the general principle as a conclusion.
explanations.D: Mis-scaled trap. The argument moves from the specific case to a general conclusion, but the general conclusion is not that a pre-existing generalization 'holds without exception.' The historian is advancing a new explanatory claim, not confirming an accepted universal.
explanations.E: Partially true trap describing only the first half of the argument. The eliminative step is accurately described, but this choice omits the principle-application move entirely — the historian does not stop at identifying labor supply reduction as the cause of this one case but generalizes the finding, which is the argument's main conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Three related factual observations with one clear hedged inference. Distractors are either out-of-scope or overreach into 'all'/'only' territory.
lr.stimulus: A recent survey of primary-care physicians in Valbrook found that those who had taken a one-week course on nutrition counseling were, on average, twice as likely as their colleagues to discuss diet during routine checkups. The survey also found that patients of the course-trained physicians reported making healthier food choices more often than patients of other physicians. No other differences between the two groups of physicians were noted.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every patient whose physician took the nutrition course now eats a healthier diet than before.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At least some patients make healthier food choices after their physicians discuss diet with them during checkups.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Physicians who take continuing-education courses are generally more competent than those who do not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nutrition counseling is the most effective tool a primary-care physician has for improving patient health.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients in Valbrook were less healthy than patients elsewhere before the nutrition course was offered.

explanations.correct: The stimulus links two facts — course-trained physicians discuss diet more often, and their patients report healthier choices more often. The most defensible hedged inference is that at least some patients' improved choices follow from such discussions.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'every patient' is not supported; the stimulus speaks in averages.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Out of scope — the stimulus is about one specific course, not continuing education generally.
explanations.D: Too strong and out of scope — no comparison is made to other tools.
explanations.E: Out of scope — no claim is made about Valbrook patients' prior health.

lr.difficultyReason: Two observational facts about a wetland; correct answer is a modest inference. Traps are overreach and opposite-direction.
lr.stimulus: Biologists studying the Oster Marsh report that populations of the marsh wren have grown substantially in each of the past five years. Over the same period, the marsh's native cattail reeds, in which marsh wrens build their nests, have expanded to cover roughly 30 percent more of the marsh than they did before. No other major changes to the marsh's vegetation or water levels have been recorded.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The marsh wren population would not have grown at all without the expansion of cattail reeds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any marsh with expanding cattail reeds will see a rise in marsh wren populations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The expansion of cattail reeds in Oster Marsh has probably contributed to the growth of its marsh wren population.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marsh wrens nest only in native cattail reeds and in no other vegetation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Oster Marsh contains more marsh wrens than any comparable wetland in the region.

explanations.correct: Cattails are the wrens' nesting habitat, they have expanded substantially, and no other relevant change occurred. The hedged inference that the expansion has probably contributed to the population growth is what the facts most support.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'would not have grown at all' is not supported; the stimulus allows other causes.
explanations.B: Too strong — the stimulus is about one marsh, not any marsh.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Too strong — the stimulus says wrens build nests in cattails, not that they nest nowhere else.
explanations.E: Out of scope — no comparison with other wetlands is made.

lr.difficultyReason: Two commerce facts, one clear hedged conclusion about subgroup behavior. Traps overreach to absolutes.
lr.stimulus: Sales data from Orlen Bookshop show that among customers who purchased a novel during last year's summer discount promotion, more than half also bought at least one full-price book during the same visit. Customers who did not purchase a discounted novel, by contrast, bought a full-price book during their visits less than a quarter of the time.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The summer discount promotion caused Orlen Bookshop's overall revenue to rise.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No customer who bought a full-price book last summer would have done so without the discount promotion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Customers who purchased a discounted novel tended to spend more at Orlen Bookshop per visit than customers who did not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most of Orlen Bookshop's full-price sales last year came from customers buying discounted novels.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The discount promotion will be even more successful if repeated next summer.

explanations.correct: The first group bought a discounted novel plus a full-price book over half the time; the second group bought a full-price book less than a quarter of the time and no discounted novel. The hedged comparative claim about per-visit spending is what the data most strongly support.
explanations.A: Out of scope — the stimulus compares subgroups, not overall revenue.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'no customer ... would have' goes beyond what the data show.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Too strong — the stimulus gives rates per customer group, not the composition of full-price sales overall.
explanations.E: Out of scope — no prediction about future promotions is supported.

lr.difficultyReason: Two legal facts about an appellate court; correct answer applies hedged language to the pattern observed.
lr.stimulus: Of the criminal convictions appealed to the Westhaven Court of Appeals last year, those in which the defense argued that the trial judge had improperly excluded evidence were overturned roughly twice as often as those that raised other grounds for appeal. The court handled a roughly equal number of appeals of each kind.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Trial judges in Westhaven improperly exclude evidence more often than they make other kinds of errors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any appeal arguing that a trial judge improperly excluded evidence will succeed in the Westhaven Court of Appeals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At least some of the convictions overturned last year by the Westhaven Court of Appeals were overturned on the ground that a trial judge had improperly excluded evidence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Westhaven Court of Appeals applies a less demanding standard to evidentiary-exclusion claims than to other grounds for appeal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most convictions that are appealed in Westhaven are ultimately overturned on some ground or other.

explanations.correct: If appeals citing improper exclusion are overturned at roughly twice the rate of other appeals, and the counts are roughly equal, some overturned convictions last year rested on that ground. The hedged 'at least some' claim is directly supported.
explanations.A: Out of scope — frequency of errors is not compared, only success rates on appeal.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'any appeal ... will succeed' is not supported; only a higher success rate is reported.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the stimulus does not describe the court's standards.
explanations.E: Out of scope — no overall overturn rate is given.

lr.difficultyReason: Two archaeological facts yield one hedged historical inference. Traps are scope creep and too-strong.
lr.stimulus: Archaeologists excavating a small coastal settlement dated to roughly 1200 B.C.E. uncovered storage jars containing olive oil whose chemical signature matches oils produced on an island more than 500 kilometers away. The settlement's own soil and climate are unsuitable for olive cultivation, and no evidence of olive presses has been found at the site.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Olive oil was the most widely traded commodity in the region around 1200 B.C.E.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The settlement's inhabitants obtained at least some of their olive oil through long-distance exchange.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The inhabitants of the coastal settlement were wealthier than those of inland settlements of the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No goods other than olive oil were imported into the coastal settlement from distant sources.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The island where the matching oil was produced was the largest olive-oil exporter of its era.

explanations.correct: The oil's chemical signature matches a distant source, and the settlement could not have produced olives or pressed oil locally. The hedged inference that at least some oil reached them through long-distance exchange is what the facts best support.
explanations.A: Too strong and out of scope — the stimulus says nothing about the ranking of traded commodities.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Out of scope — no comparative wealth claim is supported.
explanations.D: Too strong — the stimulus only addresses olive oil.
explanations.E: Too strong — the island's ranking as an exporter is not discussed.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward technology observation with one hedged inference; traps include absolute generalization and opposite direction.
lr.stimulus: In a controlled test, engineers measured the fuel consumption of a fleet of delivery trucks before and after installing software that automatically adjusts engine settings based on road grade and speed. Trucks using the software consumed, on average, 8 percent less fuel per kilometer than identical trucks without the software. Driving routes and cargo loads were held constant across both groups.
lr.questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Installing the software reduces fuel consumption by the same amount for every truck that uses it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any technology that adjusts engine settings automatically will lower a truck's fuel consumption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Trucks equipped with the engine-adjustment software tend to consume less fuel per kilometer than otherwise comparable trucks without it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The software reduces fuel consumption primarily by lowering engine speed on steep grades.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fleet operators who adopt the software will recoup its purchase cost within a year.

explanations.correct: Identical trucks on identical routes with identical loads differed only in whether they used the software, and the software-equipped trucks averaged 8 percent lower fuel use. The hedged comparative generalization tracks exactly what was measured.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'same amount for every truck' goes beyond an 8 percent average.
explanations.B: Too strong — the stimulus is about one specific software package.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the mechanism behind the savings is not discussed.
explanations.E: Out of scope — no claim about purchase cost or payback period is supported.

lr.difficultyReason: Two linguistics observations yield one hedged inference about an exception to a broader pattern.
lr.stimulus: In most of the world's languages, words denoting close kin such as 'mother' and 'father' tend to be short and to use only the simplest consonants. In the Ikwe language, however, the word for 'mother' is four syllables long and contains several consonants that young children acquire only after age five. Ikwe-speaking children, linguists report, typically begin using the word for 'mother' noticeably later than children acquiring other languages do.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ikwe-speaking children are generally slower than other children to acquire language overall.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A word's phonetic complexity can affect how early children acquire it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every language in which kinship terms are long and phonetically complex delays children's acquisition of those terms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ikwe speakers use a different word when addressing their mothers in everyday speech.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Short words with simple consonants are easier for adults to learn than long words with complex consonants.

explanations.correct: The stimulus presents a cross-linguistic pattern and one case where a kinship word is unusually long and complex; children in that case acquire the word later. The hedged inference that phonetic complexity can affect acquisition timing is the one most supported.
explanations.A: Out of scope — only one word's acquisition is discussed, not overall language acquisition.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — a single case does not support a universal claim.
explanations.D: Out of scope — everyday usage patterns are not discussed.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the stimulus concerns children, not adult learners.

lr.difficultyReason: Two arts facts suggest one modest inference about attendance and programming. Traps overreach or are opposite-direction.
lr.stimulus: The Mercer Civic Theater reports that performances featuring works by living local playwrights sold, on average, about 20 percent more tickets last season than performances of works by better-known historical playwrights. Ticket prices, performance dates, and marketing budgets were comparable for both kinds of program.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Works by living local playwrights are of higher artistic quality than works by historical playwrights.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mercer Civic Theater audiences last season tended to prefer works by living local playwrights over works by better-known historical playwrights.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mercer Civic Theater will stop staging works by historical playwrights in future seasons.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every performance by a living local playwright at Mercer Civic Theater sold out last season.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Audiences at other theaters in the region showed similar preferences last season.

explanations.correct: With ticket prices, dates, and marketing held comparable, the difference in average ticket sales most directly supports a hedged preference claim about Mercer's audiences last season.
explanations.A: Out of scope and too strong — artistic quality is not discussed.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Out of scope — no programming decision is supported.
explanations.D: Too strong — averages do not support a sold-out claim about every performance.
explanations.E: Out of scope — other theaters are not discussed.

lr.difficultyReason: Two policy facts with a clean hedged inference about cause. Traps include absolute claims and opposite-direction alternatives.
lr.stimulus: After the town of Halbrook began offering free evening bus service along three main routes last year, average evening car traffic on those routes decreased by about 15 percent over the following six months. On comparable routes in Halbrook that received no free evening bus service, evening car traffic during the same period was essentially unchanged.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Free evening bus service was the only factor that could have reduced evening car traffic on the three routes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Residents of Halbrook generally prefer bus travel to car travel.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every Halbrook resident who took a free evening bus along one of the three routes would otherwise have driven a car.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The introduction of free evening bus service in Halbrook likely contributed to the drop in evening car traffic on the three routes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Halbrook's free evening bus service will produce similar reductions if extended to every route in town.

explanations.correct: Traffic fell on exactly the routes that received free buses and held steady on comparable routes that did not. The hedged causal inference is what the pattern most strongly supports.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'only factor' is not supported; the comparison makes the free service a likely contributor, not the sole one.
explanations.B: Too strong — a general preference is broader than what the traffic pattern shows.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'every ... would otherwise have driven' goes well beyond the data.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Out of scope — extending the program town-wide is not addressed.

lr.difficultyReason: Two ethics-survey facts yield one natural hedged inference. Traps are too-strong universals and out-of-scope predictions.
lr.stimulus: In a recent anonymous survey of accountants at large firms, more than 70 percent reported that they had at some point been asked by a supervisor to record a transaction in a way they believed misleading. Of those respondents, a clear majority said they had complied with the request at least once because they feared professional retaliation.
lr.questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most accountants at large firms routinely misrepresent the financial position of the companies they audit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any accountant who complies with a supervisor's misleading request does so only out of fear of retaliation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At least some accountants at large firms have recorded transactions in ways they considered misleading out of fear of professional retaliation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Supervisors at large accounting firms are generally indifferent to the ethical concerns of their staff.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stronger whistleblower protections would eliminate misleading accounting at large firms.

explanations.correct: A majority of the more-than-70-percent group said they had complied at least once out of fear of retaliation. The hedged 'at least some' inference about those accountants' conduct is a direct and modest reading of the numbers.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'routinely misrepresent' goes beyond having complied at least once in some cases.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'only out of fear of retaliation' is not supported; other motives are not ruled out.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Out of scope — supervisors' general attitudes are not described.
explanations.E: Too strong and out of scope — the effect of whistleblower protections is not addressed.

lr.difficultyReason: Three simple facts establish a direct correlation with one clear hedged inference. The correct answer uses modest language ('at least some') that the data clearly support. Distractors either overreach to 'all' or are out of scope.
lr.stimulus: A longitudinal study tracked 500 regularly employed adults over five years. Those who reported taking at least two weeks of vacation time annually showed lower rates of cardiovascular disease compared to those who took less than one week of vacation time. This relationship held across different age groups and income levels.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All adults who take two weeks of vacation annually will avoid cardiovascular disease.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Taking vacation time is the primary cause of good cardiovascular health.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At least some regularly employed adults who take two weeks of vacation annually have lower cardiovascular disease rates than those taking minimal vacation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vacation time must be taken in one consecutive period to reduce cardiovascular risk.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Adults earning higher incomes benefit more from vacation time than lower-income adults.

explanations.correct: The study directly shows that those taking two or more weeks had lower cardiovascular disease rates than those taking less than one week, across multiple demographic groups. The hedged language ('at least some') accurately reflects what the data show without overclaiming causation or universality.
explanations.A: Too strong — the passage never claims all such adults will avoid disease, only that they show lower rates.
explanations.B: Too strong — the data show correlation, not causation, and 'primary cause' overstates the connection.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the stimulus says nothing about whether vacation must be consecutive.
explanations.E: Opposite of what the data support — the stimulus says the relationship held 'across different income levels,' suggesting similar patterns, not that higher earners benefit more.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple observational fact about a subgroup's behavior. Correct answer makes a modest claim about 'some' members of the group. Distractors either generalize to all, invert the finding, or add unsupported causal language.
lr.stimulus: A survey of 300 small business owners in metropolitan areas found that 67 percent use social media as part of their marketing strategy. Among those who use social media, the average business saw an increase in customer inquiries within six months of adoption.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All small business owners in metropolitan areas use social media for marketing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Social media adoption is the most effective marketing tool available to small businesses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some small business owners who use social media saw increases in customer inquiries within six months.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Small business owners who do not use social media will experience fewer customer inquiries.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Using social media guarantees a small business will see increased customer inquiries.

explanations.correct: The stimulus says that among social media users, the average business saw an increase in inquiries. This directly supports that at least some (in fact, many) of those who adopted social media experienced the reported benefit.
explanations.A: Too strong — only 67 percent use it; the passage explicitly contradicts a universal claim.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'most effective' is not supported; the data show only that users saw increases.
explanations.D: Unsupported — the passage says nothing about non-users' outcomes.
explanations.E: Too strong — 'guarantees' overstates what the data show; the passage reports an average increase, not universality.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Two facts: (1) a linguistic pattern across multiple languages, and (2) a plausible alternative explanation. Correct answer attributes the pattern to a natural constraint without dismissing the alternative. Distractors either assume causation or ignore the stated constraint.
lr.stimulus: Linguists have documented that vowel sounds at the end of words occur more frequently in Romance languages than in Germanic languages. Researchers hypothesize this is partly due to the phonological rules governing syllable structure—Romance languages permit more word-final vowels than Germanic languages. However, historical contact and borrowing patterns between language families may also play a role.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following inferences is most supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Phonological rules are the sole cause of vowel distribution differences between language families.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some of the difference in word-final vowel frequency between Romance and Germanic languages is at least partly attributable to phonological constraints.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Germanic languages are historically younger than Romance languages.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Historical borrowing has a stronger effect on vowel distribution than phonological rules do.

choices.label: E
choices.text: All vowel sounds in Romance languages derive from contact with Germanic languages.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes both (1) an observed difference and (2) a documented phonological explanation for it, while acknowledging other factors may also apply. The hedged language ('at least partly') and acknowledgment of multiple causes fit the facts precisely.
explanations.A: Too strong — the stimulus explicitly mentions contact and borrowing as additional possible factors, so phonology is not the sole cause.
explanations.C: Out of scope — age of languages is not discussed or implied.
explanations.D: Too strong — the stimulus presents both as potentially contributing; it doesn't rank their relative strength.
explanations.E: Too strong and directionally unsupported — the stimulus doesn't claim all Romance vowels derive from Germanic contact.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental observation: a species shows reduced population in a particular habitat but thrives elsewhere. Correct answer draws the modest inference that the habitat-specific pressure (not universal unsuitability) is the limiting factor. Distractors either universalize or ignore the comparative data.
lr.stimulus: Researchers monitoring populations of a migratory bird species found that nesting numbers in wetland areas of the country have declined by 40 percent over the past decade. However, the same species shows stable or growing populations in forest and grassland habitats during the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The bird species is becoming extinct across the country.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Changes in wetland habitat conditions are reducing the suitability of those areas for this bird species.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Forest and grassland habitats are superior to all other habitat types for this species.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The bird species will never return to wetland areas.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wetland conservation efforts have been entirely ineffective.

explanations.correct: The species is thriving elsewhere but declining specifically in wetlands, which most strongly suggests that something about wetland conditions (not the species' overall viability) is the problem. This hedged conclusion respects the comparative data.
explanations.A: Too strong — the species is stable or growing in other habitats, so extinction is not supported.
explanations.C: Too strong and unsupported — the stimulus doesn't compare forest and grassland to 'all other' habitat types.
explanations.D: Too strong — the passage gives no basis for claiming the bird will 'never' return; conditions can change.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the stimulus provides no data on conservation efforts, only on population trends.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Medical observation: a symptom occurs in multiple disease contexts, suggesting a common mechanism. Correct answer modestly infers a shared feature without claiming universal cause or effect. Distractors either overreach to causation, inverse the finding, or scope-creep.
lr.stimulus: Physicians have observed that patients with several different autoimmune disorders—rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and celiac disease—all report fatigue as a primary symptom. Laboratory tests show that in each condition, certain immune cells are activated abnormally. Researchers theorize that the abnormal immune activation may be responsible for the fatigue in these conditions.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Abnormal immune cell activation is the sole cause of fatigue in humans.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some autoimmune disorders with abnormal immune activation produce fatigue as a symptom.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All patients with fatigue have an autoimmune disorder.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Curing abnormal immune activation will eliminate fatigue in all patients.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fatigue can only occur in conditions with abnormal immune cell activation.

explanations.correct: The stimulus documents three autoimmune conditions, each with fatigue and abnormal immune activation. The modest inference that 'some' autoimmune disorders with this activation pattern produce fatigue directly follows from the evidence.
explanations.A: Too strong — the stimulus discusses one possible contributing factor, not the sole cause of all fatigue.
explanations.C: Inverse and too strong — the stimulus doesn't claim all fatigue stems from autoimmune disease.
explanations.D: Too strong — the stimulus posits a possible link, not a guarantee that curing the activation eliminates fatigue.
explanations.E: Too strong and contradicts common knowledge — fatigue has many causes beyond immune activation.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Economic data: two regions show different adoption rates of a technology and different economic growth rates. Correct answer avoids claiming causation and simply notes the association. Distractors assume causation, invert the relationship, or universalize.
lr.stimulus: Over the past five years, regions that have rapidly adopted digital payment systems show average economic growth rates 2 percent higher than regions with slower adoption. However, both groups of regions include wealthy and less wealthy areas, suggesting adoption levels are not entirely determined by existing wealth.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adopting digital payment systems directly causes economic growth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All regions with rapid digital payment adoption will experience higher economic growth than those with slower adoption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some regions with faster digital payment adoption show higher economic growth rates than regions with slower adoption.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Economic growth is impossible in regions that do not rapidly adopt digital payment systems.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Existing regional wealth is the primary factor driving both digital payment adoption and economic growth.

explanations.correct: The stimulus reports that rapid-adoption regions show 2 percent higher growth on average. The modest phrasing 'some regions' accurately reflects this aggregate comparison without claiming universality or causation.
explanations.A: Too strong — the data show correlation, not causation.
explanations.B: Too strong — the passage reports average differences, not that all rapid-adoption regions outperform all slow-adoption regions.
explanations.D: Too strong and unsupported — the passage implies growth occurs in both groups, just at different average rates.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the stimulus explicitly states adoption is not entirely determined by existing wealth, undermining this claim.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: History/policy: a legislative action had documented effects in some areas but documented counterexamples. Correct answer acknowledges the variation without claiming universal outcomes. Distractors either universalize or deny the documented effect.
lr.stimulus: After a city implemented a ban on plastic shopping bags, waste in city landfills decreased by 3 percent over the following year. However, a survey showed that 40 percent of residents began purchasing reusable bags elsewhere, while 30 percent switched to plastic bags from other retailers, and 15 percent shifted to online shopping with plastic packaging.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following inferences is most supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Plastic bag bans are always effective at reducing overall plastic waste.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The city's plastic bag ban had inconsistent effects, reducing some forms of waste while not eliminating plastic use entirely.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most residents of the city opposed the plastic bag ban.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reusable bags are the only effective solution to plastic waste.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The ban caused a significant increase in overall landfill waste.

explanations.correct: The stimulus documents both a measurable landfill reduction (3 percent) and evidence that residents found multiple workarounds, some of which still involved plastic. This complexity is accurately captured by the claim of 'inconsistent effects.'
explanations.A: Too strong — the passage shows only a 3 percent reduction and multiple workarounds, undermining 'always effective.'
explanations.C: Out of scope — the survey reports behavior, not expressed opposition; many may have complied willingly.
explanations.D: Too strong and unsupported — the passage mentions reusable bags as one consumer choice, not an endorsed solution.
explanations.E: Opposite direction — the passage reports a 3 percent decrease in landfill waste, not an increase.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Educational data: test performance correlates with a specific study practice. Correct answer hedges the inference to what the data permit ('students who engage in' or 'at least some'). Distractors either claim causation, invert the correlation, or overgeneralize.
lr.stimulus: A study of 200 high school students found that those who engaged in spaced repetition—reviewing material at increasing intervals over several weeks—scored on average 15 percent higher on final exams than students who used massed practice, studying intensively just before exams. The effect was observed across multiple subject areas.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Spaced repetition is the only effective study method.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Students who use massed practice are less intelligent than those who use spaced repetition.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At least some students who use spaced repetition perform better on final exams than those using massed practice.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spaced repetition causes higher test performance in all students.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Massed practice leads to poor long-term retention.

explanations.correct: The study shows that spaced-repetition users scored 15 percent higher on average. This directly supports that at least some students using that method outperformed massed-practice users.
explanations.A: Too strong — the passage discusses one effective method, not exclusivity.
explanations.B: Out of scope — the study measures study method effects, not intelligence.
explanations.D: Too strong — 'all students' overstates an average difference; some may not benefit equally.
explanations.E: Too strong — the passage compares two methods on a final exam but doesn't address long-term retention explicitly.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethical/observational: a professional group exhibits a particular behavior or standard. Correct answer makes a modest inference about the group's typical practice or tendency. Distractors either universalize, invert, or add unsupported motivational claims.
lr.stimulus: A review of codes of conduct at 50 major law firms found that 46 of them explicitly prohibit attorneys from accepting gifts valued above $50 from clients. The remaining four firms have similar prohibitions but set the threshold at $100 or higher. Interviews with partners at these firms indicate the restrictions aim to prevent conflicts of interest.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All law firms prohibit attorneys from accepting any gifts from clients whatsoever.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some law firms have adopted gift restrictions to address conflicts of interest.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Law firms that do not restrict gifts will necessarily experience ethical violations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The $50 threshold is the only ethically defensible limit for attorney gifts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Attorneys at firms without gift restrictions are more corrupt than those at firms with restrictions.

explanations.correct: The stimulus documents that 50 firms have gift restrictions, explicitly states their stated purpose is conflict-of-interest prevention, and reports partner interviews confirming this rationale. This directly supports that some (in fact, most) firms adopted these restrictions for this stated reason.
explanations.A: Too strong — four firms have a $100 threshold, not an absolute prohibition.
explanations.C: Too strong — the stimulus doesn't claim that absence of restrictions 'necessarily' causes violations.
explanations.D: Too strong and unsupported — different firms use different thresholds; the passage doesn't endorse one as uniquely defensible.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the passage discusses policies and stated intent, not attorney corruption or character.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology/arts observation: a creative medium exhibits a documented trend in how practitioners approach it. Correct answer states a modest inference about the trend without claiming universal adoption or superiority. Distractors either universalize, invert, or add historical claims.
lr.stimulus: Analysis of independent music production over the past decade shows that more than 60 percent of new artists use digital audio workstations (DAWs) rather than traditional recording studios. A survey of these artists revealed they cited lower costs, flexibility in scheduling, and ease of editing as their primary reasons for this choice.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All successful musicians record using digital audio workstations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Traditional recording studios are no longer used by any professional musicians.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some independent music artists have adopted DAWs at least partly because of practical advantages such as lower cost and scheduling flexibility.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recording quality is superior when using digital audio workstations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Traditional recording studios will become completely obsolete within the next five years.

explanations.correct: The stimulus states that more than 60 percent of new artists use DAWs and that the survey of these artists cited practical reasons. This directly supports that at least some artists adopted DAWs because of cost, scheduling, and editing advantages.
explanations.A: Too strong — the passage discusses new independent artists, not all successful musicians; many established artists may still use studios.
explanations.B: Too strong — the stimulus says 60+ percent use DAWs, which implies studios are still used by others.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the passage reports artists' stated reasons (practical advantages) but does not compare audio quality.
explanations.E: Too strong and speculative — the passage documents a current trend, not a prediction about obsolescence.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward observational stimulus with one clear quantitative fact and a simple hedged inference. The correct answer uses modest language ('some') that directly follows from the data.
lr.stimulus: A pharmaceutical company conducted a clinical trial of a new antibiotic on 500 patients with bacterial infections. After treatment, 480 patients showed full recovery within two weeks.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The antibiotic is guaranteed to cure all bacterial infections.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some patients treated with the antibiotic recovered fully within two weeks.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All patients with bacterial infections will eventually recover if given this antibiotic.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The antibiotic is more effective than older antibiotics.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients who do not recover from bacterial infections should never use this antibiotic.

explanations.correct: 480 out of 500 patients recovered, so it is certain that some patients recovered. This is a modest, hedged claim fully supported by the data.
explanations.A: Too strong — 20 patients did not recover, so the antibiotic is not guaranteed to work.
explanations.B: Correct — the data directly supports that at least some patients recovered.
explanations.C: Too strong — the stimulus says 480 recovered within two weeks; it does not address eventual recovery for all.
explanations.D: Unsupported — the stimulus provides no comparison to other antibiotics.
explanations.E: Unsupported and inverted — the fact that some patients did not recover does not mean those patients should never use it.

lr.difficultyReason: Three related facts establishing a clear correlation. The correct answer draws a modest conclusion about the relationship between the facts.
lr.stimulus: A study of workplace productivity tracked employees over six months. Workers who took regular breaks reported higher job satisfaction. These workers also completed their assigned tasks on time more often than workers who took few breaks.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Regular breaks eliminate workplace fatigue.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All workers must take regular breaks to meet deadlines.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some workers who take regular breaks complete their tasks on time more often than some workers who do not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Taking breaks is the only way to improve job satisfaction.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Employees who avoid breaks are less competent.

explanations.correct: The study found that break-takers completed tasks on time more often. The hedged phrasing 'some workers who take breaks' vs 'some workers who do not' directly follows from this comparative data.
explanations.A: Too strong — the stimulus does not say breaks eliminate fatigue, only that break-takers have higher satisfaction and better on-time completion.
explanations.B: Too strong — the stimulus shows a correlation for this group, not that all workers must take breaks.
explanations.C: Correct — the data directly supports this modest comparative claim.
explanations.D: Too strong — breaks correlate with satisfaction, but the stimulus doesn't establish they are the only way.
explanations.E: Too strong and unsupported — lower on-time completion doesn't imply lower competence.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple observational fact about plant behavior. Correct answer uses modest hedged language ('at least some') that is directly entailed by the stimulus.
lr.stimulus: Researchers observed that plants in a greenhouse wilted when watered with salt water, but remained healthy when watered with fresh water. This pattern held true across 15 different plant species.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following inferences is most supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Salt water is toxic to all plants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At least some plants wilt when exposed to salt water.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Plant species cannot survive in salt water under any circumstances.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fresh water is the ideal growing medium for all plant species.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Salt water causes permanent damage to plant roots.

explanations.correct: The observation that plants wilted with salt water across 15 species directly supports that at least some plants wilt under these conditions.
explanations.A: Too strong — the stimulus shows wilting in these 15 species, not that salt water is universally toxic.
explanations.B: Correct — the data directly supports this hedged claim.
explanations.C: Too strong — wilting is not the same as inability to survive in any circumstance.
explanations.D: Unsupported — the stimulus only contrasts salt and fresh water in this greenhouse setting.
explanations.E: Too strong — the stimulus reports wilting, not permanent root damage.

lr.difficultyReason: Economic data presented as simple fact. Correct answer is a modest inference about consumer behavior using hedged language.
lr.stimulus: Sales data from a major retailer show that the average household income of customers who purchased luxury goods was significantly higher than the average household income of customers who purchased standard goods.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All people with high incomes purchase luxury goods.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People with low incomes never purchase luxury goods.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some customers with higher household incomes purchased luxury goods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Income is the only factor that determines whether someone buys luxury goods.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Standard goods are inferior in quality to luxury goods.

explanations.correct: If the average income of luxury purchasers was significantly higher, then at least some customers with higher income purchased luxury goods. This is a direct, modest inference.
explanations.A: Too strong — not all high-income people need to purchase luxury goods.
explanations.B: Too strong — the data does not rule out any low-income luxury purchases.
explanations.C: Correct — the data directly supports this hedged claim about at least some customers.
explanations.D: Too strong — income correlates with purchase behavior, but is not established as the only factor.
explanations.E: Unsupported — the stimulus concerns purchasing patterns, not quality comparison.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental observation with clear temporal pattern. Correct answer uses hedged language about a trend that is directly supported.
lr.stimulus: Over the past decade, the average annual rainfall in a particular region has decreased by 20 percent. Local farmers report that crop yields have fallen during this same period.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased rainfall is the only cause of lower crop yields.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All farmers in the region have experienced losses in crop yields.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rainfall changes affect agricultural productivity in at least some cases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Crop yields will eventually return to previous levels.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Irrigation cannot offset the effects of reduced rainfall.

explanations.correct: The stimulus shows both a decrease in rainfall and a reported fall in crop yields over the same period. This supports a modest inference that rainfall affects yields in at least some cases.
explanations.A: Too strong — the stimulus establishes a correlation but not exclusivity.
explanations.B: Too strong — the stimulus reports that farmers report fallen yields, not all farmers.
explanations.C: Correct — the correlation between rainfall decline and yield decline supports this hedged claim.
explanations.D: Unsupported — the stimulus provides no information about future recovery.
explanations.E: Unsupported — the stimulus does not address irrigation or its effectiveness.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistic observation presenting a simple factual comparison. Correct answer uses modest language that directly follows from the data.
lr.stimulus: A survey of 200 native English speakers found that speakers from the United Kingdom used the word 'whilst' in their everyday speech, while speakers from North America rarely used this word.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All English speakers from the United Kingdom prefer 'whilst' to 'while.'

choices.label: B
choices.text: North American English is inferior to British English.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some English speakers from the United Kingdom use 'whilst' in their everyday speech.

choices.label: D
choices.text: North American speakers are incapable of understanding 'whilst.'

choices.label: E
choices.text: 'Whilst' is becoming obsolete in all varieties of English.

explanations.correct: The survey found that UK speakers used 'whilst' in everyday speech, so at least some UK speakers use this word. This is a straightforward, modest inference.
explanations.A: Too strong — the stimulus says UK speakers used the word, not that all prefer it.
explanations.B: Unsupported — linguistic differences do not establish superiority.
explanations.C: Correct — the data directly supports that at least some UK speakers use the word.
explanations.D: Unsupported — rarity of use doesn't imply inability to understand.
explanations.E: Too strong — the stimulus shows regional variation, not obsolescence across English.

lr.difficultyReason: Historical fact with a clear stated outcome. Correct answer is a modest inference about the result using appropriately hedged language.
lr.stimulus: In the 1970s, a law was enacted to restrict the use of certain pesticides known to harm the ozone layer. Following the enactment of this law, measurements of ozone concentrations in the upper atmosphere showed improvement over the next two decades.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The law was responsible for all environmental improvements during this period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pesticide restrictions are the only way to protect the ozone layer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ozone concentrations improved at least in part due to the pesticide restrictions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ozone layer has been completely restored to its original condition.

choices.label: E
choices.text: All countries adopted similar pesticide restrictions in the 1970s.

explanations.correct: The stimulus presents a temporal sequence: law enacted, then measurements show improvement. A modest inference is that restrictions contributed at least in part to the improvement.
explanations.A: Too strong — the law's causal role in all improvements is not established.
explanations.B: Too strong — the stimulus doesn't establish exclusivity of method.
explanations.C: Correct — the temporal correlation and stated improvement support this hedged claim.
explanations.D: Too strong — improvement is not the same as complete restoration.
explanations.E: Unsupported — the stimulus concerns one law, not global adoption.

lr.difficultyReason: Medical observation with a clear quantitative comparison. Correct answer is a modest inference using hedged language ('some') that directly follows.
lr.stimulus: A study examined two groups of patients: those who took a vitamin supplement daily and those who did not. The supplement group reported fewer instances of common colds during the year-long study period.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vitamin supplements prevent all common colds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some people who take vitamin supplements experience fewer colds than some people who do not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All people should take vitamin supplements to avoid colds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Colds are caused entirely by vitamin deficiency.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin supplements are more effective than medical treatments.

explanations.correct: The study found the supplement group reported fewer colds. This directly supports a modest comparison: some supplement-takers had fewer colds than some non-takers.
explanations.A: Too strong — fewer instances is not the same as prevention of all colds.
explanations.B: Correct — the data directly supports this hedged comparative claim.
explanations.C: Too strong — the stimulus shows a correlation for one group, not a universal recommendation.
explanations.D: Unsupported and backwards — the stimulus does not establish causation from deficiency.
explanations.E: Unsupported — no comparison to medical treatments is provided.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethical scenario presenting two related facts. Correct answer is a modest inference about what the facts support using appropriately cautious language.
lr.stimulus: A study found that children who participated in community service programs developed stronger senses of civic responsibility compared to children who did not participate. Additionally, these children later voted at higher rates as adults.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following inferences is most supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Community service is the only way to foster civic responsibility.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All children who participate in community service will become engaged citizens.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some children who participate in community service programs develop stronger civic responsibility.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Voting is more important than community service.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Civic responsibility causes people to vote.

explanations.correct: The stimulus states that participants in service programs developed stronger senses of civic responsibility. At least some children had this outcome, making this modest claim strongly supported.
explanations.A: Too strong — the stimulus establishes a correlation, not exclusivity.
explanations.B: Too strong — while the group showed higher rates, not all will follow the pattern.
explanations.C: Correct — the data directly supports that at least some participants developed stronger responsibility.
explanations.D: Unsupported — the stimulus does not rank the importance of these outcomes.
explanations.E: Unsupported — the data shows a correlation but not causal direction.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology observation with clear practical outcome. Correct answer is a simple, hedged inference that directly follows from the stated facts.
lr.stimulus: A software company tested two versions of its application on groups of users. Version A included a simplified interface. Users of Version A reported spending less time learning the application and completed tasks more quickly than users of Version B.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All software should use simplified interfaces.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Simplified interfaces make software universally better.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some users experienced faster task completion with the simplified interface.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Version B is inherently flawed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Interface design is irrelevant to user experience.

explanations.correct: Users of Version A (simplified interface) completed tasks more quickly. This directly supports that at least some users experienced this advantage.
explanations.A: Too strong — the finding applies to this context, not universally to all software.
explanations.B: Too strong — simplification helped with speed and learning, but 'universally better' overstates this.
explanations.C: Correct — the data directly supports that some users completed tasks more quickly with Version A.
explanations.D: Unsupported — slower task completion does not make Version B inherently flawed.
explanations.E: Contradicted — the stimulus shows interface design does affect user performance.

lr.difficultyReason: Three straightforward facts with one clear hedged inference. A study found a specific correlation; correct answer draws a modest conclusion about what tends to occur. Distractors overreach or are irrelevant.
lr.stimulus: A pharmaceutical study followed 300 patients with moderate arthritis over 12 months. Those who took a new anti-inflammatory medication reported pain reduction within two weeks. Patients who took the medication consistently for at least eight weeks showed sustained improvement in mobility. The study found no serious side effects in any participant.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The new anti-inflammatory medication will eliminate arthritis pain in all patients who take it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At least some patients with moderate arthritis may experience sustained improvement in mobility from consistent use of the medication.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patients who take the medication for less than eight weeks will not benefit from it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The medication is safer than all other arthritis treatments currently available.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pain reduction is the most important symptom to address in arthritis treatment.

explanations.correct: The stimulus states that patients who took the medication consistently for at least eight weeks showed sustained improvement. This directly supports that at least some patients (those in the study) experienced this benefit. The answer uses appropriate hedging ('may experience') and respects the scope of the data.
explanations.A: Too strong — the stimulus says patients 'reported pain reduction,' not that it will eliminate pain. Also says 'no serious side effects,' not that it is entirely safe or effective for all.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — the stimulus does not say that patients taking it for less than eight weeks will not benefit. Some may still benefit; the study only notes what happened with those who took it for at least eight weeks.
explanations.D: Unsupported scope creep — the stimulus compares only to a control or baseline within the study, not to 'all other arthritis treatments.'
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported — the stimulus never argues that pain reduction is the most important symptom relative to mobility.

lr.difficultyReason: Three related facts about linguistic patterns in a specific region. Clear factual basis for a modest inference about how speakers in that region tend to use language. Distractors either overreach to absolute claims or apply the finding beyond the stated scope.
lr.stimulus: A linguistic survey of 450 speakers in northern coastal towns found that roughly 80 percent of those speakers use a distinctive pronunciation of the vowel in words like 'bath' and 'path.' In the same towns, approximately 75 percent of speakers aged 18 to 35 use this pronunciation, as do approximately 85 percent of speakers over age 50. The pronunciation has remained stable across these age groups for at least two decades.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All speakers in northern coastal towns pronounce 'bath' and 'path' with the distinctive vowel sound.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The distinctive pronunciation is found in fewer than half of all English speakers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Speakers over age 50 in northern coastal towns are more likely than younger speakers to use the distinctive pronunciation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The distinctive pronunciation will eventually disappear from northern coastal towns.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Linguistic features that remain stable for two decades will never change.

explanations.correct: The stimulus directly states that approximately 85 percent of speakers over age 50 use the pronunciation, while approximately 75 percent of speakers aged 18 to 35 use it. This supports the claim that speakers over 50 are more likely (by about 10 percentage points) to use the pronunciation than younger speakers.
explanations.A: Too strong — the stimulus says roughly 80 percent use the pronunciation, not all.
explanations.B: Unsupported scope creep — the stimulus concerns only speakers in northern coastal towns, not English speakers generally.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Opposite direction — the stimulus says the pronunciation has remained stable, not that it will disappear.
explanations.E: Too strong — stability over two decades does not entail that something will never change.

lr.difficultyReason: Requires integrating the adherence statistic with the subgroup finding to infer a hedged claim about adherence, not a blanket claim about the diet's efficacy. Trap (A) overreaches on efficacy; trap (D) inverts the direction.
lr.stimulus: A recent clinical trial assigned patients with elevated cholesterol either to a plant-based diet or to a standard low-fat diet. Across the full sample, average cholesterol levels dropped by similar amounts in both groups. However, fewer than half of the patients assigned to the plant-based diet reported sticking to it for the full twelve weeks, while the overwhelming majority of patients on the standard diet reported complying. Among patients who reported full adherence, those on the plant-based diet showed markedly greater reductions than those on the standard diet.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A plant-based diet is the most effective dietary intervention available for patients with elevated cholesterol.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At least some patients who would benefit substantially from a plant-based diet are unlikely to follow it long enough to do so.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patients assigned to a standard low-fat diet will always report higher rates of adherence than those assigned to a plant-based diet.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dietary interventions are generally less effective at reducing cholesterol than medication-based interventions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The standard low-fat diet is as effective as the plant-based diet when both are followed consistently.

explanations.correct: Two facts combine to support (B): fewer than half of plant-based patients adhered, and among those who did, reductions were markedly greater. So at least some patients who would have benefited substantially did not stick with it. The hedged 'at least some' is well within what the data support.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'most effective available' makes a superlative claim well beyond a two-arm comparison.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'will always' extrapolates a single trial's adherence pattern into an absolute rule.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the stimulus says nothing about medication.
explanations.E: Opposite direction — the adherent-subgroup data show the plant-based diet produced markedly greater reductions, not equal ones.

lr.difficultyReason: Must integrate the earnings comparison with the hours datapoint to reach a hedged productivity-per-hour claim. Trap (E) overreaches to all drivers; trap (B) confuses the direction of the earnings comparison.
lr.stimulus: A survey of rideshare drivers in several large metropolitan areas found that drivers who work primarily during weekday commuting hours earn, on average, roughly the same total weekly income as drivers who work primarily on weekend evenings. The commuting-hour drivers, however, spend on average about 25 percent more hours logged into the rideshare application per week than the weekend-evening drivers do.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most rideshare drivers prefer working weekend evenings to working weekday commuting hours.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Weekend-evening drivers earn less per week than weekday commuting-hour drivers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some rideshare drivers earn more per hour logged into the application on weekend evenings than they would during weekday commuting hours.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rideshare passengers tip more generously on weekend evenings than during weekday commuting hours.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any driver who switches from weekday commuting hours to weekend evenings will increase his or her total weekly income.

explanations.correct: Similar total weekly income combined with substantially fewer logged-in hours implies a higher per-hour rate, at least on average, for weekend-evening drivers. 'Some drivers earn more per hour' is a hedged claim that follows cleanly from these two facts.
explanations.A: Out of scope — preferences aren't discussed.
explanations.B: Opposite direction — total weekly incomes are described as roughly equal, not lower for weekend drivers.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Unsupported — tipping is one possible source of the earnings pattern, but the stimulus doesn't establish it.
explanations.E: Too strong — 'any driver' switching guarantees no increase in earnings; the data describe averages, not individuals.

lr.difficultyReason: Combines the restoration outcome with the species-specific exception to support a hedged claim about restoration's limits. Trap (A) overreaches; trap (D) drops the qualifier about what drainage accomplishes.
lr.stimulus: When drained wetlands in the coastal region of Ferndale were re-flooded as part of a restoration program, populations of most native waterbird species rebounded to levels comparable to those recorded before drainage. One species, the banded bittern, had nested almost exclusively in a particular type of dense reed bed that had grown up during the decades of drainage. Ten years after re-flooding, banded bittern numbers in Ferndale remain less than half their pre-drainage levels.
