lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wetland restoration programs are generally ineffective at reviving native bird populations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The banded bittern is in greater need of conservation attention than any other waterbird in Ferndale.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Re-flooding drained wetlands is not by itself sufficient to restore every native bird species that was historically present.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drainage of wetlands typically benefits the bird species that inhabit them.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The reed beds that grew during drainage are more valuable habitat than the original wetlands were.

explanations.correct: Most species rebounded after re-flooding, but the banded bittern did not — it depended on reed beds that only emerged during drainage. This supports the hedged claim that re-flooding alone is not sufficient for every species. 'Not sufficient' is exactly the language MSS favors.
explanations.A: Opposite direction — most species rebounded, which is evidence restoration is generally effective.
explanations.B: Unsupported — relative conservation priority is not established by the stimulus.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Too strong and opposite — 'typically benefits' overreaches from one species' dependence on reed beds to a general claim about drainage.
explanations.E: Too strong — one species' preference doesn't show the reed beds are more valuable overall.

lr.difficultyReason: Integrates the borrowing pattern with the timing observation to support a hedged inference about cultural contact. Trap (B) overreaches on causation; trap (E) scope-creeps from maritime terms to the whole lexicon.
lr.stimulus: The Kaldari language contains dozens of words for types of sails, fishing equipment, and navigational landmarks that are clearly borrowed from Old Merenni, the language of a now-vanished seafaring people who lived along a coast several hundred miles to the south. By contrast, Kaldari retains no Merenni-derived words for agriculture, food preparation, or family relations. Linguists have dated the borrowed maritime terms to a period roughly a century before the first written records of regular trade between the two peoples.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Speakers of Kaldari had some maritime contact with Merenni speakers before trade between the two peoples was formally recorded.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Merenni people taught the Kaldari most of what they knew about sailing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The two peoples had no significant cultural contact of any kind prior to the period of recorded trade.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Kaldari speakers borrowed words only from languages of peoples they encountered through trade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most Kaldari vocabulary was shaped by contact with the Merenni.

explanations.correct: Borrowed maritime terms predating the first records of regular trade support an inference that some maritime contact existed before the recorded trade period. The hedged 'some' fits the data well.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — borrowing vocabulary is evidence of contact, not of being taught 'most' of what one knows.
explanations.C: Opposite direction — the borrowed terms are themselves evidence of some prior contact.
explanations.D: Too strong — 'only' rules out all other sources of borrowing without support.
explanations.E: Scope creep — dozens of maritime terms aren't 'most' of the vocabulary.

lr.difficultyReason: Must connect the coin-distribution pattern with the absence of a local mint to support a hedged trade-route inference. Trap (C) overreaches from 'some' contact to 'primary'; trap (D) inverts the natural inference.
lr.stimulus: Archaeologists excavating a twelfth-century settlement in the inland region of Arvath have uncovered coins minted in the distant port of Daemos, in quantities comparable to those found at sites along the well-documented Daemos–Arvath trade road. Daemos coins have also been found in smaller quantities at several sites along a mountain pass route that historians had previously assumed was used only for seasonal herding. No mint is known to have operated in Arvath itself during the twelfth century.
lr.questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At least some of the Daemos coins found at the mountain-pass sites arrived there through commercial exchange rather than seasonal herding alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mountain pass route was used more heavily for trade than the well-documented Daemos–Arvath road was.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Daemos was the primary source of currency for inland Arvath during the twelfth century.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Arvath produced its own coins but did so secretly to avoid Daemos's influence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Daemos–Arvath trade road fell out of regular use during the twelfth century.

explanations.correct: Coins from a distant port turning up along a pass route previously thought to serve only herding supports a hedged inference that at least some exchange occurred along that route — consistent with coins being a standard indicator of commerce.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Opposite direction — the pass sites show smaller quantities than the road sites.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'primary source' is a superlative claim not supported by the quantities alone.
explanations.D: Directly contradicted — no mint is known to have operated in Arvath.
explanations.E: Unsupported — the road sites still show trade-road-level coin quantities.

lr.difficultyReason: Combines the reuse statistic with the breach-source data to support a hedged claim about password managers as insufficient rather than harmful. Trap (A) inverts; trap (D) overreaches on a tool's sufficiency.
lr.stimulus: A survey of corporate employees found that those who regularly used a password manager were significantly less likely to reuse the same password across multiple work accounts than those who did not. Nonetheless, a study of recent security breaches at the same companies found that employees who used password managers accounted for nearly as large a share of breached accounts as those who did not. In most of these breaches, the point of compromise was a phishing attack rather than a guessed or stolen password.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Password managers tend to make corporate accounts less secure overall.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Corporate employees who use password managers are no more cautious about phishing attempts than their coworkers who do not use such tools.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phishing attacks are the most common cause of password reuse in corporate settings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adopting a password manager is sufficient to protect an employee from the most common forms of account compromise.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Companies would experience fewer breaches if they banned the use of password managers.

explanations.correct: If managers reduce reuse but breach rates stay comparable — and most breaches are phishing-based — then use of a manager doesn't correspond to a lower phishing-compromise rate. That supports the hedged claim that manager users are no more cautious about phishing than non-users.
explanations.A: Opposite direction — the data don't show managers make things worse; they show they don't help against phishing in particular.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Category error — phishing causes breaches in this data, not password reuse.
explanations.D: Too strong, and the stimulus supports the opposite (managers don't prevent phishing-based compromise).
explanations.E: Opposite direction — a ban would restore password reuse, which the stimulus implies managers reduce.

lr.difficultyReason: Integrates the recording constraint with the soloist behavior to support a hedged inference about early jazz conventions. Trap (B) creeps to 'any recording'; trap (E) is a plausible worldly truth not anchored in the facts.
lr.stimulus: In the early days of commercial jazz recording, a single side of a 78-rpm disc could hold only about three minutes of music, far less than the typical length of a live jazz performance. Historians have observed that recordings made in this period contain noticeably fewer and shorter instrumental solos than eyewitness accounts describe as typical of the same ensembles' live performances. Several prominent soloists of the period complained in print that the recording format forced them to omit material they considered essential to their playing.
lr.questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The recording format of the era probably shaped the form in which some early jazz solos have been preserved.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any recording made during this period misrepresents the ensemble that produced it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Live jazz performances of the era were always substantially longer than three minutes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most jazz soloists of the period preferred live performance to studio recording.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Technological constraints have generally done more to shape music than to preserve it.

explanations.correct: The length limit, the gap between recordings and live accounts, and the soloists' own complaints together support the hedged inference that the format shaped what was preserved. 'Probably' and 'some' fit the level of warrant.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'any recording misrepresents' overreaches from 'fewer and shorter solos' to universal misrepresentation.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'always' and 'substantially' overreach the word 'typical.'
explanations.D: Unsupported — preference between media isn't established.
explanations.E: Plausible-but-unsupported worldly generalization — the stimulus speaks only to a specific case.

lr.difficultyReason: Must combine the checkout decline with the program-use rise to support a hedged inference about library function. Trap (A) inverts; trap (C) extends from 'at least one' to 'most.'
lr.stimulus: Over the past decade, the number of books checked out from the public library system of Porthaven has fallen by more than a third. During the same period, however, the total number of people who use at least one library facility in a given month has grown substantially, and library programs that do not involve borrowing books — such as tax-preparation clinics, job-search workshops, and children's story hours — have seen sharp increases in attendance.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following inferences is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Residents of Porthaven are reading fewer books than they did a decade ago.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At least some Porthaven residents now rely on the library primarily for services other than borrowing books.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most people who visit the Porthaven library no longer check out any books at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The library system would attract even more users if it stopped offering non-book programs.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Public libraries in other cities are experiencing trends similar to those in Porthaven.

explanations.correct: Total monthly users have grown substantially while checkouts have fallen, and non-borrowing programs have grown sharply. That combination supports the hedged claim that at least some residents now rely on the library primarily for non-book services.
explanations.A: Unsupported — people can read books obtained from sources other than the library (bookstores, e-books, etc.).
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'most' visitors no longer checking out anything goes beyond what declining-but-still-substantial checkouts can support.
explanations.D: Opposite direction — non-book programs are correlated with rising usage.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the stimulus addresses only Porthaven.

lr.difficultyReason: Integrates the sleep recommendation, the self-report finding, and the device data to support a hedged claim about under- rather than over-estimation of sleep. Trap (D) overreaches to the clinical category; trap (A) is the opposite.
lr.stimulus: Health authorities generally recommend that adults sleep between seven and nine hours each night. In a recent large survey, a majority of respondents reported that they typically slept less than the recommended amount. A subsequent study of participants who wore sleep-tracking devices for several weeks, however, found that nearly half of those who had earlier reported getting less than seven hours of sleep were in fact averaging more than seven hours per night according to the devices.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sleep-tracking devices systematically overstate the amount of time their users spend asleep.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The number of adults who actually sleep fewer than seven hours per night may be smaller than survey results have suggested.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most adults who believe themselves to be sleep-deprived are in fact getting adequate sleep.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adult sleep deprivation is not a genuine health concern.

choices.label: E
choices.text: People who use sleep-tracking devices tend to sleep longer than people who do not.

explanations.correct: If nearly half of self-reported under-sleepers were actually averaging more than seven hours, the survey-based picture probably overstates the number of adults sleeping too little. 'May be smaller' is appropriately hedged.
explanations.A: Unsupported — the stimulus doesn't say devices overstate; it says self-report and device data diverge, with no basis to privilege self-report.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'most adults who believe themselves sleep-deprived' overreaches from 'nearly half of one subgroup.'
explanations.D: Too strong — the stimulus doesn't dismiss the concern, only suggests its magnitude may be overstated.
explanations.E: Unsupported — the stimulus doesn't compare device users to non-users.

lr.difficultyReason: Connects the larval-survival datapoint with the protection-status contrast to support a hedged inference about the role of reserve size. Trap (A) overreaches on reserves' general effectiveness; trap (E) is a plausible worldly claim not anchored in the stimulus.
lr.stimulus: Marine biologists studying a coral reef system have found that the abundance of several commercially valuable fish species is substantially higher inside small protected reserves than in adjacent unprotected waters. Larvae of these species, however, drift on ocean currents for weeks before settling, and genetic analyses indicate that larvae produced within the reserves are regularly carried far beyond reserve boundaries. In nearby reef systems where no reserves have been established, populations of the same species have continued to decline.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Small marine reserves are sufficient to halt the decline of commercially valuable fish species throughout any reef system in which they are established.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some populations of commercially valuable fish outside small marine reserves benefit from the existence of those reserves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Larval dispersal is the main factor determining fish abundance within marine reserves.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most commercial fishers prefer to fish just outside the boundaries of marine reserves.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Expanding existing marine reserves would produce proportionally greater benefits for fish populations.

explanations.correct: Reserves contain more abundant populations; larvae produced there regularly drift beyond the boundaries; and unprotected reef systems without reserves continue to decline. Together these support the hedged claim that at least some outside populations benefit from the reserves. 'Some' is the right level of warrant.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'sufficient to halt decline throughout any reef system' overreaches from localized abundance findings.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'the main factor' is a superlative not supported by the stimulus.
explanations.D: Plausible-but-unsupported — fisher behavior isn't addressed.
explanations.E: Plausible-but-unsupported — proportionality of benefits isn't established.

lr.difficultyReason: Stimulus presents quantitative medical data with a qualification about subgroups. Correct answer respects the hedge; traps drop a qualifier or overclaim causation.
lr.stimulus: A ten-year study of patients diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes found that those who engaged in at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise per week showed, on average, a 0.8% reduction in hemoglobin A1c levels compared to those who did not exercise regularly. However, among patients who were also being treated with insulin, the reduction in A1c levels associated with exercise was less than 0.2% — a difference the study authors described as clinically negligible. The study did not examine whether exercise affected the required insulin dosages of patients in the insulin-treated group.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aerobic exercise reduces hemoglobin A1c levels in all patients diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The benefit of aerobic exercise on blood glucose control may be smaller for insulin-treated diabetic patients than for those not on insulin therapy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Insulin therapy eliminates the physiological mechanisms through which aerobic exercise improves blood glucose control.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Physicians should not recommend aerobic exercise to patients who are being treated with insulin for Type 2 diabetes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The ten-year study's findings establish that aerobic exercise is the most effective non-pharmacological intervention for managing Type 2 diabetes.

explanations.correct: The study shows a meaningful A1c reduction (0.8%) in non-insulin-treated patients but only a negligible reduction (0.2%) in insulin-treated patients. This directly supports the hedged claim that the benefit 'may be smaller' for insulin-treated patients — respecting the limitation that causation is not fully established.
explanations.A: Too strong — the stimulus shows the benefit in insulin-treated patients is clinically negligible, so the claim that exercise reduces A1c 'in all patients' is not supported.
explanations.B: Correct — a hedged comparative claim that directly follows from the data contrast between the two subgroups.
explanations.C: Causal mechanism overreach — the study says nothing about whether insulin eliminates the physiological pathway; it only reports outcome data.
explanations.D: Policy prescription not supported — the stimulus explicitly does not examine all effects of exercise on insulin-treated patients (e.g., dosage changes), so a blanket recommendation against it is unwarranted.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the study compares exercise to no exercise, not to other non-pharmacological interventions, so no 'most effective' ranking is established.

lr.difficultyReason: Economics stimulus with relative vs. absolute confusion as a key trap. Correct answer makes a hedged comparative claim; one distractor reads the relative data as absolute.
lr.stimulus: Data from a regional housing authority covering 47 municipalities show that in municipalities where rent-stabilization ordinances were enacted between 2010 and 2015, the median monthly rent increased by 12 percent over the following five years. In municipalities in the same region that did not enact such ordinances during that period, median monthly rent increased by 31 percent over the same five years. The data do not indicate whether the municipalities that enacted ordinances had higher or lower baseline rents at the start of the period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Renters in municipalities with rent-stabilization ordinances paid lower monthly rents than renters in municipalities without such ordinances.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rent-stabilization ordinances caused rents to rise more slowly than they would have otherwise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the municipalities studied, the rate of rent increase was lower where rent-stabilization ordinances were in effect than where they were not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enacting rent-stabilization ordinances is the most reliable method for controlling rent increases in a municipality.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rent-stabilization ordinances benefit low-income renters more than they benefit middle-income renters.

explanations.correct: The data directly show a 12% increase in ordinance municipalities vs. 31% in non-ordinance municipalities — a straightforward comparative claim about rates of increase that the data plainly support.
explanations.A: Relative/absolute confusion trap — the data track rates of increase, not absolute rent levels. Without knowing baseline rents, we cannot say which group paid lower absolute amounts.
explanations.B: Causal overreach — the data show correlation; the stimulus does not rule out confounding variables that might explain the difference in growth rates.
explanations.D: Superlative overreach — 'most reliable method' implies a comparison with other methods, none of which are discussed in the stimulus.
explanations.E: Out of scope — income levels of renters are never mentioned in the stimulus.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science stimulus with a counterintuitive finding. The correct answer draws a modest inference from an apparent paradox; traps include opposite-direction and plausible-but-unsupported answers.
lr.stimulus: Researchers monitoring a coastal estuary found that concentrations of nitrogen — a key nutrient for algal growth — increased significantly after a wetland restoration project was completed upstream. Despite this increase in nitrogen, algal bloom frequency in the estuary declined by approximately 30 percent over the three years following restoration, compared to the three years preceding it. Water salinity and temperature in the estuary remained stable across both periods.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Algal blooms in coastal estuaries are primarily caused by elevated water temperatures rather than by nitrogen concentrations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The wetland restoration project reduced algal bloom frequency by filtering nitrogen before it reached the estuary.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nitrogen concentration is not the only factor that determines the frequency of algal blooms in the estuary studied.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Wetland restoration projects always reduce algal bloom frequency in nearby coastal estuaries.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increases in nitrogen concentration generally lead to increases in algal bloom frequency in coastal estuaries.

explanations.correct: Nitrogen increased yet algal blooms declined — this directly demonstrates that nitrogen alone does not determine bloom frequency in this estuary. Some other factor must also be at work, so nitrogen is not the only determinant.
explanations.A: Too strong and unsupported — temperature remained stable across both periods, so it cannot explain the change; and 'primarily caused by' is an extreme, unsupported causal claim.
explanations.B: Causal mechanism overreach — the stimulus says nitrogen concentrations actually increased after restoration, making the claim that the project filtered nitrogen directly contradicted.
explanations.D: Scope creep with absolute language — 'always' and the generalization to 'all nearby coastal estuaries' far exceeds what one estuary's data can support.
explanations.E: Opposite direction — the data show nitrogen rose while blooms declined, which is the reverse of what this choice claims.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics stimulus with a controlled twist about a specific language subgroup diverging from a broader trend. Correct answer must scope correctly to that subgroup.
lr.stimulus: A cross-linguistic survey of 94 languages found that the vast majority use word order as the primary means of conveying grammatical relationships between subjects and objects. However, among languages in the survey that employ an extensive system of morphological case markers — suffixes or prefixes attached to nouns to indicate their grammatical role — flexible word order was far more common than in languages lacking such a system. In the survey, no language with a fully fixed word order was found to also employ a comprehensive case-marking system.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Languages that rely on morphological case markers do not need word order to convey grammatical relationships.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Among the languages surveyed, having a comprehensive case-marking system was associated with greater flexibility in word order.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All languages with flexible word order use morphological case markers to signal grammatical relationships.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Morphological case-marking systems developed because early languages lacked fixed word-order rules.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Word order is a less reliable grammatical device than morphological case marking across all human languages.

explanations.correct: The survey directly shows that languages with extensive case-marking systems exhibited flexible word order far more commonly than those without — a hedged associative claim that stays within the scope of the survey data.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'do not need word order' is an absolute claim; the stimulus only says flexible order is more common, not that these languages abandon word order as a grammatical device entirely.
explanations.C: Reversal of direction — the data say case-marking languages tend to have flexible order, not that all flexible-order languages have case marking. This confuses the direction of the association.
explanations.D: Historical causal speculation — the stimulus presents synchronic survey data and makes no claims about historical development or causation.
explanations.E: 'Less reliable' and 'all human languages' both overreach; the stimulus makes a comparative frequency claim about a specific survey sample, not a universal evaluative ranking.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy/law stimulus with statistical data on sentencing. Correct answer is a hedged comparative; traps include one that drops a crucial qualifier and one that makes an unsupported normative claim.
lr.stimulus: A review of sentencing records in a state's superior courts from 2015 to 2022 found that defendants convicted of felony drug offenses who had retained private counsel received custodial sentences in 38 percent of cases. Defendants convicted of the same category of offenses who were represented by public defenders received custodial sentences in 61 percent of cases. The review controlled for the defendants' prior criminal records but did not control for the severity of the specific offense within the felony drug category.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following inferences is most supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Private attorneys are more skilled than public defenders at representing clients charged with drug offenses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Among defendants with similar prior records convicted of felony drug offenses in the state studied, those with private counsel were less likely to receive custodial sentences than those with public defenders.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The type of legal representation a defendant obtains is the primary determinant of the sentence imposed in felony drug cases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Public defenders in the state studied are inadequately funded and overworked.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Defendants with private counsel receive lighter sentences than defendants with public defenders in all categories of criminal cases in the state.

explanations.correct: The review controlled for prior criminal records and found a 23-percentage-point gap in custodial sentence rates. The correct answer faithfully reflects what was controlled for ('similar prior records') and hedges appropriately ('less likely'), staying within the data's scope.
explanations.A: Plausible but unsupported — the data show an outcome difference but do not isolate attorney skill as the cause; offense severity was not controlled, and many other factors could explain the gap.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'primary determinant' implies this factor outweighs all others, which the data cannot establish since offense severity was not controlled.
explanations.D: Out of scope — resource levels and workload of public defenders are never mentioned; this is a plausible worldly belief not derivable from the stimulus.
explanations.E: Scope creep — the data cover only felony drug offenses; extending the conclusion to 'all categories of criminal cases' goes beyond what the review examined.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology stimulus with a surprising subgroup finding. Correct answer captures a hedged inference about a specific subgroup; traps include an absolute claim and an opposite-direction answer.
lr.stimulus: An independent audit of a widely used algorithmic hiring tool found that the system's accuracy in predicting six-month job retention was 74 percent when evaluated across all applicants. However, for applicants who had gaps of 12 months or longer in their employment history, the algorithm's predictions were accurate only 51 percent of the time — barely above random chance. The audit noted that applicants with employment gaps constituted roughly 18 percent of the total applicant pool reviewed.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The algorithmic hiring tool performs less reliably for applicants with extended employment gaps than for the overall applicant pool.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Applicants with employment gaps of 12 months or longer are less likely to be retained for six months than applicants without such gaps.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The algorithm's overall accuracy of 74 percent is driven primarily by its strong performance on applicants without employment gaps.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Algorithmic hiring tools are inherently biased against applicants with non-traditional career histories.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tool's predictions about applicants with employment gaps are more accurate than those about applicants without such gaps.

explanations.correct: 74% overall vs. 51% for the employment-gap subgroup directly supports the claim that the tool performs less reliably for that subgroup — a straightforward comparative inference from the numbers given.
explanations.B: Opposite direction / unsupported — the audit measures the accuracy of predictions about retention, not actual retention rates. Nothing in the stimulus says gap applicants are actually retained at lower rates.
explanations.C: Plausible but not fully supported — while mathematically plausible given the numbers and proportions, the stimulus does not provide the breakdown needed to confirm what 'drives' the overall accuracy; this requires calculation the stimulus does not invite.
explanations.D: Too strong and out of scope — 'inherently biased' and 'algorithmic hiring tools' (plural, universal) go far beyond what one audit of one tool establishes.
explanations.E: Opposite direction — the data show 51% accuracy for the gap subgroup versus 74% overall, so this choice directly inverts the finding.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: History stimulus with multiple data points across time periods. Correct answer makes a temporally scoped inference; a key trap extends the conclusion beyond the stated time period.
lr.stimulus: Between 1880 and 1910, the proportion of the urban workforce in Western European industrializing cities employed in textile manufacturing declined from approximately 35 percent to 18 percent, while the proportion employed in metalworking and machine production rose from roughly 12 percent to 29 percent. Wages in metalworking averaged 40 percent higher than those in textile work throughout this period. Census records from the same cities indicate that average household income among urban factory workers increased modestly — by approximately 8 percent in real terms — over those three decades.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The shift in employment from textiles to metalworking contributed to the modest rise in average household income among urban factory workers between 1880 and 1910.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Urban factory workers in Western Europe were better off economically in 1910 than at any other point in the nineteenth or twentieth centuries.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Textile manufacturing was no longer an economically significant industry in Western European cities by 1910.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Workers who transferred from textile manufacturing to metalworking during this period each experienced a 40 percent increase in their personal wages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The growth of metalworking industries in Western European cities was caused by deliberate government policy during this period.

explanations.correct: Higher-wage metalworking employment expanded while lower-wage textile employment contracted, and household incomes rose modestly. It is strongly supported that the compositional shift contributed to the income rise — a hedged causal inference consistent with the direction and magnitude of the data.
explanations.B: Temporal scope creep — the data only cover 1880–1910; claiming workers were better off 'than at any other point' in both the nineteenth and twentieth centuries goes far beyond what these records establish.
explanations.C: Too strong — textile employment at 18% of the urban workforce still represents a substantial share; 'no longer economically significant' is not supported.
explanations.D: Misapplication of average to individuals — the 40% figure is an average sectoral wage difference, not a guarantee about individual worker outcomes; workers switching jobs might have entered at lower pay grades.
explanations.E: Causal overreach — government policy is never mentioned; attributing the industrial shift to deliberate policy introduces a cause the stimulus does not supply.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics/policy stimulus presenting research on moral judgment with a qualification. Correct answer stays within the qualification; traps generalize improperly or introduce unsupported normative claims.
lr.stimulus: Researchers presented participants with a series of moral dilemmas in which causing harm to one person would prevent greater harm to several others. Participants who had been asked to first perform arithmetic tasks solved correctly were significantly more likely to endorse harm-causing actions in these dilemmas than participants who had not done such tasks. The researchers noted, however, that this effect was observed only for dilemmas involving strangers — it did not appear when the potential harm target was described as a family member or close friend.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Performing arithmetic tasks causes people to reason more carefully about moral dilemmas in all contexts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Utilitarian moral reasoning is superior to other forms of moral reasoning for resolving dilemmas involving strangers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The effect of prior analytical activity on moral judgment may depend on the relationship between the judge and the potential harm target.

choices.label: D
choices.text: People who perform arithmetic tasks are more ethical than those who do not when confronting real-world moral dilemmas.

choices.label: E
choices.text: People are more likely to endorse causing harm to family members than to strangers in order to prevent greater overall harm.

explanations.correct: The study found the arithmetic-task effect only for stranger dilemmas, not for family/friend dilemmas — directly supporting the hedged claim that the effect of prior analytical activity on moral judgment may depend on the relationship between the judge and the target.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'in all contexts' contradicts the finding that the effect disappeared for family/friend dilemmas; the stimulus explicitly limits the effect's scope.
explanations.B: Normative overreach — the stimulus describes what participants endorsed, not which form of reasoning is 'superior'; normative ranking is not derivable from descriptive experimental data.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported — being more likely to endorse a utilitarian trade-off in an abstract dilemma does not imply greater overall ethical behavior; 'more ethical' is a value judgment the stimulus does not support.
explanations.E: Opposite direction — the effect (endorsing harm-causing actions) was observed for stranger dilemmas and not for family/friend dilemmas, so if anything the data suggest the reverse of this claim.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts/economics stimulus with a counterintuitive revenue finding. Correct answer is a hedged inference about a specific market segment; traps include a too-strong generalization and a plausible-but-unsupported claim.
lr.stimulus: A survey of 200 independent recording artists who released albums between 2018 and 2023 found that artists who made their music available exclusively through paid-download platforms generated average annual revenues of approximately $4,200 from recorded music. Artists who made their music available for free streaming in addition to paid downloads generated average annual revenues of approximately $7,800 — nearly double — from recorded music during the same period. The survey excluded artists signed to major record labels and did not measure revenue from live performances or merchandise.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: For at least some independent recording artists, making music available for free streaming is associated with higher recorded-music revenue than relying solely on paid downloads.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Free streaming platforms increase total revenue for all musicians, including those signed to major record labels.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Independent recording artists should always distribute their music through free streaming platforms rather than relying exclusively on paid downloads.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The recorded-music industry as a whole generates more revenue from free streaming than from paid downloads.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Independent artists who use free streaming earn more from live performances and merchandise than those who rely only on paid downloads.

explanations.correct: The survey data show that the free-streaming group averaged nearly double the revenue of the paid-download-only group. The hedged 'for at least some' phrasing correctly captures that these are averages across surveyed independent artists, without overclaiming universality.
explanations.B: Scope creep — the survey explicitly excluded major-label artists; extending the finding to 'all musicians including those signed to major labels' goes beyond the data.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'should always' is a prescriptive absolute; the survey shows averages, not a universal relationship, and individual circumstances could differ substantially.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the survey measured individual artist revenues, not industry-wide totals; and the comparison between streaming and paid-download revenue in aggregate is not addressed.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the survey explicitly did not measure live performance or merchandise revenue, so no inference about those income streams is possible.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science / policy stimulus with data on conservation outcomes. The correct answer draws a modest comparative inference; traps include causal overreach and a temporal scope error.
lr.stimulus: An analysis of 63 marine protected areas (MPAs) established worldwide between 1990 and 2005 found that fish biomass within MPA boundaries was, on average, 2.3 times greater than in comparable unprotected areas of the same ocean regions after 15 years of protection. The analysis also found, however, that MPAs established in regions with active pre-existing enforcement of fishing regulations showed a biomass ratio of only 1.4 — substantially lower than the overall average. MPAs established in regions with little prior regulatory enforcement showed a biomass ratio of 3.1.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Marine protected areas are the most effective conservation tool available for rebuilding depleted ocean fish populations globally.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fish biomass in unprotected ocean areas will decline relative to that in MPAs for as long as MPAs remain in force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The magnitude of the fish biomass increase associated with MPA establishment tends to be greater in regions where pre-existing fishing regulations were weakly enforced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Establishing an MPA causes fish populations to recover more rapidly in regions with weak prior enforcement than in regions with strong prior enforcement.

choices.label: E
choices.text: In regions with active pre-existing enforcement of fishing regulations, establishing an MPA provides no meaningful conservation benefit.

explanations.correct: The data directly show a biomass ratio of 3.1 in low-enforcement regions vs. 1.4 in high-enforcement regions — a clear pattern supporting the hedged claim that biomass gains 'tend to be greater' where prior enforcement was weak.
explanations.A: Too strong and out of scope — 'most effective conservation tool globally' compares MPAs to all other possible tools, none of which are discussed in the stimulus.
explanations.B: Temporal scope creep — the study covers a specific 15-year window; projecting that the trend will continue 'for as long as MPAs remain in force' extrapolates beyond the data.
explanations.D: Causal overreach — the data show a correlation between prior enforcement levels and biomass ratios, but do not establish that MPA establishment itself causes more rapid recovery; baseline conditions could explain much of the difference.
explanations.E: Too strong — a ratio of 1.4 still represents a 40% greater biomass within MPAs compared to unprotected areas, which constitutes a meaningful difference; 'no meaningful benefit' is contradicted by the data.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Stimulus presents mixed quantitative data with a key qualification about subgroups. The correct answer requires respecting that qualification rather than overgeneralizing. Trap answers either drop the qualifier or scope-creep to the general population.
lr.stimulus: A regional health authority tracked outcomes for patients treated with a new antihypertensive drug over 24 months. Among patients under 60 years of age, the drug reduced systolic blood pressure by an average of 18 mmHg — roughly twice the reduction observed in patients 60 and older, whose average reduction was 9 mmHg. In both age groups, approximately 12 percent of patients discontinued the drug due to side effects. The overall rate of major cardiovascular events during the study period was lower in the treated group than in a matched untreated comparison group, though the difference was statistically significant only for patients under 60.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The antihypertensive drug is ineffective for patients 60 and older.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients under 60 are more likely to experience side effects from the drug than patients 60 and older.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drug's blood-pressure-lowering effect is not uniform across all age groups.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Major cardiovascular events are more common among untreated patients than among any patient receiving antihypertensive treatment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The drug's tolerability is better in younger patients than in older patients.

explanations.correct: The stimulus directly states that patients under 60 experienced twice the blood-pressure reduction of those 60 and older (18 mmHg vs. 9 mmHg). This directly supports the hedged claim that the effect is not uniform across age groups — a modest, well-grounded inference.
explanations.A: Too strong and opposite-direction trap. The drug did reduce blood pressure by 9 mmHg in older patients; the stimulus does not say it is ineffective, only less effective.
explanations.B: Scope creep / unsupported. The stimulus states discontinuation rates due to side effects were approximately 12 percent in both groups — providing no basis for a difference in tolerability by age.
explanations.C: Correct. The differential reduction (18 mmHg vs. 9 mmHg) directly and plainly supports that the effect varies by age group.
explanations.D: Too strong. The statistically significant cardiovascular benefit was observed only in the under-60 group; overgeneralizing to 'any patient' goes beyond the data.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported. Tolerability, as measured by discontinuation due to side effects, was identical across age groups at roughly 12 percent each.

lr.difficultyReason: Stimulus contains an economic dataset with a counterintuitive finding. Correct answer draws a hedged comparative inference. Traps include an absolute claim, a causal overreach, and a plausible-but-unsupported economic generalization.
lr.stimulus: Data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics show that in manufacturing sectors with the highest rates of automation, average wages grew at 3.2 percent annually over the past decade, compared with 1.4 percent annually in sectors with the lowest rates of automation. However, total employment in high-automation sectors fell by roughly 8 percent over the same period, while employment in low-automation sectors remained essentially flat. The wage data reflect averages across all workers who remained employed in each sector.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Automation causes wages to rise in every industry in which it is introduced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Workers who remained employed in high-automation sectors fared better in wage growth than those in low-automation sectors, even as total employment in those sectors declined.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Automation is the primary driver of wage growth in manufacturing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Workers displaced by automation in high-automation sectors ultimately found better-paying jobs elsewhere.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Low-automation sectors will eventually adopt the same wage-growth rates as high-automation sectors.

explanations.correct: The stimulus states that average wages grew faster in high-automation sectors (3.2% vs. 1.4%) while total employment fell. Because the wage data cover only those still employed, the inference that remaining workers in high-automation sectors saw stronger wage growth — even amid declining total employment — is directly grounded in the data.
explanations.A: Too strong and causal overreach. The data show a correlation in manufacturing sectors; extending to 'every industry' and asserting causation is not supported.
explanations.B: Correct. This hedged comparative claim is precisely what the two data points together support.
explanations.C: Too strong. The stimulus identifies a correlation but does not establish automation as the primary driver; other factors could explain the wage differential.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported. The stimulus provides no information about where displaced workers went or what they earned subsequently.
explanations.E: Scope creep / future projection. The stimulus covers a past decade; no basis for predicting convergence is provided.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science stimulus with multiple qualifications. The correct answer is a modest directional inference. Traps use absolute language or invert the direction of effect.
lr.stimulus: Researchers monitoring a coastal wetland found that plots treated with controlled burns every three years maintained plant species diversity scores approximately 40 percent higher than unburned control plots over a ten-year period. However, in the two years immediately following each burn, diversity scores in treated plots dropped below those of unburned plots before recovering. Migratory bird counts in treated plots were consistently higher than in unburned plots throughout the full ten-year period, including the two years following burns.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Controlled burns eliminate all plant species that cannot tolerate fire in coastal wetlands.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Migratory birds prefer habitats with the highest plant species diversity scores.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the long run, controlled burns tend to support greater plant species diversity in this wetland than no burning does, despite causing short-term diversity losses.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unburned wetland plots are better habitats for migratory birds than burned plots immediately after a burn event.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Controlled burns are the most effective conservation tool available for coastal wetland management.

explanations.correct: The ten-year average shows 40% higher diversity in burned plots, but the stimulus acknowledges short-term dips post-burn. The correct answer accurately captures both the long-term benefit and the short-term cost, making it the most precisely supported inference.
explanations.A: Too strong. 'Eliminate all' is not supported; diversity recovers, implying surviving species.
explanations.B: Opposite direction / unsupported. Bird counts were higher in treated plots even in the two years when diversity scores were lower, which contradicts the idea that birds track diversity scores.
explanations.C: Correct. This hedged claim respects both the long-term gain and the acknowledged short-term dip.
explanations.D: Opposite direction. Migratory bird counts in treated plots were consistently higher throughout, including in the post-burn years.
explanations.E: Too strong and out of scope. The stimulus compares only burning versus no burning; it does not compare burning to other conservation tools.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal policy stimulus with a nuanced empirical finding. The correct answer requires recognizing a specific subgroup result that diverges from the general trend. Traps include a too-strong generalization and a scope-creep answer.
lr.stimulus: A state bar association study examined outcomes in civil cases in which one party was represented by an attorney and the opposing party was self-represented. In approximately 62 percent of such cases, the attorney-represented party prevailed. However, in cases involving landlord-tenant disputes specifically, self-represented tenants prevailed in 54 percent of cases against attorney-represented landlords. The study also noted that self-represented parties in all case types spent, on average, three times as many hours preparing for hearings as attorney-represented parties reported for comparable hearings.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Self-represented litigants always prevail when they invest sufficient preparation time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attorney representation provides no meaningful advantage in civil litigation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The advantage associated with attorney representation in civil cases does not extend uniformly to all case types.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Landlords who hire attorneys in landlord-tenant disputes are less competent litigants than self-represented tenants.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Self-represented litigants would win more cases overall if courts provided them with additional preparation time.

explanations.correct: The overall rate favors attorney-represented parties (62%), but in landlord-tenant cases the self-represented party actually prevails more often (54%). This divergence directly supports the hedged inference that attorney representation's advantage is not uniform across all case types.
explanations.A: Too strong. 'Always prevail' is not supported; the data show probabilities, not certainties, and many self-represented parties still lose.
explanations.B: Opposite direction. Overall, attorney-represented parties win 62% of cases, which does indicate a meaningful general advantage.
explanations.C: Correct. The landlord-tenant exception directly shows the advantage is not uniform.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported. The study measures outcomes, not litigant competence; many factors besides competence influence results.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported. The stimulus notes preparation-time differences but does not establish that more time would improve outcomes.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology stimulus with a counterintuitive correlation. Correct answer is a hedged claim about the correlation. Traps include causal overreach and a plausible-but-unsupported inference about user behavior.
lr.stimulus: Usage data from a major streaming platform show that subscribers who watch fewer than five hours of content per week are significantly more likely to cancel their subscriptions within six months than subscribers who watch between five and twenty hours per week. Subscribers who watch more than twenty hours per week cancel at roughly the same rate as those watching five to twenty hours. The platform's internal surveys indicate that subscribers who watch fewer than five hours per week most commonly cite 'not enough time to watch' rather than 'not enough content I enjoy' as their reason for canceling.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Subscribers who cancel their subscriptions do so because they are dissatisfied with the platform's content library.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Among low-usage subscribers who cancel, limited viewing time is a more commonly cited reason than dissatisfaction with available content.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increasing the amount of content available on the platform would substantially reduce cancellation rates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Subscribers who watch more than twenty hours per week are the platform's most loyal customers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cancellation risk decreases steadily as weekly viewing hours increase across all usage levels.

explanations.correct: The internal survey data directly state that low-usage subscribers who cancel most commonly cite 'not enough time to watch' rather than content dissatisfaction. This is a direct, hedged restatement of the survey finding.
explanations.A: Opposite direction. The surveys show time constraints, not content dissatisfaction, are the dominant reason among low-usage cancelers.
explanations.B: Correct. This is a careful, hedged restatement of what the surveys directly report for the low-usage canceler group.
explanations.C: Plausible but unsupported and causal overreach. Because time constraints, not content quality, are cited, adding content may not reduce cancellations among this group.
explanations.D: Too strong. The data show high-usage subscribers cancel at similar rates to moderate users; 'most loyal' is an absolute label not supported by the data.
explanations.E: Opposite direction / scope creep. The data show high-usage (>20 hrs) subscribers cancel at the same rate as moderate users, not a lower rate — so the decrease does not continue steadily at all usage levels.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics stimulus with a comparative finding across language groups. Correct answer respects the scope of the study. Traps include overgeneralization and a plausible-but-unsupported historical claim.
lr.stimulus: A study of 40 unrelated languages found that languages with a larger inventory of distinct phonemes — the smallest units of sound that distinguish meaning — tended to be spoken in smaller geographic areas and by smaller communities of speakers. Languages with fewer phonemes tended to be spoken over wider geographic ranges and by larger populations. The researchers noted that the correlation was moderate (r = 0.52) and that several languages with large phoneme inventories are spoken by millions of people.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following inferences is most supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Languages spoken by larger populations always develop simpler sound systems over time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The number of phonemes in a language is determined primarily by the geographic range over which it is spoken.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A language's phoneme inventory size tends to be associated with the size and range of its speaker community, though the relationship is not absolute.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Languages with large phoneme inventories are linguistically superior to those with smaller inventories.

choices.label: E
choices.text: All languages with small geographic ranges have large phoneme inventories.

explanations.correct: The stimulus reports a moderate correlation between phoneme inventory and speaker community size and range, while explicitly noting exceptions. The correct answer incorporates both the observed tendency and the noted exceptions, making it a well-calibrated inference.
explanations.A: Too strong and causal overreach. 'Always develop' introduces absolute language and a developmental claim the stimulus does not make.
explanations.B: Too strong and causal overreach. The stimulus reports correlation (r = 0.52), not determination; 'primarily determined by' overstates the relationship.
explanations.C: Correct. 'Tends to be associated' and 'not absolute' accurately reflect the moderate correlation and the acknowledged exceptions.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported value judgment. The stimulus makes no evaluative claims about linguistic superiority.
explanations.E: Too strong. The stimulus describes a tendency with exceptions; 'all languages' eliminates the exceptions the stimulus explicitly acknowledges.

lr.difficultyReason: History stimulus presenting two divergent trends within the same era. Correct answer captures the tension without overclaiming. Traps involve collapsing the distinction or projecting a causal claim.
lr.stimulus: Historical records from several northern European cities in the late seventeenth century show that real wages — adjusted for price inflation — for skilled artisans rose modestly during the period from 1670 to 1700, while real wages for unskilled laborers fell during the same period. At the same time, the overall price of basic foodstuffs declined by roughly 15 percent in those cities, partly due to improved grain storage technology. Historians have noted that unskilled laborers typically spent a far higher proportion of their income on food than skilled artisans did.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Skilled artisans in late seventeenth-century northern Europe were uniformly prosperous.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The decline in food prices during this period may have partially offset the deterioration in unskilled laborers' real wages.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Improved grain storage technology was the primary cause of rising real wages for skilled artisans.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unskilled laborers in late seventeenth-century northern Europe were worse off in every measurable respect than skilled artisans.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Real wages are a more reliable measure of economic well-being than nominal wages in all historical periods.

explanations.correct: The stimulus states that food prices fell ~15%, and that unskilled laborers spent a higher share of income on food. Even though their real wages fell, the food price drop would have moderated the impact on their purchasing power for food. The hedged language 'may have partially offset' correctly reflects that this is a supportable inference, not a certainty.
explanations.A: Too strong. 'Uniformly prosperous' is an absolute claim; the stimulus only says skilled artisans' real wages rose modestly.
explanations.B: Correct. The combination of the food price decline and unskilled laborers' high food expenditure share supports this hedged inference.
explanations.C: Causal overreach and opposite direction for scope. The stimulus attributes the food price decline partly to grain storage technology but does not link this technology to skilled artisan wages at all.
explanations.D: Too strong and scope creep. 'Every measurable respect' is not supported; the stimulus provides only wage and food price data.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported and out of scope. The stimulus uses real wages but makes no comparative methodological claim about measurement reliability across all historical periods.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics/policy stimulus with a survey-based finding and a key qualification. Correct answer is a modest inference about attitudes. Traps include a causal policy claim and an absolute characterization of views.
lr.stimulus: A survey of 1,200 adults asked respondents whether they would support a proposed city ordinance requiring restaurants to display calorie counts on menus. Overall, 68 percent expressed support. However, among respondents who identified as restaurant owners or food-service workers, only 31 percent expressed support. The survey also found that respondents who reported eating at restaurants more than three times per week were slightly less supportive (61 percent) than those who ate out less frequently (71 percent).
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most adults oppose government regulation of the restaurant industry.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Requiring calorie counts on menus would reduce the frequency with which people eat at restaurants.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Support for the calorie-labeling ordinance varies considerably depending on respondents' relationship to the restaurant industry.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restaurant owners and food-service workers oppose all public health regulations that affect their businesses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Frequent restaurant patrons are the most important group for policymakers to persuade when implementing dietary regulations.

explanations.correct: The data show a large gap between the general population (68% support) and restaurant industry workers (31% support), directly supporting the inference that support varies considerably based on one's relationship to the industry. This is a well-anchored, hedged inference.
explanations.A: Opposite direction. Overall, 68 percent of adults support this regulatory measure; saying 'most oppose government regulation' inverts the finding.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported causal policy claim. The survey measures attitudes toward the ordinance, not behavioral changes that would result from it.
explanations.C: Correct. The 37-percentage-point gap between the general population and industry workers directly supports 'varies considerably.'
explanations.D: Too strong and scope creep. The survey addresses one ordinance; 'all public health regulations' is an unsupported absolute generalization.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported. The stimulus does not discuss policymaker strategy or which groups matter most for implementation.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts/cultural economics stimulus with a counterintuitive finding about funding and output. Correct answer captures a hedged comparative claim. Traps include causal overreach and a plausible-but-unsupported conclusion about artistic quality.
lr.stimulus: An analysis of nonprofit theater companies in a large metropolitan area found that companies receiving more than 60 percent of their operating budgets from government grants produced an average of 4.2 original productions per year, compared with 6.8 original productions per year for companies that relied primarily on private donations and ticket revenues. However, productions by heavily grant-funded companies were reviewed more favorably in publications covering the arts, receiving an average critic score of 78 out of 100, compared with 64 out of 100 for companies relying primarily on private funding.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Government grants cause theater companies to produce fewer but more critically acclaimed productions than private funding does.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Theater companies funded primarily by private sources are more financially stable than those relying on government grants.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In this metropolitan area, theater companies that relied primarily on government grants tended to produce fewer original works per year but received higher average critical scores than those relying on private funding.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The most artistically successful theater companies are always those with the most secure funding sources.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Private donors and ticket buyers prefer a higher volume of productions over the artistic quality of individual productions.

explanations.correct: This answer is a precise, hedged restatement of the two key findings: grant-funded companies produced fewer works (4.2 vs. 6.8) but received higher critic scores (78 vs. 64). It respects the scope ('in this metropolitan area') and uses 'tended to,' avoiding causal claims.
explanations.A: Causal overreach. The data show correlations; establishing that grants cause the pattern requires ruling out confounds the stimulus does not address.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported. The stimulus provides no information about financial stability; funding source composition is described, not financial security.
explanations.C: Correct. This is a carefully scoped, hedged restatement of the two central data comparisons.
explanations.D: Too strong. 'Always' is absolute, and the stimulus does not discuss funding security or rank companies by artistic success comprehensively.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported. The stimulus does not report audience preferences; higher output may reflect other strategic or operational factors.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science and policy crossover stimulus with a proportional finding and a temporal qualification. Correct answer requires recognizing what the temporal qualification implies. Traps include a too-strong projection and an absolute claim.
lr.stimulus: A federal agency's annual water quality reports show that the proportion of monitored rivers classified as 'impaired' — meaning they fail to meet basic ecological standards — declined from 44 percent in 2000 to 29 percent in 2020. The largest improvements occurred in rivers adjacent to agricultural land, where impairment rates fell by more than half. Rivers near urban industrial zones showed only modest improvement. Over the same period, total funding for water quality enforcement programs increased by 180 percent in real terms, though agency reports note that enforcement activity was concentrated in agricultural regions.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By 2030, fewer than 20 percent of monitored rivers will be classified as impaired if current funding trends continue.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Industrial pollution is a less significant contributor to river impairment than agricultural runoff.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The concentration of enforcement activity in agricultural regions is at least partly responsible for the larger improvements seen in rivers near agricultural land.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Water quality enforcement programs are ineffective at improving conditions in rivers near urban industrial zones.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased funding for water quality programs always produces proportional improvements in river quality.

explanations.correct: The stimulus reports that the largest improvements occurred in agricultural-adjacent rivers, and that enforcement was concentrated there. The hedged inference that this concentration is 'at least partly responsible' is well supported by the parallel between where enforcement was focused and where improvements were greatest, without asserting full causation.
explanations.A: Scope creep / future projection. The stimulus covers 2000–2020; extrapolating a specific rate to 2030 goes beyond what the data support.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported. The stimulus compares improvement rates by region, not the relative contribution of pollution sources to overall impairment.
explanations.C: Correct. The alignment between enforcement concentration in agricultural regions and the largest improvement in those same regions supports this hedged causal inference.
explanations.D: Too strong. The stimulus says industrial zone rivers showed 'only modest improvement,' not no improvement; 'ineffective' is an absolute claim the data do not support.
explanations.E: Too strong and contradicted by the data. Industrial-zone rivers improved only modestly despite the overall funding increase, showing the relationship is not always proportional.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents mixed quantitative data with an important qualification about a subgroup. The correct answer respects a hedged qualification that several trap answers either drop or invert. Test-takers must identify the modest inference that survives the stated exception.
lr.stimulus: A survey of 1,200 adults conducted by a public health institute found that people who reported sleeping fewer than six hours per night were approximately twice as likely to report persistent fatigue during daytime hours as those sleeping seven or more hours. However, among adults who engaged in vigorous aerobic exercise at least four times per week, the association between short sleep duration and daytime fatigue was substantially weaker — short-sleeping exercisers reported daytime fatigue at only a slightly elevated rate compared to well-rested non-exercisers. Adults in the survey who both slept fewer than six hours and did not exercise regularly reported the highest rates of daytime fatigue of any group. The survey did not assess diet or caffeine intake.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Regular vigorous exercise eliminates the negative effects of insufficient sleep on daytime energy levels.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For at least some adults, engaging in regular vigorous exercise may reduce, though not necessarily eliminate, fatigue associated with sleeping fewer than six hours per night.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adults who sleep fewer than six hours per night will experience persistent daytime fatigue regardless of their exercise habits.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Insufficient sleep is a less significant contributor to daytime fatigue than a sedentary lifestyle.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Caffeine intake is the primary reason that some short-sleeping exercisers avoid persistent daytime fatigue.

explanations.correct: The survey shows that among short-sleeping adults who exercise vigorously, daytime fatigue rates were only slightly elevated compared to well-rested non-exercisers — substantially weaker than the general short-sleep association. This supports a hedged inference that regular exercise may reduce (but not necessarily eliminate) fatigue for at least some short sleepers. The language 'at least some' and 'may reduce' correctly respects both the positive finding and the absence of certainty.
explanations.A: Too strong. The stimulus says the association was 'substantially weaker,' not absent. 'Eliminates' overclaims the effect.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Opposite direction. The data specifically show that short-sleeping exercisers do NOT report the same high rates as short-sleeping non-exercisers, directly contradicting this absolute claim.
explanations.D: Relative/absolute confusion and scope creep. The stimulus compares subgroups of short sleepers, not sleep versus exercise as independent variables across the full population. No such ranking of contributors is established.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported. The stimulus explicitly states that caffeine intake was not assessed, so no inference about caffeine's role can be drawn from these data.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus contains economic data with a counterintuitive finding about a specific industry subgroup. Trap answers include a too-strong absolute claim, a scope-creep answer that generalizes beyond the stated data, and a plausible-but-unsupported causal explanation. Test-takers must isolate the modest comparative inference the data actually license.
lr.stimulus: Data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics covering the period from 2010 to 2022 show that, in the United States, wages in the software development sector rose by an average of 34 percent in inflation-adjusted terms, while wages across all private-sector occupations rose by an average of 8 percent over the same period. Yet among software developers employed at firms with fewer than ten employees, inflation-adjusted wages rose by only 11 percent — barely above the all-sector average. Firms with more than 500 employees in the software sector accounted for the majority of the outsized wage growth. The data do not include freelance or contract workers.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Software developers at large firms earned more in absolute terms than software developers at small firms throughout the period from 2010 to 2022.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The overall wage growth in the software sector during this period was driven largely by wage increases at large firms rather than small ones.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Software developers who work as freelancers experienced wage growth comparable to that of developers at large firms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Employees at small software firms would have seen higher wage growth had they moved to larger firms during this period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The wage premium enjoyed by large-firm software developers reflects their superior technical skills compared to small-firm developers.

explanations.correct: The stimulus states that large firms (500+ employees) accounted for the majority of the outsized wage growth in the software sector, while small firms saw growth barely above the all-sector average. This directly and strongly supports the inference that the sector-wide figure was driven primarily by large-firm wage increases.
explanations.A: Relative/absolute confusion. The data describe rates of wage growth, not absolute wage levels. Nothing in the stimulus establishes which group earned more in absolute dollars at any point.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Plausible but unsupported. The stimulus explicitly excludes freelance and contract workers from the dataset, so no inference about their wages is warranted.
explanations.D: Scope creep and unsupported counterfactual. The data describe aggregate trends, not the outcomes that individual workers would have experienced by switching employers. No basis exists for this individual-level causal claim.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported. The stimulus offers no information about the skills or qualifications of developers at different firm sizes; attributing the differential to skill differences introduces an explanation the data do not address.

lr.difficultyReason: The environmental science stimulus presents data about a counterintuitive trend in a specific ecosystem, with a qualification that limits the scope of any inference. Trap answers include one that generalizes to all ecosystems (scope creep), one that inverts the finding, one that introduces an unsupported causal mechanism, and one using absolute language the data do not warrant.
lr.stimulus: Ecologists monitoring a temperate coastal wetland over a 15-year period documented a steady increase in overall plant species diversity, despite a concurrent rise in average water salinity attributed to reduced freshwater inflow. Closer analysis revealed that this diversity increase was confined almost entirely to a narrow transitional zone at the wetland's inland edge, where salt-tolerant species were colonizing areas previously dominated by a single freshwater sedge. In the wetland's central and seaward zones, species diversity either held steady or declined slightly over the same period. The ecologists noted that similar long-term salinity data were not available for comparable wetlands in the region.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rising salinity in coastal wetlands generally promotes plant species diversity by enabling salt-tolerant species to colonize new areas.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The freshwater sedge that previously dominated the transitional zone was probably less salt-tolerant than the species that replaced it.

choices.label: C
