choices.text: In the wetland studied, the overall increase in plant species diversity masked divergent trends in different zones of the wetland.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced freshwater inflow will ultimately eliminate plant diversity in the central and seaward zones of the wetland.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Salt-tolerant plant species are more resilient than freshwater species and will eventually dominate all zones of this wetland.

explanations.correct: The stimulus explicitly shows that the wetland's overall diversity increase was driven entirely by the transitional zone, while the central and seaward zones held steady or declined slightly. This directly supports the inference that the aggregate figure concealed divergent zone-level trends — an inference that follows cleanly from the data without overclaiming.
explanations.A: Scope creep. The data concern a single wetland over 15 years, and the ecologists explicitly note that comparable data from other wetlands are unavailable. Generalizing to 'coastal wetlands generally' goes well beyond what the evidence supports.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported. While this is a biologically reasonable hypothesis, the stimulus describes colonization patterns but never compares the salt tolerance of the displaced sedge to the colonizing species. This is an appealing worldly inference not grounded in the stated facts.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Too strong and opposite direction on certainty. The data show slight or stable trends in those zones, not a trajectory toward elimination. 'Will ultimately eliminate' introduces both a future projection and absolute language unsupported by the 15-year record.
explanations.E: Too strong. The stimulus describes colonization of one transitional zone, not a trend across all zones. 'Eventually dominate all zones' overclaims both the scope and the trajectory of the observed changes.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents mixed quantitative data with a key qualification about a subgroup. The correct answer respects those qualifications with hedged language. Traps include one absolute claim and one that drops the subgroup qualifier.
lr.stimulus: A clinical review of 4,200 patients treated for hypertension at regional hospitals found that patients who adhered to low-sodium diets reduced their systolic blood pressure by an average of 11 mmHg over six months. However, among patients who were also prescribed diuretics, dietary sodium reduction produced an average systolic reduction of only 3 mmHg — roughly one-quarter the effect seen in the broader group. Patients with chronic kidney disease were excluded from the analysis because their sodium metabolism differs markedly from that of the general hypertensive population.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Low-sodium diets are the most effective single intervention for reducing systolic blood pressure in hypertensive patients.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For at least some hypertensive patients taking diuretics, a low-sodium diet produces a smaller reduction in systolic blood pressure than it does for hypertensive patients not taking diuretics.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Diuretics cancel out all of the blood-pressure benefits of a low-sodium diet in hypertensive patients.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients with chronic kidney disease would show no improvement in blood pressure from a low-sodium diet.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hypertensive patients who are not prescribed diuretics should always adopt low-sodium diets before any other treatment is attempted.

explanations.correct: The data directly show that diuretic patients averaged only 3 mmHg reduction versus 11 mmHg for the broader group, so there are hypertensive patients on diuretics for whom the dietary effect is smaller. The hedged 'at least some' accurately captures this without overclaiming.
explanations.A: Too strong and unsupported — the stimulus makes no comparison between sodium restriction and other interventions.
explanations.B: Correct. The comparative data directly support this hedged inference.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'cancel out all' goes beyond the data, which show a diminished but still present effect (3 mmHg).
explanations.D: Opposite direction / unsupported — kidney disease patients were excluded precisely because their sodium metabolism differs; the stimulus does not say they would receive no benefit.
explanations.E: Too strong and normative — 'always' and 'before any other treatment' are not supported by the data.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus contains a counterintuitive economic finding with a temporal qualification. Traps exploit the tendency to generalize across all time periods or to invert the direction of the finding.
lr.stimulus: Data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics covering the period 1980–2022 show that in years when the national unemployment rate rose by more than two percentage points, consumer spending on live entertainment — concerts, theater, and sporting events — declined by an average of 8 percent. During the same years, however, consumer spending on home entertainment technology, including streaming subscriptions and gaming hardware, rose by an average of 14 percent. In years of stable or declining unemployment, no consistent pattern emerged between unemployment and either category of entertainment spending.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consumers always substitute home entertainment for live entertainment when economic conditions worsen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Live entertainment is a luxury good, while home entertainment technology is a necessity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: During periods of sharply rising unemployment, spending on home entertainment technology has tended to increase even as spending on live entertainment has declined.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rising unemployment causes consumers to spend less on all discretionary goods.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Home entertainment and live entertainment are always in direct economic competition with one another.

explanations.correct: The data establish that in years of sharp unemployment increases, live entertainment spending fell while home entertainment spending rose. The hedged 'has tended to' accurately reflects the pattern without overclaiming causation or universality.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'always' is not justified; the data cover specific conditions (unemployment rises >2 points), not all economic downturns.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported — the luxury/necessity economic classification is not derivable from these spending patterns alone.
explanations.C: Correct. Directly summarizes the documented pattern with appropriately hedged language.
explanations.D: Too strong and out of scope — the data don't address all discretionary goods, only two entertainment categories.
explanations.E: Too strong — 'always' and 'direct economic competition' go beyond what the data support; no consistent pattern was found in stable/declining unemployment years.

lr.difficultyReason: The environmental science stimulus presents multiple data points with a specific geographic qualifier. The correct answer draws a modest comparative inference; traps either drop the geographic qualifier or make an absolute causal claim.
lr.stimulus: Water quality monitoring conducted along three major river systems in the Pacific Northwest between 2010 and 2023 detected elevated concentrations of microplastic particles in reaches located downstream of urban centers, with median concentrations approximately six times higher than in upstream reaches of the same rivers. Agricultural reaches — those running primarily through farmland rather than urban areas — showed median microplastic concentrations intermediate between upstream and urban-downstream readings. Testing methodology was standardized across all sampling sites.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Urban centers are the sole source of microplastic contamination in Pacific Northwest river systems.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Microplastic concentrations in these rivers tend to be higher in reaches near urban centers than in reaches near agricultural areas.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reducing plastic use in urban areas would eliminate microplastic pollution in downstream river reaches.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Agricultural runoff contains no microplastic particles.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Microplastic concentrations in all rivers worldwide are higher downstream of urban areas than downstream of agricultural areas.

explanations.correct: The data establish that urban-downstream reaches had the highest median concentrations and agricultural reaches had intermediate concentrations, directly supporting the hedged comparative claim in B.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'sole source' is not supported; agricultural reaches also showed elevated concentrations.
explanations.B: Correct. Directly follows from the comparison of median concentrations between urban-downstream and agricultural reaches.
explanations.C: Too strong — the data don't address what elimination of plastic use would achieve, nor do they identify reduction as sufficient.
explanations.D: Contradicted by the data — agricultural reaches had intermediate (elevated) concentrations, implying some microplastic presence.
explanations.E: Scope creep — the data cover three Pacific Northwest rivers only; extending the claim to 'all rivers worldwide' is unsupported.

lr.difficultyReason: The linguistics stimulus presents a specific observational finding with a clear exception. Traps include overgeneralizing to all languages and inverting the directionality.
lr.stimulus: Linguists studying phoneme acquisition in bilingual children aged two to four found that children exposed to two languages from birth reached phonemic milestones — the ability to consistently distinguish and produce the distinct sounds of each language — at roughly the same age as monolingual peers for each individual language, though they showed greater variability in milestone timing. Children who began regular exposure to a second language after age two, however, showed consistent delays of three to five months in producing phonemes unique to the second language, delays not observed for their first language.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following inferences is most supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bilingual children are generally slower to develop language skills than monolingual children.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The age at which a child first receives regular exposure to a language can affect how quickly that child acquires phonemes specific to that language.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Children who learn two languages from birth will eventually outperform monolingual children on all phonemic tasks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Delays in phoneme acquisition for a second language necessarily indicate a broader cognitive deficit.

choices.label: E
choices.text: After age two, no child can fully acquire the phonemic system of a second language.

explanations.correct: The contrast between from-birth bilinguals (no delays) and late-exposure bilinguals (3–5 month delays in the second language's unique phonemes) directly supports the inference that timing of exposure influences phoneme acquisition speed.
explanations.A: Opposite direction — the data show from-birth bilinguals reach milestones at roughly the same age as monolinguals for each language; this answer misrepresents the finding.
explanations.B: Correct. The observed delay in late-exposure children but not in from-birth bilinguals strongly supports this modest causal inference.
explanations.C: Too strong and unsupported — the data show similar milestone timing, not eventual superiority.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported — the stimulus provides no information about broader cognitive deficits.
explanations.E: Too strong — 'no child can fully acquire' is an absolute claim not supported by data that show delays, not permanent incapacity.

lr.difficultyReason: The policy stimulus contains two findings that are in mild tension; the correct answer draws a modest, qualified inference that respects both findings. Traps exploit the tension by treating one finding as absolute.
lr.stimulus: A statewide evaluation of mandatory minimum sentencing laws found that counties that adopted such laws saw a 12 percent average reduction in the targeted offense categories during the first two years of implementation. Over a ten-year period, however, the same counties showed no statistically significant difference in those offense rates compared with counties that had not adopted mandatory minimums. Jurisdictions that paired mandatory minimums with funded rehabilitation programs showed sustained reductions — averaging 9 percent — over the full ten-year period.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mandatory minimum sentencing laws, on their own, may not produce lasting reductions in targeted offense rates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mandatory minimum sentencing laws always increase public safety in the short term.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rehabilitation programs alone are sufficient to reduce crime rates in any jurisdiction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Counties that did not adopt mandatory minimums experienced rising offense rates over the ten-year period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The short-term reduction in offense rates caused by mandatory minimums is entirely due to incapacitation of offenders.

explanations.correct: The ten-year data show no significant difference between mandatory-minimum and non-mandatory-minimum counties, while paired programs did produce sustained results. This supports the inference that mandatory minimums alone may not sustain reductions — a properly hedged claim.
explanations.A: Correct. The ten-year convergence in offense rates directly supports this modest, hedged conclusion.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'always' overstates the finding; the 12% reduction is an average, not a universal outcome.
explanations.C: Too strong and out of scope — the data address paired programs, not rehabilitation programs alone; 'any jurisdiction' is unsupported.
explanations.D: Unsupported — 'no statistically significant difference' doesn't tell us that comparison counties saw rising rates; they may have been stable.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported — the mechanism behind the short-term reduction is not addressed in the data.

lr.difficultyReason: The technology stimulus presents a specific engineering finding with a narrow domain qualifier. The correct answer draws a hedged comparative inference; traps either widen the domain or reverse the direction of the finding.
lr.stimulus: Engineers testing lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) and nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) battery cells under simulated rapid-charging conditions found that LFP cells retained approximately 91 percent of their original capacity after 2,000 charge cycles, while NMC cells retained approximately 74 percent under the same conditions. Both cell types performed comparably — within two percentage points — in tests involving standard overnight charging. The tests were conducted at a uniform temperature of 25°C; performance at higher temperatures was not evaluated.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: LFP batteries last longer than NMC batteries under all real-world usage conditions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Under rapid-charging conditions, LFP cells tend to degrade more slowly than NMC cells.

choices.label: C
choices.text: NMC batteries are inferior to LFP batteries for all commercial applications.

choices.label: D
choices.text: At elevated temperatures, LFP cells retain more capacity than NMC cells after 2,000 rapid-charge cycles.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Standard overnight charging destroys battery capacity more quickly than rapid charging in both LFP and NMC cells.

explanations.correct: The rapid-charging test data directly show LFP retained 91% versus NMC's 74% after 2,000 cycles, supporting the hedged claim that LFP degrades more slowly under those conditions.
explanations.A: Too strong and scope creep — 'all real-world usage conditions' is unsupported; standard charging showed comparable performance.
explanations.B: Correct. Directly supported by the rapid-charging cycle data with appropriately hedged language.
explanations.C: Too strong — the data don't address all commercial applications, and standard charging performance was comparable.
explanations.D: Unsupported — the stimulus explicitly states elevated temperature performance was not evaluated.
explanations.E: Opposite direction — the data don't compare overnight vs. rapid charging degradation rates; overnight charging showed comparable performance, not faster degradation.

lr.difficultyReason: The history stimulus involves a documented correlation with a temporal scope limitation. The correct answer is a modest hedged inference; traps either extend the scope or posit unsupported causal mechanisms.
lr.stimulus: Records from Mediterranean port cities during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries show that periods of prolonged drought in the North African interior, lasting three or more consecutive years, were followed within five years by measurable increases in the volume of grain shipped into those port cities from Iberian and Italian sources. Shorter droughts — lasting one to two years — show no consistent correlation with shifts in grain import volumes. Shipping records from Northern European ports during the same period do not display the same pattern.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Prolonged drought in North Africa during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries sometimes coincided with increased grain imports to Mediterranean port cities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Short droughts in North Africa had no effect on agricultural output during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mediterranean port cities depended entirely on North African grain supplies during drought years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The same relationship between North African drought and grain trade patterns held throughout all European port cities in this period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Northern European grain merchants were unaffected by Mediterranean climate conditions during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

explanations.correct: The records establish a documented correlation between prolonged droughts (3+ years) and increased grain imports to Mediterranean ports within five years — supporting the hedged 'sometimes coincided' formulation, which accurately reflects the pattern without asserting causation.
explanations.A: Correct. 'Sometimes' and 'coincided' are appropriately hedged; the data directly document the correlation.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported — the data show no consistent correlation with import volumes, but this doesn't mean short droughts had no effect on agricultural output; those are different measures.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'entirely' is unsupported; the data show increased imports, not total dependence.
explanations.D: Scope creep and opposite direction — the stimulus explicitly states Northern European ports did not show the same pattern.
explanations.E: Too strong and plausible-but-unsupported — 'unaffected' is an absolute claim; the data only address grain import volume patterns, not all possible effects.

lr.difficultyReason: The ethics/policy stimulus presents survey data on moral reasoning with a specific demographic qualifier. Traps exploit either the demographic qualifier or the direction of the finding.
lr.stimulus: A survey of 1,800 adults asked respondents to evaluate the moral acceptability of five types of deception — ranging from white lies to fraud — in professional contexts. Among respondents who identified as having frequent direct client contact in their work, approximately 68 percent rated at least one form of deception as morally acceptable in certain professional circumstances. Among respondents in administrative roles with minimal client contact, that figure was 41 percent. The survey did not control for respondents' professional field.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following inferences is most supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: People who interact directly with clients are more likely to regard at least some professional deception as morally acceptable than are people in administrative roles.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Client-facing professionals are more likely to engage in deceptive behavior than administrative workers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most adults believe that all forms of deception are morally unacceptable in professional contexts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Professional field is the primary determinant of attitudes toward deception in the workplace.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Administrative employees universally oppose deception, while client-facing employees universally accept it.

explanations.correct: The data directly show 68% of client-contact respondents vs. 41% of administrative respondents rated at least one form of deception as acceptable — a straightforward comparative inference with no overclaiming.
explanations.A: Correct. Directly reflects the percentage comparison between the two groups, hedged by 'more likely.'
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported — the survey measures attitudes, not actual behavior; inferring behavior from reported moral attitudes is not warranted by the data.
explanations.C: Opposite direction — the data show majorities or large minorities of both groups accepting some deception, contradicting this claim.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported — the survey explicitly did not control for professional field, so this causal primacy claim cannot be derived.
explanations.E: Too strong — 'universally' is contradicted by the data (32% of client-facing and 59% of administrative respondents did not rate any deception as acceptable).

lr.difficultyReason: The arts stimulus presents critical reception data with a period qualification. Traps include absolute claims about artistic quality and a scope-creep error extending findings beyond the stated period.
lr.stimulus: An analysis of critical reviews published in major English-language periodicals between 1950 and 1975 found that works by composers who had trained under the serialist tradition received substantially fewer favorable reviews — averaging 2.1 favorable per composer per decade — than works by composers associated with neo-Romantic styles, who averaged 5.8 favorable reviews per composer per decade. After 1975, the gap in favorable review rates between the two groups narrowed considerably, with serialist composers averaging 4.3 and neo-Romantic composers averaging 5.1 favorable reviews per composer per decade.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Between 1950 and 1975, serialist composers tended to receive less favorable critical attention in major English-language periodicals than neo-Romantic composers did.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Serialist music is objectively less artistically meritorious than neo-Romantic music.

choices.label: C
choices.text: After 1975, critical reception of serialist music exceeded that of neo-Romantic music in major English-language periodicals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Critical opinion of serialist music has always been negative in English-language publications.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The same pattern of critical reception holds for non-English-language periodicals during both periods.

explanations.correct: The data directly support a comparative claim about favorable review rates during the 1950–1975 period, and 'tended to receive' hedges appropriately against treating averages as universal rules.
explanations.A: Correct. Directly summarizes the pre-1975 comparison (2.1 vs. 5.8 favorable reviews per decade) with hedged language.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported — critical reception data measure reviewer preferences, not objective artistic merit; the link between the two is not established.
explanations.C: Opposite direction — after 1975, neo-Romantic composers still averaged more favorable reviews (5.1) than serialist composers (4.3); the gap narrowed but did not reverse.
explanations.D: Too strong — 'always been negative' is not supported; after 1975 serialists averaged 4.3 favorable reviews per decade, which is not a negative reception.
explanations.E: Scope creep — the analysis covered only major English-language periodicals; extending to non-English publications is unsupported.

lr.difficultyReason: The environmental science/economics stimulus presents data with a counterintuitive finding about a specific regulatory mechanism. Traps include an absolute causal claim, a scope error, and a reversal of the finding's direction.
lr.stimulus: An economic analysis of cap-and-trade programs implemented in twelve jurisdictions between 1995 and 2020 found that industries covered by these programs reduced their emissions by an average of 19 percent over ten years. Industries in the same jurisdictions that were exempt from cap-and-trade but subject to flat-rate emissions taxes reduced their emissions by an average of 11 percent over the same period. However, in three of the twelve jurisdictions — those where permit prices fell below a threshold of $15 per ton — covered industries showed no statistically significant emissions reduction.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cap-and-trade programs are, in at least some jurisdictions, associated with greater emissions reductions than flat-rate emissions taxes over a ten-year period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flat-rate emissions taxes always produce smaller emissions reductions than cap-and-trade programs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cap-and-trade programs universally reduce emissions regardless of permit price levels.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the three jurisdictions where permit prices fell below $15 per ton, flat-rate taxes also failed to reduce emissions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Emissions taxes produce greater reductions than cap-and-trade programs when permit prices are low.

explanations.correct: Across the twelve jurisdictions overall, cap-and-trade averaged 19% versus 11% for flat-rate taxes. 'In at least some jurisdictions' and 'associated with' correctly hedge the claim to avoid overstating causation or universality.
explanations.A: Correct. The 19% vs. 11% average difference supports this hedged comparative claim without overclaiming universality (which would be undercut by the three low-permit-price exceptions).
explanations.B: Too strong — 'always' is directly undermined by the three jurisdictions where cap-and-trade showed no significant effect; in those cases, the flat-rate tax may have outperformed.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'universally' and 'regardless of permit price' is directly contradicted by the three low-price jurisdictions showing no significant reduction.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported — the data do not address flat-rate tax performance specifically in the three low-permit-price jurisdictions.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported — the data indicate cap-and-trade underperformed in low-permit-price jurisdictions, but no comparison to flat-rate tax performance in those specific jurisdictions is provided.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents a mix of quantitative data and a notable subgroup exception. The correct answer makes a hedged comparative inference that respects the qualification. Trap answers either drop the qualifier (too strong), reverse the direction, or introduce plausible but unsupported worldly claims about the exception subgroup.
lr.stimulus: A survey of 2,400 urban households found that those with at least one member who commutes by bicycle report lower annual transportation costs, on average, than households in which all members commute by car. However, among households with annual incomes below $30,000, the pattern reverses: bicycle-commuting households in this income bracket report transportation costs roughly equal to, or in some cases higher than, those of car-commuting households in the same bracket. The survey also found that bicycle-commuting households at all income levels report purchasing more health and fitness products annually than car-commuting households at comparable income levels.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bicycle commuting reduces transportation costs for all households regardless of income level.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The transportation cost savings associated with bicycle commuting do not apply equally across all income groups.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low-income households would be better served financially by switching from bicycle commuting to car commuting.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spending on health and fitness products is the primary reason bicycle-commuting households have higher overall expenses than car-commuting households.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urban households that commute by bicycle tend to have higher incomes than those that commute by car.

explanations.correct: The survey shows that, overall, bicycle commuters have lower transportation costs than car commuters, but this advantage disappears or reverses in the lowest income bracket. This directly and strongly supports the hedged claim that the cost savings associated with bicycle commuting do not apply equally across all income groups — a modest, well-anchored inference that respects both the general trend and the exception.
explanations.A: Too strong. This is the dominant trap. The stimulus explicitly states that the cost advantage reverses among households earning below $30,000, which contradicts the claim that bicycle commuting reduces transportation costs 'for all households regardless of income level.'
explanations.B: Correct. The general finding (lower costs for bicycle commuters) combined with the exception at lower incomes directly supports the claim that the savings are not uniform across income groups. The hedged, comparative phrasing matches what the data actually show.
explanations.C: Opposite direction / unsupported. The stimulus reports that low-income bicycle-commuting households have costs roughly equal to or higher than low-income car-commuting households, but it does not establish that switching to car commuting would reduce their costs — costs could simply be comparable. This overreads the data and implies a prescriptive conclusion the stimulus does not support.
explanations.D: Scope creep and mis-scoped. The stimulus says bicycle-commuting households spend more on health and fitness products, but it never identifies this as the 'primary reason' for any cost difference, nor does it establish that bicycle-commuting households have higher overall expenses across the board.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported. While the data could be consistent with this, the stimulus makes no direct comparison of income levels between bicycle- and car-commuting households. The survey reports cost patterns within income brackets, not the income distribution of commuting choices.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus blends quantitative data with a qualifying exception (urban versus rural patients). The correct answer respects both the general trend and the exception. Traps include one too-strong answer that drops the qualifier, one that inverts the direction, and one plausible-but-unsupported claim about treatment access.
lr.stimulus: A county health department reviewed hospital admission records for patients diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes over a five-year period. Among patients living in urban areas, roughly 60 percent had received a formal nutritional counseling session within the twelve months preceding diagnosis. Among patients living in rural areas, fewer than 20 percent had received such counseling in the same window. Across both groups, patients who had received counseling were, on average, diagnosed at an earlier stage of the disease than those who had not. The department also noted that rural hospitals in the county had, on average, half as many registered dietitians on staff per one hundred beds as urban hospitals.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nutritional counseling prevents the onset of Type 2 diabetes in patients who would otherwise develop the condition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rural patients in the county had less access to nutritional counseling services than urban patients did.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increasing the number of dietitians at rural hospitals would eliminate the disparity in diabetes outcomes between rural and urban patients.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Urban patients who did not receive nutritional counseling were diagnosed at a later stage of diabetes than rural patients who did receive it.
choices.text2: Urban patients who did not receive nutritional counseling were diagnosed at a later stage of diabetes than rural patients who did receive it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Among patients in the county, receiving nutritional counseling is the most important factor in achieving an early diabetes diagnosis.

explanations.correct: The stimulus states that fewer than 20% of rural patients received counseling versus roughly 60% of urban patients, and that rural hospitals have half as many dietitians per bed. Together these facts strongly support the claim that rural patients had less access to such services — a hedged, comparative inference grounded directly in the data.
explanations.A: Too strong and out-of-scope: the stimulus shows a correlation between counseling and earlier-stage diagnosis, not that counseling prevents onset. This commits the opposite-direction trap by implying prevention rather than detection timing.
explanations.B: Correct. Both the lower counseling rate and the lower dietitian staffing ratio in rural areas directly support this comparative, hedged claim.
explanations.C: Too strong: the stimulus provides no basis for concluding that adding dietitians would 'eliminate' the disparity. This is a scope-creep and absolute-language trap.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus gives group-level averages for counseled versus non-counseled patients across both groups combined; it does not provide a cross-group comparison of urban non-counseled patients versus rural counseled patients.
explanations.E: Too strong: 'most important factor' introduces a ranking that the stimulus never establishes. This is an extreme-language trap.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents economic data with a controlled twist: a general trend (rising automation correlates with lower wages for low-skill work) coexists with an exception (one sector where automation correlates with higher wages). The correct answer draws a hedged inference from the exception. Traps include an inversion of the general trend, an absolute overclaim, and a plausible-but-unstated policy conclusion.
lr.stimulus: An analysis of manufacturing employment data from thirty-two countries between 2005 and 2020 found that in twenty-six of those countries, the introduction of automated assembly systems correlated with a decline in average hourly wages for workers classified as low-skill. In five countries, no statistically significant wage change was observed. In one country — a small economy with a highly specialized electronics sector — automation correlated with a substantial increase in average hourly wages for low-skill workers, a pattern researchers attributed to a concurrent sharp reduction in the available labor pool caused by demographic contraction.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In most of the countries studied, the introduction of automated assembly systems was associated with lower average hourly wages for low-skill manufacturing workers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Automation of manufacturing processes invariably reduces wages for low-skill workers unless the labor supply simultaneously contracts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Countries that introduce automated assembly systems should expect low-skill wages to decline within five years.
choices.text2: Countries that introduce automated assembly systems should expect low-skill wages to decline within five years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The negative effect of automation on low-skill wages is stronger in large economies than in small, specialized ones.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Demographic contraction is the primary driver of wage growth in low-skill manufacturing sectors across the countries studied.

explanations.correct: Twenty-six of thirty-two countries showed a correlation between automation and declining low-skill wages. 'Most' accurately captures 26/32 (over 80%), and 'associated with' is appropriately hedged — no causal claim is made. This is a direct, proportional inference from the data.
explanations.A: Correct. 26 out of 32 countries clearly constitutes 'most,' and the language mirrors the correlational framing of the stimulus.
explanations.B: Too strong: 'invariably' is an absolute claim. The stimulus shows five countries with no significant change, meaning wage decline is not invariable even setting aside the exceptional case. This is an extreme-language trap.
explanations.C: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus provides historical correlations but does not support a forward-looking prescriptive prediction with a specific timeline. This is a scope-creep trap.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus describes only one small-economy outlier and attributes the anomaly to labor-pool contraction, not to size per se. No systematic comparison by economy size is offered.
explanations.E: Too strong and mis-scoped: the stimulus mentions demographic contraction only in connection with one country's exceptional outcome; it says nothing about demographic contraction as a driver across the broader sample.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents linguistic fieldwork data with a qualification about language contact. The correct answer draws a modest inference about a subgroup. Traps include one too-strong universal claim, one inversion, one that introduces unsupported causal direction, and one plausible-but-unstated generalization about language endangerment.
lr.stimulus: Fieldwork conducted among speakers of seventeen endangered languages in the Pacific region documented the phonological features of each language as spoken by its oldest surviving fluent speakers (those aged 65 and above) and by its youngest fluent speakers (those aged 18 to 30). In eleven of the seventeen languages, the youngest speakers used a reduced consonant inventory compared with the oldest speakers — a pattern the researchers attributed to prolonged contact with a regional trade language that itself has a relatively sparse consonant inventory. In the six remaining languages, no significant difference in consonant inventory was observed between age groups, and none of those six languages had experienced sustained contact with the trade language.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Contact with a language that has a sparse consonant inventory will eventually cause any endangered language to lose consonant distinctions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Among the endangered languages studied, those that had sustained contact with the regional trade language were more likely to show a reduction in consonant inventory across generations than those that had not.
choices.text2: Among the endangered languages studied, those that had sustained contact with the regional trade language were more likely to show a reduction in consonant inventory across generations than those that had not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Younger speakers of endangered languages are generally less proficient in those languages than older speakers are.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The regional trade language expanded its consonant inventory as a result of contact with the endangered languages in the study.
choices.text2: The regional trade language expanded its consonant inventory as a result of contact with the endangered languages in the study.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A language's consonant inventory is the phonological feature most susceptible to change under conditions of language contact.

explanations.correct: All eleven languages that showed consonant reduction had trade-language contact; none of the six languages without such contact showed reduction. This perfectly aligns the contact condition with the outcome, strongly supporting a comparative claim about likelihood within the study sample. The answer is appropriately scoped to 'the endangered languages studied' and uses hedged comparative language ('more likely').
explanations.A: Too strong: 'will eventually cause any endangered language' is a universal, predictive absolute. The stimulus shows a correlation in a specific sample and cannot sustain that sweeping claim. This is an extreme-language trap.
explanations.B: Correct. The data show 11/11 contact languages with reduction and 0/6 non-contact languages with reduction, directly supporting this hedged comparative inference scoped to the study.
explanations.C: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus documents differences in consonant inventory, not overall proficiency levels. This introduces a concept — proficiency — absent from the stimulus, making it a plausible-but-unsupported trap.
explanations.D: Opposite direction: the stimulus describes influence flowing from the trade language to the endangered languages (reduced consonant inventory in the latter), not the reverse. This is a classic inversion trap.
explanations.E: Too strong and unsupported: the stimulus examines only consonant inventory and offers no comparison to other phonological features. Claiming it is the 'most susceptible' feature goes far beyond what the data establish. This is an absolute-ranking trap.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents a mix of quantitative findings and a qualifying subgroup exception. The correct answer respects both the main trend and the qualification. Trap answers either drop the qualification (too strong) or over-apply the subgroup finding to the whole population (scope creep).
lr.stimulus: A five-year study tracking 4,200 adults who regularly consumed fermented dairy products found that approximately 60 percent showed measurably lower markers of systemic inflammation compared to adults who consumed no fermented dairy. However, among participants who had previously been diagnosed with a specific autoimmune condition, those who consumed fermented dairy showed no significant difference in inflammation markers relative to those who did not. The study did not measure participants' overall diet quality or exercise frequency.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consuming fermented dairy products reduces systemic inflammation in all adults who do not have autoimmune conditions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For at least some adults, regular consumption of fermented dairy products is associated with lower levels of systemic inflammation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Diet quality and exercise frequency are the primary factors determining systemic inflammation levels in adults.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adults with autoimmune conditions experience higher baseline levels of systemic inflammation than other adults.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fermented dairy products are more effective at reducing inflammation than any other dietary intervention.

explanations.correct: The study found that roughly 60 percent of regular consumers of fermented dairy showed lower inflammation markers, which directly and strongly supports a hedged claim that for at least some adults, consumption is associated with lower inflammation. This respects the observational (correlational) nature of the data without overclaiming causation or universality.
explanations.A: Too strong — the stimulus establishes a majority finding among a study sample, not a universal rule. It also does not isolate autoimmune status as the only moderating variable, and the phrase 'all adults who do not have autoimmune conditions' goes far beyond what the data establish.
explanations.B: Correct. The 60 percent figure provides strong inductive support for the hedged claim that at least some adults show the association.
explanations.C: Plausible but unsupported — the stimulus explicitly notes that diet quality and exercise were not measured, so no conclusion about their relative importance can be drawn from these data.
explanations.D: Opposite/scope creep — the study compared inflammation within each group (consumers vs. non-consumers), not between the autoimmune group and the general population. No baseline comparison across groups is reported.
explanations.E: Too strong and out of scope — the study makes no comparison to other dietary interventions whatsoever.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus contains an economic trend alongside a counterintuitive exception for a specific sector. The correct answer draws a modest comparative inference. Traps include an absolute over-claim, a reversal of the direction of support, and a plausible economic truism not grounded in the stimulus.
lr.stimulus: Data from a regional commerce bureau show that during the three years following a significant rise in interest rates, the number of new small-business registrations in the region declined by 22 percent. During the same period, new registrations in the home-repair and renovation sector increased by 14 percent. The bureau's report notes that many homeowners in the region chose not to sell their homes during the period of high rates, electing instead to invest in renovations.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rising interest rates invariably cause a decline in new small-business registrations across all economic sectors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The home-repair and renovation sector is unaffected by changes in interest rates.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Not all small-business sectors responded in the same way to the rise in interest rates in this region.

choices.label: D
choices.text: High interest rates ultimately benefit regional economies by redirecting consumer spending toward home improvement.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Homeowners who renovate rather than sell their homes generate more regional economic activity than homeowners who sell.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes two divergent sector-level outcomes during the same period: overall small-business registrations fell 22 percent while home-repair registrations rose 14 percent. This directly and strongly supports the claim that not all sectors responded identically — a straightforward comparative inference that does not require any step beyond the data.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'invariably' and 'all economic sectors' overreach. The data cover one region over one period, and the home-repair exception is explicitly presented in the stimulus.
explanations.B: Too strong and opposite in spirit — the sector did respond to higher rates (positively, via homeowner behavior), meaning it was not unaffected. The stimulus provides a causal mechanism linking rate changes to renovation activity.
explanations.C: Correct. The overall decline versus the sector-specific increase directly supports this modest comparative claim.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported — the stimulus does not evaluate net regional economic benefit or compare the value of renovation spending to other forms of economic activity.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the stimulus provides no data comparing economic activity generated by renovating homeowners versus selling homeowners.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents linguistic fieldwork data with a qualification about data collection conditions. The correct answer requires integrating the main finding with the qualifier. Distractors include an absolute over-claim, a plausible-but-unsupported linguistic generalization, and a mis-scoped inference that extends the finding beyond the study's population.
lr.stimulus: Linguists conducting fieldwork among speakers of an endangered language in a mountainous region of Central Asia documented that speakers under the age of 35 used the language's traditional tonal distinctions inconsistently in casual conversation, while speakers over the age of 60 maintained those distinctions consistently. Speakers between the ages of 35 and 60 showed intermediate patterns. The fieldwork was conducted exclusively in village settings; no data were collected from speakers who had migrated to urban areas.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In at least some endangered languages, younger village-dwelling speakers tend to preserve tonal distinctions less consistently than older speakers do.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tonal distinctions in endangered languages are always better preserved among rural populations than among urban populations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tonal distinctions of this language will be entirely absent from the speech of the next generation of speakers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Urban migrants from this language community have abandoned tonal distinctions more thoroughly than village-dwelling speakers have.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Languages with tonal distinctions are more vulnerable to extinction than languages without such distinctions.

explanations.correct: The fieldwork data directly show that younger village-dwelling speakers used tonal distinctions inconsistently while older speakers maintained them consistently. The hedged phrasing 'in at least some endangered languages' and 'tend to' respects both the single-language scope of the study and the observational (rather than absolute) nature of the finding. This is the most defensible inference from the data.
explanations.A: Correct. The hedge 'at least some' limits the claim to what the one documented case licenses, and 'tend to' matches the probabilistic nature of the consistency data.
explanations.B: Too strong and out of scope — the study explicitly collected no data from urban speakers, so no rural-versus-urban comparison can be made. 'Always' is an extreme claim unsupported by data from a single language community.
explanations.C: Too strong — the data show inconsistent use, not complete absence, among younger speakers. Projecting total disappearance in the next generation goes well beyond what inconsistency patterns license.
explanations.D: Opposite/unsupported — the stimulus explicitly states no data were collected from urban migrants, so any claim about their speech patterns relative to village speakers is entirely unsupported.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported — the stimulus provides no comparative data about extinction rates of tonal versus non-tonal languages; it documents patterns within a single language.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus blends quantitative data with a specific subgroup qualification. The correct answer requires tracking a comparative claim (urban vs. rural) while respecting hedged language. Trap answers either drop the hedges, invert the comparison, or apply the subgroup finding to the general population.
lr.stimulus: A survey of nearly 4,000 adults conducted by the National Institute of Environmental Health tracked participants' reported daily sodium intake and blood pressure readings over five years. Among participants who resided in rural areas, those whose daily sodium intake exceeded 3,500 milligrams showed markedly higher rates of hypertension than rural participants with lower sodium intake — a pattern that held even after adjusting for age and body mass index. Among urban participants, however, the association between high sodium intake and hypertension was substantially weaker and, in several age brackets, statistically negligible. Researchers noted that rural participants were, on average, significantly less likely than urban participants to consume potassium-rich foods, and dietary potassium is known to blunt the blood-pressure-raising effects of sodium.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High sodium intake causes hypertension in rural adults but has no effect on the blood pressure of urban adults.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reducing sodium intake is the most effective dietary intervention for lowering blood pressure in any population.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Differences in potassium consumption may help explain why high sodium intake is more strongly associated with hypertension among rural adults than among urban adults.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Urban adults who consume high levels of sodium are at no greater risk of hypertension than urban adults with low sodium intake.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dietary potassium eliminates the risk of hypertension in adults who consume more than 3,500 milligrams of sodium per day.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes two facts that together support this inference: (1) the sodium–hypertension link is stronger in rural adults than in urban adults, and (2) rural adults consume significantly less potassium, and potassium is known to blunt sodium's blood-pressure effects. Combining these facts, the potassium gap is a plausible—and well-supported—partial explanation for the rural–urban difference. The hedged language ('may help explain') correctly reflects that this is a supported inference, not a proven cause.
explanations.A: Too strong and opposite-direction on the second half. The stimulus says the urban association is 'substantially weaker' and 'negligible' in several brackets—not that sodium has 'no effect' on urban adults. The word 'no effect' converts a hedged comparison into an absolute, which the stimulus does not support. Also, 'causes' overstates a correlation.
explanations.B: Out of scope and too strong. The stimulus says nothing about comparing sodium reduction to other dietary interventions (e.g., increasing potassium, reducing saturated fat). This is a plausible worldly belief but is not derivable from the stimulus.
explanations.D: Too strong. The stimulus says the sodium–hypertension association is 'statistically negligible' in 'several age brackets' among urban adults—not across all urban adults or at all sodium levels. Claiming 'no greater risk' for all urban adults drops the qualification and overclaims.
explanations.E: Too strong and scope creep. The stimulus says potassium 'blunts' sodium's blood-pressure-raising effects—not that it 'eliminates' the risk. Replacing 'blunts' with 'eliminates' converts a partial mitigation into a complete one, which the evidence does not support.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Requires chaining three facts (antibody prevalence, post-exposure infection rate, severity finding) and recognizing a tension between high exposure and mild outcomes to support a hedged claim about protective factors. Trap (B) overreaches from 'some' to 'most'; trap (D) points opposite to what the severity data imply.
lr.stimulus: In a community where a newly identified respiratory virus circulated last winter, serological testing later revealed that more than 70 percent of adult residents had been exposed to the virus at some point during the season. Yet the local clinic recorded confirmed symptomatic infections in only about a quarter of the adult population. Of the symptomatic cases that were recorded, those in residents who had received the previous season's standard influenza vaccine were, on average, markedly milder than those in unvaccinated residents, even though the new virus is not closely related to any influenza strain.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At least some adult residents exposed to the new virus had some immune response that either prevented symptomatic infection or reduced its severity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most adult residents of the community who were exposed to the new virus experienced no symptoms at all.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The previous season's influenza vaccine confers specific immunity against the newly identified respiratory virus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Residents who received the previous season's influenza vaccine were more likely to become symptomatically infected with the new virus than unvaccinated residents were.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The newly identified respiratory virus is less dangerous than the influenza strains targeted by the previous season's vaccine.

explanations.correct: Three facts combine: exposure was widespread (over 70%), symptomatic infection was far less common (about a quarter), and among those who were symptomatic, prior flu-vaccine recipients had milder illness. Together they support the hedged claim that at least some exposed residents had an immune response that either blocked symptoms or dampened them. 'At least some' and 'either...or' match what the data can carry.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong and slightly off-scope — the stimulus gives community-wide exposure and symptomatic rates but not the specific fraction of exposed residents who were asymptomatic; 'most' is not warranted, and the stimulus speaks to recorded symptomatic cases, not a clean asymptomatic tally.
explanations.C: Too strong — milder severity in vaccinated residents is consistent with nonspecific immune effects; 'confers specific immunity' overreaches.
explanations.D: Opposite direction — the severity finding suggests vaccinated residents fared better, not worse.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported — no comparison of the new virus's overall danger to influenza strains is given.

lr.difficultyReason: Must integrate three qualifications — effort-level reporting, confidence ratings, and the subgroup reversal — to support a hedged claim about the relationship between overconfidence and actual performance. Trap (C) treats a comparative as absolute; trap (E) drops the effort qualification.
lr.stimulus: In a large study of undergraduates preparing for standardized exams, students who reported studying fewer than ten hours per week rated themselves, on average, more confident about their readiness than students who reported studying twenty or more hours per week. On the exam itself, the high-study group outperformed the low-study group by a substantial margin. However, within the low-study group, those students who had rated themselves least confident scored about as well as the average student in the high-study group.
lr.questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Among students who study relatively little, those who are less confident about their readiness tend to perform better on the exam than their more confident peers in the same study-hours group.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Confidence about readiness is a more reliable predictor of exam performance than reported study hours are.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any student who studies twenty or more hours per week will score higher on the exam than any student who studies fewer than ten.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Students tend to overestimate how much time they actually spend studying for standardized exams.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Students who rate themselves least confident about their readiness will score about as well as students who study twice as many hours.

explanations.correct: Within the low-study group, the least-confident subset matched the average of the high-study group, while the low-study group on the whole trailed the high-study group. That subgroup reversal supports the hedged claim that, within the low-study group, lower confidence tracks with stronger performance. 'Tend to' respects the averaging in the data.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — the stimulus gives no direct comparison of predictive reliability across the two variables.
explanations.C: Absolute claim from comparative data — the stimulus reports group averages, not per-individual guarantees.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the stimulus uses reported study hours and does not address their accuracy.
explanations.E: Drops the crucial qualifier that the match holds for the least-confident students within the low-study group; the inference would be stronger and misapplied as stated.

lr.difficultyReason: Requires chaining the rainfall datum, the staple-crop yield, and the household-garden finding to support a hedged inference about crop mix. Trap (B) is the plausible-but-unsupported worldly truth; trap (D) inverts the direction by treating the overall decline as uniform.
lr.stimulus: Data from agricultural monitoring stations in the semi-arid province of Marenda show that the past decade has been, on average, the driest of any decade since record-keeping began. Overall yields of the province's main staple crop, sorghum, have declined by roughly 15 percent relative to the previous decade. However, yields from small household gardens in the same region, in which farmers typically plant a mix of drought-tolerant vegetables alongside smaller amounts of sorghum, have held roughly steady over the same period.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some agricultural plots in Marenda have been less affected by the decade's drier conditions than the province's overall sorghum yield would suggest.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Household gardens are generally more productive per unit of land than commercial sorghum fields.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If commercial farms in Marenda shifted entirely away from sorghum to drought-tolerant vegetables, their yields would rise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All sorghum plots in Marenda have shown comparable declines in yield over the past decade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rainfall is the only agricultural factor that has changed in Marenda over the past decade.

explanations.correct: Overall sorghum yields fell by about 15 percent as conditions grew drier, yet household gardens — which mix drought-tolerant vegetables with smaller amounts of sorghum — held steady. That supports the hedged claim that some plots have been less affected than the headline sorghum figure suggests. The inference chains three facts without overreaching.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported — productivity per unit of land isn't established; the stimulus compares yield changes, not absolute productivity.
explanations.C: Too strong — a full shift of commercial farms is a policy prediction the stimulus does not support.
explanations.D: Opposite direction — the household-garden finding shows not all plots declined uniformly.
explanations.E: Too strong — the stimulus notes dry conditions but does not rule out other changes.

lr.difficultyReason: Must chain the settlement statistic, the docket-composition datum, and the contingency-fee observation, recognizing the tension between case mix and outcome mix, to support a hedged claim about plaintiff representation. Trap (A) overreaches to 'more skilled'; trap (C) mis-scopes the plaintiff-defendant comparison.
lr.stimulus: A recent review of civil cases filed in the Hargreave County trial court found that cases in which the plaintiff was represented by an attorney settled before trial roughly twice as often as cases in which the plaintiff appeared without counsel. The review also found that represented plaintiffs' cases disproportionately involved claims for which attorneys are willing to work on contingency — that is, claims with a relatively high expected monetary value. Among cases that were not settled and went to trial, represented and unrepresented plaintiffs prevailed at similar rates.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Attorneys who represent plaintiffs in Hargreave County are, on average, more skilled at litigation than attorneys who represent defendants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The higher settlement rate among represented plaintiffs is likely due at least in part to features of their cases other than the quality of their representation at trial.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Plaintiffs without counsel in Hargreave County win at trial more often than defendants without counsel do.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any plaintiff who retains an attorney in Hargreave County is more likely to receive a monetary award than one who does not.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Attorneys working on contingency refuse to take cases unless a pretrial settlement is likely.

explanations.correct: Three facts: represented plaintiffs settle about twice as often; their cases disproportionately involve high-value, contingency-eligible claims; yet at trial, represented and unrepresented plaintiffs prevail at similar rates. The similar trial-win rates tug against a pure 'lawyering makes plaintiffs win' story, and the case-mix fact offers another driver. Together these support the hedged claim that the settlement gap is at least partly due to non-trial-quality features of the cases themselves.
explanations.A: Out of scope — the stimulus says nothing about defense attorneys' skill.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Mis-scoped — unrepresented defendants are not addressed.
explanations.D: Too strong — 'any' and 'more likely' extrapolate beyond averages and ignore the similar trial-win finding.
explanations.E: Too strong — contingency-fee behavior is described only as a pattern, not as a rigid refusal rule.

lr.difficultyReason: Requires integrating the subscription data, the reading-time finding, and the recall-score result to recognize a tension between volume consumed and retention. Trap (E) is a plausible worldly truth; trap (B) overreaches from 'some' to 'most'.
lr.stimulus: A survey of readers of general-interest news publications found that subscribers to a high-volume daily news service reported, on average, consuming more articles per week than subscribers to a weekly news digest. The daily-service subscribers also reported spending, on average, less time per article than the digest subscribers did. When both groups were asked a week later to recall substantive details from articles they had read during the survey period, digest subscribers scored noticeably higher than daily-service subscribers on recall of policy-oriented articles, while the two groups scored comparably on recall of articles about entertainment.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reading a larger number of news articles per week tends to improve a reader's retention of details from those articles.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most daily-service subscribers would retain more policy-oriented details if they spent more time per article.

choices.label: C
choices.text: For at least some categories of news, the amount of time spent per article is more closely associated with retention than is the sheer number of articles read.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Digest subscribers are, on the whole, more interested in policy issues than daily-service subscribers are.

choices.label: E
choices.text: News services that deliver fewer but longer articles should be preferred by readers who want to stay informed.

explanations.correct: Digest subscribers read fewer articles but spent more time per article; their recall of policy articles exceeded that of daily-service subscribers, though entertainment recall was comparable. This supports a hedged, category-scoped claim: for at least some kinds of news (policy), time-per-article tracks with retention more closely than article count does. The 'at least some categories' hedge and 'more closely associated' match what the data carry.
explanations.A: Opposite direction — daily-service subscribers read more articles but recalled less in the policy category.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'most' and 'would retain more' make a counterfactual and universal claim the data do not reach.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported — no interest data are reported; the stimulus gives only recall scores.
explanations.E: Normative overreach — the stimulus does not license a recommendation about which service readers 'should' prefer.

lr.difficultyReason: Must chain three ethical-practice facts — the nondisclosure rate, the patient-preference survey, and the follow-up finding — to support a hedged claim about the gap between professed preferences and realized outcomes. Trap (A) overreaches; trap (D) relies on a misreading of which group showed the follow-up effect.
lr.stimulus: In a survey of physicians practicing in a large urban hospital system, roughly a third reported that they had at some point declined to disclose a minor error to a patient when they believed the error had caused no lasting harm. A separate survey of patients of the same system found that an overwhelming majority said they would want to be told of any error affecting their care, even if the error caused no lasting harm. A follow-up study found that patients who had later learned of an undisclosed minor error expressed, on average, only modestly lower trust in their physician than patients who had been promptly informed of a comparable error.
lr.questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At least some physicians in the hospital system are not currently meeting the disclosure preferences of the patients they treat.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most patients in the hospital system have at some point been the subject of an undisclosed minor medical error.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Promptly disclosing minor errors to patients maximally preserves patients' trust in their physicians.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients who learn belatedly of an undisclosed error lose trust in their physicians as sharply as patients who are told promptly would have.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Physicians who withhold disclosure of minor errors do so primarily out of concern for preserving patient trust.

explanations.correct: A third of physicians have at some point withheld disclosure of a minor error; an overwhelming majority of patients say they would want to be told of any error. That gap supports the hedged claim that at least some physicians are not meeting their patients' stated disclosure preferences. 'At least some' fits comfortably within the reported figures.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — the stimulus gives the physician side ('at some point' withheld) and a preference survey, not the share of patients who have been affected.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'maximally preserves' is a superlative the follow-up study does not establish.
explanations.D: Opposite direction — the follow-up found only modestly lower trust among those who learned belatedly.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported — physicians' reasons for nondisclosure are not described.

lr.difficultyReason: Requires chaining the pricing rule, the sales pattern, and the restocking observation to infer a hedged claim about demand in a specific category. Trap (B) is stimulus-neutral plausibility; trap (E) reverses direction by assuming the pattern generalizes.
lr.stimulus: An online retailer adjusts prices on many items daily according to an automated algorithm that raises a listed item's price whenever the number of units sold in the previous 24 hours exceeds a threshold. Records show that over the past year the algorithm raised the price of a popular model of wireless headphones roughly three times as often as it raised the price of a competing model from the same manufacturer, even though the two models were initially listed at the same price. Staff also reported restocking the first model noticeably more often than the second during the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first model of wireless headphones was, over the past year, in greater demand at the retailer than the competing model was.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first model of wireless headphones is of higher quality than the competing model.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The retailer's pricing algorithm raises prices only for items whose sales exceed the threshold on several consecutive days.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first model of wireless headphones is now priced considerably higher than the competing model.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any item whose price is raised three times as often as another item's price must be restocked three times as often as well.

explanations.correct: The algorithm raises prices when daily unit sales exceed a threshold; the first model's price was raised about three times as often as the competing model's, and staff restocked it noticeably more often. Together these facts support the hedged claim that the first model was in greater demand at this retailer over the year. 'Greater demand' is scoped to this retailer and this period, matching the evidence.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported — quality is not addressed; demand could reflect branding, promotion, or other factors.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'only' and 'several consecutive days' add conditions not stated.
explanations.D: Too strong — more frequent price increases don't guarantee the current listed price is considerably higher; prices can also fall.
explanations.E: Too strong — the inference overgeneralizes the relationship between price increases and restocking frequency.

lr.difficultyReason: Requires chaining emission, air-quality, and hospitalization data while recognizing the juxtaposition between lower emissions and stable hospitalizations to support a hedged claim about non-local pollution sources. Trap (A) flips direction; trap (C) over-applies the air-quality finding.
lr.stimulus: Since the city of Polford adopted stricter emission limits on its municipal power plants a decade ago, measured emissions of fine particulate matter from those plants have declined by nearly half. Air-quality monitoring stations in residential neighborhoods near the plants have recorded only a modest improvement in average particulate levels during the same period. Hospital admissions in Polford for conditions linked to airborne particulates have remained roughly constant.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The stricter emission limits imposed on Polford's municipal power plants have caused residential air-quality monitors to record a sharp improvement in particulate levels.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sources of airborne particulates other than Polford's municipal power plants are likely contributing substantially to the particulate levels measured in Polford's residential neighborhoods.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Particulate pollution is no longer a significant contributor to hospital admissions in Polford.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Emission limits similar to those adopted by Polford would fail to improve air quality in any city that adopted them.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Residents of neighborhoods near Polford's power plants have become less likely to seek hospital care for airborne-particulate-related conditions.

explanations.correct: Plant emissions fell by nearly half, yet residential particulate levels improved only modestly and hospitalizations were roughly constant. The gap between a large emissions drop and a small air-quality change supports the hedged claim that other sources are likely contributing substantially to local particulate levels. 'Likely' and 'substantially' fit the data without overreaching.
explanations.A: Opposite direction — the stimulus reports only a modest improvement in monitoring stations' readings.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — roughly constant admissions do not show particulates are no longer a significant contributor.
explanations.D: Too strong — a universal failure claim goes well beyond one city's experience.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported — admissions rates in specific neighborhoods are not broken out.

lr.difficultyReason: Chains the playwright's output pattern, the revival-frequency data, and the critical-reception datum, with a tension between later popularity and earlier acclaim. Trap (A) misreads 'among the most' as 'the most'; trap (D) drops the revival qualifier.
lr.stimulus: A comprehensive survey of twentieth-century theater records shows that the playwright Helena Orsi produced more than forty full-length plays during her career. Of these, only eight have been professionally revived more than twice since her death, and nearly all of those eight premiered during the first decade of her career. Contemporary reviewers of Orsi's later-career plays had, on average, praised them more highly than her early-career plays, describing several as among the most formally inventive works of their decade.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The most formally inventive of Helena Orsi's plays is one of the eight that have been revived more than twice since her death.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Plays that are highly praised by contemporary reviewers tend to be revived more frequently after the playwright's death than plays that are not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Frequency of posthumous professional revival and contemporary critical praise do not always track each other closely in the case of Helena Orsi's work.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Helena Orsi's early-career plays have been revived more often than her later-career plays.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Critics in Helena Orsi's later career systematically overrated her work.
