explanations.correct: Nearly all of Orsi's frequently revived plays premiered in her first decade, yet her later-career plays received, on average, higher critical praise, with several described as among the most formally inventive of their decade. That juxtaposition supports the hedged claim that, in Orsi's case, revival frequency and critical praise do not always track each other closely. 'Not always' and 'closely' are appropriately hedged.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'among the most formally inventive' does not single out one play, and the stimulus describes several later works that way.
explanations.B: Opposite direction — the Orsi data run the other way: more-praised later plays were revived less often.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Correct reading but extrapolated — we know nearly all of the frequently revived plays are early ones, but not the aggregate revival counts across eras; the stronger comparative may not hold.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported — 'systematically overrated' imputes a critical failure the stimulus does not establish.

lr.difficultyReason: Requires integrating the bandwidth-throttling policy, the queueing observation, and the peak-hour latency figure to support a hedged claim about a bottleneck's location. Trap (B) overreaches from 'some evidence' to 'primary cause'; trap (D) misreads the throttling condition.
lr.stimulus: A regional internet service provider implemented a policy in which residential connections whose monthly traffic exceeds a threshold are throttled to a lower speed until the next billing cycle. Network engineers have observed that during peak evening hours, outbound queues at the provider's core routers fill up more quickly than at any other time, even though total traffic during peak hours is only modestly greater than at late-morning hours. Average latency measured at customer endpoints rises sharply during peak evening hours, including for customers whose connections are not being throttled.
lr.questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At least some of the peak-hour latency experienced by the provider's customers is due to conditions at the provider's core routers rather than to the throttling policy alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The throttling policy is the primary cause of the elevated latency that customers experience during peak evening hours.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eliminating the throttling policy would substantially reduce average peak-hour latency for the provider's customers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every customer whose monthly traffic exceeds the threshold experiences higher average latency than every customer whose traffic does not.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Expanding capacity at the core routers would eliminate peak-hour latency for all of the provider's customers.

explanations.correct: Core-router outbound queues fill up fastest during peak evening hours despite only modestly higher traffic than late morning, and peak-hour latency rises sharply even for non-throttled customers. Together these support the hedged claim that at least some of the peak-hour latency comes from conditions at the core routers, not only from the throttling policy. 'At least some' and 'rather than...alone' fit the data.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'primary cause' goes beyond what the non-throttled latency rise supports; it is evidence against sole-cause attribution, not for primary attribution.
explanations.C: Too strong — a counterfactual policy prediction not established by the data.
explanations.D: Mis-scoped — the stimulus does not give a throttled-versus-non-throttled latency comparison across all customers.
explanations.E: Too strong — 'eliminate...for all' overreaches from a contributing-cause inference.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents two datasets in apparent tension — a drug that reduces biomarker levels more aggressively also produces worse long-term outcomes in a subgroup. Test-takers must navigate the tension without overclaiming. The correct answer makes a hedged inference about sufficiency; the dominant trap answer uses the data to draw an absolute causal reversal.
lr.stimulus: A five-year clinical trial tracked patients with elevated arterial inflammation who were assigned to one of two cholesterol-lowering regimens. Patients on Regimen A achieved, on average, a 42 percent reduction in the inflammatory biomarker CRP, compared with a 19 percent reduction for patients on Regimen B. Despite this, patients on Regimen A who also had a history of Type 2 diabetes experienced significantly higher rates of major adverse cardiac events (MACE) than did patients on Regimen B with the same diabetic history. Among patients without diabetes, MACE rates were statistically indistinguishable between the two regimens.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reducing CRP levels is not sufficient, by itself, to guarantee lower rates of major adverse cardiac events in all patient populations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Regimen B is a more effective treatment than Regimen A for patients with elevated arterial inflammation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: CRP reduction and cardiac event rates are unrelated in patients who do not have Type 2 diabetes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients with Type 2 diabetes should never be prescribed Regimen A under any circumstances.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The mechanisms by which Regimen A reduces CRP levels are fundamentally different from those by which Regimen B does so.

explanations.correct: The diabetic subgroup on Regimen A achieved greater CRP reduction yet had worse cardiac outcomes than the same subgroup on Regimen B. This directly shows that aggressive CRP reduction did not produce better MACE outcomes for these patients — i.e., CRP reduction alone is not sufficient to guarantee lower cardiac event rates in all populations. The hedged language ('not sufficient, by itself') and the qualifier ('in all patient populations') make this strongly supported without overclaiming.
explanations.A: Correct. The data show that greater biomarker reduction in diabetic patients coincided with worse, not better, cardiac outcomes — directly undercutting any claim that CRP reduction alone guarantees benefit across all groups.
explanations.B: Too strong and mis-scoped. The stimulus says Regimen A outperforms on CRP reduction overall and that non-diabetic MACE rates are indistinguishable. Regimen B is only preferable within the diabetic subgroup; calling it 'more effective' globally overreaches the data.
explanations.C: Opposite direction / unsupported. The fact that MACE rates were indistinguishable between regimens in non-diabetics does not entail that CRP and MACE are unrelated for that group — it may simply mean both regimens produce similar CRP effects in that group. The stimulus provides no basis to infer unrelatedness.
explanations.D: Too strong. 'Never... under any circumstances' is an absolute prohibition not supported by a single subgroup finding in one trial. The stimulus shows a statistical difference, not a universal harm.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported. The stimulus describes outcomes and biomarker percentages but says nothing about the biochemical mechanisms of either regimen. This is a worldly inference the stimulus cannot support.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus contains a counterintuitive economic finding (a tariff designed to protect domestic producers actually benefited a competing import sector) alongside a quantitative nuance about firm size. The correct answer draws a precise hedged inference about the differential effect; traps include an absolute causal claim, a scope-creep answer, and a plausible-but-unsupported macroeconomic conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Following the introduction of a 25 percent import tariff on foreign-manufactured steel, domestic steel producers saw profit margins increase by an average of 11 percent over three years. However, data from the same period show that domestic automobile manufacturers — who purchase large quantities of steel — experienced a net decrease in export competitiveness, with their share of key overseas markets falling by roughly 8 percent. Smaller domestic manufacturers that used steel as an input reported no statistically significant change in export performance, though their domestic sales volumes rose modestly.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The tariff on imported steel produced benefits for some domestic industries while imposing competitive costs on others.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Import tariffs on raw materials invariably harm the export performance of downstream manufacturers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Domestic automobile manufacturers would have maintained their overseas market share had the steel tariff not been imposed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The steel tariff was, on balance, economically harmful to the domestic economy as a whole.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Smaller domestic manufacturers benefited from the tariff primarily because they compete in different markets than automobile manufacturers.

explanations.correct: The stimulus shows that domestic steel producers (one domestic industry) saw profit margin increases — a benefit — while domestic automobile manufacturers (another domestic industry) saw export competitiveness decline — a cost. The smaller manufacturers saw mixed but not clearly harmful results. Answer A captures this asymmetry with appropriately hedged language ('some... while... others') and is directly supported by the data.
explanations.A: Correct. Steel producers benefited; automobile exporters were harmed. This is the central, well-supported asymmetry in the stimulus, stated with appropriate hedging.
explanations.B: Too strong and over-generalized. 'Invariably' is an absolute claim based on one tariff applied to one raw material in one country over three years. The smaller manufacturers showed no significant export harm, further undercutting universality.
explanations.C: Unsupported counterfactual. The stimulus documents a correlation between the tariff period and falling export share, but provides no basis to rule out other causes of the decline, making this causal counterfactual unsupported.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported. Drawing a net balance sheet for the entire domestic economy would require aggregating gains and losses across all sectors — information the stimulus does not supply. This is an appealing economic judgment that goes beyond the data.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported. The stimulus identifies a divergence in outcomes between smaller manufacturers and automakers but gives no information about whether this stems from market-type differences. Introducing 'different markets' as an explanation adds a premise the stimulus does not provide.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents linguistic fieldwork data with a temporal twist: a grammatical feature thought to be archaic is actually more prevalent among younger speakers in one dialect region but not in another. The correct answer requires integrating both the age-distribution finding and the regional qualification without over-generalizing. Traps include a scope-creep answer that drops the regional qualifier, a too-strong answer about language change directionality, and a plausible-but-unsupported claim about language prestige.
lr.stimulus: Fieldwork conducted among speakers of two regional dialects of a minority language — the Northern dialect and the Coastal dialect — found that a particular verb-final word-order construction, long considered a marker of archaic speech, appeared more frequently in the spontaneous conversation of speakers under age 35 than in speakers over age 60 in the Northern dialect. In the Coastal dialect, however, frequency of the construction showed no statistically significant correlation with speaker age. Interviews revealed that younger Northern speakers were largely unaware that the construction carried any social or stylistic valence.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In at least one dialect of the minority language, the verb-final construction is not straightforwardly undergoing the pattern of decline that its characterization as archaic would predict.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Linguistic features perceived as archaic will eventually be reappropriated by younger speakers across all dialects of a language.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The verb-final construction is more grammatically complex than the alternative constructions used by older Northern speakers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Social awareness of a construction's stylistic valence is the primary driver of generational language change in minority languages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Coastal dialect is more conservative than the Northern dialect in its overall grammatical structure.

explanations.correct: In the Northern dialect, younger speakers use the verb-final construction more frequently than older speakers — the opposite of what 'archaic decline' would predict. Answer A captures this with appropriately hedged language ('at least one dialect,' 'not straightforwardly undergoing... decline') without over-generalizing to the Coastal dialect or to all minority languages. The qualifier 'at least one' is critical: the Coastal dialect shows no such reversal, so A correctly limits its scope.
explanations.A: Correct. The Northern dialect data directly contradict the expected trajectory of an archaic feature, and the answer's scoping ('at least one dialect') respects the fact that the Coastal dialect behaved differently.
explanations.B: Too strong and scope-creep. 'Eventually... across all dialects' is an absolute prediction about the future that goes far beyond what two data points from one language can support. The Coastal dialect alone shows no such trend.
explanations.C: Plausible but unsupported. The stimulus contains no information about the grammatical complexity of the verb-final construction relative to alternatives. This introduces content not present in the data.
explanations.D: Opposite direction / unsupported. The interviews reveal younger Northern speakers are largely unaware of the construction's social valence — yet they use it more. This actually suggests social awareness is not driving the change, making the answer contrary to what the stimulus most supports.
explanations.E: Scope-creep and unsupported. The stimulus addresses one specific construction in one age cohort within each dialect. Inferring the Coastal dialect's overall grammatical conservatism from the absence of an age effect in a single feature vastly overgeneralizes the data.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents tension between two sets of data — antibiotic resistance rates rising while prescriptions fall — requiring the student to identify the hedged inference that correctly resolves the tension without overclaiming causation or direction. Traps include an opposite-direction answer and a too-strong absolute claim.
lr.stimulus: A longitudinal study tracked antibiotic prescription rates and antibiotic-resistant infection rates across seventeen hospitals over a twelve-year period. In hospitals where prescription rates declined by more than 20 percent, antibiotic-resistant infection rates nonetheless increased during the first five years of the study. After the fifth year, however, those same hospitals began showing smaller increases in resistance rates than hospitals where prescription rates had remained stable or risen. Hospitals that had never reduced prescription rates showed the steepest and most consistent increases in resistance rates over the full twelve years.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reducing antibiotic prescriptions eliminates the development of antibiotic-resistant infections within five years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibiotic-resistant infections are more dangerous in hospitals that never reduced prescription rates.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reducing antibiotic prescription rates may slow the growth of antibiotic resistance over time, even if resistance continues to increase initially.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antibiotic resistance rates are determined primarily by prescription practices within individual hospitals.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hospitals that reduced prescriptions the most aggressively will eventually see antibiotic resistance rates decline to zero.

explanations.correct: The stimulus shows that hospitals with reduced prescriptions still saw rising resistance early on but smaller increases later compared to non-reducing hospitals. This hedged pattern — continued increase, but at a slower rate — directly supports the inference that reduction may slow resistance growth over time without eliminating it. 'May' and 'even if' correctly hedge against the early-period anomaly.
explanations.A: Too strong: the stimulus shows resistance still increased in the first five years in reducing hospitals; it was never eliminated.
explanations.B: Scope creep and unsupported: the stimulus measures resistance rates, not danger or severity of individual infections. No comparison of danger is offered.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Too strong: 'determined primarily' is an absolute causal claim the stimulus does not support; many other factors could influence resistance rates.
explanations.E: Too strong and opposite extrapolation: the stimulus shows resistance continued rising even in reducing hospitals; projecting it to 'zero' inverts and overclaims the trend.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus involves an economic subgroup exception (small manufacturers diverging from the broader manufacturing trend) requiring the student to pick the inference that correctly scopes the claim to that subgroup without generalizing or inverting the finding. Trap answers generalize to all manufacturers or assign an incorrect causal direction.
lr.stimulus: Data from a national trade association survey show that overall manufacturing output declined by 8 percent last year, yet manufacturers with fewer than fifty employees reported a 3 percent increase in output over the same period. The survey also found that small manufacturers — those with fewer than fifty employees — were nearly twice as likely as large manufacturers to have introduced a new product line within the preceding eighteen months. Large manufacturers, by contrast, concentrated resources on streamlining existing production processes.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Introducing new product lines is the primary driver of output growth for all manufacturing firms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Large manufacturers will eventually adopt the same strategies used by small manufacturers in order to reverse their output declines.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At least some manufacturers were able to increase output during a period of general manufacturing decline.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Streamlining existing production processes consistently reduces manufacturing output.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Small manufacturers outperform large manufacturers across all major economic indicators.

explanations.correct: The survey explicitly states that small manufacturers (fewer than 50 employees) saw a 3 percent output increase during a period when overall manufacturing output fell 8 percent. Therefore, at least some manufacturers (specifically small ones) increased output during general decline — a direct, hedged inference from the data.
explanations.A: Too strong and scope creep: 'primary driver for all manufacturing firms' is not established; the stimulus only reports a correlation for small manufacturers, and no causal primacy is stated.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus makes no predictions about future strategy adoption by large manufacturers.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Opposite direction / too strong: the stimulus says large manufacturers focused on streamlining, but does not establish that streamlining caused their decline or that it consistently reduces output.
explanations.E: Scope creep and too strong: the stimulus addresses only output; 'all major economic indicators' vastly overgeneralizes.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus involves environmental data with a counterintuitive directional twist: a species thrives in degraded habitat under certain conditions but not others. The correct answer requires tracking two interacting variables. Traps include an opposite-direction answer and one that confuses necessary vs. sufficient conditions.
lr.stimulus: Field surveys in a coastal wetland region found that populations of the spotted marsh wren were larger in moderately degraded wetlands — those affected by agricultural runoff but retaining native vegetation — than in pristine wetlands with no runoff exposure. However, in severely degraded wetlands where native vegetation had been replaced by invasive species, spotted marsh wren populations were nearly absent. Ornithologists noted that moderately degraded wetlands tended to have elevated insect populations, a primary food source for the wren, while pristine wetlands had insect populations of average density.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Agricultural runoff benefits all wetland bird species by increasing insect populations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The spotted marsh wren thrives in any wetland environment that has been exposed to agricultural runoff.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Native vegetation is more important to spotted marsh wren population size than insect abundance alone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The presence of native vegetation may be a necessary condition for agricultural runoff to support spotted marsh wren populations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wetland degradation is, on balance, beneficial to the spotted marsh wren's long-term survival as a species.

explanations.correct: The stimulus shows that runoff + native vegetation → larger wren populations, but runoff + no native vegetation (severe degradation) → nearly absent populations. This pattern supports the inference that native vegetation may be a necessary condition for runoff to benefit wrens — without it, runoff alone does not support the population. 'May be' appropriately hedges the causal claim.
explanations.A: Too strong and scope creep: the stimulus addresses only the spotted marsh wren, not all wetland bird species, and does not establish a universal benefit.
explanations.B: Too strong: the severely degraded wetlands also had runoff exposure, yet wren populations were nearly absent — directly contradicting this claim.
explanations.C: This inverts or misweights the data: the stimulus suggests insect abundance (elevated in moderately degraded wetlands) does help wrens, but the critical variable distinguishing the two degraded wetland types is native vegetation. The answer form ('more important than insect abundance alone') isn't cleanly supported because insect abundance and vegetation are confounded in the data; D is the more precise and better-supported inference.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Too strong and opposite direction: severe degradation nearly eliminates wren populations; calling degradation 'on balance beneficial' to the species' long-term survival is not supported.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus involves a policy evaluation with a counterintuitive finding: a mandatory disclosure law reduced the targeted behavior in large firms but increased it in small firms. The correct answer must be scoped precisely to one subgroup. Traps include answers that generalize across firm size or that assign causation the stimulus does not establish.
lr.stimulus: A state legislature passed a law requiring all businesses to disclose the wages paid to employees in each job category. An independent evaluation conducted two years after implementation found that the gender wage gap — the difference between average pay for men and women in equivalent positions — narrowed significantly at firms with more than 500 employees. At firms with fewer than 100 employees, however, the gender wage gap widened slightly in the two years following the law's implementation, a change the evaluators attributed to increased male retention bonuses at those firms rather than to reduced female wages.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mandatory wage disclosure laws reliably narrow the gender wage gap across all firm sizes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The wage disclosure law failed to achieve its intended effect and should be repealed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The gender wage gap narrowed at large firms following the implementation of the wage disclosure law.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Small firms deliberately used retention bonuses to circumvent the intent of the wage disclosure law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mandatory wage disclosure is more effective than any other policy intervention at closing the gender wage gap.

explanations.correct: The evaluation directly states that the gender wage gap narrowed significantly at firms with more than 500 employees in the two years after the law. This is a straightforward factual inference from the stimulus, precisely scoped to large firms.
explanations.A: Too strong: the stimulus shows the gap did not narrow — indeed widened — at small firms, directly contradicting universal applicability across all firm sizes.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus doesn't identify the law's 'intended effect' or make a normative recommendation about repeal. The law had mixed effects; calling it a failure and recommending repeal goes beyond the data.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Too strong / unsupported intent: the evaluators attribute the gap widening to increased male retention bonuses, but 'deliberately circumvent' imputes motive that the stimulus does not establish.
explanations.E: Scope creep and too strong: no comparison to other policy interventions is made in the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents historical data about a technology adoption pattern with a counterintuitive finding: early adopters fared worse than late adopters in one dimension. The correct inference must track the specific dimension without overgeneralizing. Multiple plausible but unsupported answers are available.
lr.stimulus: Historical records from the early railroad era in North America indicate that the first companies to build steam-powered rail lines in a given region frequently went bankrupt within fifteen years, while companies that entered the same regional markets ten to twenty years later tended to remain solvent for significantly longer periods. Engineers of the later period benefited from design improvements developed by earlier firms, and the later companies' rail lines required substantially less maintenance expenditure per mile than those of pioneer firms. Passenger volumes on both early and late lines were comparable during their respective first decades of operation.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following inferences is most supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Early railroad companies in North America were poorly managed compared to later entrants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Being the first to enter a regional railroad market was, in at least some cases, a financial disadvantage rather than an advantage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Technological innovation in rail engineering was the sole cause of the financial failures among pioneer railroad companies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passenger demand for rail travel was insufficient to sustain early railroad companies in any North American region.

choices.label: E
choices.text: All later-entering railroad companies ultimately outperformed their pioneer counterparts across every financial metric.

explanations.correct: The stimulus shows that first-mover railroad companies frequently went bankrupt while later entrants remained solvent longer, despite comparable passenger volumes. This supports the hedged conclusion that early entry was, in at least some cases, a financial disadvantage — a direct reading of the pattern with appropriately hedged language.
explanations.A: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus attributes the disadvantage to design inefficiencies and maintenance costs, not management quality. Attributing failure to poor management adds information not in the stimulus.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong: 'sole cause' is an absolute causal claim. The stimulus mentions maintenance costs and design improvements but does not rule out other contributing factors.
explanations.D: Opposite direction: passenger volumes were 'comparable' for early and late lines in their first decades, suggesting demand was not insufficient. This choice contradicts the stimulus.
explanations.E: Too strong and scope creep: 'all later-entering companies' and 'every financial metric' are absolute claims; the stimulus describes general tendencies, not universal outcomes.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus involves linguistic data with a two-group comparison and a qualifier about context. The correct answer requires integrating both the comparison and the qualifier without dropping either. Traps include answers that drop the contextual qualifier or generalize the finding to all languages.
lr.stimulus: A study of bilingual speakers who acquired both languages before age seven found that when asked to name objects in their weaker language, these speakers produced the correct word significantly faster when the object was presented in a familiar indoor context than when the same object appeared in an unfamiliar outdoor setting. By contrast, when naming objects in their dominant language, response times did not differ between familiar and unfamiliar contexts. The researchers noted that both languages showed comparable accuracy rates regardless of context.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bilingual speakers are always slower to name objects in their weaker language than in their dominant language.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For bilingual speakers, contextual familiarity appears to affect word retrieval speed in a weaker language but not in a dominant language.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Contextual familiarity improves accuracy as well as speed in object-naming tasks for bilingual speakers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Children who acquire two languages simultaneously before age seven will never experience retrieval difficulties in either language.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The effect of context on language processing is uniform across all bilingual populations regardless of acquisition age.

explanations.correct: The study directly shows that context affected naming speed in the weaker language (faster in familiar contexts) but not in the dominant language (no difference across contexts). The word 'appears' appropriately hedges the causal claim, making this a strong but not absolute inference from the data.
explanations.A: Too strong: 'always slower' is an absolute claim. The study reports response times in specific conditions; it does not establish that the weaker language is always slower across all possible conditions.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Opposite direction / unsupported: the stimulus explicitly states that accuracy rates were comparable regardless of context; context did not improve accuracy.
explanations.D: Too strong and unsupported: 'never experience retrieval difficulties' is an absolute claim not supported by the study, which describes response time differences, not the elimination of all retrieval difficulties.
explanations.E: Scope creep: the study examined early bilinguals (before age seven); generalizing to 'all bilingual populations regardless of acquisition age' goes beyond the data.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents an ethics/law tension in which a legal standard and a common moral intuition diverge across cases, requiring students to identify the inference about the relationship between the two standards rather than affirming either as correct. Traps include answers that endorse one standard as definitively superior or conflate the descriptive and normative claims.
lr.stimulus: Courts in several jurisdictions have held that a person has no legal duty to rescue a stranger in peril, even when rescue would pose no risk to the rescuer. Surveys conducted in those same jurisdictions find that roughly 85 percent of residents believe a bystander who fails to attempt a low-risk rescue of a drowning stranger has acted immorally. Legal scholars who have examined these surveys note that the jurisdictions with no-duty-to-rescue rules have not experienced measurable increases in bystander rescues following the rare enactment of legal duties to rescue in neighboring jurisdictions.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In at least some jurisdictions, the legal standard for rescue duty does not reflect the moral views of the majority of residents.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Legal duties to rescue should be enacted in all jurisdictions because most residents believe rescue failures are immoral.

choices.label: C
choices.text: People are more likely to attempt a rescue when there is a legal duty to do so than when there is no such duty.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Moral intuitions about rescue are unreliable guides to the formulation of legal standards.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Legal scholars unanimously agree that no-duty-to-rescue rules should be abolished.

explanations.correct: The stimulus directly establishes that in jurisdictions with no legal duty to rescue, approximately 85 percent of residents believe failing to attempt a low-risk rescue is immoral. This creates a documented gap between the legal rule (no duty) and the moral view of the majority — a gap that, in at least those jurisdictions, is straightforwardly supported by the data.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported normative claim: the stimulus is purely descriptive. Drawing a prescriptive conclusion ('should be enacted') about what law ought to be goes beyond what the facts support.
explanations.C: Opposite direction: the stimulus states that enacting legal duties to rescue in some jurisdictions did NOT produce measurable increases in bystander rescues in neighboring no-duty jurisdictions — suggesting legal duty does not reliably increase rescue attempts.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus notes a discrepancy between law and moral intuition but does not evaluate moral intuitions as unreliable guides. This is an interpretive judgment not derivable from the facts given.
explanations.E: Too strong and unsupported: the stimulus cites legal scholars' observations about survey data and behavioral effects, but does not describe any scholarly consensus in favor of abolishing the rule.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus involves arts/economics data with a counterintuitive finding: critical acclaim and commercial performance diverge by genre in a specific streaming context. The correct answer must track the divergence precisely. Traps include an answer that conflates critical and commercial success and one that generalizes beyond the streaming context.
lr.stimulus: An analysis of streaming platform data covering a five-year period found that documentary films receiving major festival awards averaged roughly 40 percent fewer total streams than non-award-winning documentaries released in the same calendar year. Among narrative fiction films, however, festival awards were positively associated with streaming volume: award-winning narrative films averaged approximately 25 percent more streams than non-award-winning narrative films released the same year. Platform analysts noted that award-winning documentaries were predominantly acquired by niche subscription services, while award-winning narrative films were acquired predominantly by large general-audience platforms.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Festival awards reliably increase the commercial streaming success of all film genres.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Niche subscription services offer lower-quality content than large general-audience platforms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: For at least one film genre, festival recognition was associated with lower streaming volume rather than higher streaming volume.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Documentary filmmakers should avoid submitting their films to major festivals if they wish to maximize streaming audiences.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The relationship between critical acclaim and streaming performance is identical across documentary and narrative fiction genres.

explanations.correct: The stimulus directly states that award-winning documentaries averaged roughly 40 percent fewer streams than non-award-winning documentaries — a clear case of festival recognition correlating with lower, not higher, streaming volume for that genre. 'At least one genre' hedges appropriately, and the inference is a direct reading of the data.
explanations.A: Too strong and opposite direction: the stimulus shows festival awards were associated with fewer streams for documentaries, directly contradicting the claim that awards 'reliably increase' streaming success 'for all genres.'
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus notes where award-winning films were acquired but makes no claim about the quality of content on different platform types.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Plausible but normative and unsupported: the stimulus reports a correlation; inferring a prescriptive recommendation for filmmakers adds a practical judgment not warranted by the data alone.
explanations.E: Opposite direction: the stimulus explicitly contrasts the two genres, showing the relationship runs in opposite directions — awards are negatively associated with documentary streams but positively associated with narrative fiction streams.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus involves technology/environmental science data with a multi-variable tension: a renewable energy technology reduces one type of environmental harm while increasing another. The correct inference must acknowledge both dimensions without dismissing either. Traps include answers that credit only one dimension or that make absolute net-benefit or net-harm claims.
lr.stimulus: A lifecycle assessment of utility-scale solar panel installations found that over a 30-year operational period, such installations produce approximately 95 percent less carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour generated than coal-fired plants of equivalent capacity. The same assessment found, however, that manufacturing the panels required substantial quantities of cadmium, a toxic heavy metal, and that disposal of decommissioned panels at the end of their operational life poses documented risks of cadmium leaching into soil and groundwater at landfill sites. The assessment did not evaluate the relative toxicity risk of coal plant emissions to groundwater.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Utility-scale solar installations are environmentally superior to coal-fired plants in every measurable respect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The environmental costs of cadmium disposal from solar panels outweigh the carbon reduction benefits over a 30-year period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Solar panel installations present at least one environmental benefit and at least one environmental risk not shared by their carbon reduction advantage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Coal-fired plants pose no significant risk of heavy metal contamination to soil or groundwater.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulators should prohibit the construction of new utility-scale solar installations until cadmium disposal methods are improved.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes both a clear environmental benefit (95% less CO₂ per kWh) and a distinct environmental risk (cadmium leaching at disposal). The correct answer acknowledges both dimensions precisely — 'at least one benefit and at least one risk not shared by their carbon reduction advantage' — without requiring a net judgment the data cannot support.
explanations.A: Too strong: the stimulus explicitly identifies a risk (cadmium contamination) associated with solar panels that is not present in the operational phase of coal plants, so solar is not superior 'in every measurable respect.'
explanations.B: Unsupported and opposite direction: the assessment did not quantify or compare the magnitude of cadmium risk against carbon benefits; making a net-cost-versus-benefit claim goes well beyond the data.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported: the assessment explicitly states it did not evaluate the relative toxicity risk of coal plant emissions to groundwater, so no conclusion about coal's groundwater risk can be drawn.
explanations.E: Normative and unsupported: the stimulus presents data, not a policy recommendation. Drawing a prescriptive regulatory conclusion requires value judgments the stimulus does not supply.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus involves historical/economic data about price controls with a finding that contradicts the standard economic prediction in a specific market subtype. The correct answer must be scoped to that subtype and hedged. Traps include answers that generalize to all price controls, invert the direction, or assign causation without support.
lr.stimulus: Economic historians examining rent control policies in four major European cities between 1920 and 1960 found that in cities where rent controls applied exclusively to housing units occupied before 1925, overall housing construction rates in those cities were not significantly lower than in comparable cities without any rent controls during the same period. Controlled units, however, experienced substantially less maintenance investment than uncontrolled units in the same cities. Additionally, the ratio of controlled to total housing units declined steadily over time as new construction added uncontrolled stock.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rent controls, when applied only to existing housing stock rather than new construction, may not depress overall housing construction rates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rent controls universally reduce maintenance investment in all types of rental housing markets.

choices.label: C
choices.text: European cities that enacted rent controls during this period had higher living standards than those that did not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The economic historians concluded that rent control policies were net beneficial to urban residents in the cities studied.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The ratio of controlled to total housing units increased over time as landlords converted uncontrolled units into controlled ones.

explanations.correct: The stimulus shows that rent controls applied only to pre-1925 units did not significantly depress overall housing construction — which runs counter to the standard economic prediction that controls reduce construction. The inference is hedged with 'may not' and correctly scoped to the specific policy design (existing stock only, not new construction), making it a direct and appropriately cautious reading of the data.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong and scope creep: the stimulus shows reduced maintenance in controlled units in these specific cities under this specific policy; 'universally' and 'all types of rental housing markets' vastly overgeneralizes.
explanations.C: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus addresses construction rates and maintenance, not living standards. No comparison of living standards is made.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported: the historians described the data; no net-beneficial conclusion is attributed to them by the stimulus.
explanations.E: Opposite direction: the stimulus states the ratio of controlled to total housing declined over time as new (uncontrolled) construction added stock — directly contradicting this answer.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents two datapoints in tension — a drug effective against a bacterial strain in vitro shows diminished efficacy in clinical trials — alongside a specific subgroup finding. The correct answer resolves the tension with a modest, hedged inference. The dominant trap (B) is a near-miss that drops a crucial qualifier; trap (D) is an opposite-direction error; trap (E) invokes a plausible but stimulus-unsupported mechanism.
lr.stimulus: A pharmaceutical research team tested a newly synthesized antibiotic compound against Staphylococcus aureus cultures in laboratory conditions and found that the compound eliminated 98 percent of bacterial colonies within 24 hours. In subsequent clinical trials involving 340 hospitalized patients with confirmed S. aureus infections, the compound reduced bacterial load significantly in only 61 percent of patients. However, among the subset of 80 patients who had not previously received any antibiotic treatment, the compound reduced bacterial load in 89 percent of cases. Patients in the broader trial who had received prior antibiotic treatment showed no statistically significant difference in outcomes compared to the control group.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The compound is more likely to be effective against S. aureus in patients who have not previously been treated with antibiotics than in patients who have.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prior antibiotic treatment invariably renders patients resistant to newly developed antibiotic compounds.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Laboratory testing of antibiotics against bacterial cultures is an unreliable method for predicting clinical efficacy in any patient population.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients with prior antibiotic exposure are more likely to benefit from the new compound than patients without such exposure.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The compound's reduced clinical efficacy is caused by immune system suppression in patients who have undergone previous antibiotic treatment.

explanations.correct: The stimulus shows that antibiotic-naive patients responded at 89%, while patients with prior antibiotic treatment showed no statistically significant benefit over controls. This directly supports the hedged comparative claim in (A) — that the compound is more likely to be effective in antibiotic-naive patients than in previously treated ones.
explanations.A: Correct. This is a carefully hedged comparative inference directly licensed by the 89% vs. no-significant-benefit contrast between the two subgroups.
explanations.B: Too strong. The stimulus shows no significant benefit in prior-treatment patients for this compound, but it does not support the absolute claim that prior treatment 'invariably' causes resistance to any newly developed antibiotic. This is the dominant too-strong trap.
explanations.C: Scope creep and overreach. The stimulus shows a gap between lab and clinical results for this compound but does not support the sweeping claim that lab testing is unreliable for 'any patient population.' The antibiotic-naive subgroup actually showed results more consistent with the lab data.
explanations.D: Opposite-direction trap. The data show the opposite: patients with prior antibiotic exposure showed no significant benefit, while antibiotic-naive patients had high response rates.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported. The stimulus provides no information about immune system function or suppression; attributing the efficacy gap to immune suppression is a mechanistic speculation not derivable from the data given.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents economic data on two trade policy regimes with a counterintuitive sub-finding: the regime with lower average tariffs nevertheless produces higher consumer prices in one key sector. The correct answer draws a narrow, hedged inference about that sector. Traps include an absolute-language near-miss (C), a scope-creep answer (D) that generalizes the sector finding to all sectors, and a plausible-but-unsupported causal explanation (E).
lr.stimulus: An economic study compared two neighboring countries, Valdoria and Mestran, over a ten-year period. Valdoria maintained an average import tariff rate of 18 percent across all goods, while Mestran's average tariff rate was 7 percent. Despite this difference, consumer prices for domestically produced electronics were, on average, 14 percent higher in Mestran than in Valdoria over the same period. In every other major goods category tracked by the study, Mestran consumers paid lower prices than Valdoria consumers. The study also noted that Mestran's domestic electronics industry received substantial production subsidies from the national government throughout the period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In at least one sector, factors other than import tariff rates may have contributed to higher consumer prices in the lower-tariff country.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Government subsidies to domestic industries always result in higher consumer prices for the subsidized goods.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mestran's low tariff policy was responsible for the higher electronics prices its consumers faced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Consumers in countries with lower average tariff rates generally pay higher prices than consumers in countries with higher tariff rates.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mestran's government subsidized its electronics industry specifically in order to offset the price-reducing effects of its low tariff policy.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes that Mestran has lower tariffs overall yet has higher electronics prices — a pattern that diverges from the trend in every other sector. The stimulus also notes Mestran's domestic electronics subsidies. Together, these facts most strongly support the hedged inference in (A): that in at least one sector (electronics), factors beyond tariff rates — plausibly those subsidies — may help explain the price anomaly. The language 'may have contributed' and 'at least one sector' is appropriately cautious.
explanations.A: Correct. The electronics anomaly (higher prices despite lower tariffs) combined with the mention of production subsidies supports the inference that non-tariff factors are at play in at least this one sector. The hedged language ('may have contributed,' 'at least one sector') keeps the claim within what the data justify.
explanations.B: Too strong. The stimulus does not establish that subsidies always cause higher consumer prices — only that one subsidized sector shows higher prices. The word 'always' makes this an overreach and the dominant too-strong trap.
explanations.C: Opposite direction / misattribution. Mestran's low tariff policy would be expected to lower prices, not raise them. Attributing the higher electronics prices directly to the low-tariff policy inverts the expected causal direction and ignores the subsidy information.
explanations.D: Scope creep. The electronics finding is the exception, not the rule — the stimulus explicitly states every other major category showed lower prices in Mestran. Generalizing the electronics anomaly to 'generally higher prices' in lower-tariff countries contradicts the bulk of the data.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported. The stimulus notes the subsidies existed but provides no information about the government's purpose or intent in granting them. Inferring the subsidies were designed to 'offset' the tariff policy imports a causal story the data do not support.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents three data points in partial tension — antibiotic use correlates with resistance in one setting but not another, with a subgroup exception. The correct answer resolves this tension via a hedged, carefully scoped inference. Distractors include a too-strong causal claim, an opposite-direction trap, a plausible-but-unsupported worldly claim, and a scope-creep trap that overgeneralizes to all pathogens.
lr.stimulus: Data from a network of regional hospitals show that wards with the highest rates of broad-spectrum antibiotic use tend to have the highest rates of antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections, with one notable exception: pediatric intensive care units (PICUs) in those same hospitals show no such correlation. In PICUs, antibiotic use rates vary widely, but resistant-infection rates remain uniformly low across all facilities surveyed. Infection-control specialists note that PICUs universally enforce hand-hygiene and barrier-precaution protocols far more stringently than other wards do.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Strict enforcement of hand-hygiene and barrier-precaution protocols may reduce resistant-infection rates enough to offset the effect of high antibiotic use in some clinical settings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reducing broad-spectrum antibiotic use is the most effective strategy for lowering antibiotic-resistant infection rates in all hospital wards.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria cannot spread among patients in settings where hand-hygiene protocols are strictly enforced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: PICUs have lower rates of antibiotic-resistant infections than other wards because their patients are younger and therefore less susceptible to resistant strains.

choices.label: E
choices.text: High rates of broad-spectrum antibiotic use are the primary driver of antibiotic resistance in hospitals worldwide.

explanations.correct: The PICU data show that even with variable and sometimes high antibiotic use, resistant-infection rates remain uniformly low — and the one distinguishing feature of PICUs is rigorous infection-control protocols. This strongly supports the hedged inference in A: strict protocols may offset the effect of antibiotic use in some settings. The hedge ('may,' 'some') respects the inductive, non-entailed nature of the inference.
explanations.A: Correct. This is the most defensible inference: the PICU exception is best explained by the one variable that distinguishes PICUs from other wards — stringent infection-control protocols — and the answer is appropriately hedged.
explanations.B: Too strong and mis-scoped. The stimulus shows that reducing antibiotic use correlates with lower resistance in most wards, but the PICU exception reveals that other factors can dominate. Claiming this strategy is 'most effective in all wards' ignores the exception and uses absolute language the stimulus doesn't support.
explanations.C: Too strong. 'Cannot spread' is an absolute claim; the stimulus shows only that resistant infections are uniformly low in PICUs, not that transmission is impossible. This is the dominant 'too strong' trap.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported. Patient age and susceptibility are never mentioned in the stimulus; this introduces outside reasoning not derivable from the information given.
explanations.E: Scope creep and relative/absolute confusion. The stimulus covers regional hospital data; extrapolating to 'hospitals worldwide' exceeds the evidence. Additionally, labeling antibiotic use as the 'primary driver' globally overstates what the correlation in non-PICU wards can establish.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents an economic dataset with a counterintuitive divergence between two related indicators: consumer confidence rises while discretionary spending falls among a specific income bracket, with a temporal complication. The correct answer must navigate the tension without overclaiming causation or generalizing beyond the scoped group. Distractors exploit opposite-direction confusion, absolute language, and plausible-but-unsupported economic reasoning.
lr.stimulus: A national survey conducted over three consecutive quarters tracked consumer confidence and discretionary spending among households in the middle-income bracket. Consumer confidence scores rose steadily across all three quarters. Discretionary spending, however, declined in the second and third quarters, despite the rising confidence scores. During those same quarters, both mortgage refinancing activity and personal savings deposit rates increased substantially among the same households. The survey excluded households in the top and bottom income quartiles.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: For at least some middle-income households, rising consumer confidence does not always translate into increased discretionary spending within the same period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumer confidence is a poor predictor of discretionary spending across all income groups.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Middle-income households reduced discretionary spending because they were pessimistic about future economic conditions despite their reported confidence scores.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased personal savings and mortgage refinancing caused middle-income households to feel more confident about their finances.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Discretionary spending among households in the top and bottom income quartiles followed a similar pattern to that observed among middle-income households.

explanations.correct: The stimulus directly shows that confidence rose while spending fell for this group across two quarters. Answer A draws the appropriately hedged inference — 'for at least some' and 'does not always' — that the two indicators can diverge within the same period. This respects both the data and the scope of the survey.
explanations.A: Correct. The divergence between rising confidence and falling spending for the surveyed group directly supports this hedged inference. The qualifier 'at least some' and 'does not always' ensure the claim stays within what the data establish.
explanations.B: Scope creep. The survey explicitly excluded the top and bottom quartiles, so no inference about 'all income groups' is warranted. This is the classic scope-creep trap — applying a finding to a population larger than the one studied.
explanations.C: Opposite direction and unsupported. The stimulus says confidence scores rose, contradicting the premise that households were pessimistic. Introducing hidden pessimism beneath confident scores adds unsupported psychological reasoning.
explanations.D: Inverts the direction of support. The stimulus presents savings and refinancing as coinciding with the spending decline, not as a cause of confidence. This answer also asserts a causal relationship the stimulus does not establish.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported. The stimulus expressly excluded the top and bottom quartiles from measurement. Any claim about their spending pattern is beyond what the data can support.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents linguistic fieldwork data in tension: a grammatical feature appears in unrelated language families but is absent in several languages within a family that typically exhibits it. The correct answer requires recognizing what the distribution pattern does and does not imply about language contact versus inheritance, while staying hedged. Distractors include a too-strong universalist claim, an opposite-direction inference about inheritance, a plausible typological claim unsupported by these data, and a scope-creep generalization.
lr.stimulus: Linguists studying evidentiality — grammatical marking that indicates the source of a speaker's information — have documented the following: the feature appears in languages from at least six unrelated language families distributed across four continents. Within the Tibeto-Burman family, however, where evidential marking is considered a characteristic feature, three recently studied languages in geographically peripheral subregions entirely lack it, though they retain other hallmark features of the family. No documented cases of evidentiality emerging through language contact between unrelated families have been identified in the dataset.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Evidentiality can be lost in some languages even when that feature is typical of the broader language family to which they belong.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Evidentiality arises independently in unrelated languages and is never transmitted through contact between speakers of different language families.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Languages that lack evidential marking are more likely to be found in geographically peripheral regions than in central ones.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The presence of evidential marking in a language is sufficient evidence that the language belongs to the Tibeto-Burman family.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The three Tibeto-Burman languages lacking evidentiality are more closely related to each other than to other members of the Tibeto-Burman family.

explanations.correct: The three Tibeto-Burman languages demonstrate that a feature characteristic of a family can be absent in some of that family's members. Answer A captures this with appropriate hedging — 'can be lost,' 'some languages,' 'even when typical of the broader family.' This is the most defensible inference the data yield.
explanations.A: Correct. The Tibeto-Burman data directly support this: despite evidentiality being a hallmark of the family, at least three member languages have lost it. The hedged phrasing ('can be lost,' 'some') keeps the claim within the evidence.
explanations.B: Too strong. The dataset shows no documented contact-transmission cases, but 'never transmitted through contact' is an absolute universal claim that the absence of cases in one dataset cannot establish. This is the dominant too-strong trap.
explanations.C: Plausible but unsupported. The three languages are described as geographically peripheral, but the stimulus provides no comparative data on central languages' rates of lacking evidentiality. Concluding a general tendency from a single directional observation is unwarranted.
explanations.D: Opposite direction and too strong. The stimulus shows evidentiality across at least six unrelated families, making it clear that Tibeto-Burman membership is neither necessary nor sufficient to predict evidentiality. This inverts the logic of the data.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported. The internal phylogenetic relationships among the three peripheral languages are never discussed in the stimulus. Inferring closer relatedness among them introduces information not derivable from the facts given.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents two datasets in apparent tension — a drug that reduces mortality in one population subgroup but not in the overall trial population. The correct answer resolves the tension with a hedged inference about subgroup effects. Traps include a too-strong causal claim (D), an opposite-direction inference (B), a scope-creep answer that generalizes beyond the subgroup (C), and a plausible-but-unsupported claim about trial design (E).
lr.stimulus: A large randomized clinical trial tested a new antihypertensive drug on two thousand adult patients over five years. Overall, the trial found no statistically significant difference in cardiovascular mortality between the drug group and the placebo group. However, among the roughly four hundred trial participants who also had type 2 diabetes, those assigned to the drug group experienced cardiovascular mortality at a rate approximately 35 percent lower than diabetic participants in the placebo group. Among the remaining non-diabetic participants, cardiovascular mortality rates were nearly identical between the drug and placebo groups.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The antihypertensive drug is more likely to reduce cardiovascular mortality in patients with type 2 diabetes than in patients without that condition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Non-diabetic patients who take the antihypertensive drug are at greater risk of cardiovascular mortality than non-diabetic patients who do not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antihypertensive drugs in general are more effective at reducing cardiovascular mortality in diabetic patients than in non-diabetic patients.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Type 2 diabetes causes patients to respond more favorably to antihypertensive medications.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The trial was poorly designed because it failed to stratify participants by diabetic status before randomization.

explanations.correct: The stimulus directly establishes a 35% lower cardiovascular mortality rate for diabetic drug-group participants versus diabetic placebo-group participants, while non-diabetic participants showed no such difference. This strongly supports the hedged comparative claim in (A) — that the drug is more likely to reduce cardiovascular mortality in diabetics than in non-diabetics. The language 'more likely' appropriately hedges the probabilistic inference without overclaiming.
explanations.A: Correct. This is a hedged comparative inference drawn directly from the divergent results across the two subgroups.
explanations.B: Opposite direction. The stimulus says non-diabetic mortality rates were 'nearly identical' between drug and placebo groups — not that the drug group fared worse. This inverts the support.
explanations.C: Scope creep. The stimulus covers only this one specific antihypertensive drug; generalizing to 'antihypertensive drugs in general' extends far beyond what the data establish.
explanations.D: Too strong / causal overclaim. The stimulus establishes a correlation between diabetic status and differential drug response, but does not support the causal claim that diabetes 'causes' more favorable responses to antihypertensive medications.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported. The stimulus gives no information about how randomization was conducted or whether stratification was attempted; this is a judgment about trial quality that cannot be inferred from the reported outcomes alone.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus involves economic data with a counterintuitive twist — regions with higher minimum wages show lower small-business closure rates overall, but the effect reverses in rural counties. The correct answer draws the most defensible inference about the relationship between geography and minimum-wage effects on small businesses. Traps include an absolute overclaim (B), an opposite-direction answer (D), a plausible worldly truth (E), and a mis-scoped generalization (C).
lr.stimulus: A regional economic survey tracked small-business closure rates across 200 counties over a decade during which several states incrementally raised their minimum wages. In counties classified as urban or suburban, higher minimum wages were associated with modestly lower small-business closure rates — roughly 8 percent fewer closures per year on average compared with counties where minimum wages remained at the federal floor. In counties classified as rural, the pattern was reversed: rural counties with higher minimum wages showed small-business closure rates approximately 12 percent higher than rural counties at the federal minimum-wage floor. Across all 200 counties combined, small-business closure rates were statistically indistinguishable between higher-minimum-wage and federal-floor counties.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The relationship between minimum-wage levels and small-business closure rates appears to differ depending on whether a county is urban or rural.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Raising the minimum wage always reduces small-business closures in urban areas and always increases them in rural areas.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Higher minimum wages harm small businesses more than they harm large businesses across all regions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rural small businesses are generally better managed than urban small businesses and therefore less sensitive to wage increases.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Minimum-wage policy should be set at the local level rather than the federal level.

explanations.correct: The stimulus reports opposite associations between minimum-wage levels and small-business closures in urban/suburban counties versus rural counties. This directly and strongly supports (A)'s hedged claim that the relationship 'appears to differ' depending on urban or rural classification. The hedged language ('appears to differ') matches the inferential bar for most-strongly-supported.
explanations.A: Correct. The divergent directional findings across county types straightforwardly support this hedged comparative claim.
explanations.B: Too strong. The word 'always' is not warranted — the stimulus reports averages and associations, not universal rules. A single exception would falsify this claim, yet the data cannot rule that out.
explanations.C: Scope creep / unsupported. The survey tracks only small-business closures; no information about large businesses is provided, making any comparison impossible.
explanations.D: Opposite direction and plausible but unsupported. The stimulus shows rural businesses close more often under higher minimum wages — suggesting greater sensitivity, not less. The claim about management quality has no basis in the stimulus.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported. This is a policy prescription that may appeal as a real-world inference, but the stimulus presents descriptive economic data and draws no normative conclusions about how policy should be structured.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents findings from historical linguistics about language-contact zones with a controlled counterintuitive finding: the communities with more prolonged contact borrowed fewer grammatical structures than those with briefer, more intense contact. The correct answer draws a careful inference about the relationship between contact type and grammatical borrowing. Traps include an absolute overclaim (B), an opposite-direction answer (C), a scope-creep answer extending to all contact situations (D), and a causal overclaim (E).
lr.stimulus: Linguists studying fifteen historically documented language-contact zones found that communities in prolonged, low-intensity contact with a neighboring language — typically spanning several generations of bilingualism — most commonly borrowed vocabulary items such as nouns and verbs, but rarely adopted the grammatical structures of the neighboring language. By contrast, communities in briefer but more socially intense contact situations, such as those arising from conquest or forced resettlement, more often showed substantial grammatical borrowing from the dominant language, including changes in word order and morphological paradigms. In nine of the fifteen contact zones studied, communities under intense short-term contact showed greater grammatical restructuring than communities in prolonged low-intensity contact.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In at least some language-contact situations, the social intensity of contact may be more closely associated with grammatical borrowing than the sheer duration of that contact is.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prolonged bilingual contact never results in grammatical borrowing between languages.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Communities under intense short-term contact borrow fewer total linguistic features than communities under prolonged low-intensity contact.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In all language-contact situations, social dominance determines the direction of grammatical influence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Intense social contact causes grammatical restructuring by suppressing speakers' native grammatical intuitions.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes that in nine of fifteen contact zones, brief but socially intense contact produced more grammatical restructuring than prolonged low-intensity contact. This supports the hedged claim in (A) that 'in at least some language-contact situations' social intensity may be more closely associated with grammatical borrowing than duration. The phrase 'at least some' is carefully calibrated to the 9-of-15 finding without overgeneralizing.
explanations.A: Correct. This is a precisely hedged inference — 'at least some situations,' 'may be more closely associated' — that the nine-of-fifteen finding directly supports without overclaiming about all contact zones.
explanations.B: Too strong. The stimulus says prolonged contact communities 'rarely' adopted grammatical structures — not never. 'Never' is an absolute that the stimulus explicitly does not establish.
explanations.C: Opposite direction. The stimulus says intense short-term contact communities showed more grammatical borrowing; (C) claims they borrow fewer total linguistic features — a reversal unsupported by the data. The stimulus also distinguishes vocabulary from grammar, but does not establish a total-feature count favoring either group.
explanations.D: Scope creep and too strong. 'All language-contact situations' goes far beyond the fifteen zones studied, and the stimulus does not claim social dominance is the determining factor in every contact scenario.
explanations.E: Causal overclaim. The stimulus documents an association between intense contact and grammatical restructuring but offers no mechanistic explanation involving the suppression of native grammatical intuitions; this is an unsupported causal hypothesis.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents two datasets in apparent tension — a drug reduces mortality in the overall trial population yet shows no benefit in the largest subgroup. The correct answer resolves this tension by drawing a carefully hedged inference about subgroup heterogeneity, while four traps respectively overclaim causation, invert the direction of support, scope-creep to the general population, or introduce a plausible but unstated mechanism.
lr.stimulus: A clinical trial enrolled 1,200 patients with moderate renal failure and randomly assigned them to receive either a new diuretic compound or a placebo. Overall, patients receiving the compound had a 22 percent lower rate of cardiovascular mortality over 36 months than patients receiving the placebo. However, when researchers stratified the data by age, patients over 65 — who constituted 58 percent of the trial population — showed no statistically significant difference in cardiovascular mortality between the compound and placebo groups. The mortality reduction was concentrated almost entirely among patients aged 65 and under. The compound produced no serious adverse events in either age group.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The new diuretic compound is an effective treatment for cardiovascular disease in patients of all ages with moderate renal failure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cardiovascular benefit associated with the compound in this trial was not uniform across the age groups studied.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Older patients with moderate renal failure metabolize diuretic compounds less efficiently, which explains their failure to benefit from the treatment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because the compound showed no benefit in the majority of trial participants, it should not be approved for use in patients with moderate renal failure.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Diuretic compounds are generally more effective at reducing cardiovascular mortality in younger patients than in older patients.

explanations.correct: The stimulus states that the overall 22% mortality reduction was 'concentrated almost entirely' among patients aged 65 and under, while the over-65 group — comprising 58% of the trial — showed no significant benefit. This directly and strongly supports the claim that the compound's cardiovascular benefit was not uniform across age groups. The hedged language ('not uniform across the age groups studied') matches the scope of the data without overclaiming.
explanations.A: Too strong / opposite direction for the older subgroup. The stimulus explicitly states that patients over 65 showed no significant benefit, so the compound is not supported as effective 'in patients of all ages.' This is the dominant too-strong trap.
explanations.B: Correct. The contrast between the overall benefit and the age-stratified data is precisely what this hedged, comparative claim captures.
explanations.C: Plausible but unsupported. The stimulus identifies the age-based difference in outcomes but provides no information about metabolic mechanisms. Introducing metabolic efficiency is a scope-creep trap that adds unstated causal content.
explanations.D: Inverts the direction of support. The fact that the majority subgroup showed no benefit does not mean the drug should not be approved — the overall trial showed a 22% mortality reduction, and the compound had no serious adverse events. This answer also introduces a regulatory conclusion that the stimulus cannot support.
explanations.E: Scope creep / overgeneralization. The stimulus covers one compound in one trial population with one specific condition. Concluding that diuretic compounds as a class are 'generally' more effective in younger patients extends far beyond what the data support.

lr.difficultyReason: Two simple categorical facts with a single transitive step; the credited inference follows directly from substituting one set into the other.
lr.stimulus: All licensed pharmacists in the province are required to complete thirty hours of continuing education annually. Every employee at Harbor Drug whose nametag reads 'RPh' is a licensed pharmacist in the province.
lr.questionStem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
