choices.text: Many of those arrested for burglary in previous years were repeat offenders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Last year judges in Oakridge County imposed longer sentences for burglary than in any recent year.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Defense attorneys in Oakridge County are widely regarded as among the most effective in the state.

explanations.correct: When only strong-evidence cases go to trial, a much higher share convict. Even with fewer arrests feeding the pipeline, that higher conviction share can yield more total convictions.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: A baseline rate doesn't explain a year-over-year change.
explanations.C: Repeat-offender status is a background fact; it doesn't address why convictions rose.
explanations.D: Sentence length is about punishment, not whether convictions occur.
explanations.E: Strong defense attorneys would tend to lower, not raise, conviction counts — deepening the paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethicists publicly endorse a principle yet privately decline to follow it — resolved by a single clear distinction between the principle they endorse and the one the situation would require.
lr.stimulus: In a recent survey, 90 percent of professional ethicists publicly endorsed the principle that people have a strong duty to give substantial portions of their income to charity. Yet when asked about their own practice, nearly all of those same ethicists reported giving only a very small share of their income to charity.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent paradox?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most of the ethicists surveyed work at universities where salaries are lower than those in comparable professions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The principle that most of the ethicists endorsed applies, by its own terms, only to people whose income is many times higher than any of the surveyed ethicists earn.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Charities in the ethicists' communities have received less total funding this year than last year.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ethicists surveyed in previous years endorsed the same principle at a similar rate.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most people who donate to charity give without first consulting any ethical principle.

explanations.correct: If the endorsed principle by its own terms applies only to much higher earners, the ethicists' low giving is consistent with their endorsement — the duty they accept simply doesn't bind people at their income level.
explanations.A: Lower salaries might explain small gifts but not why the ethicists endorse a demanding duty they appear to ignore.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Community-wide funding totals don't address the ethicists' individual giving.
explanations.D: Historical endorsement rates don't reconcile the gap between words and deeds.
explanations.E: A claim about most donors doesn't speak to ethicists, who are defined by engaging with principles.

lr.difficultyReason: Two facts with one obvious confounding variable: museum attendance declined despite renovation, but a competing attraction explains both halves.
lr.stimulus: The Metropolitan Museum's renovated East Wing attracted record foot traffic in its opening month. Yet overall museum attendance fell by 12% in the same period. Visitors had simply shifted from the existing galleries to the new East Wing, with no net increase in total visitors.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Metropolitan Museum is the largest art museum in the Western Hemisphere.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The new East Wing galleries charged admission fees in addition to general museum entry.

choices.label: C
choices.text: During the same period, a major competing museum opened across the street and drew large audiences away from the Metropolitan.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Metropolitan Museum's renovation was completed on schedule and under budget.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The East Wing featured works by contemporary artists that were popular among younger visitors.

explanations.correct: A competing museum opening explains why total attendance fell despite the new East Wing's appeal. The East Wing itself can draw record foot traffic from existing visitors, while the competing museum siphons off visitors who would otherwise have come. Both facts become consistent.
explanations.A: Irrelevant to the discrepancy between the East Wing's success and overall attendance decline.
explanations.B: Additional fees would discourage visitors from the new gallery, but this doesn't reconcile the paradox of renovated-wing success with overall attendance loss.
explanations.D: Project completion is unrelated to the attendance discrepancy.
explanations.E: Popularity with younger visitors explains why the East Wing was successful, but doesn't explain why total museum attendance fell.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple self-selection confound: employees who choose flexible schedules may differ systematically from those who don't. One obvious answer identifies this selection effect.
lr.stimulus: A recent survey found that employees with flexible work schedules report higher job satisfaction than those with fixed schedules. Yet when a tech company mandated flexible schedules for all staff, overall employee satisfaction scores actually declined.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent conflict above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Flexible schedules can reduce collaboration and team cohesion if not implemented thoughtfully.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only highly motivated and engaged employees opt into flexible schedules in the first place.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tech company that mandated flexible schedules also raised employee health insurance costs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Employees with flexible schedules work an average of three hours per week more than those with fixed schedules.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Flexible work schedules have become increasingly popular across the technology industry over the past five years.

explanations.correct: If only highly motivated employees self-select into flexible schedules, their higher satisfaction reflects their motivation, not the schedule itself. Mandating flexibility for unmotivated staff won't boost their satisfaction. This resolves the paradox.
explanations.A: While true, this would deepen the paradox by giving a reason flexible schedules harm satisfaction. We need to explain why voluntary users report higher satisfaction despite this drawback.
explanations.C: A confounding policy change that affects satisfaction, but doesn't explain the original survey finding or resolve the core discrepancy.
explanations.D: Longer hours would reduce satisfaction, making it harder to explain why voluntary users are more satisfied initially.
explanations.E: Industry trends are irrelevant to the discrepancy between voluntary and mandatory adoption outcomes.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Medical intervention paradox: a successful treatment for one group fails at the population level. Simple confound: the treatment is given to sicker patients.
lr.stimulus: A newly approved antihypertensive drug proved highly effective in clinical trials, reducing blood pressure in 85% of patients who took it. Yet in hospitals across the country, the drug has had no measurable effect on overall patient mortality rates.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The antihypertensive drug can occasionally cause harmful side effects in patients over age 70.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clinical trials for the drug were conducted in a controlled environment with carefully selected participants.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In hospitals, the drug is typically prescribed only to the most severely hypertensive patients, whose other comorbidities were the primary cause of death.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The drug works best when combined with lifestyle modifications such as dietary changes and exercise.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many competing antihypertensive drugs have been on the market for over a decade.

explanations.correct: In trials, the drug reduced blood pressure (measured outcome). In hospitals, it's given to the sickest patients, whose mortality is driven by other comorbidities, not hypertension alone. Lower blood pressure doesn't prevent death from other causes. This explains the discrepancy.
explanations.A: Side effects would worsen outcomes, deepening the paradox rather than resolving it.
explanations.B: Explains why trials succeeded, but not why hospital outcomes differ—doesn't bridge the paradox.
explanations.D: Lifestyle factors outside the drug's control don't explain the gap between trial efficacy and hospital outcomes.
explanations.E: Competition is irrelevant to the discrepancy between the drug's efficacy and its impact on mortality.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Economic paradox: price reduction fails to increase sales. Obvious confound: external market shift (e.g., competitor or changed demand).
lr.stimulus: A retailer reduced prices on winter coats by 20% in January to clear inventory. Yet sales of winter coats actually fell by 8% compared to the same month last year.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this unexpected result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: January is typically a slow month for coat sales because much of the winter season has already passed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The retailer's competitors offered summer clothing at discount prices during the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An unusually warm January that year reduced consumer demand for winter coats across the entire market.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The retailer's coat inventory consisted of styles that were considered outdated by current fashion standards.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Winter coat manufacturers increased their wholesale prices by 15% earlier that fiscal year.

explanations.correct: Unusually warm weather reduces demand for coats across the market, not just at this retailer. Even with a 20% price cut, fewer people want coats. This explains why the price reduction failed to boost sales.
explanations.A: Irrelevant; January seasonality doesn't explain why prices down but sales down too.
explanations.B: Competitor discounts are a market shift, but summer clothes aren't substitutes for winter coats.
explanations.D: Outdated styles explain slow sales, but not why prices down and sales down—this deepens the paradox.
explanations.E: Wholesale price increases wouldn't cause retail prices to drop or explain the sales decline.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple temporal/compositional shift: reading scores improved overall but appear to fall for a subgroup. Resolution: student population composition changed.
lr.stimulus: State educational data show that test scores in mathematics rose by 6% on average over five years. Yet mathematics teachers report that the students in their classrooms are less prepared and struggle more than students did five years ago.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to reconcile this apparent conflict?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The state's standardized mathematics test was redesigned to be slightly easier two years into the five-year period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A significant influx of students from schools with weaker mathematics curricula transferred into the state's public school system during this period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many experienced mathematics teachers retired and were replaced by less experienced teachers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Students now spend more time on mathematics homework than they did five years ago.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enrollment in advanced mathematics courses has declined in the state over the past five years.

explanations.correct: If the student population changed (influx of less-prepared students), average state scores could rise due to improved performance by original students, while classroom composition feels weaker. Teachers see a less-prepared cohort within their classrooms even as state averages rise.
explanations.A: Easier test would artificially raise scores, but doesn't explain why teachers see weaker students.
explanations.C: Less experienced teachers would likely lower performance, not raise state averages while students struggle.
explanations.D: More homework might improve performance, but not explain why teachers report students are less prepared.
explanations.E: Lower advanced enrollment doesn't explain the discrepancy between rising averages and weaker students in classrooms.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental paradox: conservation effort fails at scale. Simple confound: underlying problem worsens or offsetting behavior emerges.
lr.stimulus: A city promoted residential water conservation with rebates for low-flow faucets and toilets. Participating households reduced water use by 18% per household. Yet the city's total water consumption remained unchanged.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Low-flow faucets require more frequent use because they deliver less water per minute.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Non-participating households increased their water consumption to offset the conservation gains of their neighbors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The rebate program was more popular in wealthy neighborhoods than in lower-income neighborhoods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Water treatment and delivery infrastructure in the city was upgraded during the same period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The city's population grew by 18% during the conservation program period.

explanations.correct: Population growth of 18% would offset the 18% per-household savings exactly, leaving total consumption flat. Both facts become consistent: households conserve successfully, but the city's total consumption stays the same due to more households overall.
explanations.A: More frequent use would reduce the benefit of low-flow devices, but doesn't explain why total city consumption didn't drop.
explanations.B: Offsetting consumption by non-participants is implausible and poorly motivated.
explanations.D: Infrastructure upgrades don't explain why the conservation gains vanished at the city level.
explanations.C: Unequal program uptake doesn't fully explain zero net change in total consumption.
explanations.E: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal/ethical paradox: rule intended to improve fairness produces opposite effect. Resolution: definitional or scope mismatch.
lr.stimulus: A law was enacted to reduce racial disparities in criminal sentencing by limiting judges' discretion. Yet analysis found that sentences remained equally disparate after the law took effect.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this apparent conflict?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Judges have been receiving additional training on implicit bias since the law was passed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prosecutors gained greater discretion in charging decisions and began charging defendants from certain racial groups with more serious crimes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The law applied only to crimes that carry a sentence of more than ten years imprisonment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Criminal defense lawyers became more experienced at negotiating plea agreements after the law took effect.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The law was widely publicized and was well understood by all members of the judiciary.

explanations.correct: Limiting judicial discretion pushed disparity-creation upstream: prosecutors charged defendants differently by race, producing the same disparities before judges even sentenced. The law reduced judicial discretion but prosecutors filled the gap. Disparities persist.
explanations.A: Bias training would likely reduce disparities, not explain their persistence.
explanations.C: Scope limitation doesn't explain equal disparities in covered versus uncovered crimes.
explanations.D: Better plea negotiations don't explain why disparities persisted after the law.
explanations.E: Public understanding doesn't explain why disparities remained unchanged.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology adoption paradox: efficiency improvement doesn't increase output. Obvious resolution: productivity gains redirected to other uses or quality improvements.
lr.stimulus: A manufacturing plant installed new automated machinery that increased production efficiency by 25%. Yet the plant's total output of finished goods remained the same as before the equipment was installed.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this unexpected outcome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The automated machinery required substantial retraining of the plant's workforce.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The new machinery was designed to reduce manufacturing defects and improve product quality.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The plant had previously operated at maximum capacity given market demand for its products.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maintenance costs for the new equipment were higher than for the old equipment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The new machinery is expected to have a useful lifespan of at least twenty years.

explanations.correct: If the plant was already operating at maximum capacity and market demand hadn't increased, the efficiency gain allows it to maintain output while reducing labor hours or costs—not increase output. Output stays flat because demand, not capacity, was the constraint.
explanations.A: Retraining costs don't explain why output stayed the same despite 25% efficiency gain.
explanations.B: Quality improvement is orthogonal to the discrepancy between efficiency and output quantity.
explanations.D: Higher maintenance costs affect profit, not output quantity.
explanations.E: Equipment lifespan is irrelevant to the output paradox.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistic/definitional paradox: word frequency rises but usage declines. Resolution: definition or measurement scope shift (e.g., frequency in one corpus but actual speech different).
lr.stimulus: Linguists have found that the word "utilize" appears more frequently in published academic writing today than it did twenty years ago. Yet surveys of academic speakers indicate that fewer scholars actually use the word when speaking in professional settings.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve this apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The word "utilize" is easier to type than to pronounce in a natural-sounding way.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Academic journals have explicitly encouraged authors to use more varied and sophisticated vocabulary in recent years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The word "utilize" was already at a high frequency in academic writing twenty years ago.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spoken academic discourse and written academic prose have diverged, with written work becoming increasingly formal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The word "utilize" is derived from Latin, whereas most common English words are derived from Germanic roots.

explanations.correct: If written prose has become more formal and "utilize" more frequent in writing, but speech has become less formal and "utilize" less frequent in speaking, both observations are consistent. The domains diverged—writing and speech follow different trends.
explanations.A: Typing versus pronunciation ease doesn't explain the frequency difference between writing and speech.
explanations.B: Encouragement to use varied vocabulary doesn't target "utilize" specifically.
explanations.C: High baseline frequency doesn't explain why it rose in writing but fell in speech.
explanations.E: Etymological origin is unrelated to frequency trends or the written-spoken distinction.
explanations.D: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Historical paradox: same action produces different outcomes. Simple resolution: contextual or temporal difference that changes the meaning of the action.
lr.stimulus: In the early twentieth century, many nations extended voting rights to women, expecting this to transform political landscapes dramatically. Yet in most of these nations, electoral outcomes and policy priorities shifted only marginally after women gained the vote.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this apparent conflict?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Women's voting patterns tended to reflect the voting patterns of male family members in their household.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many nations also reformed their tax codes in the early twentieth century.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Women's literacy rates were generally higher in nations that granted voting rights earlier.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The extension of voting rights to women was celebrated by many international observers as a moral victory.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many nations also expanded public education around the same time women gained the vote.

explanations.correct: If women's votes aligned with men's—reflecting household patriarchal influence or shared socioeconomic interests—then women voting wouldn't change electoral outcomes. Adding votes for the same preferences doesn't shift results. Both facts become consistent.
explanations.B: Tax code reforms are orthogonal to the impact of female suffrage on electoral outcomes.
explanations.C: Higher literacy would predict greater political independence, not explain why outcomes stayed stable.
explanations.D: Moral celebration doesn't explain why electoral results remained marginal.
explanations.E: Educational expansion is unrelated to the narrowness of female suffrage's electoral impact.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Clear paradox with one obvious confounding variable. A town's park attendance fell despite expansion; a new entertainment complex opened nearby. Only one answer addresses both horns: competing attraction.
lr.stimulus: The Riverside Park was expanded by 40 percent last year, adding new trails and recreational facilities. Yet the total number of park visitors declined by 15 percent. Curiously, surveys show most residents still view the park favorably.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The park's survey asked only residents who lived within one mile of the park.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A new indoor recreation complex opened nearby during the same year and charges lower admission than the park.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The park's expansion project created temporary disruptions that lasted several months.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Residents who use the park consider it one of the town's most important community assets.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The park's maintenance budget did not increase proportionally with the expansion.

explanations.correct: If a competing attraction (cheaper rec complex) opened the same year, it explains why attendance fell despite the park's expansion. The park improved, but visitors migrated to a cheaper alternative. Both facts are now consistent.
explanations.A: Survey methodology doesn't explain the actual decline in visitor numbers.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Temporary disruptions might explain a short-term dip, but the question implies a sustained decline.
explanations.D: Favorable views don't resolve why actual attendance dropped.
explanations.E: Maintenance budget doesn't address the core paradox of expanded facilities yet fewer visitors.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward paradox: expensive drug reduces treatment costs overall. One obvious confound: drug prevents a much costlier downstream condition. Only answer addressing both halves.
lr.stimulus: A new pharmaceutical treatment costs three times as much as the standard therapy for early-stage hypertension. Yet hospitals that adopted the new treatment reported a 20 percent decrease in their overall treatment costs for hypertensive patients within two years.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent paradox?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The new treatment is covered by most major insurance plans.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients taking the new treatment are more likely to adhere to their medication regimen.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The new treatment reduces the incidence of stroke and heart attack, which are far more expensive to treat than hypertension itself.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hospitals began tracking treatment costs more carefully after adopting the new treatment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The standard therapy has been in use for over thirty years.

explanations.correct: If the new treatment prevents much more expensive complications (stroke, heart attack), it saves money downstream despite its upfront cost. This reconciles the high per-patient cost with lower overall costs.
explanations.A: Insurance coverage doesn't explain why hospitals' overall costs decreased.
explanations.B: Adherence alone doesn't explain the cost savings without addressing what the drug prevents.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Accounting practices don't create actual cost savings.
explanations.E: Age of the standard therapy is irrelevant to the cost paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: Clear two-part discrepancy: book sales up, but bookstore locations down. One obvious resolution: online retail diverted traffic. Direct confounding variable.
lr.stimulus: Over the last decade, book sales in the United States increased by 12 percent. However, the number of independent bookstores declined by 30 percent during the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Large bookstore chains have also experienced a decline in the number of their retail locations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The average price of books has increased over the last decade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Online retailers and digital formats have captured a growing share of the book market.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many independent bookstore owners have retired and not been replaced.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Readers are purchasing books from a wider variety of genres than they did ten years ago.

explanations.correct: If online retailers and digital formats have grown, they explain how total book sales can increase while brick-and-mortar locations decline. Books are still selling; the channel has shifted.
explanations.A: Chain decline doesn't resolve the discrepancy; it deepens it.
explanations.B: Price increases might explain some sales growth, but don't address store closures.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Retirement of owners is a causal factor in closures, but doesn't explain why total sales rose.
explanations.E: Genre diversity doesn't relate to the sales-vs.-locations paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple paradox: test scores up, student satisfaction down. One clear confound: test difficulty increased, so higher scores reflect harder test, not better teaching.
lr.stimulus: In recent years, students' standardized test scores at Lincoln High School have risen steadily, yet student satisfaction surveys indicate that academic morale is at its lowest point in a decade.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The school hired several new teachers with advanced degrees in their respective subjects.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The standardized test was redesigned to be significantly more difficult, and the scoring scale was adjusted upward accordingly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Student satisfaction surveys were administered online, which may have increased response rates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The school increased the frequency of standardized testing from twice a year to three times a year.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many of the school's most experienced teachers retired during this period.

explanations.correct: If the test became harder and the scale adjusted upward, higher scores don't reflect improved student learning—they reflect a measurement artifact. Students may feel stressed by harder material, explaining lower satisfaction.
explanations.A: New credentialed teachers should improve satisfaction, contradicting the data.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Survey administration method doesn't address the content paradox.
explanations.D: More frequent testing might explain lower satisfaction, but not the score rise directly.
explanations.E: Teacher retirements should lower scores, not raise them.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward paradox: restaurant hours reduced, but profit increased. One obvious resolution: reduction eliminated unprofitable late-night hours. Single confounding factor.
lr.stimulus: A downtown restaurant recently reduced its operating hours by closing late-night service. Yet the owner reports that monthly profits have increased since the change was implemented.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent paradox?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The restaurant had been using the same suppliers for over five years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The late-night customers typically ordered less food than daytime customers and tipped smaller amounts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The restaurant is located in an area with high pedestrian traffic during the day.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Other restaurants in the area remain open late at night.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The owner reduced prices on breakfast items after eliminating late-night service.

explanations.correct: If late-night customers spent less and tipped less, eliminating those hours removes unprofitable business. Profits rise despite fewer operating hours. Both facts are reconciled.
explanations.A: Supplier relationships don't explain the profit paradox.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Daytime traffic is good, but doesn't explain why profits rose when hours decreased.
explanations.D: Competitor hours don't affect this restaurant's profit paradox.
explanations.E: Price reductions would lower profits, not raise them.

lr.difficultyReason: Clear paradox: forest area stable, but biodiversity declining. One obvious confound: remaining forest is fragmented and degraded. Environmental science example with single clear resolution.
lr.stimulus: According to recent surveys, the total forest area in the region has remained relatively constant over the past fifteen years. Yet the number of native bird species inhabiting those forests has declined by 25 percent.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some migratory bird species have altered their migration patterns in response to climate change.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The remaining forests have been fragmented into smaller, isolated patches due to development, reducing habitat quality for many native species.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Local hunting regulations were relaxed during the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: New forest management policies have increased the harvesting of deadwood, which was previously left on the forest floor.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The surveys were conducted using different methodologies in the early and late periods.

explanations.correct: If forests are fragmented into isolated patches, the total area may be constant but habitat quality and connectivity decline, explaining the loss of bird species despite stable forest acreage.
explanations.A: Climate-driven migration changes don't explain habitat loss in a stable forest.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Relaxed hunting might further harm populations, but doesn't explain species loss in stable forests.
explanations.D: Deadwood harvesting is a management detail; doesn't address the quantity-vs.-quality paradox.
explanations.E: Methodological differences don't explain real ecological decline.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple paradox: museum admission free, but operating costs up. One obvious resolution: free admission increased volume, raising facility and staffing costs. Direct causal link.
lr.stimulus: The Riverside Museum eliminated its admission fee last year to increase attendance. The museum did indeed see a 35 percent increase in visitors. However, the museum's annual operating costs increased by 40 percent.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this apparent paradox?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The museum did not adjust its staff levels when the admission fee was eliminated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many of the museum's visitors are residents of the surrounding neighborhood.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cost of maintaining the museum's exhibits has not changed significantly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Free admission required increased custodial, utility, and security resources to accommodate more visitors.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The museum conducted a survey before eliminating the admission fee.

explanations.correct: If higher visitor volume requires more custodial, utility, and security resources, costs rise despite the loss of admission revenue. This explains why visitor numbers up by 35% but costs up by 40%.
explanations.A: Fixed staffing doesn't explain the cost increase beyond visitor volume.
explanations.B: Neighborhood composition doesn't explain the cost paradox.
explanations.C: If maintenance costs unchanged, other operational costs (utilities, custodial, security) must have risen.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Pre-policy surveys don't address the actual cost paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: Clear paradox: country exports more, trade deficit grows. One obvious confound: imports grew even faster. Simple arithmetic-based discrepancy with one clear resolution.
lr.stimulus: The country's exports increased by 8 percent last year, yet the overall trade deficit grew to its highest level in a decade.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exchange rates have become more stable in recent years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The country's imports increased by 15 percent during the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The country's largest trading partners also increased their exports to other nations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Government trade policies were relatively unchanged during the past year.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Consumer confidence in the country increased significantly last year.

explanations.correct: If imports grew 15% while exports only grew 8%, the deficit gap widens. Both facts are consistent: exports up but imports up faster, net negative gap grows.
explanations.A: Exchange rate stability doesn't explain the trade deficit growth.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Other nations' exports don't directly affect this country's trade balance.
explanations.D: Policy consistency doesn't address the paradox.
explanations.E: Consumer confidence might affect imports, but doesn't directly resolve the discrepancy.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward paradox: technology investment high, worker productivity unchanged. One obvious resolution: transition period and retraining costs offset immediate gains. Clear temporal confound.
lr.stimulus: Apex Manufacturing invested heavily in new automation technology last year, yet measurements of worker productivity per hour showed no significant improvement.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The company's competitors have not yet adopted similar automation technology.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Workers required extensive retraining and the company experienced startup inefficiencies during the first year of implementation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The new technology was purchased from an international supplier.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The company's profit margins decreased slightly during the same period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Worker satisfaction surveys showed improved morale after the technology was installed.

explanations.correct: If retraining and startup inefficiencies offset the technology's gains in the first year, productivity shows no net improvement despite the investment. Gains should materialize later.
explanations.A: Competitor status doesn't affect this company's productivity paradox.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Supplier location is irrelevant to productivity outcomes.
explanations.D: Profit margins don't directly explain worker productivity stagnation.
explanations.E: Worker morale doesn't resolve why measured productivity didn't improve.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple paradox: popular law yet enforcement rare. One obvious resolution: law is symbolic/political, with low enforcement resources. Clear discrepancy between adoption and implementation.
lr.stimulus: A city council unanimously passed a new environmental ordinance that was hailed as groundbreaking by environmental advocates. Yet city officials report that the ordinance is almost never enforced due to resource constraints.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The city council consists of eight members, all of whom support environmental protection.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Environmental ordinances in neighboring cities have also faced enforcement challenges.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The environmental ordinance contained detailed requirements that are expensive to monitor and enforce.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Advocates plan to challenge the ordinance in court if it is strictly enforced.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The city has experienced budget cuts in recent years.

explanations.correct: If the ordinance is expensive to monitor and enforce, the city council could unanimously support it (politically popular) while enforcement remains impractical (resource-intensive). Both facts coexist.
explanations.A: Council support doesn't explain why enforcement is lacking.
explanations.B: Other cities' challenges don't explain this city's specific paradox.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Legal challenges don't explain current non-enforcement.
explanations.E: While budget cuts might enable the paradox, they don't explain why the council passed an unenforceable law, or define the relationship between passage and enforcement.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple two-fact conflict with one obvious confounder: park attendance fell despite expansion. Correct answer identifies a competing attraction opened simultaneously. Only one choice addresses both horns.
lr.stimulus: Riverside Park expanded its facilities by 40 percent last year, yet attendance actually declined by 15 percent. However, a new entertainment complex opened two blocks away the same month the park's expansion was completed.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Riverside Park raised its admission fee by 10 percent when the expansion was completed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The new entertainment complex offered free admission during its first three months of operation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The park's new facilities were not yet fully operational at the time of the attendance measurement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Other parks in the region reported stable attendance figures during the same period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The park's original facilities remained open and functional throughout the expansion project.

explanations.correct: If the new entertainment complex offered free admission, this explains why people visited it instead of the expanded park, even though the park expanded. Both facts—expansion and attendance decline—are now reconciled by competition from the free alternative.
explanations.A: A fee increase would explain the attendance decline, but it doesn't explain why the park expanded in the first place, leaving the scenario still counterintuitive.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Operational delays would explain lower attendance but don't resolve why the park bothered expanding immediately, and doesn't touch the real cause.
explanations.D: Other parks' stability doesn't explain why this park's attendance fell despite its own improvements.
explanations.E: Keeping original facilities operational is irrelevant to the conflict between expansion and declining attendance.

lr.stimulus_note: Two-part stimulus: (1) park expanded 40%, (2) attendance declined 15%. Stimulus triggers paradox structure.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward medical case: drug reduces symptom severity yet doesn't improve patient outcomes. Correct answer identifies that patients stop taking drug early because symptoms improve, leaving underlying condition untreated. Single obvious mechanism resolves both facts.
lr.stimulus: A new antifever medication reduces fever severity in 85 percent of patients who take it, yet clinical trials show it does not improve overall patient recovery rates. Despite this, doctors continue to prescribe it.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The medication has fewer side effects than older fever-reducing drugs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients often stop taking the medication once their fever subsides, before the underlying infection is fully resolved.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fever is a symptom that naturally subsides over time in most patients.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The medication works by stimulating the immune system rather than by lowering body temperature.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Insurance companies readily cover the cost of this medication.

explanations.correct: If patients quit taking the medication as soon as symptoms improve, they interrupt the course of treatment before the underlying infection is cured. This explains why symptom relief doesn't translate to better outcomes—the medication works, but patients stop prematurely.
explanations.A: Fewer side effects explains why doctors prefer it, but doesn't reconcile the symptom relief vs. no-outcome-improvement paradox.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: If fever subsides naturally, this would question why the medication gets credit for symptom relief at all, deepening rather than resolving the paradox.
explanations.D: The mechanism of action doesn't explain why symptom relief doesn't improve recovery.
explanations.E: Insurance coverage is irrelevant to the symptom relief vs. patient outcomes conflict.

lr.stimulus_note: Medication reduces fever severity (85%) but doesn't improve recovery outcomes. Doctors still prescribe. Paradox structure is clear.

lr.difficultyReason: Economics domain: handmade goods priced higher than mass-produced alternatives, yet handmade market is growing. Correct answer identifies luxury/status signal mechanism. Clear single confounder.
lr.stimulus: Handmade pottery sells for three times the price of machine-produced pottery, yet sales of handmade pottery have increased 35 percent in the past two years. Machine-produced pottery sales have remained flat.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Machine-produced pottery is sold in more retail locations than handmade pottery.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumers increasingly view handmade goods as status symbols and are willing to pay premiums for them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The prices of both handmade and machine-produced pottery have risen over the past two years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Handmade pottery is more durable than machine-produced pottery.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mass production has become more efficient, lowering the cost of machine-produced pottery.

explanations.correct: If handmade goods are now valued as status symbols, higher prices no longer deter purchase—they actually attract buyers seeking exclusivity and prestige. This explains why raising prices coincides with growing sales.
explanations.A: Distribution differences don't explain why higher prices drive growth in handmade sales.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Price increases apply to both categories, so this doesn't explain why handmade sales grew while machine-produced sales stagnated.
explanations.D: Superior durability might justify higher prices but doesn't explain why sales grew despite the price premium.
explanations.E: Lower machine-produced prices would make the flat sales even more paradoxical, not less.

lr.stimulus_note: Handmade pottery is 3x more expensive yet sales grew 35%. Contrast setup is explicit.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science: conservation effort preserves species yet total wild population stable. Correct answer identifies that without effort, population would have crashed. Obvious temporal/counterfactual logic.
lr.stimulus: An endangered bird species was protected through strict hunting bans and habitat restoration spanning twelve years. Yet the species' total population in the wild has remained stable rather than increasing noticeably.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The bird species reproduces slowly and only reaches sexual maturity after five years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Without the hunting bans and habitat restoration, the species would have become extinct within the same twelve-year period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Other endangered bird species in the same region have shown population increases after similar conservation efforts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The bird species has no natural predators in its habitat.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Illegal hunting of the species continues in remote areas despite the official ban.

explanations.correct: If the population would have crashed without intervention, maintaining stability is actually a conservation success. The paradox dissolves when we recognize that 'no growth' in the context of prevention is not a failure.
explanations.A: Slow reproduction explains why growth is slow, but doesn't reconcile why a costly, multi-year effort produced no noticeable gains.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Other species' success doesn't explain this species' lack of growth.
explanations.D: Absence of predators doesn't explain why strict protection didn't yield population increases.
explanations.E: Ongoing poaching would actually explain the lack of growth, but this makes the story worse, not better resolved.

lr.stimulus_note: Strict 12-year conservation effort on endangered bird, yet stable (not growing) population. Paradox about effort and outcome.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology domain: tech company acquired for high price yet posted losses. Correct answer identifies acquisition valued intellectual property/patents, not current earnings. Single, obvious mechanism.
lr.stimulus: A technology startup was acquired by a major corporation for 500 million dollars, yet the startup had posted significant financial losses in each of the three years prior to acquisition.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Technology startups typically operate at a loss during their first five years of operation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The acquiring corporation anticipated that the startup's patents and technology would generate substantial future revenues.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The startup had been founded by engineers who previously worked at the acquiring corporation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The technology sector experienced rapid growth in the years immediately preceding the acquisition.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Other startups in the same field were acquired at lower prices during the same period.

explanations.correct: If the acquirer valued the startup's intellectual property and future potential rather than its current earnings, the high acquisition price makes sense despite losses. The price reflects future value, not past performance.
explanations.A: That startups commonly run at a loss explains the pattern generally but doesn't explain why this specific unprofitable startup commanded such a high price.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The founders' history doesn't explain the valuation premium.
explanations.D: Sector growth might encourage acquisitions generally but doesn't explain why losses don't reduce valuation.
explanations.E: Other companies' prices don't explain this company's valuation.

lr.stimulus_note: Startup with 3-year losses acquired for $500M. Paradox: why pay so much for a losing company?

lr.difficultyReason: History/policy: law intended to increase voter participation yet voter turnout declined in following election. Correct answer identifies confounding factor (competing election distraction). Single clear mechanism.
lr.stimulus: A state legislature passed a law making voter registration simpler and more accessible. Yet in the election held immediately after the law took effect, voter turnout in that state decreased by 5 percent compared to the previous election.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The state legislature also passed laws reducing the length of the voting period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The previous election had coincided with a highly contested gubernatorial race, while the subsequent election involved primarily local and state legislative races.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Voter registration has been shown to increase voter participation in some states but not others.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The new registration law was passed by the state legislature only weeks before the election.

choices.label: E
choices.text: In neighboring states, voter turnout also declined during the same election cycle.

explanations.correct: If the previous election featured a high-stakes gubernatorial race while the subsequent one did not, the lower turnout reflects reduced voter interest in the contest, not a failure of registration reform. The easier registration couldn't overcome voter apathy toward less prominent races.
explanations.A: Voting period restrictions would explain lower turnout directly, but this contradicts the stimulus's assumption that registration was the intended driver.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: That registration helps in some states but not others is too vague and doesn't resolve the specific paradox here.
explanations.D: Late passage explains why registration uptake might be slow, but doesn't directly reconcile the turnout decline.
explanations.E: Regional turnout patterns don't explain the state-specific paradox.

lr.stimulus_note: Law simplifying registration passed, yet turnout declined in next election. Paradox structure clear.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics: new grammar rule taught in schools yet standardized test scores declined. Correct answer identifies that scores measure older writing standard, creating temporal mismatch. Single obvious resolution.
lr.stimulus: A school district implemented a new grammar curriculum emphasizing clearer sentence structure, yet student performance on standardized writing tests declined by 8 percent in the year following implementation.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The new curriculum required students to learn significantly more grammar rules than the previous curriculum.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The standardized test had not been updated in ten years and continued to assess writing skills according to older grammatical standards.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Student writing improved in other measures such as paragraph organization and use of evidence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The new curriculum was developed by linguists with expertise in sentence composition.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Other school districts that implemented the same curriculum also saw declining test scores.

explanations.correct: If the test hasn't been updated and measures an older standard, the new curriculum's improved structure might conflict with what the outdated test assesses. Students taught the new way perform worse on a test designed for the old way—a measurement mismatch, not a curriculum failure.
explanations.A: Learning more rules might explain why scores dipped initially, but this doesn't resolve the paradox; it deepens it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Improvements in other areas don't explain why the tested measure declined.
explanations.D: Expert development doesn't explain poor test performance.
explanations.E: Other districts' results don't explain the local paradox.

lr.stimulus_note: New grammar curriculum emphasizing clarity, yet writing test scores declined. Paradox stem present.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics/law: company's ethical code expanded yet employee ethics complaints increased. Correct answer identifies that expanded code awareness enables more complaints to be filed. Single obvious mechanism.
lr.stimulus: A corporation revised its ethics code to be more comprehensive and established a new confidential complaint hotline. Yet the number of ethics violations reported by employees nearly tripled in the following year.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The corporation's profits declined significantly during the year following the ethics code revision.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Employees who previously feared retaliation for reporting violations were now confident that the anonymous hotline would protect their identity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ethics violations in the corporation's industry increased overall during the same time period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The corporation hired a new chief ethics officer to oversee compliance with the code.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Other corporations in the industry did not establish confidential complaint mechanisms.

explanations.correct: If employees were previously afraid to report violations but now feel protected by anonymity, the tripling of reports reflects not an increase in actual violations but an increase in *reporting* of pre-existing violations. The ethics code enabled disclosure, not misconduct.
explanations.A: Profit decline might explain increased unethical behavior, but doesn't address why a better code and safer reporting channel would increase complaints.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Industry-wide increase doesn't explain why this specific corporation's reported violations tripled after policy changes.
explanations.D: A new officer might oversee code enforcement but doesn't explain why violations nearly tripled specifically after the changes.
explanations.E: Competitors' lack of mechanisms doesn't explain this corporation's reported increase.

lr.stimulus_note: Comprehensive ethics code and anonymous hotline established, yet ethics complaints tripled. Paradox stem clear.

lr.difficultyReason: Vaccination coverage rose while the proportion of hospitalized flu patients who were vaccinated also rose — a genuine tension that dissolves only once one recognizes the base-rate shift: when nearly everyone is vaccinated, most of the unavoidable residual cases will by arithmetic be among vaccinated people. The trap answers each explain the rise in coverage or the rise in hospitalizations in isolation.
lr.stimulus: Public-health officials report that the share of adults in Kerrow Province who received the annual flu vaccine rose from 40 percent to 85 percent over the past decade. Nevertheless, the proportion of patients hospitalized for influenza during that period who had been vaccinated also rose sharply — from 18 percent to 70 percent.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The influenza vaccine substantially reduces, but does not eliminate, a vaccinated person's risk of contracting the flu.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hospitals in Kerrow Province have expanded their capacity to treat influenza patients over the past decade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Public-health officials in Kerrow Province encouraged older adults, who are more likely to be hospitalized if infected, to receive the vaccine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: New strains of influenza circulating in the past decade have been more virulent than those circulating earlier.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients who are vaccinated against influenza typically recover from hospitalization more quickly than unvaccinated patients do.

explanations.correct: When 85 percent of adults are vaccinated, the unvaccinated pool is tiny; any residual hospitalizations are drawn mostly from the vaccinated majority even though each vaccinated person is individually at lower risk. Both facts coexist once one sees that a large vaccinated share produces a large vaccinated share of cases by sheer base rate.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Expanded hospital capacity doesn't explain the composition of the hospitalized population by vaccination status.
explanations.C: Deepens the paradox — if the people most likely to be hospitalized were prioritized for vaccination, one would expect vaccination to reduce their share of hospitalizations.
explanations.D: Would explain a rise in hospitalizations overall but does not explain why the vaccinated share of them rose so sharply.
explanations.E: Recovery time doesn't bear on the proportion of hospitalized patients who had been vaccinated.

lr.difficultyReason: Raising the minimum wage should, on the standard story, reduce employment in low-wage sectors; yet employment rose. Resolution requires noticing a confounder — the low-wage sector expanded because consumers had more money to spend. Traps explain only half the picture or invoke the wrong mechanism.
lr.stimulus: Two years ago, the state of Velmar raised its minimum wage by 35 percent. Economists had predicted that employment in low-wage sectors such as food service and retail would fall. However, employment in those sectors has since risen by 8 percent, even as the predicted wage floor was strictly enforced.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most low-wage workers in Velmar spend nearly all their additional earnings on goods and services provided by the food-service and retail sectors, increasing demand for those sectors' workers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inflation in Velmar has outpaced that of neighboring states over the past two years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The minimum wage in Velmar is now higher than that of any neighboring state.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some low-wage employers in Velmar have responded to the increase by reducing their employees' weekly hours.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Before the wage increase, food-service and retail businesses in Velmar had unusually high rates of employee turnover.

explanations.correct: The predicted drop assumed demand for low-wage labor would be roughly fixed. If raising wages routes money right back into the sectors that employ those workers, demand for their labor actually grows, absorbing the higher wage cost and producing net hiring. Both the wage increase and the employment rise are explained by a single mechanism.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Higher inflation might erode the real value of the wage increase but doesn't explain why employment rose.
explanations.C: A cross-state comparison doesn't explain within-Velmar employment changes.
explanations.D: Deepens the paradox in a sense — hour reductions would point toward employers cutting back on labor, the opposite of what was observed.
explanations.E: Prior turnover rates don't explain why employment levels rose after the wage increase.

lr.difficultyReason: Pesticide use fell dramatically yet pollinator populations continued to decline — a tension that resolves once a second environmental factor (habitat loss from agricultural expansion driven by the same policy) is introduced. Distractors cite unrelated environmental stressors or re-describe the decline.
lr.stimulus: Over the past decade, farmers in the Landry River basin, following a widely adopted voluntary program, reduced their use of bee-toxic pesticides by nearly two-thirds. Yet during the same period, populations of native bees and other pollinators in the basin continued to decline at roughly the same rate as before the program began.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Other regions that did not adopt the voluntary pesticide-reduction program have also seen pollinator populations decline, though at a slower rate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To offset lower yields from reduced pesticide use, farmers in the Landry basin cleared large tracts of hedgerow and wildflower meadow to plant additional crop acreage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many of the pesticides that remained in use after the reductions are still moderately harmful to pollinators.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some farmers in the Landry basin adopted the voluntary program only in its final years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pollinator populations are difficult to count accurately because the insects range widely across agricultural landscapes.

explanations.correct: If the very program that reduced pesticide exposure also drove farmers to destroy the wild habitats pollinators depend on, the lost habitat offsets the chemical benefit. Both facts — reduced pesticide use and continued decline — become mutually consistent once the habitat-loss channel is made visible.
explanations.A: A slower decline elsewhere actually suggests the program helped a little, but doesn't explain why the program's basin continued to decline at the prior rate.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Residual harm would slow the expected gains, not eliminate them — and wouldn't explain continued decline at the prior rate.
explanations.D: Late adoption might delay benefits for some farms but can't account for a basin-wide two-thirds reduction producing no effect.
explanations.E: Measurement difficulty calls the data into question rather than explaining it.

lr.difficultyReason: More automated tests yet more bugs in production — resolved by a measurement artifact: the automated tests surface bugs that were previously shipping undetected, so 'bugs found' grew even as shipped-bug quality rose. Trap answers invoke the wrong direction of causation or target the wrong metric.
lr.stimulus: At Horizon Software, the engineering team doubled its investment in automated testing over the past year, and the number of tests run before each release more than tripled. Even so, the number of bugs reported by users within 30 days of each release rose by 20 percent over the same year.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most of Horizon's engineers have been writing automated tests for less than two years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Horizon's main competitors have also reported rising user bug counts over the past year.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The expansion of automated testing allowed Horizon to confidently ship four times as many new features as it did the previous year.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some categories of bugs can be caught only through manual testing, which Horizon reduced as automation expanded.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Users have become more likely to file bug reports than they were a year ago.

explanations.correct: If automated testing let Horizon ship four times as many features, each feature carrying even a modest bug rate would yield many more total bugs overall. Automated tests can raise per-feature reliability while the sheer volume of shipped features increases bug totals. Both facts are then jointly true.
explanations.A: If anything, this weakens automated testing's value but doesn't explain how a tripling of tests still let more bugs through — unless paired with some offsetting factor the answer doesn't supply.
explanations.B: Industry-wide trends don't explain Horizon's specific year-over-year change.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Provides a plausible partial mechanism — reduced manual testing could leak bugs — but doesn't explain why the team's overall testing program, which tripled total tests, failed to prevent a net rise; it is too narrow and depends on an undisclosed tradeoff.
explanations.E: A reporting-propensity change would explain the rise in reports without assuming any real change in bugs, but it doesn't connect to the expansion in automated testing that is the other half of the tension.

lr.difficultyReason: Average reading scores fell despite curriculum improvements — resolved by a selection-effect shift in which students were tested. Distractors invoke plausible but orthogonal causes.
lr.stimulus: The Brookford school district overhauled its elementary reading curriculum three years ago, incorporating methods that independent studies have shown to improve reading proficiency. Yet the average reading scores of Brookford fifth-graders on the statewide assessment have fallen each year since the new curriculum was introduced.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The statewide assessment is administered each spring by independent proctors, not by Brookford teachers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Since the new curriculum was introduced, Brookford schools have stopped exempting struggling readers from the assessment, whereas previously such students were routinely excused.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several neighboring districts have since adopted the same reading curriculum that Brookford adopted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The statewide assessment was redesigned seven years ago to emphasize inferential reasoning over decoding skills.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Brookford teachers received training in the new curriculum only during the summer before it was introduced.

explanations.correct: If the pool of test-takers now includes students who used to be excused, the tested population is weaker on average even though each individual student may be improving. The curriculum can be working while the average score falls because the measured sample has shifted.
explanations.A: Independent proctoring was presumably also in place before and so doesn't distinguish the before-and-after periods.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Neighboring districts' choices don't bear on Brookford's year-over-year scores.
explanations.D: An assessment change seven years ago predates the curriculum overhaul and so can't explain the trend beginning three years ago.
explanations.E: Limited training might blunt the curriculum's impact but wouldn't produce falling scores beyond the baseline — and doesn't reconcile improved methods with worsening results.

lr.difficultyReason: Reported burglaries fell while actual burglaries may not have — a reporting artifact that reconciles falling stats with unchanged or rising victimization. Distractors attribute the drop to policing or target neighboring jurisdictions.
lr.stimulus: According to statistics released by the Haldin Police Department, the number of residential burglaries reported in Haldin fell by 22 percent last year. Nonetheless, an anonymous survey of Haldin residents conducted by an independent research institute found that the proportion of households that had experienced a break-in during the same year was essentially unchanged from the previous year.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Last year, many Haldin insurers began requiring that policyholders file a police report within 24 hours of a burglary to remain eligible for reimbursement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Last year, several Haldin residents announced they would stop filing police reports after a widely publicized case in which officers were slow to respond to burglary calls.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Haldin Police Department last year reassigned a significant number of officers from burglary investigation to traffic enforcement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neighboring cities have reported modest increases in residential burglary over the past year.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most Haldin burglaries involve the theft of items valued at less than one thousand dollars.

explanations.correct: If a public loss of confidence caused fewer victims to file reports, the official count falls while the underlying rate of break-ins — captured by the anonymous survey — stays the same. Both datasets can be accurate: one measures reporting, the other measures incidence.
explanations.A: Deepens the paradox — tying insurance reimbursement to reports would increase reporting rates, which should raise, not lower, the official count.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Reduced investigation resources don't explain a drop in reports filed; victims file regardless of what investigators do afterward.
explanations.D: Cross-city trends don't reconcile the within-Haldin discrepancy.
explanations.E: The value of stolen items is irrelevant to whether burglaries are reported or occurring.

lr.difficultyReason: Surgeons with higher complication rates publish better outcomes — resolved by a selection effect: top surgeons take the hardest cases. Distractors invoke unrelated factors about training or publication practices.
lr.stimulus: A review of cardiac surgical data from ten major hospitals found that surgeons whose published long-term survival rates were the highest also had, on average, the highest rates of serious intraoperative complications. Ordinarily one would expect surgeons with fewer complications to achieve better long-term outcomes.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The surgeons with the highest published long-term survival rates are routinely referred the most complex and high-risk cases, which carry an inherently elevated risk of intraoperative complications.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intraoperative complications are reported more consistently by surgeons who also publish long-term survival data.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Long-term survival is determined not only by surgical outcomes but also by patients' post-operative care.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Surgeons with the lowest intraoperative complication rates tend to perform the highest volume of routine procedures.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cardiac surgeons generally receive more specialized training than surgeons in other fields.

explanations.correct: Top surgeons' case mix is skewed toward the hardest cases, which carry higher baseline complication risk, even as their skill yields superior long-term survival. The two statistics move together not because complications cause survival but because both track case difficulty and surgeon expertise.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Might make complication data look higher for some surgeons without any real difference, but doesn't explain why the same surgeons have the best survival rates.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant — post-operative care doesn't explain the within-surgeon link between intraoperative complications and published survival.
explanations.D: Explains why low-complication surgeons have low complications but not why their long-term survival is lower.
explanations.E: Cross-specialty training comparisons are beside the point.

lr.difficultyReason: Learners who spend more time immersed score worse on grammar tests — resolved by a subpopulation contrast: more-immersed learners are the less advanced ones who were placed in immersion precisely because they needed help. Distractors target test design or motivation.
lr.stimulus: A language institute reports that its intermediate Spanish students who spend the greatest number of hours each week in conversational immersion sessions score lower on the institute's end-of-term grammar exam than students who spend fewer hours in those sessions. The institute's director is surprised, since immersion is widely credited with improving grammar.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The institute assigns students with weaker entry-level grammar skills to more hours of conversational immersion than those with stronger skills.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The end-of-term grammar exam covers material that is also practiced in immersion sessions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students who enroll in the institute's intermediate program differ widely in their prior exposure to Spanish.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Conversational immersion sessions at the institute are led by native speakers of Spanish.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The institute's grammar exam is generally regarded as more difficult than similar exams at comparable schools.

explanations.correct: If weaker students are routed into more immersion, they may still score lower at term's end than stronger peers even if immersion helps each of them. The hours–score correlation reflects placement by need, not a harmful effect of immersion. This is the textbook confound.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Would make the grammar exam fairer to immersion students, deepening the paradox rather than resolving it.
explanations.C: Variation in prior exposure is a generic fact that doesn't connect hours of immersion to exam performance.
explanations.D: Native instruction if anything supports immersion's value and deepens the puzzle.
explanations.E: Exam difficulty applies uniformly to all students and so doesn't explain the difference between more- and less-immersed students.

lr.difficultyReason: A bike-lane network expansion coincided with an increase in cyclist injuries — resolved by an exposure effect: the lanes drew far more people to ride, so aggregate injuries rose even as per-rider injury risk fell. Traps misattribute the rise to infrastructure flaws or deepen the paradox.
lr.stimulus: The city of Marston built 85 miles of new protected bike lanes between 2020 and 2024. Studies of other cities' bike-lane networks have consistently found that such lanes reduce a cyclist's chance of being injured in traffic. Yet during those four years in Marston, the total number of cyclists injured in traffic accidents rose by 60 percent.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: As the protected lane network expanded, the number of residents who commuted regularly by bicycle in Marston more than tripled.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The protected bike lanes in Marston are not physically separated from car traffic at intersections.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marston's traffic enforcement staff was reduced during the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Studies of bike-lane safety in other cities focused on lanes used primarily for recreational rather than commuter cycling.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The injury statistics for Marston include only injuries serious enough to require medical attention.

explanations.correct: A threefold rise in cyclists absorbs a smaller per-rider risk and still yields many more total injuries. The per-rider safety benefit and the aggregate injury increase are compatible once exposure is factored in.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: If intersections are the weak link, that might partially weaken the benefit — but alone it doesn't reconcile a 60 percent rise with a well-documented safety effect from completed lane segments.
explanations.C: Reduced enforcement is a plausible confound but doesn't specifically target the cyclist injury rise tied to lane construction.
explanations.D: Undermines the applicability of prior studies but doesn't explain the injury rise by itself.
explanations.E: A consistent reporting threshold applies across years and thus doesn't explain a 60 percent change.

lr.difficultyReason: Ticket sales fell while ticket revenue rose — resolved by a price-composition shift that altered average ticket price upward. Distractors address attendance growth, marketing, or adjacent venues.
lr.stimulus: The Granville Symphony Orchestra reports that the number of tickets sold to its concerts fell by 15 percent this season compared with last season. Even so, total revenue from ticket sales rose by nearly 25 percent over the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The orchestra eliminated its least expensive ticket tier this season and added a new premium tier priced at more than three times the previous top price.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The orchestra presented several of its most popular programs this season.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ticket prices at comparable orchestras in other cities also rose this season.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The orchestra's hall underwent renovations midway through last season, reducing available seating.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Season subscribers make up a larger share of the orchestra's audience than single-ticket buyers do.
