explanations.correct: Removing the cheapest seats and adding a much more expensive top tier raises the average price paid per ticket sharply, so revenue can climb even as tickets sold fall. The seating-mix shift reconciles the two figures directly.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Popular programming should raise attendance, deepening the paradox that fewer tickets were sold.
explanations.C: Cross-orchestra pricing doesn't explain Granville's specific revenue-versus-attendance split.
explanations.D: A renovation last season would reduce last season's baseline attendance, which should make this season's 15 percent drop larger in context, not explain the revenue surge.
explanations.E: Subscriber share is steady across both seasons and thus doesn't account for the year-over-year change.

lr.difficultyReason: Statistical paradox requiring recognition of a self-selection confound: patients who seek out experimental treatments differ systematically from the general patient population. Distractors plausibly address one horn only.
lr.stimulus: Patients who voluntarily enroll in experimental cancer drug trials at a major research hospital have a 20 percent higher five-year survival rate than patients treated with standard therapies at the same hospital. Yet when the hospital made the experimental drug available to all cancer patients as a standard treatment, overall five-year survival rates did not improve.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The experimental drug was significantly more expensive to administer than the standard therapies it was intended to replace.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only patients whose cancer was detected at an early stage were eligible to enroll in the experimental drug trials.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some patients declined the experimental drug even after it became available as a standard treatment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The research hospital had a larger oncology staff than most comparable institutions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients who enrolled in experimental trials were more likely to comply with their full course of treatment than those who did not.

explanations.correct: If only early-stage patients were eligible for the trials, the trial group was systematically healthier from the outset, explaining their higher survival rate without any contribution from the drug itself. When the drug was extended to all patients — including late-stage — the survival benefit disappeared because the drug was never the cause of the difference.
explanations.A: Cost explains a potential barrier to access but doesn't account for why broader availability produced no survival improvement; it also doesn't explain the original higher survival rate.
explanations.B: Correct. This is a selection-effect resolution: the trial group was restricted to early-stage patients who had inherently better prognoses, dissolving the apparent contradiction.
explanations.C: Patients declining the drug addresses uptake but leaves unexplained why the original trial group fared so much better; it resolves one horn at most.
explanations.D: Staff size is irrelevant to the comparison between the trial group and the general patient population.
explanations.E: Compliance differences explain the trial group's better outcomes through behavior, not the drug — this deepens the paradox by suggesting the drug still isn't responsible, but it doesn't explain why universal access failed to improve rates if compliance is spread across the broader group.

lr.difficultyReason: Reverse-causation paradox in economics. The apparent conflict — raising the minimum wage correlates with lower teen unemployment — requires identifying a confounding economic trend rather than accepting the surface causal story. Distractors include one that deepens the paradox.
lr.stimulus: Economic analysts expected that cities raising their minimum wage above the national level would see an increase in teen unemployment, since employers would hire fewer low-skilled workers. However, in cities that enacted such raises, teen unemployment rates actually fell in the two years following the wage increase.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the surprising phenomenon described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Teen workers in cities with higher minimum wages reported greater job satisfaction than those in cities with lower wages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cities that enacted minimum wage increases were those already experiencing robust economic growth and falling unemployment across all age groups.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Employers in high-minimum-wage cities invested more heavily in automation than employers in other cities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The national minimum wage was itself raised during the same two-year period in which the city-level raises took effect.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Teen workers are more likely than adult workers to be employed in industries directly affected by minimum wage legislation.

explanations.correct: If only already-booming cities chose to raise the minimum wage, the decline in teen unemployment reflects the pre-existing economic expansion, not the wage increase. This confounding variable dissolves the paradox by revealing a selection effect at the policy level.
explanations.A: Job satisfaction does not explain employment rates and addresses neither horn of the paradox.
explanations.B: Correct. This is a classic confounding-variable resolution: cities that raised wages were those with strong economies, so falling unemployment tracks economic growth, not wage policy.
explanations.C: Greater automation would predict more unemployment, not less — this deepens the paradox.
explanations.D: A national wage increase affects all cities equally and therefore cannot explain why only the cities that enacted local raises saw the decline.
explanations.E: This confirms teens are affected by minimum wage laws but does not explain why unemployment fell rather than rose; it addresses why teens are relevant, not the direction of the effect.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science paradox involving a temporal/contextual difference. The conflict between local air quality improvement and worsening regional air quality is non-obvious; correct answer introduces a displacement mechanism.
lr.stimulus: After a major industrial city installed new emission-control filters at its largest factories, measured air pollution levels within the city dropped by 30 percent over three years. Yet regional air quality monitors located 50 to 100 kilometers downwind of the city recorded a corresponding increase in particulate pollution over the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The emission-control filters were more effective at removing certain pollutants than others.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Regional air quality monitors use a different measurement scale than the city's own monitoring stations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The filters trap particulates within dense filtration media that must be transported to and processed at facilities located downwind of the city.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several smaller cities in the region also increased industrial output during the same three-year period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Residents of the industrial city reported measurable improvements in respiratory health following the installation of the filters.

explanations.correct: If the filters concentrate pollutants that are then transported to processing facilities downwind, the pollution is not eliminated but physically relocated. This explains both the city's cleaner air and the region's dirtier air through a single hidden mechanism — a displacement effect.
explanations.A: Selective effectiveness explains partial improvement within the city but does not account for the increase downwind; resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: A measurement-scale difference could explain why the numbers look different, but a 'corresponding increase' implies the regional monitors are calibrated — this is too vague to resolve the paradox and functions as an irrelevant distractor.
explanations.C: Correct. The pollution is displaced, not destroyed — the filter medium is transported downwind, introducing a hidden causal pathway that reconciles both observations.
explanations.D: Other cities' industrial growth could explain regional pollution increases independently, but it doesn't connect to the city's filter installation or explain the correspondence in timing; this resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: Health improvements corroborate the city's lower pollution but do nothing to explain the regional increase; this is irrelevant to resolving the paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: Law/policy paradox with a definitional mismatch as the resolution. Students must recognize that the same term ('recidivism') is being measured differently across the two data sets, not that one data set is wrong.
lr.stimulus: A state department of corrections reports that prisoners who complete an in-prison vocational training program are 40 percent less likely to be reincarcerated within five years of release than prisoners who do not complete such a program. Yet independent criminologists studying the same prison system found that the vocational training program had no statistically significant effect on recidivism.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The vocational training program costs the state significantly less per participant than alternative rehabilitation programs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The department of corrections measures recidivism only as reincarceration, while the criminologists' study counted any subsequent arrest — including those not resulting in conviction — as recidivism.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prisoners who completed the vocational program were more likely to find employment within six months of release.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The criminologists studied a different five-year period than the one covered by the department's report.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Not all prisoners who began the vocational training program completed it within their sentence term.

explanations.correct: If the department counts only reincarceration while criminologists count any arrest, the two studies are measuring different outcomes. The program may genuinely reduce reincarceration (perhaps graduates evade reimprisonment even when rearrested) while not reducing arrests overall. This definitional mismatch dissolves the apparent conflict.
explanations.A: Program cost is entirely irrelevant to the discrepancy in recidivism findings.
explanations.B: Correct. This is a definitional/measurement-artifact resolution: the same word 'recidivism' refers to different phenomena in the two reports, explaining why outcomes diverge.
explanations.C: Employment outcomes might explain how the program reduces reincarceration, but this simply corroborates one horn of the paradox without addressing why the criminologists found no effect; resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: A different time period could introduce historical variation, but without knowing how conditions differed it does not specifically resolve the conflict; functions as an irrelevant distractor.
explanations.E: Non-completion rates explain why the program's effect might be diluted but don't account for the sharp divergence in findings across two measurement systems.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology paradox involving reverse causation. The paradox — better safety software correlates with more reported data breaches — is counterintuitive; the resolution requires recognizing that detection, not incidence, drives reporting.
lr.stimulus: Companies that have adopted the latest generation of cybersecurity software report, on average, three times as many data breaches per year as companies still using older security systems. Yet cybersecurity experts maintain that the newer software provides substantially stronger protection against unauthorized data access.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The newer cybersecurity software is considerably more expensive than older systems, limiting its adoption to larger companies with more data to protect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The newer software includes advanced breach-detection and logging tools that identify and record intrusion attempts that older systems would have failed to detect.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Companies using newer security systems tend to operate in industries with stricter regulatory requirements for breach disclosure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cybercriminals frequently target companies known to hold large volumes of sensitive financial data.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The cybersecurity experts who recommend the newer software are sometimes employed by the companies that manufacture it.

explanations.correct: If the newer software detects breaches that older systems miss entirely, then higher reported breach counts reflect superior detection capability rather than worse security. The actual incidence of unauthorized access may be lower; only measured reports are higher. This measurement-artifact resolution dissolves the paradox.
explanations.A: Size and data volume explain why larger companies might be more targeted but don't account for why better software correlates with more reported breaches; resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Correct. The newer software produces more breach reports because it detects more, not because it protects less — a measurement artifact that reconciles both facts.
explanations.C: Stricter disclosure requirements could contribute to higher reported numbers, but this is a weaker explanation than B because it doesn't address whether actual breaches are higher or lower; functions as a partial/one-horn resolution.
explanations.D: Targeting explains why certain companies are attacked more but does not explain the correlation with software generation specifically.
explanations.E: Expert bias undermines the experts' claims but doesn't resolve the statistical discrepancy; this is an irrelevant distractor that attacks a source rather than the data.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics paradox with a temporal-scope resolution. The conflict between a language losing native speakers and gaining overall speakers requires recognizing the distinction between native and second-language acquisition.
lr.stimulus: Linguists studying Catalan have documented a steady decline in the number of people who speak Catalan as their first language over the past three decades. Yet census data from the same period show that the total number of Catalan speakers — including those who learned it later in life — has increased by over 30 percent.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several regional governments have funded Catalan-language broadcasting and media over the past three decades.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The decline in native Catalan speakers is concentrated among elderly populations in rural communities.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Government education policies introduced Catalan as a compulsory subject in schools, producing a large cohort of fluent second-language speakers who outnumber the native-speaker losses.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many linguists consider second-language speakers to be less proficient in Catalan than native speakers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The region where Catalan is spoken experienced significant population growth due to immigration over the past three decades.

explanations.correct: Compulsory school instruction created a large pool of second-language speakers whose numbers exceed native-speaker losses. This introduces a confounding category — second-language learners — that explains how total speakers can rise even as native speakers decline, resolving both horns simultaneously.
explanations.A: Media funding may encourage learning but doesn't specify a mechanism large enough to explain a 30 percent increase in total speakers; too vague to fully resolve the paradox.
explanations.B: Geographic concentration of native-speaker decline explains where but not why total speakers rose; resolves one horn only.
explanations.C: Correct. Mandatory school instruction generates a large, quantifiable second-language cohort that accounts for the numerical increase despite native-speaker loss — a hidden-category resolution.
explanations.D: Proficiency distinctions are irrelevant to the speaker-count discrepancy; this is an irrelevant distractor.
explanations.E: Population growth through immigration could add speakers of other languages but doesn't specifically explain the increase in Catalan speakers unless immigrants learned Catalan — too speculative to fully resolve the paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: History/policy paradox requiring a contextual-difference resolution. The conflict — a tax cut producing more revenue — is the classic supply-side paradox; the resolution requires identifying a behavioral mechanism that increases the tax base, not just the rate.
lr.stimulus: When a European nation reduced its top marginal income tax rate from 75 percent to 45 percent in the early 1980s, the government's total income tax revenue increased substantially over the following decade. Critics had predicted that the rate reduction would cause a significant decline in revenue.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent conflict between the critics' prediction and the actual outcome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The government simultaneously increased tax rates on corporate profits to offset the income tax reduction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: High-income earners who had previously sheltered income in tax havens abroad repatriated substantial funds once the domestic rate fell below the effective rate of concealment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The reduction in the top marginal rate was politically popular and helped the incumbent government win reelection.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several neighboring countries also reduced their top marginal tax rates during the same decade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Government spending on social programs increased substantially during the decade following the tax cut.

explanations.correct: If wealthy taxpayers previously hid income offshore and the lower rate made domestic taxation cheaper than concealment, taxable income expanded dramatically. The tax base grew enough to offset the rate reduction, producing higher total revenue. This behavioral mechanism — increased tax-base participation — dissolves the apparent paradox.
explanations.A: A compensating corporate tax increase would explain stable total revenue through a different revenue stream, not through income tax specifically; this resolves the paradox through a different mechanism than the one described but attributes the gain to a different tax, making it only a partial explanation.
explanations.B: Correct. Repatriation of sheltered income expands the taxable base sufficiently to increase total income tax revenue despite the lower rate — a confounding behavioral-response mechanism.
explanations.C: Political popularity is entirely irrelevant to the revenue outcome; this is an irrelevant distractor.
explanations.D: Neighboring countries' rate reductions provide context but don't explain why this nation's revenue rose; irrelevant distractor.
explanations.E: Increased spending is a government decision orthogonal to revenue; it deepens concern about fiscal balance but doesn't explain the revenue increase.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts/policy paradox with a selection-effect resolution. The conflict — attendance subsidies reduce average audience satisfaction scores — is counterintuitive; resolution requires identifying a compositional change in the audience population.
lr.stimulus: A metropolitan opera company introduced a ticket subsidy program that reduced seat prices by 60 percent for low-income patrons. Following the program's introduction, the opera company's post-performance audience satisfaction surveys showed a statistically significant decline in average satisfaction scores compared to pre-subsidy surveys.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The opera company reduced its production budget in the same season it introduced the subsidy program.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Low-income patrons who attended under the subsidy program were attending opera for the first time and were unfamiliar with conventions such as not applauding between movements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The satisfaction surveys were completed voluntarily, and before the subsidy program, only the most enthusiastic attendees — those with the highest baseline satisfaction — chose to complete them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several prominent critics gave the opera company's productions negative reviews during the subsidy period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The subsidy program was funded by a government arts grant that required the opera company to serve a minimum number of low-income patrons per season.

explanations.correct: If pre-subsidy surveys were completed only by the most devoted — and therefore most satisfied — audience members, the baseline scores were inflated by self-selection. The subsidy brought in a broader audience, more of whom completed surveys, diluting the average with more representative, and lower, satisfaction scores. The program didn't cause dissatisfaction; it changed who responded.
explanations.A: A reduced production budget could lower quality and thus satisfaction, explaining the score decline without reference to the subsidy program's audience change — this resolves one horn only and doesn't engage the paradox's full structure.
explanations.B: First-time attendees' unfamiliarity with conventions might explain behavioral issues but doesn't resolve the survey-score paradox; it merely attributes dissatisfaction to newcomers without explaining the measurement artifact.
explanations.C: Correct. Pre-subsidy surveys were completed by a self-selected, highly satisfied subset; post-subsidy surveys captured a broader population, lowering the measured average. This is a classic self-selection/measurement-artifact resolution.
explanations.D: Negative critical reviews might influence audience perceptions but are too indirect and unrelated to the subsidy mechanism to fully resolve the paradox.
explanations.E: The funding mechanism and grant requirements are irrelevant to why satisfaction scores fell; this is an irrelevant distractor.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics/policy paradox involving a reverse-causation mechanism. The conflict — mandatory ethics training correlating with more violations — requires distinguishing increased detection from increased incidence.
lr.stimulus: After a large financial firm made ethics and compliance training mandatory for all employees, the number of internal ethics violations reported to the firm's compliance office rose by 45 percent in the first year. Yet the firm's external auditors found no evidence of an increase in actual unethical conduct during the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The ethics training modules were developed by the same compliance office that receives and records reported violations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mandatory training sessions informed employees about the types of conduct that qualify as ethics violations and encouraged them to report suspected misconduct, increasing both awareness and willingness to report.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several employees who completed the mandatory training subsequently left the firm to work for competitors.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The compliance office hired additional staff in the year following the training mandate to handle the expected increase in reports.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Financial firms in the same sector that did not adopt mandatory ethics training saw their violation rates remain stable during the same period.

explanations.correct: Training both taught employees what counts as a violation and encouraged reporting. Pre-training, many violations went unreported because employees didn't recognize them or feared reporting. Post-training, more violations were reported even though actual unethical conduct was unchanged — exactly what the auditors confirmed. Increased reporting reflects better awareness and reporting culture, not more misconduct.
explanations.A: The compliance office developing its own training might raise questions of bias but doesn't explain the discrepancy between reported violations and actual conduct; irrelevant to the paradox.
explanations.B: Correct. Training increased both definitional awareness and reporting propensity, causing reports to rise while actual violations stayed flat — a detection-versus-incidence resolution.
explanations.C: Employee departures are irrelevant to the violation reporting rate; this is an irrelevant distractor.
explanations.D: Hiring additional compliance staff might facilitate processing more reports, but if violations were truly rising, auditors would have found evidence — this doesn't explain the auditors' finding and resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: Stable rates elsewhere highlight the correlation but don't explain the mechanism; this is an irrelevant comparison that leaves the paradox unresolved.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science/economics paradox requiring a temporal-scope distinction. Higher fuel efficiency standards correlating with higher total fuel consumption is counterintuitive; the resolution involves a behavioral rebound effect that students must identify.
lr.stimulus: In a large industrialized country, government regulations requiring significantly higher fuel efficiency in new automobiles were enacted fifteen years ago. Yet total national gasoline consumption has increased by 18 percent since those regulations took effect, despite the fact that the average fuel efficiency of vehicles on the road has improved substantially.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fuel efficiency regulations apply only to new vehicles, and many households continue to drive older, less efficient cars purchased before the regulations took effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fuel efficiency regulations were opposed by automobile manufacturers at the time of their enactment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because more fuel-efficient vehicles cost less to operate per kilometer, drivers have increased the total number of kilometers they drive each year, more than offsetting the per-kilometer fuel savings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The country's population increased by 12 percent during the fifteen years since the regulations took effect.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hybrid and electric vehicles, which consume little or no gasoline, have become more widely available since the regulations were enacted.

explanations.correct: This is the classic rebound effect: lower per-kilometer costs induced by greater efficiency cause drivers to drive more total kilometers, increasing absolute fuel consumption even as consumption per kilometer falls. The behavioral response to cheaper driving offsets and exceeds the efficiency gains, resolving both horns of the paradox.
explanations.A: Older vehicles still on the road could limit the efficiency improvement's impact, but the stimulus stipulates that average efficiency has improved substantially — this resolves one horn only and contradicts the premise slightly.
explanations.B: Manufacturer opposition is entirely irrelevant to consumption outcomes; this is an irrelevant distractor.
explanations.C: Correct. The rebound effect — increased driving due to lower per-kilometer cost — explains how total fuel use rises even as per-vehicle efficiency improves; a behavioral confounding mechanism.
explanations.D: A 12 percent population increase could contribute to higher consumption, but a larger population of more efficient drivers should still consume less per capita — this only partially resolves the paradox and does not account for the full 18 percent increase given the efficiency improvements.
explanations.E: Wider availability of electric vehicles would predict lower gasoline consumption, not higher — this deepens the paradox rather than resolving it.

lr.difficultyReason: Statistical paradox requiring recognition of a self-selection effect: patients who seek out experimental treatments differ systematically from those who don't, so the raw survival comparison is misleading. Distractors explain one horn only or deepen the paradox.
lr.stimulus: Patients at a major cancer center who enrolled in experimental drug trials had a 12 percent higher five-year survival rate than patients at the same center who received only standard treatments. Yet when the hospital began offering the experimental drugs to all eligible patients, the overall five-year survival rate did not improve.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The experimental drugs used in the trials were considerably more expensive than standard treatments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients who voluntarily enrolled in drug trials tended to be younger and in better overall health than those who did not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cancer center expanded its clinical trial program the same year it began offering experimental drugs to all eligible patients.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some patients who were offered the experimental drugs declined them and continued with standard treatments.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Experimental drug trials at other hospitals showed similarly high survival rates among enrolled patients.

explanations.correct: If trial enrollees were already younger and healthier, their higher survival rate reflects pre-existing advantages, not the drug's efficacy. Extending the drug to all patients — including the older, sicker majority — would not replicate the same advantage, explaining why overall rates didn't improve. Classic self-selection confound.
explanations.A: Cost explains a barrier to access but does not explain why broad access failed to improve outcomes. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Correct. Identifies a self-selection confound: the trial group's superior survival was attributable to pre-existing health advantages, not the drug itself.
explanations.C: Expanding the trial program in parallel is irrelevant to whether survival rates improved under broad drug access. Does not address the discrepancy.
explanations.D: Some patients declining the drugs would reduce uptake but does not explain why survival rates were unchanged even for those who did take them. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: Consistent patterns elsewhere only confirm the paradox without resolving it — it deepens the puzzle by ruling out a center-specific anomaly.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy paradox with a reverse-causation structure: the apparent protective effect of a policy disappears when causal direction is examined. Distractors offer plausible-sounding but incomplete explanations.
lr.stimulus: Cities that adopted strict rent-control ordinances in the 1990s had significantly lower rates of resident displacement over the following decade than cities without such ordinances. Yet economists who studied the same period found that rent control did not, on average, reduce displacement rates in the cities that adopted it.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rent control ordinances are typically accompanied by other tenant-protection measures that independently reduce displacement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cities that adopted rent control in the 1990s were, on average, already experiencing lower displacement pressures before the ordinances took effect.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Landlords in rent-controlled cities sometimes converted residential units to commercial use, reducing the overall housing supply.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The economists' studies relied on different displacement metrics than those used in the cross-city comparison.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rent control ordinances vary considerably in their specific provisions from one city to another.

explanations.correct: If cities that adopted rent control already had lower displacement pressures before the ordinances, the cross-city comparison reflects pre-existing conditions rather than the policy's effect. Within those cities, rent control still added nothing — consistent with the economists' finding. This dissolves the paradox via a pre-selection confound.
explanations.A: Companion measures could explain lower displacement, but then rent control itself is still doing no work — this would deepen rather than resolve the economists' finding that rent control specifically didn't help.
explanations.B: Correct. Pre-existing lower displacement rates explain the cross-city difference without crediting rent control, reconciling both findings.
explanations.C: Unit conversion would tend to worsen displacement, deepening rather than resolving the paradox.
explanations.D: Different metrics could create an appearance of disagreement, but the stimulus contrasts raw rates vs. economist findings — a definitional mismatch that doesn't explain the underlying data discrepancy.
explanations.E: Variation in provisions might explain inconsistent effects but does not account for why rent-control cities as a group showed lower displacement. Resolves one horn only.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science paradox requiring identification of a confounding temporal variable. The student must recognize that baseline conditions differ between the two observed periods, not just compare the two stated outcomes.
lr.stimulus: A coastal wetland restoration project replanted native marsh grasses across 400 hectares. Water quality measurements taken immediately after planting showed no improvement over pre-restoration levels. Yet five years later, water quality in the same wetland had improved substantially compared to similar, unrestored wetlands in the region.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to explain the surprising phenomenon described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Native marsh grasses require several years to establish root systems capable of filtering significant quantities of pollutants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The restoration project also included installation of sediment barriers along the wetland's northern boundary.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Water quality in unrestored regional wetlands declined sharply over the same five-year period due to increased agricultural runoff.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The funding agency required water quality measurements immediately after planting as a condition of the grant.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several migratory bird species returned to the restored wetland within two years of the planting project.

explanations.correct: If grasses need years to develop filtration capacity, the immediate absence of improvement is expected — the mechanism simply hadn't activated yet. The later substantial improvement is then fully explained. Both horns of the paradox are dissolved by this temporal lag.
explanations.A: Correct. The temporal lag between planting and filtration capacity directly explains both the immediate non-improvement and the later substantial improvement.
explanations.B: Sediment barriers might contribute to later improvement, but this leaves unexplained why there was no immediate improvement from barriers that were installed at the same time. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.C: If unrestored wetlands declined, the restored wetland's comparative improvement could reflect others getting worse rather than it getting better. This is a possible confound for the five-year comparison, but it doesn't explain the immediate non-improvement. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: The funding requirement explains why measurements were taken but not why they showed no improvement. Irrelevant to the substance of the paradox.
explanations.E: Bird return is a downstream ecological indicator and does not address water quality mechanisms at all. Irrelevant.

lr.difficultyReason: Economics paradox involving a composition fallacy — aggregate data obscures a subgroup reversal. Recognizing that two distinct populations are being merged requires careful reasoning about measurement scope.
lr.stimulus: A nationwide survey found that workers who regularly telecommute report higher job satisfaction than workers who commute to an office every day. Yet companies that shifted their entire workforce to mandatory remote work saw no increase — and often a decrease — in overall employee satisfaction scores.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Workers who telecommute voluntarily tend to have jobs that are particularly well-suited to remote work and personal circumstances that make working from home advantageous.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mandatory remote work policies are more common in large corporations than in small businesses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Job satisfaction surveys typically measure satisfaction along multiple dimensions, including compensation and career advancement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some employees who were required to work remotely lacked adequate home office equipment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Employee satisfaction scores at companies with mandatory remote work declined most sharply in the first six months of implementation.

explanations.correct: Voluntary telecommuters are a self-selected group whose jobs and home situations are favorable to remote work. They report higher satisfaction because of those pre-existing advantages, not because remote work inherently raises satisfaction. Forcing all workers — including those with unsuitable jobs or home situations — into remote work removes the selection advantage, explaining why mandatory policies don't raise and often lower satisfaction.
explanations.A: Correct. Identifies the self-selection confound: voluntary remote workers differ systematically from the general workforce, dissolving the paradox.
explanations.B: Company size is irrelevant to the core mechanism of why voluntary vs. mandatory remote work produces different satisfaction outcomes.
explanations.C: Multi-dimensional surveys would apply equally to both comparisons and so cannot explain the divergent results. Irrelevant.
explanations.D: Equipment shortages partially explain some dissatisfaction but do not explain why satisfaction doesn't rise for employees who do have adequate equipment. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: The timing of dissatisfaction only specifies when mandatory remote work hurt satisfaction; it doesn't explain why voluntary telecommuters showed higher satisfaction in the first place. Resolves one horn only.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology paradox with a measurement-artifact resolution. The two data points use incompatible reference classes, so apparent inconsistency dissolves once the definitional mismatch is recognized.
lr.stimulus: A cybersecurity firm reported that companies using its advanced intrusion-detection software experienced 40 percent fewer confirmed data breaches last year than companies without it. Nevertheless, an independent audit found that companies using the software suffered more total data security incidents than comparable companies without it.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cybersecurity firm's software is significantly more expensive than competing products on the market.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The software detects and logs minor unauthorized access attempts that would go unnoticed — and therefore unreported — at companies lacking such detection capability.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Companies that purchase advanced intrusion-detection software tend to store more sensitive data than companies that do not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Data breach notification laws require companies to disclose only breaches that result in the theft of personal information.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The independent audit was commissioned by a competitor of the cybersecurity firm.

explanations.correct: The firm reports fewer confirmed data breaches (serious, successful intrusions), while the audit counts total security incidents (including minor, detected attempts). The software reveals incidents that would otherwise go undetected and unreported, inflating the total-incident count. Both findings are thus consistent: the software reduces serious breaches while increasing recorded incidents by detecting previously invisible minor ones.
explanations.A: Cost is irrelevant to reconciling breach and incident rates. Irrelevant.
explanations.B: Correct. The definitional mismatch between 'confirmed breaches' and 'total incidents' is resolved by recognizing the software surfaces minor events that would otherwise be invisible, inflating the incident count without reflecting worse actual security.
explanations.C: Storing more sensitive data makes these companies more attractive targets and might explain more attacks, but it would predict more breaches too — deepening rather than resolving the paradox.
explanations.D: Disclosure laws affect reporting of breaches, not the total incident count measured by the audit. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: Audit sponsorship is irrelevant to the content of the findings and does not reconcile the two data points. Irrelevant.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics paradox requiring a hidden-mechanism explanation. The student must identify why a usage pattern diverges between naturalistic and experimental settings — a contextual confound that takes careful reading to isolate.
lr.stimulus: Linguistic studies consistently show that bilingual children switch between their two languages — a phenomenon called code-switching — far more frequently when speaking informally with family than when speaking with peers at school. Yet in controlled laboratory settings, the same children code-switch at nearly identical rates regardless of whether they are speaking with a researcher who is also a family member or one who is a stranger.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Code-switching is considered a mark of bilingual fluency rather than a sign of language confusion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Children who code-switch frequently in informal settings tend to have larger total vocabularies across both languages.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The formal laboratory environment itself suppresses the children's natural speech patterns, neutralizing context effects that would otherwise produce different rates of code-switching.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Schools in bilingual communities often have explicit policies discouraging code-switching in the classroom.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Children who spoke with researcher family members in the lab had met those researchers on fewer than three prior occasions.

explanations.correct: In natural settings, context (home vs. school) drives large differences in code-switching. In the lab, the formal setting overrides the social relationship cue entirely, so both the family-researcher and stranger-researcher produce the same, artificially suppressed rate. This confounding effect of the lab environment explains why naturalistic and experimental findings diverge.
explanations.A: The characterization of code-switching as fluent is irrelevant to why rates differ across contexts. Irrelevant.
explanations.B: Vocabulary size is a correlate of code-switching frequency but does not explain why the family vs. stranger distinction has no effect in the lab. Irrelevant.
explanations.C: Correct. The lab setting is itself a confounding variable that neutralizes the social-context effect, reconciling the divergent findings.
explanations.D: School policies explain why school rates are lower than home rates — consistent with the first finding — but do not explain why the lab shows equal rates regardless of researcher relationship. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: The number of prior meetings would affect familiarity but does not explain why the overall lab rates are equalized and suppressed. Does not address both horns.

lr.difficultyReason: History/policy paradox requiring a reverse-causation resolution. The apparent protective correlation between a practice and a negative outcome inverts when the causal direction is examined.
lr.stimulus: Historical records show that medieval European towns with larger permanent garrisons of soldiers had significantly higher rates of violent crime than towns with smaller garrisons. Yet contemporary accounts and modern historians agree that the larger garrisons were deployed specifically to reduce violence and maintain order.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medieval soldiers stationed in towns were frequently recruited from the same regions as the local population.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Towns that already had high levels of violence were precisely the ones that authorities chose to garrison with larger numbers of soldiers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Larger garrisons required greater provisioning, which strained local economies and created resentment among townspeople.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some soldiers stationed in medieval towns engaged in criminal activity themselves, contributing to local crime rates.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Historical records of violent crime in medieval towns were compiled primarily by ecclesiastical authorities rather than secular administrators.

explanations.correct: If authorities deployed larger garrisons in response to already-high violence, the correlation between garrison size and crime reflects the pre-existing violence, not any failure of the garrison. The deployment was a reaction to the problem, not its cause. This reverse-causation explanation reconciles the statistical pattern with historians' accounts of garrisons being intended to reduce violence.
explanations.A: Shared regional origins of soldiers and locals is irrelevant to the crime-rate correlation. Irrelevant.
explanations.B: Correct. Reverse causation: high-crime towns attracted large garrisons, so the correlation runs the opposite direction from causation.
explanations.C: Economic strain and resentment could cause crime, but this would mean garrisons actually caused the crime, contradicting historians' benign accounts and deepening the paradox.
explanations.D: Criminal soldiers partially explain elevated crime but leave unresolved why authorities described garrisons as crime-reducing. Deepens the paradox by implying garrisons were counterproductive.
explanations.E: Record-keeping methodology might affect accuracy but does not account for the systematic direction of the discrepancy. Irrelevant.

lr.difficultyReason: Law/ethics paradox with a scope-difference resolution. The apparent contradiction between two legal outcomes dissolves once the different jurisdictional or definitional scopes are recognized.
lr.stimulus: In a series of rulings, the appellate courts of a particular country consistently found that warrantless searches of individuals' digital communications did not violate constitutional privacy protections. Yet over the same period, civil juries in the same country routinely awarded substantial damages to plaintiffs who sued government agencies for conducting those identical searches.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Appellate judges in the country are appointed by the executive branch, while civil jury members are drawn from the general public.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The constitutional privacy standard applied by appellate courts is narrower than the statutory privacy right codified in the civil tort law under which plaintiffs sued.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Civil damages awards were frequently reduced on appeal to lower amounts than juries initially awarded.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The volume of warrantless digital searches increased substantially over the period in question.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several of the plaintiffs who won civil damages had also filed unsuccessful criminal suppression motions based on the same searches.

explanations.correct: The appellate courts applied a constitutional standard (narrower), while civil juries applied a statutory tort standard (broader). A search can be constitutional yet still violate a separate statutory privacy right, making both outcomes simultaneously correct under different legal frameworks. The definitional mismatch between two distinct legal standards resolves the apparent conflict.
explanations.A: The different selection mechanisms for judges vs. jurors might correlate with different outcomes, but mere institutional difference doesn't explain how both legal outcomes can be legally correct simultaneously. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Correct. Two distinct legal standards — constitutional and statutory — can yield different outcomes for the same conduct without contradiction. Definitional mismatch resolution.
explanations.C: Reductions on appeal do not eliminate the awards or reconcile the finding that both outcomes were legally valid. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: Volume of searches is irrelevant to why different legal bodies reached different conclusions about the same type of search. Irrelevant.
explanations.E: Failed suppression motions confirm the constitutional finding but don't explain the separate civil damages awards. Resolves one horn only.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts/economics paradox with a hidden third-factor explanation. The student must identify that a variable correlated with both success and the outcome creates a spurious relationship.
lr.stimulus: A survey of professional musicians found that those who had received formal conservatory training earned, on average, 30 percent less annually than professional musicians who were self-taught. Yet music industry analysts consistently report that conservatory training substantially increases a musician's likelihood of sustained professional employment.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conservatory-trained musicians are disproportionately employed in orchestras and teaching positions, which offer stable but lower salaries than the top-earning self-taught performers in popular genres.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cost of conservatory training leaves many graduates with significant debt that reduces their net earnings over time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Self-taught musicians often cite conservatory-trained musicians as artistic influences.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Music industry analysts focus primarily on rock and pop genres when assessing employment trends.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conservatory programs have become more selective over the past two decades, admitting fewer students each year.

explanations.correct: Conservatory training channels musicians into stable, moderately-paid careers (orchestras, teaching) with high employment rates. Self-taught musicians face more precarious employment overall, but the top earners in popular genres skew the average income of successful self-taught professionals upward. Average income is thus lower for conservatory-trained musicians even though their employment stability is higher — both findings are simultaneously correct.
explanations.A: Correct. Genre and role channeling explains the income gap: stable employment in classical/educational roles pays less than the highest-earning popular genre performers who are disproportionately self-taught among the employed. This reconciles both findings.
explanations.B: Debt reduces net earnings but doesn't explain why gross annual earnings from employment are lower, and doesn't address the employment stability finding. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.C: Artistic influence patterns are irrelevant to the earnings and employment discrepancy. Irrelevant.
explanations.D: If analysts focus on pop/rock, their employment findings would favor self-taught musicians, deepening rather than resolving the paradox.
explanations.E: Selectivity affects the pool of conservatory graduates but not the income or employment dynamics described. Irrelevant.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science/policy paradox with a temporal-scope confound. The two observations are both accurate but cover different time windows, and the student must recognize that a lagged mechanism makes both consistent.
lr.stimulus: Following a ban on a particular industrial solvent, atmospheric concentrations of the solvent in the affected region dropped by 60 percent within two years. However, rates of the respiratory illness most closely associated with solvent exposure continued to rise for four years after the ban took effect before finally declining.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to explain why illness rates continued rising after solvent concentrations fell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The respiratory illness associated with solvent exposure typically takes several years to manifest clinically after initial exposure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Industrial use of the solvent was replaced by a chemically similar substitute that also poses respiratory risks.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The region's population grew substantially in the years following the ban, increasing the absolute number of people at risk.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Medical screening programs for the respiratory illness were expanded significantly in the same year the ban took effect.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enforcement of the solvent ban was inconsistent during the first six months after it was enacted.

explanations.correct: If the illness takes years to develop after exposure, then cases diagnosed in the four years following the ban reflect exposures that occurred before the ban reduced concentrations. The disease pipeline was already filled. Once that cohort clears, rates decline — exactly as observed. The temporal lag between exposure and clinical manifestation dissolves the paradox.
explanations.A: Correct. A multi-year latency period between exposure and clinical manifestation explains why illness rates continued rising from pre-ban exposures even as atmospheric concentrations fell post-ban.
explanations.B: A substitute solvent would explain continued illness indefinitely, contradicting the eventual decline in illness rates described in the stimulus. Deepens one horn of the paradox.
explanations.C: Population growth would raise absolute case counts but the stimulus refers to rates, which are population-adjusted. Irrelevant to the rate paradox.
explanations.D: Expanded screening would increase detected cases without changing actual illness rates — this could explain apparent continued increase, but only if the stimulus were describing detected cases rather than actual illness rates. As a partial definitional artifact answer, it is less complete than A, which explains both the rise and the eventual decline.
explanations.E: Inconsistent early enforcement might extend solvent exposure slightly but cannot account for four full years of rising illness rates after a 60 percent concentration drop. Resolves one horn only.

lr.difficultyReason: Statistical paradox requiring identification of a self-selection confound: patients who seek out experimental treatments differ systematically from those who don't, so trial success doesn't translate to population-wide benefit.
lr.stimulus: Patients with chronic migraines who voluntarily enroll in experimental acupuncture trials report a 40 percent reduction in headache frequency, a rate far exceeding that seen in standard pharmaceutical treatments. Yet when health insurers began covering acupuncture for all chronic migraine patients — not just volunteers — average headache frequency across the covered population decreased by less than 5 percent.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acupuncture requires multiple sessions before any therapeutic effect is observed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only patients who already believe strongly in acupuncture's efficacy choose to enroll in experimental trials, and such belief itself contributes significantly to treatment success.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Health insurers covering acupuncture reimburse practitioners at lower rates than trials do.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chronic migraine is more prevalent among women than among men.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The acupuncture protocols used in experimental trials are more rigorous than those used in standard clinical settings.

explanations.correct: If trial enrollees are self-selected believers whose belief itself drives improvement, their superior outcomes reflect the selection effect rather than the treatment. Mandatory coverage extends acupuncture to skeptics who lack that belief-driven boost, collapsing the population-wide effect. Both facts are reconciled.
explanations.A: This applies equally to trial participants and to the broadly covered population, so it cannot explain why one group improves far more than the other.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Lower reimbursement might affect practitioner quality, but this addresses only the covered-population side without explaining the magnitude of the trial benefit — a 'resolves one horn only' trap.
explanations.D: Gender prevalence is irrelevant to the discrepancy between trial outcomes and population outcomes.
explanations.E: Protocol rigor could partly explain the difference, but it doesn't account for why trial volunteers see a 40% improvement that is independently linked to their being volunteers — it leaves the self-selection mechanism unnamed and thus resolves only one horn.

lr.difficultyReason: Economic paradox involving reverse causation: the direction of causality between the observed variables is the opposite of what the surface reading implies.
lr.stimulus: In the Ralston manufacturing sector, firms that pay wages in the top quartile for their industry experience employee turnover rates roughly half those of firms paying median wages. Yet when the Ralston government mandated an industry-wide wage floor that raised median pay to the former top-quartile level, overall employee turnover rates did not decline at all.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High-wage firms in Ralston also tend to offer better retirement benefits than low-wage firms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The wage floor was difficult to enforce in small manufacturing firms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Firms that originally paid top-quartile wages did so because they also maintained distinctive cultures of employee recognition and career development that lower-wage firms never adopted when wages were equalized.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some Ralston manufacturing firms relocated operations to neighboring regions following the wage mandate.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Employee turnover in Ralston increased slightly in the year before the wage mandate was introduced.

explanations.correct: High-wage firms retained employees because of a bundle of advantages — recognition, career development, culture — that accompanied high wages but were not caused by them. When lower-wage firms were forced to match wages without adopting those other practices, the retention benefit did not transfer. Both facts are explained.
explanations.A: Better retirement benefits could be part of a confounding bundle, but this answer alone is too narrow to dissolve the paradox; it still leaves unexplained why equalizing wages didn't equalize retention.
explanations.B: Enforcement difficulty is irrelevant to the discrepancy unless we know firms actually circumvented the floor, which is not stated — a classic 'irrelevant' trap.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Relocation would reduce the number of firms but doesn't explain unchanged turnover rates among remaining firms — 'resolves one horn only.'
explanations.E: A pre-mandate trend worsens rather than resolves the paradox by suggesting conditions were already deteriorating before wages rose.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science paradox requiring identification of a temporal scope difference: short-term and long-term ecological dynamics operate by different mechanisms.
lr.stimulus: Forests that experience low-intensity prescribed burns every three years have significantly higher biodiversity than unburned forests in the same region. Yet ecologists monitoring the same burned forests report that immediately following each burn, the total number of animal species observed drops sharply for a period of six to eight months.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to explain the surprising phenomenon described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Prescribed burns are conducted during seasons when most migratory species have already departed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drop in observed species immediately after a burn reflects temporary displacement rather than mortality, and the periodic clearing of underbrush allows habitat diversity to increase over the longer term, attracting more species than were present before burning began.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Unburned forests accumulate leaf litter that eventually suppresses ground-cover plant growth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prescribed burn programs are expensive to administer and require specialized forestry personnel.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some animal species are attracted to forest areas immediately after a burn because of increased food availability.

explanations.correct: The answer bridges both time scales: the short-term drop is displacement (not extinction), and the long-term gain is structural habitat improvement. This reconciles the immediate post-burn decline with the superior overall biodiversity of burned forests.
explanations.A: Migratory departure explains a subset of the post-burn count decline, but doesn't address why burned forests ultimately have higher biodiversity than unburned ones — 'resolves one horn only.'
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Leaf litter suppression helps explain why unburned forests are less biodiverse, but says nothing about the immediate post-burn species drop — still 'resolves one horn only.'
explanations.D: Administrative cost is entirely irrelevant to the ecological paradox.
explanations.E: This actually deepens the paradox by suggesting species numbers should rise, not fall, immediately after a burn.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal/policy paradox involving a definitional mismatch: what 'compliance' means in the statute versus what prosecutors measure differs in a way that explains the divergent outcomes.
lr.stimulus: A study of contract disputes in Verano found that firms using standardized legal templates drafted by certified attorneys lose arbitration proceedings at a rate 30 percent lower than firms drafting their own contracts. Nonetheless, after Verano enacted a law requiring all commercial contracts to use certified templates, the overall rate at which firms lost arbitration proceedings was unchanged.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arbitration panels in Verano are composed of retired judges who are familiar with standardized template language.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Before the law, only firms with sophisticated legal departments chose to use certified templates, and those firms also prepared stronger documentary evidence and negotiated more favorable contract terms independently of the templates themselves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Certified legal templates are updated annually to reflect changes in Verano commercial law.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cost of hiring certified attorneys to draft templates increased after the mandate took effect.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Arbitration proceedings in Verano increased in number following the enactment of the template requirement.

explanations.correct: Firms that voluntarily used templates were already legally sophisticated; the templates correlated with, but did not cause, arbitration success. When all firms were required to use templates, legally unsophisticated firms gained the template but not the surrounding expertise, so the population-wide loss rate stayed flat. Both facts are reconciled.
explanations.A: Panel familiarity with template language would predict improvement after the mandate, deepening rather than resolving the paradox.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Annual updates are irrelevant to the discrepancy between voluntary-use outcomes and mandatory-use outcomes.
explanations.D: Increased cost might deter compliance but doesn't explain why mandatory templates failed to improve outcomes for compliant firms — 'resolves one horn only.'
explanations.E: A volume increase in proceedings is irrelevant to the rate at which firms lost those proceedings.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology paradox requiring a measurement artifact explanation: what is being counted differs between the two contexts in a non-obvious way.
lr.stimulus: Software engineers who use AI-assisted coding tools complete individual programming tasks roughly 55 percent faster than engineers who do not use such tools. Yet companies that have fully deployed AI coding assistants across their engineering teams report no significant reduction in the time required to ship completed software products.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: AI-assisted code requires more extensive peer review and quality-assurance testing because it produces a higher volume of code — including bugs — per unit time, consuming the hours saved in individual task completion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: AI coding tools are more effective for routine tasks than for novel algorithmic problems.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Companies that adopt AI tools tend to be larger and therefore have more complex coordination requirements.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Engineers who use AI tools report higher job satisfaction than those who do not.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The cost of AI coding tool licenses is partially offset by reductions in engineer overtime hours.

explanations.correct: If AI tools accelerate code production but simultaneously generate more defects requiring review and testing, the downstream QA bottleneck absorbs the upstream time savings. Individual task speed rises while total product delivery time stays constant — both facts are reconciled by this measurement-scope mechanism.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Task-type limitations explain why gains might be modest, but do not explain why overall delivery time shows zero reduction at all — 'resolves one horn only.'
explanations.C: Company size is a confounding variable for coordination, but this introduces an entirely separate factor rather than explaining how faster individual tasks fail to produce faster shipping — an 'irrelevant' trap.
explanations.D: Job satisfaction is entirely unrelated to the delivery-time discrepancy.
explanations.E: Cost offsets and overtime say nothing about delivery timelines — irrelevant to the stated paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics paradox requiring a contextual difference explanation: the populations compared differ in a hidden dimension that explains divergent outcomes.
lr.stimulus: Children raised in bilingual households acquire their first language's vocabulary more slowly on average than children raised in monolingual households, as measured at age three. Yet by age seven, bilingual children perform as well as or better than monolingual peers on standardized tests of first-language vocabulary.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Standardized vocabulary tests administered at age seven are calibrated to monolingual norms and may undercount bilingual children's total lexical knowledge.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In bilingual households, children allocate cognitive resources across two languages simultaneously, slowing early first-language acquisition; however, the cross-linguistic structural knowledge built during this period accelerates vocabulary acquisition in both languages during the school years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bilingual children are more likely than monolingual children to attend multilingual school programs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: First-language vocabulary size at age three is not a reliable predictor of academic performance in secondary school.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Parents in bilingual households read aloud to their children less frequently than parents in monolingual households.

explanations.correct: The answer explains the age-three lag (split cognitive resources across two languages) and the age-seven catch-up (cross-linguistic knowledge accelerates later acquisition), bridging both halves of the paradox through a single developmental mechanism.
explanations.A: If tests undercount bilingual knowledge, that would predict bilingual children actually score lower even at seven — this resolves one horn but potentially deepens the other by questioning whether the age-seven parity is real.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Multilingual school programs might accelerate catch-up but don't explain the early lag, leaving the first horn unaddressed — 'resolves one horn only.'
explanations.D: Academic performance in secondary school is outside the scope of the vocabulary paradox entirely — irrelevant.
explanations.E: Less frequent read-alouds would predict persistent deficits, deepening the paradox rather than resolving it.

lr.difficultyReason: History/policy paradox requiring a reverse-causation or hidden-third-factor explanation: the relationship between two historical variables runs contrary to intuition.
lr.stimulus: Historical records show that in the Aldenmoor region during the 1800s, towns with the highest rates of church attendance also had the highest rates of property crime. Yet sociologists universally agree that shared moral frameworks reduce antisocial behavior.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Churches in the Aldenmoor region during this period preached sermons that explicitly condemned property crime.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The towns with the highest church attendance in Aldenmoor were also the most densely populated and economically impoverished, conditions independently associated with elevated property crime rates.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Property crime records from the 1800s are less accurate than modern crime statistics because reporting rates were lower.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some Aldenmoor residents attended church specifically to establish trustworthy reputations that they then exploited for financial gain.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Church attendance in Aldenmoor declined significantly during periods of economic prosperity.

explanations.correct: A hidden confounding variable — urban density and poverty — independently drives both high church attendance (community institution in struggling areas) and high property crime. Once that common cause is identified, the correlation between church attendance and crime no longer conflicts with the sociological principle, because church attendance is not reducing crime relative to what it would be without churches in those conditions.
explanations.A: Churches condemning crime is consistent with the sociological principle but deepens the paradox by making it even harder to explain why high-attendance towns still had more crime.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Lower historical reporting accuracy might mean crime was even higher elsewhere, but this attacks data quality rather than explaining the correlation — a 'presupposes what needs to be resolved' trap.
explanations.D: Strategic church attendance as reputation cover is an interesting mechanism but applies to only a small subset of attendees and cannot explain the broader correlation — 'resolves one horn only' at best.
explanations.E: Attendance declining during prosperity confirms a poverty-attendance link but doesn't by itself bridge to crime rates without the second leg of the argument, making this incomplete.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics/policy paradox where a definitional distinction between two superficially similar populations explains divergent moral outcomes.
lr.stimulus: Surveys consistently show that professional ethicists — philosophers who study moral reasoning for a living — are no more likely than non-specialists to donate to charity or to engage in volunteer work. Yet the same ethicists score significantly higher than non-specialists on standardized tests of moral reasoning ability.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Moral reasoning ability, as measured by standardized tests, assesses skill at identifying logical inconsistencies in ethical arguments rather than motivational commitment to acting altruistically.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Professional ethicists earn salaries comparable to those of other academic philosophers, limiting their disposable income for charitable giving.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Charitable donation rates vary significantly across different academic disciplines.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some professional ethicists specialize in metaethics rather than applied or normative ethics.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Standardized moral reasoning tests are administered in controlled laboratory settings that may not reflect real-world decision-making.

explanations.correct: The paradox dissolves once 'moral reasoning ability' is recognized as measuring analytical skill at ethical argumentation, not motivation to act morally. Ethicists' high test scores and average donation behavior are entirely consistent because the test measures cognition, not behavioral disposition — a definitional mismatch resolution.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Salary comparability might explain lower donations but doesn't address volunteer work, which requires no financial outlay — 'resolves one horn only.'
explanations.C: Cross-disciplinary variation is irrelevant to why ethicists in particular score higher but don't give more — an irrelevant-comparison trap.
explanations.D: Metaethics specialization might predict lower applied moral concern, but this applies to only a subset and doesn't resolve the general discrepancy — partial at best.
explanations.E: Lab-setting caveats question the test's validity but don't explain how ethicists can score higher yet behave identically — this merely dismisses one data point rather than reconciling both.

lr.difficultyReason: Economics paradox with a self-selection and composition-effect explanation: aggregate statistics mask shifts in the composition of the measured population.
lr.stimulus: The average salary of workers who leave Portsmith's technology sector for jobs in other industries has risen steadily over the past decade. Yet average salaries within Portsmith's technology sector itself have also risen over the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Workers who leave the technology sector do so primarily for reasons of work-life balance rather than for higher compensation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Over the decade, only the highest-paid technology workers — those who commanded premium salaries in both sectors — chose to leave, so departing workers' rising average salary reflects an increasingly elite outflow rather than rising pay in destination industries.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Portsmith's cost of living has risen substantially over the past decade, reducing real wages in both the technology sector and other industries.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Workers who remain in the technology sector tend to have more years of experience than those who leave.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Portsmith's government offers tax incentives to technology firms that retain workers for more than five years.

explanations.correct: The rising average salary of departing workers reflects a composition shift: over time, only increasingly well-compensated workers choose to leave, pulling up the departing cohort's average. Meanwhile, in-sector salaries also rise due to standard wage growth. There is no contradiction — the two trends operate independently. Both facts are reconciled by the changing composition of the departing group.
explanations.A: If workers leave for balance rather than pay, this makes it harder to explain why their salaries rose — it doesn't resolve why both averages climb simultaneously and could deepen the paradox.
explanations.B: Correct.
