explanations.C: Rising cost of living affects real wages uniformly and therefore cannot explain the differential pattern between departing and remaining workers — irrelevant to the specific discrepancy.
explanations.D: Experience levels of stayers versus leavers don't directly explain why departing workers' salaries trend upward alongside sector salaries — an incomplete resolution.
explanations.E: Retention incentives might affect who stays but don't address the salary trends of those who depart — 'resolves one horn only.'

lr.difficultyReason: Arts/policy paradox requiring a temporal-scope or funding-mechanism explanation that bridges an apparent contradiction between individual success and institutional decline.
lr.stimulus: Over the past fifteen years, the number of individual visual artists in Grenwick who earn a living solely from the sale of their work has increased by 20 percent. Yet over the same period, the total number of commercial art galleries operating in Grenwick has declined by nearly 40 percent.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cost of renting gallery space in Grenwick has increased substantially over the past fifteen years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Online sales platforms and social media have allowed Grenwick artists to sell directly to collectors worldwide, reducing dependence on physical galleries as intermediaries while simultaneously expanding artists' earning potential.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several large Grenwick galleries that closed were replaced by museum annexes that exhibit but do not sell artwork.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Grenwick's municipal government reduced its arts subsidy budget by 15 percent over the same period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Artists who earn a living solely from artwork sales in Grenwick tend to specialize in portraiture and commissioned pieces.

explanations.correct: Online platforms and social media eliminated the gallery's role as the required sales intermediary. More artists can now earn a living by selling directly to buyers, so artist income rises even as physical gallery numbers fall. The same technological shift explains both horns of the paradox simultaneously.
explanations.A: Rising rental costs explain why galleries closed (one horn) but not why more artists are nonetheless earning a living from their work — 'resolves one horn only.'
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Museum annexes explain some gallery closures but don't address why artist income increased — another 'resolves one horn only' trap.
explanations.D: Reduced subsidies would predict both fewer galleries and fewer self-supporting artists, which deepens the paradox rather than resolving it.
explanations.E: Specialization in portraiture and commissioned work is irrelevant to the gallery-decline trend — an irrelevant distractor.

lr.difficultyReason: Statistical paradox requiring recognition of a self-selection confound: patients who seek experimental treatment differ systematically from those who do not, making raw survival comparisons misleading.
lr.stimulus: Patients with advanced-stage cancer who voluntarily enroll in experimental drug trials have, on average, longer post-diagnosis survival times than patients with the same diagnosis who receive only standard care. Yet independent clinical analyses consistently show that the experimental drugs being tested in those trials provide no statistically significant survival benefit over standard treatment.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Experimental drug trials are conducted at major academic medical centers, which also provide higher-quality standard care than community hospitals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only patients who are healthy enough to tolerate aggressive experimental regimens are eligible to enroll in clinical drug trials.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patients enrolled in experimental trials are monitored more frequently by physicians than are patients receiving standard care.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some experimental drugs have significant side effects that reduce patients' quality of life even when survival time is extended.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The cost of enrolling in an experimental trial is often subsidized by pharmaceutical companies conducting the research.

explanations.correct: If only relatively healthier patients can enroll in trials, then trial participants begin with a survival advantage independent of any drug effect. Their longer survival thus reflects patient selection, not drug efficacy — dissolving the paradox.
explanations.A: This explains a quality-of-care difference at the institutional level but applies equally to trial and non-trial patients at those centers, so it does not explain why trial participants specifically outlive standard-care patients elsewhere.
explanations.B: Correct. The eligibility filter (health-status requirement) creates a self-selected subgroup that would survive longer regardless of treatment, reconciling both facts.
explanations.C: More frequent monitoring might catch complications earlier but does not explain why the drugs themselves show no survival benefit; it resolves only one horn and introduces a separate mechanism.
explanations.D: Reduced quality of life is irrelevant to the survival-time discrepancy and does not address the conflict.
explanations.E: Cost subsidies affect who can afford to enroll but do not explain why drugs show no clinical benefit — this is an irrelevant financial detail.

lr.difficultyReason: Economic policy paradox involving a minimum-wage increase that correlates with rising employment — counterintuitive to standard supply-demand reasoning. Resolution requires a confounding macroeconomic variable.
lr.stimulus: Following a significant increase in the regional minimum wage, the unemployment rate in that region fell by two percentage points over the next year. Yet economists' models predict that raising the minimum wage should reduce total employment by making labor more expensive for businesses.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some businesses in the region reduced employee hours rather than laying off workers after the wage increase took effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The minimum wage increase was accompanied by a major regional infrastructure project that created tens of thousands of new jobs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Workers earning the new minimum wage tend to spend a higher fraction of their income locally than do higher-wage earners.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The economists' models were developed using data from regions with stronger union representation than the region in question.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several large employers in the region had already been paying wages above the new minimum before the increase took effect.

explanations.correct: A simultaneous infrastructure project that generated massive job creation explains why unemployment fell even though the wage increase, in isolation, would have been expected to reduce employment. The confounding variable — independent job creation — reconciles both facts.
explanations.A: Reduced hours rather than layoffs is consistent with the model's prediction of reduced labor demand; it does not explain why unemployment actually fell.
explanations.B: Correct. A large external job-creation event is a confounding variable that explains the employment gain independent of the minimum wage's effect.
explanations.C: Higher local spending by low-wage workers could theoretically stimulate demand, but the stimulus presents this as an economist's model prediction that wages reduce employment — this choice resolves one horn weakly and does not address why the models are wrong.
explanations.D: A limitation in the models' data source casts doubt on the models but does not explain the specific mechanism behind the observed employment increase.
explanations.E: If large employers already paid above the new minimum, the wage increase affected fewer workers — this would predict even less disruption, not the observed employment growth, and does not resolve the paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science paradox: a protected marine reserve shows declining fish populations despite a ban on fishing. Resolution depends on identifying an external ecological variable unrelated to the fishing ban.
lr.stimulus: A coastal marine reserve has prohibited all commercial fishing within its boundaries for the past decade. Nevertheless, populations of the fish species the reserve was established to protect have declined by nearly 30 percent over that same period, while fish populations in adjacent unrestricted fishing zones have remained stable.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The fish species in question migrate seasonally outside the reserve's boundaries, where they remain subject to commercial fishing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reserve authorities have increased enforcement patrols, resulting in fewer illegal fishing incidents within reserve waters.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A deep-water coral disease that specifically affects the habitat of the protected species has spread rapidly within the reserve over the past decade.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Commercial fishing operations in the adjacent zones use more selective gear that reduces bycatch of non-target species.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Marine reserves elsewhere in the country have successfully increased fish populations of similarly protected species.

explanations.correct: A coral disease specific to the protected species' habitat inside the reserve explains why that population declined despite the fishing ban, while species in adjacent zones — unaffected by the disease — remained stable. This third factor resolves both horns simultaneously.
explanations.A: Seasonal migration into fishing zones could explain some decline, but the question notes that adjacent-zone populations are stable — if fishing in those zones maintained stable populations of other fish, migrating fish should face no unusual pressure, leaving the specific decline unexplained.
explanations.B: Fewer illegal fishing incidents inside the reserve should help the population, not harm it — this deepens the paradox rather than resolving it.
explanations.C: Correct. A habitat-specific disease is a confounding ecological variable that accounts for the decline inside the reserve while leaving adjacent zones unaffected.
explanations.D: Selective gear in adjacent zones explains stability there but does not explain why the reserve population fell — this resolves only one horn.
explanations.E: Success of reserves elsewhere is irrelevant to the specific decline in this reserve and does not address the conflict.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology paradox: a software security patch reduces reported vulnerabilities yet total system breaches increase. Requires identifying a reverse-causation or displacement mechanism.
lr.stimulus: After a widely used operating system released a comprehensive security patch last year, the number of publicly reported software vulnerabilities in that system dropped by 40 percent. Yet the total number of successful cyberattacks on systems running that operating system increased by 25 percent over the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The security patch was made available free of charge to all registered users of the operating system.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many organizations running the operating system delayed installing the patch for months due to compatibility concerns, leaving their systems exposed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Security researchers who previously reported vulnerabilities publicly began submitting findings directly to the software company under a private disclosure program introduced alongside the patch.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The operating system's market share grew substantially in the year following the patch release, attracting more attackers to the platform.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cyberattackers increasingly used social engineering tactics rather than software exploits to breach systems during the same period.

explanations.correct: If researchers shifted from public disclosure to private reporting, the drop in publicly reported vulnerabilities reflects a change in reporting behavior — not an actual reduction in vulnerabilities. Attackers could still exploit undisclosed flaws, explaining the rise in successful attacks. Both facts are reconciled.
explanations.A: Free availability of the patch should reduce breaches if users installed it; this does not explain why breaches increased.
explanations.B: Delayed installation explains continued vulnerability but does not explain why reported vulnerabilities dropped — it resolves only one horn.
explanations.C: Correct. A shift to private disclosure is a measurement artifact: fewer public reports do not mean fewer real vulnerabilities, explaining both the drop in reports and the rise in breaches.
explanations.D: Greater market share attracting more attackers could explain more breaches but does not explain the 40 percent drop in reported vulnerabilities — it resolves only one horn.
explanations.E: Social engineering is a different attack vector; it might explain more breaches but does not explain the reduction in reported software vulnerabilities.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy paradox involving a literacy program that raises average test scores but leaves individual student outcomes unchanged. Resolution requires a compositional or demographic shift explanation.
lr.stimulus: A national reading initiative introduced five years ago required all public schools to adopt a structured literacy curriculum. Average reading test scores across the country have risen by eight points since the program's introduction. Yet longitudinal studies tracking the same individual students over the five-year period show no measurable improvement in their reading scores.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The structured literacy curriculum requires more instructional time than the programs it replaced, reducing time available for mathematics.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several states exempted their highest-performing school districts from the mandate, concentrating the curriculum in lower-performing schools.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A large influx of students from countries with stronger early literacy traditions enrolled in public schools during the same five-year period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reading test scores typically fluctuate by several points from year to year due to variations in test difficulty.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Teachers who implemented the structured curriculum received less professional development support than program designers had recommended.

explanations.correct: If a large cohort of students who were already high readers enrolled in public schools, the national average would rise even though no existing student improved. The aggregate statistic changed due to a compositional shift in the student population, not due to individual gains — resolving both facts.
explanations.A: Trade-offs with mathematics instruction are irrelevant to the reading-score discrepancy and do not address either horn of the paradox.
explanations.B: Concentrating the curriculum in lower-performing schools would, if anything, predict a smaller average gain — this makes the observed aggregate rise harder to explain, potentially deepening the paradox.
explanations.C: Correct. A demographic influx of stronger readers raises the national average without any individual student improving, reconciling the aggregate increase with the flat longitudinal data.
explanations.D: Year-to-year test fluctuation might explain a small or inconsistent change but cannot explain a consistent eight-point rise over five years while individual scores remained flat.
explanations.E: Insufficient professional development predicts the curriculum would be ineffective — consistent with no individual gains — but does not explain why the national average still rose.

lr.difficultyReason: Historical paradox: a medieval city's population records show rising birth rates yet declining total population. Requires identifying a mortality mechanism that outpaced births.
lr.stimulus: Historical parish records from a fourteenth-century European city show that the number of baptisms — a reliable proxy for births — increased by roughly 15 percent during a particular twenty-year period. Yet the same records document that the city's total registered population shrank by nearly a quarter over that same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Parish priests sometimes recorded baptisms from neighboring villages in the city's registers when those villages lacked their own clergy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recurring outbreaks of plague during that period killed adults at far higher rates than infants, producing both elevated births relative to survivors and steep overall population loss.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The city expanded its administrative boundaries during this period, incorporating several smaller settlements into its official records.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Church authorities encouraged larger families during this period as a response to earlier population losses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many wealthy families left the city for rural estates during this period, taking their household servants with them.

explanations.correct: If plague selectively killed adults at very high rates, the surviving adult population — still biologically capable of reproduction — could produce more births than before, while total population nonetheless collapsed due to the massive adult death toll. This single mechanism accounts for both facts simultaneously.
explanations.A: Recording baptisms from neighboring villages would inflate the baptism count artificially, potentially explaining the rise in baptisms — but it does not explain the population decline and leaves open whether births actually rose.
explanations.B: Correct. Age-selective mortality (adults dying faster than infants) explains rising birth rates among survivors alongside a sharp population decline — a single confounding mechanism resolving both horns.
explanations.C: Boundary expansion would increase registered population, contradicting the observed decline — this deepens the paradox.
explanations.D: Church encouragement of larger families might explain more births but does not explain the simultaneous population decline; it resolves only one horn.
explanations.E: Wealthy family emigration could reduce total registered population but would also likely reduce birth registrations, making the simultaneous rise in baptisms harder to explain.

lr.difficultyReason: Law/criminal-justice paradox: a city installs more streetlights to deter crime, but reported nighttime crime rates rise. Resolution requires a reporting-behavior or visibility mechanism.
lr.stimulus: A city installed high-intensity streetlights in its highest-crime neighborhoods last year as part of a crime-deterrence initiative. However, police data show that reported nighttime crimes in those neighborhoods increased by 18 percent in the year following installation, compared to a 3 percent increase in neighborhoods without new lighting.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High-intensity streetlights are more expensive to maintain than conventional streetlights, diverting funds from other public-safety programs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Criminals who previously operated in the now-lit neighborhoods relocated their activities to darker, adjacent areas.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Better lighting made criminal incidents more visible to witnesses, substantially increasing the likelihood that residents reported crimes to police.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The neighborhoods selected for the lighting initiative had higher baseline crime rates than the comparison neighborhoods.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Police officers patrolling well-lit streets can cover larger areas per shift, reducing total officer hours spent in lit neighborhoods.

explanations.correct: If better lighting increased the visibility of criminal acts, witnesses became more likely to report them. The rise in reported crimes thus reflects improved reporting, not more actual crimes — explaining why reported incidents rose in lit areas while actual crime may have stayed the same or fallen.
explanations.A: Diverted funding is a long-term concern that does not explain the immediate rise in reported crimes after installation — irrelevant to the specific discrepancy.
explanations.B: Criminal displacement would explain a drop in the lit neighborhoods, but the data show an increase in those neighborhoods — this resolves the wrong direction of the paradox.
explanations.C: Correct. Improved visibility raises the reporting rate, creating a measurement artifact: more reports do not mean more crimes, reconciling the deterrence rationale with the observed data.
explanations.D: Higher baseline crime rates in selected neighborhoods are expected, but this was true before installation — it does not explain the post-installation increase relative to the pre-installation trend.
explanations.E: Fewer officer hours might reduce deterrence in lit areas, consistent with more crime, but does not explain why crimes are being reported more — it resolves only one horn.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics paradox: a language immersion program produces students with stronger vocabulary but weaker grammatical accuracy than traditional instruction. Resolution requires a trade-off or attention-resource mechanism.
lr.stimulus: Students taught a foreign language through full immersion — in which the target language is the sole medium of instruction — consistently score higher on vocabulary assessments than students taught through traditional grammar-translation methods. Yet immersion students score significantly lower on tests of grammatical accuracy in that same language.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vocabulary breadth and grammatical accuracy are both considered essential components of language proficiency by most applied linguists.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immersion environments expose students to a wide range of authentic vocabulary in context but provide little explicit instruction in grammatical rules, while grammar-translation courses do the reverse.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students in immersion programs spend more total hours engaged with the target language than students in grammar-translation courses.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many immersion programs are offered only at schools with above-average funding, attracting students from higher socioeconomic backgrounds.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Grammar-translation students are more likely than immersion students to pursue advanced language study after completing the program.

explanations.correct: If immersion programs inherently maximize vocabulary exposure through authentic use but omit explicit grammar instruction — while grammar-translation programs do the opposite — then each method produces the outcomes it is designed to produce. The apparent contradiction dissolves because the two programs optimize different skills.
explanations.A: Stating that both skills matter is background information; it does not explain why one method excels at one skill and fails at the other.
explanations.B: Correct. A definitional/methodological distinction — immersion teaches vocabulary implicitly while grammar-translation teaches rules explicitly — directly explains the divergent outcomes on each test type.
explanations.C: More total hours in immersion might predict across-the-board superiority, but immersion students still score lower on grammar — this deepens rather than resolves the grammatical accuracy gap.
explanations.D: Socioeconomic background is a confound for overall academic performance, not specifically for the vocabulary-vs.-grammar split — it does not resolve the paradox.
explanations.E: Post-program choices about further study are irrelevant to the performance outcomes observed during the program.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts/economics paradox: a museum raises ticket prices substantially yet attendance increases. Requires identifying a demand-side or signaling mechanism that runs counter to basic price-demand intuition.
lr.stimulus: A contemporary art museum raised its general admission ticket price by 60 percent two years ago. Despite this steep increase, the museum's annual attendance figures have risen by 22 percent over the same two-year period, while attendance at comparable museums with stable prices has remained flat.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The museum used revenue from the price increase to fund a major renovation and the acquisition of several internationally prominent art collections.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Art museum attendance is generally less sensitive to price than attendance at movie theaters or sporting events.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The museum introduced a free-admission day once per month at the same time it raised ticket prices, drawing new visitors who had never attended before.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Higher ticket prices at the museum led some visitors to perceive the institution as more prestigious, prompting them to recommend it to others.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The city in which the museum is located experienced significant population growth over the same two-year period.

explanations.correct: If the price increase funded a major renovation and high-profile acquisitions, the museum's product improved dramatically — attracting visitors who would not previously have attended. The enhanced appeal explains rising attendance despite higher prices, reconciling both facts.
explanations.A: Correct. The revenue from higher prices was reinvested in the museum's offerings, making the museum substantially more attractive — a confounding quality improvement that explains attendance growth despite the price hike.
explanations.B: Low price sensitivity in general would predict flat attendance, not a 22 percent increase — this mitigates the paradox slightly but does not explain the positive growth, especially relative to flat attendance elsewhere.
explanations.C: A free monthly admission day could increase attendance by drawing price-sensitive visitors, explaining the rise — but the question asks which most helps to resolve the discrepancy, and this only partially accounts for it without explaining why paying attendance also rose.
explanations.D: A prestige-signaling effect is a plausible mechanism but speculative; it does not explain why comparable museums with stable prices failed to attract similar word-of-mouth growth.
explanations.E: Population growth could explain more visitors across all museums, but comparable museums with stable prices saw flat attendance — a citywide population increase should affect them too, leaving the discrepancy unexplained.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics/policy paradox: a company's voluntary environmental commitments receive high public praise yet its total carbon emissions increase. Resolution requires a scope or growth-rate mechanism.
lr.stimulus: A multinational corporation widely praised for its voluntary carbon-reduction commitments has reduced the carbon emissions per unit of product it manufactures by 35 percent over the past five years. Yet the company's total annual carbon emissions have increased by 20 percent over that same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The corporation's carbon-reduction commitments were developed in consultation with independent environmental auditors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The corporation more than doubled its total production volume over the five-year period, manufacturing far more units than before.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several of the corporation's competitors made no voluntary emissions commitments during the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Government regulations requiring emissions reductions were not enacted in the countries where the corporation operates.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Consumers increasingly prefer to purchase products from companies perceived as environmentally responsible.

explanations.correct: If the corporation more than doubled production volume, then even a 35 percent reduction in emissions per unit would result in higher total emissions: efficiency gains were outpaced by absolute growth in output. This explains how both the per-unit improvement and the total-emissions increase can simultaneously be true.
explanations.A: The involvement of independent auditors speaks to the credibility of commitments, not to why total emissions rose — irrelevant to the conflict.
explanations.B: Correct. A large increase in total production volume is the scaling mechanism: per-unit improvements are real, but multiplied across a much larger number of units, absolute emissions still rise — resolving the paradox.
explanations.C: Competitor behavior is irrelevant to the corporation's own emissions trajectory and does not address the conflict between per-unit improvement and total-emissions increase.
explanations.D: The absence of regulatory requirements might explain why the corporation's reduction is voluntary, but does not explain why total emissions rose despite per-unit reductions.
explanations.E: Consumer preference for green companies could motivate the commitments, but it does not explain the paradox of falling per-unit emissions alongside rising total emissions.

lr.difficultyReason: Statistical paradox requiring a self-selection explanation: patients who seek out experimental treatment may have more severe disease, masking the drug's real benefit. Distractors plausibly explain one horn only.
lr.stimulus: Participants in a clinical trial who voluntarily enrolled in an experimental cancer drug program had a 20 percent lower five-year survival rate than cancer patients in the general population who received standard treatment. Yet the drug has been shown in laboratory settings to be significantly more effective at destroying cancer cells than any currently approved therapy.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The experimental drug has fewer side effects than most currently approved cancer therapies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients who enrolled in the experimental program were, on average, diagnosed at a significantly more advanced stage of cancer than patients in the general population receiving standard treatment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Laboratory conditions do not perfectly replicate the environment of the human body.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The experimental drug was administered at several hospitals across different regions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some patients in the general population also received experimental treatments not captured by the standard-treatment statistics.

explanations.correct: If trial enrollees had more advanced cancer at diagnosis, their lower survival rate reflects disease severity rather than drug inefficacy. The drug can be genuinely superior in destroying cancer cells while still failing to overcome the disadvantage of later-stage disease — dissolving the apparent conflict.
explanations.A: Side-effect profiles do not explain why the drug's superior cell-destruction ability fails to produce better survival rates in the trial group. This resolves neither horn.
explanations.B: Correct. Self-selection into the trial by sicker patients explains the survival gap without contradicting the lab evidence.
explanations.C: This weakens the lab evidence rather than reconciling the two facts; it deepens rather than resolves the paradox.
explanations.D: Geographic breadth of administration is irrelevant to explaining the survival-rate discrepancy.
explanations.E: This potentially narrows the gap in the comparison group but does not explain why experimental-drug patients fared worse, leaving the paradox intact.

lr.difficultyReason: Economic paradox: a city raises the minimum wage but poverty rates rise. Resolution requires a confounding labor-market variable (employment loss). Distractors target one horn or deepen the paradox.
lr.stimulus: A major city raised its minimum wage by 30 percent over three years, intending to reduce poverty among low-income workers. Despite this increase, the city's official poverty rate rose by four percentage points during the same period, even as the regional economy as a whole was expanding.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the surprising outcome described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Workers who retained their jobs at the new minimum wage earned substantially more than they had previously.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The city's poverty threshold is calculated using a formula that has remained unchanged for decades.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many low-wage employers in the city reduced hours or eliminated entry-level positions in response to the wage increase, leaving thousands of previously employed workers without income.

choices.label: D
choices.text: City residents at all income levels reported greater satisfaction with their financial situations after the wage increase took effect.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The regional economy's expansion was driven primarily by high-technology industries that employ very few minimum-wage workers.

explanations.correct: If the wage hike caused employers to eliminate jobs, the workers who lost employment would have no income at all — pushing the poverty rate up despite the remaining workers earning more. This reconciles both facts: wages rose and poverty rose simultaneously.
explanations.A: This explains why some workers benefited but does not account for why overall poverty increased. It resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: An outdated formula could distort the poverty measurement, but the answer does not specify how this would cause the measured rate to rise, making it too vague to resolve the paradox.
explanations.C: Correct. Job losses due to the wage hike provide the confounding mechanism that explains rising poverty despite higher wages.
explanations.D: Self-reported satisfaction contradicts rather than explains a rising poverty rate, and actually deepens the paradox.
explanations.E: This context about tech expansion tells us the broader economy doesn't directly help low-wage workers, but it does not explain the mechanism by which poverty increased — it resolves one horn only.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental-science paradox: a river's fish population declined after a factory closed. Resolution via reverse causation/alternative mechanism (a competing stressor). Distractors explain closure consequences but not the fish decline.
lr.stimulus: After a chemical manufacturing plant on the Aldren River closed its operations, discharge of industrial pollutants into the river ceased entirely. Yet within two years of the closure, the river's native fish population had declined by nearly 40 percent compared to pre-closure levels.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The plant had employed a water-treatment process that, as a byproduct, maintained elevated oxygen levels in the river downstream of the facility.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fish populations in rivers without chemical plants also fluctuate from year to year due to seasonal changes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Environmental regulators conducted water-quality tests for two years after the plant closed and found no remaining chemical contamination.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The chemical plant had operated on the Aldren River for more than fifty years before its closure.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fish in the Aldren River had developed partial resistance to the chemicals previously discharged by the plant.

explanations.correct: If the plant's water-treatment process was inadvertently oxygenating the river and that byproduct disappeared with the closure, fish habitat quality may have worsened despite the elimination of chemical pollution — reconciling cleaner water with a declining fish population.
explanations.A: Correct. A hidden beneficial byproduct of the plant that vanished upon closure explains why removing pollution still led to worse ecological outcomes.
explanations.B: Normal year-to-year fluctuations cannot account for a 40-percent decline following a specific event; this is irrelevant to the paradox.
explanations.C: Confirming the absence of residual chemicals actually deepens the paradox: if the water is clean, why are fish declining?
explanations.D: The plant's operating history does not explain the post-closure decline; this is irrelevant to the paradox.
explanations.E: Partial resistance to chemicals that are no longer present does not explain the decline — it resolves neither horn of the paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology paradox: users who receive spam filters get more unwanted email. Self-selection/reverse causation: filters attract heavy email users. Distractors sound plausible but address only one horn.
lr.stimulus: Users of a major email service who opted into the provider's new AI-powered spam filter received, on average, 35 percent more unwanted commercial emails per month than users who did not activate the filter. Yet internal tests conducted by the provider confirmed that the filter accurately blocks over 95 percent of detected spam.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Users who activated the spam filter were primarily heavy email users who had already subscribed to far more commercial mailing lists than average users.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The spam filter was offered free of charge to all users of the email service.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Spam filters from competing email providers perform at similar accuracy rates to the provider's new AI filter.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The provider's internal testing was conducted on a sample of emails specifically curated to represent a wide variety of spam types.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some users who activated the filter subsequently reported feeling less concerned about email security.

explanations.correct: If users who opted in were already receiving far more spam-eligible emails due to extensive mailing-list subscriptions, the 35-percent excess reflects a pre-existing differential in exposure rather than filter failure. Even a 95-percent-effective filter leaves more spam reaching heavy users than lightly subscribed non-filter users receive in total.
explanations.A: Correct. Self-selection explains that the filter group had far greater baseline spam exposure, reconciling the outcome data with the filter's proven accuracy.
explanations.B: The cost of the filter is irrelevant to whether it works or why filtered users receive more spam.
explanations.C: Competitor performance does not explain the internal discrepancy; this is irrelevant.
explanations.D: Test methodology explains the 95-percent figure but does not account for why filter users receive more unwanted email — it resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: Changed user attitudes may suggest behavioral changes, but no mechanism linking reduced concern to more spam received is established; too speculative to resolve the paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy paradox: speed cameras in school zones reduced speeding but increased pedestrian injuries. Hidden mechanism (driver attention distraction) explains both. Distractors deepen or address only one horn.
lr.stimulus: After a city installed speed cameras in all school zones, the percentage of drivers exceeding the posted speed limit dropped from 42 percent to 11 percent. Nevertheless, the number of pedestrian injuries in those same school zones increased by 18 percent in the year following camera installation.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Speed cameras of the type installed by the city have been used successfully in other jurisdictions to reduce pedestrian fatalities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many drivers, upon noticing the cameras, slowed abruptly and then directed their attention toward the camera rather than toward the road, causing a sharp increase in distraction-related collisions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The school zones where cameras were installed had historically lower pedestrian-injury rates than zones without cameras.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pedestrian injuries in school zones without cameras remained unchanged during the same period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Drivers who received speeding fines from the cameras tended to challenge them in administrative hearings.

explanations.correct: If cameras caused drivers to brake suddenly and look away from the road, a new form of collision risk emerged that offset the benefit of lower speeds. This accounts for both facts: fewer speeders yet more injuries, because driver distraction became the new hazard.
explanations.A: Evidence that cameras work elsewhere actually deepens the paradox — if they work in other cities, why do injuries rise here?
explanations.B: Correct. Camera-induced distraction introduces a confounding mechanism that explains rising injuries despite falling speeding rates.
explanations.C: Lower historical injury rates in camera zones set up a regression-to-the-mean possibility but do not explain the post-installation increase; this resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: Stable injuries in non-camera zones confirm the camera zones worsened but do not explain why — this deepens rather than resolves the paradox.
explanations.E: Administrative challenges to fines are irrelevant to pedestrian injury rates.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics paradox: a language-immersion program improves test scores but students show weaker everyday conversational fluency. Resolution requires a definitional/measurement distinction (tests measure formal accuracy; conversation requires informal register). Distractors address only one metric.
lr.stimulus: Students enrolled in an intensive foreign-language immersion program scored, on average, 22 points higher on standardized proficiency exams than students who received traditional classroom instruction. Yet teachers and native speakers who interacted with immersion students consistently rated those students' conversational fluency as noticeably weaker than that of traditionally taught students at the same proficiency-exam level.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The standardized proficiency exams used in the comparison focus exclusively on formal grammar, reading comprehension, and written composition, and do not assess informal spoken registers or colloquial expression.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immersion programs are generally more expensive to operate than traditional classroom instruction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some immersion students had prior exposure to the language before enrolling in the program.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Native speakers tend to rate non-native conversational fluency more harshly than trained language teachers do.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Traditional classroom instruction incorporates more hours of writing practice than immersion programs typically provide.

explanations.correct: If proficiency exams measure only formal written skills and immersion training emphasizes those same formal skills, immersion students can score higher on exams while still being weaker in the informal conversational register that native speakers and teachers are actually evaluating. The two metrics measure different things, dissolving the apparent conflict.
explanations.A: Correct. A definitional/measurement mismatch between what the exam tests and what conversational fluency requires reconciles both halves of the paradox.
explanations.B: Program cost is irrelevant to the discrepancy between exam scores and conversational ratings.
explanations.C: Prior exposure could inflate immersion students' scores, but it does not explain why their conversational fluency is weaker relative to score-matched traditionally taught students.
explanations.D: If native speakers rate everyone more harshly, this does not explain why immersion students are rated lower than traditionally taught students at the same score level — it resolves neither horn.
explanations.E: Greater writing practice in traditional programs would predict lower immersion exam scores, not higher — this actually deepens the paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: Historical paradox: a medieval city's population grew rapidly during a period of documented famine. Temporal/contextual resolution: refugees from worse-affected regions inflated local numbers. Distractors address only the famine or only the growth.
lr.stimulus: Historical records show that the city of Velmoor experienced its fastest population growth during the decade-long famine of the 1340s, when grain harvests across the region failed repeatedly and the death toll in surrounding villages was catastrophic. Yet Velmoor's own grain stores were reported by contemporary chroniclers to be no better supplied than those of the surrounding areas.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Velmoor was a walled city, which gave its residents a sense of security unavailable to inhabitants of surrounding open villages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Survivors from the devastated surrounding villages fled to Velmoor in such large numbers that immigration exceeded the city's own famine mortality, producing a net population increase.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The famine of the 1340s was less severe in Velmoor than in any other location in the region.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Velmoor's chroniclers were known to exaggerate the city's prosperity in their written records.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Population counts in medieval cities were typically conducted by ecclesiastical authorities rather than civic officials.

explanations.correct: If large-scale refugee immigration to Velmoor outpaced famine deaths within the city, the net population would rise despite identical food scarcity conditions. This reconciles rapid growth with equally bad grain supplies: the city grew not because conditions were better but because outsiders arrived faster than insiders died.
explanations.A: A sense of security from walls may explain why refugees chose Velmoor, but the answer must explain actual population growth — this alone is insufficient and resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Correct. Immigration exceeding internal mortality is the confounding mechanism that reconciles population growth with dire food conditions.
explanations.C: This directly contradicts the stimulus, which states Velmoor's supplies were no better than surrounding areas — this answer presupposes the opposite of what is given.
explanations.D: If chroniclers exaggerated prosperity, the grain-store data may be unreliable, but this undermines the stimulus rather than resolving the paradox within its given facts.
explanations.E: The method of census-taking is irrelevant to whether population actually grew during a famine.

lr.difficultyReason: Law/policy paradox: mandatory sentencing laws reduced recidivism rates among released offenders but total crime rates in affected jurisdictions rose. Requires recognizing that longer sentences keep more people incarcerated (not released), so the released-offender pool is a biased sample of low-risk individuals.
lr.stimulus: After several jurisdictions adopted mandatory minimum sentencing laws for repeat offenders, the recidivism rate among offenders released from those jurisdictions' prisons fell by 14 percent compared to pre-law rates. However, total violent crime rates in those same jurisdictions increased by 9 percent over the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mandatory minimum sentencing laws are politically popular in the jurisdictions that adopt them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mandatory sentencing laws kept a large population of high-risk, repeat offenders incarcerated for longer periods, while releasing primarily first-time or lower-risk offenders, whose recidivism rates were already low.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prison conditions in the affected jurisdictions improved during the same period, which may have reduced the motivation to reoffend.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some offenders subject to mandatory sentencing were convicted of nonviolent offenses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Jurisdictions without mandatory sentencing laws also experienced increases in violent crime during the same period.

explanations.correct: If mandatory sentences kept the highest-risk repeat offenders incarcerated, those never released could not recidivate during the measurement period. The released pool thus consisted disproportionately of lower-risk individuals, artificially lowering the measured recidivism rate. Meanwhile, the large number of still-incarcerated high-risk offenders did not reduce crime that was already occurring, and the removal of deterrence for new first-time offenders may have contributed to the rise in total crime — reconciling both statistics.
explanations.A: Political popularity is irrelevant to the statistical discrepancy between recidivism and total crime rates.
explanations.B: Correct. Sample-composition bias explains the recidivism drop, and the continued absence of deterrence for new offenders explains the crime rise.
explanations.C: Improved prison conditions could explain lower recidivism but does not explain why total crime increased — this resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: Nonviolent offenders under mandatory sentencing is a tangential detail that does not reconcile the two statistics.
explanations.E: If other jurisdictions also saw crime rise, this context suggests an external cause but does not explain the simultaneous recidivism drop in the affected jurisdictions — this resolves one horn only.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts/economics paradox: ticket prices for a regional theater rose substantially yet total revenue fell. Resolution requires understanding that demand is price-elastic in this market (higher prices drove away enough attendees to reduce total receipts).
lr.stimulus: The Haverford Regional Theater raised average ticket prices by 25 percent in an effort to increase revenue and fund building renovations. In the season following the price increase, however, total ticket revenue fell by 11 percent compared to the previous season, even though no competing theaters had opened in the area.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Season-ticket subscribers, who purchased tickets at a locked-in rate, accounted for a majority of the theater's revenue in the previous season.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attendance at the theater fell by 29 percent after the price increase, as many patrons chose to stay home or substitute other leisure activities.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The theater had planned to use renovation funds to attract higher-profile productions that would command premium ticket prices.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Theater attendance across the country declined modestly during the same season due to an economic slowdown.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Building renovation costs had increased significantly since the theater first announced its pricing strategy.

explanations.correct: A 29-percent drop in attendance means that even at 25 percent higher prices, total receipts (price × quantity) fell — because the percentage loss in quantity exceeded the percentage gain in price. This identifies the elastic-demand mechanism that reconciles the two facts: prices rose, yet revenue fell.
explanations.A: Season-ticket subscribers at locked-in rates would buffer revenue against price increases rather than explain a revenue fall; this may even deepen the paradox.
explanations.B: Correct. The attendance collapse quantitatively accounts for why higher per-ticket prices still produced lower total revenue, resolving both horns.
explanations.C: Future programming plans are irrelevant to the revenue outcome already observed — this resolves neither horn.
explanations.D: A modest national attendance decline is insufficient to explain an 11-percent revenue drop following a 25-percent price hike at a theater without new competitors; this resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: Rising renovation costs affect spending, not revenue, and are irrelevant to the discrepancy.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics/policy paradox: a charity that reduced its administrative overhead percentage saw a drop in donor contributions. Resolution involves a measurement-artifact/reverse-causation explanation: donors use overhead ratio as a quality signal, and a suspiciously low ratio triggered distrust.
lr.stimulus: A well-known charitable organization reduced its administrative overhead from 18 percent of total expenditures to 6 percent, a figure that independent auditors confirmed as accurate. Nonetheless, annual donations to the organization declined by 22 percent in the two years following the announcement of this improvement.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Donors who give to charitable organizations generally prefer that most of their contributions go directly to the stated cause rather than to administration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Major donors and watchdog groups interpreted an overhead ratio as low as 6 percent as implausible, concluding that the organization was likely underreporting expenses, and consequently withdrew their support.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The organization announced the overhead reduction through a press release that received wide media coverage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Charitable giving in the organization's primary funding region declined by approximately 5 percent over the same two-year period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The reduction in administrative overhead was achieved partly by reclassifying some administrative costs as program expenses.

explanations.correct: If donors and watchdogs saw the 6-percent figure as implausibly low and inferred fraudulent accounting, their rational response would be to withdraw contributions — explaining the donation decline despite (and because of) the announced improvement. The very accuracy of the figure was unpersuasive, resolving both horns through a reverse-causation trust mechanism.
explanations.A: This explains why donors generally prefer low overhead, making the donation decline more paradoxical rather than less — it deepens the paradox.
explanations.B: Correct. Perceived implausibility of the improvement triggered donor distrust, reconciling genuine overhead reduction with declining donations.
explanations.C: Wide media coverage would, if anything, be expected to increase donations by publicizing the improvement; this deepens rather than resolves the paradox.
explanations.D: A 5-percent regional decline in giving cannot account for a 22-percent drop in donations to one specific organization; this resolves one horn only and insufficiently.
explanations.E: If this were true, the auditor-confirmed figure would be misleading — but the stimulus states auditors confirmed accuracy. This answer contradicts the stimulus rather than resolving the paradox within its given facts.

lr.difficultyReason: Statistical paradox requiring a reverse-causation resolution: patients receiving the more aggressive treatment have worse outcomes, yet the treatment itself is effective. Test-takers must recognize that severity of illness, not treatment, drives the correlation.
lr.stimulus: At a large urban hospital, patients who received an aggressive antibiotic regimen for bacterial pneumonia had a 30-percent higher in-hospital mortality rate than patients who received a standard regimen. Yet clinical trials conducted under controlled conditions consistently show that the aggressive regimen is more effective at eliminating the bacteria responsible for the pneumonia.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The aggressive antibiotic regimen is significantly more expensive than the standard regimen and is therefore used less frequently overall.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Physicians at the hospital prescribed the aggressive regimen primarily to patients whose pneumonia was already at an advanced or critical stage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several of the antibiotics used in the aggressive regimen have known side effects that can worsen certain pre-existing heart conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The clinical trials that evaluated the aggressive regimen were conducted at teaching hospitals with above-average staffing ratios.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bacterial pneumonia accounts for a smaller proportion of pneumonia cases at urban hospitals than at rural ones.

explanations.correct: If the aggressive regimen was reserved for the most critically ill patients, those patients were already more likely to die regardless of treatment. The higher mortality rate reflects patient severity, not treatment failure — dissolving the conflict between hospital outcomes and clinical-trial results.
explanations.A: Cost and frequency of use explain how often the regimen is prescribed but not why those who receive it have worse outcomes. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Correct. Identifies a confounding variable — pre-treatment severity — that accounts for both the worse hospital outcomes and the genuine clinical efficacy of the aggressive regimen.
explanations.C: Side effects on heart conditions could partially worsen outcomes, but this explains only some deaths and only in a subpopulation; it doesn't reconcile the broad discrepancy with consistently superior clinical-trial results.
explanations.D: The conditions under which the trials were conducted might affect trial generalizability, but this deepens the paradox by suggesting the hospital context is less optimal — it doesn't explain why aggressive-regimen patients die at higher rates.
explanations.E: The urban/rural distribution of pneumonia types is irrelevant to the discrepancy between hospital outcomes and clinical-trial efficacy within the same institution.

lr.difficultyReason: Economic policy paradox with a self-selection / composition-effect resolution. Test-takers must identify that the businesses surveyed after the minimum-wage increase are a biased sample — only survivors remain — making aggregate wage data appear favorable despite the policy's costs.
lr.stimulus: Following a significant increase in the regional minimum wage, a survey of businesses in the region found that the average hourly wage paid to employees had risen by less than the amount of the minimum-wage increase. Yet economists confirm that every business in the region is complying fully with the new minimum wage law.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The minimum wage increase was phased in gradually over an 18-month period rather than taking effect all at once.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many businesses in the region responded to the minimum wage increase by reducing the total number of hours worked by their employees.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A substantial number of businesses that had employed large numbers of minimum-wage workers closed permanently before the survey was conducted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The survey methodology relied on self-reported payroll data, which some economists consider less reliable than tax-record data.

choices.label: E
choices.text: In the years before the minimum-wage increase, average wages in the region had been rising steadily at approximately two percent per year.

explanations.correct: If businesses that heavily employed minimum-wage workers shut down before the survey, the surviving businesses — which had fewer minimum-wage employees to begin with — would show a smaller average wage increase even while fully complying with the new law. This survival-bias effect reconciles full compliance with a below-expected average wage rise.
explanations.A: A phase-in period might slow the full impact, but full compliance is confirmed, so the average wage should still reflect the full new minimum among current employees. This resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Reducing hours affects total compensation but not the hourly wage rate. A lower hourly average is still unexpected if all firms comply with the minimum; this doesn't explain why the average hourly wage rose less than the minimum-wage increase.
explanations.C: Correct. A classic survivor/selection-bias resolution: the post-increase business sample is biased toward firms with fewer minimum-wage workers, producing a lower measured average increase despite universal compliance.
explanations.D: Potential measurement unreliability would cast doubt on the survey results generally, but it doesn't explain the specific directional discrepancy — it equally might cause overestimates. This is an irrelevant-methodology distractor.
explanations.E: Pre-increase wage trends are irrelevant to why, after a confirmed compliance, the measured average increase falls short of the statutory increase.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental policy paradox with a temporal/scope-difference resolution. Test-takers must identify that aggregate pollution figures conceal a compositional shift: the reduction in one source is offset by a growth in another, explaining why national totals are unchanged despite the regulated sector's compliance.
lr.stimulus: After regulations requiring a 40-percent reduction in sulfur dioxide emissions from coal-fired power plants took effect, the power industry achieved exactly the required reduction. Nonetheless, total sulfur dioxide emissions measured across the nation remained unchanged from pre-regulation levels.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sulfur dioxide is one of several pollutants regulated under the same environmental statute.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The monitoring equipment used to measure national sulfur dioxide levels was upgraded in the same year the regulations took effect.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several environmental advocacy groups had lobbied for a 60-percent reduction rather than the 40-percent reduction that was enacted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: During the period when the regulations were being implemented, the number of diesel-powered industrial vehicles operating nationwide increased sharply, substantially raising sulfur dioxide output from that sector.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Power plants that burn natural gas emit far less sulfur dioxide per unit of energy produced than do coal-fired plants.

explanations.correct: A compensating increase in sulfur dioxide from a different, unregulated source — diesel vehicles — would offset the power industry's verified reduction, leaving national totals flat. This confounding variable reconciles both halves of the apparent contradiction.
explanations.A: The existence of other regulated pollutants doesn't address why sulfur dioxide specifically remained unchanged. Irrelevant.
explanations.B: Upgraded monitoring equipment could affect what is detected, but if anything more sensitive equipment would record lower totals after a genuine reduction. This doesn't explain unchanged national totals and potentially deepens the paradox.
explanations.C: Whether 60 percent would have been preferable is entirely irrelevant to why a confirmed 40-percent reduction failed to lower national totals. Irrelevant.
explanations.D: Correct. Identifies a confounding variable — a contemporaneous increase in emissions from an unregulated sector — that fully accounts for unchanged national totals despite genuine compliance by the regulated sector.
explanations.E: Natural gas versus coal emission rates might be relevant to policy choices, but the stimulus concerns coal-plant compliance and national totals; this fact doesn't explain why verified power-plant reductions were offset at the national level.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology-domain paradox requiring recognition of a definitional / measurement-scope distinction. Test-takers must see that 'customer satisfaction' and 'customer retention' measure different populations at different points in the product lifecycle, creating an apparent but not genuine contradiction.
lr.stimulus: A software company introduced an extensively redesigned version of its flagship product. Surveys conducted three months after the launch showed that customer satisfaction scores for the new version were significantly higher than scores for the previous version. Yet the company's overall customer retention rate dropped noticeably in the same three-month period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to explain the surprising phenomenon described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The satisfaction surveys were completed only by customers who had already chosen to continue using the product after the redesign.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The company increased the subscription price of the product at the same time it released the redesigned version.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Software products typically receive higher satisfaction scores immediately after a major redesign than they do after several months of use.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some longtime customers reported that they preferred the visual layout of the previous version of the product.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The company's customer support staff received additional training in the months preceding the product launch.

explanations.correct: If only customers who stayed with the product filled out the satisfaction survey, those respondents are a self-selected group — precisely the customers who liked the redesign enough to keep using it. Customers who were dissatisfied and left would not appear in the survey. This selection effect explains why satisfaction scores are high (only happy stayers were surveyed) while retention dropped (many customers left without being counted in the satisfaction data).
explanations.A: Correct. Classic self-selection / survivorship bias: the high satisfaction scores reflect only the retained, satisfied subset, not the full customer base, reconciling high measured satisfaction with lower overall retention.
explanations.B: A price increase could cause customers to leave, explaining lower retention, but it would not explain why satisfaction scores among remaining customers are higher than before. This resolves one horn only (retention drop) while deepening the other (why would satisfaction rise if the price went up?).
explanations.C: A honeymoon effect on satisfaction scores would predict scores drop over time, but it doesn't reconcile simultaneously high satisfaction scores with simultaneously low retention in the same three-month window. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: A subset of longtime customers preferring the old layout could contribute to departures, but 'some' customers is too vague to account for a noticeable retention drop, and it does nothing to explain why satisfaction scores rose. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: Better customer support training would tend to improve both satisfaction and retention, if anything deepening the paradox of why retention fell while satisfaction rose.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-fact tension: a new drug outperforms placebo in trials, patients prescribed the drug in general practice recover no faster than untreated patients, yet hospitals that adopted the drug report shorter average stays. Resolution hinges on a selection effect at the hospital level — only the sickest patients are admitted and treated, so hospital averages are driven by case mix rather than drug efficacy.
lr.stimulus: In randomized trials, patients taking the antiviral drug Reviran recovered from severe influenza two days faster than patients given a placebo. In general practice, however, patients prescribed Reviran recovered no faster than patients who received no antiviral treatment. Nonetheless, hospitals that adopted Reviran as standard care for admitted flu patients reported that average length of stay fell by nearly a full day after the drug was introduced.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: General practitioners prescribe Reviran primarily to patients whose flu symptoms are already improving, whereas hospitals administer it only to patients whose symptoms are severe enough to require admission.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reviran is significantly more expensive than other antiviral drugs currently on the market.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hospitals that adopted Reviran also expanded their outpatient follow-up programs during the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The placebo used in the randomized trials was indistinguishable in appearance from Reviran tablets.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most patients who are prescribed Reviran by a general practitioner do not complete the full course of treatment.

explanations.correct: If general practitioners prescribe Reviran mainly to patients already on the mend, the 'treated' group in general practice is biased toward mild cases who would have recovered quickly regardless — wiping out the drug's apparent edge. Hospitals, by contrast, give it to severe cases for whom the trial-proven two-day shortening translates into meaningfully shorter admissions. Both patterns arise from who receives the drug, not whether it works.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Cost is irrelevant to recovery speed or length of stay.
explanations.C: Expanded follow-up could explain shorter hospital stays but says nothing about why general practice showed no benefit while trials did.
explanations.D: Blinding quality supports the trial result but doesn't reconcile it with the general-practice and hospital data.
explanations.E: Non-adherence would explain why general practice saw no benefit but would leave the hospital and trial results unreconciled — and if anything deepens the contrast.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-layer paradox: nationwide worker productivity rose, average hourly wages also rose, yet median household income fell. Resolution requires recognizing a compositional shift — high earners working more hours and low earners dropping out of the labor force — which a simple productivity-wage story cannot explain.
lr.stimulus: Over the past decade, output per hour worked in the country of Alvara rose by 22 percent, and average hourly wages, adjusted for inflation, rose by 9 percent. Despite these gains, the median household's annual income fell by 4 percent during the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cost of housing in Alvara rose faster than either wages or productivity over the decade.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A substantial number of lower-wage workers left the labor force during the decade, while many higher-wage workers increased their hours; the average wage figure reflects only those still employed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Productivity gains were concentrated in export industries, whose goods were sold mostly to customers outside Alvara.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most of the hourly wage gains were driven by increases at the top of the wage distribution, while wages at the bottom rose more slowly.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Average household size in Alvara increased slightly over the decade, spreading household income over more people.

explanations.correct: If many low-wage workers exited the labor force, their zero earnings drag median household income down even as the remaining employed workers — a wealthier slice — push the average wage up. Meanwhile, higher-wage workers working more hours raise productivity. The three statistics measure different populations, so all three can move as described simultaneously.
explanations.A: Rising housing costs don't affect income measurements.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Export concentration could explain productivity gains but doesn't explain why median household income fell despite rising wages.
explanations.D: Top-heavy wage growth raises the average, but without an exit from the labor force it cannot pull median household income below its starting point.
explanations.E: Household size affects per-person income, not household income; and the stated increase is 'slight,' insufficient for a 4 percent drop.

lr.difficultyReason: Three facts: firms that adopted the new security protocol experience the same number of successful intrusions as those that didn't, security auditors unanimously rate the protocol as stronger, and yet the average dollar loss per intrusion at adopting firms is substantially lower. Resolution requires a definitional distinction between types of intrusion events — counted attacks versus data loss.
lr.stimulus: Cybersecurity researchers report that firms that adopted the new Sentinel authentication protocol suffer, on average, the same number of successful intrusions per year as comparable firms that did not adopt it. Auditors unanimously rate Sentinel as more resistant to unauthorized access than the industry standard. Nevertheless, the average dollar loss per intrusion at adopting firms is only about one-fifth of the loss at nonadopting firms.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sentinel blocks the most sophisticated intrusion techniques but allows certain low-level intrusions — such as benign automated probes that briefly access harmless files — to be logged as 'successful' even though no sensitive data is reached.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Firms that adopt Sentinel tend to be larger and hold more valuable data than firms that do not adopt it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cost of implementing Sentinel is substantially higher than the cost of maintaining the industry-standard protocol.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Auditors who rated Sentinel were not informed of the dollar-loss data when making their assessments.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many firms that adopted Sentinel also increased their spending on employee cybersecurity training in the same year.

explanations.correct: If Sentinel lets trivial probes be recorded as 'successful intrusions' while blocking the damaging ones, adopting firms can match nonadopters in raw count while losing far less per event. The auditors' favorable rating — keyed to blocking serious breaches — is also consistent. All three facts reconcile once 'successful intrusion' is understood to cover heterogeneous severity.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Larger, more valuable targets would raise, not lower, losses per intrusion at adopters — deepening the paradox.
explanations.C: Implementation cost doesn't affect intrusion counts or per-intrusion losses.
explanations.D: Blinding of auditors addresses rating integrity but not the count-vs.-loss mismatch.
explanations.E: A confounded training effect could lower losses, but it leaves unexplained why intrusion counts didn't also fall at adopting firms.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-way tension: habitat protection expanded, documented populations of the target species rose, yet field biologists report fewer sightings in the wild than before protection. Resolution requires a temporal-methodological shift — population figures derive from new surveying techniques that count animals previously invisible to observers.
lr.stimulus: When the Mersin government declared the coastal cedar forest a protected reserve ten years ago, the goal was to aid the recovery of the Mersin loris, a small nocturnal primate. Official population estimates for the loris have since risen from roughly 1,200 to over 4,000 individuals. Yet naturalists who have walked the reserve regularly for decades report seeing the loris far less often than they did before protection began.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Shortly after the reserve was created, biologists began using infrared camera traps placed deep in the forest interior, which detect lorises that human observers, restricted to trails, never encounter.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Mersin loris is more active on moonless nights than on moonlit ones.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cedar forest contains several other nocturnal primate species besides the Mersin loris.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Visitor access to parts of the reserve has been restricted since its creation, reducing the number of trails naturalists may walk.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mersin loris populations in unprotected neighboring forests have declined sharply over the past ten years.
