explanations.correct: If new camera-trap surveys detect lorises hidden from trail-bound human observers, the official population figure can climb even as naturalists' sightings on the trails fall — perhaps because behavioral change, disturbance avoidance, or simply the trails no longer intersecting dense habitat. The apparent mismatch is an artifact of two different counting methods.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Moonlight variation is a constant factor and cannot explain a directional change.
explanations.C: Presence of other species doesn't affect loris sightings or counts of lorises specifically.
explanations.D: Restricted trail access could explain fewer sightings but doesn't on its own explain the large rise in population estimates.
explanations.E: Decline in neighboring forests explains nothing about sightings in the reserve, and a loris influx would tend to raise, not lower, on-trail encounters.

lr.difficultyReason: Three interlocking facts about a reform: arrests for fraud fell, prosecutors filed charges in a higher percentage of referred cases, yet the absolute number of fraud convictions also fell. Resolution requires spotting that the reform narrowed what qualifies as a chargeable fraud case, affecting the pipeline at the front.
lr.stimulus: Five years ago, the state legislature overhauled its fraud statutes, narrowing the definition of criminal fraud to exclude certain deceptive but non-malicious business practices. Since the overhaul, arrests for fraud have fallen by 30 percent statewide. Prosecutors, however, now file formal charges in 85 percent of cases referred to them, up from 60 percent before the overhaul. Despite this higher charging rate, the absolute number of fraud convictions has fallen by nearly 20 percent.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The statutory overhaul eliminated from fraud law a large class of minor, easily-proven offenses, so the cases that remain are fewer in number but more likely to survive a prosecutor's screen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Defendants charged with fraud under the new statute are more likely to request jury trials than defendants charged under the old statute.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prosecutors' offices received a budget increase in the year following the overhaul.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many businesses responded to the overhaul by increasing their internal compliance audits.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The overhaul lengthened the average sentence for fraud convictions.

explanations.correct: If the overhaul removed a large tier of low-grade offenses from fraud law, total arrests drop and the surviving cases are concentrated in serious, well-evidenced conduct — exactly the cases prosecutors readily charge, explaining the higher charging percentage. Convictions still fall in absolute terms because the pool of chargeable conduct shrank. All three statistics reconcile through the narrowed definition.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Trial choice doesn't determine how many cases are charged or arrested.
explanations.C: A budget increase should raise, not lower, conviction counts and doesn't explain the charging-rate shift.
explanations.D: Private compliance work might reduce fraud, but it doesn't explain why prosecutors' charging rate rose.
explanations.E: Sentence length is about punishment, not conviction counts or charging decisions.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-way historical paradox: printed book production surged, documented literacy rates climbed, yet surviving personal correspondence from ordinary citizens during the period is far scarcer than from the decade preceding it. Resolution requires a differential-survival confounder: paper quality or conservation practices changed in a way that disproportionately destroyed the later correspondence.
lr.stimulus: Historians studying the kingdom of Voren note that between 1620 and 1640 the annual output of printed books in the kingdom tripled and documented literacy rates among free citizens rose from roughly 25 percent to over 50 percent. Nevertheless, the number of surviving personal letters written by ordinary Vorenian citizens during 1620–1640 is substantially smaller than the number surviving from the decade 1610–1620.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Around 1620, Vorenian papermakers began using a new wood-pulp process whose acidic output becomes brittle and disintegrates within a century, whereas the rag paper used in the preceding decade has survived intact.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Literacy rates among enslaved persons in Voren, who could not legally write letters, remained near zero throughout both periods.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The printed books produced during 1620–1640 were mostly religious tracts rather than works of secular correspondence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Historians have studied the decade 1610–1620 far more intensively than the subsequent two decades.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The price of paper rose sharply after 1640, making private correspondence a luxury only the wealthy could afford.

explanations.correct: A shift to acidic wood-pulp paper in 1620 would cause letters written on it to disintegrate, while earlier rag-paper letters endure. The count of 'surviving' letters is then a measure of paper chemistry, not of how many letters were written. Rising literacy and book production can coexist with a shrinking surviving corpus once differential survival is in view.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Enslaved persons' literacy is held constant, so it cannot produce the observed change between the two periods.
explanations.C: Book content doesn't affect how many personal letters survive.
explanations.D: If anything, more intensive study of the earlier period could raise the count of surviving letters from it, but it doesn't explain why the later period shows fewer surviving letters in absolute terms.
explanations.E: This concerns the period after 1640, not the period of the paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-way linguistic paradox: immersion-program learners outscore classroom-only learners on grammar tests, classroom-only learners outscore immersion learners on vocabulary tests, yet in unscripted conversation native speakers rate the immersion learners as substantially more fluent. Resolution turns on a hidden confounder — the vocabulary test penalizes register-appropriate word choices that immersion learners acquire.
lr.stimulus: Researchers compared two groups of adult Vethan-language learners. On standardized grammar tests, students who had completed a six-month immersion program in Vethea outperformed students who studied only in classrooms. On standardized vocabulary tests, however, the classroom-only students outperformed the immersion students. Yet in recorded unscripted conversations, native Vethan speakers rated the immersion students as substantially more fluent than the classroom-only students.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The standardized vocabulary test rewards knowledge of formal and literary Vethan words, while native speakers in everyday conversation use — and expect — colloquial and regional words that immersion students acquire and classroom students do not.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The immersion program included more hours of instruction per week than the classroom-only program.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students who enroll in immersion programs tend to have higher baseline language-learning aptitude than students who choose classroom programs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vethan grammar is widely considered among the most difficult features of the language to master.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Native Vethan speakers who served as raters were not informed which learners had completed immersion.

explanations.correct: If the vocabulary test rewards formal words but native speakers use — and grade for — colloquial ones, immersion students can look weaker on the test while sounding more fluent in conversation. This hidden register mismatch simultaneously explains lower test scores, higher conversational ratings, and is fully compatible with the immersion group's stronger grammar.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: More instructional hours could raise all scores but cannot explain why the immersion group does worse on vocabulary while doing better on grammar and conversation.
explanations.C: Higher aptitude predicts better performance across all three measures, deepening rather than resolving the vocabulary anomaly.
explanations.D: Grammar's difficulty doesn't reconcile the vocabulary-vs.-conversation gap.
explanations.E: Blinding supports the conversational ratings' credibility but doesn't explain the vocabulary test result.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-fact policy paradox: housing subsidies expanded, the absolute number of unsheltered residents fell, yet the rate of unsheltered homelessness per capita in the city rose. Resolution requires recognizing a migration-driven base-rate change — the population denominator fell faster than the numerator, producing a rise in rate despite falling counts.
lr.stimulus: Five years ago the city of Porthaven tripled its housing subsidy budget. Since then, the number of residents classified as unsheltered — people living on the streets or in vehicles — has fallen from 4,800 to 3,900. Despite this decline, the rate of unsheltered homelessness in Porthaven, measured as unsheltered residents per 10,000 total residents, has risen by more than 15 percent during the same five years.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During the five-year period, the total population of Porthaven fell sharply as many working-age residents moved to neighboring cities with lower costs of living.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most of the new subsidies were used by residents to remain in existing housing rather than to move into previously vacant units.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Residents classified as 'sheltered homeless' — those in shelters or transitional housing — also declined over the five-year period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Porthaven's unsheltered count is conducted during a single night in January each year.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several neighboring cities reduced their own housing subsidy programs during the same period.

explanations.correct: A rate is a ratio. If Porthaven's total population fell faster in percentage terms than its unsheltered count, the rate per 10,000 rises even as the numerator falls. The subsidies plausibly helped drive the numerator down, while outmigration of working-age residents shrinks the denominator faster still. All three facts are reconciled through the denominator change.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: This concerns how subsidies were used and wouldn't explain a rate that rises while counts fall.
explanations.C: Parallel decline in sheltered homelessness doesn't affect the per-capita unsheltered rate's direction.
explanations.D: Counting methodology is held constant across years.
explanations.E: Neighboring cuts might push homeless populations toward Porthaven, which would raise the count — but Porthaven's count fell, so this deepens the paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-fact arts paradox: ticket prices fell, the number of exhibitions offered increased, yet total paid attendance dropped. Resolution requires seeing that a new free-admission policy for the permanent collection diverted visitors who would previously have purchased tickets.
lr.stimulus: The Kellerstrom Museum of Modern Art reports that over the past three years it reduced the price of a single-day admission ticket by 20 percent and increased the number of special exhibitions it hosts each year from six to nine. Nevertheless, total paid attendance at the museum fell by nearly 25 percent during the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Three years ago the museum began offering free admission to its permanent collection, with tickets required only for the special exhibitions; most visitors report coming primarily to see the permanent collection.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The museum's three-year operating budget has remained essentially flat in inflation-adjusted terms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attendance at other art museums in the region has also declined over the past three years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several of the museum's special exhibitions have received enthusiastic reviews in major publications.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The museum's ticket price reduction was smaller, in percentage terms, than the price reductions announced by several of its peer institutions during the same period.

explanations.correct: If admission to the permanent collection became free and most visitors come primarily for it, those visitors no longer appear in paid-attendance figures. Meanwhile, the cheaper tickets and increased exhibition count draw visitors specifically to special exhibitions. Total paid attendance drops because the mass of general visitors has been redirected to free admission — a category shift, not a falling interest in the museum.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: A flat budget doesn't explain visitor choices.
explanations.C: A regional decline could explain lower attendance but leaves unexplained why the museum's own price cut and added exhibitions failed to offset it — and the choice resolves one half only.
explanations.D: Favorable reviews would raise, not lower, paid attendance; deepens the paradox.
explanations.E: Relative price position doesn't explain a 25 percent drop on top of an absolute price cut.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-fact ethical-policy paradox: an opt-out organ donation policy produces higher registered donor rates than the prior opt-in policy, public attitude surveys show approval of donation unchanged, yet the number of transplants actually performed per year has declined. Resolution rests on a temporal-logistical confounder — the policy also inadvertently shortened the window for family consultation, causing more registered donors' organs never to be recovered.
lr.stimulus: Three years ago, the nation of Berwick replaced its opt-in organ donation policy with an opt-out policy, under which citizens are presumed donors unless they register a refusal. Since the change, the proportion of adults counted as registered donors has risen from 38 percent to 74 percent, and public opinion surveys show that popular approval of organ donation has remained essentially unchanged. Yet the number of organ transplants actually performed in Berwick each year has declined by about 10 percent since the policy took effect.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The opt-out policy was accompanied by a new hospital protocol that reduced the time families are given to consent to organ recovery after a relative's death; as a result, recovery teams now miss the narrow medical window for retrieval in many more cases than before.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A majority of Berwick citizens who became registered donors under the new policy did not learn of their registration until after the policy took effect.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Other nations that adopted opt-out policies have reported varying effects on transplant numbers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Berwick's population has grown slightly since the policy change.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The opt-out policy was introduced alongside a public information campaign emphasizing the benefits of organ donation.

explanations.correct: Transplants require two things: a donor on the books and a successful, timely recovery. If the opt-out reform came packaged with a protocol that shortens family consultation and medical retrieval windows, registered donor numbers can climb while recoveries — and thus transplants — fall. Popular approval stays flat because approval isn't the bottleneck. All three facts reconcile once the recovery-window change is introduced.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Late-notice registration would still produce registered donors available at death; it doesn't explain why transplants fell.
explanations.C: Reports from other nations don't explain Berwick's specific outcome.
explanations.D: Slight population growth would tend to raise, not lower, the absolute transplant count; deepens the paradox.
explanations.E: A favorable information campaign should raise donation and transplant numbers, sharpening rather than resolving the conflict.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox involves two interacting mechanisms: a medication that reduces average hospital stay lengths yet simultaneously increases total bed-days consumed. Resolution requires recognizing a compound demographic shift — the drug enables previously untreatable (and therefore unhospitalized) patients to now receive inpatient care, expanding the patient pool. Distractors include one that deepens the paradox and one that resolves only one horn.
lr.stimulus: A new antibiotic reduces the average length of hospital stays for bacterial pneumonia patients by 30 percent compared to the previous standard treatment. Yet in the three years since the antibiotic was introduced nationwide, the total number of bed-days consumed annually by bacterial pneumonia patients has increased by 15 percent.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The antibiotic is significantly more expensive than the previous standard treatment, causing some hospitals to use it only selectively.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Since the antibiotic's introduction, the number of patients hospitalized for bacterial pneumonia each year has grown by more than 60 percent, partly because the drug makes survival probable for previously unsurvivable cases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The antibiotic requires intravenous administration for the first two days of treatment, after which patients may switch to oral medication.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bacterial pneumonia has become more prevalent in the general population over the same three-year period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hospitals that adopted the antibiotic earliest also implemented stricter discharge protocols that tend to extend average stays for all respiratory illnesses.

explanations.correct: If the hospitalized patient pool grew by over 60% while individual stay length fell 30%, total bed-days still rise substantially. This compound explanation accounts for both horns simultaneously: shorter stays per patient AND more total bed-days consumed.
explanations.A: Selective use might limit the antibiotic's reach, but this doesn't explain why total bed-days increased — it would more likely keep bed-days flat. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Correct. A 60%+ increase in patient volume more than offsets a 30% reduction in stay length, explaining the rise in total bed-days despite shorter individual stays.
explanations.C: The administration route is irrelevant to the paradox; it doesn't explain why total bed-days increased.
explanations.D: Greater prevalence is consistent with the increase in bed-days, but it doesn't explain why bed-days rose despite shorter stays — it resolves only one horn and leaves the mechanism vague.
explanations.E: This deepens the paradox: if early adopters also extended stays, the average reduction of 30% should be harder to achieve, making the data internally inconsistent rather than resolved.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox involves a policy outcome (stricter sentencing) that correlates with rising crime rates. Resolution requires a reverse-causation plus confounding-variable mechanism: jurisdictions adopted stricter sentencing in response to already-rising crime, and the crime rate reflects a lag. Distractors include a 'deepens' trap and a definitional-mismatch near-miss.
lr.stimulus: Over the past decade, jurisdictions that adopted mandatory minimum sentencing laws for drug offenses consistently show higher rates of drug-related crime than jurisdictions that did not adopt such laws. Yet criminologists agree that incarceration does reduce individual recidivism rates for those actually imprisoned.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to explain the surprising phenomenon described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mandatory minimum sentencing laws were disproportionately adopted by jurisdictions that already had the highest drug-crime rates at the time of adoption.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Incarceration of low-level drug offenders frees up investigative resources, allowing police to detect more drug crimes than they could previously.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Criminologists who study recidivism typically focus on violent offenders rather than drug offenders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some jurisdictions with mandatory minimum sentencing have larger urban populations, where drug activity is inherently more concentrated.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mandatory minimum sentencing laws are widely known to the public, which should deter first-time drug offenders more effectively than discretionary sentencing.

explanations.correct: If jurisdictions with mandatory minimums already had higher drug-crime rates before adopting the laws, the observed correlation reflects selection bias — high-crime jurisdictions chose the policy — rather than any causal effect of the laws. This reconciles higher post-adoption rates with the individual-level recidivism finding.
explanations.A: Correct. This is a classic selection/reverse-causation resolution: the laws were a response to high crime, not its cause. The correlation does not indicate failure of the policy on its own terms.
explanations.B: This deepens the paradox: if incarceration frees resources to detect more crime, reported crime should rise regardless of the policy's effectiveness, making it even harder to evaluate — but it doesn't resolve the inconsistency between aggregate and individual data.
explanations.C: A definitional mismatch trap: it weakens the recidivism evidence but doesn't explain why adopting jurisdictions have higher crime rates overall.
explanations.D: Urban-population size is a partial confounder, but it only addresses one horn — why crime is higher in those jurisdictions — without explaining why the aggregate rate didn't fall after the law's adoption.
explanations.E: This opposite-direction trap predicts the policy should work as a deterrent, which deepens rather than resolves the paradox by making the higher crime rates even more surprising.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox involves an environmental observation: a river's fish population declined sharply after a pollution cleanup. Resolution requires a compound mechanism — invasive species previously suppressed by the pollutant now thrive and outcompete native fish. Multiple distractors exploit plausible-sounding ecological mechanisms that resolve only one horn.
lr.stimulus: After a decade-long program successfully reduced industrial pollutant levels in the Harrow River to near-pristine standards, researchers expected native fish populations to recover. Instead, annual fish-population surveys showed a 40 percent decline in native species over the five years following the cleanup's completion.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The pollutants removed from the river had been acutely toxic to an invasive aquatic plant species that, now unchecked, has densely colonized the riverbed, destroying the spawning habitat native fish require.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduced pollutant levels have attracted increased recreational fishing activity, raising the total annual catch of native species.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Native fish populations often take longer than five years to recover from chronic pollution exposure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some industrial facilities upstream were granted temporary exemptions and continued discharging low levels of the pollutant during the five-year survey period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The cleanup program focused primarily on heavy metals, leaving organic chemical pollutants at levels still harmful to fish larvae.

explanations.correct: The pollutant, while harmful in general, also suppressed an invasive plant. Removing it unleashed the invasive species, which destroyed spawning habitat. This compound mechanism explains why cleaner water still produced a population decline — both horns are resolved.
explanations.A: Correct. The hidden variable (invasive plant previously suppressed by the pollutant) explains why cleaner water paradoxically harmed native fish: the ecological balance shifted against them.
explanations.B: This deepens the paradox: increased fishing due to cleaner water could reduce populations, but it frames the decline as a consequence of success — this worsens rather than resolves the inconsistency with researcher expectations.
explanations.C: This resolves one horn only — it explains why populations haven't recovered — but doesn't explain the active 40% decline. Slow recovery is not the same as sharp decrease.
explanations.D: Continued low-level discharge might explain stagnant recovery, but not a 40% decline below pre-cleanup baselines. This resolves one horn only and doesn't account for the magnitude.
explanations.E: Residual organic pollutants could harm larvae, but this implies the cleanup was incomplete — it explains the failure to recover but not the sharp active decline, resolving one horn only.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox involves an economic finding: workers in a region earned higher wages after their primary employer downsized dramatically. The resolution requires identifying a compositional effect — low-wage workers were disproportionately laid off, raising the average wage of those remaining. Distractors include a 'deepens' trap and a misleading 'resolves partially' answer.
lr.stimulus: When Veltran Manufacturing reduced its regional workforce by 45 percent over two years, economists predicted that average wages in the region would fall sharply due to oversupply of labor. Instead, regional wage surveys conducted immediately after the downsizing showed average wages had risen by 8 percent.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The workers Veltran laid off were disproportionately entry-level and lower-skilled employees, whose departure raised the statistical average wage of the remaining regional workforce.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Veltran Manufacturing offered generous severance packages to laid-off workers, temporarily sustaining consumer spending in the region.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several technology firms announced plans to open facilities in the region within six months of the Veltran downsizing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Labor economists distinguish between median and average wages, and the surveys in question measured average wages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Veltran retained its highest-paid engineers and managers while outsourcing production, which increased output per remaining employee.

explanations.correct: If the laid-off workers were predominantly lower-wage, their removal from the sample pool mathematically raises the average wage of those remaining — a classic compositional/measurement-artifact resolution. The 'average wage' figure reflects who is still employed, not any real wage increase for individuals.
explanations.A: Correct. This is a compositional effect: removing the lower end of a wage distribution raises the average. Economists' predictions assumed wages of remaining workers would fall, but the average was skewed by who left.
explanations.B: Severance sustaining consumer spending might slow economic contraction, but it doesn't explain why measured wages rose. This is irrelevant to the wage paradox.
explanations.C: Future tech-firm arrivals are consistent with eventual wage recovery, but they hadn't yet arrived — this resolves neither horn of the immediate post-downsizing data.
explanations.D: This identifies the measurement type (average vs. median) but doesn't explain why average wages rose — it merely restates a condition without providing the resolving mechanism.
explanations.E: Retaining high earners is part of the resolution mechanism but is less complete than A: it explains why high-wage workers remained but doesn't specify that lower-wage workers left in large numbers, which is the critical compositional driver.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox involves a technology outcome: a software security patch reduced the rate of successful intrusions, yet total data breaches at patched organizations increased. Resolution requires a two-part mechanism: the patch redirected attackers toward a different, unpatched vulnerability class, and the newly exposed attack vector was more damaging. Distractors include a 'deepens' option and a 'one horn only' near-miss.
lr.stimulus: A widely deployed cybersecurity patch successfully reduced successful network intrusions via malware injection by 55 percent at organizations that installed it. Yet in the year following the patch's deployment, those same organizations reported 30 percent more total data breaches than they had in the prior year.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The patch contained a configuration error that inadvertently disabled logging features, preventing organizations from detecting breaches in real time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attackers who were blocked by the patch shifted their efforts toward phishing campaigns targeting employee credentials, a vector the patch did not address, and phishing-based breaches increased fivefold.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cybersecurity budgets at patched organizations increased substantially in the year following deployment, enabling more thorough breach audits.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The patch was most rapidly adopted by large organizations that handle greater volumes of sensitive data, making them more attractive targets overall.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The definition of 'data breach' used by regulators was expanded during the year in question to include previously unreported incident types.

explanations.correct: If attackers redirected efforts to phishing — an unaddressed vector — after the patch blocked malware injection, then malware intrusions fell while a different breach type surged, explaining both the reduction in intrusions and the net increase in total breaches. Both horns are resolved.
explanations.A: Disabled logging would cause under-detection of breaches, not more breaches — and if anything would make reported breaches fall, which deepens rather than resolves the paradox.
explanations.B: Correct. Attacker substitution to a new unpatched vector (phishing) explains why closing one vulnerability led to a net increase in breaches — the patch was effective at what it targeted, but displaced rather than eliminated attacks.
explanations.C: Better auditing could explain discovering more breaches, which is a partial resolution, but this is a 'resolves one horn only' trap — it doesn't explain why actual breaches increased, only why more were detected.
explanations.D: Large organizations being more attractive targets could explain higher breach rates at adopters, but it deepens the paradox by implying that the very act of patching increased targeting — without resolving the inconsistency.
explanations.E: An expanded regulatory definition is a definitional-mismatch resolution candidate, but it resolves only the reporting increase without explaining the actual breach data, and it doesn't account for the simultaneous drop in malware intrusions.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox involves a historical pattern: literacy rates in a colony rose sharply during a period when the colonial government actively banned local-language education. The compound resolution involves a hidden variable: missionary organizations operating outside government control expanded vernacular literacy programs precisely in response to the ban. Distractors include a temporal mismatch and a deepens-the-paradox option.
lr.stimulus: Between 1880 and 1900, the colonial administration of Northaven Province banned instruction in indigenous languages at all government-funded schools, mandating that all education occur exclusively in the colonial language. Yet census records show that literacy in indigenous languages among Northaven's adult population increased by 22 percent during this same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Many adult residents of Northaven Province had already learned to read in the colonial language before 1880, which made learning to read in indigenous languages easier for them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The colonial administration's ban applied only to government-funded schools, while independent missionary societies, which operated outside government funding, dramatically expanded indigenous-language literacy programs after 1880 in direct response to the ban.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Literacy in the colonial language also increased during the same period, suggesting that overall educational attainment rose in Northaven Province between 1880 and 1900.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Census officials in 1900 used a broader definition of 'literacy' than their 1880 counterparts, counting partial reading ability as full literacy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The colonial government increased funding to government schools between 1880 and 1900, raising enrollment and improving educational outcomes in the colonial language.

explanations.correct: The ban applied only to government-funded schools. Missionary organizations — operating outside that funding — expanded indigenous-language programs in response to the ban, creating an alternative channel for literacy growth. This resolves both horns: the ban was real and enforced in its domain, yet literacy still rose through an independent, unregulated sector.
explanations.A: Transfer-of-literacy skills might facilitate learning a second script, but this is speculative and doesn't explain the institutional mechanism by which indigenous literacy rose despite the ban. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Correct. The scope restriction (government-funded only) combined with the missionary expansion is a compound mechanism resolving both horns: the ban was effective within its scope, but the scope was limited, and other actors filled the gap.
explanations.C: Rising colonial-language literacy deepens rather than resolves the paradox — if colonial-language education was displacing indigenous education, we'd expect indigenous literacy to fall, not rise.
explanations.D: A definitional mismatch trap: an expanded census definition could inflate reported literacy, but it addresses only the measurement and doesn't explain the real-world educational dynamic. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: Increased colonial-school funding and enrollment deepens the paradox: if more children entered colonial-language-only schools, indigenous-language literacy should have been further suppressed, making the 22% increase even harder to explain.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox involves a linguistic finding: speakers of a language with grammatically obligatory evidential markers (words indicating how a speaker knows something) perform worse on source-monitoring memory tests than speakers of languages without such markers. Resolution requires recognizing that habitual outsourcing of source-tracking to grammar reduces the development of independent memory-based source monitoring. Distractors include a circular resolution and a deepens option.
lr.stimulus: Languages that grammatically require speakers to mark whether their knowledge is firsthand, reported, or inferred — a feature linguists call evidentiality — are often assumed to sharpen speakers' attention to the source of their information. Yet controlled experiments consistently show that native speakers of obligatory-evidential languages perform significantly worse on laboratory source-monitoring memory tasks than speakers of languages without this feature.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to explain the surprising phenomenon described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Speakers of obligatory-evidential languages rely on grammatical markers at the time of speaking to signal source information, which reduces the need to independently encode source details in memory during comprehension.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Laboratory source-monitoring tasks were originally developed and normed using speakers of non-evidential languages, introducing a potential cultural bias in task design.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Evidential markers in many languages are acquired early in childhood, suggesting they are deeply embedded in native speakers' cognitive processing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Speakers of obligatory-evidential languages are more likely to correctly identify information as 'reported' versus 'inferred' in their daily communication than speakers of non-evidential languages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The evidential languages studied are spoken primarily in regions with oral rather than literate traditions, which may affect memory strategies independently of grammatical structure.

explanations.correct: If grammatical markers handle source-signaling at the moment of speaking, speakers are not required to store source information deeply in memory — the grammar does the work. Consequently, independent memory-based source monitoring is less practiced and less developed, explaining the worse laboratory performance. Both horns are resolved.
explanations.A: Correct. This is a reverse-causation/cognitive-offloading mechanism: grammar's efficiency as a signaling system actually atrophies the independent memory capacity it was assumed to enhance.
explanations.B: Cultural bias in task design is a plausible methodological critique, but it resolves only the measurement horn — it doesn't explain why the effect is consistent across multiple controlled experiments or why evidential speakers perform worse rather than differently.
explanations.C: Early acquisition of evidential markers deepens rather than resolves the paradox: if the feature is deeply embedded cognitively, speakers should be even more attuned to source information, making the poor performance more surprising.
explanations.D: Better real-world source labeling in communication is consistent with evidentiality's function, but it resolves only one horn — it doesn't explain why this advantage doesn't transfer to memory tasks. This is a 'resolves one horn only' trap.
explanations.E: Oral tradition affecting memory strategies is a confounding-variable candidate, but it doesn't directly address the evidentiality mechanism and leaves the specific grammatical-feature paradox unexplained. Resolves one horn only.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox involves a policy outcome: a city's ban on single-use plastic bags reduced plastic-bag litter but increased total plastic waste tonnage. Resolution requires a compound mechanism: consumers switched to reusable bags that require far more plastic per unit to manufacture, and the replacement rate was high enough that lifecycle plastic use increased. Distractors include a 'deepens' option and a partial-resolution near-miss.
lr.stimulus: After Clearwater City banned single-use plastic bags at retail checkouts, surveys confirmed a 70 percent reduction in plastic-bag litter in the city's parks and waterways. Yet municipal solid-waste data showed that total plastic waste tonnage collected in Clearwater increased by 12 percent in the two years following the ban.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The reusable bags that consumers purchased in response to the ban are made primarily of polypropylene, requiring roughly 40 times more plastic by weight per bag than single-use bags, and the majority of consumers replaced their reusable bags within 18 months rather than using them long-term.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The ban prompted Clearwater retailers to increase their use of plastic clamshell packaging for produce, which had previously been sold in bags that were exempt from the ban.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Municipal solid-waste collection in Clearwater expanded its coverage area in the same two-year period, annexing several suburban districts that had previously handled their own waste.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Clearwater residents who remembered to bring reusable bags used them consistently, while residents who forgot brought reusable bags less often over time.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The 70 percent litter reduction was measured by visual survey, which may undercount small plastic fragments that make up a significant portion of plastic pollution.

explanations.correct: Reusable bags require 40x more plastic per unit, and consumers discarded them within 18 months — well before the lifecycle offset point. This compound mechanism explains both horns: litter fell (fewer lightweight bags escaping into the environment) while total plastic tonnage rose (heavier replacement bags accumulating in solid waste at high turnover rates).
explanations.A: Correct. The high per-unit plastic weight of reusable bags combined with rapid replacement creates a net plastic-tonnage increase, while the physical properties of single-use bags (light, wind-borne) explain the independent litter reduction. Both horns resolved.
explanations.B: Increased clamshell packaging is a partial resolution — it could explain some of the tonnage increase — but it doesn't account for the specific mechanism tied to the bag ban and doesn't resolve both horns together. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.C: Expanded waste-collection coverage (annexing suburbs) would inflate reported tonnage regardless of the ban's effect. This is a measurement-artifact resolution, but it resolves only the tonnage horn and doesn't address the litter data. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: Inconsistent reusable-bag usage describes consumer behavior but doesn't explain the tonnage increase — it would more likely suggest lower reusable-bag purchases, not higher plastic waste. Irrelevant to the paradox.
explanations.E: Undercounting litter fragments addresses measurement validity in the litter survey, potentially weakening one horn, but it doesn't resolve why total plastic tonnage increased. Resolves one horn only and weakens rather than resolves.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox involves an arts/economics observation: auction prices for works by living artists rose sharply during a period when those artists' critical reputations, as measured by museum acquisitions and scholarly citations, declined. The compound resolution involves market segmentation: a new class of speculative collectors, uncorrelated with critical assessment, entered the market and drove prices up through demand that operated independently of institutional prestige.
lr.stimulus: During the 1990s, average auction prices for works by living contemporary artists rose by over 200 percent in real terms. Over the same decade, the number of works by living contemporary artists acquired by major public museums fell by 35 percent, and scholarly citations of these artists in peer-reviewed art-history journals declined sharply.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Museum acquisition budgets were sharply reduced during the 1990s due to government arts-funding cuts, preventing museums from purchasing works regardless of their critical standing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Art-history scholarship in the 1990s shifted its focus toward historical periods and deceased artists, reducing citations of living artists across the board independently of those artists' commercial trajectories.

choices.label: C
choices.text: During the 1990s, a large cohort of high-net-worth investors entered the contemporary art market treating works as financial assets, bidding prices up through speculative demand that was largely independent of institutional critical assessment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The auction houses that reported rising prices in the 1990s represented only the top tier of the contemporary art market, excluding mid-career and emerging artists whose prices remained flat.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some major museums shifted from outright acquisition to long-term loan agreements, which would not appear in acquisition statistics but still reflected institutional engagement with living artists.

explanations.correct: A new class of speculative investors valuing art as a financial instrument drove auction prices independently of critical or institutional evaluation. This resolves both horns simultaneously: prices rose because of market demand from a new buyer segment, while critical and institutional indicators fell because scholarly and curatorial taste was moving in a different direction — the two metrics were measuring different things driven by different actors.
explanations.A: Budget cuts explain reduced museum acquisitions (one horn), but don't explain why auction prices rose. This is a resolves-one-horn-only trap.
explanations.B: A shift in scholarly focus explains declining citations (one horn) but doesn't explain the price surge. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.C: Correct. Speculative investors constitute a new, independent demand driver for prices that operates outside the critical-prestige system measured by museum acquisitions and citations. Both horns are resolved by identifying the market segmentation.
explanations.D: A sampling artifact (top-tier auction data) could challenge the price-rise finding, but it resolves neither horn and introduces doubt about the stimulus's factual basis rather than explaining the discrepancy. Irrelevant.
explanations.E: Long-term loans partially address the museum-acquisition horn by suggesting institutional engagement didn't fall as much as the data indicate, but it doesn't explain the price surge and resolves only one horn incompletely.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox involves an ethics/policy finding: a country that implemented a comprehensive national ethics code for public officials saw an increase in the number of prosecuted corruption cases in the years following implementation. Resolution requires recognizing a compound mechanism: the code created enforceable legal standards and independent oversight bodies where none existed, increasing detection and prosecution capacity rather than indicating more corruption. Distractors include a deepens option and a temporal-scope trap.
lr.stimulus: Rendovia enacted a sweeping national ethics code for public officials in 2005, establishing mandatory disclosure requirements, an independent oversight commission, and criminal penalties for violations. Yet in the five years following the code's enactment, the number of public officials prosecuted for corruption in Rendovia increased by nearly 80 percent compared to the five years prior.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Before 2005, Rendovia had no independent oversight body with subpoena power, and most corrupt acts by public officials were never investigated, let alone prosecuted; the new commission's authority and investigative resources substantially increased the detection and prosecution of conduct that had previously gone undetected.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The ethics code was drafted with input from international anti-corruption organizations, whose best-practice recommendations are widely regarded as effective in the long term.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several high-profile corruption scandals involving senior officials were exposed by investigative journalists in 2006 and 2007, drawing public attention to corruption issues.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Public officials in Rendovia were initially uncertain about the scope of the new disclosure requirements and may have inadvertently failed to comply, resulting in technical violations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rendovia's economy grew substantially between 2005 and 2010, increasing the total funds available to public officials and thereby raising the monetary stakes — and temptations — associated with public positions.

explanations.correct: The 80% increase in prosecutions reflects improved detection capacity — an independent commission with subpoena power investigating previously invisible conduct — rather than a genuine increase in corrupt behavior. This resolves both horns: the ethics code is consistent with anti-corruption goals because it exposed pre-existing corruption, and the rise in prosecutions is a success indicator, not a failure.
explanations.A: Correct. The prior absence of effective investigative infrastructure meant corruption was underprosecuted; the new commission's capacity explains the prosecution surge as a detection artifact, not an increase in actual corruption. Both horns resolved.
explanations.B: International best-practice credentials are irrelevant to the prosecution data — this doesn't explain why prosecutions rose after implementation. Irrelevant trap.
explanations.C: Journalist-driven scandals might explain a few high-profile cases, but they don't account for an 80% systemic increase across all prosecutions, and they don't explain the mechanism by which the ethics code coexists with rising prosecutions. Resolves one horn only partially.
explanations.D: Technical violations from compliance confusion could contribute to some prosecutions, but this would suggest the code was poorly designed — a 'deepens the paradox' option implying the code itself generated the corruption it was meant to prevent.
explanations.E: Economic growth raising temptation is a reverse-causation trap: it implies corruption actually did increase, deepening rather than resolving the paradox by suggesting the ethics code failed to prevent corruption that genuinely worsened.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox involves two interacting mechanisms — a demographic shift and a policy change — both of which must be held in mind simultaneously to evaluate each answer. Distractors include one that deepens the paradox and one that resolves only the first horn.
lr.stimulus: A large urban hospital began a program five years ago requiring all surgeons to use a standardized pre-operative checklist. Post-operative infection rates at the hospital dropped by 18 percent in the first year after implementation. Yet over the same five-year period, the hospital's overall patient mortality rate has risen steadily each year.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The standardized checklist was developed by a team of senior surgeons with decades of combined experience.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The hospital's reputation for surgical excellence has attracted a growing proportion of critically ill patients who have exhausted treatment options elsewhere, a population with inherently higher mortality regardless of care quality.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Post-operative infections are among the leading causes of preventable in-hospital deaths nationwide.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several competing hospitals in the region adopted similar checklists during the same five-year period, reducing their own infection rates by comparable margins.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The checklist program was expanded in the third year to cover non-surgical procedures, which account for the majority of patient admissions.

explanations.correct: If the hospital's improved surgical reputation drew an increasingly severe patient population — people who are sicker to begin with — then overall mortality could rise even as infection-specific outcomes improve. The checklist genuinely reduces infections, but the case-mix shift drives aggregate mortality upward. Both facts are simultaneously true.
explanations.A: The checklist's provenance is irrelevant to explaining why mortality rose despite the infection improvement. Does not address either horn.
explanations.B: Correct. A selection effect (sicker patients self-selecting into the hospital) explains why aggregate mortality rises even as a specific, measurable complication declines.
explanations.C: This deepens the paradox: if infections are a leading cause of preventable death, a large infection-rate drop should produce a mortality drop, making the mortality increase even more puzzling.
explanations.D: Regional adoption by competitors is irrelevant to this hospital's internal mortality trend.
explanations.E: Expanding the checklist to non-surgical procedures might affect outcomes in that population, but it doesn't explain why mortality rose — if anything, broader quality improvement should help, deepening the paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: Resolution requires recognizing a temporal scope difference combined with a compositional fallacy trap. One distractor resolves the second horn only; another subtly deepens the paradox by implying the tax should have worked.
lr.stimulus: A city introduced a congestion tax on all vehicles entering the downtown core during peak hours. Traffic volume in the downtown core fell by 22 percent in the six months following the tax's introduction. Nevertheless, average commute times for workers traveling into downtown increased by nearly 15 percent over the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to explain the surprising phenomenon described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The congestion tax revenue was earmarked exclusively for road maintenance rather than for expanding public transit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many commuters who abandoned private vehicles in response to the tax switched to buses, which share the same road lanes and now run less frequently due to increased passenger loads.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The congestion tax applies only during peak hours, so leisure drivers can still enter the downtown core at no charge during off-peak times.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Traffic engineers predicted before the tax was introduced that congestion would decrease by at least 25 percent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several major employers relocated their offices to the downtown core after the tax was introduced, citing improved street conditions.

explanations.correct: Fewer cars entered downtown, but the displaced commuters crowded onto buses that use the same lanes. Slower, overcrowded buses increase total commute time even as vehicle count drops. Both horns are resolved: volume fell (fewer cars) yet commutes lengthened (bus slowdown).
explanations.A: The allocation of tax revenue addresses a different policy question and does not explain why commute times rose despite lower traffic volume.
explanations.B: Correct. Modal shift to buses that share road space — and that slow under overcrowding — simultaneously explains falling vehicle counts and rising commute times.
explanations.C: Off-peak leisure driving is irrelevant to peak-hour commute times, which are the focus of the paradox.
explanations.D: Pre-implementation predictions are irrelevant to explaining the observed outcome.
explanations.E: This deepens the paradox: if employers relocated downtown because streets improved, demand for downtown travel rose, which should worsen congestion — yet the stimulus already notes congestion fell. This makes the commute-time increase even harder to explain through this chain.

lr.difficultyReason: The resolution requires a measurement-artifact explanation combined with an understanding of ecological fallacy. The paradox has two quantitative horns that resist simple causal explanations, and the best distractor addresses only the aggregate trend while ignoring the individual-level finding.
lr.stimulus: Researchers studying a coastal estuary found that average water salinity levels declined by 12 percent over a decade, a change they attributed to increased freshwater runoff from upstream agriculture. Yet fish species diversity in the estuary increased significantly over the same ten-year period, even though most estuarine fish species are known to be highly sensitive to salinity changes.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The agricultural operations upstream use fertilizers that are known to be harmful to many species of fish when present in high concentrations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The decline in average salinity masked an increase in salinity variability across the estuary's micro-zones, creating a broader range of distinct habitats that support different specialist species simultaneously.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Estuarine fish diversity is typically measured only during the summer months, when salinity levels tend to be higher than the annual average.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The freshwater fish species that migrated into the estuary from upstream rivers are not classified by researchers as estuarine species.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some of the fish species recorded in the estuary during the study period had not been observed there in over thirty years.

explanations.correct: A drop in average salinity does not mean all zones became uniformly less saline. If variability across micro-zones increased, the estuary now contains some very-low-salinity zones and some moderate-salinity zones simultaneously, supporting a wider range of specialist species than a uniform environment would. Average salinity fell and diversity rose — both facts hold.
explanations.A: High fertilizer concentrations would harm fish, which deepens rather than resolves the paradox by giving an additional reason diversity should have declined.
explanations.B: Correct. Increased spatial heterogeneity in salinity — hidden by the average metric — creates more ecological niches, resolving the paradox via a measurement-artifact and habitat-diversity mechanism.
explanations.C: If diversity is measured during high-salinity months, it would capture salinity-sensitive species well, but this doesn't explain why diversity increased over time — it addresses measurement timing, not the trend direction.
explanations.D: Excluding freshwater migrants from the count would reduce the measured diversity, not increase it, and thus resolves one horn in the wrong direction.
explanations.E: Species returning after absence is consistent with the diversity increase but doesn't explain why the return occurred despite — or because of — changed salinity. Resolves one horn only.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox requires disentangling a reverse-causation mechanism from a selection effect, and involves an economics domain with two quantitative facts. Distractors exploit common intuitions about supply and demand.
lr.stimulus: Economic analysts noted that in a particular metropolitan housing market, neighborhoods where landlords voluntarily reduced rents by an average of 8 percent saw vacancy rates fall to near zero over the following year. Yet when the city government enacted a rent-control ordinance capping all rents at 8 percent below pre-ordinance levels, vacancy rates across the city rose by 11 percent within the same timeframe.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Landlords who voluntarily reduced rents did so specifically in neighborhoods that already had high vacancy rates and strong unmet housing demand, while the rent-control ordinance applied uniformly to all neighborhoods including those with low vacancy rates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The rent-control ordinance included provisions requiring landlords to obtain city permits before converting residential units to commercial use.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most economists predicted before the ordinance was enacted that rent control would increase overall housing supply within two years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city's population grew by approximately 3 percent during the year following the rent-control ordinance.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several landlords who had voluntarily reduced rents before the ordinance subsequently raised them back to controlled levels once the ordinance took effect.

explanations.correct: Voluntary rent reductions were a targeted response to high-vacancy, high-demand neighborhoods — the rent cut matched market conditions and filled empty units. The ordinance applied everywhere, including low-vacancy markets where landlords, facing capped returns, responded by converting, abandoning, or reducing supply of rental units. Self-selection in voluntary cuts versus uniform mandate explains both outcomes.
explanations.A: Correct. Voluntary reductions were targeted at undersupplied neighborhoods (reversing the vacancy problem), while the blanket ordinance disrupted markets that were already balanced, causing landlords to exit the rental market and raise vacancies.
explanations.B: Conversion restrictions would tend to keep units as rentals, which would reduce vacancy — the opposite of what the ordinance produced. This resolves one horn in the wrong direction.
explanations.C: Pre-enactment economist predictions are irrelevant to explaining the observed outcomes and do not address either horn.
explanations.D: Population growth would increase demand and should lower vacancy rates, which deepens the paradox of rising vacancies under rent control.
explanations.E: Raising rents back to controlled levels still means controlled rents were maintained; this doesn't explain why vacancy rose — the mechanism is unclear and resolves neither horn.

lr.difficultyReason: The resolution requires a definitional distinction combined with a temporal scope difference. Both horns involve legal outcomes with quantitative support. The trap answer deepens the paradox by implying a mechanism that should make the paradox worse.
lr.stimulus: Prosecutors in a state that adopted mandatory minimum sentencing for drug offenses secured convictions in 94 percent of drug cases brought to trial — a rate significantly higher than the national average. Nevertheless, the total number of individuals incarcerated for drug offenses in that state declined by 30 percent in the decade following the law's adoption.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Defense attorneys in the state successfully challenged the constitutionality of several mandatory minimum provisions, and courts struck down the longest sentences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The high conviction rate at trial induced most defendants facing drug charges to accept plea agreements for lesser, non-drug offenses, dramatically reducing the number of cases actually going to trial and thus the number resulting in mandatory drug sentences.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mandatory minimum sentences are generally regarded by legal scholars as an ineffective deterrent to drug-related criminal activity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The state's prison system expanded its capacity by 40 percent during the decade in question to accommodate expected increases in the inmate population.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prosecutors in neighboring states without mandatory minimums reported lower conviction rates but similar levels of drug-offense incarceration.

explanations.correct: Mandatory minimums created such a credible conviction threat at trial that defendants accepted plea deals to non-drug charges. The trial conviction rate is genuinely high — among the few who went to trial — but the population going to trial shrank enormously. Fewer drug convictions resulted, so incarceration for drug offenses fell. Both facts are simultaneously true.
explanations.A: Striking down only the longest sentences would reduce sentence length but not the number of people incarcerated for drug offenses — it resolves one horn only and incompletely.
explanations.B: Correct. The high trial conviction rate is real but applies to a tiny, self-selected pool of cases; the plea-deal mechanism converts drug charges to non-drug charges before trial, collapsing the number of drug incarcerations.
explanations.C: Scholarly opinion on deterrence is irrelevant to explaining the statistical discrepancy between conviction rates and incarceration numbers.
explanations.D: Expanded prison capacity would facilitate more incarcerations, not fewer — this deepens the paradox by removing a supply-side constraint that might otherwise explain the decline.
explanations.E: Comparisons to neighboring states address a different population and do not explain the internal paradox within this state's own data.

lr.difficultyReason: Resolution requires identifying both a compositional effect and a reverse-causation element. The paradox involves technology adoption data with two distinct quantitative claims, and distractors include a 'resolves one horn only' and an 'opposite-direction' trap.
lr.stimulus: A major software company found that engineers who completed its voluntary advanced coding certification scored, on average, 35 percent higher on annual performance reviews than uncertified colleagues. However, when the company made the same certification program mandatory for all engineers, overall team productivity scores declined over the following two years.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The certification exam was updated to include more challenging material just before the mandatory program was introduced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only the company's highest-performing engineers sought the certification voluntarily, so the performance differential reflected pre-existing ability rather than the certification's effect; mandatory enrollment displaced billable work hours for all engineers, including average and below-average performers who gained little benefit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several engineers who had voluntarily obtained the certification left the company for higher-paying positions after the program became mandatory.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The company's clients reported higher satisfaction with products built by certified engineers than with those built by uncertified engineers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The certification program was designed by an external vendor with limited familiarity with the company's proprietary development environment.

explanations.correct: Voluntary uptake was a self-selected sample of high performers; their superiority was pre-existing, not caused by the certification. When made mandatory, the program consumed work hours for all engineers while delivering little benefit to average performers, net-lowering productivity. Both facts hold: voluntary certified engineers outperform (selection effect) and mandatory certification hurts productivity (opportunity cost plus negligible marginal gain for most).
explanations.A: A harder exam affects pass rates and difficulty but doesn't explain why mandatory participation would reduce productivity — it resolves neither horn adequately.
explanations.B: Correct. A two-part resolution: self-selection explains the voluntary performance gap; opportunity cost for the full population explains the productivity decline under mandatory enrollment.
explanations.C: High performers leaving after mandatory rollout would worsen productivity, which is consistent with one horn, but doesn't explain why the voluntary program showed positive results — resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: Client satisfaction corroborating the performance data for voluntary participants deepens the paradox by reinforcing that certification appears valuable, making the mandatory decline more puzzling.
explanations.E: Vendor unfamiliarity might reduce the program's quality, but this would also weaken the voluntary participants' performance advantage — it resolves neither horn cleanly.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox involves a historical counterfactual structure requiring a hidden third-factor explanation. Distractors include a plausible economic cause that actually deepens the paradox and a one-horn resolution involving trade policy.
lr.stimulus: Historians note that during a prolonged period of agricultural prosperity in medieval Flanders — when grain prices were high and harvests were above average for over a decade — the number of documented famines in the region actually increased compared to the preceding decade of poor harvests and low grain prices.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High grain prices during the prosperous period incentivized wealthy landowners to export surplus grain to foreign markets, leaving local peasant populations with less access to food despite abundant harvests.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medieval famines were often caused by factors other than grain shortages, including outbreaks of livestock disease and disruptions to trade routes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Historical records of famines from the earlier decade were less reliably maintained, meaning fewer famines may have been documented even if similar numbers occurred.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The prosperous decade coincided with a rapid population increase in the region, which outpaced the growth in food production and concentrated hunger among the landless poor.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Grain prices in neighboring regions remained low throughout both decades, reducing Flemish merchants' incentives to import food during shortfalls.

explanations.correct: High grain prices and good harvests benefit producers but harm consumers who must buy food. Wealthy landowners, incentivized by high prices, exported grain, reducing local supply available to subsistence populations. Abundance at the aggregate level coexisted with scarcity at the distribution level. Both facts hold: there was genuine agricultural prosperity and genuinely more famines.
explanations.A: Correct. Export incentivization during high-price periods explains how a surplus harvest can simultaneously produce local food scarcity — a confounding variable in the distribution chain resolves the paradox.
explanations.B: This suggests famines can have non-grain causes, but doesn't explain why famine frequency would specifically increase during a period of grain abundance rather than decrease — it resolves one horn only and weakly.
explanations.C: Under-documentation of the earlier decade's famines means the comparison baseline may be artificially low, but this is a methodological note — it doesn't address why abundance coincided with famine, merely questioning the data rather than resolving the conflict.
explanations.D: Population growth outpacing food production could cause famine, but this deepens one aspect of the paradox: if harvests were above average for a decade, food production was growing, and population growth alone would need to be extreme to outpace it — this explanation is implausible given the stimulus's characterization of prosperity.
explanations.E: Low prices in neighboring regions reducing import incentives explains why shortfalls couldn't be remedied by imports, but it presupposes shortfalls occurred — which contradicts the 'above-average harvests' in the stimulus. This resolves one horn in a direction opposite to the stated facts.

lr.difficultyReason: Requires recognizing that an aggregate improvement statistic masks a Simpson's Paradox-style reversal across subgroups. Both horns involve hard outcome data. Distractors include a genuine-sounding medical mechanism that resolves only one horn.
lr.stimulus: A clinical trial of a new antidepressant found that among patients with mild depression, the drug produced a 40 percent greater symptom reduction than placebo, and among patients with severe depression, the drug produced a 25 percent greater symptom reduction than placebo. Yet when trial results were reported for all patients combined, the drug showed no statistically significant advantage over placebo.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The placebo effect is generally stronger in patients with mild depression than in patients with severe depression, inflating the baseline for comparison.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The trial enrolled a disproportionately large share of patients with severe depression — a group that shows high placebo response rates — so the overall combined analysis was dominated by a subgroup in which the drug's absolute improvement over placebo was small, diluting the drug's aggregate advantage to non-significance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Regulatory agencies require antidepressant trials to report combined results across all severity categories regardless of differential efficacy by subgroup.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some patients initially classified as mildly depressed were reclassified as severely depressed midway through the trial following re-evaluation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The drug's manufacturer funded the trial, raising questions about whether the subgroup analyses were pre-specified or conducted after the aggregate result was known.

explanations.correct: When a subgroup with a smaller drug-vs.-placebo advantage (severe depression) heavily dominates the sample, the aggregate statistic is pulled toward that smaller difference. Even though both subgroups show a positive drug effect, the combined result loses significance because the large-N subgroup has a modest absolute advantage. This is a Simpson's Paradox-type compositional effect. Both facts are true.
explanations.A: A stronger placebo effect in mild depression would shrink the drug-vs.-placebo gap in that subgroup, which actually deepens the paradox: if mild patients have a strong placebo effect, the 40% advantage for the drug is even more remarkable — yet the overall result is non-significant. This worsens the inconsistency.
explanations.B: Correct. Enrollment imbalance weighting the aggregate toward the severe group (lower absolute advantage) produces a diluted combined result despite clear subgroup benefits — a compositional/weighting resolution.
explanations.C: Regulatory reporting requirements explain the reporting structure but not the statistical outcome itself. Irrelevant to why the aggregate shows no significance.
explanations.D: Reclassification of some patients between groups could affect the numbers, but without knowing which direction the reassignments went and how many were involved, this doesn't reliably explain the aggregate non-significance — resolves one horn only, and weakly.
explanations.E: Funding source and analytic sequence raise bias concerns but are irrelevant to explaining the mathematical discrepancy between subgroup and aggregate results. Does not touch the statistical paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox hinges on a definitional mismatch between two metrics that appear to track the same outcome but do not, combined with a population-scope difference. Strong distractors include a temporal explanation that is close but resolves only one horn.
lr.stimulus: Linguists studying language endangerment report that the number of languages classified as 'critically endangered' globally has decreased by roughly 200 over the past twenty years. Critics, however, point out that the total number of fluent adult speakers of the world's minority languages has also declined sharply over the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Many of the 200 languages removed from the critically endangered list were reclassified as 'extinct' after their last known fluent speakers died, so the category shrank because languages graduated to a worse status, not a better one.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Revitalization programs funded by international organizations have successfully increased the number of children learning several dozen endangered languages in formal school settings.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The criteria used to classify a language as critically endangered have been revised twice over the past twenty years, each time raising the threshold number of speakers required for that classification.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Linguists disagree about whether a language with only written but no oral tradition should be counted as a living language for the purposes of endangerment classification.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The decline in minority-language speakers has been most pronounced in regions undergoing rapid urbanization, where dominant national languages are adopted for economic reasons.

explanations.correct: The 'critically endangered' count fell not because languages recovered but because they moved to the worse category of 'extinct.' Fewer critically endangered languages plus fewer total speakers are perfectly consistent: languages are dying off, exiting critical endangerment through extinction rather than through recovery. Both facts are simultaneously true and mutually reinforcing.
explanations.A: Correct. A definitional-category movement (critically endangered → extinct) explains why the critically endangered count fell while speaker totals also fell. The apparent good news in the statistics is illusory.
explanations.B: Successful revitalization of a few dozen languages would increase the number of speakers and might move some languages off the critically endangered list, but this resolves one horn only (the falling critically-endangered count) while making the falling speaker totals more paradoxical.
