explanations.C: Changing the threshold to require more speakers for critical-endangerment classification would move languages down the threat scale, appearing to reduce the count even if conditions worsened — this offers a competing definitional explanation, but it does not account for the simultaneous decline in total speakers across all minority languages. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: Disagreement about classification of written-only languages is a scholarly dispute irrelevant to explaining the directional trends in the data.
explanations.E: Urbanization explains the mechanism behind falling speaker counts but does not address why the critically endangered classification count fell — resolves one horn only.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox requires identifying a temporal-scope mechanism interacting with a demographic factor. Distractors include one that deepens the paradox (by suggesting arts funding was adequate) and one that conflates correlation with causation in the opposite direction.
lr.stimulus: After a national arts council tripled its grant funding to regional theater companies over a five-year period, the number of professional theater productions staged annually across the country increased by 45 percent. Yet surveys conducted at the end of that period showed that the percentage of adults who reported attending live theater at least once in the past year had declined by 8 percent compared to surveys taken before the funding increase.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The tripling of grant funding allowed many theater companies to reduce ticket prices substantially, making productions more accessible to lower-income audiences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The grant funding was concentrated in rural and small-town regions that previously lacked professional theater, producing many new productions attended by populations not previously surveyed as theatergoers, while simultaneously the urban middle-class demographic that historically attended theater shifted to streaming entertainment, reducing the overall attendance percentage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several major theater companies in large cities closed during the same five-year period, citing rising real estate costs that even increased grants could not offset.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The arts council also increased funding to opera and dance companies during the same period, suggesting that the performing arts sector as a whole was a policy priority.

choices.label: E
choices.text: International tours by foreign theater companies increased during the same period, providing additional live performance options that may have competed with domestically produced theater.

explanations.correct: More productions were staged in newly served rural areas, increasing total output. But the established urban demographic that historically drove the percentage-attendance figure shifted away from theater to streaming. The percentage of adults attending fell because the historically theater-going demographic declined, even though raw production count rose among new audiences in underserved regions. Both facts coexist via demographic substitution and geographic expansion.
explanations.A: Lower ticket prices should increase attendance, not decrease the percentage of adults attending — this resolves one horn in the wrong direction and deepens the paradox of declining attendance percentages.
explanations.B: Correct. Geographic expansion of productions (raising the count) combined with attrition of the traditional urban attendance demographic (lowering the percentage) resolves both horns through a compound demographic and distributional mechanism.
explanations.C: Major urban companies closing helps explain declining attendance percentage (one horn), but it also implies fewer productions — which conflicts with the observed 45 percent increase in productions. This resolves one horn in a direction inconsistent with the other facts.
explanations.D: Broader arts-sector funding priorities are irrelevant to explaining the discrepancy between production counts and attendance percentages in theater specifically.
explanations.E: Foreign competition might slightly reduce domestic theater attendance but doesn't explain the 45 percent production increase — resolves one horn only and weakly.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox involves interacting mechanisms: a drug reduces average hospital stays yet total bed-days occupied by that patient population increase. Resolution requires understanding that the drug enables survival of previously fatal cases, expanding the treated population — a compound demographic-plus-policy interaction that most test-takers miss.
lr.stimulus: A new antibiotic reduces the average length of hospital stay for patients with drug-resistant infections from 18 days to 11 days. Yet in the three years since the antibiotic was introduced, the total number of hospital bed-days consumed annually by patients with drug-resistant infections has increased by nearly 40 percent.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The antibiotic is significantly more expensive than the treatments it replaced, increasing the overall cost of care for each patient.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hospitals in several regions adopted infection-control protocols at the same time the antibiotic was introduced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The antibiotic successfully treats infections that previously killed patients within days of hospitalization, resulting in a much larger number of surviving patients who require extended care.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drug-resistant infections are more common in patients who have already been hospitalized for other conditions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Physicians have begun prescribing the antibiotic for a broader range of infections than those for which it was initially approved.

explanations.correct: If the antibiotic saves patients who previously died within days, those survivors now complete full treatment courses. The treated population grows dramatically, so even though each stay is shorter, the total bed-days rise — both halves of the paradox are dissolved.
explanations.A: Higher cost per patient explains a financial puzzle, not the bed-days discrepancy. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Infection-control protocols would reduce new cases, which would decrease total bed-days — this deepens rather than resolves the paradox.
explanations.C: Correct. Population expansion (new survivors) fully accounts for the rise in aggregate bed-days despite shorter individual stays.
explanations.D: Pre-existing hospitalization status is a background fact about the patient mix; it does not explain why total bed-days rose after the drug's introduction.
explanations.E: Broader prescribing could increase patient numbers, but 'broader range of infections' is too vague — it doesn't explain why the increase is 40% while stays fell 39%, and it fails to connect the two halves causally the way C does.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox pairs an economic statistic (median household income rose) with a social outcome (poverty rate rose), requiring test-takers to recognize that median and rate statistics can diverge when income distribution shifts — a subtle measurement-artifact resolution most test-takers conflate with 'inequality' distractors.
lr.stimulus: In Northvale County, median household income increased by 12 percent over the past decade, after adjusting for inflation. Yet over the same period, the percentage of households living below the federal poverty line increased from 11 percent to 16 percent.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The federal poverty line threshold has not been meaningfully updated to reflect modern living costs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A large influx of very high-income households into Northvale County raised the median while leaving the lower portion of the income distribution largely unchanged.

choices.label: C
choices.text: County residents increasingly rely on two-income households to maintain their standard of living.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Northvale County's total population grew substantially over the decade, primarily through immigration.

choices.label: E
choices.text: State tax policy changes reduced take-home pay for middle-income earners in Northvale County.

explanations.correct: If wealthy newcomers pulled the median upward without improving incomes at the bottom, the median rises while the share of households below the poverty line also rises. This demographic shift explains both statistics simultaneously — a classic measurement-artifact resolution.
explanations.A: An outdated poverty threshold would, if anything, undercount poverty, making a rise in the measured rate harder to explain, not easier. This deepens the paradox.
explanations.B: Correct. High-income in-migration skews the median upward while the lower tail of the distribution is unaffected or worsened, reconciling both data points.
explanations.C: Two-income reliance describes a coping mechanism but doesn't explain why poverty rates rose alongside the median. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: Population growth through immigration could increase the number of low-income residents, but without specifying that immigrants are disproportionately low-income, this answer is too vague to dissolve the paradox.
explanations.E: Reduced take-home pay for middle earners would likely lower the median as well, making the rising median harder to explain. This deepens the paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox involves a policy outcome in environmental science: a city's total carbon emissions fell after a congestion tax, yet air quality in the city center worsened. Distractors address one horn each; the correct answer requires recognizing a spatial-redistribution mechanism.
lr.stimulus: After Millford City introduced a congestion tax on vehicles entering the city center, traffic volume in that area fell by 22 percent and the city's total vehicular carbon emissions declined measurably. However, air quality monitors in the city center recorded higher concentrations of particulate matter in the two years following the tax than in the two years before it.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to explain the surprising phenomenon described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Revenue from the congestion tax was used to subsidize electric-vehicle purchases by city residents.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The congestion tax exempted delivery trucks, which tend to produce higher particulate emissions per mile than private vehicles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Drivers who avoided the city center began using older, poorly maintained vehicles on peripheral routes, increasing emissions in residential neighborhoods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city center's remaining vehicles, now traveling at higher speeds on less congested roads, burn fuel more efficiently, reducing their individual emissions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Construction of a new transit hub in the city center during the same period generated substantial dust and particulate matter.

explanations.correct: Construction of a transit hub would introduce a large independent source of particulate matter in the city center, explaining why local air quality worsened even as overall vehicle emissions fell. Both horns of the paradox are dissolved by this concurrent confounding event.
explanations.A: EV subsidies would reduce emissions further, which deepens the puzzle of why city-center air quality worsened.
explanations.B: Exempting delivery trucks explains some continued emissions but cannot explain why particulate levels were higher after the tax than before, since delivery traffic presumably existed before the tax as well.
explanations.C: Peripheral emissions worsening is a geographic shift, not a city-center phenomenon — this resolves neither horn within the city center and actually deepens the city-center paradox.
explanations.D: More efficient fuel burn by remaining vehicles would improve air quality, deepening rather than resolving the paradox.
explanations.E: Correct. An independent particulate source (construction) in the city center accounts for the local air-quality decline despite the citywide emissions reduction.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox involves law and policy: mandatory sentencing guidelines increased average sentences for drug offenses, yet the prison population for drug offenders declined. This counter-intuitive result requires a compound explanation involving prosecutorial behavior — a hidden behavioral-response mechanism.
lr.stimulus: After a state enacted mandatory minimum sentencing guidelines for drug offenses, the average prison sentence imposed on convicted drug offenders increased from 2.4 years to 4.1 years. Nonetheless, within five years of the guidelines taking effect, the total number of inmates serving time for drug offenses in that state's prisons had fallen by 18 percent.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mandatory minimum sentences are widely regarded by legal scholars as an ineffective deterrent to drug crimes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prosecutors in the state dramatically increased their use of plea agreements that reduce charges to non-drug offenses in order to avoid triggering the mandatory minimums.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The state simultaneously expanded drug-treatment diversion programs available to first-time offenders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Federal courts began handling an increasing share of drug prosecutions in that state after the guidelines were enacted.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prison overcrowding led officials to release some drug offenders early under a compassionate-release provision.

explanations.correct: If prosecutors systematically reduced charges to avoid mandatory minimums, far fewer defendants would be convicted of drug offenses at all. Sentences for those convicted would be longer (consistent with the data), but the number entering prison on drug charges would drop sharply — explaining the declining inmate population despite harsher sentences.
explanations.A: Whether mandatory minimums deter crime is a normative assessment; it doesn't explain the mechanical paradox of longer sentences coexisting with fewer inmates.
explanations.B: Correct. Charge reduction deflects convictions away from drug-offense categories, simultaneously explaining both the longer average sentences (only the most serious cases proceed) and the smaller drug-inmate population.
explanations.C: Diversion programs could reduce the number of convictions, partially addressing the second horn, but they don't explain why average sentence length increased. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: Federal handling of more cases would reduce state drug-offense convictions, but it doesn't explain why average sentences rose. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: Early release would lower the current inmate count but does not explain why the total population sentenced fell, nor why average sentence length rose.

lr.difficultyReason: The technology paradox — a company's servers consume less energy per computation yet its total energy bill is higher — requires recognizing Jevons paradox (efficiency gains induce greater usage), a non-obvious economic principle layered with a computational-demand interaction.
lr.stimulus: A major data company upgraded its server infrastructure so that each server now consumes 30 percent less electricity per unit of computation than before the upgrade. Yet the company's total monthly electricity expenditure is 25 percent higher than it was prior to the infrastructure upgrade.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Electricity rates in the region where the company's data centers are located increased by approximately 8 percent following the upgrade.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The upgraded servers require more skilled technicians to maintain, increasing the company's overall operating costs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The lower cost per computation enabled the company to offer cheaper services, attracting far more customers and causing the total volume of computations performed each month to more than double.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some of the old servers were retained as backup systems and continue to draw a small amount of electricity on standby.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The new servers require a more powerful cooling system, which itself consumes substantial electricity.

explanations.correct: If efficiency gains lowered the cost per computation sufficiently to more than double total computation volume, total electricity consumption would rise even though each unit of work is cheaper — a textbook Jevons paradox resolution. Both the efficiency gain and the higher total bill are explained.
explanations.A: An 8% rate increase alone cannot account for a 25% rise in expenditure if efficiency improved by 30%; the numbers don't close the gap. This is a partial, arithmetic-inconsistent resolution.
explanations.B: Technician costs affect labor expenditure, not electricity expenditure. Irrelevant to the discrepancy.
explanations.C: Correct. Doubling-plus computation volume overwhelms the 30% per-unit efficiency gain, explaining the net 25% rise in electricity costs.
explanations.D: Standby power for old backup servers would add a modest increment but cannot plausibly account for a 25% increase in total electricity expenditure. Resolves one horn only, insufficiently.
explanations.E: Enhanced cooling adds electricity demand. However, this is typically factored into server-efficiency measurements; without ruling that out, this answer is weaker than C, and it doesn't explain why the increase is specifically tied to higher usage volume.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox involves linguistics and historical policy: a regional language that received official government recognition and funding saw its number of fluent native speakers decline more rapidly after recognition than before. Distractors include a plausible 'prestige effect' wrong answer and a deepens-the-paradox choice.
lr.stimulus: A regional language spoken in an isolated highland community had been losing fluent native speakers at a rate of roughly 3 percent per year for two decades. After the national government granted the language official recognition and funded immersive school programs, the rate of fluency loss accelerated to nearly 8 percent per year over the following decade.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to explain the surprising phenomenon described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Official recognition increased the language's prestige, motivating more young people to study it formally.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The school programs taught a standardized written form of the language that differed significantly from the spoken vernacular, causing community elders — the primary fluent speakers — to disengage from transmission and stop teaching the language at home.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Government funding for the language programs was insufficient to cover the cost of training qualified teachers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several neighboring communities that spoke related dialects also began losing speakers at higher rates after the recognition decree.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The highland community experienced significant economic growth following official recognition, which reduced emigration of working-age residents.

explanations.correct: If the standardized school form diverged from the vernacular, elders — who were the living transmission source — felt alienated and withdrew from informal home teaching. The school programs thus replaced organic intergenerational transmission with an inferior formal substitute, accelerating net fluency loss. Both the existence of programs and the worsened decline are explained.
explanations.A: Increased prestige and formal study would predict slower decline, not faster. This deepens the paradox rather than resolving it.
explanations.B: Correct. Displacement of home transmission by an alienating standardized form is a documented mechanism in language endangerment; it simultaneously accounts for program existence and accelerated decline.
explanations.C: Underfunding would make the programs ineffective but cannot on its own explain acceleration beyond the pre-recognition baseline rate. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: Neighboring dialect communities declining faster is a separate phenomenon and does not explain the acceleration in the target community. Irrelevant.
explanations.E: Reduced emigration would keep more working-age speakers in the community, which would predict slower decline, not faster. This deepens the paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox pairs an arts-funding outcome with an audience statistic: a city tripled arts subsidies and professional theater companies multiplied, yet average per-performance audience size fell sharply. Multiple plausible distractors target one horn; the correct answer invokes a market-saturation mechanism requiring test-takers to synthesize supply-demand reasoning with audience-behavior data.
lr.stimulus: Over a ten-year period, a city tripled its annual arts subsidies, and the number of professional theater companies operating in the city increased from 8 to 27. However, over the same period, the average audience size per performance across all city theaters fell from 310 patrons to 190 patrons.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several of the new theater companies specialize in experimental works that appeal to smaller, niche audiences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The total number of performances staged annually in the city increased by more than 200 percent, while the total number of theatergoers grew by only about 30 percent — meaning the same audience pool was spread across far more performances.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theater ticket prices rose an average of 20 percent over the decade due to increased production costs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city's population declined slightly over the ten-year period as residents relocated to suburban areas.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Arts subsidies were distributed unevenly, with the largest established companies receiving the majority of funding.

explanations.correct: If the number of performances more than tripled while the audience pool grew only 30%, simple division yields a dramatic fall in average per-performance attendance — exactly as observed. The growth in companies (and thus performances) is directly caused by the subsidies, and the per-performance decline follows arithmetically. Both horns are resolved.
explanations.A: Niche experimental audiences explain why some new companies draw fewer patrons, but this addresses only part of the average-decline horn and doesn't explain why the original eight companies would also see declining averages. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Correct. A 200%-plus supply increase against a 30% demand increase mathematically produces the observed per-performance decline while fully accounting for the subsidy-driven company growth.
explanations.C: Higher ticket prices would reduce demand and lower attendance, but this doesn't explain why companies multiplied. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: A slight population decline could modestly reduce theatergoers, but it cannot account for a drop from 310 to 190 patrons per performance when the total audience grew. This is an opposite-direction distractor for the audience-size horn.
explanations.E: Uneven distribution of subsidies would predict that large companies thrived while small ones struggled — not that 19 new companies emerged. This actually deepens the proliferation half of the paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: The paradox involves history and policy: a wartime rationing program reduced per-capita caloric consumption by 20 percent, yet population-level malnutrition rates fell during the same period. The resolution requires recognizing that pre-rationing inequality meant most calories went to the wealthy, so rationing redistributed intake upward for the previously under-fed majority — a distributional-equity mechanism test-takers often overlook.
lr.stimulus: During a prolonged wartime rationing program, average per-capita caloric consumption in the affected country fell by 20 percent compared to pre-war levels. Yet rates of malnutrition-related illness in that country's hospitals declined steadily throughout the rationing period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wartime governments typically invest heavily in public health infrastructure, which reduces hospital admission rates independent of nutritional status.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Before rationing was introduced, food distribution was highly unequal: a small wealthy minority consumed far more than adequate nutrition while a large portion of the population consumed far less, and rationing reallocated food to the previously under-fed majority.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The rationing program also restricted the consumption of sugar and alcohol, which can contribute to certain nutritional deficiencies when consumed in excess.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many residents in rural areas were exempt from rationing because they could produce their own food, maintaining their pre-war caloric intake.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wartime labor demands caused many previously sedentary workers to take on physically demanding jobs, increasing their caloric needs substantially.

explanations.correct: If pre-rationing food distribution was grossly unequal, the overall average concealed widespread under-nutrition among the majority. Rationing compressed consumption — reducing excess at the top and increasing sufficiency at the bottom — so even though the mean fell, the share of the population with adequate nutrition rose, explaining fewer malnutrition cases. Both statistical facts are reconciled.
explanations.A: Improved public-health infrastructure could reduce hospital admissions for many reasons, but it doesn't explain why malnutrition-specific illness declined while calories fell. Resolves one horn only, and weakly.
explanations.B: Correct. A distributional reallocation from over-fed elites to the under-fed majority explains how average calories can fall while population health on the malnutrition dimension improves.
explanations.C: Reduced sugar and alcohol could improve some nutritional markers, but this is a secondary mechanism that doesn't address the core paradox of fewer total calories yet less malnutrition. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: Rural exemptions would mean rural caloric intake was unchanged, but this actually makes the average-calorie decline harder to account for and does nothing to explain improved urban malnutrition rates. Deepens one horn.
explanations.E: Greater caloric needs from physical labor would predict more malnutrition under reduced caloric availability, not less. This deepens the paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: Transparent correlation-to-causation flaw in a short, two-sentence stimulus. Only (C) replicates the exact move — an observed correlation treated as proof of causation. Other choices commit obviously different errors or are valid.
lr.stimulus: Students who eat breakfast every day score higher on math tests than students who skip breakfast. Therefore, eating breakfast causes students to do better in math.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Runners who wear expensive shoes tend to finish races faster than those who don't. So expensive shoes must be worth the money.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every swan I have ever seen has been white. Therefore, all swans are white.

choices.label: C
choices.text: People who own dogs tend to live longer than people who do not. Therefore, owning a dog causes people to live longer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If it rains, the grass will be wet. The grass is wet, so it must have rained.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The new drug worked for my neighbor. Therefore, it should be approved for everyone.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: observed correlation (breakfast-eaters score higher) is treated as proof that breakfast causes the higher scores. (C) replicates the exact move: correlation between dog ownership and longevity is treated as proof that owning a dog causes longer life.
explanations.A: Tempting because it sounds causal, but the conclusion is evaluative ('worth the money'), not a causal claim. Different structure.
explanations.B: Unwarranted generalization from a sample, not correlation-to-causation.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent — a conditional flaw, not a causal one.
explanations.E: Generalization from a single case, not correlation-to-causation.

lr.difficultyReason: Sufficient-necessary confusion stated plainly. Only (B) reverses a conditional in the same way. Other answers are valid or commit transparently different errors.
lr.stimulus: If a plant receives sunlight, it will grow. The fern in my kitchen is growing. Therefore, it must be receiving sunlight.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a student studies hard, she will pass the exam. Dana studied hard, so Dana passed the exam.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If it snows, the schools close. The schools are closed today. Therefore, it must be snowing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most people who exercise feel healthier. Marcus exercises, so Marcus probably feels healthier.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All mammals have lungs. A whale is a mammal. Therefore, a whale has lungs.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The more you practice piano, the better you get. Elena practices every day, so she is improving.

explanations.correct: Stimulus form: 'If P then Q; Q; therefore P' — affirming the consequent, a sufficient-necessary confusion. (B) runs the identical move: 'If snow then schools close; schools are closed; therefore snowing.'
explanations.A: Valid reasoning — if studying hard is sufficient, then a hard-studying student passes. No flaw.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No conditional reversal; a probabilistic inference applied straightforwardly.
explanations.D: Valid categorical syllogism. No flaw.
explanations.E: No flaw — applying a stated pattern to a case.

lr.difficultyReason: Unwarranted generalization from a tiny, unrepresentative sample. Only (D) replicates the same leap from a handful of cases to a sweeping claim.
lr.stimulus: I've read three novels by contemporary British authors, and I disliked all three. Contemporary British fiction is clearly not worth reading.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The last two movies directed by Silva flopped at the box office. Therefore, Silva's next movie will also flop.

choices.label: B
choices.text: This restaurant serves excellent pasta. Therefore, it probably serves excellent risotto as well.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a painting is by Goya, it is valuable. This painting is valuable, so it must be by Goya.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I've eaten at four Vietnamese restaurants in the city, and all four had slow service. Vietnamese restaurants in this city are just slow.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Jazz venues have been closing in our city. Therefore, live music in general is dying out.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: a few personal experiences (three novels) are used to condemn an entire category (contemporary British fiction). (D) does the same: four restaurant visits used to condemn every Vietnamese restaurant in the city.
explanations.A: Predicts a future event from a pattern — different structure (forecast, not sweeping generalization about a category).
explanations.B: Compositional extension from one dish to another — not a sample-to-population move.
explanations.C: Affirming the consequent — a conditional flaw, not generalization.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Scope shift from one subcategory (jazz) to a broader category (live music), not a small-sample generalization.

lr.difficultyReason: Plain equivocation on a single word ('natural') across premise and conclusion. Only (A) shifts meaning of one term between premise and conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Everything natural is good for you. Poison ivy grows naturally in the forest. Therefore, poison ivy is good for you.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nothing is better than eternal happiness. A cold sandwich is better than nothing. Therefore, a cold sandwich is better than eternal happiness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All fruits are healthy. An apple is a fruit. Therefore, an apple is healthy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most athletes train daily. Priya is an athlete. Therefore, Priya probably trains daily.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a law is unjust, it should not be obeyed. This law is unjust. Therefore, it should not be obeyed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Exercise improves health. Marta exercises. Therefore, Marta is healthy.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: 'natural' shifts meaning from 'wholesome / good-for-you natural' (premise 1) to 'occurring in nature' (premise 2). (A) equivocates on 'nothing' — 'no thing is better' vs. 'is better than no food at all.' Same meaning-shift flaw.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Valid categorical syllogism — no equivocation, no flaw.
explanations.C: Valid probabilistic inference; no shift in meaning.
explanations.D: Valid modus ponens — no flaw.
explanations.E: Overreaches from 'improves health' to 'is healthy,' but no single word shifts meaning — different flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: Correlation-to-causation in an economics setting. Only (E) treats a co-occurring trend as proof of causation. Other answers are valid or commit clearly different errors.
lr.stimulus: In countries where citizens drink more coffee, average life expectancy is higher. Drinking more coffee, therefore, must increase life expectancy.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following most closely parallels the flawed reasoning above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a country has a high GDP, it tends to have low unemployment. This country has low unemployment, so it must have a high GDP.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two of my coworkers caught colds this week. Everyone at work is going to get sick.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All European nations use the euro. Germany is a European nation. Therefore, Germany uses the euro.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The stock market rose last year, and so did housing prices. The stock market rise must have caused the housing prices to climb.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A used car that looks clean is probably well-maintained. This car looks clean. So it's probably well-maintained.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: two things rise together (coffee consumption, life expectancy) and the author concludes one causes the other. (D) is the same move: stock market and housing prices both rose, so one caused the other.
explanations.A: Affirming the consequent — a conditional flaw, not correlation-to-causation.
explanations.B: Hasty generalization from two cases, not a causal leap from correlation.
explanations.C: Valid categorical reasoning. The premise is actually false, but the structure is not flawed.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Applies a general pattern to a specific case — no flaw, and not causal reasoning.

lr.difficultyReason: Classic affirming-the-consequent in a legal context. Only (B) reverses a stated conditional. The other answers present valid reasoning or different fallacies.
lr.stimulus: Any defendant who forged the signature had access to the notary's office. Ms. Lowe had access to the notary's office. Therefore, Ms. Lowe forged the signature.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anyone who wins the marathon trains daily. Ravi did not train daily. Therefore, Ravi did not win the marathon.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any hiker who reached the summit carried a rope. Dana carried a rope. Therefore, Dana reached the summit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All licensed pilots have passed the medical exam. Kira is a licensed pilot. Therefore, Kira has passed the medical exam.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most violinists in the orchestra studied abroad. Tomas is a violinist in the orchestra. Therefore, Tomas probably studied abroad.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If the window is open, the alarm will sound. The alarm is sounding, so the window is open — unless the sensor is broken.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: having access was necessary for forgery, not sufficient; treating it as sufficient commits sufficient-necessary confusion. (B) makes the same error: carrying a rope was necessary for reaching the summit, but the argument treats it as sufficient.
explanations.A: Valid — denying the necessary condition. No flaw.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Valid categorical reasoning — no flaw.
explanations.D: Valid probabilistic inference from 'most' — no flaw.
explanations.E: Hedges the conclusion; the 'unless' clause avoids the flaw the stimulus commits.

lr.difficultyReason: Unwarranted generalization in a technology context. Only (A) jumps from a single case to a sweeping verdict on a whole category. Other answers commit transparently different flaws.
lr.stimulus: My new tablet froze twice in the first week. Clearly, tablets from this manufacturer are unreliable.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first two chapters of this textbook contained errors. The whole textbook must be poorly edited.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a phone battery is damaged, it drains quickly. This phone's battery drains quickly, so it must be damaged.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most users of this software report bugs. Teo is a user, so he has probably reported a bug.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Apps that go viral usually have clever marketing. This app has clever marketing. Therefore, it will go viral.

choices.label: E
choices.text: New cars with high safety ratings sell well. This car has a high safety rating, so it will sell well — if people hear about it.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: a tiny experience (two freezes in one unit) is projected onto an entire manufacturer's product line. (A) mirrors the move: defects in two chapters are projected onto the whole textbook.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Affirming the consequent — different flaw.
explanations.C: Valid probabilistic inference.
explanations.D: Sufficient-necessary confusion — treats marketing as sufficient when it's only typical.
explanations.E: Hedges the conclusion and therefore is not clearly flawed.

lr.difficultyReason: Equivocation on the word 'right' across premise and conclusion in an ethics stimulus. Only (C) matches by shifting the meaning of a single term between premises.
lr.stimulus: Every citizen has a right to free speech. Whatever a person has a right to do is the right thing to do. Therefore, whatever a citizen says is the right thing to say.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All triangles have three sides. This figure has three sides. Therefore, this figure is a triangle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People who skip meals are often tired. Lin skips meals. So Lin is often tired.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A sound investment is a safe one. Soundproof walls keep noise out. Therefore, walls that keep noise out are safe investments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most voters prefer candidate Reyes. Maria is a voter. So Maria probably prefers Reyes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: When temperatures drop, ice forms. Ice has formed. So temperatures have dropped.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: 'right' shifts from 'entitled/permitted' to 'morally correct.' (C) equivocates on 'sound': 'safe/sensible investment' vs. 'sound as in noise.' Same single-word meaning shift across premises.
explanations.A: Valid structure except that having three sides is sufficient for being a triangle — no equivocation.
explanations.B: Valid probabilistic inference. No meaning shift.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Valid reasoning from 'most' — no flaw.
explanations.E: Affirming the consequent — different flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: Correlation-to-causation in an environmental-policy setting. Only (B) treats co-occurrence as causation. Others commit different errors or reason validly.
lr.stimulus: Cities that installed more bike lanes last decade saw air quality improve over the same period. Installing bike lanes, therefore, causes air quality to improve.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Recent graduates who attended networking events got jobs within six months. Attending networking events must make graduates more competent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neighborhoods that planted more street trees last year reported lower crime rates. Planting street trees must cause crime to drop.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any runner who finishes the race gets a medal. Oskar got a medal, so Oskar must have finished the race.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every play I've seen at this theater has been disappointing. The theater must never put on good plays.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A solar panel works when it receives light. This panel is working, so it must be receiving light.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: two trends co-occurred in the same places (more bike lanes, better air) and the author concludes causation. (B) is the same move: tree-planting and crime drops co-occurred, and the author infers causation.
explanations.A: Tempting, but the conclusion shifts topic to 'competence' rather than to getting jobs — scope shift rather than pure correlation-to-causation.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Affirming the consequent — different flaw.
explanations.D: Unwarranted generalization from a sample, not correlation-to-causation.
explanations.E: Valid — requires light, has light, so it works. No flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: Sufficient-necessary confusion in a linguistics context. Only (E) reverses a stated conditional. Others are valid or commit different fallacies.
lr.stimulus: Anyone fluent in Portuguese can understand some written Spanish. Carla can understand some written Spanish. Therefore, Carla is fluent in Portuguese.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every experienced translator knows at least two languages. Yuki is not an experienced translator. So Yuki doesn't know two languages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most native speakers of a language speak it without an accent. Sven is a native speaker, so Sven probably speaks without an accent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: People who read a lot have large vocabularies. Reading, therefore, causes vocabulary to grow.

choices.label: D
choices.text: My two roommates are studying German. Everyone in our building must be studying German.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Everyone who has taken the advanced class can recite the declensions. Nadia can recite the declensions. Therefore, Nadia has taken the advanced class.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: fluency in Portuguese is sufficient for understanding some written Spanish, but the argument treats it as necessary — classic sufficient-necessary reversal. (E) runs the same move: taking the advanced class is sufficient for reciting the declensions, but the argument treats it as necessary.
explanations.A: Denying a necessary condition — different structure (and valid, if one reads the conditional as stated).
explanations.B: Valid probabilistic inference from 'most.' No flaw.
explanations.C: Correlation-to-causation — different flaw.
explanations.D: Unwarranted generalization — different flaw.
explanations.E: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Transparent circular reasoning flaw. The stimulus concludes that vitamins help recovery because they contain recovery-promoting substances. This is circular: assuming the premise to reach the conclusion. Only one answer (D) replicates this exact self-supporting structure with different content. Other answers either contain valid reasoning or commit obviously different errors.
lr.stimulus: All vitamins contain substances that promote recovery from illness. Vitamin C is a vitamin. Therefore, vitamin C promotes recovery from illness.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All minerals are beneficial to health. Some beneficial substances are not minerals. Therefore, some beneficial substances might be minerals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All cells contain DNA. Cancer is caused by mutated cells. Therefore, cancer is caused by mutated DNA.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All universities have professors. The University of Chicago is a university. Therefore, the University of Chicago has professors.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All honest people tell the truth. Jim tells the truth. Therefore, Jim is honest.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most birds can fly. Penguins are birds. Therefore, penguins can probably fly.

explanations.correct: The stimulus commits affirming the consequent: 'All X have property P → If something has P, is it X?' The conclusion assumes the inverse of the conditional. D does the same: 'All honest people tell the truth' does not imply that all truth-tellers are honest, but the argument assumes it does. Both are classical logical fallacies of conditional reversal.
explanations.A: Valid reasoning with proper quantifiers; no flaw.
explanations.B: Combines two premises to reach a valid intermediate conclusion; not a conditional reversal.
explanations.C: Valid application of a universal premise to a member of the category; this is sound reasoning.
explanations.D: Correct. Stimulus: All P are Q; X is Q; therefore X is P (affirming the consequent). D: All honest are truth-tellers; Jim is a truth-teller; therefore Jim is honest. Exact same flaw.
explanations.E: Different flaw — quantifier mismatch (probabilistic generalization to a specific case), not a conditional reversal.

lr.difficultyReason: Transparent false dichotomy. The stimulus presents only two options (study hard or fail) and eliminates one, concluding the other must be true. This is transparent because the structure is immediately visible and no other answer replicates it. Trap answers introduce unrelated fallacies or valid reasoning.
lr.stimulus: Either you study hard for the exam or you will fail. Since you did not study hard, you will definitely fail.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments contains flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Either the defendant is guilty or innocent. The evidence shows the defendant acted with intent. Therefore, the defendant is guilty.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A restaurant is either expensive or cheap. Since this restaurant is not expensive, it must be cheap.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If you do not exercise regularly, you will gain weight. You exercise regularly. Therefore, you will not gain weight.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All successful companies innovate. This company is successful. Therefore, this company innovates.

choices.label: E
choices.text: People are either optimists or pessimists. Research shows most people are adaptable. Therefore, most people are neither optimists nor pessimists.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: False dilemma—assumes only two options (study hard OR fail), eliminates one, concludes the other. B: False dilemma—assumes only two options (expensive OR cheap), eliminates one, concludes the other. Identical structure and identical flaw.
explanations.A: Premises do not establish a dichotomy; the reasoning is invalid for different reasons.
explanations.B: Correct. Both stimulus and B set up a false binary choice, eliminate one option, and conclude the remaining option must be true.
explanations.C: This is a conditional premise with a negated antecedent; not a false dichotomy.
explanations.D: Valid categorical reasoning; no flaw of false dichotomy.
explanations.E: Introduces a contradiction but doesn't use the dichotomy flaw in the way the stimulus does.

lr.difficultyReason: Transparent ad hominem. The stimulus rejects a claim solely because of who made it (a competitor), not by engaging with the claim itself. Only one answer (C) commits the same ad hominem error. Other answers are valid arguments or commit different logical errors.
lr.stimulus: The rival pharmaceutical company claims that our drug is ineffective. But the rival company has a financial incentive to discredit us. Therefore, our drug must be effective.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dr. Smith claims that the new vaccine is safe. Dr. Smith has conducted extensive research on vaccines. Therefore, the new vaccine is safe.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The defense attorney argues that the witness is unreliable. The witness has been convicted of perjury in the past. Therefore, the defense attorney's argument is valid.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The activist claims that the factory pollutes the environment. But the activist is known for exaggerating problems. Therefore, the factory does not pollute the environment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The economist predicts a recession. The economist has never been accurate in the past. Therefore, there will be no recession.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The politician supports the tax increase. The politician is wealthy. Therefore, the tax increase is unjust.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: Ad hominem—rejects a claim (drug is ineffective) by attacking the source (rival has incentive to lie), then concludes the opposite of the claim. D: Ad hominem—rejects a claim (recession will occur) by attacking the source's character (never accurate), then concludes the opposite. Both assume that discrediting the source proves the claim false, which is the ad hominem flaw.
explanations.A: Appeals to the source's credibility; valid reasoning, not ad hominem.
explanations.B: Legitimately questions reliability; not the same ad hominem structure as stimulus.
explanations.C: Correct. Stimulus: Source has incentive to lie, therefore claim is false. C: Source exaggerates, therefore claim is false. Both reject a claim via ad hominem attack.
explanations.D: Correct. Stimulus: Rival is biased, so our drug works. D: Economist is inaccurate, so no recession. Both attack the messenger to refute the message.
explanations.E: Attacks the source's motives but doesn't conclude the claim is false; different structure.

lr.difficultyReason: Transparent necessary/sufficient confusion. The stimulus treats a necessary condition as sufficient: if something is required for success, the stimulus assumes having it guarantees success. Only one answer (B) replicates this exact reversal. Other answers either use conditionals correctly or commit different errors.
lr.stimulus: A college degree is necessary for a successful career in law. Therefore, anyone with a college degree will have a successful law career.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Water is necessary for plant growth. Therefore, some plants cannot grow without water.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A valid passport is necessary for international travel. Therefore, anyone with a valid passport can travel internationally.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Practice is necessary for mastering an instrument. Therefore, you should practice every day.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sleep is necessary for health. Most healthy people sleep regularly. Therefore, most healthy people are well-rested.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A license is necessary to drive legally. Most licensed drivers follow traffic laws. Therefore, most drivers are licensed.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: Necessary condition stated (college degree is necessary for law success), then treated as sufficient (anyone with degree → success). B: Necessary condition stated (passport is necessary for international travel), then treated as sufficient (anyone with passport → can travel). Both confuse a requirement with a guarantee.
explanations.A: Correctly states a necessary condition without treating it as sufficient; valid reasoning.
explanations.B: Correct. Stimulus: College degree is necessary for law success, so having a degree guarantees success. B: Passport is necessary for travel, so having a passport guarantees ability to travel. Same flaw.
explanations.C: Normative claim, not a logical flaw of conditional confusion.
explanations.D: Introduces a separate premise about frequency; not a simple necessary/sufficient confusion.
explanations.E: Reverses the direction of the necessary condition; different structure.

lr.difficultyReason: Transparent begging the question (circular reasoning). The stimulus asserts that the novel is well-written because it received critical praise, but critical praise is itself a measure of literary quality. The conclusion restates the premise. Only one answer (E) replicates this circularity. Other answers use premises and conclusions logically distinct from each other.
lr.stimulus: This novel must be well-written because it has received critical acclaim from major literary magazines. After all, critical acclaim is a sign of literary excellence.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is flawed in the same way as the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: This restaurant must serve excellent food because the chef trained at a prestigious culinary school and uses only fresh ingredients.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The president's policy must be effective because it was voted on by Congress. Voting is how Congress passes laws.

choices.label: C
choices.text: This athlete must be talented because he won multiple championships. Championships are competitive events.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The movie must be entertaining because millions of people watched it. Large audiences indicate popularity.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The scientific theory must be true because experts accept it. Acceptance by experts is how we identify true theories.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: Novel is well-written (conclusion) because of critical acclaim (premise), and critical acclaim = literary excellence (which is what well-written means). The justification for the premise is simply a restatement of the conclusion. E: Theory is true (conclusion) because experts accept it (premise), and expert acceptance = identifying true theories (which is what truth means in this context). Both beg the question.
explanations.A: Provides distinct grounds (training, ingredients) for the conclusion; not circular.
explanations.B: Attempts a logical move but the second sentence doesn't truly justify the first; different type of flaw.
explanations.C: Championships are evidence of talent, but the argument doesn't assume championships = talent; valid structure.
explanations.D: Popularity is a distinct property from entertainment; not begging the question.
explanations.E: Correct. Stimulus: Well-written because of critical acclaim, and critical acclaim is a sign of literary excellence (begs the question). E: True because experts accept it, and expert acceptance is how we identify truth (begs the question). Identical flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: Transparent equivocation. The stimulus uses 'state' in two different senses (a nation-state versus an emotional state) in a single argument, creating an invalid inference. Only one answer (C) replicates equivocation on a word with multiple meanings. Other answers either avoid equivocation or commit different errors.
lr.stimulus: Countries with strong states are politically stable. Psychology shows that people with a strong state of mind are resilient. Therefore, psychology explains political stability.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Banks offer interest on savings. Interest in history is common among scholars. Therefore, banks and scholars share similar motivations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The right to free speech is protected by law. Some people have a right to remain silent. Therefore, silence is protected by law.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Newspapers have political authority in democracies. Some news reports have political authority. Therefore, democracies are influenced by news reports.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Trees absorb carbon dioxide. Some carbon dioxide affects the climate. Therefore, trees affect the climate.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Successful investments require patience. Patients in hospitals require medical care. Therefore, successful investments require medical care.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: Uses 'state' to mean both 'nation-state' (premise 1) and 'mental/emotional state' (premise 2), then conflates them to reach an invalid conclusion. A: Uses 'interest' to mean both 'financial interest' (banks) and 'intellectual interest' (scholars), then conflates them. Both equivocate on a word with multiple meanings.
explanations.A: Correct. 'Interest' means financial return in the first sentence and intellectual curiosity in the second; conflating them is equivocation, matching the stimulus's equivocation on 'state.'
explanations.B: Uses distinct homonyms ('right' as right to speak vs. right to silence) but in a way that doesn't create the same equivocal flaw.
explanations.C: Conflates 'political authority' of newspapers (institutional) with authority of news reports (content), but the logical structure differs from the stimulus.
explanations.D: Moves from 'trees absorb CO2' to 'CO2 affects climate' to 'trees affect climate'—a chain of valid premises, not equivocation.
explanations.E: Correct. This is a clear equivocation on 'require': patience (required for success) vs. medical care (required for patients). Matches stimulus's equivocation on 'state.'

lr.difficultyReason: Transparent composition fallacy. The stimulus attributes a property of the parts (individual scientists are fallible) to the whole (the scientific community), reaching an invalid conclusion. Only one answer (D) replicates this part-to-whole error. Other answers either reason validly about wholes or commit different fallacies.
lr.stimulus: Individual scientists are sometimes wrong in their reasoning. Therefore, the scientific consensus must be wrong.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each chess piece has limited mobility. Therefore, no meaningful chess strategy is possible.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some economists disagree about tax policy. Therefore, economics as a field is not a valid discipline.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every brick in the wall is small. Therefore, every wall is small.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Individual musicians in an orchestra are not perfect. Therefore, orchestral performances are not excellent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some athletes are not intelligent. Therefore, athletic competition requires no intelligence.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: Individual parts (scientists) have a property (fallibility), so the whole (scientific consensus) must lack the opposite property (be wrong). D: Individual parts (musicians) have a property (imperfection), so the whole (orchestral performance) must lack the opposite property (be excellent). Both commit the composition fallacy.
explanations.A: Correctly infers a limitation of the whole from a property of parts, but the flaw is different from the stimulus.
explanations.B: Attributes disagreement of individuals to invalidity of the field; related but different structure.
explanations.C: Composition fallacy, but concludes something obviously true (small bricks → small wall), making it less transparent.
explanations.D: Correct. Stimulus: Individual scientists are fallible, so scientific consensus is wrong. D: Individual musicians are imperfect, so orchestral performances are not excellent. Both wrongly infer that a property of parts determines the opposite property of the whole.
explanations.E: Commits an unsupported generalization; different flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: Transparent division fallacy (inverse of composition). The stimulus attributes a property of the whole (the team is successful) to each part (every player is successful), reaching an invalid conclusion. Only one answer (E) replicates this whole-to-part error. Other answers reason validly or commit different fallacies.
lr.stimulus: The basketball team won the championship. Therefore, every player on the team must be an excellent basketball player.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments contains flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: This company is profitable. Therefore, the company must have a large number of employees.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The orchestra performed beautifully. Therefore, every instrument in the orchestra sounded beautiful.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The novel is long. Therefore, every chapter in the novel is long.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The committee is efficient. Therefore, the committee has efficient decision-making procedures.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The board of directors made a profitable investment. Therefore, each director individually made a profitable investment.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: Whole property (team won championship) → Individual part property (every player is excellent). B: Whole property (orchestra performed beautifully) → Individual part property (every instrument sounded beautiful). Both commit division fallacy by attributing the whole's property to all of its parts.
explanations.A: Attributes a property to the whole that doesn't necessarily follow from profitability; different flaw.
explanations.B: Correct. Stimulus: Team's success → each player's excellence. B: Orchestra's beauty → each instrument's beauty. Both wrongly infer that a property of the whole applies to each part.
explanations.C: Attributes the whole's length to parts; division fallacy, but less transparent because the conclusion is absurd.
explanations.D: Infers a method or structure from a property; different type of inference.
explanations.E: Correct. Stimulus: Team's championship → each player's excellence. E: Board's profitable investment → each director's profitable investment. Both wrongly distribute a collective achievement to individuals.

lr.difficultyReason: Transparent false cause. The stimulus confuses temporal sequence (A happens before B) with causal relation (A causes B), reaching an invalid conclusion. Only one answer (C) replicates this post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy. Other answers either reason validly about causation or commit different errors.
lr.stimulus: The company implemented new management practices in January. The company's profits increased in February. Therefore, the new management practices caused the increase in profits.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The government raised interest rates on Tuesday. The stock market declined on Thursday. Therefore, higher interest rates caused the stock market to decline.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A medication was prescribed in the morning. The patient felt better in the afternoon. Therefore, the medication was effective.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The city installed new traffic lights in March. Traffic accidents decreased in April. Therefore, the new traffic lights reduced traffic accidents.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The school hired new teachers in September. Student test scores improved in October. Therefore, the new teachers caused the improvement.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Interest rates are rising. Unemployment is also rising. Therefore, rising interest rates cause unemployment to rise.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: Post hoc ergo propter hoc—event A happens, then event B happens, so A caused B. No control for other factors. A: Interest rates raised (A), market declined (B), therefore A caused B. C and D are similar, but A is the most transparent because the temporal gap and alternate explanations are most obvious.
explanations.A: Correct. Stimulus: Management change → profit increase (assumes causation from sequence). A: Interest rate increase → market decline (assumes causation from sequence). Both commit post hoc ergo propter hoc.
explanations.B: Temporal sequence with a plausible causal link; not the same flaw as stimulus.
explanations.C: Correct. Stimulus: New practices → profit increase. C: New traffic lights → accident decrease. Both post hoc ergo propter hoc.
explanations.D: Correct. Stimulus: New management → profit increase. D: New teachers → test score improvement. Both post hoc ergo propter hoc.
explanations.E: Correlation without causation, but lacks the temporal sequence element that makes post hoc fallacy transparent.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: the stimulus treats a sufficient condition as though it were necessary and then generalizes from one instance to a population. Two choices match one half of the flaw but not both; the correct answer replicates both moves in a different domain.
lr.stimulus: Nutritionist: Anyone who eats a serving of oily fish each day will lower their risk of heart disease. Mira eats oily fish every day, and her cardiologist tells her that her risk of heart disease is low. It follows that lowering one's risk of heart disease requires daily consumption of oily fish, and that patients who do not eat oily fish must therefore be at elevated risk.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains flawed reasoning most similar to that in the nutritionist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Studying two hours a night is enough to pass the bar exam. Daniel studies two hours a night and passed the bar. So studying two hours a night is the only way to pass the bar, and anyone who studies less than that must fail.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Daily meditation reduces stress in those who practice it. Since Hugo reports reduced stress, he probably meditates daily.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Regular exercise lowers blood pressure. Regular exercise also improves sleep. So anyone whose blood pressure is low probably sleeps well.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Everyone who trains at high altitude builds endurance. Anika trained at high altitude, so Anika built endurance. Therefore, high-altitude training is widely available to athletes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reading aloud to children improves their vocabulary. Most parents who read aloud to their children are well educated. So well-educated parents produce children with the best vocabularies.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: (i) flips sufficient (oily fish is enough to lower risk) into necessary (required), and (ii) generalizes from one person's case to all patients. (A) flips sufficient (two hours is enough to pass) into necessary (only way) and generalizes from Daniel's case to everyone who studies less.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Parallel topic (health habit) but a different flaw — concluding from an effect back to its cause, not a sufficient/necessary swap.
explanations.C: Different flaw — treating two separate effects of one cause as though they caused each other.
explanations.D: Has the right structural opening but the conclusion drifts to an unrelated claim about availability, so the flaw is in the wrong position rather than parallel.
explanations.E: Correlational overreach about educated parents — a different flaw dressed in similar vocabulary.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw combining a part-to-whole (compositional) error with a category shift from 'some' to 'every.' Three choices are surface-parallel; only one replicates both the composition move and the universalization.
lr.stimulus: Each player on the Riverton chess club has won at least one regional tournament. Therefore, the Riverton chess club as a whole has won every regional tournament, and any team that includes a Riverton member is assured of a regional title.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each musician in the Halden Quartet has performed at Carnegie Hall. So the Halden Quartet has performed at Carnegie Hall as an ensemble, and any group that includes a Halden musician must have performed there too.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most of the dancers in the Astoria company trained in Paris. So the company's style is probably Parisian, and dancers who leave the company will carry that style with them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Velaris law firm has won every major antitrust case it has argued. So each of its partners has personally won a major antitrust case.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each scientist on the Terra team has published in a leading journal. So at least one Terra paper has appeared in a leading journal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every runner on the Corbel track squad has finished a marathon under three hours. Therefore, the squad's average marathon time is under three hours.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: attributes an individual-member property ('won a tournament') to the collective, then extends it universally to any group containing a member. (A) attributes 'performed at Carnegie Hall' from individuals to the quartet and then to any group containing one — identical compound move.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Starts from 'most,' not 'each,' and the flaw is a stylistic generalization rather than a compositional leap.
explanations.C: Reverses the direction — whole-to-part rather than part-to-whole — so the flaw is in the wrong structural position.
explanations.D: Valid inference — if each scientist has published, then at least one paper has appeared. Not flawed at all.
explanations.E: Valid inference — a universal property of members can legitimately yield a claim about the group's average. Not flawed.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: correlation-to-causation fused with a scope shift from a single country to the global economy. Trap choices replicate one move but not the other.
lr.stimulus: In Norway, as the share of electric vehicles on the road has risen, urban air quality has improved. It follows that electric vehicles cause cleaner air, and that worldwide adoption of electric vehicles is therefore the primary means by which humanity will solve global air pollution.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In Japan, as broadband speeds have risen, small-business productivity has risen. So faster broadband causes higher productivity, and expanding broadband globally will be the chief driver of worldwide economic growth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In Denmark, cycling rates have increased while obesity rates have fallen. So cycling probably causes weight loss.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In several European countries, reading scores have risen alongside increased library funding. Therefore, library funding must be the main cause of rising literacy in those particular countries.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many nations have reduced smoking rates through taxation. Therefore, taxation of unhealthy products is the most effective public-health tool available to governments everywhere.

choices.label: E
choices.text: In Finland, school meal programs are associated with better student health. So Finland's particular meal program improves health, and its specific curriculum should be exported worldwide.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: (i) treats a within-one-country correlation as causation, then (ii) inflates a local effect into the primary global solution. (A) replicates both: a Japan-internal correlation treated as causal, then inflated to the chief driver of worldwide economic growth.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Commits only the causation-from-correlation half; no global scope shift.
explanations.C: Stays within the same set of countries and stops at the causal claim. Only half the flaw.
explanations.D: Starts from a generalization across many nations, so the scope shift isn't there; the flaw is different.
explanations.E: Has a geographic expansion but leaps to a curriculum claim the premise doesn't touch — the flaw is a substitution in the conclusion, not a compound correlation/scope error.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw combines equivocation on 'right' (legal right vs. moral entitlement) with an unwarranted move from 'some' to 'all.' Traps include a valid analog and an equivocation without the quantifier move.
lr.stimulus: Legal scholar: Some citizens have a right to carry firearms, in the sense that the law permits them to do so. But a right, properly understood, is a moral entitlement. Therefore, all citizens have a moral entitlement to carry firearms, and any restriction on that entitlement is unjust.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some workers have a duty to report safety violations, in the sense that company policy requires them to. But a duty, properly understood, is a binding moral obligation. Therefore, every worker has a moral obligation to report safety violations, and any worker who does not report them is acting immorally.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most judges have a duty to recuse themselves when they have a personal interest in a case. A duty is a moral obligation. Therefore, judges who fail to recuse themselves in such cases act immorally.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some drivers have a license to operate commercial trucks, and a license is a form of permission. So every driver has permission to operate commercial trucks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some doctors are authorized to prescribe controlled substances. Since authorization is a form of trust, these doctors are trusted by the community, and patients should therefore follow any of their recommendations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Certain parents are permitted by law to homeschool their children. Since a legal permission is a form of choice, every parent has the choice to homeschool, and any parent who does not is failing their children.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: equivocates on 'right' (legal permission → moral entitlement) and expands 'some' to 'all,' concluding any restriction is unjust. (A) equivocates on 'duty' (policy-required → moral obligation) and expands 'some' to 'every,' concluding that non-reporters act immorally — identical compound move.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Starts from 'most' and omits the equivocation — duty is already used morally in both premises. The quantifier shift is also minor.
explanations.C: Has the some-to-every move but no equivocation: 'license' and 'permission' aren't being traded on two distinct senses.
explanations.D: Accurate reasoning is disguised as flawed by the final overreach, but the core move is a chained inference about trust, not a sense-shift on a single term.
explanations.E: Equivocates on 'choice,' but the conclusion is a moral indictment that doesn't parallel 'any restriction is unjust' — the flaw lands in a different structural slot.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: absence of evidence treated as evidence of absence, combined with a shift from 'in our samples' to 'in this region.' Several answer choices nail one half but miss the other.
lr.stimulus: Field biologist: In our three summer surveys of the Dorval wetlands, we never observed the marsh wren. Our surveys covered only the eastern portion of the wetlands. Since we did not detect the marsh wren in those surveys, the species must be absent from the wetlands entirely, and conservation plans for the Dorval marsh wren should therefore be canceled.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the field biologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In three spot checks of the company's eastern warehouse, auditors found no expired inventory. Since the auditors did not find expired inventory during those checks, there must be none anywhere in the company, and the firm's expired-inventory write-off policy should be eliminated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several recent dives of the Pelos reef found no evidence of the striped grouper, though divers covered only a small area. It is therefore possible that the species is rarer than previously thought.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Surveys of a small southern district failed to detect the rust moth. Since the rust moth has never been detected there, it must be rare in that district, though it may thrive elsewhere.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Audits of the eastern branch of a bank revealed no fraud. So the eastern branch is free of fraud, and the bank's other branches should adopt its procedures.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Our annual inspections of the northern bridge have never uncovered structural defects. The inspections are thorough and cover the whole bridge. So the northern bridge is probably structurally sound, and scheduled inspections can continue at the current interval.
