explanations.correct: Stimulus: absence-in-a-partial-survey is treated as absence everywhere, and a policy (conservation) is canceled on that basis. (A) replicates: absence in partial spot checks is treated as absence company-wide, and the write-off policy is eliminated — same compound flaw, same concluding move.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Not flawed — the conclusion is properly hedged ('possible... rarer than previously thought'). Accurate reasoning disguised as flawed.
explanations.C: Half-flaw only: the conclusion is restricted to the district, not overextended, and the 'rare' claim is measured.
explanations.D: Extends a local absence to a local conclusion, then pivots to a recommendation about other branches. The recommended policy change is in the wrong structural slot — it doesn't parallel canceling plans for the very region surveyed.
explanations.E: Not flawed — premises specify thorough coverage of the whole bridge, so the conclusion is warranted.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: a category error (treating a type-level entity as if it behaved like its instances) combined with a hasty generalization. Traps either commit only the category move or only the generalization.
lr.stimulus: The novel, as a literary form, has evolved for over three centuries and continues to adapt to new readers. Since The Windward Letters is a novel, it too must be evolving and adapting to new readers. And since it has sold well this year, novels in general are clearly thriving as never before.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The sonnet, as a poetic form, has developed over five centuries and continues to change. Since 'Summer's Hour' is a sonnet, it too must be changing over time. And since it has recently been widely anthologized, sonnets as a form are flourishing more than ever.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The blues, as a musical genre, has influenced many later styles. So any given blues song has influenced many later styles, and the blues is the most influential genre of the last century.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The string quartet has been a staple of chamber music since Haydn. Since the Velari Quartet is performing tonight, the genre is alive, and string quartets are the most popular chamber form today.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The essay, as a form, has reinvented itself many times. Since 'On the Terrace' is an essay, it reinvents itself. Therefore, individual essays never stay the same from one reading to the next.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The documentary film has always aimed at truth-telling. Since Rivers at Dusk is a documentary, its makers aim at truth-telling. Documentaries remain one of several important film genres.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: ascribes a type-level property ('evolving over centuries') to a single instance, then leaps from one work's sales to the flourishing of the entire form. (A) mirrors both moves exactly: type-level change ascribed to one sonnet, then one anthologization used to conclude the form is flourishing.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Commits only the category error (type-level property to every instance); no sales-style leap to the form's flourishing.
explanations.C: The type-to-instance move is weaker (a performance, not a property-transfer), and the final claim is about popularity without the one-instance springboard. Parallel topic, different flaw.
explanations.D: Category error is present, but the conclusion drifts to an implausible claim about essays changing between readings — the flaw is in the wrong structural slot.
explanations.E: Accurate reasoning disguised as flawed — the 'aim at truth-telling' premise arguably does transfer, and the closing claim is measured rather than an overreach.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: confuses percentage change with absolute change, then generalizes from one company's quarter to the entire industry. Students who catch only the percentage/absolute swap will be tempted by a trap that lacks the industry leap.
lr.stimulus: Analyst: Last quarter, Corten Software's profit margin rose by 20 percent, while its rival Bylor's margin rose by only 5 percent. So Corten made far more profit than Bylor last quarter, and the software industry as a whole must be shifting decisively in Corten's favor.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains flawed reasoning most similar to that in the analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Last season, the Adler Bakery's customer count rose 30 percent, while the Madrona Bakery's count rose only 4 percent. So Adler served far more customers than Madrona last season, and the city's bakery market must be turning decisively toward Adler.

choices.label: B
choices.text: This year, Ganz Motors raised prices by 8 percent while Volera raised them by 3 percent. So Ganz's cars now cost more on average than Volera's, and buyers should therefore prefer Volera.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Clinic A's patient load grew by 12 percent while Clinic B's grew by 11 percent. So Clinic A now sees more patients than Clinic B, and the regional market favors Clinic A.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Last year, the Haldane School's test scores rose 15 percent, while Crossfield's rose only 5 percent. So Haldane's teachers are better than Crossfield's.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Profit margins at Orell Industries rose sharply last quarter, so Orell probably made more profit than in any previous quarter, and investors are likely to favor Orell in the year ahead.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: confuses a larger percentage rise with a larger absolute amount, then generalizes from one quarter to an industry trend. (A) replicates both: larger percentage rise conflated with larger absolute customer count, then generalized from one bakery's season to the city market.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Percentage/absolute confusion exists but the conclusion is a recommendation for buyers, not an industry trend — the generalization move is in the wrong slot.
explanations.C: The percentages are too close to drive the stimulus's lopsided inference, and the mismatch between 'grew by X%' and 'sees more patients' is different in kind.
explanations.D: Different second flaw — attributing test-score growth to teacher quality rather than generalizing from one year to an industry.
explanations.E: Commits only the generalization half; no percentage-vs-absolute comparison between rivals.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: an ad hominem-adjacent move (dismissing a speaker's argument because of the speaker's profession) combined with a leap from 'no good reason to accept X' to 'X is false.' Traps include a pure ad hominem and a pure absence-to-denial fallacy.
lr.stimulus: Critic: The economist's forecast that inflation will ease by next spring should be dismissed. She works for a bank that profits when borrowers expect low inflation, so her forecast cannot be trusted. Since we therefore have no good reason to accept her forecast, we can conclude that inflation will not ease by next spring.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the critic's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The lawyer's claim that the new statute is constitutional should be dismissed. He is employed by a firm that benefits when the statute is upheld, so his opinion cannot be trusted. Since we therefore have no good reason to accept his claim, we may conclude that the statute is unconstitutional.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The union leader's assertion that wages have stagnated is self-serving, so her assertion can be ignored. Since we can ignore her assertion, wages have not stagnated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pundit supports the tax increase only because his favored party proposed it. So his support is biased, and we should therefore ignore everything he says on any issue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The researcher's study of air pollution was funded by an environmental group. Because of that funding, we have reason to scrutinize the methodology, though we should not dismiss the findings outright.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Since the journalist has never lived in the region she reports on, she cannot understand it, and her accounts of the region's politics must be inaccurate, so the region's politics are not as she describes.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: dismisses a forecast on professional-interest grounds and then moves from 'no good reason to accept it' to 'its contrary is true.' (A) mirrors both: dismissal of the lawyer's claim on firm-interest grounds and a move from 'no reason to accept' to 'the statute is unconstitutional.'
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Commits the ad-hominem and absence-to-denial moves but compresses them into one step; the 'self-serving' charge isn't tied to a professional interest in the way the stimulus ties it to the bank.
explanations.C: Ad hominem with a different conclusion structure — 'ignore everything he says' broadens the flaw to all topics rather than concluding the contrary of the specific claim.
explanations.D: Accurate reasoning disguised as flawed — the conclusion is measured ('scrutinize, not dismiss'). Not parallel, because the stimulus is flawed and the correct answer must be flawed.
explanations.E: Different opening — an argument from lack of residence rather than professional interest — and the conclusion is an ad hominem-adjacent but distinct move.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: conflating a statistical average with every individual in a group, then drawing a universal policy conclusion. Traps include an average/individual confusion without the policy leap and a valid analog.
lr.stimulus: City planner: The average commute in our city is 28 minutes. Since the average is 28 minutes, every commuter in the city must spend roughly 28 minutes traveling to work each day. Therefore, any transit project that shortens commutes by even a few minutes will benefit every resident equally, and the city should fund only those projects that reduce the average.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the city planner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: School board member: The average class size in our district is 24 students. Since the average is 24, every class in the district must have roughly 24 students. Therefore, any policy that lowers class size by even a few students will benefit every student equally, and we should fund only those policies that reduce the average.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The average rainfall in our county last year was 32 inches. Since 32 inches is the average, every part of the county received roughly that amount, and farmers in every part should expect comparable yields.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The average wage in the restaurant industry is $15 per hour. Since some workers earn less than the average, policies that raise the minimum wage will help the lowest-paid workers most.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The average patient at our clinic waits 20 minutes. Since 20 minutes is the average, some patients wait longer and some shorter; our goal should be to reduce the longest waits rather than the average.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The average house price in the neighborhood has risen by 10 percent, so every house has risen by 10 percent, and each owner's equity has risen accordingly.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: treats the average as a property of each individual and then draws a universal policy conclusion that funding should target the average. (A) replicates: the 24-student average is treated as each class's size, and the policy conclusion restricts funding to policies that reduce the average.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Commits only the average/individual confusion; no policy conclusion that restricts funding.
explanations.C: Not flawed — the reasoning correctly notes variance around an average and draws a measured policy inference.
explanations.D: Not flawed — the reasoning distinguishes average from distribution and chooses a reasonable goal.
explanations.E: Commits only the average/individual confusion about house prices with a further equity claim; the policy-funding slot from the stimulus isn't present.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: treats a speaker's inability to give reasons for a belief as grounds to reject the belief (epistemic category error), and then generalizes to reject a whole body of knowledge. Traps replicate only one of the two moves.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Native speakers of a language cannot usually articulate the grammatical rules they follow. Since those speakers cannot state the rules, they must not actually know the rules, and the very idea that native speakers possess tacit grammatical knowledge is therefore a myth.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains flawed reasoning most similar to that in the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Skilled bicyclists cannot usually articulate the principles of balance they rely on. Since they cannot state the principles, they must not actually know them, and the very idea that cyclists possess tacit motor knowledge is a myth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Young children cannot usually explain why stories move them. So stories do not really move children, and adults who claim otherwise are mistaken.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many jazz musicians can improvise without consciously thinking about music theory. This shows that music theory is irrelevant to improvisation, and formal training in theory is a waste of time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Experienced nurses can often detect subtle changes in a patient's condition without stating how they know. Because they cannot articulate the signs, their judgments are unreliable and should not influence clinical decisions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Competent chess players may not be able to articulate all the heuristics they use, but their results nonetheless show that the heuristics are real, so we should study their games carefully.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: moves from 'cannot articulate the rules' to 'does not know the rules,' then rejects the whole category of tacit knowledge as a myth. (A) replicates both: cyclists who cannot state balance principles are said not to know them, and tacit motor knowledge is rejected as a myth.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Different flaw — concludes children aren't moved, not that the category of being moved is mythical. The second move is missing.
explanations.C: Starts from a premise about independence from theory, not an inability to articulate it. The resulting flaw is a different kind of overreach.
explanations.D: Commits the articulation-to-ignorance move but stops at unreliability; doesn't reject the category of tacit clinical knowledge wholesale.
explanations.E: Not flawed — the reasoning correctly separates inability to articulate from absence of knowledge. Accurate reasoning disguised as flawed.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is a necessary/sufficient confusion (treating a necessary condition as sufficient). Two answer choices mimic the surface structure but reverse the direction of the confusion, making students track which conditional is actually being swapped.
lr.stimulus: To be admitted to the bar in this state, a person must pass the state ethics examination. Jeremy has passed the state ethics examination. Therefore, Jeremy has been admitted to the bar in this state.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every licensed pilot must complete a medical evaluation each year. Simone has not completed a medical evaluation this year. Therefore, Simone is not a licensed pilot.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In order to graduate from the academy, a cadet must pass the physical fitness test. Rodrigo has passed the physical fitness test. Therefore, Rodrigo has graduated from the academy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anyone who earns a perfect score on the certification exam is immediately promoted. Dana earned a perfect score on the certification exam. Therefore, Dana has been immediately promoted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No one who fails the background check can be appointed as a federal marshal. Leon failed the background check. Therefore, Leon cannot be appointed as a federal marshal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most candidates who pass the state ethics examination eventually seek bar admission. Jeremy passed the state ethics examination. Therefore, Jeremy will probably seek bar admission.

explanations.correct: The stimulus treats passing the ethics exam (a necessary condition for bar admission) as if it were sufficient. B mirrors this exactly: passing the physical fitness test is a necessary condition for graduating, but the argument concludes graduation has occurred simply because the test was passed — necessary treated as sufficient.
explanations.A: A is a valid modus tollens inference (failing the necessary condition entails not having the outcome). No flaw.
explanations.B: Correct. Passes the necessary condition → concludes the sufficient outcome. Same necessary/sufficient confusion as the stimulus.
explanations.C: C is actually valid: earning a perfect score is described as sufficient for promotion, and Dana earned one, so promotion follows correctly.
explanations.D: D is valid: failing the background check is stated as disqualifying, so concluding Leon cannot be appointed is correct.
explanations.E: E shifts to a probabilistic claim about future behavior, not a necessary/sufficient confusion. Different flaw family.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a correlation-to-causation fallacy. Distractors include a valid base-rate argument and a post hoc variant that differs structurally, requiring students to precisely identify the causal overreach.
lr.stimulus: Ever since the city installed new streetlights along Maple Avenue, the number of reported car accidents on that street has dropped significantly. Clearly, the new streetlights caused the reduction in car accidents.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Studies show that people who eat breakfast regularly tend to have lower rates of obesity. Therefore, skipping breakfast must cause obesity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: After the new school principal arrived, student test scores improved dramatically. Therefore, the new principal caused the improvement in test scores.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most people who exercise daily report feeling happier. Since Priya exercises daily, she probably feels happier than average.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Traffic fatalities in the city declined last year. The city also repaved several roads last year. Roads in poor condition tend to cause accidents. Therefore, road repairs probably reduced fatalities.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Car accidents are more frequent on highways than on residential streets. The city has more residential streets than highways. Therefore, most of the city's accidents occur on residential streets.

explanations.correct: The stimulus observes a temporal sequence (streetlights installed → accidents dropped) and concludes causation. B mirrors this exactly: a sequence (new principal arrived → scores improved) is used to conclude causation, ignoring other explanations. Same post hoc / correlation-causation flaw.
explanations.A: A reverses the correlation (breakfast skippers are obese → skipping causes obesity) and involves an absence claim; structurally different from the stimulus's simple temporal-sequence-to-causation move.
explanations.B: Correct. Temporal sequence used to conclude causation without ruling out alternative explanations.
explanations.C: C is a base-rate application to an individual — a different flaw family (statistical generalization to a case), not a causal claim.
explanations.D: D provides an intermediate causal mechanism (poor roads cause accidents; roads were repaired), making it a reasoned causal argument rather than a bare correlation-to-causation leap.
explanations.E: E commits a percentage/absolute-number confusion, a different flaw entirely.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus uses an ad hominem (attacking the source rather than the argument). Distractors include a valid credibility challenge and a circumstantial variant, making students distinguish between undermining an argument and dismissing a person.
lr.stimulus: The nutritionist who testified before the committee argued that the new dietary guidelines are scientifically unsound. But this nutritionist receives substantial funding from the processed food industry. Therefore, the dietary guidelines are not scientifically unsound.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The economist who claims that the tax cut will stimulate growth has been wrong about economic predictions before. Therefore, the tax cut probably will not stimulate growth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The engineer who evaluated the bridge argued that it is structurally sound. Since this engineer was paid by the company that built the bridge, we cannot be certain the bridge is structurally sound.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The historian who disputes the traditional account of the battle has written several well-regarded books. Therefore, the traditional account of the battle is probably incorrect.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The auditor who reported financial irregularities at the firm has a personal grievance against the firm's CEO. Therefore, there are no financial irregularities at the firm.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The chemist who argues that the compound is unstable works in a lab that has never published peer-reviewed research. Therefore, before accepting the claim, the committee should request independent verification.

explanations.correct: The stimulus dismisses the nutritionist's conclusion (guidelines are unsound) by attacking the nutritionist's funding source, then asserts the opposite conclusion as true. D mirrors this: the auditor's personal grievance is used to dismiss the finding and assert its opposite (no irregularities). Same ad hominem → affirm-opposite structure.
explanations.A: A attacks the economist's track record (past errors), not a personal interest. Also concludes 'probably will not' rather than definitively asserting the opposite — structurally different strength and type.
explanations.B: B is a valid epistemic caution: noting a potential conflict of interest to justify uncertainty ('cannot be certain'), not asserting the opposite conclusion. No flaw of the same kind.
explanations.C: C is an appeal to authority (positive), concluding the historian is correct because they wrote good books — a different flaw.
explanations.D: Correct. Personal motivation dismissed → opposite conclusion asserted. Same ad hominem structure as stimulus.
explanations.E: E recommends further verification rather than asserting a conclusion, and the basis is institutional credibility rather than personal bias. Different flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a composition fallacy (properties of parts attributed to the whole). Distractors include a division fallacy and a valid generalization, requiring students to track the direction of the part-whole inference.
lr.stimulus: Each module in the new software package has been individually tested and found to be highly efficient. Therefore, the complete software package is highly efficient.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The national orchestra is considered world-class. Yuki plays in the national orchestra. Therefore, Yuki is a world-class musician.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every player on the championship team is an exceptional athlete. Therefore, the championship team is composed of exceptional athletes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each ingredient in this recipe is low in calories. Therefore, the dish made from this recipe is low in calories.

choices.label: D
choices.text: This alloy is extremely strong. Therefore, each of the metals used to make this alloy is extremely strong.

choices.label: E
choices.text: All the studies conducted on this drug used small sample sizes. The drug has nevertheless been approved. Therefore, the approval process was flawed.

explanations.correct: The stimulus infers a property of the whole (efficient package) from properties of each part (efficient modules) — composition fallacy. C mirrors this: each ingredient is low-calorie (parts), therefore the dish is low-calorie (whole). The whole may exceed the sum of parts in caloric terms, just as integrated modules may interact inefficiently.
explanations.A: A is a division fallacy — inferring a property of a member from a property of the group. The direction is reversed from the stimulus.
explanations.B: B is actually valid: if every player is exceptional, then the team is composed of exceptional athletes. Tautological, not flawed.
explanations.C: Correct. Parts → whole composition fallacy, mirroring the stimulus.
explanations.D: D is a division fallacy — inferring properties of the components from a property of the whole. Reversed direction.
explanations.E: E is a different flaw: inferring process failure from methodological weakness in supporting studies. Not a part-whole inference.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus uses a false dichotomy. Distractors include a valid either/or elimination and a disjunction that is exhaustive, requiring students to identify whether the two options genuinely exhaust the possibilities.
lr.stimulus: Either the government must raise taxes or it must cut social services. The government has decided not to raise taxes. Therefore, the government must cut social services.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A patient must either have a bacterial infection or a viral infection to explain her symptoms. Tests have ruled out a bacterial infection. Therefore, she has a viral infection.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The company can succeed only if it either improves its product or reduces its prices. The company has decided not to reduce its prices. Therefore, the company must improve its product to succeed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Either the painting is authentic or it is a forgery. Experts have confirmed the painting is authentic. Therefore, it is not a forgery.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either the defendant was at the crime scene or the defendant is innocent. Witnesses place the defendant elsewhere. Therefore, the defendant is innocent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Either the new bridge design is structurally sound or it should not be built. The design has not been certified as structurally sound. Therefore, the bridge should not be built.

explanations.correct: The stimulus presents a false dichotomy — raise taxes or cut services — ignoring other options (borrowing, reducing waste, growing the economy, etc.). B mirrors this: improve product or reduce prices ignores other paths to success (marketing, new markets, etc.). The disjunction is presented as exhaustive when it is not, and the same elimination-of-one-option structure follows.
explanations.A: A is actually valid if the medical premise that only bacterial or viral infections explain these symptoms is accepted. The disjunction is stated as exhaustive. Not a false dichotomy.
explanations.B: Correct. The two options do not exhaust all routes to success; presenting them as exclusive and exhaustive is the same false dichotomy as the stimulus.
explanations.C: C is valid: authentic and forgery are genuinely mutually exclusive and exhaustive categories for a painting's status. Correct inference.
explanations.D: D involves a false dichotomy (being at the scene vs. innocence ignores other scenarios), but the reasoning form is valid modus tollens given the premise — the flaw lies in the premise's implicit gap, not in the same structural move as the stimulus.
explanations.E: E's disjunction is arguably exhaustive: a bridge design is either sound or it shouldn't be built. This reads as a valid conditional. Not a false dichotomy.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a base-rate reversal (most A's have property B; this thing has B; therefore it is probably an A). Two distractors use probabilistic language but reverse the direction or apply it validly, requiring careful tracking of quantifier direction.
lr.stimulus: Most successful entrepreneurs dropped out of college before completing their degrees. Marcus dropped out of college before completing his degree. Therefore, Marcus will probably be a successful entrepreneur.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most competitive marathon runners train more than 60 miles per week. Fatima trains more than 60 miles per week. Therefore, Fatima is probably a competitive marathon runner.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most people who live past age 90 have maintained a healthy diet throughout their lives. Therefore, maintaining a healthy diet probably increases longevity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most pediatricians recommend limiting screen time for children under two. Dr. Singh is a pediatrician. Therefore, Dr. Singh probably recommends limiting screen time for children under two.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most of the students who failed the exam had not attended the review session. Paulo did not attend the review session. Therefore, Paulo probably failed the exam.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Successful entrepreneurs tend to take calculated risks. Marcus has launched three businesses, each involving considerable financial risk. Therefore, Marcus exhibits the behavior typical of successful entrepreneurs.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: most successful entrepreneurs (A) dropped out (B); Marcus dropped out (B); therefore Marcus is probably a successful entrepreneur (A). The flaw reverses the base rate — having property B shared by most A's doesn't make B-havers likely to be A's. A mirrors this exactly: most competitive runners (A) train 60+ miles (B); Fatima trains 60+ miles (B); therefore Fatima is probably a competitive runner (A).
explanations.A: Correct. Identical base-rate reversal structure.
explanations.B: B infers a causal relationship from a correlation among centenarians — a different flaw (correlation to causation).
explanations.C: C is valid: if most pediatricians hold a view and Dr. Singh is a pediatrician, inferring she probably holds that view is a correct base-rate application (group → member), not a reversal.
explanations.D: D has the structure: most failures (A) skipped the session (B); Paulo skipped (B); therefore Paulo probably failed (A). This is the same base-rate reversal — but note A is 'failures,' making it structurally identical to the correct answer A. However, the base rate stated is 'most who failed had not attended' which maps directly; A is the cleaner, more parallel match with a non-trivially large reference class.
explanations.E: E draws an observational conclusion (Marcus exhibits typical behavior) without concluding he is a successful entrepreneur. The conclusion type differs from the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus generalizes from a sample that is explicitly unrepresentative (selection bias). Distractors include a valid inductive generalization and a hasty generalization without selection bias, requiring students to spot the specific bias in sampling.
lr.stimulus: A survey of visitors to the city's art museum found that 85 percent consider the arts to be an important priority for public funding. Clearly, the vast majority of the city's residents support increased public funding for the arts.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A poll of randomly selected registered voters found that 60 percent favor stricter environmental regulations. Therefore, a majority of registered voters probably favor such regulations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A questionnaire distributed at a gun show found that 90 percent of respondents oppose new firearm restrictions. Therefore, most citizens oppose new firearm restrictions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A study surveyed 50 people in a major city and found that 70 percent preferred public transit to driving. Therefore, about 70 percent of all urban residents prefer public transit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Exit polls at three rural precincts showed strong support for the incumbent. Therefore, the incumbent will probably win the statewide election.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A telephone survey reached 1,000 randomly chosen households nationwide and found that 55 percent support the proposed healthcare bill. Therefore, a slight majority of households probably support the bill.

explanations.correct: The stimulus surveys art museum visitors — a group self-selected for interest in the arts — and projects their views onto all city residents. This is a selection-bias generalization. B mirrors this: surveying gun show attendees — a group self-selected for strong views on firearms — and projecting their views onto all citizens. Same biased-sample structure.
explanations.A: A uses a randomly selected sample of registered voters and projects to registered voters — the population matches the sample. Valid inference, no selection bias.
explanations.B: Correct. Self-selected, non-representative sample projected onto a broader population.
explanations.C: C involves a small sample and projects to all urban residents — a hasty generalization issue, but the flaw is sample size, not selection bias. The sample is not systematically skewed in the way the stimulus's is.
explanations.D: D is a selection-bias generalization (rural precincts → statewide), and the sample is non-representative. This is a plausible trap, but the flaw is geographic unrepresentativeness (subset of locations) rather than self-selection by interest/attitude, which is the precise mechanism in the stimulus.
explanations.E: E uses a large, randomly selected nationwide sample — the gold standard of polling. Valid inference.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a circular reasoning (begging the question) flaw. Distractors include a near-circular argument that provides a separate supporting premise and a valid argument with a strong conclusion, requiring careful parsing of whether the premise independently supports the conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Freedom of speech is a fundamental right because every person has a basic entitlement to express themselves freely. After all, free expression is simply what freedom of speech means.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Honesty is virtuous because people who are honest act in accordance with virtue. Acting in accordance with virtue is precisely what it means to be virtuous, and honesty requires telling the truth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The death penalty is unjust because it deprives a person of life without adequate justification, and any punishment that does so is a violation of human rights.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Democracy is the best form of government because it gives power to the people, and giving power to the people produces better outcomes than concentrating it in a few individuals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: This investment is risky because risky investments are those that may not return principal, and this investment may not return principal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Exercise is beneficial because physical activity has been demonstrated to improve cardiovascular health and reduce the risk of chronic disease.

explanations.correct: The stimulus defines freedom of speech as free expression, then claims free expression is the reason freedom of speech is fundamental — the conclusion is smuggled into the premise by definition. D mirrors this: 'this investment is risky' (conclusion) is supported by 'risky investments may not return principal, and this investment may not return principal' — the definition of risk is used as the reason the investment is risky. The conclusion is contained in the premise through definitional substitution.
explanations.A: A contains a near-circular element but also adds an independent factual claim ('honesty requires telling the truth'), giving it some non-circular content. Not as purely circular as the stimulus.
explanations.B: B offers an independent evaluative premise (deprivation of life without justification violates human rights) that does not merely restate the conclusion. Valid argument structure.
explanations.C: C provides a causal premise (giving power to people produces better outcomes) that independently supports the conclusion. Not circular.
explanations.D: Correct. The definition of 'risky' is used as the sole reason the investment is risky — the conclusion is embedded in the premise by definition. Same circular structure.
explanations.E: E is a valid argument supported by empirical evidence. No circularity.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a division fallacy (attributing a property of the whole to each of its parts). Distractors include a composition fallacy (the reverse direction) and a valid statistical inference, requiring students to track the direction of the part-whole inference.
lr.stimulus: The Millbrook Symphony Orchestra is one of the most celebrated orchestras in the country. Therefore, each musician in the Millbrook Symphony Orchestra must be one of the most celebrated musicians in the country.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each chapter of this novel is beautifully written. Therefore, the novel as a whole is beautifully written.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Thornfield University is one of the most prestigious universities in the world. Therefore, every professor at Thornfield University must be among the most prestigious academics in the world.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every member of the city council voted in favor of the new zoning law. Therefore, the city council as a body supports the new zoning law.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The national cycling team has won more Tour de France titles than any other team. Most members of the national cycling team are from the same region. Therefore, that region produces the best cyclists.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most top-ranked law firms have at least one partner who clerked for a Supreme Court justice. Hartley & Brown is a top-ranked law firm. Therefore, at least one partner at Hartley & Brown probably clerked for a Supreme Court justice.

explanations.correct: The stimulus attributes prestige of the whole (the orchestra) to each of its parts (individual musicians) — a division fallacy. B mirrors this exactly: prestige of the whole (Thornfield University) is attributed to each of its parts (individual professors).
explanations.A: A is a composition fallacy — inferring a property of the whole (novel) from properties of its parts (chapters). The direction is the reverse of the stimulus.
explanations.B: Correct. Property of the whole attributed to each part — same division fallacy.
explanations.C: C is actually valid: if every member voted for something, the body as a whole supports it. This is a valid composition inference, not a flaw.
explanations.D: D is a hasty causal generalization, not a part-whole inference. Different flaw.
explanations.E: E is a valid base-rate inference applied to a specific firm. No flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus confuses a sufficient condition for a necessary one (affirming the consequent in conditional form). Distractors include a valid modus ponens and a necessary/sufficient confusion in the other direction, requiring careful attention to conditional structure.
lr.stimulus: If a river ecosystem is healthy, then it will support diverse fish populations. The Alderton River supports diverse fish populations. Therefore, the Alderton River ecosystem is healthy.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a company is well-managed, it will show consistent profits. Verdant Technologies has shown consistent profits for five consecutive years. Therefore, Verdant Technologies is well-managed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If the soil is fertile, crops will grow abundantly. The crops on this farm are growing abundantly. Therefore, the soil here is fertile.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a patient has been vaccinated against measles, the patient will test negative for measles antibodies of the active infection type. This patient tests negative for such antibodies. Therefore, this patient has been vaccinated against measles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a language is classified as endangered, then fewer than 1,000 native speakers remain. Linguists have classified Tharric as endangered. Therefore, fewer than 1,000 native speakers of Tharric remain.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If an athlete trains at altitude for at least six weeks, her red blood cell count will increase. Mira's red blood cell count has increased. Therefore, Mira probably trained at altitude for at least six weeks.

explanations.correct: The stimulus has the form: If healthy → diverse fish; diverse fish present; therefore healthy. This is affirming the consequent — a sufficient condition (healthy ecosystem) is treated as necessary because its consequent (diverse fish) is observed. A mirrors this: If well-managed → consistent profits; consistent profits observed; therefore well-managed. Same affirming-the-consequent structure.
explanations.A: Correct. If P then Q; Q; therefore P — affirming the consequent, identical to the stimulus.
explanations.B: B has the same logical form (If fertile → abundant crops; crops abundant; therefore fertile) as A and the stimulus. However, A is the cleaner parallel because B's conclusion (soil is fertile) and the mechanism involved make it a near-duplicate; A uses a distinct domain (corporate management) and is the intended best answer.
explanations.C: C also has the affirming-the-consequent form and is a strong parallel. However, the conditional in C is more complex (vaccination → test negative for specific antibodies), and the conclusion is absolute rather than hedged. A remains the closest structural match to the stimulus.
explanations.D: D is a valid modus ponens: If endangered → fewer than 1,000 speakers; Tharric is endangered; therefore fewer than 1,000 speakers. Valid inference, no flaw.
explanations.E: E adds the hedge 'probably,' softening the conclusion, and the conditional in E describes a sufficient (not necessary) antecedent more ambiguously. Less precise match than A.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is necessary/sufficient confusion — taking a sufficient condition as necessary. Two answer choices replicate a conditional-logic error with surface plausibility; students must track the exact direction of the reversal to distinguish the correct match from the near-miss.
lr.stimulus: To receive a research grant from the Halcyon Foundation, an applicant must hold an advanced degree. Dr. Renata Voss holds an advanced degree. Therefore, Dr. Voss will receive a research grant from the Halcyon Foundation.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In order to be certified as an organic farm, a farm must pass a soil-quality inspection. The Whitmore farm failed its soil-quality inspection. Therefore, the Whitmore farm will not be certified as an organic farm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only employees who have completed the safety training are permitted to operate the heavy machinery. Fortunately, Delia has completed the safety training. Therefore, Delia is permitted to operate the heavy machinery.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every student who passes the qualifying exam is eligible for the scholarship. Marcus passed the qualifying exam. Therefore, Marcus will receive the scholarship.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All medications approved by the regulatory board have undergone clinical trials. This medication has undergone clinical trials. Therefore, it has been approved by the regulatory board.

choices.label: E
choices.text: To join the honors society, a student must maintain a grade point average above 3.5. Priya's grade point average has fallen below 3.5. Therefore, Priya will be removed from the honors society.

explanations.correct: The stimulus treats a necessary condition (holding an advanced degree) as if it were sufficient for receiving a grant. D replicates the same flaw: 'approved → undergone trials' (holding a necessary condition), then argues backward: 'undergone trials → approved.' The same necessary/sufficient confusion is committed at matching strength.
explanations.A: This is valid reasoning. If passing the inspection is necessary for certification, then failing it correctly entails non-certification (modus tollens). No flaw.
explanations.B: The phrase 'only employees who have completed safety training are permitted' establishes that training is necessary for permission. Concluding that Delia is permitted because she completed training treats a necessary condition as sufficient — close, but the conclusion is 'permitted,' which is the same direction as the stimulus. However, 'Only X are permitted' means 'permitted → completed training,' so 'completed training → permitted' is a sufficient/necessary reversal. This mirrors the stimulus's flaw. However, compared to D, this choice uses 'only' language, which can be parsed as making training sufficient in context. The cleaner parallel is D because its conditional direction is unambiguous: 'approved → trials,' and the argument reverses to 'trials → approved.'
explanations.C: This is a valid inference. 'Every student who passes is eligible' means passing is sufficient for eligibility. Concluding eligibility from passing is correct. But then inferring receipt of the scholarship from mere eligibility introduces a new unsupported leap rather than a conditional reversal — a different flaw (gap between eligibility and receipt).
explanations.E: This is valid reasoning by modus tollens: maintaining above 3.5 is necessary to join; falling below 3.5 entails removal. No logical flaw is committed.
explanations.D: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is correlation/causation — inferring that because two things co-occurred, one caused the other. Two answer choices involve causal language with surface plausibility, requiring students to identify which one commits the same unwarranted causal inference from mere correlation rather than a different error.
lr.stimulus: In the decade after the city of Millbrook installed a network of bicycle lanes, traffic fatalities in the city decreased by 30 percent. The bicycle lanes must therefore have caused the reduction in traffic fatalities.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ever since the national government imposed stricter emissions standards, air quality in the country's major cities has improved. Stricter emissions standards must therefore be responsible for the improved air quality.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Studies show that people who eat breakfast regularly tend to have lower rates of obesity. Therefore, eating breakfast regularly prevents obesity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Alderton pharmaceutical company increased its marketing budget last year, and its sales increased as well. Because no other changes were made to the company's operations, the marketing increase must have caused the sales growth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: As the global average temperature has risen over the past century, the rate of species extinction has also increased. Clearly, rising temperatures are not the only factor contributing to the increase in extinction rates.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The rate of smartphone adoption in Veldrin County increased significantly between 2010 and 2020. During that same period, the county's literacy rate also increased. Therefore, increased smartphone adoption was a consequence of the rising literacy rate.

explanations.correct: The stimulus notes that bicycle lanes were installed and fatalities later fell, then concludes the lanes caused the reduction — inferring causation from temporal co-occurrence alone, with no consideration of alternative explanations. A replicates this exactly: emissions standards were imposed, air quality improved, therefore the standards caused the improvement. Same structure: two correlated events, same unwarranted causal conclusion, same failure to consider confounds.
explanations.B: This also involves a correlation-to-causation error, but it additionally ignores the possibility of reverse causation (people who are not obese may find it easier to eat breakfast) and confounds (healthier lifestyle in general). More importantly, B draws on a statistical study rather than a temporal sequence of policy and outcome — a slightly different structure. Close, but A more precisely mirrors the stimulus's specific move of a single timed intervention followed by a measured change.
explanations.C: This argument explicitly rules out alternative explanations ('no other changes were made'), which actually strengthens the causal inference and makes it less flawed — or at least differently structured. The stimulus makes no such elimination of alternatives.
explanations.D: This argument actually resists overclaiming causation, concluding that temperature is not the only factor. It does not commit a correlation-causation flaw; it is closer to a valid hedged inference.
explanations.E: This commits a correlation-causation error but reverses the expected causal direction (literacy → smartphones rather than smartphones → literacy), introducing a reverse-causation twist that is a distinct, additional error not present in the stimulus.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is an ad hominem (circumstantial) — dismissing an argument by attacking the arguer's self-interest rather than addressing the reasoning. Two answer choices involve credibility challenges, requiring students to distinguish a circumstantial ad hominem from an abusive ad hominem or a legitimate bias objection.
lr.stimulus: Professor Langholm's study concludes that universities should increase funding for humanities departments. But Professor Langholm teaches in a humanities department, so she would personally benefit from such an increase. Her conclusion is therefore unwarranted.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The lead researcher on the new climate model argues that governments must dramatically cut carbon emissions. However, the researcher has never worked in industry and therefore lacks practical expertise. We should not accept his recommendations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The president of the pharmaceutical company testified before Congress that the proposed drug pricing regulations would harm innovation. Since the company would lose revenue under those regulations, his testimony should be dismissed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Senator Avora claims that the proposed tax cut will stimulate economic growth. But Senator Avora has been wrong about economic forecasts before. Her claim should therefore be treated with skepticism.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The building contractor recommended that the city hire his firm to repair the damaged bridge. Of course he would say that — recommending his own firm is simply what any contractor in his position would do. His recommendation should be disregarded.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dr. Fontaine argues that patients should not be allowed to refuse certain life-saving treatments. Dr. Fontaine, however, holds an unusual view within the medical community. Most physicians disagree with her position, so her argument should be rejected.

explanations.correct: The stimulus dismisses Professor Langholm's conclusion solely because she stands to benefit personally from it — a circumstantial ad hominem. B replicates this exactly: the pharmaceutical executive's testimony is dismissed not because his reasoning is refuted but because his company would lose revenue under the policy he opposes. Same structure: arguer has financial self-interest → conclusion dismissed without engaging the argument.
explanations.A: This attacks the arguer's qualifications (lack of practical experience) rather than his self-interest. This is an abusive or appeals-to-authority ad hominem, a different species of the ad hominem family. The flaw type does not match the stimulus's circumstantial variety.
explanations.C: This dismisses the senator's claim based on her past track record of error — an appeal to prior unreliability, which is a different flaw (though sometimes reasonable). Crucially, there is no self-interest motive invoked; the challenge is to her competence, not her bias.
explanations.D: This is a close trap. The contractor does have self-interest, but the argument explicitly notes that recommending one's own firm is simply what any contractor would do — making the dismissal sound almost logical. More importantly, the argument's rhetorical move is slightly different: it naturalizes the behavior ('of course he would') rather than straightforwardly inferring that self-interest invalidates the recommendation. Compared to B, which cleanly parallels the stimulus, D introduces a 'you'd expect anyone to do this' move that is not in the stimulus.
explanations.E: This dismisses Dr. Fontaine's argument by appeal to majority opinion within her field — an appeal to authority (or appeal to consensus), not an ad hominem based on self-interest. Different flaw category entirely.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a clear necessary/sufficient confusion (treating a sufficient condition as necessary). Two answer choices are designed to share surface plausibility by involving conditionals; the student must track which one reverses the same conditional direction.
lr.stimulus: Dr. Reyes noted that every patient who receives the new antiviral drug Velozine recovers from the infection within three days. Marcus recovered from his infection within three days. Therefore, Marcus must have received Velozine.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every employee who passes the certification exam is eligible for promotion. Daniela is eligible for promotion. Therefore, Daniela must have passed the certification exam.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every employee who passes the certification exam is eligible for promotion. Tomás passed the certification exam. Therefore, Tomás is eligible for promotion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No employee who fails the certification exam is eligible for promotion. Yuki failed the exam. Therefore, Yuki is not eligible for promotion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some employees who are eligible for promotion have not yet passed the certification exam. Renata is eligible for promotion. Therefore, Renata has probably not passed the certification exam.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most employees who pass the certification exam receive a salary increase within a year. Jerome received a salary increase within a year. Therefore, Jerome probably passed the certification exam.

explanations.correct: The stimulus treats a sufficient condition (receiving Velozine → recovery) as if it were also necessary (recovery → received Velozine). This is affirming the consequent: if P then Q; Q; therefore P. Choice A commits the identical flaw — passing the exam is sufficient for eligibility, but the argument concludes from eligibility alone that the exam was passed.
explanations.A: Correct. Mirrors the stimulus exactly: the sufficient condition (passing exam → eligible) is treated as necessary (eligible → must have passed). This is affirming the consequent.
explanations.B: This is a valid modus ponens inference: if P then Q; P; therefore Q. No flaw.
explanations.C: This is a valid modus ponens with a negative conditional: no P→Q; Yuki is P; therefore Yuki is not Q. No flaw.
explanations.D: This introduces the quantifier 'some' and draws a probabilistic conclusion in the wrong direction, which resembles a base-rate reversal rather than a necessary/sufficient confusion. Different flaw.
explanations.E: This involves 'most' rather than 'every,' making it a base-rate reversal (Carpaccio-type flaw) rather than affirming the consequent. The stimulus uses a universal conditional, not a probabilistic claim.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a part-to-whole (compositional) fallacy — inferring that a property of each part must belong to the whole. Two answer choices involve similar subject matter and quantifier language, requiring the student to distinguish the compositional fallacy from a valid generalization and from a different quantifier error.
lr.stimulus: Each individual chapter of Professor Aldana's new economics textbook is concise and easy to read. Therefore, the textbook as a whole must be concise and easy to read.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each tile in the mosaic is small and lightweight. Therefore, the mosaic as a whole is small and lightweight.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each tile in the mosaic was crafted by a skilled artisan. Therefore, the mosaic as a whole was crafted by skilled artisans.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mosaic contains hundreds of tiles. Most of the tiles are blue. Therefore, the mosaic is predominantly blue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each ingredient in the dish is healthful when eaten alone. However, some combinations of healthful ingredients can produce harmful chemical reactions. Therefore, this dish may not be healthful.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every individual musician in the orchestra performed flawlessly. Therefore, the audience gave the orchestra a standing ovation.

explanations.correct: The stimulus assumes that a property true of each part (concise, easy to read) must be true of the whole — the classic compositional fallacy. Choice A replicates this exactly: each tile is small and lightweight, but the whole mosaic need not be small or lightweight. The predicate 'small' is paradigmatically non-compositional.
explanations.A: Correct. Attributes 'small' and 'lightweight' to each tile and then illegitimately attributes the same properties to the whole mosaic — same compositional fallacy as the stimulus.
explanations.B: This is actually a valid inference for 'crafted by skilled artisans' — if each part was crafted by skilled artisans, the whole was crafted by skilled artisans. This is a distributive property that does transfer to the whole. No flaw.
explanations.C: This is a valid probabilistic inference from a majority of parts. No compositional fallacy — the conclusion ('predominantly blue') is appropriately hedged and follows from 'most tiles are blue.'
explanations.D: This explicitly acknowledges the non-compositional nature of the whole, making it an argument against the compositional fallacy. It does not commit the error; it warns against it.
explanations.E: This is a different flaw — it conflates the quality of individual performances with the audience's reaction, which involves an unwarranted causal leap rather than a part-to-whole attribution of properties.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a correlation-to-causation flaw in a policy context. Answer choices include one that reverses the causal direction (a related but distinct flaw) and one that is a valid inference, requiring students to identify the specific causal overreach rather than merely any causal misstep.
lr.stimulus: Ever since the city of Hartwell introduced its community policing program two years ago, rates of reported property crime have dropped significantly. Clearly, the community policing program is responsible for the reduction in property crime.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Since the Morrow Valley school district began requiring students to wear uniforms three years ago, student test scores have risen steadily. The uniform policy must be the reason test scores have improved.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Economists have found that cities with higher average incomes tend to have lower crime rates. Therefore, high incomes must prevent residents from committing crimes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The number of specialty coffee shops in Hartwell has grown in every year that the community policing program has been in place. Therefore, the coffee shops are causing crime rates to fall.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hartwell's property crime rate is now lower than it was two years ago. The police chief was appointed two years ago. Therefore, the police chief must have been appointed because crime rates were falling.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hartwell's community policing program has been in place for two years and remains well-funded. Programs that remain well-funded for two or more years are generally considered successful. Therefore, the program is probably considered successful.

explanations.correct: The stimulus observes a temporal correlation (program introduced, then crime fell) and concludes the program caused the drop, ignoring alternative explanations. Choice A replicates this exactly: a policy was introduced, a positive outcome followed, and the policy is credited as the cause — the same post hoc, correlation-to-causation flaw.
explanations.A: Correct. Mirrors the stimulus: a new policy (uniforms) preceded an improvement (test scores), and the policy is concluded to be the cause — identical correlation-to-causation overreach with no consideration of confounding factors.
explanations.B: This commits a different causal flaw — it interprets a cross-sectional correlation (high income and low crime co-occur) as evidence that one prevents the other. Unlike the stimulus, which uses temporal sequence, this conflates correlation with causation in a non-temporal, cross-sectional way. Also, 'prevent' introduces a stronger causal claim than the stimulus's structure warrants.
explanations.C: This is a different flaw — it attributes causation to a factor (coffee shops) that is clearly a parallel trend, not even the policy being evaluated. The implausibility of the causal agent distinguishes this from the stimulus, which at least involves a plausible candidate.
explanations.D: This reverses the causal direction: it concludes the appointment was caused by the crime trend, whereas the stimulus concludes the policy caused the crime trend. This is reverse causation, a distinct flaw.
explanations.E: This is a valid deductive inference: the program meets the stated criteria for being considered successful. No causal claim and no flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is a classic necessary/sufficient confusion — the stimulus treats a sufficient condition as if it were necessary. Two answer choices mirror the surface topic or structure superficially, requiring the student to track the exact conditional direction.
lr.stimulus: Dr. Huang has noted that patients who recover quickly from knee surgery always follow the prescribed physical therapy regimen. Marcus followed the prescribed physical therapy regimen after his knee surgery. Therefore, Marcus will probably recover quickly.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All prize-winning roses are fertilized with a specific compound. The roses in the Bellview Garden have been fertilized with that compound. Therefore, the roses in the Bellview Garden will probably win a prize.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most students who graduate with honors studied at least three hours per day. Yolanda studied at least three hours per day. Therefore, Yolanda probably graduated with honors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whenever a medication causes drowsiness, it carries a warning label. This medication carries a warning label. Therefore, this medication probably causes drowsiness.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Employees who are promoted within one year of being hired are always assigned a mentor during their first month. Priya was assigned a mentor during her first month. Therefore, Priya will probably be promoted within one year.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Engineers who design award-winning bridges always have advanced degrees. Since Kenji has an advanced degree, he will probably design an award-winning bridge.

explanations.correct: The stimulus states that quick recovery always accompanies following therapy (quick recovery → therapy), then notes Marcus did follow therapy, and concludes he will recover quickly — affirming the consequent. Choice A mirrors this exactly: prize-winning → fertilized with compound; the roses were fertilized; therefore they will win a prize. The same necessary/sufficient swap (affirming the consequent) is committed at the same probability strength.
explanations.A: Correct. Prize-winning roses are always fertilized with the compound (prize → fertilized), but the argument treats the fertilizer as sufficient for winning, which it is not. This is the same affirming-the-consequent flaw as the stimulus.
explanations.B: Close trap — uses 'most' rather than 'always/all,' making this a base-rate reversal flaw rather than a strict affirming-the-consequent. The quantifier difference changes the flaw category.
explanations.C: This reverses a sufficient condition ('causes drowsiness → warning label') and concludes back to the antecedent — structurally the same direction, but the conclusion adds a label that merely 'carries a warning' without the 'probably' qualifier on the same term, and the setup uses 'whenever' symmetrically. More importantly, the argument is affirming the consequent, which matches — but the probability language is absent, making the flaw slightly stronger than the stimulus's. Tempting, but A matches both structure and probability strength more precisely.
explanations.D: Different direction: promotion → mentor assigned (not mentor → promotion). The argument then says Priya was assigned a mentor and concludes she'll be promoted — this is also affirming the consequent, but the conditional stated is 'promoted → mentor,' so the consequent is 'mentor assigned,' which is what we observe. This is structurally parallel but the conclusion drawn ('will probably be promoted') is identical in structure to A. However, the stimulus's conditional is stated as 'always follows therapy → recovers quickly' — the universal claim is about quick recoverers always following therapy (quick recovery → therapy), not the reverse. D's conditional runs promoted → mentor, then observes mentor, concluding promoted — this is affirming the consequent just as in A. Both A and D are close; however, A uses 'all' matching the stimulus's 'always,' while D's conclusion drops to a future event without the same base universal, making A the cleaner parallel.
explanations.E: Same flaw family (affirming the consequent: award-winning → advanced degree; has degree → will win award), but the conclusion 'will probably design an award-winning bridge' introduces a future-achievement framing absent in the stimulus. More critically, E's universal is about a specific professional outcome linked to credentials, making it a plausible but slightly off match compared to A's tighter replication of the all-X-have-Y-therefore-Y-implies-X structure.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a correlation-to-causation flaw. The answer choices include one valid causal argument supported by mechanism, one that mistakes cause and effect, one that is a different flaw (hasty generalization), and one that precisely replicates the correlation-causation error. Students must distinguish these at moderate speed.
lr.stimulus: In cities where bicycle lane networks were expanded, average commute times decreased over the following two years. Clearly, expanding bicycle lane networks causes commute times to decrease.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In school districts that introduced daily reading programs, standardized test scores improved over the next three years. It follows that daily reading programs cause standardized test scores to improve.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hospitals that perform more surgeries per year tend to have lower patient mortality rates for those surgeries. Therefore, performing more surgeries must improve a surgical team's technique, which reduces mortality.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every time unemployment rates fell in the Westbrook region, consumer spending rose. Hence, low unemployment is always followed by high consumer spending in that region.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the three neighborhoods where new community gardens were established, reported incidents of vandalism declined. Therefore, establishing community gardens causes vandalism to decline.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Researchers observed that children who eat breakfast regularly perform better in school. Since breakfast consumption and academic performance are correlated, neither one causes the other.

explanations.correct: The stimulus observes a correlation between two variables across multiple locations and concludes a causal relationship without ruling out confounding factors, reverse causation, or coincidence. Choice D mirrors this exactly: a correlation between a new feature in neighborhoods (community gardens) and a subsequent decline in another variable (vandalism) is treated as proof of direct causation.
explanations.A: Close trap — same surface structure (program introduced; scores improved; therefore the program caused improvement). However, reading programs have a plausible, direct instructional mechanism, making the causal inference significantly more defensible. This is not a valid argument — confounders still exist — but the flaw is less egregious than in D, where the causal connection between gardens and vandalism is more remote. More importantly, A is constructed to feel parallel, but on the LSAT the 'most similar' match is D, which involves a more counterintuitive and clearly unjustified causal leap of the same formal type.
explanations.B: Different flaw — the argument here provides a causal mechanism ('improves technique') to explain the correlation rather than simply asserting causation from correlation. The structure differs: the premise is a correlation, but the argument adds an explanatory step. This is a different — and partially legitimate — reasoning pattern.
explanations.C: This argument does not commit the correlation-causation flaw. It merely redescribes the observed pattern ('every time X, Y') as a general regularity ('X is always followed by Y') — a different error (treating a temporal sequence as a universal law) or arguably a valid descriptive generalization. It does not assert that X causes Y.
explanations.D: Correct. Three neighborhoods observed; a subsequent change noted; direct causation concluded. No mechanism, no confounders addressed — a precise structural and logical match to the stimulus.
explanations.E: This argument moves in the opposite direction: it acknowledges a correlation and then denies causation altogether, concluding neither variable causes the other. This is a different flaw (or possibly a valid cautionary move), not the same error as asserting causation from correlation.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a hasty generalization — drawing a universal conclusion from a small and potentially unrepresentative sample. Answer choices include one valid inductive argument with a large representative sample, one that confuses correlation with causation, one that commits a false dichotomy, and one that precisely replicates the hasty generalization.
lr.stimulus: The three tech entrepreneurs I interviewed for my economics thesis all reported that they dropped out of college before founding their companies. It is therefore safe to conclude that most successful tech entrepreneurs drop out of college.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A survey of 10,000 randomly selected voters across all fifty states found that 54 percent favor the proposed tax reform. We can therefore conclude that a majority of voters in the country probably favor the tax reform.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Either a language acquires new loanwords through trade contact, or its vocabulary remains static. Since Mandarin has acquired many loanwords, it must have undergone extensive trade contact.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The four law review articles I read this semester all argued against expanding judicial review. It is therefore safe to conclude that most legal scholars oppose expanding judicial review.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In countries where literacy rates rose sharply, economic growth followed within a decade. Therefore, increasing literacy rates must cause economic growth.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every language I have studied has irregular verbs, so there are probably some irregular verbs in every human language.

explanations.correct: The stimulus draws a sweeping universal conclusion about 'most' successful tech entrepreneurs based on a sample of three self-selected interviewees — a classic hasty generalization from a small, likely biased sample. Choice C replicates this exactly: from four law review articles (a tiny, non-representative sample), the arguer concludes that 'most legal scholars' hold a particular view. Same flaw, same structure, same probability language ('most'), same non-representative sampling problem.
explanations.A: This is a valid inductive inference. A large, randomly selected sample of 10,000 voters across all states is methodologically sound; concluding a majority probably favor the reform is a legitimate probabilistic generalization. This is a 'valid analog' trap — it superficially resembles the stimulus's move (sample → general conclusion) but commits no flaw.
explanations.B: This commits a false dichotomy — the premise presents only two options for how a language acquires loanwords, then eliminates one to assert the other. This is a different flaw category entirely, unrelated to sampling or generalization.
explanations.C: Correct. Four articles, unrepresentative sample, sweeping conclusion about 'most' scholars — hasty generalization matching the stimulus's flaw precisely.
explanations.D: This is a correlation-to-causation flaw: observing that literacy rises preceded economic growth and concluding causation. Different flaw family from hasty generalization.
explanations.E: Tempting trap — also a generalization from a personal sample ('languages I have studied') to a universal conclusion ('every human language'). However, the conclusion is 'probably some irregular verbs in every language,' which is structurally an overgeneralization. The key difference is that E's conclusion uses 'every' (a universal quantifier) rather than 'most' (a majority quantifier), and the sample in E could plausibly be a diverse linguistic cross-section, making the flaw slightly different in character. C more precisely mirrors the stimulus: small named sample → 'most' members of a professional class hold a view.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is a classic necessary/sufficient confusion — a condition stated as necessary is treated as sufficient in the conclusion. Two answer choices have surface plausibility by sharing quantifier language, requiring the student to track the exact conditional reversal.
lr.stimulus: Only researchers who have received institutional ethics board approval may conduct studies involving human subjects. Dr. Vasquez has received institutional ethics board approval. Therefore, Dr. Vasquez may conduct studies involving human subjects.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only licensed electricians are permitted to install residential wiring in this city. Marchetti is a licensed electrician. Therefore, Marchetti is permitted to install residential wiring in this city.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only registered voters are eligible to serve on a jury. Fontaine is eligible to serve on a jury. Therefore, Fontaine is a registered voter.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only applicants with a graduate degree are considered for senior analyst positions. Huang has a graduate degree. Therefore, Huang will be hired as a senior analyst.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only board-certified surgeons are allowed to perform this procedure. Dr. Okonkwo performed this procedure. Therefore, Dr. Okonkwo is a board-certified surgeon.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only students who pass the qualifying exam advance to the dissertation stage. Reyes did not pass the qualifying exam. Therefore, Reyes will not advance to the dissertation stage.

explanations.correct: The stimulus treats ethics board approval as sufficient for being permitted to conduct human-subjects research, when the 'only' statement establishes it as merely necessary. C replicates this exactly: having a graduate degree is only a necessary condition for being considered, but the conclusion treats it as sufficient to guarantee being hired.
explanations.A: This is actually a valid inference. 'Only licensed electricians are permitted' means being licensed is necessary and (in this localized claim) the 'only' licenses permission, so having the license does permit the activity. No flaw is committed.
