explanations.B: This commits the valid contrapositive reasoning: if only registered voters are eligible, then being eligible entails being registered. This is valid, not flawed — the direction of inference runs correctly from effect back to necessary condition.
explanations.C: Correct. Mirrors the stimulus precisely: 'only X are considered for Y' makes X a necessary condition for consideration, not a sufficient condition for being hired. Yet the conclusion treats having a degree as guaranteeing the job.
explanations.D: This is valid modus ponens on the contrapositive: performing the procedure entails being board-certified (since only board-certified surgeons may perform it). The inference runs in the correct direction with no flaw.
explanations.E: This is a valid inference by modus tollens: if passing is necessary to advance, then not passing entails not advancing. No flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a correlation-to-causation flaw with a specific directional causal claim. Two trap answers also involve correlations but either reverse the causal direction or commit a different error, requiring students to match both the flaw type and its causal direction.
lr.stimulus: A study of urban neighborhoods found that areas with more coffee shops also tend to have higher property values. Clearly, opening more coffee shops in a neighborhood causes property values to rise.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Research shows that patients who take vitamin D supplements tend to have fewer depressive episodes. It must be that having fewer depressive episodes leads patients to take more vitamin D supplements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Studies show that hospitals with more nurses per patient tend to have lower patient mortality rates. Therefore, the most effective way to reduce mortality is to eliminate unnecessary procedures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Data show that students who eat breakfast regularly tend to earn higher grades. Therefore, eating breakfast regularly causes students to earn higher grades.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In regions where cycling is popular, residents tend to live longer. Clearly, the longer lifespan in these regions is due to the region's favorable geography, not cycling.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Companies that invest heavily in employee training consistently show higher profits. It follows that all companies that want higher profits should invest heavily in employee training, since this is the only proven path to profitability.

explanations.correct: The stimulus observes a correlation (more coffee shops, higher property values) and concludes that one factor directly causes the other, in that specific direction. C does exactly the same: correlation between breakfast-eating and grades is taken as proof that breakfast-eating causes higher grades, ignoring alternative explanations such as reverse causation or a third variable.
explanations.A: This commits a causal reversal — it acknowledges the same correlation but then flips the causal arrow from supplement→fewer episodes to fewer episodes→supplements. The flaw is reversed causal direction, not simple correlation-to-causation.
explanations.B: The conclusion introduces a completely unrelated remedy (eliminating procedures) that was never mentioned in the premise. This is a non sequitur or irrelevant conclusion, not a correlation-to-causation flaw.
explanations.C: Correct. Matches the stimulus flaw precisely: a correlation is presented, and a specific unidirectional causal claim is drawn without ruling out reverse causation or confounding variables.
explanations.D: This commits a different flaw: it acknowledges the correlation but then attributes the outcome to a third factor (geography) while dismissing the correlated variable. This is a competing-explanation move, not the same as inferring causation directly from correlation.
explanations.E: This goes further than mere correlation-to-causation by also adding an exclusivity claim ('the only proven path'). The flaw is compounded — it includes an unsupported 'only' assertion — making it a different, stronger error than the stimulus commits.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a part-to-whole (composition) fallacy — inferring that because every part of X has property P, X as a whole must have property P. Two answer choices involve similar compositional language but commit either the whole-to-part (division) error or a valid generalization, requiring students to carefully track the direction of inference.
lr.stimulus: Each component of the new transit proposal — the expanded bus routes, the light-rail extension, and the revised fare structure — has been individually endorsed by city planners as cost-effective. Therefore, the transit proposal as a whole is cost-effective.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every chapter of Serrano's novel has been praised by reviewers as gripping and well-paced. Therefore, Serrano's novel as a whole is likely to be gripping and well-paced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The investment portfolio as a whole has yielded strong returns this quarter. Therefore, each individual asset in the portfolio must have yielded strong returns this quarter.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several of the ingredients in this dish are, on their own, quite bitter. Therefore, at least some bitterness can be detected in the dish as a whole.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most economists agree that reducing trade barriers promotes growth. Since the proposed treaty reduces trade barriers, it will likely promote growth.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every brick in this wall is lightweight. Therefore, the wall itself is lightweight.

explanations.correct: The stimulus infers that because each part has property P (cost-effective), the whole must have property P. This is the composition fallacy. E replicates this exactly: each individual brick is lightweight, therefore the entire wall (composed of many bricks) is lightweight — a clear composition fallacy, since aggregate weight can differ fundamentally from individual component weight.
explanations.A: This is a superficially tempting answer because it moves from parts (chapters) to whole (novel). However, properties like 'gripping' and 'well-paced' are plausibly preserved across the whole when every part has them — this is closer to a valid inference. More importantly, it lacks the clear quantitative mismatch that makes composition a fallacy. It does not match the flaw as precisely as E.
explanations.B: This commits the opposite error: division fallacy — inferring from a property of the whole to a property of each part. The direction of inference is reversed relative to the stimulus.
explanations.C: This is actually a valid (or near-valid) inference: if several components are bitter, detecting some bitterness in the whole is a reasonable, cautious conclusion. The conclusion is hedged ('at least some') and does not overstate, so no composition fallacy is committed.
explanations.D: This is a straightforward deductive application of a general principle to a specific case (modus ponens structure). No part-to-whole reasoning is involved; this argument is valid.
explanations.E: Correct. Each part (brick) has property P (lightweight); conclusion: the whole (wall) has property P (lightweight). This is the composition fallacy in its clearest form, directly mirroring the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a classic necessary/sufficient confusion — treating a sufficient condition as necessary. Two or three answer choices replicate a conditional error but differ in direction; students must track which one swaps in the same way.
lr.stimulus: To be admitted to the honors program at Westfield University, a student must have a GPA of at least 3.8. Marcus has a GPA of 3.8, so he will certainly be admitted to the honors program.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every finalist in the regional debate competition must have won at least one preliminary round. Jordan won three preliminary rounds, so Jordan is definitely a finalist in the competition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No one who fails the safety certification exam is permitted to operate the machinery. Sasha failed the exam, so Sasha will not be permitted to operate the machinery.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most students who are admitted to the honors program maintain their GPA throughout their first year. Priya was admitted to the honors program, so she will probably maintain her GPA through her first year.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To qualify for the scholarship, applicants must submit a recommendation letter. Elena submitted a recommendation letter, so she qualifies for the scholarship.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Students who complete the advanced seminar are guaranteed a passing grade in the course. Tomás did not complete the advanced seminar, so he will not receive a passing grade.

explanations.correct: The stimulus treats a necessary condition (GPA ≥ 3.8) as if it were sufficient, concluding that meeting the minimum guarantees admission. D mirrors this exactly: submitting a recommendation letter is a necessary condition for the scholarship, but Elena concludes she qualifies simply by satisfying that requirement — the same necessary-for-sufficient swap.
explanations.A: Same flaw on the surface, but the premise says every finalist MUST have won a preliminary round (necessary condition for being a finalist). Jordan won rounds, so Jordan is a finalist — this is the same flaw. However, the conditional direction is identical to D, making D the cleaner match because it preserves the institutional-requirement framing and the word 'qualifies' mirrors 'admitted.' Close trap — but D is structurally identical and tonally cleaner.
explanations.B: This is valid reasoning: failing the exam is a sufficient condition for being denied permission, and Sasha failed. No flaw is present — affirming the antecedent correctly.
explanations.C: This commits a different flaw — reasoning from a majority/base-rate premise to a conclusion about a specific individual. It is not a necessary/sufficient confusion.
explanations.D: Correct. Submitting a letter is necessary but not sufficient; concluding it is sufficient mirrors the stimulus's error.
explanations.E: This commits denying the antecedent: completing the seminar is sufficient for passing; Tomás did not complete it, so the argument incorrectly concludes he won't pass. Different conditional error from the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a correlation-to-causation flaw in a medical context. Answer choices include one that replicates the error, one that is a valid causal inference, and two that commit superficially similar but distinct errors (reversed causation, confounding variable ignored differently).
lr.stimulus: In a recent survey, people who reported eating breakfast every morning also reported lower rates of workplace absenteeism. Clearly, eating breakfast every morning causes people to miss fewer days of work.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Employees at companies that offer flexible scheduling report higher job satisfaction. It must be that higher job satisfaction leads employees to advocate for flexible scheduling at their companies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Research shows that children who own more books tend to score higher on reading assessments. Therefore, owning more books causes children to become better readers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A controlled experiment demonstrated that patients who received the new drug recovered from the infection faster than those given a placebo. Therefore, the drug accelerates recovery from the infection.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Studies consistently find that wealthier neighborhoods have more trees. This is probably because city planners tend to invest more in green infrastructure in higher-income areas.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most marathon runners maintain strict sleep schedules. Since maintaining a strict sleep schedule is difficult, most marathon runners have strong willpower.

explanations.correct: The stimulus observes a correlation (breakfast-eating and lower absenteeism) and concludes one causes the other, without ruling out confounds or reverse causation. B does the same: it observes a correlation (owning more books, higher reading scores) and concludes ownership causes the outcome, ignoring that better-reading families may buy more books, or that a third factor (parental involvement) explains both.
explanations.A: This commits reversed causation — it takes the same correlation and attributes it to the effect causing the cause. This is a different version of the causal flaw, not the same one as the stimulus, which infers the more intuitive causal direction without justification.
explanations.B: Correct. Mirrors the stimulus: correlation observed → direct causal conclusion drawn without eliminating alternatives.
explanations.C: This is valid reasoning. A controlled experiment with a placebo comparison is standard scientific methodology for establishing causation; no flaw is committed.
explanations.D: This provides a specific causal explanation for a correlation, but it hedges with 'probably' and supplies a plausible mechanism (city planner investment). It does not commit a bare correlation-to-causation inference the way the stimulus does.
explanations.E: This commits a different flaw — an unsupported inference about willpower from a behavioral pattern. It is not a correlation-to-causation error but rather an unwarranted assumption about an underlying trait.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a part-to-whole (compositional) fallacy. Answer choices include one that replicates the fallacy, one that commits the reverse (whole-to-part/division), and two with plausible surface similarity but different errors. Students must distinguish composition from division and from valid inferences.
lr.stimulus: Each individual scene in the new film has been praised by critics as visually stunning. Therefore, the film as a whole must be a visually stunning work of art.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every player on the national soccer team is among the most skilled athletes in the country. Therefore, the national soccer team is the most skilled team in the country.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The university's economics department is ranked first in the nation. Therefore, every professor in the economics department is among the nation's top economists.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The novel's plot has been universally admired by reviewers. Moreover, novels with universally admired plots tend to win literary awards. Therefore, this novel will probably win a literary award.

choices.label: D
choices.text: This alloy is composed entirely of lightweight metals. Each of those metals is inexpensive to produce. Therefore, the alloy itself is inexpensive to produce.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several of the chapters in this history textbook contain factual errors. Therefore, the textbook's overall historical narrative is unreliable.

explanations.correct: The stimulus infers a property of the whole (the film is stunning) from a property shared by each part (each scene is stunning). A replicates this exactly: each individual player is highly skilled (part), therefore the team as a whole is the most skilled (whole). The fallacy is that assembling individually skilled parts does not guarantee the whole has that same property — team chemistry, coordination, and comparative ranking are separate questions.
explanations.A: Correct. Each part (player) has property P; therefore the whole (team) has property P. Identical compositional fallacy.
explanations.B: This commits the fallacy of division — reasoning from the whole (top-ranked department) to its parts (individual professors). This is the inverse of the stimulus's error.
explanations.C: This is valid probabilistic reasoning: a true general trend (admired plots → awards) is applied to a specific instance that fits the trend. No fallacy is committed.
explanations.D: Close trap — D does attribute properties of parts to the whole (lightweight, inexpensive), but the two premises attribute different properties (lightweight and inexpensive), while the conclusion draws only on the inexpensive premise. This is a different structural error from a clean compositional fallacy and introduces a scope shift between the two properties.
explanations.E: This is a hasty generalization or unwarranted extrapolation — from some flawed chapters to the entire narrative being unreliable. It is not a compositional fallacy; it moves from some parts having a flaw to the whole having a flaw, which is more akin to an overextended inductive inference.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is necessary/sufficient confusion — treating a sufficient condition as necessary. Two answer choices involve similar conditional language, requiring careful tracking of which direction the error runs.
lr.stimulus: Whenever a patient is admitted to Riverside Hospital with acute appendicitis, the surgical team is immediately assembled. Dr. Lena Hartwick is a member of the surgical team, and she has just been called in. Therefore, a patient with acute appendicitis must have been admitted.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The city's emergency notification system is activated whenever a Category 3 hurricane makes landfall nearby. The notification system was just activated, so a Category 3 hurricane must have made landfall nearby.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All competitive swimmers train for at least two hours daily. Marcus trains for at least two hours daily. Therefore, Marcus is a competitive swimmer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a building receives a historic preservation designation, its exterior cannot be altered. The facade of Alderton House has not been altered, so it must have received a historic preservation designation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every employee who passes the advanced certification exam receives a pay raise. Fatima passed the advanced certification exam. Therefore, Fatima will receive a pay raise.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whenever the municipal pool is closed for maintenance, the parks department sends an announcement to all residents. No announcement was sent this week, so the pool was not closed for maintenance this week.

explanations.correct: The stimulus infers that the only cause of the surgical team being assembled is acute appendicitis — it treats 'appendicitis → team assembled' as if it were 'team assembled → appendicitis,' confusing a sufficient condition for a necessary one. Choice A commits the same error: 'Category 3 hurricane → notification system activated' is treated as 'notification activated → Category 3 hurricane.' The sufficient condition is mistakenly read as the only possible cause.
explanations.A: Correct. Same flaw: the sufficient condition (hurricane) is treated as the necessary/only explanation for the effect (notification), mirroring the stimulus exactly.
explanations.B: This confuses a necessary condition ('at least two hours of training' is necessary for competitive swimmers) with a sufficient one — a slightly different directional error. The stimulus errs by reversing a sufficient condition, not by elevating a necessary condition.
explanations.C: Close trap. 'Historic designation → no alteration' is reversed to conclude designation from no alteration. This is structurally similar but the premise in the stimulus describes an action triggered by an event; here the conditional is a restriction, not a triggered response. Also, the conclusion is about an exterior feature being unaltered, making it a converse error on a prohibition rather than on an activating cause.
explanations.D: This is a valid modus ponens inference — no flaw. The employee passed the exam (sufficient condition met), so the consequent (pay raise) follows correctly.
explanations.E: This is a valid modus tollens inference — if the notification system is the necessary signal of closure, the absence of notification validly implies no closure. No flaw is committed.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is correlation-to-causation. Two answer choices involve causal language in familiar domains; students must distinguish a genuine causal inference error from a valid statistical inference and from a different flaw (sampling bias).
lr.stimulus: A study of school districts found that districts with more after-school tutoring programs tend to have higher average standardized test scores. Clearly, the tutoring programs are raising students' test scores.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neighborhoods with more coffee shops per capita also tend to have lower rates of unemployment. Coffee shops must therefore be creating jobs and reducing unemployment in those neighborhoods.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The regions of the country that consume the most olive oil also report the lowest rates of cardiovascular disease. Therefore, at least some of the people in those regions consume olive oil.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because the survey sample was drawn entirely from urban residents, its finding that most people support public transit funding cannot be reliably extended to rural residents.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sales of umbrellas rise every autumn. Therefore, umbrella purchases must be causing the seasonal change in weather that autumn brings.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every city that has adopted a congestion-pricing scheme has seen a reduction in downtown traffic. We can therefore predict that the next city to adopt congestion pricing will also see reduced downtown traffic.

explanations.correct: The stimulus observes a correlation between tutoring programs and test scores, then concludes the programs cause the scores to rise — ignoring that wealthier or better-resourced districts might independently produce both outcomes. Choice A does the same: it observes a correlation (more coffee shops, lower unemployment) and concludes the coffee shops are causing the employment benefit, ignoring that both variables could stem from a common cause (e.g., economic prosperity).
explanations.A: Correct. Observes a correlation and infers a specific causal direction without ruling out confounding variables — identical flaw to the stimulus.
explanations.B: This is a valid inference: 'regions consume the most' entails that some people in those regions consume olive oil. No flaw is present; it's merely weak existential reasoning from a known fact.
explanations.C: This correctly identifies a sampling-bias problem, which is a different flaw — failure of representativeness — not correlation-to-causation.
explanations.D: This is a reversed-causation error (umbrella sales causing weather), which is technically a correlation-causation flaw, but the causal direction is backwards and the conclusion is absurd rather than merely unwarranted. It differs from the stimulus in that the stimulus infers plausible-seeming causation from correlation; D infers implausible reverse causation. The closer match remains A.
explanations.E: This is an inductive generalization from past cases to a future case — a valid (though defeasible) predictive inference. No specific flaw in causal attribution is committed.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is a part-to-whole (composition) fallacy. Three answer choices involve property-transfer reasoning; students must distinguish the composition fallacy from a valid generalization and from a division fallacy (whole-to-part).
lr.stimulus: Each individual chapter of Professor Okafor's new linguistics textbook is concise and easy to follow. Therefore, the textbook as a whole must be concise and easy to follow.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every molecule of water is odorless and tasteless. Therefore, a glass of pure water must be odorless and tasteless.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The national economy is healthy and growing. Therefore, each sector of the economy must be healthy and growing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every ingredient in this stew was fresh when purchased. Therefore, this stew must be fresh and delicious.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each musician in the chamber ensemble is a highly skilled soloist. Therefore, the ensemble's performances as a group must be outstanding.

choices.label: E
choices.text: This documentary film is engaging and informative. Therefore, each individual segment of the film must be engaging and informative.

explanations.correct: The stimulus attributes a property of each individual part (each chapter is concise and easy to follow) to the whole (the textbook). This is the composition fallacy. Choice D does the same: each individual musician is a skilled soloist (part-level property), so the ensemble as a whole must be outstanding (whole-level conclusion). Individual excellence does not guarantee collective excellence — ensemble performance requires coordination, balance, and interaction that go beyond individual skill.
explanations.A: This is actually a valid inference, not a flaw. Properties of individual water molecules (odorlessness, tastelessness) do aggregate to the bulk substance by the nature of molecular uniformity. No fallacy is committed.
explanations.B: This is the division fallacy — inferring a property of the parts from a property of the whole — the reverse of the composition fallacy in the stimulus. The stimulus argues from parts to whole; B argues from whole to parts.
explanations.C: Close trap. Inferring 'fresh and delicious' from 'each ingredient was fresh' does move from parts to whole, but the conclusion adds 'delicious,' which requires an evaluative leap beyond the stated premise. This mixes composition with an unsupported additional claim, making it a slightly different error. More importantly, freshness genuinely does aggregate (fresh ingredients → fresh stew is at least partially valid), diluting the fallacy. D's error is purer.
explanations.D: Correct. Pure composition fallacy: individual skill (part) attributed to ensemble quality (whole), ignoring that group performance is an emergent, non-additive property.
explanations.E: This is the division fallacy — inferring properties of each segment from properties of the whole film — the reverse of the composition fallacy in the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus weaves three errors together: equivocation on 'natural' (uncultivated vs. chemical-free), a universal generalization from a non-representative sample of heirloom tomatoes, and a sufficient-for-necessary swap turning 'naturalness suffices for nutritional value' into 'natural crops are the only nutritious crops.' The correct answer replicates all three moves.
lr.stimulus: Heirloom tomatoes grown in the wild woods near Asheville contain none of the synthetic pesticides applied on industrial farms, so they are entirely natural. And since everything natural is nutritionally superior, we may conclude that only wild-grown heirloom tomatoes are nutritionally superior to their cultivated counterparts.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Old-growth cedar harvested from the remote Alaskan coast has no artificial preservatives, and so it is entirely pure. Since everything pure is structurally stronger than its alternatives, we may conclude that only coastal old-growth cedar is structurally stronger than kiln-dried pine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the vineyards of the Mosel Valley use no herbicides, their Rieslings contain no residues. Rieslings with no residues are widely preferred by sommeliers, so Mosel Rieslings are widely preferred by sommeliers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Raw honey from alpine meadows contains no added sugars. Therefore, since consumers prefer foods with no added sugars, consumers prefer raw alpine honey to processed honey.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Handwoven rugs from rural Anatolia use no synthetic dyes, so they are entirely authentic. Because authentic rugs appreciate in value, handwoven Anatolian rugs appreciate in value more than machine-made rugs do.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wild salmon caught off the Kenai Peninsula are free of farm-pen antibiotics, and so they are purer than farmed salmon. Since purer fish are healthier, wild Kenai salmon are healthier than farmed salmon.

explanations.correct: A mirrors all three moves: it equivocates on 'pure' (free of preservatives vs. unadulterated in any sense), generalizes from a narrow example to a universal 'everything pure is stronger,' and flips a sufficient condition ('purity suffices for strength') into a necessary one ('only this cedar is stronger'). The compound flaw is identical in structure to the stimulus.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Contains a linking chain but no equivocation and no sufficient/necessary reversal — the conclusion follows validly from the premises as stated.
explanations.C: A single correlation-to-preference step; no universal claim and no 'only' reversal in the conclusion.
explanations.D: Equivocates on 'authentic' but concludes with a comparative claim, not an 'only' exclusivity claim; it is missing the sufficient/necessary flip.
explanations.E: Valid chain: free of antibiotics → purer → healthier. No equivocation, no universal overreach, no exclusivity reversal.

lr.difficultyReason: Three compounding errors: (1) composition fallacy (what is true of a part of the orchestra is ascribed to the whole); (2) ambiguity on 'balanced' (acoustic balance vs. repertoire balance); (3) the conclusion then inverts the conditional, treating 'balance implies acclaim' as 'only balanced orchestras are acclaimed.' Each answer choice replicates some but not all of these moves.
lr.stimulus: Every section of the Prague Chamber Orchestra — strings, winds, brass — produces a balanced sound on its own. So the orchestra as a whole must be balanced. Because only balanced orchestras win international acclaim, the Prague Chamber Orchestra must be among the acclaimed ensembles of its generation.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each of the attorneys at Merton & Voss is persuasive in oral argument, so Merton & Voss is a persuasive firm. Because persuasive firms win most of their trials, Merton & Voss wins most of its trials.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every department at Halloran College — humanities, sciences, arts — is rigorous on its own. So the college as a whole is rigorous. And because only rigorous colleges produce Rhodes Scholars, Halloran must be among the colleges producing Rhodes Scholars.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each player on the Winfield hockey team has excellent stickhandling, so the team must have excellent stickhandling. Teams with excellent stickhandling tend to win championships, so Winfield will probably win the championship.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every chapter in Professor Lin's new book is clearly written, so her book is clearly written. Clearly written books sell well, so her book will sell well.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Each division of Volterra Motors meets its quarterly targets, so Volterra meets its annual targets. Since companies that meet annual targets are admired by investors, Volterra is admired by investors.

explanations.correct: B replicates all three moves: composition (each department rigorous → college rigorous); equivocation on 'rigorous' (department-level rigor vs. institutional reputation); and the 'only rigorous colleges produce Rhodes Scholars' conditional flipped into a claim that Halloran is among the Rhodes-producing colleges. The compound flaw matches precisely.
explanations.A: Composition is present, but there is no 'only' conditional reversal; the chain is linear.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Hedged conclusion ('probably') and no equivocation on 'stickhandling'; missing two of the three moves.
explanations.D: Simple composition followed by a valid inference; no ambiguity and no reversal.
explanations.E: Contains a different compositional flaw (quarterly vs. annual) and a scope shift, but no sufficient/necessary reversal in the final step.

lr.difficultyReason: Three stacked errors: (1) correlation mistaken for causation between statin use and reduced cardiac events; (2) the causal claim is then universalized beyond the study population; (3) base-rate reversal — because most patients with low cardiac events are on statins, a patient on statins is presumed to have low cardiac event risk. The correct answer must stack all three.
lr.stimulus: A ten-year observational study in Uppsala found that patients taking statins had 30% fewer cardiac events than those not taking them. It follows that statins prevent cardiac events in any patient population. Since most low-risk cardiac patients in our clinic are on statins, any patient we place on statins will likely be a low-risk cardiac patient.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A longitudinal survey in Oslo showed that readers of literary fiction score higher on empathy tests than non-readers. Therefore, literary fiction cultivates empathy in any reader. Because most empathic professionals read literary fiction, any professional who begins reading literary fiction will likely become empathic.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A city-wide study found that neighborhoods with more trees have lower asthma rates. So trees must improve respiratory health. Therefore, planting trees in any city will reduce its asthma rates.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Surveys show that frequent meditators report lower stress. Since meditation calms the mind, anyone who meditates will feel less stressed. Most people who feel less stressed have stable relationships, so meditation stabilizes relationships.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A regional audit found that firms using agile methodology deliver software faster than those using waterfall. Agile therefore accelerates delivery universally. Anyone who adopts agile will deliver software faster than their waterfall competitors.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A decade-long trial showed that communities consuming more olive oil had lower rates of stroke. So olive oil prevents stroke. Since most stroke-free communities consume olive oil, any community that begins consuming olive oil will be stroke-free.

explanations.correct: A matches all three moves: (1) correlation-to-causation (readers scoring higher → fiction cultivates empathy); (2) universal overreach ('in any reader'); (3) base-rate reversal — 'most empathic professionals read fiction, so any professional who reads will be empathic.' The compound is exact.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Correlation-to-causation plus universalization, but no base-rate reversal — the final step is a straightforward (if unwarranted) generalization.
explanations.C: Introduces a second causal chain (meditation → relationships) rather than a base-rate inversion; the flaw pattern diverges on the third step.
explanations.D: Two moves only — correlation-to-causation and universalization. Missing the base-rate reversal step.
explanations.E: Close, but the conclusion is 'stroke-free,' a certainty claim, while the stimulus concludes a probabilistic 'likely be low-risk.' The strength mismatch makes E off-by-one.

lr.difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) ad hominem dismissal that slides into (2) a genetic fallacy generalized into a universal claim about a field, which in turn (3) inverts a conditional — from 'biased sources cannot establish truth' to 'only unbiased sources can.' The correct answer must replicate the slide from personal attack through field-level generalization to necessary-condition inversion.
lr.stimulus: The historian Ackroyd was a lifelong royalist, so his account of the Glorious Revolution cannot be trusted. Indeed, because any historian with political loyalties is biased, the entire field of political history is compromised. It follows that only accounts by politically unaffiliated historians can give us genuine historical knowledge.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following exhibits a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The critic Beaumont was a declared modernist, so his review of the new opera is biased. Because biased critics misjudge opera, Beaumont misjudged this opera, and so his review should be disregarded.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The economist Halvarsson advised a sitting government, so her forecasts cannot be trusted. Since any economist advising a government is compromised, the entire discipline of macroeconomic forecasting is unreliable. Therefore, only forecasts produced by economists with no governmental ties can qualify as legitimate forecasts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The journalist Ruiz has taken corporate sponsorship, so his coverage of that corporation should be discounted. Sponsored journalism is often biased, and biased journalism misleads readers. Therefore, Ruiz's readers are likely misled about the corporation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Pelham once consulted for an industrial client, and so his published findings are suspect. Because published findings by consultants are frequently disputed, Dr. Pelham's findings will probably be disputed as well.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The statistician Okoro worked briefly for a polling firm, so she is biased. Since bias invalidates polling, her polls are invalid. The only valid polls are those she did not design.

explanations.correct: B mirrors the slide: personal attack on Halvarsson → universal claim about all economists with government ties → field-wide compromise → only unaffiliated economists produce 'legitimate' forecasts. All three moves match the stimulus structure.
explanations.A: Personal attack plus a chain, but no field-level generalization and no inversion to 'only X can produce knowledge.'
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Hedged throughout ('often,' 'likely') and stops at a reader-level conclusion; no 'only' reversal.
explanations.D: Two moves, not three — no field-wide claim.
explanations.E: Personal attack and 'only' reversal, but the scope is restricted to Okoro's own polls rather than being universalized across a field.

lr.difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) hasty generalization from one startup to all startups; (2) equivocation on 'fail' (bankruptcy vs. failing to reach projections); (3) denying the antecedent — from 'poor management leads to failure' to 'without poor management, no failure.' The correct answer must compound all three.
lr.stimulus: Morrow Analytics missed its revenue projections last quarter and was labeled a failure. It follows that every startup that misses projections has failed. And since poor management is what causes startups to fail, any startup with competent management will meet its projections.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments displays a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Riverton public library closed after its budget was cut, which proves that budget cuts destroy libraries. Every library facing budget cuts is at risk of being destroyed, and since inadequate public support causes library destruction, libraries with adequate public support are safe.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kessler Foods recalled a batch of soup contaminated with listeria, which shows it cut corners on inspection. Therefore, every food manufacturer that recalls a batch has cut corners on inspection. Because corner-cutting causes recalls, any manufacturer that does not cut corners will never issue a recall.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The manuscript Vellum & Ink was rejected by its publisher, so it was deemed unpublishable. Every manuscript rejected by a publisher is unpublishable, and since a weak premise causes rejection, manuscripts without weak premises are never rejected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Santillan's clinic was cited by the regulator last year, meaning her clinic was compromised. Every clinic cited by regulators is compromised, and because lax protocols cause citations, any clinic with strict protocols will never be cited.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The engineering firm Aldebaran lost its bid on the bridge contract, so it is uncompetitive. Since every firm that loses a major bid is uncompetitive, and uncompetitive firms have poor leadership, Aldebaran's leadership is poor.

explanations.correct: B compounds the same three moves: hasty generalization (Kessler's recall → every recall means cut corners); equivocation on 'recall' (one batch vs. manufacturer reputation); and denying the antecedent (corner-cutting causes recalls → no corner-cutting, no recalls). The strength of the conclusion ('never') matches the stimulus's universal closure.
explanations.A: Generalization and denial-of-antecedent are present, but 'destroy' and 'at risk of being destroyed' are not equivocal — the argument holds 'destruction' constant. Two of three moves.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Close, but the final step shifts the dimension: 'weak premise causes rejection' is inverted, but without the equivocation on 'rejected' vs. 'unpublishable' being fully carried through.
explanations.D: The conclusion retains the same term ('cited') throughout — no equivocation. And the final 'never' is a denial of antecedent, but only two of three moves.
explanations.E: Runs the chain forward rather than inverting the final conditional; the structure is linear rather than compound-flawed in the stimulus's way.

lr.difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) percentage-vs-absolute confusion (share of workforce vs. head count); (2) universalization across a region; (3) affirming the consequent — from 'automation reduces manufacturing share' to 'because manufacturing share has declined, automation must have caused it.' The correct answer must stack all three.
lr.stimulus: In the Ruhr region, manufacturing has fallen from 40% of the workforce to 25% over two decades, meaning fewer people than ever work in manufacturing there. This pattern must therefore hold across all industrialized regions. And since automation reduces manufacturing's share of the workforce, the decline in the Ruhr must have been caused by automation.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In Kyoto, tourism has fallen from 30% of service-sector employment to 15% over a decade, so fewer residents than ever work in tourism there. The same must be true of all historic cities in Asia. And because budget airlines draw tourism away from traditional hubs, Kyoto's decline must have been caused by budget airlines.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In several European capitals, the share of cycling commuters has risen above 20%. This trend holds across all urban centers. Because bike lanes increase cycling share, the rise in these capitals must have been caused by bike lane construction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Across the Midwest, family farms now account for 10% of agricultural output, down from 25% thirty years ago. This must be true nationwide. Consolidation reduces the family farm share, and so consolidation caused the decline.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In Lombardy, the textile industry's workforce share dropped from 35% to 20%, which means fewer workers than ever are in textiles. This pattern extends across all Mediterranean economies. Since offshoring reduces textile employment share, offshoring must explain the Lombardy decline.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Coal mining in Appalachia fell from 18% of regional employment to 6%, so coal employs fewer people than ever in the region. The same must be true in every coal-producing country. And because environmental regulation reduces coal's share of employment, regulation caused the Appalachian decline.

explanations.correct: D mirrors all three moves precisely: percentage-to-absolute confusion ('35% to 20%' → 'fewer workers than ever'); universalization ('all Mediterranean economies'); and affirming the consequent (offshoring reduces textile share; share fell; therefore offshoring caused it). The compound matches the stimulus closely, and the domain is economics — distinct from the stimulus's industrial context but structurally identical.
explanations.A: Present all three moves but the causal agent named ('budget airlines') and the quantity ('service-sector employment') introduce a scope mismatch — the stimulus's causal agent is more tightly tied to the dependent variable than A's is.
explanations.B: Missing the percentage-to-absolute confusion — the rise in cycling share is stated as a share, not translated into absolute counts.
explanations.C: Lacks the 'fewer than ever' absolute-number mistranslation; the argument stays in percentage terms. Two of three moves.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Close, but 'fewer people than ever' is a stronger absolute claim and the scope ('every coal-producing country') is broader than the stimulus's 'all industrialized regions' — off-by-one in breadth.

lr.difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) false dichotomy (either strict liability or no accountability); (2) this dichotomy is supported by an equivocation on 'accountability' (legal liability vs. moral responsibility); (3) the necessary condition is then flipped into a sufficient one. The correct answer must replicate all three in a new domain.
lr.stimulus: Either manufacturers are held strictly liable for defective products, or there is no product accountability at all. Strict liability is therefore the only way to ensure accountability. And since accountability is necessary for consumer trust, imposing strict liability will by itself be enough to restore consumer trust in our markets.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Either a university enforces a strict plagiarism policy, or it has no academic integrity. A strict policy is thus the only route to integrity. And because integrity is necessary for scholarly reputation, a strict plagiarism policy by itself will restore the university's scholarly reputation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Either a newspaper has a strong editorial board, or it has no standards at all. Therefore, a strong editorial board is the only way to maintain standards. Because standards are important to readers, a strong editorial board will make readers loyal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A museum either charges admission or it cannot maintain its collection. Charging admission is thus the only viable model. Since funds are necessary for maintenance, charging admission will be sufficient for maintenance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either a city has strong zoning or it has chaotic development. Zoning is the only cure for chaotic development. And because orderly development is desirable, zoning will make the city's development orderly.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Either athletes are subject to random drug testing, or doping goes unchecked. Random testing is thus the only remedy. Because unchecked doping harms the sport's credibility, random testing will by itself restore the sport's credibility.

explanations.correct: A mirrors all three moves: false dichotomy (strict policy vs. no integrity); equivocation on 'integrity' (policy enforcement vs. scholarly integrity); and the necessary-to-sufficient flip (integrity necessary for reputation → strict policy sufficient for reputation). The domain shift to academia leaves the structure intact.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: False dichotomy and a chain, but the final inference is a reasonable probabilistic claim — no necessary-to-sufficient inversion of the right shape.
explanations.C: Explicitly labels the necessary-to-sufficient move, but lacks the equivocation step that makes the stimulus a three-error compound.
explanations.D: All three moves are present in broad outline but the equivocation on 'orderly' vs. 'zoning' is thin; the argument reads more like a two-step chain.
explanations.E: Very close, but shares a domain with the stimulus (legal/regulatory accountability) and keeps the word 'credibility' stable throughout — no equivocation. Two of three moves.

lr.difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) appeal to authority by a non-expert (a successful poet pronouncing on neuroscience); (2) that authority claim is then generalized across a whole field; (3) circular reasoning — the conclusion ('creativity requires solitude') is smuggled in as a premise ('creative work only happens alone'). The correct answer must replicate all three in a new domain.
lr.stimulus: The celebrated poet Vernier has said that he composes only in solitude, so all neuroscience of creativity must treat solitude as essential. Indeed, creative work — being work that can only happen alone — requires solitude; and since what requires solitude cannot flourish in collaborative settings, genuine creativity cannot flourish in collaborative settings.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The renowned chef Kilbane insists that great cuisine demands only the freshest local produce, so all food science must treat freshness as the decisive variable. Great cuisine — being cuisine that only local produce can produce — requires local produce; and since what requires local produce cannot come from long supply chains, genuine cuisine cannot come from long supply chains.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The celebrated architect Nesbitt has said that great buildings require symmetry, so architectural theory must prioritize symmetry. Symmetrical buildings tend to last longer than asymmetrical ones, so the best-lasting buildings are symmetrical.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The acclaimed composer Viana claims that rhythm is the heart of music, so music theorists must agree. Since rhythm is the heart of music, a piece without rhythm is not music. Therefore a piece without rhythm cannot be called music.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The renowned physicist Hertzen has argued that quantum effects dominate at small scales, so quantum theory should focus there. Because quantum effects dominate at small scales, and what dominates at small scales must be studied there, quantum theory belongs at small scales.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The celebrated novelist Orellana has written that novels must have strong characters, so critics should weight characterization highly. Since strong characters require depth, and depth comes from solitude, novelists must work alone.

explanations.correct: A matches all three moves: non-expert authority (a chef on food science); field-wide generalization ('all food science must treat freshness as decisive'); and circular reasoning ('cuisine that only local produce can produce' smuggled in to conclude 'genuine cuisine cannot come from long supply chains'). The compound is identical.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Authority plus a causal chain, but no circularity — the conclusion 'best-lasting buildings are symmetrical' is independent of the premises.
explanations.C: Contains circularity but lacks the field-wide generalization step; the argument stays narrow.
explanations.D: The conclusion is a tautological restatement of the premise rather than a smuggled-in circular claim; the structure is flatter than the stimulus.
explanations.E: Authority and a chain, but the final inference borrows the stimulus's own vocabulary ('solitude') without replicating its three-step compound flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) appeal to tradition; (2) a slippery-slope inference from one regulatory change to civilizational decline; (3) conflation of 'legal permission' with 'moral endorsement.' The correct answer must match all three.
lr.stimulus: For centuries, common law has treated inherited property as a fundamental right, and so it must remain so. Any reform that narrows inheritance will inevitably unravel the entire edifice of private property. Because the law permits inheriting property, the state clearly endorses the moral goodness of transferring wealth across generations, and any challenge to that endorsement is a challenge to civilization itself.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: For decades, our municipal code has permitted single-family zoning, and so it must remain so. Any reform that allows multifamily housing will inevitably unravel the entire neighborhood character. Because zoning permits single-family homes, the city endorses the moral goodness of that way of life, and any challenge to it is a challenge to community itself.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For generations, our university has required a Latin examination for all graduates, and so the requirement should remain. Removing Latin will weaken classical education. Because the university tests Latin, it values classical learning, and challenging the test is challenging classical learning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Our courts have long allowed juries to decide capital cases, so they must continue to do so. Removing the jury will undermine confidence in the legal system, and because juries are used, the legal system clearly endorses lay decision-making.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The constitution permits free assembly, so free assembly must be preserved. Restricting assembly would unravel democratic culture. Since the constitution permits assembly, the state approves of assembly, and assembling is therefore a civic virtue.

choices.label: E
choices.text: For a century the tax code has exempted certain charitable gifts, and so this exemption must persist. Narrowing it will slowly erode all philanthropy, and because the code permits the exemption, the government formally approves of charitable giving.

explanations.correct: A replicates all three moves: appeal to tradition (decades of single-family zoning); slippery slope (any reform unravels neighborhood character); conflation of legal permission with moral endorsement ('the city endorses the moral goodness' of single-family living). Closes with the civilizational-stakes rhetoric matching the stimulus.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Tradition and a weak consequence claim, but the slope is not 'unraveling' scale and the legal-moral conflation is weakly drawn.
explanations.C: Tradition and conflation present, but no slippery slope — the consequence claim is bounded ('confidence in the legal system').
explanations.D: Conflation and a slope, but the tradition appeal is replaced by a straight appeal to the constitution; the third move is missing its traditional framing.
explanations.E: Tradition and conflation, but the slope is described as 'erode' rather than the stimulus's systemic-unraveling frame, and the civilizational stakes are absent — off-by-one in scope.

lr.difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) survivorship bias (only surviving languages are studied); (2) the resulting pattern is generalized into a universal linguistic claim; (3) the generalization is then used to predict the future — past success becomes a guarantee of continued success. The correct answer must replicate all three.
lr.stimulus: Every surviving European language today has a written tradition going back at least five hundred years, so all European languages have always had long written traditions. Since languages with long written traditions persist, and since written tradition guarantees persistence, Basque — with its long written tradition — is guaranteed to persist for another five centuries.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every established monastery in Ireland has continuously kept a scriptorium for at least eight centuries, so all Irish monasteries have always kept scriptoria. Since monasteries with scriptoria endure, and because a scriptorium guarantees endurance, Glendalough Monastery — with its eight-century scriptorium — is guaranteed to endure another eight centuries.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every skyscraper still standing in Chicago was built before 1960, so Chicago skyscrapers have always been built in that era. Because pre-1960 skyscrapers are sturdy, the Monadnock Building, which predates 1960, will continue to stand.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every bank that survived the 2008 crisis had diversified holdings, so all banks at that time had diversified holdings. Since diversified banks tend to weather downturns, Commerzbank, which is diversified, will weather any future downturn.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All surviving Etruscan bronzes show a high tin content, so Etruscan bronzes uniformly contained high tin. Because high-tin bronzes resist corrosion, the Arezzo Chimera — a high-tin Etruscan bronze — will resist corrosion for centuries to come.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every jazz standard still performed today was composed before 1970, so jazz standards have always dated to that era. Because pre-1970 standards have lasting appeal, 'Mood Indigo' will continue to be performed.

explanations.correct: A replicates all three moves: survivorship bias ('every established monastery' = those that survived); universal generalization ('all Irish monasteries have always kept scriptoria'); and the leap from 'guarantees endurance' to a future-prediction certainty ('guaranteed to endure another eight centuries'). The compound is identical and the domain shift (language to religious institutions) is clean.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Survivorship and generalization, but the conclusion is softer ('will continue to stand') and lacks the certainty language — off-by-one in strength.
explanations.C: Survivorship and generalization, but the final claim is narrowed ('any future downturn') and depends on a tendency rather than a guarantee — two of three moves.
explanations.D: Survivorship and generalization present, but the conclusion concerns a material property rather than a temporal persistence claim — the domain of the third move doesn't match.
explanations.E: Survivorship and a generalization, but the conclusion 'will continue to be performed' is a tendency-style claim, not a guarantee-level prediction; the third move is weaker than the stimulus's.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is a necessary/sufficient confusion embedded in a medical context. All five answer choices are dense mini-arguments; two plausible traps replicate the surface vocabulary without matching the directional swap. Students who misidentify the flaw as base-rate reversal will select a wrong answer.
lr.stimulus: Dr. Alvarez argues that anyone who has Rennick syndrome will test positive on the Halpern screening. Marcus tested positive on the Halpern screening. Therefore, Marcus probably has Rennick syndrome.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anyone who completes the advanced licensing exam is qualified to practice independently. Yolanda is qualified to practice independently. Therefore, Yolanda probably completed the advanced licensing exam.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anyone who studies abroad for at least one semester will become fluent in the local language. Priya studied abroad for one semester. Therefore, Priya is probably fluent in the local language.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most people who score highly on the aptitude test go on to excel in engineering. Tomás excels in engineering. Therefore, Tomás probably scored highly on the aptitude test.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Anyone who receives the merit scholarship must have an outstanding academic record. Devon has an outstanding academic record. Therefore, Devon will probably receive the merit scholarship.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No one who has completed the detoxification protocol will test positive for trace compounds. Simone has not completed the protocol. Therefore, Simone will probably test positive for trace compounds.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: If Rennick syndrome → positive test (sufficient condition). Marcus has positive test → therefore Marcus has Rennick syndrome. This treats a sufficient condition as if it were also necessary — affirming the consequent. Answer A replicates this exactly: If complete advanced exam → qualified (sufficient). Yolanda is qualified → therefore she completed the exam. Same affirming-the-consequent flaw at matching probabilistic strength.
explanations.A: Correct. If completing the exam is sufficient for qualification, being qualified does not entail completing the exam — other routes to qualification may exist. The argument affirms the consequent, exactly as the stimulus does.
explanations.B: This is a valid modus ponens inference: the premise establishes a sufficient condition (study abroad → fluent), and the conclusion follows by applying that condition to Priya. No flaw — trap for students who focus only on surface conditionals without checking validity.
explanations.C: This commits base-rate reversal ('most X have Y; this thing has Y; so it's probably an X'), not affirming the consequent. The stimulus's premise is a universal conditional, not a 'most' statement. Different flaw family.
explanations.D: This confuses necessary with sufficient in the opposite direction: the stimulus affirms the consequent, but D draws a conclusion about obtaining a sufficient cause from possessing what is only a necessary precondition — treating a necessary condition as sufficient. The directional error is different from the stimulus's.
explanations.E: This denies the antecedent: 'If completed protocol → not positive; Simone has not completed protocol → Simone will probably test positive.' Related conditional fallacy, but structurally distinct from affirming the consequent.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a composition fallacy — inferring a property of the whole from properties of the parts. All five answer choices are dense mini-arguments in varied domains; one answer commits a valid inference from an analogous structure, one commits division (the inverse fallacy), and one is a different quantifier error. Students who misidentify the flaw will be lured by the division-fallacy trap.
lr.stimulus: Every section of Hargrove's new economic policy proposal has been praised by independent analysts as carefully reasoned and internally consistent. Therefore, the proposal as a whole is almost certainly carefully reasoned and internally consistent.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each chapter of Delacroix's biography of Empress Theodora is historically accurate and meticulously sourced. Therefore, the biography as a whole is almost certainly historically accurate and meticulously sourced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rowan's symphony is widely regarded as a masterpiece of modern composition. Therefore, each movement of the symphony is almost certainly a masterpiece in its own right.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every ingredient in Chef Marconi's signature dish has been certified as organic and locally sourced. Therefore, Chef Marconi's restaurant probably uses only organic and locally sourced ingredients in all its dishes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most of the essays in the anthology were written by established scholars. Therefore, the anthology as a whole was probably written by established scholars.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Each member of the investigative panel has demonstrated expertise in financial regulation. Therefore, the panel as a whole almost certainly has the expertise needed to conduct the investigation.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: every part (section) has property P → the whole (proposal) has property P. This is the fallacy of composition — properties of parts do not automatically transfer to the whole, because section-level coherence doesn't guarantee cross-section coherence. Answer A mirrors this exactly: every part (chapter) has property P (accurate, sourced) → the whole (biography) has property P. A biography could have inaccuracies or inconsistencies arising from how chapters relate to one another, even if each chapter is internally accurate.
explanations.A: Correct. Replicates the composition fallacy: part-level property (accurate chapter) → whole-level property (accurate biography). The whole can fail to be accurate even when each part is, due to contradictions or gaps between chapters.
explanations.B: This commits the fallacy of division — inferring a property of the parts from a property of the whole. That is the inverse of the composition fallacy in the stimulus. Close structural relative but a different error.
explanations.C: This is a scope expansion error — from a property of one dish to a property of the entire restaurant's menu. Not composition (part→whole) but rather generalization from one instance to a broader class. Different flaw.
explanations.D: This uses the quantifier 'most' rather than 'every/each,' and the inference is from a statistical majority among parts to a property of the whole. This is a weaker version of the error, but the premise is probabilistic rather than universal, making the flaw structurally distinct.
explanations.E: This is a valid inference. Panel-level expertise in a domain is constituted by the expertise of its members; when each member has the relevant expertise, the collective body plausibly has that expertise. No flaw — trap for students who assume any part→whole inference is flawed.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits base-rate reversal in a linguistics/history context: 'Most X's have property Y; this thing has property Y; therefore it is probably an X.' Each answer choice is a dense five-line mini-argument. One trap commits the same quantifier move but reverses direction; one is a valid base-rate inference; one changes absolute vs. proportional framing. Students must track quantifier direction precisely.
lr.stimulus: Most ancient inscriptions that originated in the Keldaran trading network were written on fired clay tablets. The newly excavated inscription at Mervasa was written on a fired clay tablet. Therefore, the Mervasa inscription was probably produced within the Keldaran trading network.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most prize-winning wines from the Corenne valley are aged in French oak barrels. The Domaine Pelletier reserve is aged in French oak barrels. Therefore, the Domaine Pelletier reserve is probably a prize-winning wine from the Corenne valley.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most manuscripts produced in the Aldric scriptorium were written on vellum. The Aldric scriptorium produced the Hartwell Psalter. Therefore, the Hartwell Psalter was probably written on vellum.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The majority of architectural features found in Velmorian temples also appear in Dassine civic buildings. The Harwell colonnade contains several features found in Dassine civic buildings. Therefore, the Harwell colonnade was probably built by Velmorian craftsmen.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most structural engineers who specialize in seismic retrofitting have completed graduate-level coursework in geotechnical analysis. Petra has completed such coursework. Therefore, Petra is probably a structural engineer who specializes in seismic retrofitting.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Sorvaine Bridge was constructed using techniques documented in most Fenwick-era engineering manuals. Most bridges built using those techniques have remained structurally sound for over two centuries. Therefore, the Sorvaine Bridge has probably remained structurally sound for over two centuries.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: Most [category] have [property Y]; this item has [property Y]; therefore this item is probably [category]. This is base-rate reversal — the frequency of Y within the Keldaran network tells us nothing about the frequency of Keldaran-origin among all Y-bearing objects; other networks may also use fired clay. Answer A replicates this exactly: Most prize-winning Corenne wines have [property Y = French oak]; Domaine Pelletier has [property Y]; therefore it is probably a prize-winning Corenne wine. Many non-prize-winning or non-Corenne wines are also aged in French oak, so the inference reverses the base rate.
explanations.A: Correct. Mirrors the stimulus's base-rate reversal: most members of category X have property Y → item with Y is probably in category X. Ignores that property Y may be widespread outside category X.
explanations.B: This is a valid inference. The premise states most items produced by a specific source have property Y, and the conclusion is that a known product of that source probably has Y. Modus ponens from base rate — no flaw. Trap for students who focus on the 'most … therefore probably' surface structure without checking inferential direction.
explanations.C: The argument involves an additional inferential step (shared features imply shared craftsmen) that introduces a causal attribution error — not base-rate reversal. The property in question (Dassine civic features) is shared across both Velmorian and Dassine contexts, but the flaw is misattributing causation rather than reversing a base rate.
explanations.D: This commits base-rate reversal using a universal-ish 'most … have completed coursework' → 'Petra has coursework → Petra is probably in the specialization.' Structurally close, but notice the subject and predicate are reversed relative to the stimulus in a different way: in the stimulus the category is a geographic-cultural network; here the category is a professional specialization defined partly by the very credential cited, making the flaw slightly different in kind. More importantly, this answer is a strong trap — students should recognize that answer A more cleanly replicates the stimulus because the property (French oak aging) is widely shared outside the target category, exactly as fired clay tablets were shared outside the Keldaran network.
explanations.E: This chains two 'most' premises toward a conclusion about a specific item — a different quantifier-chain structure. The first premise links the bridge to a technique; the second links the technique to longevity. Neither premise reverses a base rate; the argument's flaw (if any) is in how two probabilistic premises combine, not in reversing part-to-whole frequency.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is a necessary/sufficient confusion: the stimulus treats a sufficient condition as necessary. Each answer is a dense mini-argument; two choices involve similar subject matter but commit different errors (one valid, one correlation-causation), and one is off-by-a-quantifier, requiring careful structural analysis.
lr.stimulus: All patients who receive the experimental drug Veratol show marked improvement in their cognitive function within three weeks. Helena has shown marked improvement in her cognitive function over the past three weeks. Therefore, Helena must have received Veratol.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every employee who completes the advanced certification program receives a salary increase. Tomás received a salary increase last quarter. Therefore, Tomás must have completed the advanced certification program.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most patients who undergo physical therapy after knee surgery regain full mobility within six months. Daniela regained full mobility six months after knee surgery. Therefore, Daniela probably underwent physical therapy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any student who studies abroad for a full year becomes fluent in the host country's language. Priya studied abroad in France for a full year. Therefore, Priya is fluent in French.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All children who are exposed to a second language before age five develop superior pattern-recognition skills. Since children who develop superior pattern-recognition skills tend to excel in mathematics, early second-language exposure must cause mathematical excellence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whenever river sediment levels rise sharply, the local fish population declines within two seasons. The local fish population has declined this season. Therefore, river sediment levels must have risen sharply recently.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: All A → B; X has B; therefore X is A. This treats a sufficient condition (Veratol → improvement) as if it were also necessary (improvement → Veratol). Choice A replicates this exactly: All A (complete certification) → B (salary increase); Tomás has B; therefore Tomás is A. Same necessary/sufficient confusion at the same strength ('must').
explanations.A: Correct. Mirrors the flaw precisely: affirming the consequent, treating a sufficient condition as necessary, and using the same categorical strength ('must').
explanations.B: Uses 'most' rather than 'all' in the first premise, making this a base-rate reversal flaw (the Carpaccio flaw), not the necessary/sufficient confusion in the stimulus. Different flaw.
explanations.C: This is a valid modus ponens inference: All A → B; X is A; therefore X is B. No flaw — a trap 'valid analog' choice.
explanations.D: This chains two general claims to reach a causal conclusion — a correlation-to-causation error, structurally distinct from the stimulus's affirming-the-consequent flaw.
explanations.E: Same affirming-the-consequent structure as the stimulus but uses 'whenever' (a universal conditional), which closely parallels the stimulus. However, the domain and causal direction differ subtly — this is the close distractor. The key distinction: Choice A more precisely mirrors 'all … must have' categorical strength and the institutional/individual structure of the stimulus. Choice E remains a strong parallel but is less clean because 'whenever' introduces a temporal/conditional nuance rather than a pure class-membership conditional.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a composition fallacy: what is true of every individual part is assumed to be true of the whole. Answer choices involve superficially similar aggregation language; one commits a valid statistical inference, one commits a division fallacy (the mirror image), and one conflates percentage with absolute magnitude — traps from §6.3 and §6.8 of the dossier.
lr.stimulus: Every chapter of Professor Aldane's new economics textbook has been praised by reviewers as brilliantly argued and highly accessible. It follows that Professor Aldane's textbook, taken as a whole, is a brilliantly argued and highly accessible work.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each individual instrument in the Meridian Chamber Orchestra is precisely tuned to concert pitch. Therefore, the Meridian Chamber Orchestra, as an ensemble, will produce perfectly harmonious music.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Meridian Chamber Orchestra as a whole has won three consecutive national competitions. Therefore, each individual musician in the orchestra must be among the finest performers in the country.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every scene in Director Volkov's new film has been shot with exceptional technical precision. Since technical precision in every component scene is a reliable indicator of overall cinematic quality, the film is probably of high overall quality.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The unemployment rate fell in each of the nation's twelve largest cities last quarter. Therefore, the national unemployment rate must have fallen last quarter.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Each player on the Harwick rugby team performed flawlessly in last Saturday's match. Therefore, the Harwick rugby team played a flawless match last Saturday.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: every individual part has property P → the whole has property P. This is a composition fallacy. Choice E replicates it exactly: every individual player (part) performed flawlessly → the team (whole) played flawlessly. The same move from distributed parts to the collective whole.
explanations.A: Close distractor — each instrument is tuned (property P) → ensemble produces harmonious music. This resembles composition, but the conclusion introduces a new property (harmonious music) not equivalent to the parts' property (being in tune), making it slightly different in structure. More precisely, it's a composition fallacy with a domain shift in the predicate. Choice E keeps the predicate identical across parts and whole ('flawless'), which more cleanly mirrors the stimulus's 'brilliantly argued and highly accessible' remaining constant.
explanations.B: This is a division fallacy — inferring a property of each part from a property of the whole — the structural mirror image of the composition fallacy, not the same flaw.
explanations.C: This argument includes an explicit bridging premise ('technical precision in every component scene is a reliable indicator of overall cinematic quality'), which makes the inference valid rather than fallacious. Trap: valid analog.
explanations.D: A classic percentage-vs.-absolute distractor. Even if unemployment fell in the twelve largest cities, those cities' labor forces could represent a minority of national employment — the flaw is about aggregation of rates, not composition of properties. This is the §6.8 relative-vs.-absolute trap, a different error.
explanations.E: Correct. Mirrors composition fallacy precisely: part-level property ('each player performed flawlessly') to whole-level conclusion ('the team played a flawless match').
