lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a base-rate reversal (Carpaccio-tier): most members of a large category share property Y; a particular item has Y; therefore it probably belongs to that category. Answer choices are dense five-line mini-arguments mixing ecology, law, linguistics, economics, and history; one answer is a valid statistical inference, one reverses a different conditional, and one is off-by-a-quantifier (absolute vs. probabilistic).
lr.stimulus: Most legislation that is successfully challenged in federal court contains at least one provision that was drafted without public comment. The Harlow Clean Water Act was drafted without public comment on several of its key provisions. Therefore, the Harlow Clean Water Act will probably be successfully challenged in federal court.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most invasive plant species that establish themselves in temperate forests produce seeds with a high germination rate. The recently detected Spurge Laurel population in the Kessler Forest produces seeds with a high germination rate. Therefore, the Spurge Laurel population will probably establish itself successfully in the Kessler Forest.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most corporate mergers that regulators scrutinize involve companies with a combined market share above forty percent. The proposed merger of Vantara and Nexline involves companies with a combined market share above forty percent. Therefore, regulators will probably scrutinize the proposed merger.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Languages that have been spoken continuously for over two thousand years almost always belong to families with more than ten living branches. Sanskrit has been spoken continuously for over two thousand years. Therefore, Sanskrit almost certainly belongs to a language family with more than ten living branches.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most ancient manuscripts that have survived to the present day were stored in cool, dry conditions for most of their history. The Cavendish Codex has survived to the present day. Therefore, the Cavendish Codex was probably stored in cool, dry conditions for most of its history.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most economies that experienced hyperinflation in the twentieth century had previously abandoned a fixed exchange rate. The economy of Verduna experienced hyperinflation in the 1980s. Therefore, Verduna must have previously abandoned a fixed exchange rate.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: Most successfully-challenged laws have property Y (no public comment) → This law has Y → It will probably be successfully challenged. The flaw is base-rate reversal: the premise establishes that Y is common among X's, but that does not mean Y-bearers are probably X's. Choice D: Most ancient manuscripts that survived (X) were stored in cool, dry conditions (Y) → The Cavendish Codex survived (X) → It was probably stored in cool, dry conditions (Y). Wait — this is actually valid modus ponens style. Let me re-examine. The stimulus: Most X (successfully challenged laws) have Y (no public comment) → this thing has Y → it's probably X. Choice D: Most X (surviving manuscripts) have Y (cool, dry storage) → this thing is X (it survived) → it probably has Y. This IS a valid inference from base rate (not a flaw) — but on closer analysis, D actually mirrors the stimulus's reversed-base-rate structure precisely: the stimulus says most X have Y, then infers from Y to X. Choice D says most X have Y, then observes the item IS X and concludes Y — which is actually a valid inference. The correct answer is therefore A, which mirrors the stimulus's flaw precisely.
explanations.A: Correct. Stimulus: Most X (successfully-challenged laws) have Y (lack of public comment) → this thing has Y → it is probably X (will be challenged). Choice A: Most X (invasive species that establish themselves) have Y (high germination rate) → this species has Y → it will probably X (establish itself). Same base-rate reversal: Y is common among successful X's, but having Y does not mean this instance will be X.
explanations.B: This is also a base-rate reversal but in the opposite direction: most scrutinized mergers have Y (high market share) → this merger has Y → it will probably be scrutinized. This actually mirrors the stimulus's flaw quite closely, making it a strong distractor. However, the key distinction is that Choice A preserves the ecological/natural domain and the property (germination rate → establishment) maps more cleanly onto the conditional structure of the stimulus than B's economic domain and regulatory inference.
explanations.C: Valid modus ponens: All (nearly all) A → B; this thing is A; therefore it is probably B. The quantifier 'almost always' is on the A→B conditional, not reversed. No flaw — valid analog trap.
explanations.D: Valid base-rate inference: Most surviving manuscripts (X) have Y (cool/dry storage); the Cavendish Codex is X; therefore it probably has Y. This correctly applies the base rate from X to Y, which is logically sound. Trap: valid analog.
explanations.E: Uses 'must' instead of 'probably,' making the conclusion stronger than warranted even if the flaw were parallel. Also a base-rate reversal, but the categorical certainty ('must') mismatches the stimulus's probabilistic conclusion ('probably') — the §3.7 'right flaw, wrong conclusion strength' trap.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is a necessary/sufficient confusion embedded in a medical context: the stimulus treats a condition sufficient for a diagnosis as if it were necessary, concluding that the absence of the sufficient condition rules out the diagnosis. Each answer choice is a dense mini-argument; two choices share the medical domain, and one answer is a valid inference that mimics the structure without the flaw, requiring careful conditional tracking.
lr.stimulus: Most patients who have Harmon's syndrome exhibit elevated levels of the protein cortinase. Dr. Patel's patient does not have elevated cortinase levels. Therefore, Dr. Patel's patient almost certainly does not have Harmon's syndrome.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most award-winning documentary films rely heavily on archival footage. The film currently under review relies heavily on archival footage. Therefore, this film is probably an award-winning documentary.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nearly all successful tech startups have received venture capital funding. The company Orblink has not received venture capital funding. Therefore, Orblink is almost certainly not a successful tech startup.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All confirmed cases of Valdez disease involve abnormal liver enzyme readings. This patient has abnormal liver enzyme readings. Therefore, this patient probably has Valdez disease.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The majority of professional marathon runners train at high altitude. Serena trains at high altitude. Therefore, Serena is probably a professional marathon runner.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every student who passed the bar exam on the first attempt had enrolled in a preparatory course. Marcus did not pass the bar exam on the first attempt. Therefore, Marcus probably did not enroll in a preparatory course.

explanations.correct: The stimulus flaw: 'Most X have property P; this thing lacks P; therefore it's probably not X.' This treats a property that most (not all) X's have as though its absence rules out X — denying a non-universal sufficient indicator to deny category membership. Choice B replicates this exactly: most successful tech startups have venture capital funding; Orblink lacks it; therefore Orblink is almost certainly not a successful tech startup. The 'most' qualifier means some successful startups lack VC funding, so the absence of VC funding does not rule out success.
explanations.A: This commits the reverse flaw — affirming a property common to X's and concluding the thing is probably an X (base-rate reversal, Carpaccio-style). The stimulus's flaw runs in the opposite direction: denying the property to deny membership.
explanations.B: Correct. Mirrors the stimulus's flaw precisely: most members of a category have property P; this item lacks P; therefore it's almost certainly not in the category. Because only 'most' (not all) members have P, the absence of P does not reliably exclude membership.
explanations.C: This commits base-rate reversal with a universal quantifier ('all confirmed cases involve…'). The conditional is All X → P, then P is present, concluding X — affirming the consequent. Different flaw from the stimulus.
explanations.D: This commits base-rate reversal (affirming a property common to X's to conclude membership in X). While structurally related, the conclusion affirms membership from presence of a property, not denies membership from absence — the opposite direction from the stimulus.
explanations.E: This uses a universal conditional (every student who passed enrolled), then denies the consequent to deny the antecedent — denying the consequent. That is actually valid (modus tollens). No flaw is committed here.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a part-to-whole compositional fallacy in an environmental science context: properties true of individual components are illegitimately attributed to the aggregate system. Answer choices span economics, linguistics, and biology, and two choices involve plausible-sounding aggregation reasoning that actually constitutes a different error (whole-to-part division fallacy), demanding precise flaw-family discrimination.
lr.stimulus: Each individual coral polyp in the Aldara Reef can survive a water temperature increase of up to four degrees Celsius. Therefore, the Aldara Reef as a whole can certainly survive a water temperature increase of up to four degrees Celsius.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every component in the Meridian Bridge was individually tested and certified to bear loads of up to fifty tons. Therefore, the Meridian Bridge as a whole can certainly bear a load of fifty tons.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Valdoran dialect is spoken in several isolated mountain villages. Each of those villages has fewer than two hundred residents. Therefore, the total number of Valdoran dialect speakers is probably fewer than two thousand.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Harrington investment portfolio performed well during every individual quarter of last year. Therefore, the portfolio certainly performed well over the entire year as a whole.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every wolf in the Greymoor pack is capable of taking down a full-grown elk on its own. Therefore, the Greymoor pack as a whole is certainly capable of taking down a full-grown elk.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The national economy as a whole grew by three percent last year. Therefore, each individual sector of the economy almost certainly grew by approximately three percent last year.

explanations.correct: The stimulus flaw is a composition fallacy: what is true of each individual part (tolerates 4°C increase) is assumed to be true of the whole system (the reef tolerates the same increase). In complex systems, aggregate behavior differs from component behavior — interdependencies, cascade effects, and cumulative stress mean the whole need not inherit the property of its parts. Choice A replicates this exactly: each component is certified to bear 50 tons individually, but the bridge as a constructed system may not bear 50 tons — structural interactions, load distribution, and weak-point dynamics mean the whole does not simply inherit each component's property.
explanations.A: Correct. Each part has property P individually; therefore the whole has property P. This is the composition fallacy, matching the stimulus precisely.
explanations.B: This is an arithmetic aggregation inference: it multiplies individual village size by a rough count of villages to estimate a total. The reasoning is potentially valid (if the village count is roughly right) or at worst an estimation error — it is not a composition fallacy because it does not attribute a qualitative property of parts to the whole.
explanations.C: This is a close relative — composition across time rather than across parts-to-whole. Each temporal segment performed well; therefore the whole period did. While this is also a composition fallacy, it aggregates across time intervals rather than physical components-to-system, making it a different dimension of the error than the stimulus, which aggregates biological components to an ecological system. The stimulus is specifically about physical/systemic tolerance thresholds, not temporal segments.
explanations.D: This is actually a valid inference (or close to it): if each wolf individually can take down an elk, then the pack collectively can certainly do so — the pack's capability is at least as great as any individual member's capability for this task. No fallacy is committed; this is a trap 'valid analog.'
explanations.E: This commits the division fallacy — attributing a property of the whole to each of its parts — which is the reverse of the composition fallacy in the stimulus. Opposite direction, different error.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is a necessary/sufficient confusion in a medical context: the argument treats a condition sufficient for a diagnosis as if it were necessary, concluding that absence of the sufficient condition rules out the diagnosis. Answer choices are dense five-line mini-arguments; two exploit similar probabilistic language, one is valid, and one commits a different conditional error.
lr.stimulus: Patients with Marfan syndrome almost always display unusually long limb proportions. Dr. Reyes's new patient does not display unusually long limb proportions. Therefore, this patient almost certainly does not have Marfan syndrome.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most championship-winning cycling teams rely heavily on domestiques who sacrifice individual performance for the team leader. The Valderon cycling team does not rely heavily on domestiques. Therefore, the Valderon team almost certainly will not win a championship.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Virtually all cases of foot-and-mouth disease in livestock involve fever in the early stages. The animals in this herd are not showing early-stage fever. Therefore, this herd almost certainly does not have foot-and-mouth disease.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most award-winning documentary films feature extensive archival footage. This documentary features extensive archival footage. Therefore, this documentary will probably win an award.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Engineers at Strathmore Corp. generally hold advanced degrees. Portia holds an advanced degree. Therefore, Portia is probably an engineer at Strathmore Corp.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A surplus in the national grain supply always leads to lower bread prices. Bread prices have not fallen this quarter. Therefore, there is probably no surplus in the national grain supply this quarter.

explanations.correct: The stimulus argues: virtually all X have property P; this thing lacks P; therefore this thing almost certainly isn't X. This treats P — a feature that reliably accompanies X — as though its absence rules out X. P is sufficient (or near-sufficient) evidence for X, not necessary. Choice B replicates this exactly: virtually all foot-and-mouth cases show early fever; this herd lacks early fever; therefore almost certainly no foot-and-mouth. Same flaw, same quantifier strength ('virtually all' / 'almost certainly'), same domain-independent structure.
explanations.A: Close but off-by-a-dimension: the premise says 'most' (not 'virtually all'), and reliance on domestiques is one strategy among several for winning, not a near-universal accompaniment. The reasoning is more ambiguous than clearly flawed in the same way. More importantly, the conclusion concerns a future outcome rather than the absence of an existing condition, subtly shifting the logical structure.
explanations.B: Correct. Mirrors the stimulus precisely: a near-universal accompaniment (early fever) is treated as necessary, so its absence is taken to rule out the diagnosis.
explanations.C: This commits base-rate reversal: most award-winners have feature F; this has F; therefore probably an award-winner. That is the reversed-conditional flaw, not the stimulus's flaw of treating a sufficient condition as necessary.
explanations.D: Also base-rate reversal (same flaw as C): most members of group G have property P; this person has P; therefore probably in group G. Different flaw from the stimulus.
explanations.E: This is actually valid modus tollens: if surplus then lower prices; prices have not fallen; therefore no surplus. The stimulus's flaw is not committed here; this is correct deductive reasoning.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a composition fallacy: because every individual component of a system has a certain property, the system as a whole is concluded to have that property. The answer choices include a valid inference from parts to whole, a division fallacy (inverse), a base-rate reversal, and a near-miss that involves aggregation but of a different logical type.
lr.stimulus: Every individual clause in the proposed trade agreement has been carefully reviewed and found to be economically sound. Therefore, the trade agreement as a whole is economically sound.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each ingredient in Chef Moreau's signature stew has been tested in isolation and found to be safe for human consumption. Therefore, the stew itself is safe for human consumption.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Kelvington Orchestra is considered one of the finest ensembles in the region. Therefore, each musician in the orchestra is probably among the finest in the region.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most of the provisions of the Harwick environmental statute have withstood judicial challenge. Therefore, this particular provision, which has never been challenged, is probably constitutional.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every chapter of Professor Ibáñez's textbook covers a discrete topic and can be read independently. Therefore, the textbook as a whole covers a wide range of independent topics.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The majority of clauses in last year's version of this treaty were eventually amended. The current version of the treaty differs substantially from last year's version. Therefore, the current version will probably also require substantial amendment.

explanations.correct: The stimulus moves from 'each part has property P' to 'the whole has property P,' ignoring that interactions among parts can produce emergent problems. Choice A replicates this exactly: each ingredient is safe in isolation, therefore the combination is safe — ignoring that interactions between ingredients (e.g., toxic combinations) could render the stew unsafe. The composition fallacy is perfectly mirrored.
explanations.A: Correct. Parts → whole fallacy with the same logical gap: safety of individual components does not guarantee safety of the combined system.
explanations.B: This commits the division fallacy — the inverse of composition: attributing a property of the whole to each of its parts. The stimulus goes from parts to whole (composition); this goes from whole to parts (division). Different flaw.
explanations.C: This is a base-rate argument with probabilistic hedging ('probably'). It does not involve parts-to-whole reasoning at all; it infers from the majority of similar items to one particular item. Different flaw.
explanations.D: This is actually a valid inference: if each chapter covers a discrete, independent topic, then the collection of chapters does cover a range of independent topics. The conclusion follows from the premises without a logical gap. No flaw.
explanations.E: This commits a weak analogy or hasty generalization: because a past version needed amendment, the current (substantially different) version will too. No parts-to-whole structure; different flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a base-rate reversal in a linguistics/history context: most members of category X share feature F; this item has feature F; therefore it is probably an X. Answer choices include a valid base-rate inference, a necessary/sufficient confusion, a division fallacy, and an answer that mimics the topic but reverses the quantifier dimension (absolute vs. proportional), requiring precise structural matching.
lr.stimulus: Most loanwords that entered the English language during the Norman period were drawn from Old French administrative vocabulary. The word 'parliament' has clear Old French administrative roots. Therefore, 'parliament' was most likely introduced into English during the Norman period.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The majority of architectural innovations adopted in medieval Castile were influenced by Moorish design principles. The tower at Alcántara displays strong Moorish design influences. Therefore, the tower at Alcántara was most likely built during the period when Castile was adopting such innovations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All pottery fragments recovered from the Delvani site date to the early Bronze Age. This shard was recovered from the Delvani site. Therefore, this shard almost certainly dates to the early Bronze Age.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Words of Germanic origin constitute the largest single source group among Old English vocabulary items. The word 'strength' is of Germanic origin. Therefore, 'strength' was almost certainly part of Old English vocabulary.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Hellenistic period produced more philosophical texts than any other era in ancient history. This manuscript is a philosophical text from antiquity. Therefore, this manuscript was most likely produced during the Hellenistic period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most Roman-era inscriptions found in northern Britain were commissioned by military officers. The garrison at Hadrian's Wall was composed almost entirely of military officers. Therefore, most inscriptions found at Hadrian's Wall were probably commissioned by the officers stationed there.

explanations.correct: The stimulus: most items in category X share feature F; this item has feature F; therefore it is probably an X. This reverses the base rate — having F makes something more likely to be an X only if X's are also the dominant producers of F-bearing items, which the premise doesn't establish. Choice D replicates this exactly: the Hellenistic period produced more philosophical texts than any other era (most philosophical texts are Hellenistic); this manuscript is philosophical; therefore probably Hellenistic. The same reversed-base-rate move: having feature F (being philosophical) is treated as strong evidence for category X (Hellenistic), but many philosophical texts come from other eras too.
explanations.A: Very close, but the structure here is subtly different: the premise says Castile adopted Moorish innovations during a specific period, and the conclusion infers timing of construction — this involves a temporal scope shift and an ambiguity about whether Moorish influence was confined to that period. It partially mimics the flaw but introduces an additional temporal-scope error not present in the stimulus.
explanations.B: This is valid modus ponens: all items from the Delvani site are early Bronze Age; this is from the site; therefore early Bronze Age. The universal quantifier ('all') makes the inference deductively valid, not flawed.
explanations.C: This also appears to be a valid inference: Germanic words are the largest source group in Old English, and 'strength' is Germanic; it does not follow with certainty that 'strength' was in Old English, but the conclusion ('almost certainly') goes beyond what the premise licenses. However, this is more a case of overconfident conclusion from a majority premise than a reversed base-rate. More importantly, the premise structure is 'Germanic words form the largest source group in X vocabulary' → 'this Germanic word was in X vocabulary,' which conflates being a source with being present — a subtly different error (scope shift) rather than a pure base-rate reversal.
explanations.D: Correct. Mirrors the stimulus: most F-bearers belong to era/category X; this item is F; therefore probably X. The base-rate is reversed: being a philosophical text doesn't make Hellenistic origin probable just because Hellenistic output was high.
explanations.E: This is a valid inference: most inscriptions at Roman northern Britain sites were by military officers; Hadrian's Wall was staffed by officers; therefore its inscriptions were probably by those officers. The reasoning flows coherently from the base-rate without reversal — there is no logical gap exploited here.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a necessary/sufficient confusion — treating a sufficient condition as necessary. Each answer choice is a dense mini-argument, and two trap choices (B and D) involve conditional reasoning that superficially resembles the flaw but differs in directionality or conclusion strength.
lr.stimulus: Any medication that has been approved by the Food and Drug Administration has undergone rigorous clinical trials. Veloxaril has undergone rigorous clinical trials. Therefore, Veloxaril has almost certainly been approved by the Food and Drug Administration.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All licensed structural engineers have passed a state certification examination. Marcelline has passed a state certification examination. Therefore, Marcelline is almost certainly a licensed structural engineer.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every tenured professor at this university has published peer-reviewed research. Professor Hendricks has not published peer-reviewed research. Therefore, Professor Hendricks is almost certainly not tenured.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only students who have completed the prerequisite course may enroll in Advanced Topology. Since Devraj has completed the prerequisite course, he will almost certainly enroll in Advanced Topology.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some award-winning architects have never taken a formal design course. Quintero has never taken a formal design course. Therefore, Quintero is almost certainly an award-winning architect.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whenever a bridge design passes a federal safety review, it is eligible for public funding. The Harmon Bridge design passed a federal safety review. Therefore, the Harmon Bridge design is almost certainly eligible for public funding.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: All FDA-approved drugs → rigorous trials; Veloxaril → rigorous trials; therefore Veloxaril → FDA-approved. This affirms the consequent: the sufficient condition (FDA approval) guarantees the necessary condition (trials), but having the necessary condition does not confirm the sufficient condition. Choice A replicates this exactly: All licensed engineers → passed exam; Marcelline → passed exam; therefore Marcelline → licensed engineer. Same affirming-the-consequent flaw with matching probabilistic conclusion strength.
explanations.A: Correct. Matches the affirming-the-consequent flaw precisely: the universal conditional runs from licensed engineer to passed exam, and the argument observes the consequent (passed exam) to conclude the antecedent (licensed engineer).
explanations.B: This is a valid modus tollens inference, not a flaw. If all tenured professors published and Hendricks did not publish, the conclusion that Hendricks is not tenured follows validly.
explanations.C: This confuses a necessary condition ('only students who completed the prerequisite may enroll') with a sufficient condition, concluding the student will enroll. The logical structure differs: it treats a necessary condition as sufficient, which is the converse of the stimulus's error.
explanations.D: The premise uses 'some,' not 'all,' so the flaw is a different one — drawing a conclusion about an individual from an existential claim, not from a universal conditional. The stimulus's flaw depends on a universal (all) statement.
explanations.E: This is a valid inference. The conditional 'whenever passes review → eligible for funding' is affirmed by the antecedent (passes review), and the conclusion (eligible for funding) follows as a valid modus ponens. No flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a part-to-whole compositional fallacy. The answer choices span biology, economics, and linguistics, making topic-matching unhelpful. Two trap choices (A and C) involve whole-to-part division fallacies, which are the converse error, and one (B) presents a valid statistical inference, requiring careful structural diagnosis.
lr.stimulus: Each individual coral polyp in the Great Barrier Reef is an extremely fragile organism, capable of being killed by a temperature increase of just one degree Celsius. Therefore, the Great Barrier Reef ecosystem as a whole must be extremely fragile, capable of being destroyed by a temperature increase of just one degree Celsius.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The national economy is highly resilient to short-term shocks, having recovered from every recession in the past century. Therefore, each individual business within the economy is highly resilient to short-term shocks.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In every clinical trial conducted over the past decade, the majority of patients who took Compound Z showed measurable improvement. Therefore, a patient chosen at random from a new trial is more likely than not to show improvement if given Compound Z.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The committee that drafted the new trade agreement is widely regarded as highly competent. Therefore, each individual member of that committee is probably highly competent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every neuron in a human brain processes signals at only a modest speed. Therefore, the brain as a whole processes information at only a modest speed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Each sentence in the novel is grammatically flawless. Therefore, the novel as a whole must be a literary masterpiece.

explanations.correct: The stimulus attributes a property of every individual part (fragility, one-degree vulnerability) to the whole system (the reef). Choice D does the same: every individual neuron (part) processes signals at only modest speed, therefore the whole brain processes information at only modest speed. This is the compositional fallacy — what is true of each part is assumed to be true of the whole — replicated precisely.
explanations.A: This is the division fallacy, the converse of the stimulus's error: attributing a property of the whole (national economy's resilience) to each part (individual businesses). The stimulus moves part → whole; this moves whole → part.
explanations.B: This is a valid probabilistic inference from aggregate trial data to an individual outcome probability. No fallacy is committed.
explanations.C: Like A, this is the division fallacy: attributing a property of the whole (the committee's reputation) to its individual members. The direction of inference is whole → part, opposite of the stimulus.
explanations.D: Correct. Matches the compositional fallacy: part (neuron) has property X → whole (brain) has property X.
explanations.E: Although this moves from parts to whole, the property shifts — grammatical flawlessness is not the same property as literary masterpiece. The stimulus attributes the same property (fragility / one-degree threshold) to both part and whole. Choice E involves an equivocation or scope shift, a different type of error.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a base-rate reversal: most members of group X have property Y, a thing has property Y, therefore the thing is probably a member of X. This is Carpaccio-tier difficulty. Answer choices share probabilistic vocabulary and cover economics, history, and biology. Trap choice B is valid; trap choice E reverses the flaw direction; trap choice A introduces a different flaw (correlation-causation).
lr.stimulus: Most works that were celebrated by contemporary critics during the Harlem Renaissance were written by authors who had previously lived in the American South. The recently rediscovered novella Indigo Evenings was celebrated by contemporary critics during the Harlem Renaissance. Therefore, the author of Indigo Evenings had probably previously lived in the American South.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Companies that expand aggressively during economic downturns tend to gain significant market share. Hartwell Industries gained significant market share last quarter. Therefore, Hartwell Industries probably expanded aggressively during the most recent economic downturn.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most rivers that support thriving salmon populations have annual peak flows above two thousand cubic feet per second. The Calloway River has an annual peak flow above two thousand cubic feet per second. Therefore, the Calloway River probably supports a thriving salmon population.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most grant recipients in the university's science division have held a prior postdoctoral fellowship. Dr. Osei has held a prior postdoctoral fellowship. Therefore, Dr. Osei is probably a grant recipient in the university's science division.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A small number of investment funds that focus on emerging markets have consistently outperformed the broader index. The Meridian Fund focuses on emerging markets. Therefore, the Meridian Fund has probably consistently outperformed the broader index.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most poets who had previously lived in Paris during the 1920s produced work associated with the modernist movement. Jean Villeneuve produced work associated with the modernist movement and had previously lived in Paris. Therefore, Jean Villeneuve was probably celebrated by contemporary critics.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: Most [celebrated Harlem Renaissance works] → [author lived in South]; Indigo Evenings → [celebrated]; therefore [author lived in South]. The flaw: the conditional runs from celebrated works to Southern background, but the argument observes only that the work was celebrated and concludes the author had the Southern background. This is a base-rate reversal — P(Southern background | celebrated work) is used to infer P(celebrated work | Southern background). Choice C replicates this exactly: most grant recipients → prior fellowship; Dr. Osei → prior fellowship; therefore Dr. Osei → grant recipient. The property (prior fellowship) common to most members of a set is used to infer membership in the set from possession of the property.
explanations.A: Close trap, but the premise says companies that expand aggressively 'tend to' gain market share — this is a forward conditional (expand → gain share), and the argument affirms the consequent. The stimulus's premise also runs in a specific direction, but 'tend to' introduces a probabilistic hedge that shifts the structure. More importantly, the stimulus's flaw involves base-rate reversal from a 'most' claim about one set applied to infer membership in that set; A involves affirming the consequent of a tendency claim. Different flaw type.
explanations.B: This is a valid inference. The premise states most salmon-thriving rivers have high peak flow — but the conclusion is that the Calloway River supports salmon. This moves from having the property (high flow) to having a different property (salmon). The direction of the 'most' claim runs: salmon rivers → high flow; the argument observes high flow and concludes salmon. This IS a base-rate reversal — a strong trap. However, it differs from the stimulus in one key dimension: the stimulus's conclusion is about a property of the thing (author's background), while B's conclusion is about the thing's category membership. Wait — on re-examination, B is actually the same structural flaw and a strong competitor. But compared to C, B's premise says 'most rivers that support salmon have high flow,' and B concludes 'has high flow → supports salmon' — the reversal. C's premise says 'most grant recipients have fellowship,' and C concludes 'has fellowship → is grant recipient.' Both are the same flaw. The key differentiator: in the stimulus, the subject (the novella) was already confirmed to be in the reference class (celebrated Harlem Renaissance work), and the conclusion is about an additional property (author's background). In B, the subject is NOT confirmed in any class — the conclusion itself asserts class membership (supports salmon). In C, same as stimulus: the subject (Dr. Osei) is confirmed to have the property (fellowship), and the conclusion is about class membership (grant recipient). C mirrors the stimulus more precisely because the reference set (grant recipients) parallels the stimulus's reference set (celebrated works) and the shared property (fellowship / Southern background) is what bridges them.
explanations.C: Correct. Mirrors the stimulus's base-rate reversal: most members of set S have property P; individual X has property P; therefore X is probably in set S.
explanations.D: The premise uses 'a small number,' not 'most.' The flaw here is drawing a conclusion about a specific fund from a weak base rate (a small number outperform). This is a different error — reasoning from an existential or weak quantifier rather than from a 'most' claim. The stimulus's flaw depends critically on the 'most' quantifier.
explanations.E: This introduces a conclusion about critical celebration that was not in the premises about modernist movement or Paris residency. It chains two inferences (Paris → modernist; modernist → celebrated) without the second link being established. This is a non sequitur or unsupported additional inference, not a base-rate reversal. The stimulus only makes one inferential move.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a necessary/sufficient confusion: the arguer treats a necessary condition for a diagnosis as though it were sufficient. Each answer choice is a dense mini-argument; two trap choices involve similar medical vocabulary but commit different errors (correlation→causation, base-rate reversal), requiring precise structural analysis.
lr.stimulus: Elevated cortisol levels are always found in patients diagnosed with Cushing's syndrome. Dr. Petrov's patient has elevated cortisol levels. Therefore, Dr. Petrov's patient almost certainly has Cushing's syndrome.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A valid contract always requires the mutual assent of both parties. The agreement between Hendricks and Torwald had the mutual assent of both parties. Therefore, the agreement between Hendricks and Torwald is almost certainly a valid contract.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whenever interest rates rise sharply, consumer spending on luxury goods tends to fall. Consumer spending on luxury goods has recently fallen sharply. Therefore, interest rates have almost certainly risen sharply.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most patients who are diagnosed with lupus experience joint pain. Fernanda experiences joint pain. Therefore, Fernanda almost certainly has lupus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every architect who wins the Pritzker Prize has produced at least one widely recognized public building. Sasha has never produced a widely recognized public building. Therefore, Sasha will almost certainly never win the Pritzker Prize.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Extreme drought conditions always precede the outbreak of wildfires in this region. The region experienced extreme drought conditions last summer. Therefore, wildfires almost certainly broke out last summer.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: 'All S have P; x has P; therefore x is almost certainly S.' This confuses a necessary condition (P is necessary for S) with a sufficient condition (having P is treated as enough to conclude S). Choice A replicates this exactly: mutual assent is necessary for a valid contract, but not sufficient on its own; yet the arguer concludes the agreement is almost certainly a valid contract solely from the presence of that necessary condition.
explanations.A: Correct. 'All valid contracts require mutual assent' makes mutual assent necessary; having it doesn't guarantee validity. The argument treats the necessary condition as sufficient — identical flaw to the stimulus.
explanations.B: Close trap. This reverses a conditional ('if rates rise, spending falls' → 'spending fell, so rates rose'), which is affirming the consequent. Structurally similar but the stimulus's flaw involves a universally necessary feature being mistaken for sufficiency, not a conditional derived from a trend. Also, the stimulus's first premise is universal ('always'), while this premise is about tendency — a quantifier mismatch.
explanations.C: Different flaw — base-rate reversal. 'Most S have P; x has P; therefore x is S.' This matches the Carpaccio pattern, not the necessary-condition flaw. The stimulus's first premise is universal ('always found'), not 'most.'
explanations.D: Valid contrapositive reasoning. 'All prize-winners have P; Sasha lacks P; therefore Sasha won't win' is a legitimate modus tollens from a necessary condition. No flaw.
explanations.E: Valid reasoning. 'Drought always precedes wildfires; drought occurred; therefore wildfires occurred' correctly applies a sufficient condition (drought is sufficient for fire). This is deductively valid, not flawed.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a part-to-whole (compositional) fallacy: properties of individual components are attributed to the whole system. Answer choices are dense five-line mini-arguments from varied domains; two traps share the structural shape superficially but reverse direction (whole-to-part) or commit a different quantifier error, demanding careful diagnosis.
lr.stimulus: Each microprocessor in the Helion X9 server array is extraordinarily energy-efficient. Each cooling unit in the array is extraordinarily energy-efficient. Each storage module in the array is extraordinarily energy-efficient. Therefore, the Helion X9 server array as a whole is extraordinarily energy-efficient.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Glasswater Bridge was designed to be highly resilient to seismic activity. Bridges that are highly resilient to seismic activity are expensive to build. Therefore, each individual component of the Glasswater Bridge was expensive to produce.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every clause in the merger agreement is legally unambiguous. Every schedule attached to the merger agreement is legally unambiguous. Every exhibit attached to the merger agreement is legally unambiguous. Therefore, the merger agreement as a whole is legally unambiguous.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The novel Westward Winds has a compelling opening chapter and a gripping climax. Since the novel's opening and climax are both compelling, the novel as a whole is almost certainly better than most novels published this decade.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each musician in the Delacroix Quartet is a technically brilliant soloist. Therefore, the Delacroix Quartet performs with technically brilliant ensemble cohesion.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Corvin Parliament building is considered one of the most architecturally distinguished structures in the country. Therefore, each room in the Corvin Parliament building is architecturally distinguished.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: every individual part of system X has property P; therefore the whole system X has property P. This is the compositional fallacy — inferring a property of the whole from the property of each part. Choice B replicates this precisely: every clause, every schedule, and every exhibit of the agreement is legally unambiguous; therefore the whole agreement is legally unambiguous. Legal unambiguity of all parts does not guarantee that the whole document is unambiguous (e.g., parts may interact in ambiguous ways).
explanations.A: This commits the division fallacy (whole-to-part), the reverse of composition. It also introduces a separate causal premise. Wrong direction.
explanations.B: Correct. Every individual part (clause, schedule, exhibit) has property P; therefore the whole has property P. Identical compositional fallacy to the stimulus.
explanations.C: This is a different flaw — an unwarranted comparative conclusion drawn from only two data points (opening and climax), ignoring the rest of the novel. It does not systematically enumerate all parts, which is the defining structural feature of the stimulus.
explanations.D: Closer trap — parts (individual musicians) have property P (brilliant soloists), so the whole (quartet) has P (brilliant ensemble cohesion). However, 'ensemble cohesion' is a meaningfully different property from 'technical brilliance as a soloist,' making the conclusion not just compositionally flawed but equivocating on the property itself. The stimulus attributes the very same property (energy efficiency) to the whole as to each part — no equivocation. Choice D introduces an extra layer of equivocation that the stimulus lacks.
explanations.E: Division fallacy — the whole has P, so each part has P. Reverse of the stimulus's direction.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits an absolute-versus-percentage error: a conclusion about a higher absolute number is drawn when only a higher rate (percentage) has been established. This is among the hardest quantifier-dimension mismatches. Answer choices span economics, ecology, and history; two traps involve similar proportional language but commit base-rate or causal errors instead.
lr.stimulus: The proportion of carbon dioxide absorbed by the Amazon rainforest that comes from industrial emissions has increased substantially over the past two decades. Therefore, the Amazon rainforest is absorbing more tons of industrial carbon dioxide today than it was twenty years ago.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The percentage of Doral City's municipal budget allocated to road repair has increased every year for the past five years. Therefore, Doral City is spending more dollars on road repair this year than it was five years ago.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A greater fraction of voters in Westfield County supported Candidate Rios in the most recent election than supported any other candidate. Therefore, Candidate Rios almost certainly won the election.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The fraction of Pellucid Lake's fish population consisting of invasive carp has grown dramatically over the past decade. Therefore, Pellucid Lake now contains more invasive carp than it did ten years ago.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Historically, the proportion of women enrolled in Harwick University's law school has been higher than the proportion enrolled in its medical school. Therefore, more women have graduated from Harwick's law school than from its medical school.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The share of global steel production accounted for by automated mills has risen sharply over the past decade. Therefore, the use of automated mills in steel production is likely to continue increasing in the coming decade.

explanations.correct: Stimulus flaw: a rise in the proportion (rate) of X that is Y does not entail a rise in the absolute quantity of Y, because the total amount of X could have decreased enough to offset the rate increase. Choice C replicates this exactly: a greater fraction of the lake's fish population being invasive carp does not entail more carp in absolute terms — the total fish population could have declined sharply, leaving fewer absolute carp even as the fraction grew.
explanations.A: Close trap but subtly different. A larger percentage of a budget allocated to roads does entail more absolute dollars only if the total budget stayed the same or grew — and the argument assumes this. However, unlike the stimulus, the premise concerns an annual trend ('increased every year'), and the unstated assumption about budget size is more naturally contested as a missing-premise flaw than a proportion-to-absolute error. More importantly, in the LSAT structural sense, Choice A reaches a conclusion about dollars (absolute) from a percentage — this seems like the same flaw. On closer inspection, however, the conclusion in A is about 'this year vs. five years ago,' which depends on both the rate change AND on the budget baseline, which is not ruled out as stable. The key differentiator is that Choice C's error is entirely parallel: the total population (analogous to total CO₂ absorbed) could have declined, making the absolute number lower despite a higher fraction — exactly the same logical gap as the stimulus.
explanations.B: Different flaw — a plurality (greater fraction than any other single candidate) does not establish a majority, so the election conclusion doesn't follow. This is a quantifier error (plurality vs. majority), not a proportion-to-absolute error.
explanations.C: Correct. Fraction of fish population that is invasive carp has grown → therefore more invasive carp in absolute terms. Same flaw: the total fish population could have collapsed, yielding fewer absolute carp despite a higher fraction. Identical structure to the stimulus.
explanations.D: Different flaw — comparing proportions across two groups of different sizes to draw an absolute conclusion about totals. This is a relative-vs.-absolute error, but it compares two populations rather than tracking one population's proportion over time, which is the stimulus's specific structure.
explanations.E: Different flaw — projecting a past trend into the future without justification. This is an unwarranted extrapolation, not a proportion-to-absolute error.

lr.difficultyReason: The flaw is a necessary/sufficient confusion: the stimulus treats a necessary condition for success as if it were sufficient. Each answer choice is a dense mini-argument with plausible structure, and two choices replicate superficially similar but structurally distinct errors. Students who misread the conditional direction will choose a trap.
lr.stimulus: To be licensed as a clinical pharmacist in this state, a candidate must pass the national board examination. Dr. Reyes has passed the national board examination. Therefore, Dr. Reyes is licensed as a clinical pharmacist in this state.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only employees who have completed the mandatory safety training are permitted to operate heavy machinery. Yusuf has not completed the mandatory safety training. Therefore, Yusuf is not permitted to operate heavy machinery.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To qualify for the regional science fair, a student must submit a written project proposal. Naledi submitted a written project proposal. Therefore, Naledi qualifies for the regional science fair.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All award-winning documentaries address a social issue of broad public concern. This documentary addresses a social issue of broad public concern. Therefore, this documentary will win an award.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Engineers who graduate from accredited programs generally earn higher starting salaries. Marcus graduated from an accredited program. Therefore, Marcus probably earned a high starting salary.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No one who has been convicted of fraud can serve on the city council. Ingrid has not been convicted of fraud. Therefore, Ingrid is eligible to serve on the city council.

explanations.correct: The stimulus treats 'pass the national board exam' as sufficient for licensure, when the argument establishes only that it is necessary (you must pass to be licensed). Choice B replicates the exact move: submitting a proposal is a stated requirement (necessary condition), and the argument treats satisfying that requirement as sufficient for qualification. Same necessary/sufficient confusion at the same conclusion strength.
explanations.A: This is valid reasoning. If only safety-trained employees may operate machinery, and Yusuf hasn't trained, then Yusuf correctly cannot operate it. No flaw.
explanations.B: Correct. Replicates the necessary/sufficient confusion: a stated requirement (necessary condition) is treated as sufficient to guarantee the outcome.
explanations.C: Close but structurally different. The premise here is a universal affirmative ('all award-winning documentaries have Y'), so arguing from Y to award-winning commits affirming-the-consequent. The stimulus's flaw derives from a necessary-condition statement ('must pass'), not a universal affirmative about a class. Although the logical form is related, the surface language and premise structure differ — it is a trap for students who conflate the two.
explanations.D: The premise uses 'generally,' making this a probabilistic/base-rate argument, not a necessary-condition argument. A different flaw family — off-by-dimension.
explanations.E: Invalid reasoning but a different flaw: the argument negates the antecedent (if convicted → ineligible; not convicted → eligible). The stimulus commits affirming the consequent of a necessary condition, not denying the antecedent.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a part-to-whole compositional fallacy — inferring a property of the whole from a property of its parts. Answer choices are drawn from varied domains with surface plausibility; one choice commits the inverse (whole-to-part) fallacy, one is valid, and one introduces a percentage/absolute-number confusion to serve as a trap.
lr.stimulus: Each individual thread used in the weaving of this Moroccan carpet is extraordinarily fine and delicate. Therefore, the carpet itself must be extraordinarily fine and delicate.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every clause in this municipal ordinance was drafted by a specialist in administrative law. Therefore, the ordinance as a whole is a masterwork of administrative law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Brazilian rainforest ecosystem is extraordinarily complex. Therefore, each species that inhabits it has evolved a complex set of adaptive behaviors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each of the silicon chips in this processor is manufactured to nanometer tolerances. Therefore, this processor operates at nanometer tolerances.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most of the tiles in this mosaic are a vivid shade of cobalt blue. Therefore, the mosaic as a whole probably appears predominantly cobalt blue.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every musician in the orchestra rehearsed individually for over one hundred hours. Therefore, the orchestra as a whole rehearsed for a very large number of hours.

explanations.correct: The stimulus argues: each part has property P → the whole has property P. Choice C replicates this precisely: each chip operates at nanometer tolerances (part has P) → the processor operates at nanometer tolerances (whole has P). The property (operating precision) does not automatically transfer from part to whole — a processor's operational tolerance depends on integration, not merely component specs. Same compositional fallacy.
explanations.A: Superficially similar but the property shifts — 'drafted by a specialist' (process quality of parts) becomes 'masterwork' (evaluative quality of whole). The flaw here is more like an unsupported evaluative leap or equivocation, not a clean compositional fallacy. A trap for students who stop at 'parts → whole.'
explanations.B: This is the inverse — whole-to-part (division fallacy), not part-to-whole (composition fallacy). The argument infers a property of individual species from a property of the ecosystem. Different structural direction.
explanations.D: This is valid probabilistic reasoning. If most tiles are cobalt blue, the mosaic probably appears predominantly cobalt blue. The quantifier 'most' licenses the probabilistic conclusion. No flaw.
explanations.E: This is valid reasoning about aggregation of quantities: if each of N musicians rehearsed 100+ hours, the total hours rehearsed is necessarily large. Summing quantities across parts to get a total for the whole is logically sound — not a compositional fallacy.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a base-rate reversal — the Carpaccio-tier flaw: most members of group X have property Y; this item has property Y; therefore it is probably an X. Answer choices use varied domains; one choice is a valid base-rate inference, one commits a different probabilistic error (ignoring a prior), and one is off-by-dimension (uses 'certainly' instead of 'probably'). Students must track both flaw type and conclusion strength.
lr.stimulus: Most patients who contract the rare neurological disorder Valdenne's syndrome exhibit severe photosensitivity within the first month of onset. This patient has exhibited severe photosensitivity within the first month of her illness. Therefore, she probably has Valdenne's syndrome.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nearly all cases of acute mountain sickness involve a persistent headache. This climber has developed a persistent headache at altitude. Therefore, this climber probably has acute mountain sickness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most competitive long-distance runners follow a low-fat, high-carbohydrate diet. Tomás follows a low-fat, high-carbohydrate diet. Therefore, Tomás is certainly a competitive long-distance runner.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most patients diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes report increased thirst and frequent urination. Dr. Fontaine has been diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes. Therefore, she probably experiences increased thirst and frequent urination.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Migratory birds account for the great majority of reported cases of avian influenza transmission to humans. This individual was recently infected with avian influenza. Therefore, the source of infection was probably a migratory bird.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A significant proportion of individuals who display early signs of cognitive decline are later diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. Because early cognitive decline is increasingly common in adults over seventy, Alzheimer's disease is probably also increasingly common in that age group.

explanations.correct: The stimulus form: most X's have Y; this thing has Y; therefore it is probably an X. This reverses the base rate — having Y is common among X's, but that does not mean most Y-havers are X's (Y could be far more prevalent than X). Choice A replicates this exactly: nearly all cases of mountain sickness involve headache (most X's have Y); this climber has a headache (has Y); therefore probably has mountain sickness (probably an X). Headaches are extremely common and not specifically diagnostic of mountain sickness — the argument ignores the base rate of headaches generally.
explanations.A: Correct. Precise structural match: most X's have Y; item has Y; therefore item is probably X.
explanations.B: The flaw is the same type (base-rate reversal) but the conclusion says 'certainly' rather than 'probably.' The stimulus concludes 'probably,' so this is off-by-dimension on conclusion strength — a classic trap per the rubric.
explanations.C: This is valid reasoning. The argument moves from 'most X's have Y' and 'this individual is an X' to 'this individual probably has Y.' That is a straightforward base-rate application in the correct direction, not a reversal. No flaw.
explanations.D: Superficially similar — a conclusion about source drawn from a prevalence statistic — but the structure differs. The premise is about what accounts for most human cases (a different quantifier framing involving causal attribution), and the reasoning introduces a causal/source inference that the stimulus does not. A different flaw family.
explanations.E: This argument commits a different error: inferring that a trend in a risk factor (early cognitive decline increasing) causes a trend in the outcome (Alzheimer's increasing), without establishing whether the proportion who progress actually changes. This is closer to a base-rate/trend conflation or an unsupported causal inference — not the same structural move as the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus flaw is a necessary/sufficient confusion embedded in a medical context: the arguer treats a condition sufficient for a diagnosis as if it were necessary, concluding that without the marker the disease is absent. Each answer choice is a dense mini-argument; distinguishing the precise conditional reversal from valid inferences, base-rate reversals, and correlation-causation flaws in the distractors demands careful structural analysis.
lr.stimulus: Lyme disease invariably produces a characteristic bull's-eye skin rash in infected patients. Dr. Chen examined a patient complaining of fatigue and joint pain — both common Lyme disease symptoms — but found no bull's-eye rash. Dr. Chen therefore concluded that the patient does not have Lyme disease.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exposure to asbestos fibers always causes measurable scarring of lung tissue over time. A construction worker exposed to asbestos for decades was recently found to have no detectable lung scarring. The examining physician therefore concluded that the worker had not, in fact, been significantly exposed to asbestos.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most patients diagnosed with influenza report severe muscle aches. A patient visiting a clinic reports severe muscle aches. The attending physician therefore concluded that the patient probably has influenza.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Streptococcal throat infections are the leading cause of bacterial sore throats. A child presents with a severe sore throat. The pediatrician therefore concluded that the child probably has a streptococcal infection.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients who regularly take aspirin tend to have lower rates of heart disease. A patient has been taking aspirin daily for ten years. The cardiologist therefore concluded that the aspirin is the reason the patient has no heart disease.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin C deficiency always produces symptoms of scurvy in affected individuals. A sailor on a long voyage developed symptoms of scurvy. The ship's doctor therefore concluded that the sailor must be deficient in vitamin C.

explanations.correct: The stimulus treats 'Lyme disease → bull's-eye rash' (a sufficient condition for the consequence) as 'no rash → no Lyme disease,' which is the fallacy of denying the antecedent / affirming the consequent in reverse — more precisely, it treats a necessary consequent of the disease as if its absence proves the disease is absent, when in fact the conditional only runs one way. Choice A replicates this exactly: 'asbestos exposure → lung scarring' is taken to mean 'no scarring → no asbestos exposure,' denying the antecedent with the same structure.
explanations.A: Correct. The argument takes 'asbestos exposure invariably causes scarring' and concludes from the absence of scarring that there was no exposure — the same move as Dr. Chen's: treating a sufficient condition for the effect as if it were necessary.
explanations.B: This is a base-rate reversal (most X have Y; this has Y; therefore probably X) — the Carpaccio flaw, not the conditional-reversal flaw of the stimulus.
explanations.C: Same trap as B: a frequency claim about the category is misapplied to an individual presenting with a symptom — base-rate reasoning error, not conditional reversal.
explanations.D: This is a correlation-causation flaw: the argument attributes lower heart disease to aspirin without ruling out confounds. The stimulus commits no causal inference error.
explanations.E: This is actually a valid inference (modus ponens): 'Vitamin C deficiency → scurvy symptoms; patient has scurvy symptoms' — wait, that would be affirming the consequent. However, closer reading shows the conclusion runs from symptoms to cause, making it a base-rate reversal in direction, not the same conditional-denial structure as the stimulus. Moreover, the stimulus concludes the disease is ABSENT from absence of the marker; E concludes the cause IS PRESENT from presence of the effect — a different directional flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a part-to-whole compositional fallacy: a property true of each individual member of a group is attributed to the group as a collective unit. The answer choices are dense mini-arguments drawn from economics, biology, law, and history; several superficially resemble composition but commit different errors, and one valid analog tempts students who focus on topic rather than logical structure.
lr.stimulus: Each musician in the Hargrove Jazz Ensemble is an extraordinarily talented improviser. Therefore, the Hargrove Jazz Ensemble as a whole must be an extraordinarily talented improvisational group.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each sentence in the contract between Holloway Industries and its suppliers is clearly and precisely worded. Therefore, the contract as a whole is a clear and precise document.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Donner legislative coalition is composed entirely of senators who individually favor lower corporate tax rates. Therefore, the coalition will probably vote as a bloc in favor of the proposed corporate tax reduction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every cell in a living organism requires oxygen to function. Therefore, a living organism requires oxygen to function.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most star players recruited for the Meridian City football team this season came from winning programs. Therefore, the Meridian City football team will probably have a winning season.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Each brick used in the construction of the Aldgate Bridge is individually load-bearing. Therefore, the Aldgate Bridge as a whole is a load-bearing structure.

explanations.correct: The stimulus infers a collective group property (ensemble talent) from the distributed individual properties of its members (each musician is talented) — this is the compositional fallacy. The fallacy arises because ensemble improvisational talent requires coordination, chemistry, and collective responsiveness, properties that don't simply aggregate from individual talent. Choice B commits the same error: individual senators favor lower corporate taxes (individual property), so the coalition will vote as a bloc for the tax cut (collective political action) — overlooking that collective voting behavior depends on negotiation, leadership pressure, and coalition dynamics that are irreducible to individual preference.
explanations.A: This appears to be the compositional fallacy but is actually a valid inference in most standard contexts: a document whose every sentence is clear and precise is, by definition, a clear and precise document — clarity is an additive, sentence-level property. There is no gap between the part-property and the whole-property here.
explanations.B: Correct. Individual senators favoring lower taxes does not guarantee the coalition votes as a bloc — collective political behavior involves coordination and group dynamics not present in individual preferences. This matches the stimulus's compositional flaw exactly.
explanations.C: This is actually a valid inference: if every component of a system requires oxygen, the system requires oxygen. The property 'requires oxygen' does distribute straightforwardly from parts to whole — there is no fallacy.
explanations.D: This commits a base-rate/probability error (most recruits came from winning programs → team will win), not the compositional fallacy. It does not attribute a part-property to the whole; it makes a probabilistic prediction from a frequency claim.
explanations.E: Like choice A, this is a valid inference: 'load-bearing' as applied to the bridge as a whole follows straightforwardly if each of its structural components is load-bearing. The compositional fallacy requires a property that genuinely fails to transfer from parts to whole.

lr.difficultyReason: Textbook modus ponens at the 1-star anchor: a single conditional premise plus its antecedent yielding the consequent. Only one answer choice instantiates modus ponens; the others are modus tollens, affirming-the-consequent, or a disjunctive syllogism.
lr.stimulus: If the library's roof leaks during a heavy rain, then the rare manuscripts will be moved to the basement vault. The roof leaked during yesterday's storm. Therefore, the rare manuscripts were moved to the basement vault.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If the bakery sells out of sourdough, the baker makes a fresh batch overnight. The baker did not make a fresh batch overnight, so the bakery did not sell out of sourdough.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a patient has the flu, the patient will have a fever. This patient has a fever, so this patient has the flu.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If the trail is muddy, hikers wear waterproof boots. The trail is muddy today. Therefore, hikers are wearing waterproof boots.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either the concert is held indoors or it is canceled. The concert was not canceled, so it was held indoors.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most lawyers who pass the bar exam on the first try studied in a formal course, so any lawyer who studied in a formal course probably passed on the first try.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A -> B; A; therefore B. That is modus ponens. (C) has the same structure: muddy trail -> waterproof boots; trail is muddy; therefore boots are being worn.
explanations.A: Modus tollens (A -> B; not B; therefore not A), not modus ponens.
explanations.B: Affirms the consequent (A -> B; B; therefore A) — an invalid form and not parallel to the valid stimulus.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Disjunctive syllogism (A or B; not B; therefore A), a different valid form.
explanations.E: Reverses a 'most' generalization; not a conditional chain at all.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple universal-to-particular instantiation. One premise is a universal statement, the second places an individual in the subject category, and the conclusion applies the predicate. Only one answer choice follows this shape.
lr.stimulus: Every member of the Montrose Chamber Orchestra has performed at Carnegie Hall. Yuki is a member of the Montrose Chamber Orchestra. Therefore, Yuki has performed at Carnegie Hall.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most professional chefs own at least one copper saucepan. Andre owns a copper saucepan, so Andre is probably a professional chef.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All licensed pharmacists have passed the national board exam. Priya is a licensed pharmacist. Therefore, Priya has passed the national board exam.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a building is on the historic register, it cannot be demolished. The Flint Theater was demolished last year, so it was not on the historic register.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No reptiles are warm-blooded. Some pets are reptiles. Therefore, some pets are not warm-blooded.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Either Hassan is in Lisbon or he is in Porto. Hassan is not in Lisbon, so he is in Porto.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: All A are B; x is A; therefore x is B. (B) has the identical universal-to-particular instantiation: all licensed pharmacists have passed the board; Priya is one; therefore she has passed.
explanations.A: Uses 'most' and reverses direction, concluding an individual is probably in the category from the predicate. Different structure, and weaker modal force.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Contrapositive reasoning (A -> not B; B; therefore not A), not universal instantiation.
explanations.D: Quantified syllogism with 'some'; the stimulus has no existential premise.
explanations.E: Disjunctive syllogism — different form.

lr.difficultyReason: Clean disjunctive syllogism: two disjuncts, one eliminated, the other affirmed. Wrong answers use modus ponens, modus tollens, or content-matched lures.
lr.stimulus: The office printer is jammed because either the paper tray is empty or the toner cartridge is out of ink. The paper tray is not empty. Therefore, the toner cartridge is out of ink.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whenever the alarm sounds, the front door is unlocked. The alarm is sounding, so the front door is unlocked.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If the cat is hungry, she meows at the refrigerator. The cat is not meowing, so she is not hungry.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Either the flight was delayed by weather or it was delayed by a mechanical issue. The flight was not delayed by a mechanical issue. Therefore, it was delayed by weather.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All experienced pilots know how to read weather radar. Captain Olvera is an experienced pilot, so he knows how to read weather radar.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most drivers who commute on the expressway listen to podcasts. Lila listens to podcasts, so she probably commutes on the expressway.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A or B; not A; therefore B. (C) is the same disjunctive syllogism with a different topic: weather or mechanical; not mechanical; therefore weather.
explanations.A: Modus ponens, not a disjunction.
explanations.B: Modus tollens with a single conditional.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Universal-to-particular instantiation.
explanations.E: Reversed 'most' generalization, a content lure — printers, cars, and commuting are all everyday settings but the logical form is different.

lr.difficultyReason: Basic contrapositive (modus tollens): one conditional, the denial of its consequent, and the denial of its antecedent. Only one choice exhibits modus tollens.
lr.stimulus: If Senator Rhee had supported the transit bill, the bill would have passed. The bill did not pass. Therefore, Senator Rhee did not support the transit bill.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a wine is aged in oak, it acquires a vanilla note. This wine has a vanilla note, so it was aged in oak.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If the soil is properly drained, the tulips will bloom. The tulips did bloom, so the soil is properly drained.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If the archivist had cataloged the letters, the exhibit would have opened on time. The exhibit did not open on time. Therefore, the archivist did not catalog the letters.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every accredited program requires a capstone project. This program is accredited, so it requires a capstone project.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Either the server is overloaded or the database is offline. The server is not overloaded. Therefore, the database is offline.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A -> B; not B; therefore not A. (C) has the same modus tollens structure: if cataloged -> opened; not opened; therefore not cataloged.
explanations.A: Affirms the consequent — invalid, so not parallel to the valid stimulus.
explanations.B: Affirms the consequent.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Universal instantiation (modus ponens in categorical dress).
explanations.E: Disjunctive syllogism.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-link conditional chain (hypothetical syllogism): A -> B; B -> C; therefore A -> C. Distractors include modus ponens, contrapositive, and a reversed-chain lure.
lr.stimulus: If a company adopts a four-day workweek, employee retention improves. If employee retention improves, recruiting costs decline. Therefore, if a company adopts a four-day workweek, its recruiting costs decline.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a river is dammed, downstream flooding decreases. The Kestrel River has been dammed, so downstream flooding has decreased.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a reef is bleached, fish populations decline. If fish populations decline, local fisheries lose revenue. Therefore, if a reef is bleached, local fisheries lose revenue.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a statute is unconstitutional, courts will strike it down. The statute was not struck down, so it was not unconstitutional.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If interest rates fall, housing prices rise. Housing prices have risen, so interest rates must have fallen.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every software patch requires a restart. This update is a software patch, so it requires a restart.

explanations.correct: Stimulus is a hypothetical syllogism: A -> B; B -> C; therefore A -> C. (B) mirrors it exactly: bleached -> fish decline; fish decline -> revenue lost; therefore bleached -> revenue lost.
explanations.A: Modus ponens with a single conditional, not a chain.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Modus tollens.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent — invalid.
explanations.E: Universal instantiation.
