lr.stimulus: A language will retain its native speaker base only if younger generations continue to acquire it as a first language. Younger generations in this community have stopped acquiring the language as a first language. Therefore, this language will not retain its native speaker base.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A theater company survives only if it attracts new audiences each season. This theater company has not attracted new audiences this season. Therefore, this theater company will not survive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a language loses its native speaker base, it becomes a dead language. This language has lost its native speaker base. Therefore, this language will become a dead language.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whenever younger generations stop learning a language, cultural traditions tied to it disappear. Younger generations have stopped learning this language. Therefore, the cultural traditions tied to it will disappear.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A language retains its speakers only if it is taught in schools. This language is taught in schools. Therefore, this language will retain its speakers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Either a language is supported by government policy or it gradually disappears. This language is not supported by government policy. Therefore, it will gradually disappear.

explanations.correct: The stimulus uses 'only if,' which means: retains base → younger generations acquire it. The second premise denies the consequent (younger generations have NOT acquired it), yielding modus tollens: not consequent, therefore not antecedent (will not retain base). Choice A has identical structure: survives → attracts new audiences; has NOT attracted new audiences; therefore will not survive.
explanations.A: Correct. 'Only if' conditional plus denial of the consequent (modus tollens). Structure is identical to the stimulus.
explanations.B: This is modus ponens (if loses base → dead language; has lost base; therefore dead language). Different direction of inference. The 'only if' structure is absent.
explanations.C: This is a standard conditional chain affirming the antecedent (modus ponens with 'whenever'). No 'only if' construction; the direction of inference differs from the stimulus.
explanations.D: This commits the fallacy of affirming the consequent (retains speakers → taught in schools; taught in schools; therefore retains speakers). This is invalid reasoning, whereas the stimulus is valid.
explanations.E: Disjunctive syllogism structure (A or B; not A; therefore B). Valid, but a different logical form from the stimulus's modus tollens via 'only if.'

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus uses a two-premise analogy structure (X is like Y in relevant ways; Y has property R; therefore X has property R). Distractors include a universal instantiation that superficially resembles an analogy, and a topic-similar choice with an additional unsupported premise.
lr.stimulus: Crowdfunding platforms operate in the same regulatory environment and serve the same investor base as traditional securities exchanges. Traditional securities exchanges are required to disclose all material risks to investors. Therefore, crowdfunding platforms should also be required to disclose all material risks to investors.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Community-supported agriculture programs operate under the same food safety standards and serve the same consumers as licensed grocery stores. Licensed grocery stores must display nutritional information on all products. Therefore, community-supported agriculture programs should also display nutritional information.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All financial institutions that accept deposits from the public must carry deposit insurance. Crowdfunding platforms accept deposits from the public. Therefore, crowdfunding platforms must carry deposit insurance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Securities exchanges and crowdfunding platforms are both profit-driven. Profit-driven institutions sometimes prioritize revenue over investor protection. Therefore, crowdfunding platforms may sometimes prioritize revenue over investor protection.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Traditional securities exchanges were once unregulated and experienced frequent fraud. Since crowdfunding platforms are currently unregulated, they will also experience frequent fraud.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Crowdfunding platforms raise capital from the public, as do municipal bond issuers. Municipal bond issuers are subject to audit requirements. The public deserves protection. Therefore, crowdfunding platforms should be subject to audit requirements.

explanations.correct: The stimulus argues by analogy: X and Y share the same regulatory environment and investor base (relevant similarities); Y has requirement R; therefore X should have R. Choice A mirrors this exactly: CSA programs and grocery stores share the same food safety standards and consumer base; grocery stores must display nutritional info; therefore CSA programs should too.
explanations.A: Correct. Two stated relevant similarities followed by a parallel obligation. Matches the analogy structure of the stimulus in both form and premise count.
explanations.B: This is universal instantiation (all A must carry insurance; crowdfunding platforms are A; therefore they must carry insurance). No analogy is drawn; the argument proceeds from a universal rule directly applied to a particular.
explanations.C: Shares only one similarity ('profit-driven'), not two. More importantly, the conclusion is weakened to 'may sometimes,' whereas the stimulus concludes with a definite normative obligation. Strength mismatch and structural shortfall.
explanations.D: This reasons from historical precedent to a causal prediction, not from shared characteristics to a shared obligation. Different argument form; also potentially invalid (post hoc).
explanations.E: Introduces an additional unsupported premise ('the public deserves protection') that the stimulus does not have. Three-premise structure does not match the stimulus's two-premise analogy.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus is a disjunctive syllogism where the disjunction is presented as an exhaustive 'either…or.' One distractor uses a non-exhaustive 'either…or' that invalidates the inference; another uses the same subject matter but adds an unneeded premise. Students must check exhaustiveness.
lr.stimulus: The sculpture was created either during the artist's early period or during the late period. Experts have conclusively established that it was not created during the late period. Therefore, the sculpture was created during the artist's early period.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The treaty was negotiated either under the current administration or the previous one. Historians have conclusively shown it was not negotiated under the current administration. Therefore, it was negotiated under the previous administration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The policy was introduced either to reduce crime or to increase tax revenue. It has not reduced crime. Therefore, it must have been introduced to increase tax revenue.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The sculpture may have been created during the early period. If created in the early period, it would exhibit rough textures. The sculpture has rough textures. Therefore, it was likely created during the early period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The composer wrote the symphony either in Vienna or Prague. The symphony was written in Vienna. Therefore, it was not written in Prague.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The painting was created in either the Renaissance or the Baroque period. Baroque characteristics are present. Therefore, the painting was created in the Baroque period.

explanations.correct: The stimulus is a clean disjunctive syllogism: A or B (exhaustive); not B; therefore A. Choice A mirrors this exactly: treaty under current or previous administration; not current; therefore previous. Two-premise structure, eliminates one disjunct, concludes the other.
explanations.A: Correct. Disjunctive syllogism with the same two-premise structure. The disjunction is exhaustive (only two possible administrations), and one is eliminated, so the other must be true.
explanations.B: The disjunction ('to reduce crime or to increase revenue') is a stated purpose, not necessarily exhaustive — the policy could have been introduced for both reasons or neither. The elimination of one purpose does not conclusively establish the other. Structurally parallel in surface form but the exhaustiveness condition is weaker.
explanations.C: Uses probabilistic reasoning ('may have been,' 'likely') and affirms the consequent (if early → rough textures; has rough textures; therefore early). Different form and invalid structure.
explanations.D: Affirms one disjunct to deny the other, which is valid but inverts the inferential direction (not the same as eliminating one to conclude the other). The premise affirms rather than eliminates.
explanations.E: Affirms the consequent of an implicit conditional rather than eliminating a disjunct: presence of Baroque characteristics does not logically entail the Baroque period without a universal premise. Subtly different in inferential basis.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus is a conditional chain using 'unless' (equivalent to 'if not'): unless A, B; B leads to C; not A; therefore C. The 'unless' formulation trips students who translate it incorrectly. Distractors use straightforward 'if…then' chains that seem equivalent but differ in premise structure.
lr.stimulus: Unless a clinical trial includes a control group, its results cannot be considered scientifically valid. The results of this trial cannot be considered scientifically valid if they are to be published in a peer-reviewed journal. This trial does not include a control group. Therefore, its results cannot be published in a peer-reviewed journal.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Unless a contractor is licensed, the work performed cannot be legally certified. Work that cannot be legally certified cannot be included in a public infrastructure bid. This contractor is not licensed. Therefore, this contractor's work cannot be included in a public infrastructure bid.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a clinical trial lacks a control group, it is invalid. All invalid trials are rejected by peer reviewers. This trial lacks a control group. Therefore, this trial will be rejected by peer reviewers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A trial's results are publishable only if its methodology is sound. This trial's methodology is not sound. Therefore, its results are not publishable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either a trial includes a control group or it relies on observational data. This trial does not include a control group. Therefore, it relies on observational data.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unless funding is approved, the research program cannot proceed. The research program has not proceeded. Therefore, funding was not approved.

explanations.correct: The stimulus has the form: unless A → not valid; not valid → not publishable; not A; therefore not publishable. It is a three-premise conditional chain triggered by the 'unless' condition. Choice A mirrors this: unless licensed → not certified; not certified → not in bid; not licensed; therefore not in bid.
explanations.A: Correct. Three-premise conditional chain with 'unless' triggering the first conditional, a second conditional extending the consequence, and a factual premise denying the 'unless' condition. Identical structure.
explanations.B: Uses 'if…lacks' rather than 'unless,' making it a standard modus ponens chain. While logically equivalent in content, the stimulus has three premises including an explicit 'unless' construction; this has the same three steps but lacks the 'unless' framing that defines the structure. More importantly, the conclusion ('rejected') differs in nature from the stimulus's conclusion ('cannot be published').
explanations.C: Only two premises (only if + factual denial = modus tollens). The stimulus has three premises. Premise-count mismatch.
explanations.D: Disjunctive syllogism — completely different logical form from the stimulus's conditional chain.
explanations.E: Three premises but the reasoning is modus tollens applied to the 'unless' (unless funding → cannot proceed; has not proceeded; therefore no funding). The stimulus affirms the 'unless' condition (no control group) and chains forward; this denies the consequent and chains backward.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus employs a universal negative (No A are B) combined with a particular premise (x is A) to yield a particular negative conclusion (x is not B). Distractors substitute 'some' for 'no' or invert the subject and predicate of the universal premise, trapping students who scan loosely.
lr.stimulus: No ethical investment fund holds shares in companies that manufacture landmines. The Verdant Growth Fund is an ethical investment fund. Therefore, the Verdant Growth Fund does not hold shares in any company that manufactures landmines.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No peer-reviewed journal publishes articles that lack empirical support. The Annals of Cognitive Science is a peer-reviewed journal. Therefore, the Annals of Cognitive Science does not publish articles lacking empirical support.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some ethical funds avoid fossil fuel stocks. The Verdant Growth Fund is an ethical fund. Therefore, the Verdant Growth Fund may avoid fossil fuel stocks.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No fund that holds landmine stocks has been certified as ethical. The Verdant Growth Fund holds no landmine stocks. Therefore, the Verdant Growth Fund can be certified as ethical.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All ethical funds are transparent about their holdings. The Verdant Growth Fund is transparent about its holdings. Therefore, the Verdant Growth Fund is an ethical fund.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No investment fund is both ethical and profitable without compromise. The Verdant Growth Fund is profitable without compromise. Therefore, the Verdant Growth Fund is not ethical.

explanations.correct: The stimulus uses: No A are B (universal negative); x is A; therefore x is not B. Choice A follows the same form: No peer-reviewed journal publishes unsupported articles; Annals is peer-reviewed; therefore Annals does not publish unsupported articles.
explanations.A: Correct. Universal negative ('no peer-reviewed journal…') plus particular affirmative ('Annals is a peer-reviewed journal') yields particular negative conclusion. Identical structure.
explanations.B: Uses 'some' instead of 'no,' making the universal premise a particular affirmative. The conclusion is accordingly weakened to 'may,' creating a strength mismatch with the stimulus's certain conclusion.
explanations.C: Inverts the subject and predicate: the universal premise is 'No fund with landmine stocks is ethical' (no B are A), while the particular premise affirms the predicate (holds no landmine stocks), not the subject. This commits a structural inversion and is actually invalid reasoning (denying the antecedent).
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent: all ethical funds are transparent; Verdant is transparent; therefore Verdant is ethical. This is an invalid inference and differs structurally from the valid universal negative reasoning in the stimulus.
explanations.E: Uses 'no A are both B and C' — a different universal negative form. The particular premise denies one conjunct to conclude the other conjunct is absent. Different structure from the stimulus's simpler no-A-are-B form.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus uses a conditional with a necessary condition ('only if') plus modus tollens. One distractor uses 'only if' correctly but commits modus ponens (affirming the antecedent of the derived conditional), which is invalid. Students must carefully distinguish sufficient from necessary conditions.
lr.stimulus: A renewable energy project receives federal subsidies only if it meets the efficiency threshold established by the Energy Department. The solar installation at Pine Ridge did not meet that efficiency threshold. Therefore, the Pine Ridge installation does not receive federal subsidies.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A pharmaceutical drug is approved for sale only if it passes clinical trials administered by a licensed body. The drug Varentix did not pass such clinical trials. Therefore, Varentix is not approved for sale.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A renewable energy project meets the efficiency threshold only if it uses certified components. The Pine Ridge installation uses certified components. Therefore, it meets the efficiency threshold.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a project receives federal subsidies, it must report its energy output annually. The Pine Ridge project does not report its energy output annually. Therefore, it does not receive federal subsidies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All projects that meet the efficiency threshold are eligible for federal subsidies. The Pine Ridge project meets the efficiency threshold. Therefore, the Pine Ridge project is eligible for federal subsidies.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Federal subsidies are granted only to projects approved by the regional board. This project was approved by the regional board. Therefore, this project will receive federal subsidies.

explanations.correct: The stimulus: receives subsidies only if meets threshold → (receives subsidies → meets threshold); did not meet threshold (not Q); therefore does not receive subsidies (not P). This is modus tollens via 'only if.' Choice A: approved only if passes trials → (approved → passes trials); did not pass trials (not Q); therefore not approved (not P). Identical structure.
explanations.A: Correct. 'Only if' creates a necessary condition; denial of that condition via modus tollens yields the conclusion. Premise count, conditional direction, and conclusion strength all match.
explanations.B: Same 'only if' vocabulary but commits the fallacy of affirming the consequent. The 'only if' makes passing clinical trials necessary for approval; meeting the threshold is affirmed; concluding approval follows is invalid. The stimulus is valid; this choice is not.
explanations.C: This is straightforward modus tollens on a sufficient-condition conditional ('if receives subsidies → reports output'; does not report; therefore does not receive). Valid but different structure: the conditional direction differs from the stimulus's 'only if' (where the necessary condition is what is denied).
explanations.D: Universal instantiation (all meeting threshold are eligible; Pine Ridge meets threshold; therefore eligible). Affirms the antecedent of a sufficient-condition universal, not a necessary-condition 'only if.' Different logical form.
explanations.E: Affirms the consequent: subsidies only if approved by board (approved → ??? — actually, 'only if approved' means receives subsidies → approved by board); was approved; therefore will receive subsidies. This affirms the consequent and is invalid reasoning.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus uses a disjunctive syllogism (A ∨ B; ¬A; ∴ B), which requires the student to formalize the argument before scanning answer choices. Several distractors share surface topic similarity or use a similar conclusion but differ in logical form (e.g., conditional rather than disjunctive structure), making it moderately challenging.
lr.stimulus: The contamination in the reservoir originated either from agricultural runoff or from a malfunctioning treatment facility. Investigators have confirmed that there was no agricultural runoff during the relevant period. Therefore, the contamination must have originated from the malfunctioning treatment facility.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The budget shortfall was caused either by declining tax revenue or by increased municipal spending. Since increased municipal spending has been ruled out by auditors, the shortfall must have been caused by declining tax revenue.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If the treatment facility malfunctioned, then contamination would enter the reservoir. The facility did malfunction, so contamination must have entered the reservoir.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Agricultural runoff typically causes reservoir contamination. Because there was significant agricultural activity upstream, the reservoir contamination was most likely caused by runoff.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The contamination in the reservoir could not have come from the treatment facility unless the facility had malfunctioned. The facility did not malfunction, so the contamination must have come from somewhere other than the facility.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whenever both agricultural runoff and treatment-facility failures occur simultaneously, reservoir contamination is inevitable. Both events occurred, so the reservoir became contaminated.

explanations.correct: The stimulus has the form: A ∨ B; ¬A; ∴ B (disjunctive syllogism). Choice A matches exactly: either declining tax revenue (A) or increased spending (B) caused the shortfall; increased spending has been ruled out (¬B... wait — ¬B here is 'spending ruled out,' which parallels ¬A in the stimulus); therefore declining tax revenue is responsible (A). The structure is: X ∨ Y; ¬Y; ∴ X — a clean disjunctive syllogism with the same two-premise structure and a necessary conclusion ('must have been').
explanations.A: Correct. Matches the disjunctive syllogism perfectly: two exclusive alternatives, one is eliminated, therefore the other must be the cause. The conclusion's modal force ('must have been') also matches the stimulus.
explanations.B: Wrong structure. This is modus ponens (If P then Q; P; ∴ Q), not a disjunctive syllogism. It introduces a conditional premise that does not appear in the stimulus.
explanations.C: Wrong structure and wrong strength. This uses an analogical/probabilistic inference from general tendencies ('typically causes') to a 'most likely' conclusion. The stimulus has two exhaustive alternatives and reaches a necessary conclusion, not a probabilistic one.
explanations.D: Wrong structure. This is modus tollens (A → B; ¬B; ∴ ¬A), applied to a conditional derived from the disjunct. It also reaches a weaker, open-ended conclusion ('somewhere other than the facility') rather than identifying a specific positive cause.
explanations.E: Wrong structure. This is a conjunctive sufficient condition (A ∧ B → C; A ∧ B; ∴ C) — modus ponens with a conjunctive antecedent. There is no disjunction and no elimination of alternatives.

lr.difficultyReason: Four-step chain with a biconditional hinge and modus tollens: All A are B; every B has C; C iff D; the specimen does not have D; therefore it cannot be A. Students must process a universal, a universal, a biconditional, and a negated particular before concluding with necessity. Traps preserve three of the four structural features while reversing one.
lr.stimulus: Every case of bacterial meningitis involves inflammation of the meninges. Any patient with inflammation of the meninges exhibits elevated cerebrospinal protein. A patient exhibits elevated cerebrospinal protein if, and only if, a lumbar puncture yields a cloudy sample. The lumbar puncture performed on this patient yielded a clear sample. It follows that this patient cannot have bacterial meningitis.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in the argument above is most parallel to that in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every genuine Ming porcelain contains kaolin clay from Jingdezhen. Any object containing kaolin clay from Jingdezhen shows a distinctive thermoluminescence signature. An object shows a distinctive thermoluminescence signature if, and only if, its firing temperature exceeded 1300 degrees Celsius. The firing temperature of the disputed vase did not exceed 1300 degrees Celsius. It follows that the disputed vase cannot be a genuine Ming porcelain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every genuine Ming porcelain contains kaolin clay from Jingdezhen. Most objects containing kaolin clay from Jingdezhen show a distinctive thermoluminescence signature. An object shows a distinctive thermoluminescence signature if, and only if, its firing temperature exceeded 1300 degrees Celsius. The disputed vase did not exceed 1300 degrees Celsius. So the disputed vase is probably not genuine Ming porcelain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every genuine Ming porcelain contains kaolin clay from Jingdezhen. Any object containing kaolin clay from Jingdezhen shows a distinctive thermoluminescence signature. The disputed vase shows a distinctive thermoluminescence signature. It follows that the disputed vase is a genuine Ming porcelain.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every genuine Ming porcelain contains kaolin clay from Jingdezhen. Any object containing kaolin clay from Jingdezhen shows a distinctive thermoluminescence signature. An object shows a distinctive thermoluminescence signature only if its firing temperature exceeded 1300 degrees Celsius. The firing temperature of the disputed vase did not exceed 1300 degrees Celsius. So the disputed vase may not be genuine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every genuine Ming porcelain contains kaolin clay from Jingdezhen. The disputed vase does not contain kaolin clay from Jingdezhen. It follows that the disputed vase cannot be a genuine Ming porcelain.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: ∀x(Ax → Bx); ∀x(Bx → Cx); ∀x(Cx ↔ Dx); ¬Dp; ∴ ¬Ap (with necessity). (A) replicates each step — two universals, a biconditional, a negated particular, and a necessity conclusion — simply reskinned in the porcelain domain.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Weakens the second premise from 'any/every' to 'most' and weakens the conclusion from necessity to probability — two quantifier/modal mismatches.
explanations.C: Only three premises, and the third step affirms the consequent rather than running modus tollens through a biconditional. Structurally reversed.
explanations.D: Replaces the biconditional with a one-way conditional ('only if') and softens the conclusion to 'may not' — both modal force and connective strength are off.
explanations.E: Two premises, not four; skips the inflammation and biconditional steps entirely.

lr.difficultyReason: Four-step mixed-quantifier argument: some A are B; all B require C; C iff D; x is both A and B; therefore x probably requires D. The argument moves from existential to universal to biconditional and ends with a hedged conclusion that tracks the 'probably' licensed by instantiation from an existential base.
lr.stimulus: Some medical studies that yield statistically significant results nevertheless have low replication rates. Every study with a low replication rate requires independent pre-registration to warrant continued funding. A study requires independent pre-registration if, and only if, its effect size falls below a conventional threshold. The Harmon study yielded statistically significant results and has a low replication rate. Therefore, the Harmon study's effect size probably falls below the conventional threshold.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some charitable organizations that report high donor retention nevertheless show thin program margins. Every organization with thin program margins requires a restructuring plan to maintain its rating. An organization requires a restructuring plan if, and only if, its overhead ratio exceeds a conventional threshold. The Ardent Fund reports high donor retention and shows thin program margins. Therefore, the Ardent Fund's overhead ratio probably exceeds the conventional threshold.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most charitable organizations that report high donor retention show thin program margins. Every organization with thin program margins requires a restructuring plan. An organization requires a restructuring plan if, and only if, its overhead ratio exceeds a conventional threshold. The Ardent Fund reports high donor retention. Therefore, the Ardent Fund's overhead ratio exceeds the conventional threshold.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some charitable organizations that report high donor retention nevertheless show thin program margins. Most organizations with thin program margins require a restructuring plan. An organization requires a restructuring plan only if its overhead ratio exceeds a conventional threshold. The Ardent Fund reports high donor retention. So the Ardent Fund's overhead ratio probably exceeds the conventional threshold.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some charitable organizations that report high donor retention nevertheless show thin program margins. Every organization with thin program margins requires a restructuring plan. An organization requires a restructuring plan if, and only if, its overhead ratio exceeds a conventional threshold. The Ardent Fund's overhead ratio exceeds the conventional threshold. Therefore, the Ardent Fund probably shows thin program margins.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every charitable organization that reports high donor retention shows thin program margins. Every organization with thin program margins requires a restructuring plan. An organization requires a restructuring plan if, and only if, its overhead ratio exceeds a conventional threshold. The Ardent Fund reports high donor retention and shows thin program margins. Therefore, the Ardent Fund's overhead ratio exceeds the conventional threshold.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: ∃x(Ax ∧ Bx); ∀x(Bx → Cx); ∀x(Cx ↔ Dx); Ah ∧ Bh; ∴ probably Dh. (A) preserves all four elements: existential opener, universal middle, biconditional hinge, instantiation of both openers, hedged conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Converts the existential to 'most' and drops the hedge, then omits the second instantiation ('shows thin program margins'). Two shifts off parallel.
explanations.C: Weakens the second premise from 'every' to 'most' and the third from biconditional to one-way conditional.
explanations.D: Same premise set, but the conclusion reverses direction — it instantiates the consequent to derive the antecedent side, which is structurally a different move.
explanations.E: Opens with 'every' instead of 'some' and drops the hedge — conclusion shifts from probable to definite.

lr.difficultyReason: Four-link contrapositive chain: A→B, B→C, C→D, ¬D, ∴ ¬A. Students must run modus tollens through three conditionals in succession. Traps shorten the chain, reverse a single step, or swap quantifier strength on one premise.
lr.stimulus: If a currency union permits unlimited capital mobility, then its members must coordinate fiscal policy. If members must coordinate fiscal policy, then each member will need to cede some budgetary sovereignty. If each member cedes some budgetary sovereignty, then a central authority will have to ratify national budgets. No central authority has the power to ratify the member states' national budgets. Therefore, this currency union does not permit unlimited capital mobility.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a manuscript was typeset by the Aldine press, then it uses a Bembo-derived typeface. If it uses a Bembo-derived typeface, then its lowercase 'e' carries a slanted crossbar. If its lowercase 'e' carries a slanted crossbar, then its ink will contain a distinctive iron-gall residue. This manuscript's ink does not contain iron-gall residue. Therefore, this manuscript was not typeset by the Aldine press.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a manuscript was typeset by the Aldine press, then it uses a Bembo-derived typeface. If it uses a Bembo-derived typeface, then its lowercase 'e' carries a slanted crossbar. This manuscript's lowercase 'e' does not carry a slanted crossbar. Therefore, this manuscript was not typeset by the Aldine press.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a manuscript was typeset by the Aldine press, then it uses a Bembo-derived typeface. If it uses a Bembo-derived typeface, then its lowercase 'e' carries a slanted crossbar. Most Bembo-derived manuscripts contain iron-gall residue. This manuscript's ink does not contain iron-gall residue. Therefore, this manuscript was probably not typeset by the Aldine press.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a manuscript was typeset by the Aldine press, then it uses a Bembo-derived typeface. If it uses a Bembo-derived typeface, then its lowercase 'e' carries a slanted crossbar. If its lowercase 'e' carries a slanted crossbar, then its ink contains iron-gall residue. This manuscript's ink contains iron-gall residue. Therefore, this manuscript was typeset by the Aldine press.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If a manuscript was typeset by the Aldine press, then it uses a Bembo-derived typeface. If it uses a Bembo-derived typeface, then its lowercase 'e' carries a slanted crossbar. If its lowercase 'e' carries a slanted crossbar, then its ink contains iron-gall residue. This manuscript was not typeset by the Aldine press. Therefore, its ink does not contain iron-gall residue.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A→B; B→C; C→D; ¬D; ∴ ¬A. (A) matches all four premises with the same conditional directions and ends with modus tollens through the full chain to deny the antecedent of the first premise.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Only three premises — the chain is shortened by one link, so the structure is three-step tollens, not four-step.
explanations.C: Replaces one premise with a 'most' quantifier and hedges the conclusion to 'probably' — two features off parallel.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent at the end — this is an invalid move, and the stimulus is valid, so the parallel fails.
explanations.E: Denies the antecedent to derive denial of the consequent — also invalid, and runs the chain in the reverse direction.

lr.difficultyReason: Universal disjunctive plus a 'most' elimination plus instantiation, ending with a hedged positive conclusion. Four components: a universal conditional into a disjunction, a most-quantified negation of one disjunct, a particular instance, and a 'likely' conclusion on the surviving disjunct.
lr.stimulus: Every contract that is unconscionable at the time of signing is either procedurally defective or substantively one-sided. Most contracts that are unconscionable at the time of signing are not procedurally defective. The Marsden agreement was unconscionable at the time of its signing. Therefore, the Marsden agreement is likely substantively one-sided.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every alloy that fractures under cyclic loading is either crystallographically flawed or chemically contaminated. Most alloys that fracture under cyclic loading are not crystallographically flawed. The bracket from the Hargrove bridge fractured under cyclic loading. Therefore, the bracket is likely chemically contaminated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every alloy that fractures under cyclic loading is either crystallographically flawed or chemically contaminated. Most alloys that fracture under cyclic loading are chemically contaminated. The bracket from the Hargrove bridge fractured under cyclic loading. Therefore, the bracket is chemically contaminated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most alloys that fracture under cyclic loading are either crystallographically flawed or chemically contaminated. Most such alloys are not crystallographically flawed. The bracket from the Hargrove bridge fractured under cyclic loading. Therefore, the bracket is likely chemically contaminated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every alloy that fractures under cyclic loading is either crystallographically flawed or chemically contaminated. No alloy that fractures under cyclic loading is crystallographically flawed. The bracket from the Hargrove bridge fractured under cyclic loading. Therefore, the bracket is chemically contaminated.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every alloy that fractures under cyclic loading is both crystallographically flawed and chemically contaminated. Most alloys that fracture under cyclic loading are not crystallographically flawed. The bracket from the Hargrove bridge fractured under cyclic loading. Therefore, the bracket is likely chemically contaminated.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: ∀x(Ax → (Bx ∨ Cx)); most A are ¬B; a is A; ∴ a is likely C. (A) matches each piece: a universal with a disjunctive consequent, a 'most' negation of one disjunct, an instantiation, and a hedged positive conclusion on the remaining disjunct.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Runs the 'most' in the opposite direction (most A are C, not most A are ¬B) and drops the hedge.
explanations.C: Softens the first premise from 'every' to 'most', weakening the universal backbone of the argument.
explanations.D: Replaces 'most' with 'no' — a universal negative rather than a hedged majority — and strengthens the conclusion from 'likely' to categorical.
explanations.E: Turns the disjunction into a conjunction, so the second premise (most aren't B) contradicts the first rather than narrowing it.

lr.difficultyReason: Biconditional plus chain plus existential generalization: A ↔ B; B → C; some A are D; therefore some D are C. Students must combine a biconditional (treat as A → B), a conditional, and an existential subject to yield an existential conclusion — an inference type that hinges on carrying the existential through two universals.
lr.stimulus: A wetland is classified as a vernal pool if, and only if, it dries completely for part of each year. Every wetland that dries completely for part of each year supports at least one obligate indicator species. Some vernal pools in the Redclay reserve also exhibit fairy-shrimp egg banks. Therefore, some wetlands in the Redclay reserve that exhibit fairy-shrimp egg banks support at least one obligate indicator species.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in the argument above is most parallel to that in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A language is classified as tonal if, and only if, it uses pitch to distinguish lexical meaning. Every language that uses pitch to distinguish lexical meaning has at least one minimal tone pair. Some tonal languages in the Sahel survey also employ vowel harmony. Therefore, some languages in the Sahel survey that employ vowel harmony have at least one minimal tone pair.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A language is classified as tonal if, and only if, it uses pitch to distinguish lexical meaning. Most languages that use pitch to distinguish lexical meaning have at least one minimal tone pair. Some tonal languages in the Sahel survey also employ vowel harmony. Therefore, most languages in the Sahel survey that employ vowel harmony have at least one minimal tone pair.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A language is classified as tonal only if it uses pitch to distinguish lexical meaning. Every language that uses pitch to distinguish lexical meaning has at least one minimal tone pair. Some tonal languages in the Sahel survey employ vowel harmony. Therefore, some languages in the Sahel survey that employ vowel harmony have at least one minimal tone pair.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A language is classified as tonal if, and only if, it uses pitch to distinguish lexical meaning. Every language that uses pitch to distinguish lexical meaning has at least one minimal tone pair. Every tonal language in the Sahel survey employs vowel harmony. Therefore, every language in the Sahel survey that employs vowel harmony has at least one minimal tone pair.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A language is classified as tonal if, and only if, it uses pitch to distinguish lexical meaning. Every language that has at least one minimal tone pair uses pitch to distinguish lexical meaning. Some tonal languages in the Sahel survey employ vowel harmony. Therefore, some languages in the Sahel survey that employ vowel harmony are tonal.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: Ax ↔ Bx; ∀x(Bx → Cx); ∃x(Ax ∧ Dx restricted to region R); ∴ ∃x(Dx ∧ Cx in R). (A) preserves the biconditional opener, the universal second step, the existential subject, and the existential conclusion at the same scope.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Downgrades the second premise from 'every' to 'most' and the conclusion from existential to 'most', changing two features.
explanations.C: Replaces the biconditional with a one-way 'only if' conditional — the biconditional strength is lost.
explanations.D: Strengthens both the existential premise and conclusion to universals ('every'), changing quantifier type.
explanations.E: Reverses the direction of the second premise, then draws a conclusion about being tonal rather than about the minimal-tone-pair property.

lr.difficultyReason: Four-step argument mixing two universal conditionals, a 'most' generalization over the chain's endpoint, an instantiation, and a hedged conclusion. Students must recognize that the conclusion's 'probably' is licensed not by 'most' alone but by chaining two universals before meeting the 'most' premise.
lr.stimulus: Any operating system that ships with the latest kernel patch supports hardware-level memory tagging. Every system that supports hardware-level memory tagging can run the new sandboxed runtime. Most systems that can run the new sandboxed runtime pass the FlexBench security audit. The server in our datacenter ships with the latest kernel patch. Therefore, the server in our datacenter will probably pass the FlexBench security audit.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any vineyard that uses biodynamic practices maintains a closed compost cycle. Every vineyard that maintains a closed compost cycle meets the Demeter soil standard. Most vineyards that meet the Demeter soil standard earn an export license. The Salin estate uses biodynamic practices. Therefore, the Salin estate will probably earn an export license.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any vineyard that uses biodynamic practices maintains a closed compost cycle. Every vineyard that maintains a closed compost cycle meets the Demeter soil standard. Every vineyard that meets the Demeter soil standard earns an export license. The Salin estate uses biodynamic practices. Therefore, the Salin estate will probably earn an export license.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most vineyards that use biodynamic practices maintain a closed compost cycle. Every vineyard that maintains a closed compost cycle meets the Demeter soil standard. Most vineyards that meet the Demeter soil standard earn an export license. The Salin estate uses biodynamic practices. Therefore, the Salin estate will earn an export license.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any vineyard that uses biodynamic practices maintains a closed compost cycle. Every vineyard that maintains a closed compost cycle meets the Demeter soil standard. Most vineyards that meet the Demeter soil standard earn an export license. The Salin estate earns an export license. Therefore, the Salin estate probably uses biodynamic practices.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any vineyard that uses biodynamic practices maintains a closed compost cycle. Every vineyard that maintains a closed compost cycle meets the Demeter soil standard. Most vineyards that earn an export license meet the Demeter soil standard. The Salin estate uses biodynamic practices. Therefore, the Salin estate will probably earn an export license.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: ∀x(Ax → Bx); ∀x(Bx → Cx); most Cx are Dx; Aa; ∴ probably Da. (A) mirrors all four steps: two universal conditionals forming a chain, a 'most' generalization over the chain endpoint, an instantiation of A, and a hedged conclusion of D.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Strengthens the third premise from 'most' to 'every' while keeping the conclusion hedged — the 'probably' no longer matches the now-universal chain.
explanations.C: Weakens the first premise from 'any' to 'most' and promotes the conclusion from 'probably' to categorical.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent at the end of the chain — concludes about the antecedent from the endpoint, reversing direction.
explanations.E: Reverses the direction of the third premise (most D are C, not most C are D) — cannot yield the same inference.

lr.difficultyReason: Four-step argument combining a universal conditional, a contrapositive observation, and a disjunctive syllogism with a particular in one of the disjuncts. The contrapositive move eliminates one disjunct and forces the positive conclusion on the other.
lr.stimulus: Every Indo-European language retains at least one trace of laryngeal consonants in its oldest strata. The language recorded on the Boglath tablets shows no trace of laryngeal consonants in any stratum. The Boglath language is either Indo-European or Pre-Hurrian. Therefore, the Boglath language is Pre-Hurrian.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every true comet released from the Oort cloud exhibits a measurable hyperbolic excess velocity at its first observed perihelion. The object designated 2031 FQ exhibited no measurable hyperbolic excess velocity at its first observed perihelion. The object is either a true comet released from the Oort cloud or a Jupiter-family interloper. Therefore, the object is a Jupiter-family interloper.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most true comets released from the Oort cloud exhibit a measurable hyperbolic excess velocity at first perihelion. The object designated 2031 FQ exhibited no such velocity. The object is either a true comet released from the Oort cloud or a Jupiter-family interloper. Therefore, the object is probably a Jupiter-family interloper.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every true comet released from the Oort cloud exhibits a measurable hyperbolic excess velocity at first perihelion. The object designated 2031 FQ exhibited a measurable hyperbolic excess velocity at first perihelion. The object is either a true comet released from the Oort cloud or a Jupiter-family interloper. Therefore, the object is a true comet released from the Oort cloud.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every true comet released from the Oort cloud exhibits a measurable hyperbolic excess velocity at first perihelion. The object designated 2031 FQ exhibited no measurable hyperbolic excess velocity. Therefore, the object is not a true comet released from the Oort cloud.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every true comet released from the Oort cloud exhibits a measurable hyperbolic excess velocity at first perihelion. The object designated 2031 FQ is a Jupiter-family interloper. The object is either a true comet released from the Oort cloud or a Jupiter-family interloper. Therefore, the object exhibited no measurable hyperbolic excess velocity.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: ∀x(Ax → Bx); ¬Ba; A∨C for a; ∴ C for a. (A) matches: a universal conditional, a negated particular consequent, a binary disjunction containing the class, and a positive conclusion on the alternative disjunct.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Weakens the first premise from 'every' to 'most' and hedges the conclusion to 'probably' — two structural features change.
explanations.C: Affirms the consequent and concludes on the wrong disjunct (Indo-European analog rather than the alternative) — reverses direction.
explanations.D: Only two premises, ending at the modus tollens negation; the disjunctive-syllogism step is missing entirely.
explanations.E: Uses the disjunction with an asserted disjunct as a premise rather than deriving it, and concludes about the consequent property, not the category.

lr.difficultyReason: Four-step analogical argument with an embedded universal conditional and a hedged conclusion. Two cases share two properties; a universal links those properties to a third; one case has the third property; the conclusion transfers the property to the other case with 'likely'.
lr.stimulus: The reform movements of eighteenth-century Denmark and eighteenth-century Tuscany shared two features: both were led by enlightened monarchs, and both enacted agrarian reforms before any constitutional reform. Every eighteenth-century reform movement that was led by an enlightened monarch and enacted agrarian reforms before constitutional reforms eventually produced a durable legal code. The Danish movement eventually produced a durable legal code. Therefore, the Tuscan movement likely produced a durable legal code as well.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The composition curricula of Rosedale Academy and Finch Academy shared two features: both were designed by former novelists, and both sequenced revision instruction before stylistic instruction. Every composition curriculum designed by a former novelist that sequenced revision before stylistic instruction eventually produced a signature student magazine. Rosedale's curriculum eventually produced a signature student magazine. Therefore, Finch's curriculum likely produced a signature student magazine as well.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The composition curricula of Rosedale Academy and Finch Academy shared two features. Every composition curriculum designed by a former novelist that sequenced revision before stylistic instruction eventually produced a signature student magazine. Rosedale's curriculum eventually produced a signature student magazine. Therefore, Finch's curriculum produced a signature student magazine.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The composition curricula of Rosedale Academy and Finch Academy shared two features: both were designed by former novelists, and both sequenced revision instruction before stylistic instruction. Most composition curricula designed by former novelists that sequence revision before stylistic instruction eventually produce a signature student magazine. Rosedale's curriculum eventually produced a signature student magazine. Therefore, Finch's curriculum produced a signature student magazine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The composition curricula of Rosedale Academy and Finch Academy shared two features: both were designed by former novelists, and both sequenced revision instruction before stylistic instruction. Every composition curriculum designed by a former novelist that sequenced revision before stylistic instruction eventually produced a signature student magazine. Finch's curriculum eventually produced a signature student magazine. Therefore, Rosedale's curriculum likely produced a signature student magazine — before Finch's did.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The composition curricula of Rosedale Academy and Finch Academy share several features. Rosedale's curriculum produced a signature student magazine. Therefore, Finch's curriculum likely produced a signature student magazine as well.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: X and Y share properties P and Q; ∀z((Pz ∧ Qz) → Rz); X has R; ∴ Y likely has R. (A) mirrors the shared-property opener, the universal conditional over both properties, the single-case confirmation of R, and the hedged transfer to Y.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Drops the explicit naming of the two shared features and strips the hedge from the conclusion — two structural gaps.
explanations.C: Weakens the universal premise from 'every' to 'most' and promotes the conclusion from 'likely' to categorical.
explanations.D: Keeps all premises intact but adds an extra temporal claim ('before Finch's did') to the conclusion — an unlicensed addition.
explanations.E: Vague analogical premise ('several features') and no universal conditional — drops two of the four structural elements.

lr.difficultyReason: Nested-conditional argument: if all A are B, then C; C is false; therefore some A are not B. Four structural elements to match — a conditional whose antecedent is itself a universal, a contrapositive application, the existential generalization licensed by the negation of a universal, and the explicit 'at least one' phrasing.
lr.stimulus: If every eligible voter in Callenhurst registered by the deadline, then the preliminary turnout estimate would exceed 40,000. The preliminary turnout estimate does not exceed 40,000. Therefore, at least one eligible voter in Callenhurst did not register by the deadline.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in the argument above is most parallel to that in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If every licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge completed the refresher course, then the continuing-education log would contain over 400 entries. The continuing-education log does not contain over 400 entries. Therefore, at least one licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge did not complete the refresher course.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If every licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge completed the refresher course, then the continuing-education log would contain over 400 entries. The continuing-education log contains over 400 entries. Therefore, every licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge completed the refresher course.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If most licensed pharmacists at Greerbridge completed the refresher course, then the continuing-education log would contain over 400 entries. The continuing-education log does not contain over 400 entries. Therefore, most licensed pharmacists at Greerbridge did not complete the refresher course.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If every licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge completed the refresher course, then the continuing-education log would contain over 400 entries. At least one licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge did not complete the refresher course. Therefore, the continuing-education log does not contain over 400 entries.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If every licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge completed the refresher course, then the continuing-education log would contain over 400 entries. The continuing-education log does not contain over 400 entries. Therefore, no licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge completed the refresher course.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: (∀x Ax → Bx) → C; ¬C; ∴ ∃x(Ax ∧ ¬Bx). (A) replicates the nested conditional whose antecedent is a universal, runs modus tollens to deny the universal antecedent, and correctly draws the existential ('at least one ... did not') conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Affirms the consequent — concludes the universal from the numerical fact being true, an invalid move.
explanations.C: Replaces 'every' with 'most' in both antecedent and conclusion, so the negation of a 'most' claim is drawn instead of an existential.
explanations.D: Runs the conditional in the opposite direction: denies the universal to conclude the consequent's negation, reversing cause and effect.
explanations.E: Overshoots from 'at least one did not' to 'no one did' — a quantifier strength error at the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Four-step conjunctive-consequent plus biconditional structure: A → (B ∧ C); ¬B; B ↔ D; ∴ ¬A and ¬D. Students must derive two distinct negations — one by contrapositive of a conjunction and one through the biconditional — both with necessity.
lr.stimulus: If a symphony is genuinely by Grazia, it has both a modulation to the flat mediant in its exposition and a triple-meter trio in its scherzo. The symphony on this score does not modulate to the flat mediant in its exposition. A symphony contains a modulation to the flat mediant in its exposition if, and only if, its autograph manuscript bears a triadic cipher in the margin. It follows that the symphony on this score is not genuinely by Grazia, and its autograph manuscript does not bear a triadic cipher in the margin.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a coin is a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, it has both a quadriga on the obverse and a facing Arethusa on the reverse. The coin in this collection does not bear a quadriga on the obverse. A coin bears a quadriga on the obverse if, and only if, its die has a microscopic anchor mark at the seven o'clock position. It follows that the coin in this collection is not a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, and its die does not have a microscopic anchor mark at the seven o'clock position.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a coin is a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, it has either a quadriga on the obverse or a facing Arethusa on the reverse. The coin in this collection does not bear a quadriga. A coin bears a quadriga if, and only if, its die has a microscopic anchor mark at the seven o'clock position. It follows that the coin is not a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, and its die does not have a microscopic anchor mark.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a coin is a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, it has both a quadriga on the obverse and a facing Arethusa on the reverse. The coin in this collection does not bear a quadriga on the obverse. A coin bears a quadriga on the obverse only if its die has a microscopic anchor mark at the seven o'clock position. It follows that the coin is not a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, and its die probably lacks the anchor mark.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a coin is a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, it has both a quadriga on the obverse and a facing Arethusa on the reverse. The coin in this collection does not bear a facing Arethusa on the reverse. A coin bears a facing Arethusa if, and only if, its die has a microscopic anchor mark at the seven o'clock position. It follows that the coin bears a quadriga on the obverse, and its die does not have a microscopic anchor mark.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If a coin is a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, it has both a quadriga on the obverse and a facing Arethusa on the reverse. The coin in this collection is not a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm. A coin bears a quadriga if, and only if, its die has a microscopic anchor mark. It follows that the coin does not bear a quadriga, and its die does not have the anchor mark.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A → (B ∧ C); ¬B; B ↔ D; ∴ ¬A ∧ ¬D. (A) preserves each step: a conditional with a conjunctive consequent, a negated conjunct, a biconditional binding that conjunct to a fourth property, and a two-part necessary conclusion negating both A and D.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Converts the conjunction in the consequent to a disjunction — denying one disjunct no longer licenses denying the conditional's antecedent on its own.
explanations.C: Replaces the biconditional with a one-way 'only if' conditional and softens one half of the conclusion to 'probably', breaking both connective strength and modal match.
explanations.D: Runs the negation on the wrong conjunct (Arethusa, not quadriga), then draws an unlicensed positive conclusion that the coin bears a quadriga — an inversion of the stimulus's moves.
explanations.E: Uses ¬A as a premise rather than deriving it, then draws ¬B as a conclusion — running the conditional in the wrong direction (denying the antecedent to derive a negated conjunct).

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus uses a nested conditional chain (A→B, B→C, A; ∴C) embedded in dense medical prose. Answer choices share premise counts but differ in conditional direction or conclusion strength, requiring students to track all four structural criteria simultaneously.
lr.stimulus: Every patient who receives immunosuppressive therapy following a transplant must be monitored for opportunistic infections. Any patient monitored for opportunistic infections will have blood cultures drawn weekly. Harmon received immunosuppressive therapy following his recent transplant. Therefore, Harmon will have blood cultures drawn weekly.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All contracts signed under duress are voidable. Any voidable contract may be rescinded by the aggrieved party. The agreement Lena signed was signed under duress. Therefore, Lena may rescind the agreement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most investors who hold volatile assets diversify their portfolios. Anyone who diversifies holds bonds. Petra holds volatile assets. Therefore, Petra probably holds bonds.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any musician trained in counterpoint understands harmonic tension. Marcus understands harmonic tension. Therefore, Marcus was trained in counterpoint.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every species that loses habitat will decline in population. The spotted warbler has declined in population. Therefore, the spotted warbler must have lost habitat.

choices.label: E
choices.text: All employees who miss three consecutive shifts are placed on probation. Yolanda was placed on probation. Therefore, Yolanda must have missed three consecutive shifts.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: All A→B; All B→C; x is A; ∴ x is C. Choice A: All A→B (contracts signed under duress are voidable); All B→C (voidable contracts may be rescinded); Lena's contract is A; ∴ Lena may C. Identical three-premise conditional chain with universal quantifiers and a particular instantiation. Conclusion strength ('may rescind') matches the permitted/required language exactly.
explanations.A: Correct. Perfect structural match: universal conditional chain (A→B, B→C), particular instantiation, valid conclusion.
explanations.B: Strength-shift trap. Uses 'most' and 'probably' rather than universal quantifiers, changing the argument from deductive to inductive and weakening the conclusion.
explanations.C: Affirming-the-consequent trap. Two-premise structure with the wrong conditional direction: knows B, concludes A, which is invalid and structurally unlike the stimulus.
explanations.D: Modus tollens trap (invalid version). Concludes from effect back to cause using 'must have,' reversing the conditional direction of the stimulus.
explanations.E: Same trap as D — affirms the consequent. From 'placed on probation' it concludes the antecedent, the opposite conditional direction from the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: Disjunctive syllogism stimulus with a negated universal embedded in environmental prose. Distractors use apparent disjunctions but shift quantifier strength or introduce a third disjunct, requiring careful formalization.
lr.stimulus: Either the algal bloom in Lake Merin was caused by agricultural runoff or it was caused by thermal stratification. The bloom cannot have been caused by thermal stratification, because water temperature records show the lake was fully mixed throughout the season. Therefore, the algal bloom was caused by agricultural runoff.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The budget shortfall resulted either from reduced tax revenue or from increased expenditures. Increased expenditures did not occur, since all departmental budgets were frozen. Therefore, the shortfall resulted from reduced tax revenue.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The server failure was caused either by a hardware fault, a software bug, or a power surge. There was no power surge and no software bug. Therefore, the server failure was caused by a hardware fault.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The decline in bee populations is probably due to pesticide exposure or habitat loss. Habitat loss is the more likely explanation. Therefore, habitat loss is probably the primary cause.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If the disease spread through contaminated water, then the downstream villages would have been affected. The downstream villages were not affected. Therefore, the disease did not spread through contaminated water.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Either the artifact is a forgery or it dates to the Ming dynasty. Experts have authenticated it as genuine. Therefore, the artifact dates to the Ming dynasty.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A ∨ B; ¬B (established by evidence); ∴ A. Choice A: A ∨ B (reduced revenue or increased expenditures); ¬B (expenditures did not increase, established by evidence); ∴ A. Exact two-disjunct disjunctive syllogism with an evidentially grounded negation of one disjunct.
explanations.A: Correct. Two-disjunct exclusive disjunction, one disjunct eliminated by positive evidence, valid conclusion of the remaining disjunct.
explanations.B: Wrong premise count trap. Uses three disjuncts (A ∨ B ∨ C) rather than two, requiring elimination of two disjuncts. Structurally distinct from the stimulus.
explanations.C: Strength-shift trap. Uses 'probably' and comparative likelihood rather than categorical elimination, making the argument inductive rather than deductive.
explanations.D: Different argument form trap. This is modus tollens (A→B; ¬B; ∴¬A), not a disjunctive syllogism. No disjunction appears.
explanations.E: Same form but the negation is established differently — 'experts authenticated it as genuine' eliminates 'forgery' not by direct evidence of ¬A but by establishing the contradictory of A through testimony. Structurally close but the elimination method relies on an implicit double-negation rather than a direct factual claim, making A a cleaner structural match.

lr.difficultyReason: Contrapositive stimulus (modus tollens) in an ethics context. Multiple distractors use valid argument forms (modus ponens, disjunctive syllogism) that share premise-count but differ in conditional direction, punishing students who do not check direction.
lr.stimulus: If a public official acts in a manner that serves only private interests, then that official has violated the public trust. The inspector general did not violate the public trust. Therefore, the inspector general did not act in a manner that serves only private interests.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a compound is soluble in water, it will dissolve when placed in an aqueous solution. This compound did not dissolve when placed in an aqueous solution. Therefore, this compound is not soluble in water.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a regulation is enacted without public comment, it is procedurally invalid. This regulation was enacted without public comment. Therefore, this regulation is procedurally invalid.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a firm engages in predatory pricing, its competitors will suffer losses. Ralston's competitors have suffered losses. Therefore, Ralston has engaged in predatory pricing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either a treaty is ratified by the senate or it lacks legal force. This treaty lacks legal force. Therefore, this treaty was not ratified by the senate.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If an investment carries high risk, a prudent advisor will disclose that risk to clients. If a prudent advisor discloses risk to clients, the clients can make informed decisions. Fenchurch carries high-risk investments. Therefore, Fenchurch's clients can make informed decisions.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A→B; ¬B; ∴¬A (modus tollens). Choice A: If soluble→dissolves; did not dissolve (¬B); ∴ not soluble (¬A). Perfect structural match: single conditional premise, denial of consequent, denial of antecedent as conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Modus tollens: A→B; ¬B; ∴¬A. Two premises, same conditional direction, same conclusion strength.
explanations.B: Modus ponens trap. A→B; A; ∴B. Same premise count and conditional direction, but affirms the antecedent rather than denying the consequent — the opposite argument form.
explanations.C: Affirming-the-consequent trap. A→B; B; ∴A. Invalid argument that resembles modus tollens structurally but reverses which element is negated.
explanations.D: Disjunctive syllogism trap. A∨B; B; ∴¬A. Valid, but a different argument form entirely — no conditional premise appears.
explanations.E: Conditional chain (modus ponens on a chain) trap. A→B; B→C; A; ∴C. Three premises rather than two, and affirms rather than denies — structurally distinct.

lr.difficultyReason: Universal-to-particular syllogism (All A are B; All B are C; x is A; ∴ x is C) with quantifier-strength distractors. The correct answer must match on two universal premises plus a particular, and students must resist answers that use 'most' or 'some.'
lr.stimulus: Every treaty ratified by a two-thirds Senate majority becomes binding federal law. All binding federal law supersedes conflicting state statutes. The Meridian Convention was ratified by a two-thirds Senate majority. Therefore, the Meridian Convention supersedes any conflicting state statutes.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All peer-reviewed studies meet publication standards. All studies meeting publication standards may be cited in court proceedings. The Okafor study is peer-reviewed. Therefore, the Okafor study may be cited in court proceedings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most peer-reviewed studies meet high methodological standards. Any study meeting high standards can be cited authoritatively. The Brennan study is peer-reviewed. Therefore, the Brennan study can probably be cited authoritatively.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every federally listed endangered species receives habitat protections. The gray wolf is a federally listed endangered species. Therefore, the gray wolf receives habitat protections.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All organic compounds contain carbon. Benzene is an organic compound. Therefore, benzene contains carbon. Similarly, all aromatic compounds are organic, so all aromatic compounds contain carbon.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some legislative acts that pass with broad bipartisan support achieve lasting policy change. The Clean Air Act passed with broad bipartisan support. Therefore, the Clean Air Act may have achieved lasting policy change.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: All A→B; All B→C; x is A; ∴ x is C. Three premises, two universal conditionals, one particular instantiation. Choice A replicates this exactly with peer-reviewed → publication standards → citable; Okafor is peer-reviewed; ∴ Okafor is citable.
explanations.A: Correct. Two universal premises, one particular instantiation, deductively certain conclusion — perfect structural match.
explanations.B: Quantifier-shift trap. Uses 'most' and 'probably,' converting the argument from deductive to inductive. Fails on quantifier type and conclusion strength.
explanations.C: Wrong premise count trap. Only one universal premise (not two), making this a simple universal instantiation rather than a two-step chain.
explanations.D: Extended analogy trap. The argument chains correctly but then adds a second conclusion drawn from a new universal premise, making it structurally more complex than the two-chain stimulus.
explanations.E: Double quantifier-shift trap. Uses 'some' in the first premise and 'may have' in the conclusion — both weaker than the stimulus's universals and deductive conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Analogy stimulus with two structural similarities cited before a transferred conclusion. Distractors replicate the surface form (two similarities then a conclusion) but shift the direction of transfer or introduce a disanalogy, requiring careful tracking of analogy structure.
lr.stimulus: The economies of Valdoria and Seltham are similar in that both have export-dependent manufacturing sectors and both experience sharp contractions when global demand falls. Valdoria successfully stabilized its economy by implementing countercyclical fiscal policy. Therefore, Seltham would likely stabilize its economy by implementing countercyclical fiscal policy.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Compounds X and Y both have hexagonal molecular structures and both exhibit high thermal stability. Compound X became superconducting when doped with nitrogen. Therefore, compound Y would likely become superconducting when doped with nitrogen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Raptors and owls both hunt prey and both have sharp talons. Because owls are nocturnal, raptors are probably also nocturnal hunters.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Larkspur Bridge and the Fenwick Viaduct were both built in the 1920s and both use riveted steel construction. The Fenwick Viaduct required reinforcement after fifty years. Therefore, the Larkspur Bridge may also require reinforcement, since it shares those structural features.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients with condition A and condition B both show elevated inflammatory markers and both respond to corticosteroids. A patient presenting with only elevated inflammatory markers is therefore likely to have both condition A and condition B.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Silvopasture and agroforestry both integrate trees with agriculture and both improve soil health. Since silvopasture has been shown to sequester carbon effectively, agroforestry has also been shown to sequester carbon effectively.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: X and Y share property P and property Q; X has result R; ∴ Y would likely have result R. Choice A: Compounds X and Y share hexagonal structure (P) and thermal stability (Q); X became superconducting under condition R; ∴ Y would likely become superconducting under R. Exact analogical structure with two shared properties and a transferred conclusion using 'likely.'
explanations.A: Correct. Two shared structural properties cited, a result observed in one entity, and the same result projected onto the other entity with matching 'likely' hedging.
explanations.B: Direction-of-transfer trap. The two properties cited (hunting prey, sharp talons) belong to both, but the conclusion (nocturnal) is transferred from owls to raptors based on a property of owls alone — the analogy breaks because raptors are diurnal, and the structure imports a property not shared as a similarity.
explanations.C: Close match but conclusion-strength shift. Uses 'may also require' (weaker hedge) vs. 'would likely.' Also, the two shared properties (age, construction type) are cited before the observation, but the argument explicitly labels them as the basis for the projection, making it structurally close yet subtly weaker in confidence than A.
explanations.D: Reversal trap. The argument runs in the wrong direction — from a shared symptom back to the presence of both conditions, rather than from shared properties forward to a projected outcome.
explanations.E: Factual-claim trap. The conclusion is stated as an established fact ('has also been shown') rather than a projection ('would likely'), eliminating the analogical hedge that matches the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: Nested modus tollens with an intermediate conclusion used as a premise. Students must recognize that the intermediate conclusion functions as a suppressed premise and that the overall form is (A→B)→C; ¬C; ∴¬(A→B), which is rare and easily confused with simpler two-step arguments.
lr.stimulus: If the neural network's training data is representative of real-world inputs, then the network's error rate on deployment will be low. If the network's error rate on deployment is low, the product will receive regulatory approval. The product did not receive regulatory approval. Therefore, the neural network's training data was not representative of real-world inputs.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If the soil amendment improves nitrogen retention, then crop yields will increase. If crop yields increase, the cooperative will turn a profit this season. The cooperative did not turn a profit this season. Therefore, the soil amendment did not improve nitrogen retention.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If the vaccine induces an immune response, then antibody levels will rise. If antibody levels rise, the patient is protected. The patient's antibody levels did rise. Therefore, the patient is protected.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If the manuscript predates the printing press, it was copied by hand. This manuscript was not copied by hand. Therefore, this manuscript does not predate the printing press.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If the funding proposal meets all eligibility criteria, it will be reviewed. The proposal was not reviewed. Therefore, the proposal did not meet all eligibility criteria. The agency should revise its submission guidelines accordingly.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If infrastructure investment is adequate, economic growth will follow. Economic growth has not followed in the northern region. Therefore, infrastructure investment in the northern region was not adequate. Since it was not adequate, federal intervention is warranted.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A→B; B→C; ¬C; ∴¬A. Two conditional premises forming a chain, denial of the final consequent, denial of the original antecedent — modus tollens applied through a chain. Choice A replicates this exactly: soil amendment→yield increase (A→B); yield increase→profit (B→C); no profit (¬C); ∴ soil amendment did not work (¬A).
explanations.A: Correct. A→B; B→C; ¬C; ∴¬A — modus tollens applied through a two-step conditional chain. Premise count, conditional direction, and conclusion strength all match.
explanations.B: Modus ponens trap. A→B; B→C; A (antibody levels rose); ∴C. Affirms the antecedent of the second conditional rather than denying the final consequent — opposite direction.
explanations.C: Wrong premise count trap. Only one conditional premise, making this a simple two-premise modus tollens rather than the three-premise chain-tollens of the stimulus.
explanations.D: Added-conclusion trap. Matches the chain-tollens structure through the third sentence but then appends a separate practical recommendation, making the argument structurally more complex than the stimulus.
explanations.E: Same trap as D — a valid chain-tollens followed by a second evaluative conclusion, adding a premise and changing the argument's scope beyond the stimulus's form.
