lr.difficultyReason: Universal negative syllogism (No A are B; x is A; ∴ x is not B) in a linguistics context. Distractors include 'some A are not B' premises that produce weaker conclusions, and universal affirmatives with affirmed-consequent errors, all requiring precise quantifier tracking.
lr.stimulus: No language that lacks a system of recursive embedding can produce sentences of unbounded length. Ancient Pirahã, as documented by linguists, lacks any system of recursive embedding. Therefore, ancient Pirahã cannot produce sentences of unbounded length.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No investment vehicle that lacks FDIC insurance can guarantee depositor protection against bank failure. Municipal bond funds lack FDIC insurance. Therefore, municipal bond funds cannot guarantee depositor protection against bank failure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some ecosystems lacking apex predators cannot maintain stable prey populations. The Glenmore Reserve lacks apex predators. Therefore, the Glenmore Reserve probably cannot maintain stable prey populations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No algorithm that requires exponential time can solve problems efficiently at scale. This sorting algorithm has been shown to solve problems efficiently at scale. Therefore, this sorting algorithm does not require exponential time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No certification that lacks an accreditation body is recognized by professional licensing boards. This certification is recognized by professional licensing boards. Therefore, this certification has an accreditation body.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No process that bypasses quality control produces consistently defect-free output. This assembly line produces consistently defect-free output. Therefore, this assembly line does not bypass quality control.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: No A is B; x is A; ∴ x is not B. Universal negative major premise, particular affirmative minor, particular negative conclusion — a valid universal-negative syllogism. Choice A replicates this: No [vehicle lacking FDIC] can guarantee protection (No A is B); municipal bond funds lack FDIC (x is A); ∴ municipal bond funds cannot guarantee protection (x is not B).
explanations.A: Correct. No A is B; x is A; ∴ x is not B. Universal negative syllogism, exact structural match.
explanations.B: Quantifier-shift trap. Uses 'some' rather than 'no,' degrading the first premise from a universal negative to a particular negative, and 'probably' weakens the conclusion from certain to probable.
explanations.C: Modus tollens trap. No A is B rewritten as A→¬B; then ¬(¬B) = B; ∴¬A. This is a two-premise modus tollens on the contrapositive, structurally different — it affirms the consequent (B) to deny A, whereas the stimulus affirms the subject (A) to conclude ¬B.
explanations.D: Affirming-the-consequent trap. No A is B → A→¬B; the argument then says B (recognized), concludes ¬A (has accreditation body) — this is actually valid (contrapositive) but runs in the opposite direction from the stimulus.
explanations.E: Same trap as D — valid contrapositive reasoning from consequent to antecedent, opposite direction from the stimulus's affirmation of the antecedent.

lr.difficultyReason: Biconditional-derived argument in a history context: A if and only if B; A; ∴ B. Distractors include one-directional conditionals (A→B but not B→A) that yield the same surface conclusion but from a structurally different premise, and a 'not A; ∴ not B' modus tollens on a biconditional.
lr.stimulus: A Roman provincial governor wielded executive military authority if and only if the Senate granted him imperium. Governor Cassius Longinus wielded executive military authority during his tenure in Syria. Therefore, the Senate had granted Cassius Longinus imperium.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A gene is expressed in a given tissue if and only if the relevant transcription factors are present in that tissue. The BRCA1 gene is expressed in mammary tissue. Therefore, the relevant transcription factors are present in mammary tissue.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A physician may prescribe a controlled substance only if the physician holds a DEA registration. Dr. Mbeki holds a DEA registration. Therefore, Dr. Mbeki may prescribe controlled substances.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An athlete qualifies for the national team if and only if the athlete scores above the qualifying threshold. Renata did not score above the qualifying threshold. Therefore, Renata did not qualify for the national team.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A contract is enforceable only if it includes consideration. This contract includes consideration. Therefore, this contract is enforceable.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A building permit is issued if and only if the plans comply with zoning regulations. The plans for the Harwick development comply with zoning regulations. Therefore, a building permit will be issued for the Harwick development.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A↔B; A; ∴B — specifically, the biconditional is used in its reverse direction: A (wielded authority) is given, and B (had imperium) is concluded. This requires the B→A direction of the biconditional. Choice A: expressed↔transcription factors present; BRCA1 is expressed (A); ∴ transcription factors present (B) — same direction of inference on the same biconditional form.
explanations.A: Correct. A↔B; A; ∴B — biconditional used in the reverse (B←A) direction. Premise count, biconditional form, and conclusion direction all match.
explanations.B: One-directional conditional trap. 'Only if' creates A→B (not a biconditional); the argument then affirms B to conclude A — affirming the consequent, which is invalid. Structurally distinct from the valid biconditional inference.
explanations.C: Opposite direction on biconditional trap. A↔B; ¬B; ∴¬A — uses the same biconditional but the modus tollens direction (denying B to deny A) rather than the affirmation direction used in the stimulus.
explanations.D: 'Only if' trap again — 'enforceable only if consideration' yields enforceable→consideration; the argument then gives consideration and concludes enforceable, which affirms the consequent on a one-directional conditional. Invalid and structurally distinct.
explanations.E: Correct form (A↔B; B; ∴A) but wrong direction — it affirms B (plans comply) to conclude A (permit issued), using the forward direction of the biconditional, while the stimulus uses the reverse direction (affirms A to conclude B).

lr.difficultyReason: Argument by exclusion across multiple alternatives (process of elimination with three alternatives, two eliminated): A ∨ B ∨ C; ¬A; ¬B; ∴ C. Distractors use two-alternative disjunctions or eliminate only one alternative, requiring students to match exact premise count.
lr.stimulus: The masonry failure in the cathedral's north transept was caused either by seismic stress, by water infiltration, or by substandard mortar composition. Seismic records confirm no significant tremors in the region over the relevant period, ruling out seismic stress. Engineering analysis of the drainage system confirms no water infiltration occurred. Therefore, the failure was caused by substandard mortar composition.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The price spike in lithium can be explained by increased demand, decreased supply, or speculative trading. Data show that global lithium production rose during this period, ruling out decreased supply. Market surveillance found no evidence of coordinated speculative trading. Therefore, the price spike was caused by increased demand.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The patient's fever is caused either by a bacterial infection or by a viral infection. Laboratory tests show no bacterial pathogens. Therefore, the fever is caused by a viral infection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The manuscript error resulted from scribal misreading, a copyist substitution, or a deliberate editorial change. Paleographic analysis rules out a deliberate editorial change. Therefore, the error was caused either by scribal misreading or by a copyist substitution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either the algorithm failed due to a data error, a coding flaw, or inadequate hardware. A code review found no coding flaws, and a hardware audit confirmed adequate processing capacity. Therefore, the algorithm failed due to a data error.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The harvest shortfall was due to drought, pest infestation, or early frost. Regional climate data rule out drought. Therefore, the shortfall was due to either pest infestation or early frost, and since pest damage is far more common, pest infestation is the likely cause.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A ∨ B ∨ C; ¬A (evidence); ¬B (evidence); ∴ C. Three alternatives, two eliminated by positive evidence, conclusion is the remaining alternative. Choice A matches exactly: increased demand ∨ decreased supply ∨ speculative trading; ¬decreased supply (production rose); ¬speculative trading (surveillance data); ∴ increased demand.
explanations.A: Correct. Three-alternative disjunction, two alternatives eliminated by independent evidentiary claims, deductively certain remaining conclusion.
explanations.B: Wrong premise count trap. Two alternatives, only one eliminated — simpler disjunctive syllogism (A ∨ B; ¬A; ∴ B) rather than the three-alternative elimination of the stimulus.
explanations.C: Incomplete elimination trap. Three alternatives but only one eliminated, yielding a disjunctive conclusion (A ∨ B) rather than a single certain conclusion. Structurally weaker than the stimulus.
explanations.D: Very close structural match — three alternatives, two eliminated by evidence. However, the two eliminations are presented as a conjunction in a single sentence rather than in separate sentences as in the stimulus and choice A. Content-wise nearly parallel, but A more precisely mirrors the stimulus's structure of sequencing separate evidential eliminations.
explanations.E: Incomplete elimination plus probabilistic inference trap. Only one alternative is eliminated deductively; the second elimination is achieved through a probability judgment ('far more common'), making the overall argument inductive.

lr.difficultyReason: Nested sufficient-necessary argument: 'Only if' premise (A only if B) plus a universal (All C are A) plus a particular (x is C), yielding x must be B. Distractors confuse 'only if' with 'if,' reversing the conditional, or omit the intermediate universal link.
lr.stimulus: A clinical trial result is publishable in a peer-reviewed journal only if it includes a pre-registered methodology. All double-blind randomized trials include a pre-registered methodology. The Vexler study is a double-blind randomized trial. Therefore, the Vexler study is publishable in a peer-reviewed journal.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A contractor may bid on federal projects only if the contractor holds a valid performance bond. All licensed general contractors hold a valid performance bond. Dunmore Construction is a licensed general contractor. Therefore, Dunmore Construction may bid on federal projects.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A student may graduate with honors only if the student maintains a GPA above 3.7. Yusuf maintained a GPA above 3.7. Therefore, Yusuf may graduate with honors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An architectural design receives landmark status only if the city council approves it. All designs submitted by registered historic preservation firms are approved by the city council. This design was submitted by a registered historic preservation firm. Therefore, this design will receive landmark status.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A drug receives FDA approval only if clinical trials demonstrate safety and efficacy. The trials for Compound Z did not demonstrate efficacy. Therefore, Compound Z will not receive FDA approval.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A musician is eligible for the grant only if the musician is a citizen. All conservatory graduates are citizens. Therefore, all conservatory graduates are eligible for the grant.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: P only if Q (publishable only if pre-registered = publishable→pre-registered); All R are Q (all double-blind trials include pre-registration); x is R; ∴ x is publishable (P). The inference runs: x is R → x is Q → x satisfies the necessary condition for P; and since R guarantees Q which is necessary for P, and the stimulus treats R as sufficient for P via Q. Formally: P→Q; All R→Q; x is R; ∴ x is Q; and since R is stipulated to guarantee P (all double-blind trials are publishable because they meet the only necessary condition), ∴ x is P. Choice C mirrors this exactly: landmark only if council approves (P→Q); all historic preservation firm designs are approved (R→Q); this design is by such a firm (x is R); ∴ landmark status (x is P).
explanations.A: Extremely close structural match — three premises with 'only if,' universal link, and particular instance. However, the subject matter proximity to choice C and the identical structure mean we must check: A says 'only if performance bond' (bid→bond); all licensed GCs have bond (R→Q); Dunmore is R; ∴ Dunmore may bid. This is structurally identical to C and the stimulus. C is preferred because its intermediate class (historic preservation firms) maps more cleanly onto the stimulus's intermediate class (double-blind trials), and 'landmark status' maps onto 'publishable' as a gatekept status — but structurally both A and C are valid parallels. C is the credited answer because the 'only if' condition and the categorical approval by a governing body (city council / peer-reviewed journal) more precisely mirror the stimulus's institutional gatekeeping logic.
explanations.B: Wrong premise count trap. Only two premises — missing the intermediate universal link (All R are Q). This is a simple: P only if Q; x is Q; ∴ x is P — which actually affirms the necessary condition to conclude the sufficient, a fallacy not present in the stimulus.
explanations.C: Correct. Three-premise argument with 'only if,' universal intermediate link, and particular instantiation — exact structural match to the stimulus.
explanations.D: Modus tollens on 'only if' trap. P only if Q; ¬Q; ∴¬P — valid but structurally different: two premises, denies the necessary condition to deny the sufficient. Opposite inference direction from the stimulus.
explanations.E: Universal conclusion trap. Draws a universal conclusion ('all conservatory graduates') from universal premises rather than a particular conclusion about a specific individual, making it structurally distinct from the stimulus's particular-instantiation conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus is a nested conditional chain (A→B, B→C, A; ∴C) wrapped in policy language. Several answer choices use valid but differently shaped arguments (modus tollens, disjunctive syllogism) that share surface policy vocabulary. Students must track all three premises and verify conditional direction.
lr.stimulus: Any regulation that increases compliance costs without producing measurable public benefit ought to be repealed. The recently enacted disclosure rule increases compliance costs for small businesses. No study has identified any measurable public benefit produced by the disclosure rule. Therefore, the disclosure rule ought to be repealed.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any surgical procedure that carries serious risk without a documented therapeutic purpose should be discontinued. The Lassen technique carries serious risk and has no documented therapeutic purpose. Therefore, the Lassen technique should be discontinued.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any policy that raises taxes must be approved by a legislative supermajority. The infrastructure bill has not been approved by a supermajority. Therefore, the infrastructure bill must not raise taxes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any regulation that burdens small businesses should be reviewed. The disclosure rule burdens small businesses. Therefore, the disclosure rule should be reviewed, and further study is warranted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either the disclosure rule produces public benefit or it should be repealed. It produces no public benefit. Therefore, it should be repealed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most regulations that increase compliance costs are eventually challenged in court. The disclosure rule increases compliance costs. Therefore, the disclosure rule will probably be challenged in court.

explanations.correct: The stimulus has the form: (i) For all X: if X increases costs AND produces no benefit, then X ought to be repealed; (ii) this rule increases costs; (iii) this rule produces no benefit; ∴ this rule ought to be repealed. Answer A matches exactly: universal conditional with two conjunctive antecedent conditions (carries serious risk AND no documented therapeutic purpose), both conditions are confirmed for the specific case, and the conclusion applies the universal rule to that case.
explanations.A: Correct. Matches the universal-to-particular form with two conjunctive antecedent conditions, both instantiated, yielding the same prescriptive conclusion structure.
explanations.B: Wrong structure. This is modus tollens (A→B; ¬B; ∴¬A), not a universal instantiation with a conjunctive antecedent. The conclusion denies the antecedent by denying the consequent — opposite direction from the stimulus.
explanations.C: Wrong conclusion. The stimulus's conclusion is a specific prescriptive directive (repeal it), while this choice adds an open-ended rider ('further study is warranted') that has no basis in the stated premises, changing the conclusion's scope.
explanations.D: Wrong form. This is a disjunctive syllogism (A∨B; ¬A; ∴B), not a universal instantiation. It uses only two premises, whereas the stimulus uses three.
explanations.E: Wrong quantifier and strength. The stimulus uses a universal ('any') and a certain conclusion ('ought to'), while this choice uses 'most' and a probabilistic conclusion ('probably'). Both quantifier and modal force are mismatched.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus is a contrapositive argument (A→B; ¬B; ∴¬A) embedded in scientific language. Distractors include a modus ponens choice with the same topic and a disjunctive syllogism that reaches an identical conclusion, making surface-level scanning unreliable.
lr.stimulus: If a newly identified compound is soluble in water, it will react with the catalyst in the standard assay. The compound designated RX-7 did not react with the catalyst in the standard assay. Therefore, RX-7 is not soluble in water.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a contractor is licensed in this state, the contractor's work is covered by the state warranty program. Halcyon Construction's work is covered by the state warranty program. Therefore, Halcyon Construction is licensed in this state.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a student passes the qualifying examination, the student is admitted to the doctoral program. Soren did not pass the qualifying examination. Therefore, Soren was not admitted to the doctoral program.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a manuscript is accepted by the editorial board, it is scheduled for publication. The manuscript titled Meridian was not scheduled for publication. Therefore, Meridian was not accepted by the editorial board.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either a specimen reacts with the catalyst or it is classified as inert. RX-7 did not react with the catalyst. Therefore, RX-7 is classified as inert.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If a compound is soluble in water, laboratory technicians will detect it during routine screening. RX-7 is soluble in water. Therefore, laboratory technicians will detect RX-7 during routine screening.

explanations.correct: The stimulus is: soluble → reacts; did not react; ∴ not soluble — a pure modus tollens (contrapositive). Answer C: accepted → scheduled; not scheduled; ∴ not accepted. Identical form: A→B; ¬B; ∴¬A.
explanations.A: Affirms the consequent — a formal fallacy. Licensed→covered; covered; ∴licensed. Different (and invalid) structure.
explanations.B: Denies the antecedent — also a formal fallacy. Pass→admitted; did not pass; ∴not admitted. Different (and invalid) structure.
explanations.C: Correct. Pure modus tollens matching the stimulus's contrapositive form.
explanations.D: Disjunctive syllogism (A∨B; ¬A; ∴B). Different form even though subject matter echoes the stimulus.
explanations.E: Modus ponens (A→B; A; ∴B). Affirms the antecedent rather than denying the consequent — opposite direction from the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus is a disjunctive syllogism nested within an analogy context, and the conclusion is prescriptive. Several distractors also feature disjunctions but differ in whether the disjunction is inclusive or exclusive, or whether the negated disjunct is a premise versus embedded.
lr.stimulus: The orchestral score must have been composed either before the composer's departure from Vienna or during her later years in Prague. Archival records conclusively show it was not composed before her departure from Vienna. Therefore, the score was composed during her later years in Prague.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The theft was committed either by an employee with access to the safe or by someone who bypassed the alarm. Security logs confirm that the alarm was bypassed. Therefore, the theft was not committed by an employee with access to the safe.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The ancient inscription was carved either by craftspeople from the northern province or by those from the coastal settlements. Linguistic analysis rules out craftspeople from the coastal settlements. Therefore, the inscription was carved by craftspeople from the northern province.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If the fresco was painted before 1510, it predates the artist's mature period. The fresco does predate the artist's mature period. Therefore, the fresco was painted before 1510.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either the symphony was composed in F major or the manuscript was mislabeled. The symphony was composed in F major. Therefore, the manuscript was not mislabeled.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The libretto was written either by the lead soprano or by the company's house poet, or possibly by both. The house poet has denied writing it. Therefore, the lead soprano alone wrote the libretto.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A∨B; ¬A; ∴B — a clean disjunctive syllogism. Answer B: northern∨coastal; ¬coastal; ∴northern. Same form, same two-premise structure, same exclusive disjunction resolved by elimination.
explanations.A: Wrong direction of elimination. The logs confirm the alarm was bypassed (affirming one disjunct), and the conclusion denies the other. This is a non sequitur — affirming one disjunct does not eliminate the other in a non-exclusive disjunction.
explanations.B: Correct. Pure disjunctive syllogism: A∨B; ¬B; ∴A.
explanations.C: Affirms the consequent (fallacy). If painted before 1510→predates; predates; ∴before 1510. Different and invalid structure.
explanations.D: Affirms one disjunct to deny the other — valid only in an exclusive disjunction, but presented here without that premise, making it structurally distinct from the stimulus's elimination of a disjunct.
explanations.E: The disjunction is stated as inclusive ('or possibly by both'), so eliminating one disjunct does not establish the other alone. The conclusion overreaches the premises — structurally non-parallel.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus is a three-link conditional chain (A→B, B→C, A; ∴C) in an environmental science context. Distractors include a two-link chain reaching the same conclusion, a chain in which the antecedent is not affirmed, and a chain with reversed final conditional.
lr.stimulus: Whenever atmospheric particulate levels exceed the threshold set by the regional authority, air quality monitoring stations are required to issue public alerts. Whenever public alerts are issued, local schools must shift to remote instruction. Atmospheric particulate levels in the valley exceeded the regional threshold yesterday. Therefore, local schools in the valley had to shift to remote instruction yesterday.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a river's flow rate drops below minimum levels, irrigation permits are suspended. If irrigation permits are suspended, crop yields in the delta region decline. The river's flow rate dropped below minimum levels last spring. Therefore, crop yields in the delta region declined last spring.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whenever water temperature exceeds safe limits, fish populations migrate downstream. Whenever fish populations migrate downstream, commercial fishing yields decline. Water temperature has not exceeded safe limits this season. Therefore, commercial fishing yields have not declined this season.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a forest fire burns more than 10,000 acres, federal emergency funding is triggered. Federal emergency funding was triggered after the Ridgeline fire. Therefore, the Ridgeline fire burned more than 10,000 acres.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whenever particulate levels exceed safety limits, authorities issue health warnings. Particulate levels in the city exceeded safety limits on Tuesday. Therefore, authorities issued health warnings on Tuesday.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If an estuary's salinity drops, migratory birds avoid the area. If migratory birds avoid the area, ecotourism revenue falls. If ecotourism revenue falls, conservation funding is reduced. The estuary's salinity dropped this year. Therefore, conservation funding was reduced this year.

explanations.correct: Stimulus form: A→B; B→C; A; ∴C — a three-link conditional chain with the antecedent affirmed. Answer A: flow drops→permits suspended; permits suspended→yields decline; flow dropped; ∴yields declined. Identical three-premise, two-conditional chain.
explanations.A: Correct. Three-premise conditional chain (two conditionals plus affirmation of the initial antecedent), yielding the terminus of the chain.
explanations.B: Denies the antecedent (A→B; ¬A; ∴¬B) across a two-conditional chain — a formal fallacy. Different both in validity and in the direction of inference.
explanations.C: Only two premises; affirms the consequent of a single conditional to affirm the antecedent — a fallacy. Wrong form and wrong premise count.
explanations.D: Only two premises (one conditional plus affirmation of antecedent). Modus ponens with a single link — structurally shorter than the stimulus's three-link chain.
explanations.E: Four premises — three conditionals plus affirmation of the first antecedent. One link longer than the stimulus. Premise count mismatch.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus is a universal-to-particular inference with a negative universal quantifier ('no'). Distractors use 'some,' 'most,' and 'all' quantifiers that share surface plausibility. Students must identify the 'no X is Y; Z is X; ∴ Z is not Y' structure precisely.
lr.stimulus: No economic policy that disproportionately burdens low-income households can be considered equitable. The proposed value-added tax disproportionately burdens low-income households. Therefore, the proposed value-added tax cannot be considered equitable.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No testimony obtained without proper Miranda warnings is admissible in a federal proceeding. The confession given by the defendant was obtained without proper Miranda warnings. Therefore, the defendant's confession is not admissible in a federal proceeding.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most dietary supplements that lack clinical trials cannot be marketed as treatments. The compound Veratol lacks clinical trials. Therefore, Veratol probably cannot be marketed as a treatment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some financial instruments that carry hidden fees are not transparent to consumers. The structured note issued by Alderon Bank carries hidden fees. Therefore, the structured note is not transparent to consumers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All tax measures that reduce the deficit are fiscally responsible. The capital gains surcharge reduces the deficit. Therefore, the capital gains surcharge is fiscally responsible.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No policy that raises revenue can be both equitable and efficient simultaneously. The proposed value-added tax raises revenue. Therefore, the proposed tax cannot be both equitable and efficient simultaneously.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: No X is Y; Z is X; ∴ Z is not Y. Answer A: No testimony-without-Miranda is admissible; this confession is testimony-without-Miranda; ∴ this confession is not admissible. Exact match on the negative universal quantifier and the two-premise instantiation.
explanations.A: Correct. Matches the 'No X is Y; this is X; ∴ this is not Y' form precisely.
explanations.B: Quantifier mismatch: 'most' instead of 'no,' and conclusion is probabilistic ('probably') rather than certain. Both modal force and quantifier are wrong.
explanations.C: Quantifier mismatch: 'some X are not Y' does not allow inference about a particular X. The stimulus uses a universal negative ('no'), which does support instantiation; 'some' does not.
explanations.D: Uses a positive universal ('all X are Y'; this is X; ∴ this is Y) rather than a negative universal. The conclusion affirms a property rather than denying one.
explanations.E: Same-topic trap. The subject matter echoes the stimulus (equitable, value-added tax), but this is a distractor designed to exploit content familiarity. The structure is also valid universal instantiation, but the conclusion's content is different from just 'not equitable.'

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus uses an analogical structure with two shared properties grounding a transferred conclusion. Distractors share one but not two properties with the analog, or transfer a different type of conclusion, requiring students to check both the number of analogy bases and the type of conclusion transferred.
lr.stimulus: The ruins at Qalat Mudiq have the same stratigraphy and the same ceramic typology as the ruins at Tell Afis, which have been dated to the early Iron Age. Since Qalat Mudiq shares these two dating indicators with Tell Afis, the ruins at Qalat Mudiq should also be dated to the early Iron Age.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The falcon species nesting in the northern canyon has the same wing morphology and the same prey specialization as the peregrine falcon, which is known to migrate annually. Since the canyon falcon shares these two characteristics with the peregrine, the canyon falcon probably migrates annually as well.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The compound isolated from the deep-sea organism has a molecular weight and a solubility profile similar to those of compound X, which is toxic to nerve tissue. Therefore, the newly isolated compound may have some toxic properties.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The medieval manuscript found in Bruges has the same binding technique as the manuscript known as the Ghent Codex, which was produced in Flanders. Since they share this binding technique, the Bruges manuscript was also produced in Flanders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The newly discovered asteroid has the same albedo and orbital period as asteroid 1999 RQ36, which is composed primarily of carbonaceous material. Since they share two properties, the new asteroid is probably composed primarily of carbonaceous material.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The architectural style of the temple at Priene is identical to that of the temple at Didyma. The temple at Didyma was built by the architect Pytheos. Therefore, the temple at Priene was probably also built by Pytheos.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: X and Y share property P1 AND P2; Y has conclusion-property C; ∴ X has C. The analog has two shared properties explicitly cited. Answer D: new asteroid and 1999 RQ36 share albedo AND orbital period (two properties); 1999 RQ36 has composition C; ∴ new asteroid probably has C. Same two-property analogical structure transferring the same type of factual conclusion.
explanations.A: Close, but the conclusion is probabilistic ('probably') while also being about behavior (migration) rather than a classification/dating property. More importantly, the shared properties are biological traits used to infer a behavioral pattern — subtly different analogical base.
explanations.B: Uses 'similar to' rather than identical properties, and the conclusion is weakened to 'may have some toxic properties' — hedged more than the stimulus's 'should also be dated.' Strength mismatch.
explanations.C: Only one shared property (binding technique), not two. Premise count mismatch in the analogy's basis.
explanations.D: Correct. Two explicitly shared properties (albedo, orbital period) grounding a transferred classification conclusion, matching the stimulus's structure.
explanations.E: Only one shared property (architectural style), and the conclusion infers authorship — a different type of transferred conclusion from a classification inference.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus is a hypothetical syllogism (pure conditional chain with no affirmed antecedent, yielding a conditional conclusion). This form is rare and easily confused with modus ponens. Distractors either affirm the antecedent to produce a categorical conclusion or use the same premises with the antecedent denied.
lr.stimulus: If the legislature passes the new budget, the education ministry will receive additional funding. If the education ministry receives additional funding, teacher salaries across the public sector will increase. Therefore, if the legislature passes the new budget, teacher salaries across the public sector will increase.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If the harvest is abundant, grain prices will fall. If grain prices fall, the cost of livestock feed decreases. The harvest was abundant. Therefore, the cost of livestock feed decreased.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a proposed merger is approved by regulators, the combined firm will dominate the market. If the combined firm dominates the market, smaller competitors will exit. Therefore, if the proposed merger is approved by regulators, smaller competitors will exit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If infrastructure investment increases, economic growth accelerates. Economic growth has accelerated. Therefore, infrastructure investment must have increased.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either the budget will pass or social services will be cut. The budget did not pass. Therefore, social services will be cut.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If trade tariffs rise, domestic manufacturing expands. If domestic manufacturing expands, unemployment decreases. Tariffs have not risen. Therefore, unemployment will not decrease.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A→B; B→C; ∴A→C — hypothetical syllogism producing a conditional conclusion without affirming the antecedent. Answer B: merger approved→dominates; dominates→competitors exit; ∴merger approved→competitors exit. Same two-conditional premise structure yielding a conditional (not categorical) conclusion.
explanations.A: Uses the same two conditionals but also affirms the antecedent (modus ponens extension), producing a categorical conclusion rather than a conditional one. Premise count is three, not two.
explanations.B: Correct. Pure hypothetical syllogism: A→B; B→C; ∴A→C. The conclusion is conditional, not categorical.
explanations.C: Affirms the consequent fallacy (A→B; B; ∴A). Different structure and invalid.
explanations.D: Disjunctive syllogism (A∨B; ¬A; ∴B). Completely different form.
explanations.E: Denies the antecedent (A→B; B→C; ¬A; ∴¬C) — a formal fallacy. Three premises plus a categorical conclusion. Different form and invalid.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus combines a universal affirmative with a particular negative to yield a particular negative conclusion (All A are B; some C are not B; ∴ some C are not A) — a standard syllogistic form that is hard to spot under paraphrase. Distractors use 'some C are B' (affirming instead of denying) or reverse the universal.
lr.stimulus: All antibiotics approved for pediatric use have been tested in clinical trials involving subjects under twelve years of age. Some of the compounds in the hospital's new formulary have not been tested in clinical trials involving subjects under twelve years of age. Therefore, some of the compounds in the hospital's new formulary are not antibiotics approved for pediatric use.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All licensed civil engineers have passed the state professional examination. Some contractors working on the harbor project have not passed the state professional examination. Therefore, some contractors working on the harbor project are not licensed civil engineers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All board-certified surgeons have completed an accredited residency. Some physicians at the clinic have completed an accredited residency. Therefore, some physicians at the clinic are board-certified surgeons.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All heirloom seeds in the collection are certified organic. Some seeds purchased at the market are certified organic. Therefore, some seeds purchased at the market are heirloom seeds from the collection.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All compounds cleared by the FDA have undergone phase-three trials. This compound has undergone phase-three trials. Therefore, this compound has been cleared by the FDA.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some approved antibiotics have not been tested on pediatric populations. All compounds in the formulary are approved antibiotics. Therefore, some compounds in the formulary have not been tested on pediatric populations.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: All A are B; some C are not B; ∴ some C are not A. Answer A: All licensed engineers passed exam (All A are B); some harbor contractors have not passed exam (some C are not B); ∴ some harbor contractors are not licensed engineers (some C are not A). Perfect quantifier and structural match.
explanations.A: Correct. All A are B; some C are ¬B; ∴ some C are ¬A — exact match.
explanations.B: Affirms the consequent in quantified form: All A are B; some C are B; ∴ some C are A. This is invalid. The stimulus's second premise uses a negative ('have not'), which is essential to the valid inference.
explanations.C: Same trap as B — affirms the consequent in quantified form (All A are B; some C are B; ∴ some C are A). Invalid structure.
explanations.D: Single-instance affirms-the-consequent fallacy. Completely different structure: All A are B; this is B; ∴ this is A.
explanations.E: Same-topic trap using medical language. The form is different: some A are ¬B; all C are A; ∴ some C are ¬B — valid but a different syllogistic form (particular-universal, not universal-particular-negative).

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus is a contrapositive chain — two conditionals used in their contrapositive forms to reach a conclusion. Distractors include a forward chain using the same conditionals, a single-contrapositive modus tollens, and a chain with one conditional reversed.
lr.stimulus: If a language lacks a grammatical marker for evidentiality, its speakers do not systematically distinguish direct from indirect knowledge in their grammar. If speakers do not systematically distinguish direct from indirect knowledge in their grammar, the language cannot be classified as epistemically transparent. The language spoken in the isolated highland community has no grammatical marker for evidentiality. Therefore, the language spoken in the highland community cannot be classified as epistemically transparent.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a corporation lacks an independent audit committee, its financial disclosures are not fully transparent. If its financial disclosures are not fully transparent, the corporation cannot be listed on the regulated exchange. Teknon Corp. lacks an independent audit committee. Therefore, Teknon Corp. cannot be listed on the regulated exchange.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a corporation is listed on the regulated exchange, it has an independent audit committee. If it has an independent audit committee, its financial disclosures are fully transparent. Teknon Corp. is not listed on the regulated exchange. Therefore, Teknon Corp. does not have transparent financial disclosures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a country adopts a common currency, it surrenders independent monetary policy. Valdoria has not surrendered independent monetary policy. Therefore, Valdoria has not adopted a common currency.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a treaty lacks an enforcement mechanism, signatory nations will not comply with its terms. If signatory nations do not comply, the treaty's objectives will not be achieved. The Carlen Accord lacks an enforcement mechanism. Therefore, the Carlen Accord's objectives will not be achieved.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If a language has been documented by linguists, a grammar of it exists in print. If a grammar exists in print, the language can be taught in formal instruction. The highland language has been documented by linguists. Therefore, the highland language can be taught in formal instruction.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: ¬E→¬D; ¬D→¬C; ¬E (the antecedent); ∴¬C — a three-premise chain where both conditionals have negative antecedents and consequents, and the antecedent of the first is affirmed. Answer A: ¬audit→¬transparent; ¬transparent→¬listed; ¬audit; ∴¬listed. Same form: both conditionals run negative-to-negative, and the first antecedent (negative condition) is affirmed, yielding the final negative conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Three-premise chain with negative-antecedent conditionals throughout, matching the stimulus's logical structure precisely.
explanations.B: Uses contrapositives of A's conditionals (positive chain), then denies the antecedent — a fallacy. Different form and invalid.
explanations.C: Only two premises — a single modus tollens. Matches on contrapositive direction but lacks the second conditional link, making the chain shorter than the stimulus.
explanations.D: Three-premise chain, but the conditionals have a positive antecedent leading to a negative consequent (lacks enforcement → won't comply), which differs structurally from the stimulus's negative-antecedent-to-negative-consequent form. The chain is valid but the conditional polarity differs.
explanations.E: Three-premise modus ponens chain with all positive antecedents and positive consequents — the forward chain form, not the negative-chain form of the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus uses a biconditional-like structure: a sufficient-and-necessary condition stated as two separate conditionals to yield a classification inference. Distractors use only one direction of the biconditional, causing students who miss the double-conditional structure to select an affirms-the-consequent answer.
lr.stimulus: A sculpture can be attributed to the Lydian school if and only if it exhibits both the characteristic drapery folds and the distinctive facial proportions associated with that school. The recently excavated figure exhibits both the characteristic drapery folds and the distinctive facial proportions. Therefore, the recently excavated figure can be attributed to the Lydian school.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A vine qualifies as a heritage cultivar if and only if it is over seventy-five years old and is registered with the national viticulture authority. The vine in plot seven is over seventy-five years old and is registered with the national authority. Therefore, the vine in plot seven qualifies as a heritage cultivar.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A contract is enforceable only if it was signed by both parties and witnessed. The contract in question was signed by both parties and witnessed. Therefore, the contract in question is enforceable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An employee is eligible for the bonus if she has met her quarterly targets. Daria has met her quarterly targets. Therefore, Daria is eligible for the bonus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A building may be designated a historic landmark only if it is at least one hundred years old. The Aldren Building is at least one hundred years old. Therefore, the Aldren Building may be designated a historic landmark.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A gemstone is classified as investment grade if it has both ideal cut proportions and a clarity rating above SI-1. This sapphire has ideal cut proportions. Therefore, this sapphire may be classified as investment grade.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: X qualifies IFF (P1 AND P2); this has P1 AND P2; ∴ this qualifies. The biconditional's sufficient-and-necessary structure means affirming both conjunctive conditions licenses the conclusion. Answer A: heritage IFF (>75 years AND registered); vine has both; ∴ vine qualifies. Same biconditional with two conjunctive conditions, both affirmed.
explanations.A: Correct. Biconditional (if and only if) with two conjunctive conditions, both satisfied, yielding the classification conclusion.
explanations.B: Uses 'only if' — a necessary condition statement, not a biconditional. Affirming necessary conditions does not establish sufficiency; this is an affirms-the-consequent fallacy presented deceptively. Different structure.
explanations.C: Single sufficient condition (if she met targets → eligible); only one condition, not a conjunctive biconditional. Premise count and biconditional structure both mismatch.
explanations.D: Uses 'only if' — a necessary but not sufficient condition. Same trap as B: affirming a necessary condition does not license the conclusion. Structurally different from the biconditional stimulus.
explanations.E: Has two conjunctive conditions but only one is affirmed (cut proportions), not both. The conclusion is also hedged ('may be'), whereas the stimulus's conclusion is certain. Both condition-count and modal force are mismatched.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus uses a nested conditional chain (A→B, B→C, C→D; A; ∴ D) embedded in medical prose. Answer choices each present five-line arguments with similar surface complexity; the correct answer must match on all four nodes of the chain, premise count, and conclusion strength ('must').
lr.stimulus: Every drug that inhibits enzyme X will reduce inflammation. Every compound that reduces inflammation will lower the patient's fever. Every substance that lowers a patient's fever will shorten the illness duration. Compound Z inhibits enzyme X. Therefore, Compound Z must shorten the illness duration.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every legislation that caps emissions will reduce pollution. Every policy that reduces pollution will lower health-care costs. Every measure that lowers health-care costs will increase worker productivity. Bill 7 caps emissions. Therefore, Bill 7 must increase worker productivity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every drug that inhibits enzyme X will reduce inflammation. Every compound that reduces inflammation will lower fever. Drug W reduces inflammation. Therefore, Drug W must lower fever.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every treatment that reduces fever will shorten illness. Every illness that is shortened improves patient morale. Treatment Q reduces fever. Therefore, Treatment Q probably improves patient morale.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every compound that inhibits enzyme X will reduce inflammation. Compound Z does not inhibit enzyme X. Therefore, Compound Z will not reduce inflammation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every drug that reduces inflammation will lower fever. Every drug that lowers fever will shorten illness. Drug Y lowers fever. Therefore, Drug Y must shorten illness.

explanations.correct: The stimulus chains four universals (A→B, B→C, C→D), then asserts A of a particular, concluding D with 'must.' Choice A mirrors this exactly: caps emissions → reduces pollution → lowers costs → increases productivity; Bill 7 caps emissions; therefore Bill 7 must increase productivity. Four nodes, three conditional links, same conclusion force.
explanations.A: Correct. Four-node chain (A→B→C→D), particular asserts A, conclusion asserts D with 'must.' Structure is identical.
explanations.B: Wrong premise count. B drops one link in the chain (only A→B→C, not A→B→C→D) and starts the minor premise at a later node; the chain has only three nodes. Trap: same topic domain as stimulus.
explanations.C: Strength-shift trap. The conclusion says 'probably improves' rather than 'must improve,' and the chain is only two links long, not three.
explanations.D: Wrong argument form. D denies the antecedent (¬A; ∴ ¬B), which is an invalid form entirely different from the valid four-node modus ponens chain in the stimulus.
explanations.E: Missing-premise trap. E uses only a two-link chain (A→B→C), but the minor premise asserts B (not A), making it a valid two-step modus ponens — still one node short of the stimulus's three-link chain.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus uses a contrapositive applied to a universal ('All A that are B are C; x is A and not C; ∴ x is not B'). Distractors share environmental vocabulary or use modus ponens on the same universals, forcing careful attention to contrapositive direction and quantifier scope.
lr.stimulus: All ecosystems that receive sufficient rainfall support diverse plant communities. The highland plateau is an ecosystem that does not support a diverse plant community. Therefore, the highland plateau does not receive sufficient rainfall.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All software systems that receive regular updates remain secure. The payroll system does not remain secure. Therefore, the payroll system does not receive regular updates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All ecosystems with diverse plant communities receive sufficient rainfall. The coastal wetland has a diverse plant community. Therefore, the coastal wetland receives sufficient rainfall.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most ecosystems that receive sufficient rainfall support diverse plant communities. The valley floor does not support a diverse plant community. Therefore, the valley floor probably does not receive sufficient rainfall.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All ecosystems that support diverse plant communities have stable soil. The rainforest supports a diverse plant community. Therefore, the rainforest has stable soil.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No ecosystem that lacks rainfall can support animal life. The desert lacks sufficient rainfall. Therefore, the desert cannot support animal life.

explanations.correct: Stimulus form: All A→B; x is A and ¬B; ∴ x is ¬(sufficient rainfall) — modus tollens on a universal. Choice A: All (systems receiving updates)→(secure); payroll is not secure; ∴ payroll does not receive updates. Identical contrapositive structure.
explanations.A: Correct. Universal conditional, negative minor premise on the consequent, conclusion denies the antecedent via valid modus tollens.
explanations.B: Affirms the consequent trap. B's minor premise asserts the consequent (has diverse community), and the conclusion asserts the antecedent — that is affirming the consequent, which is invalid and structurally different.
explanations.C: Quantifier-shift trap. C weakens 'all' to 'most' and concludes 'probably,' matching neither the universality of the stimulus's premise nor the certainty of its conclusion.
explanations.D: Wrong argument form. D applies modus ponens (affirms the antecedent, concludes the consequent) rather than modus tollens. The logical direction is reversed from the stimulus.
explanations.E: Surface-similar topic, different structure. E uses a negative universal ('No A can B') and modus ponens, which differs from the stimulus's affirmative universal with modus tollens.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus is a disjunctive syllogism nested within a universal: 'Every X is either A or B; x is X and not A; ∴ x is B.' Distractors use similar vocabulary but apply the disjunction to the wrong level (universal vs. particular) or add an extra premise, requiring careful parsing of quantifier scope.
lr.stimulus: Every contract before this court is either enforceable or void. The lease agreement before this court is not enforceable. Therefore, the lease agreement is void.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every chemical reaction in this experiment is either exothermic or endothermic. Reaction 4 in this experiment is not exothermic. Therefore, Reaction 4 is endothermic.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some contracts before this court are either enforceable or void. The mortgage before this court is not enforceable. Therefore, the mortgage is probably void.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every statute passed by the legislature is either constitutional or subject to review. Statute 12 is subject to review. Therefore, Statute 12 is not constitutional.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every document in this archive is authentic or a reproduction. Document 7 is authentic. Therefore, Document 7 is not a reproduction.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every contract is enforceable if both parties consent and the terms are legal. This contract's terms are not legal. Therefore, this contract is not enforceable.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: Universal disjunction over a set (every X is A or B); particular x belongs to the set and is ¬A; conclude x is B. Choice A: universal disjunction (every reaction is exothermic or endothermic); Reaction 4 is ¬exothermic; conclude it is endothermic. Perfect structural match.
explanations.A: Correct. Universal disjunction applied to a set member; negative minor premise eliminates one disjunct; conclusion affirms the remaining disjunct. Mirrors the stimulus exactly.
explanations.B: Quantifier-shift trap. 'Some' replaces 'every,' weakening the universal premise, and 'probably' softens the conclusion — two mismatches with the stimulus.
explanations.C: Affirms one disjunct trap. C's minor premise asserts one disjunct (is subject to review) and concludes the other is false, which is an invalid inference when the disjunction is inclusive.
explanations.D: Same-direction flaw. D affirms one disjunct positively and concludes the negation of the other — identical invalid form to C. Also treats the disjunction as exclusive without justification.
explanations.E: Different argument form. E uses a conjunctive conditional (A ∧ B → C; ¬B; ∴ ¬C) — a modus tollens on a conjunctive antecedent — not a disjunctive syllogism.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus is a two-premise analogy argument: X and Y share two relevant properties P and Q; Y has property R; ∴ X has R. Distractors share either one property or the conclusion, but not the full two-property analogical base, or they reverse which entity has R.
lr.stimulus: The economies of both Northland and Southland have high household debt ratios and contracting manufacturing sectors. Southland's currency depreciated sharply last year. Therefore, Northland's currency will likely depreciate as well.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both species Corvid A and Corvid B have identical nesting behaviors and equivalent foraging ranges. Corvid B has shown population decline in fragmented habitats. Therefore, Corvid A will likely show population decline in fragmented habitats as well.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Northland's economy has a high household debt ratio. Economies with high household debt ratios tend to have currency depreciation. Therefore, Northland's currency will likely depreciate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Southland's currency depreciated last year. Northland's manufacturing sector is contracting just as Southland's was before its depreciation. Therefore, Northland's currency will likely depreciate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both Northland and Southland have contracting manufacturing sectors. Northland's currency depreciated last year. Therefore, Southland's currency will likely depreciate as well.

choices.label: E
choices.text: All countries with high household debt and contracting manufacturing sectors eventually see currency depreciation. Northland has both conditions. Therefore, Northland's currency must depreciate.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: X and Y share two properties (P and Q); Y has R; ∴ X has R (analogical inference). Choice A: Corvid A and B share two properties (nesting behavior and foraging range); Corvid B has R (population decline); ∴ Corvid A has R. Two shared properties, correct entity direction, 'likely' conclusion — perfect match.
explanations.A: Correct. Two entities share exactly two properties; one entity is shown to have outcome R; the other is predicted to have R via analogy. Conclusion strength ('likely') matches.
explanations.B: Wrong form. B is a two-premise syllogism using a statistical universal ('tend to'), not an analogy between two named entities sharing properties. Only one shared property is cited.
explanations.C: Only one shared property trap. C cites only the contracting manufacturing sector as the basis for analogy; the debt ratio is absent. The stimulus requires two shared properties as the analogical foundation.
explanations.D: Reversed entity trap. D shares one property and makes the correct entity Y (Southland) the one whose conclusion is drawn, rather than X (Northland) — direction is reversed relative to the stimulus.
explanations.E: Different argument form and strength-shift. E uses a universal generalization with deductive force ('must'), not an analogy between two named entities. 'Must' vs. 'likely' is a conclusion-strength mismatch.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus uses a universal-to-particular syllogism with an intermediate universal ('All A are B; all B are C; x is A; ∴ x is C'), but the middle term is negated in some distractors or the minor premise is placed at a different node, forcing students to trace the chain carefully.
lr.stimulus: All published works that contain original expression are protected by copyright. All works protected by copyright require the author's permission before reproduction. The novel Evergreen contains original expression and is a published work. Therefore, reproducing Evergreen requires the author's permission.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All licensed physicians who perform surgery must carry malpractice insurance. All those who carry malpractice insurance must register with the state board. Dr. Osei is a licensed physician who performs surgery. Therefore, Dr. Osei must register with the state board.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All published works require the author's permission before reproduction. Evergreen is a published work. Therefore, reproducing Evergreen requires the author's permission.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All works with original expression are copyrighted. All copyrighted works require permission before reproduction. Evergreen does not require permission. Therefore, Evergreen lacks original expression.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All licensed physicians must carry malpractice insurance. Dr. Kim is not a licensed physician. Therefore, Dr. Kim need not carry malpractice insurance.

choices.label: E
choices.text: All works containing original expression are protected by copyright. Evergreen is protected by copyright. Therefore, Evergreen contains original expression.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: All A→B; All B→C; x is A; ∴ x is C. Three premises (two universals + one particular), valid AAA-1 syllogistic chain. Choice A: All (licensed surgeons)→(carry insurance); All (carry insurance)→(register with board); Dr. Osei is a licensed surgeon; ∴ Dr. Osei must register. Identical three-premise, two-link chain.
explanations.A: Correct. Two universal premises chain A→B and B→C; minor premise places a particular at A; conclusion places it at C. Three premises, two links, certain conclusion.
explanations.B: Wrong premise count trap. B collapses the two-step chain into one universal premise (A→C directly) and one minor premise — only two premises total, missing the intermediate link.
explanations.C: Different argument form. C uses modus tollens (¬C; A→B→C; ∴ ¬A) — a contrapositive application — rather than the forward-direction modus ponens chain of the stimulus.
explanations.D: Denies the antecedent. D's minor premise negates A (¬A) and concludes ¬B, which is the fallacy of denying the antecedent — an invalid form structurally distinct from the stimulus.
explanations.E: Affirms the consequent. E's minor premise asserts B (is copyrighted) and concludes A (has original expression) — affirming the consequent, an invalid form entirely different from the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus combines a biconditional premise with a universal ('A language preserves a cultural practice if and only if it retains the relevant vocabulary; Language L retains the vocabulary; ∴ L preserves the practice'). Distractors exploit the biconditional by reversing direction or replacing it with a one-way conditional, requiring recognition of both directions of the if-and-only-if.
lr.stimulus: A linguistic community preserves a traditional practice if and only if its language retains the vocabulary associated with that practice. The Valeri community's language retains the vocabulary associated with its weaving tradition. Therefore, the Valeri community preserves its weaving tradition.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal right is enforceable if and only if it is codified in statute. The right to quiet enjoyment is codified in statute. Therefore, the right to quiet enjoyment is enforceable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A traditional practice is preserved if the community teaches it to children. The Valeri community teaches weaving to its children. Therefore, the Valeri community preserves its weaving tradition.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A linguistic community preserves a traditional practice only if its language retains the relevant vocabulary. The Valeri community does not retain the vocabulary. Therefore, the Valeri community does not preserve the practice.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A legal right is enforceable if and only if it is codified in statute. The right to privacy is not enforceable. Therefore, the right to privacy is not codified in statute.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A linguistic community preserves a traditional practice if and only if its language retains the vocabulary. The Doru community does not preserve its fishing tradition. Therefore, the Doru community's language does not retain fishing vocabulary.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A ↔ B (biconditional); B is asserted; ∴ A. Choice A: legal right enforceable ↔ codified in statute (biconditional); right to quiet enjoyment is codified; ∴ it is enforceable. Same biconditional premise structure, same direction (assert B, conclude A), identical form.
explanations.A: Correct. Biconditional premise; minor premise asserts the right-hand side (B); conclusion affirms the left-hand side (A). Mirrors the stimulus's use of the biconditional's B→A direction.
explanations.B: One-way conditional trap. B replaces the biconditional with a simple 'if' (sufficient condition only), which is a weaker, structurally different premise. The inference is valid but not parallel.
explanations.C: Wrong direction of biconditional. C uses only the 'only if' half (A→B), then applies modus tollens (¬B; ∴ ¬A). The stimulus uses the other direction (B→A) with modus ponens. Different conditional direction.
explanations.D: Same biconditional, wrong direction trap. D asserts ¬A and concludes ¬B — this uses modus tollens on the A→B half of the biconditional — the opposite direction from the stimulus's B→A modus ponens.
explanations.E: Same biconditional, wrong direction and negative minor premise. E asserts ¬A and concludes ¬B (modus tollens on A→B direction), which differs from the stimulus's positive assertion of B to conclude A.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus is a three-premise argument combining a universal negative with an existential: 'No A is B; some C are A; ∴ some C are not B.' Distractors flip the quantifier type, reverse the negative, or use modus ponens on a universal, requiring careful tracking of both the negative universal and the existential.
lr.stimulus: No algorithm that relies solely on historical data can accurately predict unprecedented market events. Some risk-assessment tools used by this bank rely solely on historical data. Therefore, some risk-assessment tools used by this bank cannot accurately predict unprecedented market events.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No vaccine developed without clinical trials can be approved for public use. Some vaccines currently in distribution were developed without clinical trials. Therefore, some vaccines currently in distribution cannot be approved for public use.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No historical data set can predict unprecedented events. All risk-assessment tools rely on historical data. Therefore, no risk-assessment tool can predict unprecedented events.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No algorithm relying solely on historical data can predict unprecedented events. No risk-assessment tool at this bank relies solely on historical data. Therefore, all risk-assessment tools at this bank can predict unprecedented events.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some algorithms cannot predict unprecedented events. Some risk-assessment tools are algorithms. Therefore, some risk-assessment tools cannot predict unprecedented events.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No historical model is completely reliable. This bank's risk-assessment tool is a historical model. Therefore, this bank's risk-assessment tool is not completely reliable.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: No A is B (universal negative); some C are A (existential affirmative); ∴ some C are not B (existential negative). Choice A: No (vaccine without trials) is (approved); some (vaccines in distribution) are (vaccines without trials); ∴ some (vaccines in distribution) are not (approved). Identical EIO syllogism.
explanations.A: Correct. Universal negative major premise, existential affirmative minor premise, existential negative conclusion — EIO syllogism matching the stimulus precisely.
explanations.B: Quantifier-shift trap. B uses 'all' in the minor premise instead of 'some,' producing an AEE syllogism with a universal negative conclusion ('no risk tool') rather than the existential negative conclusion of the stimulus.
explanations.C: Invalid form and negative minor premise. C negates the minor premise (No C are A) rather than asserting some C are A, and draws a universal positive conclusion — both the form and conclusion type differ from the stimulus.
explanations.D: Missing universal negative premise. D uses two existential/particular premises ('some algorithms cannot…; some tools are algorithms'), which is an undistributed-middle fallacy and structurally distinct from the valid EIO form of the stimulus.
explanations.E: Different argument form and quantifier. E applies a universal negative to a singular term ('this bank's tool'), drawing a singular conclusion. This is a universal-to-particular modus tollens pattern, not the existential syllogism of the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus uses a conditional with a conjunctive antecedent (A ∧ B → C; A is present; B is present; ∴ C) across three explicit premises. Distractors either use only one conjunct, deny one conjunct to draw a negative conclusion, or switch to a disjunctive antecedent, requiring students to verify that both conjuncts are affirmed.
lr.stimulus: Whenever a historical monument is both listed on the national registry and located within a protected zone, federal preservation funds are automatically allocated to it. The Alderton Clocktower is listed on the national registry, and it is located within a protected zone. Therefore, federal preservation funds are automatically allocated to the Alderton Clocktower.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whenever a manuscript is both authenticated by a certified archivist and catalogued in the national database, it qualifies for digitization funding. The Morrow Letters have been authenticated by a certified archivist and catalogued in the national database. Therefore, the Morrow Letters qualify for digitization funding.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whenever a monument is listed on the national registry, it may receive preservation funds. The Alderton Clocktower is listed on the national registry. Therefore, the Alderton Clocktower may receive preservation funds.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whenever a historical monument is listed on the national registry or located in a protected zone, it receives federal attention. The Alderton Clocktower is listed on the national registry. Therefore, the Alderton Clocktower receives federal attention.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whenever a historical monument is both listed on the national registry and in a protected zone, it receives federal funds. The Barton Bridge is not located in a protected zone. Therefore, federal funds are not allocated to the Barton Bridge.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whenever a manuscript is authenticated and catalogued, it qualifies for funding. The Morrow Letters have not been catalogued. Therefore, the Morrow Letters do not qualify for funding.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: (A ∧ B) → C; A; B; ∴ C. Three premises (one conditional + two conjunct-affirmers), valid modus ponens on a conjunctive antecedent. Choice A: (authenticated ∧ catalogued) → qualifies; Morrow Letters are authenticated; Morrow Letters are catalogued; ∴ qualify. Identical structure — both conjuncts explicitly affirmed.
explanations.A: Correct. Conjunctive antecedent conditional; both conjuncts explicitly affirmed in two separate minor premises; conclusion follows by modus ponens. Mirrors the stimulus exactly.
explanations.B: Missing conjunct trap. B reduces the conjunctive antecedent to a single condition ('listed on registry'), dropping the second conjunct entirely. It also weakens the consequent from automatic allocation to 'may receive,' a strength mismatch.
explanations.C: Disjunctive antecedent trap. C replaces the conjunction ('and') with a disjunction ('or'), making a weaker antecedent. The inference is valid but structurally different — the stimulus requires both conditions, not just one.
explanations.D: Denies one conjunct trap. D's minor premise negates one conjunct (¬B) and concludes the negation of the consequent (¬C). This attempts modus tollens on an incomplete basis — denying one conjunct of a conjunctive antecedent does not entail ¬C if A could still obtain with another route.
explanations.E: Denies antecedent trap. E negates one conjunct (not catalogued) and concludes ¬C — the same structural error as D but in a different domain. Denying one element of a conjunctive antecedent does not validly entail denial of the consequent.

lr.difficultyReason: Short two-speaker dialogue with sharply opposed positions on one central claim. Martina says home cooking is healthier than restaurant food; Reggie explicitly denies this. Four distractors are off-topic or only one speaker addresses them.
lr.stimulus: Martina: People who cook most of their meals at home eat healthier food than people who eat out often. Home cooks control the amount of salt, oil, and sugar in their meals, and restaurant kitchens almost always use more of each than a home cook would. Reggie: That's a myth. Restaurants now publish nutrition information and many of them prepare meals with less salt and oil than the average home cook does. People who eat out regularly are not eating less healthily than those who cook at home.
lr.questionStem: On the basis of their statements, Martina and Reggie are committed to disagreeing about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: restaurants are required by law to publish nutrition information

choices.label: B
choices.text: people who cook at home eat more healthily than people who eat out often

choices.label: C
choices.text: eating too much salt is unhealthy

choices.label: D
choices.text: home cooks enjoy preparing their own meals

choices.label: E
choices.text: restaurants charge more for healthy meals than for unhealthy ones

explanations.correct: Martina asserts that home cooks eat healthier than people who eat out often; Reggie explicitly denies it. That is exactly the proposition at issue.
explanations.A: Neither speaker addresses whether the disclosure is legally required.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Both would agree that excess salt is unhealthy; no disagreement there.
explanations.D: Neither speaker addresses enjoyment of cooking.
explanations.E: Neither speaker addresses menu pricing.

lr.difficultyReason: Direct disagreement about whether a specific policy should be adopted. Speakers use the same vocabulary and contradict each other on the central proposal; distractors are out-of-scope or mutual-agreement traps.
lr.stimulus: Councilor Dent: Our city should ban gasoline-powered leaf blowers. They produce more pollution per hour of use than most cars, and the noise is a nuisance to every neighbor within two blocks. Councilor Vu: A ban is the wrong response. Electric leaf blowers are already widely available, and landscapers are switching to them on their own. The city should not outlaw a tool that is already being phased out voluntarily.
lr.questionStem: Dent and Vu disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: gasoline-powered leaf blowers produce more pollution per hour than most cars

choices.label: B
choices.text: electric leaf blowers are quieter than gasoline-powered ones

choices.label: C
choices.text: the city should prohibit gasoline-powered leaf blowers

choices.label: D
choices.text: landscapers should be free to choose their own equipment

choices.label: E
choices.text: noise from leaf blowers bothers neighbors

explanations.correct: Dent says the city should ban them; Vu says a ban is the wrong response. That is a direct contradiction about the policy.
explanations.A: Dent asserts this claim; Vu does not address it, so their disagreement cannot be established.
explanations.B: Neither speaker compares the noise of electric and gas blowers directly.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Neither speaker takes a general position on landscaper autonomy.
explanations.E: Dent says neighbors are bothered; Vu does not deny this.

lr.difficultyReason: Two historians dispute a factual claim about cause. One says the invention of the printing press was the primary driver of rising literacy; the other flatly denies it and assigns primacy to schooling. Distractors are off-topic or agreed-upon.
lr.stimulus: Alenka: The rise in European literacy rates between 1500 and 1800 was driven primarily by the printing press. Once books became cheap and abundant, ordinary people had both the opportunity and the incentive to learn to read. Bertil: The printing press mattered, but it was not the primary driver. Literacy rates rose mainly because governments and churches invested in schools that taught children to read. Without that schooling, cheap books would have sat unread.
lr.questionStem: Alenka and Bertil disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: books became cheaper after the printing press was invented

choices.label: B
choices.text: the printing press had any effect on European literacy rates

choices.label: C
choices.text: the printing press was the primary cause of rising literacy in Europe from 1500 to 1800

choices.label: D
choices.text: governments funded schools during the early modern period

choices.label: E
choices.text: literacy rates in Europe rose between 1500 and 1800

explanations.correct: Alenka says the press was primarily responsible; Bertil explicitly denies that it was primary and assigns primacy to schools.
explanations.A: Both would accept that books became cheaper.
explanations.B: Bertil concedes the press 'mattered'; he doesn't deny any effect.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Bertil asserts it; Alenka does not deny it.
explanations.E: Both speakers accept that literacy rates rose.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics-domain disagreement about a single evaluative claim: whether it is morally permissible to eat animals. Speakers take opposite positions in plain language; distractors are agreement or out-of-scope.
lr.stimulus: Parisa: It is morally wrong to eat animals. Animals can suffer, and we now have abundant, nutritious plant foods available. Causing suffering to a sentient creature when we have good alternatives cannot be justified. Quentin: It is not morally wrong. Humans evolved as omnivores, and raising and eating animals in humane conditions is a long-standing and legitimate practice. Causing some harm is acceptable when the practice serves a genuine human interest.
lr.questionStem: Parisa and Quentin disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: animals are capable of suffering

choices.label: B
