choices.text: plant-based foods are nutritionally adequate

choices.label: C
choices.text: humans evolved as omnivores

choices.label: D
choices.text: eating animals is morally wrong

choices.label: E
choices.text: factory farming is humane

explanations.correct: Parisa says it is morally wrong; Quentin says it is not. Direct contradiction of the central claim.
explanations.A: Parisa asserts it; Quentin does not deny it — he accepts that some harm is caused.
explanations.B: Parisa asserts it; Quentin says nothing about plant nutrition.
explanations.C: Quentin asserts it; Parisa does not deny it.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Neither speaker addresses factory farming specifically.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental-science dispute where each speaker makes one explicit central claim about wind power's sufficiency. Direct contradiction; distractors are out-of-scope technical points.
lr.stimulus: Sunita: Wind power alone could supply all of our country's electricity needs. Studies estimate that the wind resources across our plains and coastlines could generate several times our current total demand if fully developed. Tomas: Wind cannot supply all of our electricity. The wind does not blow reliably everywhere at once, and without enormous advances in storage we will always need some other source to fill the gaps.
lr.questionStem: Sunita and Tomas disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the country's plains and coastlines have significant wind resources

choices.label: B
choices.text: wind power can supply all of the country's electricity needs

choices.label: C
choices.text: battery storage technology has improved in recent years

choices.label: D
choices.text: wind turbines are a form of renewable energy

choices.label: E
choices.text: electricity demand is growing in the country

explanations.correct: Sunita asserts wind alone could supply all electricity needs; Tomas explicitly denies it. Direct contradiction.
explanations.A: Sunita asserts this; Tomas does not deny it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Neither speaker addresses recent storage improvements specifically.
explanations.D: Neither speaker addresses the classification of wind as renewable.
explanations.E: Neither speaker addresses demand growth.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics domain with a crisp prescriptive versus descriptive disagreement. Speakers contradict each other over one explicit claim about whether 'literally' should be used non-literally.
lr.stimulus: Professor Holm: Using the word 'literally' to mean 'figuratively,' as in 'I literally died laughing,' is simply incorrect. 'Literally' means 'in a literal sense,' and using it to mean the opposite undermines the distinction the word exists to mark. Professor Iyer: That use is not incorrect. Words change meaning through ordinary use, and 'literally' as an intensifier is now so widespread and well understood that it is a legitimate sense of the word.
lr.questionStem: Holm and Iyer disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the non-literal use of 'literally' is widespread

choices.label: B
choices.text: words can change meaning over time

choices.label: C
choices.text: using 'literally' to mean 'figuratively' is incorrect

choices.label: D
choices.text: 'literally' has a literal sense

choices.label: E
choices.text: listeners are usually confused by the non-literal use of 'literally'

explanations.correct: Holm says the use is simply incorrect; Iyer says it is not incorrect. Direct contradiction.
explanations.A: Iyer asserts it; Holm does not deny that it is widespread.
explanations.B: Iyer asserts it; Holm does not deny it in general.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Both speakers accept that 'literally' has a literal sense.
explanations.E: Neither speaker addresses listener confusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal-domain dispute with one clear evaluative claim on each side. Speakers directly contradict each other about whether jury trials produce fairer outcomes than bench trials. Distractors are mutual-agreement or off-topic.
lr.stimulus: Wren: Jury trials produce fairer outcomes than bench trials. A jury of twelve ordinary citizens brings a broader range of perspectives than any single judge and is harder for a skilled attorney to manipulate. Xavier: Jury trials are not fairer. Juries are swayed by emotional appeals and often do not understand complex evidence. A seasoned judge is more likely to reach a fair verdict in difficult cases.
lr.questionStem: Wren and Xavier disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: jury trials produce fairer outcomes than bench trials

choices.label: B
choices.text: jurors are ordinary citizens

choices.label: C
choices.text: complex evidence is sometimes presented at trial

choices.label: D
choices.text: attorneys are sometimes skilled at persuasion

choices.label: E
choices.text: judges are appointed rather than elected

explanations.correct: Wren claims jury trials are fairer than bench trials; Xavier explicitly denies that claim. Direct contradiction.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Both accept that jurors are ordinary citizens.
explanations.C: Xavier implies it; Wren does not deny it.
explanations.D: Wren asserts it; Xavier does not deny it.
explanations.E: Neither speaker addresses how judges are selected.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology domain. Clear disagreement on one factual claim: whether social media has, on balance, worsened teen mental health. Distractors are agreement traps or single-speaker claims.
lr.stimulus: Ori: Widespread social media use has, on balance, worsened teenage mental health over the past fifteen years. Rates of anxiety and depression among teens began climbing at precisely the time smartphones and social platforms became ubiquitous, and many clinicians report a clear link. Petra: Teen mental health has not been worsened by social media on balance. The rise in diagnoses largely reflects greater awareness and willingness to seek treatment, not a real increase in underlying problems caused by these platforms.
lr.questionStem: Ori and Petra disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: smartphones have become ubiquitous among teenagers

choices.label: B
choices.text: social media use has worsened teen mental health on balance

choices.label: C
choices.text: teens should be restricted from using social media

choices.label: D
choices.text: rates of diagnosis for anxiety and depression have risen among teens

choices.label: E
choices.text: clinicians treat teenagers for anxiety and depression

explanations.correct: Ori asserts social media has worsened teen mental health on balance; Petra explicitly denies it. Direct contradiction.
explanations.A: Both accept that smartphones became ubiquitous.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Neither speaker takes a position on restricting use.
explanations.D: Both accept diagnoses have risen; they dispute the cause, not the fact.
explanations.E: Neither speaker disputes that clinicians treat such conditions.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts-domain evaluative disagreement. Speakers make one explicit claim each about whether a museum should return a specific artifact. Direct contradiction; distractors are off-topic or agreed-upon.
lr.stimulus: Curator Ambrose: Our museum should return the bronze statue to its country of origin. It was removed during a colonial expedition without the consent of the local community, and holding onto it today perpetuates that injustice. Director Basile: We should not return it. The statue has been carefully preserved and publicly displayed here for over a century, and returning it now would mean fewer people could see and study it. Our obligation is to public access.
lr.questionStem: Ambrose and Basile disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the bronze statue was removed without local consent

choices.label: B
choices.text: the museum should return the bronze statue to its country of origin

choices.label: C
choices.text: the statue has been preserved at the museum

choices.label: D
choices.text: public access to artifacts is a consideration for museums

choices.label: E
choices.text: colonial-era acquisitions were sometimes carried out without consent

explanations.correct: Ambrose says the museum should return the statue; Basile says it should not. Direct contradiction of the central proposal.
explanations.A: Ambrose asserts this; Basile does not deny it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Both accept the statue has been preserved at the museum.
explanations.D: Both treat public access as a legitimate consideration; they weigh it differently.
explanations.E: Both would accept this general point.

lr.difficultyReason: Economics domain with a straightforward disagreement about whether raising tariffs will help domestic manufacturers. Direct contradiction; distractors are out-of-scope or agreement traps.
lr.stimulus: Diego: Raising tariffs on imported steel will help our domestic steel manufacturers. With foreign steel made more expensive, buyers will turn to domestic mills, and our producers will gain customers and revenue. Elise: Raising tariffs will not help our domestic manufacturers. Most of them use imported steel as an input, and higher tariffs will raise their production costs enough to more than offset any gains from reduced foreign competition.
lr.questionStem: Diego and Elise disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: tariffs on imported steel would make foreign steel more expensive for domestic buyers

choices.label: B
choices.text: domestic manufacturers use imported steel as an input

choices.label: C
choices.text: raising tariffs on imported steel will help domestic steel manufacturers

choices.label: D
choices.text: the government has the authority to impose tariffs

choices.label: E
choices.text: consumers prefer products made from domestic steel

explanations.correct: Diego asserts the tariff will help domestic manufacturers; Elise explicitly denies it. Direct contradiction of the central claim.
explanations.A: Both accept that tariffs would make imported steel more expensive.
explanations.B: Elise asserts it; Diego does not deny it.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Neither speaker addresses the government's legal authority.
explanations.E: Neither speaker addresses consumer preferences.

lr.difficultyReason: Short, sharply opposed positions on a single topic. Speakers use clear language and directly contradict on whether video games have educational value.
lr.stimulus: Dr. Chen: Video games are primarily entertainment products, and their educational value is incidental. Schools should focus resources on proven teaching methods rather than adopting games in classrooms. Dr. Okonkwo: You underestimate games' potential. Research shows they develop problem-solving skills and engagement. Schools should explore games as educational tools.
lr.questionStem: Dr. Chen and Dr. Okonkwo disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: video games can develop certain cognitive skills

choices.label: B
choices.text: schools currently use traditional teaching methods

choices.label: C
choices.text: video games should play a role in schools' educational approach

choices.label: D
choices.text: entertainment products lack any value to society

choices.label: E
choices.text: problem-solving is an important skill for students

explanations.correct: Chen denies schools should adopt games; Okonkwo affirms schools should explore games as tools. This is a direct disagreement on whether games should play a role in schools' educational approach.
explanations.A: Both speakers implicitly accept that games can develop skills. Chen concedes educational value; Okonkwo asserts it. This is agreement, not disagreement.
explanations.B: Neither speaker clearly takes a position on this factual claim about current practice.
explanations.C: Correct. Chen opposes schools exploring games; Okonkwo advocates for it.
explanations.D: Neither speaker makes or denies a claim about entertainment products lacking value.
explanations.E: Both speakers would likely agree problem-solving is important. This is not a point of disagreement.

lr.difficultyReason: Two speakers with plainly opposing views on a single clear issue. No shared assumptions; the disagreement is transparent and vocabulary is straightforward.
lr.stimulus: Moreno: Preserving wilderness areas is a luxury we cannot afford. As populations grow, we must convert natural land to housing and agriculture to meet human needs. Peña: That reasoning ignores ecological costs. Destroyed ecosystems cannot be restored, and their loss threatens the survival of countless species and human well-being alike. We must prioritize preservation.
lr.questionStem: Moreno and Peña disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: human population is increasing in many regions

choices.label: B
choices.text: ecosystems can recover once damaged

choices.label: C
choices.text: preservation of wilderness should take priority over immediate human needs

choices.label: D
choices.text: species extinction has occurred

choices.label: E
choices.text: housing and agriculture are necessary for human survival

explanations.correct: Moreno prioritizes development for human needs; Peña prioritizes preservation. They directly disagree on whether preservation should take priority over immediate human demands.
explanations.A: Moreno asserts this; Peña does not dispute it. One-sided claim.
explanations.B: Peña denies this; Moreno does not address it explicitly. One-sided.
explanations.C: Correct. Moreno says preservation is a luxury we cannot afford (denies priority); Peña says we must prioritize preservation (affirms priority).
explanations.D: Neither speaker disputes that extinction occurs; this is background fact.
explanations.E: Both speakers appear to accept this. No disagreement.

lr.difficultyReason: Clear dialogue with opposing stances on a single axis. Speakers have distinct and incompatible positions on the merits of a proposal.
lr.stimulus: Laird: Remote work policies undermine team cohesion and company culture. Employees need in-person collaboration to build trust and share knowledge effectively. Kim: You ignore the data. Studies show remote workers are equally productive and less stressed. Companies should embrace flexibility because it benefits employees without sacrificing output.
lr.questionStem: Laird and Kim disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: remote work reduces employee stress levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: company culture is important for business success

choices.label: C
choices.text: remote work arrangements should be a standard company policy

choices.label: D
choices.text: employees value workplace flexibility

choices.label: E
choices.text: in-person collaboration enables knowledge sharing

explanations.correct: Laird opposes remote work policies, saying they harm culture; Kim advocates for them. They disagree on whether remote work should be standard policy.
explanations.A: Kim affirms this; Laird does not explicitly deny it. One-sided.
explanations.B: Both speakers seem to accept this. Not a disagreement.
explanations.C: Correct. Laird rejects remote work policies; Kim says companies should embrace them.
explanations.D: Both speakers could accept this. Not a clear disagreement.
explanations.E: Laird affirms this; Kim does not directly deny it. One-sided.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward dialogue with opposing positions on a concrete topic. The disagreement is explicit and unmistakable.
lr.stimulus: Dr. Okonkwo: Mandatory standardized testing in schools wastes instructional time and narrows curriculum. It measures only a limited set of skills and has not improved student learning outcomes. Schools should eliminate these tests. Dr. Chen: Testing provides essential accountability data. Without standardized measures, schools cannot identify which students need help or compare performance across districts. Testing must continue.
lr.questionStem: Dr. Okonkwo and Dr. Chen disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: standardized testing measures a wide range of student skills

choices.label: B
choices.text: some students struggle academically

choices.label: C
choices.text: schools should retain standardized testing requirements

choices.label: D
choices.text: accountability in education serves a purpose

choices.label: E
choices.text: testing narrows what subjects are taught in schools

explanations.correct: Dr. Okonkwo argues schools should eliminate tests; Dr. Chen argues they must continue. They directly disagree on whether tests should be retained.
explanations.A: Dr. Okonkwo denies this; Dr. Chen does not address it. One-sided.
explanations.B: Neither speaker disputes this premise. Both would likely agree.
explanations.C: Correct. Okonkwo opposes retention; Chen supports it.
explanations.D: Both speakers recognize accountability has some value. Not a disagreement.
explanations.E: Okonkwo asserts this; Chen does not directly deny it. One-sided.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple, opposed statements on a single issue. Speakers reach directly contradictory conclusions about the same topic.
lr.stimulus: Peña: Artificial intelligence should be designed to mimic human judgment as closely as possible. If AI systems cannot explain their decisions the way humans do, they are unreliable and unsafe for critical applications. Moreno: That expectation is misguided. AI does not need to think like humans to be effective. AI systems can be reliable even if they operate through processes we do not fully understand. The focus should be on verifiable outcomes, not on replicating human reasoning.
lr.questionStem: Peña and Moreno disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: artificial intelligence has been deployed in critical applications

choices.label: B
choices.text: AI systems that operate through processes humans do not understand can still be reliable

choices.label: C
choices.text: human judgment is a valuable decision-making approach

choices.label: D
choices.text: verifiable outcomes are important for assessing AI performance

choices.label: E
choices.text: AI should be easier for humans to understand

explanations.correct: Peña denies that AI with unexplainable processes is reliable; Moreno affirms that such systems can be reliable. Direct disagreement on whether AI can be reliable without human-like reasoning.
explanations.A: Neither speaker clearly disputes this factual claim.
explanations.B: Correct. Peña says unexplainable AI is unreliable; Moreno says it can be reliable.
explanations.C: Both speakers implicitly accept human judgment has value. No disagreement.
explanations.D: Moreno affirms this; Peña does not deny it. One-sided.
explanations.E: Moreno does not address whether AI should be easier to understand. One-sided.

lr.difficultyReason: Direct opposition on a central topic with clear supporting reasoning. The speakers reach opposite conclusions about a simple factual and evaluative question.
lr.stimulus: Laird: The historical novel is a legitimate form of serious literature. Blending historical facts with imaginative narrative allows authors to explore human experience in ways pure history cannot. This hybrid approach enriches understanding. Kim: Historical novels mislead readers. By mixing fact and fiction without clear boundaries, they obscure what actually happened. Readers should study history through factual sources, not novels.
lr.questionStem: Laird and Kim disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: historical novels contain some factual elements

choices.label: B
choices.text: understanding human experience is valuable

choices.label: C
choices.text: historical novels should be considered a serious literary form

choices.label: D
choices.text: factual sources exist about historical events

choices.label: E
choices.text: authors sometimes incorporate imagination into their work

explanations.correct: Laird affirms the historical novel is a legitimate serious literary form; Kim denies it, recommending readers avoid novels in favor of factual sources. They disagree on whether novels deserve recognition as serious literature.
explanations.A: Both speakers implicitly accept that novels contain historical facts. No disagreement.
explanations.B: Both speakers would accept this. Not a point of disagreement.
explanations.C: Correct. Laird endorses novels as serious literature; Kim rejects them as such.
explanations.D: Both speakers acknowledge factual historical sources exist. No disagreement.
explanations.E: Both speakers recognize authors use imagination. No disagreement.

lr.difficultyReason: Clear, opposing proposals with distinct reasoning. Speakers take unambiguous positions on the same evaluative question.
lr.stimulus: Dr. Chen: Patent laws should protect pharmaceutical innovations for longer periods to incentivize drug development. The high cost of research justifies extended monopolies that let companies recoup investments. Dr. Okonkwo: Longer patents delay generic competition and keep life-saving drugs unaffordable for most patients. Access to medicine matters more than pharmaceutical profits. Patents should be shorter to speed generic availability.
lr.questionStem: Dr. Chen and Dr. Okonkwo disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: developing new pharmaceuticals requires significant financial investment

choices.label: B
choices.text: generic drugs are less effective than brand-name drugs

choices.label: C
choices.text: patent protections should be extended to incentivize pharmaceutical innovation

choices.label: D
choices.text: access to medicine is important

choices.label: E
choices.text: pharmaceutical companies have costs they must recover

explanations.correct: Dr. Chen advocates for longer patents to incentivize innovation; Dr. Okonkwo opposes extended patents because they restrict access. They disagree on whether patent protections should be extended.
explanations.A: Both speakers accept this. Dr. Chen uses it as justification; Dr. Okonkwo does not dispute it. No disagreement.
explanations.B: Neither speaker claims this. Not addressed.
explanations.C: Correct. Chen supports extension; Okonkwo opposes it.
explanations.D: Both speakers clearly accept this. No disagreement.
explanations.E: Both speakers implicitly recognize this. No disagreement.

lr.difficultyReason: Opposing evaluations of a single proposal. Speakers differ sharply on whether a policy is warranted, with clear supporting statements.
lr.stimulus: Moreno: Public funding for museums is wasteful. Museums serve only affluent patrons who can afford to visit. Governments should redirect resources to essential services like healthcare and schools. Peña: Museums educate the entire community and preserve cultural heritage that belongs to everyone. Subsidized admission allows poor families to access culture. Public funding for museums is a worthwhile investment in social well-being.
lr.questionStem: Moreno and Peña disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: museums have visitors from different economic backgrounds

choices.label: B
choices.text: government resources are limited

choices.label: C
choices.text: public funding of museums is a justified expenditure

choices.label: D
choices.text: cultural heritage has value

choices.label: E
choices.text: healthcare and education are important public services

explanations.correct: Moreno calls public museum funding wasteful; Peña calls it a worthwhile investment. They disagree on whether public funding of museums is justified.
explanations.A: Moreno asserts museums serve mainly the affluent; Peña implies subsidized access helps poor families. However, the core disagreement is not about current visitor composition but about whether funding is justified.
explanations.B: Neither speaker disputes this. Both accept it implicitly.
explanations.C: Correct. Moreno opposes the expenditure; Peña supports it as worthwhile.
explanations.D: Peña asserts this; Moreno does not deny it. One-sided.
explanations.E: Both speakers likely accept this. No disagreement.

lr.difficultyReason: Plainly opposed positions on a single question. Speakers use straightforward language and reach directly contradictory conclusions.
lr.stimulus: Dr. Okonkwo: Bilingual education programs are essential. They allow non-English-speaking students to learn academic content while developing English proficiency. Students educated bilingually perform better academically than those in English-only classrooms. Dr. Chen: Immersion in English is faster and more efficient. Bilingual programs dilute instruction and slow English acquisition. Students benefit more from intensive English instruction without the distraction of a second language.
lr.questionStem: Dr. Okonkwo and Dr. Chen disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: English language proficiency is important for students

choices.label: B
choices.text: bilingual education programs improve academic performance compared to English-only approaches

choices.label: C
choices.text: non-English-speaking students exist in schools

choices.label: D
choices.text: some instructional approaches are more efficient than others

choices.label: E
choices.text: students can learn multiple languages simultaneously

explanations.correct: Dr. Okonkwo affirms that bilingual students perform better academically; Dr. Chen denies this, claiming English-only immersion is more effective. They directly disagree on the comparative academic outcomes.
explanations.A: Both speakers accept English proficiency is important. No disagreement.
explanations.B: Correct. Okonkwo claims bilingual students perform better; Chen claims English-only is more effective.
explanations.C: Both speakers acknowledge these students exist. No disagreement.
explanations.D: Both speakers implicitly accept this general principle. No disagreement.
explanations.E: Both speakers implicitly accept this is possible. No disagreement.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers accept the premise that animal testing has produced medical benefits and both grant that alternatives are improving; the disagreement is specifically about whether the current benefits justify continuing the practice. Trap (A) is an agreement in disguise; trap (E) shifts to a claim only Farooq addresses.
lr.stimulus: Farooq: Animal testing has unquestionably delivered important medical advances, and I would not deny that. But we now have cell-culture and computational methods that approximate many of those results, and continuing to subject animals to painful trials when those alternatives exist is no longer defensible. Hollister: The alternatives you cite are promising but remain unreliable for many systemic effects. Until that changes, the medical gains from animal studies still outweigh the welfare costs, even granting that those costs are real.
lr.questionStem: Farooq and Hollister disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: animal testing has historically contributed to medical progress

choices.label: B
choices.text: the current welfare costs of animal testing are outweighed by its medical benefits

choices.label: C
choices.text: cell-culture methods will eventually supplant animal testing entirely

choices.label: D
choices.text: subjecting laboratory animals to painful procedures causes genuine harm

choices.label: E
choices.text: regulators have been too slow to approve computational alternatives

explanations.correct: Farooq says the practice is no longer defensible given that alternatives exist; Hollister says the medical gains still outweigh the welfare costs. That is a direct disagreement about the current cost-benefit balance.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Farooq explicitly grants that animal testing has delivered important advances, and Hollister presupposes the same.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Neither speaker addresses complete replacement; both only compare current reliability.
explanations.D: Both would accept that the welfare costs are real; Hollister even concedes this explicitly.
explanations.E: Only Farooq gestures toward the availability of alternatives, and neither speaker takes a position on regulatory pace.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers grant that standardized tests correlate with later outcomes and both acknowledge that the correlation is imperfect; the disagreement is specifically over whether the tests should be used as admissions gatekeepers. Trap (D) is a point only one speaker addresses.
lr.stimulus: Ramsey: Standardized admissions tests correlate with first-year college grades, but the correlation is modest and the tests also track family income closely. Given that, we should not let these scores function as gatekeepers for admission. Okafor: The correlation with grades, while imperfect, is still the best single predictor we have, and no admissions office I know of uses the scores as a sole criterion. They belong in the mix precisely because they add information that transcripts alone do not.
lr.questionStem: Ramsey and Okafor's statements most strongly support the claim that they disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: standardized admissions test scores are perfectly correlated with first-year college grades

choices.label: B
choices.text: admissions offices currently use standardized test scores as the sole basis for admission

choices.label: C
choices.text: standardized test scores should be used as a factor in college admissions decisions

choices.label: D
choices.text: transcripts alone are sufficient to predict first-year college grades

choices.label: E
choices.text: standardized test scores correlate with the family income of test-takers

explanations.correct: Ramsey denies the tests should function as gatekeepers; Okafor affirms that they belong in the admissions mix. That is a disagreement about whether the scores should be a factor in admissions.
explanations.A: Both would deny this — Ramsey calls the correlation modest and Okafor calls it imperfect.
explanations.B: Only Okafor addresses current practice; Ramsey takes no position on what offices actually do.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Only Okafor implies transcripts alone are insufficient; Ramsey says nothing about transcripts.
explanations.E: Agreement in disguise — Ramsey asserts this and Okafor does not contest it.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers grant that training data includes copyrighted work and both concede the outputs are often novel; the disagreement turns on whether the training itself constitutes infringement. Trap (A) is a factual point both accept; trap (E) shifts to a normative claim only one addresses.
lr.stimulus: Dex: AI image models are trained on vast archives of copyrighted artwork without the artists' consent. Even when the resulting images look nothing like any single source, the training itself is a use of the works, and that use is an infringement. Vera: The training process analyzes statistical features of the images, not the images themselves, and the outputs are typically novel. Reading a book to learn a writing style is not infringement; training on images to learn visual style is analogous.
lr.questionStem: Dex and Vera disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: AI image models are trained on archives that include copyrighted work

choices.label: B
choices.text: the images generated by AI models are typically copies of specific source artworks

choices.label: C
choices.text: training an AI image model on copyrighted artwork constitutes copyright infringement

choices.label: D
choices.text: reading a copyrighted book to study the author's style constitutes infringement

choices.label: E
choices.text: artists should be compensated when their work is used to train AI image models

explanations.correct: Dex says the training itself is infringement; Vera's analogy is meant to show that such training is not infringement. They take opposite positions on exactly this proposition.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers presuppose that copyrighted works are included in the training data.
explanations.B: Both would deny this — Dex says the outputs look nothing like any single source and Vera says outputs are typically novel.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Only Vera addresses the book analogy; Dex does not commit to a position on reading books.
explanations.E: Neither speaker addresses compensation; the debate is about the legal/conceptual status of training, not about remedy.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that some offset projects fail to deliver the promised carbon reductions and both accept that emissions reduction at the source is desirable. The disagreement concerns whether a well-designed offset program can meaningfully substitute for on-site reductions. Trap (B) is an agreement.
lr.stimulus: Mendez: Independent audits have repeatedly found that many forest-based carbon offset projects overstate their actual carbon reductions, sometimes by an order of magnitude. A company buying such offsets instead of cutting its own emissions is not genuinely addressing its climate impact. Halligan: Audit failures have certainly tarnished offset markets, but the problem is poor measurement, not the concept. With rigorous monitoring and verification, a well-designed offset program can achieve real reductions that firms could not practically achieve on-site.
lr.questionStem: Mendez and Halligan disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: forest-based offset projects have sometimes overstated their carbon reductions

choices.label: B
choices.text: reducing emissions at the source is, in principle, a desirable goal

choices.label: C
choices.text: a well-designed offset program can substitute for a company's on-site emissions reductions

choices.label: D
choices.text: current verification protocols are adequate to detect overstated reductions

choices.label: E
choices.text: companies have a legal obligation to purchase carbon offsets

explanations.correct: Mendez claims that buying offsets instead of cutting emissions is not genuinely addressing climate impact; Halligan claims a well-designed offset program can achieve real reductions firms cannot practically make on-site. They disagree about whether offsets can substitute for on-site cuts.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Halligan concedes that audit failures have occurred.
explanations.B: Both accept this; Mendez frames cutting one's own emissions as the genuine response, and Halligan does not deny its desirability.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Only Mendez alludes to audit findings; neither takes a position on whether current protocols are adequate in general.
explanations.E: Legal obligation is out of scope — neither speaker mentions any legal requirement.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that antibiotic resistance is rising and both accept that over-prescription contributes. The disagreement turns on where the primary responsibility for reform should fall. Trap (A) is a shared premise; trap (E) splits the speakers the wrong way.
lr.stimulus: Dr. Bae: Antibiotic resistance is rising, and over-prescription in primary care is a major driver. The most effective lever is stricter prescribing guidelines enforced at the clinical level, where individual prescribing decisions actually get made. Dr. Ilundain: Physician-level guidelines alone will not be enough. The bulk of antibiotic use is in livestock agriculture, not human medicine, and regulating agricultural use is where reform will make the biggest difference.
lr.questionStem: On the basis of their statements, Dr. Bae and Dr. Ilundain are committed to disagreeing about which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibiotic resistance in humans is a growing problem.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Primary-care physicians sometimes prescribe antibiotics when they are not clinically warranted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The most effective target for reducing antibiotic resistance is prescribing practices in primary care.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Livestock agriculture accounts for the bulk of antibiotic use.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulation of antibiotic use by farmers would, by itself, solve the problem of antibiotic resistance.

explanations.correct: Dr. Bae says the most effective lever is clinical-level prescribing guidelines; Dr. Ilundain denies this by saying the biggest difference will come from regulating agricultural use. That is a direct disagreement about where the most effective target lies.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers take resistance as a given problem worth addressing.
explanations.B: Only Dr. Bae addresses primary-care prescribing specifically; Dr. Ilundain says nothing about whether individual prescriptions are clinically unwarranted.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Only Dr. Ilundain asserts this; Dr. Bae does not deny it and takes no position on the share.
explanations.E: This splits them the wrong way — Dr. Ilundain says agricultural regulation will make the biggest difference, not that it would solve the problem alone; Dr. Bae does not address it at all.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that rent control protects current tenants and that housing supply is strained. The disagreement is specifically about the net effect on renters overall. Trap (B) is a shared premise; trap (D) is a claim only one speaker addresses.
lr.stimulus: Navarro: Rent control protects the tenants who are already in regulated units, and I grant that. But when landlords can't adjust rents on existing stock, developers build fewer new units, and renters who are not yet in the system end up paying more for worse housing. On balance, rent control hurts renters as a group. Sung: Protecting the tenants already in place is not a minor thing — it's the whole point. Displacement is catastrophic for those affected, and a policy that prevents it benefits renters, even if supply effects are real at the margin.
lr.questionStem: Navarro and Sung disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: rent control, taken as a whole, benefits renters as a group

choices.label: B
choices.text: tenants currently living in rent-controlled units are protected by the policy

choices.label: C
choices.text: housing supply effects from rent control are entirely negligible

choices.label: D
choices.text: displacement of tenants imposes severe costs on those affected

choices.label: E
choices.text: developers should be encouraged to build more housing than they currently do

explanations.correct: Navarro concludes that on balance rent control hurts renters as a group; Sung concludes that the policy benefits renters. They take opposite positions on the net effect.
explanations.B: Agreement in disguise — Navarro explicitly grants this and Sung affirms it.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.C: Sung calls supply effects 'real at the margin,' so neither speaker denies the effects exist.
explanations.D: Only Sung characterizes displacement as catastrophic; Navarro does not deny this — he simply doesn't address it directly.
explanations.E: Neither speaker makes recommendations about developer incentives.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that the traditional literary canon is narrow in its demographic origins and both accept that canonical works have literary merit. The disagreement is about whether the curriculum should be reorganized around broader representation. Trap (C) is an agreement; trap (E) splits them the wrong way.
lr.stimulus: Acheampong: The traditional literary canon taught in our universities is overwhelmingly drawn from a narrow slice of authors. That is a fact, and it limits students' sense of what literature can do. A curriculum organized around broader representation would serve students better. Pilsen: The canon is narrow in origin, but the works in it have earned their place through sustained literary power. Reorganizing the curriculum around representation risks replacing one criterion for inclusion with another that has little to do with how good the writing is.
lr.questionStem: Acheampong and Pilsen's statements commit them to disagreeing about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the works in the traditional literary canon possess any literary merit

choices.label: B
choices.text: the university literature curriculum should be reorganized to emphasize broader authorial representation

choices.label: C
choices.text: the traditional literary canon is drawn from a narrow demographic range

choices.label: D
choices.text: literary merit is a criterion that can be applied objectively

choices.label: E
choices.text: students currently have an accurate sense of what literature can do

explanations.correct: Acheampong endorses a curriculum reorganized around broader representation; Pilsen opposes reorganizing on those grounds. They take directly opposing positions on the reorganization proposal.
explanations.A: Neither speaker denies the canon has literary merit — Pilsen affirms it and Acheampong does not deny it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Agreement in disguise — both speakers grant the canon's narrow origin.
explanations.D: Neither speaker addresses objectivity of merit directly.
explanations.E: Only Acheampong claims students' sense is limited; Pilsen does not affirm that students currently have an accurate sense — he just doesn't address it.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers grant that juries historically have engaged in nullification and both accept that judges instruct juries to apply the law. The disagreement is about whether jurors have a legitimate right to nullify, not whether they are able to or whether it happens. Trap (A) is an agreement.
lr.stimulus: Yusuf: A jury's power to acquit against the evidence — so-called nullification — has been exercised throughout the history of common law. When a jury's conscience tells it a conviction under a particular statute would be unjust, the jury is entitled to refuse to convict, regardless of the judge's instructions. Leclerc: Jurors have the raw power to acquit against the evidence, and no one disputes that juries have done so. But a power is not a right. The law binds the juror just as it binds the judge, and exercising nullification violates the oath the juror has taken.
lr.questionStem: Yusuf and Leclerc disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: juries have historically acquitted defendants against the weight of the evidence

choices.label: B
choices.text: a juror is entitled to refuse to convict when the juror believes conviction would be unjust

choices.label: C
choices.text: judges instruct juries to apply the law as given

choices.label: D
choices.text: a juror who nullifies can be legally punished for doing so

choices.label: E
choices.text: nullification has ever produced a just outcome in a particular case

explanations.correct: Yusuf says the juror is entitled to refuse to convict when conscience so dictates; Leclerc denies this entitlement, distinguishing raw power from right. That is exactly their point of disagreement.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Leclerc concedes that no one disputes juries have done this.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Both accept this as background; neither disputes it.
explanations.D: Neither speaker addresses punishment of nullifying jurors.
explanations.E: Neither speaker takes a position on the outcomes of particular historical cases.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that reenactments engage the public and that they involve simplification. The disagreement is specifically about whether simplification for engagement produces a net educational gain. Trap (C) is an agreement; trap (E) is a point only one speaker addresses.
lr.stimulus: Professor Okonkwo: Historical reenactments draw large audiences and generate interest in the past, and I grant that this engagement is valuable. But reenactors simplify and sanitize the events they stage, and audiences walk away with tidier versions of history than the record supports. The net educational effect is negative. Curator Holst: Reenactors do simplify — they must, to stage anything at all. But an oversimplified encounter that leaves a visitor curious enough to read further is a net gain over no encounter at all.
lr.questionStem: Professor Okonkwo and Curator Holst disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: historical reenactments tend to draw large audiences

choices.label: B
choices.text: historical reenactments, on balance, have a positive educational effect on their audiences

choices.label: C
choices.text: reenactors simplify the events they stage

choices.label: D
choices.text: the historical record of the events reenactors stage is well-documented

choices.label: E
choices.text: audiences of reenactments sometimes read further about the events afterward

explanations.correct: Okonkwo concludes that the net educational effect is negative; Holst concludes that the result is a net gain. They disagree squarely on the net educational effect.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Okonkwo asserts this and Holst does not contest it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Agreement in disguise — both speakers affirm that simplification occurs.
explanations.D: Neither speaker addresses the state of the historical record.
explanations.E: Only Holst mentions post-reenactment reading; Okonkwo does not deny it happens.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that a universal basic income would relieve acute poverty and both accept that it is costly. The disagreement concerns whether the work-disincentive concern should block the policy. Trap (A) is an agreement; trap (D) splits the speakers the wrong way.
lr.stimulus: Patel: A universal basic income would dramatically reduce acute poverty, and the pilot programs we have seen bear this out. The main objection — that recipients would stop working — has not materialized in any rigorous study. We should not let an empirically unsupported worry block a policy with documented benefits. Reyna: The pilots have indeed shown little aggregate decline in work effort. I concede that. But pilots are temporary, and people behave differently when they know a benefit is permanent. The work-disincentive concern is not refuted by short-run pilots; it just hasn't been properly tested yet.
lr.questionStem: Patel and Reyna disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: universal basic income pilot programs have reduced poverty among participants

choices.label: B
choices.text: the existing evidence about pilots is sufficient to set aside the work-disincentive concern

choices.label: C
choices.text: pilot participants in universal basic income studies showed significant aggregate declines in work effort

choices.label: D
choices.text: people behave identically whether a benefit is temporary or permanent

choices.label: E
choices.text: a universal basic income would eliminate poverty entirely

explanations.correct: Patel says the empirically unsupported worry should not block the policy — i.e., current evidence suffices to set the concern aside. Reyna says the concern is not refuted by short-run pilots, meaning the evidence does not suffice. That is their exact point of disagreement.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Patel asserts poverty reduction and Reyna does not contest it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Agreement in disguise — Reyna concedes that pilots showed little aggregate decline, and Patel asserts the same.
explanations.D: This splits them the wrong way — Patel does not commit to the 'identically' claim; his point is that the empirical evidence should carry weight. Reyna rejects identity of behavior, but Patel never affirms it.
explanations.E: Neither speaker claims UBI would eliminate poverty entirely; Patel says only that it would dramatically reduce acute poverty.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that antibiotic resistance is a serious problem; disagreement is on a specific axis (whether overprescription by physicians is the primary driver), requiring the test-taker to isolate the real point of contention from shared premises.
lr.stimulus: Dr. Fenn: The alarming rise in antibiotic-resistant bacteria is driven primarily by physicians overprescribing antibiotics for viral infections. If we restrict prescriptions more aggressively, resistance rates will begin to fall. Dr. Osei: You are focusing on the wrong culprit. Agricultural overuse of antibiotics — feeding livestock subtherapeutic doses to accelerate growth — releases far greater quantities of antibiotics into the environment than overprescription does. Restricting physician prescriptions alone will accomplish little.
lr.questionStem: Dr. Fenn and Dr. Osei disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: antibiotic resistance poses a serious threat to public health

choices.label: B
choices.text: agricultural antibiotic use contributes to antibiotic resistance

choices.label: C
choices.text: physician overprescription is the principal cause of rising antibiotic resistance

choices.label: D
choices.text: restricting antibiotic prescriptions would have any effect on resistance rates

choices.label: E
choices.text: governments have an obligation to regulate antibiotic use in livestock farming

explanations.correct: Dr. Fenn explicitly identifies physician overprescription as the primary driver; Dr. Osei explicitly identifies agricultural use as the greater source and says physician overprescription is not the main culprit. Both speakers directly address and take opposing positions on this proposition.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers treat resistance as a serious problem; neither disputes this.
explanations.B: One-sided — Dr. Osei asserts agricultural use contributes; Dr. Fenn does not deny that agricultural use contributes, only that physician overprescription is the bigger factor.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the precise axis of disagreement.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — Dr. Osei says restricting prescriptions 'alone' will accomplish little, not that it will have zero effect. Dr. Fenn says it will cause resistance to fall. The nuance in Dr. Osei's 'alone' makes this a near-miss trap, not the clearest point of issue.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses governmental regulatory obligations.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers support some form of carbon taxation; the disagreement is about revenue allocation, a specific sub-issue that test-takers may overlook in favor of the superficially broader agreement on carbon taxes.
lr.stimulus: Moreno: A carbon tax is the most efficient tool we have for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Revenue from the tax should be returned directly to citizens as dividends, ensuring that lower-income households are not disproportionately burdened. Peña: I agree that a carbon tax is the right approach. However, returning revenue as citizen dividends squanders an opportunity. That revenue should be invested in green infrastructure — renewable energy grids and public transit — which will reduce emissions far more effectively over the long term.
lr.questionStem: Moreno and Peña disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: a carbon tax is an efficient mechanism for reducing greenhouse gas emissions

choices.label: B
choices.text: lower-income households are disproportionately affected by carbon pricing

choices.label: C
choices.text: green infrastructure investment would reduce emissions over the long term

choices.label: D
choices.text: carbon tax revenue should be distributed to citizens rather than invested in infrastructure

choices.label: E
choices.text: governments are capable of administering a carbon tax effectively

explanations.correct: Moreno explicitly advocates returning revenue as citizen dividends; Peña explicitly argues that revenue should fund green infrastructure instead. Both speakers directly address and take opposing stances on this allocation question.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers explicitly agree that a carbon tax is the right approach.
explanations.B: One-sided — Moreno raises this concern as a reason for dividends; Peña does not address whether lower-income households are disproportionately burdened.
explanations.C: One-sided — Peña asserts this; Moreno does not address the long-term emission impact of infrastructure investment.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker discusses governmental capacity to administer the tax.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that social media affects adolescent mental health; they differ on whether the relationship is primarily causal or correlational, a conceptually nuanced distinction that generates plausible wrong answers.
lr.stimulus: Aldridge: Research consistently shows that heavy social media use causes depression and anxiety in teenagers. The mechanism is clear: constant social comparison and cyberbullying directly harm developing self-esteem. Platforms should be required to implement use-limiting features for minors. Burak: The data do not support that conclusion. Studies showing a correlation between social media use and poor mental health cannot establish causation — teenagers who are already struggling with depression may simply be more likely to spend time online. Mandatory use restrictions are premature.
lr.questionStem: Aldridge and Burak disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: teenagers who use social media heavily are more likely to report symptoms of depression

choices.label: B
choices.text: social media platforms have any responsibility for the well-being of their users

choices.label: C
choices.text: social comparison is a feature of adolescent social interaction generally

choices.label: D
choices.text: social media use is a cause, rather than merely a correlate, of depression in adolescents

choices.label: E
choices.text: legislators should be permitted to regulate the design features of social media platforms

explanations.correct: Aldridge asserts a clear causal mechanism; Burak directly disputes causation by arguing that correlational studies cannot establish it and that the relationship may be reversed. Both speakers explicitly take opposing positions on this proposition.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Aldridge's argument presupposes this correlation, and Burak explicitly references studies showing it; neither disputes the correlation itself.
explanations.B: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses platform responsibility in general terms.
explanations.C: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses adolescent social comparison beyond the social media context.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Shift in subject — both mention mandatory restrictions, but neither addresses the broader constitutional or legal question of legislative authority to regulate platform design.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers value judicial independence; their disagreement targets a specific institutional design question. One trap answer is an agreement; another is one-sided.
lr.stimulus: Laird: Judicial elections undermine the independence of the courts. When judges must campaign for votes, they inevitably tailor their rulings to please the electorate rather than faithfully applying the law. Appointment by a merit-selection commission is the only way to preserve impartiality. Kim: Judicial elections are not the problem you describe. Accountability to the public is itself a democratic value, and elected judges are no less faithful to the law than appointed ones. Insulating judges entirely from democratic input creates its own risks of unresponsive, elitist jurisprudence.
lr.questionStem: Laird and Kim disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: judicial impartiality is an important value in a legal system

choices.label: B
choices.text: judicial elections compromise the impartiality of judges

choices.label: C
choices.text: merit-selection commissions produce judges who are more qualified than elected judges

choices.label: D
choices.text: democratic accountability is a legitimate concern in the design of judicial systems

choices.label: E
choices.text: judges appointed by commissions have longer terms than elected judges

explanations.correct: Laird explicitly argues that elections force judges to tailor rulings to voters, compromising impartiality; Kim explicitly denies this, arguing that elected judges are no less faithful to the law. Both take clear opposing positions.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers treat impartiality as important; Laird defends it by opposing elections, and Kim invokes it implicitly by denying elections undermine it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: One-sided — Laird does not argue that commission-appointed judges are more qualified, only more impartial; Kim does not address qualifications.
explanations.D: Agreement in disguise — Laird does not deny that democratic accountability is a legitimate value; Kim explicitly invokes it. Laird's preference for commissions is about a different concern.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker discusses term lengths.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree the rainforest has ecological value; disagreement is specifically about whether sustainable logging can preserve that value, a nuanced axis surrounded by apparent common ground.
lr.stimulus: Nkosi: Sustainable logging practices allow us to harvest timber commercially while preserving the ecological integrity of rainforests. Certification programs that enforce strict harvest limits and reforestation requirements have proven effective. Rainforests managed under such programs retain their biodiversity. Vega: That is wishful thinking. No logging operation, however carefully managed, can replicate the ecological complexity of an old-growth forest. Once primary forest is disturbed, the biodiversity losses are effectively permanent on any human timescale. True ecological preservation requires leaving these forests entirely untouched.
lr.questionStem: Nkosi and Vega disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: rainforest biodiversity has significant ecological value

choices.label: B
choices.text: certification programs for sustainable logging have been implemented in some regions

choices.label: C
choices.text: commercial logging operations generate economic benefits for local communities

choices.label: D
choices.text: sustainably managed logging can preserve the biodiversity of rainforests

choices.label: E
choices.text: governments have an obligation to protect old-growth forests from commercial development

explanations.correct: Nkosi explicitly asserts that certified sustainable logging preserves biodiversity; Vega explicitly denies that any managed logging can replicate or preserve old-growth ecological complexity. Both speakers directly address and oppose each other on this proposition.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers treat rainforest biodiversity as valuable; their dispute is about whether sustainable logging threatens it.
explanations.B: One-sided — Nkosi references the existence of certification programs; Vega does not address whether such programs exist, only whether they succeed.
explanations.C: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses economic benefits to local communities.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker discusses governmental obligations specifically.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers acknowledge that Renaissance art reflects its historical context; the disagreement concerns whether biographical knowledge of the artist is necessary for full aesthetic appreciation — a nuanced interpretive claim that creates plausible traps.
lr.stimulus: Chandra: To fully appreciate a Renaissance painting, one must understand the biographical context of the artist — the patron relationships, personal hardships, and theological commitments that shaped each work. Without that knowledge, a viewer grasps only the surface. Torres: I disagree. A great painting communicates its meanings visually, through composition, color, and form. Viewers who know nothing of an artist's biography regularly have profound aesthetic experiences before such works. Biographical context may enrich appreciation, but it is not necessary for it.
lr.questionStem: Chandra and Torres disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: Renaissance paintings reflect the theological beliefs of the era in which they were created

choices.label: B
choices.text: biographical knowledge of an artist can enhance a viewer's appreciation of the artist's work

choices.label: C
choices.text: an understanding of artistic composition is relevant to aesthetic appreciation

choices.label: D
choices.text: knowledge of an artist's biography is necessary for a full appreciation of that artist's painting

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renaissance patrons exerted significant influence over the content of commissioned artworks

explanations.correct: Chandra says biographical context is necessary for full appreciation; Torres explicitly denies necessity while conceding biographical context may enrich appreciation. Both speakers directly address whether biographical knowledge is necessary.
explanations.A: One-sided — Chandra references theological commitments; Torres does not address whether Renaissance paintings reflect theological beliefs.
explanations.B: Agreement in disguise — Torres concedes biographical context 'may enrich appreciation'; Chandra clearly agrees. Neither disputes that it can enhance appreciation — only whether it is required.
explanations.C: One-sided — Torres references composition, color, and form; Chandra does not address whether composition knowledge is relevant.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses patron influence on content in general terms.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers support universal basic income in principle; their disagreement targets work incentives specifically, creating a clear but narrow axis that test-takers may miss when distracted by the broader shared premise.
lr.stimulus: Reyes: A universal basic income — a guaranteed monthly payment to every citizen regardless of employment status — would eliminate the poverty trap created by means-tested benefits and give workers the bargaining power to refuse exploitative jobs. Critics worry it will discourage work, but people have intrinsic motivations to contribute; the evidence from pilot programs shows employment levels remain stable. Hartmann: The pilot program evidence is too limited to be reassuring. When a program is universal and permanent rather than temporary and localized, the incentive effects are amplified. A guaranteed income with no work requirement will meaningfully reduce labor force participation over time.
lr.questionStem: Reyes and Hartmann disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: means-tested benefit programs create disincentives that trap recipients in poverty

choices.label: B
choices.text: a universal basic income would reduce the bargaining power of low-wage workers

choices.label: C
choices.text: pilot programs studying universal basic income have been conducted

choices.label: D
choices.text: a permanent universal basic income would significantly reduce labor force participation

choices.label: E
choices.text: citizens in a wealthy society have a right to a guaranteed minimum income

explanations.correct: Reyes argues that evidence shows employment levels remain stable and that intrinsic motivation preserves labor force participation; Hartmann argues that a permanent, universal program would meaningfully reduce labor force participation. Both speakers directly address and take opposing positions on this proposition.
explanations.A: One-sided — Reyes asserts means-tested programs create poverty traps; Hartmann does not address this claim.
explanations.B: Shift in subject — Reyes argues UBI increases workers' bargaining power; neither speaker discusses a reduction in bargaining power.
explanations.C: Agreement in disguise — both speakers acknowledge pilot programs exist; Hartmann's criticism is about the adequacy of such evidence, not whether programs occurred.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses rights-based arguments for guaranteed income.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that indigenous languages are disappearing; they disagree specifically about whether formal schooling in those languages is effective at reversing decline — a targeted claim requiring careful reading of each speaker's position.
lr.stimulus: Wolfe: The most effective way to revitalize an endangered indigenous language is to integrate it into formal schooling. When children are immersed in a language through structured instruction from an early age, they achieve genuine fluency rather than mere familiarity. Immersion schools have demonstrably reversed language decline in several communities. Clearwater: Formal schooling alone cannot save a language. Language vitality depends on its use in everyday community life — in markets, ceremonies, and homes. When a language is spoken only in classrooms, children learn it as an academic subject rather than as a living means of communication, and it continues to decline outside school walls.
lr.questionStem: Wolfe and Clearwater disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: indigenous languages are disappearing at an alarming rate

choices.label: B
choices.text: children who attend immersion schools achieve some degree of fluency in the target language

choices.label: C
choices.text: the use of a language in daily community life contributes to its vitality

choices.label: D
choices.text: formal schooling is sufficient on its own to reverse the decline of an endangered language

choices.label: E
choices.text: governments should fund immersion school programs for speakers of endangered languages

explanations.correct: Wolfe argues that immersion schooling has demonstrably reversed language decline, implying formal schooling is an effective and sufficient tool; Clearwater explicitly argues that formal schooling alone cannot save a language. Both speakers address and oppose each other on the sufficiency of formal schooling.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers treat language decline as a real problem they wish to address; neither disputes that languages are disappearing.
explanations.B: One-sided — Wolfe asserts immersion produces fluency; Clearwater does not dispute that children learn the language in school, only that school-based learning is insufficient for vitality.
explanations.C: One-sided — Clearwater asserts this; Wolfe does not deny that community use matters, only that formal schooling is effective.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses governmental funding obligations.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers value historical accuracy; disagreement targets whether presentism in historical judgment is appropriate, a nuanced normative claim that generates near-miss traps about shared values.
lr.stimulus: Okafor: Historians should evaluate historical figures by the moral standards of their own time, not ours. Judging a seventeenth-century slaveholder by twenty-first-century norms is anachronistic — it distorts our understanding of the past and imposes a false moral clarity on genuinely complex historical situations. Svensson: That approach conveniently excuses atrocities. The wrongness of enslaving another person does not depend on when in history it occurred. If we restrict moral judgment to the standards contemporaries applied, we lose the ability to say that any historical injustice was truly wrong, and history becomes a chronicle without moral meaning.
lr.questionStem: Okafor and Svensson disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: slavery was widely practiced and economically significant in the seventeenth century

choices.label: B
choices.text: historians have an obligation to understand historical figures in their own context

choices.label: C
choices.text: applying contemporary moral standards to historical figures distorts historical understanding

choices.label: D
choices.text: some actions are morally wrong regardless of the era in which they were committed

choices.label: E
choices.text: moral standards have changed significantly between the seventeenth and twenty-first centuries

explanations.correct: Okafor explicitly argues that judging past figures by present standards distorts our understanding of history; Svensson explicitly rejects this, arguing instead that restricting judgment to contemporary standards loses moral meaning. Both speakers directly address and oppose each other on whether applying modern standards distorts historical understanding.
explanations.A: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses the economic or demographic dimensions of seventeenth-century slavery.
explanations.B: Agreement in disguise — Okafor explicitly endorses understanding figures in their own context, and Svensson does not deny that contextual understanding is valuable, only that it should substitute for moral judgment.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — Svensson implies this, and Okafor's view suggests standards are era-relative, but Okafor's argument is about historical methodology, not a direct denial of universal moral truths. This is a near-miss that focuses on the underlying metaphysical claim rather than the methodological disagreement both speakers address.
explanations.E: One-sided — Okafor's argument presupposes standards differ across eras; Svensson does not address whether standards have changed, only that change in standards does not affect the wrongness of certain acts.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree open-source software has benefits; their disagreement focuses on whether it produces more secure software than proprietary alternatives — a specific technical claim with plausible agreement traps on both sides.
lr.stimulus: Drayton: Open-source software is more secure than proprietary software. Because the source code is publicly available, a global community of developers can identify and patch vulnerabilities far more quickly than any single company's internal team. The sheer number of independent reviewers means that bugs are shallow — quickly found and fixed. Lim: That logic is flawed. Having source code publicly available means that malicious actors can study it just as easily as defenders can. Many open-source projects are maintained by tiny volunteer teams with no resources for systematic security auditing. Proprietary software teams, by contrast, can dedicate full-time security professionals to the task.
lr.questionStem: Drayton and Lim disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: open-source software projects are sometimes maintained by small volunteer teams

choices.label: B
choices.text: the public availability of source code provides any advantage in identifying software vulnerabilities

choices.label: C
choices.text: proprietary software development companies employ professional security teams

choices.label: D
choices.text: open-source software is, on balance, more secure than proprietary software

choices.label: E
choices.text: software security is an important consideration for both individual users and organizations

explanations.correct: Drayton explicitly argues that open-source software is more secure due to community review; Lim explicitly argues that public code availability aids attackers as much as defenders and that proprietary teams are better resourced — directly contesting the superiority claim. Both speakers address and oppose each other on the overall security comparison.
explanations.A: One-sided — Lim asserts this; Drayton does not address team size or resources.
explanations.B: Shift in subject — Drayton argues public availability is an advantage; Lim argues it is a double-edged sword. This is close, but Lim's claim is not that public code provides no advantage for defenders, only that it equally benefits attackers, making the net effect negative. The cleaner disagreement is the overall comparative security claim in D.
explanations.C: One-sided — Lim references proprietary security professionals; Drayton does not address proprietary team structures.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses whether security matters to users generally; both presuppose it does.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that antibiotic resistance is a serious problem; disagreement hinges on a specific causal axis (agricultural vs. clinical use) rather than a total contradiction. One trap answer captures their shared concern.
lr.stimulus: Moreno: The overuse of antibiotics in livestock farming is the primary driver of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Farmers administer these drugs not just to treat illness but to accelerate growth, exposing entire herds to antibiotics and creating ideal conditions for resistance to evolve. Reducing agricultural antibiotic use would therefore do more to protect public health than any clinic-based intervention. Peña: Antibiotic resistance is indeed a grave threat, but the main culprit is the inappropriate prescribing of antibiotics by physicians. Patients demand prescriptions for viral infections, and many doctors comply. Agricultural reform is worthwhile, but curbing clinical overprescription would yield the greatest public health gains.
lr.questionStem: Moreno and Peña disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: antibiotic resistance poses a serious threat to public health

choices.label: B
choices.text: reducing antibiotic use in agriculture would have any public health benefit

choices.label: C
choices.text: the primary source of antibiotic resistance is the agricultural rather than the clinical sector

choices.label: D
choices.text: physicians are capable of correctly diagnosing viral infections

choices.label: E
choices.text: antibiotic-resistant bacteria can be transmitted from livestock to humans

explanations.correct: Moreno explicitly argues agricultural overuse is the primary driver; Peña explicitly argues inappropriate clinical prescribing is the main culprit. Both directly take opposing positions on which sector is the primary source.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers acknowledge antibiotic resistance is a serious threat.
explanations.B: Shift in subject — Peña calls agricultural reform 'worthwhile,' so both actually agree it has some benefit. Only one speaker denies primacy, not all benefit.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: One-sided — neither speaker directly addresses physicians' diagnostic accuracy; Peña mentions patient demand and physician compliance, not diagnostic skill.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses the transmission mechanism from livestock to humans.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers share common ground on carbon pricing in principle; their disagreement is about which mechanism — tax or cap-and-trade — is superior in practice. A trap answer exploits their shared endorsement of carbon pricing.
lr.stimulus: Nakamura: A carbon tax is the most effective tool for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. It sets a clear price signal that businesses can plan around, and revenues can be returned to citizens as dividends, making the policy politically durable. Cap-and-trade schemes, by contrast, are vulnerable to price volatility and political manipulation of permit allocations. Osei: Carbon taxes sound appealing in theory, but cap-and-trade systems are superior in practice. By setting a firm emissions ceiling, cap-and-trade guarantees a specific environmental outcome regardless of how firms respond. A carbon tax only changes incentives — it cannot ensure that actual emissions will fall to any particular level.
lr.questionStem: Nakamura and Osei disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: placing a price on carbon emissions is an appropriate policy response to climate change

choices.label: B
choices.text: carbon taxes provide businesses with a predictable price signal

choices.label: C
choices.text: cap-and-trade systems are more effective than carbon taxes at reducing greenhouse gas emissions

choices.label: D
choices.text: governments should return carbon tax revenues to citizens

choices.label: E
choices.text: greenhouse gas emissions are the leading cause of climate change

explanations.correct: Nakamura argues the carbon tax is the most effective tool and criticizes cap-and-trade; Osei argues cap-and-trade is superior in practice. This is the direct axis of disagreement.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers endorse carbon pricing as an appropriate response; they only disagree about which mechanism is better.
explanations.B: One-sided — Nakamura affirms this, but Osei does not address the predictability of the price signal; Osei's critique concerns outcome certainty, not price predictability.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: One-sided — Nakamura mentions revenue dividends; Osei never addresses what should be done with tax revenues.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses the causal relationship between emissions and climate change.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that the jury system has value; disagreement centers on whether professional judges would deliver more accurate verdicts. A trap answer captures their shared premise about the importance of accurate verdicts.
lr.stimulus: Hartley: The jury system, while democratic in spirit, frequently produces inaccurate verdicts. Jurors lack legal training, are susceptible to emotional appeals, and often misunderstand complex evidence. Replacing jury trials with panels of professional judges in serious criminal cases would yield more reliable outcomes and better serve justice. Drummond: Professional judges are not infallible, and their decisions can reflect institutional biases acquired over years on the bench. Juries bring diverse perspectives that help guard against such bias. The occasional inaccuracy that comes with lay judgment is an acceptable price for verdicts that reflect community values rather than professional insularity.
lr.questionStem: Hartley and Drummond disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: accurate verdicts are an important goal of a criminal justice system

choices.label: B
choices.text: professional judges are entirely free from bias in their decision-making

choices.label: C
choices.text: juries are susceptible to emotional appeals during trials

choices.label: D
choices.text: replacing juries with professional judges would produce more accurate verdicts in serious criminal cases

choices.label: E
choices.text: the jury system should be abolished in all civil as well as criminal proceedings

explanations.correct: Hartley explicitly argues professional judges would yield more reliable outcomes; Drummond argues judges carry institutional biases and that lay judgment, despite occasional inaccuracy, is preferable. They directly oppose each other on whether switching to judges improves accuracy.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers treat accurate verdicts as an important goal; they disagree about how best to achieve them.
explanations.B: Shift in subject — Hartley does not claim judges are entirely bias-free; Hartley only claims they are more reliable than juries. The proposition in (B) is stronger than Hartley's actual claim.
