explanations.C: One-sided — Hartley asserts this; Drummond does not directly contest whether juries are susceptible to emotional appeals.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses civil proceedings; Hartley limits the proposal to serious criminal cases.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers value preserving endangered languages; they disagree on whether immersive school programs are the most effective preservation method. A trap presents their shared concern about language loss as a disagreement.
lr.stimulus: Vasquez: Endangered languages are best preserved through immersive school programs that teach children entirely in the heritage language. Schools create a new generation of fluent speakers, and fluency — not just cultural memory — is what keeps a language alive. Community events and digital archives, while helpful, are supplementary at best. Lindqvist: Immersive schooling can actually alienate families if parents themselves are not fluent, creating a divide between home and classroom. The most effective preservation happens when communities integrate the language into daily life — through markets, local governance, and inter-generational conversation. Schools matter, but they are not the primary engine of revitalization.
lr.questionStem: Vasquez and Lindqvist disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the preservation of endangered languages is a worthwhile social goal

choices.label: B
choices.text: digital archives have any role to play in language preservation

choices.label: C
choices.text: immersive school programs are the most effective means of preserving endangered languages

choices.label: D
choices.text: children must achieve full fluency for a language to survive

choices.label: E
choices.text: governments should fund endangered language programs

explanations.correct: Vasquez argues immersive school programs are the best preservation tool; Lindqvist argues community integration into daily life is more effective and that schools are not the primary engine. Both take clear opposing positions.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers clearly treat language preservation as worthwhile; neither questions its value.
explanations.B: One-sided — Vasquez calls digital archives supplementary; Lindqvist does not address digital archives at all.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: One-sided — Vasquez implicitly endorses full fluency as the goal; Lindqvist's position concerns where language integration occurs, not whether fluency is needed.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses government funding.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that the gig economy has changed labor markets; they share the view that workers deserve protections. Disagreement lies in whether classifying gig workers as employees is the right mechanism for delivering those protections.
lr.stimulus: Chandra: Gig workers — drivers, delivery couriers, freelance taskers — deserve the same protections as traditional employees: minimum wage guarantees, access to unemployment insurance, and employer contributions to health benefits. The only way to achieve this is to reclassify them as employees. Their nominal independence is a legal fiction that benefits corporations at workers' expense. Bellamy: Gig workers genuinely value the flexibility that comes with independent contractor status, and mandatory reclassification would destroy that. Worker protections should instead be extended through portable benefits legislation — policies that attach benefits to individuals rather than to employment relationships. Reclassification is neither necessary nor desirable for protecting these workers.
lr.questionStem: Chandra and Bellamy disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: gig workers are entitled to some form of labor protections

choices.label: B
choices.text: reclassifying gig workers as employees is the appropriate means of securing their labor protections

choices.label: C
choices.text: many gig workers prefer flexible working arrangements to fixed schedules

choices.label: D
choices.text: corporations benefit financially from the independent contractor classification

choices.label: E
choices.text: portable benefits legislation has been successfully implemented in any jurisdiction

explanations.correct: Chandra says reclassification is the only way to achieve worker protections; Bellamy says reclassification is neither necessary nor desirable, preferring portable benefits instead. Both directly address and oppose each other on this mechanism.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers agree gig workers deserve protections; the dispute is over method, not entitlement.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: One-sided — Bellamy asserts workers value flexibility; Chandra calls their independence a 'legal fiction' but does not directly address whether workers subjectively prefer it.
explanations.D: One-sided — Chandra asserts this; Bellamy does not dispute or address it.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker discusses the historical track record of portable benefits laws.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers share concern about social media's effects on democratic discourse; they diverge on whether algorithmic content ranking is the cause. A trap answer presents their shared worry as a point of contention.
lr.stimulus: Eriksson: Social media platforms' algorithmic ranking systems are the root cause of political polarization online. By prioritizing emotionally provocative content, these algorithms drive users into ideological echo chambers, eroding the shared factual foundation that democratic deliberation requires. Regulating algorithmic design should therefore be a top legislative priority. Walcott: Political polarization predates social media and would persist without it. Research shows that most people encounter more cross-cutting political content online than they do in their offline social circles. The algorithms are not the villain — pre-existing partisan identities drive users to select polarizing content regardless of how feeds are ranked.
lr.questionStem: Eriksson and Walcott disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: political polarization is a threat to democratic deliberation

choices.label: B
choices.text: social media platforms use algorithms to rank the content users see

choices.label: C
choices.text: social media algorithms are a primary cause of political polarization

choices.label: D
choices.text: legislatures have the authority to regulate the design of social media algorithms

choices.label: E
choices.text: users encounter any politically diverse content through social media feeds

explanations.correct: Eriksson asserts algorithms are the root cause of polarization; Walcott argues polarization predates social media and that pre-existing partisan identities, not algorithms, drive polarizing content consumption. They directly oppose each other on this causal claim.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both treat polarization as a problem; Eriksson explicitly and Walcott implicitly treat it as something to be concerned about.
explanations.B: One-sided — Eriksson discusses algorithmic ranking; Walcott does not dispute that platforms use such algorithms; this is shared background.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: One-sided — Eriksson calls for legislative regulation; Walcott does not address legislative authority.
explanations.E: Shift in subject — Walcott says users encounter more cross-cutting content online, which implies (E) is true; Eriksson does not deny that any diverse content appears, only that algorithms suppress it relative to provocative content.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that the New Deal had economic effects; the disagreement is whether deficit spending was responsible for ending the Depression. A trap answer captures shared acceptance of New Deal spending programs.
lr.stimulus: Ferreira: The New Deal's deficit spending pulled the United States out of the Great Depression by injecting demand into a collapsed economy. Federal employment programs put money in workers' pockets, which they spent on goods and services, generating a multiplier effect that gradually restored economic confidence. Without this fiscal intervention, the Depression would have lasted far longer. Stanton: The New Deal alleviated suffering and reformed financial institutions, but it did not end the Depression — the economy remained deeply depressed through the late 1930s. Full recovery came only with the enormous defense spending triggered by World War II. New Deal deficits were too modest and inconsistent to generate the demand needed for complete recovery.
lr.questionStem: Ferreira and Stanton disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: New Deal programs alleviated economic suffering during the 1930s

choices.label: B
choices.text: World War II military spending boosted the American economy

choices.label: C
choices.text: the federal government ran budget deficits during the New Deal era

choices.label: D
choices.text: New Deal deficit spending was sufficient to end the Great Depression

choices.label: E
choices.text: demand stimulus can in principle restore a depressed economy

explanations.correct: Ferreira argues New Deal deficit spending did pull the economy out of the Depression; Stanton argues it was insufficient and that recovery only came with WWII defense spending. Both directly address and oppose each other on whether New Deal spending was enough to end the Depression.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Stanton explicitly grants that the New Deal alleviated suffering; Ferreira affirms this as well. Neither denies it.
explanations.B: One-sided — Stanton credits WWII spending with full recovery; Ferreira does not address WWII spending at all.
explanations.C: Out of scope — neither speaker disputes the historical fact of deficit spending; Stanton even mentions deficits were 'too modest,' presupposing they occurred.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: One-sided — Ferreira implicitly endorses demand stimulus; Stanton's argument concerns the scale of the specific stimulus, not whether demand stimulus can work in principle.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers value artistic integrity; they disagree on whether commercial success is compatible with it. A trap answer presents their shared valuation of integrity as a point of disagreement.
lr.stimulus: Inoue: An artist who tailors work to market demands has surrendered the creative independence that makes art meaningful. Commercial success requires producing what audiences already expect, which inevitably narrows the artist's vision and homogenizes culture. The most enduring art has almost always been created in defiance of prevailing tastes, not in service of them. Adjei: Commercial success and artistic integrity are not mutually exclusive. Many artists have reached wide audiences precisely because their genuine vision resonated broadly, not because they compromised it. Financial independence from commercial success can actually free an artist from dependence on institutional patrons, who impose their own constraints on creative work.
lr.questionStem: Inoue and Adjei disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: artistic integrity is a valuable quality in creative work

choices.label: B
choices.text: institutional patronage places constraints on artists' creative freedom

choices.label: C
choices.text: commercial success necessarily compromises an artist's creative integrity

choices.label: D
choices.text: the most enduring artworks have typically been created without regard for market demand

choices.label: E
choices.text: artists should seek to expand the audience for their work

explanations.correct: Inoue argues that tailoring work to the market 'inevitably' narrows vision, implying commercial success necessarily compromises integrity; Adjei directly counters that the two are 'not mutually exclusive.' Both take clear opposing positions on this proposition.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers treat artistic integrity as valuable; neither dismisses it.
explanations.B: One-sided — Adjei raises institutional patronage as a constraining force; Inoue does not address patrons at all.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: One-sided — Inoue asserts this historical claim; Adjei does not directly contest the historical record, only the general relationship between commerce and integrity.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses whether artists should seek wider audiences as a goal.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that mandatory minimum sentences have costs; disagreement is about whether prosecutorial discretion adequately corrects for their harshness. A trap answer captures their shared critique of rigid sentencing.
lr.stimulus: Okafor: Mandatory minimum sentencing laws produce unjust outcomes by stripping judges of the discretion needed to account for individual circumstances. A first-time, low-level drug offender can face the same prison term as a violent repeat offender. Prosecutors cannot fix this problem — their charging decisions introduce inconsistency without restoring principled case-by-case fairness. Reyes: Mandatory minimums do constrain judges, but prosecutors retain substantial power to calibrate outcomes by choosing which charges to file. In practice, prosecutorial discretion functions as a release valve, allowing the system to avoid the most egregious applications of these laws. The real solution lies in better training prosecutors, not in abolishing mandatory minimums.
lr.questionStem: Okafor and Reyes disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: mandatory minimum sentencing laws limit the discretion available to judges

choices.label: B
choices.text: some mandatory minimum sentences produce outcomes that are disproportionately harsh

choices.label: C
choices.text: prosecutorial discretion adequately compensates for the inflexibility of mandatory minimum laws

choices.label: D
choices.text: violent repeat offenders deserve longer prison sentences than first-time offenders

choices.label: E
choices.text: mandatory minimum laws should be abolished entirely

explanations.correct: Okafor explicitly argues prosecutors cannot fix the harshness of mandatory minimums and that their decisions introduce inconsistency without principled fairness; Reyes explicitly argues prosecutorial discretion functions as an effective 'release valve.' Both take opposing positions on this specific claim.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers accept that mandatory minimums constrain judges; Reyes affirms this while focusing on prosecutorial power as compensation.
explanations.B: Agreement in disguise — Okafor argues minimums are unjust; Reyes grants that 'most egregious applications' must be avoided, implying some outcomes are too harsh.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses the normative question of what sentences violent offenders deserve.
explanations.E: Shift in subject — Okafor critiques mandatory minimums and implies reform, but does not call for total abolition; Reyes opposes abolition. The disagreement in the stimulus is not about total abolition.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers endorse the use of cost-benefit analysis in policy; they diverge on whether it should be the decisive criterion when environmental values are at stake. A trap presents their shared endorsement of cost-benefit analysis as a point of contention.
lr.stimulus: Prasad: Cost-benefit analysis should be the decisive criterion in environmental policymaking. When we quantify the costs of regulation against the economic value of the benefits — cleaner air, reduced health costs, preserved ecosystems — we can make rational, transparent decisions rather than ones driven by emotion or political pressure. Every environmental protection can and should be evaluated on these terms. Delacroix: Cost-benefit analysis is a useful tool, but treating it as decisive in environmental policy is a mistake. Many ecological values — the existence of a species, the integrity of a wilderness — cannot be adequately captured in monetary terms. When cost-benefit calculations exclude or undervalue these things, following them blindly leads to policies that are economically tidy but ethically indefensible.
lr.questionStem: Prasad and Delacroix disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: cost-benefit analysis has any legitimate role in environmental policymaking

choices.label: B
choices.text: environmental regulations impose costs on businesses and the broader economy

choices.label: C
choices.text: the preservation of wild species has value that policymakers should take into account

choices.label: D
choices.text: cost-benefit analysis should serve as the decisive criterion in making environmental policy decisions

choices.label: E
choices.text: some environmental decisions are influenced by political pressure rather than rational analysis

explanations.correct: Prasad argues cost-benefit analysis should be the decisive criterion; Delacroix argues it is a useful tool but must not be treated as decisive because it cannot capture all ecological values. Both take clear, opposing positions on this precise proposition.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Delacroix explicitly calls cost-benefit analysis 'a useful tool,' affirming it has a legitimate role; Prasad obviously endorses it. Neither denies it has any role.
explanations.B: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses the distribution of regulatory costs; Prasad mentions economic value of benefits but not costs imposed on businesses specifically.
explanations.C: Agreement in disguise — Prasad includes 'preserved ecosystems' among benefits and Delacroix argues species existence has value that cost-benefit analysis undervalues. Both treat such value as real; they disagree about whether cost-benefit analysis captures it.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: One-sided — Prasad raises political pressure as something rational analysis should replace; Delacroix does not address political pressure at all.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers share common ground (vaccines benefit public health), but disagree on one specific axis — whether mandating vaccines is justified. A trap answer presents their area of agreement; another is one-sided.
lr.stimulus: Moreno: Vaccination programs have dramatically reduced the incidence of infectious disease, and the evidence for their effectiveness is overwhelming. But compelling individuals to receive vaccines crosses an ethical line — personal medical decisions must remain voluntary, or we compromise the very autonomy that defines a free society. Peña: I share your admiration for what vaccines have achieved. What you miss, however, is that personal autonomy cannot be invoked to justify choices that put other people's lives at risk. Mandatory vaccination is not a restriction on freedom; it is a basic obligation to the community.
lr.questionStem: Moreno and Peña disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: vaccination programs have been effective at reducing infectious disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: individuals have an obligation to consider the well-being of others when making personal decisions

choices.label: C
choices.text: mandatory vaccination is an ethically permissible policy

choices.label: D
choices.text: the scientific evidence supporting vaccines is reliable

choices.label: E
choices.text: governments ever have legitimate authority to regulate individual behavior

explanations.correct: Moreno explicitly denies that mandating vaccines is ethically permissible, grounding the denial in individual autonomy. Peña explicitly affirms that mandatory vaccination is an ethical obligation to the community. Both take clear, opposed positions on this proposition.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers affirm that vaccination programs have been effective. Moreno's opening sentence concedes this point, and Peña's opening echoes it.
explanations.B: One-sided trap — Peña's argument presupposes individuals have obligations to others, but Moreno never denies this general principle; Moreno's objection is specifically about medical compulsion, not about whether obligations to others exist at all.
explanations.D: Out of scope — neither speaker disputes the reliability of vaccine science; both treat it as settled.
explanations.E: Out of scope and one-sided — neither speaker addresses the general question of government regulatory authority; the dialogue is confined to the specific question of medical mandates.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that AI has economic consequences; disagreement is localized to whether automation produces net job loss. One trap is an agreement; another is one-sided.
lr.stimulus: Okafor: Automation driven by artificial intelligence will eliminate far more jobs than it creates. History shows that technological transitions displace workers, and there is no guarantee that the new industries spawned by AI will absorb the labor force quickly enough to prevent widespread unemployment. Shen: That historical narrative is selective. Every major wave of automation has ultimately generated more employment than it eliminated, because lower production costs expand markets, and expanding markets demand more workers. AI will follow the same pattern.
lr.questionStem: Okafor and Shen disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: artificial intelligence will have significant economic consequences for workers

choices.label: B
choices.text: automation driven by AI will result in a net reduction in employment

choices.label: C
choices.text: lower production costs can lead to the expansion of existing markets

choices.label: D
choices.text: previous waves of automation displaced some workers in the short term

choices.label: E
choices.text: governments should intervene to retrain workers displaced by automation

explanations.correct: Okafor explicitly claims AI automation will eliminate more jobs than it creates — a net reduction. Shen explicitly denies this, arguing every wave of automation has ultimately produced more employment than it eliminated. Both take clear, opposed positions.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers clearly believe AI will have significant economic consequences for workers; they differ only on the direction and magnitude of the net effect.
explanations.C: One-sided trap — Shen's argument relies on lower costs expanding markets, but Okafor neither affirms nor denies this mechanism; Okafor's concern is about the speed of reabsorption, not whether market expansion occurs.
explanations.D: Agreement in disguise — Okafor implies past displacement occurred, and Shen's framing ('ultimately generated more employment') concedes short-term displacement. Neither disputes that past displacement happened.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses government retraining policy; the dialogue concerns economic outcomes, not policy prescriptions.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Speakers share agreement on the value of biodiversity but diverge specifically on whether economic development is the primary driver of deforestation. Trap includes an agreement and a one-sided answer.
lr.stimulus: Dr. Vasquez: Deforestation remains the gravest threat to tropical biodiversity. The primary engine is not poverty, as is often assumed, but large-scale commercial agriculture driven by global commodity markets. Addressing deforestation requires regulating those markets, not merely funding local conservation programs. Dr. Liang: Biodiversity loss is certainly alarming, but attributing it mainly to commercial agriculture oversimplifies a complex problem. Subsistence farming, illegal logging, and infrastructure development each account for substantial forest loss. No single driver dominates, and policy must address all of them simultaneously.
lr.questionStem: Dr. Vasquez and Dr. Liang disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: tropical deforestation poses a serious threat to biodiversity

choices.label: B
choices.text: subsistence farming contributes to forest loss

choices.label: C
choices.text: commercial agriculture is the principal cause of tropical deforestation

choices.label: D
choices.text: conservation policy should take economic factors into account

choices.label: E
choices.text: global commodity markets influence land-use patterns in tropical regions

explanations.correct: Dr. Vasquez explicitly identifies large-scale commercial agriculture as the primary engine of deforestation. Dr. Liang explicitly denies that any single driver dominates, rejecting the claim that commercial agriculture is the principal cause. Both take directly opposed positions on this proposition.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Dr. Vasquez calls deforestation the gravest threat to tropical biodiversity, and Dr. Liang describes biodiversity loss as certainly alarming. Neither disputes the seriousness of the threat.
explanations.B: One-sided trap — Dr. Liang mentions subsistence farming as a contributing cause, but Dr. Vasquez says nothing about whether subsistence farming contributes; Vasquez's argument is about what is primary, not about ruling out other causes entirely.
explanations.D: Out of scope — neither speaker directly addresses what factors conservation policy should weigh; Dr. Vasquez discusses market regulation, but neither explicitly argues about whether economic factors should or should not be considered in policy.
explanations.E: One-sided trap — Dr. Vasquez's argument presupposes that global commodity markets influence land use, but Dr. Liang does not deny this; Liang's disagreement is about relative causal weight, not about whether markets have any influence.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers value artistic originality but disagree specifically on whether constraints imposed by patrons historically enhanced or diminished the quality of art produced. One trap is agreement; another is a subject-shift.
lr.stimulus: Laird: The great works of the Renaissance were produced under conditions of strict patronage — artists worked within prescribed religious and political constraints. Far from limiting artistic genius, those constraints gave artists a clear framework that focused their creativity and elevated the quality of their work. Kim: You romanticize the past. Many Renaissance artists chafed bitterly under patronage demands, and the works we celebrate most were often produced in spite of those constraints, not because of them. External demands imposed by patrons diminished, rather than enhanced, the artistic quality of the work.
lr.questionStem: Laird and Kim disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: Renaissance artists sometimes worked under constraints imposed by patrons

choices.label: B
choices.text: the works produced during the Renaissance are among the greatest in Western art

choices.label: C
choices.text: artistic creativity can flourish in any historical period

choices.label: D
choices.text: patronage constraints enhanced rather than diminished the quality of Renaissance art

choices.label: E
choices.text: some Renaissance artists expressed dissatisfaction with the demands of their patrons

explanations.correct: Laird explicitly argues that patronage constraints focused creativity and elevated quality. Kim explicitly argues those constraints diminished artistic quality. Both take directly opposed positions on this proposition.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers accept that Renaissance artists worked under patron-imposed constraints; this is the shared premise of their debate, not the point of disagreement.
explanations.B: Agreement in disguise — Laird cites great Renaissance works admiringly, and Kim's argument ('the works we celebrate most') similarly presupposes those works are celebrated. Neither disputes their greatness.
explanations.C: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses whether creativity can flourish in any historical period; the debate is specific to the effect of Renaissance patronage constraints.
explanations.E: One-sided trap — Kim explicitly states that many artists 'chafed bitterly,' but Laird does not deny that some artists were dissatisfied; Laird's argument is about the net effect on quality, not about artists' emotional experience.
explanations.D: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that plea bargaining reduces court costs; disagreement is focused on whether it produces just outcomes. A trap presents shared common ground; another is one-sided on a different axis.
lr.stimulus: Renata: Plea bargaining is a pragmatic necessity in any functioning criminal justice system. It reduces court costs, spares victims the ordeal of trials, and allows prosecutors to focus resources on the most serious cases. Crucially, defendants are not coerced — they agree to plead guilty in exchange for a known, reduced sentence. Dominic: Calling plea bargaining voluntary ignores the enormous pressure defendants face. When the alternative is risking a far harsher sentence at trial, many innocent people plead guilty simply to avoid that risk. A process that systematically produces false convictions cannot be called just, regardless of its administrative efficiencies.
lr.questionStem: Renata and Dominic disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: plea bargaining reduces the administrative costs of processing criminal cases

choices.label: B
choices.text: defendants who accept plea agreements are ever innocent of the charges against them

choices.label: C
choices.text: the criminal justice system requires some mechanism for resolving cases without full trials

choices.label: D
choices.text: plea bargaining produces outcomes that are consistent with justice

choices.label: E
choices.text: prosecutors should be permitted to offer sentence reductions in exchange for guilty pleas

explanations.correct: Renata argues that plea bargaining is a legitimate, just practice because defendants voluntarily accept reduced sentences. Dominic argues that it systematically produces false convictions and therefore cannot be called just. Both take directly opposed positions on whether plea bargaining produces just outcomes.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Renata cites reduced court costs as a benefit, and Dominic concedes 'administrative efficiencies' exist. Neither disputes that plea bargaining lowers administrative costs.
explanations.B: One-sided trap — Dominic argues innocent people plead guilty, but Renata does not address or deny this possibility; Renata's argument concerns voluntariness, not the factual innocence of those who plea.
explanations.C: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses whether some case-resolution mechanism short of full trials is necessary; Dominic objects to plea bargaining specifically, not to alternatives in general.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the debate concerns whether the practice is just, not the separate legal/policy question of whether prosecutors should be permitted to make such offers.
explanations.D: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Speakers share agreement that language shapes thought; the disagreement is localized to whether a language's grammatical structure determines the limits of its speakers' conceptual range. One trap is agreement; another is a subject-shift.
lr.stimulus: Torres: The grammar of a language does more than reflect the way its speakers think — it actively constrains what they can think. Languages that lack tense markers, for instance, make certain temporal distinctions genuinely inaccessible to their speakers. The structure of language is the structure of thought itself. Nakamura: Language obviously influences how we habitually frame our experience, and I wouldn't deny that. But 'influences' is far weaker than 'determines.' Speakers can and regularly do grasp concepts for which their native language provides no dedicated grammatical structure — through borrowing, metaphor, and context. Grammar sets tendencies, not limits.
lr.questionStem: Torres and Nakamura disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: language has some influence on the way its speakers habitually think

choices.label: B
choices.text: speakers of any language can acquire vocabulary from other languages

choices.label: C
choices.text: grammatical structure determines the conceptual limits of a language's speakers

choices.label: D
choices.text: languages differ from one another in their grammatical structures

choices.label: E
choices.text: the study of linguistics provides insight into human cognition

explanations.correct: Torres explicitly claims that grammatical structure sets hard limits — certain distinctions are 'genuinely inaccessible' — which is the claim that grammar determines conceptual limits. Nakamura explicitly denies this, arguing that grammar sets tendencies, not limits, and that speakers routinely grasp concepts without dedicated grammatical structure. Both take directly opposed positions.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Torres argues grammar shapes thought, and Nakamura explicitly says 'language obviously influences how we habitually frame our experience.' Both accept that language influences thought.
explanations.B: One-sided trap — Nakamura mentions borrowing as evidence against strict determination, but Torres never addresses whether speakers borrow vocabulary; this is not a point Torres takes a position on.
explanations.D: Out of scope — neither speaker debates whether languages differ grammatically; both assume this as background.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker addresses the value of linguistics as a discipline.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that carbon taxes change behavior; they diverge specifically on whether a revenue-neutral carbon tax is sufficient to achieve meaningful emissions reductions. One trap is agreement; another is a subject-shift to a point neither addresses.
lr.stimulus: Eriksson: A revenue-neutral carbon tax is the most efficient tool available for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. By pricing carbon accurately, it changes behavior across the entire economy simultaneously, without requiring the government to pick winners among competing clean technologies. Returning the revenue as dividends ensures it is politically sustainable. Mbeki: I support pricing carbon, but a revenue-neutral tax alone will not achieve the emissions reductions the climate crisis demands. The scale of investment required in clean infrastructure — grids, transit, storage — can only come from directing carbon revenue into those systems, not distributing it as consumer dividends.
lr.questionStem: Eriksson and Mbeki disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: placing a price on carbon emissions alters the behavior of economic actors

choices.label: B
choices.text: governments should avoid directing investment toward specific clean technologies

choices.label: C
choices.text: a revenue-neutral carbon tax is sufficient to achieve the necessary scale of emissions reductions

choices.label: D
choices.text: the climate crisis requires significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions

choices.label: E
choices.text: carbon tax revenue should be returned to the public in some form

explanations.correct: Eriksson argues that a revenue-neutral carbon tax is the most efficient tool available and implicitly sufficient on its own. Mbeki explicitly denies sufficiency, arguing a revenue-neutral tax alone will not achieve the required emissions reductions and that revenue must be directed into infrastructure. Both take directly opposed positions on sufficiency.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Eriksson's entire argument rests on carbon pricing changing behavior, and Mbeki supports pricing carbon as well. Neither disputes that a carbon price alters economic behavior.
explanations.B: One-sided trap — Eriksson argues against government picking winners among technologies, but Mbeki does not directly address this principle; Mbeki's argument is about directing revenue into infrastructure categories, not selecting specific technologies.
explanations.D: Agreement in disguise — both speakers treat the urgency of the climate crisis as given; Mbeki explicitly invokes it, and Eriksson's argument presupposes it. Neither disputes that significant emissions reductions are required.
explanations.E: Subject-shift trap — Eriksson advocates returning revenue as dividends; Mbeki advocates directing it into infrastructure. Both envision revenue going somewhere public, but they disagree about where. The proposition as stated ('returned to the public in some form') is too broad to capture the disagreement and could be construed as something both accept.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that the placebo effect is real; their disagreement is specifically about whether physicians are ever ethically justified in prescribing placebos without patient knowledge. One trap offers agreement; another is one-sided.
lr.stimulus: Dr. Okonkwo: The placebo effect is a genuine, measurable physiological response, and harnessing it can meaningfully reduce patient suffering. When a physician prescribes an inert treatment knowing it will trigger that response, and the patient benefits, the deception involved is a minor cost outweighed by real therapeutic gain. Dr. Chen: The placebo effect is real, but that does not justify deceiving patients. Informed consent is not a bureaucratic formality — it is the foundation of the physician-patient relationship. A physician who withholds information to manipulate a patient's physiology, however well-intentioned, has violated the patient's right to make autonomous medical decisions.
lr.questionStem: Dr. Okonkwo and Dr. Chen disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the placebo effect produces measurable physiological changes in patients

choices.label: B
choices.text: physicians are ever ethically justified in prescribing placebos without a patient's knowledge

choices.label: C
choices.text: informed consent is a component of the physician-patient relationship

choices.label: D
choices.text: patient suffering can be reduced by means other than pharmacologically active treatments

choices.label: E
choices.text: medical ethics should give greater weight to patient outcomes than to procedural rules

explanations.correct: Dr. Okonkwo explicitly argues that prescribing a placebo without disclosure is justified when therapeutic benefit outweighs the minor cost of deception. Dr. Chen explicitly denies this, arguing such deception violates patient autonomy regardless of outcome. Both take directly opposed positions on whether such prescribing is ever ethically justified.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Dr. Okonkwo calls the placebo effect 'genuine and measurable,' and Dr. Chen concedes 'the placebo effect is real.' Both accept this premise; it is the shared starting point of their debate.
explanations.C: One-sided trap — Dr. Chen explicitly affirms that informed consent is foundational to the physician-patient relationship, but Dr. Okonkwo does not deny this general principle; Okonkwo argues only that in certain cases therapeutic benefit can outweigh the cost of deception.
explanations.D: Agreement in disguise — both speakers accept that placebo treatments reduce suffering without pharmacologically active ingredients; this is presupposed by both sides of the argument.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker directly addresses the meta-ethical question of how to weigh outcomes against procedural rules as general categories; the debate is about a specific practice, not about the relative weight of ethical frameworks.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that the new antibiotic reduces mortality in the trial, agree side effects are non-trivial, and agree resistance is a concern. The disagreement is implicit: Tanaka's reasoning commits her to the view that the trial's mortality benefit should govern approval now, while Ruiz's commits him to the view that it should not, because resistance risks are a current decision-input, not a future one. Trap (B) is agreement in disguise; (D) swaps 'current decision' for 'future prescribing'.
lr.stimulus: Dr. Tanaka: The phase III trial showed a thirty-percent drop in mortality from drug-resistant pneumonia, and the side effect profile, while not trivial, is manageable with monitoring. The agency should approve the drug on that record. Future resistance is a real worry, but it is a worry about what comes next, and can be handled through prescribing guidelines. Dr. Ruiz: A thirty-percent mortality reduction is significant, and I would not dispute the safety data. But broad approval will drive the very resistance we are both concerned about, and once that resistance is entrenched, no prescribing guideline will undo it. The trial result tells us the drug works today; it does not tell us we should authorize it today.
lr.questionStem: Dr. Tanaka and Dr. Ruiz are committed to disagreeing over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the risk that broad approval will accelerate resistance is a sufficient reason to withhold approval now

choices.label: B
choices.text: the drug reduced mortality from drug-resistant pneumonia in the phase III trial

choices.label: C
choices.text: prescribing guidelines can completely eliminate the risk of antibiotic resistance

choices.label: D
choices.text: physicians should restrict their prescribing of the drug once it has been approved

choices.label: E
choices.text: the drug's side effects rule out approval on safety grounds alone

explanations.correct: Tanaka treats resistance as a downstream worry handleable by guidelines, so it is not a reason to withhold approval now; Ruiz treats resistance as the decisive reason to withhold approval now. Piecing together their full statements, they are committed to opposite yes/no answers on exactly this proposition.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Agreement in disguise — Tanaka asserts it and Ruiz calls it significant.
explanations.C: Neither speaker claims complete elimination; Tanaka only says guidelines can handle it, and Ruiz denies guidelines would fix entrenched resistance, not that they aim to eliminate it.
explanations.D: The dialogue is about whether to approve, not about post-approval prescribing behavior; neither speaker takes a position on what individual physicians should do after approval.
explanations.E: Both speakers agree the safety data is acceptable; Tanaka calls side effects manageable and Ruiz says he would not dispute the safety data.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree the defendant lied under oath, agree the lie was material, and agree a conviction would be legally sustainable. The disagreement is whether the prosecutor was ethically required to bring the charge, which has to be reconstructed from Lund's 'duty to pursue' reasoning and Abebe's 'discretion to decline where the social cost exceeds the marginal deterrent gain'. Trap (C) is an apparent disagreement that dissolves; (E) is a shift of subject.
lr.stimulus: Lund: The defendant lied under oath about a material fact. A prosecutor who has uncontested evidence of perjury has a duty to pursue that charge; the integrity of sworn testimony depends on people knowing such lies will be prosecuted. Whether a jury convicts is a separate question. Abebe: The evidence here was uncontested, and yes, a conviction would almost certainly have been sustained on appeal. But prosecutorial resources are finite, and when the marginal deterrent value of one more perjury case is small compared to the cases it displaces, the office is entitled to decline. That is not a failure of integrity; it is a judgment about where public harm is greatest.
lr.questionStem: Lund and Abebe's statements commit them to disagreeing about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: a prosecutor faced with uncontested evidence of material perjury is ethically required to bring the charge

choices.label: B
choices.text: the defendant's false statement concerned a material fact

choices.label: C
choices.text: prosecutorial offices operate under genuine resource constraints

choices.label: D
choices.text: a perjury conviction in this case would have been sustained on appeal

choices.label: E
choices.text: declining to prosecute the case would weaken public trust in sworn testimony

explanations.correct: Lund asserts a duty to pursue perjury where the evidence is uncontested; Abebe asserts the office is entitled to decline when deterrent value is low. The two positions cannot both be held.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Both speakers grant materiality — Lund asserts it and Abebe does not contest it.
explanations.C: Only Abebe invokes resource constraints; Lund takes no position either way on whether such constraints exist, only on their relevance.
explanations.D: Agreement in disguise — Lund implies a conviction was available and Abebe concedes it would likely be sustained.
explanations.E: Lund implies integrity is served by prosecution, but does not claim declining would weaken trust; Abebe's view is that declining is not a failure of integrity. Neither speaker commits to the specific trust-erosion claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that the Phillips curve has weakened empirically and both agree that low unemployment has coincided with low inflation in the last decade. The disagreement is implicit: Haugen treats weakened correlation as evidence the underlying mechanism is gone, while Desai treats it as evidence the mechanism is masked by favorable supply conditions that may not persist. Trap (A) is agreement in disguise; (D) is out of scope.
lr.stimulus: Haugen: For most of the past decade, unemployment has been historically low without any meaningful pickup in inflation. The Phillips curve, which predicted exactly such a pickup, has lost its predictive grip, and central banks should stop designing policy around a relationship that the data no longer bears out. Desai: I grant that the simple textbook curve has been a poor forecaster recently. But that stretch coincided with uniquely favorable supply conditions — globalization, flexible labor markets, stable commodity prices. Those conditions are fading. Writing off the underlying relationship now is exactly the wrong lesson to draw from a decade of good luck.
lr.questionStem: Haugen and Desai's statements provide the most support for the claim that they would disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the Phillips curve has been a poor empirical forecaster over the past decade

choices.label: B
choices.text: the relationship between unemployment and inflation the Phillips curve describes still operates as an underlying mechanism

choices.label: C
choices.text: supply-side conditions over the past decade have been unusually favorable

choices.label: D
choices.text: central banks' current policy frameworks should place more weight on commodity prices

choices.label: E
choices.text: low unemployment has coincided with low inflation in recent years

explanations.correct: Haugen treats the weakened correlation as evidence the underlying relationship is gone; Desai explicitly resists 'writing off the underlying relationship' and attributes the weakness to temporary conditions. That is a direct disagreement about whether the mechanism still operates.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Haugen calls the curve's predictive grip lost and Desai grants the textbook curve has been a poor forecaster recently.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Only Desai takes a position on supply-side conditions; Haugen does not address them.
explanations.D: Neither speaker takes a position on commodity prices as a policy input; Desai only cites stable commodity prices as one favorable condition.
explanations.E: Both speakers accept this — Haugen states it outright, Desai does not dispute it.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree carbon pricing reduces emissions, both agree regressive effects on low-income households are real, and both agree dividends can be paid. The disagreement is about whether dividends fully neutralize the distributive objection — Olander treats dividends as sufficient; Ibarra treats them as insufficient because the harm is not only in aggregate income but in exposure timing. Trap (A) is agreement; (E) is out of scope.
lr.stimulus: Olander: A carbon price reduces emissions efficiently, and the revenue can be rebated as equal per-person dividends. Once you do that, the typical low-income household comes out ahead in net terms, because their direct carbon footprint is smaller than average. The distributive concern about carbon pricing is, for practical purposes, solved. Ibarra: Aggregate net-positive numbers hide a timing problem. The price rise hits heating, gas, and groceries immediately every month, while the dividend arrives quarterly or annually. A family living paycheck to paycheck is not made whole by a refund that shows up after an eviction notice.
lr.questionStem: Olander and Ibarra are committed to disagreeing over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: a carbon price reduces emissions

choices.label: B
choices.text: equal per-person dividends funded by carbon pricing revenue adequately address the policy's distributional impact on low-income households

choices.label: C
choices.text: the direct carbon footprint of low-income households is smaller than the population average

choices.label: D
choices.text: carbon pricing dividends should be paid monthly rather than less frequently

choices.label: E
choices.text: the government should expand heating subsidies independently of any carbon pricing scheme

explanations.correct: Olander concludes the distributive concern is for practical purposes solved by equal dividends; Ibarra's paycheck-to-paycheck counter is precisely that dividends do not adequately address the impact. Piecing together each speaker's full statement is required.
explanations.A: Both would agree; Olander asserts it and Ibarra does not contest it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Only Olander invokes this claim; Ibarra does not address the comparative footprint.
explanations.D: Ibarra highlights the timing mismatch but does not explicitly advocate monthly payments; Olander does not address payment frequency at all. No clear yes/no disagreement.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker takes a position on heating subsidies as a separate program.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree restoration is feasible in principle, both agree the watershed has been severely degraded, and both agree native species have declined. The implicit disagreement is whether restoration is worth doing given the baseline question: Quince treats the pre-dam ecosystem as the operative target; Reyes treats it as an arbitrary benchmark not entitled to special authority. Trap (C) is an apparent disagreement that evaporates; (D) is one-sided.
lr.stimulus: Quince: The dam has transformed the watershed, and native salmon runs are down by over ninety percent. Dam removal is engineering-feasible now, and a decade of restoration would let the river return to something close to its pre-dam condition. Given what we have lost, that outcome is clearly worth pursuing. Reyes: I agree removal is feasible, and I do not contest the decline figures. But 'pre-dam condition' is just the state the river happened to be in when someone started measuring. Restoring it favors the species that were dominant then over the species that are dominant now, and I see no reason the earlier configuration has a stronger claim on us.
lr.questionStem: Quince and Reyes disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: dam removal on this river is engineering-feasible at present

choices.label: B
choices.text: restoring the pre-dam ecosystem would succeed on ecological grounds

choices.label: C
choices.text: native salmon populations have declined by over ninety percent

choices.label: D
choices.text: the current species composition of the watershed should be preserved as it now stands

choices.label: E
choices.text: the pre-dam ecosystem is the appropriate target for restoration of this watershed

explanations.correct: Quince treats pre-dam condition as the outcome clearly worth pursuing; Reyes explicitly denies that the earlier configuration has a stronger claim on us than the current one. Each speaker's full argument has to be integrated to see this.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers grant feasibility.
explanations.B: Neither speaker questions ecological success on its own terms; the dispute is whether that target is the right one.
explanations.C: Both accept the decline — Quince asserts it and Reyes does not contest it.
explanations.D: Only Reyes implicitly defends the current configuration; Quince takes no position on preservation as an independent goal.
explanations.E: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree recommendation algorithms shape what users see, both agree platforms make editorial-like choices, and both agree user autonomy matters. The implicit disagreement is whether users' revealed consent to opaque ranking defeats an autonomy-based objection — which requires combining Kuroda's 'consent via continued use' with Ferreira's 'consent presupposes the very transparency the system withholds'. Trap (A) is shared; (D) is shift of subject.
lr.stimulus: Kuroda: Every platform that ranks content is making editorial choices; that is unavoidable. Users know this in broad outline, and they continue to use the platforms. Continued use under roughly accurate public descriptions of how ranking works is the kind of consent that settles the autonomy objection to algorithmic curation. Ferreira: Platforms do make editorial choices, and autonomy is exactly what is at stake. But the 'broad outline' users have is a press release, not a mechanism. Meaningful consent to being ranked requires knowing what is being optimized and how, and that is precisely what users are not told. What you are calling consent is compliance.
lr.questionStem: Kuroda and Ferreira's statements most strongly support the claim that they disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: recommendation algorithms make choices analogous to editorial decisions

choices.label: B
choices.text: users' continued use of ranked platforms under current disclosure practices constitutes consent sufficient to defeat the autonomy objection

choices.label: C
choices.text: users currently know the precise optimization targets of recommendation algorithms

choices.label: D
choices.text: platforms should be legally required to publish their ranking source code

choices.label: E
choices.text: autonomy is a consideration that any evaluation of algorithmic ranking must take into account

explanations.correct: Kuroda says continued use under broad public descriptions settles the autonomy objection; Ferreira says that what Kuroda is calling consent is merely compliance and does not defeat the objection. Each speaker's position has to be assembled from multiple sentences.
explanations.A: Both agree platforms make editorial-like choices.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Both would deny that users know the precise optimization — Kuroda says users have only a broad outline and Ferreira agrees that is all users have.
explanations.D: Neither speaker takes a position on publishing source code; the dispute is about consent, not disclosure remedies.
explanations.E: Agreement in disguise — Kuroda frames his argument around the autonomy objection and Ferreira explicitly says autonomy is at stake.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree the newly discovered letters are authentic, both agree the conventional account of the treaty's origins has explanatory gaps, and both agree the letters fill some of those gaps. The implicit disagreement is whether the letters warrant overturning the conventional account: Balan treats filling gaps as sufficient; Ostrow treats it as insufficient absent corroboration from independent sources. Trap (A) is agreement; (E) is a shift.
lr.stimulus: Balan: The newly discovered Hartwell letters are authentic, and they fill the awkward gaps in the standard account of the treaty's negotiation — especially the chancellor's silence in the spring of 1827. Historians have been working around those gaps for a century; the letters supply what was missing, and the standard account should be revised accordingly. Ostrow: The letters are genuine, and yes, they plug exactly the gaps you name. But a single correspondent writing from one side of the negotiation is not enough to rewrite the record. Until the Hartwell material is corroborated by sources outside his circle, the most we should say is that a rival account is now plausible, not that the standard one is wrong.
lr.questionStem: Balan and Ostrow are committed to disagreeing about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the Hartwell letters are genuine documents

choices.label: B
choices.text: the conventional account of the treaty's negotiation should be revised in light of the newly discovered letters

choices.label: C
choices.text: the chancellor's silence in the spring of 1827 has gone unexplained in the standard account

choices.label: D
choices.text: corroboration from sources outside Hartwell's circle would strengthen any revised account

choices.label: E
choices.text: the treaty's terms as signed differ from those the chancellor originally favored

explanations.correct: Balan concludes the standard account should be revised accordingly; Ostrow concludes that the most we should say is that a rival account is plausible, not that the standard one is wrong — a direct denial of the revision conclusion.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers affirm authenticity.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Both accept this — Balan names the gap and Ostrow says the letters 'plug exactly the gaps you name.'
explanations.D: Only Ostrow invokes corroboration as a standard; Balan does not take a position on whether further corroboration would strengthen a revision.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the debate is about whether to revise the account, not about the chancellor's preferences over terms.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree grammaticality judgments shift across speakers, both agree some shifts reflect change in progress, and both agree that 'standard' usage is partly a social artifact. The implicit disagreement is whether prescriptive judgments ever track a genuine property of the language rather than social positioning. Arriaga says yes (where a construction violates a deep pattern common to most dialects); Pell says no. Trap (C) is shared; (E) is one-sided.
lr.stimulus: Arriaga: Many prescriptive rules, I grant, are just prestige dialect dressed up as grammar. But not all of them. When a construction violates a pattern that shows up in nearly every dialect of the language — say, a word-order constraint that every speaker I have tested respects below the level of awareness — calling that construction ungrammatical is tracking something real about the language, not scoring social points. Pell: Speakers' judgments shift, and what most dialects now share was once shared by fewer. 'Respected by most speakers below awareness' is a description of current distribution, which is itself a social fact. I see no version of 'genuinely ungrammatical' that is not, in the end, a statement about whose usage currently counts.
lr.questionStem: Arriaga and Pell disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: some prescriptive rules reflect prestige dialect dressed up as grammatical rules

choices.label: B
choices.text: any classification of a construction as ungrammatical can track a property of the language rather than a social fact about whose usage counts

choices.label: C
choices.text: grammaticality judgments can shift across generations of speakers

choices.label: D
choices.text: word-order constraints are operative in every dialect of the language

choices.label: E
choices.text: speakers' current usage has the same authority as their grandparents' usage

explanations.correct: Arriaga gives a case where ungrammaticality tracks a genuine property of the language; Pell asserts he sees no version of 'genuinely ungrammatical' that is not a social fact. Resolving this requires reading across each speaker's reasoning.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Arriaga concedes it and Pell plainly endorses it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Both accept this — Pell asserts judgments shift and Arriaga does not dispute it.
explanations.D: Arriaga hedges to 'nearly every dialect' and Pell does not take a position on universality; no clean yes/no disagreement.
explanations.E: Only Pell hints at this; Arriaga does not address generational authority.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree the work is aesthetically accomplished, both agree the artist held views most would find odious, and both agree the views influenced the work's content. The implicit disagreement is whether aesthetic merit can be evaluated independently of the moral defects expressed in the content. Merton says yes (craft and content separate at the level of evaluation); Salazar says no. Trap (A) is shared; (D) is shift.
lr.stimulus: Merton: The novel is, on any ordinary craft measure, a major achievement — structurally daring, prose of extraordinary control. Everyone grants the author's published views were repellent, and those views do shape what the characters argue. But the quality of the book as a made thing is one judgment, and the moral content it carries is another, and we evaluate them separately. Salazar: Structural daring, prose control, yes. And the views inflect the characters' arguments, as you say. But the book's architecture is built around a sympathetic portrait of those same views. The craft is not hovering above the content; it is how the content is made persuasive. You cannot rate the craft high and the content low and call yourself done.
lr.questionStem: Merton and Salazar's statements provide the most support for the claim that they disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the author's published views are morally objectionable

choices.label: B
choices.text: the aesthetic quality of the novel can be evaluated separately from the moral content the novel expresses

choices.label: C
choices.text: the novel's prose is unusually controlled

choices.label: D
choices.text: novels whose authors hold repellent views should be removed from school curricula

choices.label: E
choices.text: the views of the author shape what the characters of the novel argue

explanations.correct: Merton treats the quality judgment as one thing and the moral content as another, evaluated separately; Salazar says you cannot rate craft high and content low and call yourself done — i.e., the two cannot be evaluated separately. That is the implicit yes/no axis.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Merton calls the views repellent and Salazar does not contest it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Both agree the prose has extraordinary control.
explanations.D: Out of scope — neither speaker takes a position on curricular inclusion.
explanations.E: Both accept this — Merton says the views shape what characters argue and Salazar agrees the views inflect the characters' arguments.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree the firm's conduct was legal, both agree it caused significant harm to a third party, and both agree the harm was foreseeable. The implicit disagreement is whether foreseeable but lawful harm to a third party triggers moral obligation to compensate — which requires combining Essien's 'legality is the limit of enforceable duty' with Yavuz's 'foreseeability plus causation grounds a moral duty even where law is silent'. Trap (C) is agreement; (D) is a shift.
lr.stimulus: Essien: The firm operated within every rule on the books, and the harm to the downstream community, while real and foreseeable, resulted from conduct no regulator had chosen to prohibit. Where the law draws the line is where enforceable duty ends; beyond that, you may disapprove, but you may not demand payment. Yavuz: I will stipulate the conduct was legal and that the harm was foreseeable — those are precisely my premises. If a firm knowingly acts in a way that predictably injures an identifiable third party, the absence of a statute does not dissolve the obligation to make that party whole. A duty is not only what a legislature has written down.
lr.questionStem: Essien and Yavuz are committed to disagreeing about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the firm's conduct violated any statute or regulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: a firm has a moral obligation to compensate a third party for foreseeable harm caused by conduct that is not prohibited by law

choices.label: C
choices.text: the harm caused to the downstream community was foreseeable at the time the firm acted

choices.label: D
choices.text: legislatures should enact new statutes prohibiting the firm's type of conduct

choices.label: E
choices.text: regulators have been lax in not prohibiting the firm's conduct

explanations.correct: Essien holds that beyond the law's line you may not demand payment — a denial of obligation to compensate; Yavuz holds the absence of a statute does not dissolve the obligation to make the injured party whole — an affirmation. The pieces have to be assembled from each speaker's full argument.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers stipulate the conduct was lawful.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Both accept foreseeability — Essien calls the harm real and foreseeable and Yavuz stipulates the same.
explanations.D: Neither speaker takes a position on future statutes; the debate is about obligation given the current legal landscape.
explanations.E: Only Essien implicitly defends the regulators by saying no regulator chose to prohibit; Yavuz does not take a position on regulator conduct.

lr.difficultyReason: The speakers share substantial common ground — both endorse carbon taxes as a policy tool — but disagree on a conditional presupposition about whether effectiveness requires revenue neutrality. Three near-miss answers describe positions only one speaker takes or positions both accept.
lr.stimulus:
Moreno: Carbon taxes are among the most efficient tools for reducing emissions, but only if the revenue generated is returned to households as dividends. Without that neutrality, businesses absorb the cost by reducing wages rather than reducing emissions, defeating the policy's purpose.
Peña: I agree that carbon taxes can reduce emissions effectively. But making revenue neutrality a precondition is too restrictive. Governments need that revenue to fund the clean-energy infrastructure that actually drives the transition away from fossil fuels.
lr.questionStem: Moreno and Peña's statements provide the most support for the claim that they disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: carbon taxes are capable of reducing greenhouse gas emissions

choices.label: B
choices.text: governments should invest in clean-energy infrastructure

choices.label: C
choices.text: carbon tax revenue should be directed toward household dividends rather than public investment

choices.label: D
choices.text: carbon taxes are the most efficient available tool for environmental policy

choices.label: E
choices.text: revenue neutrality is a necessary condition for carbon taxes to achieve their emissions-reduction purpose

explanations.correct: Moreno explicitly argues that revenue neutrality is required for carbon taxes to work — without it, businesses reduce wages instead of emissions. Peña explicitly denies this, calling it 'too restrictive' and arguing effectiveness does not require revenue neutrality. This is a direct disagreement about a conditional presupposition.
explanations.A: Both speakers agree carbon taxes can reduce emissions — Peña explicitly says so, and Moreno assumes it. This is a point of agreement, not disagreement.
explanations.B: Only Peña addresses clean-energy infrastructure investment. Moreno does not take a position on it. One-sided trap.
explanations.C: This is a near-miss: Moreno favors dividends and Peña does not, but the question of whether revenue should go to dividends versus public investment is broader than what Moreno argues. Moreno's actual claim is about the necessity of revenue neutrality for effectiveness — not a direct prescription about where all revenue goes. E captures the precise axis of disagreement more faithfully.
explanations.D: Moreno uses 'among the most efficient,' not 'the most efficient.' Peña does not address this comparative ranking. One-sided and misstates Moreno's claim.
explanations.E: Correct. See explanation above.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers endorse procedural fairness in criminal sentencing, creating a strong agreement-in-disguise trap. The disagreement is about a presupposition regarding whether algorithmic tools can be made transparent enough to satisfy due process — a nuanced conditional claim that requires close reading.
lr.stimulus:
Dr. Chen: Algorithmic risk-assessment tools used in criminal sentencing must be banned. Even if they could be made accurate, defendants have a due-process right to challenge the evidence used against them, and proprietary algorithms cannot be meaningfully examined or rebutted by defense counsel.
Dr. Okonkwo: Procedural fairness is essential, and I share your concern about opacity. But the solution is mandatory disclosure of algorithmic source code to defense teams, not an outright ban. With sufficient transparency requirements, these tools can satisfy due process while also improving sentencing consistency.
lr.questionStem: On the basis of their statements, Dr. Chen and Dr. Okonkwo are committed to disagreeing about which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: whether defendants have a right to challenge evidence used in their sentencing

choices.label: B
choices.text: whether algorithmic risk-assessment tools currently used in sentencing lack sufficient transparency

choices.label: C
choices.text: whether algorithmic risk-assessment tools can be made compatible with defendants' due-process rights

choices.label: D
choices.text: whether sentencing consistency is a value worth pursuing in the criminal justice system

choices.label: E
choices.text: whether proprietary algorithmic tools are currently used in criminal sentencing

explanations.correct: Dr. Chen holds that even if made accurate, algorithmic tools cannot satisfy due process because they cannot be meaningfully examined — implying no reform short of a ban is adequate. Dr. Okonkwo explicitly argues that with transparency requirements, these tools can satisfy due process. This is a direct disagreement about a conditional possibility.
explanations.A: Both speakers accept that defendants have due-process rights to challenge evidence. This is a point of agreement — agreement-in-disguise trap.
explanations.B: Both appear to agree current tools lack sufficient transparency. Dr. Chen says they 'cannot be meaningfully examined'; Dr. Okonkwo calls for disclosure reforms, implying current opacity is a problem. Another agreement-in-disguise trap.
explanations.D: Only Dr. Okonkwo mentions sentencing consistency as a value. Dr. Chen takes no position on it. One-sided trap.
explanations.E: Neither speaker disputes this factual premise — it is a shared background assumption. Out-of-scope trap.
explanations.C: Correct. See explanation above.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that indigenous languages are valuable and worth preserving, creating agreement-in-disguise traps. The subtle disagreement is about whether formal schooling is a sufficient mechanism for language revitalization — a degree-of-sufficiency claim that requires careful inference from each speaker's reasoning.
lr.stimulus:
Laird: The most effective way to revitalize an endangered indigenous language is immersive community use — daily speech in homes, markets, and ceremonies. Formal schooling in the language is helpful but plays only a supporting role. Without organic intergenerational transmission, institutional programs merely preserve a linguistic artifact.
Kim: Formal schooling is central, not peripheral. Communities often lack the critical mass of fluent speakers needed for organic transmission, so structured educational programs are what create the new generation of speakers who can then sustain community use. Schooling is not a supplement — it is the foundation.
lr.questionStem: Laird and Kim disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: endangered indigenous languages have cultural value worth preserving

choices.label: B
choices.text: formal schooling in an endangered language is beneficial to revitalization efforts

choices.label: C
choices.text: intergenerational transmission within communities contributes to language survival

choices.label: D
choices.text: formal schooling alone is sufficient to sustain an endangered language as a living community tongue

choices.label: E
choices.text: institutional programs for language preservation should be government-funded

explanations.correct: Laird explicitly argues that without organic intergenerational transmission, institutional programs only preserve a 'linguistic artifact' — implying formal schooling alone is insufficient for living revitalization. Kim argues that schooling is 'the foundation' that creates the next generation of speakers who sustain community use — implying it can be sufficient as the primary driver. This is a disagreement about sufficiency.
explanations.A: Both speakers clearly value indigenous language preservation — this is shared common ground. Agreement-in-disguise trap.
explanations.B: Laird calls schooling 'helpful'; Kim calls it 'central.' Both agree it is beneficial — they disagree about its degree of importance and sufficiency. Agreement-in-disguise trap.
explanations.C: Both speakers acknowledge community transmission contributes to language survival. Laird emphasizes it; Kim does not deny it but argues it cannot occur without schooling first. Agreement-in-disguise trap.
explanations.E: Neither speaker addresses government funding. Out-of-scope trap.
explanations.D: Correct. See explanation above.

lr.difficultyReason: The speakers agree on the value of historical accuracy but diverge on whether artistic license in historical fiction constitutes a form of harm or a legitimate interpretive freedom. The correct answer identifies a presupposition one speaker holds and the other rejects, while three distractors exploit shared premises or one-sided claims.
lr.stimulus:
Nakamura: Historical fiction that invents motivations for real figures, or alters documented outcomes, does a disservice to audiences. Readers who lack independent knowledge of the period will form false impressions that are very difficult to dislodge. The entertainment value does not justify that epistemic cost.
Foster: Historical fiction has always been an interpretive art, not a documentary record, and audiences understand this. The genre's conventions are well established. When authors imagine a historical figure's inner life or adjust events for narrative coherence, they are not deceiving anyone — they are doing what the form requires.
lr.questionStem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Nakamura and Foster disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: historical accuracy has value in works that engage with real historical events

choices.label: B
choices.text: historical fiction authors should disclose in an author's note when events have been altered

choices.label: C
choices.text: audiences of historical fiction generally understand that the genre involves artistic invention

choices.label: D
choices.text: historical fiction that alters documented events can have significant entertainment value

choices.label: E
choices.text: historical fiction writers have the same obligations to accuracy as documentary filmmakers

explanations.correct: Nakamura's entire argument depends on the premise that audiences lack independent knowledge and form false impressions — implying they do not understand that the genre involves invention. Foster directly contradicts this, asserting that 'audiences understand this' and that genre conventions are 'well established.' This is a direct disagreement about an empirical presupposition.
explanations.A: Both speakers implicitly value historical accuracy to some extent — Nakamura explicitly, Foster does not dispute it but argues the genre operates differently. This is not a clean disagreement; agreement-in-disguise trap.
explanations.B: Neither speaker addresses author's notes or disclosure practices. Out-of-scope trap.
explanations.D: Nakamura concedes entertainment value ('The entertainment value does not justify...'); Foster agrees the form serves narrative purposes. Both accept entertainment value — agreement-in-disguise trap.
explanations.E: Neither speaker makes this direct comparison. Out-of-scope trap.
explanations.C: Correct. See explanation above.

lr.difficultyReason: Both economists agree that monopolies harm consumers but disagree about whether market self-correction is reliable enough to substitute for antitrust enforcement — a degree-of-reliability claim embedded in conditional reasoning. The trap choices include an agreement about consumer harm and a one-sided claim about regulatory costs.
lr.stimulus:
Vasquez: Antitrust enforcement is indispensable in technology markets. Network effects and high switching costs mean that dominant platforms entrench themselves in ways the market cannot self-correct. Without regulatory intervention, monopoly power in these markets becomes self-perpetuating.
Hartley: Markets are more dynamic than regulators acknowledge. Even in technology sectors, the history of seemingly invincible platforms being displaced by nimble competitors shows that monopoly power is temporary. Heavy antitrust enforcement risks chilling the very innovation that produces those disruptive challengers.
lr.questionStem: Vasquez and Hartley disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: monopoly power in technology markets can harm consumers

choices.label: B
choices.text: network effects and high switching costs are present in technology markets

choices.label: C
choices.text: antitrust enforcement can sometimes reduce incentives for innovation

choices.label: D
choices.text: competitive market forces are sufficient to correct monopoly power in technology sectors without regulatory intervention

choices.label: E
choices.text: dominant technology platforms have ever been displaced by smaller competitors

explanations.correct: Vasquez argues that market self-correction cannot occur in technology markets given network effects and switching costs, making regulation indispensable. Hartley argues that market dynamics are sufficient, citing historical displacement of dominant platforms. This is a direct disagreement about whether market forces alone are sufficient.
explanations.A: Neither speaker denies that monopoly power harms consumers — both implicitly accept this as the reason monopoly power matters. Agreement-in-disguise trap.
