lr.stimulus: An employer is obligated to accommodate an employee's religious practice only when the employee has formally notified the employer of the need for accommodation and the accommodation would not impose undue hardship on the business's operations. Absent either condition, no obligation arises.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A retail manager refuses to adjust a Muslim employee's break schedule to allow Friday prayers, even though the employee submitted a written accommodation request and rescheduling would cost the store nothing. The manager's refusal violates the employer's obligation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A factory supervisor denies a Seventh-day Adventist worker's request to avoid Saturday shifts, citing the difficulty of finding replacements. The worker submitted the request in writing two weeks ago. Because the hardship is undue, no obligation exists, and the supervisor's denial is appropriate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An office manager learns informally that a Jewish employee observes the Sabbath and unilaterally adjusts the schedule, concluding that the adjustment costs nothing. The employee never made a formal request. The manager's action fulfills the employer's obligation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A company declines to permit an employee to wear a religious head covering, noting that no formal policy on religious dress exists. The employee has repeatedly asked verbally. Because no written policy exists, no obligation arises.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A department head accommodates a Hindu employee's request to observe a religious holiday, even though covering the absence requires costly overtime. The head concludes that the moral importance of religious practice always overrides business cost concerns.

explanations.correct: Choice B satisfies both conditions: the employee formally notified the employer in writing, and the accommodation would impose undue hardship (difficulty finding replacements). When undue hardship exists, the principle confirms no obligation arises, making the denial appropriate and conforming to the principle.
explanations.A: Violates-the-principle trap. Both conditions for obligation are met (formal notice, no undue hardship), yet the employer refuses. This scenario illustrates a violation of the principle, not conformance.
explanations.B: Correct. Formal notification was given, but undue hardship exists; therefore no obligation arises. The denial conforms to the principle.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. The cost condition is satisfied (no undue hardship), but the employee never formally notified the employer. Only one condition is met, so no obligation exists — the manager's voluntary action cannot 'fulfill an obligation' that hasn't arisen.
explanations.D: Outside-scope / extra-fact misdirection. The principle's trigger is formal notification by the employee, not the existence of a written company policy. The employee's verbal requests may or may not constitute formal notification, but the reasoning given (no written policy) is irrelevant to the principle.
explanations.E: Violates/misapplies-scope trap. The department head acts on a moral override not present in the principle. The principle does not say religious importance overrides cost; it limits obligation to cases of no undue hardship.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in environmental policy: a government agency is justified in imposing an emission fine only if (a) the facility exceeded its permitted emission level and (b) the facility had been given prior written notice of the violation. Traps satisfy only one condition or invert the rule.
lr.stimulus: A government environmental agency is justified in imposing a fine on an industrial facility for emissions violations only if the facility's recorded emissions exceeded its permitted level during the relevant period and the agency had previously issued the facility a written notice of violation. Unless both conditions are satisfied, imposition of the fine is not justified.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An agency fines a chemical plant after finding its sulfur dioxide output 30 percent above the permitted ceiling. The agency had sent the plant a written violation notice the previous quarter. The fine is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An agency fines a power station whose nitrogen oxide emissions were within permitted limits, on the grounds that the station had received a prior written notice related to a different pollutant. The fine is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An agency fines a refinery that exceeded its permitted emission level last year, even though the refinery received only a verbal warning at the time and no written notice was ever issued. The fine is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An agency declines to fine a smelting facility that exceeded permitted emission levels, because the agency had already issued a written notice and considers one enforcement action sufficient. The agency's restraint is justified under the principle.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An agency issues a written notice to a factory whose emissions are currently within permitted limits, in anticipation of future violations. Because the notice was properly issued, any subsequent fine would be justified regardless of future emission levels.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both antecedents: the facility's recorded emissions exceeded the permitted level (30% above ceiling), and the agency had previously issued a written notice of violation. Both conditions being met, the principle confirms the fine is justified.
explanations.A: Correct. Emissions exceeded permitted level AND prior written notice was given — both conditions satisfied.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. The written notice was for a different pollutant; the current emissions are within permitted limits. The first condition (exceeding permitted level for the relevant period) is not satisfied.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. The facility exceeded permitted levels, but only a verbal warning was given — not a written notice of violation. The second condition is not met, so the fine is not justified under the principle.
explanations.D: Outside-scope / violates-principle trap. Both conditions are met (exceeded levels + written notice), yet the agency declines to fine. The principle says the fine is justified when both are met; it does not say fining is mandatory, but the reasoning given (prior notice makes further action unnecessary) is not supported by the principle and misapplies it.
explanations.E: Reversed/extra-fact trap. The principle requires that emissions actually exceeded permitted levels during the relevant period before a fine is justified. A prospective notice cannot pre-authorize a future fine regardless of future emission levels; that inverts the principle's structure.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in ethics/education: a teacher is warranted in reporting a student's misconduct to administration only if (a) the misconduct poses a risk of harm to other students and (b) the teacher has first attempted to resolve the matter directly with the student. Traps address only one condition.
lr.stimulus: A teacher is warranted in reporting a student's misconduct to the school administration only if the misconduct poses a genuine risk of harm to other students and the teacher has first made a good-faith attempt to resolve the matter directly with the student. If only one of these conditions obtains, reporting to administration is not warranted.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A history teacher reports a student to the principal for repeatedly talking during lectures after speaking with the student privately twice. Because disruption harms classroom learning, the teacher's report is warranted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A science teacher discovers that a student has been tampering with lab equipment in ways that could injure classmates. After a private conversation with the student yields no change in behavior, the teacher reports the matter to the administration. The report is warranted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A gym teacher, alarmed that a student threatened a classmate, immediately reports the threat to the principal without speaking to the student first, reasoning that the risk of harm is too serious to delay. The report is warranted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An art teacher reports a student for plagiarizing a class project, having spoken with the student about the issue, because plagiarism ultimately harms the academic community. The report is warranted.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A math teacher attempts to resolve a cheating incident directly with a student but, finding the conversation unproductive, reports the student to administration. Because the teacher made a good-faith attempt first, the report is warranted.

explanations.correct: Choice B satisfies both conditions: tampering with lab equipment poses a genuine risk of harm to other students (physical injury), and the teacher made a good-faith direct attempt to resolve the matter before reporting. Both antecedents are met, so reporting is warranted.
explanations.A: Partial fit trap. The teacher did attempt direct resolution (two private conversations), but talking during lectures does not constitute a genuine risk of harm to other students as the principle requires. Only the second condition is met.
explanations.B: Correct. Risk of physical harm to classmates (first condition) and prior direct conversation (second condition) are both satisfied.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. The risk of harm condition is met (a threat to a classmate), but the teacher skipped the direct-resolution attempt entirely. Only the first condition is satisfied; the report is not warranted under the principle.
explanations.D: Partial fit / outside-scope trap. The teacher did speak with the student first, but plagiarism harming the 'academic community' is not equivalent to posing a genuine risk of harm to other students as specified in the principle. The first condition is not clearly satisfied.
explanations.E: Partial fit trap. A good-faith direct attempt was made, satisfying the second condition. However, cheating (as described) does not pose a genuine risk of harm to other students; the first condition is not met. The teacher's reasoning conflates procedural compliance with full satisfaction of the principle.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in economics/consumer protection: a consumer is entitled to a full refund only if (a) the product failed to perform its advertised function and (b) the consumer returns the product within the warranty period. Distractors fail one condition or misapply the consequent.
lr.stimulus: A consumer is entitled to a full refund on a purchased product only if the product failed to perform the function advertised by the manufacturer and the consumer returns the product within the manufacturer's stated warranty period. If either condition is not met, the consumer is not entitled to a full refund.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yolanda purchases a blender advertised as capable of crushing ice. Within the warranty period, she finds it can crush ice but dislikes the noise level. She returns it and demands a full refund. She is entitled to the refund.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Marcus buys a waterproof watch advertised as water-resistant to 50 meters. The watch stops functioning after brief submersion at 10 meters. He returns it three months after the one-year warranty expired. He is entitled to a full refund.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Priya purchases a space heater advertised to heat rooms up to 400 square feet. The heater fails to warm her 300-square-foot room. She returns it within the warranty period. She is entitled to a full refund.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tomás buys a printer advertised as compatible with his operating system. After the warranty expires, he discovers it was never compatible. He returns it promptly. He is entitled to a full refund.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renata returns a coffee maker within the warranty period because she prefers a different brand. The machine brews coffee exactly as advertised. She is entitled to a full refund because she acted within the warranty period.

explanations.correct: Choice C satisfies both conditions: the heater failed to perform its advertised function (heating rooms up to 400 sq ft, but failing to heat a smaller 300 sq ft room), and Priya returned it within the warranty period. Both antecedents are met, so she is entitled to a full refund.
explanations.A: Partial fit trap. Yolanda returned the blender within the warranty period (second condition met), but the blender did perform its advertised function — crushing ice. She is dissatisfied for a reason unrelated to the advertised function, so the first condition is not met.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. The watch failed to perform its advertised function (first condition met), but Marcus returned it after the warranty expired. The second condition is not satisfied; he is not entitled to a refund.
explanations.C: Correct. Both conditions satisfied: advertised function failed and return within warranty period.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. The printer failed to perform its advertised function (first condition met), but Tomás returns it after the warranty has expired. The second condition is not met; no entitlement arises.
explanations.E: Partial fit / violates-principle trap. Renata returned within the warranty period (second condition met), but the product performed exactly as advertised. The first condition is not met; she is not entitled to a full refund under the principle.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in technology/privacy policy: a data company is obligated to delete a user's personal data upon request only if (a) the data was collected without the user's explicit consent and (b) the user can demonstrate that retaining the data causes ongoing harm to the user. Traps satisfy only one condition.
lr.stimulus: A technology company is obligated to delete a user's personal data upon request only if the data was originally collected without the user's explicit consent and the user can demonstrate that continued retention of the data causes the user ongoing harm. If only one of these conditions is satisfied, no deletion obligation exists.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A user requests deletion of browsing data that was collected after the user clicked 'I agree' to the site's data policy. The user argues that retaining the data is embarrassing. The company is obligated to delete the data.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A user discovers that a social-media platform collected location data without any consent notification. The user shows that advertisers are using the data to target the user with content that aggravates the user's anxiety disorder. The company is obligated to delete the data.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A user requests deletion of purchase-history data collected without consent. The user cannot identify any specific harm from its retention but objects on principle. The company is obligated to delete the data.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A user requests deletion of health data that was collected with full explicit consent. The user demonstrates that a data breach has caused the user's insurance premiums to rise. The company is obligated to delete the data.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A user requests deletion of email data that was collected without consent. The company argues that deletion would be technically burdensome. Because deletion is burdensome, the company has no obligation to delete.

explanations.correct: Choice B satisfies both conditions: the location data was collected without any consent notification (no explicit consent), and the user demonstrates ongoing harm — advertisers using the data aggravate the user's anxiety disorder. Both antecedents are met; the company is obligated to delete.
explanations.A: Partial fit trap. The user clicked 'I agree,' giving explicit consent; the first condition is not satisfied. The company has no deletion obligation regardless of the embarrassment claim.
explanations.B: Correct. No consent was given, and ongoing harm is demonstrated. Both conditions are met.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. Data was collected without consent (first condition met), but the user cannot identify any specific ongoing harm. The second condition is not satisfied; no obligation exists.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. The data breach demonstrates ongoing harm (second condition met), but the data was collected with full explicit consent. The first condition is not met; no obligation exists under the principle.
explanations.E: Outside-scope / extra-fact trap. Technical burden is not a condition addressed by the principle. The principle's conditions concern consent and harm; the company's technical difficulty is irrelevant to whether the obligation exists.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in arts/intellectual property: a court should award damages to an artist for unauthorized reproduction of a work only if (a) the reproduction was made for commercial gain and (b) the artist had registered the work with the appropriate copyright authority before the reproduction occurred. Distractors fail one condition.
lr.stimulus: A court should award damages to an artist for unauthorized reproduction of the artist's work only if the reproduction was made for commercial gain by the reproducing party and the artist had registered the work with the appropriate copyright authority prior to the unauthorized reproduction. If either condition is absent, an award of damages is not appropriate.
lr.questionStem: The principle above, if valid, most helps to justify which one of the following judgments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A graphic novelist's work was reproduced without authorization in a for-profit merchandise line. The artist had registered the copyright two years before the reproduction. A court awards damages to the artist.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A sculptor's work was photographed without permission and displayed on a nonprofit museum's website with no admission charge. The sculptor had registered the work before the photograph was taken. A court awards damages to the sculptor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A photographer's images were used without authorization in a commercial advertising campaign. The photographer registered the copyright three months after the campaign launched. A court awards damages to the photographer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A composer's melody was reproduced commercially without consent. The composer had not registered the work at the time of reproduction but registered it the following year. A court awards damages to the composer.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A painter's work was reproduced without consent in a for-profit art book. The painter had not yet registered the copyright at the time of reproduction. Because the reproduction generated substantial revenue, a court awards damages to the painter.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both conditions: the reproduction was made for commercial gain (for-profit merchandise line), and the artist had registered the copyright prior to the reproduction (two years before). Both antecedents are met; the damages award is justified.
explanations.A: Correct. Commercial gain and prior registration are both present.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. The sculptor had prior registration (second condition met), but the museum's display was nonprofit with no admission charge — the first condition (commercial gain) is not satisfied. Damages are not appropriate under the principle.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. The reproduction was for commercial gain (first condition met), but registration occurred three months after the campaign launched — not prior to the reproduction. The second condition is not met; damages are not appropriate.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. The reproduction was commercial (first condition met), but the composer had not registered the work before the reproduction. Post-hoc registration does not satisfy the principle's prior-registration requirement.
explanations.E: Partial fit / extra-fact trap. The reproduction was for commercial gain (first condition met), but the painter had not registered the copyright before the reproduction occurred. Revenue generated is irrelevant to the principle; the second condition is not satisfied.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in linguistics/academic policy: a journal editor is justified in rejecting a submitted manuscript without external peer review only if (a) the manuscript falls entirely outside the journal's stated scope and (b) the manuscript contains no original empirical data. Traps satisfy only one condition or misread the consequent.
lr.stimulus: A journal editor is justified in rejecting a submitted manuscript without sending it to external peer reviewers only if the manuscript falls entirely outside the journal's stated subject-matter scope and the manuscript contains no original empirical data. If either condition is not met, the manuscript must be sent to external peer review before a rejection decision.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An editor at a linguistics journal receives a manuscript on quantum physics that includes a novel dataset of particle-collision measurements. The editor rejects it without peer review, reasoning that quantum physics is outside the journal's scope.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An editor at a history journal receives a purely theoretical essay arguing for a new periodization of the Renaissance; it contains no original empirical data. The essay addresses Renaissance history, which is within the journal's scope. The editor rejects it without peer review.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An editor at an economics journal receives a manuscript on marine biology that reviews existing literature but includes no new datasets or original observations. The editor rejects it without peer review.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An editor at a medical journal receives a manuscript on pharmacology — squarely within scope — with original clinical trial data. The editor finds the methodology weak and rejects it without peer review.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An editor at a sociology journal receives a manuscript on cultural anthropology — adjacent to but not within the journal's scope — that includes original survey data. The editor sends it to peer review before deciding. The editor's decision is justified.

explanations.correct: Choice C satisfies both conditions: marine biology is entirely outside an economics journal's stated scope, and the manuscript contains no original empirical data (reviews only existing literature). Both antecedents are met; rejection without peer review is justified.
explanations.A: Partial fit trap. Quantum physics is outside a linguistics journal's scope (first condition met), but the manuscript contains a novel dataset of original empirical data. The second condition is not satisfied; the manuscript must go to peer review.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. The manuscript contains no original empirical data (second condition met), but Renaissance history is within the history journal's scope. The first condition is not met; the editor must send it to peer review.
explanations.C: Correct. Marine biology is outside an economics journal's scope AND no original empirical data is present. Both conditions satisfied.
explanations.D: Violates-principle trap. Pharmacology is within the medical journal's scope, so the first condition fails immediately. Sending the manuscript out — or in this case wrongly rejecting it without review — is not justified by the principle regardless of methodological concerns.
explanations.E: Outside-scope / conforms-to-different-outcome trap. The editor sends the manuscript to peer review, which is actually the correct action under the principle when a condition is not met (original data is present). This scenario is consistent with the principle but asks whether peer review is justified, not whether rejection without review is — a subtle mismatch with the principle's framing, and it doesn't describe a rejection decision.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in history/governance: a head of state is morally justified in declaring a state of emergency only if (a) a threat to national security that cannot be addressed through ordinary legislative means is imminent and (b) the declaration is submitted for legislative ratification within 72 hours. Traps miss one condition.
lr.stimulus: A head of state is morally justified in declaring a state of emergency only if an imminent threat to national security exists that cannot be adequately addressed through ordinary legislative processes and the declaration is submitted to the legislature for ratification within seventy-two hours of issuance. Both conditions must be satisfied for the declaration to be morally justified.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Facing an imminent cyberattack on critical infrastructure that legislators cannot convene quickly enough to address, a president declares a state of emergency and submits it to the legislature for ratification 48 hours later. The declaration is morally justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A prime minister declares a state of emergency in response to widespread labor strikes, arguing that normal legislative debate would take too long. The declaration is submitted for ratification after 96 hours. The declaration is morally justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alarmed by a sudden economic downturn, a president declares a state of emergency and submits it for legislative ratification within 24 hours. The legislature could have convened an emergency session to address the downturn ordinarily. The declaration is morally justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A chancellor declares a state of emergency in response to a terrorist organization's credible threat of imminent attacks on multiple cities. The threat cannot be addressed through ordinary legislation in time. The chancellor submits the declaration for ratification after one week. The declaration is morally justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Responding to a severe flood that kills dozens, a governor declares a state of emergency. An emergency legislative session could have been convened to authorize relief funds within hours. The declaration is submitted for ratification within 12 hours. The governor's declaration is morally justified.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both conditions: an imminent national security threat (cyberattack on critical infrastructure) exists that cannot be addressed through ordinary legislative means (legislators cannot convene quickly enough), and the declaration was submitted for ratification within 72 hours (48 hours). Both antecedents are met.
explanations.A: Correct. Imminent security threat unaddressable by ordinary legislation, and ratification submitted within 72 hours.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. Labor strikes may not constitute an imminent national security threat in the principle's sense, and critically, the declaration was submitted after 96 hours — exceeding the 72-hour window. The second condition is not met.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. The declaration was submitted within 24 hours (second condition met), but the legislature could have addressed the economic downturn through ordinary legislative processes. The first condition (ordinary means insufficient) is not satisfied.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. The imminent terrorist threat unaddressable by ordinary legislation satisfies the first condition, but the declaration was submitted after one week — far exceeding the 72-hour requirement. The second condition is not met.
explanations.E: Partial fit trap. The declaration was submitted within 72 hours (second condition met), but an emergency legislative session could have been convened ordinarily within hours. The first condition (threat cannot be adequately addressed through ordinary legislative processes) is not satisfied.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in policy/social ethics: a city government is justified in demolishing a privately owned historic structure only if (a) the structure poses a documented and imminent public safety hazard and (b) the owner has been given reasonable opportunity to remediate the hazard but failed to do so. Distractors each omit one condition.
lr.stimulus: A city government is justified in demolishing a privately owned historic structure only if the structure poses a documented, imminent hazard to public safety and the property owner has been given reasonable opportunity to remediate the hazard but has failed to do so within the time allotted. If either condition is unmet, demolition is not justified.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A city demolishes a century-old warehouse whose crumbling façade poses an imminent risk of collapse onto a busy pedestrian street. The city gave the owner 60 days to make repairs; the owner made no repairs and the deadline passed. The demolition is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A city demolishes a historic theater that engineers have cited as structurally unsound. The city notified the owner of the hazard but demolished the building the next morning before the owner had any opportunity to respond. The demolition is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A city demolishes a Victorian mansion that neighborhood residents consider an eyesore. The city provided the owner 90 days to restore the façade, but the owner declined. Because the owner was given ample time, the demolition is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A city demolishes a historic mill building whose foundation inspectors believe may become hazardous within the next decade. The owner was given 30 days to remediate and failed to act. The demolition is justified because the owner had opportunity to remediate.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A city demolishes a landmarked bridge that poses an imminent collapse risk to motorists. Because the bridge is publicly owned, the city proceeds without notifying any private party. The demolition is justified under the same principle.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both conditions: the structure poses a documented, imminent public safety hazard (crumbling façade, imminent collapse risk over a pedestrian street), and the owner was given reasonable opportunity (60 days) to remediate but failed to act within the allotted time. Both antecedents are met; demolition is justified.
explanations.A: Correct. Imminent documented hazard and reasonable opportunity to remediate with owner's failure to act both present.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. The structure poses an imminent hazard (first condition met), but the owner was given no reasonable opportunity to remediate — the building was demolished the following morning. The second condition is not satisfied.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. The owner was given reasonable opportunity and failed to act (second condition met), but aesthetic concerns — being an 'eyesore' — do not constitute a documented, imminent public safety hazard. The first condition is not met.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. The owner was given opportunity to remediate (second condition met), but the foundation hazard is prospective — becoming hazardous within the next decade — not imminent. The first condition (documented, imminent hazard) is not satisfied.
explanations.E: Outside-scope trap. The principle concerns privately owned historic structures and notification of the private owner. A publicly owned bridge involves no private owner, so the principle's conditions (particularly giving the owner opportunity to remediate) cannot apply. The scenario is outside the principle's scope.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent: a physician is justified in withholding information only if (a) disclosure would cause direct psychological harm and (b) the patient has not explicitly requested full disclosure. Traps satisfy only one condition.
lr.stimulus: A physician is justified in withholding a diagnosis from a patient only if two conditions are both met: the disclosure of that diagnosis would foreseeably cause the patient direct psychological harm, and the patient has not explicitly requested complete information about his or her medical condition.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dr. Osei withholds a terminal diagnosis from a patient who has signed a form requesting full disclosure of all medical findings, because Dr. Osei believes the news will cause the patient severe depression.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dr. Reyes withholds a cancer diagnosis from a patient who has never asked about her condition and whose psychiatrist has documented that learning of the diagnosis would trigger a severe anxiety episode.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dr. Pham discloses a serious diagnosis to a patient who has not asked for information, reasoning that withholding information is generally paternalistic.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Novak withholds a minor diagnosis from a patient who explicitly asked for complete information, on the grounds that the patient seemed emotionally fragile during the appointment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dr. Chen withholds a diagnosis from a patient who has not requested information, even though Dr. Chen believes the disclosure would cause no psychological harm whatsoever.

explanations.correct: Dr. Reyes satisfies both conditions: the patient has never requested full disclosure (condition 2 met) and the psychiatrist's documentation establishes that disclosure would cause direct psychological harm (condition 1 met). The withholding is therefore justified under the principle.
explanations.A: Partial fit / violates the principle: the patient explicitly requested full disclosure, so condition 2 is not met. Withholding is not justified regardless of the anticipated harm.
explanations.B: Correct. Both conditions are satisfied.
explanations.C: Outside the principle's scope: the principle governs when withholding is justified; this answer describes disclosure and offers a separate rationale. Neither condition is evaluated.
explanations.D: Partial fit: the patient explicitly asked for complete information, so condition 2 fails. The principle does not justify withholding here.
explanations.E: Partial fit: condition 2 is met (no request for information), but condition 1 fails because disclosure would cause no psychological harm. Withholding is not justified.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent: a tenant is entitled to withhold rent only if (a) the landlord has been notified of the defect in writing and (b) the landlord has failed to remedy the defect within a reasonable time. Traps omit one condition.
lr.stimulus: A residential tenant is entitled to withhold rent from a landlord only if the tenant has previously notified the landlord of the defect in writing and the landlord has failed to remedy the defect within a reasonable period of time after receiving that notice.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Margolis withholds rent after verbally telling her landlord three times about a broken heating system that has gone unrepaired for four months.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tremblay withholds rent after sending a written notice about a leaking roof; his landlord repairs the roof within one week of receiving the notice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Okonkwo sends a written notice about a faulty electrical panel and, after the landlord takes no action for three months, withholds rent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Svensson withholds rent immediately upon discovering a mold problem, intending to notify the landlord by letter the following day.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Petrakis sends a written notice about a pest infestation and withholds rent the very next day before the landlord has had any opportunity to respond.

explanations.correct: Okonkwo sent written notice (condition 1 met) and the landlord took no action for three months, which constitutes failure to remedy within a reasonable time (condition 2 met). Withholding rent is therefore justified.
explanations.A: Partial fit: the defect went unrepaired for four months (condition 2 met), but Margolis only notified verbally, not in writing (condition 1 not met). Withholding is not justified.
explanations.B: Partial fit / violates the principle: written notice was given (condition 1 met), but the landlord remedied the defect within one week — a reasonable time — so condition 2 is not met.
explanations.C: Correct. Both conditions are satisfied.
explanations.D: Violates the principle: Svensson withholds before sending any written notice. Neither condition is met at the time of withholding.
explanations.E: Partial fit: written notice was sent (condition 1 met), but withholding occurred the very next day — not after a reasonable period for the landlord to respond (condition 2 not met).

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent: a government agency should release a document only if (a) the request is made by an identifiable individual or organization and (b) the document contains no information that would compromise ongoing law-enforcement operations.
lr.stimulus: A government agency should release a requested document to the public only if the request is made by an identifiable individual or recognized organization and the document does not contain information that would compromise an ongoing law-enforcement operation.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The agency releases a document to an anonymous requester because the document concerns a completed investigation with no bearing on current operations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The agency releases a document to a registered nonprofit organization, having confirmed that the document references no active investigations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The agency withholds a document from an identifiable journalist because the agency director personally dislikes the journalist's reporting.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The agency releases a document to an identifiable university research center, even though the document contains details of surveillance methods currently in use.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The agency releases a document to an identifiable law firm, reasoning that law firms are officers of the court and therefore always entitled to government records.

explanations.correct: The request comes from a registered nonprofit organization (identifiable/recognized — condition 1 met), and the document references no active investigations (condition 2 met). Release is justified.
explanations.A: Partial fit: the document condition is met, but the request is anonymous, so condition 1 is not met. Release is not justified.
explanations.B: Correct. Both conditions are satisfied.
explanations.C: Outside the principle's scope / violates: the requester is identifiable and the principle is silent on personal animosity; the principle would actually support release if condition 2 were met, but that condition is not addressed here. The withholding is based on an impermissible reason not sanctioned by the principle.
explanations.D: Partial fit / violates the principle: the requester is identifiable (condition 1 met), but the document contains details of currently active surveillance methods, so condition 2 is not met. Release is not justified.
explanations.E: Extra-fact misdirection: the requester is identifiable (condition 1 met), but the answer introduces a separate rationale ('officers of the court') that bypasses the principle's second condition, which is left unsatisfied.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent: a corporation is obligated to compensate a worker for an injury only if (a) the injury occurred on company premises during working hours and (b) the worker had complied with all relevant posted safety protocols.
lr.stimulus: A corporation is obligated to compensate an injured worker only if the injury occurred on company premises during scheduled working hours and the worker had complied with all relevant safety protocols posted by the company at the time of the injury.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Drummond injures her back while lifting boxes in the company warehouse during her shift, having followed all posted lifting-safety guidelines. The corporation is obligated to compensate her.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ibarra injures his hand on company machinery during his shift, but he had removed a required safety guard moments before the accident. The corporation is obligated to compensate him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Weston slips on ice in the company parking lot during her lunch break while complying with all posted protocols. The corporation is obligated to compensate her.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Callahan injures his wrist at home while completing a work assignment sent by his supervisor, having followed all company protocols. The corporation is obligated to compensate him.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nguyen injures her shoulder during an after-hours company social event held on company premises; she had followed all posted protocols. The corporation is obligated to compensate her.

explanations.correct: Drummond's injury occurred on company premises during her scheduled shift (condition 1 met) and she complied with all posted safety protocols (condition 2 met). The corporation is obligated to compensate her.
explanations.A: Correct. Both conditions are satisfied.
explanations.B: Partial fit: the injury occurred on premises during working hours (condition 1 met), but Ibarra removed a required safety guard, violating posted protocols (condition 2 not met). No obligation arises.
explanations.C: Partial fit / ambiguous timing: compliance is met (condition 2), but 'lunch break' may not constitute 'scheduled working hours.' Even if it did, this is the intended trap for condition 1.
explanations.D: Partial fit: protocols were followed (condition 2 met), but the injury occurred at home, not on company premises (condition 1 not met). No obligation arises.
explanations.E: Partial fit: the injury occurred on company premises (part of condition 1 met) and protocols were followed (condition 2 met), but an after-hours social event is not 'scheduled working hours' (condition 1 not fully met).

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent: an art museum is justified in refusing to display a donated work only if (a) the donor's conditions of display conflict with the museum's established curatorial policies and (b) the museum's governing board has formally reviewed and rejected those conditions.
lr.stimulus: An art museum is justified in refusing to display a donated artwork only if the donor's conditions for display conflict with the museum's established curatorial policies and the museum's governing board has formally reviewed and rejected those conditions.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A museum refuses to display a donated sculpture because the curator personally finds the work aesthetically unappealing, without consulting the governing board.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A museum refuses to display a donated painting because the donor insists it be shown alongside works from a specific period, a condition incompatible with the museum's rotation policy; the board formally voted to reject the condition.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A museum refuses to display a donated photograph because the donor's condition — that it never be loaned to other institutions — conflicts with curatorial policy; the director rejects the condition without board review.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A museum refuses to display a donated tapestry because the donor's lighting requirements are unusual, even though the board approved the donation and the lighting requirement is not addressed in curatorial policy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A museum refuses to display a donated mosaic after the board reviews the donation file, even though the donor imposed no conditions and the refusal is based solely on lack of gallery space.

explanations.correct: The donor's condition conflicts with the museum's established rotation policy (condition 1 met) and the board formally voted to reject that condition (condition 2 met). The refusal is justified.
explanations.A: Violates the principle: the curator's personal preference is not a conflict with curatorial policy, and the board was not consulted. Neither condition is met.
explanations.B: Correct. Both conditions are satisfied.
explanations.C: Partial fit: the conflict with curatorial policy exists (condition 1 met), but the director — not the board — rejected the condition without formal board review (condition 2 not met). Refusal is not justified.
explanations.D: Partial fit / reversed: the board reviewed the donation (condition 2 partially met), but the lighting requirement is not addressed in curatorial policy, so there is no conflict (condition 1 not met). Refusal is not justified.
explanations.E: Outside the principle's scope: the principle governs refusals when donor conditions conflict with policy. Here there are no donor conditions; the refusal is based on lack of space, a scenario the principle does not address.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent: a scientist should retract a published finding only if (a) the scientist has discovered a methodological error that materially affects the conclusions and (b) a correction rather than retraction cannot adequately address that error.
lr.stimulus: A scientist should retract a published finding only if the scientist has discovered a methodological error that materially affects the study's conclusions and a published correction would be insufficient to adequately address that error.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dr. Falcone retracts a study after discovering that a mislabeled axis on one figure would mislead readers, even though issuing a corrected figure would fully resolve the problem.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dr. Huang retracts a study after discovering that a transcription error in the data tables fundamentally undermines all of the paper's principal conclusions and cannot be fixed by issuing a correction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dr. Mbeki retracts a study after learning that a rival lab has published contradictory findings, even though Dr. Mbeki can find no error in her own methodology.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Sorensen retracts a study after a peer reviewer raises concerns about the sample size, even though the sample size is consistent with accepted norms in the field and does not affect the conclusions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dr. Ivanova retracts a study upon discovering a methodological flaw that affects a secondary analysis but leaves all primary conclusions intact, determining that a correction would be an adequate remedy.

explanations.correct: Dr. Huang discovered a transcription error (a methodological error) that fundamentally undermines all principal conclusions (condition 1: materially affects conclusions — met) and cannot be fixed by a correction (condition 2: correction insufficient — met). Retraction is justified.
explanations.A: Partial fit / violates: there is a methodological error (condition 1 arguably met), but issuing a corrected figure would fully resolve the problem, meaning a correction is sufficient (condition 2 not met). Retraction is not justified.
explanations.B: Correct. Both conditions are satisfied.
explanations.C: Outside the principle's scope: contradictory external findings are not a methodological error in the original study. Condition 1 is not met.
explanations.D: Partial fit / violates: the peer reviewer's concern does not constitute a discovered methodological error affecting conclusions (condition 1 not met). Retraction is not justified.
explanations.E: Partial fit: a methodological flaw was found, but it affects only a secondary analysis and the scientist determined a correction is adequate (condition 2 not met). The principle does not justify retraction.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent: a school is justified in expelling a student only if (a) the student has committed a violation that is explicitly enumerated in the school's published code of conduct and (b) the student was given a formal warning for a prior violation of the same rule.
lr.stimulus: A school is justified in expelling a student only if the student has committed a violation explicitly enumerated in the school's published code of conduct and the student had previously received a formal written warning for violating the same rule.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A school expels Tarrant for cheating on an exam, an offense listed in the code of conduct, after issuing him a formal written warning for cheating earlier in the semester.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A school expels Brennan for repeated tardiness, an offense listed in the code of conduct, after issuing formal written warnings for plagiarism on two prior occasions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A school expels Hollis for using unauthorized software during an exam — conduct not specifically enumerated in the code of conduct — after issuing a written warning for the same conduct.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A school expels Kimura for plagiarism, listed in the code of conduct, without issuing any prior warning because the school principal considers plagiarism a serious offense.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A school expels Oduya for disruptive behavior, listed in the code of conduct, after informally cautioning her about the same behavior at a parent-teacher meeting.

explanations.correct: Cheating is explicitly enumerated in the code of conduct (condition 1 met), and Tarrant had previously received a formal written warning for cheating — the same rule (condition 2 met). Expulsion is justified.
explanations.A: Correct. Both conditions are satisfied.
explanations.B: Partial fit: tardiness is listed in the code (condition 1 met), but the prior written warnings were for plagiarism, not tardiness — not the same rule (condition 2 not met). Expulsion is not justified.
explanations.C: Partial fit: a formal written warning was issued for the same conduct (condition 2 met), but using unauthorized software is not enumerated in the code of conduct (condition 1 not met). Expulsion is not justified.
explanations.D: Partial fit: plagiarism is listed in the code (condition 1 met), but no prior formal warning was given (condition 2 not met). The principal's view of seriousness is irrelevant to the principle.
explanations.E: Partial fit: disruptive behavior is listed (condition 1 met), but the prior caution was informal, not a formal written warning (condition 2 not met). Expulsion is not justified.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in a technology domain: a software company is obligated to issue a free patch only if (a) the vulnerability was present in the product at the time of sale and (b) the vulnerability exposes user data to unauthorized external access.
lr.stimulus: A software company is obligated to issue a free security patch to its customers only if the security vulnerability was present in the product at the time it was originally sold and the vulnerability exposes customer data to unauthorized external access.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nexara Software issues a free patch after discovering that a feature added in a post-sale update created a flaw allowing outsiders to access user data.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vortex Technologies issues a free patch after finding that its product, as originally sold, contained a bug that slows processing speeds but does not expose any user data.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Paragon Systems issues a free patch after discovering that its product, as originally sold, contained a flaw that allows unauthorized third parties to extract stored customer records.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lumicon issues a free patch for a vulnerability introduced by a third-party plug-in, not present at sale, which allows outsiders to monitor user keystrokes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: ClarityTech issues a free patch for a vulnerability that was present at the time of sale but that only permits internal employees — not outsiders — to access user data without authorization.

explanations.correct: The flaw was present in the product as originally sold (condition 1 met) and it allows unauthorized third parties to extract customer records, constituting unauthorized external access (condition 2 met). The obligation to issue a free patch is established.
explanations.A: Partial fit: external access to user data exists (condition 2 met), but the flaw was introduced by a post-sale update, not present at time of sale (condition 1 not met). No obligation under the principle.
explanations.B: Partial fit: the vulnerability was present at time of sale (condition 1 met), but it slows processing speeds without exposing user data (condition 2 not met). No obligation under the principle.
explanations.C: Correct. Both conditions are satisfied.
explanations.D: Partial fit: external access to user data exists (condition 2 met), but the vulnerability was introduced by a third-party plug-in after the sale (condition 1 not met). No obligation under the principle.
explanations.E: Partial fit: the vulnerability was present at time of sale (condition 1 met), but only internal employees — not unauthorized external parties — can access the data (condition 2 not met). No obligation under the principle.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in a linguistics/history domain: a lexicographer is justified in labeling a word 'archaic' only if (a) the word has not appeared in any widely circulated publication within the past fifty years and (b) the word lacks any living community of speakers who use it in ordinary discourse.
lr.stimulus: A lexicographer is justified in labeling a word 'archaic' only if the word has not appeared in any widely circulated publication within the past fifty years and no living community of speakers uses the word in ordinary discourse.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A lexicographer labels 'sooth' archaic after confirming that it has not appeared in any widely circulated publication in over sixty years, even though a small regional dialect community still uses it regularly in conversation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A lexicographer labels 'forsooth' archaic after confirming that it appears only in scholarly articles about Middle English — not in widely circulated publications — and that no living dialect community uses it in everyday speech.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A lexicographer labels 'prithee' archaic because it sounds old-fashioned, without researching whether it appears in current publications or is used by any speaker community.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A lexicographer labels 'perchance' archaic after finding that it appeared in a major newspaper's crossword column last year, reasoning that crossword usage does not constitute serious discourse.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A lexicographer labels 'yclept' archaic after discovering that a popular fantasy novel published fifteen years ago used the term, but no speaker community uses it in ordinary discourse.

explanations.correct: Scholarly articles about Middle English do not constitute widely circulated publications in the relevant sense, so condition 1 is met; and no living dialect community uses 'forsooth' in everyday speech (condition 2 met). The 'archaic' label is justified.
explanations.A: Partial fit: condition 1 is met (not in widely circulated publications for 60+ years), but a small regional dialect community still uses the word in conversation (condition 2 not met). The label is not justified.
explanations.B: Correct. Both conditions are satisfied.
explanations.C: Outside the principle's scope / violates: the lexicographer applies no relevant inquiry. Neither condition is verified. The label cannot be justified under the principle.
explanations.D: Partial fit / violates: no living speaker community uses the word (condition 2 met), but the word appeared in a major newspaper last year — a widely circulated publication (condition 1 not met). The label is not justified.
explanations.E: Partial fit: no speaker community uses 'yclept' in ordinary discourse (condition 2 met), but a popular fantasy novel published fifteen years ago — a widely circulated publication — used the term (condition 1 not met). The label is not justified.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in an environmental policy domain: a regulatory agency is justified in imposing an emergency pollution moratorium only if (a) monitoring data show that pollutant levels have exceeded the established safety threshold and (b) the source of the exceedance has been identified as a specific regulated facility.
lr.stimulus: A regulatory agency is justified in imposing an emergency pollution moratorium on a facility only if current monitoring data show that pollutant levels in the affected area have exceeded the established safety threshold and the agency has identified that specific facility as the source of the exceedance.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The agency imposes a moratorium on the Hartwell plant after monitoring data confirm that pollutant levels in the surrounding watershed exceed the safety threshold and isotopic analysis identifies the Hartwell plant as the source.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The agency imposes a moratorium on the Crestline refinery after receiving citizen complaints about odors, even though current monitoring data show pollutant levels below the safety threshold.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The agency imposes a moratorium on the Delphi chemical plant after monitoring data confirm that safety thresholds are exceeded, even though the agency has not yet determined which facility in the industrial corridor is responsible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The agency imposes a moratorium on the Solaris factory after identifying it as the source of elevated emissions, even though current data show pollutant levels still within the established safety threshold.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The agency imposes a moratorium on all facilities in a region after a general modeling study predicts that future pollutant levels may exceed the threshold, without having identified any specific source.

explanations.correct: Monitoring data confirm that pollutant levels exceed the safety threshold (condition 1 met), and isotopic analysis identifies the Hartwell plant as the specific source (condition 2 met). The moratorium is justified.
explanations.A: Correct. Both conditions are satisfied.
explanations.B: Partial fit / violates: the source is presumably identified (condition 2 arguably met), but monitoring data show levels below the threshold (condition 1 not met). The moratorium is not justified.
explanations.C: Partial fit: monitoring data confirm threshold exceedance (condition 1 met), but the agency has not identified which specific facility is responsible (condition 2 not met). The moratorium is not justified.
explanations.D: Partial fit: the facility has been identified as a source (condition 2 met), but current pollutant levels remain within the safety threshold (condition 1 not met). The moratorium is not justified.
explanations.E: Violates both conditions: modeling predictions are not current monitoring data exceeding the threshold (condition 1 not met), and no specific facility has been identified (condition 2 not met). The moratorium is not justified.

lr.difficultyReason: The principle has a two-part antecedent (product failed within warranty AND failure was not caused by misuse); correct answer satisfies both conditions while traps satisfy only one or invert the conditional.
lr.stimulus: A manufacturer is obligated to replace a defective product at no charge to the consumer only if the product failed under normal use conditions and the consumer purchased the product within the past two years.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A homeowner purchased a lawn mower eighteen months ago and used it exclusively for mowing her own grass. The mower's engine seized during normal operation. The manufacturer is obligated to replace the mower at no charge.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A contractor purchased a power drill three years ago and used it only on light-duty projects. The drill's chuck broke during routine use. The manufacturer is obligated to replace the drill at no charge.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A student purchased a laptop fourteen months ago and accidentally dropped it, cracking the motherboard. Because the student had no history of careless behavior, the manufacturer is obligated to replace the laptop at no charge.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A chef purchased a stand mixer eleven months ago. She modified the mixer to run at higher voltages than the manufacturer recommends, and the motor burned out. The manufacturer is obligated to replace the mixer at no charge because the purchase was recent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A cyclist purchased a bicycle pump two years and one month ago. The pump's pressure gauge failed during a routine inflation. The manufacturer is obligated to replace the pump at no charge because the failure was not the cyclist's fault.

explanations.correct: The homeowner's mower (a) failed under normal use conditions and (b) was purchased within the past two years (eighteen months ago). Both antecedent conditions are satisfied, so the obligation to replace at no charge follows directly from the principle.
explanations.A: Correct. Both conditions are met: normal use and purchase within two years.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. The drill was purchased three years ago, which violates the two-year condition. Only one antecedent is satisfied.
explanations.C: Violates the principle. The laptop's failure resulted from being dropped — not a normal-use failure but misuse (accidental abuse). The principle requires failure under normal use conditions, which is not met here.
explanations.D: Violates the principle. The chef modified the mixer to run beyond manufacturer specifications, meaning the failure did not occur under normal use conditions. The recency of purchase alone is insufficient.
explanations.E: Partial fit trap. The pump was purchased two years and one month ago, which falls outside the two-year window. The non-fault reasoning introduces an irrelevant consideration not addressed by the principle.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent principle in an ethics domain; traps use reversal, partial fit, and scope errors to mislead test-takers who read only part of each scenario.
lr.stimulus: A researcher is justified in withholding the results of a study from publication only if disclosing those results would directly endanger identifiable individuals and no method of anonymization would adequately protect those individuals.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A sociologist studied gang activity in a small town. Publishing her data would allow readers to identify specific gang members, and no technique could obscure their identities without destroying the study's value. She withholds the results from publication.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A psychologist fears that his findings on anxiety disorders might be misinterpreted by the public and cause unnecessary alarm. He withholds the results from publication to prevent widespread anxiety.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A public-health researcher discovers that publishing disease-cluster data would embarrass a local hospital. To protect the hospital's reputation, she withholds the results from publication.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An economist's research reveals insider-trading patterns at a specific firm. He believes the firm's executives could face reputational harm if identified, so he publishes the results anyway, with executive names redacted.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A geneticist finds that her data on rare hereditary conditions could reveal participants' identities, but she publishes the results after confirming that data aggregation adequately protects participant anonymity.

explanations.correct: Both conditions are met: (1) publication would directly endanger identifiable individuals (gang members could be identified and targeted), and (2) no anonymization method would adequately protect them. Withholding is therefore justified under the principle.
explanations.A: Correct. Both antecedent conditions are satisfied, and the action (withholding) matches the principle's consequent.
explanations.B: Outside the principle's scope. The harm feared is diffuse public alarm, not danger to identifiable individuals. The principle specifically requires direct endangerment of identifiable people.
explanations.C: Outside the principle's scope. Reputational harm to an institution is not danger to identifiable individuals. The principle does not justify withholding for institutional protection.
explanations.D: Reversed application trap. The researcher publishes (with redactions) rather than withholds, and the scenario describes a possible anonymization solution (redaction), so even if withholding were at issue, the second condition would fail.
explanations.E: Violates the principle. The geneticist publishes after confirming that anonymization adequately protects participants, which means the second condition (no adequate anonymization) is not met. The principle would not justify withholding in this case, and the researcher does not withhold — this scenario is fully consistent with the principle but illustrates publication, not withholding.

lr.difficultyReason: Economics-domain principle with a two-part antecedent involving both market position and consumer harm; distractors employ partial fit, converse error, and extra-fact misdirection.
lr.stimulus: A regulatory agency is justified in imposing price controls on a company only if the company holds a dominant market position in the relevant industry and there is credible evidence that the company's pricing is causing measurable harm to consumers.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A pharmaceutical company controls 80 percent of the market for a critical medication. An independent audit confirms that the company's pricing has forced thousands of patients to forgo the medication. The agency imposes price controls on the company.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A regional grocery chain controls 15 percent of local food sales. Several consumer groups allege, without supporting data, that its prices are too high. The agency imposes price controls on the chain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An internet service provider holds a dominant market position in a rural county. Customers in the area are dissatisfied with service quality but have not experienced measurable financial harm from the provider's pricing. The agency imposes price controls.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A streaming platform commands a dominant share of the video market. Because the platform has not yet raised prices, consumers have not been harmed. The agency declines to impose price controls.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A small regional airline controls 70 percent of routes out of a mid-sized airport. A consumer advocacy group believes fares are high, but the agency finds no credible evidence of measurable consumer harm. Concluding that dominant market position alone justifies intervention, the agency imposes price controls.

explanations.correct: Both antecedent conditions are satisfied: the pharmaceutical company holds a dominant market position (80 percent market share) and there is credible evidence (an independent audit) of measurable consumer harm (patients forgoing medication). Price controls are therefore justified.
explanations.A: Correct. Dominant position and credible evidence of measurable harm are both present.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. Consumer harm allegations exist but lack supporting data (not credible evidence), and a 15 percent market share does not constitute a dominant position. Neither antecedent condition is clearly met.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. The ISP holds a dominant position but there is no measurable financial harm from pricing — only service-quality dissatisfaction. Only one of the two required conditions is met.
explanations.D: Outside the principle's scope / reversal trap. The agency declines to impose controls, which is consistent with the principle (no harm yet), but the scenario tests the converse: the principle tells us when controls ARE justified, not when they should be withheld.
explanations.E: Violates the principle. The agency imposes controls based on dominant market position alone, explicitly acknowledging no credible evidence of measurable harm. This directly contradicts the principle's requirement that both conditions be satisfied.

lr.difficultyReason: Law/evidence domain with a two-part antecedent; traps use partial fit, converse error, and extra-fact misdirection to create plausible-seeming wrong answers.
lr.stimulus: A judge is warranted in excluding a witness's testimony only if the testimony was obtained through a process that violated the witness's legal rights and the testimony would not have been discovered through lawful means independent of that violation.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Investigators coerced a witness into testifying by threatening her with false charges. Prosecutors later established that no independent lawful investigation would have uncovered her account. The judge excludes the testimony.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A witness was questioned without being informed of his right to remain silent. However, detectives had already scheduled an interview with the same witness through a routine lawful canvass of the neighborhood. The judge excludes the testimony.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A witness gave testimony voluntarily and was fully informed of her rights throughout the process. Because the testimony is damaging to the defendant, the defense counsel argues it should be excluded. The judge excludes the testimony.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Testimony was gathered in a manner that violated a witness's rights, and the prosecution concedes that no independent lawful means would have produced the testimony. The judge admits the testimony because it is highly probative.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A witness's statement was obtained unlawfully, but police had an independent tip from a confidential informant that would have led them to the same witness through lawful channels. The judge excludes the testimony.

explanations.correct: Both conditions are satisfied: (1) the testimony was obtained through a process that violated the witness's legal rights (coercion via false threats), and (2) it would not have been discovered through independent lawful means. Exclusion is therefore warranted under the principle.
explanations.A: Correct. Both antecedent conditions are met, and the judge's action (exclusion) matches the principle's consequent.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. The first condition (rights violation) is met, but the second condition fails — an independent lawful canvass was already underway, meaning the testimony would have been discovered through lawful means. Exclusion is not warranted under the principle.
explanations.C: Violates the principle. No rights violation occurred; the witness testified voluntarily and was fully informed. The first antecedent condition is not met, so exclusion is not warranted. The judge's exclusion contradicts the principle.
explanations.D: Violates the principle. Both antecedent conditions are met, yet the judge admits rather than excludes the testimony. This is the inverse of what the principle requires and directly contradicts it.
explanations.E: Partial fit trap. The first condition (unlawful obtainment) is met, but the independent-tip information establishes that lawful means would have discovered the testimony — negating the second condition. Exclusion is not warranted, making the judge's action inconsistent with the principle.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental policy principle with a two-part antecedent (ecological harm and feasibility of mitigation); traps use scope error, partial fit, and converse error across varied scenario contexts.
lr.stimulus: A government agency is entitled to require a private developer to modify a construction project only if the project poses a demonstrable risk of significant ecological harm and there exists a feasible modification that would substantially reduce that harm.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An environmental review concludes that a proposed marina will destroy critical wetland habitat, and engineers have identified a redesign that would preserve most of the wetlands at modest additional cost. The agency requires the developer to adopt the redesign.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A developer plans to build a hotel near a protected forest. Local residents object to the visual impact on the landscape, but environmental scientists find no demonstrable ecological risk. The agency requires modifications to reduce the visual impact.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A mining company's proposed expansion poses a significant risk of contaminating a river ecosystem. Environmental engineers determine that no feasible modification could substantially reduce the contamination risk given the site's geology. The agency requires the company to modify its plans.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A developer's wind-farm project creates demonstrable risks of significant harm to migratory bird populations. Although turbine-placement modifications would substantially reduce bird mortality, these modifications would more than double the project's cost, making the project economically infeasible. The agency declines to require modifications.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A planned highway extension poses significant risk of fragmenting a wildlife corridor. Ecologists confirm that no modification would substantially reduce this harm. The agency declines to require modifications and instead offers the developer tax incentives to voluntarily adopt mitigation measures.

explanations.correct: Both antecedent conditions are satisfied: (1) the marina poses a demonstrable risk of significant ecological harm (destruction of wetland habitat confirmed by environmental review), and (2) a feasible modification exists that would substantially reduce that harm (the redesign). The agency's requirement to modify is therefore entitled under the principle.
explanations.A: Correct. Both conditions are met — demonstrable significant ecological harm and a feasible, substantially-reducing modification — and the agency acts in accordance with the principle.
explanations.B: Outside the principle's scope. The objection is aesthetic (visual impact), not ecological. No demonstrable ecological risk exists, so the first antecedent condition is not met. The agency's requirement is not justified by the principle.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. The project poses significant ecological harm (first condition met), but no feasible modification exists that would substantially reduce it (second condition fails). Requiring modification is therefore not warranted under the principle.
explanations.D: Extra-fact misdirection / partial fit. The principle requires a 'feasible' modification; the scenario raises the question of whether economic infeasibility counts. However, the principle does not specify economic feasibility — this answer introduces cost considerations not addressed by the principle, making it a distractor. More critically, the agency declines to act, which may or may not conform; the ambiguity is the trap. The agency's declination is not clearly what the principle supports when both conditions appear met if 'feasible' is read as technically feasible.
explanations.E: Partial fit trap. The first condition (demonstrable significant ecological harm) appears met, but the second condition fails — no modification would substantially reduce the harm. The agency correctly declines to require modifications, which is consistent with the principle, but the agency's substituted action (tax incentives) is irrelevant to whether the principle is conformed to. This scenario tests the converse rather than a direct application.

lr.difficultyReason: Three compound antecedent conditions, an 'unless' exception whose own antecedent must be checked, and a proportionality clause. Correct answer must satisfy all three conditions, show the exception does not trigger, and confirm the punishment scales with the harm. Traps satisfy the main conditions but fall under the exception, invert the proportionality requirement, or rely on a different subsidiary principle.
