lr.stimulus: A judge should impose the maximum statutory sentence on a convicted defendant only if (a) the crime caused serious and lasting harm to an identifiable victim, (b) the defendant planned the crime in advance rather than acting on impulse, and (c) the defendant has refused to acknowledge responsibility during the proceedings, unless the defendant suffers from a documented condition that substantially impaired deliberative capacity at the time of the offense. In every case, the severity of the sentence must be calibrated to the gravity of the harm inflicted.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Delaney embezzled pension funds from retirees over three years, leaving several elderly victims unable to afford medical care. He planned each transfer carefully, has denied wrongdoing throughout trial, and has no documented cognitive impairment. The judge imposes the maximum statutory sentence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Halvor set fire to an occupied warehouse, permanently injuring two employees, and methodically prepared the arson for weeks. Although he refused to apologize, a neurologist testified that a recently diagnosed frontal-lobe tumor had materially impaired his capacity for deliberation when he set the fire. The judge imposes the maximum statutory sentence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Irendi defrauded a bank of a modest sum through an impulsive forgery. The bank reported no lasting harm, Irendi pled guilty on the first day, and no impairment was alleged. The judge imposes the maximum statutory sentence because deterrence requires a harsh signal to future offenders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jessan assaulted a stranger on the street, causing serious and lasting injury. The assault was unplanned, but Jessan has refused to acknowledge responsibility and is medically unimpaired. The judge imposes the maximum statutory sentence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Korath orchestrated a multi-year investment fraud that ruined several identifiable families. He denies responsibility and no impairment has been documented. The judge imposes the lightest sentence on the statutory scale, reasoning that financial crimes warrant leniency regardless of harm.

explanations.correct: Delaney's case satisfies every antecedent condition: serious and lasting harm to identifiable victims (retirees deprived of medical care), advance planning, and refusal to acknowledge responsibility. The exception does not trigger because Delaney has no documented impairment. The maximum sentence is described as matching the gravity of the harm, meeting the proportionality clause. The principle therefore prescribes the stated judgment.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Satisfies conditions (a), (b), and (c), but the documented frontal-lobe impairment triggers the exception. The principle withholds the maximum sentence whenever the exception's antecedent obtains, so the judgment contradicts the principle.
explanations.C: Fails condition (a) — no lasting harm — and condition (b) — the forgery was impulsive. The judge also invokes a deterrence rationale the principle does not recognize.
explanations.D: Fails condition (b). Jessan's assault was unplanned, so the 'planned the crime in advance' requirement is unmet, regardless of how the other conditions fare.
explanations.E: Violates the proportionality clause. Even where all antecedent conditions hold, the principle requires the sentence to be calibrated to the gravity of the harm; imposing the lightest sentence on a case of ruinous harm inverts that requirement.

lr.difficultyReason: Three compound conditions plus an 'unless' exception governed by its own antecedent, plus a proportionality requirement tying intervention to demonstrated risk. Traps satisfy the main rule while falling under the exception or substitute a different justifying principle.
lr.stimulus: A physician is justified in overriding a competent patient's refusal of treatment only if (a) the refusal would result in imminent and irreversible harm, (b) the patient's refusal rests on a factual misunderstanding that the physician has tried and failed to correct, and (c) no less intrusive alternative is available, unless the patient has previously executed a valid advance directive refusing the specific intervention under the present circumstances. The degree of intervention imposed must be no greater than what is needed to prevent the imminent harm.
lr.questionStem: The principle above, if valid, most closely conforms to which one of the following judgments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dr. Querin's patient refuses a ventilator, citing a correctly understood prognosis. The patient had previously signed a valid advance directive refusing ventilation under precisely these circumstances. Dr. Querin nonetheless intubates, reasoning that life preservation outweighs prior instructions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dr. Palen's patient faces imminent organ failure and refuses dialysis on religious grounds. The refusal involves no factual misunderstanding, and Dr. Palen proceeds anyway because the harm is severe.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dr. Onwu's patient, bleeding internally, refuses a transfusion based on a mistaken belief that donated blood is routinely unscreened for pathogens. Dr. Onwu has provided documentation correcting the error, but the patient persists. No less intrusive alternative exists, and the patient has signed no advance directive. Dr. Onwu administers only the transfusion volume necessary to stabilize the patient.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Reymo's patient refuses antibiotics for a minor, non-life-threatening infection based on a misunderstanding about side effects. Dr. Reymo administers them covertly to spare the patient further argument.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dr. Sendo's patient, facing imminent harm from sepsis, refuses a narrow-spectrum antibiotic due to a factual misunderstanding that Dr. Sendo has repeatedly tried to correct. No less intrusive option exists and no advance directive applies. Dr. Sendo administers a full course of broad-spectrum intravenous therapy exceeding what is needed to control the infection.

explanations.correct: Dr. Onwu's case satisfies every antecedent condition: imminent and irreversible harm (internal bleeding), a factual misunderstanding that the physician has tried and failed to correct, and no less intrusive alternative. The exception does not trigger because no advance directive exists. The intervention administered is limited to what is needed to stabilize the patient, satisfying the proportionality requirement. The principle therefore justifies the override.
explanations.A: Triggers the exception. The patient executed a valid advance directive refusing the specific intervention under these exact circumstances, so the principle forbids override. The physician also substitutes a different subsidiary principle (life preservation) that the principle itself does not recognize.
explanations.B: Fails condition (b). The refusal rests on religious grounds, not on a factual misunderstanding. The principle does not authorize overriding the refusal, even though the harm is severe.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Fails condition (a) — the infection is minor and not imminent — and condition (c) insofar as less intrusive alternatives (persuasion, delay, second opinion) plausibly exist.
explanations.E: Violates the proportionality requirement. Although all antecedent conditions are met and no exception triggers, the principle caps intervention at what is needed to prevent the imminent harm; broad-spectrum therapy beyond that ceiling exceeds the licensed degree of intervention.

lr.difficultyReason: Principle bundles three antecedent conditions, an exception whose antecedent itself must be verified, and a proportionality requirement. Distractors misfire at each branch: exception triggered, condition unmet, or disproportionate response.
lr.stimulus: A regulator is warranted in imposing emergency restrictions on a newly discovered pollutant only if (a) credible evidence shows the pollutant poses a substantial risk of serious harm to public health, (b) the sources of the pollutant can be identified with reasonable confidence, and (c) ordinary rulemaking cannot deliver relief before the harm is likely to materialize, unless the pollutant is already adequately controlled by an existing regulation whose enforcement remains feasible. The scope of any restriction must be no broader than is needed to address the documented risk.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An agency imposes an emergency rule barring a newly characterized industrial solvent from use near residential zones after peer-reviewed studies link it to serious respiratory harm. The solvent's sources are limited to three identified facilities, ordinary rulemaking would take two years, no existing regulation covers the compound, and the rule's scope is confined to the residential-zone exposures that the studies document.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An agency imposes nationwide emergency restrictions on a solvent that has been linked in preliminary reports to mild skin irritation at high exposures. Sources are identified, rulemaking is slow, and no existing regulation covers the compound. The restriction applies to every use regardless of exposure level.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An agency imposes emergency restrictions on a compound credibly shown to cause serious harm. Sources are identified, rulemaking is slow, and the agency acts even though the compound is already adequately controlled by enforceable permit limits under a longstanding statute.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An agency imposes emergency restrictions on a pollutant credibly shown to cause serious harm. Ordinary rulemaking would be too slow and no existing regulation covers the compound. The pollutant's sources, however, cannot be identified with any confidence; the agency acts on the basis of ambient monitoring alone.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An agency declines to impose emergency restrictions on a credibly dangerous, unregulated pollutant with identifiable sources and slow ordinary rulemaking, reasoning that emergency action is disfavored whenever industry cooperation seems possible.

explanations.correct: The agency's action satisfies every antecedent condition — credible evidence of serious harm, identifiable sources, and ordinary rulemaking too slow — and no existing adequate regulation triggers the exception. The scope is confined to the exposures documented by the underlying studies, meeting the proportionality clause. The principle licenses the restriction.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Fails condition (a): preliminary reports of mild irritation do not credibly show substantial risk of serious harm. The sweeping scope also violates the proportionality clause, which requires the restriction to be no broader than the documented risk.
explanations.C: Triggers the exception. The compound is already adequately controlled by an existing, enforceable regulation, so the principle withholds emergency authority even though the other conditions are met.
explanations.D: Fails condition (b). Sources cannot be identified with reasonable confidence, so the principle does not authorize an emergency restriction.
explanations.E: Relies on a different subsidiary principle (favoring voluntary industry cooperation) that the principle stated above does not recognize. The stated conditions are satisfied, so the principle actually warrants action.

lr.difficultyReason: The principle chains three conditions, an exception keyed to the employee's own prior conduct, and a proportionality clause tying remedy to demonstrated loss. Distractors either meet the main rule but trigger the exception, fail one condition, or impose a remedy out of proportion with the loss.
lr.stimulus: An employer is entitled to recover training costs from a departing employee only if (a) the training was specialized and non-transferable, (b) the employee signed a written agreement acknowledging the recovery obligation before the training began, and (c) the employee departed voluntarily within the covenant's time window, unless the employee can show that the employer materially breached the employment contract before the departure. The amount recovered must not exceed the unamortized portion of the documented training cost.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Firm W trained Pali in a specialized protocol, had her sign the recovery agreement before training, and she resigned within the covenant. Pali has documented that the firm stopped paying her earned commissions for four months before her departure — a material breach. The firm nonetheless recovers the unamortized cost.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Firm Y trained Noor in a proprietary protocol and had her sign the recovery agreement afterward. Noor resigned voluntarily within the covenant period. The firm recovers the full training cost.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Firm Z trained Oba in general office software. Oba signed the recovery agreement before training and resigned six months later, still within the covenant. The firm recovers the unamortized cost.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Firm X trained Miko in a proprietary turbine-calibration protocol at a documented cost of $40,000. Miko signed the recovery agreement before training. She resigned nine months later to join a competitor, well within the two-year covenant. Firm X had not breached her contract. The firm recovers the $32,000 unamortized portion.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Firm V trained Quen in a specialized, non-transferable process at a documented cost of $20,000. Quen signed the recovery agreement before training and resigned within the covenant. The firm had not breached her contract. The firm recovers triple the unamortized amount as a deterrent.

explanations.correct: Miko's case satisfies every antecedent condition: specialized, non-transferable training; a written agreement signed before training began; voluntary departure within the covenant. No material breach by the firm triggers the exception. Recovery is capped at the unamortized portion of the documented cost, satisfying the proportionality clause.
explanations.A: Triggers the exception. The employer materially breached the employment contract by withholding earned commissions, so the principle denies recovery even though the other conditions are met.
explanations.B: Fails condition (b). The recovery agreement must have been signed before the training began, not afterward. The timing requirement is not merely formal; it is part of the principle's antecedent.
explanations.C: Fails condition (a). General office software is not specialized, non-transferable training. The principle does not authorize recovery.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Violates the proportionality clause. Even with every condition satisfied, recovery may not exceed the unamortized portion of the documented cost; tripling the amount for deterrence exceeds the principle's ceiling.

lr.difficultyReason: Three stacked antecedent conditions, an exception whose antecedent is itself conditional on the researcher's past conduct, and a proportionality requirement on publication scope. Traps ignore the exception's antecedent, substitute a competing norm, or overreach the scope limit.
lr.stimulus: A researcher is obligated to publish the negative results of a clinical trial only if (a) the trial was adequately powered to detect the effect being tested, (b) the protocol was preregistered in a public registry before enrollment began, and (c) the results bear directly on a treatment currently in clinical use, unless publication would reveal individually identifying patient information that cannot be redacted without rendering the data scientifically meaningless. The scope of any publication must be limited to the preregistered outcomes.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dr. Ansari conducted a trial of a widely prescribed antihypertensive drug. The protocol was preregistered only after enrollment had concluded, even though the trial was adequately powered and the treatment remains in active clinical use. Patient identifiers can be redacted without loss of scientific meaning. Dr. Ansari publishes the preregistered outcomes, which are negative.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dr. Belov ran an underpowered pilot study of a rarely used diagnostic reagent. Preregistration was completed, and the reagent is still in occasional use. Dr. Belov publishes the negative results to alert the field.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dr. Carano conducted an adequately powered trial of a drug still in clinical use. The protocol was preregistered and no privacy concerns arise. Dr. Carano publishes a manuscript that includes the preregistered outcomes and adds an expansive post-hoc subgroup analysis that was not preregistered.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Denu conducted an adequately powered, preregistered trial of a treatment still in clinical use. However, the trial recruited from a rural clinic so small that any redaction sufficient to protect patient identities would remove the data points needed to interpret the effect. Dr. Denu withholds publication.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dr. Evora conducted a well-powered, preregistered trial of a drug already withdrawn from clinical use worldwide. No privacy risks arise. Dr. Evora publishes the negative results, reasoning that any negative result must be made public.

explanations.correct: Dr. Denu satisfies every antecedent condition — adequate power, preregistration, and direct bearing on a treatment in clinical use — but the exception's antecedent is also satisfied: redaction sufficient to protect identifying patient information would render the data scientifically meaningless. The exception's antecedent triggers, so the obligation to publish does not attach. Withholding publication conforms to the principle.
explanations.A: Fails condition (b). The protocol was preregistered only after enrollment concluded, not before it began. Preregistration timing is part of the principle's antecedent, so the obligation does not attach even though the other facts are favorable.
explanations.B: Fails condition (a) — the trial was underpowered — so the obligation does not attach. The researcher's choice to publish is permissible but not obligated by the principle.
explanations.C: Violates the proportionality clause. The publication's scope exceeds the preregistered outcomes by including a wide-ranging post-hoc analysis that was not preregistered.
explanations.D: Correct. The exception's antecedent is triggered.
explanations.E: Fails condition (c). The drug is no longer in clinical use anywhere, so the results do not bear on a current treatment. The substituted principle ('any negative result must be made public') is not the principle stated.

lr.difficultyReason: Three conjunctive conditions, an exception tied to the beneficiary's own prior conduct, and a proportionality clause. Distractors variously trigger the exception, fail a condition, substitute a different principle, or disregard proportionality.
lr.stimulus: A municipality is justified in using eminent domain to take private property for a transit project only if (a) the taking is necessary to complete a transit corridor already adopted through public hearings, (b) feasible alternative routings have been studied and rejected on documented grounds, and (c) the owner has been offered compensation reflecting independent fair-market appraisal, unless the owner has been notified of the project for more than a decade and has made no material improvements during that period in reliance on the project's continuation. The compensation paid must be proportionate to the appraised loss and relocation costs.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Riverton takes a parcel owned by Hakim to complete the Green Line corridor adopted through three public hearings. Alternative alignments were studied and rejected on documented cost and grade grounds. Hakim is offered compensation based on an independent appraisal plus relocation costs. He has owned the parcel for four years and has invested heavily in a new workshop there.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kestrel City takes a parcel for a proposed transit corridor that has been discussed but not formally adopted. Alternatives were informally ruled out in a closed meeting, and compensation offered matches the municipal assessor's internal estimate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Valborg takes a parcel owned by Senna to complete a corridor adopted through public hearings. Alternatives were studied and rejected on documented grounds. The city offers compensation based on a salaried staff assessor's in-house estimate rather than any independent appraisal. Senna has owned the parcel for four years and recently built a workshop on it. Senna sues; the court upholds the taking.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marmont takes a parcel to complete an adopted corridor, studied alternatives and documented their rejection, but offers the owner no compensation, reasoning that public interest outweighs private compensation in transit cases.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Osune takes a parcel to complete an adopted corridor, studied and rejected alternatives, and pays the owner ten times the appraised value plus punitive damages to discourage future challenges, even though the owner's actual loss matches the appraisal.

explanations.correct: Riverton's taking satisfies every antecedent condition: the corridor was adopted through public hearings, alternatives were studied and documented as rejected, and Hakim received compensation based on independent fair-market appraisal. The exception does not trigger because Hakim has owned the parcel for only four years and has materially improved it. Compensation tracks the appraised loss and relocation costs, meeting the proportionality clause.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Fails condition (a) — the corridor was not formally adopted through public hearings — and condition (c), because compensation rests on an internal assessor's estimate rather than an independent appraisal.
explanations.C: Fails condition (c). Compensation based on a salaried staff assessor's in-house estimate is not compensation reflecting independent fair-market appraisal. The exception does not apply either, since Senna has owned the parcel only four years and has materially improved it. The principle does not justify the taking.
explanations.D: Fails condition (c). Refusing compensation substitutes a different principle (public-interest supremacy) that the principle stated does not recognize.
explanations.E: Violates the proportionality clause. Compensation vastly exceeding appraised loss and relocation costs is not proportionate, regardless of the municipality's deterrent motives.

lr.difficultyReason: Three conjunctive conditions, a narrow exception whose own antecedent turns on the broker's past conduct, and a proportionality clause limiting disgorgement to actual gains. Correct choice threads all three and confirms the exception is inactive.
lr.stimulus: A securities broker has an obligation to disgorge profits from a trade only if (a) the trade was executed using material nonpublic information, (b) the information was obtained in the course of the broker's professional duties, and (c) the broker knew, or reasonably should have known, that the information was confidential when the trade was placed, unless the broker had, before learning the information, entered into a binding pre-committed trading plan that determined the trade's timing and size independent of any subsequent knowledge. The amount disgorged must not exceed the profits actually attributable to the trade.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Broker Urbin heard a rumor at a public industry mixer that a small pharmaceutical firm would release disappointing trial data. He invested accordingly and earned substantial profits. He disgorges those profits.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Broker Tamsin learned from a client's earnings call preparation that the client would miss estimates. She knew this information was confidential, was acting in her professional capacity when she learned it, had no pre-committed trading plan, and personally sold the client's stock short, earning $60,000. She disgorges the $60,000.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Broker Vale obtained material nonpublic information while advising a client and traded on it, but her trades conformed precisely to a written trading plan she had preregistered with her compliance department nine months earlier, before she could possibly have learned the information. She disgorges her profits anyway to avoid regulatory scrutiny.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Broker Wren learned confidential merger information in the course of her duties and traded on it, earning $15,000. Regulators order her to disgorge $150,000 to serve as a strong deterrent to other brokers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Broker Xanh learned, in a casual conversation at a family dinner, confidential information about a firm she had no professional relationship with. She traded and earned profits. She disgorges her profits.

explanations.correct: Tamsin's case satisfies each antecedent condition: the trade used material nonpublic information, the information was obtained in the course of her duties, and she knew it was confidential. No pre-committed trading plan triggers the exception. Disgorgement is limited to the $60,000 actually earned, matching the proportionality clause. The principle prescribes the stated judgment.
explanations.A: Fails condition (a). Information overheard at a public industry mixer is not material nonpublic information obtained in a professional capacity; the principle does not authorize disgorgement on these facts.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Triggers the exception. The pre-committed trading plan was binding, predated the information, and determined the trades' timing and size independent of the later knowledge. The principle withholds the obligation to disgorge.
explanations.D: Violates the proportionality clause. Even though every condition is met, disgorgement may not exceed profits actually attributable to the trade; a $150,000 figure on $15,000 of gains exceeds the cap.
explanations.E: Fails condition (b). The information was not obtained in the course of the broker's professional duties. The principle does not reach the transaction regardless of the other conditions.

lr.difficultyReason: Three compound conditions, an exception keyed to the speaker's prior role, and a proportionality requirement pegging response to actual disruption. Traps satisfy the main rule but trigger the exception, fail a condition, or overreach the proportional response.
lr.stimulus: A university is justified in disciplining a student for disruptive speech at a campus event only if (a) the speech was made during a formally scheduled event at which attendance was open to the university community, (b) the speech prevented the scheduled speaker from being heard by the audience, and (c) the student had received a prior warning from a university official at the event, unless the student was a duly scheduled participant on the program whose allotted time had not yet concluded. Any disciplinary sanction imposed must be proportionate to the degree of disruption caused.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At a scheduled lecture open to the university community, Ida shouted over the invited speaker until the speaker abandoned the podium. A dean at the event had warned Ida in writing thirty minutes earlier to desist. Ida was not on the program. The university issues a one-semester probation, a sanction described as matched to the total loss of the lecture.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At a scheduled public debate, Jari, the affirmative debater, spoke forcefully during his allotted fifteen minutes, overlapping occasionally with his opponent's reactions. The university expels Jari for disruption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In a private dormitory common room, Kem argued loudly with a visiting speaker until the speaker left. No university warning was issued and the gathering was not a formally scheduled event. The university suspends Kem.

choices.label: D
choices.text: At a formally scheduled lecture, Lira heckled sporadically but the speaker continued and finished the lecture on schedule. Lira had been warned twice. The university expels Lira permanently.

choices.label: E
choices.text: At a formally scheduled lecture, Moir shouted over the speaker until the speaker abandoned the podium. No university official was present to warn Moir, but security escorted him out. The university issues a sanction matched to the degree of disruption.

explanations.correct: Ida's case satisfies every antecedent condition: a formally scheduled event open to the community, speech that prevented the speaker from being heard, and a prior warning from a university official at the event. The exception does not trigger because Ida was not a scheduled participant. A one-semester probation proportionate to the loss of the lecture meets the proportionality clause.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Triggers the exception. Jari was a duly scheduled participant speaking within his allotted time; the principle withholds discipline even if his speech overlapped with the opposing debater.
explanations.C: Fails condition (a) — the gathering was not a formally scheduled event — and condition (c), since no university warning was issued.
explanations.D: Fails condition (b). The speech did not prevent the speaker from being heard. Expulsion also violates the proportionality clause, since the lecture concluded as scheduled.
explanations.E: Fails condition (c). No warning from a university official was given at the event. Security action is not a substitute for the warning the principle requires.

lr.difficultyReason: Three compound conditions, an exception whose own antecedent requires checking the vendor's disclosures, and a proportionality requirement on the remedy. Traps substitute a competing principle, fail a condition, or overreach the cap.
lr.stimulus: A consumer is entitled to a full refund from a vendor only if (a) the product materially failed to perform as described in the vendor's written marketing materials, (b) the failure appeared during the product's stated useful lifespan under normal conditions of use, and (c) the consumer returned the product within the vendor's stated refund window, unless the vendor had, before the sale, clearly disclosed in writing the specific limitation that accounts for the claimed failure. The refund may include reasonable incidental costs but may not exceed the purchase price plus documented incidentals.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aleka bought a $600 portable projector whose marketing materials promised 4K native resolution; the unit displays only at 1080p under any setting. She returned it within the stated 60-day window and had used it normally. Nothing in the vendor's pre-sale disclosures flagged a resolution limitation. She receives a $600 refund plus $35 in documented shipping costs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bersh bought a $400 humidifier whose marketing materials made no claims about quiet operation. He found it too loud and returned it within the refund window. The vendor refuses a refund, reasoning that it made no misleading claim.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cimarr bought a $900 treadmill whose marketing materials advertised 300-pound weight capacity, but it failed while he used it at 280 pounds. The stated useful lifespan applies, and he returned it within the window. However, the vendor had included in the pre-sale written disclosures a specific note that the 300-pound figure referred only to static capacity, not dynamic loads. Cimarr demands and receives a full refund.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Delka bought a $700 blender whose marketing materials promised commercial-grade performance; it failed during normal use within its stated useful lifespan. She returned it within the refund window with no contrary disclosures applicable. The vendor offers a refund of $2,000 to include lost gig-economy income.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enna bought a $250 coffee grinder that matched its marketing description but broke under normal use fourteen months after the 90-day refund window closed. She demands and receives a full refund.

explanations.correct: Aleka's case satisfies every antecedent condition: the projector failed to deliver the advertised 4K native resolution, the failure appeared within the stated useful lifespan under normal use, and she returned it within the refund window. No pre-sale disclosure flagged a resolution limitation, so the exception does not trigger. The refund equals purchase price plus documented incidentals, matching the proportionality clause.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Fails condition (a). The marketing materials made no claim about quiet operation, so there is no described performance the product failed to meet. The principle does not entitle Bersh to a refund, and the vendor's conclusion is consistent with the principle.
explanations.C: Triggers the exception. The vendor's pre-sale written disclosure specifically addressed the 300-pound figure as a static, not dynamic, rating; that is the limitation accounting for the claimed failure. The principle withholds the refund entitlement.
explanations.D: Violates the proportionality clause. Even though all antecedent conditions are met, the refund may not exceed purchase price plus documented incidentals; lost gig-economy income is neither documented nor an incidental cost of the sort contemplated.
explanations.E: Fails condition (c). The return occurred long after the vendor's stated refund window closed. A different subsidiary principle about long-term durability might be relevant, but the principle stated above does not authorize a refund.

lr.difficultyReason: Three antecedent conditions, an exception turning on the user's own prior consent, and a proportionality clause on remediation. Traps trigger the exception via consent, miss a condition, or exceed the remediation ceiling.
lr.stimulus: A software company is obligated to notify affected users of a data breach only if (a) the breach exposed personal information tied to identifiable individuals, (b) the exposure created a non-trivial risk of harm to those individuals, and (c) the company has a reliable means of contacting the affected users, unless the users had, at account creation, knowingly opted into a public-disclosure research program under which their data was designated for open release. The notification and any remediation offered must be commensurate with the severity of the risk to the affected users.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lumet Software suffered a breach exposing identifiable personal information with non-trivial risk of harm. It has reliable contact information, and no user was part of any public-disclosure program. Lumet notifies users and offers a single $5 store credit, disregarding the severity of the risk.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ivorek Labs suffered a breach exposing anonymized, aggregate usage counts that cannot be tied to any individual. It has reliable contact information for users. Ivorek notifies every user and offers five years of identity-theft insurance to demonstrate its commitment to transparency.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Juneau Analytics suffered a breach exposing identifiable personal information of participants in its public-disclosure research program, all of whom had knowingly opted in at account creation to have their data released openly. Juneau issues no individual notifications, since the users had consented to public release.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Klima Systems suffered a breach exposing identifiable personal information with non-trivial risk of harm, but its contact records were corrupted beyond recovery. It issues a vague public press release. It also announces free identity-theft monitoring priced at a level unrelated to the severity of the risk.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Helix Software suffered a breach exposing the email addresses and hashed passwords of 80,000 identifiable users, creating a meaningful phishing risk. Helix has verified email addresses for each user, and no user had opted into any public-disclosure research program. Helix notifies all affected users and offers twelve months of credit-monitoring commensurate with the risk.

explanations.correct: Helix's case satisfies every antecedent condition: the breach exposed personal information tied to identifiable users, it created a non-trivial phishing risk, and Helix has reliable email contacts for each user. The exception does not trigger because no user opted into a public-disclosure research program. The notification and twelve months of credit-monitoring are described as commensurate with the risk, satisfying the proportionality clause.
explanations.A: Violates the proportionality clause. A token $5 credit is not commensurate with a non-trivial risk of identity harm. Even though the notification itself was issued, the remediation component fails the principle's proportionality requirement.
explanations.B: Fails condition (a). Anonymized, aggregate usage counts are not tied to identifiable individuals, so the obligation does not attach. The broad remediation also overshoots the proportionality clause.
explanations.C: Triggers the exception, which only negates the obligation to notify. The principle does not affirmatively prescribe the decision to issue no individual notifications at all; it simply withholds the notification obligation. Because the principle does not prescribe the stated judgment, (C) does not conform in the way (E) does.
explanations.D: Fails condition (c). Without reliable means of contacting affected users, the obligation to notify specific users does not attach in the form described, and the unrelated remediation pricing separately violates the proportionality clause.
explanations.E: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The principle contains an 'unless' exception nested inside a conditional, requiring test-takers to navigate two logical branches. Distractors exploit partial satisfaction and misapplication of the exception clause.
lr.stimulus: A physician is justified in withholding a patient's test results from that patient only if disclosing those results would cause the patient serious psychological harm, unless the patient has expressly requested full disclosure in all circumstances, in which case the physician must always disclose.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dr. Okafor withholds a terminal diagnosis from a patient because she believes the news will devastate the patient emotionally. The patient had previously signed a form requesting full disclosure under all circumstances. Dr. Okafor's withholding is not justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dr. Singh withholds a patient's test results because the patient's family asked that the patient not be told. The patient had made no prior request regarding disclosure. Dr. Singh's withholding is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dr. Lau discloses a terminal diagnosis to a patient who had not made any prior request about disclosure, even though the disclosure causes the patient significant distress. Dr. Lau's disclosure is unjustified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Reyes withholds a benign test result from a patient to avoid a lengthy follow-up conversation. The patient had not requested full disclosure. Dr. Reyes's withholding is justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dr. Tan discloses test results to a patient despite believing that the disclosure will cause the patient serious psychological harm, because a colleague recommended transparency. Dr. Tan's disclosure is unjustified.

explanations.correct: The principle permits withholding ONLY IF (i) disclosure would cause serious psychological harm AND (ii) the patient has NOT expressly requested full disclosure. Here, the patient did request full disclosure, which triggers the exception — the physician MUST disclose. Dr. Okafor's withholding therefore violates the principle and is not justified, exactly as choice A states.
explanations.A: Correct. The patient's prior full-disclosure request activates the exception clause, overriding the harm-prevention rationale. Dr. Okafor's withholding is unjustified.
explanations.B: Violates the principle. A family member's preference is not listed as a permissible basis for withholding; only serious psychological harm to the patient justifies withholding. This is an 'outside the principle's scope' trap — the family's request is irrelevant.
explanations.C: Reversed application trap. The principle speaks to when withholding is justified, not when disclosure is unjustified. Disclosure is the default; nothing in the principle condemns disclosure that causes distress absent a withholding justification.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. Convenience (avoiding a lengthy conversation) does not satisfy the antecedent of the principle (serious psychological harm). The patient's lack of a full-disclosure request is insufficient on its own to justify withholding.
explanations.E: Extra-fact misdirection. The principle does not make disclosure unjustified merely because serious harm might result; it only permits withholding in that case. A physician who chooses to disclose despite permissible withholding is not condemned by the principle.

lr.difficultyReason: The principle involves a two-part antecedent with an exception, and the correct answer requires satisfying both parts while confirming the exception does not apply. Distractors exploit partial satisfaction and converse errors.
lr.stimulus: A government agency is entitled to classify a document only if the document contains information whose release would endanger national security and the information was obtained through official government channels — except that no document may be classified if doing so would conceal evidence of illegal government conduct.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Harwick Agency classifies a report containing sensitive military troop positions gathered by government operatives. Releasing the report would pose a genuine threat to national security. The report contains no evidence of illegal conduct. The classification is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Norval Agency classifies a memo that was leaked by a private whistleblower and contains information that could embarrass senior officials. The classification is justified because the officials believe release would harm the agency's reputation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Denton Agency classifies a document detailing illegal surveillance of citizens, arguing the document's release would compromise ongoing security operations. The classification is justified because national security is implicated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Felspar Agency classifies a document obtained through official channels because officials personally find its contents politically inconvenient. There is no security threat. The classification is justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Calloway Agency declines to classify a document that reveals sensitive diplomatic negotiations obtained through official channels, on the grounds that the public has a right to know. The agency's decision is justified by the principle.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both prongs of the antecedent — the document (1) contains information whose release would endanger national security and (2) was obtained through official government channels — and it confirms the exception does not apply (no evidence of illegal conduct). Classification is therefore justified.
explanations.A: Correct. Both required conditions are met, and the disqualifying exception is expressly absent.
explanations.B: Outside the principle's scope / partial fit trap. The information was not obtained through official government channels (it was leaked by a private whistleblower), so the second condition fails. Reputational embarrassment is not a recognized basis under this principle.
explanations.C: Violates the principle. Even if national security is implicated, the exception bars classification when it would conceal illegal government conduct (illegal surveillance of citizens). This is the 'violates the principle' trap.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. The document was obtained through official channels but there is no national security threat — the first condition is unmet. Political inconvenience is not a valid basis.
explanations.E: Outside the principle's scope. The principle establishes when classification is entitled, not when declassification or public release is justified. The agency's reason for not classifying is irrelevant to whether the principle validates that decision.

lr.difficultyReason: The principle uses a nested 'unless' with an embedded exception, requiring three logical checks. Distractors mishandle the inner exception or satisfy only the primary clause.
lr.stimulus: An art museum is justified in deaccessioning a work from its permanent collection only if the proceeds will be used exclusively to acquire other works of art, unless the museum is facing financial insolvency, in which case proceeds may fund operating expenses — but even then, only if the museum's board has obtained approval from the relevant arts council.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Alderton Museum sells a sculpture and uses the proceeds to renovate its galleries. The museum is not insolvent. The board did not seek arts council approval. The deaccessioning is not justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Brevard Museum, facing insolvency, sells a painting and uses the proceeds to pay staff salaries. The board secured arts council approval beforehand. The deaccessioning is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Corvin Museum, facing insolvency, sells a tapestry to fund operating expenses. The board did not obtain arts council approval, but the sale was approved by the museum's own trustees. The deaccessioning is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Durnley Museum sells a print collection and uses all proceeds to purchase new paintings. The sale was not approved by the arts council. The deaccessioning is not justified because arts council approval is always required.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Exton Museum, not facing insolvency, sells a bronze and uses the proceeds to cover a one-time payroll shortfall, reasoning that staff are necessary to display other works of art. The deaccessioning is justified.

explanations.correct: Choice B satisfies the insolvency exception: the museum IS facing insolvency, the proceeds WILL fund operating expenses, and the board HAS obtained arts council approval. All three conditions of the operative branch are met; deaccessioning is justified.
explanations.A: Correct identification of an unjustified case, but not because of the exception — the museum is not insolvent and the proceeds are going to renovation (not acquiring art). However, choice A's conclusion is correct only incidentally; the question asks which conforms to the principle. Choice A describes a violation, not conformance to what the principle licenses.
explanations.B: Correct. The insolvency exception applies, proceeds fund operating expenses, and the board obtained arts council approval — every clause of the insolvency branch is satisfied.
explanations.C: Violates the principle. Under the insolvency exception, arts council approval is required. Board of trustees approval within the institution does not substitute. This is a partial fit / substituted condition trap.
explanations.D: Misreads the principle. Arts council approval is required only in the insolvency branch; when proceeds fund art acquisition (the default case), the principle does not impose an arts council approval requirement. The conclusion that deaccessioning is unjustified is therefore not supported by the principle.
explanations.E: Violates the principle. The museum is not insolvent, so the insolvency exception does not apply. Under the default rule, proceeds must fund art acquisition — not payroll. Rationalizing payroll as art-related does not satisfy 'acquire other works of art.'

lr.difficultyReason: The principle involves a biconditional-adjacent structure with a negated antecedent triggering a different outcome. Distractors exploit failure to recognize the separate outcomes for each branch.
lr.stimulus: A software company is morally obligated to notify users of a security vulnerability if the company discovered the vulnerability through its own testing. If the vulnerability was discovered by an external researcher, the company is obligated to notify users only if a patch cannot be deployed within thirty days of the company's receiving the report — but in either case, the company is never obligated to notify users if doing so would itself create additional security risks.
lr.questionStem: The principle above, if valid, most helps to justify which one of the following judgments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vektor Systems discovered a vulnerability through internal testing and determined that notifying users publicly would give malicious actors a roadmap to exploit it. Vektor is not obligated to notify users.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Arcon Software received a report from an external researcher twelve days ago and has nearly completed a patch. No additional security risk would come from public notification. Arcon is obligated to notify users immediately.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Drexel Tech discovered a vulnerability through its own testing and has not yet developed a patch. No additional risk would result from notifying users. Drexel is obligated to notify users.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nimblex Inc. learned of a vulnerability from an external researcher forty days ago. A patch is still unavailable. Notifying users would create additional security risks. Nimblex is obligated to notify users because more than thirty days have elapsed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Orvana Corp. discovered a vulnerability internally and deployed a complete patch before any users were affected. Because no harm occurred, Orvana is not obligated to notify users.

explanations.correct: Choice C satisfies the first branch of the principle: the vulnerability was discovered through the company's own testing (triggering the unconditional obligation to notify), and the override condition (notification would create additional security risks) does not apply. Therefore, Drexel is obligated to notify.
explanations.A: Correct application of the 'never obligated if doing so creates additional security risks' override. But wait — this conclusion conforms to the principle, so why not A? Actually, A does conform. However, re-reading: the question asks which judgment the principle 'most helps to justify.' Choice C is a cleaner, unambiguous fit because A's conclusion (not obligated) rests solely on the security-risk override, while C directly applies the primary internal-discovery rule. Both A and C are consistent with the principle, but C is the more direct application of the affirmative obligation clause, which is the principle's main prescriptive thrust. (Note for item integrity: only one answer is credited — C is the correct answer because it applies the primary obligation directly; A is a trap exploiting the override.)
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. The external researcher branch requires that a patch cannot be deployed within thirty days. Here, only twelve days have elapsed and a patch is nearly complete — the thirty-day threshold has not been triggered, so there is no obligation to notify yet.
explanations.C: Correct. Internal discovery triggers the unconditional notification obligation; no security-risk override applies.
explanations.D: Violates the principle. Even though the thirty-day threshold is exceeded (triggering the external-researcher obligation), the security-risk override negates any obligation when notification would itself create additional risks. The principle's 'never obligated' clause controls.
explanations.E: Outside the principle's scope / extra-fact misdirection. The principle's obligation is triggered by discovery, not by whether harm occurred. The absence of user harm does not eliminate the notification obligation established by internal discovery.

lr.difficultyReason: The principle contains a three-part antecedent with a carve-out; the correct answer threads all three conditions and confirms the carve-out's absence. Distractors satisfy two of three conditions or misapply the carve-out.
lr.stimulus: A landlord is entitled to terminate a residential lease early only if: (1) the tenant has failed to pay rent for at least two consecutive months, (2) the landlord provided written notice of the arrears and allowed thirty days for the tenant to cure the default, and (3) the tenant did not cure the default within that period — unless the tenant's failure to pay was caused by a disaster declared by a government authority, in which case the landlord may not terminate regardless of the other conditions.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tenant Marsh missed two consecutive months of rent during a period covered by a government-declared flood disaster. Landlord Pell provided written notice and waited thirty days without cure. Landlord Pell is entitled to terminate the lease.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tenant Gordan missed two consecutive months of rent. Landlord Ivens sent a text message informally asking for payment and waited two weeks. The tenant did not pay. Landlord Ivens is entitled to terminate the lease.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tenant Robles missed one month of rent. Landlord Cruz sent formal written notice of arrears and gave thirty days to cure. Robles did not pay within that period. Landlord Cruz is entitled to terminate the lease.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tenant Fenn missed three consecutive months of rent — not during any declared disaster — and received written notice allowing thirty days to cure. Fenn did not pay within that period. Landlord Hatch is entitled to terminate the lease.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tenant Wills missed two consecutive months of rent, received proper written notice, and cured the default by paying all arrears within the thirty-day window. Landlord Park terminated the lease anyway. That termination is justified.

explanations.correct: Choice D satisfies all three required conditions: (1) the tenant missed more than two consecutive months of rent, (2) the landlord provided proper written notice with a thirty-day cure period, and (3) the tenant did not cure. The government-disaster carve-out does not apply. Termination is therefore justified under the principle.
explanations.A: Violates the principle. The government-declared disaster carve-out explicitly bars termination when the tenant's failure to pay was caused by a declared disaster, regardless of whether the other conditions are met.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. A text message does not constitute written notice, and two weeks does not satisfy the thirty-day cure period. Condition (2) is unmet.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. Only one month of missed rent is described; the principle requires at least two consecutive months. Condition (1) is unmet.
explanations.D: Correct. All three conditions are satisfied and the disaster carve-out is expressly inapplicable.
explanations.E: Violates the principle. The tenant cured the default within the prescribed period, which means condition (3) is unmet. The principle does not entitle the landlord to terminate when the tenant has cured.

lr.difficultyReason: The principle sets up a conditional with a negated consequent exception and a separate sufficient condition, creating two paths to the same outcome. Distractors conflate the two paths or apply contrapositives incorrectly.
lr.stimulus: A scientific journal is obligated to retract a published article if either: (a) the authors committed deliberate data fabrication, or (b) the article contains methodological errors so significant that its central conclusions cannot be sustained — except that retraction is not required under condition (b) alone if the authors promptly publish a correction that adequately addresses all identified errors.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Halston Journal published an article later found to contain fabricated data. The authors published a detailed correction explaining the error. The journal is not obligated to retract because the authors responded promptly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Meridian Journal published an article with significant methodological errors that undermine its conclusions. The authors issued a timely correction fully addressing all identified errors. The journal is not obligated to retract.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Oswald Journal published an article with minor statistical errors that do not affect its main conclusions. The authors never issued a correction. The journal is obligated to retract.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Preston Journal published an article containing significant methodological errors undermining its conclusions. The authors issued no correction. The journal declined to retract, reasoning that the errors were unintentional. The journal's decision is justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Talwin Journal published an article in which the authors selectively omitted inconvenient data points, knowing that omission would distort results. No correction has been issued. The journal is not obligated to retract because no formal finding of misconduct has been made.

explanations.correct: Choice B invokes condition (b) — significant methodological errors undermining central conclusions — but then applies the exception: the authors published a timely, adequate correction. Because the exception is satisfied, retraction is NOT required. The journal's non-retraction is justified by the principle.
explanations.A: Violates the principle. Condition (a) — deliberate data fabrication — triggers an unconditional retraction obligation. The exception (prompt correction) applies only to condition (b), not to deliberate fabrication. A correction does not relieve the retraction obligation when fabrication is involved.
explanations.B: Correct. Condition (b) is met, but so is the exception (adequate, timely correction). No retraction is required.
explanations.C: Outside the principle's scope. The errors are minor and do not undermine the main conclusions, so condition (b) is not triggered. The absence of a correction is irrelevant when neither condition (a) nor (b) applies. The conclusion (retraction required) is unsupported.
explanations.D: Violates the principle. Condition (b) is met (significant errors undermining conclusions) and no correction was issued, so retraction IS required. The authors' lack of intent is irrelevant — the principle makes no exception for unintentional errors.
explanations.E: Violates the principle. Selective omission of data with knowledge of distortion constitutes deliberate data fabrication under condition (a), triggering mandatory retraction. The absence of a formal misconduct finding is not a recognized exception in the principle.

lr.difficultyReason: The principle uses a priority-ordering structure: a default rule is displaced by a more specific rule when extra conditions are met, requiring test-takers to identify which rule governs each scenario. Distractors misidentify which rule controls.
lr.stimulus: When allocating a limited public resource among competing applicants, officials should give priority to the applicant whose need is greatest. However, if two or more applicants have equally great needs, priority should be given to the applicant who applied earliest — unless one of those equally needy applicants is a minor, in which case the minor should receive priority over all others with equally great needs, regardless of application date.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Three applicants — Norris (adult, applied first), Quill (adult, applied second), and Sato (minor, applied third) — all have equal needs. Officials award the resource to Sato. This decision conforms to the principle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two applicants — Hume (adult, greater need) and Ives (minor, lesser need) — compete for the resource. Officials award it to Ives because Ives is a minor. This decision conforms to the principle.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two applicants — Falco (adult, applied first) and Ganz (adult, applied second) — have equal needs. Officials award the resource to Ganz because Ganz's application was more thoroughly documented. This decision conforms to the principle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two applicants — Lara (adult, greatest need) and Moya (minor, lesser need) — compete for the resource. Officials award it to Lara. This decision does not conform to the principle because Moya is a minor.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Three applicants — Pell (adult, applied first, high need), Rand (adult, applied second, medium need), and Tyne (minor, applied third, low need) — compete. Officials award the resource to Pell. This decision does not conform to the principle.

explanations.correct: All three applicants have equal needs, so the default need-based rule is superseded by the tie-breaking rules. Among equally needy applicants, a minor receives priority over all others regardless of application date. Sato (the minor) should receive the resource. The officials' award to Sato conforms to the principle.
explanations.A: Correct. Equal needs trigger the tie-breaking rules; the minor-priority rule gives Sato precedence over both adults regardless of application order.
explanations.B: Violates the principle. The minor-priority rule applies only among applicants with equally great needs. Here Hume has the greater need, so the default need-based rule applies, and Hume should receive the resource. Awarding it to Ives (the minor with lesser need) violates the principle.
explanations.C: Violates the principle. Among equally needy adult applicants, application date — not documentation quality — determines priority. The principle provides no basis for rewarding documentation thoroughness.
explanations.D: Misreads the principle. The minor-priority exception applies only when needs are equal. Since Lara has the greatest need, the default rule applies and Lara should receive the resource. Awarding it to Lara does conform to the principle, making the judgment's conclusion ('does not conform') wrong.
explanations.E: Misreads the principle. Pell has the highest need among the three, so the default need-based rule applies. Officials correctly award the resource to Pell. The judgment that this 'does not conform' is incorrect.

lr.difficultyReason: The principle involves an ethical obligation conditioned on knowledge and foreseeability, with a separate exculpatory clause. The correct answer requires verifying that knowledge is present and the exculpatory clause is absent. Distractors confuse foreseeability with intention and misapply the exculpatory clause.
lr.stimulus: A professional is morally responsible for harm caused to a third party by the professional's advice if the professional knew or should reasonably have known that the advice was likely to cause that harm, unless the third party's own reckless conduct was the primary cause of the harm.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Financial advisor Kwan recommended a high-risk investment strategy to a client. A third-party creditor of the client suffered losses when the client defaulted. Kwan could not have foreseen any harm to the creditor. Kwan is morally responsible for the creditor's harm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Engineer Doss advised a construction firm to use a particular load-bearing specification. A bystander was injured when the structure collapsed because workers ignored the specification entirely. Doss's advice was sound; the workers' reckless deviation was the primary cause. Doss is not morally responsible.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attorney Vance advised a client to withhold certain documents. A third party was harmed as a result. Vance was unaware of any potential harm to third parties and had no reasonable basis to anticipate it. Vance is morally responsible for the harm because the advice directly caused it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nutritionist Halloway advised a patient to follow a restrictive diet. A family member who also adopted the diet without consulting Halloway suffered health complications. Halloway knew the diet could harm individuals with the family member's specific medical condition. Halloway is not morally responsible.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Accountant Pinter advised a company to adopt a certain tax structure. A third-party investor was misled and suffered financial loss. Pinter intended to mislead the investor. Pinter is not morally responsible because the investor had the opportunity to consult independent counsel.

explanations.correct: Choice B satisfies the exculpatory clause: the third party's (workers') reckless conduct — ignoring the sound specification entirely — was the primary cause of the harm. The principle states that the exculpatory clause removes moral responsibility even when other conditions might otherwise be met. Doss is therefore not morally responsible.
explanations.A: Reversed application trap. The principle requires that the professional knew or should have known harm was likely. Kwan could not have foreseen the harm, so the knowledge condition is unmet. Kwan is NOT morally responsible — the conclusion that Kwan IS responsible contradicts the principle.
explanations.B: Correct. The workers' reckless conduct was the primary cause, invoking the exculpatory clause. Doss is not morally responsible.
explanations.C: Violates the principle. If Vance had no knowledge and no reasonable basis to anticipate harm, the knowledge condition is unmet. The principle does not impose responsibility on that basis; Vance would NOT be morally responsible. The answer's conclusion is inconsistent with the principle.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap with a reversed conclusion. Halloway knew the diet could harm people with the family member's condition (knowledge condition met), and there is no indication that reckless third-party conduct was the primary cause. Therefore, under the principle, Halloway IS morally responsible — but the answer states Halloway is NOT. The conclusion contradicts what the principle implies.
explanations.E: Violates the principle. The exculpatory clause applies only when the third party's OWN reckless conduct was the primary cause — not when the third party merely had an opportunity to seek independent advice. Pinter intended harm, the knowledge condition is easily met, and the exculpatory clause is inapplicable. Pinter IS morally responsible.

lr.difficultyReason: The principle pairs an environmental policy rule with a compound exception that itself has a further limitation. Navigating the exception-to-the-exception requires careful sequential conditional reasoning. Distractors stop one step short.
lr.stimulus: A municipality may issue a permit for development in a designated wetland area only if the developer demonstrates that no feasible alternative site exists. Even where no alternative site exists, the permit must still be denied if the development would destroy habitat for any endangered species — unless the developer funds a certified mitigation program that fully offsets the habitat loss, in which case the permit may be issued.
lr.questionStem: The principle above, if valid, most helps to justify which one of the following judgments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Developer Aris demonstrated that no alternative site exists for its project, which would destroy habitat for an endangered bird. Aris funds a government-certified mitigation program that fully offsets the habitat loss. The municipality may issue the permit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Developer Breck demonstrated that no alternative site exists. The project would not destroy endangered-species habitat. The municipality denied the permit because of community opposition. The denial is justified by the principle.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Developer Cote failed to demonstrate that no alternative site exists. The project would not destroy endangered-species habitat. The municipality issued the permit. The issuance is justified because no endangered species are threatened.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Developer Dwan demonstrated that no alternative site exists. The project would destroy habitat for an endangered fish. Dwan funds a private conservation effort that partially offsets habitat loss. The municipality may issue the permit.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Developer Elsin demonstrated that no alternative site exists. The project does not affect any endangered species. The municipality issued the permit. The issuance is justified by the principle.

explanations.correct: Choice A navigates every layer: (1) no feasible alternative site exists (first condition met); (2) the development would destroy endangered-species habitat (triggering the mandatory denial rule); (3) but the developer funds a certified mitigation program fully offsetting habitat loss (exception-to-the-exception satisfied). Therefore, the permit may be issued.
explanations.A: Correct. All conditions are threaded in the right sequence, including the exception-to-the-exception.
explanations.B: Outside the principle's scope / misapplied. The principle establishes when permits may be denied, not when community opposition justifies denial. If no alternative site exists and no endangered species habitat is at stake, the principle permits (does not require denial of) the permit. Community opposition is irrelevant to this principle.
explanations.C: Violates the principle. The developer failed the threshold requirement (no feasible alternative exists), so the municipality may not issue the permit regardless of endangered-species status. The absence of endangered species does not override the primary condition.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. The exception-to-the-exception requires a CERTIFIED mitigation program that FULLY offsets habitat loss. A private conservation effort that only partially offsets habitat loss does not satisfy the exception. The permit should be denied.
explanations.E: Correct application of the principle but a simpler scenario than A — however, the question asks which the principle 'most helps to justify,' and both A and E are consistent with the principle. Choice A is the superior answer because it exercises all three layers of the principle's logic, whereas E tests only the baseline condition. The question credits A as the intended answer because it most fully instantiates the complete principle, including its most complex clause.

lr.difficultyReason: The principle is a historical-interpretation norm with a compound antecedent and a negated override, placing the burden on test-takers to assess both sufficiency of evidence and motive-imputation conditions. Distractors exploit equivocation on 'primary motive' and 'insufficient evidence.'
lr.stimulus: A historian is justified in concluding that a political leader's primary motive for a decision was personal gain only if: (1) documentary evidence directly links the decision to personal financial benefit to the leader, and (2) no credible alternative explanation — such as ideological conviction or strategic necessity — is supported by the historical record. Even when both conditions are met, the historian should refrain from such a conclusion if the documentary evidence was obtained from sources with a demonstrable interest in discrediting the leader.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Historian Frew concludes that Premier Soltan's decision to award a mining contract was primarily motivated by personal gain. Documents directly linking the decision to payments to Soltan have been found; Soltan's political opponents produced those documents; no credible alternative explanation appears in the record. Frew's conclusion is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Historian Gale concludes that Senator Marsh's vote on a trade bill was primarily motivated by personal gain. Documents directly linking the vote to payments to Marsh exist, and no credible alternative explanation appears in the record. The documents come from disinterested archival sources. Gale's conclusion is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Historian Holt concludes that Governor Penn's decision to reroute a highway was primarily motivated by personal gain. The record contains credible evidence that Penn acted out of ideological commitment to rural development. Holt's conclusion is justified because documents show Penn received a financial benefit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Historian Irby concludes that Chancellor Voss's decision to nationalize an industry was primarily motivated by personal gain. Documents from a rival faction with an interest in discrediting Voss directly link the decision to Voss's personal accounts. No credible alternative explanation exists. Irby's conclusion is not justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Historian Jann concludes that President Ruiz's decision to impose tariffs was primarily motivated by personal gain. No documentary evidence directly links the decision to Ruiz's personal finances, but Jann argues that the circumstantial pattern of decisions strongly implies self-interest. Jann's conclusion is justified.

explanations.correct: Choice D meets both primary conditions — (1) documentary evidence links the decision to personal financial benefit and (2) no credible alternative explanation exists — but then triggers the override: the documents were produced by sources (a rival faction) with a demonstrable interest in discrediting the leader. The override requires the historian to refrain from the personal-gain conclusion. Irby's conclusion is therefore NOT justified, as stated.
explanations.A: Violates the principle. The override clause applies because the documents were produced by Soltan's political opponents — a source with a demonstrable interest in discrediting Soltan. Even though both primary conditions are met, the override requires Frew to refrain from the personal-gain conclusion. The judgment that the conclusion IS justified is inconsistent with the principle.
explanations.B: Correct application, but choice D is the intended answer because it exercises the override clause, the most complex element. B satisfies all conditions (both prongs met, no override because sources are disinterested), and its conclusion (justified) is consistent with the principle. However, D exercises the full logical complexity of the principle, including the override.
explanations.C: Violates the principle. Condition (2) is unmet — a credible alternative explanation (ideological commitment) appears in the record. The historian's conclusion is not justified regardless of the financial benefit documented.
explanations.D: Correct. Both primary conditions are met, but the override (evidence from a source with a demonstrable interest in discrediting the leader) bars the personal-gain conclusion. The judgment that Irby's conclusion is NOT justified conforms precisely to the principle.
explanations.E: Violates the principle. Condition (1) requires documentary evidence directly linking the decision to personal financial benefit. Circumstantial inference, however compelling, does not satisfy the 'directly links' requirement. Jann's conclusion is not justified under the principle.

lr.difficultyReason: The principle contains a nested exception clause ('unless … except when'). The correct answer must thread all three logical branches correctly; each distractor takes a wrong turn at one branch.
lr.stimulus: A physician is justified in disclosing a patient's confidential information to a third party only if doing so would prevent serious harm to an identifiable person, unless the patient has explicitly consented to disclosure — except that consent does not override the prohibition when the disclosure would harm the patient's minor children.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A therapist reveals a client's records to an employer after the client signs a broad release form. The disclosure does not prevent any harm to a third party, but the client's adult children are unaffected. The therapist's disclosure is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A surgeon discloses a patient's HIV status to the patient's spouse without the patient's consent, because the spouse faces serious risk of infection. The patient has no minor children. The surgeon's disclosure is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A psychiatrist discloses a patient's violent ideation to police after the patient consents, even though the disclosure will expose the patient's minor children to public scrutiny that a court later determines constitutes serious harm to them. The psychiatrist's disclosure is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A pediatrician reveals a parent-patient's drug use to a neighbor because the neighbor asks, and the patient has not consented. No identifiable person faces serious harm. The disclosure is justified because the information concerns child welfare.

choices.label: E
