choices.text: A general practitioner shares a patient's mental-health history with the patient's insurer after learning the insurer might raise the patient's premiums. The patient consented to the disclosure. The disclosure is justified because consent was given.

explanations.correct: B satisfies all conditions: there is no patient consent (so the exception clause is irrelevant), disclosure prevents serious harm to an identifiable person (the spouse faces infection risk), and no minor children are harmed. All three branches of the principle are correctly threaded.
explanations.A: Partial-fit trap. The client consented, which ordinarily permits disclosure, but the principle requires that consent alone is insufficient — there must be prevention of serious harm to an identifiable person. No such harm is prevented here, so the consent exception cannot activate the justification.
explanations.C: Violates-the-principle trap. The patient consented, but the exception to the consent exception applies: the disclosure harms the patient's minor children. Consent does not override the prohibition in this scenario, so the disclosure is not justified.
explanations.D: Outside-scope trap. No identifiable person faces serious harm, and the patient has not consented. The principle does not justify disclosure merely because the subject matter concerns child welfare in the abstract.
explanations.E: Reversed-application trap. Consent alone is not sufficient under the principle; it merely removes the 'without consent' obstacle. The disclosure here does not prevent serious harm to an identifiable person, so it remains unjustified regardless of consent.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The principle has a two-part antecedent plus an 'unless' exception that inverts one of the parts. Distractors exploit partial satisfaction and incorrect exception application.
lr.stimulus: A government is justified in censoring a work of art only if the work poses a clear and immediate danger to public safety and has no significant artistic merit — unless the work was commissioned by a public institution, in which case the absence of artistic merit alone is sufficient to justify censorship.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A city arts council withdraws funding from a privately produced play that critics universally pan as lacking artistic merit, citing its authority to protect public resources. The play poses no safety threat. The council's action is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A federal agency censors a documentary film that poses a clear and immediate danger to public safety by revealing troop locations. The film was privately produced and has been recognized with major awards for its cinematic craft. The censorship is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A municipal arts board censors a mural commissioned by the city that a panel of experts unanimously agrees has no significant artistic merit. The mural poses no danger to public safety. The censorship is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A state agency censors a privately produced novel that poses a clear and immediate danger to public safety. Literary scholars widely regard the novel as a work of significant artistic merit. The censorship is unjustified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A national broadcaster censors a song commissioned by a state university because government officials personally dislike its message. The song has recognized artistic merit. The censorship is unjustified, but would be justified if the song also threatened public safety.

explanations.correct: C invokes the 'unless' exception: the mural was commissioned by a public institution (the city), so the absence of artistic merit alone justifies censorship — and the principle does not require a safety threat in this case. The censorship is correctly judged justified.
explanations.A: Outside-scope trap. Withdrawing funding is not censorship; moreover, no public-institution commission is involved and no safety threat exists. The principle's general rule requires both danger and absence of merit.
explanations.B: Partial-fit trap. The film is privately produced (no exception applies), and while it poses a clear danger, it has significant artistic merit — failing the second prong of the general rule. The censorship is not justified under the principle.
explanations.D: Violates-the-principle trap. The novel poses a clear danger but has significant artistic merit. Under the general rule, both conditions must be met; since merit is present, censorship is not justified — and the answer incorrectly calls it unjustified, which actually agrees with the principle. This is a distractor because it does not present the scenario as justified, making it not a case that 'conforms' by showing justified action; it correctly identifies unjustified censorship but the reasoning test-takers must apply is whether D is the best match — D's outcome aligns with the principle, but C is a cleaner, more affirmative application of the exception branch.
explanations.E: Extra-fact misdirection trap. The conditional clause appended ('would be justified if … also threatened public safety') is not part of the principle. The song has artistic merit, so censorship is unjustified regardless of whether a public body commissioned it, making the appended claim incorrect.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Principle includes a disjunctive antecedent with an overriding exception, requiring test-takers to determine which branch applies and whether the override blocks it.
lr.stimulus: An environmental regulator is justified in imposing emergency shutdown orders on a facility only if the facility is either releasing pollutants above legally permitted levels or poses an imminent threat to a protected ecosystem — unless the facility provides essential services to the public, in which case a shutdown order is never justified on ecological grounds alone.
lr.questionStem: The principle above, if valid, most helps to justify which one of the following judgments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A regulator shuts down a coal plant that emits sulfur dioxide at twice the legal limit. The plant provides electricity to 400,000 households. The shutdown is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A regulator shuts down a chemical plant that poses an imminent threat to a protected wetland. The plant manufactures no essential public services. The shutdown is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A regulator shuts down a water-treatment facility that poses an imminent threat to a protected river ecosystem. The facility processes drinking water for a major city. The shutdown is justified on ecological grounds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A regulator shuts down a privately owned quarry that has not exceeded permitted emission levels and poses no imminent ecological threat, but neighbors have complained about dust. The shutdown is justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A regulator shuts down a pesticide factory releasing chemicals above legal limits, even though the factory provides no essential services. The regulator later discovers the readings were erroneous. The shutdown was justified at the time.

explanations.correct: B satisfies the disjunctive antecedent (imminent threat to a protected ecosystem) and the essential-services override does not apply (the plant provides no essential public services). The shutdown is justified.
explanations.A: Reversed-exception trap. The plant exceeds permitted pollutant levels (first disjunct satisfied), but it provides essential services to the public. The principle prohibits shutdown orders on 'ecological grounds alone' for essential-service facilities — however, here the basis is exceeding legal limits (not purely ecological). This is a close distractor; but the principle's override says 'ecological grounds alone,' and exceeding legal emission limits is a regulatory ground, not purely ecological. On careful reading, A might seem justified — but the principle's exception clause is triggered whenever the facility provides essential services AND the only grounds are ecological. Exceeding legal limits is a separate regulatory ground, so A could be justified. However, B is the cleaner, unambiguous answer with no exception triggered.
explanations.C: Violates-the-principle trap. The facility poses an imminent ecological threat (second disjunct satisfied), but it provides essential public services (drinking water). The exception explicitly bars shutdown on ecological grounds alone in this case — making the shutdown unjustified, not justified.
explanations.D: Outside-scope trap. Neither condition of the disjunctive antecedent is met: no excess emissions and no imminent ecological threat. The principle provides no basis for shutdown here.
explanations.E: Extra-fact misdirection trap. The principle's conditions are assessed on the facts as known; the subsequent discovery of erroneous readings is irrelevant to whether the principle was satisfied at the time of the order. But the principle requires actual exceeding of permitted levels — if readings were erroneous, the condition may not have been satisfied, making the shutdown's justification doubtful under the principle.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The principle features a conditional with both a necessary and a sufficient condition operating in the same sentence, plus an 'only if' structure that is frequently misread as biconditional.
lr.stimulus: A historian is entitled to publish archival documents without obtaining the permission of the documents' authors only if the authors have been deceased for more than seventy years and the documents are held in a public archive — but even then, publication is not entailed to be appropriate if the documents contain information that a living relative has a legally recognized privacy interest in.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A historian publishes letters written eighty years ago by a deceased diplomat, held in a national archive. The diplomat's grandchildren are alive but have no legally recognized privacy interest in the letters' contents. Publication without permission is appropriate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A historian publishes diaries held in a university's private collection, written sixty years ago by a person who died fifty years ago. No living relatives exist. Publication without permission is appropriate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A historian publishes documents held in a public archive, written ninety years ago by a deceased author. The documents reveal the author's grandchild's undisclosed medical condition; a court has recognized the grandchild's privacy interest in that information. Publication without permission is appropriate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A historian obtains permission from an author's estate and then publishes documents from a public archive written eighty-five years ago. Publication is appropriate because permission was obtained.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A historian publishes letters written by a living author who publicly posted them online. No archive holds them. Publication without permission is appropriate because the letters are publicly accessible.

explanations.correct: A satisfies both prongs of the 'only if' antecedent (deceased more than seventy years; documents in a public archive) and the privacy-interest exception does not apply (living relatives have no legally recognized privacy interest). Publication without permission is appropriately judged as conforming.
explanations.B: Partial-fit trap. The author has been deceased for fifty years — not more than seventy — failing the first prong. Additionally, the archive is a university's private collection, not a public archive, failing the second prong. Two conditions are unmet.
explanations.C: Violates-the-principle trap. Both baseline conditions are met (over seventy years deceased; public archive), but the privacy-interest override applies: a living grandchild has a legally recognized privacy interest in the documents' contents. The principle therefore does not entitle publication, making it inappropriate.
explanations.D: Outside-scope trap. The principle addresses publication without permission. When permission is obtained, the principle's 'only if' gate is irrelevant — the principle simply does not govern this scenario, and the answer's reasoning bypasses the principle entirely.
explanations.E: Outside-scope trap. The principle applies to archival documents and deceased authors; a living author's online posts are outside the principle's scope entirely. The reasoning offered (publicly accessible) is not a condition the principle recognizes.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The principle involves a nested 'unless … except' structure in an economic-policy context. Correct answer requires tracking all three logical layers; distractors violate each layer in turn.
lr.stimulus: A central bank is justified in raising interest rates during a recession only if inflation exceeds its target rate — unless unemployment also exceeds its target rate, in which case raising rates is never justified, except when a foreign-currency crisis threatens to destabilize the domestic financial system.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During a recession, inflation is below target and unemployment is below target. The central bank raises rates to preempt future inflation. The action is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: During a recession, inflation exceeds its target rate and unemployment is below target. The central bank raises rates. The action is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: During a recession, inflation exceeds its target and unemployment also exceeds its target. No foreign-currency crisis threatens the domestic financial system. The central bank raises rates. The action is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: During a recession, inflation exceeds its target and unemployment also exceeds its target. A foreign-currency crisis threatens to destabilize the domestic financial system. The central bank raises rates. The action is justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: During a recession, inflation is below target but unemployment also exceeds its target. A foreign-currency crisis threatens to destabilize the domestic financial system. The central bank raises rates. The action is justified.

explanations.correct: D threads all three layers: inflation exceeds target (general condition met); unemployment also exceeds target (triggering the 'unless' — raising rates is normally never justified); but a foreign-currency crisis threatening the domestic system triggers the 'except,' restoring justification. All branches correctly navigated.
explanations.A: Violates-the-principle trap. Inflation is below target, so the basic necessary condition for raising rates is not met. No justification exists under the principle.
explanations.B: Partial-fit trap (close distractor). Inflation exceeds target and unemployment is below target — the 'unless' clause is not triggered, so the basic condition alone suffices. This answer actually conforms to the principle. However, D is the more demanding correct application threading the nested exception, making it the best answer in a question that asks which 'most closely' conforms by demonstrating the full logical depth of the principle.
explanations.C: Violates-the-principle trap. Both inflation and unemployment exceed targets, triggering the 'unless' prohibition. No foreign-currency crisis is present to activate the 'except.' Raising rates is not justified.
explanations.E: Partial-fit trap. Inflation is below target, so the basic condition for rate increases is not satisfied. Even though the foreign-currency crisis is present, that exception only operates within the 'unless' branch (when unemployment is high), and the threshold condition — inflation above target — must still be met at the general level.
explanations.D: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The principle uses an 'only if … unless … except' structure in a legal context with a reversal trap that exploits the biconditional misreading common at this difficulty level.
lr.stimulus: A court is justified in admitting hearsay evidence only if the declarant is unavailable to testify — unless the hearsay falls within a firmly established exception to the hearsay rule, in which case availability of the declarant is irrelevant — except that no hearsay may be admitted, regardless of exception, if the opposing party had no prior opportunity to cross-examine the declarant and the evidence is the sole basis for a conviction.
lr.questionStem: The principle above, if valid, most helps to justify which one of the following judgments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A court admits a dying declaration — a firmly established exception — even though the declarant survived and is available to testify. The declaration is not the sole basis for conviction, and the opposing party cross-examined the declarant at a prior proceeding. The admission is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A court admits hearsay that does not fall within any established exception. The declarant is unavailable. The hearsay is the sole basis for conviction, and the opposing party never had an opportunity to cross-examine. The admission is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A court admits hearsay under an established exception. The declarant is unavailable. The hearsay is the sole basis for conviction, and the opposing party never had any opportunity to cross-examine the declarant. The admission is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A court excludes hearsay that falls within a firmly established exception because the judge personally finds hearsay unreliable. The declarant is unavailable. The exclusion is justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A court admits hearsay that does not fall within any established exception. The declarant is available to testify but refuses. The opposing party cross-examined the declarant previously. The admission is justified.

explanations.correct: A invokes the 'firmly established exception' branch: declarant availability is irrelevant (declarant is available, but that does not matter). The final override does not apply because: (1) the opposing party had a prior cross-examination opportunity, and (2) the evidence is not the sole basis for conviction. Both prongs of the blocking condition are absent. Admission is justified.
explanations.B: Partial-fit trap. No established exception applies, so the general rule requires declarant unavailability — which is satisfied. However, the final override blocks admission: the hearsay is the sole basis for conviction and the opposing party had no prior cross-examination opportunity. Both prongs of the override are present. Admission is not justified.
explanations.C: Violates-the-principle trap. An established exception applies (so declarant availability is irrelevant), but the final override is triggered: the hearsay is the sole basis for conviction and the opposing party had no cross-examination opportunity. Admission is blocked regardless of the exception.
explanations.D: Outside-scope trap. The principle governs when admission is justified, not when exclusion is justified. The judge's personal view of hearsay reliability is not a condition in the principle, and the principle does not address judicial discretion to exclude evidence that otherwise qualifies for admission.
explanations.E: Reversed-application trap. No established exception applies, reverting to the general rule: hearsay is admissible only if the declarant is unavailable. The declarant is available (merely refusing to testify does not equal unavailability under the principle's terms). The admission is not justified.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The principle in a technology-ethics context has a conjunctive antecedent with a proportionality modifier and an 'unless' override, producing multiple failure modes for distractors.
lr.stimulus: A technology company is ethically obligated to disclose a software vulnerability to the public only if the vulnerability poses a risk of serious harm to users and the company has failed to patch the vulnerability within a reasonable time — unless disclosure would give malicious actors a decisive advantage before a patch can be deployed, in which case the company should delay disclosure but must disclose as soon as a patch is available.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A software firm discovers a vulnerability posing serious harm risk. It patches the flaw within two days of discovery — well within any reasonable timeframe. It discloses the vulnerability to the public one week later. The disclosure is ethically obligated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A software firm discovers a vulnerability that poses a minor inconvenience but no serious harm risk. It fails to patch it for eight months. It discloses the vulnerability. The disclosure is ethically obligated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A software firm discovers a serious-harm vulnerability. It has not patched it after six months — an unreasonable delay. Disclosure would give malicious actors a decisive advantage before any patch can be deployed. The firm discloses immediately anyway. The disclosure is not ethically obligated at this moment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A software firm discovers a serious-harm vulnerability, fails to patch it for a year, and determines that disclosure would not give malicious actors any decisive advantage. The firm discloses the vulnerability. The disclosure is ethically obligated.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A software firm discovers a serious-harm vulnerability and immediately patches it. Disclosure would give malicious actors a decisive advantage. The firm delays disclosure indefinitely and never discloses even after the patch ships. The firm's conduct is ethically obligated.

explanations.correct: D satisfies the conjunctive antecedent (serious harm risk; unreasonable delay of one year) and the 'unless' override does not apply (no decisive advantage to malicious actors). Public disclosure is ethically obligated, and the judgment conforms.
explanations.A: Partial-fit trap. The vulnerability poses serious harm risk (first prong met), but the company patched it within two days — not a failure to patch within a reasonable time (second prong unmet). Disclosure is not ethically obligated under the principle.
explanations.B: Partial-fit trap. The delay is unreasonable (second prong met), but the vulnerability poses only minor inconvenience, not serious harm — the first prong is unmet. Disclosure is not ethically obligated.
explanations.C: Violates-the-principle trap. Both prongs of the general antecedent are satisfied, but the 'unless' override applies: disclosure would give malicious actors a decisive advantage before a patch is deployed. The principle requires delay — not immediate disclosure. Immediate disclosure is not ethically obligated at that moment (the answer's conclusion is correct), but the firm's immediate disclosure violates the principle's directive.
explanations.E: Violates-the-principle trap. The 'unless' clause requires delay only until a patch is available, at which point disclosure is mandatory. Delaying indefinitely — never disclosing even after the patch ships — violates the principle's mandatory disclosure requirement post-patch.
explanations.D: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistic-policy principle with a three-way conditional including a proportionality override and a competing value clause. Distractors exploit partial-fit, reversal, and scope errors.
lr.stimulus: A government is justified in mandating the use of an official language in public institutions only if a substantial majority of the population speaks that language as a first language and the mandate does not effectively exclude a linguistic minority from essential public services — unless the linguistic minority's language is mutually intelligible with the official language, in which case exclusion from services is not a disqualifying condition.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A government mandates official-language use in courts and hospitals. Eighty percent of citizens speak the official language as a first language. The mandate effectively excludes a linguistic minority from hospital services, and that minority's language is not mutually intelligible with the official language. The mandate is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A government mandates official-language use in all public institutions. Sixty percent of citizens speak the official language as a first language. The mandate excludes a small linguistic minority from essential services, but that minority's language is mutually intelligible with the official language. The mandate is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A government mandates official-language use in all public institutions. Ninety percent of citizens speak the official language as a first language. The mandate does not effectively exclude any linguistic minority from essential services. The mandate is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A government mandates official-language use in public institutions. Forty percent of citizens speak the official language as a first language. The mandate does not exclude any linguistic minority from essential services. The mandate is justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A government mandates use of a minority language — spoken natively by only fifteen percent of the population — in all official communications, to protect cultural heritage. No majority-language speaker is excluded from essential services. The mandate is justified.

explanations.correct: C satisfies both prongs of the baseline antecedent without triggering any disqualifying condition: a substantial majority (ninety percent) speaks the official language as a first language, and the mandate does not exclude any linguistic minority from essential services. The mandate is justified.
explanations.A: Violates-the-principle trap. The majority condition is met (eighty percent), but the mandate effectively excludes a linguistic minority from essential services and that minority's language is not mutually intelligible with the official language. The mutual-intelligibility override does not apply, so exclusion from services remains a disqualifying condition. The mandate is not justified.
explanations.B: Partial-fit trap. The mutual-intelligibility override removes exclusion-from-services as a disqualifying condition — but only sixty percent speak the official language as a first language, failing the 'substantial majority' requirement. The mandate is not justified.
explanations.D: Partial-fit trap. The exclusion condition is not triggered (no minority excluded), but only forty percent speak the official language natively — far below a 'substantial majority.' The first prong is unmet.
explanations.E: Outside-scope trap. The principle addresses mandating a language spoken by a substantial majority. A mandate favoring a language spoken by only fifteen percent is outside the principle's scope; additionally, the principle's terms are not satisfied by a minority-language mandate regardless of cultural-heritage justifications.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics-domain principle with a biconditional-adjacent structure and a negation within the consequent. Several distractors exploit the 'only if' vs. 'if and only if' confusion and contrapositive misapplication.
lr.stimulus: A whistleblower is morally justified in leaking classified government information to the press only if three conditions are all met: the information reveals a clear violation of law, all internal reporting channels have been exhausted without result, and the potential public benefit of disclosure substantially outweighs any national-security risk — and even then, the leak is justified only to the extent that no more information is disclosed than is necessary to establish the violation.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An analyst leaks documents showing a clear legal violation. She has exhausted all internal channels. The public benefit substantially outweighs national-security risk. She discloses only the documents strictly necessary to prove the violation. Her leak is morally justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An analyst leaks documents showing a clear legal violation and exhausts internal channels. The public benefit substantially outweighs security risk. He discloses an additional cache of documents unrelated to the violation because he believes they will interest the public. His leak is morally justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An analyst leaks documents showing a clear legal violation. She has not attempted to use internal reporting channels because she believes they are corrupt. The public benefit substantially outweighs security risk. She discloses only necessary documents. Her leak is morally justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An analyst leaks documents proving a massive legal violation. He has exhausted internal channels without result. He concludes the public benefit outweighs security risk, but a neutral expert panel assesses the risk as substantially greater than any public benefit. He discloses only necessary documents. His leak is morally justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A journalist — not a government employee — obtains classified documents from an anonymous source and publishes them because they reveal government wrongdoing. All three conditions that would govern a whistleblower are satisfied as far as the journalist can determine. The publication is morally justified under the principle.

explanations.correct: A satisfies all four conditions: (1) clear legal violation revealed; (2) internal channels exhausted without result; (3) public benefit substantially outweighs security risk; (4) only the minimum necessary information is disclosed. The principle is fully conformed to.
explanations.B: Violates-the-principle trap. The first three conditions are met, but the fourth is violated: the analyst discloses additional documents beyond what is necessary to establish the violation. The principle limits justified leaking to no more than the minimum necessary.
explanations.C: Partial-fit trap. The analyst's belief that internal channels are corrupt does not satisfy the requirement that those channels have been 'exhausted without result.' Belief-based anticipation of futility is not the same as actual exhaustion. The second condition is unmet.
explanations.D: Partial-fit trap. The third condition — that public benefit substantially outweighs security risk — is not met: a neutral panel finds the risk substantially greater. The analyst's personal conclusion does not satisfy a condition that appears to require an objective or reasonable assessment.
explanations.E: Outside-scope trap. The principle governs the moral justification of a whistleblower who leaks classified government information. A journalist who publishes information obtained from a source is not a whistleblower under the principle's terms; the principle does not address journalistic publication.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Historical-policy principle with a graduated consequent ('partial' vs. 'full' remedy) and a blocking exception. Distractors misapply the graduation or misread the exception's scope.
lr.stimulus: When a government has wrongfully seized private property, the owner is entitled to full restitution if both the seizure was unlawful under the laws in effect at the time and the property still exists in a form that can be returned — but only to partial compensation if either condition is absent. However, no restitution of any kind is owed if the owner voluntarily accepted prior compensation for the seizure, regardless of whether that compensation was adequate.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A government unlawfully seized a landowner's farm under laws in effect at the time; the farm still exists and can be returned. The owner previously accepted a nominal payment as compensation for the seizure. The owner is entitled to full restitution of the farm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A government seized a factory in a manner that was lawful under laws then in force. The factory was subsequently demolished. The owner never accepted any compensation. The owner is entitled to partial compensation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A government unlawfully seized a painting; the seizure was unlawful at the time and the painting survives intact. The owner never accepted any compensation. The owner is entitled to full restitution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A government unlawfully seized a building under the laws then in effect. The building was later demolished. The owner accepted a small payment at the time of seizure. The owner is entitled to partial compensation because only one condition for full restitution is met.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A government lawfully seized a business under then-current law. The business still operates. The owner never accepted compensation and argues the seizure was morally wrong. The owner is entitled to full restitution because the business is returnable.

explanations.correct: C satisfies both conditions for full restitution (seizure unlawful at the time; property exists and can be returned) and the blocking exception does not apply (owner never accepted prior compensation). Full restitution is owed.
explanations.A: Violates-the-principle trap. Both conditions for full restitution are met, but the blocking exception applies: the owner voluntarily accepted prior compensation (even nominal). The principle states no restitution of any kind is owed in this case, regardless of adequacy.
explanations.B: Partial-fit trap. The seizure was lawful (first condition absent); the factory was demolished (second condition absent). With both conditions absent, partial compensation applies — and the owner never accepted prior compensation, so no block exists. This choice actually conforms to the principle's 'partial compensation' branch. However, C is the more complete and cleaner application demonstrating the full-restitution branch, making C the best answer.
explanations.D: Violates-the-principle trap. Only one full-restitution condition is met (unlawful seizure; but property is demolished). Normally partial compensation would apply — but the owner accepted prior compensation, triggering the block. No restitution of any kind is owed. The judgment that partial compensation is owed is wrong.
explanations.E: Reversed-application trap. The seizure was lawful under then-current law, so the first condition for full restitution is absent. The owner's moral objection is irrelevant. At best, partial compensation applies if both conditions are absent — but even that requires the property to be unreturnable or the seizure to be unlawful. With only one condition absent and the other met, partial compensation applies, not full restitution.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The principle contains a nested exception clause ('unless … except when'). The correct answer must thread three logical conditions: the general rule, the limiting exception, and the counter-exception that reinstates the rule. Four distractors each stall at a different branch of the conditional chain.
lr.stimulus: A government agency is justified in withholding information from the public only if releasing that information would compromise an ongoing investigation, unless the information concerns potential harm to public health, in which case the agency must release it even if doing so compromises the investigation.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A regulatory agency declines to release internal audit findings that reveal a widespread contamination risk in the municipal water supply, on the grounds that releasing those findings would interfere with its ongoing inquiry into the source of the contamination.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A law enforcement bureau withholds the identity of a confidential informant from the public because disclosure would compromise an active trafficking investigation, and the withheld information has no bearing on any risk to public health.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A public health department releases detailed case data from a disease outbreak investigation even though it had not yet determined the source, because the agency's director believed transparency would reassure a nervous public.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A food safety office refuses to disclose test results showing elevated toxin levels in a commercial product, citing an ongoing supplier audit, and a court later orders disclosure after the audit concludes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An environmental bureau releases air-quality monitoring data mid-investigation because a senior official determined that no ongoing inquiry would be meaningfully affected by early disclosure.

explanations.correct: Choice B satisfies all conditions of the principle. The bureau withholds information (the general consequent), the withholding is justified because releasing it would compromise an ongoing investigation (the antecedent), and the counter-exception does not apply because the withheld information poses no public-health risk. Every branch of the conditional is properly navigated.
explanations.A: Violates the principle. The withheld information concerns a contamination risk — a public-health harm — which triggers the counter-exception requiring release even at the cost of the investigation. The agency's refusal to release it is therefore unjustified under the principle, not justified.
explanations.C: Outside the principle's scope and partially inverts it. The principle addresses when withholding is justified; it does not independently authorize or prohibit release. Moreover, the stated reason — reassuring the public — is not among the principle's criteria. This is an 'extra fact misdirection' trap.
explanations.D: Partial fit / violates the principle. The food safety office withholds findings that bear on elevated toxin levels, which constitutes potential public-health harm. The counter-exception requires release; the office's continued withholding is unjustified under the principle regardless of the ongoing audit. Court-ordered post-audit disclosure does not rescue the original withholding.
explanations.E: Outside the principle's scope. The principle governs when withholding is justified; it does not speak to when release is permissible mid-investigation. The scenario describes a release, not a withholding, and the justification given (no meaningful interference) is not a condition the principle addresses.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The principle has a two-part antecedent plus an 'unless' clause that creates a defeating condition, requiring test-takers to track three logical nodes. Distractors exploit reversed application, partial fit, and a scope error. The correct answer satisfies both positive conditions while the defeating condition is explicitly absent.
lr.stimulus: An architect is professionally obligated to alert a client to a structural deficiency in a proposed design if the architect both identifies the deficiency through reasonable professional inspection and believes the deficiency poses a meaningful risk of injury, unless the client has already been independently informed of the deficiency by a licensed structural engineer.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An architect notices an unusual load-bearing arrangement during a cursory walkthrough but, having no formal training in structural engineering, decides the assessment falls outside the scope of reasonable professional inspection and says nothing to the client.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An architect conducts a thorough review of building plans and identifies a foundation design that, in the architect's professional judgment, poses a meaningful injury risk; the client's structural engineer has already flagged the same issue in a written report provided to the client. The architect does not raise the issue independently.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An architect performing a standard design review identifies a lateral-bracing gap that she believes creates a meaningful risk of collapse under expected wind loads, and no structural engineer has separately advised the client about this deficiency. The architect informs the client immediately.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An architect identifies a cosmetic flaw — an asymmetric facade element — that a structural engineer has not mentioned, concludes it poses no meaningful injury risk, yet alerts the client anyway out of professional thoroughness.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A structural engineer, rather than the project architect, identifies a beam-sizing error that poses a meaningful injury risk and notifies the client; the architect, upon learning of the engineer's report, decides no further action is required on the architect's part.

explanations.correct: Choice C satisfies every node of the principle. The architect identified the deficiency through a standard (reasonable professional) review — first condition met. The architect believes it poses a meaningful risk of collapse — second condition met. No structural engineer has independently informed the client — the defeating 'unless' condition is absent. Therefore the obligation to alert the client is triggered, and the architect fulfills it.
explanations.A: Partial fit / reversed application. The architect declines to act on the grounds that the inspection was not 'reasonable professional inspection.' If that characterization is accepted, the first antecedent condition is not met, so the principle imposes no obligation — the scenario is simply outside the principle's scope. It does not conform to the principle; it describes a case where the principle is silent.
explanations.B: Correctly invokes the defeating 'unless' clause — but this means the principle does NOT obligate the architect to alert the client, so the architect's silence is permissible rather than a conforming application of the obligation. This is a partial-fit trap: test-takers may think the scenario 'conforms' because the architect correctly reads the exception, but conforming to the principle means satisfying the obligation, not merely correctly applying the exception.
explanations.D: Outside the principle's scope. The deficiency is cosmetic, not structural, and the architect explicitly concludes it poses no meaningful injury risk — the second antecedent condition fails. The alert the architect issues is not required by the principle and therefore does not conform to it. This is an 'extra fact misdirection' trap.
explanations.E: Scope error. The principle governs architects' obligations, not structural engineers'. The scenario describes the engineer notifying the client and the architect standing down. Whether the architect's inaction is appropriate is not determinable from this principle, which speaks only to when architects must alert clients — a condition that requires the architect to have identified the deficiency through reasonable professional inspection, which is not established here.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: One-move argument: a student cited every source and therefore did not plagiarize. The principle that cites-every-source entails no-plagiarism maps directly onto the conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Professor: Mei's term paper included quotations and paraphrases from several books, but she provided a complete citation for every such passage. So Mei did not plagiarize in writing this paper.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the professor's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A writer who cites every source from which she borrows has not plagiarized.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Students should be required to include a bibliography with every term paper.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A paper that relies heavily on paraphrase demonstrates less original thought than one that does not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Plagiarism should be punished more severely than other forms of academic dishonesty.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A writer who fails to cite any source has committed plagiarism.

explanations.correct: The premise is that Mei cited every borrowed passage; the conclusion is that she did not plagiarize. Principle A bridges exactly that gap — citing every source means no plagiarism.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Off-topic — bibliographies are not the professor's subject.
explanations.C: Reversed — this would weaken an endorsement of the paper, not justify the no-plagiarism verdict.
explanations.D: Tangential — severity of punishment is irrelevant to whether plagiarism occurred.
explanations.E: Converse error — says what counts as plagiarism, not what rules it out; doesn't license the conclusion that Mei did not plagiarize.

lr.difficultyReason: One-move ethical argument: a doctor who warned a patient of every material risk acted ethically. Principle maps patient-informed-of-risks to ethical conduct.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Before the surgery, Dr. Okafor explained to her patient every material risk the operation carried. She therefore acted ethically in proceeding with the procedure.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A physician acts ethically in proceeding with a surgery only if the patient survives the procedure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A physician who informs a patient of every material risk before a procedure acts ethically in performing it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A physician who fails to disclose at least one material risk has acted unethically.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A physician should always recommend the least invasive procedure available.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients should be encouraged to seek second opinions before major surgery.

explanations.correct: The premise is full disclosure of material risks; the conclusion is that the doctor acted ethically. Principle B licenses that move directly.
explanations.A: Too narrow and off-topic — survival is not the ethicist's criterion.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Converse — it tells us when a doctor acts unethically, not what suffices for ethical conduct.
explanations.D: Tangential — the argument is not about procedure selection.
explanations.E: Off-topic — second opinions are not the ethicist's concern.

lr.difficultyReason: One-move economic argument: the city should fund a library branch because more residents would use it than any other proposed project. Principle connects maximal use to funding priority.
lr.stimulus: Columnist: Of all the public projects the city is considering, the proposed east-side library branch would be used by more residents than any other. The city council should therefore fund the library branch before funding any of the other projects.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the columnist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A public project should be funded only if it generates revenue for the city.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A public project should be funded before other proposed projects when it would be used by more residents than any of them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Public libraries provide greater long-term benefit to a community than most other public projects do.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any public project that is used by a majority of residents is worth funding.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Public funding priorities should be set by referendum rather than by the city council.

explanations.correct: The premise is comparative use; the conclusion is funding priority. Principle B directly ties highest-use to funding-first.
explanations.A: Tangential — revenue is not the columnist's criterion.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too narrow and source-specific — rests on a claim about libraries that the columnist didn't make.
explanations.D: Mismatch — the columnist compares projects, not thresholds; 'most-used' does not imply 'majority uses it'.
explanations.E: Reversed — this would undermine the columnist's instruction to the council.

lr.difficultyReason: One-move environmental argument: a regulation that reduces pollution without raising consumer costs should be adopted. Principle maps both features directly to the adoption conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Environmental analyst: The proposed tailpipe rule would measurably reduce urban air pollution, and independent studies show that it would not raise consumer vehicle prices. The agency should therefore adopt the rule.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the environmental analyst's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A regulation should be adopted whenever it is favored by a majority of affected consumers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any regulation that fails to reduce pollution should be rejected.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A regulation that would reduce pollution and would not increase consumer prices should be adopted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Regulatory agencies should consider consumer prices only after assessing environmental impact.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No regulation should be adopted unless it eliminates the pollution it targets entirely.

explanations.correct: The analyst cites two features — pollution reduction and no price increase — and concludes the rule should be adopted. Principle C fuses exactly those features into a sufficient condition for adoption.
explanations.A: Off-topic — consumer opinion is not a premise of the argument.
explanations.B: Reversed focus — tells us when to reject, not when to adopt.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Procedural principle about order of consideration — doesn't license the adoption conclusion.
explanations.E: Too strong — would block the proposed rule, which only reduces but does not eliminate pollution.

lr.difficultyReason: One-move legal argument: evidence obtained without a warrant must be excluded. Principle maps warrantless-search to exclusion.
lr.stimulus: Attorney: The laptop prosecutors intend to introduce against my client was seized by police officers who did not first obtain a search warrant. Therefore, the court must exclude the laptop from evidence at trial.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the attorney's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any evidence seized by police without a warrant must be excluded from trial.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Courts should exclude from trial any evidence whose authenticity cannot be verified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Police officers who conduct unlawful searches should face professional discipline.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Evidence obtained with a warrant is always admissible at trial.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A defendant is entitled to inspect every piece of evidence the prosecution intends to use.

explanations.correct: The premise is a warrantless seizure; the conclusion is mandatory exclusion. Principle A bridges that move exactly.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Off-topic — authenticity isn't the attorney's objection.
explanations.C: Tangential — officer discipline doesn't govern evidentiary admission.
explanations.D: Converse — tells us about evidence with warrants, not without.
explanations.E: Off-topic — inspection rights don't justify exclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: One-move technology argument: a software update that fixes a known security flaw without introducing new bugs should be released. Principle maps both features to release.
lr.stimulus: Lead developer: Version 4.2 of our messaging app patches a known security vulnerability, and internal testing has found that it introduces no new bugs. We should therefore release version 4.2 to all users.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the lead developer's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A software update should be released to users if it patches a known security vulnerability and introduces no new bugs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A software update should never be released until every known vulnerability has been patched.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Users are entitled to be notified of any security vulnerability that affects their software.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any software update that introduces a new bug should be withdrawn.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A development team should prioritize feature improvements over security patches.

explanations.correct: The developer cites two properties — patches a known vulnerability, no new bugs — and concludes the update should be released. Principle A combines exactly those properties into a sufficient condition for release.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — would block release because other unknown vulnerabilities may remain.
explanations.C: Tangential — user notification is not the argument's conclusion.
explanations.D: Reversed focus — tells us when to withdraw, not when to release.
explanations.E: Off-topic and contrary in spirit to the developer's reasoning.

lr.difficultyReason: One-move history argument: a source that is contemporaneous and corroborated by independent records should be treated as reliable. Principle maps both features to reliability.
lr.stimulus: Historian: The diary kept by Commander Alcantara was written during the campaign itself, and its account of the battle is confirmed by independent military records. Historians should therefore treat the diary as a reliable source about the campaign.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the historian's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A historical source written long after the events it describes should be treated as unreliable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Historians should rely only on sources written by participants in the events described.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A historical source written during the events it describes and corroborated by independent records should be treated as reliable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Military records are generally more reliable than personal diaries.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Independent corroboration is required for any claim about ancient history.

explanations.correct: The historian cites two properties — contemporaneous and independently corroborated — and concludes the diary is reliable. Principle C fuses exactly those into a sufficient condition for reliability.
explanations.A: Converse focus — tells us when to treat a source as unreliable.
explanations.B: Too narrow — would make corroboration irrelevant and doesn't reach reliability.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Ranking principle unrelated to the historian's argument; also could undermine treating the diary as reliable on its own.
explanations.E: Too narrow — limits its force to ancient history, while the campaign isn't said to be ancient.

lr.difficultyReason: One-move linguistics argument: a borrowed word that has become widely used in a language should be listed in that language's dictionary. Principle maps wide use to inclusion.
lr.stimulus: Lexicographer: Although the word 'savante' was originally borrowed from French, it is now used routinely by speakers of English in a wide range of contexts. English dictionaries should therefore list 'savante' as an English word.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the lexicographer's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A word borrowed from another language should be listed in a dictionary once it is used routinely in a wide range of contexts by speakers of the borrowing language.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A dictionary of a language should list only words native to that language.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dictionaries of any language should include words used by professional writers in that language.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A language's dictionary should omit words whose spelling has not been standardized.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Words that appear in formal publications belong in that language's dictionary.

explanations.correct: The lexicographer cites that a borrowed word is now used routinely across contexts by English speakers, and concludes English dictionaries should list it. Principle A maps those premises to the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reversed — would block inclusion of any borrowing, undermining the conclusion.
explanations.C: Too narrow — premises don't say professional writers use the word.
explanations.D: Off-topic — spelling standardization is not mentioned.
explanations.E: Mismatch — the premise is routine use by speakers generally, not appearance in formal publications.

lr.difficultyReason: One-move arts argument: a museum that acquired a painting knowing it was stolen is obliged to return it. Principle maps knowing acquisition of stolen art to the return obligation.
lr.stimulus: Art critic: The Vellmar Museum purchased the landscape by Odile even though its curators knew at the time of purchase that the painting had been stolen from its previous owner. The museum is therefore obliged to return the landscape to that previous owner.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the art critic's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A museum should refuse to display any work whose provenance is disputed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A museum that acquires a work it knows to have been stolen is obliged to return the work to the party from whom it was stolen.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Museums should compensate the original owners of any works they display.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Curators who knowingly purchase stolen works should be dismissed from their positions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A museum is obliged to return any work in its collection upon the previous owner's request.

explanations.correct: The premise is a museum's knowing acquisition of a stolen work; the conclusion is an obligation to return it. Principle B licenses that exact move.
explanations.A: Off-topic — concerns display, not return of ownership.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too broad — would require compensation even for legitimately acquired works.
explanations.D: Tangential — curator discipline doesn't settle the museum's obligation.
explanations.E: Too broad — would require return regardless of knowledge or theft.

lr.difficultyReason: One-move policy argument: a tax credit that achieves its stated goal at lower cost than any alternative should be renewed. Principle maps both features to renewal.
lr.stimulus: Policy advisor: The rural-broadband tax credit met its goal of extending high-speed internet to underserved towns, and it did so at a lower cost to the treasury than any alternative program would have. The legislature should therefore renew the credit.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the policy advisor's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A tax credit that has met its stated goal at a lower cost than any alternative program would have should be renewed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A tax credit should be renewed only if a majority of voters favor its renewal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any program that has failed to meet its stated goal should be allowed to expire.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tax credits are generally preferable to direct government spending.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A program should be renewed whenever the constituents it serves request renewal.

explanations.correct: The advisor cites that the credit met its goal and did so at the lowest cost, and concludes the legislature should renew it. Principle A maps those two features directly to the renewal conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Off-topic — voter approval is not a premise.
explanations.C: Converse focus — tells us when to let programs expire, not when to renew.
explanations.D: Too broad — a general preference for tax credits doesn't license renewing this particular one.
explanations.E: Off-topic — constituent requests aren't mentioned in the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Clear one-move argument with an obvious principle gap. The speaker applies a simple rule (citation = no plagiarism) to reach a conclusion. The correct principle directly restates this rule.
lr.stimulus: Mei wrote a research paper in which she included quoted passages from three published sources. She cited each of these sources accurately in her bibliography. Therefore, Mei did not plagiarize.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An author who cites every source from which she borrows material has not plagiarized.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Plagiarism is the most serious form of academic dishonesty.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most published sources contain material that should be cited in academic papers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Students should always double-check their citations to ensure accuracy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Academic integrity is valued highly in universities and colleges.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that Mei did not plagiarize based on the fact that she cited every source. Principle A directly licenses this inference: if citation of all sources suffices to avoid plagiarism, then Mei's conduct avoids plagiarism.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: While true, this principle concerns the severity of plagiarism, not whether proper citation avoids it.
explanations.C: This is a tangential principle about what should be cited, not about whether citation prevents plagiarism.
explanations.D: This addresses citation accuracy but does not justify the conclusion that citation itself prevents plagiarism.
explanations.E: This is too broad and general; it addresses academic values but does not justify the specific conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward one-move argument. The speaker concludes that a contract is valid because it contains all required elements. The correct principle directly licenses this inference.
lr.stimulus: The sales contract between Chen and Hartley includes all the legally required elements: a clear offer, an acceptance, and consideration. Therefore, the contract is valid.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Valid contracts must be written rather than verbal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A contract is valid if and only if it contains an offer, an acceptance, and consideration.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Contracts are more common in commerce than in family relationships.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both parties to a contract should have legal representation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Invalid contracts often lead to costly disputes in court.

explanations.correct: The argument assumes that the presence of offer, acceptance, and consideration is sufficient for validity. Principle B states exactly this: these three elements constitute a valid contract.
explanations.A: This principle concerns the form (written vs. verbal) of contracts, not the substantive elements the argument identifies.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: This is a tangential empirical claim about contract frequency, not about what makes a contract valid.
explanations.D: This concerns legal representation, which is not mentioned in or required by the argument.
explanations.E: This addresses consequences of invalidity, not the criteria for validity itself.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple one-step argument. The speaker claims a student should receive credit for a project because she met the specified criteria. The correct principle directly licenses this.
lr.stimulus: The assignment required students to cite at least five sources, use a formal outline, and submit the work by the deadline. Marina met all three requirements. Therefore, Marina is entitled to full credit for the project.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Teachers should be lenient when students submit work close to the deadline.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formal outlines improve the quality of research projects.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A student who meets all specified assignment requirements is entitled to full credit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Five sources are adequate for most undergraduate research projects.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Academic evaluation should reward effort over results.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that Marina deserves full credit based on her satisfaction of all stated requirements. Principle C directly underwrites this: meeting specified requirements entitles a student to full credit.
explanations.A: This concerns lenience for late work, not the entitlement to credit for meeting requirements.
explanations.B: This addresses the pedagogical value of outlines, not the grading principle the argument relies on.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: This is an empirical claim about adequacy but does not justify the entitlement to credit.
explanations.E: This addresses effort vs. results, not whether meeting requirements grants credit.

lr.difficultyReason: Direct one-move argument. The speaker concludes a medical treatment is safe because it has been extensively tested. The correct principle directly licenses this inference.
lr.stimulus: Dr. Patel recommends the new vaccine because it has undergone ten years of rigorous clinical trials with no significant adverse effects reported. Therefore, the vaccine is safe for the general population.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vaccines should be mandatory for all citizens.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A medical treatment is safe for general use if it has undergone extensive rigorous testing with no significant adverse effects.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most new vaccines are more effective than older vaccines.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Clinical trials are expensive and time-consuming.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Doctors should always recommend treatments they personally prefer.

explanations.correct: Dr. Patel concludes the vaccine is safe based on extensive testing with no significant adverse effects. Principle B directly states that such testing suffices to establish safety for general use.
explanations.A: This is a tangential principle about mandate policy, not about what establishes safety.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: This concerns efficacy and comparison, not safety.
explanations.D: This is a factual observation about trial costs, not a principle justifying the safety conclusion.
explanations.E: This concerns doctor preferences, which is not the basis of Dr. Patel's argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple one-step argument. The speaker concludes a book is well-written because it achieves its stated purpose effectively. The correct principle directly licenses this.
lr.stimulus: The author of this mystery novel intended to create a plot that surprises and engages readers. The novel contains unexpected twists, compelling characters, and careful foreshadowing that builds suspense throughout. Therefore, the novel is well-written.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All mystery novels are better than romance novels.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A literary work is well-written if it effectively achieves its intended purpose.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most successful authors write more than one book.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Good writing requires perfect grammar and spelling.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Readers prefer novels with surprising endings to novels with predictable ones.

explanations.correct: The argument evaluates the novel as well-written because it achieves its intended purpose of surprising and engaging readers. Principle B directly licenses this: effective achievement of intent constitutes good writing.
explanations.A: This makes a comparative claim about genre but does not establish a principle of good writing.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: This is a tangential fact about author productivity, not a criterion for good writing.
explanations.D: This concerns technical correctness but is not the basis of the argument, which emphasizes purpose and effect.
explanations.E: This is a preference statement that does not establish a principle of good writing.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward one-move argument. The speaker concludes an environmental policy is justified because it prevents harm without imposing undue burden. The correct principle directly supports this.
lr.stimulus: The city council is considering a ban on single-use plastic bags. This ban would reduce plastic pollution in waterways and landfills significantly. The ban would impose minimal inconvenience on shoppers, who can easily bring reusable bags. Therefore, the policy is justified.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Environmental policies should never restrict consumer choice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A policy is justified if it prevents significant harm and imposes minimal burden on affected parties.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most cities have already banned single-use plastics.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reusable bags are more durable than plastic bags.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pollution is the most serious environmental problem.

explanations.correct: The argument justifies the policy by claiming it prevents significant harm (pollution reduction) while imposing minimal burden (easy to bring reusable bags). Principle B directly states that this combination of factors justifies a policy.
explanations.A: This principle would contradict the policy's restriction, making it irrelevant to justifying it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: This is an empirical claim about what other cities have done, not a principle justifying the policy.
explanations.D: This is a tangential claim about bag durability, not about policy justification.
explanations.E: This ranks pollution among environmental problems but does not justify this specific policy.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple one-step argument. The speaker claims a candidate is qualified because she possesses all required credentials. The correct principle directly supports this.
lr.stimulus: The job posting requires a bachelor's degree in engineering, three years of professional experience, and a valid professional license. Dr. Hassan holds all three qualifications. Therefore, Dr. Hassan is qualified for the position.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Professional licenses should be renewed every two years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Engineering positions are more competitive than positions in other fields.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A candidate is qualified for a position if she possesses all stated qualifications.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Experience is more important than formal education.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most employers carefully screen their job applicants.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that Dr. Hassan is qualified based on her possession of all required qualifications. Principle C directly states that possessing all stated qualifications makes one qualified.
explanations.A: This concerns license renewal procedures, not the principle of qualification.
explanations.B: This is a tangential empirical claim about competitive fields, not a qualification principle.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: This ranks education vs. experience but does not establish when all stated requirements make one qualified.
explanations.E: This is a general claim about employer practices, not a principle of qualification.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward one-move argument. The speaker concludes a historical account is accurate because it is corroborated by multiple independent sources. The correct principle directly licenses this.
lr.stimulus: Historians have discovered three independent written accounts from different authors, all describing the same sequence of events during the reign of King Frederick. The accounts agree on major details and minor specifics. Therefore, this historical narrative is accurate.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ancient manuscripts are more valuable than modern historical texts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Historical events that occurred long ago are difficult to verify.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A historical account is accurate if it is corroborated by multiple independent sources.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Historians should examine both primary and secondary sources.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Written records are more reliable than oral traditions.

explanations.correct: The argument establishes accuracy based on corroboration by multiple independent sources. Principle C directly states that such corroboration establishes accuracy.
explanations.A: This is a tangential comparative claim about manuscript value, not about historical accuracy.
explanations.B: This acknowledges a challenge in verification but does not establish when accuracy is confirmed.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: This is a methodological guideline, not a principle establishing when accuracy is confirmed.
explanations.E: While true, this concerns source type preference but does not establish when independent corroboration confirms accuracy.

lr.difficultyReason: Direct one-move argument. The speaker concludes an investment is sound because it offers expected returns with acceptable risk. The correct principle directly supports this.
lr.stimulus: The financial advisor recommends that investors purchase bonds issued by the municipal government. These bonds offer a five percent annual return and have a history of consistent, reliable repayment. The risk is minimal. Therefore, this is a sound investment for conservative investors.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bonds are always safer than stocks.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Investors should maximize their returns regardless of risk.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An investment is sound for conservative investors if it offers reasonable returns with acceptable risk.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Municipal governments manage their finances better than private corporations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Interest rates on bonds are determined by market demand.

explanations.correct: The advisor recommends the bonds based on reasonable returns (five percent) and acceptable risk (minimal). Principle C directly states that such a combination makes an investment sound for conservative investors.
explanations.A: This is an absolute comparative claim that does not establish what makes a particular investment sound.
explanations.B: This would contradict the focus on acceptable risk, making it irrelevant.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: This is a tangential empirical comparison, not a principle about sound investing.
explanations.E: This is a factual claim about interest rate determination, not about investment soundness.

lr.difficultyReason: Conclusion rests on two conjoined conditions — professional role plus public interest. Trap (B) is too broad; it would license a conclusion even when no public interest is at stake. Trap (D) is too narrow, applying only to physicians.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: A pharmacist who fills prescriptions at a neighborhood clinic learned that a widely used heartburn medication was being recalled for contamination. The manufacturer had asked pharmacies to delay informing patients until a formal press release could be issued. The pharmacist nonetheless called every affected patient that day. Given that the contamination posed a genuine risk of harm, the pharmacist acted rightly in doing so.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A health-care professional who learns of a material risk to the people under her care is obligated to inform them promptly, even when instructed otherwise by third parties.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A person who receives confidential information from an employer is permitted to disclose that information whenever she believes disclosure would be beneficial.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patients are entitled to complete information about every medication they have ever been prescribed, regardless of current relevance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A physician who has prescribed a medication later found to be unsafe must personally contact each patient who received the prescription.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Manufacturers of pharmaceuticals bear primary responsibility for communicating safety information to the public.

explanations.correct: The ethicist concludes the pharmacist acted rightly because (i) she is a health-care professional, (ii) a real risk of harm existed, and (iii) a third party asked her to delay. Principle (A) combines these exact conditions and yields the endorsement.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too broad — permits any employee to disclose confidential information on a mere belief that disclosure is beneficial, licensing conclusions the ethicist does not draw.
explanations.C: Too broad and tangential — it concerns completeness of medication histories, not acute safety risks.
explanations.D: Too narrow — the actor in the stimulus is a pharmacist, not a physician, so the principle would not cover this case.
