explanations.E: Shifts the subject to manufacturer responsibility, which is not what the ethicist is defending.

lr.difficultyReason: Argument depends on both foreseeability and counterfactual avoidability. Trap (C) inverts the direction; trap (E) applies only to intentional harm.
lr.stimulus: Columnist: The city's transit agency continued to run its oldest subway cars for two years after internal engineers reported that a brake component was prone to failure at high speed. A derailment last month, caused by precisely that component, injured dozens of riders. The agency's leadership argues that the derailment was a freak accident for which no one is to blame. That defense fails: the agency is culpable for the harm.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the columnist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An organization is culpable for a harm when it has been warned of a specific risk and continues a practice that could have been altered to prevent that harm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An organization is culpable for a harm only if its leadership directly intended the harmful outcome.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An organization that cannot rule out every possible mechanical failure must cease operations until its equipment is certified safe.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Public agencies bear a heavier duty of care than private firms performing comparable services.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No one is to blame for harms that arise from accidents the responsible parties did not foresee.

explanations.correct: The columnist stresses (i) the agency was warned of this specific brake risk and (ii) could have withdrawn the cars but did not. Principle (A) combines warning plus avoidability to yield culpability — exactly the move the columnist makes.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too narrow — would acquit the agency in this case, since intent is not alleged.
explanations.C: Too broad — would license halting operations in any case of residual uncertainty, a conclusion the columnist does not draw.
explanations.D: Tangential — comparison of public versus private duty is not what the columnist is defending.
explanations.E: Addresses a different aspect — defines when no one is to blame, not when culpability attaches; and the stimulus shows the risk was foreseen.

lr.difficultyReason: Requires a principle matching both the consent gap and the material-effect condition in the researcher's critique. Trap (B) is too broad; trap (D) is reversed.
lr.stimulus: Researcher: A recent linguistic study recorded casual conversations in public cafés to document regional slang, informing only the café owners and not the patrons being recorded. The investigators claim that because no names were published, no harm was done. But patrons could be identified by voice in the audio files released with the paper, and several later reported embarrassment when colleagues recognized them. The study's method was ethically indefensible.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the researcher's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Researchers must secure informed consent from participants whenever the research materials released could reasonably be used to identify them and affect their standing with others.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All social-science research involving human subjects must obtain written consent from every subject before any data collection begins.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Research is ethically defensible only when its scientific value clearly outweighs any inconvenience to the subjects.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants need not consent to research so long as their personal names are withheld from publication.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Public spaces afford no expectation of privacy, and research conducted in them is therefore exempt from consent requirements.

explanations.correct: The researcher's complaint rests on two facts: patrons were identifiable from the released audio, and that identification produced real social harm. Principle (A) joins identifiability and adverse standing into a consent requirement, licensing the 'ethically indefensible' verdict.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too broad — a blanket written-consent rule would condemn studies the researcher is not condemning and ignores the identifiability criterion she actually invokes.
explanations.C: Tangential — cost-benefit weighing is not the basis of the researcher's critique.
explanations.D: Reversed — this principle would exonerate the investigators, since names were indeed withheld.
explanations.E: Reversed — would license the study's design rather than condemn it.

lr.difficultyReason: Conclusion blames a regulator on grounds of available knowledge plus preventable magnitude. Trap (A) is too broad; trap (E) shifts the subject to industry.
lr.stimulus: Economist: The financial regulator had ample data showing that a particular class of mortgage-backed securities was badly mispriced, and it had the statutory authority to require banks to mark these holdings down. Choosing not to act, the regulator allowed losses to mount until several mid-sized banks failed, costing taxpayers billions. The regulator is properly faulted for the scope of those losses.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the economist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A public official is to blame for any adverse outcome occurring within the sphere of that official's authority.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A regulator who possesses both the evidence of a growing harm and the authority to mitigate it is properly faulted for the portion of the harm that its inaction allowed to continue.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Financial regulators ought to privilege market stability over the enforcement of individual accounting rules.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Private firms, not public regulators, bear ultimate responsibility for the soundness of their own balance sheets.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Industries whose failures impose large costs on taxpayers should face stricter oversight than industries whose failures do not.

explanations.correct: The economist faults the regulator on two specific grounds: it had the data (evidence) and the authority (power to mitigate), and its inaction allowed additional harm. Principle (B) joins these exact conditions to fault.
explanations.A: Too broad — would fault the regulator even when it lacked relevant evidence or lawful tools, licensing conclusions stronger than the economist's.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Tangential — the economist is not making a claim about how to rank stability against accounting rules.
explanations.D: Reversed — this principle shifts blame away from the regulator the economist is faulting.
explanations.E: Shifts the subject from regulator conduct to the design of oversight regimes generally.

lr.difficultyReason: Judgment depends jointly on genuine effort and on outcome-independent acknowledgment. Trap (C) is too narrow to primary caregivers; trap (E) is reversed.
lr.stimulus: Teacher: Priya spent weeks tutoring a younger student in algebra, preparing customized worksheets and meeting twice a week even during exam season. The younger student's grades did not substantially improve, and the school's tutoring coordinator argues that Priya therefore deserves no recognition. The coordinator is mistaken: Priya deserves recognition for her tutoring work.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the teacher's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anyone who volunteers to assist another student deserves formal recognition from the school, whatever their methods.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A person who devotes sustained and conscientious effort to helping another deserves recognition for that effort, whether or not the effort produces its intended outcome.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Primary caregivers and teachers who guide a child's long-term development deserve public acknowledgment for that guidance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recognition should be reserved for students whose assistance measurably improves the academic performance of those they help.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tutors should be evaluated primarily on the test-score gains of the students they tutor.

explanations.correct: The teacher endorses recognition because Priya expended genuine, sustained effort, and does so despite the absence of a measurable outcome. Principle (B) joins effort-and-conscientiousness to recognition and explicitly decouples it from outcomes.
explanations.A: Too broad — 'whatever their methods' licenses recognition for haphazard or counterproductive efforts the teacher is not endorsing.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too narrow — Priya is a peer tutor, not a primary caregiver, so the principle does not cover her case.
explanations.D: Reversed — would deny Priya recognition, since grades did not improve.
explanations.E: Reversed — endorses the coordinator's view, not the teacher's.

lr.difficultyReason: Preservation judgment rests on two linked criteria — historical function and irreplaceability. Trap (B) is too broad; trap (D) is reversed.
lr.stimulus: Preservationist: The nineteenth-century glass conservatory in Marston Park is structurally unsound and would cost nearly as much to restore as to demolish and replace. The parks department therefore favors demolition. But the conservatory is the only surviving example of a glazing technique once central to the city's industrial identity, a technique no living craftsperson can fully reconstruct. The parks department should restore, not demolish, the conservatory.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the preservationist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When a structure is both a unique surviving exemplar of a historically significant technique and cannot be reconstructed using contemporary methods, it should be restored rather than demolished.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All structures more than a century old should be preserved whenever doing so is physically possible.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Public parks should allocate funds equally between new construction and the maintenance of existing structures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When restoration and replacement costs are comparable, a municipality should choose whichever option yields greater future utility for visitors.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cities have a duty to commemorate their industrial heritage through public monuments and explanatory plaques.

explanations.correct: The preservationist's conclusion rests on (i) the conservatory's uniqueness as a surviving exemplar of the glazing technique and (ii) the technique's non-reconstructibility today. Principle (A) joins those exact conditions to a restoration duty.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too broad — a blanket century-old rule would mandate preservation in many cases the preservationist does not discuss and ignores uniqueness and reconstructibility.
explanations.C: Tangential — budget allocation policy doesn't speak to this specific demolish-or-restore choice.
explanations.D: Reversed — future-utility weighing could favor demolition-plus-replacement and would not license the preservationist's conclusion.
explanations.E: Tangential — plaques and monuments are a different preservation strategy than structural restoration.

lr.difficultyReason: Verdict requires both the content-creator relationship and the commercial-use condition. Trap (A) is too broad; trap (E) is too narrow.
lr.stimulus: Critic: A regional museum scanned three hundred paintings by local artists to generate an interactive exhibit, then licensed the same scans to a textile company that printed the images on scarves sold at a substantial profit. The artists, most of whom had donated the originals for exhibition purposes, received nothing. The museum's decision to license the scans for commercial resale was wrong.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the critic's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An institution that acquires any work of art acquires along with it the right to use the work in any manner the institution sees fit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An institution that obtains works from their creators for a specified noncommercial purpose acts wrongly in subsequently licensing those works for commercial profit without the creators' involvement.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Museums should prioritize public access to artworks over the financial interests of the artists who created them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Digital reproductions of artworks must be identified as reproductions whenever they are displayed to the public.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A museum that sells original paintings it owns outright must share the proceeds with the living artists who painted them.

explanations.correct: The critic's verdict rests on two facts: the artists transferred the works for a specific noncommercial purpose (exhibition), and the museum then licensed them for commercial profit without the artists. Principle (B) joins those conditions to wrongdoing.
explanations.A: Reversed — would exonerate the museum.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Tangential — access-versus-income is not the axis of the critic's complaint, which is about scope of use.
explanations.D: Tangential — labeling reproductions is a different issue.
explanations.E: Too narrow — addresses sale of original paintings, not licensing of digital scans, and so would not cover the case at hand.

lr.difficultyReason: Conclusion rests on both disproportionate burden and availability of less restrictive means. Trap (A) is too broad; trap (D) is too narrow.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: The state's new rule requires anyone wishing to braid hair professionally to complete 1,500 hours of cosmetology training and pass a chemistry exam covering dyes the braiders never use. The rule is meant to protect consumers from unsanitary practices, but the same safety outcome could be achieved through a short sanitation course and a simple inspection regime. The state's rule is unjustified.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the policy analyst's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A government regulation is unjustified unless it is supported by a majority of the workers in the regulated trade.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A government regulation that imposes significant burdens on those it regulates is unjustified when a substantially less burdensome alternative would achieve the same legitimate purpose.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Consumer-protection regulations should be tailored to the specific risks of each trade rather than modeled on unrelated trades.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Occupational licensing requirements for hair braiders must exclude material on chemical hair dyes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any regulation motivated by a legitimate safety interest is justified regardless of the costs it imposes on workers.

explanations.correct: The analyst's verdict rests on (i) the rule's heavy burden on braiders and (ii) the availability of a much less burdensome alternative that achieves the same safety aim. Principle (B) joins those exact conditions to an unjustified verdict.
explanations.A: Too broad and off-point — would condemn many rules regardless of whether less burdensome alternatives exist, and majority approval is not the analyst's criterion.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Tangential — captures a related intuition (tailoring) but does not join burden and least-restrictive-means, which are the analyst's actual grounds.
explanations.D: Too narrow — a rule about hair-dye content on licensing exams would justify only part of the analyst's critique, leaving the 1,500-hour burden unaddressed.
explanations.E: Reversed — would license the rule, not condemn it.

lr.difficultyReason: Entitlement depends on both the voluntary disclosure and the absence of countervailing third-party harm. Trap (B) is too broad; trap (E) is reversed.
lr.stimulus: Librarian: A patron who checked out several books on computer security asked the library to delete his borrowing records for the past year, citing concerns that an employer-conducted background check might misread them. The library's records contain no information about anyone other than the patron himself, and erasing them would compromise no other patron's interests. The library should honor the request.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the librarian's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An institution should, upon the voluntary request of the person to whom records exclusively pertain, erase those records whenever doing so harms no one else's legitimate interests.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Libraries should accede to any patron request that does not violate state or federal law.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Institutions should retain borrowing records indefinitely so that patterns of misuse can be detected retrospectively.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An individual's reading history is among the most sensitive categories of personal information and deserves the highest level of legal protection.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Employers performing background checks are entitled to access library borrowing records that would otherwise be confidential.

explanations.correct: The librarian's conclusion rests on (i) the patron's own voluntary request about records that pertain only to him and (ii) the absence of harm to others' interests. Principle (A) combines both conditions to yield erasure.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too broad — 'any request that doesn't violate law' would license many requests the librarian does not endorse and ignores the harm-to-others condition she relies on.
explanations.C: Reversed — would counsel against erasure.
explanations.D: Tangential — a claim about legal status of reading history does not license erasure in this particular case.
explanations.E: Reversed and tangential — authorizes disclosure to employers rather than erasure for the patron.

lr.difficultyReason: Permission depends on reversibility joined with lack of viable alternatives. Trap (A) is too broad; trap (D) is tangential.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientist: Some ecologists object to the release of genetically modified mosquitoes engineered to suppress populations carrying a deadly fever, worrying that releases could disrupt local ecosystems. In the island region under discussion, however, the engineered mosquitoes' modifications fade within a few generations if releases are halted, and no other method has reduced the fever there despite decades of effort. Releasing the engineered mosquitoes in this region is permissible.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the environmental scientist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any intervention that may save human lives from a deadly disease is permissible regardless of its ecological consequences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An ecological intervention addressing a serious public-health threat is permissible when its effects can be halted and no established alternative has proven effective in the affected region.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scientific research involving genetic modification must first be tested in contained laboratory settings before any field deployment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Regions affected by a mosquito-borne disease should adopt the intervention proven most effective in other regions with comparable climates.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Once an ecological intervention has shown any adverse effect in a pilot trial, it should not be expanded to wider release.

explanations.correct: The scientist's permission rests on two joined facts: the intervention is reversible (modifications fade) and alternatives have long failed in this region. Principle (B) combines serious threat, reversibility, and lack of proven alternatives, licensing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Too broad — ignores ecological consequences entirely and would license interventions the scientist is not endorsing.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Tangential — contained-lab testing is not the question; the stimulus concerns a field release already past that stage.
explanations.D: Tangential — the scientist's argument hinges on this region's failure history and on reversibility, not on transplanting methods from other regions.
explanations.E: Reversed — would forbid the release.

lr.difficultyReason: Requires identifying the principle that licenses a normative claim about medical disclosure; distractors invoke plausible but tangential duties.
lr.stimulus: Physician: A patient asked me whether a new cholesterol medication I was prescribing carries any risk of liver damage. I told her it does not, even though recent trial data suggest a small but nonzero risk. My reason was that disclosing a very small risk would cause the patient needless anxiety and would likely lead her to refuse a treatment she genuinely needs. This was the right decision.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the physician's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A physician is obligated to tell patients only information that the physician has verified through direct clinical experience.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients should always be given the opportunity to seek a second opinion before beginning any new course of treatment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Withholding information from a patient is justified when disclosing it would cause harm that outweighs the benefit of the patient's being informed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A physician who deceives a patient for any reason violates the fundamental duty of medical practice.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Medical decisions should be guided primarily by the financial interests of the healthcare system rather than by the preferences of individual patients.

explanations.correct: The physician's argument rests on a harm-benefit calculation: the harm of the patient's anxiety and treatment refusal outweighs the benefit of knowing a tiny risk. Principle C captures this balancing logic directly and licenses the conclusion that withholding was right.
explanations.A: Tangential — the issue is not verification of information but whether to disclose it. This principle addresses a different condition entirely.
explanations.B: Tangential — second opinions are not mentioned or implied by the physician's reasoning.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Reversed — this principle would condemn the physician's action, not justify it.
explanations.E: Too broad and mismatched — financial interests of the healthcare system play no role in the physician's stated reasoning.

lr.difficultyReason: Argument turns on a specific normative move about regulatory burden; distractors are plausibly related to environmental policy but miss the argument's core.
lr.stimulus: Environmentalist: The proposed coastal development project would destroy approximately forty hectares of protected wetlands. Developers argue that the economic benefits to the region justify proceeding. But the project should not be approved. The economic gains will accrue primarily to a small group of private investors, while the ecological losses — erosion protection, flood mitigation, and biodiversity — will be borne by the entire coastal community for generations.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the environmentalist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Economic development should never be permitted in areas designated as protected habitat.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A project that concentrates benefits among a few private parties while distributing its costs broadly across the public is not justified on economic grounds alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ecological value of wetlands is always greater than any economic benefit a development project could produce.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Private investors who profit from development projects should be required to compensate local communities for any resulting inconvenience.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulatory agencies are obligated to solicit public comment before approving any coastal construction project.

explanations.correct: The environmentalist's argument hinges on an asymmetry: private parties capture the benefits while the public bears the costs. Principle B — that such asymmetric distribution defeats an economic justification — licenses the conclusion that approval is unwarranted.
explanations.A: Too broad — the environmentalist does not claim all development in protected areas is impermissible; the objection is specifically about who bears costs versus who gains benefits.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too broad — the environmentalist does not argue that ecological value universally trumps economic benefit; the argument is specifically about the distribution of gains and losses.
explanations.D: Tangential — compensation mechanisms are not what the environmentalist invokes; the argument opposes approval, not inadequate compensation.
explanations.E: Tangential — procedural public-comment requirements are unrelated to the substantive cost-benefit reasoning offered.

lr.difficultyReason: The normative claim involves authenticity and artistic intent; distractors exploit adjacent aesthetic concepts without licensing the specific conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Critic: The symphony orchestra's decision to use computer-generated sound effects during a live performance of a contemporary orchestral work is artistically indefensible. The composer explicitly scored the piece for acoustic instruments only, and the audience paid to hear a live acoustic performance. Substituting synthesized sounds — even imperceptible ones — misrepresents what the audience is experiencing.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the critic's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Contemporary composers should always collaborate with performers to determine the final sonic character of a new work.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An arts organization acts wrongly when it presents a performance in a manner that misrepresents the nature of what the audience will experience.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Computer-generated music is inherently inferior in artistic quality to music performed by live acoustic instruments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ticket prices for orchestral performances should reflect the full costs of production, including any technology used.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A composer's intentions are relevant to a performance's artistic merit only when those intentions are communicated to the audience in advance.

explanations.correct: The critic's argument centers on misrepresentation: the audience believes they are hearing an acoustic performance but are not. Principle B — that presenting a performance in a way that misrepresents what the audience experiences is wrong — directly licenses the conclusion that the orchestra's decision is indefensible.
explanations.A: Tangential — composer-performer collaboration during composition is not what the critic invokes; the issue is what occurs during a live performance.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too broad — the critic does not claim synthesized sound is inherently inferior; the objection is about misrepresentation, not the quality of the technology.
explanations.D: Tangential — ticket pricing and cost transparency are unrelated to the critic's misrepresentation argument.
explanations.E: Reversed — this principle would weaken the critic's position by implying the composer's intent is irrelevant unless disclosed to the audience.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument involves a normative claim about legal accountability; distractors invoke related legal concepts but fail to match the argument's logical structure.
lr.stimulus: Legal Scholar: A software company released a security update that it knew contained an unpatched vulnerability, reasoning that the vulnerability was unlikely to be exploited before a full fix was ready. When the vulnerability was exploited two weeks later and users' financial data was stolen, the company claimed it bore no legal responsibility because it had acted in good faith. This claim is wrong. The company was aware of the risk it was imposing on its users and chose to impose it anyway.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the legal scholar's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Software companies should be held to a higher standard of care than other technology firms because of the sensitive nature of financial data.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Good faith is a complete defense to legal liability whenever a party lacked the intent to cause harm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A party that knowingly imposes a risk of harm on others bears legal responsibility if that risk materializes, regardless of the party's intentions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Companies operating in the technology sector are responsible for ensuring that all software they release is completely free of security vulnerabilities.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Legal liability arises only when a party's conduct falls below the standard that a reasonable person would observe in the same situation.

explanations.correct: The scholar's argument is that knowing about a risk and choosing to impose it defeats the good-faith defense — awareness of risk, not intent to harm, is what matters. Principle C captures this precisely: knowingly imposing a risk that materializes grounds liability regardless of intentions.
explanations.A: Too narrow — heightened standards for financial-data companies are not the scholar's basis for rejecting the good-faith defense; the argument applies to knowing risk-imposition generally.
explanations.B: Reversed — this principle would support the company's claim, which is exactly what the scholar is arguing against.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Too broad — requiring zero vulnerabilities is far stronger than the scholar's claim, which is only about knowing about a risk; the scholar does not require perfection.
explanations.E: Tangential — the reasonable-person standard may be relevant in negligence law, but the scholar's argument is specifically about the legal effect of the company's actual knowledge of the risk.

lr.difficultyReason: Argument involves a normative claim about economic policy and individual circumstance; one distractor is temptingly close but addresses a different normative dimension.
lr.stimulus: Economist: The proposed flat consumption tax would impose the same percentage rate on all purchases regardless of the buyer's income level. Proponents argue that equal percentage rates constitute equal treatment. But the policy is unfair. A family spending ninety percent of its income on necessities loses a far greater share of its discretionary resources to such a tax than does a household spending thirty percent of its income on those same goods.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the economist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tax policy is fair only when it raises sufficient revenue to fund essential government services for all citizens.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Equal numerical treatment does not constitute equal treatment when the practical burden it imposes differs substantially across individuals due to differences in their circumstances.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Governments should never impose any form of taxation on goods that qualify as basic necessities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A tax policy is fair if and only if wealthier individuals pay a higher total dollar amount in taxes than do lower-income individuals.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Economic policies should be evaluated primarily by whether they promote overall growth in gross domestic product.

explanations.correct: The economist's argument is that identical percentage rates are not genuinely equal because the actual burden differs based on income and spending patterns. Principle B — that equal numerical treatment can fail to constitute genuine equality when circumstances differ — licenses that critique directly.
explanations.A: Tangential — revenue sufficiency is not the economist's concern; the argument is about the distributive fairness of the rate structure.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too broad — the economist does not argue against all taxation of necessities; the argument is about the flat rate's unequal effective burden, not the taxability of necessities per se.
explanations.D: Too narrow and mismatched — the principle concerns total dollar amounts rather than the proportional burden on discretionary resources, which is the economist's actual focus.
explanations.E: Tangential — GDP growth is unrelated to the fairness argument the economist advances.

lr.difficultyReason: Requires identifying the principle behind a normative claim about linguistic preservation policy; distractors address related cultural or political concerns without licensing the specific argument.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Several regional governments have adopted policies that fund instruction exclusively in the dominant national language, eliminating support for minority language education. Officials justify this by arguing that fluency in the national language improves employment prospects. But these policies are misguided. A community's language is inseparable from its cultural identity and oral traditions; extinguishing the language extinguishes the community itself.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the linguist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Government education policy should be designed to maximize the average employment income of graduates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Policies that produce measurable economic benefits are justified even if they involve some cultural costs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A policy that eliminates something constitutive of a community's identity is not justified solely by the economic benefits it may produce.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minority communities are entitled to representation in any government body that makes decisions affecting their linguistic rights.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Governments should promote bilingualism rather than monolingualism as the standard for national educational systems.

explanations.correct: The linguist argues that the economic justification is insufficient because eliminating minority language education destroys something constitutive of the community's identity. Principle C — that a policy eliminating something constitutive of community identity cannot be justified by economic benefits alone — licenses that conclusion directly.
explanations.A: Reversed — this principle supports the officials' justification rather than the linguist's critique.
explanations.B: Reversed — this principle would undermine the linguist's argument by allowing economic benefits to override cultural costs.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Tangential — procedural representation rights are not part of the linguist's substantive argument about the policy's justification.
explanations.E: Too narrow — advocating bilingualism is a specific policy recommendation that goes beyond what the linguist's argument requires; the linguist's point is about the insufficiency of an economic rationale, not about a preferred policy alternative.

lr.difficultyReason: Argument involves a historical judgment about moral responsibility; distractors invoke temporal or institutional distinctions that are plausible but don't license the specific claim.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Some have argued that leaders of the colonial administration in question cannot be judged by contemporary moral standards because they acted in accordance with the norms of their era. But this reasoning fails. Those leaders had access to dissenting voices within their own society — abolitionists, indigenous advocates, and dissident clergy — who articulated precisely why the policies were wrong. Choosing to ignore those voices does not excuse the moral failure.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the historian's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Historical figures should be evaluated only by the standards that were dominant in their own societies, not by standards developed afterward.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A person who deliberately disregards a moral critique that was available to them at the time of their actions cannot claim ignorance as a defense against moral judgment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The existence of dissent within a society is sufficient evidence that the majority view at the time was morally wrong.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Colonial administrators should be held to the same legal standards as elected government officials in democratic states.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Moral progress requires that later generations recognize and correct the errors of their predecessors.

explanations.correct: The historian's argument turns on the fact that the leaders had access to moral criticism and chose to ignore it, making the 'different era' defense inapplicable. Principle B — that deliberately disregarding available moral critique forfeits the ignorance defense — licenses this conclusion precisely.
explanations.A: Reversed — this principle supports the position the historian is arguing against.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too broad — the historian does not claim the existence of dissent proves the majority was wrong; the point is narrower: that the leaders personally had access to the critique and ignored it.
explanations.D: Tangential — legal standards for colonial administrators versus elected officials are not what the historian invokes; the argument is about moral judgment.
explanations.E: Tangential — the duty of later generations to correct past errors is a different normative claim than the one licensing the historian's specific argument about individual moral responsibility.

lr.difficultyReason: Normative claim about technology and privacy requires the right scope of principle; one distractor is temptingly close but applies to a broader class of cases than the argument requires.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: A major social media platform recently began using its users' private messages to train its artificial intelligence models, relying on a clause buried in its terms of service that users had agreed to when signing up. The platform argues it acted within its legal rights. Nonetheless, the practice is ethically wrong. Users who agreed to those terms had no reasonable expectation that their private conversations would be used in this way.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Technology companies should be prohibited by law from training artificial intelligence systems on any user-generated content.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consent obtained through terms of service is legally valid and therefore sufficient to render any subsequent use of user data ethically permissible.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Acting within one's legal rights is sufficient to establish that one's conduct is ethically acceptable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Using information in a way that reasonable people who provided it would not have anticipated is ethically impermissible, regardless of legal authorization.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The ethical permissibility of data use depends on whether the data was collected from users in a domain that is inherently public rather than private.

explanations.correct: The ethicist's argument is that legal authorization does not settle the ethical question when users' reasonable expectations were violated. Principle D — that using information in ways users could not reasonably have anticipated is ethically impermissible regardless of legal authorization — licenses the conclusion that the platform acted wrongly.
explanations.A: Too broad — an absolute prohibition on AI training from user content goes far beyond the ethicist's specific claim, which is about reasonable expectations, not the technology itself.
explanations.B: Reversed — this principle would support the platform's position, contradicting the ethicist's conclusion.
explanations.C: Reversed — the ethicist explicitly rejects the inference from legal permission to ethical permissibility; this principle would undermine the argument.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Tangential — the public/private domain distinction is not the basis of the ethicist's argument; the argument is about reasonable expectations at the time of consent, not the inherent nature of the domain.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument involves a normative claim about scientific communication policy; distractors invoke plausible epistemic or institutional norms that don't license the specific conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Science Journalist: A government health agency recently declined to publish a completed study on the long-term effects of a widely used food additive, citing concerns that the findings might cause public alarm before further research could confirm them. This decision was wrong. The public has been consuming the additive for decades and has a legitimate interest in knowing what researchers have found, even if the findings are preliminary.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the science journalist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Scientific findings that have not been replicated by independent researchers should not be released to the public under any circumstances.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A public agency may withhold research findings only when releasing them would create a risk of harm that outweighs the public's interest in having the information.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Government agencies have an absolute duty to publish all research they fund, regardless of the content or stage of the findings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The potential to cause public alarm is never a legitimate reason for a government agency to withhold any type of information from the public.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Preliminary scientific findings on matters that directly affect public health should not be suppressed by the agency responsible for that health domain solely to avoid causing concern.

explanations.correct: The journalist argues that the public's legitimate interest in research directly affecting their health overrides the agency's concern about premature alarm — particularly when the public has been exposed to the substance for decades. Principle E captures this precisely: health-relevant preliminary findings should not be suppressed by the responsible agency merely to prevent concern.
explanations.A: Reversed — this principle would support withholding findings that lack replication, directly contradicting the journalist's position.
explanations.B: This principle is compatible with the journalist's argument but does not license the conclusion as directly as E. It is a harm-balancing framework that could cut either way; E more precisely targets the journalist's specific claim about suppression to avoid concern.
explanations.C: Too broad — requiring publication of all funded research regardless of circumstances goes well beyond the journalist's argument, which is limited to research on public-health matters affecting current consumers.
explanations.D: Too broad — the journalist does not claim that preventing alarm is never a legitimate reason for any agency to withhold any information; the argument is specifically about a health agency withholding relevant health research.
explanations.E: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Argument involves a normative claim about institutional conflict of interest; distractors are closely related to ethics of funding but differ in scope or direction.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: A prominent nutrition research institute regularly publishes dietary guidelines that are adopted by public health agencies worldwide. The institute receives more than half of its annual funding from companies that manufacture processed food products. Even if the institute's researchers act in complete good faith, the institute should not be the body responsible for issuing these guidelines. The source of an institution's funding shapes the questions it asks and the conclusions it emphasizes, regardless of individual researchers' intentions.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Research institutions that accept private funding should disclose the identity of all donors in any publication resulting from that funding.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An institution whose structural incentives are misaligned with the public interest should not hold authority over decisions that directly affect that public interest, even if its individual members act in good faith.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nutrition researchers who receive industry funding are more likely to produce biased results than researchers funded exclusively by government grants.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Public health agencies should evaluate the quality of dietary research solely on the basis of the methodological rigor of the studies they consider.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any institution that publishes guidelines adopted by government bodies must be subject to direct governmental oversight and regular independent audits.

explanations.correct: The ethicist's argument is that structural funding misalignment — not individual bad faith — disqualifies the institute from holding guideline authority. Principle B captures this structural logic: an institution with misaligned incentives should not hold public-interest authority regardless of its members' personal integrity.
explanations.A: Tangential — disclosure of donors is a transparency measure but does not address the disqualification claim the ethicist makes; the ethicist argues the institute should not hold authority, not merely that it should disclose funders.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Premise mismatch — the ethicist explicitly sets aside individual bad faith and bias; a principle about the likelihood of biased results is not what licenses the structural disqualification argument.
explanations.D: Reversed — this principle would support the institute's authority if its methodology is sound, which is precisely what the ethicist argues is insufficient.
explanations.E: Too narrow and tangential — governmental oversight and audits are procedural remedies that do not address whether the institution should hold authority in the first place.

lr.difficultyReason: Requires identifying the principle that licenses a normative claim about individual patient autonomy over aggregate policy outcomes. Distractors invoke plausible-sounding medical ethics principles that don't match the argument's core move.
lr.stimulus: Physician: A hospital administration recently proposed requiring all patients with a certain chronic condition to follow a single standardized treatment protocol in order to reduce overall costs. This policy is unjustified. Even if the protocol produces the best average outcome across all patients, it would force some individuals to forgo treatments better suited to their particular circumstances.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the physician's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medical institutions should adopt policies that maximize the overall health of the patient population they serve.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A health policy is unjustified if it prioritizes cost reduction over the improvement of patient health outcomes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A medical policy is unjustified if it compels individuals to accept worse outcomes for themselves in order to serve aggregate goals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients should not be required to follow any treatment they have not explicitly chosen, regardless of the clinical evidence supporting it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Standardizing medical procedures is acceptable only when every patient would benefit equally from the procedure.

explanations.correct: The physician's argument turns on the fact that some individuals would be made worse off by the protocol in order to serve the aggregate goal of cost reduction. Principle C — a policy is unjustified when it forces individuals to accept worse outcomes for aggregate goals — directly licenses that conclusion.
explanations.A: This is the principle the hospital administration is using, not the one that justifies the physician's critique. Tangential principle trap.
explanations.B: The physician does not claim that cost reduction is an illegitimate goal per se; the objection is about individuals being harmed, not about the motivation being cost. Too narrow and misidentifies the argument's core claim.
explanations.C: Correct. This principle precisely covers the physician's reasoning: some patients are forced to accept worse individual outcomes for an aggregate (cost) goal.
explanations.D: The physician does not argue that explicit patient consent is the criterion; the concern is about worsened outcomes, not unchosen treatment. Principle–premise mismatch.
explanations.E: Equal benefit for every patient is a stricter standard than what the physician argues — the physician only objects because some patients are made worse off, not because benefits are unequal. Too broad trap.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument involves a specific economic fairness claim. The correct principle must capture the relationship between original contribution and entitlement to gains; distractors invoke related but mismatched economic principles.
lr.stimulus: Economist: When a startup company's value increases substantially after an early employee joins and contributes innovative work, that employee is entitled to a meaningful share of the resulting gains even if the initial employment contract specified only a fixed salary. The gains would not have materialized without that employee's specific contributions.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the economist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Employment contracts are binding only if both parties fully understood the potential value of the work at the time of signing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Workers are entitled to a share of gains they were causally responsible for producing, even when prior agreements specified otherwise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Companies that achieve substantial growth owe a debt of gratitude to all employees who worked for them during that period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fixed-salary contracts are inherently unfair to employees whose skills significantly exceed the market rate at which they were hired.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The value of an employee's contribution to a company should be assessed at the time the contribution is made, not in retrospect.

explanations.correct: The economist's claim is that causal responsibility for the value gain entitles the employee to a share of it, even over the contract's terms. Principle B — workers are entitled to gains they causally produced, even when prior agreements say otherwise — directly underwrites this reasoning.
explanations.A: The economist's argument does not depend on whether parties understood the contract's implications at signing; the argument is about who caused the gains. Principle–premise mismatch.
explanations.B: Correct. This principle captures both the causal element ('responsible for producing') and the override of prior contractual terms ('even when prior agreements specified otherwise').
explanations.C: Gratitude is not the same as entitlement to gains, and 'all employees' is too broad — the economist singles out the employee whose specific contributions drove the growth. Too broad trap.
explanations.D: The economist's argument is about causal contribution to value, not about whether the salary undervalued the employee at hire. Tangential principle trap.
explanations.E: This principle would actually undermine the economist's position by discounting retrospective assessment of contribution value. Reversed trap.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental policy argument with a normative claim about precautionary action. Correct principle must match the specific structure: acting under uncertainty when irreversible harm is possible. Distractors use plausible environmental language but miss the irreversibility criterion.
lr.stimulus: Environmental Scientist: A proposed mining operation would extract minerals from a region where several species' habitats have not yet been fully studied. Even though we cannot yet confirm that the operation would cause lasting ecological damage, the project should not be approved. If the habitat is later found to be critical and has already been destroyed, the loss cannot be undone.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the environmental scientist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Industrial projects should not be approved unless their proponents can demonstrate net economic benefit to the surrounding communities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The potential economic benefits of a project do not outweigh the environmental costs if those costs affect endangered species.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When an action risks irreversible harm, the inability to confirm that harm in advance is not sufficient justification for proceeding.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Projects that affect wildlife habitats must be preceded by complete ecological studies of all potentially affected species.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Environmental protection should take precedence over economic development whenever the two goals come into conflict.

explanations.correct: The scientist's argument structure is: the harm may be irreversible, and our inability to confirm it now is not a reason to proceed. Principle C — inability to confirm irreversible harm in advance doesn't justify proceeding — directly licenses this conclusion.
explanations.A: The scientist does not mention economic benefit or community impact; the argument rests on the risk of irreversible harm. Tangential principle trap.
explanations.B: The scientist does not invoke endangered species specifically, and the principle requires weighing economic benefits against costs — a framing the argument doesn't use. Principle–premise mismatch.
explanations.C: Correct. This captures both the irreversibility element and the epistemic uncertainty the scientist identifies as insufficient grounds for approval.
explanations.D: The scientist's conclusion is that the project should not be approved, not merely that a study must precede it. This principle is too narrow and leaves open the possibility that a complete study would justify the project. Too narrow trap.
explanations.E: This principle would justify the scientist's conclusion in any environmental-vs.-economic conflict, making it too broad — and the scientist does not frame the conflict as economic development versus environment. Too broad trap.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal reasoning about the limits of precedent. The correct principle must cover the argument's claim that a precedent should not apply when conditions that justified it no longer exist. Distractors include plausible legal principles that don't match the specific structure.
lr.stimulus: Legal Scholar: A court recently invoked a nineteenth-century precedent to deny liability in a case involving an online platform's role in spreading harmful misinformation. That ruling was wrong. The precedent was established to protect publishers who exercised no control over independently produced content. Today's platforms, however, actively curate and algorithmically amplify content, exercising far greater control than any traditional publisher.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the legal scholar's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Courts should not apply legal precedents established before the advent of modern technology to cases that involve digital platforms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal precedent should not be applied to a case when the factual conditions that originally justified that precedent no longer obtain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Entities that profit from the distribution of harmful content bear legal liability for the harms that content causes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Courts have an obligation to update legal precedents whenever advances in technology have made those precedents obsolete.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Legal liability for misinformation should depend on whether the entity disseminating it knew the content was false.

explanations.correct: The scholar's argument is that the precedent was justified by a specific factual condition — lack of editorial control — which no longer holds. Principle B — a precedent shouldn't apply when the conditions that justified it no longer exist — directly licenses that argument.
explanations.A: The scholar's objection is not that the precedent is old or that digital platforms are categorically different, but that the specific justifying condition (no editorial control) is absent. Too narrow and misidentifies the basis of the argument.
explanations.B: Correct. This principle precisely captures the scholar's reasoning: the precedent applied when publishers had no control; platforms now have extensive control, so the condition is gone.
explanations.C: The scholar does not argue that profiting from harmful content is the criterion for liability. This introduces a different standard not found in the argument. Tangential principle trap.
explanations.D: The scholar argues this precedent shouldn't apply in this case, not that courts must update all outdated precedents. Too broad trap.
explanations.E: The scholar does not address the knowledge condition for liability; the argument concerns editorial control and the basis for the precedent. Principle–premise mismatch.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics argument about when deception in art is permissible. Correct principle must capture the relationship between disclosure of artistic intent and permissibility of staged content. Distractors invoke related artistic freedom or honesty principles that miss the argument's hinge.
lr.stimulus: Art Critic: A documentary filmmaker secretly staged several scenes — depicting them as spontaneous — without informing viewers. Even though the staged scenes conveyed truths about the subjects' lives, this practice was wrong. Audiences consented to watch a documentary, a genre whose value rests on the representation of unscripted reality.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the art critic's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Filmmakers who stage scenes in documentaries should always disclose which scenes were staged in the film's credits.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Artistic expression is permissible only when the artist does not misrepresent the factual content of the work.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deceiving an audience is wrong when the audience's consent to engage with a work depends on a representation about that work's nature that the creator knowingly violates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Documentary filmmakers have an absolute obligation to present only footage that was captured without any directorial intervention.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The moral value of an artwork is determined primarily by whether it conveys accurate truths about its subject matter.

explanations.correct: The critic's argument hinges on the audience having consented to watch a documentary — a genre premised on unscripted reality — and the filmmaker violating that premise by secretly staging scenes. Principle C captures this: deception is wrong when it violates a representation about the work's nature on which audience consent was based.
explanations.A: The critic does not argue that post-hoc disclosure in credits would remedy the wrong; the objection is to the act of secret staging itself. Too narrow trap.
explanations.B: The critic does not claim the staged scenes were factually inaccurate; they are said to convey truths. This principle would actually favor the filmmaker. Reversed trap.
explanations.C: Correct. The principle covers both the consent element and the violated representation about genre, which is exactly the structure of the critic's argument.
explanations.D: 'Absolute obligation' and 'any directorial intervention' are stronger than what the critic claims, and the critic's argument is specifically about deception of audience, not about directorial purity. Too broad trap.
explanations.E: The critic explicitly concedes the staged scenes conveyed truths, so a principle about truth-telling cannot explain why the practice was wrong. Principle–premise mismatch.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology policy argument about algorithmic accountability. Correct principle must license the normative claim that opacity in automated decisions is impermissible when individuals are adversely affected. Distractors use adjacent tech-ethics language but address different concerns.
lr.stimulus: Policy Analyst: Several government agencies now use automated algorithms to make decisions about citizens' eligibility for social benefits, yet these agencies refuse to disclose how the algorithms work. This practice is unacceptable. When an automated system determines that a person is ineligible for support they need, that person has no way to identify or challenge any errors in the decision.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the policy analyst's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Government agencies should prefer human decision-makers over automated systems whenever the decisions affect individuals' access to public resources.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Automated systems used by governments should be tested for bias against protected demographic groups before deployment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A decision-making process that prevents affected individuals from identifying and contesting errors is unacceptable in contexts where those individuals stand to be significantly harmed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transparency in government operations is a fundamental requirement of democratic governance, regardless of the nature of the decisions being made.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Individuals should not be denied access to social benefits unless their ineligibility has been confirmed by at least two independent assessments.

explanations.correct: The analyst's argument is that opacity prevents error detection and challenge by affected individuals, making the practice unacceptable. Principle C — a process that blocks error identification and contestation is unacceptable when significant harm is at stake — directly licenses this conclusion.
explanations.A: The analyst does not argue that automated systems are categorically inferior to human decision-makers; the concern is specifically about opacity and inability to challenge errors. Tangential principle trap.
explanations.B: Bias testing addresses a different concern (demographic fairness at design) rather than the specific problem of opacity preventing individual error challenges. Principle–premise mismatch.
explanations.C: Correct. This principle covers all the structural elements of the argument: inability to identify and challenge errors, and the significant harm of losing needed support.
explanations.D: Democratic governance transparency is too broad a principle — it would apply regardless of harm potential, whereas the analyst's argument is grounded in the specific harm to affected individuals. Too broad trap.
explanations.E: The analyst does not call for a dual-confirmation standard; the argument is about the right to understand and challenge decisions. Principle–premise mismatch.

lr.difficultyReason: History argument about attributing responsibility across generations. Correct principle must license the specific normative claim about inherited institutional benefit and current obligation, without covering too much or too little.
lr.stimulus: Historian: A contemporary university continues to occupy land that was seized from indigenous communities through documented fraudulent transactions in the nineteenth century. University administrators argue they bear no responsibility because they did not personally participate in the original seizure. This argument is unpersuasive. The university as an institution has continuously benefited from and built upon those fraudulent transactions for over a century.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the historian's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Institutions that were founded using unjust means are morally obligated to dissolve and transfer their assets to the wronged parties.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An institution bears responsibility for a historical wrong when it has continuously derived benefits from that wrong, even if its current members were not party to it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Current administrators of an institution inherit both the achievements and the obligations incurred by their predecessors in the same role.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fraudulent transactions that dispossessed communities of land should be voided and the land returned regardless of how much time has passed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A party cannot evade moral responsibility for a harmful outcome by claiming ignorance of the circumstances that produced it.

explanations.correct: The historian's argument is that the university's continuous benefit from the fraudulent transactions — not personal participation — is what grounds current institutional responsibility. Principle B captures this precisely: an institution that has continuously benefited from a historical wrong bears responsibility for it.
explanations.A: The historian argues that the administrators' defense is unpersuasive, not that the institution must dissolve or transfer assets. This goes further than the historian's conclusion. Too broad trap.
explanations.B: Correct. This principle directly addresses institutional (not individual) responsibility and grounds it in continuous benefit rather than personal participation — exactly the structure of the historian's argument.
explanations.C: The historian's target is the institution, not individual administrators; this principle focuses on personal role succession rather than institutional benefit. Principle–premise mismatch.
explanations.D: The historian does not argue that the land must be returned; the argument is only that the administrators' defense is unpersuasive. Too broad trap.
explanations.E: The administrators claim they were not participants, not that they were ignorant; ignorance is not the basis of the defense the historian is refuting. Principle–premise mismatch.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics argument about the appropriate basis for prescriptive language rules. Correct principle licenses the claim that usage patterns of speakers — not tradition — should determine correct grammar. Distractors invoke related but distinct claims about language authority.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Many style guides still classify the construction 'they' as a singular pronoun to be incorrect, citing centuries of grammatical tradition. But these guides are wrong to prohibit this usage. The construction has been in continuous use by native speakers of English for over four centuries and is now nearly universal in everyday speech.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the linguist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Language rules established by non-native speakers of a language have no legitimate authority over the usage of native speakers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A grammatical prescription is unjustified when it prohibits a construction that has been consistently and broadly used by the speakers of that language.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The correct criterion for evaluating language is clarity of communication, not conformity to historical tradition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Style guides should adopt only those grammatical rules that have been validated by formal linguistic research.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No form of language use should be classified as incorrect if it serves the communicative purposes of the speakers who use it.

explanations.correct: The linguist argues that prohibiting a construction that has been consistently and broadly used by native speakers for centuries is unjustified. Principle B — a prescription is unjustified when it prohibits a consistently and broadly used construction — directly licenses this conclusion.
explanations.A: The linguist does not identify who created the style guides or whether they are native speakers; the objection is about usage patterns, not the identity of rule-makers. Tangential principle trap.
explanations.B: Correct. This principle captures the two key elements of the linguist's evidence — consistency of use and breadth — and directly links them to the conclusion that the prohibition is unjustified.
explanations.C: The linguist's argument rests on usage patterns, not on the clarity of the construction. This principle introduces a different criterion not found in the argument. Principle–premise mismatch.
explanations.D: The linguist does not argue for a research-validation standard; the argument is about actual speaker usage. Principle–premise mismatch.
explanations.E: This is too broad — it would prohibit classifying any usage as incorrect if it serves communicative purposes, a much stronger position than the linguist's, which is grounded in the specific evidence of four centuries of broad use. Too broad trap.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy argument about the permissibility of restricting one group's activity to benefit another. Correct principle must capture the relationship between demonstrated harm to others and justified restriction of liberty. Distractors invoke vague balancing tests or unrelated policy goals.
lr.stimulus: Urban Planner: A city ordinance that restricts short-term rental platforms in residential neighborhoods is justified. Residents of these neighborhoods have documented that the proliferation of short-term rentals has driven up rents and displaced long-term tenants, undermining the residential character of the areas where they have built their lives.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the urban planner's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Municipal governments are entitled to regulate economic activity within their jurisdictions whenever doing so increases local tax revenue.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The freedom to conduct a commercial activity may be legitimately restricted when that activity has been shown to harm others who depend on the affected resource.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Residential neighborhoods should be protected from commercial development in order to preserve the architectural character of cities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Economic activities that displace vulnerable populations are morally impermissible and should be prohibited by law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Government regulations are justified only when they impose the minimum restrictions necessary to achieve a compelling public interest.

explanations.correct: The planner's argument is that short-term rentals have demonstrably harmed long-term residents who depend on the housing resource, justifying restriction of that commercial activity. Principle B — commercial freedom may be restricted when activity harms others who depend on the resource — directly licenses this conclusion.
explanations.A: The planner's argument is grounded in harm to residents, not in tax revenue. Introducing a revenue rationale misidentifies the argument's basis. Tangential principle trap.
explanations.B: Correct. This principle covers demonstrated harm ('has been shown to harm'), the identity of those harmed ('others who depend on the affected resource'), and the permissibility of restriction — matching the argument's structure precisely.
explanations.C: The planner's concern is about rent displacement and loss of residential character in the social sense, not architectural preservation. Tangential principle trap.
explanations.D: 'Vulnerable populations' is not specified by the planner, and 'morally impermissible and should be prohibited by law' is a stronger conclusion than the planner draws. Too broad trap.
explanations.E: The minimum-restriction standard adds a condition not present in the planner's argument; the planner argues only that the restriction is justified, not that it is the least restrictive option. Principle–premise mismatch.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics argument about promise-keeping when circumstances have materially changed. Correct principle must license the specific claim that a promise does not bind when fulfilling it would produce harms the promisee could not have foreseen and would not have intended. Distractors exploit general promise-keeping language.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: A person promised a close friend that she would manage the friend's financial affairs if the friend ever became incapacitated. The friend is now incapacitated, but the financial affairs have grown far more complex than either party could have anticipated, and managing them would require the person to commit serious professional ethics violations. The person is not morally obligated to keep this promise.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promises made informally between friends carry less moral weight than those made in official or contractual contexts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A person is not bound by a promise when fulfilling it would require actions that are themselves morally impermissible.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Promises made in anticipation of future circumstances become void when those circumstances do not materialize as expected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Moral obligations to friends are always secondary to one's professional duties and obligations to employers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No one can be held to a promise made on the basis of information that later turns out to have been incomplete.

explanations.correct: The ethicist's core claim is that the person cannot be obligated to keep the promise because doing so would require committing serious professional ethics violations — actions that are themselves morally impermissible. Principle B — a promise does not bind when fulfillment requires morally impermissible actions — directly licenses this conclusion.
explanations.A: The ethicist does not argue that the promise's informality diminishes its force; the argument is about the impermissibility of what fulfillment would require. Tangential principle trap.
explanations.B: Correct. This principle states precisely the condition the ethicist relies on: the required action (ethics violations) is itself morally impermissible, which releases the promisor from obligation.
explanations.C: The ethicist does not argue that the circumstances failed to materialize — the friend is indeed incapacitated as contemplated. The problem is the unforeseen complexity requiring ethics violations. Principle–premise mismatch.
explanations.D: The ethicist does not invoke a general hierarchy between friendship and professional duties; the specific concern is that keeping the promise requires acting unethically. Too broad and misidentifies the argument's structure.
explanations.E: This principle would release anyone from any promise made on incomplete information — a far broader condition than the ethicist argues, which is specifically tied to moral impermissibility of the required action. Too broad trap.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument turns on a specific normative claim about individual consent versus aggregate benefit. Distractors include a plausible but over-broad utilitarian principle and a reversed principle about institutional authority.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: A hospital recently enrolled terminally ill patients in a drug trial without obtaining each patient's individual consent, arguing that the aggregate benefit to future patients outweighs the inconvenience of the consent process. But this practice is indefensible. A patient's willingness to accept risk is a matter of that patient's own values and circumstances, not a calculation that administrators can make on the patient's behalf.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medical institutions should prioritize treatments that produce the greatest benefit for the largest number of patients.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether a person may be subjected to medical risk is determined by that person's own assessment of their situation, not by the collective judgment of others.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Administrators who make decisions on behalf of patients are obligated to act in those patients' best medical interests.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients who participate in drug trials should be compensated for the risks they bear.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The benefits that research produces for society cannot justify the harm that research causes to individual participants.

explanations.correct: The ethicist's argument hinges on the claim that individual risk-tolerance is personal and cannot be substituted by administrative calculation. Principle B — that subjection to medical risk is determined by one's own assessment, not collective judgment — directly licenses this critique of the hospital's consent-bypassing practice.
explanations.A: Too broad and reversed: this utilitarian principle would actually support the hospital's rationale, not the ethicist's critique.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Tangential: 'best medical interests' shifts the subject to clinical outcomes, not individual autonomy over risk — the ethicist's actual concern.
explanations.D: Too narrow: compensation addresses a consequence of participation, not the threshold question of whether enrollment without consent is permissible.
