choices.text: It is a general economic principle cited to explain why the survey findings are reliable.

explanations.correct: The claim is supported by the survey data (households cite job-security concerns even at low rates) and itself supports the 'consequently' conclusion that rate cuts are the wrong instrument. It is a textbook intermediate conclusion.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is introduced by 'consequently' and concerns policy (rate cuts as wrong instrument). Treating the spending-determinant claim as the main conclusion misreads the argument's architecture — this is the 'confuses intermediate with main conclusion' trap.
explanations.B: The claim is explicitly supported by the survey evidence, so it is not unsupported. This is the 'accurate content, wrong function' trap.
explanations.D: The claim does not concede anything to the view that interest rates matter; it directly contradicts that view using evidence. There is no subsequent reversal — this is the 'opposing view confusion' trap.
explanations.E: The claim does not explain why the survey findings are reliable; causally the survey findings explain the claim, not the reverse.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: An ethics argument about whistleblower protection uses a three-step inferential chain. The intermediate conclusion — that employees who disclose organizational wrongdoing act in the public interest — is supported by a premise about democratic accountability and itself supports the main conclusion about legal protection. Trap choices isolate only one of its two roles.
lr.stimulus: Democratic accountability requires that citizens have access to accurate information about the conduct of powerful institutions. Employees who disclose organizational wrongdoing are often the only available source of such information; hence, they act in the public interest when they make such disclosures. It follows that employees who disclose organizational wrongdoing in good faith deserve robust legal protection from retaliation.
lr.questionStem: The claim that employees who disclose organizational wrongdoing act in the public interest plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument, supported by the claims about democratic accountability and the uniqueness of employee disclosures as information sources.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a premise offered directly in support of the main conclusion, and no support is given for it in the argument.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is an opposing view that the argument ultimately rejects in favor of a narrower conception of employee obligations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a conclusion supported by evidence about democratic accountability and employees' unique informational role, and it is itself used to support the conclusion about legal protection.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is background context that motivates the argument without functioning as a logical step in the inferential chain.

explanations.correct: The claim follows ('hence') from the premises about democratic accountability and employees' unique role as information sources, and it then licenses ('it follows that') the main conclusion about legal protection. It is an intermediate conclusion, and D accurately captures both its supported and supporting functions.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is about legal protection, introduced by 'it follows that.' Treating the public-interest claim as the main conclusion is the 'confuses intermediate with main conclusion' trap.
explanations.B: The claim is supported within the argument by two preceding premises, so it cannot be characterized as unsupported — this is the 'partial function' trap.
explanations.C: The argument nowhere treats this claim as an opposing view; it affirmatively defends it. This is the 'opposing view confusion' trap.
explanations.E: The claim does operative logical work as an intermediate step; calling it mere background misclassifies its function — this is the 'background vs. support' trap.
explanations.D: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: An environmental science argument about carbon sequestration features a two-level inferential chain. The intermediate conclusion — that peatland degradation is releasing sequestered carbon faster than forests can absorb it — is supported by comparative flux data and supports the main conclusion that wetland preservation must take priority over reforestation in climate policy.
lr.stimulus: Measurements of carbon flux show that degraded peatlands emit roughly ten times more carbon per hectare annually than equivalent areas of temperate forest absorb. Given these figures, peatland degradation is releasing sequestered carbon faster than reforestation efforts can compensate. Therefore, climate policy that prioritizes new tree planting over peatland preservation is systematically misdirected.
lr.questionStem: The claim that peatland degradation is releasing sequestered carbon faster than reforestation efforts can compensate plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a premise offered in support of the main conclusion, with no inferential support provided for it within the argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument, for which the carbon-flux measurements serve as evidence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a conclusion drawn from carbon-flux data, and it functions as the key premise supporting the main conclusion about policy priorities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a concession acknowledging the limits of peatland preservation that the argument then reframes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is contextual information explaining what carbon sequestration is, rather than a logically operative claim.

explanations.correct: The claim is supported by the carbon-flux measurement data ('given these figures') and then supports the 'therefore' conclusion about policy. Both functions are captured by C, identifying it as an intermediate conclusion.
explanations.A: The argument does provide inferential support for the claim (the flux measurements). Calling it an unsupported premise is the 'partial function' trap — it misses the conclusion role.
explanations.B: The main conclusion is the policy claim introduced by 'therefore.' Treating this as the main conclusion is the 'confuses intermediate with main conclusion' trap.
explanations.D: No concession structure exists here; the argument never acknowledges a contrary view about peatland preservation. This is the 'opposing view confusion' trap.
explanations.E: The claim is not definitional background; it is a substantive inferential step. This is the 'background vs. support' trap.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: A technology argument about algorithmic content moderation uses a three-step chain. The intermediate conclusion — that automated moderation systems cannot reliably distinguish political satire from sincere incitement — is supported by empirical error-rate data and used to support the main conclusion that platforms should not rely solely on automated moderation for political content.
lr.stimulus: Error-rate analyses of major platforms' automated moderation systems show that these systems misclassify satirical political content as incitement at rates exceeding forty percent. Automated moderation systems therefore cannot reliably distinguish political satire from sincere incitement. Platforms that rely exclusively on such systems for political content thus risk systematically suppressing protected speech, which means they must incorporate human review for any content flagged in political categories.
lr.questionStem: The claim that automated moderation systems cannot reliably distinguish political satire from sincere incitement plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument, for which the error-rate analysis and the risk of suppressing protected speech both serve as support.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a conclusion supported by error-rate data, and it in turn supports the conclusion that platforms risk suppressing protected speech, which itself supports the main conclusion about human review.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a premise offered directly in support of the main conclusion, with no inferential basis provided for it within the argument.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a position the argument attributes to critics of automated moderation but does not itself endorse.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is background context about the technical limitations of machine learning, introduced to frame the subsequent policy recommendation.

explanations.correct: The argument is a three-step chain: error-rate data → (intermediate 1) automated systems cannot reliably distinguish satire from incitement → (intermediate 2) platforms risk suppressing protected speech → (main conclusion) platforms must incorporate human review. The target claim is the first intermediate conclusion, supported by data and supporting the next link. B captures this.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the requirement for human review. The target claim is an intermediate step, not the endpoint — this is the 'confuses intermediate with main conclusion' trap.
explanations.C: The error-rate data provides inferential support for the target claim, so it is not unsupported — this is the 'partial function' trap.
explanations.D: The argument endorses this claim; it does not attribute it to critics. This is the 'opposing view confusion' trap.
explanations.E: The claim does operative inferential work; it is not mere framing background — this is the 'background vs. support' trap.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: A linguistics argument about language extinction turns on an intermediate conclusion — that the loss of a language entails the loss of irreplaceable conceptual distinctions encoded in it — which is derived from fieldwork evidence and used to support the main conclusion that language preservation warrants dedicated institutional funding.
lr.stimulus: Linguistic fieldwork consistently documents that many endangered languages encode spatial, temporal, and kinship distinctions for which no equivalent expressions exist in dominant languages. The loss of such a language therefore entails the loss of irreplaceable conceptual distinctions that cannot be reconstructed from surviving records. Accordingly, language preservation programs deserve the same category of institutional support that is routinely granted to the preservation of unique biological species.
lr.questionStem: The claim that the loss of such a language entails the loss of irreplaceable conceptual distinctions plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument, supported by the fieldwork findings about untranslatable distinctions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a premise offered directly in support of the main conclusion, for which no support is provided in the argument.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a conclusion the argument draws from fieldwork evidence, and it functions as the premise supporting the institutional-funding conclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a view the argument concedes to critics of language preservation before rebutting it with the fieldwork data.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a general principle used to evaluate competing claims about the relative merits of biological versus linguistic preservation.

explanations.correct: The claim follows ('therefore') from the fieldwork evidence about untranslatable distinctions and itself supports ('accordingly') the main conclusion about institutional funding. C correctly identifies both its supported and supporting functions — it is an intermediate conclusion.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the institutional-funding claim, introduced by 'accordingly.' The target claim is an intermediate step — this is the 'confuses intermediate with main conclusion' trap.
explanations.B: The fieldwork evidence does support the target claim within the argument, so calling it unsupported is the 'partial function' trap.
explanations.D: No concession-rebuttal structure exists; the argument never attributes this claim to critics. This is the 'opposing view confusion' trap.
explanations.E: The claim is not a general evaluative principle; it is a specific empirical-inferential step about what language loss entails. This is the 'accurate content, wrong function' trap.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: A history argument about the decline of the Roman Western Empire uses a two-level inferential chain. The intermediate conclusion — that the economic contraction of the third century fundamentally weakened the empire's capacity to field professional armies — is drawn from fiscal evidence and used to support the main conclusion that military overextension alone cannot explain the empire's collapse.
lr.stimulus: Papyrological records from the third century CE document a severe contraction in tax revenues collected across western provinces, coinciding with currency debasement and a collapse of long-distance trade networks. This economic contraction fundamentally weakened the empire's capacity to fund and sustain professional armies along its borders. Attributing Rome's eventual collapse solely to military overextension therefore ignores the deeper fiscal deterioration that had already undermined the very instrument of that military capacity.
lr.questionStem: The claim that the economic contraction fundamentally weakened the empire's capacity to fund and sustain professional armies plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument, for which the papyrological records and the critique of military overextension accounts both serve as evidence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a premise for which no support is offered in the argument, used to refute the military-overextension explanation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a conclusion supported by the fiscal evidence, and it is itself used to support the main conclusion that military overextension alone cannot explain Rome's collapse.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a concession the argument makes to proponents of the military-overextension thesis before arguing that both factors are equally important.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is background historical context establishing the chronological setting for the main argument.

explanations.correct: The papyrological fiscal evidence supports the target claim, and the target claim then supports ('therefore') the main conclusion that military overextension alone is insufficient as an explanation. C captures both inferential roles correctly.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the anti-reductionist thesis about military overextension, introduced by 'therefore.' The target claim is an intermediate step — this is the 'confuses intermediate with main conclusion' trap.
explanations.B: The papyrological records provide explicit support for the target claim within the argument, so it is not unsupported — this is the 'partial function' trap.
explanations.D: The argument does not concede that military overextension is equally important; it argues fiscal factors are the deeper cause. This is the 'opposing view confusion' trap.
explanations.E: The claim is not mere chronological context; it does substantive inferential work as the intermediate conclusion — this is the 'background vs. support' trap.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: A law argument about prosecutorial disclosure obligations features a two-level chain. The intermediate conclusion — that withholding forensic evidence favorable to the defense compromises the fairness of criminal proceedings — is derived from due-process principles and used to support the main conclusion that courts should impose automatic reversals when such evidence is concealed.
lr.stimulus: Due process requires that criminal proceedings be genuinely adversarial, which in turn demands that each side have meaningful access to the evidence bearing on guilt or innocence. When prosecutors withhold forensic evidence favorable to the defense, that requirement is violated, and the fairness of the proceedings is fundamentally compromised. Courts should therefore treat such concealment as grounds for automatic reversal of any conviction obtained in those proceedings, without requiring the defendant to demonstrate prejudice from the specific omission.
lr.questionStem: The claim that the fairness of the proceedings is fundamentally compromised plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument, supported by the due-process principle and the observation that prosecutorial concealment violates adversarial requirements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a conclusion drawn from due-process principles and the violation of adversarial requirements, and it supports the main conclusion that courts should impose automatic reversals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is an unsupported premise the argument assumes in order to justify automatic reversals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a view endorsed by critics of prosecutorial misconduct rules that the argument evaluates but ultimately finds insufficient.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a general legal principle invoked to clarify what due process requires, rather than a substantive inferential step.

explanations.correct: The target claim follows from the due-process principle and the observation that adversarial requirements are violated when evidence is withheld. It then supports ('therefore') the main conclusion about automatic reversals. B correctly identifies it as an intermediate conclusion serving both functions.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the automatic-reversal rule, introduced by 'therefore.' The target claim is an intermediate step — this is the 'confuses intermediate with main conclusion' trap.
explanations.C: The due-process principle and the adversarial-requirement violation provide support for the target claim; it is not unsupported — this is the 'partial function' trap.
explanations.D: The argument does not attribute this claim to critics; it affirmatively asserts it. This is the 'opposing view confusion' trap.
explanations.E: The claim is not merely clarifying what due process requires; it is a substantive conclusion about the effects of prosecutorial concealment — this is the 'accurate content, wrong function' trap.
explanations.B: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: An arts-policy argument about public funding for experimental theater uses a three-step chain. The intermediate conclusion — that experimental theater generates aesthetic innovations later adopted by commercial productions — is supported by historical examples and used to support the main conclusion that public funding for experimental theater produces broad cultural benefits, not merely niche ones.
lr.stimulus: Historical records show that staging techniques now standard in commercial theater — including thrust stages, non-realistic lighting, and ensemble-devised scripts — were pioneered by publicly funded experimental companies in the mid-twentieth century. Experimental theater thus generates aesthetic innovations that commercial productions eventually adopt and disseminate to broad audiences. Public funding for experimental theater therefore produces cultural benefits far beyond the small audiences who attend experimental performances directly, and this breadth of benefit justifies substantial public subsidy.
lr.questionStem: The claim that experimental theater generates aesthetic innovations that commercial productions eventually adopt and disseminate to broad audiences plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument, supported by the historical examples of staging techniques and by the claim about the breadth of cultural benefits.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a premise offered in support of the main conclusion, for which no evidence or support is provided within the argument.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a conclusion drawn from the historical record of staging techniques, and it is used to support the main conclusion that public funding produces broad cultural benefits justifying subsidy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a position the argument attributes to advocates of commercial theater and then appropriates to support arts funding.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a concession to the view that experimental theater has limited direct audience reach, which the argument then reframes as an advantage.

explanations.correct: The historical staging-technique examples support ('thus') the target claim, and the target claim then supports ('therefore') the main conclusion about breadth of cultural benefit justifying subsidy. C correctly identifies both its supported and supporting functions as an intermediate conclusion.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the justification for substantial public subsidy, introduced by 'therefore.' The target claim is an intermediate step — this is the 'confuses intermediate with main conclusion' trap.
explanations.B: The historical records do provide support for the target claim; it is not unsupported — this is the 'partial function' trap.
explanations.D: The argument does not attribute the claim to advocates of commercial theater; it derives it from historical evidence. This is the 'opposing view confusion' trap.
explanations.E: No concession about limited direct audiences is made in the argument's structure; the target claim is not a reframed concession — this is the 'opposing view confusion' trap.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: A policy argument about urban heat-island mitigation uses a two-level inferential chain. The intermediate conclusion — that dark impervious surfaces in dense urban areas absorb and retain heat in ways that significantly elevate local temperatures — is drawn from thermal imaging data and used to support the main conclusion that municipal building codes should mandate reflective roofing materials.
lr.stimulus: Thermal imaging surveys of major cities consistently show that surface temperatures in densely built neighborhoods exceed those of surrounding rural areas by as much as eight degrees Celsius, even when ambient weather conditions are identical. Dark impervious surfaces in such neighborhoods absorb and retain heat in ways that significantly elevate local temperatures — a finding that directly follows from the thermal imaging data. Municipal building codes should therefore mandate reflective roofing and paving materials in high-density zones, since doing so would reduce the heat retention responsible for these dangerous temperature differentials.
lr.questionStem: The claim that dark impervious surfaces in such neighborhoods absorb and retain heat in ways that significantly elevate local temperatures plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a premise offered directly in support of the main conclusion about building codes, with no supporting evidence provided for it in the argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument, for which the thermal imaging data and the policy recommendation both serve as evidence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a concession to urban planners who dispute the degree to which surface materials affect local temperatures, which the argument then rebuts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a conclusion supported by the thermal imaging data, and it serves as the key premise supporting the main conclusion that building codes should mandate reflective materials.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is background scientific information explaining the urban heat-island phenomenon, offered to orient the reader rather than to support any specific policy claim.

explanations.correct: The argument states that the heat-absorption claim 'directly follows from the thermal imaging data,' establishing its supported role. It then underlies ('therefore') the mandate for reflective materials, establishing its supporting role. D correctly identifies it as an intermediate conclusion serving both functions.
explanations.A: The thermal imaging data explicitly supports the target claim within the argument, so it is not unsupported — this is the 'partial function' trap.
explanations.B: The main conclusion is the building-code mandate, introduced by 'therefore.' The target claim is an intermediate step — this is the 'confuses intermediate with main conclusion' trap.
explanations.C: No concession-rebuttal structure involving urban planners exists; the argument presents this as an affirmative finding. This is the 'opposing view confusion' trap.
explanations.E: The claim does operative inferential work connecting the data to the policy conclusion; it is not mere background orientation — this is the 'background vs. support' trap.
explanations.D: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument has a two-level chain: empirical evidence supports an intermediate conclusion (that urban heat island effects are driven primarily by surface albedo changes), which in turn supports the main conclusion (that reflective roofing mandates are the most cost-effective climate intervention for cities). The target claim is the intermediate conclusion, and two trap choices partially describe its function — one calls it a premise only, another calls it the main conclusion — requiring test-takers to recognize it simultaneously serves both roles.
lr.stimulus: Cities seeking to reduce their contributions to climate change often weigh a wide range of interventions, from expanded transit systems to building electrification. Measurements taken across dozens of metropolitan areas confirm that localized temperature increases of up to 4°C above surrounding rural areas are overwhelmingly attributable to reduced surface reflectivity rather than to waste heat from machinery or vehicles. Therefore, surface albedo is the dominant driver of urban thermal loading — a finding that, in turn, establishes that mandating highly reflective roofing materials is the most cost-effective climate intervention available to municipal governments, since albedo modification requires no ongoing energy expenditure and can be implemented through existing building codes.
lr.questionStem: The claim that surface albedo is the dominant driver of urban thermal loading plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the argument's main conclusion, supported by measurements taken across metropolitan areas.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a premise offered directly in support of the claim that cities should weigh a wide range of climate interventions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a conclusion drawn from empirical evidence and used in turn to support the argument's main conclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is background information establishing the context within which the argument's main conclusion is to be understood.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a position the argument is designed to discredit by appealing to measurements from metropolitan areas.

explanations.correct: The claim is explicitly flagged by 'Therefore' as a conclusion drawn from the metropolitan measurement data. It then functions as a premise — signaled by 'a finding that, in turn, establishes' — supporting the main conclusion that reflective roofing mandates are the most cost-effective intervention. This dual function (supported conclusion + supporting premise) defines an intermediate conclusion, exactly what C describes.
explanations.A: This is the partial-function trap. The claim is indeed supported by empirical data, but it is not where the argument stops — the author uses it to establish a further conclusion about roofing mandates. Calling it the main conclusion ignores its supporting role in the argument's second inferential step.
explanations.B: The claim does not support the opening observation about cities weighing interventions; that sentence is scene-setting context. The target claim supports the specific recommendation about reflective roofing, not the general framing remark.
explanations.D: Background information does not carry inferential weight — it neither follows from evidence nor supports a conclusion. The target claim does both, so labeling it mere background misidentifies its structural role entirely.
explanations.E: The target claim is not a position the author is attacking; it is a position the author is asserting and using. The measurements support this claim rather than refute it. This choice confuses the author's own intermediate conclusion with an opposing view.
explanations.C: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus contains a three-part inferential chain in a legal-policy domain. The target claim — that jurors who deliberate longer reach verdicts better aligned with evidentiary weight — is an intermediate conclusion supported by comparative trial data and itself supports the main conclusion that voir dire should screen for deliberative patience. Two trap answers capture only one of the target claim's two inferential roles, and a third trap mislabels it as a concession.
lr.stimulus: Critics of jury reform proposals often argue that extended voir dire procedures waste court resources without improving verdict quality. However, the data tell a different story. Comparative analyses of trial outcomes show that juries composed of members who score highly on deliberative-patience assessments reach verdicts whose alignment with the weight of the presented evidence is measurably superior to those of juries lacking such members. It follows that jurors who deliberate longer and more carefully produce outcomes that more faithfully reflect the evidence — and this conclusion, once accepted, makes clear that voir dire screening for deliberative patience is a justified and efficient use of court resources, since it directly enhances the very purpose for which juries exist.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the statement that jurors who deliberate longer and more carefully produce outcomes that more faithfully reflect the evidence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a premise offered directly in support of the main conclusion, without itself being supported by any other claim in the argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the argument's main conclusion, for which the comparative analyses of trial outcomes serve as the sole support.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a claim the argument concedes to critics of jury reform before ultimately rejecting it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a conclusion supported by the comparative trial data and is itself used to support the claim that voir dire screening for deliberative patience is justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is background context that clarifies the meaning of deliberative patience without bearing directly on the argument's conclusion.

explanations.correct: The phrase 'It follows that' marks the target claim as a conclusion drawn from the comparative analyses of trial outcomes. Immediately after, 'this conclusion, once accepted, makes clear that' signals that the target claim then serves as a premise supporting the main conclusion about voir dire screening. D captures both inferential roles — supported by data, and itself supporting the main conclusion — which is the defining structure of an intermediate conclusion.
explanations.A: This is the partial-function trap. The target claim does support the main conclusion, but it is also itself supported by the comparative trial data (introduced by 'It follows that'). Saying it is offered 'without itself being supported by any other claim' is demonstrably false given the explicit 'It follows that' signal.
explanations.B: This is the main-conclusion confusion trap. The argument does not end with the target claim — it proceeds to a further conclusion about voir dire screening being justified. Treating the intermediate step as the destination ignores the argument's second inferential move.
explanations.C: The target claim is the author's own assertion, not a concession to critics. The critics' position — that extended voir dire wastes resources — is introduced in the first sentence and is the view the argument rebuts. The target claim is part of the rebuttal, not a concession.
explanations.E: The target claim is not definitional or contextual; it carries direct inferential weight, flowing from the data and flowing into the main conclusion. Background context plays no such role in an argument's logical chain.
explanations.D: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Single causal inference with one visible alternative — seasonal flu. Correct answer rules out the alternative; traps are irrelevant facts or strengthen a neighboring claim.
lr.stimulus: A hospital cafeteria switched from serving raw salad bar items to only cooked vegetables last March. In the three months that followed, reported cases of gastrointestinal illness among cafeteria regulars fell by nearly half compared with the same period the previous year. The cafeteria's dietitian concluded that eliminating the raw items was probably what caused the decline in illness.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the dietitian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rates of seasonal gastrointestinal illness in the surrounding community were roughly the same in both years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several cafeteria regulars said they preferred the variety offered by the old salad bar.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cafeteria's cooked vegetables are sourced from the same suppliers as the former raw items.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hospitals that maintain salad bars report higher patient satisfaction with food service.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gastrointestinal illness had been trending downward at the hospital for several years before the change.

explanations.correct: The obvious alternative is that a milder flu season in the community, not the menu change, explains the drop. (A) rules that alternative out by showing community rates were unchanged, leaving the cafeteria's switch as the more plausible cause.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — preferences don't speak to what caused illnesses to fall.
explanations.C: If anything, weakens by suggesting the supplier, not the raw/cooked distinction, would matter — but the relevant contamination risk is in raw handling, so this is at best neutral and does not strengthen.
explanations.D: Strengthens a different conclusion — about patient satisfaction, not about the cause of reduced illness.
explanations.E: Opposite answer — a pre-existing downward trend suggests the drop would have happened without the menu change.

lr.difficultyReason: Single causal inference about a charitable-giving norm. Correct answer closes the obvious analogical gap; traps include an accurate-but-irrelevant detail and an unwarranted comparison.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: A community foundation found that when donors were sent a handwritten thank-you note after their first gift, they were far more likely to give again the following year than donors who received only a printed acknowledgment. The foundation's director therefore recommends that every charity adopt handwritten notes to encourage repeat giving.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the director's recommendation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Handwritten notes cost more to produce than printed acknowledgments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Donors to the foundation gave, on average, larger first-time gifts than donors to peer organizations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The foundation's donors did not differ systematically from donors to other charities in age, income, or giving history.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some donors said they appreciated receiving any kind of acknowledgment after giving.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many large charities already use printed acknowledgments as their standard practice.

explanations.correct: The director generalizes from one foundation's donors to donors at every charity. (C) closes that analogical gap by ruling out the worry that foundation donors are an unusual sample, making the generalization more plausible.
explanations.A: Opposite answer — higher cost is a reason not to adopt the practice.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — first-gift size doesn't speak to whether handwritten notes drive repeat giving elsewhere.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — appreciating any acknowledgment doesn't distinguish handwritten from printed.
explanations.E: Unwarranted comparison — what other charities do now doesn't support the claim that switching would help them.

lr.difficultyReason: Single causal inference about a retail promotion. Correct answer rules out the only visible alternative (holiday traffic); traps include a disguised weakener and an accurate-but-irrelevant distractor.
lr.stimulus: The owner of a bookstore began offering a 10 percent discount to customers who signed up for a loyalty card. Over the next quarter, sales at the store rose by 15 percent compared with the same quarter the previous year. The owner concluded that the loyalty-card program was probably the main cause of the sales increase.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the owner's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Foot traffic at the mall housing the bookstore was nearly identical in both quarters.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A popular new novel was released during the quarter and sold well at the bookstore.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several competing bookstores in the area also run loyalty programs of their own.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Customers who signed up for the loyalty card most often bought paperback fiction.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The bookstore's profit margins were lower during the quarter of the discount than in the preceding quarter.

explanations.correct: The obvious alternative is that more shoppers were in the mall, driving sales regardless of the card. (A) rules that out, leaving the loyalty program as the better explanation for the sales bump.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Introduces an alternative cause — the new release, not the card, could explain the increase.
explanations.C: Unwarranted comparison — competitor programs don't bear on why this store's sales rose.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — what cardholders bought doesn't speak to whether the card caused the sales bump.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — margins address profitability, not what caused sales volume to rise.

lr.difficultyReason: Single causal inference about a legal deterrent. Correct answer rules out the visible alternative (police staffing); traps include a disguised weakener and a different-conclusion distractor.
lr.stimulus: After the city raised the fine for running a red light from $100 to $400, the number of red-light violations at monitored intersections fell by nearly a third in the following year. A traffic commissioner argued that the higher fine was probably what drove the decline.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most supports the commissioner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some drivers said they were unaware the fine had changed until they received a citation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The city added no additional traffic officers or cameras during the year in question.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fines for other moving violations, such as speeding, remained unchanged during the year.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pedestrian injuries at crosswalks near monitored intersections also decreased during the year.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neighboring cities with unchanged fines saw small increases in red-light violations over the same period.

explanations.correct: The natural alternative is that more enforcement — more officers or cameras — produced the drop. (B) rules that out, leaving the fine increase as the more plausible cause.
explanations.A: Opposite answer — if some drivers didn't know about the higher fine, the fine itself couldn't have deterred them, weakening the argument.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — unchanged fines for other violations don't speak to why red-light violations fell.
explanations.D: Strengthens a different conclusion — about pedestrian safety outcomes, not about what caused the drop in red-light violations.
explanations.E: At best weakly consistent; without a comparable baseline it doesn't rule out a confound and doesn't address why this city's drop occurred.

lr.difficultyReason: Single causal inference about a wetland restoration project. Correct answer rules out the visible alternative (regional weather); traps include a disguised weakener and an irrelevant fact.
lr.stimulus: Environmentalist: Three years ago, volunteers restored native plants along a two-mile stretch of Otter Creek. This spring, biologists counted more than twice as many nesting songbirds along that stretch as they had counted the year before the restoration. The restoration effort was probably responsible for the increase in nesting birds.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the environmentalist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Volunteers also removed trash from the creek bed during the restoration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Songbird populations in the surrounding region have held steady over the past decade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The restored plants are native to the creek's watershed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nearby Birch Creek, where no restoration has taken place, also saw a slight rise in nesting songbirds this spring.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some of the volunteers had no previous experience with ecological restoration.

explanations.correct: A natural alternative is that something regional — a favorable season, a weather pattern — caused songbird numbers to rise. (B) rules that out by showing regional populations were stable, leaving the restored stretch's doubling attributable to the restoration.
explanations.A: Introduces an alternative cause — trash removal, not replanting, might explain the increase.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — using native plants was part of the restoration, not something that distinguishes a causal explanation.
explanations.D: Weakens — if unrestored creeks also saw more nesting, something besides the restoration is likely at work.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — volunteer experience doesn't bear on whether the restoration caused the increase.

lr.difficultyReason: Single causal inference about a software change. Correct answer rules out the visible alternative (a separate performance upgrade); traps include an unwarranted comparison and an irrelevant fact.
lr.stimulus: After a video streaming service redesigned its homepage to recommend shows based on each viewer's watch history, the average length of a viewing session grew by roughly 20 percent. The company's product manager concluded that the new personalized recommendations were probably what caused viewers to watch longer.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the product manager's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The service's video playback speed and streaming quality were not changed during the period studied.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Competing streaming services have also begun experimenting with personalized recommendations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Viewers on the service tend to use mobile devices more often than televisions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some viewers reported that the new homepage looked visually more cluttered than the old one.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The service's catalog of available shows grew by roughly 30 percent during the same period.

explanations.correct: A plausible alternative is that faster playback or better streaming quality kept viewers watching longer. (A) rules that out, making the new recommendations the better-supported cause of the longer sessions.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Unwarranted comparison — what competitors are doing doesn't address why this service's sessions grew.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — device usage doesn't speak to what caused viewing times to increase.
explanations.D: If anything, weakens — a cluttered-looking homepage would be a reason viewers might watch less, not more.
explanations.E: Introduces an alternative cause — a larger catalog, not the recommendations, could explain longer sessions.

lr.difficultyReason: Single causal inference about a classroom intervention. Correct answer confirms a load-bearing mechanism; traps include an irrelevant fact and an answer that strengthens a different conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: A third-grade teacher introduced a daily 10-minute session in which students read aloud to a classmate. By the end of the term, students' scores on a standardized reading-comprehension test had risen well beyond the usual year-over-year gain. The teacher concluded that the read-aloud sessions were probably what improved her students' comprehension.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the teacher's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reading aloud to a peer has been shown to improve young readers' grasp of sentence structure and meaning.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Parents of students in the class reported that their children were excited about reading this year.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The teacher has more than a decade of experience teaching third grade.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Students in the class also showed improvement on the math portion of the standardized test.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Other third-grade classrooms at the same school did not adopt a read-aloud routine.

explanations.correct: The teacher's claim assumes that reading aloud actually does something to comprehension. (A) confirms that mechanism by linking the specific practice to comprehension gains, making it more likely that the sessions — not some other factor — drove the improvement.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — enthusiasm doesn't establish the causal link between the sessions and comprehension gains.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — teacher experience doesn't distinguish this year's intervention as the cause.
explanations.D: Strengthens a different conclusion — math gains point to a broader change, not specifically to read-aloud driving comprehension.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant on its own — without comparative data on those classrooms, the absence of the routine elsewhere tells us nothing.

lr.difficultyReason: Single causal inference about a historical shift. Correct answer rules out the visible alternative (climate); traps include an unwarranted comparison and an irrelevant fact.
lr.stimulus: Historian: In the decades after a new canal opened between two inland towns in the 1830s, grain shipments from the northern town rose fivefold. The northern town's farmers were already expanding production before the canal, but most historians now agree that the canal, rather than any prior trend, was probably the main driver of the shipping surge.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the historians' view?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Climate records show that growing-season weather in the region was similar before and after the canal's opening.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A later canal, built in a different region, also coincided with rising grain shipments.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The northern town's population roughly doubled during the decades after the canal opened.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Grain was the most valuable commodity shipped on the canal in its first decade of operation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The canal was financed in part by merchants from the southern town, who expected to benefit from trade.

explanations.correct: The salient alternative is that better growing weather, not the canal, produced the shipping surge. (A) rules that out by showing weather was similar, leaving the canal as the more plausible driver.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Unwarranted comparison — a different canal in a different region doesn't explain this town's surge.
explanations.C: Introduces an alternative cause — a doubling population could itself have expanded agricultural output and shipping.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — grain's share of canal shipments doesn't bear on why shipments grew.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — financing arrangements don't speak to what caused the subsequent rise in shipments.

lr.difficultyReason: Single causal inference about a housing policy. Correct answer rules out the visible alternative (general rental market); traps include a disguised weakener and a different-conclusion distractor.
lr.stimulus: The city council of Ambrose passed an ordinance last year limiting short-term vacation rentals to 90 nights a year. In the following twelve months, the number of long-term rental apartments listed in Ambrose rose by nearly 25 percent. A council member concluded that the ordinance was probably what drove the increase in long-term listings.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the council member's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In nearby cities that did not adopt such ordinances, the number of long-term rental listings stayed roughly flat over the same period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A new apartment building with more than 300 units opened in Ambrose two months before the ordinance took effect.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ambrose's median rent for long-term apartments rose during the year after the ordinance was passed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some short-term rental owners opposed the ordinance during public hearings.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The council is now considering further regulations on short-term rentals elsewhere in the city.

explanations.correct: A natural alternative is that long-term listings were rising everywhere for reasons unrelated to the ordinance. (A) rules that out: comparable cities without the ordinance saw no such rise, so the ordinance is the better-supported cause of the jump in Ambrose.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Introduces an alternative cause — a large new building could itself account for much of the 25 percent rise.
explanations.C: Strengthens a different conclusion — about rent levels, not about what caused the rise in long-term listings.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — opposition at hearings doesn't bear on whether the ordinance caused the listing increase.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — future regulatory plans don't speak to what caused the past year's change.

lr.difficultyReason: Single causal inference about a museum exhibit. Correct answer rules out the visible alternative (school-break traffic); traps include an unwarranted comparison and an accurate-but-irrelevant fact.
lr.stimulus: The Varro Museum of Modern Art opened a new interactive sculpture exhibit in October. Over the following three months, the museum's total visitor numbers were roughly 40 percent higher than during the same three months the year before. The museum's director concluded that the new exhibit was probably the main reason for the jump in visitors.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the director's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The school-holiday calendar in the Varro area was essentially the same during both three-month periods.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Museums in other cities that opened new interactive exhibits have also reported rising attendance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Varro Museum raised the price of general admission shortly before the exhibit opened.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many visitors to the new exhibit posted photographs of it on social media.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The museum hosted a highly publicized free-admission weekend during the three months in question.

explanations.correct: A natural alternative is that a longer or earlier school holiday drove more family visits during the later period. (A) rules that out, leaving the new exhibit as the more plausible driver of the 40 percent jump.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Unwarranted comparison — what other museums have experienced doesn't establish that this exhibit caused Varro's increase.
explanations.C: Opposite answer — a price increase, all else equal, would tend to depress visits, not raise them.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — social media activity doesn't distinguish the exhibit from other possible causes of the attendance rise.
explanations.E: Introduces an alternative cause — a free-admission weekend could itself account for a substantial share of the attendance bump.

lr.difficultyReason: Single causal inference with one visible alternative. Correct answer rules out the alternative explanation (bad weather) for increased crop yields.
lr.stimulus: Farmer Chen increased the amount of irrigation to her wheat fields this season. The wheat yield from her fields this year is significantly higher than last year. Chen concludes that the increased irrigation caused the higher yield.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Other farmers in the region also increased their wheat yields this year.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Weather conditions this year were generally similar to those of last year.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Wheat is one of the most common crops grown in the region.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased irrigation often requires significant upfront investment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Chen's fields were planted with the same wheat variety as in previous years.

explanations.correct: If weather conditions were similar between the two years, this rules out the alternative explanation that better weather caused the higher yield. Since the only major variable that changed was irrigation, the causal claim is strengthened.
explanations.A: Irrelevant — what other farmers did does not explain whether Chen's increased irrigation caused her higher yield.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — the commonality of wheat farming has no bearing on what caused Chen's yield increase.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — cost considerations do not address whether irrigation caused the yield increase.
explanations.E: Does not strengthen; if anything, it leaves open the question of whether yield would have increased anyway due to other factors.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple causal inference where the correct answer rules out a rival cause (laboratory contamination).
lr.stimulus: Researchers found elevated levels of a harmful bacteria in water samples from a coastal region. Since the region experienced an unusual algal bloom earlier this year, the researchers conclude that the algal bloom caused the bacterial increase.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Algal blooms typically last several months in coastal environments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Harmful bacteria can reduce the clarity of water in coastal regions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In nearby regions without algal blooms, water samples show no increase in harmful bacteria levels.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The researchers used standardized laboratory techniques for all water samples.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Algal blooms have occurred in this coastal region before this year.

explanations.correct: By showing that regions without algal blooms do not have bacterial increases, this rules out other environmental factors and strengthens the causal link between the bloom and the bacteria.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant — the duration of blooms does not explain causation.
explanations.B: Irrelevant — the relationship between bacteria and clarity does not address causation.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Addresses methodology but does not rule out an alternative cause for the bacterial increase.
explanations.E: Weakens if anything — if prior blooms did not cause bacterial increases, why would this one?

lr.difficultyReason: Direct causal claim with one alternative explanation. Correct answer confirms a load-bearing premise about the mechanism.
lr.stimulus: A pharmaceutical company introduced a new medication to treat insomnia. Sales of the medication increased sharply within the first month. The company concludes that patients found the medication to be effective.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to support the company's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The medication was aggressively advertised on television and in medical journals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients who used the medication reported improved sleep quality.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Insomnia affects millions of people in the country.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The medication is more expensive than competing insomnia treatments.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Previous insomnia medications on the market had limited side effects.

explanations.correct: By showing that patients actually experienced improved sleep, this directly supports the conclusion that effectiveness drove sales, rather than marketing or other factors.
explanations.A: Introduces an alternative explanation (advertising, not effectiveness) and thus weakens the argument.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — market size does not explain why this medication sold well.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — price does not explain effectiveness or sales.
explanations.E: Irrelevant — the side effects of previous medications have no bearing on this medication's effectiveness.

lr.difficultyReason: Single causal inference where the correct answer rules out a confounding variable (time).
lr.stimulus: A school introduced a new reading program. Students' reading scores improved significantly over the following academic year. School administrators conclude that the new program improved student reading performance.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Many schools in the country have adopted similar reading programs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The school's student population did not change significantly during the year.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Control schools that did not adopt the new program showed no significant improvement in reading scores.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reading is considered an essential skill by most educators.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The school had attempted other reading interventions in the past without success.

explanations.correct: By showing that schools without the new program did not improve, this rules out the alternative explanation that scores improved simply due to student maturation or general trends, thereby strengthening the causal claim.
explanations.A: Irrelevant — what other schools did does not prove this school's program worked.
explanations.B: Accurate but does not address whether the program caused the improvement.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — the importance of reading does not explain improvement.
explanations.E: Somewhat supportive but weaker than a direct control comparison; past failure doesn't prove current success caused the improvement.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple predictive argument where the correct answer confirms a key assumption about the mechanism linking the premise to the conclusion.
lr.stimulus: A technology company released a new smartphone with an innovative feature. Tech reviewers praised the feature in early reviews. The company predicts that the new smartphone will sell very well.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tech reviewers' opinions have strongly influenced consumer purchases in the smartphone market in the past.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The company spent millions on developing the innovative feature.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Smartphones are one of the most popular consumer electronics products.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many competing companies also offer smartphones with innovative features.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The company has a history of releasing products that appeal only to tech enthusiasts.

explanations.correct: By confirming that tech reviewers' praise historically translates to consumer purchases, this strengthens the link between the positive reviews and the predicted sales success.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — development cost does not predict sales success.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — market popularity does not explain this specific product's success.
explanations.D: Introduces a competitive threat and weakens the prediction.
explanations.E: Weakens if anything — a history of niche appeal contradicts the prediction of high sales.

lr.difficultyReason: Single causal inference where the correct answer rules out an alternative explanation (pre-existing health difference).
lr.stimulus: A fitness center claims that their new exercise program causes significant weight loss. They point out that members who completed the program lost an average of 15 pounds.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Weight loss is important for overall health.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Members who did not complete the program gained weight on average.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The exercise program is offered at multiple locations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Exercise programs are becoming increasingly popular nationwide.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many fitness centers offer similar weight-loss programs.

explanations.correct: By showing that non-completers gained weight, this rules out the alternative that participants would have lost weight anyway due to other lifestyle factors, strengthening the causal claim about the program.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant — the importance of weight loss does not prove the program causes it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Irrelevant — the number of locations does not prove efficacy.
explanations.D: Irrelevant — overall trends do not explain this program's effectiveness.
explanations.E: Introduces the idea that other programs exist but does not strengthen the causal claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward causal argument where the correct answer bridges a key assumption about how the cause produces the effect.
lr.stimulus: A museum installed brighter lighting in its ancient artifacts exhibit. Museum staff observed that visitor attendance in the exhibit increased by 20 percent. The museum concludes that the brighter lighting caused the increase in attendance.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Brighter lighting reduces eyestrain for visitors viewing artifacts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ancient artifacts are popular attractions in museums worldwide.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The lighting installation was completed during the summer tourist season.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Other exhibits in the museum also received new lighting installations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Attendance at other museums remained stable during the same period.

explanations.correct: By showing that the brighter lighting improves the visitor experience, this supports the mechanism by which lighting would cause increased attendance.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — popularity in general does not explain this specific lighting change.
explanations.C: Introduces a confounding variable (seasonal tourism) that weakens rather than strengthens.
explanations.D: Irrelevant — other exhibits' lighting does not explain the artifacts exhibit's attendance increase.
explanations.E: Supports the argument somewhat but is weaker than confirming the mechanism.

lr.difficultyReason: Causal inference with a visible alternative (pre-existing preference). Correct answer rules out this alternative.
lr.stimulus: A restaurant introduced a new organic menu option. Orders of the organic menu items increased significantly in the weeks following the introduction. The restaurant manager concludes that the availability of organic options caused the increase in orders.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Organic foods are generally more expensive than conventional foods.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Before the organic menu was introduced, customers had not requested organic options.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many restaurants in the city offer organic menu items.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Organic menu items are prepared by the same kitchen staff as conventional items.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The restaurant's total number of customers decreased during the same period.

explanations.correct: By showing that customers had not previously requested organic options, this rules out the alternative that existing demand caused the orders, strengthening the conclusion that the availability itself caused the increase.
explanations.A: Accurate but raises the question of why customers would pay more; does not strengthen.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Introduces competitive alternatives that would weaken the causal claim.
explanations.D: Irrelevant — preparation methods do not explain demand.
explanations.E: Weakens the argument — if total customers decreased, the organic orders increase seems anomalous.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple causal claim with one obvious alternative. Correct answer rules out the alternative (timing coincidence).
lr.stimulus: A government agency began a campaign to encourage citizens to conserve water. Two months after the campaign launched, water consumption in the city decreased by 10 percent. The agency claims that the campaign caused the reduction.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to support the agency's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Water conservation is important for environmental sustainability.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Similar campaigns in other cities did not result in measurable decreases in water consumption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neighboring cities that did not run conservation campaigns showed no decrease in water consumption.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The campaign included both television and radio advertisements.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Water rates in the city had remained stable for the preceding year.

explanations.correct: By showing that neighboring cities without the campaign did not experience decreased consumption, this rules out the alternative explanation that the decrease was due to external factors like drought or seasonal changes.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant — the importance of conservation does not prove the campaign caused the reduction.
explanations.B: Introduces doubt about the campaign's effectiveness and weakens the claim.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Irrelevant — the media used does not address causation.
explanations.E: Accurate but does not address whether the campaign (rather than rate changes) caused the decrease.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward causal argument where the correct answer confirms that the proposed mechanism actually produces the effect.
lr.stimulus: A language school changed its teaching method from grammar-focused instruction to conversation-based practice. Students' spoken fluency scores improved significantly on standardized tests administered six months later. The school attributes the improvement to the new teaching method.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the school's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Grammar is an important component of language learning.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversation-based practice provides more opportunities for students to produce spoken language.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many other language schools also use conversation-based teaching methods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Students' written grammar scores did not change significantly.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Standardized language tests have been used for decades.

explanations.correct: By confirming that conversation-based practice provides more opportunities for producing spoken language, this supports the mechanism by which the new method would improve spoken fluency.
explanations.A: Accurate but does not explain why conversation-based practice would improve spoken fluency.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Irrelevant — what other schools do does not prove this school's method caused the improvement.
explanations.D: Consistent with the argument but does not strengthen the causal claim.
explanations.E: Irrelevant — the history of testing does not address the new method's effectiveness.

lr.difficultyReason: Single causal inference with an obvious alternative explanation. The correct answer rules out that the increased fruit production was caused by seasonal rainfall rather than the new irrigation system.
lr.stimulus: The introduction of a new irrigation system at Maple Farm resulted in a 40 percent increase in fruit production over the following season. Therefore, the new irrigation system is responsible for the increase in production.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Maple Farm had used irrigation systems at various points in its history.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rainfall in the region was below average during the season in which production increased.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Other farms in the region also experienced increased production that season.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The new irrigation system was more expensive than the old one.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased fruit production is common when irrigation systems are first installed.

explanations.correct: By showing that rainfall was below average, this eliminates the alternative explanation that the increased production came from natural rainfall rather than the new irrigation system. This directly strengthens the causal claim.
explanations.A: Irrelevant to whether this particular new system caused the recent production increase.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Weakens the argument by suggesting a common regional cause rather than the unique new system at this farm.
explanations.D: Concerns cost, not whether the system caused the production increase.
explanations.E: While topical, this does not eliminate alternatives and actually suggests the increase might be a general phenomenon rather than caused specifically by this system.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward causal argument where an obvious alternative explanation (existing technical ability) can be ruled out. Correct answer confirms the mechanism at work.
lr.stimulus: After the hospital implemented a mandatory training program on patient safety procedures, the rate of medication errors dropped significantly. This suggests that the training program was the cause of the improvement.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to support the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most hospital employees are willing to participate in training programs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Before the training program was implemented, staff members frequently made the same types of medication errors that the program addressed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Other hospitals have offered similar patient safety training to their staff.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The hospital's medication error rate had been stable for the five years before the training program.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some hospital staff members had prior experience with patient safety issues.

explanations.correct: By establishing that the error rate was stable before the training program, this rules out the alternative that some other gradual change (equipment upgrade, staffing change) caused the improvement. This directly strengthens the causal claim.
explanations.A: Irrelevant — willingness to participate doesn't establish the training caused the reduction.
explanations.B: While relevant to whether the training addressed the right problems, it doesn't eliminate alternative explanations for the improvement.
explanations.C: Other hospitals' practices are irrelevant to whether this hospital's training caused its improvement.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Doesn't address whether the training program caused the improvement.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple causal argument about economic behavior. The correct answer rules out the alternative that price alone explains the sales increase, supporting the claim that advertising caused it.
lr.stimulus: Last month, TechnoGear Company launched an aggressive advertising campaign for its new smartphone. Sales increased by 30 percent in the month following the campaign. Therefore, the advertising campaign was responsible for the sales increase.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The price of the smartphone remained unchanged during and after the advertising campaign.

choices.label: B
choices.text: TechnoGear Company had advertised previous products with moderate success.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The smartphone was more durable than competing products.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The advertising campaign reached millions of potential customers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sales of other TechnoGear products also increased that month.

explanations.correct: By eliminating the alternative that a price reduction drove sales, this strengthens the claim that advertising was responsible. It shows the causal mechanism wasn't price-based.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Tells us about past campaigns but doesn't eliminate alternatives for this specific increase.
explanations.C: Product quality is a different alternative explanation that isn't ruled out by this choice.
explanations.D: Reach is consistent with advertising but doesn't rule out other causes of the sales increase.
explanations.E: Suggests a company-wide phenomenon rather than campaign-specific causation.

lr.difficultyReason: Direct causal claim in environmental science with a clear alternative explanation. Correct answer rules out seasonal variation as the cause, strengthening the link to the new policy.
lr.stimulus: Since the coastal city adopted a new waste-management policy that reduced plastic disposal in landfills, the amount of plastic debris in the nearby ocean has declined by 20 percent. Therefore, the policy directly reduced ocean plastic pollution.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ocean currents can transport plastic debris across thousands of miles.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Before the policy was adopted, the amount of plastic debris in the ocean had been increasing for consecutive years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Other cities have implemented similar waste-management policies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some of the plastic pollution in the ocean comes from sources outside the city.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Plastic debris in the ocean can harm marine wildlife.

explanations.correct: By showing a prior consistent upward trend, this rules out the alternative that ocean plastic naturally fluctuates seasonally or that the decline is unrelated to the policy. It strengthens the causal link.
explanations.A: Irrelevant to whether this city's policy caused the local decline.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Other cities' actions don't establish causation for this city.
explanations.D: While true, this doesn't rule out the policy being responsible for the decline.
explanations.E: Establishes the importance of the issue but not the causal claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Causal argument in educational context with one clear alternative: student motivation rather than the new teaching method. Correct answer rules out this alternative.
lr.stimulus: After introducing a new interactive teaching method, student performance on standardized tests improved by 15 percent. Consequently, the new teaching method is responsible for the performance improvement.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The new teaching method requires less preparation time than the traditional method.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Student motivation levels were comparable before and after the introduction of the new method.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many schools have attempted to introduce new teaching methods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The standardized test measures core academic skills.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Interactive teaching methods are popular in educational research.

explanations.correct: By establishing that student motivation remained constant, this rules out the alternative explanation that students simply became more motivated (rather than the method being more effective). This strengthens the causal claim.
explanations.A: Irrelevant to whether the method caused performance improvements.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Whether other schools use new methods doesn't establish causation here.
explanations.D: Confirms what the test measures but doesn't eliminate alternative explanations.
explanations.E: Popularity in research doesn't establish this method caused the improvement.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple policy argument where the most obvious alternative is that external circumstances changed. Correct answer confirms the policy itself was the driver.
lr.stimulus: The city enacted a new traffic law requiring mandatory traffic safety courses for repeat offenders. In the year following the law's implementation, traffic violations declined by 25 percent. The traffic law is therefore responsible for the reduction in violations.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
