lr.stimulus: A regional bank introduced a new mobile app last spring and found that customers who installed the app visit branch offices 30 percent less often than customers who have not installed it. The bank's chief executive concluded that the app is probably reducing customers' need to visit branches in person.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the executive's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Before installing the app, the two groups of customers visited branch offices at nearly identical rates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The app received generally positive reviews in several consumer technology publications.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The bank reduced the opening hours of several branch offices shortly after releasing the app.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The app was developed jointly with a software firm that has built similar apps for other banks.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Among customers under 30, app installers visit branch offices considerably less than non-installers.

explanations.correct: A critical reader suspects that app installers were already less branch-dependent. (A) rules out that selection-effect alternative by showing the two groups had the same visit rate before the app existed.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — reviews don't establish that the app is reducing in-person visits.
explanations.C: Opposite answer — shorter hours could independently explain fewer visits, weakening the causal attribution to the app.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — the app's development history doesn't bear on its causal effect.
explanations.E: Strengthens a different conclusion — about under-30 customers specifically, rather than the overall customer base.

lr.difficultyReason: Confirms a premise about causal direction in a linguistics argument. Trap (C) is an unwarranted comparison; trap (A) strengthens a different conclusion about a different contact situation.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Over the past three centuries, the English spoken in the coastal town of Hadrell has acquired a number of distinctive vowel pronunciations not found in neighboring towns. Hadrell historically hosted a large community of Dutch sailors, and the distinctive vowels closely resemble those of seventeenth-century Dutch. The distinctive vowels in Hadrell English probably originated through contact with Dutch speakers.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In another English port that hosted French-speaking sailors, English developed several borrowed vocabulary items from French.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The distinctive vowel pronunciations first appear in Hadrell written records only after Dutch sailors had been settling there for several decades.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The dialect spoken in a coastal town two hundred miles from Hadrell shares some lexical items with Dutch.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hadrell residents remain proud of their town's maritime heritage and often display Dutch-language signs at local festivals.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Seventeenth-century Dutch itself underwent vowel changes that distinguished it from earlier Dutch dialects.

explanations.correct: The argument needs the distinctive vowels to come from Dutch contact, not to predate it. (B) establishes the causal timing — the vowels emerged after Dutch sailors arrived — which strongly supports Dutch-to-English transmission.
explanations.A: Strengthens a different conclusion — about a different town and vocabulary rather than vowels in Hadrell.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Unwarranted comparison — a separate town with different contact conditions doesn't support the Hadrell claim.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — modern pride doesn't establish historical linguistic transmission.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — internal Dutch history doesn't show that Hadrell English borrowed from it.

lr.difficultyReason: Confirms a causal mechanism in a historical argument. Trap (D) is the opposite answer; trap (B) is accurate but irrelevant to the specific causal claim.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Why did the Verran Republic collapse in 1783? One traditional account blames a crop failure that year. I suspect, instead, that the collapse was driven primarily by the republic's decision a decade earlier to devalue its currency, which drove foreign creditors to withdraw investment in the years that followed. Tax receipts from the republic's port cities had been shrinking steadily since the devaluation.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several contemporary pamphleteers in the republic blamed the collapse on an incompetent military.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Verran Republic had experienced two earlier currency devaluations in the previous century.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Records show that foreign creditors pulled nearly two-thirds of their investments from Verran ventures in the years between the devaluation and the collapse.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 1783 crop failure was among the most severe the republic had recorded in its history.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neighboring republics that did not devalue their currency experienced modest growth during the same decade.

explanations.correct: The historian's chain runs from devaluation to creditor withdrawal to collapse. (C) directly confirms the crucial middle link — that creditors did in fact pull out on a large scale — making the causal chain substantially more credible.
explanations.A: Introduces a third explanation (military incompetence) that doesn't bear on devaluation vs. crop failure.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — earlier devaluations don't bear on whether this one caused the collapse.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Opposite answer — a severe crop failure makes the traditional crop-failure account more plausible, undermining the historian.
explanations.E: Weak support: speaks generally to devaluation's effects but doesn't tie withdrawal to the Verran collapse specifically.

lr.difficultyReason: Closes an analogical gap in a public-policy argument. Trap (A) strengthens a different claim about fiscal cost; trap (E) is accurate but irrelevant to educational outcomes.
lr.stimulus: Education policy advisor: The Nortongate school district saw substantial gains in elementary reading scores after adopting a phonics-focused curriculum two years ago. The neighboring Westfell district is now considering the same curriculum and should probably expect similar gains in its own elementary reading scores.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the advisor's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Implementing the phonics-focused curriculum in Nortongate cost less than the district's previous reading program.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nortongate and Westfell have comparable class sizes, teacher-experience distributions, and student demographics.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reading scores across the state have risen modestly over the past five years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Westfell's teachers have expressed concern about the time required to retrain for a new curriculum.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nortongate voters recently approved additional bond funding for school library resources.

explanations.correct: The advisor extrapolates from one district to another. (B) confirms the relevant similarities between the districts, tightening the analogy and making comparable gains more likely.
explanations.A: Strengthens a different conclusion — about cost rather than about reading-score gains.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Opposite answer — a statewide rise could independently explain Nortongate's gains, weakening the attribution to the curriculum.
explanations.D: If anything, weakens — teacher resistance could undermine implementation in Westfell.
explanations.E: Introduces an alternative cause — extra library funding, not the phonics curriculum, may have driven Nortongate's gains.

lr.difficultyReason: Confirms a premise about artistic influence. Trap (E) is accurate but irrelevant; trap (A) strengthens a different conclusion about a later period.
lr.stimulus: Art historian: Several compositions in the early works of the painter Ilse Krevel — particularly the use of foreground lanterns to frame crowds — closely parallel compositions in the etchings of the seventeenth-century Dutch printmaker Adriaen van Ostade. Although Krevel never acknowledged van Ostade as an influence, her early compositions were probably shaped by familiarity with his work.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Krevel's late paintings abandoned lantern-framing compositions in favor of flatter, more diffuse lighting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Krevel spent the two years before painting her earliest works as a student at an academy whose library held a well-used collection of van Ostade etchings.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Van Ostade's etchings were reprinted in inexpensive editions during the twentieth century and were widely available to art students in Krevel's era.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several other painters of Krevel's generation have been shown to have drawn on seventeenth-century Dutch printmakers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Krevel's later critical writings describe van Ostade's work in generally dismissive terms.

explanations.correct: The argument depends on Krevel having been familiar with van Ostade before painting her early works. (B) specifically places van Ostade's etchings in her study environment just before the relevant paintings, directly supporting the familiarity premise.
explanations.A: Strengthens a different conclusion — about her late style rather than the early compositions the historian concerns.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Weaker support — general availability doesn't establish Krevel's own familiarity the way documented access does.
explanations.D: Accurate but weak — what other painters did doesn't show what Krevel did.
explanations.E: If anything, weakens, by suggesting Krevel was unfamiliar with or uninterested in van Ostade.

lr.difficultyReason: Rules out an alternative cause in an economic argument. Trap (C) is an unwarranted comparison; trap (D) strengthens a different conclusion about a related but distinct industry.
lr.stimulus: Last year, online retailer Parvest doubled the number of fulfillment warehouses serving its largest metropolitan market. Average delivery times for Parvest orders in that market have since fallen from 48 hours to 22 hours. The company's operations director concluded that the additional warehouses are probably responsible for the faster deliveries.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the director's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Parvest hired a new chief logistics officer three months before the warehouses opened.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Order volume in the metropolitan market did not change appreciably before or after the warehouses opened.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A competing retailer that did not add warehouses also saw its delivery times improve, but by a smaller margin.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parvest's grocery subsidiary, which uses a separate distribution network, has also seen faster deliveries.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The new warehouses are located closer, on average, to the neighborhoods receiving the most Parvest orders.

explanations.correct: A natural alternative is that order volume changed in a way that eased the existing network (fewer orders would shorten times even without new warehouses). (B) rules that out, making the new warehouses the more plausible cause of faster delivery.
explanations.A: Introduces an alternative cause — the new logistics officer could have implemented other changes responsible for faster delivery.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Unwarranted comparison — a competitor's improvement suggests industry-wide factors and doesn't isolate the warehouses.
explanations.D: Strengthens a different conclusion — about the grocery subsidiary's separate network.
explanations.E: Tempting, but closer-to-customer proximity largely restates what adding warehouses accomplishes; without ruling out alternative causes such as a volume change, it doesn't anchor the causal claim as directly as (B).

lr.difficultyReason: The argument rests on a load-bearing assumption about a mechanism (drug metabolism). The correct answer confirms that mechanism, while distractors offer topical but structurally irrelevant facts or introduce alternative explanations.
lr.stimulus: A clinical trial found that patients who took Drug X recovered from a particular bacterial infection significantly faster than patients who took a placebo. The researchers concluded that Drug X accelerates recovery by directly inhibiting the growth of the bacteria responsible for the infection.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patients in the Drug X group reported higher satisfaction with their treatment than patients in the placebo group.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Laboratory tests confirm that Drug X prevents the bacteria from reproducing when introduced to bacterial cultures at the concentrations achieved in patients' bloodstreams.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The bacterial infection studied is more common in older patients than in younger ones.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients who took Drug X also slept more hours per night on average, which is known to support immune function.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Drug X was developed by the same research team that discovered a widely used antiviral medication.

explanations.correct: The argument's conclusion rests on the claim that Drug X works by directly inhibiting bacterial growth. Choice B provides direct laboratory evidence confirming this mechanism at clinically relevant concentrations, thus bridging the observed outcome (faster recovery) to the proposed causal mechanism.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant — patient satisfaction speaks to subjective experience, not to whether Drug X inhibits bacterial growth.
explanations.B: Correct. Confirms the load-bearing mechanistic premise of the argument.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — age distribution of the infection does not support the mechanism by which Drug X works.
explanations.D: Introduces an alternative cause — if Drug X improved sleep, and sleep boosts immunity, that would be a rival explanation for faster recovery, weakening rather than strengthening the argument.
explanations.E: Unwarranted comparison — the research team's prior success is irrelevant to whether this drug works via bacterial inhibition.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy argument with a predictive conclusion. The correct answer rules out a key alternative explanation; distractors are plausible but structurally mismatched.
lr.stimulus: A city government reduced speed limits on residential streets from 30 mph to 20 mph. In the two years following the change, the number of pedestrian injuries on those streets fell by 25 percent. The city council concluded that the lower speed limit caused the reduction in pedestrian injuries.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pedestrian injury rates on the city's highways, where speed limits were unchanged, remained the same over the same two-year period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drivers generally prefer lower speed limits in school zones than in other residential areas.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The number of registered vehicles in the city increased by 10 percent during the same two-year period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Other cities that reduced residential speed limits saw improvements in air quality as well as pedestrian safety.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pedestrian traffic on residential streets increased by 20 percent during the same two-year period.

explanations.correct: If pedestrian traffic on those streets rose by 20 percent yet injuries still fell 25 percent, the reduction in injuries is even more impressive and cannot be explained by fewer people walking. This rules out the alternative that fewer pedestrians (rather than the speed limit change) caused the decline in injuries, strongly supporting the causal claim.
explanations.A: Strengthens a different conclusion — it shows the effect is specific to altered streets, which is mildly relevant but does not address why injuries fell the way choice E does.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — driver preferences about school zones do not speak to the causal claim about residential injury rates.
explanations.C: If anything, more vehicles would be expected to increase injury risk, making the reduction harder to explain — this is a mild opposite-direction distractor that does not clearly strengthen.
explanations.D: Unwarranted comparison — what happened in other cities neither confirms nor denies whether the speed limit change caused the reduction in this city.
explanations.E: Correct. Rules out the alternative explanation that fewer pedestrians account for the drop in injuries.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science argument with an analogical gap. The correct answer closes the analogy by confirming a shared relevant feature. Distractors are domain-plausible but do not close the gap.
lr.stimulus: Researchers studying a lake in northern Canada found that the introduction of an invasive fish species caused a collapse of the native zooplankton population. They argued that a similar introduction of the same invasive species into a comparable lake in Scandinavia would probably cause an equally severe collapse of its zooplankton population.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the researchers' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Scandinavian lake has a surface area and depth nearly identical to those of the Canadian lake, and its zooplankton species rely on the same feeding strategies as those in Canada.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Invasive fish species have caused ecological damage in river systems as well as in lakes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Scandinavian lake is located in a region with stricter environmental protection laws than Canada.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The invasive fish species reproduces at a faster rate in warmer water, and the Canadian lake is warmer than average.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Zooplankton populations in lakes generally recover within a decade if the invasive species is removed.

explanations.correct: The argument is analogical: what happened in Canada will happen in Scandinavia. The critical gap is whether the two lakes are relevantly similar. Choice A closes this gap by confirming that the Scandinavian lake shares the physical and ecological features most relevant to the predicted outcome, making the analogy much stronger.
explanations.A: Correct. Confirms the relevant similarity needed to support the analogical prediction.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — damage in rivers does not support predicting damage in this specific Scandinavian lake.
explanations.C: Potentially weakens by suggesting regulation might prevent the introduction or mitigate the effect.
explanations.D: This undermines the analogy — if the Canadian lake is unusually warm and the invasion effect depends on temperature, the result might not transfer to a colder Scandinavian lake.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — recovery timelines do not speak to whether a collapse would occur in the first place.

lr.difficultyReason: Economics argument with a predictive conclusion about wage policy. The correct answer rules out an alternative mechanism; distractors are plausible economic facts that do not address the argument's key gap.
lr.stimulus: A study of manufacturing firms found that companies that voluntarily raised wages above the regional minimum experienced lower employee turnover than similar firms that did not. The study's authors concluded that higher wages caused the reduction in turnover at those firms.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The firms that raised wages were located in regions with faster-growing local economies, where workers generally have more job options.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The firms that raised wages did not simultaneously introduce other retention initiatives, such as improved benefits or flexible scheduling.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Manufacturing turnover rates vary significantly across different industries and regions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Higher wages are associated with increased worker productivity in sectors other than manufacturing.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several of the firms that raised wages had previously experienced unusually high turnover rates.

explanations.correct: The main threat to the causal conclusion is that the wage-raising firms may have also implemented other retention measures, which could be the true cause of lower turnover. Choice B rules out this confounding explanation, leaving the wage increase as the most plausible cause.
explanations.A: Introduces an alternative cause — a faster-growing economy means more job options, which would normally increase turnover, not decrease it. This is mildly strengthening in a roundabout way, but does not address the key confound the way B does.
explanations.B: Correct. Rules out the confounding explanation of simultaneous non-wage retention initiatives.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — industry-wide variation in turnover does not speak to whether wages caused the specific reduction observed.
explanations.D: Strengthens a different conclusion — productivity benefits in other sectors do not support the causal claim about turnover in manufacturing.
explanations.E: Potentially undermines the argument via regression to the mean — firms with unusually high prior turnover might have shown improvement regardless of wage changes.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics argument requiring the correct answer to confirm an implicit mechanism about language acquisition. Distractors include a plausible-sounding fact that strengthens a neighboring claim and an opposite answer.
lr.stimulus: Children who are exposed to two languages from birth consistently demonstrate stronger executive function skills — such as attention switching and impulse control — than monolingual children of the same age. Researchers have argued that managing two languages simultaneously exercises the brain's executive control systems, thereby strengthening those skills.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to support the researchers' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bilingual children tend to have larger vocabularies in their dominant language than monolingual children of the same age.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Brain-imaging studies show that bilingual individuals activate executive control regions more frequently during everyday tasks than monolingual individuals do.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Children who learn a second language after age seven show smaller executive function advantages than those exposed to two languages from birth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some researchers have proposed that bilingual children's executive function advantages diminish by early adulthood.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Families in which two languages are spoken tend to have higher average household incomes than monolingual families.

explanations.correct: The researchers' argument depends on a mechanism: managing two languages exercises executive control systems. Choice B provides neuroimaging evidence that bilingual individuals do in fact engage executive control regions more, directly supporting the proposed mechanism and therefore the conclusion.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant — vocabulary size in the dominant language does not speak to whether language management exercises executive control.
explanations.B: Correct. Confirms the mechanistic claim that bilingual language management activates executive control systems.
explanations.C: Consistent with the argument but strengthens a related point about timing rather than the core mechanism; does not directly confirm that managing two languages is what produces the benefit.
explanations.D: Potentially weakens by suggesting the benefit is temporary, casting doubt on whether the mechanism produces lasting strengthening.
explanations.E: Introduces an alternative cause — higher socioeconomic status is independently associated with stronger executive function, providing a rival explanation for the observed advantage.

lr.difficultyReason: History argument with a predictive-causal structure. The correct answer bolsters a load-bearing premise about comparative conditions. Distractors are historically plausible but structurally off.
lr.stimulus: Historians have argued that the rapid spread of the printing press through 15th-century Europe was primarily caused by existing high levels of literacy among the urban merchant class, which created immediate commercial demand for printed materials. They point out that the press spread fastest in cities where merchant literacy rates were highest.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the historians' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In cities where printing presses appeared earliest, merchant literacy rates had been rising steadily for at least two decades before the press arrived.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gutenberg's original press was designed primarily for the reproduction of religious texts rather than commercial documents.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Catholic Church initially attempted to regulate the content of printed materials in several European cities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several cities with early printing presses also had active universities, which independently encouraged literacy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The cost of producing a printed book fell significantly within two decades of the press's introduction.

explanations.correct: The historians' argument requires that high merchant literacy preceded and drove adoption of the press, rather than resulting from it. Choice A confirms that literacy was already rising before the press arrived in those cities, establishing the correct causal direction and bolstering the premise that pre-existing literacy created demand.
explanations.A: Correct. Confirms temporal precedence of literacy over press adoption, supporting the causal direction of the argument.
explanations.B: Potentially weakens — if the press was designed for religious texts, the commercial literacy demand explanation is less compelling.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — Church regulation speaks to content control, not to what drove the press's geographic spread.
explanations.D: Introduces an alternative cause — universities independently encouraging literacy suggests a rival explanation for why literacy was high in early-press cities.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — falling production costs explain later diffusion but do not address what drove the initial rapid spread among early adopter cities.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology argument about software reliability with a methodological gap. The correct answer confirms that the study's measurement method captures what it claims to measure. Distractors are topical but structurally inert.
lr.stimulus: A software company analyzed error logs from its two main product lines and found that Product A had three times as many reported bugs per thousand lines of code as Product B. The company concluded that Product A's codebase is significantly less reliable than Product B's.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Product A has been on the market for twice as long as Product B, giving users more time to discover and report bugs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Product A and Product B have user bases of similar size and technical sophistication, and both user bases report bugs through the same logging system at similar rates.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The engineering teams responsible for Product A and Product B use the same coding languages and development frameworks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Software bugs in financial applications tend to have more serious consequences than bugs in entertainment applications.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Product B has received more investment in automated testing infrastructure than Product A in the past year.

explanations.correct: The argument uses reported bugs as a proxy for reliability. A key threat is that the difference in reported bugs could reflect differences in user behavior or reporting systems rather than actual reliability. Choice B rules this out by confirming that both user bases are comparable in size, sophistication, and reporting rates, validating the measurement method.
explanations.A: Undermines the argument — if Product A has been on the market longer, its higher bug count might reflect more exposure time, not lower reliability.
explanations.B: Correct. Rules out the alternative explanation that reporting disparities account for the difference in logged bugs.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — using the same tools does not address whether the reported bug counts reflect actual reliability differences.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — the severity of consequences in different domains does not speak to whether Product A is less reliable than Product B.
explanations.E: Potentially weakens — if Product B recently received more testing investment, that could explain its lower bug count rather than its underlying code quality.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics/law argument about the effect of mandatory disclosure requirements. The correct answer rules out an alternative explanation for observed behavior change. Distractors include one that strengthens a neighboring claim and one that introduces a confound.
lr.stimulus: After a jurisdiction enacted a law requiring attorneys to disclose any financial relationships with expert witnesses they retain, the rate at which opposing counsel challenged expert witness testimony in civil cases dropped by nearly 30 percent. Legal scholars have argued that the disclosure requirement caused this drop by reducing the use of financially compromised experts.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the legal scholars' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Surveys of attorneys conducted after the law took effect showed that most had stopped retaining expert witnesses with whom they had financial relationships.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The same jurisdiction also experienced a significant decline in the overall number of civil cases filed during the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Expert witness testimony has been shown to be highly influential on jury verdicts in civil cases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mandatory disclosure requirements for financial conflicts of interest are used in several other legal contexts in the same jurisdiction.

choices.label: E
choices.text: In jurisdictions without the disclosure requirement, rates of expert witness challenges remained stable over the same period.

explanations.correct: The scholars argue the disclosure law caused a drop in challenges by reducing the use of compromised experts. Choice A confirms the intermediate causal link: attorneys actually changed their behavior in response to the law by dropping financially connected experts, making it far more plausible that fewer challenges stemmed from cleaner expert selection.
explanations.A: Correct. Confirms the intermediate mechanism — attorneys stopped retaining financially connected experts — that links the disclosure law to fewer challenges.
explanations.B: Introduces an alternative explanation — fewer cases overall could mean fewer opportunities to challenge experts, which would be a rival cause for the drop in challenges.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — jury influence of expert testimony does not speak to why the challenge rate changed after the disclosure law.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — the use of disclosure requirements in other legal contexts does not support the causal claim about this specific law's effect on challenge rates.
explanations.E: Strengthens, but less directly than A — stable rates elsewhere suggest the drop was not due to a general trend, but this does not confirm the specific mechanism the scholars propose.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts/cultural argument with a predictive conclusion about audience behavior. The correct answer rules out an alternative explanation. Distractors include one that subtly introduces a confound and one that strengthens a peripheral claim.
lr.stimulus: A performing arts center introduced a program offering significantly discounted tickets to patrons under 30. Within two years, the percentage of audiences aged 18–29 rose from 11 percent to 22 percent. The center's director argued that the discount program was responsible for attracting younger audiences.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the director's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The center's programming — the types of performances offered — did not change significantly during the two years the discount program was in place.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Other performing arts centers in the region do not offer similar discount programs and have not seen comparable increases in young adult attendance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Young adults who attended the center through the discount program rated their experience highly on post-show surveys.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city's population of residents aged 18–29 grew substantially during the same two-year period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Performing arts centers that offer educational outreach programs also tend to attract more diverse audiences.

explanations.correct: One alternative explanation for higher young adult attendance is that the center began programming more content appealing to younger audiences. Choice A rules this out by establishing that programming remained stable, leaving the discount program as the most plausible explanation for the demographic shift.
explanations.A: Correct. Rules out the alternative explanation that programming changes (rather than the discount) attracted younger audiences.
explanations.B: Provides supporting comparison but is weaker than A — other centers' situations may differ in many ways beyond the discount program, making the comparison less probative about this center's specific causal claim.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — high satisfaction among discount attendees does not address whether the discount program caused the increase in young attendance.
explanations.D: Introduces an alternative explanation — a growing young adult population in the city could independently account for higher young adult attendance regardless of the discount program.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — educational outreach programs and audience diversity are not at issue in this argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science/policy argument about a conservation intervention. The correct answer confirms the load-bearing assumption that the control group is a valid comparison. Distractors are plausible environmental facts that fail to address the argument's key inferential gap.
lr.stimulus: A conservation organization reintroduced wolves to a national park that had been without them for decades. Over the following ten years, the park's riverbank vegetation recovered substantially, which researchers attributed to wolves limiting deer overgrazing near rivers. They compared the park to an adjacent protected area of similar size that had not received wolf reintroduction and showed no comparable vegetation recovery.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wolves are apex predators whose effects on ecosystems often extend beyond their direct prey.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The adjacent protected area had deer population densities and riverbank soil composition comparable to those of the national park prior to wolf reintroduction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The national park received increased rainfall in the years following wolf reintroduction relative to historical averages.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reintroduction of wolves into ecosystems in other countries has yielded mixed results depending on prey availability.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Riverbank vegetation provides important habitat for fish and migratory birds in temperate ecosystems.

explanations.correct: The argument relies on comparing the park with and without wolves using the adjacent area as a control. For this comparison to be valid, the two areas must have been ecologically similar before wolf reintroduction. Choice B confirms exactly this — that deer density and soil composition were comparable — making the control group a legitimate baseline and strengthening the causal inference.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant — a general statement about wolves as apex predators does not confirm that vegetation recovery in this specific park was caused by wolves limiting deer grazing.
explanations.B: Correct. Validates the control comparison by confirming the two areas were ecologically similar before the intervention.
explanations.C: Introduces an alternative explanation — increased rainfall could independently account for the vegetation recovery, undermining the causal claim rather than strengthening it.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — mixed results elsewhere do not speak to the specific causal claim about this park's vegetation recovery.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — the ecological value of riverbank vegetation does not address whether wolves caused its recovery.

lr.difficultyReason: Scientific/methodological argument requiring the test-taker to identify a load-bearing assumption about instrument capability and rule out an alternative explanation. Trap choices include one that superficially supports the field of study rather than the specific conclusion, and one that introduces a plausible but irrelevant historical detail.
lr.stimulus: Archaeologists excavating a Bronze Age settlement in central Anatolia found no traces of iron tools at any stratum dated before 1200 BCE, despite conducting an extensive survey of all known habitation layers. Because iron corrodes more slowly in arid conditions than in humid ones, and the site's soil is notably dry, any iron tools present should have survived long enough to leave detectable remnants. The archaeologists therefore concluded that the inhabitants of this settlement did not use iron tools before 1200 BCE.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Iron artifacts from the same period have been successfully recovered at other Bronze Age sites located in regions with similarly arid soil conditions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The settlement was occupied continuously from approximately 2500 BCE until its abandonment around 1150 BCE.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bronze tools found at the site show sophisticated craftsmanship consistent with a culture capable of working with multiple metals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron smelting technology was known to have existed in neighboring regions before 1200 BCE.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Archaeologists have used the same excavation methods at dozens of other Bronze Age sites throughout the eastern Mediterranean.

explanations.correct: The argument's key assumption is that iron tools, if present, would have survived and been detectable in this site's arid soil. Choice A confirms this assumption by establishing that iron artifacts from the same era have in fact been found at other sites with similarly arid conditions — directly showing that the detection method works and that absence of evidence is genuinely evidence of absence here. This closes the gap between 'no iron found' and 'no iron used.'
explanations.A: Correct. Rules out the alternative explanation that the dry conditions somehow still failed to preserve iron; confirms the load-bearing premise that iron would have survived in this soil type.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant trap. The continuous occupation timeline tells us the site was inhabited throughout the relevant period, but it doesn't address whether iron tools would have been detectable if they existed. This does not strengthen the no-iron-tools conclusion.
explanations.C: Strengthens a different conclusion trap. The sophistication of bronze craftsmanship might suggest the culture was metallurgically advanced, but it says nothing about whether iron was or wasn't used — a culture capable of working multiple metals could include or exclude iron.
explanations.D: Introduces an alternative explanation / opposite answer trap. Knowing that iron smelting existed nearby before 1200 BCE makes it more plausible that the inhabitants could have acquired iron tools, which actually weakens the argument by suggesting the absence is surprising and in need of further explanation.
explanations.E: Unwarranted comparison trap. That the same excavation methods were used at other sites tells us nothing about whether those methods are sensitive enough to detect iron remnants in this specific arid environment, nor does it confirm the conclusion about this settlement's inhabitants.

lr.difficultyReason: Scientific/methodological argument where the correct answer confirms a load-bearing assumption about instrument sensitivity. Four distractors are topically plausible but fail to close the premise-to-conclusion gap.
lr.stimulus: Researchers recently discovered that a newly identified deep-sea bacterium produces an enzyme capable of breaking down certain persistent pesticides. They observed this activity only in water samples taken from depths below 800 meters, where sunlight does not penetrate. They therefore concluded that sunlight inhibits the enzyme's activity, preventing the bacterium from degrading pesticides in shallower waters.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The bacterium has been found in water samples collected from several different ocean basins.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When water samples from below 800 meters were exposed to artificial light in a laboratory, the enzyme's degradation activity ceased.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Other deep-sea bacteria are known to produce enzymes that break down various industrial pollutants.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The concentration of pesticides in ocean water is highest at depths above 800 meters.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The bacterium is unable to survive at water temperatures exceeding those typically found below 800 meters.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that sunlight inhibits the enzyme's activity. Choice B directly confirms this causal mechanism: introducing light to deep-water samples halts the enzyme's activity, demonstrating that light itself — not depth or some other variable — is the operative factor.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant. Geographic distribution of the bacterium says nothing about whether sunlight inhibits its enzyme activity.
explanations.B: Correct. Replicating the inhibition effect under controlled light conditions confirms that sunlight is the causal factor, directly strengthening the conclusion.
explanations.C: Introduces an unwarranted comparison — what other bacteria do in analogous situations does not bear on this bacterium's sensitivity to sunlight.
explanations.D: This is a potential weakener in disguise: if pesticide concentration is highest above 800 m, one might wonder whether the bacterium simply moves away from them, introducing an alternative explanation for the depth pattern.
explanations.E: Introduces an alternative explanation — temperature tolerance, not sunlight, could explain why the bacterium is absent from shallower waters, which weakens rather than strengthens the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy argument with a load-bearing comparative assumption. Correct answer confirms the key premise that the proposed alternative achieves the stated goal. Distractors include an opposite answer and an accurate-but-irrelevant choice.
lr.stimulus: A city transportation department has proposed replacing its fleet of diesel buses with electric buses, arguing that this switch will meaningfully reduce particulate matter emissions in the downtown corridor. Critics have noted that the city's electrical grid is largely powered by coal. However, the department insists that even accounting for emissions at the power plant, total particulate matter released per passenger kilometer will be lower for electric buses than for diesel buses.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the transportation department's position?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several other cities that use electric buses have reported significant improvements in downtown air quality.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The coal-fired power plants supplying the city's grid are located outside the downtown corridor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Life-cycle analyses show that modern electric buses produce, on a per-passenger-kilometer basis, substantially less total particulate matter than equivalent diesel buses, even when upstream power-generation emissions are included.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Electric buses require less maintenance than diesel buses and have a longer operational lifespan.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Residents of the downtown corridor have expressed strong support for the transition to electric buses.

explanations.correct: The department's central claim is that total particulate matter per passenger kilometer is lower for electric buses even accounting for power-plant emissions. Choice C directly confirms this load-bearing premise with life-cycle analysis data, closing the gap between the argument's assertion and the critics' objection.
explanations.A: Unwarranted comparison — other cities may differ in grid composition, ridership, and baseline conditions, so their experience does not directly confirm the department's claim about this city's net emissions.
explanations.B: This shifts the downtown air quality argument, but the department's stated position concerns total particulate matter released, not geographic distribution of emissions. This addresses a different conclusion.
explanations.C: Correct. Directly bolsters the load-bearing claim that net particulate output is lower for electric buses even after accounting for coal-fired generation.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — maintenance and lifespan bear on cost and fleet management, not on particulate matter emissions.
explanations.E: Public opinion does not bear on whether the emissions reduction claim is accurate.

lr.difficultyReason: Medical/causal argument where the correct answer rules out a prominent alternative explanation. Distractors include a plausible-sounding trap that strengthens an adjacent claim rather than the actual conclusion.
lr.stimulus: A clinical team observed that patients who took a daily low-dose aspirin regimen for at least five years had a significantly lower incidence of a particular type of colorectal polyp compared to patients who did not take aspirin. The team concluded that long-term low-dose aspirin use reduces the formation of this polyp type.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aspirin is known to inhibit cyclooxygenase enzymes, which play a role in the inflammatory pathways associated with colorectal polyp development.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients who took aspirin daily for five or more years were no more likely than non-aspirin users to follow a low-fiber diet, which is associated with increased polyp risk.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The colorectal polyp type in question is a known precursor to colorectal cancer in a significant proportion of cases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several anti-inflammatory medications other than aspirin have been studied for their effects on colorectal health.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients in the aspirin group had, on average, more frequent colonoscopies, which could affect polyp detection rates.

explanations.correct: The greatest threat to a causal conclusion from an observational study is that a confounding variable — not aspirin — explains the difference. If aspirin users happened to eat more fiber, fiber (not aspirin) could be responsible for fewer polyps. Choice B rules out this dietary confound, strengthening the causal claim.
explanations.A: This confirms a plausible mechanism, which does help, but it strengthens the biological plausibility of the claim rather than ruling out the most pressing threat to a causal inference from an observational study. Choice B more directly addresses the logical gap. (Mechanism confirmation is weaker than confound elimination here.)
explanations.B: Correct. Eliminates a dietary confound that would otherwise rival aspirin as the causal explanation for the lower polyp incidence.
explanations.C: Strengthens the clinical importance of the finding but not the causal argument — relevance to cancer doesn't bear on whether aspirin caused fewer polyps.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — what studies exist on other drugs says nothing about aspirin's specific causal role here.
explanations.E: This is a disguised weakener: more colonoscopies in the aspirin group could mean polyps are detected and removed more often, making lower incidence an artifact of screening rather than true prevention.

lr.difficultyReason: Economics argument requiring the correct answer to close an analogy gap. Distractors include an unwarranted comparison and an opposite answer.
lr.stimulus: After a neighboring country eliminated tariffs on imported agricultural goods, domestic food prices in that country fell by an average of twelve percent within two years. An economist argues that if our country eliminates similar tariffs, domestic food prices here will likely fall by a comparable margin.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The neighboring country's agricultural sector lobbied strongly against tariff elimination before it was enacted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Our country's current tariff rates on agricultural imports are set at levels comparable to those that the neighboring country eliminated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Food prices in the neighboring country have continued to fall in the years following the initial two-year period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Our country imports a much smaller proportion of its food supply than the neighboring country did before its tariff elimination.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Economists generally agree that free trade in agricultural goods benefits consumers in developing nations.

explanations.correct: The economist's argument is analogical: what happened in the neighboring country will happen here. The analogy depends on the two countries having similar tariff structures. Choice B confirms that our current tariff levels are comparable to those eliminated in the neighboring country, closing the key analogical gap.
explanations.A: Irrelevant to the price prediction — political opposition to a policy doesn't bear on whether eliminating tariffs will lower prices.
explanations.B: Correct. Confirms that the tariff conditions are sufficiently similar between the two countries to support the analogical inference.
explanations.C: Strengthens a different conclusion — that long-term prices will continue falling — rather than the argument that an initial comparable reduction will occur in our country.
explanations.D: This is an opposite answer: if our country imports much less of its food supply, eliminating tariffs may have a smaller price effect, weakening the analogy.
explanations.E: An overly broad generalization that does not specifically support the claim about this particular country's expected price reduction magnitude.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal/evidentiary argument where the correct answer rules out an alternative explanation for the observed evidence. Distractors include a choice that strengthens a neighboring claim and an accurate-but-irrelevant choice.
lr.stimulus: Prosecutors argued that a defendant's fingerprints found on a safe in the victim's home indicate that the defendant had been inside the victim's home at some point before the crime. The defense countered that the fingerprints might have been transferred indirectly — for example, via an object touched by both the defendant and the safe. The prosecutor responded that indirect transfer of legible fingerprints is extremely rare under ordinary circumstances.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to support the prosecutor's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Forensic analysts confirmed that the fingerprints on the safe matched the defendant's prints in twelve distinct ridge characteristics.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The defendant had no known legitimate reason to have visited the victim's home prior to the crime.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Studies of fingerprint transfer in laboratory settings show that indirect transfer rarely produces prints with sufficient clarity for identification.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The safe was located in a locked room within the victim's home, accessible only through the main living area.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fingerprint evidence has been used successfully in numerous criminal convictions over the past century.

explanations.correct: The prosecutor's claim that indirect transfer of legible prints is extremely rare is a key premise that defeats the defense's alternative explanation. Choice C provides empirical backing for that premise — lab studies confirm that indirect transfer rarely yields identifiable prints — directly strengthening the prosecutor's reasoning.
explanations.A: Confirms print quality and identity but does not address the defense's indirect-transfer theory; it strengthens a different sub-claim (that the prints belong to the defendant) rather than ruling out the alternative explanation.
explanations.B: Relevant to guilt but not to the specific argument about fingerprint evidence and indirect transfer; strengthens a different conclusion about motivation.
explanations.C: Correct. Provides empirical support for the prosecutor's key premise that indirect transfer of identifiable prints is rare, neutralizing the defense's alternative explanation.
explanations.D: Strengthens the inference that the defendant was in the home but via spatial reasoning rather than by addressing the indirect-transfer argument, making it weaker than C.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — general admissibility of fingerprint evidence does not bear on whether indirect transfer could explain these particular prints.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology/causal argument where the correct answer confirms the implicit mechanism linking the cause to the effect. Trap choices include an opposite answer and a choice that introduces an alternative cause.
lr.stimulus: Software engineers at a firm noticed that after deploying a patch that reduced the frequency of background synchronization processes, the average battery life of users' devices increased by roughly 20 percent. They concluded that the frequent background synchronization processes had been the primary drain on battery life.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Battery life on devices running the updated software remained stable even when users increased their screen brightness settings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Energy consumption logs collected from devices before the patch showed that background synchronization processes accounted for the largest share of power draw among all running processes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The patch also disabled several non-essential notification features that had previously run continuously in the background.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Users reported higher satisfaction with the device's performance after the patch was deployed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Devices manufactured in prior years had longer battery lives before similar synchronization features were introduced.

explanations.correct: The engineers concluded that synchronization processes were the primary battery drain. Choice B directly confirms this by showing pre-patch energy logs identified synchronization as the largest power consumer, providing mechanical evidence that the causal attribution is correct.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant — screen brightness behavior after the patch does not bear on whether synchronization was the primary drain before the patch.
explanations.B: Correct. Pre-patch energy data directly confirm that synchronization processes were the dominant draw, strengthening the causal conclusion.
explanations.C: Introduces an alternative explanation — the disabled notification features, not the reduced synchronization, could account for the battery improvement, weakening rather than strengthening the argument.
explanations.D: User satisfaction is an accurate but irrelevant measure; performance perception does not confirm the causal mechanism linking synchronization to battery drain.
explanations.E: Consistent with synchronization being a drain over time, but the historical comparison is too indirect — it doesn't confirm that synchronization (versus other features added simultaneously) was the primary cause.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics/historical argument requiring the correct answer to close a gap between observed data and a causal conclusion about language change. Includes a trap that strengthens a different conclusion and an opposite answer.
lr.stimulus: Linguistic historians have documented that in a dialect of a medieval Germanic language, the second-person plural pronoun gradually replaced the second-person singular pronoun in formal address over roughly 150 years. They attribute this change to increased contact with neighboring Romance-speaking populations, who used a similar plural-for-singular honorific form. Therefore, the change was most likely the result of direct borrowing from Romance speech conventions.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The same dialect underwent several other phonological changes during the same 150-year period that are unrelated to Romance influence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Historical records show that bilingual speakers who regularly conversed in both the Germanic dialect and neighboring Romance languages were disproportionately represented among the social elites who first adopted the new honorific form.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several other Germanic dialects that had no significant contact with Romance speakers also shifted from singular to plural in formal address during the medieval period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The plural-for-singular honorific convention is attested in written Romance texts predating the Germanic shift by at least two centuries.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Linguistic borrowing of grammatical features is generally considered more difficult to document than borrowing of vocabulary items.

explanations.correct: The argument claims the change resulted from direct borrowing via contact with Romance speakers. Choice B identifies the social mechanism of transmission: bilingual elites who used both languages were the first adopters, directly supporting the contact-borrowing hypothesis and closing the gap between 'contact existed' and 'borrowing occurred.'
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant — other unrelated phonological changes do not bear on whether this particular pronominal change was borrowed from Romance.
explanations.B: Correct. Establishes the social transmission pathway that connects Romance contact to adoption of the new honorific form, strengthening the direct-borrowing conclusion.
explanations.C: Opposite answer — if isolated Germanic dialects made the same shift independently, this suggests an internal grammatical tendency rather than Romance borrowing, weakening the argument.
explanations.D: Confirms the feature existed in Romance before the Germanic shift but does not establish that the shift resulted from borrowing rather than independent development; strengthens plausibility but less directly than B.
explanations.E: A methodological observation about linguistics in general; does not support the specific causal claim about this dialect change.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics/policy argument where the correct answer bolsters a load-bearing factual premise. Distractors include an accurate-but-irrelevant choice and a choice that strengthens a neighboring conclusion.
lr.stimulus: An ethics board argued that a hospital's policy of routinely notifying family members when a patient is admitted with a life-threatening condition — even without the patient's explicit consent — is justified because, in emergency situations, patients are typically unable to make informed decisions about notification preferences. The board concluded that presuming consent to family notification in these cases respects patient welfare more than strict non-disclosure would.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the ethics board's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Surveys of patients who survived life-threatening emergencies show that a large majority report being glad that their family members were notified during the crisis.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Privacy laws in the relevant jurisdiction permit hospitals to disclose patient information to family members in genuine emergencies without prior consent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many hospitals have adopted similar notification policies, suggesting broad professional consensus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients who are notified of a family member's emergency admission report feeling less anxious than those who learn of the admission after the fact.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Medical ethicists generally hold that patient autonomy is the primary value to be weighed in any hospital policy decision.

explanations.correct: The board's argument rests on the claim that presuming consent to notification better serves patient welfare. Choice A directly supports this by showing that most patients, once able to reflect, endorse the notification — confirming the welfare justification and supporting the presumed-consent inference.
explanations.A: Correct. Post-hoc patient endorsement of notification provides evidence that the presumed preference aligns with actual preferences, directly strengthening the welfare-based justification.
explanations.B: Confirms legal permissibility but not ethical justification — that a policy is permitted by law does not strengthen the argument that it respects welfare better than non-disclosure.
explanations.C: Broad professional adoption is an appeal to consensus, not a substantive reason to think patient welfare is served; it does not close the argument's logical gap.
explanations.D: Addresses family members' anxiety, not patients' welfare — this strengthens a different conclusion about the family's experience rather than the patient-centered claim the board makes.
explanations.E: If anything, this weakens the argument: emphasizing patient autonomy as the primary value undercuts the board's rationale for overriding explicit consent requirements.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science/predictive argument where the correct answer rules out an alternative explanation for the observed correlation. Distractors include a choice that introduces a competing cause and an accurate-but-irrelevant comparison.
lr.stimulus: Ecologists studying a coastal wetland found that plots where an invasive reed species had been manually removed showed a threefold increase in native plant diversity within four growing seasons. They concluded that the invasive reed's dominance had been suppressing native plant diversity in those plots.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The invasive reed is known to release allelopathic compounds into the soil that inhibit seed germination in many native plant species.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Adjacent plots from which the invasive reed was not removed showed no significant increase in native plant diversity over the same four growing seasons.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The removal process involved mechanical cutting, which also disturbed the soil surface and may have created additional germination opportunities for native species.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Invasive reed species have been documented suppressing native biodiversity in freshwater wetlands in other regions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The four growing seasons during which the study was conducted were characterized by above-average rainfall, which generally promotes plant diversity.

explanations.correct: Without a control comparison, the diversity increase could be due to weather, natural succession, or other factors. Choice B provides the necessary control: plots where the reed was not removed showed no improvement, isolating removal — and thus the reed's prior presence — as the cause of the change.
explanations.A: Confirms a plausible suppression mechanism but does not rule out that the diversity increase was caused by something other than reed removal (e.g., the soil disturbance from the removal process itself).
explanations.B: Correct. The control-group comparison eliminates alternative explanations for the diversity increase, directly strengthening the causal conclusion.
explanations.C: Introduces an alternative explanation — soil disturbance during removal, not the reed's absence, could have caused the diversity increase, weakening the argument.
explanations.D: Unwarranted comparison — evidence from other regions does not confirm the causal mechanism in this specific wetland.
explanations.E: Introduces another alternative cause — above-average rainfall could explain the diversity increase independently of reed removal, weakening the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: History/predictive argument requiring the correct answer to close a gap between a historical precedent and a current policy prediction. Traps include a choice strengthening a neighboring claim and an unwarranted comparison.
lr.stimulus: Historians of early modern Europe have noted that when city-states in the region reduced guild restrictions on apprenticeship length in the sixteenth century, the rate of new craft workshop formation increased substantially within a generation. A policy analyst argues that if a contemporary city reduces similar occupational licensing barriers, the number of new small businesses in licensed trades will likely increase within a comparable timeframe.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the policy analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The sixteenth-century guild restrictions and the contemporary city's occupational licensing requirements both function primarily by increasing the time and cost required before a newcomer may legally operate independently.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Small business formation rates in licensed trades are currently lower in the contemporary city than in cities with fewer licensing requirements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Historians have debated whether the increase in workshop formation in sixteenth-century city-states was driven primarily by reduced apprenticeship barriers or by concurrent population growth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The contemporary city's licensed trades include several sectors, such as food service and personal care, that did not exist in recognizable form in sixteenth-century city-states.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Economists widely agree that reducing barriers to entry in any market tends to increase the supply of goods and services over time.

explanations.correct: The analyst's argument is analogical: what happened when guild restrictions were reduced in the sixteenth century will happen when licensing barriers are reduced today. This analogy only holds if the mechanisms are relevantly similar. Choice A confirms that both sets of restrictions work the same way — by raising entry costs and time — closing the critical analogical gap.
explanations.A: Correct. Establishes that the historical and contemporary barriers are functionally equivalent, validating the analogy and strengthening the prediction.
explanations.B: Shows that licensing correlates with lower business formation compared to other cities today, but this is a different comparison from the historical analogy; it strengthens a neighboring claim about licensing effects generally rather than the specific analogical argument.
explanations.C: Weakens the argument by casting doubt on whether the historical precedent was actually caused by reduced barriers, undercutting the foundation of the analogy.
explanations.D: Highlights a disanalogy between the two contexts — different trade sectors — which weakens rather than strengthens the argument.
explanations.E: An overly broad economic generalization that is too abstract to directly support the specific historical-analogy argument; it does not address whether the analogy between guild restrictions and licensing barriers is valid.

lr.difficultyReason: Scientific argument that requires confirming an implicit assumption about measurement reliability. The correct answer rules out an alternative explanation (soil composition rather than rainfall) by confirming the experimental controls. Four distractors include a plausible irrelevant fact, an opposite-direction answer, a choice that strengthens a neighboring premise, and an unwarranted comparison.
lr.stimulus: Researchers studying drought tolerance compared two strains of wheat grown in identical greenhouse conditions. Strain A consistently produced 30 percent more grain than Strain B when water was reduced to half the normal level. The researchers concluded that Strain A has superior drought tolerance.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Strain A was developed in an arid region where low rainfall is common throughout the growing season.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Under normal water conditions, Strain A and Strain B produce comparable grain yields.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The greenhouse soil used in the experiment was identical in nutrient composition for both strains.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several other drought-tolerant wheat strains have been developed over the past decade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Strain B is known to produce higher yields than Strain A in cold climates.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that Strain A is superior specifically under drought conditions. If Strain A also outperformed Strain B under normal water conditions, the 30-percent advantage might simply reflect Strain A's generally higher productivity rather than drought tolerance. Showing that yields are comparable under normal conditions isolates water reduction as the key variable, directly strengthening the conclusion.
explanations.A: This introduces an alternative explanation — Strain A may have been selectively bred for arid conditions for reasons unrelated to the mechanism tested, which is more of a background fact than a strengthener for the experimental conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct. Ruling out the possibility that Strain A simply always outperforms Strain B isolates the reduced-water condition as the cause of the yield difference, strengthening the drought-tolerance conclusion.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant to the conclusion. The researchers already stated identical greenhouse conditions; this merely reiterates a control that does not directly bridge the premise-to-conclusion gap about drought tolerance.
explanations.D: An unwarranted comparison — the existence of other drought-tolerant strains is irrelevant to whether Strain A's advantage specifically reflects drought tolerance.
explanations.E: This introduces a tangential fact about cold-climate performance that does not speak to the drought-condition comparison at issue.

lr.difficultyReason: Medical/pharmacological argument where the correct answer confirms the load-bearing mechanism linking drug uptake to cognitive outcome. Distractors include a choice that strengthens a side premise, a plausible irrelevancy, an opposite-direction trap, and a comparison that doesn't close the gap.
lr.stimulus: A clinical trial found that patients who took a daily low-dose aspirin for two years showed significantly less cognitive decline than a control group that received a placebo. The trial's lead physician concluded that low-dose aspirin probably slows cognitive aging.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Low-dose aspirin has well-documented anti-inflammatory effects throughout the body, including in brain tissue.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Participants in the aspirin group were, on average, two years younger than those in the placebo group at the start of the trial.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cognitive decline is one of the most common complaints among patients over the age of sixty.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several participants in the placebo group reported higher-than-average levels of daily stress during the trial period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Other anti-inflammatory drugs have been shown to slow cognitive decline in animal models.

explanations.correct: The argument needs a plausible mechanism connecting aspirin to slower cognitive aging. Confirming that aspirin reduces inflammation in brain tissue supplies the missing causal link — neuroinflammation is associated with cognitive decline — making the conclusion more likely to hold.
explanations.A: Correct. Confirming the biological mechanism (anti-inflammatory action in brain tissue) bridges the gap between taking aspirin and experiencing less cognitive decline.
explanations.B: This is actually a weakener disguised as context: if the aspirin group was younger at baseline, the observed difference in cognitive decline may reflect the age difference rather than aspirin's effect.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. The prevalence of cognitive complaints among older patients does not make aspirin's causal role more likely.
explanations.D: This introduces an alternative explanation for the placebo group's decline (stress) rather than confirming the aspirin mechanism, and does not straightforwardly strengthen the causal claim.
explanations.E: An unwarranted comparison — animal-model results for different drugs do not confirm that aspirin works in humans through the same pathway.

lr.difficultyReason: Economics argument about minimum-wage policy where the correct answer rules out an alternative explanation for the observed employment stability. Traps include a choice that only strengthens a background premise, a topically related but irrelevant fact, and an opposite-direction answer.
lr.stimulus: After a coastal city raised its minimum wage by 15 percent, economists observed that restaurant employment in the city remained stable over the following year. They concluded that the wage increase did not cause significant job losses in the restaurant sector.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Restaurant revenues in the city increased during the same year, driven by a spike in tourism.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neighboring cities that did not raise their minimum wage saw restaurant employment decline slightly over the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The city's overall unemployment rate fell by one percentage point in the year following the wage increase.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restaurant owners in the city reported that the wage increase was smaller than they had anticipated.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Low-wage workers generally spend a higher proportion of their income locally than higher-wage workers do.

explanations.correct: A rival explanation for stable employment is that broader economic trends would have kept restaurant employment stable regardless of the wage increase. Showing that cities without the wage increase actually saw employment decline rules out a favorable economic tide as the explanation, strengthening the conclusion that the wage increase itself did not cause job losses.
explanations.A: This introduces an alternative explanation — tourism may have bolstered employment independently of the wage effect — which actually undermines rather than strengthens the conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct. A comparison group that declined without the wage increase rules out the possibility that employment stability was simply a regional trend, isolating the wage policy as consistent with stable employment.
explanations.C: Strengthens a related claim about overall employment but does not specifically address restaurant-sector job losses or rule out confounds in that sector.
explanations.D: Speaks to restaurant owners' expectations but does not directly confirm that the wage increase lacked negative employment effects.
explanations.E: Introduces a spending-multiplier argument that is tangential; it might explain why revenues held up but does not directly address employment stability.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal/policy argument about eyewitness reliability where the correct answer confirms the load-bearing empirical premise. Traps include a choice that merely restates the conclusion, an irrelevant statistic, a comparison that doesn't close the gap, and an opposite-direction trap.
lr.stimulus: Defense attorneys have argued that eyewitness testimony obtained more than 48 hours after an event is likely to be less accurate than testimony obtained within 24 hours. Memory researchers have documented that stress hormones released during a traumatic event interfere with long-term memory consolidation. Based on this, attorneys claim that delayed eyewitness accounts should be given less weight in criminal trials.
