Choice B provides a within-period comparison: performing arts that lack streaming alternatives did not see the same decline. This contrast rules out a general arts-attendance trend and supports the conclusion that streaming specifically drove theater's decline.
explanations.A: A demographic pattern that could be consistent with either streaming competition or other generational factors; it does not rule out an alternative cause.
explanations.B: Correct. Rules out a general arts-attendance downturn by showing that non-streamed performing arts held their audience — strongly implicating streaming as the differentiating factor.
explanations.C: Introduces marketing investment as an alternative variable; it may even suggest that other factors (not streaming) explain variation in declines.
explanations.D: Introduces a rival causal explanation — price increases — that could account for the attendance drop, making this a disguised weakener.
explanations.E: The corporate pedigree of streaming services is irrelevant to whether streaming caused the attendance decline.

lr.difficultyReason: Medicine/public health predictive argument. The correct answer confirms an implicit assumption that the proposed intervention will generalize to the target population. Traps include an accurate-but-irrelevant epidemiological fact and a choice that introduces a confounding mechanism.
lr.stimulus: A large randomized controlled trial conducted in Finland found that adults with elevated cholesterol who took a daily low-dose aspirin regimen for five years had a 25 percent lower rate of first-time heart attacks than those in the control group. Finnish public health officials are now recommending that adults in Finland with elevated cholesterol adopt this aspirin regimen to reduce heart attack risk.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aspirin has also been shown to reduce the risk of certain types of stroke in populations with elevated cardiovascular risk.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Finnish adults enrolled in the trial were demographically and medically similar to the broader Finnish adult population with elevated cholesterol.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low-dose aspirin is widely available and inexpensive in Finland.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some participants in the aspirin group experienced gastrointestinal side effects that led them to discontinue the regimen before the five-year trial concluded.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Heart attack rates in Finland have been declining gradually over the past two decades due to improved dietary habits.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from trial results to a population-wide recommendation. The critical assumption is that the trial population represents the people who will follow the recommendation. Choice B directly confirms this by establishing that trial participants were demographically and medically similar to the broader target population, justifying the generalization.
explanations.A: Establishes a separate benefit (stroke reduction) that is irrelevant to whether the heart-attack-prevention result applies to the target population.
explanations.B: Correct. Confirms the representativeness assumption that allows the trial results to be generalized to the broader Finnish population with elevated cholesterol.
explanations.C: Addresses accessibility/feasibility rather than whether the intervention will work for the broader population — relevant to policy adoption but not to the medical argument's conclusion.
explanations.D: Introduces a compliance problem that could reduce real-world effectiveness — a mild weakener of the recommendation's expected impact.
explanations.E: A declining baseline rate is an alternative explanation for any future reduction in heart attacks observed after the policy is adopted, potentially weakening attribution to aspirin.

lr.difficultyReason: Scientific/medical argument where the correct answer confirms a load-bearing assumption about a study's control conditions. Distractors are topically plausible but address neighboring claims or introduce irrelevant comparisons.
lr.stimulus: A clinical trial tested whether a new antibiotic reduced recovery time from bacterial pneumonia. Patients who received the antibiotic recovered, on average, four days faster than patients who did not. The researchers concluded that the antibiotic itself was responsible for the faster recoveries.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The antibiotic has been shown to be effective against several other bacterial infections besides pneumonia.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients in both the antibiotic group and the control group received the same standard supportive care throughout the trial.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The antibiotic is less expensive to manufacture than most currently approved antibiotics for pneumonia.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some patients who did not receive the antibiotic also recovered within the average time recorded for the antibiotic group.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bacterial pneumonia is more common in elderly patients than in younger adults.

explanations.correct: The argument's conclusion rests on the antibiotic — not confounding differences in care — causing faster recovery. Confirming that both groups received identical supportive care rules out the alternative that better ancillary treatment explains the difference, directly strengthening the causal claim.
explanations.A: Accurate-but-irrelevant trap: effectiveness against other infections does not bear on whether the antibiotic caused the specific outcome in this trial.
explanations.B: Correct. Rules out the alternative explanation that differential care — rather than the antibiotic — produced the observed difference.
explanations.C: Irrelevant: manufacturing cost has no bearing on whether the antibiotic caused faster recovery.
explanations.D: This actually weakens the inference slightly by suggesting recovery without the antibiotic is possible within the same timeframe.
explanations.E: Unwarranted comparison: demographic epidemiology of pneumonia does not address the causal mechanism within the trial.

lr.difficultyReason: Economics argument requiring the correct answer to close an analogy gap between two different market contexts. Distractors include a plausible-but-irrelevant statistic and a choice that strengthens a neighboring claim.
lr.stimulus: A city government is considering capping rents on residential apartments, citing the success of a similar policy in a neighboring city where median rents fell by twelve percent within two years of implementation. Critics argue the cities are too different for the comparison to hold, because the neighboring city has a much larger rental housing stock. The policy's proponents contend the cap would still reduce rents here.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the proponents' contention?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rent control policies have been attempted in several countries with widely varying outcomes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The neighboring city's rental housing stock has grown by fifteen percent since the policy was introduced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Studies of cities with small rental housing stocks show that rent caps reduce median rents as effectively as in cities with large stocks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city government has successfully capped prices in the commercial real estate sector in the past.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The median income of renters in the two cities is approximately the same.

explanations.correct: The critics' objection is that housing-stock size makes the comparison invalid. Evidence that rent caps work equally well in small-stock cities directly closes that analogy gap and supports the proponents' claim.
explanations.A: Accurate-but-irrelevant: varying outcomes globally does not address whether the cap will work in this specific city.
explanations.B: Strengthens a neighboring claim about the neighboring city's housing supply, not the proponents' contention about this city.
explanations.C: Correct. Directly answers the critics' objection by showing that stock size does not impair the policy's effectiveness.
explanations.D: Unwarranted comparison: commercial real estate price caps operate under different mechanisms than residential rent control.
explanations.E: Irrelevant: income parity does not bear on whether the policy mechanism will reduce rents regardless of stock size.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science argument with a causal conclusion about pollution source. Correct answer rules out an alternative pollution source. Distractors include a choice that merely confirms the pollution exists and one that addresses a different conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Elevated mercury levels were detected in fish sampled from a river downstream from a coal-fired power plant. No such elevation was found in fish sampled from the same river upstream from the plant. The environmental agency concluded that the power plant's emissions are responsible for the mercury contamination in the downstream fish.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mercury contamination in fish poses a well-documented health risk to humans who consume them regularly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The power plant has been operating at the same capacity for the past decade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There are no other industrial facilities, mining operations, or known natural mercury deposits between the upstream and downstream sampling sites.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Coal-fired power plants in other regions have been linked to elevated mercury levels in nearby waterways.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The downstream fish samples were collected during the same season as the upstream samples.

explanations.correct: The agency's causal claim requires that no other source between the two sampling points explains the downstream elevation. Ruling out all other industrial, mining, and natural sources between those points directly supports the conclusion that the power plant is responsible.
explanations.A: Accurate-but-irrelevant: health risks of mercury do not bear on whether the plant caused this particular contamination.
explanations.B: Irrelevant to source attribution; operational consistency does not rule out alternative pollution sources.
explanations.C: Correct. Eliminates alternative explanations for the downstream elevation, strengthening the causal inference.
explanations.D: Strengthens a general claim about coal plants and mercury, not the specific causal conclusion about this plant and this river.
explanations.E: Controls for seasonal variation in sampling method — useful but a minor methodological point that does not rule out alternative pollution sources, which is the critical gap.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology/linguistics argument where the correct answer confirms a key mechanism linking the premise to the conclusion. Distractors include an opposite answer and an unwarranted comparison.
lr.stimulus: A software company recently released an updated version of its voice-recognition application. Following the update, the number of user complaints about transcription errors dropped by forty percent. The company attributed this improvement to a new machine-learning model incorporated in the update.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the company's attribution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The new machine-learning model was trained on a dataset three times larger than the one used to train the previous model.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Voice-recognition technology in general has improved steadily over the past decade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The update contained no other changes to the application besides the new machine-learning model.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some users continued to report transcription errors even after installing the update.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The company's competitors also released updates around the same time, which reduced errors in their own applications.

explanations.correct: If the update included only the new machine-learning model and nothing else, then the model is the only candidate cause for the improvement, directly supporting the company's attribution.
explanations.A: Confirms a feature of the model but does not rule out that other changes in the update also contributed to the improvement.
explanations.B: Unwarranted comparison: industry-wide improvement trends do not establish that this specific model caused this specific drop in complaints.
explanations.C: Correct. Eliminates all other within-update alternative causes, making the machine-learning model the only viable explanation.
explanations.D: Opposite-answer trap: continued errors among some users is consistent with the update helping but does not strengthen the attribution.
explanations.E: Irrelevant and potentially weakening: competitors' simultaneous improvements suggest industry trends may explain outcomes, not the specific model.

lr.difficultyReason: History/policy argument where the correct answer confirms a load-bearing premise about intent. Distractors include one that strengthens a different conclusion and one that is accurate but irrelevant.
lr.stimulus: Historians have long debated whether the Roman Senate's decision in 59 BCE to grant Julius Caesar an extended military command in Gaul was primarily motivated by a desire to remove a politically dangerous rival from Rome rather than by genuine strategic necessity. Proponents of the rivalry thesis note that Caesar's command was unusually lengthy and that several senators who supported it were known political adversaries of Pompey, Caesar's main rival at the time.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the rivalry thesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rome faced no documented external military threat from Gaul at the time the command was granted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Caesar's campaigns in Gaul ultimately expanded Roman territory significantly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Senate had previously granted extended commands to generals for documented strategic reasons.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Caesar wrote detailed commentaries on his Gallic campaigns that are still read today.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several senators who opposed the extended command were among Caesar's closest political allies.

explanations.correct: The rivalry thesis holds that political rivalry, not strategic necessity, motivated the Senate. Evidence that no genuine military threat existed at the time undermines the strategic-necessity alternative and directly supports the rivalry thesis.
explanations.A: Correct. Eliminates the strategic-necessity explanation, leaving political rivalry as the more plausible motivation.
explanations.B: Irrelevant to motivation: the eventual outcome does not speak to why the command was granted in the first place.
explanations.C: Weakens slightly by suggesting the Senate had legitimate precedent for extended commands, making strategic necessity more plausible.
explanations.D: Accurate-but-irrelevant: the literary legacy of Caesar's commentaries has no bearing on senatorial motivation.
explanations.E: This detail slightly weakens the rivalry thesis by complicating the political picture — if Caesar's allies opposed the command, the pattern of support is less clearly explained by rivalry alone.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics/policy argument with an implicit analogical assumption. Correct answer confirms the mechanism connecting the policy premise to the moral conclusion. Distractors include a strengthener of a neighboring claim and an opposite answer.
lr.stimulus: A bioethics committee recommended that hospitals be required to obtain explicit written consent from patients before using their anonymized medical records in research studies. The committee argued that patients have a right to control how their personal information is used, even when that information has been stripped of identifying details.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the committee's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Research studies that use anonymized medical records have produced significant medical advances over the past two decades.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients who are informed about research uses of their records are no less willing to consent than patients who are not informed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anonymization techniques used by hospitals do not completely eliminate the possibility of re-identifying individual patients from their records.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Written consent requirements increase administrative burdens for hospital research departments.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most patients are unaware that their records may be used for research purposes.

explanations.correct: The committee argues that patients retain a right to control their information even after anonymization. If anonymization is imperfect and re-identification remains possible, the records are not truly de-personalized — this confirms that the patient's interest in controlling the information persists even after the stripping process, directly strengthening the committee's reasoning.
explanations.A: Opposite-answer trap: benefits of the research practice could be used to argue against requiring consent, weakening the committee's position.
explanations.B: Accurate-but-irrelevant: willingness to consent once informed does not bear on whether consent should be required.
explanations.C: Correct. Bolsters the implicit premise that anonymized records still retain a meaningful connection to the patient, justifying the right-to-control argument.
explanations.D: Weakens the argument by introducing a cost of the proposed requirement.
explanations.E: Somewhat supports the case for informing patients but strengthens the procedural argument for notification rather than the ethical argument for a right to control.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics argument with a predictive conclusion. Correct answer confirms a load-bearing premise about the relevant population. Distractors include an unwarranted comparison and a choice that is topically relevant but addresses the wrong claim.
lr.stimulus: A linguist studying language acquisition found that children raised in bilingual households achieve full grammatical proficiency in their second language significantly earlier than children who begin formal instruction in a second language at age seven or older. The linguist predicted that children raised in bilingual households would also demonstrate stronger long-term retention of their second language in adulthood.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the linguist's prediction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adults who learned a second language early in childhood show greater neural activation in language-processing regions than those who learned it later.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Children in bilingual households are exposed to both languages in a wider variety of social contexts than are students in formal language classes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Early grammatical proficiency in a second language is strongly correlated with stronger retention of that language in adulthood.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bilingual children often outperform monolingual children on tests of cognitive flexibility.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Formal second-language instruction programs vary widely in quality across different school districts.

explanations.correct: The linguist's prediction links early proficiency (the observed advantage) to stronger adult retention. Confirming that early grammatical proficiency directly correlates with adult retention supplies the missing causal bridge, strengthening the prediction.
explanations.A: Confirms a neurological correlate but does not establish that the neural difference translates into stronger retention specifically.
explanations.B: Confirms the mechanism for why bilingual children acquire the language earlier but does not connect early acquisition to long-term retention.
explanations.C: Correct. Directly links the established advantage (early proficiency) to the predicted outcome (adult retention), closing the inferential gap.
explanations.D: Unwarranted comparison: cognitive flexibility advantages are unrelated to second-language retention.
explanations.E: Accurate-but-irrelevant: variation in instructional quality does not bear on the relationship between early proficiency and adult retention.

lr.difficultyReason: Law/policy argument where the correct answer rules out an alternative legal explanation. Distractors include a choice that strengthens a different conclusion and a classic opposite-answer trap.
lr.stimulus: A legal scholar argues that the dramatic increase in patent litigation over the past fifteen years is primarily attributable to the rise of patent assertion entities — companies that acquire patents solely to license or litigate them rather than to manufacture products. The scholar notes that the share of all patent lawsuits filed by such entities rose from twelve percent to nearly sixty percent during this period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the scholar's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The total number of patents granted by the patent office increased substantially over the same fifteen-year period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patent litigation brought by manufacturing companies did not increase significantly over the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patent assertion entities tend to target smaller technology companies that lack the resources to mount a vigorous defense.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several countries with fewer patent assertion entities have also seen increases in patent litigation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The cost of filing a patent lawsuit has declined over the past fifteen years due to procedural reforms.

explanations.correct: The scholar argues that patent assertion entities drove the overall increase. If litigation by manufacturing companies did not increase, the overall rise must be attributable to the entity category that did grow — patent assertion entities — directly supporting the scholar's claim.
explanations.A: Introduces an alternative explanation: more patents could independently drive more litigation, weakening the attribution to assertion entities.
explanations.B: Correct. Rules out the alternative that manufacturing-company litigation also surged, leaving assertion entities as the primary driver of the increase.
explanations.C: Provides detail about litigation targets but does not bear on whether assertion entities caused the overall increase in litigation volume.
explanations.D: Opposite-answer trap: if countries without assertion entities also saw increases, that suggests other factors drive litigation, weakening the scholar's claim.
explanations.E: Introduces an alternative explanation for the overall increase — reduced filing costs — rather than supporting the assertion-entity explanation.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts/cultural argument with an analogical conclusion. Correct answer closes the analogy gap. Distractors include an accurate-but-irrelevant historical fact and a choice that strengthens a neighboring but distinct claim.
lr.stimulus: A musicologist argues that the commercial failure of atonal classical compositions in the mid-twentieth century was primarily due to audience unfamiliarity with the style rather than to any intrinsic aesthetic deficit in the music. As evidence, the musicologist cites the initial hostile reception given to now-celebrated Romantic composers such as Beethoven and Wagner, whose works were ultimately embraced once audiences became accustomed to them.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the musicologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atonal compositions that have been repeatedly broadcast on public radio stations have attracted growing and appreciative audiences over time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beethoven and Wagner were both prolific composers who produced works in multiple genres.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The music industry in the mid-twentieth century was dominated by a small number of record labels that preferred commercially safe repertoire.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several atonal composers were also distinguished music theorists who wrote extensively about their compositional methods.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Audiences in the nineteenth century had access to live performances of new compositions far more frequently than modern audiences do.

explanations.correct: The musicologist's analogy predicts that atonal music, like Romantic music, would be embraced once audiences became accustomed to it. Evidence that repeated exposure has already begun producing appreciative audiences for atonal music directly confirms the analogy and supports the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Confirms that increased familiarity with atonal music produces the same reception shift predicted by the Romantic analogy.
explanations.B: Accurate-but-irrelevant: the compositional output of Beethoven and Wagner does not bear on whether unfamiliarity explains the reception of atonal music.
explanations.C: Introduces an alternative explanation — industry gatekeeping — for the commercial failure of atonal music, weakening the unfamiliarity thesis.
explanations.D: Irrelevant: composers' theoretical writings do not address whether audience unfamiliarity drove commercial failure.
explanations.E: Unwarranted comparison: differences in concert-attendance patterns between centuries do not address the unfamiliarity-versus-aesthetic-deficit question.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science/policy argument requiring the correct answer to confirm a key empirical premise. Distractors include a strengthener of a subsidiary claim and a classic opposite-answer trap.
lr.stimulus: City planners in a mid-sized metropolitan area proposed expanding the urban tree canopy to reduce the so-called urban heat island effect — the tendency of cities to be significantly warmer than surrounding rural areas due to the prevalence of heat-absorbing surfaces. The planners predicted that increasing tree coverage by twenty percent would lower peak summer temperatures in city centers by up to three degrees Celsius.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the planners' prediction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Urban trees provide additional benefits such as improved air quality and reduced stormwater runoff.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cities that increased their tree canopy by similar proportions experienced reductions in peak summer temperatures consistent with the planners' estimate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The urban heat island effect is more pronounced in cities with higher population densities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Planting trees in urban areas is significantly more costly than installing reflective roofing materials, which also reduce urban temperatures.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The metropolitan area under consideration has a climate that is cooler than that of most cities where tree-canopy studies have been conducted.

explanations.correct: The planners predict a specific temperature reduction from a specific increase in canopy coverage. Evidence that comparable canopy expansions in other cities produced comparable temperature reductions directly confirms the empirical basis for the prediction.
explanations.A: Accurate-but-irrelevant: collateral benefits of urban trees do not bear on the predicted temperature reduction.
explanations.B: Correct. Confirms the load-bearing empirical premise by showing the predicted mechanism has operated as expected in comparable real-world cases.
explanations.C: Strengthens the general claim that cities experience heat island effects but does not address whether tree canopy expansion will achieve the predicted cooling.
explanations.D: Opposite-answer trap: noting that alternative interventions also exist — and may be cheaper — does not support the planners' prediction and could be read as undermining the proposal.
explanations.E: Potentially weakens: if this city is cooler than the study cities, the generalizability of the canopy-cooling findings to this location is less secure.

lr.difficultyReason: Methodological/scientific argument where the correct answer confirms a load-bearing assumption about study design. Distractors include a plausible-but-irrelevant fact about the drug class and a choice that strengthens a neighboring claim rather than the core conclusion.
lr.stimulus: A clinical study followed two groups of patients with elevated cholesterol for three years. One group took a newly developed plant-based supplement daily; the other group took a placebo. At the end of the study, the supplement group showed a 15 percent greater reduction in LDL cholesterol than the placebo group. The researchers concluded that the supplement itself caused the additional reduction in LDL cholesterol.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The plant extract used in the supplement has been shown to inhibit cholesterol synthesis in isolated liver cells.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Participants in both groups reported no significant changes in diet or exercise habits over the course of the study.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Plant-based supplements are generally considered safer than synthetic cholesterol-lowering drugs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The researchers who conducted the study have previously published research on plant-based medicines.

choices.label: E
choices.text: LDL cholesterol levels naturally decline in some patients over a three-year period without any intervention.

explanations.correct: The argument's conclusion rests on the supplement being the cause of the difference. A rival explanation is that the supplement group independently changed diet or exercise habits. (B) eliminates that rival explanation by confirming lifestyle habits were stable across both groups, directly supporting the causal claim.
explanations.A: This confirms a possible biological mechanism, but it strengthens a neighboring claim about how the supplement could work in theory — not the conclusion that it actually caused the observed reduction in this study. Strengthens a different conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct. Rules out a confounding lifestyle variable, closing the most salient gap between the observed difference and the causal conclusion.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — safety comparisons to synthetic drugs have no bearing on whether the supplement caused LDL reduction.
explanations.D: Irrelevant; the researchers' prior publication record does not speak to whether the supplement caused the outcome in this study.
explanations.E: Introduces an alternative explanation — natural decline — which would weaken the argument by suggesting the supplement group's improvement may not have been caused by the supplement.

lr.difficultyReason: Economic/policy argument built on an analogy between two jurisdictions. The correct answer closes the analogical gap by confirming a structural similarity. Distractors include an unwarranted comparison and a choice that would actually weaken by suggesting the jurisdictions differ in a relevant way.
lr.stimulus: When the city of Harwell reduced its downtown parking fees by 40 percent three years ago, retail sales in the downtown corridor increased by 18 percent within twelve months. The city of Calderton is now considering the same fee reduction. Proponents argue that Calderton's downtown retail sector will therefore likely experience a similar boost in sales.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the proponents' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Surveys show that parking cost is one of the primary reasons residents of Calderton avoid shopping downtown.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Harwell's downtown retailers credited the parking fee reduction as the main cause of their increased revenue.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several cities that reduced downtown parking fees saw no appreciable change in retail sales.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Calderton's downtown retail sector is larger and more diversified than Harwell's was at the time of its fee reduction.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reducing parking fees is a less expensive policy intervention than constructing new parking structures.

explanations.correct: The analogical argument requires that parking cost be a deterrent to Calderton shoppers — that the mechanism driving Harwell's results also operates in Calderton. (A) directly confirms that deterrence is present in Calderton, closing the key analogical gap.
explanations.A: Correct. Confirms that the mechanism behind Harwell's success — parking cost discourages downtown visits — applies to Calderton, making the predicted outcome more likely.
explanations.B: Strengthens the claim that the fee reduction caused Harwell's results, which is a neighboring claim already accepted in the argument. It does not address whether the same effect will occur in Calderton — strengthens a different conclusion.
explanations.C: Weakens the argument by introducing counterexamples where the policy failed, undercutting the reliability of the analogy.
explanations.D: Introduces a disanalogy — Calderton's sector is structurally different — which might suggest the outcomes will differ rather than converge. This could weaken rather than strengthen.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant; cost-effectiveness comparisons among policy options don't support the prediction that sales will increase.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science argument with a causal claim about species decline. The correct answer confirms an implicit mechanism. Trap (D) sounds supportive but addresses a general principle rather than the specific causal claim; trap (E) is a disguised weakener.
lr.stimulus: Over the past two decades, populations of a freshwater mussel species in the Teller River basin have declined by more than 60 percent. During that same period, agricultural runoff containing elevated levels of phosphorus has increased substantially in the basin. Biologists studying the mussel populations concluded that the phosphorus-laden runoff is the primary cause of the decline.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the biologists' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Laboratory experiments show that mussels of this species experience significantly higher mortality rates when exposed to phosphorus concentrations matching those now found in the Teller River.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Phosphorus runoff from agriculture has increased in river basins throughout the region over the same two-decade period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Freshwater mussels are considered a keystone species because their decline can trigger broader ecosystem disruption.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elevated phosphorus levels are known to harm a wide variety of freshwater invertebrate species.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A dam constructed upstream in the Teller River basin fifteen years ago has altered the river's flow rate and sediment composition.

explanations.correct: The biologists' conclusion requires that phosphorus at the levels now present in the Teller River actually harms this mussel species. (A) provides direct experimental evidence of precisely that mechanism — mortality increases at exactly those concentrations — confirming the implicit causal link.
explanations.A: Correct. Confirms the biological mechanism at the specific phosphorus concentrations present in this case, directly supporting the causal conclusion.
explanations.B: Indicates the phenomenon is widespread, but does not establish that phosphorus caused the Teller River declines specifically. A regional trend does not rule out other local factors unique to the Teller basin.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — the ecological importance of mussels says nothing about what is causing their decline in this basin.
explanations.D: Strengthens a general claim that phosphorus harms freshwater invertebrates broadly, but does not confirm that this particular species is harmed at the concentrations in the Teller River. Strengthens a neighboring, more general conclusion rather than the specific one.
explanations.E: Introduces an alternative causal explanation — altered flow and sediment from a dam — that could account for the decline without implicating phosphorus runoff. This is a disguised weakener.

lr.difficultyReason: Scientific/methodological argument about a drug trial. The correct answer confirms a load-bearing assumption about the control group's comparability. Traps include a plausible-sounding irrelevant fact about dosage and a choice that strengthens a neighboring claim rather than the conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Researchers conducting a clinical trial found that patients who received the experimental drug Veralox recovered from moderate influenza infections an average of two days faster than patients in the control group who received a placebo. The researchers concluded that Veralox itself caused the faster recovery.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Veralox was developed using a novel antiviral compound not found in any currently approved influenza medication.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients in the Veralox group and the placebo group had similar baseline health profiles and were infected with the same influenza strain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The clinical trial was conducted at three different hospital sites to ensure geographic diversity among participants.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several participants in the placebo group sought additional over-the-counter remedies during the trial period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Veralox has also shown promising results in laboratory tests against other respiratory viruses.

explanations.correct: The argument's causal conclusion depends on the two groups being comparable — if patients in the Veralox group were healthier or had milder infections to begin with, the drug itself might not deserve credit. Choice B confirms that the groups were matched on baseline health and virus strain, closing the most obvious gap between the evidence and the causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant. The novelty of the compound's chemistry tells us nothing about whether the trial design supports a causal conclusion. This is a topical but non-supporting fact.
explanations.B: Correct. Confirms the critical load-bearing assumption that the control and treatment groups were comparable, ruling out pre-existing group differences as an alternative explanation for the faster recovery.
explanations.C: Strengthens external validity (generalizability) but does not address whether Veralox caused faster recovery versus some confound within the trial — a different conclusion than the one drawn.
explanations.D: This is a disguised weakener. If placebo patients sought additional remedies, those remedies — not the absence of Veralox — may partly explain the difference, which actually introduces an alternative cause rather than ruling one out.
explanations.E: Strengthens a neighboring claim about Veralox's general antiviral properties, not the specific causal conclusion that Veralox caused faster influenza recovery in this trial.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental/policy argument with an implicit mechanism about carbon pricing reducing industrial emissions. The correct answer closes an analogy gap between past policy and the current proposal. Traps include an irrelevant comparison and a choice that introduces a rival cause.
lr.stimulus: An environmental advocacy group argues that introducing a carbon tax on industrial emissions in the Lakewood region will significantly reduce those emissions within five years. They point to the fact that a neighboring region, Cedarvale, introduced a comparable carbon tax a decade ago and saw its industrial emissions drop by 30 percent over the following five years.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the advocacy group's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Lakewood region's industrial sector is dominated by the same types of manufacturing industries as Cedarvale's was when its carbon tax was introduced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carbon taxes have been endorsed by a majority of environmental economists as an effective tool for reducing greenhouse gas emissions globally.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cedarvale's industrial emissions continued to decline for several years after the initial five-year period following the carbon tax's introduction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Lakewood region recently enacted stricter environmental regulations that are independent of any proposed carbon tax.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several Lakewood industries have already begun exploring renewable energy options in anticipation of future environmental legislation.

explanations.correct: The argument is analogical: because Cedarvale's carbon tax worked, Lakewood's will too. The analogy's weakest link is whether the two regions' industrial sectors are sufficiently similar. Choice A closes that gap by confirming that Lakewood's industries mirror the types that responded to the tax in Cedarvale, making the analogical inference much stronger.
explanations.A: Correct. Directly confirms the analogical premise by establishing industrial-sector similarity between Lakewood and Cedarvale, the critical gap the argument needs to bridge.
explanations.B: Unwarranted comparison. This is a broad global endorsement that does not specifically address whether Lakewood's situation resembles the contexts in which carbon taxes have worked. It strengthens a general claim, not the specific prediction.
explanations.C: Strengthens a different conclusion — that Cedarvale's long-term results were positive — rather than supporting the prediction that Lakewood will see emissions drop in the next five years.
explanations.D: Introduces an alternative cause. If Lakewood already has stricter independent regulations, those regulations — not the proposed carbon tax — might drive any future emission reductions, which undermines rather than supports attributing results to the carbon tax.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant. Industry anticipation of future legislation tells us nothing decisive about whether the carbon tax specifically will cause the predicted five-year reduction.

lr.difficultyReason: Historical/linguistic argument about a causal claim regarding written language standardization. The correct answer confirms the implicit mechanism linking trade network expansion to dialect convergence. Traps include an opposite-direction causal claim and an irrelevant historical fact.
lr.stimulus: Historians of language have noted that the dialects spoken in the Aldenmere valley became significantly more uniform between the twelfth and fourteenth centuries. During this same period, long-distance trade networks connecting the valley's towns expanded considerably. The historians argue that the expansion of these trade networks caused the dialect convergence.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to support the historians' reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Written records from the thirteenth century show that Aldenmere merchants who traveled between towns began adopting vocabulary and pronunciations from each other's home dialects.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dialect convergence has also been observed in other valley regions of comparable geography during the medieval period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Aldenmere valley's population grew substantially during the twelfth through fourteenth centuries due to improved agricultural yields.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dialect convergence in the Aldenmere valley was already underway before the trade network expansion began in earnest.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The towns connected by the Aldenmere trade networks were located no more than two days' travel from one another.

explanations.correct: The historians' causal argument requires a mechanism: how would trade network expansion actually produce dialect convergence? Choice A supplies that mechanism directly — merchants traveling between towns adopted each other's linguistic features, constituting exactly the process by which trade contact would cause dialects to merge. This confirms the implicit causal link the argument depends on.
explanations.A: Correct. Supplies the missing causal mechanism — merchants engaged in cross-dialectal linguistic exchange — that bridges the premise (trade expansion) to the conclusion (dialect convergence), directly supporting the historians' causal claim.
explanations.B: Unwarranted comparison. Other valley regions experiencing dialect convergence could be explained by any number of shared geographic or demographic factors; without linking those cases to trade, this does not support the specific causal claim about Aldenmere.
explanations.C: Introduces an alternative cause. Population growth driven by agricultural yields is a rival explanation for dialect convergence (more mixing of people generally), which undermines the trade-network explanation rather than supporting it.
explanations.D: Opposite answer. If convergence was already underway before trade expansion, this directly weakens the causal claim by suggesting the trade networks were not the cause.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant. The physical proximity of towns may be a background condition, but it does not explain why trade — rather than proximity alone — drove dialect convergence, nor does it confirm the causal mechanism the argument needs.

lr.difficultyReason: Statistical inference layered over a causal claim: the argument compares two cohorts but leaves a selection-bias alternative open. The correct answer rules out that subtle third alternative. Trap (A) strengthens a neighboring claim about dosage; trap (D) introduces an unwarranted comparison.
lr.stimulus: Patients treated for hypertension at the Ledford clinic were prescribed either drug P or drug Q, depending on which was in stock the day they first visited. Over five years, patients who received drug P had 22 percent fewer cardiac events than those who received drug Q. Since the two groups were otherwise similar in age, weight, and medical history, researchers concluded that drug P probably provides better cardiac protection than drug Q.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patients who received higher doses of drug P experienced greater reductions in blood pressure than those who received lower doses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drug P and drug Q are prescribed with roughly equal frequency at other hypertension clinics in the region.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patients who received drug P were no more likely than those who received drug Q to also be taking cholesterol-lowering medications during the study.

choices.label: D
choices.text: At a different clinic, patients treated with drug P had fewer cardiac events than patients treated with a third hypertension drug.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Drug P is somewhat more expensive per dose than drug Q.

explanations.correct: The researchers controlled for age, weight, and medical history, but a concurrent cholesterol drug could be the real driver of drug P patients' better outcomes. (C) rules out that alternative, making the causal attribution to drug P substantially more plausible.
explanations.A: Strengthens a different conclusion — about dose-response for blood pressure, not about comparative cardiac protection.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — prescribing frequency elsewhere doesn't address whether drug P actually protects the heart.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Unwarranted comparison — a third drug's performance doesn't address the P-versus-Q contrast or rule out confounding at Ledford.
explanations.E: Tangential — cost has no bearing on clinical efficacy.

lr.difficultyReason: Economic argument combining an analogy with a causal claim. The correct answer closes the analogical gap by ruling out a feature unique to the reference case. Trap (B) strengthens a sister conclusion about revenue; trap (E) is an alternative cause dressed as support.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Three decades ago, the province of Harwell gradually phased out its personal income tax while raising its sales tax. Within ten years, Harwell's per capita economic output had grown substantially faster than that of neighboring provinces. The province of Brenmark is now considering a similar tax shift. Critics argue that the shift worked in Harwell only because Harwell's tourist economy absorbed the new sales tax. Still, the same tax shift would probably accelerate growth in Brenmark as well.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Brenmark has a slightly larger population than Harwell had at the time of its tax shift.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tax revenues in Harwell rose, rather than fell, during the decade following the shift.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Brenmark already attracts a proportion of its revenue from tourists that is comparable to what Harwell's tourist share was before the shift.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most of Harwell's accelerated growth during that decade occurred in sectors unrelated to tourism, such as manufacturing and software.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Around the time Harwell phased out its income tax, a neighboring province subsidized a new rail line into Harwell's largest city.

explanations.correct: The critics' objection is that tourism, not the tax shift, drove Harwell's growth. (D) undermines that alternative by showing the growth came from non-tourist sectors, closing the analogical gap between Harwell and Brenmark.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant — a modest population difference doesn't address the tourism objection.
explanations.B: Strengthens a different conclusion — about revenue, not growth.
explanations.C: Addresses tourist share but cuts both ways: it could just as easily support the critics' view that the shift depends on a tourism buffer.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Weakens — supplies a rival explanation (the rail subsidy) for Harwell's growth.

lr.difficultyReason: EXCEPT format over an ethical argument: four choices strengthen, one fails to. Test-takers under time pressure tend to pick the first strengthener rather than scanning for the odd-one-out. The non-strengthener (C) is irrelevant rather than weakening, which makes it harder to spot.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Public universities should require every undergraduate to complete a course in formal logic. Studies of college graduates consistently show that those who took such a course later reported fewer regrets about major life decisions than graduates who did not. A course in formal logic therefore probably improves students' ability to make decisions they will not later regret.
lr.questionStem: Each of the following, if true, strengthens the ethicist's argument EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Students who enter college with a preference for formal logic do not consistently report fewer regrets about life decisions than students without that preference.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exercises used in formal logic courses directly train students to identify unstated assumptions in everyday reasoning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A course in formal logic typically satisfies one of several general-education requirements at most public universities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Graduates who took a formal logic course report making the same kinds of major life decisions as graduates who did not.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Self-reported regret correlates closely with independent measures of decision quality in long-term outcome studies.

explanations.correct: (C) is accurate but irrelevant: how the course fits into graduation requirements has no bearing on whether formal logic improves decision-making. It neither rules out an alternative nor confirms any load-bearing link, so it fails to strengthen.
explanations.A: Strengthens — rules out the selection-bias alternative that logic-minded students simply regret less.
explanations.B: Strengthens — supplies the unstated mechanism connecting logic training to better decisions.
explanations.C: Correct (does not strengthen).
explanations.D: Strengthens — rules out the alternative that the two groups face different kinds of decisions.
explanations.E: Strengthens — validates the self-report measure that the study relies on.

lr.difficultyReason: Statistical inference in an environmental argument where the correct answer addresses a subtle selection threat (which sites were sampled). Trap (A) strengthens a sister claim; trap (E) introduces an alternative cause.
lr.stimulus: Ecologist: Since protected status was extended to the Morrin estuary twelve years ago, the number of adult saltmarsh sparrows counted during our annual surveys has risen by 40 percent. Sparrow populations in comparable unprotected estuaries have declined over the same period. The protected designation has therefore probably caused the sparrow population to recover at Morrin.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the ecologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At Morrin, the reproductive success rate of saltmarsh sparrows was already higher than the regional average before protection was granted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The annual surveys at Morrin have been conducted using the same survey routes and methods throughout the twelve-year period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some unprotected estuaries in the region have seen increases in the populations of other shorebird species during the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protected status at Morrin restricts public access but does not restrict the use of nearby agricultural land.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The annual surveys at Morrin were expanded to cover additional marsh areas five years after protected status was granted.

explanations.correct: A natural alternative is that the rising count reflects changes in survey methodology rather than a real population increase. (B) rules this out by confirming methodological consistency, so the 40-percent rise is more plausibly a real recovery caused by protection.
explanations.A: Weakens — a pre-existing reproductive advantage suggests the recovery might have happened without protection.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Unwarranted comparison — other species' trends don't bear on saltmarsh sparrows at Morrin.
explanations.D: Tangential — the access restriction's scope doesn't address whether the population actually rose because of protection.
explanations.E: Weakens — expanding the survey area inflates counts for reasons unrelated to population recovery.

lr.difficultyReason: Nested reasoning: a predictive claim rests on an analogy plus an implicit mechanism about consumer behavior. The correct answer confirms the mechanism rather than bolstering the analogy. Trap (A) strengthens a different conclusion about retention; trap (E) is a disguised weakener.
lr.stimulus: Technology columnist: The new Velora smart speaker displays on-screen captions for every spoken response. When an earlier model without captions was tested, users who were hard of hearing abandoned it within two weeks at three times the rate of other users. Since captions directly address that group's difficulties, the Velora will probably retain hard-of-hearing users at roughly the same rate as other users.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the columnist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Users of the earlier model who remained after two weeks tended to continue using it for at least a year.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Among users of the earlier model who abandoned it, those who were hard of hearing cited difficulty understanding spoken responses more often than any other reason.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Velora's captions can be disabled through a setting in the companion app.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Velora costs somewhat more than the earlier model but is sold through the same retail channels.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several competing smart speakers released this year also include on-screen captions for spoken responses.

explanations.correct: The columnist assumes the earlier model's high abandonment rate among hard-of-hearing users was caused by difficulty understanding speech — the exact problem captions fix. (B) confirms that mechanism, making it far more plausible that adding captions will close the retention gap.
explanations.A: Strengthens a different conclusion — about long-term retention of users who already stayed, not about the hard-of-hearing abandonment gap.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Weakens — if users can disable captions, the mechanism may not operate for them.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — price and distribution don't speak to whether captions solve the retention problem.
explanations.E: Irrelevant — competitor features don't bear on whether the Velora will retain hard-of-hearing users.

lr.difficultyReason: Historical-linguistic argument with a compared-scenarios structure. The correct answer rules out a non-obvious third alternative (prior exposure through trade). Trap (D) strengthens a neighboring claim about a different language family; trap (B) is opposite-direction.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Speakers of the now-extinct Kellish language used a suffix that marked the speaker's degree of certainty about a reported event. The same suffix, with nearly the same range of meanings, appears in texts written in Antoric, a language spoken a thousand kilometers away. Since the two languages had no known common ancestor, the simplest explanation is that Antoric borrowed the suffix from Kellish during a period of contact between the two communities.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antoric texts that use the suffix were composed at least two centuries after the earliest surviving Kellish texts that use it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several other Kellish grammatical features appear in the earliest Antoric texts that use the suffix.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most languages spoken in the broader region used some system for marking speaker certainty about reported events.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Languages descended from a common ancestor of Antoric, spoken far to the north, also use suffixes to mark speaker certainty.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trade goods of Kellish origin have been found in Antoric archaeological sites but not the other way around.

explanations.correct: If Antoric independently happened to develop a similar certainty suffix, that would undercut the borrowing claim. (B) rules that alternative out: the clustering of multiple Kellish features in the earliest Antoric texts that use the suffix is far more consistent with borrowing than with coincidence.
explanations.A: Weakly supportive but does not rule out independent development — chronology alone doesn't distinguish borrowing from coincidence.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Weakens — regional ubiquity makes independent development of such a suffix in Antoric more plausible.
explanations.D: Strengthens a different conclusion — about the Antoric family's inherited tendencies, which would actually undermine the borrowing explanation.
explanations.E: Consistent with contact but doesn't establish the linguistic borrowing specifically; it's at best weak background support.

lr.difficultyReason: Historical causal argument with compared scenarios. The correct answer addresses a subtle reverse-causation threat. Trap (A) strengthens a sister claim about a different period; trap (D) introduces an unwarranted comparison.
lr.stimulus: Historian: In the two decades after the introduction of mechanical printing in Delsar, the number of pamphlets published per capita rose fivefold, and the number of literate adults in the city's trade guilds roughly doubled. In neighboring Trelford, which did not adopt mechanical printing until much later, literacy rates in comparable guilds remained flat. Mechanical printing therefore probably caused the rise in guild literacy in Delsar.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the historian's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the two decades before printing was introduced in Delsar, literacy rates in Delsar's trade guilds had been essentially constant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several Trelford printers traveled to Delsar to learn the new technology before returning home to set up their own presses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pamphlets published in Delsar during the period in question dealt largely with matters of commercial practice relevant to guild members.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cities elsewhere in the region that adopted mechanical printing at roughly the same time as Delsar did not experience comparable literacy gains.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many Delsar guild members began sending their children to informal schools during the period in question.

explanations.correct: A natural reverse-causation worry is that guilds were already becoming more literate — and that rising demand, not the press, caused the surge in pamphlets. (A) rules out that alternative by showing pre-printing literacy was flat, so the post-printing rise is more plausibly caused by the press.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Tangential — printer mobility doesn't speak to whether printing caused the literacy rise in Delsar.
explanations.C: Tempting, but content relevance alone doesn't rule out that literate guild members demanded the pamphlets rather than the press causing the literacy.
explanations.D: Weakens — if comparable cities with printing did not see the gains, the press is unlikely to be sufficient, undermining the causal attribution.
explanations.E: Introduces an alternative cause (informal schooling) that would weaken rather than strengthen the press attribution.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy argument with a nested causal chain (program feature → behavioral change → outcome). Correct answer confirms the middle link. Trap (B) is accurate but irrelevant; trap (C) strengthens a misreading of the argument.
lr.stimulus: City planner: When Harford adopted evening parking meters on its main commercial street, foot traffic at nearby restaurants during dinner hours rose by 18 percent within six months. The meters discourage long-term parking by commuters, freeing spaces for diners. The meters are therefore probably responsible for the increase in dinner-hour foot traffic.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the city planner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The revenue from the evening meters has been earmarked for maintenance of the commercial street's sidewalks and lighting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The hourly meter rate during evening hours is the same as the rate during business hours.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Restaurants near the commercial street that offer private parking lots reported similar increases in dinner-hour foot traffic.

choices.label: D
choices.text: After the meters were installed, the average length of time parked cars remained on the commercial street during dinner hours fell sharply.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several new restaurants opened on the commercial street during the six months following the meters' installation.

explanations.correct: The planner's causal chain has two links: meters shorten parking durations, and shorter durations free spaces for diners. (D) directly confirms the first link with observed data, making the full chain substantially more plausible.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant — how the revenue is spent has no bearing on the mechanism.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — uniform pricing doesn't speak to whether the meters changed parking behavior.
explanations.C: Weakens — if restaurants with private lots saw similar gains, the meters are unlikely to be the cause.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Weakens — new restaurants supply an alternative cause for the traffic increase.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts/statistical argument where the correct answer rules out a subtle self-selection threat. Trap (E) is a plausible strengthener for a misreading about all students; trap (A) strengthens a sister conclusion about adult learners.
lr.stimulus: Music instructor: Among children at the Arris conservatory, those who begin piano lessons before age seven tend, on average, to achieve higher scores on sight-reading exams at age twelve than children who begin later. The earlier start therefore probably causes the stronger sight-reading performance.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the instructor's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adult students who begin piano lessons after age thirty tend to achieve lower sight-reading scores than those who began earlier in adulthood.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sight-reading exam at Arris is administered using the same format and difficulty level to all twelve-year-old students.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Among Arris children, age of starting piano lessons is not correlated with parental income or with prior exposure to other musical instruments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Teachers at Arris observe that early-starting students generally seem more confident during lessons than later-starting students.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Students at Arris who practice more hours per week tend to score higher on sight-reading exams than students who practice less.

explanations.correct: The natural alternative is that early-starting students are systematically different — wealthier families, more musical households — and that those factors, not the early start, drive sight-reading scores. (C) rules out both confounders, making the causal attribution to age-of-start more plausible.
explanations.A: Strengthens a sister conclusion about adult learners and doesn't bear on the causal claim about children.
explanations.B: Rules out a measurement concern but does nothing to address the underlying self-selection threat.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Accurate but tangential — confidence during lessons doesn't establish that the early start caused the exam-score gap.
explanations.E: Plausible strengthener for a misreading that practice hours explain the effect; it actually introduces an alternative cause.

lr.difficultyReason: Medical argument with a nested causal claim relying on timing. The correct answer rules out a reverse-causation alternative. Trap (A) strengthens a different conclusion; trap (D) is accurate but irrelevant.
lr.stimulus: Researcher: A large study of adults over age sixty has found that those who walk briskly for at least thirty minutes a day are significantly less likely to show early markers of cognitive decline than those who are less active. Brisk walking probably helps prevent early cognitive decline in older adults.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researcher's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Older adults who engage in strenuous cardiovascular exercise other than walking also show fewer early markers of cognitive decline than less active peers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Study participants who began walking briskly only after enrolling in the study showed fewer cognitive-decline markers five years later than those who remained inactive.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Among study participants, the difference in cognitive-decline markers between brisk walkers and less active adults grew larger with each year of follow-up.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Brisk walking has been shown to improve cardiovascular health in adults of all ages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Study participants who reported the most enjoyment of their daily activities were slightly more likely to walk briskly than those who reported less enjoyment.

explanations.correct: The central threat is reverse causation: people whose cognition is already declining may simply walk less. (B) addresses this by showing that adults who took up brisk walking after enrolling — and so could not have selected into walking on the basis of prior cognitive health — still showed fewer decline markers, strongly supporting the causal direction the researcher claims.
explanations.A: Strengthens a different conclusion — that cardiovascular exercise broadly helps cognition — rather than the specific brisk-walking claim, and doesn't rule out reverse causation.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Consistent with the conclusion but equally consistent with cognitive decline making people progressively less active; does not rule out reverse causation.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant to cognitive decline specifically.
explanations.E: Weakens — introduces mood or life satisfaction as an alternative cause of both walking and better cognition.

lr.difficultyReason: EXCEPT format. The argument involves a multi-step policy chain (legible labeling → informed consumer choice → healthier diets). Four answers strengthen distinct links; one (the correct answer) appears supportive on the surface but actually addresses a neighboring claim rather than the argument's conclusion.
lr.stimulus: A consumer advocacy group argues that requiring restaurants to display calorie counts prominently on menus will improve public health outcomes. Diners who see calorie information, the group contends, will make lower-calorie choices, and consistently lower-calorie choices lead to reduced rates of diet-related illness. The group therefore urges all municipalities to mandate prominent calorie labeling on restaurant menus.
lr.questionStem: Each of the following, if true, strengthens the consumer advocacy group's argument EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: In cities where calorie labeling was mandated, average per-meal calorie consumption at restaurants decreased significantly within two years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People who habitually consume fewer calories than the average for their demographic group have lower rates of diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Surveys show that the majority of diners report that they would choose lower-calorie options if calorie information were clearly available at the point of ordering.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restaurants that voluntarily adopted calorie labeling before any mandate reported an increase in overall customer satisfaction scores.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Longitudinal studies indicate that sustained reductions in daily caloric intake correlate strongly with decreased incidence of diet-related chronic illnesses.

explanations.correct: The argument's conclusion is that mandatory calorie labeling will improve public health. Customer satisfaction is entirely disconnected from the health-outcome chain the argument traces. D neither rules out an alternative explanation nor confirms a load-bearing premise linking labeling to healthier choices to better health. It is therefore the one answer that does NOT strengthen the argument.
explanations.A: Strengthens — directly confirms that labeling causes lower-calorie choices, a key causal link in the argument.
explanations.B: Strengthens — supports the premise that lower-calorie choices reduce diet-related illness.
explanations.C: Strengthens — supports the premise that diners will act on calorie information when displayed.
explanations.D: Correct (does not strengthen). Customer satisfaction scores are irrelevant to the health-improvement conclusion.
explanations.E: Strengthens — bolsters the premise that sustained caloric reduction leads to fewer chronic illnesses.

lr.difficultyReason: Multi-step causal chain in medicine. The correct answer addresses a non-obvious implicit assumption — that the observed biomarker reduction actually reflects the proposed mechanism rather than a confounding drug interaction. Distractors include a plausible-sounding choice that strengthens only a neighboring claim.
lr.stimulus: Researchers studying patients with chronic inflammatory arthritis found that those who began taking a new omega-3 supplement showed a marked reduction in serum levels of interleukin-6, a key inflammatory marker, after twelve weeks. The researchers concluded that omega-3 supplementation directly suppresses interleukin-6 production in joint tissue, thereby reducing inflammation.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Interleukin-6 is known to be a reliable indicator of systemic inflammation in patients with chronic arthritis.

choices.label: B
choices.text: None of the patients in the study changed their dosage of anti-inflammatory medications during the twelve-week supplementation period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Other omega-3 supplements produced by different manufacturers have also been shown to reduce inflammatory symptoms in arthritis patients.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The patients who showed the greatest reduction in interleukin-6 also reported the most significant improvements in joint mobility.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Omega-3 fatty acids have been used as dietary supplements for purposes unrelated to inflammation for several decades.

explanations.correct: The researchers attribute the IL-6 reduction to the omega-3 supplement specifically. A rival explanation is that changes in patients' anti-inflammatory medication drove the reduction. B rules out that alternative by confirming medication dosages were unchanged, directly strengthening the causal attribution to omega-3.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant — confirming IL-6 is a reliable marker doesn't establish that omega-3 caused its reduction.
explanations.B: Correct. Rules out confounding medication changes as an alternative explanation for the observed reduction.
explanations.C: Strengthens a broader claim about omega-3 supplements generally, not the specific mechanistic conclusion about this supplement suppressing IL-6 in joint tissue.
explanations.D: Shows a correlation between IL-6 reduction and symptom improvement but does not address whether omega-3 caused the IL-6 reduction in the first place.
explanations.E: Irrelevant — longevity of use for other purposes says nothing about the causal mechanism proposed.

lr.difficultyReason: Analogical argument in law/economics. The correct answer closes an analogical gap by establishing that the key structural feature making the analogy work actually holds in the target case. Distractors include a surface-plausible choice that strengthens the source case rather than the analogy.
lr.stimulus: A legal scholar argues that recent antitrust rulings against dominant social media platforms should be modeled on the landmark breakup of telecommunications monopolies in the 1980s. In that case, breaking up a single dominant provider spurred innovation, lowered consumer prices, and created a more competitive market. The scholar concludes that applying similar remedies to dominant social media companies would produce comparable benefits.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the legal scholar's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The telecommunications breakup of the 1980s is widely regarded by economists as one of the most successful antitrust interventions in American history.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Social media platforms, like telecommunications providers in the 1980s, derive their dominance primarily from network effects and control of essential infrastructure rather than from superior products alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several technology companies that emerged after previous antitrust actions in the software industry went on to become dominant platforms themselves.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Consumer advocacy groups in multiple countries have called for stricter regulation of social media companies' data practices.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The federal agencies responsible for antitrust enforcement currently have more resources than they did during the telecommunications case.

explanations.correct: The scholar's analogy depends on social media platforms sharing the structural features that made the telecom breakup effective (network effects, infrastructure control). B confirms that the same dominance-conferring mechanism applies in both cases, directly closing the analogical gap and strengthening the conclusion.
explanations.A: Strengthens only the source side of the analogy — it confirms the telecom precedent was successful, but does not establish that social media platforms are relevantly similar.
explanations.B: Correct. Establishes the shared structural feature (network effects + infrastructure control) that underpins the analogy's validity.
explanations.C: Introduces an alternative outcome (new dominant companies emerging post-breakup) that if anything raises doubt about the effectiveness of the remedy — a mild weakener.
explanations.D: Irrelevant — advocacy group calls for data regulation address a different issue than the structural antitrust argument.
explanations.E: Addresses enforcement capacity, not the structural similarity that makes the analogy work.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science causal argument with a non-obvious load-bearing assumption. The correct answer confirms a mechanism (bioaccumulation pathway) that is implicit but necessary for the conclusion. A strong distractor rules out a different alternative cause, making it appear equally valid.
lr.stimulus: Ecologists monitoring a coastal estuary found that osprey populations declined sharply following the expansion of a nearby agricultural operation. They noted elevated concentrations of organophosphate pesticides in estuary fish — the osprey's primary food source. The ecologists concluded that pesticide bioaccumulation through the food chain is responsible for the osprey population decline.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the ecologists' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No new residential development occurred near the estuary in the three years preceding the osprey population decline.

choices.label: B
