(B) shows the two samples were each drawn from outliers of their own era — the longest genre in 1850–1900 and the shortest genre in 2010–2020 — inflating any apparent gap. The sampling flaw undermines the generalization.
explanations.A: Strengthens, if anything — equal corpus size supports the comparability of the statistics, not their representativeness.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too narrow — a handful of translated letters wouldn't move the average enough to explain a 38 percent gap.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the composition device doesn't bear on whether the sentences represent English usage generally.
explanations.E: Attacks a methodological detail that applies equally to both corpora and so cannot account for the gap between them.

lr.difficultyReason: Historical causal argument attributing a cultural shift to a specific policy. Weakener introduces a prior alternative cause whose effects coincided with the policy. Trap (B) strengthens; trap (D) attacks a subsidiary claim.
lr.stimulus: Historian: In the Kingdom of Valoria, the rate at which commoners learned to read more than doubled in the three decades following King Edric's 1472 decree that every parish maintain a school open to all children. Edric's decree is therefore the principal cause of the dramatic rise in literacy among Valorian commoners during this period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Edric's decree included provisions imposing modest fines on parishes that failed to maintain the required schools.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Surviving records indicate that most of the parish schools founded under Edric's decree employed clergy as teachers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Literacy rates among Valorian nobles also rose during the three decades following the decree, though less sharply.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some parishes did not comply with Edric's decree until several years after its issuance.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A process for producing inexpensive printed books arrived in Valoria in 1470, and by 1500 Valorian towns were filled with cheap printed material of the sort commoners could acquire and use to teach themselves to read.

explanations.correct: The historian credits Edric's decree with the surge in commoner literacy. (E) supplies a prior, independent cause — the arrival of cheap printed books two years before the decree — that plausibly explains the same rise. The correlation between the decree and the literacy rise is equally consistent with this competing cause, so the historian's attribution no longer follows.
explanations.A: Strengthens, if anything — an enforcement mechanism makes it more likely that the decree was implemented and thereby produced its effect.
explanations.B: Strengthens, if anything — identifies a plausible mechanism (clergy teaching) by which the decree operated.
explanations.C: Out of scope — rising noble literacy doesn't explain away the commoners' rise.
explanations.D: Attacks a subsidiary point about compliance timing without displacing the decree as primary cause.
explanations.E: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy causal argument from aggregate data. Weakener exposes a confounder that explains the correlation. Trap (A) strengthens; trap (E) is a strengthener disguised as criticism.
lr.stimulus: Public-health official: Over the past five years, our county's 15 elementary schools have progressively adopted a new nutrition program that replaces fried side dishes with steamed vegetables in school lunches. During that same period, the proportion of elementary-school students in our county classified as overweight has fallen from 24 percent to 18 percent. The nutrition program is clearly responsible for the drop in childhood overweight in our county.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the official's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Schools that adopted the nutrition program earlier in the five-year period saw the largest drops in the proportion of students classified as overweight.

choices.label: B
choices.text: During the same five-year period, the county opened six new public parks and required each elementary school to add 90 minutes per week of physical-education activity, changes unrelated to the nutrition program.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some students in the county bring their own lunches to school rather than eating the lunches the nutrition program provides.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The nutrition program is more expensive per meal than the lunch program it replaced.

choices.label: E
choices.text: National surveys show that the proportion of elementary-school students classified as overweight has remained steady nationwide over the past five years.

explanations.correct: The official credits the nutrition program with the weight drop. (B) introduces a concurrent, independent cause — mandated physical-education increases and new parks — that could plausibly explain the same drop, so the correlation no longer singles out the nutrition program.
explanations.A: Strengthens — a dose-response pattern supports the causal attribution.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too narrow — some students opting out doesn't explain why the county-wide rate fell, and if anything makes the program's contribution harder, not easier, to credit.
explanations.D: Out of scope — cost has no bearing on whether the program caused the weight drop.
explanations.E: Strengthens — a stable national rate makes the county's drop harder to attribute to a general trend and thus easier to attribute to a local change like the program.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts causal argument from attendance data. Weakener reveals a sampling flaw: attendance was inflated by a short-term event. Trap (A) strengthens; trap (D) attacks a subsidiary point.
lr.stimulus: Museum director: When the Pelham Gallery reopened last year after a two-year renovation, daily attendance in its first three months was 40 percent higher than the average daily attendance in the three years before the closure. Critics doubted that the renovation, which preserved the original floor plan, would draw additional visitors. But these attendance figures show that the renovation has substantially increased the gallery's appeal to the public.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the museum director's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During the three months following its reopening, the Pelham Gallery charged the same admission fee that it had charged before the renovation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For the three months following its reopening, the Pelham Gallery hosted a rare traveling exhibition of Renaissance drawings that attracted unusually large crowds wherever it was shown.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several other galleries in the same city undertook renovations during the Pelham's closure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Pelham Gallery's renovation cost significantly more than its director had initially projected.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some visitors to the Pelham Gallery reported that they preferred the gallery's prior appearance.

explanations.correct: The director attributes the attendance jump to the renovation's increased appeal. (B) offers a non-obvious alternative cause — a rare traveling exhibition present during exactly the measurement window — that would draw crowds regardless of the renovation. The data no longer support the renovation-as-cause claim.
explanations.A: Strengthens, if anything — an unchanged admission fee rules out price as an alternative explanation.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too narrow — simultaneous renovations elsewhere don't, by themselves, explain why the Pelham's attendance rose.
explanations.D: Attacks a subsidiary point about cost, not about whether the renovation increased appeal.
explanations.E: Too narrow — a few dissenting visitors don't account for the 40 percent increase.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal analogical argument from one jurisdiction to another. Weakener denies the load-bearing assumption that the jurisdictions' enforcement regimes are comparable. Trap (B) strengthens; trap (A) attacks a subsidiary point.
lr.stimulus: Attorney: The state of Arlen enacted a law requiring all commercial truck drivers to install electronic logging devices that automatically record driving hours. Within two years, the rate of accidents involving Arlen commercial trucks had dropped by nearly a quarter. The state of Brennan has now enacted an identical logging-device requirement; Brennan should expect a similarly sharp reduction in its own rate of accidents involving commercial trucks.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the attorney's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arlen's commercial trucking fleet is, on average, slightly older than Brennan's.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The two states have comparable highway systems and similar weather conditions throughout the year.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At the same time as it enacted the logging-device requirement, Arlen also tripled the number of state inspectors assigned to review commercial-truck records and hired a specialized prosecutorial unit to pursue hours-of-service violations; Brennan has taken no such enforcement steps.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The electronic logging devices used in Arlen were manufactured by several different companies, some of which sell their devices at a premium.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A few Arlen trucking firms complained that the logging devices were initially unreliable.

explanations.correct: The attorney infers that Brennan will see a similar drop because it enacted the same law. (C) reveals that Arlen paired the law with a major enforcement expansion — tripled inspectors and a dedicated prosecutorial unit — that Brennan has not matched. The analogy collapses once the true cause is identified as the enforcement regime, not the law alone.
explanations.A: Attacks a subsidiary point about fleet age that, if anything, predicts more accidents in Arlen and so doesn't explain away Arlen's decline.
explanations.B: Strengthens — comparable roads and weather support the analogy.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Out of scope — device pricing has no bearing on accident reduction.
explanations.E: Too narrow — complaints from a few firms about early reliability don't undermine the two-year outcome.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain: the weakener must attack the move from 'drug reduced tumor markers' to 'drug will reduce cancer mortality,' not merely one isolated step. One distractor strengthens; one is out-of-scope.
lr.stimulus: Researchers at a prominent oncology institute administered a new compound to patients with early-stage pancreatic cancer. After six months, patients who received the compound showed a 40 percent reduction in tumor-marker levels compared to those who received a placebo. The researchers concluded that widespread adoption of the compound would significantly reduce pancreatic cancer mortality rates.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tumor-marker levels are not reliably correlated with patient survival outcomes in pancreatic cancer.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The compound produced mild gastrointestinal side effects in approximately 20 percent of trial participants.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pancreatic cancer mortality rates have declined slightly over the past decade due to improved surgical techniques.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients who received the compound also adhered more rigorously to dietary recommendations throughout the trial.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The compound reduced tumor-marker levels more effectively in female patients than in male patients.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'tumor markers decreased' to 'mortality will decrease.' If tumor-marker levels are not reliably correlated with survival, that bridge collapses — reduced markers need not mean reduced deaths, directly undermining the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Attacks the key inferential link between the measured outcome (tumor markers) and the predicted benefit (mortality reduction).
explanations.B: Out-of-scope trap. Side effects bear on tolerability, not on whether the compound reduces mortality. Does not weaken the conclusion.
explanations.C: Accurate-but-irrelevant trap. Background trends in mortality from other causes do not undermine the claim that this compound would further reduce mortality.
explanations.D: This is a confounder that weakens the premise that the compound caused the marker reduction, but it is a 'too narrow' attack — it questions the causal attribution of the marker change rather than the leap to mortality outcomes.
explanations.E: Irrelevant differential-effect detail. The argument concerns overall mortality reduction; a demographic subgroup difference doesn't weaken that claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive argument from economic data. The weakener must show that the trend cited as evidence will not produce the predicted outcome, not merely that the outcome is undesirable. Includes a strengthener trap and an adjacent-claim attack.
lr.stimulus: Over the past three years, consumer spending on domestic travel has increased by 22 percent while spending on international travel has remained flat. An economic analyst argued that this shift indicates growing consumer preference for domestic destinations and predicted that domestic airlines will post record profits within the next two years.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the analyst's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Domestic airlines have invested heavily in fleet upgrades, substantially increasing their operating costs over the same period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumer surveys confirm that travelers find domestic destinations more appealing than they did five years ago.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several international airlines have begun offering direct routes that previously required connections through domestic hubs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spending on domestic lodging has increased proportionally alongside spending on domestic travel.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The increase in domestic travel spending is primarily attributable to higher fuel surcharges passed on to consumers, not to more passengers flying.

explanations.correct: The analyst infers record airline profits from increased consumer spending on domestic travel. If that spending increase reflects higher per-ticket costs (fuel surcharges), not more passengers, airlines are not necessarily carrying more profitable volume — their costs may have risen proportionally, and the revenue increase may simply offset fuel expenses. This breaks the spending-increase-to-profit link.
explanations.A: This weakens the profit conclusion by noting rising costs, which is relevant, but E is more directly targeted: it shows the revenue increase itself does not represent new business, making A a weaker attack by comparison.
explanations.B: Opposite-answer trap. Confirms the preference shift the analyst cited, strengthening the premise rather than weakening the conclusion.
explanations.C: Shift-in-subject trap. Changes to international airline routing affect international travel competition but don't directly undermine the domestic profit prediction.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope. Parallel growth in lodging spending is consistent with the analyst's story; it doesn't undermine the airline-profit conclusion.
explanations.E: Correct. Reveals that the spending metric misrepresents actual demand growth, severing the link between the statistic and the predicted profitability.

lr.difficultyReason: Analogical argument comparing two legal systems. The weakener must identify a disanalogy that undermines the prediction, while distractors attack peripheral details or strengthen the comparison.
lr.stimulus: Legal scholars studying criminal sentencing note that the nation of Valdris reduced recidivism rates by 30 percent after replacing mandatory minimum sentences with individualized rehabilitation programs. Based on this precedent, the scholars argue that adopting similar rehabilitation-focused sentencing in the state of Crestmont would produce a comparable reduction in repeat offenses.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Valdris's rehabilitation programs were designed by corrections experts with decades of experience in criminal psychology.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Crestmont's prison population is composed predominantly of offenders convicted of drug-related crimes, whereas Valdris's was composed predominantly of property-crime offenders, for whom rehabilitation is significantly more effective.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several other nations that implemented rehabilitation-focused sentencing also experienced reductions in recidivism.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Crestmont currently spends less per inmate on correctional services than the national average.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mandatory minimum sentences were originally adopted in Crestmont in response to a spike in violent crime during the 1990s.

explanations.correct: The analogical argument assumes Crestmont resembles Valdris in the relevant respects. Choice B reveals a key disanalogy: the offender populations differ in a way that directly affects whether rehabilitation works — drug offenders respond less well than property offenders. This undermines the analogical inference.
explanations.A: This detail about Valdris's program quality doesn't weaken the argument; if anything, it's neutral or suggests quality matters, but it doesn't show Crestmont can't replicate the result.
explanations.B: Correct. Classic disanalogy weakener targeting the analogical bridge between Valdris and Crestmont.
explanations.C: Opposite-answer trap. Additional confirming cases strengthen the generalization rather than weaken it.
explanations.D: Too narrow / out-of-scope. Lower spending per inmate is weakly relevant at best and does not directly attack the recidivism-reduction claim.
explanations.E: Historical context about why mandatory minimums were adopted is irrelevant to whether replacing them now would reduce recidivism.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-cause causal argument with a well-hidden alternative explanation as the correct answer. One distractor is an opposite answer; one attacks the wrong causal direction.
lr.stimulus: A wildlife biologist reported that in the Fenwick River basin, populations of native trout declined sharply in the three years following the introduction of a non-native crayfish species. She concluded that the crayfish are responsible for the trout decline, most likely by competing for the same invertebrate food sources.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the biologist's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The non-native crayfish and the native trout have been observed feeding in overlapping areas of the river basin.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A viral pathogen lethal to trout was detected in the Fenwick River basin approximately six months before the crayfish were introduced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In laboratory conditions, trout and non-native crayfish compete directly for invertebrate prey.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Native crayfish populations in the Fenwick River basin have also declined since the non-native species was introduced.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The non-native crayfish species has caused trout declines in two other river systems where it was introduced.

explanations.correct: The biologist assumes crayfish caused the trout decline. If a viral pathogen was already present before the crayfish arrived, the pathogen is a viable alternative explanation for the decline, substantially weakening the causal attribution.
explanations.A: Opposite-answer trap. Overlapping feeding areas support the competition hypothesis, strengthening the conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct. Introduces a prior alternative cause (viral pathogen) that could explain the trout decline independently of the crayfish.
explanations.C: Opposite-answer trap. Lab evidence of direct competition bolsters the biologist's mechanism, strengthening the argument.
explanations.D: Shift-in-subject trap. Native crayfish decline is consistent with the non-native crayfish outcompeting everyone, but it neither supports nor meaningfully undermines the conclusion about trout.
explanations.E: Opposite-answer trap. Parallel outcomes in other river systems strengthen the causal claim about the Fenwick basin.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy argument predicting behavioral change. The weakener reveals that the policy's assumed mechanism won't function as described. Distractors include a narrowly scoped premise-attacker and an irrelevant comparison.
lr.stimulus: A city council member argued that installing speed cameras at the ten most dangerous intersections in the city would substantially reduce traffic fatalities. She cited evidence that cities with comparable camera programs have seen fatality rates fall by up to 25 percent at monitored intersections.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Speed cameras are more effective at deterring speeding than police patrols at the same locations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The majority of fatal accidents at Crestmont's most dangerous intersections are caused not by speeding but by drivers running red lights, a behavior speed cameras do not monitor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Installing and maintaining speed cameras is considerably less expensive than stationing police officers at intersections.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some cities that implemented speed camera programs later removed them after public opposition campaigns.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Traffic fatalities at intersections without cameras have increased in cities that installed camera programs.

explanations.correct: The argument assumes speed cameras will reduce fatalities by deterring dangerous driving. Choice B shows that the dominant cause of fatalities at these specific intersections is red-light running, not speeding — so speed cameras won't address the actual cause, breaking the mechanism linking the policy to the predicted outcome.
explanations.A: Opposite-answer trap. Showing cameras outperform patrols strengthens the case for cameras.
explanations.B: Correct. Reveals that the assumed mechanism (speed reduction → fewer fatalities) does not apply to the city's actual accident profile.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope. Cost-effectiveness is irrelevant to whether the program will reduce fatalities.
explanations.D: Accurate-but-irrelevant trap. Public opposition affects implementation, not the causal relationship between cameras and fatality rates.
explanations.E: Shift-in-subject trap. A displacement effect at non-camera intersections is a concern but doesn't directly undermine the claim that the cameras will reduce fatalities at the monitored intersections.

lr.difficultyReason: Argument from historical correlation to causal conclusion. The weakener introduces an alternative explanation for the correlation; distractors include a reversed-causation answer and an irrelevant historical detail.
lr.stimulus: Historians examining data from fifteenth-century European cities found that cities with active merchant guilds had, on average, significantly higher literacy rates than cities without such guilds. They concluded that merchant guilds promoted literacy by creating economic incentives for reading and record-keeping.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most calls into question the historians' reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Merchant guilds in some cities also sponsored the construction of churches and public buildings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cities with higher literacy rates tended to attract more merchants, who then organized into guilds, rather than the guilds developing first.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cities with the highest literacy rates also had the largest populations in fifteenth-century Europe.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Merchant guilds in different cities varied considerably in their organizational structure and membership requirements.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Literacy rates across Europe increased generally during the fifteenth century regardless of guild activity.

explanations.correct: The historians infer that guilds caused higher literacy. Choice B reverses the causal direction: pre-existing literacy attracted merchants who formed guilds. This alternative explanation — that literacy caused guilds rather than guilds causing literacy — directly undermines the causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Out-of-scope. Guild involvement in construction is irrelevant to the literacy-guild causal claim.
explanations.B: Correct. Classic reversed-causation weakener: the effect (high literacy) preceded and caused the supposed cause (guilds), not the other way around.
explanations.C: Introduces a third variable (population size) but doesn't clearly sever the guild-literacy link; it is weaker than B and more of an alternative explanation for literacy rates generally.
explanations.D: Accurate-but-irrelevant trap. Structural variation among guilds doesn't undermine the correlation or the causal claim derived from it.
explanations.E: This could introduce a common-cause explanation (general literacy trend), but it is vague — it says literacy rose everywhere, which doesn't specifically address why guild cities had higher rates, leaving the historians' correlation intact.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology-domain argument from a sample study to a general conclusion. The weakener attacks the representativeness of the sample; distractors include a strengthener and an attack on a peripheral premise.
lr.stimulus: A software company conducted a six-week pilot study in which employees were permitted to set their own work schedules rather than adhering to fixed office hours. Productivity, measured by tasks completed per week, rose by 18 percent during the pilot. Company executives concluded that abolishing fixed hours company-wide would produce a lasting increase in overall productivity.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the executives' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Employees who participated in the pilot reported higher job satisfaction than they had before the study began.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The pilot study included only volunteers, who tend to be among the company's most self-motivated employees and are therefore unrepresentative of the workforce as a whole.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The company's productivity measurement system counts tasks completed regardless of the complexity or quality of the work.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Flexible scheduling has been adopted by several other technology firms with positive results.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some departments within the company rely on synchronized team meetings that require employees to be present at specific times.

explanations.correct: The executives generalize from the pilot study to the entire company. Choice B reveals that the pilot sample was self-selected volunteers — the most motivated employees — making the sample unrepresentative. Results from this group cannot reliably predict outcomes for the full workforce, directly undermining the generalization.
explanations.A: Opposite-answer trap. Higher job satisfaction is consistent with and supportive of the productivity conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct. Attacks the generalization by exposing a sampling bias that makes the pilot results unrepresentative.
explanations.C: This weakens the validity of the productivity metric (a premise attacker), but it doesn't directly undermine the conclusion that abolishing fixed hours increases productivity — it questions how productivity is measured, not whether flexible hours cause it to rise.
explanations.D: Opposite-answer trap. Positive results elsewhere strengthen the case for the policy.
explanations.E: This identifies a practical implementation challenge but doesn't directly undermine the causal claim that flexible hours raise productivity; it's a logistical concern rather than a logical defeater.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethical/policy argument predicting a behavioral outcome from a deterrence mechanism. The weakener shows the deterrence mechanism won't operate as expected. Includes a narrowly scoped distractor and a reverse-direction trap.
lr.stimulus: A criminologist argued that publishing the names and photographs of convicted tax evaders in national newspapers would deter future tax evasion. She cited survey data showing that 68 percent of respondents said public shaming would make them less likely to evade taxes.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tax evasion causes significant harm to public finances and undermines confidence in civic institutions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People who evade taxes typically do so through complex offshore arrangements that are rarely detected and prosecuted, so few would actually be subject to public naming.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Respondents to surveys about deterrence frequently overstate how much they would be influenced by a given sanction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Countries that have implemented public-shaming programs for other offenses have sometimes seen increases in those offenses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The criminologist's survey was conducted among a nationally representative sample of adults.

explanations.correct: The deterrence argument assumes that would-be tax evaders face a realistic threat of being named publicly. Choice B reveals that tax evasion is rarely detected or prosecuted, so few evaders would ever be publicly named. Without a credible threat of exposure, the naming policy cannot deter the behavior, severing the mechanism linking the policy to the predicted outcome.
explanations.A: Out-of-scope. The harm caused by tax evasion is irrelevant to whether public naming would deter it.
explanations.B: Correct. Undermines the deterrence mechanism by showing the threat of public naming is not credible for most potential evaders.
explanations.C: This is also a genuine weakener — it attacks the reliability of the survey evidence — but it is a 'too narrow' attack on the premise rather than the conclusion. Even if survey data overstates deterrence, the naming policy might still have some deterrent effect; B more directly shows the mechanism fails entirely.
explanations.D: Relevant but weak — it concerns other offenses, not tax evasion specifically. The shift-in-subject makes this less directly applicable than B.
explanations.E: Opposite-answer trap. A representative sample strengthens the reliability of the survey evidence.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics-domain argument inferring a causal conclusion from co-occurrence data. The weakener introduces a common-cause alternative explanation. One distractor attacks a tangential premise; one is a strengthener.
lr.stimulus: Linguists studying bilingual children found that those who regularly switched between two languages during conversation — a practice known as code-switching — scored significantly higher on standardized tests of executive function than children who spoke only one language. The linguists concluded that the practice of code-switching itself enhances executive function in developing brains.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the linguists' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Executive function tests are widely regarded as reliable measures of cognitive flexibility and attention control.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Children with stronger innate executive function are better able to manage two languages simultaneously and therefore engage in code-switching more frequently.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bilingual children who code-switch frequently are exposed to a greater variety of vocabulary than monolingual children.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The bilingual children in the study came predominantly from middle-income households with high parental involvement in education.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Previous research has shown that learning a second language, regardless of code-switching, offers some cognitive benefits.

explanations.correct: The linguists attribute better executive function scores to code-switching. Choice D reveals that the bilingual children came predominantly from high-parental-involvement, middle-income households — a confounding variable. Parental educational engagement is a well-established predictor of cognitive outcomes; this alternative explanation means code-switching may not be the cause of the higher scores.
explanations.A: Opposite-answer trap. Validating the reliability of the test strengthens the evidentiary premise rather than weakening the conclusion.
explanations.B: Reversed-causation answer — tempting, but this is actually a strong weakener too. However, D is preferred because it introduces an entirely external confound (socioeconomic/parental factor) that is not entailed by the study's own variables, whereas B attacks only the direction of causation within those variables. Both weaken, but D more directly undermines the study's ability to isolate code-switching as the cause.
explanations.C: Shift-in-subject trap. Vocabulary exposure is a different outcome; it doesn't directly undermine the executive-function conclusion.
explanations.D: Correct. Identifies a confounding third variable — parental involvement and household income — that could independently explain the executive function advantage, weakening the causal attribution to code-switching.
explanations.E: Accurate-but-irrelevant trap. General bilingual benefits don't specifically undermine the claim that code-switching in particular enhances executive function.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts-domain argument predicting an economic outcome from a policy intervention. Weakener reveals that the policy mechanism depends on an assumption that does not hold. Includes one strengthener trap and one out-of-scope distractor.
lr.stimulus: The director of a regional arts council argued that increasing public subsidies for local theater companies would revitalize the downtown arts district and attract new businesses to the area. She pointed to a study showing that cities with robust live-theater scenes have higher concentrations of restaurants, hotels, and retail shops in their downtown cores.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the director's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The study cited by the director controlled for city size and regional economic conditions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the cities examined by the study, the thriving theater scenes developed after businesses had already established themselves downtown, attracted by favorable commercial rents rather than by cultural amenities.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Local theater companies have reported that increased subsidies would allow them to stage more productions and hire additional staff.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several downtown arts districts in other regions have attracted tourism revenue as well as new businesses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The regional arts council has successfully administered subsidy programs for visual artists in the past.

explanations.correct: The director's argument assumes that a strong theater scene causes business growth. Choice B reveals reversed causation: in the study cities, businesses came first (drawn by low rents), and the theater scene developed afterward. This means the study's correlation does not support the causal claim that subsidizing theater will attract businesses — the mechanism runs in the opposite direction.
explanations.A: Opposite-answer trap. Methodological controls strengthen the study's reliability, bolstering the director's evidentiary basis.
explanations.B: Correct. Reversed-causation weakener applied appropriately: the supposed cause (theater) actually followed the supposed effect (business concentration), undermining the director's causal inference.
explanations.C: Opposite-answer trap. If subsidies produce more productions and jobs, this supports the overall chain leading to revitalization.
explanations.D: Opposite-answer trap. Examples of other arts districts attracting businesses support the director's prediction.
explanations.E: Out-of-scope. The council's past administrative competence is irrelevant to whether theater subsidies will cause business growth in the downtown district.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (drug → reduced inflammation → improved outcomes). The correct weakener attacks the move from evidence to conclusion by introducing an alternative explanation for the observed improvement. Distractors include a strengthener and an out-of-scope trap about a different drug.
lr.stimulus: A clinical researcher concluded that a new anti-inflammatory drug was responsible for the significant reduction in joint pain reported by patients in a recent trial. Patients who took the drug for eight weeks reported a 40 percent decrease in pain scores compared to their scores at the start of the trial. No other treatments were administered during the study period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The trial did not include a control group of patients who received a placebo instead of the drug.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drug's active compound has been shown in laboratory studies to inhibit the specific enzyme responsible for inflammation in joint tissue.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A different anti-inflammatory drug tested in a separate trial produced only a 25 percent decrease in pain scores over the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several participants in the trial began a low-impact exercise program during the eight-week period without informing the research team.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients with more severe joint pain at the start of the trial reported greater absolute reductions in pain scores than those with milder initial pain.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes the drug caused the pain reduction. Choice D introduces an alternative explanation—an independent exercise program—that could account for the improved pain scores, directly undermining the causal attribution to the drug.
explanations.A: This is a strengthener trap: the absence of a control group actually weakens the researcher's methodology and might seem to weaken the argument, but on LSAT logic the question is whether A, if true, undermines the conclusion. Absence of a placebo group weakens the evidentiary basis—however, D is a more direct weakener because it supplies an actual competing cause rather than merely noting a methodological gap. Among the choices, D most directly attacks the causal conclusion by introducing a specific confounding variable.
explanations.B: Opposite/strengthener trap. Demonstrating a mechanism by which the drug suppresses inflammation bolsters the causal claim rather than undermining it.
explanations.C: Unwarranted-comparison trap. The argument concerns whether this drug caused the improvement; the relative performance of a different drug is irrelevant to that causal claim.
explanations.D: Correct. Introduces a concrete alternative cause (exercise) that could explain the pain reduction independent of the drug.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant trap. The distribution of improvement across severity levels does not challenge the claim that the drug caused improvement overall; it merely describes a pattern within the results.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive argument: an economist predicts future economic growth based on a historical correlation. The weakener attacks the move from past correlation to future prediction by undermining the stability of the underlying condition. One distractor strengthens; another attacks a premise without touching the conclusion.
lr.stimulus: An economist argued that the city of Harwell will experience significant economic growth over the next decade. Harwell recently completed a large-scale expansion of its public transit network, and historical data from twelve other cities show that comparable transit expansions were each followed within five years by measurable increases in commercial investment and employment rates.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the economist's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The twelve cities cited by the economist all completed their transit expansions during periods of broad national economic growth, whereas Harwell's expansion was completed during a national recession.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Harwell's transit expansion was completed under budget and on schedule, suggesting strong project management capacity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two of the twelve cities experienced their economic growth only eight years after the transit expansion, rather than within five years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some economists dispute whether increases in commercial investment are the best measure of economic growth.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Harwell's transit expansion added more total route-miles than any of the twelve comparable expansions cited by the economist.

explanations.correct: The economist's prediction depends on the historical pattern holding for Harwell. Choice A reveals that all twelve comparison cities expanded during national economic upturns, while Harwell did so during a recession—exposing a critical disanalogy that undermines the reliability of the historical pattern as a predictor for Harwell's future.
explanations.A: Correct. Attacks the analogical reasoning at the heart of the prediction by showing the comparison cases were conducted under systematically different macroeconomic conditions.
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. Demonstrating Harwell's organizational competence makes a successful outcome more likely, bolstering rather than weakening the economist's prediction.
explanations.C: Too-narrow trap. The two-year delay in a minority of cases is a minor variation that does not undermine the general pattern; the economist's claim is about the next decade, so a slight timing difference is irrelevant to whether growth will occur.
explanations.D: Shift-in-subject trap. Debating the best metric for economic growth challenges a definitional premise but does not undermine whether Harwell will experience growth as the economist defines it.
explanations.E: Unwarranted-comparison trap that actually functions as a mild strengthener—Harwell's larger expansion might predict even greater growth—so it does not weaken the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Causal-generalization argument in environmental science. The argument moves from a single regional observation to a broad policy conclusion. The correct weakener challenges the representativeness of the evidence by showing the observed outcome results from a local factor that does not generalize. Distractors include one strengthener and one irrelevant trap.
lr.stimulus: A conservation official argued that reintroducing gray wolves to wilderness areas is an effective strategy for restoring native plant diversity. In Ridgecrest Valley, where wolves were reintroduced seven years ago, the populations of elk and deer declined sharply, grazing pressure on riverbank vegetation was reduced, and the density of native shrubs and grasses increased by over 60 percent.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ridgecrest Valley contains an unusually high concentration of natural mineral springs that independently promote rapid plant growth in riparian zones.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gray wolves in Ridgecrest Valley have expanded their territory to areas outside the original reintroduction zone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several wilderness areas lacking large predators have experienced significant declines in native plant diversity over the same seven-year period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reintroduction of gray wolves required a ten-year planning process and cooperation among multiple government agencies.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The elk population in Ridgecrest Valley had already begun declining slightly before the wolves were reintroduced, due to a drought the previous year.

explanations.correct: The official generalizes from Ridgecrest Valley's outcome to a broad strategy. Choice A reveals that Ridgecrest Valley has an idiosyncratic feature—mineral springs that accelerate plant growth—that could independently account for the observed increase in plant diversity. This alternative explanation undercuts the conclusion that wolf reintroduction itself was the effective driver, and suggests the result may not generalize to other wilderness areas.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces a site-specific confounding variable (mineral springs) that could explain the plant diversity increase independent of the wolves, both providing an alternative explanation and undermining the generalizability of the single case.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant trap. The wolves' territorial expansion does not address whether their presence caused the plant diversity increase or whether the strategy works elsewhere.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. Showing that areas without predators fared worse over the same period supports the comparative case for wolf reintroduction, bolstering the official's argument.
explanations.D: Shift-in-subject trap. The difficulty and cost of the planning process bears on the policy's feasibility, not on whether wolf reintroduction effectively restores plant diversity.
explanations.E: Too-narrow / premise-attack trap. A pre-existing slight elk decline would weaken the wolf-caused-elk-decline link, but since some decline did still occur and plant diversity did increase, this choice does not substantially undercut the conclusion that the strategy produced the plant diversity outcome.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (policy → reduced cost → increased access) where the weakener attacks the move from evidence to conclusion rather than the premises in isolation. Distractors include a strengthener and an out-of-scope fact about drug pricing.
lr.stimulus: A county health official recently reported that after the county subsidized generic drug prescriptions for low-income residents, emergency-room visits among that population dropped by 22 percent over the following year. The official concluded that expanded access to affordable medications caused the decline in emergency-room use, and therefore recommended extending the subsidy program to all uninsured residents.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During the same year, the county opened two new urgent-care clinics in neighborhoods with high concentrations of low-income residents.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Generic drugs are therapeutically equivalent to their brand-name counterparts for the conditions most commonly treated among low-income patients.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several neighboring counties that did not introduce similar subsidies also saw reductions in emergency-room visits over the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Uninsured residents who are not low-income tend to visit emergency rooms less frequently than low-income residents do.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some participants in the subsidy program reported that they still had difficulty affording transportation to pharmacies.

explanations.correct: The official's argument rests on the subsidy causing the drop in ER visits. Choice A introduces an alternative explanation — the opening of urgent-care clinics — that could account for the decline independently of the subsidy, directly undermining the causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces a competing causal factor (new urgent-care clinics) that could independently explain the drop in ER visits, weakening the conclusion that the subsidy caused the decline.
explanations.B: Strengthens the argument by supporting the premise that generic drugs are effective substitutes, bolstering the claim that affordable access to them would reduce ER dependency. This is the opposite-answer trap.
explanations.C: Accurate but directed at a slightly different target: it suggests the trend was countywide rather than subsidy-specific, which does weaken — but this is a trap variant that competes with A. However, A is more direct because it provides a concrete alternative mechanism within the county itself. On reflection, C also weakens, but A is more specifically tied to the population studied.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope. This addresses utilization patterns of a different group (non-low-income uninsured), which was not the basis for the causal claim being evaluated.
explanations.E: Too narrow. Transportation difficulties might limit uptake of the subsidy, but this does not challenge the causal link between subsidy access and reduced ER visits for those who did use the program.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive argument based on historical analogy. The weakener attacks the premise-to-conclusion move by exposing a disanalogy between the historical case and the current prediction. Distractors include a strengthener and an irrelevant comparison.
lr.stimulus: An economic analyst noted that the last three times the national savings rate fell below four percent, a recession followed within eighteen months. The national savings rate has now fallen below four percent for the second consecutive quarter. The analyst therefore predicted that the economy will enter a recession within the next eighteen months.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the analyst's prediction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consumer confidence surveys conducted this quarter show lower optimism than in any of the three previous periods when the savings rate fell below four percent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In each of the three prior instances, the savings rate had been declining steadily for at least six months before falling below four percent, whereas the current decline began only last quarter.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Economists disagree about whether a savings rate below four percent is inherently harmful to long-term economic growth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The national savings rate has occasionally fallen below four percent without triggering discussions of fiscal policy reform.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Government spending as a share of GDP has remained stable over the past two years.

explanations.correct: The analyst's prediction relies on an analogy between the current situation and the three historical precedents. Choice B identifies a key disanalogy — in the prior cases the savings rate had been declining for at least six months before the threshold was crossed, whereas now the decline is very recent. This disanalogy undermines the reliability of the historical pattern as a basis for prediction.
explanations.A: Strengthens the argument. Lower consumer confidence than in prior periods suggests economic conditions are at least as worrying now, reinforcing the prediction of recession. This is the opposite-answer trap.
explanations.B: Correct. Exposes a structural disanalogy between the current episode and the historical cases on which the prediction is based, undermining the analogical inference.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope. Expert disagreement about whether a low savings rate is harmful in the abstract does not speak to the specific predictive pattern the analyst identified.
explanations.D: Irrelevant. Whether fiscal policy discussions were triggered is unrelated to whether a recession followed the savings-rate drop.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. Stable government spending is a separate economic variable; the argument concerns the savings rate as a predictor, and this fact does not engage with that causal or predictive mechanism.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step argument moving from observed correlation to causal generalization in an environmental science context. The weakener attacks the move from observed data to broad causal conclusion by showing the sample is unrepresentative. Distractors include a strengthener and a too-narrow premise attack.
lr.stimulus: Researchers studying a coastal wetland found that plots where invasive reed grass had been removed showed a 40 percent increase in native bird species diversity within two years. The researchers concluded that invasive reed grass suppresses native bird diversity throughout coastal wetlands, and that removal programs should be implemented region-wide.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The plots selected for reed-grass removal were those that already had the highest baseline densities of invasive reeds, making them atypical of most wetland areas in the region.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Native bird species that recolonized the cleared plots required, on average, eight months to establish stable breeding populations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Invasive reed grass also reduces populations of native amphibians in freshwater marshes adjacent to the studied wetlands.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reed-grass removal efforts in the studied plots were conducted by trained ecologists using methods that minimized soil disruption.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several bird species that increased in number after reed removal are listed as species of conservation concern in the region.

explanations.correct: The researchers generalize from their study plots to coastal wetlands region-wide. Choice A reveals that the study plots were selected specifically because they had the highest invasive reed densities, making them unrepresentative of the broader region. This undermines the basis for the region-wide recommendation, since results in extreme-density plots may not apply where reed invasion is less severe.
explanations.A: Correct. Demonstrates that the sample was unrepresentative (selected for atypically high reed density), weakening the generalization to all coastal wetlands in the region.
explanations.B: Too narrow. The eight-month recolonization timeline affects the pace of recovery but does not challenge the conclusion that reed grass suppresses diversity or that removal would be beneficial region-wide.
explanations.C: Shift in subject. This describes an effect of reed grass on amphibians in a different habitat type (freshwater marshes), which does not bear on whether reed grass suppresses bird diversity in coastal wetlands.
explanations.D: Strengthens the argument by ruling out an alternative explanation — that soil disruption from removal, rather than the removal itself, caused the change in bird diversity. This is the opposite-answer trap.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant. The conservation status of the rebounding bird species does not speak to whether the causal mechanism applies region-wide.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (policy → cost reduction → increased adoption). The correct weakener attacks the move from cost reduction to adoption, leaving the cost-reduction premise intact. Distractors include a strengthener, an out-of-scope economic fact, and a narrowly scoped premise attack.
lr.stimulus: A government economist argued that the new tax credit for residential solar panel installation will substantially increase the proportion of households that use solar energy. She reasoned that the credit will reduce the upfront cost of installation by nearly 30 percent, and that high upfront cost has historically been the primary barrier preventing homeowners from adopting solar technology.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A survey of homeowners who declined to install solar panels found that a majority cited concerns about long-term maintenance costs rather than upfront installation costs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The tax credit applies only to installations completed by licensed contractors, and licensed contractors are available in most regions of the country.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Countries that have offered similar upfront subsidies for solar installation have seen dramatic increases in residential solar adoption within three years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The federal government has introduced tax credits for energy-efficient appliances in the same fiscal year as the solar credit.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Solar panel technology has improved significantly over the past decade, making panels more efficient than those available when the cost barrier was first identified.

explanations.correct: The economist's argument depends on the premise that high upfront cost is the primary barrier to adoption. Answer A directly undercuts this by showing that most homeowners who declined to install solar panels cited ongoing maintenance costs—not upfront cost—as their obstacle. If the credit doesn't address the actual primary barrier, it is unlikely to drive the predicted increase in adoption.
explanations.A: Correct. This is the weakener: it attacks the load-bearing premise that upfront cost is the primary barrier, showing that maintenance costs dominate homeowner objections. Removing the upfront cost obstacle won't eliminate the actual deterrent.
explanations.B: Out-of-scope. That licensed contractors are widely available is, if anything, a mild strengthener (it rules out an access barrier), not a weakener.
explanations.C: Opposite answer / strengthener. International precedent supporting upfront subsidies bolsters the economist's prediction rather than undermining it.
explanations.D: Irrelevant / shift in subject. The existence of concurrent appliance credits doesn't bear on whether the solar credit will increase solar adoption; this is an accurate but unconnected fact.
explanations.E: Too narrow / wrong direction. Improved efficiency could, if anything, make solar more attractive—a mild strengthener—and it does not address the premise-to-conclusion move about cost barriers.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive argument based on historical correlation in a medical context. The correct weakener introduces a disanalogy between the historical sample and the target population, attacking the move from evidence to conclusion without touching either empirical premise in isolation. Distractors include a strengthener and a plausible but tangential medical fact.
lr.stimulus: Researchers at a large urban hospital observed that patients who were assigned a dedicated case manager during the first week of hospitalization had significantly shorter average stays than patients who received standard care. The hospital's administrators concluded that assigning case managers to all newly admitted patients would reduce the hospital's average length of stay system-wide.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the administrators' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Case managers at the hospital are currently assigned only to patients whose conditions are judged, at admission, to be the least medically complex.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hospitals that have universally implemented case management programs have reported reductions in average length of stay comparable to those observed at the urban hospital.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cost of hiring sufficient case managers to cover all newly admitted patients would exceed the savings generated by shorter hospital stays during the first year of implementation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several of the case managers at the hospital have advanced clinical training in addition to their administrative credentials.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients who receive standard care at the hospital are still assigned a primary nurse responsible for coordinating their discharge planning.

explanations.correct: The administrators assume the observed benefit of case management can be generalized to all patients. Answer A reveals a critical disanalogy: the case managers were assigned only to the least complex patients—precisely those most likely to have short stays regardless. The correlation between case management and shorter stays may therefore reflect patient selection, not the case managers' effect. Expanding case management to all patients, including complex ones, would not be expected to produce the same result.
explanations.A: Correct. This is the weakener: it exposes a selection-bias confound. The positive outcome was observed in a skewed sample (low-complexity patients), so the administrators cannot validly generalize the effect to the full patient population.
explanations.B: Opposite answer / strengthener. External evidence that universal case management works elsewhere directly supports the administrators' conclusion.
explanations.C: Shift in subject / irrelevant. Cost-effectiveness is a separate consideration from whether the policy would reduce length of stay; the conclusion is about clinical outcomes, not financial returns.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant. The credentials of individual case managers don't bear on whether the effect observed in the study will generalize to all new admissions.
explanations.E: Too narrow. The existence of discharge-planning nurses describes standard care but does not address the selection-bias problem or otherwise undermine the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Analogical argument in an environmental-science context predicting that a successful invasive-species intervention in one region will succeed in another. The correct weakener attacks the analogy by identifying a relevant disanalogy. Distractors include a strengthener, an out-of-scope ecological fact, and a narrowly scoped distractor that attacks a peripheral premise.
lr.stimulus: Wildlife officials in the Pacific Northwest introduced a targeted biological control agent—a host-specific parasitic wasp—to suppress populations of the invasive emerald ash borer beetle in forested areas of Oregon. Within four years, ash borer populations in treated areas declined by over 70 percent, and native ash tree survival rates improved markedly. Based on this success, conservation groups have urged officials to deploy the same wasp in the forests of the upper Midwest, where the ash borer has devastated native ash populations.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument for deploying the parasitic wasp in the upper Midwest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The parasitic wasp requires overwintering temperatures above a threshold that is regularly exceeded in Oregon but that upper Midwest forests frequently fall below, preventing the wasp from establishing a self-sustaining population.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The emerald ash borer has caused greater cumulative damage to native ash populations in the upper Midwest than in Oregon, suggesting that intervention is more urgently needed in the Midwest.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Biological control programs using host-specific parasites have, in general, a strong record of avoiding harm to non-target insect species.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oregon wildlife officials consulted with entomologists at three universities before approving the wasp introduction program.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Native ash trees in the upper Midwest belong to the same genus as those in Oregon, though they include several distinct regional species.

explanations.correct: The argument is analogical: because the wasp worked in Oregon, it will work in the Midwest. Answer A identifies a decisive disanalogy—climatic incompatibility. The wasp cannot survive Midwest winters, so it cannot establish a self-sustaining population there. This directly undermines the core premise that the Oregon intervention is a reliable model for the Midwest deployment.
explanations.A: Correct. This is the weakener: it attacks the analogy by revealing that the key mechanism (a persistent wasp population suppressing the beetle) cannot replicate in the Midwest due to climatic differences, making the Oregon success non-transferable.
explanations.B: Opposite answer / strengthener. Greater urgency of the problem in the Midwest, if anything, supports the case for deploying the wasp there, bolstering rather than undermining the argument.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. The general safety record of host-specific biological controls neither supports nor undermines the conclusion about whether this particular wasp will be effective in the Midwest. It addresses a different concern (non-target harm), not the effectiveness question.
explanations.D: Shift in subject. The procedural care taken in Oregon speaks to the quality of the Oregon program's design but has no bearing on whether conditions in the Midwest are suitable for replication.
explanations.E: Too narrow. Taxonomic similarity of the host trees is a minor point about the target ecosystem; it does not address whether the wasp can survive Midwest winters or effectively suppress the beetle there.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (policy → reduced emissions → improved air quality) where the weakener attacks the move from evidence to conclusion rather than either step in isolation. One distractor strengthens; another is accurate but out-of-scope.
lr.stimulus: A regional environmental agency reported that since the city of Morrow introduced a congestion-pricing program three years ago, vehicle traffic in the city center has declined by 22 percent. Because vehicle exhaust is the primary source of airborne particulate matter in urban areas, the agency concluded that Morrow's downtown air quality has substantially improved since the program was implemented.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During the three years since the congestion-pricing program began, a large construction project has filled Morrow's city center with dust and diesel-powered machinery.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several neighboring cities that implemented similar congestion-pricing programs have reported measurable improvements in their downtown air quality.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Morrow's congestion-pricing program generates revenue that the city has used to expand its public transit network.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vehicles that remain in Morrow's city center after the pricing program was introduced tend to be older and less fuel-efficient than the average vehicle that was diverted away.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The agency's measurement of particulate matter relies on sensors placed at fixed monitoring stations throughout the city center.

explanations.correct: The argument's conclusion depends on the chain: less traffic → less vehicle exhaust → better air quality. Choice A introduces an alternative source of airborne particulate matter — construction dust and diesel machinery — that has been operating concurrently with the traffic reduction. Even if vehicle exhaust fell, this new major source of particulates undermines the conclusion that air quality has substantially improved, directly attacking the move from reduced traffic to improved air quality.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces an alternative explanation — a major concurrent source of particulate pollution — that severs the link between reduced vehicle traffic and the predicted air-quality improvement.
explanations.B: Opposite-answer trap. Evidence that comparable programs improved air quality elsewhere actually strengthens the agency's conclusion by providing analogous support for the causal chain.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. Expanding public transit is a downstream benefit of the pricing revenue, but it says nothing about whether air quality in the city center has in fact improved. Out-of-scope.
explanations.D: Too narrow / premise attack. This challenges whether the 22% traffic reduction actually reduced total emissions proportionally, but the effect is mild and indirect; the argument can still stand if even the older remaining vehicles emit less exhaust in aggregate than the 22% more vehicles did. Choice A more directly and completely undermines the conclusion.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. This raises a methodological quibble about measurement accuracy but does not establish that air quality failed to improve — only that measurement method is fixed-location. It does not introduce an alternative explanation or attack the premise-to-conclusion move substantively.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (new medication → reduced inflammation → improved mobility). The weakener attacks the move from evidence to conclusion by offering an alternative explanation for the observed improvement. Distractors include a strengthener and an out-of-scope detail about the same medical domain.
lr.stimulus: Researchers at a clinical trial administered a new anti-inflammatory drug to patients with rheumatoid arthritis over a twelve-week period. By the end of the trial, participants reported a 40 percent improvement in joint mobility. The researchers concluded that the drug's anti-inflammatory properties were responsible for the mobility gains.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All trial participants were also enrolled in a supervised physical therapy program that began at the same time as the drug regimen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anti-inflammatory drugs have been shown in previous studies to reduce joint swelling in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some participants reported minor gastrointestinal side effects during the first two weeks of the trial.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The improvement in mobility was measured using a standardized assessment tool validated for arthritis research.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients who received a higher dose of the drug reported slightly greater mobility gains than those on the lower dose.

explanations.correct: If all participants were simultaneously enrolled in physical therapy, that program is a plausible alternative cause of the mobility improvements, undermining the researchers' causal attribution to the drug.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces a confounding variable—physical therapy—that could fully explain the observed improvement without any contribution from the drug.
explanations.B: Opposite-answer trap. Prior evidence that anti-inflammatory drugs reduce swelling strengthens the researchers' conclusion rather than weakening it.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope. Side effects in some participants are irrelevant to whether the drug caused mobility improvements in the group as a whole.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant. Validating the measurement tool bolsters the reliability of the data; it does not challenge the causal claim.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. A dose-response relationship is consistent with the drug being causally responsible for mobility gains.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive argument: economist predicts policy outcome from a single historical precedent. The weakener attacks the analogy by exposing a relevant disanalogy. Distractors include a same-topic strengthener and a too-narrow answer that questions data quality without touching the conclusion.
lr.stimulus: An economist argues that eliminating the city's commercial rent-control ordinance will stimulate new business formation. She points to Hillcrest, a neighboring municipality that repealed its rent-control law five years ago and subsequently saw a 25 percent increase in new business registrations over the following three years.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The city currently has a higher commercial vacancy rate than Hillcrest had at the time of its repeal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: During the three years following Hillcrest's repeal, the regional economy as a whole experienced unusually rapid expansion that did not affect the city.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several economists have argued that rent control can reduce the overall quality of commercial real estate stock over time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city's rent-control ordinance was enacted more recently than Hillcrest's was.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Business registration data in Hillcrest may have included renewals as well as genuinely new enterprises.

explanations.correct: If Hillcrest's business surge coincided with a regional economic boom that did not affect the city, then the repeal of rent control may not have caused the increase—and replicating the policy change in the city cannot be expected to produce the same result. This is a disanalogy that severs the analogical basis of the prediction.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant. A higher vacancy rate might even support the economist's view that loosening rent control could attract new tenants; it does not undermine the causal claim.
explanations.B: Correct. Reveals that Hillcrest's growth may have been driven by an external economic factor absent in the city, breaking the analogy.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. Supporting the view that rent control harms commercial real estate reinforces the economist's case for repeal.
explanations.D: Too narrow. The relative age of the ordinances does not bear on whether repealing the city's ordinance would replicate Hillcrest's business growth.
explanations.E: Too narrow. Even if the data overcount new registrations, the argument's core analogy stands unless we know the overcounting is systematic enough to eliminate the apparent effect.

lr.difficultyReason: Causal-predictive argument in environmental science. The weakener attacks the causal inference by offering an alternative explanation for the observed data. One distractor attacks a peripheral premise without touching the conclusion; another strengthens.
lr.stimulus: Biologists studying a coastal wetland recorded a 30 percent decline in shorebird populations over a decade. During that same period, an industrial facility upstream discharged elevated levels of heavy metals into the watershed. The biologists concluded that heavy-metal contamination was responsible for the shorebird decline.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heavy metals are known to accumulate in the small fish and invertebrates that shorebirds typically eat.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The industrial facility's discharge levels exceeded federal safety thresholds throughout the monitoring period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A highly contagious avian disease spread through shorebird populations along the entire coastline during the same decade, causing comparable declines in wetlands unaffected by industrial discharge.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The biologists used aerial surveys to count shorebird populations, a method that can undercount birds sheltering in dense vegetation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Heavy-metal contamination has been linked to reproductive failure in several other bird species studied in laboratory settings.

explanations.correct: If a contagious disease caused similar declines in unaffected wetlands, the heavy-metal contamination need not be the cause of this wetland's decline, providing a compelling alternative explanation.
explanations.A: Strengthener trap. Establishing a plausible biological mechanism for how heavy metals could harm shorebirds supports the causal conclusion.
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. Confirming that discharge levels were dangerously high bolsters the claim that contamination was the culprit.
explanations.C: Correct. Comparable declines in sites without industrial discharge indicate a region-wide alternative cause, undermining the specific causal attribution.
explanations.D: Too narrow. Undercounting due to methodology would affect the accuracy of the absolute numbers but does not explain why a decline occurred, leaving the causal claim intact.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. Laboratory evidence linking heavy metals to bird reproductive failure supports the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step policy argument: policy change caused behavioral shift, behavioral shift caused outcome. Weakener attacks the second causal link. Distractors include an opposite answer and a shift-in-subject trap.
lr.stimulus: After a city council enacted a mandatory helmet law for cyclists, emergency room admissions for serious head injuries among cyclists dropped by 35 percent over two years. A public health official concluded that the helmet law was responsible for the reduction in serious head injuries.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Studies in other cities have found that mandatory helmet laws increase overall cyclist safety.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The helmet law was accompanied by a significant increase in cycling infrastructure, including protected lanes, which substantially reduced the number of cyclist-vehicle collisions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Compliance with the helmet law among cyclists under age 18 was higher than compliance among adult cyclists.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several neighboring cities without helmet laws also recorded decreases in cyclist head injuries during the same period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Emergency room physicians noted that the head injuries they did treat during the post-law period were less severe on average.

explanations.correct: If cities without helmet laws also experienced declines in cyclist head injuries over the same period, a region-wide factor—not the helmet law—may be responsible, undermining the official's causal claim.
explanations.A: Strengthener trap. Evidence from other cities supporting helmet law effectiveness reinforces the official's conclusion.
explanations.B: Alternative explanation that could weaken, but it does not undermine the helmet law's causal role as clearly as D; moreover, improved infrastructure might explain some but not all of the reduction. However, D provides a cleaner, direct challenge by showing the effect occurred without the cause.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. Differential compliance rates by age do not address whether the law as a whole caused the injury reduction.
explanations.D: Correct. Parallel declines in cities without the law suggest a common regional factor, not the helmet law, is the real cause.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant. The severity of remaining injuries does not undermine the claim that the law reduced the number of serious injuries.
