lr.difficultyReason: Causal argument in technology. The weakener introduces a confounder that explains the correlation. Distractors include a too-narrow methodological objection and a strengthener using the same domain.
lr.stimulus: A technology firm introduced an AI-assisted code-review tool for its software engineers in January. By June of the same year, the number of software defects reaching production had fallen by 45 percent compared to the prior six-month period. The firm's engineering director concluded that the AI tool was responsible for the dramatic improvement in software quality.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most calls into question the engineering director's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The AI tool flagged an average of twelve potential defects per code review session during the six-month period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In January, the firm also replaced its most error-prone legacy codebase with a newly architected system that had been under development for two years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Software engineers at the firm reported high satisfaction with the AI tool's interface and recommendations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The defect-tracking system used by the firm counts only defects reported by end users, potentially undercounting internal testing failures.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Other technology firms that adopted similar AI code-review tools also reported reductions in production defects.

explanations.correct: Replacing the error-prone legacy codebase at the same time as the AI tool's introduction provides an alternative explanation for the defect reduction, undermining the director's attribution of the improvement to the AI tool alone.
explanations.A: Strengthener trap. Showing the AI tool actively caught defects supports the causal claim.
explanations.B: Correct. A simultaneous and highly consequential infrastructure change is a confounding variable that could fully account for the drop in production defects.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. Engineer satisfaction with the tool's interface does not establish that the tool caused fewer defects to reach production.
explanations.D: Too narrow. An undercounting issue would mean the true defect numbers are uncertain, but it does not explain why a decline occurred or attribute it to another cause.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. Corroborating evidence from other firms supports the hypothesis that AI tools reduce defects.

lr.difficultyReason: Analogical argument in law. The weakener exposes a disanalogy that severs the comparison. One distractor strengthens; another is a shift-in-subject trap.
lr.stimulus: A defense attorney argued that her client should not be held liable for defamation because a court in a neighboring jurisdiction ruled in favor of a defendant who made nearly identical statements about a public official. Since the facts of the two cases are substantially similar, the attorney contended, the outcome should be the same.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the attorney's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The plaintiff in the current case is a private individual, not a public official, and private individuals bear a lower burden of proof in defamation claims than public officials do.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The neighboring jurisdiction's court cited the defendant's lack of malicious intent as a key factor in its ruling.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Defamation law varies somewhat from jurisdiction to jurisdiction due to differences in state statutes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The statements at issue in the neighboring jurisdiction's case were made in a published newspaper article, as in the current case.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The attorney's client has no prior history of defamatory statements.

explanations.correct: The attorney's argument rests on factual similarity between the cases. If the plaintiff's status differs in a legally decisive way—private individuals have a lower burden of proof—then the cases are not truly analogous, directly undermining the analogical reasoning.
explanations.A: Correct. Identifies a material legal disanalogy (public official vs. private individual) that invalidates the comparison and weakens the attorney's conclusion.
explanations.B: Too narrow. This explains why the other defendant won, but without knowing whether the current defendant also lacked malicious intent, it does not clearly weaken the attorney's argument—it could even provide a road map for the defense.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. General jurisdictional variation is too vague to undermine this specific analogy unless the relevant statute in the current jurisdiction is shown to differ materially.
explanations.D: Strengthener trap. Confirming a factual similarity between the cases bolsters the analogy the attorney is drawing.
explanations.E: Shift-in-subject trap. The defendant's prior conduct is not relevant to whether the two cases are legally analogous.

lr.difficultyReason: Causal generalization from sample in linguistics. Weakener attacks the representativeness of the sample. Distractors include a strengthener and an out-of-scope distractor.
lr.stimulus: A linguist studied fifty bilingual children between the ages of four and six and found that those who regularly switched between their two languages during play—a behavior called code-switching—scored higher on executive function tests than those who did not code-switch. The linguist concluded that code-switching enhances executive function in bilingual children.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Children with stronger executive function are more likely to have the cognitive flexibility needed to code-switch in the first place.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Executive function tests for young children have been validated across multiple cultural and linguistic groups.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some monolingual children score as highly on executive function tests as the highest-scoring bilingual children in the study.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The bilingual children in the study spoke a variety of language pairs, including Spanish-English and Mandarin-English combinations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Other studies have found that bilingualism in general, regardless of code-switching behavior, is associated with enhanced executive function.

explanations.correct: If children with stronger executive function are already more predisposed to code-switch, the causal direction may be reversed: executive function drives code-switching, not the other way around. This reversed-causation argument directly undermines the linguist's causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Raises the possibility of reversed causation, which would explain the correlation without requiring that code-switching causes improved executive function.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant. Validation of the test instrument does not bear on whether the causal relationship runs in the direction the linguist claims.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope. Monolingual children's scores are outside the scope of an argument about bilingual children who code-switch versus those who do not.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant. Language-pair diversity in the sample may strengthen the generalizability of the findings, not weaken the argument.
explanations.E: Too narrow. If general bilingualism already boosts executive function, the linguist's claim about code-switching specifically could still hold as an additional factor; this does not clearly weaken the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive argument in ethics/policy about corporate disclosure. Weakener attacks the prediction by showing a disanalogy between predicted and actual conditions. One distractor is an unwarranted comparison; another strengthens.
lr.stimulus: A consumer advocacy group argued that requiring corporations to publicly disclose the salaries of all employees will reduce income inequality within those firms. The group cited evidence that when a financial services company voluntarily published its full salary data two years ago, its internal pay gap between the highest- and lowest-paid employees narrowed by 18 percent within twelve months.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the argument's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The financial services company that voluntarily disclosed its salaries did so specifically because its leadership was already committed to reducing pay inequality, a motivation that mandatory disclosure would not instill in resistant firms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mandatory pay-disclosure laws have been enacted in several European countries over the past decade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Income inequality in financial services firms tends to be higher than in other industries due to the prevalence of performance bonuses.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shareholders of publicly traded companies already have access to executive compensation data through annual reports.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Employees who learn that peers in comparable roles are paid more tend to negotiate more aggressively for raises.

explanations.correct: The advocacy group's argument depends on an analogy to a voluntary-disclosure case. If voluntary disclosure worked because leadership was already motivated to reduce inequality—a condition absent in firms that resist mandatory disclosure—the analogy breaks down, and the predicted effect of mandatory disclosure is undermined.
explanations.A: Correct. Exposes a critical disanalogy: the motivational context that made voluntary disclosure effective would be absent in companies compelled by law, severing the analogical basis for the prediction.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant. The existence of such laws elsewhere says nothing about whether they achieved the goal of reducing income inequality.
explanations.C: Unwarranted comparison trap. Even if financial services firms have higher baseline inequality, this does not undermine the claim that disclosure reduces whatever level of inequality exists.
explanations.D: Too narrow. Executive compensation visibility is narrower than full salary disclosure; this does not address whether mandatory full disclosure would reduce inequality.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. If disclosure prompts employees to negotiate higher wages, that mechanism supports the prediction that disclosure will narrow the pay gap.

lr.difficultyReason: Causal argument in history. Weakener introduces a confounding variable. Distractors include a premise-attacking choice that doesn't touch the conclusion and a strengthener.
lr.stimulus: Historians have noted that the Roman city of Pompeii had an unusually dense concentration of thermopolia—fast-food establishments—compared to other Roman cities of similar size. One historian argued that this high density of thermopolia indicates that Pompeii's residents had lower rates of home cooking than Romans in comparable cities, suggesting that Pompeii had a distinctive street-food culture driven by consumer preference for prepared meals.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Archaeological evidence indicates that a significant portion of Pompeii's population lived in multi-family apartment buildings that lacked kitchen facilities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The thermopolia found in Pompeii offered a wider variety of foods than those excavated in other Roman cities.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Roman cookbooks from the same era suggest that home cooking was common among wealthy households throughout the empire.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some thermopolia in Pompeii were located adjacent to large private homes, suggesting their owners were affluent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Historians have used thermopolia density as a proxy for urbanization levels in other ancient Mediterranean cities.

explanations.correct: If many residents lacked kitchen facilities due to apartment living, the high density of thermopolia would be explained by structural necessity rather than consumer preference for street food, undermining the historian's conclusion about a distinctive preference-driven culture.
explanations.A: Correct. Provides an alternative structural explanation—absence of home kitchens—that accounts for high thermopolia density without invoking a special cultural preference.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant. Variety in menu offerings does not address whether the density of thermopolia reflects consumer preference versus structural necessity.
explanations.C: Too narrow. Evidence about wealthy households cooking at home does not clearly undermine the claim about Pompeii's population broadly, and does not address the structural explanation for density.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant. The wealth of thermopolia owners does not speak to why residents used them or whether preference or necessity drove demand.
explanations.E: Shift-in-subject trap. How other historians use thermopolia data in other contexts is irrelevant to whether this historian's specific causal inference about Pompeii is valid.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive causal argument in arts/cultural policy. Weakener attacks by showing the evidence does not generalize. Distractors include an opposite answer and a too-narrow premise-attacker.
lr.stimulus: A municipal arts council proposed eliminating fees for gallery exhibitions in public museums, arguing that doing so would significantly increase attendance among lower-income residents. The council pointed to a pilot program at one city museum in which free admission on Sunday afternoons resulted in a 60 percent increase in visitors from lower-income zip codes during those hours.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Sunday afternoon free-admission program was heavily advertised through community outreach in lower-income neighborhoods, a marketing effort the council has no plans to replicate for the proposed fee elimination.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lower-income residents cited transportation costs, not admission fees, as the primary barrier to museum attendance in a survey conducted before the pilot program.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The museum that ran the pilot program is located closer to lower-income neighborhoods than most of the city's other public museums.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Eliminating fees would reduce museum revenues, potentially forcing cuts to educational programming.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several major cities that have adopted permanent free-admission policies report sustained increases in overall museum attendance.

explanations.correct: If lower-income residents themselves identify transportation—not admission fees—as the main barrier, then eliminating fees would not address the actual obstacle, making it unlikely that attendance among lower-income residents would significantly increase as predicted.
explanations.A: Weakens somewhat, but focuses on marketing as an omitted factor rather than directly undercutting the mechanism. B is stronger because it attacks the core causal assumption—that fees are the relevant barrier—whereas A only explains why the effect might be smaller in practice.
explanations.B: Correct. Directly challenges the load-bearing causal premise that admission fees are the primary barrier for lower-income residents, undermining the prediction that eliminating fees will significantly boost their attendance.
explanations.C: Too narrow. The pilot museum's location might explain why its results could be hard to replicate across all museums, but it does not undermine the core causal claim that free admission drives lower-income attendance.
explanations.D: Shift-in-subject trap. Potential budgetary consequences are a separate policy consideration; they do not weaken the prediction that attendance would increase.
explanations.E: Opposite-answer trap. Evidence from other cities sustaining increased attendance under free-admission policies strengthens the council's prediction.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (new filtration policy → reduced contaminant levels → improved public health outcomes). The weakener attacks the move from reduced contaminants to improved health by introducing an alternative explanation for the health data. Distractors include a strengthener and an out-of-scope fact about filtration technology.
lr.stimulus: A municipal water authority installed a new filtration system three years ago, after which measurements showed a 30 percent decline in waterborne contaminant levels in the city's tap water. Over the same period, rates of gastrointestinal illness among city residents dropped by 22 percent. The authority concluded that the filtration system was responsible for the reduction in illness.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The new filtration system cost significantly more to operate than the system it replaced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: During the same three-year period, a citywide public health campaign successfully increased handwashing compliance rates by 40 percent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Waterborne contaminants are known to cause gastrointestinal illness in laboratory studies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The new filtration system also reduced levels of heavy metals in the city's tap water.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several neighboring municipalities that did not install new filtration systems reported no change in gastrointestinal illness rates over the same period.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that the filtration system caused the drop in gastrointestinal illness. Choice B introduces a competing cause—a handwashing campaign that also occurred during the same period and independently could have reduced gastrointestinal illness rates. This alternative explanation undermines the authority's causal attribution to the filtration system.
explanations.A: Out-of-scope trap. Operating costs are irrelevant to whether the filtration system caused the health improvement. This does not touch the premise-to-conclusion move.
explanations.B: Correct. Introduces an alternative explanation for the decline in illness, attacking the causal link between the filtration system and improved health outcomes.
explanations.C: Opposite-answer (strengthener) trap. Confirming that waterborne contaminants cause gastrointestinal illness in lab settings actually bolsters the argument's assumption that reduced contaminants should reduce illness.
explanations.D: Too narrow / irrelevant trap. That the system reduced heavy metals is a tangential benefit; it does not address the causal relationship between the filtration system and gastrointestinal illness specifically.
explanations.E: Shift-in-subject trap. The comparison with municipalities that did not upgrade is ambiguous at best and could even be read as supporting the argument by suggesting that without new filtration, no improvement occurred—making this a mild strengthener rather than a weakener.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive argument: an economist uses historical correlation between consumer confidence index rises and GDP growth to predict that a current confidence surge will produce GDP growth. The weakener attacks the premise-to-conclusion move by identifying a structural difference that makes the historical pattern inapplicable now. Distractors include a strengthener and an irrelevant statistic.
lr.stimulus: An economist noted that over the past four decades, every time the national consumer confidence index rose by more than 10 points in a single quarter, GDP growth of at least 2 percent followed within 12 months. The consumer confidence index has now risen by 14 points this quarter. The economist therefore predicts that GDP growth of at least 2 percent will occur within the next 12 months.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the economist's prediction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consumer confidence indices are calculated using survey data collected from a random sample of households.

choices.label: B
choices.text: GDP growth of 2 percent is generally considered the minimum threshold for a healthy economy by most financial analysts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The current surge in consumer confidence is driven entirely by anticipated government subsidies that economists expect will be canceled before consumers can increase their actual spending.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In all four decades studied, the rises in consumer confidence were accompanied by low unemployment rates, which also independently predict GDP growth.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Consumer confidence has risen by more than 10 points in a single quarter on six separate occasions over the past four decades.

explanations.correct: The economist's prediction rests on the assumption that past correlations hold because rising confidence translates into increased consumer spending, which drives GDP. Choice C reveals that the current confidence rise is based on anticipated subsidies expected to be canceled, meaning actual spending—and thus GDP impact—will not follow. This attacks the mechanism linking the confidence index to GDP growth, undermining the prediction.
explanations.A: Out-of-scope trap. The methodology for calculating the index does not bear on whether the historical correlation holds or whether the current situation differs meaningfully from past instances.
explanations.B: Irrelevant trap. What analysts consider a healthy growth threshold is a definitional point that neither strengthens nor weakens the prediction about whether that growth will occur.
explanations.C: Correct. Identifies a structural difference between current conditions and all historical instances, severing the link between confidence and actual economic activity.
explanations.D: This actually weakens the argument, but less directly than C—it suggests the confidence index may be a spurious correlate rather than a cause, since low unemployment (not present in the current situation) may have been doing the real work. However, the stimulus does not specify current unemployment, making this weaker than C's direct attack on the spending mechanism. On the LSAT, C is the stronger, more targeted weakener.
explanations.E: Accurate-but-irrelevant trap. Stating how many times confidence rose in the historical sample simply restates background information consistent with the economist's premise and does nothing to weaken the prediction.

lr.difficultyReason: Analogical argument: a policy advocate argues that because a literacy program reduced recidivism in one jurisdiction, an identical program should reduce recidivism in a second jurisdiction. The weakener attacks the analogy by identifying a relevant disanalogy. Distractors include a strengthener, a premise-level attack that leaves the conclusion standing, and an out-of-scope comparison.
lr.stimulus: A policy advocate argued that a voluntary prison literacy program introduced in Westfield County reduced inmate recidivism rates by 18 percent over five years. She therefore recommended that Hartley County adopt an identical program, predicting it would achieve comparable reductions in recidivism there.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the advocate's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Westfield County literacy program was funded primarily through private donations rather than public tax revenue.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Studies in organizational behavior show that voluntary programs consistently attract participants who are already more motivated to reform than the general prison population.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hartley County's prison population has a substantially higher proportion of inmates serving sentences for violent offenses, a group for which literacy interventions have shown little effect on recidivism.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Westfield County also expanded its post-release employment support services during the same five-year period in which the literacy program operated.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recidivism rates in Hartley County have remained unchanged for the past decade despite several other reform initiatives.

explanations.correct: The argument is analogical: because the program worked in Westfield County, it will work in Hartley County. Choice C identifies a relevant disanalogy—Hartley County's population is predominantly violent offenders, for whom literacy programs have not demonstrated effectiveness. This directly undermines the assumption that the two counties are sufficiently similar for the results to transfer.
explanations.A: Out-of-scope trap. Funding source (private vs. public) is irrelevant to whether the program achieves recidivism reductions. It might affect feasibility but does not bear on the advocate's causal or analogical reasoning.
explanations.B: This is a self-selection / methodological attack on the Westfield County finding itself—it suggests the 18 percent reduction may not have been caused by the program. However, it attacks a premise (the Westfield result) rather than the analogical move to Hartley County. Even if the Westfield finding is methodologically flawed, the same flaw would apply similarly in Hartley County, leaving the comparative recommendation somewhat intact. Choice C more directly attacks the conclusion.
explanations.C: Correct. Establishes a material disanalogy between the two jurisdictions that breaks the analogical inference at its core.
explanations.D: Opposite-answer trap. That Westfield County also expanded employment support during the same period actually weakens the Westfield County finding's reliability—but this functions more as an alternative explanation for Westfield's success than as a reason the program won't work in Hartley. Paradoxically, noting this confound could be seen as mildly undermining the advocate, but it is a weaker and less targeted attack than C.
explanations.E: Irrelevant / shift-in-subject trap. The fact that prior reform initiatives failed in Hartley County is consistent with the literacy program being different in kind and does not specifically address why this particular program would fail there.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (medication → lower inflammation → improved outcomes). The weakener attacks the move from evidence to conclusion by introducing an alternative explanation for the observed improvement. Distractors include a strengthener and an out-of-scope comparison.
lr.stimulus: A clinical researcher reported that patients who took a new anti-inflammatory drug for eight weeks showed significantly lower rates of joint deterioration than patients who received a placebo. The researcher concluded that the drug's suppression of inflammatory markers was responsible for the reduced joint deterioration in the treatment group.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patients in the treatment group were, on average, ten years younger than patients in the placebo group.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drug has been shown in laboratory studies to inhibit the specific enzymes that trigger inflammation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several patients in the placebo group reported that their joint pain worsened during the study period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Anti-inflammatory drugs in the same class have produced similar results in earlier trials.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The study did not measure inflammatory marker levels in the placebo group at the end of the trial.

explanations.correct: If treatment-group patients were significantly younger than placebo-group patients, age alone could account for the lower rate of joint deterioration, severing the link between the drug's mechanism and the outcome. This is a classic confounding-variable weakener.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces a confounding variable (age difference between groups) that provides an alternative explanation for the observed difference, undermining the researcher's causal conclusion.
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. Laboratory evidence that the drug inhibits inflammation-triggering enzymes supports the proposed causal mechanism rather than weakening it.
explanations.C: Accurate-but-irrelevant trap. That placebo patients worsened is consistent with the argument's premise; it does not address whether the drug's anti-inflammatory action specifically caused the treatment group's improvement.
explanations.D: Strengthener trap. Prior similar results in related drugs bolster confidence in the conclusion rather than undermining it.
explanations.E: Too-narrow trap. The absence of placebo inflammatory data is a methodological gap, but it does not offer an alternative explanation for the outcome; it merely limits one piece of supporting evidence.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive argument based on economic trend data. The weakener attacks the inference from past correlation to future outcome. Distractors include one strengthener and one irrelevant macroeconomic fact.
lr.stimulus: An economist argued that because consumer confidence indices have risen for six consecutive quarters in Merona, household spending will increase substantially over the next year. She pointed to historical data showing that sustained rises in consumer confidence have reliably preceded spending increases in Merona's economy.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the economist's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consumer confidence indices in neighboring countries have also risen over the same six-quarter period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Merona's government recently enacted a series of credit-tightening regulations that sharply limit consumers' access to loans.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The historical periods the economist cites also featured rising consumer confidence indices.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some economists believe that consumer confidence is a lagging rather than a leading indicator of spending.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Household spending in Merona declined modestly in one of the six quarters during which confidence was rising.

explanations.correct: Even if consumer confidence is high, new credit-tightening regulations could prevent consumers from converting that confidence into actual spending. This attacks the bridge between the historical pattern and the predicted future outcome, providing a structural reason the past correlation will not repeat.
explanations.A: Out-of-scope trap. Rising confidence in neighboring countries is irrelevant to whether Merona's consumers will increase spending.
explanations.B: Correct. Credit-tightening regulations sever the mechanism by which confidence translates into spending, directly undermining the economist's prediction.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. Confirming that the historical periods featured rising confidence validates the premise rather than weakening the conclusion.
explanations.D: Too-narrow trap. A contested academic view does not establish that the correlation fails in Merona's specific case; it merely raises a theoretical doubt without concrete evidence.
explanations.E: Accurate-but-irrelevant trap. A single quarter of modest decline during a broader upward trend does not undermine the sustained-rise premise enough to weaken the conclusion significantly.

lr.difficultyReason: Analogical argument comparing two legal systems. The weakener identifies a disanalogy that breaks the comparison. Distractors include a strengthener and a premise-level attack that leaves the conclusion intact.
lr.stimulus: A legal scholar argued that Verdana's proposed mandatory sentencing guidelines should reduce judicial inconsistency, citing the example of Caltria, where similar guidelines were introduced a decade ago and led to a marked reduction in sentencing disparities across courts. Because the two countries share comparable court structures and criminal codes, the scholar concluded that Verdana can expect comparable results.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Caltria's guidelines were accompanied by an extensive judicial training program that Verdana does not plan to implement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mandatory sentencing guidelines have been adopted by several other countries with mixed results.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Verdana's criminal code closely resembles Caltria's in its classification of offenses and prescribed penalties.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some of Caltria's judges initially opposed the guidelines but later acknowledged their effectiveness.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sentencing disparities in Verdana are currently higher than they were in Caltria before its guidelines were introduced.

explanations.correct: The scholar's analogy depends on the two countries being comparable in the relevant respects. If Caltria's success depended critically on a judicial training program that Verdana will not have, the analogy breaks down — the training, not the guidelines alone, may have driven the reduction in disparities.
explanations.A: Correct. Identifies a disanalogy (training program) that could explain Caltria's success independently of the guidelines, undermining the prediction for Verdana.
explanations.B: Too-narrow trap. Mixed results elsewhere introduce doubt but do not specifically address the scholar's Caltria-to-Verdana analogy; the argument already acknowledges Caltria's success.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. Confirming a similarity between the two countries' criminal codes directly supports the analogy the scholar relies on.
explanations.D: Strengthener trap. Evidence that judges accepted the guidelines over time bolsters confidence in their practical effectiveness.
explanations.E: Accurate-but-irrelevant trap. Greater initial disparity in Verdana might actually suggest even more room for improvement, but the choice does not attack the core analogical inference.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain in environmental science: pesticide use → decline in bee population → crop yield reduction. Weakener attacks the second link. Distractors include an opposite answer and a shift-in-subject trap.
lr.stimulus: Agricultural researchers found that the use of a particular class of pesticides increased dramatically in the Denvar Valley over the past decade, during which time the local honeybee population fell by nearly 40 percent. A regional farming coalition concluded that the pesticide use caused the crop yield reductions that Valley farmers reported over the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the farming coalition's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Honeybees are the primary pollinators for most of the crops grown in the Denvar Valley.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The crops that experienced the greatest yield reductions in the Denvar Valley are largely self-pollinating and do not depend on honeybees.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pesticide use in agricultural regions adjacent to the Denvar Valley did not increase over the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some farmers in the Denvar Valley reported using the pesticides less frequently than recommended guidelines suggest.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Research has linked the same class of pesticides to colony collapse disorder in honeybee populations in other regions.

explanations.correct: The coalition's conclusion assumes that the bee decline caused the crop yield reductions. If the affected crops are self-pollinating and do not rely on bees, then even a large bee decline cannot explain the yield reductions, severing the second link in the causal chain.
explanations.A: Strengthener trap. Establishing bees as primary pollinators supports the mechanism connecting bee decline to crop yield loss.
explanations.B: Correct. Attacks the second causal link (bee decline → yield reduction) by showing the crops don't depend on bees, undermining the coalition's conclusion.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope trap. What happened in adjacent regions does not bear on whether pesticide-driven bee decline caused yield reductions in the Denvar Valley specifically.
explanations.D: Too-narrow trap. Reduced pesticide use by some farmers might weaken the first link (pesticide → bee decline) slightly, but the question asks about the coalition's specific conclusion regarding yield reductions, and this choice doesn't address that link.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. External evidence linking the pesticides to colony collapse disorder in other regions supports the first causal link in the chain.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy argument relying on a sample-to-general generalization. The weakener attacks the representativeness of the sample. Distractors include a strengthener and a premise-attack that doesn't undermine the conclusion.
lr.stimulus: A city transportation director reported that a pilot program offering free bus passes to residents of the Westbrook district resulted in a 22 percent decrease in private vehicle trips in that district over six months. The director concluded that extending the free-pass program citywide would produce a comparable reduction in private vehicle use across the entire city.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the director's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Westbrook is one of the city's most densely served transit districts, with bus routes running every eight minutes, while most other districts have service only once per hour.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Residents of Westbrook who received the free passes reported high satisfaction with the bus service.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 22 percent reduction in vehicle trips in Westbrook occurred despite a modest increase in the district's population during the pilot period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Other cities that have implemented free transit programs have seen reductions in vehicle traffic ranging from 10 to 30 percent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some Westbrook residents who received free passes continued to drive rather than use public transit.

explanations.correct: The director's generalization from Westbrook to the whole city assumes the pilot district is representative. If Westbrook has far more frequent service than other districts, residents elsewhere could not substitute bus travel for driving even with free passes — the high service frequency, not the free passes alone, likely drove the reduction.
explanations.A: Correct. Reveals that Westbrook is an unrepresentative sample because of its unusually high service frequency, undermining the generalization to the whole city.
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. High resident satisfaction supports the program's effectiveness and bolsters the case for expansion.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. A reduction even amid population growth makes the pilot result look more robust, supporting the conclusion.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope trap. Evidence from other cities does not address whether Westbrook is representative of the city's other districts.
explanations.E: Too-narrow trap. Some continued driving is consistent with a 22 percent overall reduction; this doesn't challenge the conclusion about citywide expansion.

lr.difficultyReason: Causal argument in technology policy. Two-step chain: social media algorithm change → increased exposure to misinformation → rise in measured belief in false claims. Weakener attacks the first link with a confounding timeline factor. One distractor strengthens; one is a subject-shift trap.
lr.stimulus: A media watchdog organization reported that a major social media platform changed its content-recommendation algorithm in March, and that surveys conducted in June showed a significant increase in users' belief in several widely circulated false claims compared to surveys from the previous December. The organization concluded that the algorithm change caused the increase in misinformation beliefs.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the organization's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The false claims in question were the subject of several high-profile news stories and a prominent political speech between March and June.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The platform's algorithm change was designed to increase user engagement rather than to promote any particular type of content.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Users who spent more time on the platform after the algorithm change reported encountering more misinformation than users who spent less time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The surveys used a representative sample of the platform's active users and were conducted by an independent polling firm.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Other social media platforms that did not change their algorithms also saw increases in misinformation-related content during the same period.

explanations.correct: If the specific false claims received heavy coverage in high-profile news stories and a prominent political speech between March and June, those external events provide an alternative explanation for the rise in belief — one entirely independent of the algorithm change.
explanations.A: Correct. Provides an alternative explanation (external media and political amplification) for the rise in misinformation beliefs, undermining the causal attribution to the algorithm change.
explanations.B: Out-of-scope trap. The algorithm's stated design intent does not determine whether it actually increased misinformation exposure; the conclusion concerns effects, not intent.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. A dose-response relationship between platform use and misinformation exposure after the change supports the organization's causal claim.
explanations.D: Strengthener trap. Methodological rigor in the surveys validates the data underlying the premise, bolstering the argument.
explanations.E: Accurate-but-irrelevant trap. Increases on other platforms could reflect the same external events cited in choice A, but as stated this choice does not explain why the specific platform's algorithm change was not the cause — it introduces a separate correlation without ruling out the algorithm's role.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive argument in linguistics: exposure to bilingual education → stronger executive function → better academic outcomes. The weakener attacks the move from mechanism to predicted outcome. One distractor is a classic strengthener; one is a reversed-causation misapplication trap.
lr.stimulus: A linguist argued that children enrolled in bilingual education programs develop stronger executive function skills due to the constant mental effort of managing two languages. Because executive function is a reliable predictor of academic achievement, the linguist concluded that bilingual education programs will improve students' overall academic performance.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Studies show that children with stronger executive function skills perform better on standardized academic assessments than peers with weaker executive function skills.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The executive function gains associated with bilingual education are too small in magnitude to produce measurable differences in academic achievement.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Children in bilingual programs spend more hours each week on language instruction and fewer hours on core academic subjects than children in monolingual programs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some children who perform well academically were never enrolled in bilingual education programs.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bilingual education programs are more expensive per student to operate than standard monolingual programs.

explanations.correct: Even if bilingual education improves executive function and executive function predicts achievement, those gains could be offset or overwhelmed by the reduced time spent on core academic subjects. This attacks the prediction by introducing a countervailing mechanism that undermines the expected net outcome.
explanations.A: Strengthener trap. Confirming the link between executive function and academic performance supports one of the argument's key premises.
explanations.B: This is a strong distractor — it attacks the magnitude of the executive function effect. However, it only weakens the first step (bilingual ed → meaningful executive function gain) without introducing a competing mechanism, making it less targeted than C, which directly undermines the predicted academic outcome.
explanations.C: Correct. Introduces a countervailing causal mechanism: reduced core-subject instruction time could negate the executive-function benefit, directly undermining the prediction that bilingual education improves academic performance.
explanations.D: Shift-in-subject trap. The existence of high-achieving monolingual students does not address whether bilingual education would improve bilingual students' performance.
explanations.E: Out-of-scope trap. Cost per student is irrelevant to whether bilingual education actually improves academic performance.

lr.difficultyReason: Historical causal argument. The weakener attacks the causal claim by reversing the direction of the relationship. One distractor is a strengthener; one attacks a peripheral premise without touching the conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Historians have noted that during the sixteenth century, cities in the Brennan region that had larger merchant guilds also tended to have higher rates of literacy among their adult populations. One historian concluded that the guilds promoted literacy by requiring merchants to maintain written records and conduct correspondence, thereby creating strong incentives for members and their families to become literate.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the historian's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sixteenth-century Brennan cities with higher literacy rates attracted more long-distance trade, which in turn drew migrants who formed or joined merchant guilds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Merchant guild members in sixteenth-century Brennan were required by guild charters to keep detailed written accounts of all commercial transactions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Literacy rates among non-guild members in the Brennan region also rose during the sixteenth century.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some sixteenth-century Brennan cities had high literacy rates despite the absence of large merchant guilds.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Historians disagree about the precise methods used to estimate literacy rates in sixteenth-century Brennan.

explanations.correct: The historian infers that guilds caused higher literacy. Choice A reverses the relationship: pre-existing literacy attracted trade and thus larger guilds — the literacy came first and drove guild formation rather than the reverse. This is a paradigmatic reversed-causation weakener.
explanations.A: Correct. Reverses the causal direction: literacy attracted trade which built larger guilds, meaning literacy caused guild size rather than guilds causing literacy.
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. Confirming that guilds required written record-keeping supports the historian's proposed mechanism.
explanations.C: Too-narrow trap. Rising literacy among non-guild members might suggest broader societal forces were at work, but as stated it does not directly undermine the claim that guilds drove literacy among guild populations.
explanations.D: Too-narrow trap. The existence of high-literacy cities without large guilds shows guilds are not necessary for literacy but does not address whether guilds caused the observed literacy correlation in cities that did have large guilds.
explanations.E: Accurate-but-irrelevant trap. Methodological disagreement about measuring literacy is a scholarly caveat but does not attack the causal argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethical/policy argument using a proportionality principle. The weakener identifies a relevant dissimilarity that the argument's principle cannot accommodate. One distractor strengthens the principle; one is an out-of-scope moral claim.
lr.stimulus: An ethics board member argued that a pharmaceutical company acted wrongly by charging patients in low-income countries twenty times more for a life-saving drug than it costs to manufacture. The member reasoned that it is always unethical to price a product in a way that makes it inaccessible to those who need it most, and the pricing policy clearly makes the drug inaccessible to the patients who need it.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the ethics board member's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The pharmaceutical company used the profits from higher drug prices to fund the research and development of three new life-saving drugs that would not otherwise have been developed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several consumer advocacy groups have publicly condemned the company's pricing policy as exploitative.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The manufacturing cost the member cites does not include the company's research, development, and regulatory approval expenses.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Other pharmaceutical companies charge similar prices for comparable drugs in the same low-income markets.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The drug in question is also used for non-life-threatening conditions by patients in wealthy countries who can afford the price.

explanations.correct: The ethics board member argues that pricing that makes a drug inaccessible to those who need it is always unethical. Choice A introduces a consequentialist consideration: the profits funded future life-saving research that benefits more people. This challenges the blanket 'always unethical' principle by showing a morally relevant countervailing outcome, weakening the conclusion that the company acted wrongly.
explanations.A: Correct. The future-drug-development consequence provides a morally significant reason to doubt the claim that the pricing was unethical, challenging the 'always unethical' principle underlying the argument.
explanations.B: Out-of-scope trap. Public condemnation is a sociological fact, not an ethical argument; it does not bear on whether the pricing was actually unethical.
explanations.C: Too-narrow trap. While it shows the member's cost comparison is incomplete, this does not itself establish the pricing is ethical — it only challenges one factual premise without undermining the normative conclusion.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope trap. Industry-wide pricing norms do not address the ethical principle at issue; widespread practice does not determine ethical permissibility.
explanations.E: Accurate-but-irrelevant trap. That wealthy patients can afford the drug for non-life-threatening uses is tangential; the argument concerns accessibility for those who need it for life-saving purposes.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive argument in arts/cultural policy. The argument generalizes from one city's experience to predict an outcome in another. Weakener attacks the bridge between the evidence and the prediction by identifying a structural difference. One distractor is a strengthener; one is an unwarranted comparison trap.
lr.stimulus: A city arts council proposed building a new downtown concert hall, citing the example of Fairhaven, where a similar concert hall built fifteen years ago drew a large influx of tourists and generated significant revenue for local businesses in the surrounding area. The council concluded that the new concert hall would similarly revitalize the downtown district and increase revenue for local businesses.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the arts council's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fairhaven's concert hall was the only major performance venue within a three-hour drive when it opened, whereas the city already has three large performance venues within its downtown district.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Construction costs for the proposed concert hall are estimated to be 40 percent higher than the cost of building Fairhaven's hall.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Surveys indicate that a majority of the city's residents support the construction of the new concert hall.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fairhaven's downtown businesses reported a 30 percent increase in revenue in the five years following the concert hall's opening.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some concert halls built in other cities over the past two decades have failed to attract sufficient audiences to remain financially viable.

explanations.correct: The council's analogy depends on the two cities being relevantly similar. Fairhaven's success likely owed much to satisfying unmet demand — it was the only venue for miles. If the city already has three downtown performance venues, a new hall would not fill a similar gap and would instead compete for the same audience pool, making the predicted revitalization far less likely.
explanations.A: Correct. Identifies a critical disanalogy: Fairhaven lacked competing venues while the city already has three, meaning the new hall cannot tap pent-up demand the way Fairhaven's did.
explanations.B: Unwarranted-comparison trap. Higher construction costs affect the project's financial return but do not address whether the hall will attract tourists and generate business revenue — the conclusion is about revitalization, not construction ROI.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. Majority public support suggests residents are likely to attend and patronize surrounding businesses, bolstering the prediction.
explanations.D: Strengthener trap. Quantifying Fairhaven's business revenue increase reinforces the evidence that the council's analogy draws on.
explanations.E: Too-narrow trap. The existence of failed concert halls elsewhere raises generic doubt but does not specifically address why this city's situation differs from Fairhaven's, which is the key analogical inference.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (new compound → enzyme suppression → reduced inflammation). The weakener attacks the move from lab results to clinical conclusion. Distractors include a strengthener and an out-of-scope comparison to another drug.
lr.stimulus: A pharmaceutical researcher found that a newly synthesized compound suppresses the production of an enzyme linked to chronic joint inflammation. In trials on laboratory mice, mice administered the compound showed significantly lower levels of joint inflammation than untreated mice. The researcher concluded that the compound will effectively reduce chronic joint inflammation in human patients.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The enzyme suppressed by the compound plays a substantially different role in human joint tissue than it does in mouse joint tissue.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several existing anti-inflammatory drugs also work by suppressing enzyme production.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The laboratory mice used in the trials were specially bred to develop joint inflammation rapidly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The compound suppressed enzyme production in all treated mice, not just those with chronic inflammation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Human patients with chronic joint inflammation typically have higher baseline enzyme levels than healthy individuals.

explanations.correct: The argument assumes that because the compound works on mice, it will work on humans — a direct analogical leap. If the enzyme plays a different role in human tissue, the mechanism that reduced inflammation in mice may not translate, directly undermining the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Attacks the analogy from mouse to human by exposing a disanalogy in the underlying mechanism.
explanations.B: Out of scope. The fact that other drugs work similarly neither strengthens nor weakens this compound's human efficacy.
explanations.C: This could, if anything, raise concerns about the trial's representativeness, but it doesn't directly attack the conclusion about human patients — it's too narrow a methodological quibble to undermine the conclusion.
explanations.D: Irrelevant to the human-efficacy conclusion. Universal suppression in mice doesn't bear on whether the compound will work in humans.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. Higher baseline enzyme levels in affected humans might actually support the idea that suppressing the enzyme would benefit human patients.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive argument resting on a two-step chain: carbon tax → higher energy costs → reduced consumption. Weakener attacks the second step. One distractor strengthens; one attacks a peripheral claim.
lr.stimulus: An economist argued that the federal government's newly enacted carbon tax will significantly reduce the nation's overall energy consumption. The tax raises the price of fossil-fuel-derived energy, and consumers and businesses consistently reduce their consumption of goods and services when prices rise. Therefore, the carbon tax will achieve its goal of meaningfully lowering total energy use nationwide.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the argument's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most economists agree that carbon taxes are among the most efficient tools for reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For the majority of consumers and businesses, fossil-fuel-derived energy has no readily available substitute, making demand for it highly inelastic.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The carbon tax is projected to generate billions of dollars in annual government revenue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several other nations have enacted carbon taxes at higher rates than the one now in effect in this country.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Businesses that produce renewable energy are expected to benefit financially from the carbon tax.

explanations.correct: The argument assumes the standard economic principle that price increases reduce consumption. If demand for fossil-fuel energy is highly inelastic — meaning consumers and businesses cannot easily cut back or switch — then higher prices will not produce meaningful reductions in consumption, directly undermining the conclusion.
explanations.A: Strengthener trap. Expert agreement on carbon taxes' efficiency supports, rather than weakens, the economist's claim.
explanations.B: Correct. Inelastic demand breaks the link between higher prices and reduced consumption — the key inferential step.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Revenue generation is a separate outcome; it doesn't speak to whether energy consumption will fall.
explanations.D: Unwarranted comparison trap. What other nations do at different rates doesn't bear on whether this tax will reduce domestic consumption.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Renewable energy producers' financial gains are a side effect; they don't address whether total energy consumption declines.

lr.difficultyReason: Causal argument with an alternative-explanation weakener. The stimulus infers cause from correlation. One distractor attacks a peripheral premise; one is an irrelevant historical fact.
lr.stimulus: A city's transportation authority reported that after a new light-rail line opened, traffic congestion on the two parallel highway corridors decreased by 22 percent over the following year. The authority concluded that the light-rail line was responsible for the reduction in highway congestion.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The light-rail line's opening was accompanied by a major increase in gasoline prices that prompted many commuters to abandon their cars.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ridership on the new light-rail line exceeded the authority's projections by 30 percent in its first year of operation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several businesses along the two highway corridors closed during the year following the light-rail line's opening.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The light-rail line cost significantly more to construct than the authority had initially budgeted.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Other cities that have opened light-rail lines have reported similar reductions in highway congestion.

explanations.correct: The authority infers that the light-rail line caused the congestion decrease because the two events coincided. Introducing a simultaneous gasoline price spike — an independent factor that would also reduce highway traffic — provides an alternative explanation for the observed decrease, weakening the causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Alternative explanation that accounts for the congestion drop without crediting the light-rail line.
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. High ridership is consistent with the light-rail line drawing cars off the road, supporting the authority's conclusion.
explanations.C: Too narrow. Business closures could reduce traffic, but this is a weaker and less direct alternative explanation than A; moreover, it doesn't clearly undermine the rail line as the primary cause without further inference.
explanations.D: Irrelevant. Construction cost overruns have no bearing on whether the rail line caused the congestion reduction.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. Analogous outcomes in other cities support, rather than weaken, the authority's causal claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Analogical/predictive argument in law. The weakener identifies a disanalogy between the two legal contexts compared. Distractors include a strengthener and an out-of-scope procedural fact.
lr.stimulus: A legal scholar argued that the nation's courts should recognize a constitutional right to digital privacy in personal communications, citing the precedent established in Katz v. United States, in which the Supreme Court held that individuals have a reasonable expectation of privacy in telephone conversations. Because digital communications are functionally equivalent to telephone conversations as a means of private personal exchange, the scholar concluded that courts should extend the same constitutional protection to digital communications.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most calls into question the scholar's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Unlike the contents of a telephone call, digital communications are routinely stored on third-party servers and disclosed to those servers' operators under standard user agreements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Supreme Court in Katz v. United States unanimously agreed that some form of privacy protection was warranted for telephone calls.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several foreign legal systems already extend explicit privacy protections to digital communications.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Digital communications can travel across international borders, complicating jurisdictional questions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts have become increasingly comfortable applying precedents established before the digital era to contemporary technological contexts.

explanations.correct: The scholar's argument rests on the analogy that digital communications are functionally equivalent to telephone calls for constitutional purposes. If digital communications are routinely stored on and disclosed to third-party servers — a key disanalogy — users may lack a 'reasonable expectation of privacy,' which is the very standard Katz established. This disanalogy undercuts the analogical extension.
explanations.A: Correct. Exposes a legally significant disanalogy: the third-party disclosure doctrine (established in Smith v. Maryland) applies to digital communications in a way it did not apply to Katz's phone call, undermining the functional equivalence claim.
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. Unanimous agreement in Katz reinforces the precedent the scholar is relying on.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Foreign legal systems' practices don't bear on what domestic courts should do under the U.S. Constitution.
explanations.D: Shift in subject. Jurisdictional complexity is a separate problem, not one that undermines the analogical argument about whether privacy rights should exist.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. Courts' comfort with applying older precedents to new technology supports the scholar's approach.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain in environmental science: deforestation → soil erosion → river sedimentation. Weakener attacks the second causal link. One distractor attacks the first link only; one is a strengthener.
lr.stimulus: Environmental officials in the Maren River watershed documented a 40 percent increase in riverside deforestation over the past decade. They concluded that this deforestation is responsible for the severe sedimentation recently observed in the Maren River, reasoning that deforestation leads to soil erosion, and soil erosion delivers excess sediment into adjacent waterways.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The deforested areas in the Maren River watershed are separated from the river by wide bands of intact wetland vegetation that trap eroded soil before it reaches the river.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Soil erosion rates in the Maren River watershed have increased sharply over the past decade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deforestation in neighboring watersheds has not led to measurable increases in river sedimentation in those areas.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Maren River has experienced periodic sedimentation events caused by upstream flooding throughout its recorded history.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Government agencies have logged the deforested areas under permits that require replanting within five years.

explanations.correct: Even if deforestation causes soil erosion (first link), the conclusion that this erosion reaches and sediments the river depends on a second link: eroded soil actually enters the river. If intact wetland buffers trap the eroded soil before it reaches the river, the second causal step fails, and the sedimentation must have another cause.
explanations.A: Correct. Severs the second causal link — from soil erosion to river sedimentation — by introducing a physical barrier that prevents eroded soil from reaching the river.
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. Confirming increased erosion supports the causal chain rather than weakening it.
explanations.C: Too narrow / shifts subject. Evidence from neighboring watersheds introduces an alternative comparison but does not directly explain why the erosion-to-sedimentation link fails in the Maren watershed.
explanations.D: Out of scope. Historical periodic sedimentation from flooding is a different phenomenon and doesn't undermine the officials' specific causal claim about recent deforestation.
explanations.E: Irrelevant. Future replanting commitments don't bear on whether past or current deforestation caused the observed sedimentation.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive argument in technology policy. The weakener shows the predicted mechanism will not operate as assumed. Distractors include an out-of-scope historical analogy and a strengthener.
lr.stimulus: A technology policy analyst predicted that mandating open-source software in all government agencies will substantially lower the agencies' long-term software costs. The analyst reasoned that open-source software eliminates licensing fees, which currently constitute the largest share of government software expenditure, and that the money saved on fees can be redirected to other priorities.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the analyst's prediction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Open-source software typically requires significantly more specialized technical staff to maintain and customize than commercial licensed software, and qualified personnel are costly to hire and retain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several private corporations have successfully reduced their software costs by transitioning to open-source solutions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Government agencies are subject to procurement regulations that may delay the adoption of new software platforms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Open-source software communities regularly release security updates, reducing the risk of cyberattacks on government systems.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Licensing fees for commercial software have increased at an average annual rate of 8 percent over the past decade.

explanations.correct: The analyst assumes that eliminating licensing fees translates directly into lower overall costs. If open-source software requires expensive specialized personnel whose costs offset or exceed the savings on licensing fees, the predicted net cost reduction fails — directly undermining the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces offsetting costs (personnel) that the analyst's reasoning ignores, attacking the move from 'no licensing fees' to 'lower long-term costs.'
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. Corporate success with open-source solutions supports the analyst's prediction by analogy.
explanations.C: Too narrow. Procurement delays affect the timing of adoption, not whether long-term costs will ultimately be lower — so it doesn't squarely undermine the cost-savings conclusion.
explanations.D: Strengthener trap. Security benefits are an additional advantage of open-source, reinforcing the case for the mandate.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. Rising licensing fees make the savings from eliminating them even more significant, supporting the analyst's prediction.

lr.difficultyReason: Causal argument in history/policy based on a correlation. The weakener provides an alternative historical explanation. One distractor is an accurate but irrelevant detail; one strengthens.
lr.stimulus: Historians studying the decline of the Roman Empire have noted that a series of severe grain shortages struck the empire's western provinces in the decades immediately preceding the final collapse of Roman authority in 476 CE. One prominent historian concluded that these grain shortages were the primary cause of the empire's fall, since a starving population cannot sustain the military and administrative apparatus necessary to maintain state authority.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The grain shortages affected the eastern provinces of the Roman Empire less severely than the western provinces.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The final collapse of Roman authority in the western provinces coincided with a massive influx of Gothic and Hunnic military forces that overwhelmed the Roman legions independently of any economic crisis.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ancient grain storage facilities in the western provinces had deteriorated significantly by the fourth century CE.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Historians disagree about the precise date on which Roman authority in the west should be considered to have ended.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Grain shortages of comparable severity had occurred in earlier centuries without preventing Roman military campaigns.

explanations.correct: The historian concludes the grain shortages were the primary cause of the collapse. If a massive independent military invasion — unrelated to the economic crisis — overwhelmed the legions, then military defeat, not starvation, could be the primary cause, providing a powerful alternative explanation that undermines the historian's causal claim.
explanations.A: Out of scope. The differential impact on eastern vs. western provinces is consistent with the historian's argument; it doesn't provide an alternative cause.
explanations.B: Correct. A simultaneous, independent military catastrophe constitutes an alternative explanation for the collapse that competes with the grain shortage hypothesis.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant trap. Deteriorated storage might have worsened shortages, but it doesn't undermine the conclusion — it actually supports the causal chain.
explanations.D: Irrelevant. Disagreement about the collapse's precise date doesn't address the causal claim about grain shortages.
explanations.E: This is a genuine weakener but a weaker one than B: if shortages didn't cause collapse before, it suggests shortages alone aren't sufficient — but it doesn't provide a positive alternative explanation for the fifth-century collapse. B more directly undermines the 'primary cause' claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Generalization from a sample in linguistics research. The weakener attacks the representativeness of the sample. Distractors include a strengthener and a shift-in-subject trap.
lr.stimulus: A linguist studied a group of 200 bilingual children raised in households where both English and Spanish were spoken and found that these children reached all standard language-acquisition milestones at the same ages as monolingual English-speaking children. The linguist concluded that bilingual upbringing does not delay language development in children generally.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The 200 children studied came exclusively from households with highly educated parents who engaged in frequent, structured language activities with their children — conditions rarely found in the broader population of bilingual households.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Monolingual children in the study's comparison group were drawn from the same geographic region as the bilingual children.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bilingual children in the study scored higher than monolingual children on tests measuring vocabulary breadth in their dominant language.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some researchers have argued that early bilingual exposure enhances cognitive flexibility in children.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Language-acquisition milestones are defined differently by different professional organizations, making cross-study comparisons difficult.

explanations.correct: The linguist generalizes from a sample to 'children generally.' If the sample was drawn exclusively from unusually favorable conditions — highly educated, engaged parents — it is not representative of the broader bilingual population, where developmental delays might still occur. This attacks the generalization's validity.
explanations.A: Correct. Reveals a sampling bias that makes the general conclusion unreliable.
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. Matching the comparison group geographically reduces a confound and supports the study's validity.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. Superior vocabulary scores in bilingual children further support the argument that bilingual upbringing poses no developmental disadvantage.
explanations.D: Shift in subject trap. Claims about cognitive flexibility are a different outcome than language-acquisition milestones; this doesn't weaken the conclusion about milestone timing.
explanations.E: Too narrow. Definitional disagreements complicate comparisons but don't directly undermine the study's internal finding or the generalization drawn from it.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive argument in arts/policy. The weakener attacks the assumption that the proposed mechanism will produce the predicted effect. One distractor is an irrelevant economic fact; one is a strengthener.
lr.stimulus: The director of a regional arts council argued that offering substantial cash grants to independent theaters will increase attendance at live theatrical performances across the region. The director reasoned that the grants will allow theaters to reduce ticket prices, and lower ticket prices will attract larger audiences who were previously deterred by cost.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the director's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Surveys of residents who do not attend live theater indicate that the primary barrier to attendance is unfamiliarity with theatrical programming, not ticket prices.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Independent theaters in the region have struggled financially for the past several years due to rising operating costs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cash grants of the size proposed have successfully revitalized performing arts sectors in two comparable regions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Regional arts councils in other areas have funded grant programs for museums and symphony orchestras with positive results.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some independent theaters plan to use grant funds primarily to upgrade their facilities rather than to reduce ticket prices.

explanations.correct: The director's argument depends on a two-step mechanism: grants → lower prices → higher attendance. If non-attendees stay away because of unfamiliarity, not cost, then lowering prices will not attract them, breaking the second causal link and directly undermining the predicted attendance increase.
explanations.A: Correct. Attacks the assumption that price is the key barrier to attendance, severing the link between lower prices and higher audiences.
explanations.B: Out of scope. The theaters' prior financial struggles explain why grants are needed but don't undermine whether grants will produce the predicted attendance increase.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. Comparable success elsewhere supports the director's prediction.
explanations.D: Shift in subject trap. Grants to museums and orchestras are a different context; the results don't speak to independent theater attendance.
explanations.E: This weakens the first step (grants → lower prices) in part, but it says 'some' theaters — leaving open that others will reduce prices. It is a weaker attack than A, which undermines the mechanism even if prices do drop.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethical/policy argument based on an analogy between two regulatory contexts. Weakener identifies a relevant disanalogy. One distractor strengthens; one is an accurate but irrelevant fact about one side of the analogy.
lr.stimulus: A consumer-advocacy group argued that ride-sharing drivers should be classified as employees rather than independent contractors, citing the precedent set when delivery couriers at a major logistics company were reclassified as employees after regulators determined that the company exercised sufficient control over their working conditions. Because ride-sharing platforms similarly dictate drivers' pricing, routes, and performance standards, the advocacy group concluded that ride-sharing drivers meet the same legal standard for employee classification.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
