choices.text: Unlike delivery couriers, who were required to work designated shifts set by the logistics company, ride-sharing drivers can log on and off the platform at any time of their choosing and are subject to no minimum hour requirements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The logistics company's delivery couriers were found to receive compensation below the legal minimum wage before their reclassification.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ride-sharing platforms collect data on driver behavior, including speed and route adherence, to enforce their performance standards.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Employee classification would entitle ride-sharing drivers to benefits such as health insurance and unemployment compensation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several jurisdictions have already enacted legislation specifically addressing the employment status of gig-economy workers.

explanations.correct: The advocacy group's argument rests on an analogy between delivery couriers and ride-sharing drivers. The legal standard for employee classification typically includes control over scheduling and hours as a central factor. If ride-sharing drivers have complete freedom over when they work — unlike the couriers who had mandatory shifts — this is a legally significant disanalogy that undermines the conclusion that they meet the same classification standard.
explanations.A: Correct. Identifies a key disanalogy in the degree of control exercised, specifically regarding scheduling autonomy, which is central to the legal test being applied.
explanations.B: Irrelevant. The couriers' wage violation was a separate basis for their reclassification that doesn't apply to the ride-sharing context being argued about.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. Evidence that platforms monitor and enforce performance standards supports the advocacy group's claim that control is exercised over drivers.
explanations.D: Out of scope. The entitlements that would flow from reclassification are a consequence, not a reason bearing on whether the legal standard is met.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Legislation in other jurisdictions is a separate legal development; it doesn't speak to whether ride-sharing drivers meet the specific standard used in the courier precedent.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (policy → cost reduction → improved outcomes). The weakener attacks the move from cost reduction to improved outcomes rather than the policy's cost effects directly. One distractor strengthens; one is out-of-scope.
lr.stimulus: A county health administrator argued that switching from fee-for-service reimbursement to a bundled-payment model reduced hospital spending by 12 percent over two years. She concluded that the bundled-payment model therefore improved patient health outcomes, since lower costs mean fewer unnecessary procedures and less risk of hospital-acquired infections.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the administrator's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several hospitals in neighboring counties adopted bundled payments at the same time and reported similar reductions in spending.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The reduction in spending under bundled payments was achieved primarily by discharging patients earlier, before their recoveries were fully confirmed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hospital-acquired infection rates have declined nationally over the past decade regardless of reimbursement model.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bundled-payment models require hospitals to coordinate care across multiple providers, which can increase administrative complexity.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Under fee-for-service reimbursement, physicians tend to order more diagnostic tests than under bundled payments.

explanations.correct: The administrator assumes that reduced spending signals fewer unnecessary procedures, which would improve outcomes. Answer B shows the spending reduction came from early discharges — a mechanism that could harm rather than help patient health, severing the assumed link between lower costs and better outcomes.
explanations.A: Out-of-scope: shows the trend is widespread but does nothing to challenge whether lower costs translate to better outcomes in this county.
explanations.B: Correct. Reveals an alternative explanation for the cost reduction that undermines, rather than supports, improved patient outcomes.
explanations.C: Too narrow / irrelevant: addresses only infection rates nationally and doesn't explain whether this county's outcomes improved due to the payment model.
explanations.D: Attacking a peripheral premise: administrative complexity is a cost, not evidence that patient outcomes failed to improve.
explanations.E: Opposite (strengthener): confirms that fee-for-service incentivizes unnecessary tests, which supports the administrator's premise that bundled payments reduce unnecessary procedures.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive argument with a two-step inference: reduced greenhouse emissions → slowed warming → preserved Arctic habitat. Weakener attacks the second link. Distractors include a strengthener and a subject-shift trap.
lr.stimulus: Environmental researchers at a Nordic institute reported that a newly proposed international agreement would reduce global greenhouse gas emissions by 18 percent within a decade. The researchers concluded that the agreement, if ratified, would prevent the further collapse of Arctic sea-ice habitat critical to polar bear survival.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The proposed agreement has already received preliminary endorsements from the ten largest greenhouse-gas-emitting nations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Polar bears have demonstrated some ability to adapt their hunting behaviors when sea-ice coverage decreases temporarily.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Arctic sea ice is currently losing volume at a rate driven primarily by ocean heat absorption that has already been locked in by past emissions, meaning an 18 percent future reduction would not meaningfully slow ice loss for several decades.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several Arctic species other than polar bears depend on sea-ice habitat for breeding and foraging.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some member nations have historically failed to meet their targets under prior international environmental agreements.

explanations.correct: The researchers' conclusion depends on reduced future emissions translating into preserved Arctic sea ice within a meaningful timeframe. Answer C breaks that link by establishing that sea-ice loss is driven by already-locked-in ocean heat, so the emissions reduction would not prevent further collapse for decades — directly undermining the conclusion.
explanations.A: Strengthens the argument by suggesting ratification is likely, making the researchers' conditional conclusion more relevant.
explanations.B: Shift in subject: addresses polar bear behavioral adaptation, not whether sea-ice habitat is preserved — a distractor that doesn't touch the causal chain.
explanations.C: Correct. Attacks the premise that reducing future emissions will halt imminent sea-ice collapse.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope: broadens concern to other species but does not weaken the claim about polar bear habitat.
explanations.E: Too narrow: raises doubt about whether the agreement will be honored, but the researchers' conclusion is conditional ('if ratified'), so compliance history is a peripheral issue.

lr.difficultyReason: Analogical argument comparing two technologies. Weakener introduces a disanalogy that breaks the comparison. Distractors include an accurate-but-irrelevant fact and an opposite answer.
lr.stimulus: A technology journalist argued that because voice-recognition software improved dramatically once developers began training it on data sets ten times larger than those previously used, image-recognition software will similarly achieve dramatic improvements if developers simply scale up their training data sets by the same factor.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the journalist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The leading image-recognition software already outperforms human accuracy on several standardized visual classification benchmarks.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Voice-recognition software and image-recognition software are both forms of machine-learning applications that rely on large training data sets.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Image-recognition software, unlike voice-recognition software, has reached a performance plateau where errors stem primarily from ambiguities in the images themselves rather than from insufficient training data.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scaling up training data sets is generally more expensive for image data than for audio data.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several major technology companies have announced plans to double their image-recognition training data sets within the next two years.

explanations.correct: The journalist's analogy assumes image-recognition software would respond to more data the way voice-recognition software did. Answer C breaks that analogy by identifying a key disanalogy: image recognition's errors are not data-quantity problems, so adding more data would not produce the same gains.
explanations.A: Out-of-scope: current performance level doesn't address whether more data would cause further improvement.
explanations.B: Strengthens the analogy by confirming the two technologies share relevant structural features.
explanations.C: Correct. Introduces a disanalogy that undermines the journalist's analogical reasoning.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant: addresses cost, not whether the improvement would occur — a classic 'accurate but irrelevant' trap.
explanations.E: Out-of-scope: describes plans to scale data but doesn't speak to whether doing so will produce dramatic improvement.

lr.difficultyReason: Causal argument from correlation in an economics context. Weakener provides an alternative explanation for the observed correlation. One distractor attacks a premise without touching the conclusion; one strengthens.
lr.stimulus: A financial analyst observed that in the twelve months following each of the last four recessions, companies that increased their advertising budgets grew their market share by an average of 9 percent, while companies that cut advertising budgets lost an average of 6 percent. The analyst concluded that increased advertising spending is what caused the market-share gains during post-recession recoveries.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the analyst's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Companies that increased advertising budgets during post-recession periods also tended to have stronger underlying balance sheets, which independently enabled them to pursue growth strategies unavailable to struggling competitors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The four recessions examined by the analyst varied considerably in duration and in the industries they affected most severely.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Advertising costs tend to fall during recessions, making it cheaper for financially healthy companies to increase their advertising spending.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some companies that maintained flat advertising budgets during the post-recession periods also experienced modest market-share growth.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Market-share gains are one of the most reliable indicators of long-term revenue growth for consumer-goods companies.

explanations.correct: The analyst infers causation from correlation. Answer A provides an alternative explanation — stronger balance sheets, not advertising itself, drove growth — because financially healthier companies could pursue multiple growth strategies simultaneously. This severs the causal link the analyst asserts.
explanations.A: Correct. Classic alternative-explanation weakener: a third variable (financial health) explains both the ability to increase advertising and the ability to gain market share.
explanations.B: Attacking a peripheral premise: variation across recessions raises a methodological concern about sample consistency but doesn't offer an alternative cause for the observed gains.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant to causation: lower advertising costs explains why spending increased but not whether that spending caused the gains.
explanations.D: Too narrow: flat-budget companies' modest gains are consistent with the analyst's conclusion and arguably weaken it only weakly; it doesn't provide a better causal account.
explanations.E: Shift in subject: relevance of market share to revenue is a separate claim and does nothing to challenge the advertising-causation inference.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive policy argument where the weakener attacks the assumption that the predicted mechanism will operate in this context. Distractors include a strengthener and an out-of-scope fact.
lr.stimulus: A city council member proposed mandatory minimum sentencing for repeat vandalism offenses, arguing that because mandatory minimums for repeat drunk driving reduced such incidents in three comparable cities by 30 percent over five years, the same policy applied to vandalism will produce a comparable reduction in vandalism rates in this city.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the council member's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vandalism is most frequently committed by juveniles, who are typically exempt from mandatory minimum sentencing statutes, whereas repeat drunk driving is predominantly an adult offense.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The three cities that adopted mandatory minimums for drunk driving also increased funding for public transportation during the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mandatory minimum sentencing is opposed by several civil liberties organizations on constitutional grounds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vandalism rates in this city have increased by 15 percent over the past two years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat offenders in other categories of property crime have been effectively deterred by mandatory minimum sentences in jurisdictions that have implemented them.

explanations.correct: The council member analogizes drunk-driving mandatory minimums to vandalism. Answer A breaks the analogy by identifying a critical disanalogy: the primary vandalism offenders (juveniles) are exempt from mandatory minimums, so the policy's deterrent mechanism cannot reach the offenders it needs to deter.
explanations.A: Correct. Disanalogy trap: the key population committing vandalism is not subject to the policy, so the analogized mechanism fails.
explanations.B: Too narrow: raises an alternative explanation for the drunk-driving reduction (confound), which weakens confidence in the analogy's basis but is less direct than A in attacking whether the policy will work for vandalism here.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope: constitutional opposition speaks to political feasibility, not to whether the policy would reduce vandalism rates if enacted.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant: establishing baseline trend doesn't address whether mandatory minimums will reduce vandalism going forward.
explanations.E: Strengthens: extending the pattern of deterrence to other property crimes supports the analogy the council member is drawing.

lr.difficultyReason: Medical causal argument where the weakener provides an alternative explanation for observed improvements. One distractor is an opposite answer; one is a subject-shift trap.
lr.stimulus: Researchers at a university medical center reported that patients who received acupuncture treatments twice weekly for eight weeks showed a statistically significant reduction in self-reported chronic lower-back pain. The researchers concluded that acupuncture directly reduces chronic lower-back pain.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patients who received sham acupuncture — in which needles were placed at clinically irrelevant points — reported pain reductions nearly identical to those reported by patients receiving genuine acupuncture.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some patients who completed the eight-week acupuncture regimen reported that their pain returned to prior levels within three months of stopping treatment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic lower-back pain is among the most common reasons adults in industrialized nations seek medical treatment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several patients who received acupuncture also independently began low-impact exercise routines during the eight-week study period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Acupuncture has been used as a therapeutic practice in parts of East Asia for more than two thousand years.

explanations.correct: If sham acupuncture produces the same reduction in pain, the improvement cannot be attributed to the specific mechanism of genuine acupuncture. Answer A suggests placebo effect or therapeutic attention — not the acupuncture itself — caused the pain reduction, directly undermining the causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Sham-control comparison reveals that the active ingredient in acupuncture is not responsible for the improvement, implicating placebo or non-specific effects.
explanations.B: Too narrow: addresses durability of effects, not whether acupuncture directly caused the initial reduction — a different claim than the one being evaluated.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope: prevalence of the condition is irrelevant to whether acupuncture causally reduces it.
explanations.D: Alternative explanation (confound): this also weakens the conclusion, but answer A is a more direct and controlled counterexample, making A the stronger weakener.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant: historical usage does not establish or undermine a causal claim about the mechanism of pain reduction.

lr.difficultyReason: Causal-predictive argument in linguistics. The weakener attacks the inference from a historical pattern to a future outcome by identifying a relevant dissimilarity. Distractors include a strengthener and an accurate-but-irrelevant choice.
lr.stimulus: A linguist argued that when a minority language community's children begin attending schools conducted entirely in the dominant national language, the minority language typically becomes extinct within three generations. She therefore predicted that the Veltari language, spoken by a small community whose children recently began attending exclusively national-language schools, will become extinct within three generations.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Studies of language extinction consistently show that economic pressure to assimilate accelerates the shift away from minority languages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Veltari community has established a network of after-school language immersion programs and has made Veltari literacy a condition for participation in community cultural events, practices not present in communities where extinction followed school-language shifts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Veltari has no official written orthography, which makes formal instruction in the language more difficult.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The national language in the Veltari community's country is spoken by more than forty million people.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Language extinction has been documented in communities that never shifted their school instruction to a dominant language.

explanations.correct: The linguist generalizes from past cases of language extinction following school-language shifts. Answer B identifies features of the Veltari community — immersion programs and cultural incentives for language use — that were absent in those historical cases, breaking the analogy and reducing confidence that the same outcome will follow.
explanations.A: Strengthens: confirms a factor (economic pressure) that likely operates in many language-shift contexts, supporting the extinction prediction.
explanations.B: Correct. Introduces a disanalogy between the Veltari community and the communities from which the extinction pattern was derived.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant trap: lack of a written orthography might hinder formal instruction, but this detail doesn't bear on whether the historical extinction pattern applies here — it could support the prediction as easily as undermine it.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope: the dominant language's speaker population is irrelevant to whether the Veltari-specific pattern will follow historical precedent.
explanations.E: Shift in subject: establishes that school-language shift is not necessary for extinction, not that it won't cause extinction here.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethical-economics argument where a conclusion overreaches from an observed trend to a normative recommendation. The weakener shows that the key premise rests on an incomplete comparison. One distractor strengthens; one attacks a side premise.
lr.stimulus: An economic ethicist argued that companies paying workers the minimum wage are exploiting those workers, because studies consistently show that workers paid at the minimum wage report lower well-being than workers paid above it. He concluded that all companies should be legally required to pay wages above the statutory minimum.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the ethicist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Well-being among minimum-wage workers is also strongly correlated with factors such as job security, workplace relationships, and commute time, which are independent of wage level.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In jurisdictions that have raised the minimum wage significantly, employment rates in low-wage sectors have subsequently declined.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Workers paid above the minimum wage report higher well-being than minimum-wage workers even after controlling for industry type and hours worked.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The statutory minimum wage varies considerably across jurisdictions, making a universal mandate difficult to define.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many small businesses operate on margins so thin that raising wages above the minimum would require reducing their workforce.

explanations.correct: The ethicist concludes that minimum-wage pay causes lower well-being and thus constitutes exploitation. Answer A provides an alternative explanation for the lower well-being — independent factors like job security and commute — that severs the causal link between minimum-wage pay specifically and reduced well-being, undermining the exploitation inference.
explanations.A: Correct. Alternative-explanation weakener: the correlation between minimum-wage pay and lower well-being may be driven by confounding variables, not by the wage level itself.
explanations.B: Attacking a side consideration: this is an economic consequence of raising minimums, but the ethicist's argument is about whether current minimum-wage payment is exploitative, not about the effects of raising the minimum.
explanations.C: Strengthens: the controlled comparison bolsters the claim that wage level, not just associated factors, accounts for the well-being difference.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope: definitional complexity of a universal mandate is a practical concern, not a challenge to the ethical argument about whether current minimum-wage payment is exploitative.
explanations.E: Shift in subject: small-business costs address the feasibility or economic consequences of a mandate, not whether minimum-wage payment is exploitative.

lr.difficultyReason: Historical causal argument. The weakener offers a confounding event that provides an alternative cause for the observed historical outcome. One distractor is an opposite (strengthener); one is a reversed-causation trap.
lr.stimulus: A historian argued that the introduction of the printing press to Western Europe in the mid-fifteenth century was the primary cause of the rapid spread of the Protestant Reformation in the early sixteenth century, because the Reformation's theological pamphlets reached mass audiences only after the printing press made their wide distribution feasible.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Literacy rates in Western Europe had been rising steadily for more than a century before the printing press was introduced, expanding the potential audience for written theological arguments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The printing press was also used extensively to distribute Catholic counter-Reformation literature, yet Catholicism did not experience a comparable fragmentation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Earlier reform movements in Western Europe, such as those of Jan Hus and John Wycliffe, failed to achieve lasting mass followings despite having theological arguments comparable in content to Luther's.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Protestant Reformation spread most rapidly in regions where pre-existing grievances against the institutional Church were strongest, suggesting those grievances — not print distribution — were the primary driver.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Martin Luther himself credited the printing press as an essential tool in spreading his theological critiques.

explanations.correct: The historian claims the printing press was the primary cause. Answer D offers an alternative primary cause — pre-existing anti-Church grievances — whose geographic pattern better explains where the Reformation spread most rapidly. This directly challenges the printing-press-as-primary-cause conclusion.
explanations.A: Too narrow: rising literacy supports the printing press's eventual impact but doesn't identify an alternative primary cause for the Reformation's spread.
explanations.B: Shift in subject: Catholic fragmentation vs. Protestant fragmentation are different phenomena; the fact that Catholicism didn't fragment despite print access doesn't explain what caused the Reformation to spread.
explanations.C: Strengthens, arguably: the failure of pre-printing-press reform movements supports the historian's argument that the printing press was a decisive new factor.
explanations.D: Correct. Alternative-explanation weakener providing a rival primary cause whose geographic distribution aligns better with where the Reformation took hold.
explanations.E: Opposite (strengthener): Luther's own attribution supports the historian's causal claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive argument from arts/economics context. Weakener attacks the assumption that past patterns will hold under changed conditions. Distractors include a strengthener and an accurate-but-irrelevant choice.
lr.stimulus: A museum director argued that because the museum's last three major traveling exhibitions each increased annual membership enrollment by at least 20 percent, the museum's upcoming traveling exhibition of twentieth-century graphic design will similarly produce at least a 20 percent increase in membership enrollment.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the museum director's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Graphic design is a field that has attracted significant popular interest in recent years, and the exhibition will include pieces by several internationally recognized designers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The museum's annual membership enrollment is currently near its historical peak, leaving little room for the 20 percent growth that prior exhibitions achieved from lower baseline enrollment figures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The previous three traveling exhibitions required substantially higher organizational costs than the upcoming graphic design exhibition is projected to require.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Traveling exhibitions are generally more effective at attracting new museum members than permanent collection expansions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The museum's marketing budget for the upcoming exhibition is comparable to the budgets allocated to the previous three successful exhibitions.

explanations.correct: The director assumes that the pattern of 20 percent enrollment growth will repeat. Answer B attacks that assumption by revealing a changed condition — enrollment is near its historical peak — meaning the same absolute growth is arithmetically harder to achieve and prior growth rates are not a reliable baseline for predicting future rates.
explanations.A: Strengthens: popular interest in graphic design and notable designers make it more plausible that the exhibition will attract new members.
explanations.B: Correct. Identifies a changed condition (ceiling effect on enrollment) that makes the historical pattern an unreliable predictor for this case.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant: lower exhibition costs affect profitability, not whether the exhibition will generate membership growth.
explanations.D: Strengthens: confirms traveling exhibitions as a membership-growth driver, supporting the director's prediction.
explanations.E: Out-of-scope: comparable marketing budgets are consistent with similar outcomes but don't address the ceiling-effect problem identified in B, and don't themselves weaken the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (new drug → reduced inflammation → improved outcomes). The weakener attacks the move from the clinical evidence to the conclusion by introducing a confound at the second link. One distractor strengthens, one is out-of-scope.
lr.stimulus: Researchers at a teaching hospital administered a new anti-inflammatory drug to patients recovering from knee replacement surgery. Those patients showed measurably lower inflammation markers over the following two weeks and also reported significantly less post-operative pain than patients who received a standard pain regimen. The researchers concluded that the drug's anti-inflammatory action was responsible for the reduction in reported pain.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The new drug contains an opioid compound that directly suppresses pain signals in the central nervous system, independent of any anti-inflammatory effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients who received the new drug were more likely to follow the prescribed physical therapy regimen than those who received the standard pain regimen.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inflammation markers measured in blood plasma are a reliable proxy for tissue-level inflammation in post-surgical patients.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The standard pain regimen used in the comparison group has been in clinical use for more than two decades.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients who reported less pain during recovery also tended to have shorter hospital stays.

explanations.correct: The researchers claim the drug works through its anti-inflammatory action. If the drug contains a compound that directly suppresses pain independently of inflammation, the pain reduction could be explained by that mechanism rather than anti-inflammation — directly undermining the causal claim.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces an alternative causal mechanism that explains pain reduction without invoking anti-inflammatory action, severing the link the researchers depend on.
explanations.B: Shifts subject — this would weaken the conclusion that the drug itself caused pain reduction, but it attacks a different causal path (therapy compliance) rather than the anti-inflammatory mechanism specifically claimed. Slightly relevant but weaker than A.
explanations.C: Strengthens. Validates the measurement tool the researchers used, bolstering the evidence that inflammation was actually reduced.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope. The longevity of the standard regimen's clinical use has no bearing on the mechanism by which the new drug reduces pain.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — the correlation between pain and hospital stay duration does not speak to whether anti-inflammation caused pain reduction.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive argument: economist predicts a policy outcome based on historical analogy. The weakener attacks the disanalogy between the historical case and the present one. Distractors include one that strengthens the analogy and one that is narrowly about a different time period.
lr.stimulus: An economist argues that imposing a modest tariff on imported steel will revitalize domestic steel production, pointing to a 1980s tariff that was followed by a 10 percent increase in domestic steel output within three years. Because the current tariff proposal mirrors the 1980s measure in both rate and scope, the economist predicts a comparable increase in output will follow its enactment.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the economist's prediction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Unlike in the 1980s, most domestic manufacturers today rely on imported steel components that would become significantly more expensive under the proposed tariff, reducing their demand for domestic steel.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The 1980s tariff was accompanied by a simultaneous government subsidy program for domestic steel producers that is not part of the current proposal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Steel output in several competing nations increased substantially during the years following the 1980s tariff.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The current tariff proposal has received bipartisan support in both legislative chambers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Domestic steel production has declined steadily over the past decade, reaching its lowest level in forty years.

explanations.correct: The economist's analogy depends on the two situations being sufficiently similar. If the 1980s tariff was accompanied by a subsidy program absent from the current proposal, the output increase may have been driven by the subsidy rather than (or in addition to) the tariff — breaking the analogy and undermining the prediction.
explanations.A: Plausible weakener, but it introduces a new mechanism (downstream demand reduction) rather than directly attacking the historical analogy the argument rests on. B more precisely targets the premise that the two situations are comparable.
explanations.B: Correct. Identifies a critical disanalogy — a confounding policy present in the historical case but absent now — that explains the earlier output increase and severs the analogical basis for the prediction.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope. Foreign output levels during the 1980s don't bear on whether a similar domestic tariff today will yield a similar domestic output increase.
explanations.D: Irrelevant to the economic prediction — political support says nothing about the causal mechanism or likely outcome.
explanations.E: This might seem to strengthen concern about domestic production but actually could support the tariff's rationale. It does not weaken the argument that the tariff will produce an increase comparable to the 1980s.

lr.difficultyReason: Causal argument from correlation in an environmental science context. The conclusion overreaches by declaring a pollutant the cause of declining amphibian populations. The weakener introduces an alternative explanation; distractors include a strengthener and a premise-only attacker.
lr.stimulus: A wildlife biologist documented a sharp decline in spotted salamander populations in wetlands located near an agricultural region where atrazine use has increased markedly over the past fifteen years. Water samples from those wetlands contained atrazine concentrations above levels shown in laboratory studies to impair amphibian reproduction. The biologist concluded that atrazine runoff is causing the population decline.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the biologist's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Spotted salamander populations in wetlands far from agricultural activity have remained stable over the same fifteen-year period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The wetlands near the agricultural region also border a highway whose construction over the past fifteen years has significantly reduced the surrounding forest habitat on which spotted salamanders depend for breeding migration.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Atrazine has been shown to cause hormonal disruption in multiple amphibian species in addition to spotted salamanders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Laboratory studies establishing the reproductive impairment threshold for atrazine used juvenile salamanders, whereas the biologist's field samples measured adult populations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Farmers in the agricultural region have begun voluntarily reducing atrazine application rates in response to environmental concerns.

explanations.correct: The biologist concludes atrazine caused the decline. If a major habitat disruption (highway construction reducing breeding forest) occurred simultaneously in the same area, that provides an alternative explanation for the population decline, seriously undermining the causal conclusion.
explanations.A: This actually strengthens the argument by providing a control-group comparison suggesting the decline is specific to atrazine-exposed wetlands.
explanations.B: Correct. Introduces a competing causal factor — habitat loss due to highway construction — that could independently explain the observed population decline, weakening the conclusion that atrazine is the cause.
explanations.C: Strengthens. Broadens the evidence that atrazine is harmful to amphibians, supporting the biologist's causal claim.
explanations.D: Attacks a premise (the relevance of laboratory threshold data) without fully undermining the conclusion — the field concentrations could still be causing harm even if the lab data is imperfect. This is the 'too narrow' trap.
explanations.E: Irrelevant to whether atrazine caused the past and ongoing decline; future reduction in application rates does not address the causal claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy argument predicting that a legal change will reduce a harmful outcome. The weakener shows the mechanism connecting the policy to the outcome is unreliable. One distractor is an opposite answer (strengthens); one is out-of-scope.
lr.stimulus: A state legislature is debating a bill that would mandate a minimum three-day waiting period before any firearm purchase is finalized. Proponents point to studies showing that a significant proportion of gun-related suicides involve firearms purchased within 24 hours of the act. They conclude that the waiting period will meaningfully reduce the state's gun-related suicide rate.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument for the waiting period's effectiveness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most individuals who attempt suicide using a recently purchased firearm have no prior history of diagnosed mental illness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The state already has among the highest rates of household firearm ownership in the country, meaning most residents at risk already have access to a firearm in the home.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Waiting periods for firearm purchases have been adopted in several other states over the past two decades.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Suicidal crises frequently intensify over periods longer than three days, so a waiting period would not eliminate risk.

choices.label: E
choices.text: States that have implemented waiting periods have recorded lower rates of gun-related suicides than states without such policies.

explanations.correct: The argument assumes the waiting period will reduce access to firearms at the moment of crisis. If most at-risk residents already own a firearm, the waiting period on new purchases would not meaningfully restrict access, breaking the link between the policy and the predicted reduction in suicides.
explanations.A: Irrelevant to the mechanism by which the waiting period would or would not work — prior mental illness history does not bear on firearm access at time of crisis.
explanations.B: Correct. Undermines the mechanism: if at-risk individuals already possess firearms, delaying new purchases does not reduce their access, severing the causal link between the policy and the predicted outcome.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope. The fact that other states have adopted waiting periods says nothing about whether this state's waiting period will be effective.
explanations.D: This is the 'too narrow' / straw-man trap. It attacks a stronger version of the conclusion (complete elimination of risk) rather than the actual conclusion (meaningful reduction). The argument only claims a meaningful reduction, not elimination.
explanations.E: Strengthens. Provides empirical evidence that waiting periods correlate with lower suicide rates, directly supporting the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Argument from historical evidence to a conclusion about technological causation. The weakener is a classic reverse-causation / confound attack. Distractors include one that strengthens and one that attacks an irrelevant adjacent claim.
lr.stimulus: A technology historian argues that the widespread adoption of the printing press in fifteenth-century Europe directly caused the rapid spread of Protestant ideas during the Reformation. As evidence, the historian cites the fact that the regions where printing presses were most densely concentrated also experienced the earliest and most extensive Protestant conversions.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most calls into question the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Protestant reformers were among the earliest and most prolific users of the printing press to disseminate their theological texts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The regions with the highest concentration of printing presses in fifteenth-century Europe were also major commercial centers whose populations had higher literacy rates and greater exposure to new ideas through trade networks, independent of printed materials.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several regions with few printing presses eventually adopted Protestant ideas after prolonged exposure to traveling preachers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Catholic Church attempted to restrict the distribution of Protestant pamphlets produced by printing presses in several regions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Martin Luther's Ninety-Five Theses were among the most widely printed documents of the early sixteenth century.

explanations.correct: The historian infers causation from the correlation between press density and Protestant conversion. B introduces a confounding variable — high literacy and trade-network exposure in commercial centers — that could explain both the concentration of presses and the spread of Protestant ideas, without the press being the cause.
explanations.A: Strengthens. Confirms that reformers actively used the press to spread ideas, supporting the causal claim.
explanations.B: Correct. Identifies a common cause (commercial center characteristics) that explains both variables, undermining the inference that press density caused Protestant conversion.
explanations.C: This is the 'too narrow' trap. It shows the press wasn't strictly necessary, but does not undermine the claim that the press caused early and extensive conversion in press-dense regions.
explanations.D: Irrelevant to whether the press caused conversions; Church resistance would, if anything, suggest the press was effective (consistent with the historian's view).
explanations.E: Strengthens, or at minimum is irrelevant. Confirming Luther's texts were widely printed is consistent with the historian's causal claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics/policy argument where the conclusion generalizes from one sample to a broader population. The weakener attacks the representativeness of the sample. Distractors include one strengthener and one that addresses an irrelevant demographic.
lr.stimulus: A nonprofit organization surveyed 600 adults in a large metropolitan area and found that 74 percent supported a proposed city ordinance requiring restaurants to display letter grades for food safety inspections. Citing these results, the organization concluded that the ordinance has broad public support and urged the city council to enact it without delay.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the organization's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The survey was conducted exclusively at farmers' markets and organic grocery stores, venues whose patrons tend to have unusually strong preferences for food transparency regulations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Similar letter-grading ordinances in other cities have been shown to improve restaurant hygiene compliance rates within two years of enactment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A majority of restaurant owners in the city oppose the proposed ordinance on the grounds that it unfairly penalizes establishments for minor infractions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The survey question was phrased to clearly distinguish the proposed letter-grade system from a numerical scoring system that had previously been rejected.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Seventy-four percent support among survey respondents exceeds the two-thirds threshold that city council typically requires before advancing major ordinances.

explanations.correct: The conclusion claims the ordinance has broad public support, but if the survey was conducted only at venues with self-selected, atypically food-transparency-conscious patrons, the sample is unrepresentative of the general public — directly undermining the generalization.
explanations.A: Correct. Attacks the representativeness of the sample, revealing selection bias that invalidates the inference from survey results to broad public support.
explanations.B: Out-of-scope. The effectiveness of the ordinance in other cities is irrelevant to whether this city's public broadly supports the proposed ordinance.
explanations.C: Shift in subject. Restaurant owners' opposition is a different constituency from the general public; the argument is about public (resident) support, not business-owner support.
explanations.D: Strengthens. Suggests the survey methodology was careful and results are not an artifact of question framing.
explanations.E: Strengthens. Suggests the measured support exceeds the practical threshold for council action, bolstering the case for enactment.

lr.difficultyReason: Causal argument in linguistics concluding that bilingual education causes improved cognitive outcomes. The weakener introduces a selection-effect confound. One distractor attacks a different link in the chain; one strengthens.
lr.stimulus: A school district compared standardized cognitive-flexibility test scores for students enrolled in its bilingual immersion program with scores for students in its standard monolingual curriculum. The bilingual students scored, on average, 18 percent higher on the cognitive-flexibility measures. District administrators concluded that participation in the bilingual program is responsible for the students' superior cognitive-flexibility scores.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the administrators' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enrollment in the bilingual program requires a written application, and admitted students are disproportionately drawn from households where parents have higher levels of education and place a strong emphasis on academic achievement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cognitive-flexibility tests used by the district have been validated in multiple peer-reviewed studies as reliable measures of executive function in school-age children.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students in the bilingual program spend more hours per week on structured classroom tasks than students in the standard curriculum.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cognitive-flexibility scores tend to improve naturally as children age, regardless of the curriculum they follow.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several peer-reviewed studies conducted in other countries have found a positive association between bilingualism and cognitive-flexibility measures.

explanations.correct: The conclusion attributes the score difference to the bilingual program. If enrollment is selective in a way that admits students from academically oriented households, those students may have higher cognitive-flexibility scores due to home environment rather than the program — a classic selection-effect confound that undermines the causal inference.
explanations.A: Correct. Reveals a selection bias: the bilingual group may be cognitively advantaged before the program begins due to socioeconomic and parental factors, not because of the program itself.
explanations.B: Strengthens. Validates the measurement instrument, bolstering confidence in the score difference as a real effect.
explanations.C: This is a 'too narrow' trap — it introduces an alternative explanation (instructional time) but leaves open whether that instructional time is part of what 'bilingual program participation' means. It weakens marginally but less decisively than A.
explanations.D: Irrelevant — if both groups aged equally over the study period, natural developmental improvement would not explain the difference between groups.
explanations.E: Strengthens. External evidence supports the causal claim that bilingualism improves cognitive flexibility.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive argument in technology policy where the conclusion forecasts reduced energy consumption from a software update. The weakener attacks the move from lab-measured efficiency gains to real-world consumption outcomes (rebound effect). Distractors include one out-of-scope and one strengthener.
lr.stimulus: An electronics manufacturer announced that a firmware update for its line of smart televisions reduces the power draw of each unit by 22 percent during active use. The manufacturer concluded that when owners install the update, total electricity consumption attributable to the company's televisions will decrease substantially.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the manufacturer's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The firmware update also improves picture quality, which many users have cited as a reason to increase the number of hours per day they use their televisions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The 22 percent reduction in power draw was measured in laboratory conditions that closely replicate average household viewing environments.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Smart televisions account for a growing share of residential electricity consumption relative to other consumer electronics.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The manufacturer's televisions are sold in over forty countries, each with different residential electricity pricing structures.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Other electronics manufacturers have released similar energy-efficiency updates for their smart televisions in the same period.

explanations.correct: Even if each unit draws 22 percent less power per hour, total consumption depends on total hours used. If improved picture quality causes users to watch significantly more hours, overall electricity consumption may not decrease — this is a rebound-effect weakener that attacks the inference from per-unit efficiency to aggregate consumption.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces the rebound effect: the efficiency gain per hour of use may be offset by increased usage hours, undermining the conclusion that total consumption will decrease substantially.
explanations.B: Strengthens. Validates the per-unit efficiency figure by confirming lab conditions were realistic, supporting the premise from which the conclusion is drawn.
explanations.C: Irrelevant to whether the firmware update causes a decrease; this describes a trend independent of the update's effect.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope. Pricing structures affect consumer behavior but are too remote from the causal chain to undermine the conclusion as directly as A.
explanations.E: Shift in subject — other manufacturers' updates don't bear on whether this manufacturer's update will reduce consumption of this company's televisions.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal reasoning argument where an attorney concludes a contract clause is enforceable by analogy to a precedent case. The weakener identifies a key disanalogy. One distractor strengthens the analogy; one is irrelevant.
lr.stimulus: An attorney argues that a non-compete clause in an employment contract is legally enforceable, citing a circuit court ruling that upheld an identical clause in a contract between a financial services firm and a senior analyst. Because the clause in question is worded identically and appears in a contract between a financial services firm and a senior analyst, the attorney concludes it will be upheld by the same court.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the attorney's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Since the earlier ruling, the circuit court has issued two opinions narrowing the enforceability of non-compete clauses to situations in which the employer can demonstrate that the employee had access to genuinely proprietary trade secrets.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Non-compete clauses with identical wording have been upheld in the majority of circuit courts across the country.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The employee subject to the current clause has already accepted a position with a competing firm, making the dispute more urgent than the earlier case.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The earlier ruling was issued by a three-judge panel, which is the standard composition for circuit court decisions of that type.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The financial services industry is subject to more extensive regulatory oversight than most other sectors of the economy.

explanations.correct: The attorney's conclusion rests on the precedent from the earlier ruling. If the court has since narrowed that precedent by requiring proof of access to genuine trade secrets — a condition not established in the current case — the earlier ruling no longer straightforwardly supports enforceability, directly undermining the analogical argument.
explanations.A: Correct. Identifies a legal development that changes the controlling standard since the precedent was set, breaking the analogy between the earlier ruling and the current case.
explanations.B: Strengthens. Broader appellate support for the clause reinforces the attorney's conclusion.
explanations.C: Irrelevant. The urgency of the dispute does not affect the legal enforceability of the clause.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope. The composition of the panel is procedurally standard and irrelevant to the enforceability question.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. Industry regulatory oversight is irrelevant to the enforceability of a non-compete clause unless a connection is established — none is given here.

lr.difficultyReason: Causal argument in arts policy concluding that public arts funding caused measurable economic benefits. The weakener attacks the direction of causation. Distractors include one strengthener and one that is irrelevant.
lr.stimulus: A city arts commission released a report noting that neighborhoods in which municipal arts grants were concentrated over a five-year period showed, on average, a 30 percent increase in retail foot traffic and a significant rise in new business licenses compared to other neighborhoods. The commission concluded that targeted arts funding caused the economic revitalization observed in those neighborhoods.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the commission's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The city council awarded arts grants preferentially to neighborhoods that had already been identified as emerging economic hubs by a separate urban planning initiative, which itself channeled infrastructure investment into those areas.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neighborhoods that received arts grants also experienced an influx of younger residents during the same five-year period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several of the businesses that opened in the grant-concentrated neighborhoods were arts-related, such as galleries and performance venues.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The arts commission's grant selection process was reviewed and approved by an independent auditing body.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Comparable increases in retail foot traffic were observed in similar neighborhoods in a neighboring city that implemented an identical arts-grant program over the same period.

explanations.correct: The commission concludes arts funding caused economic revitalization. If grants were directed to neighborhoods already targeted by an infrastructure investment initiative — meaning those neighborhoods were poised for economic growth regardless — the observed revitalization may be attributable to the infrastructure investment rather than the arts grants, reversing or replacing the causal direction.
explanations.A: Correct. Reveals that the grant-receiving neighborhoods were pre-selected for economic promise and received simultaneous infrastructure investment, providing an alternative (and plausibly more powerful) causal explanation for the observed economic improvements.
explanations.B: This is the 'too narrow' trap — demographic influx could be an intermediate cause or a confound, but it does not as decisively sever the causal link as A, which identifies a prior systematic selection effect.
explanations.C: Strengthens, or at minimum is consistent with the causal claim — arts-related businesses opening in arts-grant neighborhoods supports the conclusion that arts funding drove economic activity.
explanations.D: Irrelevant. The auditing of the grant process does not bear on whether the grants caused economic revitalization.
explanations.E: Strengthens. Replication of the result in a comparable city under identical conditions supports the causal inference.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (policy → reduced emissions → improved air quality outcome). The weakener attacks the move from evidence to conclusion by introducing an alternative causal factor driving the observed outcome. Distractors include one strengthener, one out-of-scope environmental fact, and one choice that attacks a peripheral premise without touching the conclusion.
lr.stimulus: A regional environmental authority enacted strict vehicle-emission standards four years ago. Since then, the average concentration of ground-level ozone in the region has declined by 22 percent. The authority's director concluded that the emission standards were responsible for the improvement in air quality.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During the same four-year period, a major industrial plant in the region—responsible for a substantial portion of local ozone precursor emissions—permanently shut down its operations one year before the emission standards took effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neighboring regions that did not adopt similar emission standards experienced no significant change in ground-level ozone concentrations over the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ground-level ozone is known to cause respiratory problems in people with pre-existing lung conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The vehicle-emission standards were more stringent than those required by national environmental law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some vehicle owners in the region delayed compliance with the new emission standards by obtaining temporary exemptions.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that the emission standards caused the 22% decline in ozone. Choice A introduces an alternative cause—the shutdown of a major industrial polluter—that preceded the standards' implementation and could independently explain the ozone reduction, thereby undermining the director's causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces a competing cause (industrial plant closure) that predates and could fully account for the observed improvement, severing the claimed link between the emission standards and the air-quality outcome.
explanations.B: This is a strengthener, not a weakener. The absence of improvement in regions without the standards supports the conclusion that the standards drove the change; it is the opposite-answer trap.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope. The health effects of ground-level ozone are irrelevant to whether the emission standards caused its decline.
explanations.D: Strengthener or irrelevant. The stringency of the standards, if anything, bolsters the claim they were effective; it does not weaken the causal conclusion.
explanations.E: Too narrow. Some delayed compliance weakens implementation fidelity only marginally and doesn't undermine the overall causal conclusion—it leaves open that sufficient compliance still drove the decline.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive argument with a two-step inferential move: historical success of a technology → adoption of that technology in a new context → predicted economic benefit. The correct weakener attacks the move from evidence to conclusion by exposing a disanalogy between the historical case and the new context. Distractors include a strengthener and an accurate-but-irrelevant economic fact.
lr.stimulus: A technology consulting firm recently advised a mid-sized retail bank to adopt an AI-driven loan-underwriting system. The firm pointed to the fact that three large investment banks that implemented the same system last year reported a 30 percent reduction in loan-default rates. The consulting firm concluded that the retail bank would also experience a significant reduction in loan defaults if it adopted the system.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the consulting firm's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The AI-driven underwriting system was originally designed to evaluate the creditworthiness of large corporate borrowers, and its predictive models have not been validated for the consumer and small-business lending that constitutes the retail bank's entire portfolio.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The three investment banks that adopted the system are headquartered in the same financial district and share several major institutional clients.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loan-default rates at large investment banks tend to fluctuate more sharply than those at retail banks because of differences in loan size and duration.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The retail bank's current loan-underwriting process relies on a combination of human judgment and rule-based software that was last updated five years ago.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several other AI-driven financial software products have successfully reduced administrative costs for retail banks in markets similar to this one.

explanations.correct: The firm's conclusion rests on an analogy: because the system worked for large investment banks, it will work for the retail bank. Choice A exposes a critical disanalogy—the system was built and validated only for large corporate borrowers, not for the consumer and small-business lending that the retail bank actually does. This directly undercuts the analogical inference.
explanations.A: Correct. Identifies a fundamental disanalogy between the cases on which the prediction is based and the target case, severing the analogical bridge the consulting firm's argument requires.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant. The shared clients and location of the investment banks don't bear on whether the system will transfer effectively to a retail-lending context; this is a shift-in-subject trap.
explanations.C: Too narrow / inaccurate target. This describes a general difference in volatility between the two types of banks but doesn't explain why the system itself would fail in the retail context; it could even be read as supporting the conclusion (retail defaults are more predictable).
explanations.D: Strengthener or irrelevant. The outdated state of the retail bank's current system might actually support the consulting firm's recommendation; it doesn't weaken the prediction.
explanations.E: Strengthener. Evidence that AI-driven systems benefit retail banks supports, rather than undermines, the consulting firm's conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Causal argument in a medical/policy context where the conclusion generalizes from a study's correlation to a population-level recommendation. The correct weakener introduces a confounding variable that explains the correlation without supporting the causal claim. One distractor strengthens by ruling out a rival explanation; another is out-of-scope.
lr.stimulus: Researchers studying a large urban hospital found that patients who were visited by a hospital social worker within 24 hours of admission had significantly shorter average hospital stays than patients who were not visited. The researchers concluded that early social-worker visits reduce the length of hospital stays and recommended that all hospitals implement mandatory early social-worker rounds.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the researchers' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Social workers at the hospital were assigned to visit patients whose medical charts indicated a straightforward, uncomplicated recovery prognosis, while patients with more complex conditions were referred to specialist case managers instead.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hospitals that have implemented mandatory social-worker rounds have reported improvements in patient satisfaction scores independent of changes in length of stay.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The hospital in the study had a higher ratio of social workers to patients than most other urban hospitals in the country.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several studies conducted at rural hospitals have found no statistically significant relationship between social-worker visits and length of stay.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Early social-worker visits help patients arrange post-discharge care, which is one mechanism by which hospital stays could plausibly be shortened.

explanations.correct: The researchers infer that early social-worker visits cause shorter stays. Choice A reveals that social workers were selectively assigned to patients already expected to recover quickly. This means the correlation could reflect patient-complexity selection bias rather than any causal effect of the visits—patients with shorter stays were predisposed to shorter stays regardless of the visits.
explanations.A: Correct. Identifies a confounding variable (case complexity / recovery prognosis) that accounts for the correlation between early social-worker visits and shorter stays without requiring any causal role for the visits, directly undermining the causal conclusion.
explanations.B: Out-of-scope. Patient satisfaction is a separate outcome; this choice neither supports nor undermines the claim that visits reduce length of stay, making it an accurate-but-irrelevant trap.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. The staff ratio might explain why the hospital could conduct early visits but says nothing about whether those visits actually caused shorter stays; this is a shift-in-subject trap.
explanations.D: Too narrow / potential strengthener of doubt, but misapplied. The absence of an effect at rural hospitals introduces a different population; it doesn't explain away the urban hospital's correlation and leaves the researchers' finding unexplained. A careful reader may think this weakens, but it doesn't attack the causal inference from the study's own data.
explanations.E: Strengthener. Providing a plausible causal mechanism by which visits could shorten stays bolsters the researchers' causal conclusion rather than weakening it; this is the opposite-answer trap.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (reduced pollutant emissions → improved river health → policy success). Correct weakener attacks the move from cleaner water to policy credit by introducing an alternative cause. Distractors include a strengthener, an out-of-scope fact about a different waterway, and an answer that attacks a premise without undermining the conclusion.
lr.stimulus: A regional environmental agency introduced strict regulations on industrial discharge into the Maren River in 2018. By 2022, measured levels of phosphorus and nitrogen in the river had dropped by nearly 40 percent, and populations of native fish species had rebounded significantly. The agency concluded that its discharge regulations were responsible for the river's ecological recovery.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several factories operating along the Maren River voluntarily reduced their discharge levels even before the 2018 regulations took effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A prolonged drought that began in 2019 reduced agricultural runoff into the Maren River by nearly 45 percent, a well-documented source of phosphorus and nitrogen.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fish populations in rivers that did not receive similar regulatory protections have continued to decline over the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The agency's inspectors documented dozens of violations of the discharge regulations between 2018 and 2022.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Environmental scientists consider a 40 percent reduction in phosphorus and nitrogen levels to be sufficient to support native fish species recovery.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that the discharge regulations caused the river's recovery. Choice B introduces a compelling alternative cause — drought-reduced agricultural runoff — that independently explains the drop in pollutant levels and the fish rebound. If the drought was the primary driver, the regulations may deserve little credit, which directly undermines the agency's conclusion.
explanations.A: This is a 'too narrow / too early' trap. Voluntary pre-2018 reductions might partially complicate attribution, but they don't introduce a competing explanation for the post-2018 improvement; they may even be part of the regulatory era's overall effect. B provides a stronger, fully independent alternative cause.
explanations.B: Correct. Introduces an alternative explanation (agricultural runoff reduction from drought) that could fully account for both the pollutant decline and the ecological recovery, severing the link between the regulations and the observed improvement.
explanations.C: Opposite-answer trap. Showing that unprotected rivers continued to decline actually strengthens the agency's conclusion by providing a comparison group that suggests the regulations made a difference.
explanations.D: Attacks a premise (regulatory compliance) but does not eliminate the conclusion. Even with violations, partial compliance could still have driven significant improvement; this choice weakens the premise without decisively undermining the conclusion the way B does.
explanations.E: Out-of-scope / irrelevant. This confirms that the magnitude of pollutant reduction is ecologically meaningful, which if anything supports the argument. It does not challenge whether the regulations caused that reduction.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive argument based on an economic analogy. The weakener attacks the analogy by exposing a relevant disanalogy. Distractors include a strengthener, a narrowly scoped fact that doesn't touch the prediction, and an out-of-scope comparison.
lr.stimulus: A financial analyst argues that the city of Daltham should expect a significant rise in property values over the next decade. The analyst points to the case of Riverford, a comparable mid-sized city that invested heavily in public transit infrastructure in the 2000s and saw property values increase by 35 percent within ten years. Daltham has recently approved a similarly scaled public transit expansion, and the analyst predicts an equivalent appreciation in Daltham's real estate market.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the analyst's prediction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Riverford's property value increase was concentrated almost entirely in neighborhoods within walking distance of the new transit lines, while Daltham's transit expansion will run exclusively through its already densely developed commercial core, where residential properties are scarce.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several other mid-sized cities that invested in public transit during the same period as Riverford also experienced significant increases in property values.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Daltham's city council debated the transit expansion for three years before approving the final plan.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Property values in Daltham have remained stable for the past five years, suggesting a resilient local real estate market.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Public transit expansions in large metropolitan areas tend to produce greater property value increases than those in mid-sized cities.

explanations.correct: The analyst's prediction rests on an analogy to Riverford: similar transit investment produced a 35% property value increase there, so Daltham should see the same. Choice A attacks the analogy by revealing a critical disanalogy — in Riverford, transit lines ran through areas with abundant residential properties (enabling value appreciation), whereas Daltham's lines will run through a dense commercial core with few residential properties. This structural difference explains why Riverford's outcome may not transfer to Daltham, directly undermining the prediction.
explanations.A: Correct. Exposes a disanalogy that severs the basis for the analogical prediction: the mechanism by which transit drives residential property appreciation cannot operate the same way in Daltham.
explanations.B: Opposite-answer trap. Showing that other cities also benefited from transit investment corroborates the pattern the analyst relies on, thereby strengthening rather than weakening the prediction.
explanations.C: Irrelevant / out-of-scope. The length of the council debate has no bearing on whether the completed transit expansion will cause property values to rise.
explanations.D: Attacking a neighboring claim trap. A stable market might suggest resilience, but it does not undermine the prediction of future appreciation from a new cause (transit investment). If anything, stability could mean there is room for growth.
explanations.E: Shift-in-subject trap. This compares large metros to mid-sized cities but doesn't address whether Daltham specifically will or won't see appreciation. The analyst's claim is about Daltham, not about a general metro-size comparison.

lr.difficultyReason: Causal argument based on a historical correlation, with a two-step inference: bilingual education → improved cognitive flexibility → better academic outcomes. The correct weakener introduces a confounding variable that undermines the move from correlation to causal credit. Distractors include a strengthener and a too-narrow answer that only partially disrupts the argument.
lr.stimulus: A school district administrator reviewed academic records and found that students who had been enrolled in the district's bilingual education program for at least three years scored, on average, 12 percentile points higher on standardized reasoning tests than students who had received only monolingual instruction. The administrator concluded that participation in the bilingual program enhanced the students' cognitive flexibility, which in turn produced the observed gains in reasoning scores.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enrollment in the bilingual program requires a parental application and is preferentially granted to students who demonstrated above-average academic aptitude in their early assessments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cognitive flexibility, as measured by standard psychological instruments, is strongly correlated with performance on standardized reasoning tests.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The bilingual program has been in operation for only six years, making long-term conclusions about its efficacy difficult to establish with certainty.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some students who scored highest on the reasoning tests had been enrolled in the bilingual program for fewer than three years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Students in the monolingual program received, on average, the same number of instructional hours per week as students in the bilingual program.

explanations.correct: The administrator concludes that the bilingual program caused the higher scores by boosting cognitive flexibility. But if enrollment is restricted to students who already showed above-average academic aptitude, then the higher scores may simply reflect the pre-existing abilities of the students selected — not any effect of the program itself. This is a classic confounding-variable / selection-bias weakener: the correlation between bilingual enrollment and higher scores is explained by prior aptitude rather than by the program's causal impact.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces selection bias as an alternative explanation: students in the bilingual program were already higher-aptitude, so the gap in reasoning scores reflects selection, not the program's effect on cognitive flexibility.
explanations.B: Opposite-answer trap. Confirming that cognitive flexibility correlates with reasoning test scores actually supports one of the links in the administrator's causal chain (flexibility → better scores), thereby strengthening the argument.
explanations.C: Too narrow / scope limitation trap. Noting the program's short history raises a mild epistemic caution but does not provide an alternative explanation for the observed 12-percentile-point gap or undermine the causal mechanism. It leaves the administrator's inference largely intact.
explanations.D: Too narrow / counterexample trap. A few high-scorers with under three years of enrollment are outliers that don't address the average gap or the causal claim. The argument is about the group-level average, so individual exceptions don't substantially weaken it.
explanations.E: Irrelevant / rules out a distractor. Equalizing instructional hours actually eliminates one possible confound (more seat time → better scores), which if anything slightly strengthens the administrator's case that the bilingual content itself, rather than mere instruction quantity, accounts for the difference.

lr.difficultyReason: Controlled-study stimulus whose conclusion rides on an unstated methodological assumption: that the enrollment criterion did not preselect for spontaneous recovery.
