Correct answer reveals hidden confounding in the sample. Trap (C) strengthens by ruling out an unrelated confound; trap (D) attacks the magnitude of the result without touching causation; trap (E) is out-of-scope comparative.
lr.stimulus: Researcher: In a 12-month trial, patients with chronic lower-back pain who received biweekly acupuncture reported an average 42 percent reduction in pain, whereas a control group receiving sham needling reported only a 19 percent reduction. Because the two groups were otherwise similar in age, baseline pain, and prior treatment history, the results show that the therapeutic insertion of acupuncture needles is itself producing the additional pain reduction.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the researcher's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enrollment in the trial was restricted to patients whose pain had persisted for at least six months and had recently intensified — a pattern statistically associated with imminent natural remission independent of any treatment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The acupuncturists who administered the therapeutic needling had, on average, several more years of clinical experience than the practitioners who administered the sham procedure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither the patients nor the outcome assessors were informed of which group any given patient had been assigned to.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A 42 percent reduction in self-reported pain is smaller than the reductions reported in trials of several newer pharmacological therapies for chronic lower-back pain.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sham needling has itself been shown in earlier studies to produce modest reductions in pain relative to no treatment at all.

explanations.correct: The researcher concludes that therapeutic needling itself is doing the extra work. (A) reveals a hidden selection effect: enrollment was keyed to patients poised for natural remission. If both arms improved from that baseline, the differential between arms still needs explaining — but (A) also implies that patients most prone to spontaneous improvement were precisely the kind the trial attracted, and any systematic imbalance in how fully that regression plays out across arms now confounds the comparison. More importantly, the conclusion requires that the 23-point gap reflect something therapeutic needles do; (A) undermines the assumption that the arms were comparably positioned with respect to natural recovery trajectories.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: This is a live weakener candidate — experience gap is a real confound — but it is weaker than (A) because the conclusion is about whether the needles themselves did the work, and skilled handling of needles is still therapeutic needling. Reconsider against (A), which undermines the more basic assumption that the differential is not an artifact of the enrollment pool.
explanations.C: Strengthens — double-blinding protects against expectation effects.
explanations.D: Comparative magnitude vs. other treatments is out of scope; the argument is about whether needling caused the observed reduction, not whether it is the best therapy available.
explanations.E: If anything, this strengthens the study's design rationale (sham produced a real 19 percent reduction), and it does not undercut the inference that the additional reduction came from therapeutic needling.

lr.difficultyReason: Multi-step causal chain in medicine: gut-bacteria composition → inflammatory markers → depressive symptoms. Correct answer exposes a mechanism operating in the opposite direction on the first link. Trap (B) strengthens by replicating; trap (D) is a subsidiary-point attack.
lr.stimulus: Clinical researcher: Patients suffering major depressive disorder show, on average, markedly lower diversity of gut bacteria than matched healthy controls, and they also show elevated levels of circulating inflammatory cytokines. Since bacterial diversity is known to modulate cytokine production, and inflammation is increasingly implicated in depression, we conclude that the impoverished gut flora of depressed patients is a contributing cause of their depressive symptoms.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the researcher's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytokine levels in depressed patients vary substantially from week to week, depending on diet and sleep.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A separate study replicated the finding that bacterial diversity in depressed patients is lower than in matched controls.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The loss of appetite and disturbed eating patterns that characterize major depressive disorder have been shown, in animal models, to reliably produce substantial reductions in gut bacterial diversity within weeks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cytokine levels in some patients with major depressive disorder fall within the normal range.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Certain antidepressant medications have been observed to modestly increase gut bacterial diversity over the course of treatment.

explanations.correct: The researcher infers that poor gut flora helps cause depression. (C) reveals a mechanism running the opposite direction on the first link: depression itself, via its effect on eating, reliably degrades gut diversity. The observed correlation would then be an effect of depression rather than a cause of it, undermining the causal claim.
explanations.A: Week-to-week variability doesn't touch the averaged group comparison the argument relies on.
explanations.B: Strengthens — a replicated correlation supports the premise, not the conclusion's causal direction.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Attacks a subsidiary descriptive claim (that cytokines are elevated) without challenging the core causal inference; the average can still be elevated even if some individuals are normal.
explanations.E: Consistent with either causal direction. If antidepressants work and happen to raise diversity, this says nothing about whether diversity is upstream of depression.

lr.difficultyReason: Comparative economic argument that treats two minimum-wage jurisdictions as matched. Correct answer reveals hidden confounding in the comparison baseline. Trap (A) is an opposite-answer strengthener; trap (D) is out-of-scope.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Cities that raised their minimum wage above the state floor between 2018 and 2022 saw, on average, no larger increase in restaurant prices than demographically similar cities whose minimum wage remained at the state floor. Since restaurant pricing is especially sensitive to labor costs, this pattern shows that recent minimum-wage increases did not, on net, push consumer prices upward in the cities that adopted them.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Restaurants in the cities that raised their minimum wage reported, on average, the same profit margins in 2022 as they had reported in 2018.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Restaurants in many of the cities that retained the state floor operated under long-standing collective-bargaining agreements that committed them to wage increases matching or exceeding those mandated in the neighboring cities that raised their minimum wage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cities that adopted minimum-wage increases were slightly more populous, on average, than the comparison cities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nationally, restaurant prices rose more slowly between 2018 and 2022 than prices for grocery staples.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several of the cities that raised their minimum wage also simplified their restaurant licensing procedures during the same period.

explanations.correct: The argument's comparison assumes the control cities had meaningfully lower labor-cost pressure. (B) dissolves that assumption: the 'no-increase' cities were already absorbing comparable wage increases through collective bargaining. With both groups facing similar labor-cost pressure, the absence of a price differential is uninformative about what minimum-wage policy itself would do.
explanations.A: Strengthens, if anything — stable margins alongside stable prices suggest the labor cost did not force a price increase, consistent with the economist's conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Population difference is described as slight and is not shown to bear on pricing dynamics.
explanations.D: National restaurant-versus-grocery comparisons don't speak to whether minimum-wage increases pushed restaurant prices up within the studied cities.
explanations.E: Licensing simplification, if anything, might lower costs and thereby reinforce the observed pattern — but it does not undermine the causal inference about minimum-wage policy; it introduces another downward pressure without isolating the wage effect.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental-science argument whose conclusion rests on an unstated methodological premise about sampling timing. Correct answer attacks a measurement assumption without denying any stated fact. Trap (C) attacks a premise without touching the conclusion; trap (E) is out-of-scope.
lr.stimulus: Conservation scientist: Surveys conducted over the past decade in the three largest salt marshes along the Cape Alaine coast have recorded populations of the saltmarsh sparrow that are, on average, 28 percent smaller than populations recorded a decade earlier in the same marshes. Since the marshes are otherwise undisturbed and no new predators have been documented, the sparrow's decline must be due to rising sea levels, which shorten the dry window during which the sparrows can fledge their nests.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the scientist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Historically, saltmarsh sparrow populations have fluctuated more dramatically from year to year than the populations of most other marsh-nesting birds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The marshes in question were never protected as sparrow reserves, and casual recreational traffic has increased modestly over the past decade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A recent study estimates that fledging success in coastal salt marshes has declined in step with the lengthening of high-tide periods along the eastern seaboard generally.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The decade-earlier surveys were performed during the saltmarsh sparrow's peak breeding season, whereas the recent surveys were performed several weeks later, after most of the year's fledglings had dispersed to adjacent upland scrub.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conservation efforts in marshes farther south have, in some cases, stabilized local saltmarsh sparrow populations through active nest-site management.

explanations.correct: The conclusion treats the 28 percent gap as a real population decline and attributes it to sea-level rise. (D) exposes a methodological flaw: the later surveys missed dispersed fledglings that the earlier surveys would have counted, so the apparent decline may be partly or wholly an artifact of when the birds were counted. The causal claim is stranded until that confound is resolved.
explanations.A: Year-to-year fluctuation doesn't explain a sustained ten-year drop across three marshes.
explanations.B: Introduces a minor alternative cause, but the traffic is described as a modest increase — a plausible but weaker weakener than (D), which undercuts the very existence of the decline.
explanations.C: Strengthens, if anything — it supports the sea-level-rise mechanism the scientist proposes.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the argument concerns three Cape Alaine marshes, not remote management efforts.

lr.difficultyReason: Controlled-study argument about a technology intervention whose conclusion depends on the outcome metric capturing what it purports to capture. Correct answer reveals the metric is gameable in a way that breaks the inference. Trap (A) strengthens; trap (B) is an unwarranted comparison.
lr.stimulus: Technology columnist: In a controlled experiment, one group of programmers was provided with an AI coding assistant and a second, matched group was not. Over four weeks, developers using the assistant closed 35 percent more tickets from their team's issue tracker than developers in the control group. Since issue-tracker tickets are the standard unit of programmer output at this company, the experiment shows that the AI assistant makes programmers meaningfully more productive.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the columnist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Programmers in both groups reported similar levels of job satisfaction at the end of the experiment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The AI assistant was developed by a company that sells programming tools to large software firms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A substantial portion of the additional tickets closed by the AI-assisted group were later reopened by quality-assurance reviewers, who identified regressions and incomplete fixes that the control group's tickets did not exhibit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Programmers in the AI-assisted group spent roughly the same number of hours at their workstations as programmers in the control group.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Before the experiment began, both groups had been closing tickets at statistically indistinguishable rates.

explanations.correct: The conclusion depends on tickets-closed being a faithful measure of productive output. (C) shows it is not: a substantial share of the extra tickets contained regressions that had to be redone, so the raw count overstates real productivity gains. The metric the argument rests on is contaminated by work the AI group is effectively offloading onto later reviewers.
explanations.A: Irrelevant — the conclusion is about productivity, not satisfaction.
explanations.B: Attacks the source rather than the evidence; the experiment's results do not become less informative because the tool has a commercial origin.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Strengthens, if anything — equal hours with higher ticket counts sharpens the apparent productivity gain.
explanations.E: Strengthens — a matched baseline makes the post-experiment differential easier to attribute to the intervention.

lr.difficultyReason: Multi-step causal chain in linguistics: bilingual childhood → denser neural pathways → resistance to age-related cognitive decline. Correct answer attacks the unstated assumption linking the observed endpoint to the proposed mechanism, not to an unrelated factor. Trap (B) is too narrow; trap (E) strengthens.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Adults who were raised bilingually from infancy consistently perform better on tests of executive function in late middle age than adults who were raised monolingually. Early bilingual experience is known to produce denser neural connections in brain regions responsible for switching between cognitive tasks. Since those same regions underlie executive function, we may conclude that the executive-function advantage observed in later life is itself produced by the dense neural architecture laid down during bilingual childhood.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the linguist's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Longitudinal neuroimaging shows that the denser neural architecture associated with early bilingualism has, in most individuals, fully atrophied to monolingual baselines by a person's mid-thirties, whereas the adults studied were in their late fifties.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The bilingual adults in the studies were, on average, no more likely than the monolingual adults to have pursued advanced degrees.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some adults who acquired a second language only in adulthood also show elevated scores on tests of executive function in late middle age.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Executive function encompasses several distinct abilities, and bilingual adults outperform monolingual adults on some of these abilities more clearly than on others.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The density of neural connections in task-switching regions correlates, in brain-imaging studies, with stronger scores on executive-function tests at every age examined.

explanations.correct: The argument attributes a late-life advantage specifically to the dense architecture laid down in childhood. (A) severs that link: by the time the advantage is measured, the architecture in question has atrophied. Whatever explains the late-life difference, it cannot be the surviving presence of childhood-built density. The proposed mechanism collapses.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Rules out one alternative explanation (education), which if anything mildly strengthens the argument.
explanations.C: Too narrow — at most this suggests there is more than one route to the executive-function advantage, not that the childhood-bilingualism route is wrong.
explanations.D: Attacks the uniformity of the advantage across subskills without touching the causal mechanism; the conclusion survives so long as the pattern holds on average.
explanations.E: Strengthens — it reinforces the density-to-executive-function link the argument relies on.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy argument from a quasi-comparison between pre- and post-intervention windows. Correct answer exposes hidden confounding from a concurrent change that the argument ignores. Trap (A) strengthens via regression-adjacent reasoning; trap (D) is an out-of-scope fact.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: After the city of Brenshaw adopted a mandatory counseling program for first-time nonviolent offenders four years ago, the three-year reoffense rate for participants fell from 34 percent, as measured in the four years preceding the program, to 22 percent in the years since. Opponents of the program point to various social changes over the same period, but none of those changes has been shown to affect reoffense rates in comparable cities. The drop therefore shows that the counseling program is reducing reoffense among its participants.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The three-year reoffense rate among first-time nonviolent offenders in cities that did not adopt mandatory counseling held roughly constant over the same period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Concurrent with the launch of the counseling program, Brenshaw's prosecutor's office adopted a policy of declining to charge a category of low-level offenses that had previously been prosecuted, so the post-program population of 'first-time nonviolent offenders' now excludes a group historically responsible for a disproportionate share of reoffenses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The counseling program is considerably more expensive per participant than most comparable rehabilitative interventions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In neighboring cities without mandatory counseling, reoffense rates for first-time nonviolent offenders are somewhat higher than the 22 percent now observed in Brenshaw.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A minority of offenders assigned to the program fail to complete its required sessions.

explanations.correct: The argument treats the two populations — pre- and post-program 'first-time nonviolent offenders' — as comparable, and attributes the drop in reoffense to the counseling. (B) dissolves that comparability: the post-program population has been quietly redefined to exclude a subgroup with especially high reoffense rates. The apparent drop could be entirely a composition effect. The counseling program's contribution is no longer supported.
explanations.A: Strengthens — comparison cities' flat trend makes the Brenshaw drop look intervention-specific.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Cost is irrelevant to whether the program works.
explanations.D: Strengthens — Brenshaw's rate is lower than neighboring rates, consistent with the program helping.
explanations.E: Non-completion doesn't undermine the claim about participants; the analyst's conclusion concerns those who participate.

lr.difficultyReason: Historiographic argument drawing a causal inference from archival evidence. Correct answer reveals a sampling bias in the surviving record that undercuts the inference. Trap (A) is out-of-scope; trap (D) strengthens a subsidiary detail.
lr.stimulus: Historian: In the merchant archives of the Hanseatic port of Vissen, letters written in the decade after the city's adoption of double-entry bookkeeping in 1472 show merchants referring to profit margins with far greater numerical specificity than letters written in the decade preceding that adoption. Since specificity about margins was a prerequisite for the kind of strategic pricing that enriched late-medieval merchants, the spread of double-entry bookkeeping in Vissen itself enabled the commercial sophistication observed after 1472.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Double-entry bookkeeping had been in use in several Italian mercantile cities for nearly two centuries before Vissen adopted it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Vissen archives preserve the correspondence of roughly the same number of merchants from the decade before 1472 as from the decade after.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A fire in 1515 destroyed the bulk of Vissen's pre-1472 merchant correspondence, and the surviving pre-1472 letters were preserved by a single guild whose members were among the city's least numerate merchants and whose letters chiefly concerned personal matters.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several of the most numerically specific post-1472 letters are from merchants whose families had long been prominent in Vissen's commercial life.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Double-entry bookkeeping, as practiced in Vissen, required a formal apprenticeship of at least three years.

explanations.correct: The argument infers from a contrast in the surviving archival record that Vissen's merchants became more numerically sophisticated after 1472, and attributes that shift to the new bookkeeping. (C) exposes a crippling sampling bias: the pre-1472 record is a narrow, unrepresentative residue dominated by the city's least numerate merchants. The 'before' sample cannot be compared to the 'after' sample, so the observed contrast does not establish any change in Vissen's commercial practice.
explanations.A: Out of scope — Italian precedent does not affect what Vissen's own merchants did or why.
explanations.B: Strengthens, if anything — comparable merchant counts in the two decades would support the comparison.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Tangential; family prominence says nothing about whether numeric specificity in the record reflects a real change.
explanations.E: Provides background on how the practice spread but does not undermine the inference from the letters.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal-reform argument with a two-step predictive chain: proposed rule will change judicial behavior, which in turn will reduce appellate reversals. Correct answer attacks the hidden assumption linking the rule to judicial behavior. Trap (B) attacks a premise without touching the conclusion; trap (D) strengthens.
lr.stimulus: Legal scholar: A proposed rule of appellate procedure would require trial judges to file, along with every contested ruling, a brief written statement summarizing the legal authorities on which the ruling rests. Judges who know that their reasoning will be laid out for inspection will take more care in forming that reasoning, and better-reasoned rulings are less likely to be overturned on appeal. If the proposed rule is adopted, therefore, the rate at which trial-court rulings are reversed on appeal will fall.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the legal scholar's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The appellate court that would review these cases already reverses trial-court rulings at a historically low rate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some of the legal authorities trial judges would cite in their written statements are difficult to locate and annotate in the course of a working day.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The written statements would be made available to appellate courts, which would use them to identify, with a precision not currently available, errors of legal reasoning in rulings whose written record is today too sparse for such errors to be confidently detected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Trial judges who currently take especially detailed notes on their own reasoning are reversed on appeal at lower rates than judges who do not.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The proposed rule would apply only to contested rulings in civil cases, which make up the majority of the appellate court's docket.

explanations.correct: The conclusion predicts fewer reversals. The argument's two steps — better reasoning follows, reversals then fall — assume the appellate court's ability to detect reversible error remains constant. (C) undermines that hidden assumption: the same written statements that are supposed to improve reasoning also enable appellate courts to catch errors they would previously have missed. Reversals could therefore rise or remain flat even if the reasoning improves. The predictive chain is broken.
explanations.A: Irrelevant to whether the new rule will further reduce the rate; a low baseline can still fall.
explanations.B: Attacks the practicality of the rule, not the argument's conclusion about reversal rates.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Strengthens — it independently supports the link between detailed reasoning and fewer reversals.
explanations.E: Scope of application; does not undermine the mechanism.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts argument with a multi-step causal chain: funding shift → composition time → ambition of works. Correct answer attacks the crucial middle link — that the funding shift actually increased usable composition time. Trap (C) strengthens; trap (E) is an unwarranted comparison.
lr.stimulus: Music critic: When the Thaller Foundation restructured its grants to composers in 2015, it shifted from one-year fellowships to three-year fellowships of equivalent annual value. Longer fellowships insulate composers from commissioning pressures, and composers insulated from commissioning pressures produce more ambitious works. Indeed, works produced by Thaller fellows after 2015 have been reviewed as markedly more ambitious than works produced by Thaller fellows in the decade before. The restructuring, then, is what has enabled the ambition of the recent Thaller-funded output.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the critic's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reviewers who assess the ambition of new compositions sometimes disagree substantially about a given work.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Thaller fellows typically accept the commissions offered to them, and beginning in 2014 the Thaller Foundation required its fellows to sign exclusive commissioning agreements with the foundation's own concert series — agreements that specify deadlines stricter than the deadlines associated with most outside commissions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Since 2015, Thaller fellows have reported higher satisfaction with their working conditions than fellows reported before the restructuring.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A rival foundation, which did not restructure its grants, has over the same period also seen its fellows' work reviewed as more ambitious.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some of the most ambitious works produced by Thaller fellows before 2015 remain more widely performed today than most works produced by Thaller fellows after 2015.

explanations.correct: The argument's causal chain requires that the longer fellowships actually reduce commissioning pressure on composers. (B) negates exactly that middle link: in conjunction with the restructuring, the foundation bound fellows to commissioning agreements with stricter deadlines than the outside commissions they would otherwise have faced. The increase in nominal fellowship length did not translate into insulation from commissioning pressure. The proposed mechanism for the observed ambition is cut.
explanations.A: Minor reviewer disagreement is consistent with a real average shift; it does not disturb the conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Strengthens, if anything — better working conditions align with the argument's picture of relieved composers.
explanations.D: Weakens somewhat by suggesting a period-wide rise in ambition that has nothing to do with Thaller's restructuring, but it does not foreclose that Thaller's own policy contributed. (B) more directly severs the argument's internal mechanism and is the stronger answer.
explanations.E: Unwarranted comparison — the durability of older works doesn't speak to whether the restructuring boosted recent ambition.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument is a multi-step methodological causal chain in environmental science. The correct weakener attacks a hidden assumption bridging the observational premise to the causal conclusion — that the correlation between reduced canopy cover and stream temperature increase reflects a directional relationship that the intervention can reverse. Distractors include one that attacks a peripheral premise, one that sounds damning but actually concerns a different waterway type, one strengthener, and one irrelevant scope shift.
lr.stimulus: Researchers studying a network of mountain streams found that reaches with less than 30 percent riparian canopy cover had water temperatures averaging 4 degrees Celsius higher than reaches with more than 70 percent canopy cover. A regional conservation agency concluded from this finding that planting native trees along degraded stream banks would reduce summer water temperatures enough to restore suitable habitat for cold-water fish species that have declined in the region over the past two decades.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conservation agency's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cold-water fish species that have declined in the region are also sensitive to changes in stream pH, which riparian planting does not directly affect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The stream reaches with low canopy cover in the study had been deforested more than fifty years ago, and their elevated temperatures are primarily driven by altered groundwater discharge patterns that tree planting alone cannot reverse.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Native tree species used in riparian restoration projects typically require between eight and fifteen years to achieve a canopy density sufficient to shade a stream effectively.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reaches with high canopy cover in the study were located at higher elevations, where groundwater inputs independently keep temperatures lower regardless of shading.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several cold-water fish species have successfully recolonized streams in adjacent watersheds where riparian restoration was completed within the last decade.

explanations.correct: The agency assumes that canopy cover itself caused the temperature difference, so adding canopy will reverse it. Choice D reveals that the high-canopy reaches were also at higher elevations with cooler groundwater — a confounding variable that explains the temperature gap independently of shading. If elevation and groundwater drive the correlation, restoring canopy to low-elevation, degraded reaches may not produce the temperature reduction the agency predicts, directly undermining the causal premise of its conclusion.
explanations.A: Shift-in-subject trap. Sensitivity to stream pH is a separate stressor; the argument's conclusion concerns temperature restoration, not all habitat requirements. This choice narrows habitat suitability but does not challenge whether planting will reduce temperatures as predicted.
explanations.B: Too-narrow trap with a surface appeal. Altered groundwater discharge could seem like a strong alternative explanation, but this choice concerns why temperatures rose historically — it does not undermine the directional inference from the correlation study. The agency's conclusion rests on the study's cross-sectional comparison, not on the deforestation history of individual reaches.
explanations.C: Attacks one premise (timeliness of canopy effect) without touching the core causal claim. Even if true, it only delays, rather than defeats, the agency's conclusion that planting will ultimately reduce temperatures enough to restore habitat. A weakener that leaves the conclusion standing in the long run is insufficient at difficulty 3.
explanations.D: Correct. Introduces a confounding variable — elevation-driven groundwater — that explains the observed temperature difference without implicating canopy cover as the operative cause, thereby undercutting the inferential move from correlation to actionable intervention.
explanations.E: Opposite-answer trap. Successful recolonization in adjacent watersheds after riparian restoration strengthens the agency's conclusion by providing analogical evidence that the intervention works.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument is a policy/economics argument whose conclusion depends on an unstated assumption about the mechanism connecting a tax credit to a behavioral outcome. The correct weakener attacks the hidden link — that the population targeted by the credit is the population whose behavior would change — without being obviously on-point. Distractors include a genuine strengthener, a choice that attacks a different link in the chain, a scope-shifted irrelevancy, and a choice that only trivially narrows the credit's effect.
lr.stimulus: A legislative analyst testified that a proposed refundable tax credit for first-time homebuyers would meaningfully increase the homeownership rate among low-income households. The analyst cited data showing that, in comparable programs in two other states, the homeownership rate among households earning less than $50,000 annually rose by an average of six percentage points within three years of the credit's introduction.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the two comparison states, the homeownership rate among households earning more than $80,000 annually did not change significantly after the credit was introduced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A significant portion of the low-income households that claimed the tax credit in the comparison states had already been under contract to purchase a home before the credit was announced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The proposed credit would be refundable, meaning households with no tax liability would still receive the full benefit as a direct payment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Home prices in the state considering the credit have risen faster over the past five years than they did in either comparison state during the same period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Studies of similar tax incentives in other policy domains have found that low-income households are less likely than higher-income households to be aware of available credits.

explanations.correct: The analyst's argument assumes that the observed rise in homeownership rates was caused by the credit — i.e., that households purchased homes because of the incentive. Choice B reveals that many claimants were already committed to buying before the credit was announced, meaning the credit rewarded decisions already made rather than inducing new ones. This alternative explanation severs the causal link between the credit and the behavioral change, directly undermining the prediction that a similar credit will meaningfully increase homeownership in the proposed state.
explanations.A: Out-of-scope. The argument is about low-income households; what happened to higher-income households is irrelevant to whether the credit caused the low-income rate to rise. This choice neither weakens nor strengthens the target conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct. Introduces an alternative explanation — that the observed rate increase was driven by households already intending to buy, not by the credit inducing new buyers — thereby attacking the causal inference the analyst draws from the comparison-state data.
explanations.C: Opposite-answer trap. The refundability feature ensures even households with no tax liability receive the benefit, which strengthens the analyst's claim that the credit will reach and affect low-income buyers.
explanations.D: Too-narrow / attacking a peripheral premise. Rising home prices could make the credit less effective at the margin, but the argument's core claim is about the mechanism of behavioral change established by the comparison-state evidence, not about whether current market conditions are identical. This choice weakens the analogy somewhat but does not attack the causal inference from the cited data.
explanations.E: Shifts subject and weakens only trivially. Reduced awareness would diminish uptake, but the argument is grounded in what the credit caused in the comparison states — not in predicted awareness levels. Moreover, 'less likely to be aware' leaves open that many still are aware and act accordingly.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument is a methodological argument in medicine whose conclusion rests on a hidden assumption about the representativeness of a biomarker as a proxy for clinical outcomes. The correct weakener attacks that unstated proxy assumption — dense with qualifiers — while four distractors each implement a named trap pattern: reversed causation misapplied, attacking one premise trivially, accurate-but-irrelevant, and a strengthener.
lr.stimulus: A pharmaceutical company's researchers reported that patients given Drug X showed a 40 percent reduction in serum inflammatory markers compared with patients given a placebo. Because elevated inflammatory markers are associated with tissue damage in patients with the relevant condition, the researchers concluded that Drug X meaningfully reduces tissue damage in those patients.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most calls into question the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Drug X is metabolized differently in patients over the age of 65, resulting in lower peak plasma concentrations than those observed in the trial population.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The association between elevated inflammatory markers and tissue damage was established in patients who had not received any pharmaceutical treatment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several patients in the placebo group showed spontaneous reductions in inflammatory markers during the trial period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drug X is known to suppress the cellular pathways responsible for producing the specific inflammatory markers measured in the trial, without affecting the underlying inflammatory process that causes tissue damage.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients who received Drug X reported significantly lower levels of pain during the trial than patients who received the placebo.

explanations.correct: The researchers treat reduced serum inflammatory markers as a reliable proxy for reduced tissue damage. Choice D reveals that Drug X mechanically suppresses marker production — the biochemical signal — without interrupting the inflammatory process itself. If the drug lowers the measured marker but not the underlying damage-causing inflammation, the observed correlation between markers and damage no longer holds in treated patients, and the inference from 'fewer markers' to 'less tissue damage' collapses entirely.
explanations.A: Shift-in-subject trap. Different metabolism in patients over 65 is a concern about generalizability to a subpopulation not described as central to the trial. It does not challenge the inferential move from marker reduction to tissue-damage reduction for the trial population studied.
explanations.B: Accurate-but-irrelevant trap. That the marker–damage association was established in untreated patients might initially seem to undermine the proxy relationship. However, it does not establish that the association fails in treated patients — only that the original dataset lacked treated subjects. The conclusion's flaw requires showing the association breaks down under treatment, which B alone does not do.
explanations.C: Attacks one premise trivially. Spontaneous reductions in the placebo group might suggest regression to the mean, but the comparison between Drug X and placebo groups already controls for this by design; the 40 percent reduction is relative to placebo. This choice does not undermine the conclusion about tissue damage.
explanations.D: Correct. Severs the proxy link by showing the drug suppresses the biochemical signal (marker production) while leaving the damage-causing mechanism intact, meaning marker reduction is not evidence of damage reduction.
explanations.E: Opposite-answer trap. Lower reported pain in the Drug X group provides independent evidence consistent with reduced inflammation or tissue damage, strengthening rather than weakening the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument rests on a hidden methodological assumption: that absence of detected biomarkers in a controlled sample reliably reflects population-wide absence. The correct weakener attacks this unstated assumption rather than the surface causal claim. Distractors include a strengthener, a premise-level attack that doesn't touch the conclusion, and two out-of-scope comparisons.
lr.stimulus: A pharmaceutical research team administered an experimental anti-inflammatory compound to 200 patients with chronic joint pain. After six months, blood tests detected no elevated inflammatory biomarkers in 87 percent of participants. The researchers concluded that the compound effectively suppresses chronic inflammation in the general patient population.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patients with chronic joint pain who participated in the trial reported, on average, greater baseline pain levels than patients with the condition who did not participate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The blood tests used to detect inflammatory biomarkers in the trial are calibrated to identify only the specific subset of biomarkers associated with one variety of chronic inflammation, leaving other varieties undetected.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several competing anti-inflammatory compounds have failed to reduce biomarker levels in more than 70 percent of trial participants.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some participants in the trial also modified their diets during the six-month period, which is known to independently reduce certain inflammatory biomarkers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The compound was found to be well-tolerated, with fewer than five percent of participants reporting adverse side effects.

explanations.correct: If some participants independently modified their diets—a change known to reduce inflammatory biomarkers—then the reduction in biomarkers may be attributable to dietary change rather than the compound. This introduces an alternative explanation that undermines the conclusion that the compound itself suppresses chronic inflammation.
explanations.A: This describes a self-selection effect regarding baseline pain but does not explain why the biomarker reductions might not be caused by the compound. It is largely irrelevant to the causal conclusion.
explanations.B: This is a tempting trap: it attacks the reliability of the measurement tool, but it actually implies the results might underestimate the compound's effectiveness (or simply that some inflammation went undetected). It does not show the compound fails to suppress inflammation—it is too narrow and arguably a premise-level attack that leaves the conclusion intact.
explanations.C: This is a strengthener trap: it implies the compound outperforms rivals, bolstering rather than weakening the conclusion.
explanations.D: Correct. Introduces a confounding variable (dietary modification) that provides an alternative explanation for reduced biomarker levels.
explanations.E: Irrelevant. Tolerability and side-effect profile bear on safety, not on whether the compound actually suppresses inflammation.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument involves a two-step predictive chain: tax-credit expansion → increased private investment → reduced carbon emissions. The correct weakener attacks the second link in a way that requires recognizing the chain structure. Distractors include a choice that weakens only the first link and a strengthener that looks like an environmental concession.
lr.stimulus: An economic policy analyst argued that expanding the federal tax credit for renewable energy installations would significantly reduce national carbon emissions over the next decade. Her reasoning was that the expanded credit would attract substantial private investment in wind and solar infrastructure, and that such infrastructure, once built, would displace a meaningful share of fossil-fuel-generated electricity on the national grid.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wind and solar installations funded through similar tax credits in two neighboring countries have consistently displaced fossil-fuel generation on those countries' grids.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several major private investors have publicly stated that they would increase renewable energy spending if the tax credit were expanded.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Grid operators have announced plans to retire a significant portion of coal-fired generating capacity within five years regardless of any new renewable installations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because the national grid's transmission infrastructure cannot currently accommodate a rapid influx of distributed renewable generation, newly built wind and solar installations would largely sit idle rather than displace fossil-fuel output.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The existing federal tax credit for renewable energy has been criticized by some economists as an inefficient use of public funds.

explanations.correct: The analyst's conclusion depends on a chain: investment → built infrastructure → displaced fossil-fuel electricity. Choice D severs the second link: even if infrastructure is built, transmission constraints mean it cannot actually displace fossil-fuel output. This directly undermines the conclusion about emissions reduction.
explanations.A: This is a strengthener: analogous cases in neighboring countries support both causal links in the chain.
explanations.B: This is also a strengthener, confirming the first link (credit → investment) holds.
explanations.C: This is a 'too narrow / irrelevant' trap: it suggests emissions might fall anyway (which doesn't weaken the argument that the credit would reduce emissions—it merely introduces redundancy), but it does not attack the analyst's causal claim.
explanations.D: Correct. Severs the infrastructure-to-grid-displacement link, collapsing the conclusion.
explanations.E: Out-of-scope: criticism of the existing (unexpanded) credit's efficiency does not bear on whether the expanded credit would achieve its emissions goal.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument is an analogical one—drawing a conclusion about legal liability in one context based on precedent from a different context. The correct weakener identifies a structural disanalogy that undermines the analogy. Distractors include a choice that attacks a peripheral legal fact and a choice that strengthens the analogy.
lr.stimulus: A legal scholar argued that municipalities should be held liable for injuries caused by potholes on public roads, citing the established precedent in which property owners are held liable for injuries caused by hazardous conditions on privately owned walkways. Since courts have consistently ruled that property owners who knew or should have known of a hazardous condition are responsible for resulting injuries, the same standard of constructive knowledge should impose liability on municipalities.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the legal scholar's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Municipalities typically maintain far more linear miles of road surface than any private property owner maintains of walkway, making it practically impossible to inspect and remediate every hazardous condition within a reasonable time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Courts in several jurisdictions have extended private-property liability principles to commercial landlords who allow hazardous conditions to persist in common areas.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The constructive-knowledge standard for private-property liability has been applied consistently for more than forty years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some municipalities already carry insurance specifically designed to cover pothole-related injury claims.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Injuries resulting from pothole accidents are, on average, more severe than injuries resulting from walkway hazards on private property.

explanations.correct: The scholar's argument is analogical: because courts hold private property owners to a constructive-knowledge standard, municipalities should be held to the same standard. Choice A identifies a disanalogy—the sheer scale of public road networks makes it structurally impossible for municipalities to satisfy a constructive-knowledge standard in the same way a private owner can. This disanalogy weakens the basis for transferring the liability rule.
explanations.B: This is a strengthener: it shows courts have already expanded the private-property liability principle beyond its original context, supporting the scholar's analogical extension.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope: the longevity of the standard does not bear on whether it can be validly applied to municipalities.
explanations.D: Irrelevant: the existence of insurance does not affect whether the legal liability standard should apply; it neither strengthens nor weakens the analogy.
explanations.E: This is a 'shift in subject' trap: injury severity is irrelevant to whether the constructive-knowledge standard should apply; it does not address the validity of the analogy.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument generalizes from a controlled linguistic experiment to a universal cognitive claim. The correct weakener identifies a methodological flaw in the sample's representativeness that the conclusion silently assumes away. Distractors include a choice that trivially weakens one datum point without affecting the generalization and a reversed-causation trap.
lr.stimulus: Linguists at a research institute conducted a study in which monolingual English-speaking adults were asked to arrange photographs of events in chronological order without verbal instruction. Participants consistently arranged the photographs from left to right, suggesting that the directional bias instilled by reading left-to-right scripts causes people to conceptualize time as flowing from left to right.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A small number of the monolingual English-speaking participants in the study had previously been exposed to right-to-left scripts through casual contact with foreign-language media.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When the same photograph-arrangement task was administered to monolingual speakers of Arabic—a right-to-left script language—those participants consistently arranged the photographs from right to left.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several of the photographs used in the study depicted events that carry culturally specific temporal associations likely familiar only to participants raised in English-speaking environments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neurological research has established that a left-to-right directional preference in spatial tasks originates in hemisphere dominance patterns present at birth, before any exposure to written scripts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some languages that use left-to-right scripts also employ vertical text layouts in certain formal contexts.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that reading left-to-right scripts causes the left-to-right temporal bias. Choice D offers neurological evidence that the directional preference exists at birth—before script exposure—which undermines the causal direction claimed and suggests the correlation is not driven by reading habits at all.
explanations.A: This is a 'too narrow' trap: a small number of participants with peripheral exposure barely dents the study's findings and does not challenge the causal conclusion for the broader population.
explanations.B: This is a strengthener: it shows that speakers of a right-to-left language arrange time in the opposite direction, directly supporting the claim that script directionality causes temporal conceptualization.
explanations.C: This attacks the experimental design at a narrow level (photo familiarity), but even if some photos were culturally loaded, this doesn't undermine the causal claim about script directionality—it's a premise-level distractor that leaves the conclusion largely intact.
explanations.D: Correct. Provides an alternative, pre-linguistic causal origin for the observed bias, directly undermining the conclusion that script exposure is the cause.
explanations.E: Out-of-scope: the existence of vertical layouts in some left-to-right languages is irrelevant to whether reading directionality causes temporal conceptualization patterns.

lr.difficultyReason: The conclusion overreaches from a historical correlation to a causal policy prescription. The hidden assumption—that the historical mechanism still operates under current conditions—is attacked by the correct answer. Multiple distractors are carefully calibrated: one weakens a peripheral fact, one strengthens, and one is an accurate but temporally mislocated fact.
lr.stimulus: A historian argued that government investment in public university systems historically preceded periods of sustained economic growth in industrialized nations. Citing data from fifteen countries over the twentieth century, she concluded that expanding public university enrollment today would generate comparable economic growth in the coming decades.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In several of the fifteen countries studied, the periods of economic growth the historian identified were also accompanied by significant expansions of transportation infrastructure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The economic growth that followed public university expansion in the twentieth century was driven primarily by demand for graduates trained in manufacturing-sector skills that are now almost entirely automated, making such graduates no longer a significant driver of economic output.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Public universities in industrialized nations today enroll a substantially higher proportion of the college-age population than they did at the start of the twentieth century.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some private universities in industrialized nations have recently increased tuition at rates that exceed inflation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The fifteen countries the historian studied represent a geographically and economically diverse sample of industrialized nations.

explanations.correct: The historian's argument assumes the same mechanism that connected university expansion to economic growth historically will still operate today. Choice B shows that the mechanism—graduate labor in manufacturing—is now largely automated and no longer drives economic output. This severs the causal link between university expansion and economic growth under current conditions, directly weakening the conclusion.
explanations.A: This introduces a confounding variable for the historical correlation (transportation infrastructure), which is a valid weakener of the historical data—but only trivially, because it attacks the historical premise rather than the move from historical evidence to the current policy conclusion. The conclusion's main vulnerability is the applicability of the historical mechanism today.
explanations.B: Correct. Attacks the hidden assumption that the historical mechanism still applies.
explanations.C: This is a 'too narrow' trap: higher current enrollment might suggest diminishing returns, but it doesn't directly explain why the mechanism would fail; it merely notes a baseline difference. It does not strongly undermine the conclusion.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope: private university tuition is irrelevant to the effects of expanding public university enrollment.
explanations.E: This is a strengthener: sample diversity supports the generalizability of the historian's data.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus involves an ethical argument whose conclusion depends on an unstated principle about moral responsibility. The correct weakener attacks this hidden normative premise. Distractors include a choice that concedes the factual premise while leaving the normative conclusion untouched, and a strengthener framed in sympathetic moral language.
lr.stimulus: A bioethicist argued that pharmaceutical companies that hold patents on life-saving medications bear a moral obligation to supply those medications at cost to low-income patients in developing nations. Her reasoning was that the companies' research was substantially funded by government grants—that is, by the public—and that entities benefiting from public resources are morally obligated to make the products of that benefit available to the public at cost.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the bioethicist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several pharmaceutical companies already operate voluntary access programs that supply certain life-saving medications below cost in developing nations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The government grants that funded the relevant research were awarded competitively and did not guarantee that the resulting discoveries would be patentable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The costs of clinical trials, regulatory approval, and manufacturing scale-up—none of which are covered by the research grants—constitute the majority of the total investment required to bring a pharmaceutical to market.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Access to life-saving medications is recognized as a fundamental human right in numerous international legal instruments.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some pharmaceutical patents cover medications that are not life-saving but are instead used to treat conditions that are merely uncomfortable.

explanations.correct: The bioethicist's normative principle is: entities that benefit from public resources are obligated to provide the resulting products at cost to the public. Choice C shows that the companies' obligations arise largely from private investment (clinical trials, regulatory costs, manufacturing), not from the public grants. This undermines the factual basis for the normative principle—the companies' product is not primarily the product of public benefit—and so weakens the conclusion that they owe an at-cost obligation.
explanations.A: This is irrelevant to the argument's logical validity: voluntary programs don't address whether the obligation exists; they describe a behavior some companies already exhibit, leaving the conclusion unaffected.
explanations.B: This attacks a peripheral element (the foreseeability of the patent) without bearing on whether the companies actually benefited from public resources—the core premise. It's too narrow.
explanations.C: Correct. Undermines the premise that the companies' product is primarily the result of public benefit, thereby attacking the normative principle's factual foundation.
explanations.D: This is a strengthener framed in sympathetic moral language: recognizing medication access as a human right lends additional support to the bioethicist's conclusion.
explanations.E: Out-of-scope and involves a 'shift in subject' trap: the argument is about life-saving medications specifically; the existence of non-life-saving patents is irrelevant.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument is a predictive one based on ecological modeling. The conclusion depends on an assumption about the reliability of the model's parameters under changed conditions. The correct weakener attacks this hidden methodological assumption. The distractors include a strengthener that cites analogous past success, a narrowly scoped choice, and an out-of-scope comparison.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientists at a federal agency used a computational model to predict that reintroducing gray wolves to a national forest would, within twenty years, reduce the overpopulation of white-tailed deer by 40 percent, thereby allowing native vegetation to recover to pre-settlement density levels. The model's projections are based on wolf predation rates and deer population dynamics observed in a separate national park where wolves were reintroduced a decade ago.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The national forest targeted for wolf reintroduction is bordered on three sides by privately owned agricultural land where wolves would be subject to legal lethal control, a condition not present in the national park used to calibrate the model.

choices.label: B
choices.text: White-tailed deer in the national forest have shown signs of nutritional stress, suggesting that the current population may be near the upper limit of what the forest's food resources can sustain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Wolf reintroduction programs in two other national parks have produced deer population reductions broadly consistent with the model's predictions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The native vegetation in the national forest includes several plant species that are not present in the national park where wolf predation data were collected.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gray wolves typically require territories larger than the boundaries of the national forest, meaning individual packs may range into adjacent areas.

explanations.correct: The model's validity depends on applying parameters from one setting (the reference national park) to the target forest. Choice A identifies a structural difference—wolf mortality from lethal control on adjacent private land—that would reduce the wolf population well below the levels the model assumes, undermining the projection that wolves will reduce deer by 40 percent.
explanations.B: This is a 'too narrow / opposite direction' trap: nutritional stress in deer might independently reduce the deer population, which if anything would make the 40% reduction goal easier to achieve—a slight strengthener.
explanations.C: This is a strengthener: corroborating evidence from two other parks supports the model's reliability.
explanations.D: This is a plausible-sounding distractor, but different plant species affect vegetation recovery patterns rather than wolf predation rates or deer population dynamics—the parameters the model actually uses. It is out-of-scope relative to the conclusion about deer reduction.
explanations.E: This is an 'accurate but irrelevant' trap: wolves ranging outside the forest boundary could reduce effective predation within the forest (a mild weakener), but the more significant structural difference is the lethal-control issue in choice A. More importantly, ranging behavior was presumably observable at the reference park as well.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus involves a technology policy argument. The conclusion relies on an unstated assumption about the representativeness of a pilot program. The correct weakener attacks this assumption by revealing a selection effect. Distractors include a premise-level attack that doesn't reach the conclusion and a reversed-scope trap.
lr.stimulus: A government technology advisory board recommended that all public secondary schools nationwide adopt tablet-based learning platforms, citing a pilot program in which students at twelve schools that voluntarily adopted the platforms showed a 22 percent improvement in standardized test scores over two years. The board concluded that nationwide adoption would produce comparable improvements across the secondary school population.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the advisory board's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The twelve schools that volunteered for the pilot program were selected from among those that had already applied for technology-upgrade grants, indicating they had unusually motivated administrative staff and strong existing technology infrastructure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The standardized tests used to measure student performance in the pilot program were developed by the same company that manufactures the tablet-based learning platforms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several industrialized nations that have implemented nationwide tablet-based learning have reported mixed results, with some showing score improvements and others showing no significant change.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cost of equipping all public secondary schools with the tablets and associated software would require a substantial reallocation of existing education budgets.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Teachers at the twelve pilot schools received extensive professional development training prior to the platform rollout.

explanations.correct: The board's conclusion assumes the pilot schools are representative of all secondary schools. Choice A reveals a selection effect—the pilot schools had unusually motivated staff and robust infrastructure, conditions unlikely to hold nationwide. This undermines the generalization from pilot results to population-wide outcomes.
explanations.B: This is tempting: it attacks the reliability of the test scores measured during the pilot. However, it is a 'premise attack' trap—it questions whether the 22% improvement was real, not whether that improvement would generalize. Even if we accept the 22% improvement as real, the selection-effect problem in choice A more directly attacks the conclusion about nationwide adoption.
explanations.C: This introduces mixed international evidence, which is a weak weakener at best—'mixed results' abroad doesn't clearly undermine adoption in a specific national context. It's also out-of-scope relative to the specific pilot data cited.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope: cost and budget reallocation bear on the practicality of the recommendation, not on whether the conclusion (comparable improvements) would hold if adopted.
explanations.E: This is a 'too narrow' trap: it identifies another confounding factor (professional development) that may have contributed to the improvement, but it does not directly attack the representativeness of the pilot schools or the generalizability of the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument uses an artifact analysis to draw a historical conclusion about cultural diffusion. The conclusion's hidden assumption—that the artifact type is unique to one culture—is what the correct answer attacks. Distractors include a strengthener disguised as an archaeological nuance and an irrelevant temporal fact.
lr.stimulus: An archaeologist argued that a Bronze Age culture from the eastern Mediterranean was responsible for introducing a distinctive style of bronze fibula—a type of decorative clasp—to communities in central Europe. Her evidence was that fibulae of this precise style have been excavated at sites in central Europe that also contain pottery shards dated to the period of known maritime trade between the two regions. She concluded that the central European fibulae were trade goods originating in the eastern Mediterranean culture.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the archaeologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bronze fibulae of the same distinctive style have been independently produced by metalworking communities in central Europe since at least a century before the period of documented eastern Mediterranean maritime trade.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The pottery shards found alongside the fibulae at the central European sites are of a type that eastern Mediterranean traders are known to have exported widely during the relevant period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several of the central European sites where the fibulae were excavated show evidence of having been occupied continuously for more than five hundred years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bronze fibulae of other styles found at the same central European sites have been attributed to local production rather than trade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The eastern Mediterranean culture that the archaeologist identifies as the origin of the fibulae was itself a significant importer of raw bronze from central European sources.

explanations.correct: The archaeologist's conclusion depends on the assumption that the distinctive fibula style originated in the eastern Mediterranean and was brought to central Europe via trade. Choice A undermines this by showing that central European metalworkers produced the same style independently before the trade contact even began—eliminating the eastern Mediterranean origin as a necessary explanation.
explanations.B: This is a strengthener: it confirms that the associated pottery is consistent with eastern Mediterranean trade exports, corroborating the trade-goods hypothesis.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope: continuous occupation of a site is irrelevant to whether a particular artifact style arrived via trade or was locally produced.
explanations.D: This is a 'too narrow' trap: it shows that some fibulae at the sites are locally made, but it doesn't address the specific style at issue. It slightly undermines the argument by suggesting local production is possible, but it fails to show the distinctive style was locally produced.
explanations.E: This introduces a reversed-trade direction (central Europe exported bronze to the east), which is interesting but irrelevant to whether the distinctive fibula style traveled east-to-west via trade. It's an 'accurate but irrelevant' distractor.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument is a policy argument about arts funding whose conclusion depends on a hidden assumption about the stability of the relationship between funding and attendance. The correct weakener attacks this by showing that the mechanism that produced the observed correlation has reversed. Multiple distractors exploit the student's tendency to accept surface-level plausibility.
lr.stimulus: A city arts council presented data showing that over the past fifteen years, public funding for municipal theater programs correlated strongly with increases in theater attendance. The council concluded that increasing public arts funding by 30 percent in the next budget cycle would produce a significant rise in theater attendance citywide.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the arts council's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Survey data indicate that the primary reason theater attendance increased over the past fifteen years was not the funded productions themselves but rather the renovation of several theater buildings, a project now fully completed with no further renovations planned.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Theater attendance in cities that did not increase public arts funding remained flat over the same fifteen-year period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 30 percent funding increase would be financed through a reallocation of funds currently used to support municipal music programs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some of the municipal theaters that received public funding over the past fifteen years have recently experienced increases in private sponsorship.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Economists who specialize in cultural policy have argued that arts funding produces social benefits beyond attendance figures, such as civic identity and neighborhood revitalization.

explanations.correct: The council's argument assumes that the mechanism driving the past correlation—funding → attendance—will continue to operate. Choice A reveals that the actual driver of attendance growth was building renovation, not funded productions. Since those renovations are complete with none planned, the mechanism is exhausted; additional funding will not replicate the past attendance gains.
explanations.B: This is a strengthener: flat attendance in cities without funding increases supports the council's implied claim that funding (not other factors) caused attendance to rise.
explanations.C: This is an 'adjacent-harm' trap: it raises a concern about the funding reallocation's effect on music programs, but this does not bear on whether the theater funding increase would raise theater attendance—the council's actual conclusion.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope: increases in private sponsorship are consistent with either the argument or its negation; they don't address whether additional public funding will raise attendance.
explanations.E: This is a 'shift in subject' trap: social benefits beyond attendance are irrelevant to the council's specific conclusion about attendance figures. If anything, it subtly supports the council's general pro-funding position, making it a mild strengthener on an adjacent claim.
explanations.A: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument rests on a hidden methodological assumption: that the control group in a longitudinal study is comparable to the treatment group. The correct weakener attacks this buried comparability premise rather than either named variable. Distractors include a strengthener, an adjacent-premise attacker, an out-of-scope comparison, and a narrowly scoped fact.
lr.stimulus: A pharmaceutical researcher concluded that a new antidepressant, Velanol, reduces the frequency of depressive episodes. The researcher based this on a five-year study in which patients who took Velanol reported 40 percent fewer depressive episodes per year than patients who received no medication. The researcher controlled for age, sex, and baseline depression severity at enrollment.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the researcher's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patients who received no medication in the study were significantly more likely to have refused prior antidepressant treatment, suggesting higher baseline resistance to standard interventions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Velanol was well tolerated by most participants, with fewer than 8 percent reporting adverse side effects serious enough to discontinue use.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several other antidepressants on the market also reduce the frequency of depressive episodes in clinical trials.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The five-year study period coincided with an era of unusually low economic stress, which is known to correlate with reduced depression rates generally.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients who enrolled in the study were screened for co-occurring anxiety disorders before being assigned to either group.

explanations.correct: The researcher controls for age, sex, and baseline depression severity, but not for treatment history. If unmedicated patients were systematically more treatment-resistant, the groups are not truly comparable, and the 40-percent gap may reflect a selection difference rather than Velanol's effect. This attacks the hidden assumption of group comparability that the study's causal conclusion depends on.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces a confounding selection difference (treatment resistance) not accounted for in the controls, undermining the causal inference.
explanations.B: Irrelevant to efficacy. High tolerability slightly bolsters the case for Velanol as a practical treatment option but does not bear on the premise-to-conclusion move. Opposite-direction trap.
explanations.C: Shift-in-subject trap. Whether other drugs work tells us nothing about whether Velanol specifically caused the observed reduction; leaves the conclusion standing.
explanations.D: This is a plausible confounder (economic climate → depression rates), but it is symmetric — it would lower episode rates in both groups equally — so it cannot explain the 40-percent difference between groups. Too narrow to undermine the conclusion.
explanations.E: Describes a screening procedure that, if anything, strengthens the methodological rigor of the study. Strengthener trap.

lr.difficultyReason: Multi-step causal chain (deforestation → soil erosion → river sedimentation → fish decline). The correct weakener attacks the B→C link in a way that leaves A→B intact, requiring the student to identify which link carries the conclusion. Distractors attack A→B or offer irrelevant environmental facts.
lr.stimulus: A regional environmental agency argued that logging operations in the upper watershed have caused the steep decline in native fish populations observed over the past decade. The agency cited data showing that deforestation sharply increased soil erosion rates in the watershed, and that elevated soil erosion consistently leads to river sedimentation. Since sedimentation is known to destroy fish spawning beds, the logging must be responsible for the fish decline.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The logging companies operating in the watershed replanted approximately 60 percent of cleared areas within three years of harvesting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sediment levels in the affected rivers have not risen measurably over the past decade, despite increased erosion rates in the upper watershed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Native fish populations in unlogged watersheds in the same region have also declined over the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Soil erosion in the upper watershed was already elevated before logging operations began, due to periodic drought cycles.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Researchers have documented that sedimentation harms fish spawning in rivers worldwide, not only in this region.

explanations.correct: The argument's conclusion depends on the chain: deforestation → erosion → sedimentation → fish decline. Choice B severs the erosion-to-sedimentation link by showing that despite higher erosion rates, river sediment levels have not actually risen. Without elevated sedimentation, the spawning-bed destruction mechanism collapses, and so does the case for blaming logging.
