explanations.A: Attacks the extent of deforestation (A→B link) but only partially — 40 percent of cleared areas were not replanted. Does not sever any single link cleanly enough to undermine the conclusion significantly.
explanations.B: Correct. Severs the critical erosion→sedimentation link, dismantling the causal mechanism the argument relies on.
explanations.C: Alternative-explanation trap, but weaker than B: fish declines elsewhere suggest a region-wide factor, but the agency's argument is specifically about the mechanism (sedimentation), not mere correlation. This choice raises doubt about correlation without attacking the stated mechanism.
explanations.D: Pre-existing erosion weakens the implied uniqueness of logging as an erosion source but does not address whether logging contributed additionally or whether sedimentation actually occurred. Too narrow.
explanations.E: Strengthens by confirming the sedimentation-to-fish-decline link is well-established. Opposite-direction trap.

lr.difficultyReason: An economics argument predicting a future outcome rests on an analogy to a prior episode. The hidden assumption is that the analogy holds. The correct weakener identifies a disanalogy that undermines the prediction. Distractors include a strengthener, an irrelevant historical fact, and one answer that weakens the analogy's premise rather than the conclusion.
lr.stimulus: An economic analyst argued that the government's planned 15-percent tariff on imported steel will reduce domestic steel prices within two years. The analyst cited the tariff imposed on imported aluminum in 2012, after which domestic aluminum prices fell by 12 percent within 18 months as domestic producers, now shielded from foreign competition, invested in efficiency-enhancing technology and passed savings on to buyers.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The domestic steel industry is currently operating at near full capacity, leaving producers little room to invest in additional efficiency improvements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The 2012 aluminum tariff was slightly lower, at 13 percent, than the steel tariff being proposed today.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several economists who opposed the 2012 aluminum tariff have since revised their assessments in light of the price data.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Domestic steel producers lobbied heavily for the proposed tariff, suggesting they anticipate increased profitability.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Consumer demand for steel has remained stable over the past five years, even as global steel production increased.

explanations.correct: The analyst's prediction depends on the same mechanism that lowered aluminum prices: protected domestic producers invest in efficiency technology and pass savings to buyers. If the steel industry is already at full capacity, that mechanism cannot operate — there is no room for efficiency investment — so the analogical prediction fails. This is a precise disanalogy attacking the causal mechanism, not just a surface difference.
explanations.A: Correct. Undercuts the efficiency-investment mechanism that drove price reduction in the aluminum case, breaking the analogy at its load-bearing assumption.
explanations.B: The 2-percentage-point difference in tariff levels is immaterial to whether the mechanism operates; it does not expose a meaningful disanalogy. Accurate-but-irrelevant trap.
explanations.C: Strengthens by adding credibility to the aluminum-tariff precedent. Opposite-direction trap.
explanations.D: If anything, strengthens the idea that producers see profit potential, which could include efficiency investment. Opposite-direction trap.
explanations.E: Stable demand establishes a baseline but does not address whether producers will invest in efficiency; irrelevant to the analogical mechanism.

lr.difficultyReason: A policy argument uses a generalization from a pilot program to a national rollout. The correct weakener shows the pilot sample is non-representative in a way that is not obvious from the stimulus. Distractors include a near-miss that attacks program design rather than representativeness, a strengthener, and an out-of-scope policy comparison.
lr.stimulus: A policy adviser urged the federal government to mandate financial literacy courses in all public high schools nationwide. As evidence, the adviser cited a three-year pilot program in forty rural school districts, in which graduating students who completed the course were 30 percent more likely than non-participants to maintain a positive savings balance one year after graduation. The adviser concluded that a nationwide mandate would produce similarly significant improvements in young adults' financial outcomes.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The forty rural districts selected for the pilot were chosen in part because their school boards had already expressed strong support for financial literacy education, making their students and teachers unusually predisposed to engagement with the curriculum.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The financial literacy curriculum used in the pilot program took three years to develop and required substantial teacher training before implementation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some students who completed the financial literacy course reported that the material was too advanced for their grade level.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several other countries that have adopted mandatory financial literacy requirements in secondary schools have reported positive outcomes for young adults.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Students in the pilot program who did not take the course had lower average household incomes than those who did.

explanations.correct: The adviser's generalization from pilot to nationwide mandate assumes the pilot sample is representative. Choice A reveals the pilot districts were self-selected for unusual institutional buy-in, making the results ungeneralizable — a mandatory rollout to all districts, including resistant ones, would not replicate the conditions that produced the 30-percent gain. This attacks the hidden representativeness assumption.
explanations.A: Correct. Exposes a critical selection bias: the pilot districts were predisposed to success, so the result cannot be generalized to all schools nationwide.
explanations.B: Attacks implementation feasibility, not the logical move from pilot results to national prediction. A difficult rollout might slow adoption but doesn't undermine the underlying causal relationship the adviser asserts. Too narrow.
explanations.C: Identifies a curriculum design issue but doesn't show the improvement outcome is wrong — students may have found it challenging yet still benefited. Irrelevant to the conclusion's scope.
explanations.D: Strengthens by providing corroborating international evidence. Opposite-direction trap.
explanations.E: This actually weakens the comparison within the pilot (the control group was poorer), but it attacks the internal validity of the pilot itself rather than the generalizability to the national level. Because the conclusion is about national rollout efficacy, this is a too-narrow trap — it raises doubt about the pilot's own numbers but leaves the generalization assumption untouched.

lr.difficultyReason: A legal argument relies on an unstated principle — that legislative silence implies permission. The correct weakener introduces evidence that undermines this interpretive principle in a way that requires understanding the implicit move from 'statute does not mention X' to 'X is therefore allowed.' Distractors include a choice that strengthens the interpretation and one that shifts to an adjacent legal question.
lr.stimulus: A defense attorney argued that her client's use of automated bidding software during an online auction did not violate the auction platform's terms of service. The attorney pointed out that the terms of service explicitly prohibit 'deceptive practices' and 'manual bid manipulation' but make no mention of automated software. Since the terms do not prohibit automated bidding, the client's conduct must be considered permissible under the agreement.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the attorney's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The platform's terms of service were drafted before automated bidding software was widely available, and the drafters have since publicly stated that all non-human bidding methods were intended to fall within the prohibition on bid manipulation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Courts in the jurisdiction have consistently held that online auction terms of service are enforceable contracts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The client used the automated software openly and did not attempt to conceal its use from the platform.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Other auction platforms operating in the same market have explicitly banned automated bidding in their terms of service.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The platform's terms of service prohibit 'deceptive practices,' a category that some courts have interpreted broadly.

explanations.correct: The attorney's argument rests on legislative/contractual silence implying permission: because automated bidding is not explicitly named, it is allowed. Choice A demolishes this by showing the silence was a drafting gap, not intentional permission — the drafters publicly stated automated bidding was meant to fall under the 'bid manipulation' prohibition. This defeats the 'not mentioned = permitted' interpretive principle that the argument depends on.
explanations.A: Correct. Shows the silence was inadvertent, not permissive, directly undermining the inference from omission to authorization.
explanations.B: Strengthens by confirming the terms are legally binding — if anything, this makes the prohibition on 'bid manipulation' more potent. Opposite-direction trap.
explanations.C: The attorney's argument is about the terms' text, not intent to deceive; openness of use is legally irrelevant to whether the terms were violated. Accurate-but-irrelevant trap.
explanations.D: Shift-in-subject trap. What competitors prohibit tells us nothing about what this platform's silence means; other platforms' rules don't interpret this contract.
explanations.E: Weakens the attorney's position only obliquely — the conclusion is about automated bidding, not 'deceptive practices.' This answer would weaken only if automated bidding were already classified as deceptive, which hasn't been established. Too narrow / shift in subject.

lr.difficultyReason: A technology argument draws a causal conclusion from a before-and-after productivity metric without ruling out a specific type of confound: a parallel organizational change. The correct weakener introduces that confound. Distractors include a strengthener disguised as a process detail, an irrelevant industry comparison, and a choice that attacks the metric's validity without touching the conclusion.
lr.stimulus: A management consultant reported that after a mid-sized software firm adopted an AI-assisted code-review tool, the average time developers spent fixing bugs dropped by 35 percent over the following year. The consultant concluded that the AI tool was responsible for the improvement in developer productivity.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The AI code-review tool was developed by a third-party vendor with extensive experience in software quality assurance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: During the same year, the firm restructured its engineering teams, reducing team sizes and pairing senior developers with junior ones — a configuration independently shown to reduce debugging time by up to 40 percent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Developers at the firm reported high satisfaction with the AI tool in anonymous surveys conducted six months after its adoption.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several competing software firms adopted similar AI code-review tools in the same period without reporting comparable productivity gains.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Time spent fixing bugs is only one component of total developer productivity, which also includes time spent on new feature development and documentation.

explanations.correct: The consultant's conclusion is causal: the AI tool caused the 35-percent drop in debugging time. Choice B introduces a simultaneous organizational change — team restructuring with senior-junior pairings — that is independently documented to reduce debugging time by a comparable or greater magnitude. This alternative explanation directly undermines the attribution of the improvement to the AI tool.
explanations.A: Vendor experience is irrelevant to whether the tool caused the improvement; it speaks to product quality, not causation. Accurate-but-irrelevant trap.
explanations.B: Correct. Classic alternative-explanation weakener: a parallel intervention with known, documented efficacy that could account for the observed improvement.
explanations.C: Strengthens the inference by suggesting developers found the tool valuable, implying use was substantive. Opposite-direction trap.
explanations.D: This might seem to weaken, but competitor results are a shift-in-subject trap — the argument is about this specific firm's results, and different firms' implementations may vary in fidelity or context.
explanations.E: Attacks the adequacy of the productivity metric but does not challenge the causal claim that the AI tool caused the observed reduction in the metric that was measured. Premise-attacker-without-touching-conclusion trap.

lr.difficultyReason: An ethics argument from a universal moral principle to a specific policy conclusion. The hidden assumption is that the principle applies to the class of cases in question. The correct weakener shows a relevant difference that exempts the case from the principle's scope — requiring students to distinguish 'weakens the principle' from 'weakens the application of the principle to this case.'
lr.stimulus: An ethicist argued that hospitals should never disclose a patient's medical information to law enforcement without explicit patient consent. The ethicist's reasoning was that respect for personal autonomy requires that individuals retain control over sensitive personal information, and medical information is among the most sensitive categories of personal data.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patient autonomy is widely recognized as a foundational principle in biomedical ethics.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Law enforcement agencies sometimes request medical information without sufficient legal justification.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When a patient poses a credible, specific threat of serious violence to an identifiable third party, the patient's autonomy interest is outweighed by the potential victim's right to protection — a conclusion the ethicist has endorsed in other contexts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many jurisdictions already have statutory frameworks that require court orders before hospitals must comply with law enforcement requests for medical records.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Medical information is defined differently under privacy law in different countries, making a universal standard difficult to implement.

explanations.correct: The ethicist's argument is that autonomy always requires patient consent before disclosure. Choice C introduces a category the ethicist has already acknowledged as an exception — credible, specific threats of violence — and applies it to this context. This shows the 'never disclose without consent' conclusion is too absolute because the ethicist's own stated values permit exceptions that would allow disclosure. This undermines the universal claim by showing a class of cases the principle, by the ethicist's own lights, does not cover.
explanations.A: Strengthens by affirming the foundational premise (patient autonomy matters). Opposite-direction trap.
explanations.B: Attacks the behavior of law enforcement, not the logical move from the autonomy principle to the 'never disclose' conclusion. Even if true, unjustified requests could be screened without a blanket prohibition. Shift-in-subject trap.
explanations.C: Correct. Shows the ethicist's own commitment to victim-protection rights in analogous cases undermines the absolute 'never' in the conclusion — the principle does not apply uniformly to all disclosure situations.
explanations.D: Addresses practical implementation and existing law, not the normative argument. Accurate-but-irrelevant trap.
explanations.E: International variation in legal definitions is irrelevant to the normative ethical argument, which does not depend on legal uniformity. Out-of-scope trap.

lr.difficultyReason: A historical argument uses a single episode to support a broad causal generalization. The correct weakener shows the episode is anomalous in a way that invalidates the generalization, but this requires recognizing the specific historical feature that made the episode unique. Distractors include a strengthener that cites a parallel episode and a too-narrow choice that addresses only one dimension of the anomaly.
lr.stimulus: A historian argued that economic depressions are the primary cause of democratic backsliding. The historian pointed to the collapse of the Weimar Republic in Germany during the early 1930s: a devastating economic depression coincided with the rise of authoritarianism, and the historian claimed this pattern demonstrates that economic hardship reliably produces conditions favorable to authoritarian takeover.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Weimar Republic was also subject to specific structural weaknesses — including a fragmented party system, provisions enabling emergency rule, and the political legacies of World War I — that made it uniquely susceptible to authoritarian capture independent of economic conditions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several democracies experienced severe economic depressions during the twentieth century without undergoing democratic backsliding.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Authoritarianism tends to produce economic decline, suggesting the causal relationship between economics and political systems may run in the opposite direction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Great Depression of the 1930s affected many countries simultaneously, producing varied political outcomes across different national contexts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Historians disagree about the relative weight of economic versus political causes in the fall of the Weimar Republic.

explanations.correct: The historian's argument is a generalization: economic depressions reliably cause democratic backsliding. Choice B directly refutes this generalization by citing counterexamples — democracies that survived severe economic depressions without backsliding. These counterexamples show the claimed reliable causal relationship does not hold universally, undermining the move from the Weimar case to the broader conclusion.
explanations.A: This identifies confounds in the Weimar case, which calls into question whether the depression — rather than structural factors — was the cause in that specific episode. However, the argument's conclusion is a general causal claim about economic depressions and democratic backsliding broadly, not just about Weimar. Choice A weakens the premise (the Weimar example) but not the broader conclusion as directly as B does. Too-narrow trap.
explanations.B: Correct. Provides direct counterexamples to the general causal claim, the most powerful form of weakening a causal generalization.
explanations.C: Reversed-causation trap. While this introduces an alternative causal direction, it does not address the specific claim that depressions cause backsliding — it would need to show the Weimar sequence ran in reverse to directly undermine the argument.
explanations.D: Similar to A — varied outcomes during the Great Depression suggest other factors matter, but this is less precise and direct than B's explicit counterexamples. Weaker version of B.
explanations.E: Scholarly disagreement about causes is meta-evidence about the difficulty of the question, not evidence about the causal relationship itself. Accurate-but-irrelevant trap.

lr.difficultyReason: A linguistics argument about language change uses corpus frequency data to infer a causal mechanism (prescriptive instruction causing decline of a grammatical form). The correct weakener shows the frequency data could reflect a different methodological artifact rather than real-world language change. Distractors include a strengthener, a shift to a different language feature, and a choice that attacks a side premise without touching the conclusion.
lr.stimulus: A linguist argued that prescriptive grammar instruction in schools is causing the decline of the subjunctive mood in English. The linguist cited corpus data showing that subjunctive constructions appeared 40 percent less frequently in written texts produced after 1990 than in texts from the 1960s. Since grammar instruction intensified in the 1970s and 1980s, the linguist concluded that teaching prescriptive rules paradoxically suppresses students' awareness of the subjunctive, leading to its disuse.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most calls into question the linguist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The corpus used to measure post-1990 written texts drew primarily from online forums and informal digital communication, whereas the 1960s corpus consisted almost entirely of formal published prose.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some linguists argue that the subjunctive mood is being replaced by modal auxiliaries such as 'might' and 'should,' rather than simply disappearing from English.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Grammar instruction in many school districts became less prescriptive after 2000, yet subjunctive use has not recovered in recent corpus analyses.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prescriptive grammar instruction in the 1970s focused primarily on punctuation and sentence structure rather than on mood distinctions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several European languages with more extensive subjunctive systems have also experienced declining subjunctive use over the same period.

explanations.correct: The linguist's argument depends on the corpus frequency drop as evidence of real-world language change caused by grammar instruction. Choice A exposes a methodological artifact: the post-1990 corpus overrepresents informal digital communication (where subjunctive use is naturally lower) while the 1960s corpus captured formal prose (where it is naturally higher). The frequency difference may reflect a genre shift in corpus composition rather than any change in language behavior driven by instruction. This undermines the data's reliability as evidence of the claimed trend.
explanations.A: Correct. Identifies a corpus composition artifact that could entirely explain the frequency difference, making the data unreliable as evidence of the claimed language change.
explanations.B: Addresses how the subjunctive may be functionally replaced, which if anything supports a real decline — it doesn't challenge the data or the causal claim about instruction. Partially-relevant but insufficient trap.
explanations.C: This actually strengthens the argument by suggesting the decline persists even when the proposed cause weakened — but it is a complex distractor because it could also suggest instruction wasn't the cause. On balance, the lack of recovery after instruction eased could suggest the decline is real and entrenched, slightly supporting the claim. Opposite-direction or ambiguous trap.
explanations.D: Weakens the premise that grammar instruction in the 1970s focused on mood distinctions — attacking the 'instruction intensified' premise. But even if instruction didn't target mood specifically, another kind of prescriptivism could have the suppressive effect. This is a too-narrow attack on one premise that leaves the broader causal conclusion standing through other routes.
explanations.E: Parallel trends in other languages suggest the change may be a broader typological shift, not caused by English-specific school instruction. This is a legitimate weakener but less precise than A, which attacks the data quality itself rather than providing an alternative explanation at the macro level. Second-best distractor.

lr.difficultyReason: An arts/cultural policy argument predicts that public arts funding cuts will cause a decline in domestic artistic output, relying on an implicit assumption about the relationship between funding and production. The correct weakener attacks this assumption by showing a structural difference that severs the link, and requires distinguishing it from a choice that strengthens the argument by confirming the funding-output relationship holds elsewhere.
lr.stimulus: A cultural policy advocate argued that the proposed 25-percent cut to the National Arts Endowment's grants program will lead to a significant decline in the production of original domestic artworks over the next five years. The advocate noted that endowment grants currently provide the primary income for nearly 60 percent of working artists in the country, and that without income, artists cannot afford to produce work.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several major private foundations have announced plans to increase arts grants by an amount that would offset the proposed endowment cuts, specifically targeting artists who currently rely on endowment funding.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The endowment's grants program has historically supported artists working in traditional media more heavily than those working in digital or emerging art forms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In countries where public arts funding was reduced sharply, artistic output declined within a similar timeframe.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many artists who receive endowment grants supplement their income with teaching, commissions, or commercial work.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The National Arts Endowment administers a separate program for arts education that is not subject to the proposed cut.

explanations.correct: The advocate's argument assumes that the funding cut will deprive artists of income and thereby reduce production. Choice A directly severs this link: if private foundations will compensate with offsetting grants specifically targeting affected artists, the income loss does not occur, and the predicted production decline has no mechanism. This is a classic 'compensating factor' weakener that attacks the crucial premise that artists will lack income.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces a compensating mechanism that prevents the predicted causal sequence from unfolding — no income loss means the production decline prediction fails.
explanations.B: Identifies a distributional feature of current grants (favoring traditional media) that is irrelevant to whether a funding cut reduces total output. Accurate-but-irrelevant trap.
explanations.C: Strengthens by providing comparative evidence that the predicted pattern (funding cut → output decline) has occurred elsewhere. Opposite-direction trap.
explanations.D: Partially weakens by suggesting some artists have income sources beyond endowment grants, but the advocate's claim was about the 60 percent who rely on grants as their primary income — supplemental income from teaching doesn't necessarily compensate for a 25-percent cut to primary income. Too-narrow trap; doesn't fully sever the link.
explanations.E: The separate arts education program is outside the scope of the argument, which concerns artistic production, not arts education. Shift-in-subject trap.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument relies on a methodological assumption buried in a premise: that the biomarker reliably tracks disease progression across all patient subgroups. The correct weakener attacks this hidden assumption without directly disputing the correlation data. Distractors include a strengthener, a too-narrow premise attacker, and two out-of-scope facts about related treatments.
lr.stimulus: A clinical researcher concluded that Drug X reduces the severity of rheumatoid arthritis by citing a study in which patients who received Drug X showed significantly lower levels of C-reactive protein (CRP) — a recognized inflammatory biomarker — after six weeks of treatment compared to a placebo group. The researcher therefore argued that Drug X effectively suppresses the inflammatory process underlying rheumatoid arthritis.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the researcher's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: C-reactive protein levels are known to fluctuate independently of joint inflammation in patients who have concurrent cardiovascular conditions, a comorbidity prevalent in the study population.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The placebo group in the study reported higher rates of self-reported pain than the Drug X group at the six-week mark.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several other anti-inflammatory drugs also reduce CRP levels in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drug X was originally developed to treat a different autoimmune condition before being repurposed for rheumatoid arthritis trials.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients in the Drug X group adhered to the treatment protocol at a higher rate than patients in the placebo group.

explanations.correct: The researcher's conclusion depends on CRP serving as a reliable proxy for joint inflammation. If CRP levels in this population drop for reasons unrelated to joint inflammation — specifically due to cardiovascular comorbidities — then lower CRP after Drug X treatment does not establish that the drug suppressed arthritic inflammation. This attacks the hidden methodological assumption that CRP tracks the targeted process.
explanations.A: Correct. Undermines the evidentiary link between CRP reduction and arthritis suppression by showing CRP is confounded by the study population's cardiovascular conditions.
explanations.B: This is a strengthener trap: it provides additional evidence consistent with Drug X working, bolstering rather than undermining the conclusion.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope. The fact that other drugs also reduce CRP says nothing about whether Drug X's CRP reduction reflects genuine arthritis suppression.
explanations.D: Irrelevant. The drug's developmental history does not bear on whether it suppresses rheumatoid inflammation in the present study.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. Higher adherence in the Drug X group if anything supports the conclusion by showing the drug effect is not diluted by non-compliance.

lr.difficultyReason: Multi-step economic argument: the conclusion rests on a chain from tariff → reduced imports → domestic job growth. The correct weakener attacks the second link (reduced imports do not translate into domestic job growth) in a non-obvious way by introducing an assumption about capital substitution. Distractors include one that attacks the first link narrowly and one that seems relevant but shifts the subject.
lr.stimulus: A government economist argued that the newly imposed steel tariff will reduce unemployment in the domestic steel industry. The economist's reasoning was that the tariff will raise the price of imported steel, making domestically produced steel more price-competitive, which will in turn increase demand for domestic steel and thereby require steel producers to hire additional workers.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Domestic steel producers have announced plans to invest their anticipated tariff-driven revenue gains in automated production equipment rather than in expanding their workforce.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The countries whose steel exports are subject to the tariff have threatened retaliatory tariffs on unrelated domestic goods.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The price difference between imported and domestic steel was smaller before the tariff than economists had estimated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several domestic steel producers have operated at below full capacity for the past three years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Studies of previous tariff regimes in other industries found that tariffs reliably increased domestic market share for protected producers.

explanations.correct: The argument's final link assumes that increased demand for domestic steel will translate into more workers being hired. Choice A breaks this link: if producers use revenue gains to automate rather than hire, increased demand need not increase employment. This directly undermines the conclusion about reduced unemployment.
explanations.A: Correct. Severs the demand-increase → job-growth link by introducing capital substitution as the more likely response.
explanations.B: Shift-in-subject trap. Retaliatory tariffs may harm other domestic industries, but that is a different conclusion than the one about steel-sector employment specifically.
explanations.C: Too-narrow trap. This attacks the premise that the tariff will meaningfully shift price competitiveness, but if some price advantage is created, the argument's chain could still hold.
explanations.D: This could appear to strengthen (spare capacity means producers can fill more orders without hiring), but it is a trap: a student might read it as weakening because unused capacity sounds like an industry problem. It actually slightly undermines the need for new hires. However, this is less directly targeted at the conclusion than A, and the reasoning is ambiguous, making A the stronger weakener.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. Past tariff success in raising domestic market share supports the premise that the tariff will increase demand for domestic steel.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science argument with a methodological hidden assumption: satellite deforestation data is treated as equivalent to ground-level canopy loss. The correct weakener reveals that the data measure different things, attacking the premise's evidentiary basis rather than the general claim. Distractors include a tempting alternative-explanation choice that addresses deforestation but not the argument's core logical gap.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientists at a policy institute argued that the Brazilian Amazon lost more forest cover during the past decade than during any prior ten-year period, concluding that current logging regulations are inadequate and must be strengthened. The scientists based their conclusion on satellite imagery data showing that the total area classified as 'non-forest' increased by 18 percent over the decade.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most calls into question the scientists' reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Satellite classification algorithms were recalibrated midway through the decade to flag previously uncounted secondary-growth areas as 'non-forest,' meaning the apparent increase substantially reflects a change in measurement standards rather than new deforestation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Logging companies operating in the Amazon are required to replant one tree for every tree felled under current regulations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Agricultural expansion, not commercial logging, accounts for the majority of Amazon deforestation in recent years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several Amazon nations other than Brazil also experienced increased deforestation over the same period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The policy institute that published the study receives partial funding from environmental advocacy organizations.

explanations.correct: The scientists' entire argument rests on the satellite data accurately representing an actual increase in deforestation. If the 18% increase is largely an artifact of a mid-decade change in measurement standards, the data do not establish that forest cover actually declined more than in prior periods, which demolishes the empirical premise supporting the conclusion that current regulations are inadequate.
explanations.A: Correct. Undermines the reliability of the key data by showing that apparent increase may reflect methodological change, not genuine deforestation.
explanations.B: Too narrow and potentially out-of-scope. Replanting requirements speak to mitigation, not to whether the 18% figure is accurate or whether regulations are adequate in total.
explanations.C: Shift-in-subject trap. Even if agricultural expansion, not logging, is the main driver, this does not undermine the claim that forest cover declined more than before — it just challenges what type of regulation is needed, not whether regulations are inadequate overall.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope. Regional comparisons to other countries do not bear on whether the Brazilian data accurately reflect new deforestation or whether current regulations are adequate.
explanations.E: Ad-hominem-adjacent trap. Funding source may raise a question about bias, but it does not directly weaken the logical connection between the satellite data and the conclusion, especially since the data's validity has not been challenged on evidentiary grounds by this choice.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal-reasoning argument whose conclusion depends on an unstated assumption that the precedent cited is legally analogous to the current case. The correct weakener identifies a legally relevant disanalogy that the argument overlooks. Distractors include one that attacks a factual premise and one that strengthens by confirming the analogy.
lr.stimulus: A defense attorney argued that her client should not be held liable for breach of contract because the client's failure to perform was caused by an unanticipated government-mandated shutdown of the client's industry — a circumstance beyond the client's control. The attorney cited a precedent in which a court excused contractual non-performance caused by an unanticipated natural disaster, reasoning that the principle governing that case applies equally here.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the attorney's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contract in the precedent case explicitly included a force majeure clause, whereas the contract at issue contains no such clause and was negotiated after industry-shutdown risks were publicly known.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The client's industry had previously experienced government-mandated shutdowns twice in the prior decade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Courts in other jurisdictions have excused contractual non-performance caused by government-mandated shutdowns on at least three occasions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The opposing party suffered significant financial losses as a result of the client's failure to perform.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Natural disasters are generally regarded by courts as more severe disruptions to commerce than government-mandated shutdowns.

explanations.correct: The attorney's argument depends on the precedent being legally analogous to the current case. Choice A introduces two disanalogies that jointly undermine the analogy: the precedent's excuse was grounded in an explicit contractual force majeure clause, which this contract lacks, and the risk was foreseeable when the contract was signed. Both factors are legally material and break the analogy the attorney relies upon.
explanations.A: Correct. Identifies a disanalogy — presence of force majeure clause and known risk at contracting — that dismantles the analogical foundation of the argument.
explanations.B: This is a narrower version of the foreseeability point in A, but it attacks only a premise (unanticipated) rather than the analogical structure of the argument as a whole, and it lacks the force majeure component. It weakens but less completely than A.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. Other courts excusing similar non-performance supports the attorney's analogical argument.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope. The extent of the opposing party's losses is relevant to damages, not to whether the defense of excuse applies — it does not bear on the strength of the analogy.
explanations.E: This choice appears to weaken but is an unwarranted-comparison trap: even if natural disasters are considered more severe, courts could still excuse government-shutdown non-performance; severity of disruption is only one factor, and this choice does not directly attack the analogical premise the attorney invoked.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology-policy argument with a two-step causal chain: encryption backdoors → law-enforcement access → reduced crime. The correct weakener attacks the hidden assumption that law enforcement currently lacks the technical ability to exploit existing vulnerabilities, making the policy redundant rather than harmful or ineffective for a different reason. Distractors include a too-narrow attacker and a politically charged but logically irrelevant distractor.
lr.stimulus: A national security official argued that legislation requiring technology companies to build government-accessible backdoors into encrypted communications software would significantly reduce serious crime by giving law enforcement agencies reliable access to suspects' communications. The official noted that encrypted communications have been cited as an obstacle in numerous recent criminal investigations.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sophisticated criminal organizations have consistently migrated to newer encryption platforms within weeks of any known government access capability becoming public, rendering backdoor access obsolete before it can be systematically exploited.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many civil liberties organizations have expressed strong opposition to mandatory encryption backdoor legislation on privacy grounds.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Technology companies operating internationally would face conflicting legal obligations if different governments imposed incompatible backdoor requirements.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Law enforcement agencies have successfully used metadata analysis, rather than message content, to prosecute criminals in several high-profile cases.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Encryption software is subject to independent security audits in several countries to ensure it meets national standards.

explanations.correct: The argument's conclusion requires that backdoor access would actually give law enforcement reliable access to criminal communications. Choice A undermines this by showing that criminal organizations adapt rapidly to any known access capability, meaning the backdoors would not in practice provide the reliable access the official promises, breaking the causal chain from backdoor legislation to reduced crime.
explanations.A: Correct. Attacks the assumption that backdoor access would be practically effective against the criminal targets law enforcement seeks to monitor.
explanations.B: Out-of-scope. Civil liberties opposition is a political and normative consideration; it does not weaken the logical claim that backdoors would reduce crime.
explanations.C: Shift-in-subject trap. International compliance complexity is a practical obstacle for technology companies, not evidence against the conclusion that backdoors would reduce crime if implemented.
explanations.D: Too-narrow trap. That metadata alone has sometimes sufficed weakens the necessity of the legislation but does not attack whether backdoors would reduce crime if enacted — the argument's actual conclusion.
explanations.E: Irrelevant. Security auditing standards have no direct bearing on whether backdoor access would reduce crime.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistic argument whose conclusion generalizes from a sample of documented language-contact cases to a universal claim about borrowing directionality. The correct weakener attacks the sample's representativeness via a selection-bias point that is methodologically subtle. Distractors include a choice that seems to confirm the sampling concern but does not actually address directionality, and one that conflates borrowing with a different linguistic phenomenon.
lr.stimulus: A linguist argued that whenever two languages come into sustained contact, the language spoken by the socially dominant group invariably borrows fewer lexical items from the subordinate-group language than vice versa. As evidence, the linguist cited eighteen documented language-contact cases drawn from colonial history in which the politically dominant language showed minimal lexical borrowing from indigenous languages.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Colonial-era contact situations are systematically over-represented in historical linguistics archives because colonial administrations kept detailed written records, whereas contact situations involving more equal power relationships are comparatively underdocumented.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several of the eighteen cases involved languages from the same language family, raising the possibility that structural similarities, rather than social dominance, constrained lexical borrowing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lexical borrowing occurs at a slower rate in written languages than in spoken languages, regardless of the social status of the language's speakers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In at least three of the eighteen documented cases, the politically dominant language eventually supplanted the subordinate language entirely.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some linguists distinguish between lexical borrowing and code-switching, arguing that the two phenomena have different social causes.

explanations.correct: The linguist generalizes from eighteen colonial cases to a universal claim about all language-contact situations. Choice A reveals that these cases are not a representative sample — they were selected through an archival bias that over-represents colonial (dominant-subordinate) contact precisely because colonial dominance generated more records. This means the sample is skewed toward cases that would show the pattern the linguist claims is universal, undermining the generalization.
explanations.A: Correct. Attacks the sample's representativeness via a selection-bias argument, undermining the generalization from colonial cases to all language-contact situations.
explanations.B: Too-narrow trap. This raises an alternative explanation for the low borrowing in some of the eighteen cases, but it attacks a premise without reaching the conclusion — even if structural similarity explains some cases, the overall pattern might still support the linguist's generalization.
explanations.C: Irrelevant distractor. Writing versus speech affects borrowing rate, not directionality, which is the subject of the linguist's claim.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope. Language replacement is a different phenomenon from lexical borrowing and does not bear on the directionality-of-borrowing conclusion.
explanations.E: Shift-in-subject trap. The distinction between borrowing and code-switching, even if valid, does not address whether the linguist's sample supports the universal claim about borrowing directionality.

lr.difficultyReason: Historical causal argument attributing the decline of a medieval trade route to a single economic cause. The correct weakener provides an alternative structural cause whose timing aligns better with the decline, requiring the student to assess explanatory adequacy rather than simply finding any alternative. Distractors include a choice that partially overlaps with the correct answer's domain but weakens only a peripheral detail, and a strengthener that confirms the stated economic cause.
lr.stimulus: A historian argued that the decline of the Silk Road trade network after the fifteenth century was primarily caused by rising Ottoman tariffs on goods transiting Anatolia, which made overland trade prohibitively expensive and pushed European merchants toward maritime alternatives. The historian cited a threefold increase in transit fees between 1453 and 1510 as key evidence.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Portuguese navigators had already established a viable sea route around Africa to South Asian spice markets by 1498, and European merchants had begun shifting to maritime trade before Ottoman tariff increases reached their highest levels.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ottoman administrators recognized that excessive tariffs could reduce trade volume and periodically reduced transit fees during diplomatic negotiations with European powers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The volume of goods transported along the Silk Road declined sharply in the decades immediately following the Ottoman tariff increases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several Central Asian cities that served as Silk Road hubs experienced significant population declines during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Other overland trade routes not subject to Ottoman tariffs, such as those through Persia, also declined during the same period.

explanations.correct: The historian argues that rising Ottoman tariffs were the primary cause of the Silk Road's decline. Choice A undermines this by showing that the maritime shift began before Ottoman tariff increases peaked — meaning an independent technological and navigational development (the Portuguese sea route, established 1498) already made maritime trade viable before tariffs became prohibitively high. This reverses the direction of the causal story and provides a better-timed alternative explanation.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces a competing cause whose timeline precedes the tariff increases, directly challenging the tariff-as-primary-cause claim.
explanations.B: Weakens a peripheral detail (that tariffs were consistently high) but not the main conclusion — even periodic reductions are consistent with tariffs still playing a primary causal role overall.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. Declining trade volume following tariff increases is consistent with and supports the historian's causal claim.
explanations.D: Ambiguous and out-of-scope. Population declines in hub cities could reflect the trade decline the historian describes, or independent causes; this choice does not attack the causal direction claimed.
explanations.E: Reversed-causation trap. If non-Ottoman routes also declined, this might suggest a systemic cause independent of Ottoman tariffs — which does weaken the argument. However, it is less targeted than A: it doesn't explain what that systemic cause was, and a student must infer the implication, making A the more direct and stronger weakener.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics-policy argument that predicts a behavioral outcome from a moral incentive program. The conclusion depends on an unstated assumption about the causal pathway from public recognition to behavioral change. The correct weakener attacks this assumption by introducing evidence about motivational crowding-out, a non-obvious psychological mechanism. Distractors include one that attacks the ethics of the program (irrelevant to the causal prediction) and one that raises a different causal mechanism without bearing on the conclusion.
lr.stimulus: A municipal ethics board proposed a public recognition program for city contractors who voluntarily disclosed minor regulatory violations before an audit. The board concluded that the program would increase total regulatory compliance across the contractor pool, because contractors who received public recognition for voluntary disclosure in one instance were likely to exercise greater care in regulatory matters going forward, motivated by the reputational benefit of being seen as transparent.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the ethics board's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Behavioral research has found that external rewards such as public recognition can displace the internal sense of moral responsibility that initially motivated compliant behavior, ultimately reducing the overall level of conscientious rule-following.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some city contractors operate in industries where regulatory violations are difficult to detect even during formal audits.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ethics board program requires contractors to document all voluntarily disclosed violations in a publicly accessible database.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Critics of the program have argued that publicly recognizing voluntary disclosure may unfairly disadvantage contractors who achieve perfect compliance and never have violations to disclose.

choices.label: E
choices.text: In the year before the program was proposed, roughly 40 percent of city contractors underwent formal regulatory audits.

explanations.correct: The board's conclusion rests on the assumption that public recognition will motivate better future compliance. Choice A introduces the phenomenon of motivational crowding-out: external rewards can undermine internal moral motivation, meaning the program could actually reduce conscientious rule-following among contractors who previously complied out of genuine ethical commitment. This directly undermines the predicted increase in total compliance.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces motivational crowding-out as a mechanism by which the recognition program could reduce rather than increase overall compliance, attacking the causal assumption linking public recognition to improved behavior.
explanations.B: Out-of-scope. Difficulty of detecting violations in some industries is independent of whether the recognition program changes contractor behavior; it does not bear on the causal pathway the board posited.
explanations.C: Could be read as either neutral or a minor strengthener (transparency mechanism in place); it does not weaken the conclusion about behavioral change.
explanations.D: Shift-in-subject trap. The fairness objection concerns relative outcomes for perfectly compliant contractors — a normative concern irrelevant to whether total compliance increases as predicted.
explanations.E: Irrelevant. Baseline audit rates provide context but do not bear on whether the recognition program's mechanism will succeed in increasing compliance.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts-funding policy argument that generalizes from an economic model to predict audience expansion. The correct weakener attacks the hidden assumption that price elasticity for live-arts attendance is high, which is embedded within an unstated premise. The student must recognize that the entire predictive argument collapses if demand is inelastic in the relevant population. Distractors include a too-narrow choice about implementation costs and a demographic red-herring.
lr.stimulus: A city arts council argued that subsidizing ticket prices for live orchestral performances — reducing average ticket prices by 30 percent — would substantially expand the audience for classical music among residents who currently do not attend such performances. The council cited surveys showing that cost is the most frequently cited barrier among non-attendees, and concluded that the subsidy would translate directly into significantly higher attendance.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the council's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Follow-up interviews with survey respondents who cited cost as a barrier revealed that most would not attend even at substantially reduced prices because their primary deterrent was unfamiliarity with the art form rather than the financial burden per se.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The subsidy program would require the arts council to redirect funds currently allocated to community arts education initiatives.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Orchestral performances in the city have maintained an average audience capacity of 78 percent over the past five years, suggesting existing demand is relatively stable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Residents between the ages of 18 and 34 are underrepresented among current orchestral audiences relative to their share of the general population.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ticket price subsidies for theatrical performances in a neighboring city resulted in a 22 percent increase in first-time attendees over two seasons.

explanations.correct: The council's argument assumes that because non-attendees cite cost as the most frequently named barrier, reducing cost will remove the primary obstacle and drive attendance. Choice A reveals that cost is not the operative barrier — it is merely the socially salient answer given, while the actual deterrent is unfamiliarity with the art form. If price reduction does not address the real barrier, attendance will not substantially increase, directly undermining the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Attacks the assumption that stated cost barriers reflect the actual operative deterrent to attendance, showing that demand is not in fact price-elastic for this population.
explanations.B: Too-narrow trap. The reallocation of funds concerns implementation trade-offs, not the logical connection between price reduction and attendance growth.
explanations.C: Partially relevant but ambiguous. Stable existing demand suggests that current attendees aren't price-sensitive, but the argument is about new attendees among non-attendees, not current ones. This does not directly attack the causal claim.
explanations.D: Demographic red-herring. The underrepresentation of young adults is a description of the current audience, not evidence about whether a price subsidy would change non-attendee behavior.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. A comparable subsidy producing a significant attendance increase in a similar domain supports the council's prediction.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental-policy argument with a two-step predictive chain: carbon tax → reduced industrial emissions → measurable atmospheric CO2 reduction. The correct weakener attacks the second link through a carbon-leakage mechanism that is empirically well-supported but non-obvious to test-takers unfamiliar with the concept. Distractors include a strengthener about domestic emissions reductions and a choice attacking the first link too narrowly.
lr.stimulus: An environmental policy analyst argued that a proposed national carbon tax set at $80 per metric ton of CO2 equivalent would meaningfully reduce atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations within two decades. The analyst cited projections showing that such a tax would reduce domestic industrial CO2 emissions by approximately 35 percent, concluding that this domestic reduction would produce a corresponding improvement in atmospheric CO2 levels.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the analyst's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When jurisdictions impose carbon taxes without equivalent international coordination, energy-intensive industries typically relocate production to countries without carbon pricing, resulting in equivalent or greater global emissions than before the tax.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Economic models projecting the emissions-reduction effects of carbon taxes have historically underestimated business adaptation to price signals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The proposed carbon tax would generate substantial government revenue that legislators have proposed directing toward renewable energy infrastructure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Atmospheric CO2 concentrations are influenced by oceanic absorption rates, which vary independently of industrial emission levels.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several peer-reviewed studies have confirmed that a $80-per-ton carbon price falls within the range economists consider sufficient to drive meaningful emissions reductions in the industrial sector.

explanations.correct: The analyst concludes that domestic emissions reductions will produce corresponding atmospheric improvements. Choice A introduces carbon leakage: if domestic taxes cause carbon-intensive industries to relocate abroad, global emissions may remain the same or increase, meaning the domestic 35% reduction does not translate into reduced atmospheric CO2. This directly severs the link between domestic emissions reduction and the atmospheric outcome the analyst predicts.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces carbon leakage as a mechanism by which domestic emissions reductions are offset by increased foreign emissions, undermining the conclusion that atmospheric CO2 will meaningfully decrease.
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. If models underestimate business adaptation, the actual domestic reduction may exceed 35%, supporting rather than undermining the analyst's conclusion.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. Revenue directed to renewable energy would further reduce emissions, bolstering the causal chain toward reduced atmospheric CO2.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope. Oceanic absorption variability affects the rate at which CO2 is removed from the atmosphere, but this is independent of the argument's causal claim linking emission reductions to atmospheric improvements; it does not undermine the analyst's specific reasoning.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. Confirmation that $80/ton is sufficient to drive emissions reductions in the industrial sector supports the first link of the analyst's chain.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument's conclusion depends on a hidden methodological assumption: that the linguistic complexity index reliably tracks cognitive load across typologically distinct languages. The correct weakener attacks this buried premise rather than the surface causal claim, while four distractors each implement a named trap — one strengthener, one too-narrow, one irrelevant, and one that undermines an adjacent premise without touching the conclusion.
lr.stimulus: A team of researchers measured the linguistic complexity of written legal documents in twelve countries, using a standardized index that scores documents on sentence length, syntactic embedding depth, and rare-vocabulary density. Countries whose legal documents scored in the top quartile of the index had court proceedings that lasted, on average, 40 percent longer than those in the bottom quartile. The researchers concluded that reducing the linguistic complexity of legal documents would significantly shorten court proceedings in high-complexity countries.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The standardized complexity index was developed using documents from languages that share the same grammatical family, and it systematically underscores complexity in languages with different morphological structures, making high-scoring countries disproportionately those with already-efficient court systems.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In several of the twelve countries studied, court proceedings grew longer over the same period in which legal documents became more complex, suggesting that the relationship between the two variables is not merely coincidental.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Legal scholars in countries with the longest court proceedings have independently advocated for plain-language reforms, indicating that practitioners themselves recognize the burden imposed by complex documents.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A pilot program in one high-complexity country reduced the rare-vocabulary density of its civil court filings by 30 percent but had no measurable effect on the duration of criminal proceedings in that country.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Countries with high linguistic complexity scores also tend to have more litigants who represent themselves without counsel, a factor that independently prolongs court proceedings regardless of document complexity.

explanations.correct: The researchers assume the index accurately identifies countries whose legal documents genuinely impose high cognitive or procedural burdens. Choice A reveals that the index is methodologically biased: it underscores complexity in morphologically distinct languages, so countries classified as 'high complexity' are actually those whose languages happen to share the index's grammatical family — and these happen to be countries with efficient courts. This means the correlation between high index scores and longer proceedings may be an artifact of measurement error rather than a genuine relationship, directly undermining the evidential basis for the causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Attacks the hidden methodological assumption that the index validly measures what it claims to measure across all twelve countries, collapsing the evidentiary foundation for the causal claim.
explanations.B: Opposite-answer trap (strengthener). Noting that complexity and proceeding length grew together over time corroborates the researchers' causal story by reinforcing the temporal correlation; it does not weaken the conclusion.
explanations.C: Shift-in-subject trap. That practitioners advocate for reform is consistent with the researchers' conclusion but does not logically support or weaken it; the source of the advocacy is irrelevant to whether simplification would actually reduce proceeding duration.
explanations.D: Too-narrow trap. The pilot affected only civil filings and measured only criminal proceedings — a scope mismatch that makes the result inconclusive. Even if taken at face value, it attacks only one application of the proposed intervention without showing that the researchers' broader conclusion is wrong.
explanations.E: Confounding-variable trap that sounds like a strong weakener but is not. While self-represented litigants could independently prolong proceedings, this would have to be shown to explain the full 40-percent gap. As stated, it is merely an additional factor that coexists with document complexity; it does not demonstrate that complexity is causally inert, leaving the researchers' conclusion largely intact.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument rests on a hidden methodological assumption: that the comparison group is equivalent in all relevant respects. The correct weakener attacks that buried premise rather than the surface causal claim. Distractors include a strengthener, an out-of-scope comparative, a choice that attacks a peripheral premise without touching the conclusion, and a plausible-sounding but irrelevant fact.
lr.stimulus: A pharmaceutical researcher reported that patients who received a new antibiotic for bacterial pneumonia recovered an average of three days faster than patients who received the standard treatment during the same period at the same hospital. The researcher concluded that the new antibiotic is more effective than the standard treatment for bacterial pneumonia.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the researcher's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patients assigned to the new antibiotic had, on average, significantly milder cases of bacterial pneumonia at the time of admission than those assigned to the standard treatment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The standard treatment has been used successfully for bacterial pneumonia for more than two decades.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The new antibiotic costs substantially more per treatment course than the standard treatment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several patients in the standard treatment group experienced minor side effects that did not affect their rate of recovery.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The hospital at which the study was conducted sees a higher volume of pneumonia cases than most hospitals in the region.

explanations.correct: The researcher assumes the two patient groups were comparable at baseline. If new-antibiotic patients had milder cases to begin with, the faster recovery could reflect disease severity rather than drug efficacy — a classic confound that severs the causal link between treatment and outcome.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces a confounding variable (baseline disease severity) that provides an alternative explanation for the faster recovery, directly undermining the conclusion that the new antibiotic is more effective.
explanations.B: Opposite-answer trap. Establishing the standard treatment's long track record slightly bolsters its credibility, which if anything weakens the case for switching — but this does not undermine the researcher's specific comparative-efficacy conclusion.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope. Cost is irrelevant to whether the new antibiotic is medically more effective; the conclusion is about efficacy, not value or prescribing policy.
explanations.D: Too narrow / attacks peripheral premise. Minor side effects that did not affect recovery rates have no bearing on the comparative recovery-speed finding that grounds the conclusion.
explanations.E: Irrelevant. Hospital case volume says nothing about whether the new antibiotic outperforms the standard treatment within that hospital's comparison.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument is a multi-step predictive chain (policy → behavioral change → economic outcome). The correct answer attacks the second link — the move from behavioral change to economic outcome — which students often overlook because the first link seems like the obvious target. Distractors include a strengthener, a choice that attacks the first link only, an irrelevant statistic, and a subject-shift trap.
lr.stimulus: A city council economist argued as follows: by eliminating the downtown parking subsidy, the city will force commuters to seek cheaper alternatives such as public transit. Because commuters who switch to public transit will no longer spend money at downtown parking garages, the revenue currently collected by those private garages will decline sharply, causing several garages to close. Therefore, eliminating the parking subsidy will ultimately reduce the total number of parking spaces available downtown.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Many commuters who currently use the subsidized parking would continue to drive downtown even if the subsidy were eliminated, because no public transit route serves their neighborhoods.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Private parking garages in cities that eliminated similar subsidies typically converted their facilities into mixed-use commercial space rather than closing them entirely.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The city's public transit system has sufficient unused capacity to accommodate a large influx of new riders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parking garage operators in the downtown area have consistently opposed the parking subsidy since it was introduced.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Eliminating the parking subsidy would reduce the city's annual budget expenditure by several million dollars.

explanations.correct: The economist's conclusion depends on the chain: subsidy removal → commuters switch to transit → garages lose revenue → garages close → fewer total spaces. Choice B cuts the final link: if garages convert to commercial space rather than close, they would no longer provide parking spaces regardless — or more precisely, the spaces are lost through conversion, not closure driven by revenue decline. More importantly, it shows the garages would not simply 'close' and be replaced by nothing; they'd repurpose, meaning the causal mechanism for space reduction is broken. The real-world comparator undermines the specific prediction that the revenue decline causes closures that reduce spaces.
explanations.A: Too narrow / attacks the first link only. If many commuters keep driving, garages may not lose as much revenue — but this only weakens the premise that commuters will switch; it does not address what happens to garages if some do switch. The conclusion could still follow from a partial shift, so this choice leaves the conclusion largely intact.
explanations.B: Correct. Attacks the critical second-to-final link by showing that even if garages lose revenue, the predicted outcome (reduction in total spaces) does not follow — garages convert rather than close, and conversions remove spaces through a mechanism independent of the economist's causal chain.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. If transit has spare capacity, the shift away from driving is more feasible, which supports the economist's predicted behavioral change and thus bolsters, rather than weakens, the argument.
explanations.D: Irrelevant. Garage operators' political stance on the subsidy has no logical bearing on whether eliminating it will reduce available parking spaces.
explanations.E: Subject shift. Budget savings are a separate consequence of the policy; whether the city saves money does not bear on whether total downtown parking spaces will decrease.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus involves a methodological argument about linguistic evidence: a hidden assumption that written records are a reliable proxy for spoken language change. The correct weakener attacks that unstated methodological premise, which students must first identify. Distractors include a strengthener, a reversed-causation misapplication, a peripheral-premise attacker, and an out-of-scope comparison.
lr.stimulus: Historians of language have long debated when the Latin spoken in the western Roman provinces began diverging into the distinct precursors of modern Romance languages. A historical linguist recently argued that this divergence began no earlier than the sixth century CE, citing evidence that written documents from the fifth century across different provinces show remarkably uniform Latin grammar and vocabulary.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most calls into question the historical linguist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Many fifth-century Latin documents were produced by a small class of highly educated scribes who were trained to write in a standardized classical Latin that differed markedly from the spoken vernacular of ordinary people.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sixth-century documents from different provinces show considerably greater variation in Latin grammar and vocabulary than fifth-century documents do.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Modern Romance languages differ from one another in phonology more than in grammatical structure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Historians have recovered relatively fewer written documents from the fifth century than from the sixth century.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some linguists believe that the divergence of Romance languages was accelerated by the migration of Germanic peoples into western Roman territories.

explanations.correct: The linguist infers that uniformity in written documents reflects uniformity in spoken language, and therefore concludes that spoken divergence had not yet begun. Choice A exposes the fatal flaw in this inference: written Latin was a standardized prestige register maintained by trained scribes, not a faithful record of vernacular speech. Uniformity in documents could coexist with substantial spoken divergence already underway, directly undermining the evidentiary basis of the sixth-century dating.
explanations.A: Correct. Attacks the hidden methodological premise — that written uniformity tracks spoken uniformity — by providing a mechanism (scribal standardization) that would produce uniform documents even if spoken dialects were already diverging.
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. If sixth-century documents show greater variation, this is consistent with the linguist's claim that divergence became apparent from the sixth century onward; it actually supports rather than undermines the argument.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope. Whether Romance languages differ more in phonology than grammar is irrelevant to when divergence of the spoken precursors began; it concerns the endpoint of divergence, not the starting point the linguist is dating.
explanations.D: Peripheral-premise attacker. Fewer fifth-century documents might raise questions about sample size, but the argument does not hinge on document quantity — it hinges on uniformity among the documents that do exist. This choice marginally complicates the evidence base without touching the core inference from written to spoken uniformity.
explanations.E: Subject shift. The claim about Germanic migration may relate to what accelerated divergence, but the linguist's conclusion concerns when divergence began, not what caused its acceleration. This choice neither attacks nor supports the sixth-century start date.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument relies on a buried methodological assumption: that the control and treatment populations in the trial were equivalent in ways that matter. The correct weakener attacks this hidden comparability assumption rather than the stated evidence or the conclusion directly. Distractors include a strengthener, an irrelevant epidemiological fact, a choice that attacks only one peripheral premise, and a plausible-sounding but logically inert shift in subject.
lr.stimulus: A large clinical trial found that patients who received the experimental drug Velaprex recovered from moderate pneumonia an average of four days faster than patients who received only supportive care. The trial's researchers concluded that Velaprex directly accelerates the immune clearance of the bacterial pathogen responsible for pneumonia and should therefore be adopted as the standard first-line treatment for the condition.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patients assigned to the Velaprex group were, on average, significantly younger and had fewer pre-existing comorbidities than patients assigned to the supportive-care group.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Velaprex has been shown in laboratory settings to inhibit the replication of the bacterial strain most commonly associated with moderate pneumonia.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several other experimental drugs currently in development target the same bacterial pathway as Velaprex.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Supportive care for pneumonia has improved substantially over the past decade, reducing average recovery times across all patient populations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some patients in the Velaprex group reported mild gastrointestinal side effects during the course of treatment.

explanations.correct: The researchers conclude Velaprex directly caused faster recovery.
