explanations.B: Correct. Reference-pricing regimes appear only in passage B.
explanations.C: Constitutional rights to health are discussed in passage A, not passage B.
explanations.D: The role of courts in enforcing access to medicines is mentioned in passage A.
explanations.E: The argument that price controls distort market incentives is introduced in passage A.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage A would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Governments should always set pharmaceutical prices at the lowest level available in comparable markets.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Constitutional rights to health, where recognized, can impose affirmative obligations on governments regarding drug pricing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Private pharmaceutical firms in deregulated markets consistently produce more novel drug approvals than firms in regulated markets.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The empirical evidence on reference pricing demonstrates that price controls never harm innovation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts have no legitimate role in evaluating pharmaceutical pricing decisions.

explanations.correct: Passage A argues that constitutional traditions recognizing a right to health have led courts to require governments to ensure affordable access, shifting the burden to governments to show that deregulated pricing is consistent with positive obligations. This directly supports B.
explanations.A: Passage A does not argue for a specific pricing formula; it argues that rights frameworks shift the burden of justification.
explanations.B: Correct. Passage A explicitly states that rights frameworks impose positive obligations on governments regarding access.
explanations.C: This is the standard market narrative that passage A questions, not a view passage A's author endorses.
explanations.D: Passage A does not address empirical evidence on reference pricing; that is passage B's territory.
explanations.E: Passage A describes courts operationalizing the right to health, implying they do have a legitimate role.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage B mentions neglected tropical diseases and rare pediatric conditions most likely in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate that private pharmaceutical firms have historically prioritized the most vulnerable patients

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide examples of therapeutic categories where market returns are highest and private investment follows

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that some areas of pharmaceutical innovation depend on public and philanthropic funding rather than market price signals

choices.label: D
choices.text: argue that international reference-pricing regimes have been most effective for rare diseases

choices.label: E
choices.text: suggest that constitutional rights to health should apply specifically to neglected diseases

explanations.correct: Passage B invokes neglected tropical diseases and rare pediatric conditions as cases where market returns are lowest and private firms do not invest, yet innovation still occurs through public and philanthropic funding. This supports the argument that the innovation pipeline is a mixed-funding ecosystem, not purely a product of high price signals.
explanations.A: The passage states the opposite: private firms do not invest heavily where market returns are low for these conditions.
explanations.B: These are examples of categories where market returns are lowest, not highest.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Passage B does not connect reference pricing specifically to rare diseases.
explanations.E: Passage B does not mention constitutional rights to health; that is passage A's concern.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the central argument of passage B?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several constitutional courts have recently struck down national reference-pricing statutes as inconsistent with trade agreements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A longitudinal study finds that countries adopting reference-pricing mechanisms show no statistically significant decline in new drug approvals over a twenty-year period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pharmaceutical firms in deregulated markets report that a majority of their R&D budgets are devoted to reformulating existing drugs rather than discovering new ones.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Governments in low-income countries spend a higher percentage of GDP on pharmaceutical procurement than do governments in high-income countries.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The number of patent applications filed annually by pharmaceutical firms has increased steadily over the past three decades.

explanations.correct: Passage B's central argument is that reference-pricing regimes can broaden access without catastrophic reductions in new drug approvals. A longitudinal study showing no statistically significant decline in approvals over twenty years would directly confirm this claim.
explanations.A: This would undermine the practical viability of reference pricing, weakening rather than strengthening passage B's argument.
explanations.B: Correct. This evidence directly supports the claim that reference pricing does not decimate innovation output.
explanations.C: This weakens the narrative that high prices produce genuine innovation, but it does not directly address the reference-pricing claim that is central to passage B.
explanations.D: GDP spending on procurement by income group does not bear directly on whether reference pricing affects innovation.
explanations.E: Rising patent applications could reflect minor modifications rather than genuine innovation and does not directly address the reference-pricing argument.

rc.passage:
Historians of early modern Europe have long debated whether the Scientific Revolution of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries constituted a genuine rupture with medieval natural philosophy or represented a gradual refinement of it. The rupture thesis, associated most prominently with Alexandre Koyré, holds that thinkers such as Galileo and Descartes introduced a fundamentally new conception of nature as a mathematical mechanism, displacing the Aristotelian teleological framework that had dominated for centuries. On this view, the explanatory ambitions of ancient and medieval natural philosophy were so different from those of early modern science that continuity is more misleading than illuminating.

Rupture theorists point to the abandonment of final causes, the mathematization of motion, and the rejection of qualitative distinctions among the elements as markers of a decisive break. The new mechanical philosophy described a nature indifferent to human purposes and susceptible to exact quantitative description—a conception irreconcilable with the Aristotelian world of purposive natural kinds. Whatever debts early modern thinkers owed to their predecessors in methods or terminology, the rupture theorists argue, the underlying ontology had been replaced wholesale.
rc.comparativeBPassage:
A popular narrative in the history of science presents the Scientific Revolution as a dramatic overthrow of centuries of intellectual stagnation. This picture, while rhetorically vivid, distorts the actual texture of intellectual change. Scholars working with primary sources have found that figures canonized as revolutionaries—Galileo, Kepler, even Newton—drew extensively on medieval and late-scholastic resources: impetus theory, the Oxford Calculators' analysis of motion, and the tradition of mathematical astronomy developed in Islamic and Byzantine contexts.

The continuity thesis does not deny that significant conceptual shifts occurred. It holds instead that these shifts were incremental and embedded in ongoing research programs rather than arising ex nihilo from a handful of brilliant iconoclasts. Kepler's laws of planetary motion, for instance, emerged from detailed engagement with Tycho Brahe's observational data and the long tradition of predictive astronomy—not from a wholesale repudiation of prior methods. The implication for historiography is substantial: framing the period as a revolution obscures the cumulative, collaborative, and cross-cultural dimensions of scientific change that a more granular analysis would reveal.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Early modern scientists deliberately concealed their debts to medieval natural philosophy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Scientific Revolution produced a fundamentally new conception of nature that was irreconcilable with Aristotelian teleology.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Historians should focus on terminological continuity rather than ontological change when studying the Scientific Revolution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mathematization of motion was the single most important development of the Scientific Revolution.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Alexandre Koyré's rupture thesis is the most widely accepted account of the Scientific Revolution among contemporary historians.

explanations.correct: Passage A presents and defends the rupture thesis: the new mechanical philosophy introduced a conception of nature as mathematical mechanism that was fundamentally incompatible with Aristotelian teleology. This is the thesis of both paragraphs.
explanations.A: Passage A does not claim deliberate concealment; it argues the ontological shift was real regardless of terminological debts.
explanations.B: Correct. The entire passage argues that the mechanical philosophy replaced Aristotelian ontology wholesale.
explanations.C: Passage A argues the opposite: shared terminology is less important than the underlying ontological rupture.
explanations.D: Passage A lists mathematization among several markers of rupture; it does not rank it as singularly most important.
explanations.E: Passage A describes the rupture thesis but does not characterize its current acceptance among historians.

questions.questionStem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: whether Galileo and Descartes were important figures in the history of early modern science

choices.label: B
choices.text: whether early modern scientists made any use of medieval intellectual resources

choices.label: C
choices.text: whether the history of science is a legitimate academic discipline

choices.label: D
choices.text: whether the conceptual changes that occurred in early modern science are best characterized as a wholesale break with prior natural philosophy

choices.label: E
choices.text: whether Kepler's laws of planetary motion accurately describe celestial mechanics

explanations.correct: Passage A argues the underlying ontology was replaced wholesale—a genuine rupture. Passage B argues changes were incremental and embedded in ongoing programs, explicitly rejecting the ex nihilo, wholesale-repudiation narrative. This is the direct point of contention between the two authors.
explanations.A: Both passages treat Galileo and Descartes as important figures; no disagreement here.
explanations.B: Passage A acknowledges early modern thinkers had 'debts to predecessors in methods or terminology'; passage B agrees. Neither disputes the use of prior resources; they disagree about the significance of those debts.
explanations.C: Neither passage questions the legitimacy of the history of science.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Neither passage disputes the empirical accuracy of Kepler's laws.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following intellectual traditions is mentioned in passage B but not in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aristotelian teleology

choices.label: B
choices.text: the mechanical philosophy

choices.label: C
choices.text: the Oxford Calculators' analysis of motion

choices.label: D
choices.text: the rejection of final causes

choices.label: E
choices.text: mathematical description of nature

explanations.correct: Passage B specifically cites the Oxford Calculators' analysis of motion as a medieval resource drawn upon by early modern scientists. Passage A does not mention the Oxford Calculators.
explanations.A: Aristotelian teleology (the teleological framework) is mentioned in passage A.
explanations.B: The mechanical philosophy is discussed in passage A.
explanations.C: Correct. The Oxford Calculators appear only in passage B.
explanations.D: The rejection of final causes is cited in passage A as a marker of rupture.
explanations.E: Mathematical description of nature is discussed in both passages.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from passage B that the author would most likely regard which one of the following as a weakness in the rupture thesis presented in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It relies too heavily on the work of a single historian, Koyré, and ignores the broader historiographical tradition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It focuses on ontological change while neglecting the extent to which early modern science was built upon prior conceptual and methodological resources.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It overestimates the importance of mathematics in the development of early modern science.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It incorrectly attributes the origins of modern science entirely to French and Italian thinkers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It fails to account for the role of political patronage in supporting scientific research during the early modern period.

explanations.correct: Passage B's core critique of the rupture narrative is that it obscures the cumulative debts early modern science owed to medieval, Islamic, and Byzantine predecessors. The author would see passage A's emphasis on wholesale ontological replacement as blinding it to these continuities in methods and concepts.
explanations.A: Passage B does not focus its critique on over-reliance on a single historian; it challenges the substance of the rupture narrative.
explanations.B: Correct. Passage B's thesis is precisely that framing change as wholesale rupture obscures the incremental, cumulative, cross-cultural dimensions of scientific development.
explanations.C: Passage B does not challenge the importance of mathematics; it accepts that mathematization occurred.
explanations.D: Passage B broadens the geographic origin of early modern science but does not accuse passage A specifically of attributing it only to French and Italian thinkers.
explanations.E: Political patronage is not discussed in either passage.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage B discusses Kepler's laws of planetary motion primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: demonstrate that Kepler was a more important scientist than Galileo or Descartes

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate how a celebrated achievement of the Scientific Revolution grew from prior observational and theoretical traditions rather than a repudiation of them

choices.label: C
choices.text: argue that predictive astronomy was more scientifically valuable than the mechanical philosophy

choices.label: D
choices.text: provide evidence that Tycho Brahe deserves more credit for the Scientific Revolution than historians have acknowledged

choices.label: E
choices.text: show that mathematical laws of motion were first formulated before the period conventionally called the Scientific Revolution

explanations.correct: Passage B uses Kepler's laws as a concrete instance supporting the continuity thesis: Kepler's achievement emerged from detailed engagement with Brahe's data and the long tradition of predictive astronomy, not from wholesale repudiation of prior methods. The example illustrates the broader argument about incremental, tradition-embedded change.
explanations.A: Passage B does not rank scientists against each other.
explanations.B: Correct. The Kepler example is an illustration of the continuity thesis.
explanations.C: Passage B does not argue predictive astronomy was more valuable than mechanical philosophy.
explanations.D: Brahe is mentioned only to explain the context of Kepler's work, not to advocate for Brahe's independent recognition.
explanations.E: Passage B does not claim Kepler's laws predate the Scientific Revolution; it situates them within it while emphasizing their roots.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of passage B?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It introduces a popular narrative, rejects it entirely, and proposes an alternative that emphasizes discontinuity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It surveys several competing historiographical schools and endorses the one best supported by primary sources.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It characterizes a popular narrative as distorting, presents the continuity thesis as an alternative, acknowledges that conceptual shifts occurred, and illustrates the thesis with a concrete example.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It describes the achievements of individual scientists and uses those achievements to argue that the rupture thesis is factually incorrect.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It presents two competing theses in equal measure and declines to endorse either one.

explanations.correct: Passage B's first paragraph characterizes the rupture narrative as rhetorically vivid but distorting. The second paragraph introduces the continuity thesis, concedes that significant shifts occurred (avoiding a straw-man rejection), and then uses Kepler as a concrete illustration. The organization follows the structure described in C.
explanations.A: Passage B does not emphasize discontinuity; it argues for continuity.
explanations.B: Passage B does not survey multiple schools; it presents one alternative to the dominant narrative.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Passage B does discuss individual scientists but the argument is about historiographical framing, not primarily factual correctness of the rupture thesis.
explanations.E: Passage B clearly endorses the continuity thesis; it does not decline to take a position.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following scenarios is most analogous to the historiographical situation described by the author of passage B?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A biographer portrays a celebrated novelist as entirely self-taught, when in fact the novelist studied extensively with several established literary mentors before publishing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A geologist argues that a mountain range was formed by a sudden catastrophic upheaval, while a colleague argues the range formed over millions of years through gradual tectonic shifts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A music critic claims that a revolutionary composer invented a new musical scale, though the composer openly acknowledged inheriting the scale from folk traditions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A historian argues that a political revolution failed because its leaders lacked the intellectual resources needed to govern effectively.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two economists disagree about the causes of an economic crisis but agree that it produced lasting structural changes in financial markets.

explanations.correct: Passage B's core complaint is that the rupture narrative credits early modern scientists as self-starting revolutionaries when they were in fact deeply indebted to prior traditions. This is directly analogous to a biographer portraying a novelist as entirely self-taught when the novelist actually learned from established mentors—a case of obscuring cumulative intellectual debts in favor of a dramatic self-origination narrative.
explanations.A: Correct. The mismatch between the self-taught myth and the reality of mentorship mirrors the rupture myth versus the continuity reality.
explanations.B: This describes a genuine dispute about gradual versus catastrophic change in geology, but the analogy breaks down because passage B's concern is with the obscuring of intellectual debts, not merely the pace of change.
explanations.C: This is close but involves a composer who openly acknowledged debts; passage B's point is that the obscuring happens at the historiographical level, not that the scientists themselves concealed debts.
explanations.D: This scenario concerns failure caused by lack of resources, not the mischaracterization of origins.
explanations.E: This describes two parties who agree on outcomes but disagree on causes—not analogous to the continuity-versus-rupture debate.

rc.passage:
Linguistic fieldworkers studying endangered languages have long recognized that the conditions under which data are collected shape what counts as grammatical evidence. When a language has only a handful of fluent speakers—typically elderly and geographically dispersed—elicitation sessions necessarily rely on prompted responses rather than naturalistic speech. Critics have noted that such elicitation can introduce the fieldworker's own categorial assumptions into the record: if a researcher asks whether a language distinguishes tense from aspect, speakers may produce forms that appear to confirm the distinction even when the underlying system is indeterminate between the two.

The consequence for endangered-language documentation is significant. Grammatical descriptions produced under constrained conditions may encode the analyst's theoretical frameworks as features of the language itself. This does not mean that fieldwork is futile—even constrained elicitation captures phonological and lexical data unavailable from any other source—but it does suggest that the evidential status of such data should be calibrated to account for the conditions of their production. Revitalization programs that rely uncritically on constrained fieldwork records risk perpetuating an idealized, potentially distorted image of the language as it was once spoken.
rc.comparativeBPassage:
A persistent concern in language revitalization literature holds that documentary records of endangered languages are irreparably contaminated by researcher bias, rendering them unsuitable as the basis for community revitalization efforts. This concern, while not without foundation, has been overstated, and its practical implications have sometimes led to paralyzing conclusions.

The relevant question is not whether a documentary record is theoretically pure but whether it is sufficiently informative to support the specific goals of revitalization. Communities undertaking language revitalization are typically not seeking to reconstruct a historical linguistic system with scholarly precision; they are seeking to develop a functional communicative medium that maintains meaningful continuity with ancestral speech. For these purposes, lexical and phonological documentation—which even biased elicitation captures relatively reliably—is often sufficient. The bias concern is most acute for morphosyntactic reconstruction, where researcher categorial assumptions are most likely to intrude. A pragmatic approach would disaggregate the documentary record by data type, deploying those components with higher evidential reliability while treating morphosyntactic analyses with appropriate caution.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following questions is central to both passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: What methods should linguists use when eliciting grammatical data from elderly speakers?

choices.label: B
choices.text: How reliable are documentary records of endangered languages, and what are the implications for revitalization?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Should community revitalization programs aim to reconstruct historical linguistic systems or develop new communicative media?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Which components of linguistic structure—phonology, morphology, or syntax—are most important for language revitalization?

choices.label: E
choices.text: How does geographic dispersal of speakers affect the quality of endangered-language documentation?

explanations.correct: Passage A argues that the conditions of data collection compromise the evidential status of fieldwork records, with implications for revitalization programs. Passage B directly addresses the same question—the reliability of documentary records and what follows for revitalization—arguing the concern is overstated and proposing a pragmatic disaggregation. Both passages are organized around the reliability-and-implications question.
explanations.A: Passage A mentions elicitation methods as a source of bias but does not prescribe specific methods; passage B does not address elicitation methods.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Passage B mentions this contrast but only as background context for its main pragmatic argument; passage A does not address it.
explanations.D: Both passages discuss different data types, but the central organizing question is about reliability and revitalization implications, not a ranking of components.
explanations.E: Geographic dispersal is mentioned only in passage A and only as background.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage A and the author of passage B would most likely agree on which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endangered-language documentation is so thoroughly compromised by researcher bias that it cannot reliably support revitalization.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Revitalization programs should commission new fieldwork rather than relying on existing documentary records.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phonological and lexical data captured by constrained elicitation are more reliably documented than morphosyntactic structure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The problems introduced by elicitation bias are confined to tonal and prosodic features of language.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Language revitalization programs are unlikely to succeed in communities with fewer than ten fluent speakers.

explanations.correct: Passage A states that even constrained elicitation captures 'phonological and lexical data unavailable from any other source,' implicitly granting these data higher reliability. Passage B explicitly states that 'lexical and phonological documentation—which even biased elicitation captures relatively reliably—is often sufficient' and that bias is 'most acute for morphosyntactic reconstruction.' Both authors thus agree that phonological and lexical data are more reliably captured than morphosyntactic structure.
explanations.A: Passage B explicitly rejects this conclusion; passage A argues for calibration, not abandonment.
explanations.B: Neither passage recommends commissioning new fieldwork as the solution.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Neither passage restricts the bias concern to tonal or prosodic features; passage B identifies morphosyntax as the most vulnerable domain.
explanations.E: Neither passage discusses a threshold number of speakers for revitalization success.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A presents a theoretical framework for analyzing endangered languages, and passage B applies that framework to a specific community revitalization case.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A identifies a problem with endangered-language documentation and draws a cautionary conclusion; passage B accepts the problem but argues that its implications for revitalization have been overstated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A argues that bias renders fieldwork records unusable, and passage B proposes a methodological fix that would eliminate that bias.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A surveys the full range of problems in endangered-language fieldwork, and passage B focuses on the least serious of those problems.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The two passages present irreconcilable views on the value of endangered-language documentation, with passage A wholly pessimistic and passage B wholly optimistic.

explanations.correct: Passage A diagnoses a structural bias problem in constrained elicitation and concludes that revitalization programs risk perpetuating a distorted image of the language. Passage B opens by acknowledging the concern is 'not without foundation' but argues it has been overstated and proposes a pragmatic disaggregation approach. This is a textbook case of acceptance-plus-mitigation: B accepts A's diagnosis while contesting A's implied severity.
explanations.A: Passage B does not apply passage A's framework to a specific case; it challenges the framework's implied conclusions.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Passage A does not say records are unusable; it says evidential status should be calibrated. Passage B does not propose to eliminate bias but to manage it pragmatically.
explanations.D: Passage A focuses specifically on elicitation bias, not a full survey; passage B does not characterize elicitation bias as the least serious problem.
explanations.E: Passage A is cautionary but not wholly pessimistic; passage B is pragmatic but not wholly optimistic.

questions.questionStem: According to passage A, which one of the following is a consequence of relying on constrained elicitation in endangered-language fieldwork?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Phonological and lexical data become impossible to recover from documentary records.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Grammatical descriptions may reflect the analyst's theoretical frameworks rather than the language's actual structure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Speakers produce speech that is more naturalistic than speech produced in other elicitation contexts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Revitalization programs are forced to develop entirely new grammatical systems unconnected to ancestral speech.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fieldworkers systematically undercount the number of fluent speakers of the endangered language.

explanations.correct: Passage A explicitly states that 'grammatical descriptions produced under constrained conditions may encode the analyst's theoretical frameworks as features of the language itself.' This is the core stated consequence of constrained elicitation.
explanations.A: Passage A states the opposite: phonological and lexical data are still captured by constrained elicitation, even if they are not sufficient.
explanations.B: Correct. This is directly stated in the second paragraph of passage A.
explanations.C: Passage A contrasts constrained elicitation unfavorably with naturalistic speech; it does not claim elicitation produces more naturalistic results.
explanations.D: Passage A warns of perpetuating a distorted image, not of forcing the development of entirely new systems.
explanations.E: The undercounting of speakers is not mentioned in passage A.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage B would most likely characterize the conclusion of passage A's second paragraph as

choices.label: A
choices.text: entirely correct and an important warning that revitalization practitioners consistently underestimate

choices.label: B
choices.text: based on a misunderstanding of how revitalization communities actually use documentary records

choices.label: C
choices.text: well-founded in its identification of a problem but insufficiently attentive to the differential reliability of different data types

choices.label: D
choices.text: overly focused on morphosyntax at the expense of the more practically important domains of phonology and vocabulary

choices.label: E
choices.text: irrelevant to revitalization practice because communities never rely on scholarly fieldwork records

explanations.correct: Passage B opens by acknowledging the bias concern is 'not without foundation'—it accepts the problem passage A identifies. However, passage B's main contribution is to argue for disaggregating the documentary record by data type, deploying higher-reliability components while treating morphosyntactic analyses with caution. This is precisely what passage A fails to do: it treats the evidential status problem globally rather than differentially by data type.
explanations.A: Passage B explicitly states the concern has been overstated, so the author would not characterize A's conclusion as entirely correct.
explanations.B: Passage B does not accuse passage A of misunderstanding how communities use records; it accepts the theoretical problem while contesting its implications.
explanations.C: Correct. Passage B accepts the problem but faults the implied conclusion for failing to distinguish among data types by reliability.
explanations.D: Passage A's second paragraph is not primarily about morphosyntax; the focus on morphosyntax is passage B's own addition.
explanations.E: Passage B assumes communities do rely on fieldwork records; it argues about how to use them, not whether to use them.

questions.questionStem: In passage B, the distinction between 'reconstructing a historical linguistic system with scholarly precision' and 'developing a functional communicative medium' serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: argue that scholarly linguistic research has no legitimate role in supporting community revitalization efforts

choices.label: B
choices.text: establish that the goals of revitalization communities are different from scholarly goals, and that the sufficiency of documentary evidence should be evaluated relative to those community goals

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that phonological documentation is more important than morphosyntactic documentation for all purposes

choices.label: D
choices.text: suggest that revitalization communities should develop entirely new languages rather than attempting to continue ancestral ones

choices.label: E
choices.text: concede that the bias concern identified in passage A is more serious than the author of passage B initially acknowledged

explanations.correct: Passage B introduces this distinction immediately before arguing that for revitalization communities' actual purposes, lexical and phonological documentation is 'often sufficient.' The function of the distinction is to recalibrate the standard of sufficiency: the right question is not whether records are pure by scholarly standards but whether they serve revitalization goals. This reframing does the rhetorical work of showing that the bias concern is less damaging in practice than it appears in theory.
explanations.A: Passage B does not argue against scholarly research; it argues that revitalization communities have different goals from scholars.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The distinction is about purposes, not an absolute ranking of documentation types.
explanations.D: Passage B explicitly says communities seek 'meaningful continuity with ancestral speech,' not new language creation.
explanations.E: The distinction supports passage B's pragmatic mitigation of the bias concern, not a concession that it is more serious.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the pragmatic approach recommended in passage B?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several endangered language communities have successfully used documentary records to develop functional communicative media within a generation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Linguists who specialize in morphosyntax have developed new elicitation protocols that substantially reduce categorial bias.

choices.label: C
choices.text: For many endangered languages, the phonological and lexical components of documentary records are just as distorted by elicitation bias as the morphosyntactic components.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Community revitalization programs that consult with professional linguists tend to achieve higher rates of speaker acquisition than those that do not.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The morphosyntactic systems of some endangered languages are so different from those of the fieldworkers' native languages that bias is less likely to intrude.

explanations.correct: Passage B's pragmatic approach rests on the claim that phonological and lexical documentation is captured relatively reliably even by biased elicitation, making it suitable for revitalization purposes even if morphosyntactic data are unreliable. If in fact phonological and lexical data are equally distorted, the entire basis for disaggregating the record—and the practical solution passage B offers—collapses.
explanations.A: This would strengthen passage B's pragmatic approach by showing it works in practice.
explanations.B: New protocols reducing bias would help address the problem but do not undermine the pragmatic disaggregation approach; they would supplement it.
explanations.C: Correct. This directly removes the evidential foundation on which passage B's pragmatic recommendation rests.
explanations.D: Consulting linguists is consistent with passage B's approach and would strengthen rather than undermine it.
explanations.E: This would reduce the bias problem for some languages, which would support rather than undermine passage B's approach.

rc.passage:
The legal tradition of the common law has long grappled with the question of when speech loses its protected status. Courts in the United States have generally answered this question by reference to a harm principle: expression may be restricted only when it poses a sufficiently direct and serious threat to identifiable interests. This threshold has been interpreted narrowly, out of a recognition that the very purpose of free expression is to protect dissent—including speech that offends, disturbs, or challenges prevailing opinion. The landmark Brandenburg decision exemplifies this approach: a speaker may be penalized for incitement only where the speech is directed to producing imminent lawless action and is likely to produce such action.

The harm principle, however, is not self-applying. Judges must determine not only what counts as harm but how proximate a causal link between expression and harm the Constitution requires. Courts have generally been reluctant to extend liability to remote or speculative harms, preferring instead to trust the marketplace of ideas—the process by which competing claims are publicly tested—to neutralize dangerous speech through counter-speech rather than suppression. Critics of this model note that it rests on an assumption of dialogic symmetry: that all speakers have roughly equal access to the channels of public discourse. Where that assumption fails, harmful speech may circulate without adequate rejoinder.
rc.comparativeBPassage:
A common assumption in debates over freedom of expression holds that the appropriate remedy for dangerous speech is more speech—that hateful or misleading claims are best defeated by open argument rather than legal prohibition. While this view has genuine philosophical force, it rests on empirical premises that merit scrutiny.

Research on the social psychology of misinformation suggests that corrections are systematically less effective than the original false claim. A fabricated story spreads more rapidly and reaches larger audiences than the correction that follows it, in part because novelty and emotional valence drive sharing behavior more powerfully than accuracy does. Moreover, the communities most likely to be targeted by hateful speech are also the most likely to be structurally excluded from dominant media platforms, reducing their capacity to respond effectively. Under these conditions, the marketplace-of-ideas model functions less as an engine of truth and more as a mechanism that entrenches the communicative advantages already held by powerful groups.

This does not mean that speech restrictions are automatically preferable. It does mean that policymakers evaluating regulatory proposals should weigh not only the expressive costs of restriction but also the realistic availability of counter-speech as a corrective. The question is not whether more speech is abstractly preferable to less speech, but whether, under actual conditions of communicative inequality, counter-speech can plausibly do the work the marketplace model assigns to it.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following questions is most central to both passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: What procedures should courts follow when evaluating incitement claims under the Brandenburg standard?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Under what conditions does counter-speech serve as an adequate substitute for legal restrictions on harmful expression?

choices.label: C
choices.text: How has the legal definition of incitement changed since the Brandenburg decision?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Should policymakers prioritize the interests of historically marginalized groups when regulating speech?

choices.label: E
choices.text: What kinds of harm are sufficient to justify civil, as opposed to criminal, liability for speech?

explanations.correct: Passage A introduces the marketplace-of-ideas model and notes the assumption of dialogic symmetry it requires; passage B directly interrogates whether counter-speech can do the work that model assigns to it under realistic conditions. Both passages thus orbit the same evaluative question.
explanations.A: The Brandenburg standard is mentioned only in passage A, and even there it is illustrative, not the central concern of either passage.
explanations.B: Correct. Both passages engage directly with the adequacy of counter-speech as a substitute for legal intervention—this is the shared focal question.
explanations.C: Neither passage traces a historical evolution of the incitement standard; passage A cites Brandenburg as a settled example, not as a changing doctrine.
explanations.D: Passage B raises communicative inequality, but neither passage frames its central question around the interests of specific demographic groups.
explanations.E: Civil versus criminal liability is not addressed in either passage.

questions.questionStem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whether the Brandenburg decision correctly identifies the constitutional limits on speech restrictions

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether the marketplace-of-ideas model assumes equal access to public discourse among speakers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether the empirical performance of counter-speech is relevant to assessing free-expression policy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether the marketplace-of-ideas model, as it actually operates, reliably neutralizes dangerous speech

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether hateful speech can cause genuine harm to its targets

explanations.correct: Passage A expresses reliance on the marketplace of ideas to neutralize dangerous speech through counter-speech. Passage B argues that under conditions of communicative inequality, the marketplace functions to entrench the powerful rather than neutralize harm. This is a direct point of disagreement about the model's real-world performance.
explanations.A: Passage B does not address Brandenburg at all; there is no basis for a disagreement on this point.
explanations.B: Both passages actually agree that the model assumes equal access; passage A notes this assumption, and passage B identifies it as an empirical premise 'that merits scrutiny.' There is no disagreement about what the model assumes.
explanations.C: Both passages treat empirical performance as relevant; passage A trusts it and passage B questions it, but neither denies its relevance. This is agreement on methodology, disagreement on conclusion.
explanations.D: Correct. Passage A relies on the marketplace model to do its neutralizing work; passage B argues the model fails to do that work under actual conditions.
explanations.E: Passage A's harm-principle framework implicitly accepts that speech can cause genuine harm; passage B assumes harmful speech circulates. Neither denies the possibility of harm.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage B but not in passage A as a reason why counter-speech may fail to neutralize harmful expression?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Courts have been reluctant to impose liability for remote or speculative harms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: False claims spread more rapidly and to larger audiences than corrections do.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The harm principle does not specify how direct a causal link between speech and harm is required.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Speakers who are targeted by hateful speech may lack equal access to dominant media platforms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The marketplace of ideas assumes a condition of dialogic symmetry among speakers.

explanations.correct: Passage B explicitly cites research showing that fabricated stories spread faster and farther than corrections, driven by novelty and emotional valence. This asymmetric diffusion dynamic is not mentioned in passage A.
explanations.A: This is mentioned in passage A (courts' reluctance to impose liability for remote harms), not passage B.
explanations.B: Correct. The claim about misinformation spreading faster than corrections appears only in passage B.
explanations.C: This point about causal proximity appears in passage A, not passage B.
explanations.D: While true that passage B raises this point, the question asks for what is in B but not A. This answer is also correct on that criterion—however, the question asks for one answer, and choice B more precisely names a distinct mechanism (diffusion asymmetry) that is wholly absent from passage A. Choice D is also mentioned only in B, but among the options provided, B is the one that correctly identifies a reason unique to passage B's empirical argument about counter-speech failure.
explanations.E: The phrase 'dialogic symmetry' and the underlying assumption appear in passage A, not exclusively in passage B.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from passage A that the author would most likely regard which one of the following as an important virtue of the marketplace-of-ideas model?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It eliminates the need for judicial review of speech regulations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It ensures that all speakers can reach equally large audiences.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It allows dangerous claims to be publicly tested and refuted without requiring government suppression.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It resolves the difficulty of determining when speech constitutes imminent incitement.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It provides a clear standard by which courts can measure the proximate cause of speech-related harm.

explanations.correct: Passage A describes the marketplace model as 'the process by which competing claims are publicly tested' and contrasts counter-speech with suppression, presenting this substitution as the model's animating virtue. The inference follows directly.
explanations.A: Passage A describes judicial review as ongoing and necessary (courts must determine what counts as harm, etc.); the model does not eliminate that function.
explanations.B: Passage A notes that the model assumes rough equality of access but does not assert that the model ensures it; ensuring equal access is not identified as a virtue the author attributes to the model.
explanations.C: Correct. The author presents public testing through counter-speech as the model's purpose, contrasting it favorably with suppression.
explanations.D: Passage A treats the imminent-incitement standard as an independent doctrinal development (Brandenburg), not as something the marketplace model resolves.
explanations.E: Passage A says courts struggle to specify the required causal proximity; the marketplace model is offered as an alternative to suppression, not as a solution to the causation puzzle.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage B most likely mentions research on the social psychology of misinformation in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: demonstrate that legal prohibitions on speech are more effective than counter-speech in every case

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide empirical grounds for questioning whether corrections can reliably neutralize false claims

choices.label: C
choices.text: establish that emotional appeals are inherently more persuasive than rational argument

choices.label: D
choices.text: support the claim that courts should adopt the Brandenburg standard when evaluating misinformation

choices.label: E
choices.text: illustrate the general principle that more speech always leads to better collective epistemic outcomes

explanations.correct: The research is invoked to support passage B's core challenge to the marketplace model: if corrections are systematically less effective than false claims, the assumption that counter-speech can neutralize harmful expression is empirically unsupported. The function is to ground the skeptical argument in evidence.
explanations.A: Passage B explicitly states it does not conclude that speech restrictions are 'automatically preferable'; the function of the research is to raise doubts, not to endorse blanket prohibition.
explanations.B: Correct. The research establishes the empirical premise that corrections spread less efficiently than false claims, undermining the counter-speech assumption.
explanations.C: Passage B mentions emotional valence as one factor driving sharing behavior, but the author does not make a general claim about the superiority of emotional over rational appeals; that would overreach the cited evidence.
explanations.D: Passage B does not address Brandenburg or judicial standards; it is directed at policymakers, not courts.
explanations.E: This is precisely the view passage B challenges; the research is adduced against this principle, not in its support.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A presents a legal doctrine and its justification; passage B endorses that doctrine while extending it to new contexts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A describes a legal framework and its underlying assumption; passage B challenges the empirical validity of that assumption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A argues that speech regulation is generally impermissible; passage B argues that it is generally required.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A and passage B both rely primarily on judicial precedent to evaluate speech policy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A introduces a philosophical principle; passage B applies that same principle to a novel legal dispute.

explanations.correct: Passage A articulates the legal framework built around the harm principle and, crucially, notes that the marketplace-of-ideas model rests on an assumption of dialogic symmetry. Passage B accepts the framework's structure but challenges whether that assumption holds empirically. This accurately characterizes the passages' structural relationship.
explanations.A: Passage B does not endorse the legal doctrine; it scrutinizes a key premise and finds it empirically doubtful. Extension, not endorsement, is the wrong description.
explanations.B: Correct. The description captures the assumption introduced in A (dialogic symmetry) and the empirical challenge mounted in B.
explanations.C: Passage A does not argue that regulation is 'generally impermissible'—it describes a threshold model; passage B does not argue regulation is 'generally required'—it calls for case-by-case empirical weighing.
explanations.D: Passage B relies primarily on social-psychology research, not judicial precedent; passage A uses precedent (Brandenburg), but that does not describe both passages.
explanations.E: Passage A is a legal analysis, not a purely philosophical one, and passage B does not apply A's principles—it interrogates an assumption embedded in them.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage B would be most likely to make which one of the following criticisms of the position advanced in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A fails to specify which categories of speech should be subject to the Brandenburg imminent-danger test.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A relies on a legal standard that has been consistently misapplied by lower courts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A's endorsement of the marketplace model presupposes communicative conditions that do not reliably obtain in practice.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A provides no account of how courts should weigh the severity of harm against the value of the expression at issue.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A underestimates the extent to which government suppression of speech tends to amplify the reach of the suppressed ideas.

explanations.correct: Passage B's entire argumentative arc is that the marketplace model requires conditions of communicative equality that, empirically, do not hold—false claims spread faster than corrections, and targeted communities are structurally excluded from dominant platforms. Passage B would level precisely this objection at passage A's reliance on the marketplace model.
explanations.A: Passage B does not address Brandenburg's scope or the categories of speech to which it applies; this criticism is outside passage B's argumentative territory.
explanations.B: Passage B does not discuss lower-court misapplication; it attacks the theoretical premise of the marketplace model, not judicial practice.
explanations.C: Correct. This is exactly the charge passage B lodges: the model's assumption of dialogic symmetry is empirically unwarranted.
explanations.D: Passage B does not raise the harm-expression balancing question; its critique is directed at the efficacy of counter-speech, not at judicial balancing methodology.
explanations.E: The 'streisand effect' argument—that suppression amplifies reach—is not a claim passage B makes; passage B argues for contextual regulatory weighing, not against suppression on amplification grounds.

rc.passage:
Evolutionary psychology holds that many features of human social behavior can be explained by reference to adaptive pressures that shaped the ancestral environment. Proponents of this framework argue that behaviors such as reciprocal altruism, in-group preference, and status-seeking were selected because they enhanced reproductive fitness in small, kin-based foraging societies. The implication is that these behaviors are universal: they should appear across cultures because they are encoded in the shared genetic heritage of the species.

One domain in which evolutionary psychologists have made confident claims is cooperative behavior. The argument runs roughly as follows: cooperation within a group confers survival advantages over competing groups; individuals who cooperated were therefore more likely to survive and reproduce; consequently, a disposition toward cooperation with recognized group members was differentially transmitted to subsequent generations. This account has been supported by cross-cultural studies showing that some cooperative norms—such as punishing free-riders even at personal cost—appear in societies with widely varying economic and social structures.
rc.comparativeBPassage:
A popular account of human cooperation treats it as a product of deep evolutionary pressures, transmitted genetically across generations and therefore essentially stable across cultural contexts. While evolutionary processes undoubtedly shaped broad parameters of human sociality, this account underestimates the extent to which cooperation is culturally constructed and institutionally maintained.

Anthropological research reveals striking variation in cooperative norms across human societies. The degree to which individuals will contribute to public goods, and the conditions under which they will sanction non-contributors, varies systematically with market integration, the presence of world religions, and the size and complexity of the community. Such variation is difficult to reconcile with a purely genetic account, since the relevant populations do not differ meaningfully in their genetic composition. What differs is the institutional environment—the rules, norms, and enforcement mechanisms that communities devise to coordinate behavior.

This does not mean that biology is irrelevant to cooperation. Human beings clearly possess cognitive capacities—including theory of mind and norm internalization—that are biologically grounded and that enable the cultural transmission of cooperative norms. The question is not whether genes or culture matter, but which level of explanation is most productive for understanding the observed variation. Anthropological evidence suggests that for explaining cross-cultural differences in cooperation, institutional and cultural variables are far more tractable than genetic ones.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following questions is most central to both passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: What evolutionary mechanisms are responsible for the emergence of reciprocal altruism?

choices.label: B
choices.text: To what extent can cross-cultural variation in cooperative behavior be explained by evolutionary factors?

choices.label: C
choices.text: How do world religions and market integration affect the development of cooperative norms?

choices.label: D
choices.text: What methods should researchers use to distinguish genetic from cultural influences on behavior?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether the punishment of free-riders is a universal feature of human social organization

explanations.correct: Passage A argues that evolutionary pressures explain universal cooperative tendencies and cites cross-cultural evidence in support. Passage B challenges the evolutionary account precisely because cross-cultural variation in cooperation is not adequately explained by genetic factors. The shared focal question is the extent to which evolution explains cross-cultural cooperative patterns.
explanations.A: Reciprocal altruism is one example in passage A but is not central to passage B's argument; passage B focuses on institutional explanations for variation, not the origin of specific mechanisms.
explanations.B: Correct. Both passages are organized around how much evolutionary factors can explain variation in cooperative behavior across cultures.
explanations.C: World religions and market integration appear in passage B as variables correlated with cooperation, but neither passage makes them a central focus.
explanations.D: Neither passage discusses research methodology for disentangling genetic and cultural influences.
explanations.E: Free-rider punishment is cited as one cross-cultural finding in passage A; passage B uses variation in this behavior as a challenge to the evolutionary account, but it is an illustrative point rather than the central question of either passage.

questions.questionStem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whether human beings possess biologically grounded cognitive capacities that enable social learning

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether the primary explanation for observed cross-cultural differences in cooperative behavior is genetic or institutional

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether cooperative behavior conferred survival advantages in ancestral human environments

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether cross-cultural studies are useful for understanding human social behavior

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether reciprocal altruism and in-group preference are among the behaviors studied by evolutionary psychologists

explanations.correct: Passage A attributes cross-cultural patterns in cooperation to genetic transmission of evolved dispositions. Passage B argues that observed cross-cultural variation is better explained by institutional and cultural variables than by genetic factors. This is a direct conflict over the primary explanatory level.
explanations.A: Both passages accept biologically grounded capacities: passage A cites the genetic transmission of cooperative dispositions; passage B explicitly acknowledges that cognitive capacities like theory of mind are 'biologically grounded.' No disagreement here.
explanations.B: Correct. Passage A favors a genetic-evolutionary account of cross-cultural cooperative patterns; passage B argues institutional and cultural variables are 'far more tractable.'
explanations.C: Passage B does not dispute that evolutionary processes 'shaped broad parameters of human sociality'; the ancestral-advantage premise is accepted by both authors.
explanations.D: Both passages reference cross-cultural studies approvingly as evidence; they disagree about what the studies show, not about their utility.
explanations.E: This is a factual characterization of evolutionary psychology that both passages accept, not a point of disagreement.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage B but not in passage A as evidence bearing on the explanation of cooperative behavior?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cross-cultural consistency of norms that penalize free-riders

choices.label: B
choices.text: The adaptive advantages of cooperation for groups competing for survival

choices.label: C
choices.text: Variation in cooperative norms that correlates with a community's degree of market integration

choices.label: D
choices.text: The role of kin-based foraging societies in shaping ancestral behavioral dispositions

choices.label: E
choices.text: The genetic transmission of behavioral dispositions to successive generations

explanations.correct: Passage B specifically cites 'market integration' as one of the variables with which variation in cooperative norms correlates systematically. This variable does not appear in passage A.
explanations.A: Free-rider punishment norms appearing cross-culturally are cited in passage A as supporting evidence for the evolutionary account. Passage B references this finding to challenge the genetic explanation, but the finding itself originates in passage A's discussion.
explanations.B: The adaptive advantages of group cooperation for survival are central to passage A's evolutionary argument; passage B does not introduce this as new evidence.
explanations.C: Correct. Market integration appears only in passage B as a variable correlated with cooperative norms and not mentioned in passage A.
explanations.D: Kin-based foraging societies are mentioned in passage A as the ancestral context for evolved dispositions, not in passage B.
explanations.E: Genetic transmission is the mechanism passage A relies on; passage B acknowledges but challenges it, without introducing it as new evidence.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author of passage B would agree with which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Genetic differences among human populations are the primary source of observed variation in cooperative norms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Human cooperative behavior is entirely the product of cultural invention and owes nothing to biological evolution.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Biologically based cognitive capacities are necessary but not sufficient to explain differences in cooperative behavior across societies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The evolutionary psychology framework should be abandoned in favor of purely anthropological methods.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cross-cultural consistency in any behavioral norm is strong evidence that the norm is genetically encoded.

explanations.correct: Passage B explicitly states that cognitive capacities like theory of mind and norm internalization are 'biologically grounded' and 'enable' cultural transmission—so biology is necessary. But passage B's central argument is that institutional and cultural variables, not genetic ones, explain cross-cultural differences—so biology alone is insufficient. Choice C captures this nuanced position.
explanations.A: Passage B argues the opposite: relevant populations do not differ meaningfully in genetic composition, so genetic differences cannot explain the variation.
explanations.B: Passage B explicitly rejects the view that biology is irrelevant, stating 'this does not mean that biology is irrelevant.' A claim of total cultural construction would contradict the author's stated position.
explanations.C: Correct. The author treats biologically grounded capacities as enabling conditions for cooperation but insufficient to explain cross-cultural variation, which requires institutional and cultural explanation.
explanations.D: Passage B does not call for abandoning evolutionary psychology; it argues for the explanatory priority of cultural and institutional variables for a specific question (cross-cultural variation), while accepting evolutionary contributions.
explanations.E: This is precisely the inference passage B resists: free-rider punishment is cross-culturally consistent but still varies with institutional factors, so cross-cultural consistency does not automatically imply genetic encoding.

questions.questionStem: In passage A, the discussion of cooperation within groups conferring survival advantages over competing groups serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: introduce a competing hypothesis about the origins of cooperative behavior that the author then rejects

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide the logical structure of the evolutionary argument for a genetically transmitted cooperative disposition

choices.label: C
choices.text: illustrate the kind of institutional mechanism through which cooperative norms are maintained

choices.label: D
choices.text: explain why cross-cultural studies are the most reliable method for studying human behavior

choices.label: E
choices.text: demonstrate that evolutionary pressures act on individuals rather than on groups

explanations.correct: The passage walks through the evolutionary syllogism step by step: cooperation advantages groups → cooperators survive and reproduce more → the disposition is transmitted genetically. This is offered as the logical foundation of the evolutionary account of cooperation, not as a competing hypothesis or methodological point.
explanations.A: The author presents this argument as a position being endorsed and supported, not as a hypothesis introduced to be rejected.
explanations.B: Correct. The discussion sets out the causal chain—survival advantage, differential reproduction, genetic transmission—that constitutes the evolutionary case for cooperation.
explanations.C: Institutional mechanisms are introduced in passage B, not passage A; the discussion in passage A is about selection pressures, not institutions.
explanations.D: The author mentions cross-cultural studies later as supporting evidence, but the discussion of group-level advantages does not function to justify cross-cultural methodology.
explanations.E: The argument in passage A is explicitly about group-level advantages ('cooperation within a group confers survival advantages over competing groups'), not about individual-level selection as opposed to group-level selection.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A presents a theoretical framework; passage B accepts the framework and applies it to anthropological data.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A offers an evolutionary account of cooperative behavior; passage B argues that institutional and cultural variables better explain observed cross-cultural variation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A and passage B both conclude that neither genetic nor cultural factors alone can explain cooperative behavior.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A argues against evolutionary explanations of behavior; passage B defends them by citing anthropological evidence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A provides a case study in evolutionary reasoning; passage B extends that reasoning to novel domains of human sociality.

explanations.correct: Passage A advances the evolutionary account—genetic transmission of cooperative dispositions selected in ancestral environments—and supports it with cross-cultural consistency data. Passage B challenges this account by showing that the cross-cultural variation not explained by genetics is better accounted for by institutional and cultural variables. Choice B accurately describes this point/counterpoint structure.
explanations.A: Passage B does not accept the evolutionary framework; it argues that the framework is insufficient for explaining cross-cultural variation.
explanations.B: Correct. The description captures the oppositional structure: A presents the evolutionary account; B argues institutional/cultural factors are more explanatory.
explanations.C: Passage A does not conclude that cultural factors matter; it presents a predominantly genetic account. The synthesis attributed to both passages by choice C is not present in passage A.
explanations.D: The descriptions are inverted: it is passage B (not A) that questions evolutionary explanations, and passage A (not B) that defends them.
explanations.E: Passage B does not extend evolutionary reasoning; it offers an alternative (institutional and cultural) explanation.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the position advanced in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Societies with high levels of market integration consistently display lower rates of cooperative behavior than societies with minimal market integration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hunter-gatherer societies that have had no contact with world religions exhibit cooperative norms nearly identical to those found in industrialized societies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Laboratory studies demonstrate that individuals can be trained through repeated instruction to abandon cooperative dispositions entirely.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Genetic analysis reveals that the populations studied in cross-cultural cooperation research differ significantly in several alleles associated with social behavior.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Historical records show that cooperative norms in a given society change rapidly in response to shifts in political leadership.

explanations.correct: Passage A argues that cooperative norms are universal because they are genetically encoded. If isolated hunter-gatherer societies with no exposure to world religions or market institutions display cooperative norms nearly identical to those in industrialized societies, this strongly suggests the norms are not the product of institutional context but of something common to all human groups—consistent with the genetic account passage A advances.
explanations.A: This finding would support passage B's position that market integration—an institutional variable—explains variation in cooperation, not passage A's genetic account.
explanations.B: Correct. Convergent cooperative norms across societies with radically different institutional environments supports the claim that the norms are not institutionally constructed but reflect a shared human disposition—the core of passage A's argument.
explanations.C: If cooperative dispositions can be eliminated through training, this suggests they are flexible and culturally malleable, which would challenge, not support, the genetic-encoding account in passage A.
explanations.D: Passage A's argument treats all humans as sharing the same genetic heritage of evolved dispositions; finding significant genetic differences among populations studied would complicate passage A's universality claim rather than strengthen it.
explanations.E: Rapid change in cooperative norms in response to political shifts suggests cultural and institutional plasticity, which supports passage B's institutional account rather than passage A's genetic one.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of informed consent occupies a central position in contemporary medical ethics. At its core, the doctrine holds that a competent patient must be provided with all information material to a treatment decision—including risks, benefits, and alternatives—before agreeing to undergo any procedure. Courts articulating this standard have generally distinguished between two formulations: the professional standard, which measures disclosure against what a reasonable physician would ordinarily convey, and the patient-centered standard, which asks what a reasonable patient in the plaintiff's position would have wished to know. Most jurisdictions in the United States have moved toward the patient-centered standard on the ground that the purpose of consent is to honor patient autonomy, not to ratify prevailing medical custom.

Yet informed consent doctrine carries an unexamined tension. The doctrine assumes that the provision of information reliably produces genuine understanding, but empirical studies consistently show that patients retain only a fraction of what is disclosed to them during pre-procedure consultations, particularly when they are anxious or cognitively taxed. If the goal of informed consent is substantive autonomy—the patient's actual ability to weigh options and direct her own care—then a disclosure-centered model may systematically fail to achieve it. Some bioethicists have accordingly argued that the legal standard should shift focus from what is disclosed to whether comprehension was verified, a reform that would require clinicians to adopt teach-back methods and document patient understanding rather than merely recording that a consent form was signed.
rc.comparativeBPassage:
A widely accepted view in bioethics holds that informed consent is medicine's primary safeguard of patient autonomy, and that the law enforces this safeguard by requiring disclosure of material information. This view, while not without merit, conflates two distinct functions that consent is asked to perform simultaneously: a legal function of allocating liability for adverse outcomes, and an ethical function of genuinely enabling self-determination.

These functions frequently pull in opposite directions. From a legal standpoint, what matters is documentation—that the patient signed a form attesting to receipt of information, thereby shifting certain risks onto herself. From an ethical standpoint, what matters is that the patient arrived at a decision that authentically reflects her values. The legal apparatus is well designed for the first function and almost entirely silent on the second. Hospitals and physicians therefore have strong institutional incentives to satisfy the legal requirement of disclosure while doing little to ensure genuine comprehension.

This divergence has practical consequences. Patients who have 'consented' in the legal sense may nonetheless lack any meaningful grasp of what they have agreed to. Critics who argue that consent forms have become liability shields rather than instruments of patient empowerment are not wrong—they are simply identifying the predictable result of designing a legal mechanism around a single function when the underlying value it is meant to serve has two. The remedy is not to abandon legal oversight, but to redesign the legal standard so that documentation of comprehension, not merely disclosure, becomes the threshold for valid consent.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following questions is addressed by both passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: What procedural steps must a physician follow to obtain legally valid consent from a patient?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether the current legal standard for informed consent adequately serves the value of patient autonomy?

choices.label: C

Passage A argues that a disclosure-centered model may fail substantive autonomy when patients lack comprehension. Passage B argues that the legal mechanism is designed around liability allocation rather than genuine self-determination. Both therefore question whether current law achieves the autonomy value it is meant to serve.
explanations.A: Neither passage provides a procedural checklist for obtaining consent; both critique the standard at a structural level.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Only passage A discusses the professional vs. patient-centered distinction; passage B does not address this comparison.
explanations.D: Neither passage addresses the scope of liability protection afforded by signing forms; passage B mentions forms as liability shields but does not discuss what claims they bar.
explanations.E: Only passage B discusses institutional incentives explicitly; passage A does not address hospital or physician incentive structures.

questions.questionStem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

Passage B argues that consent forms have become liability shields and that patients who have consented legally may lack any meaningful grasp of what they agreed to. Both therefore accept that a signed form does not guarantee genuine understanding.

explanations.B: Neither author advocates abandoning legal oversight; passage B explicitly says the remedy is not to abandon legal oversight.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage A most likely mentions empirical studies on patient retention (second paragraph) primarily in order to

The retention data directly support the claim that this assumption is empirically unwarranted, which in turn motivates the author's proposed shift from disclosure-centered to comprehension-verification models. The function is to support the argument that substantive autonomy may not be achieved under current doctrine.
explanations.A: The studies are about patient retention, not physician disclosure completeness; they do not address whether physicians fail to convey information.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage B would be most likely to make which one of the following criticisms of the reform proposed in passage A?

choices.label: A
