choices.label: E
choices.text: Computational methods are most useful when applied to paintings whose attribution has been uncontested for more than a century.

explanations.correct: Passage B's final paragraph explicitly states: 'where computation and connoisseurship converge, attribution confidence increases.' This directly supports the inference that convergence of the two methods produces greater credibility than either alone.
explanations.A: Passage B argues explicitly against replacement, proposing computational methods as 'independent checks' on connoisseurship, not substitutes.
explanations.B: Passage B's circularity concern applies to training sets based on any prior attributions, whether by consensus or a single connoisseur; there is no basis in B for preferring single-connoisseur training.
explanations.C: Correct. This follows directly from passage B's closing statement about convergence increasing attribution confidence.
explanations.D: Passage B explicitly states the circularity problem 'does not invalidate computational methods'; this choice overstates the problem.
explanations.E: Passage B focuses on using computation as a check on received attributions, not particularly on long-uncontested ones; this temporal criterion is not in the text.

questions.questionStem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: whether connoisseurship-based attribution involves a method that is independently replicable

choices.label: B
choices.text: whether disputes among connoisseurs are sometimes resolved through consensus rather than by appeal to a verifiable standard

choices.label: C
choices.text: whether computational analysis can extract features from paintings that are invisible to the unaided eye

choices.label: D
choices.text: whether the training data used in computational attribution systems has any relationship to prior connoisseurship attributions

choices.label: E
choices.text: whether computational attribution methods have a valuable role to play in the study of Renaissance painting

explanations.correct: Passage A does not discuss computational methods and presents connoisseurship as the field's operative approach, implying skepticism toward external methodological challenges (though it does not explicitly mention computation). Passage B explicitly defends computational methods as valuable independent checks. The most likely point of disagreement is over whether computational methods are valuable — passage A's author, defending the connoisseurship tradition's institutional authority, would likely resist the implication that computation can serve as a check on expert judgment.
explanations.A: Both passages effectively agree that connoisseurship is not independently replicable — passage A states this explicitly, and passage B's argument presupposes it.
explanations.B: Both passages accept this; passage A explicitly describes consensus formation as the resolution mechanism.
explanations.C: Passage A does not discuss computational methods at all, so there is no basis for a disagreement about their capabilities.
explanations.D: Passage B discusses this relationship; passage A does not address computational methods, so there is no stated disagreement on this point.
explanations.E: Correct. Passage A implies the adequacy of connoisseurship as the field's method; passage B argues computational methods have a valuable supplementary role. This is the sharpest point of potential disagreement.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage B raises the circularity problem primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: demonstrate that computational attribution is fundamentally unreliable and should not be used to challenge received attributions

choices.label: B
choices.text: concede a limitation of computational methods while ultimately arguing for their use as a complement to connoisseurship

choices.label: C
choices.text: support the critics' view that computational analysis is only as good as the connoisseurship tradition it claims to supersede

choices.label: D
choices.text: argue that the training sets used in computational attribution must be rebuilt from first principles before the method can be trusted

choices.label: E
choices.text: illustrate the general problem of circularity that afflicts all empirical methods in the humanities

explanations.correct: Passage B introduces the circularity problem through the critics' voice and then explicitly states that it 'does not invalidate computational methods.' The circularity argument functions as a concession — acknowledging a real limitation — after which passage B pivots to its constructive recommendation that computation serve as a complement to connoisseurship. The concession-then-qualification structure is the key rhetorical move.
explanations.A: Passage B explicitly rejects this conclusion; the circularity problem does not invalidate the methods.
explanations.B: Correct. The circularity problem is introduced as a concession that B then qualifies, preserving a constructive role for computation.
explanations.C: Passage B presents the circularity problem as the critics' objection but does not endorse the critics' conclusion that computation is therefore useless.
explanations.D: Passage B does not recommend rebuilding training sets; it proposes a different role (complementarity) rather than a technical fix.
explanations.E: Passage B addresses a specific epistemological problem in attribution studies, not a general claim about all humanities methods.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following scenarios most closely conforms to the principle underlying the circularity problem described in passage B?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A historian uses diaries written by a political leader to assess the accuracy of biographies that relied on those same diaries.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A musicologist attributes an anonymous Baroque score to Bach by comparing it with authenticated Bach manuscripts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A literary scholar uses a novel's internal stylistic consistency to argue that it was written by a single author rather than multiple collaborators.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A forensic document examiner uses handwriting samples known to be genuine to train a classifier that then evaluates questioned documents.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A film archivist uses digitally restored prints to attribute uncredited silent films to specific directors on the basis of visual style.

explanations.correct: Passage B's circularity problem is that the computational classifier is trained on attributions previously made by the tradition being evaluated — so the method cannot provide independent validation. In choice A, the same diaries that were used as the basis for biographies are now used to assess those biographies' accuracy: the evaluative source is the same as the source being evaluated. This mirrors the circularity structure exactly.
explanations.A: Correct. The diaries are both the source for the biographies and the instrument of their evaluation — a direct parallel to the computational classifier trained on the very attributions it purports to verify.
explanations.B: This describes a standard comparative attribution method without any circularity; the authenticated manuscripts are genuinely independent of the anonymous score.
explanations.C: Internal stylistic consistency analysis does not rely on an external training set from a prior tradition; there is no circularity.
explanations.D: This is a reasonable description of training-set-based classification, but the handwriting samples known to be genuine are presumed to be independently established, not themselves products of a tradition being evaluated — so the circularity problem does not apply.
explanations.E: Visual-style attribution from digitally restored prints does not involve a circularity problem of the type described in passage B.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A argues that connoisseurship is the only reliable method for attributing Renaissance paintings, and passage B proposes computational methods as a superior replacement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A analyzes the epistemological basis and institutional character of connoisseurship-based attribution, and passage B introduces a new method that reveals limitations of connoisseurship while arguing it should supplement rather than supplant it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A defends the Morellian method against critics who favor quantitative approaches, and passage B presents those critics' arguments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A and passage B both endorse computational approaches to attribution but differ over how training data should be assembled.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A critiques the lack of objectivity in connoisseurship, and passage B defends objectivity as achievable through computational methods.

explanations.correct: Passage A provides a critical analysis of how connoisseurship works and derives its authority (epistemological + institutional character). Passage B introduces computational methods, acknowledges the circularity problem, and concludes that computation should serve as a complement to connoisseurship. This is a generalization/instance structure in part, but primarily a point/counterpoint with a nuanced resolution: A describes a tradition, B examines a challenge to it and argues for integration.
explanations.A: Passage A does not argue connoisseurship is the 'only reliable method'; it describes how attribution authority works. Passage B argues for complementarity, not replacement.
explanations.B: Correct. This accurately captures passage A's analytical function and passage B's introduction of a new approach with a nuanced conclusion.
explanations.C: Passage A does not defend the Morellian method against critics; it analyzes the method's epistemological basis. Passage B is not presented as critics' arguments.
explanations.D: Passage A does not endorse computational approaches; they are not mentioned in it.
explanations.E: Passage A does not advocate for computational objectivity; it analyzes the existing connoisseurship tradition. Passage B acknowledges the limits of computational objectivity (circularity problem).

rc.passage:
The doctrine of informed consent emerged from mid-twentieth-century bioethics as a corrective to a paternalistic medical tradition that treated patients as passive recipients of expert judgment. Under the classical model, a physician's authority derived from technical competence: patients were expected to defer to recommendations they could not evaluate independently. Informed consent fractured this arrangement. By requiring that patients receive accurate, comprehensible information about proposed treatments — including material risks, alternatives, and the consequences of no treatment — the doctrine repositioned the patient as a decision-making agent rather than an object of beneficent care.

The moral architecture of informed consent rests on two distinct foundations. The first is autonomy: respect for persons as self-governing agents requires that decisions affecting their bodies be their own. The second is epistemic: authentic consent requires not merely the absence of coercion but genuine understanding. Courts adjudicating informed-consent claims have not always distinguished these foundations clearly. The 'reasonable physician' standard — which asks what a competent clinician would typically disclose — privileges professional norms over individual autonomy. The 'reasonable patient' standard, by contrast, measures disclosure against what a reasonable person in the patient's circumstances would want to know. The shift toward the patient standard, visible in several state appellate decisions since the 1970s, signals a deeper philosophical reorientation: the physician's judgment is no longer the terminus of the clinical encounter.
rc.comparativeBPassage:
A persistent assumption in the bioethics literature holds that informed consent, properly implemented, reliably produces autonomous choice. This assumption deserves scrutiny. Empirical research in medical decision-making consistently documents a cluster of phenomena — anchoring, framing effects, affective forecasting errors — that distort patient deliberation regardless of the accuracy or completeness of disclosed information. Patients who receive statistically identical risk information expressed as survival rates versus mortality rates reach systematically different treatment decisions. Disclosure that is technically accurate may thus be epistemically insufficient.

Proponents of informed consent have tended to respond to such findings by calling for improvements in communication: clearer language, visual aids, teach-back protocols. These responses share an implicit premise: that cognitive distortions are exogenous impurities that a well-designed disclosure process can filter out. But the evidence suggests the contrary. Many of the biases at issue are not artifacts of poorly designed communications; they are features of human cognition under uncertainty. If that is correct, the informed-consent framework's foundational promise — that adequate disclosure reliably enables autonomous choice — is not merely unfulfilled but potentially unfulfillable. The practical implication is not that informed consent should be abandoned, but that the legal and ethical frameworks built around it need to be rebuilt on more modest epistemic foundations, acknowledging that consent can at best be an approximation of true autonomy, not its realization.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following questions is most central to both passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Should courts adopt the reasonable patient standard rather than the reasonable physician standard in informed-consent litigation?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Does the informed-consent doctrine succeed in securing genuinely autonomous patient decision-making?

choices.label: C
choices.text: How should bioethicists respond to empirical research on cognitive biases in medical settings?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Is the paternalistic model of medicine morally preferable to the autonomy-based model?

choices.label: E
choices.text: What evidentiary standards should govern malpractice claims arising from inadequate disclosure?

explanations.correct: Passage A traces informed consent's goal of repositioning patients as autonomous decision-making agents; passage B directly challenges whether that goal is achievable given cognitive-bias research. The shared question is whether the doctrine actually delivers autonomous choice.
explanations.A: Only passage A discusses the two legal standards; passage B does not address litigation standards.
explanations.B: Correct. Both passages engage this question — A by articulating the autonomy goal, B by questioning whether it can be met.
explanations.C: Only passage B discusses cognitive-bias research; passage A does not address it.
explanations.D: Neither passage defends paternalism; the question is about informed consent's adequacy, not the superiority of its predecessor.
explanations.E: Malpractice evidentiary standards are not discussed in either passage.

questions.questionStem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The paternalistic medical tradition that preceded informed consent treated patients as passive recipients of expert judgment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genuine informed consent requires that patients receive accurate and comprehensible information about proposed treatments.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Accurate and comprehensible disclosure of medical information is sufficient to enable authentic autonomous choice.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human cognition under uncertainty is subject to systematic biases that affect decision-making.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The informed-consent doctrine should be preserved in some form rather than abolished entirely.

explanations.correct: Passage A's framework treats disclosure of accurate, comprehensible information as the mechanism for autonomous decision-making. Passage B explicitly argues that such disclosure is 'epistemically insufficient' because cognitive biases operate regardless of disclosure quality. This is the sharpest point of disagreement.
explanations.A: Passage A asserts this; passage B does not dispute it — the historical framing is not contested.
explanations.B: Passage A affirms this; passage B accepts it as the doctrine's premise but argues it is insufficient, not that it is wrong as a requirement.
explanations.C: Correct. Passage A implicitly affirms sufficiency; passage B explicitly denies it.
explanations.D: Passage B asserts this; passage A does not address it, but neither disputes it.
explanations.E: Passage B explicitly says informed consent should not be abandoned; passage A's entire framework presupposes its value. Neither author would disagree.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A presents a legal doctrine and passage B argues for its complete replacement with a different framework.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A articulates the philosophical foundations of a doctrine and passage B challenges whether those foundations can bear the weight placed on them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A presents a historical narrative and passage B draws policy implications from the same historical evidence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A defends a majority view in bioethics and passage B summarizes minority objections that have been largely answered.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A describes a principle and passage B supplies an illustrative case study that confirms the principle's application.

explanations.correct: Passage A establishes the autonomy and epistemic foundations of informed consent; passage B uses empirical research on cognitive bias to argue those foundations cannot reliably deliver what the doctrine promises. B challenges A's architecture without wholly rejecting the doctrine.
explanations.A: Passage B explicitly says informed consent should not be abandoned — replacement is not its argument.
explanations.B: Correct. The relationship is philosophical articulation (A) followed by critique of whether the foundations hold (B).
explanations.C: Passage B does not draw implications from the same historical evidence as A; it draws on behavioral-science research not mentioned in A.
explanations.D: Passage B does not characterize itself as summarizing minority objections, nor does it say those objections have been answered — it argues they have not been.
explanations.E: Passage B does not confirm A's principles; it undercuts them. This inverts the actual relationship.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is discussed in passage A but not in passage B?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The distinction between two different legal standards for measuring the adequacy of medical disclosure

choices.label: B
choices.text: The claim that adequate disclosure may fail to produce genuinely autonomous decisions

choices.label: C
choices.text: The argument that cognitive distortions are features of human cognition rather than artifacts of poor communication

choices.label: D
choices.text: The role of framing effects in shaping patient responses to risk information

choices.label: E
choices.text: The inadequacy of informed consent's foundational promise

explanations.correct: Passage A explicitly contrasts the 'reasonable physician' standard with the 'reasonable patient' standard for disclosure adequacy. Passage B does not discuss either legal standard.
explanations.A: Correct. The two legal standards are introduced and contrasted only in passage A.
explanations.B: This claim is central to passage B, not uniquely present in passage A.
explanations.C: This argument appears only in passage B.
explanations.D: Framing effects are mentioned only in passage B.
explanations.E: The inadequacy argument is the thesis of passage B, not passage A.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage B would most likely respond to the shift toward the 'reasonable patient' standard described in passage A by pointing out that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the reasonable patient standard is philosophically inferior to the reasonable physician standard because it undervalues clinical expertise.

choices.label: B
choices.text: even when disclosure meets the reasonable patient standard, cognitive biases may prevent patients from using that information to make autonomous choices.

choices.label: C
choices.text: courts have consistently failed to apply the reasonable patient standard in a manner consistent with its underlying autonomy rationale.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the shift toward the reasonable patient standard was motivated by economic considerations rather than by genuine concern for patient autonomy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the reasonable patient standard requires physicians to disclose information that most patients find psychologically distressing and therefore counterproductive.

explanations.correct: Passage B's central argument is that cognitive biases operate regardless of the accuracy or completeness of disclosed information, making disclosure — however well calibrated to patient needs — insufficient for autonomous choice. Applied to A's 'reasonable patient' standard, B would say the standard improves disclosure but cannot overcome inherent cognitive distortions.
explanations.A: Passage B does not defend clinical expertise or criticize patient-centered standards as philosophically inferior; its critique is epistemic, not about whose norms govern disclosure.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the direct application of passage B's thesis to the legal development described in passage A.
explanations.C: Passage B does not discuss courts' application of any standard; it focuses on the behavioral-science critique.
explanations.D: Passage B offers no claims about the motivations behind legal developments; its argument is cognitive-scientific, not sociological.
explanations.E: Passage B does not argue that any standard produces psychologically distressing disclosures; that is outside the scope of its argument.

questions.questionStem: In passage B, the discussion of survival-rate versus mortality-rate framing serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate that physicians routinely manipulate disclosure to steer patients toward preferred treatment options.

choices.label: B
choices.text: demonstrate that statistically equivalent information can produce systematically different decisions, undermining the assumption that accurate disclosure ensures autonomous choice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: introduce a criticism of the reasonable physician standard that is later extended to the reasonable patient standard.

choices.label: D
choices.text: provide an example of the kind of improvement in communication that proponents of informed consent advocate.

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that numerical presentation of risk information is inherently superior to verbal presentation.

explanations.correct: The framing-effect example is introduced immediately after the claim that 'accurate disclosure may be epistemically insufficient.' Its function is to supply concrete evidence that technically accurate, complete information fails to generate consistent autonomous decisions — the core of passage B's challenge.
explanations.A: The example is not about physician manipulation; it is about how information framing affects patients' deliberation regardless of intent.
explanations.B: Correct. The example instantiates the claim that accuracy is insufficient by showing that identical facts, framed differently, produce different decisions.
explanations.C: Passage B does not discuss either legal standard; the legal standards are confined to passage A.
explanations.D: The example is offered as a problem with disclosure, not as a model of the improved communication that proponents recommend.
explanations.E: Passage B draws no conclusion about which numerical or verbal format is superior; the point is the comparison of logically equivalent framings.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage B would be most likely to make which one of the following criticisms of the moral architecture of informed consent as described in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A's autonomy foundation is internally inconsistent because self-governance requires epistemic competence that most patients lack.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A's two foundations — autonomy and epistemic adequacy — pull in opposite directions, making informed consent structurally incoherent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A's epistemic foundation assumes that adequate understanding can be produced by disclosure alone, an assumption that behavioral research on cognitive bias does not support.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A overstates the historical novelty of the informed-consent doctrine by ignoring earlier legal protections for patient choice.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A's framing of autonomy as the primary value in medical decision-making neglects other values such as beneficence and non-maleficence.

explanations.correct: Passage B's argument targets precisely the epistemic foundation: the doctrine assumes disclosure produces genuine understanding, but behavioral research shows cognitive biases operate even when disclosure is accurate and complete. This is the criticism that passage B's own text licenses.
explanations.A: Passage B does not argue that patients generally lack self-governance capacity; it argues that cognitive biases affect deliberation regardless of capacity — a different claim.
explanations.B: Passage B does not argue the two foundations conflict with each other; it argues the epistemic foundation is empirically unachievable.
explanations.C: Correct. Passage B's thesis is that the epistemic foundation's promise — disclosure enables understanding — is not borne out by behavioral evidence.
explanations.D: Passage B does not engage with legal history or make any claim about the doctrine's historical novelty.
explanations.E: Passage B does not invoke beneficence or non-maleficence; its critique is epistemic, not a reordering of competing bioethical values.

rc.passage:
The emergence of creole languages has long been treated by linguists as a natural experiment in language genesis — a rare opportunity to observe the formation of a new grammatical system under controlled historical conditions. The standard account, associated with the bioprogram hypothesis, holds that creoles share a common grammatical core despite arising from entirely different lexifier languages in geographically separate locations. This convergence, proponents argue, is not accidental: it reflects the activation of innate linguistic capacities that children bring to the task of acquiring a pidgin input. Where adults stabilize a pidgin — a contact variety used for limited transactional purposes and lacking a native speaker community — children acquiring that pidgin as a first language enrich it with the structural complexity characteristic of full human languages. The bioprogram, on this view, is a species-level default grammar that surfaces when children receive structurally impoverished input.

The evidence offered for grammatical convergence across creoles includes parallel marking of tense-mood-aspect through preverbal free morphemes, consistent subject-verb-object ordering, and the use of reduplication to signal iterative or distributive meaning. Critics have noted that these features are not unique to creoles; they appear in many non-creole languages worldwide. Proponents respond that what matters is their systematic co-occurrence in newly formed languages rather than their individual distribution — a co-occurrence that, they argue, cannot be explained by substrate influence or by independent grammaticalization of lexifier material alone.
rc.comparativeBPassage:
A widely accepted thesis in contact linguistics holds that creole languages exhibit universal grammatical properties traceable to an innate bioprogram. Closer examination of the comparative record, however, suggests that the apparent convergences among creoles are less robust than their advocates acknowledge, and that the explanatory work attributed to the bioprogram can be done more parsimoniously by attention to substrate languages and to the general pathways of grammatical change.

The strongest cases for bioprogram universality — the preverbal tense-mood-aspect system, for instance — dissolve under scrutiny when the substrate languages of the relevant creole communities are examined carefully. Many West African languages, which supplied the majority of enslaved speakers in Atlantic creole formation, employ preverbal aspect markers in constructions that closely parallel the creole patterns. The bioprogram hypothesis, unable to accommodate this correlation, must attribute it to coincidence. That attribution becomes increasingly implausible as the number of parallel substrate features grows.

More fundamentally, the bioprogram hypothesis depends on an impoverished characterization of pidgin input. Sociolinguistic documentation of living and recently stabilized pidgin communities reveals considerably more structural variability and complexity than the hypothesis requires. If children are receiving richer input than the model assumes, the developmental jump attributed to innate specification is substantially reduced. The convergences that remain can be accounted for by universal tendencies in grammaticalization — tendencies that operate in all languages, not as evidence of a creole-specific innate grammar, but as properties of human language change generally.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of passage B?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creole languages arose under unique historical conditions that make them unsuitable for testing general hypotheses about language genesis.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The bioprogram hypothesis fails because children acquiring creoles do not differ from children acquiring other languages.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The apparent grammatical universals of creole languages are better explained by substrate influence and general grammaticalization tendencies than by innate specification.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sociolinguistic documentation of pidgin communities has revealed that pidgins are full languages and therefore cannot serve as impoverished input.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The bioprogram hypothesis should be revised to incorporate substrate influence rather than abandoned entirely.

explanations.correct: Passage B's argument runs in two stages: first, that substrate-language parallels explain the preverbal aspect-marker convergences attributed to the bioprogram; second, that pidgin input is richer than the bioprogram model assumes, leaving only convergences explicable by general grammaticalization. Both stages support the conclusion in C.
explanations.A: Passage B does not argue creoles are unsuitable for study; it argues the evidence from them supports a different explanation.
explanations.B: Passage B does not compare creole-acquiring children to other children; its critique concerns the explanation of observed convergences, not child acquisition per se.
explanations.C: Correct. This integrates both stages of passage B's argument.
explanations.D: Passage B says pidgin input is richer than assumed, not that pidgins are 'full languages'; the distinction matters because B acknowledges a developmental phenomenon, just not an innate-bioprogram one.
explanations.E: Passage B does not call for revision of the bioprogram hypothesis; it argues the hypothesis is unnecessary because alternative explanations are more parsimonious.

questions.questionStem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whether creole languages emerged from contact between speakers of mutually unintelligible languages

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether the preverbal marking of tense, mood, and aspect is attested in creole languages

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether West African substrate languages influenced the formation of Atlantic creoles

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether the systematic co-occurrence of certain grammatical features in creoles is adequately explained by substrate influence alone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether reduplication is used to signal iterative or distributive meaning in any natural language

explanations.correct: Passage A acknowledges substrate influence as one possible explanation but argues that substrate influence alone cannot account for the systematic co-occurrence of features across geographically and historically separate creoles. Passage B argues the opposite — that substrate influence, combined with general grammaticalization, is sufficient. This is the central empirical disagreement.
explanations.A: Neither passage discusses the mutual intelligibility of contact languages; both presuppose a general contact-linguistics framework.
explanations.B: Both passages acknowledge preverbal TMA marking in creoles; neither disputes the datum, only its explanation.
explanations.C: Both passages acknowledge West African substrate influence; passage A accepts it as a partial factor, passage B gives it greater explanatory weight. The acknowledgment of influence itself is not disputed.
explanations.D: Correct. Passage A says substrate influence alone is insufficient; passage B argues it is sufficient (combined with grammaticalization).
explanations.E: Neither passage disputes reduplication as a cross-linguistic phenomenon; this is not a point of disagreement.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of passage B?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Introduces a widely accepted thesis, offers two independent lines of evidence against it, and concludes that the evidence instead supports an alternative explanation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Presents a paradox, analyzes its historical origins, and proposes a legislative remedy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Summarizes a theoretical position, concedes its main empirical success, and argues that the success is explicable without the theory's central mechanism.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Identifies a gap in the literature, reviews three studies that address the gap, and synthesizes them into a unified account.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Criticizes a hypothesis on methodological grounds, rehabilitates it with new data, and restates it in a revised form.

explanations.correct: Passage B opens by identifying the bioprogram thesis as widely accepted, then presents two lines of argument against it — substrate language parallels (paragraph 2) and the richness of pidgin input (paragraph 3) — and concludes both point toward alternative explanations (grammaticalization tendencies). This matches A.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Passage B does not discuss a paradox, historical origins in a narrative sense, or legislative remedies.
explanations.C: Passage B does not concede a main empirical success of the bioprogram hypothesis; it challenges the flagship cases (e.g., preverbal TMA) directly.
explanations.D: Passage B does not identify a gap in the literature or review numbered studies; it constructs an argument from substrate evidence and sociolinguistic documentation.
explanations.E: Passage B does not rehabilitate the bioprogram hypothesis or restate it in revised form; its conclusion is that alternative explanations are more parsimonious.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage A but not in passage B as evidence offered in support of creole grammatical universals?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The correlation between West African substrate languages and Atlantic creole patterns

choices.label: B
choices.text: The use of reduplication to mark iterative or distributive meaning

choices.label: C
choices.text: The structural complexity that children impose on impoverished pidgin input

choices.label: D
choices.text: The variability of grammatical structure found in living pidgin communities

choices.label: E
choices.text: The universal tendencies in grammaticalization observed across all languages

explanations.correct: Passage A explicitly lists reduplication as one of three pieces of evidence for grammatical convergence across creoles. Passage B does not mention reduplication at all — it focuses on preverbal TMA and pidgin input richness.
explanations.A: The West African substrate correlation is introduced by passage B as a counter-explanation, not by passage A as supporting evidence.
explanations.B: Correct. Reduplication is cited as evidence only in passage A.
explanations.C: Both passages discuss children's role in enriching pidgin input, though from different evaluative perspectives.
explanations.D: Structural variability in living pidgin communities is mentioned only in passage B.
explanations.E: Universal grammaticalization tendencies are invoked only in passage B.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage A would most likely respond to the argument in the final paragraph of passage B by claiming that

choices.label: A
choices.text: universal grammaticalization tendencies are themselves evidence that an innate language faculty constrains the directions of grammatical change.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the structural variability documented in living pidgin communities is an artifact of inadequate fieldwork methodologies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: sociolinguistic documentation of living pidgins is irrelevant because historical creole formation occurred in very different social conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the systematic co-occurrence of features in creoles cannot be explained by grammaticalization tendencies that operate equally in all languages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: children acquiring impoverished input cannot use general grammaticalization pathways because such pathways require large adult speaker communities.

explanations.correct: Passage A's specific rebuttal to substrate and grammaticalization explanations is that what matters is the systematic co-occurrence of features in newly formed languages, not the distribution of individual features. If grammaticalization operates equally in all languages, it cannot explain why these specific features co-occur specifically in creoles. Passage A's author would make exactly this point against B's final paragraph.
explanations.A: Passage A does not argue that grammaticalization tendencies are themselves evidence of an innate faculty; the innate faculty in passage A is the bioprogram, not a general grammaticalization mechanism.
explanations.B: Passage A does not make any claims about fieldwork methodology; criticizing methods is outside the scope of its argument.
explanations.C: Passage A does not argue that evidence from living pidgins is irrelevant; its argument concerns the explanation of convergences, not the relevance of contemporary documentation.
explanations.D: Correct. Passage A's argument turns on co-occurrence as the distinctive datum; grammaticalization in all languages would not explain co-occurrence specific to creole formation.
explanations.E: Passage A does not claim grammaticalization requires large speaker communities; this mechanistic detail is not part of its argument.

questions.questionStem: The reference to West African languages in the second paragraph of passage B serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: introduce a new empirical domain that the bioprogram hypothesis was not designed to address.

choices.label: B
choices.text: demonstrate that the bioprogram hypothesis must resort to implausible attributions of coincidence when confronted with substrate parallels.

choices.label: C
choices.text: support the claim that Atlantic creoles are the best-documented case of language genesis in the historical record.

choices.label: D
choices.text: establish that West African languages are structurally superior to the lexifier languages of Atlantic creoles.

choices.label: E
choices.text: concede a point to proponents of the bioprogram hypothesis before restating the substrate explanation.

explanations.correct: The reference to West African preverbal aspect markers is deployed to show that the bioprogram's flagship example — preverbal TMA marking — can be traced to substrate languages, and that dismissing this correlation as coincidence becomes increasingly untenable as more parallels accumulate. The function is to expose an explanatory weakness in the bioprogram hypothesis.
explanations.A: Passage B does not claim the bioprogram hypothesis was not designed to address substrate languages; bioprogram proponents do address substrate influence, which is why passage A mentions it as a competing explanation.
explanations.B: Correct. The West African evidence forces the bioprogram hypothesis to call the correlation a coincidence — an attribution passage B argues grows implausible.
explanations.C: Passage B makes no comparative claim about which creoles are best documented; the Atlantic example is chosen for its substrate evidence, not for documentation quality.
explanations.D: Passage B draws no comparison of structural superiority between West African and lexifier languages.
explanations.E: The reference is not a concession to bioprogram proponents; it is an attack on the hypothesis's strongest case.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following hypothetical findings would most directly support the bioprogram hypothesis as described in passage A while simultaneously undermining the central objection raised in the second paragraph of passage B?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A creole formed in a region whose substrate languages lack preverbal aspect markers nonetheless displays the same preverbal TMA system found in Atlantic creoles.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sociolinguistic fieldwork reveals that the pidgin from which a newly documented creole developed was structurally complex before children began acquiring it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several non-creole languages in West Africa have recently developed preverbal aspect-marking systems similar to those found in Atlantic creoles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Comparative analysis reveals that the subject-verb-object order characteristic of creoles also predominates among the substrate languages studied.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Children acquiring a creole pass through acquisition stages identical to those of children acquiring any other language, regardless of substrate.

explanations.correct: The bioprogram hypothesis predicts TMA convergences regardless of substrate. Passage B's second-paragraph objection is that West African substrate languages supply the TMA pattern, making the bioprogram unnecessary. A finding that a creole with non-West-African substrates also displays preverbal TMA would support the bioprogram (convergence without substrate source) and undermine B's objection (substrate correlation is not the explanation).
explanations.A: Correct. This directly tests and confirms the bioprogram's substrate-independence claim while removing the substrate-correlation explanation.
explanations.B: Richer pidgin input would support passage B's third-paragraph objection (developmental jump is overstated), not A's position; it does not address the second-paragraph objection about substrate.
explanations.C: Non-creole West African languages developing similar TMA systems later would not help the bioprogram; if anything, it would show that the feature spreads through contact or grammaticalization, supporting passage B.
explanations.D: SVO order in both creoles and substrates would support the substrate-influence explanation championed by passage B, undermining the bioprogram.
explanations.E: Identical acquisition stages might suggest no special innate bioprogram; it would not clearly support passage A's hypothesis about bioprogram activation specifically in impoverished-input conditions.

rc.passage:
For much of the nineteenth century, the music of Johann Sebastian Bach was regarded primarily as the work of a learned craftsman rather than that of a great composer. Concertgoers who thrilled to Beethoven or wept at Schubert tended to speak of Bach with respect, but the respect was of the sort one offers to a teacher of harmony: he had, it was said, mastered the rules, but he had not, like the Romantics, expressed himself through them. This standard view persisted well into the early twentieth century, and it still echoes whenever Bach is described as a composer of the head rather than of the heart.

The view captures something real. Bach did devote unusual attention to technical problems, and many of his works were plainly written for instruction, including pieces he composed to help his own children learn the keyboard. But to leave the matter there is to mistake a composer's discipline for his final aim. A closer acquaintance with the music shows that Bach's technical ingenuity was almost always in the service of expressive ends. The unfolding of a fugue, which can look on the page like an exercise in pattern, functions in performance as a way of gradually disclosing a single musical idea from many angles, and the listener who follows its progress is led through something closer to an argument than to a puzzle.

The misreading of Bach as a pure craftsman has its roots in the changing place of instrumental music in the nineteenth century. For Beethoven's heirs, instrumental music was the privileged vehicle for the artist's inner life, and a composer who did not supply obvious emotional signals — sudden dynamic contrasts, yearning melodies, programmatic titles — was assumed to lack such a life. Bach, whose emotional signals are often embedded in the movement of inner voices rather than placed on the musical surface, did not announce himself in the expected ways, and listeners concluded that he had little to announce.

Yet a sympathetic ear, trained to follow several independent melodic lines at once, will find in Bach's cantatas and instrumental works an emotional range that compares favorably with that of any later composer. The pieces do not weep on cue, but they grieve, exult, reflect, and console, often in the space of a few minutes. What the nineteenth-century listener heard as coolness was in fact a particular kind of restraint, one that trusted the music's architecture to carry feeling without underlining it. Seen this way, Bach is not the craftsman of legend, nor a closet Romantic, but a composer whose expressive aims pass through his technical means rather than around them.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The view of Bach as a merely technical composer misses the fact that his technical devices serve expressive ends.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bach's reputation in the nineteenth century suffered because audiences of that era preferred Beethoven and Schubert.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bach should properly be regarded as an early Romantic composer whose emotional aims were simply misunderstood.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Understanding Bach's fugues requires a listener capable of following several independent melodic lines simultaneously.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Much of Bach's keyboard music was written for instructional purposes, including the training of his own children.

explanations.correct: The passage sets up the standard 'craftsman, not composer' view in paragraph 1 and devotes the remainder to showing that Bach's technical ingenuity is in the service of expressive aims. A captures both the view being corrected and the author's corrective.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Paragraph-restatement-not-main-point: captures a contextual observation, not the thesis about the relation between technique and expression.
explanations.C: Too-strong / opposite-of-author: the final paragraph explicitly denies that Bach is 'a closet Romantic.'
explanations.D: Too narrow: the ability to follow independent lines is mentioned once to support the thesis, not as the thesis.
explanations.E: Half-right / paragraph-restatement: true per paragraph 2 but leaves out the corrective move that defines the passage.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the nineteenth-century view of Bach as a craftsman rather than a composer can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: complete rejection as based on factual error

choices.label: B
choices.text: partial agreement combined with a judgment that the view is ultimately inadequate

choices.label: C
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement, qualified only by minor reservations

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference, since the view has little bearing on contemporary concerns

choices.label: E
choices.text: uncertainty about whether the view has any defensible content at all

explanations.correct: The author writes that the standard view 'captures something real' (paragraph 2) — Bach did devote unusual attention to technical problems — but argues that it 'mistakes a composer's discipline for his final aim.' That is exactly partial agreement plus a judgment of inadequacy.
explanations.A: Too-strong: the author explicitly concedes that the view captures something real.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Opposite-tone: the author is critical of the view overall, not endorsing it.
explanations.D: The author engages with the view at length; indifference is unsupported.
explanations.E: Opposite of the text: the author clearly identifies what the view gets right.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A longstanding view is stated, partly conceded, explained historically, and then revised.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two competing scholarly theories are presented, and one is shown to be false.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A composer's career is traced chronologically from early instruction pieces to mature works.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An interpretive principle is introduced and then applied to a sequence of unrelated cases.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A critical consensus is described, defended against recent attacks, and reaffirmed.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 states the traditional view; paragraph 2 concedes what it gets right and begins the correction; paragraph 3 explains historically why the view arose; paragraph 4 offers the author's revised reading.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Mis-sequencing: the passage is not structured as a head-to-head between two theories, and neither is shown to be 'false.'
explanations.C: No chronology of Bach's career is traced.
explanations.D: Plausible-but-unused: no single interpretive principle is applied to multiple cases.
explanations.E: Opposite-tone: the consensus is being revised, not reaffirmed.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the nineteenth-century assumption that Bach lacked an inner life rested principally on

choices.label: A
choices.text: the fact that Bach composed primarily for religious rather than concert settings

choices.label: B
choices.text: the absence in his music of the obvious emotional signals that later audiences had come to expect

choices.label: C
choices.text: the widespread belief that fugues are exercises in pattern rather than arguments

choices.label: D
choices.text: a general nineteenth-century preference for vocal music over instrumental works

choices.label: E
choices.text: a lack of documentary evidence concerning the composer's private correspondence

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that a composer who did not supply 'obvious emotional signals — sudden dynamic contrasts, yearning melodies, programmatic titles — was assumed to lack such a life,' and that Bach's signals did not announce themselves in the expected ways.
explanations.A: Plausible-world fact not stated: the passage never discusses religious versus concert settings.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Wrong sentence: the fugue-as-pattern framing appears in paragraph 2 as a misreading of the music, not as the basis for the assumption about Bach's inner life.
explanations.D: Outside scope: the passage discusses instrumental music's prestige but never a preference for vocal music.
explanations.E: Outside scope: private correspondence is never mentioned.

questions.questionStem: The author's remark in paragraph 2 that a fugue 'functions in performance as a way of gradually disclosing a single musical idea from many angles' serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate how Bach's technical devices carry out expressive aims

choices.label: B
choices.text: concede that Bach's fugues are more difficult to follow than his other works

choices.label: C
choices.text: argue that fugues should be studied from the score rather than heard in performance

choices.label: D
choices.text: compare Bach's fugues unfavorably with the emotional directness of Romantic works

choices.label: E
choices.text: suggest that Bach's fugues were composed primarily as instructional exercises

explanations.correct: The remark appears as the author's concrete example of the claim immediately above — that Bach's technical ingenuity 'was almost always in the service of expressive ends.' Its function is illustrative.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Accurate-sounding but wrong function: the passage never grades fugues by difficulty of following.
explanations.C: Opposite of the text: the remark appeals to what happens 'in performance.'
explanations.D: Wrong function / opposite-tone: the remark is used to defend Bach, not to rank him below Romantics.
explanations.E: Function from a different paragraph: instructional composition is mentioned in paragraph 2, but not as the point of this particular sentence.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A composer's emotional range cannot be judged fairly on the basis of surface features alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any composer whose music lacks programmatic titles should be classified as a formalist.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bach's keyboard works are more emotionally expressive than his cantatas.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Instrumental music became the central artistic medium only after Bach's lifetime had ended.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nineteenth-century listeners were incapable of recognizing musical emotion in any form.

explanations.correct: The author argues that Bach's emotional signals are embedded in inner voices rather than placed on the surface, and that listeners who judged by surface signals missed his range. That directly supports A.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too-strong: the author uses programmatic titles as an example of surface signals, not as a criterion for classifying composers.
explanations.C: Outside scope: the passage treats cantatas and instrumental works together and does not compare them.
explanations.D: Half-right: the passage discusses the rise of instrumental music in the nineteenth century but does not fix a moment relative to Bach's life.
explanations.E: Overreach: the author criticizes a misreading, not a general incapacity.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the interpretive pattern the author applies to Bach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A novelist once dismissed as merely ornamental is reappraised when readers notice that her elaborate sentences carry precise emotional content.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A painter long celebrated for technical skill falls out of fashion when a new generation prefers more austere styles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A poet's private letters are published, allowing scholars to confirm biographical speculations that had long circulated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A philosopher abandons an early technical vocabulary in favor of a plainer style accessible to general readers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A composer widely regarded as emotionally expressive is shown, on close analysis, to have relied heavily on formal conventions.

explanations.correct: The pattern is: an artist dismissed as technically accomplished but expressively empty is shown, on closer attention, to use technical devices as the very vehicle of expression. A mirrors this exactly.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Surface-similarity: involves fashion and technical skill but reverses the direction — the artist falls out of favor rather than being reappraised upward.
explanations.C: Wrong mechanism: the pattern concerns the relation of technique to expression, not the emergence of new biographical evidence.
explanations.D: Wrong mechanism: the pattern does not involve a change in the artist's own style.
explanations.E: Inverts the direction: this is the opposite move — reducing an expressive artist to formalism.

rc.passage:
In the study of traditional tales, the figure known as the trickster — a clever, unruly character who outwits stronger beings by guile — has long posed a puzzle for interpreters. Anansi the spider in West African tradition, Coyote in many Native American traditions, and Hermes in early Greek mythology are all commonly grouped together under this label, and the grouping has encouraged a familiar reading: the trickster, it is said, exists to entertain, and his escapades serve chiefly as comic relief from the more solemn concerns of myth. This reading is not wrong, but it is partial, and taken alone it misses what makes the figure so persistent across cultures.

To see why, consider that the trickster's victories almost always depend on his marginal position. He is smaller than his opponents, lower in the social order, or denied access to the ordinary means of getting what he wants. His tools are speech, disguise, and an eye for rules that others follow without thinking. When Anansi secures the world's stories from the sky god, or when Coyote obtains fire from beings who hoarded it, the audience laughs, but it also absorbs a lesson about how the weak can act on a world arranged for the strong. The humor, in other words, is the vehicle of something more serious, and removing the seriousness leaves only a thin residue of jokes.

A second common reading treats the trickster as a symbol of pure disorder, a figure whose appeal lies in his willingness to break every rule. This too captures a real feature of the stories: trickster tales are full of taboo violations and reversals of expectation. But the trickster does not simply destroy the order he confronts. Often, as in the fire-theft stories, his transgressions bring a benefit that the community eventually accepts as its own. The order that results is not the order that existed before, but neither is it chaos; it is an order that has been forced to make room for something previously excluded.

Seen together, these observations suggest that the trickster's cross-cultural appeal rests on neither his comic charm nor his disruptive energy, but on the way he dramatizes a problem that every tradition faces: how to acknowledge, from within its own stories, that the settled order is not the whole of what is possible. The trickster does not merely amuse, and he does not merely rebel. He holds open a small, licensed space in which the rules can be examined from outside without being abandoned, and that, rather than his cleverness, is what keeps him at home in so many different mythologies.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The trickster figure is compelling across cultures because he gives traditions a way to reflect on their own settled order without discarding it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The trickster figure is best understood as a symbol of pure disorder whose appeal lies in his willingness to break rules.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anansi, Coyote, and Hermes should not be classified together, since each arises from a distinct cultural context.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The humor in trickster tales is the principal reason these stories have been preserved across so many traditions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trickster tales function mainly to teach listeners specific lessons about how the weak can prevail over the strong.

explanations.correct: Paragraphs 2 and 3 qualify the 'comic relief' and 'pure disorder' readings, and paragraph 4 states the author's integrating thesis: the trickster holds open a licensed space in which a tradition examines its own rules. A captures that thesis.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Opposite-of-author: paragraph 3 explicitly rejects the 'pure disorder' reading as partial.
explanations.C: Outside scope: the passage accepts the grouping and uses it productively.
explanations.D: Paragraph-restatement-not-main-point: captures the first reading the author corrects, not the thesis.
explanations.E: Too narrow: the weak-versus-strong theme is one strand, subsumed by the larger claim about reflection on order.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the view that the trickster exists mainly to provide comic relief is best described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: dismissal of the view as a misreading produced by careless scholarship

choices.label: B
choices.text: acceptance of the view as capturing something real but not the whole of what matters

choices.label: C
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement, with only a single minor qualification

choices.label: D
choices.text: suspicion that the view has no defensible content and is merely conventional

choices.label: E
choices.text: neutrality, since the author considers the question ultimately unanswerable

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 concedes that the comic-relief reading 'is not wrong, but it is partial.' That is precisely acceptance-with-qualification.
explanations.A: Too-strong: the author explicitly allows that the reading captures something real.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Opposite-tone: the author is corrective rather than endorsing.
explanations.D: Too-strong in the other direction; the author credits the view with capturing a real feature.
explanations.E: The author is not neutral; a clear qualifying judgment is offered.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the trickster's victories almost always depend on

choices.label: A
choices.text: his unusual physical strength relative to his opponents

choices.label: B
choices.text: the direct assistance of more powerful mythological beings

choices.label: C
choices.text: his marginal position and his skill with speech, disguise, and rules

choices.label: D
choices.text: the willingness of his community to abandon its ordinary customs

choices.label: E
choices.text: the intervention of a divine authority that sanctions his rule-breaking

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that the trickster's victories 'almost always depend on his marginal position' and identifies his tools as 'speech, disguise, and an eye for rules that others follow without thinking.'
explanations.A: Altered qualifier / opposite: the passage specifies that he is smaller or lower in the social order.
explanations.B: Plausible world-fact not stated: the passage does not mention assistance from more powerful beings.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Wrong sentence: the passage says the community eventually accepts the benefit, not that it abandons its customs.
explanations.E: Outside scope: divine sanction is not mentioned.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of fire-theft stories in paragraph 3 functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: show that the trickster's transgressions can produce benefits the community comes to accept

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that Coyote tales are more sophisticated than other trickster traditions

choices.label: C
choices.text: establish the historical priority of Native American trickster tales over West African ones

choices.label: D
choices.text: illustrate the comic dimension of trickster tales noted in paragraph 1

choices.label: E
choices.text: demonstrate that taboo violations in trickster tales are usually punished

explanations.correct: The fire-theft example is introduced to show that the trickster's rule-breaking 'brings a benefit that the community eventually accepts as its own,' supporting the author's correction of the 'pure disorder' reading.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Outside scope: the passage does not rank traditions by sophistication.
explanations.C: Outside scope: no claim of historical priority is made.
explanations.D: Function from a different paragraph: the comic dimension is a paragraph-1 concern; in paragraph 3 the example serves the order/disorder discussion.
explanations.E: Opposite of text: the example shows benefit, not punishment.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that a story in which a trickster figure broke every rule of his society and left no lasting change behind would

choices.label: A
choices.text: confirm the author's view that the trickster represents pure disorder

choices.label: B
choices.text: fit less comfortably than usual with the author's account of trickster tales

choices.label: C
choices.text: be unintelligible to audiences outside the tradition in which it was first told

choices.label: D
choices.text: prove that the comic-relief reading of trickster tales is entirely mistaken

choices.label: E
choices.text: show that trickster tales and myths of creation share a common origin

explanations.correct: The author argues that trickster tales typically leave a changed order behind — transgression plus accepted benefit. A tale that broke every rule without lasting change would be a poor fit for that account.
explanations.A: Opposite-of-author: the author rejects the 'pure disorder' reading.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Outside scope: the passage makes no claim about cross-cultural intelligibility.
explanations.D: Too-strong: the author treats the comic-relief reading as partial, not entirely mistaken.
explanations.E: Outside scope: creation myths are not discussed.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's position that the trickster holds open a licensed space for examining settled order?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In many traditions, trickster tales were performed during festivals in which ordinary social roles were temporarily suspended.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Trickster figures in some traditions are depicted as physically small or animal in form.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some scholars have argued that Anansi tales originated before Coyote tales.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Audiences typically laugh at the moment in a trickster tale when the trickster is first outwitted.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Certain trickster tales survive only in fragments, making their endings difficult to reconstruct.

explanations.correct: If trickster tales were performed in festivals that formally suspended ordinary roles, that confirms the author's picture of a 'small, licensed space' in which the settled order can be examined from outside without being abandoned.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Off-target claim: supports the 'marginal position' observation from paragraph 2, not the licensed-space thesis of paragraph 4.
explanations.C: Outside scope: historical priority does not bear on the author's claim.
explanations.D: Wrong direction / off-target: a moment of laughter does not specifically support the licensed-examination claim.
explanations.E: Outside scope: survival of fragments does not speak to the function the author ascribes.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the role the author assigns to the trickster figure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A traditional legal system designates a ceremonial role, filled during an annual assembly, whose holder is permitted to voice complaints that other members of the community cannot.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A group of rebels overturns the government of their country and replaces its laws with entirely new ones.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A historian writes a comic biography of a political leader, drawing attention to the leader's personal eccentricities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A theater troupe entertains audiences with purely slapstick performances that avoid political subjects.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A student masters the rules of a game so thoroughly that she never violates them in competition.

explanations.correct: The trickster holds open a small, licensed space in which rules can be examined from outside without being abandoned. A ceremonial role that licenses otherwise-unpermitted complaints within a standing legal order mirrors this precisely.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Inverts the direction: the trickster does not overturn the order; he opens a space within it.
explanations.C: Surface-similarity: involves humor but lacks the licensed examination of shared rules; the biography addresses one individual's eccentricities.
explanations.D: Matches only the comic-relief strand the author treats as partial; no reflection on order.
explanations.E: Opposite of the pattern: the student never steps outside the rules.

rc.passage:
The Japanese haiku tradition, originating in the sixteenth century, represents one of literature's most refined distillations of human experience into a concentrated form. A haiku consists of three lines arranged in a 5-7-5 syllable pattern, and despite its brevity, it captures a complete moment of perception with remarkable clarity. Unlike longer poetic forms that develop themes through extended meditation, the haiku artist works through suggestion and juxtaposition, allowing the reader to complete the meaning through personal insight.

The haiku's power lies partly in its treatment of nature. Early haiku masters like Basho used seasonal images not merely as decorative elements but as windows into deeper truths about impermanence and change. A single frog jumping into a pond becomes, in Basho's famous poem, an emblem of sudden awakening. The image itself is simple, drawn from everyday observation, yet it resonates with philosophical weight. This technique—capturing the universal through the particular—distinguishes haiku from other forms of nature poetry that rely on elaborate symbolism or romantic sentiment.

Over centuries, haiku masters maintained remarkable fidelity to these essential principles even as they extended the form's range. The discipline required to work within such strict constraints actually liberated poets, forcing them to choose words with extraordinary precision. Every syllable matters; every image must earn its place. This economy of language became haiku's signature, a purity of expression that influenced modern poetry throughout the twentieth century and continues to attract poets today who seek to distill experience into its most essential elements.

questions.questionStem: The main point of the passage is that haiku

choices.label: A
choices.text: originated in sixteenth-century Japan and has remained unchanged since then

choices.label: B
choices.text: achieves its power through strict form and precise language that capture experience in concentrated form

choices.label: C
choices.text: uses nature imagery as a substitute for romantic sentiment

choices.label: D
choices.text: is an inferior form of poetry compared to longer poetic traditions

choices.label: E
choices.text: requires readers to understand complex symbolic systems to appreciate it

explanations.correct: The passage consistently emphasizes how haiku captures complete moments through strict form (5-7-5 syllables), precise word choice, and concentrated expression. B accurately captures this central thesis stated in paragraph 1 and reinforced in paragraph 3.
explanations.A: The passage notes that haiku has 'extended' and evolved over centuries; it has not remained unchanged.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage says nature imagery is used instead of 'elaborate symbolism or romantic sentiment,' but the primary point is about concentrated expression, not the rejection of sentiment.
explanations.D: The passage makes no comparative judgment about superiority; it praises haiku on its own terms.
explanations.E: The passage emphasizes simplicity and directness of images, not complexity of symbolism.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Basho's poem about a frog serves primarily as an example of

choices.label: A
choices.text: nature imagery used for purely decorative purposes

choices.label: B
choices.text: a simple image from everyday observation that resonates with deeper meaning

choices.label: C
choices.text: elaborate symbolism characteristic of haiku poetry

choices.label: D
choices.text: the romantic sentiment that dominates traditional haiku

choices.label: E
choices.text: a violation of the 5-7-5 syllable structure required in haiku

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly states that Basho's frog poem demonstrates how 'a single frog jumping into a pond becomes...an emblem of sudden awakening' and notes that 'the image itself is simple, drawn from everyday observation, yet it resonates with philosophical weight.' B directly paraphrases this.
explanations.A: The passage says nature images are used as 'windows into deeper truths,' not merely decorative.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage contrasts haiku with forms that rely on 'elaborate symbolism'; Basho's approach avoids this.
explanations.D: The passage explicitly says haiku does not rely on 'romantic sentiment.'
explanations.E: The passage does not discuss whether Basho's poem violates structural rules.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the constraints imposed by haiku's formal structure can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: disapproving, since such strict rules prevent poets from expressing themselves freely

choices.label: B
choices.text: appreciative, viewing the constraints as enabling rather than limiting artistic expression

choices.label: C
choices.text: ambivalent, seeing both benefits and drawbacks to the rigid syllable count

choices.label: D
choices.text: dismissive, suggesting that modern poets should reject traditional haiku forms

choices.label: E
choices.text: analytical, merely explaining the historical reasons for haiku's formal requirements

explanations.correct: The author states that 'The discipline required to work within such strict constraints actually liberated poets,' and praises haiku's 'purity of expression.' This demonstrates clear approval of how the formal structure enables rather than limits artistic expression.
explanations.A: The passage explicitly contradicts this by saying constraints 'liberated' poets.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage takes a clearly positive stance, not an ambivalent one.
explanations.D: The author celebrates haiku's continued influence and modern relevance, not its rejection.
explanations.E: The author goes beyond mere explanation to express admiration for the constraints' effects.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from the passage that haiku poets must

choices.label: A
choices.text: have formal training in philosophy before composing poetry

choices.label: B
choices.text: develop a keen ability to select words that achieve maximum meaning within tight constraints

choices.label: C
choices.text: avoid all references to the natural world in their compositions

choices.label: D
choices.text: imitate the style of Basho in order to be considered authentic

choices.label: E
choices.text: include elaborate symbolic systems that readers must decode

explanations.correct: The passage states that 'Every syllable matters; every image must earn its place' and that the form 'forced them to choose words with extraordinary precision.' These statements support the inference that haiku poets must develop exceptional skill in word selection within strict limits.
explanations.A: While haiku may resonate with philosophical ideas, the passage does not suggest poets need philosophical training.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage emphasizes nature imagery as central to haiku; poets do not avoid it.
explanations.D: The passage notes that haiku 'extended' and evolved over time, implying diversity beyond strict Basho imitation.
explanations.E: The passage explicitly contrasts haiku with forms that rely on 'elaborate symbolism.'

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to haiku's influence on twentieth-century poetry serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: argue that haiku is superior to modern poetry

choices.label: B
choices.text: demonstrate that haiku's principles of precision and economy continue to be valued

choices.label: C
choices.text: suggest that all modern poets should write haiku exclusively

choices.label: D
choices.text: show that Western poets have completely replaced traditional forms with haiku

choices.label: E
choices.text: prove that haiku is easier to write than other poetic forms

explanations.correct: The reference to twentieth-century influence comes at the end of a paragraph explaining haiku's 'economy of language' and 'purity of expression.' The author cites this influence to show that haiku's fundamental principles remain relevant and valued by modern poets seeking to 'distill experience.'
explanations.A: The passage makes no comparison claiming superiority.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage suggests influence, not that all poets should write exclusively in this form.
explanations.D: The passage indicates haiku influenced modern poetry without suggesting complete replacement of other forms.
explanations.E: The passage emphasizes haiku's difficulty and precision, not its ease.

questions.questionStem: The passage is organized by

choices.label: A
choices.text: presenting a definition, illustrating it with examples, and explaining its enduring influence

choices.label: B
choices.text: contrasting haiku with other poetic forms throughout history

choices.label: C
choices.text: chronologically tracing the development of haiku from the sixteenth century to the present

choices.label: D
choices.text: refuting common misconceptions about haiku's origins

choices.label: E
choices.text: analyzing the biographies of individual haiku masters
