explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 defines haiku and its essential characteristics (5-7-5 form, suggestion through juxtaposition). Paragraph 2 illustrates these principles with Basho's frog example and explains how it differs from other nature poetry. Paragraph 3 discusses haiku's enduring influence on modern poetry. A accurately describes this structure.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: While comparisons are made, the passage is not organized around contrast.
explanations.C: The passage mentions origin and modern influence but does not chronologically trace development.
explanations.D: The passage does not refute misconceptions; it explains principles.
explanations.E: Only Basho is mentioned by name; the passage is not biographical.

questions.questionStem: The passage states that the haiku form differs from longer poetic traditions in that haiku

choices.label: A
choices.text: always uses elaborate romantic symbolism

choices.label: B
choices.text: developed in Western rather than Eastern cultures

choices.label: C
choices.text: works through suggestion and juxtaposition rather than extended meditation

choices.label: D
choices.text: requires readers to have formal philosophical training

choices.label: E
choices.text: has remained completely unchanged since its sixteenth-century origins

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly states in paragraph 1: 'Unlike longer poetic forms that develop themes through extended meditation, the haiku artist works through suggestion and juxtaposition.' C directly paraphrases this distinction.
explanations.A: The passage says haiku avoids elaborate symbolism, not that it uses it.
explanations.B: The passage identifies haiku as Japanese in origin.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The passage makes no such requirement.
explanations.E: The passage notes that haiku has 'extended' over centuries.

rc.passage:
The development of Renaissance perspective in fifteenth-century Italy marked a fundamental shift in how artists understood and represented space on a two-dimensional surface. Before the systematic development of linear perspective, painters relied on intuitive approaches to spatial representation, often creating images in which the size of figures bore little relationship to their distance from the viewer. The innovation of perspective, pioneered by artists like Filippo Brunelleschi and theorized by Leon Battista Alberti, provided a mathematical system for constructing the illusion of three-dimensional depth.

Perspective, however, was more than a technical tool for achieving visual realism. It embodied a revolutionary shift in how humans understood their relationship to the visual world. By establishing a fixed viewpoint from which all spatial relationships were calculated, perspective placed the observer at the center of the visual universe. This was not merely a matter of artistic technique but reflected the broader intellectual currents of the Renaissance, which increasingly emphasized the importance of individual human perception and rationality. Artists using perspective were, in effect, asserting that objective space could be understood through systematic observation and mathematical principles—a claim that carried profound philosophical implications.

The adoption of perspective did not occur uniformly across Europe, nor did it represent an unambiguous artistic progress. Some artists deliberately rejected perspective in favor of other spatial conventions, viewing the distortions created by strict perspective—such as the diminishment of distant figures—as less artistically effective than alternative approaches. Yet even these artists who resisted perspective could not entirely escape its influence, as the technique had become the dominant visual language of European art. By the sixteenth century, perspective had become so thoroughly integrated into Western artistic practice that it seemed natural and inevitable, obscuring the fact that it was itself a culturally specific invention.

questions.questionStem: The primary purpose of the passage is to

choices.label: A
choices.text: prove that Renaissance perspective is mathematically superior to all other artistic systems

choices.label: B
choices.text: explain how Renaissance perspective developed mathematically and what its broader significance was

choices.label: C
choices.text: argue that artists should reject perspective in favor of older artistic traditions

choices.label: D
choices.text: describe the life and accomplishments of Filippo Brunelleschi

choices.label: E
choices.text: criticize the Renaissance for overemphasizing individual perception

explanations.correct: The passage explains both the technical/mathematical development of perspective (paragraphs 1-2) and its philosophical significance reflecting Renaissance values about human perception and rationality. B captures this dual focus.
explanations.A: The passage does not claim superiority but notes the technique was culturally specific.
explanations.B: Correct.

rc.passage:
West African griot traditions represent one of humanity's oldest continuous storytelling practices, with roots extending back centuries into the pre-colonial past. Griots—professional historians, musicians, and oral poets—served as keepers of communal memory, preserving genealogies, historical events, and moral teachings through performance and song. Unlike written historical records, which can be consulted in silence and solitude, the griot tradition embedded knowledge within performance, creating a dynamic relationship between narrator and audience that required active participation and emotional engagement.

The role of the griot extended far beyond entertainment. In West African societies, griots held respected positions as advisors and counselors to rulers, their authority deriving from their mastery of historical knowledge and their rhetorical skill. The griot's recitation of a ruler's genealogy served to legitimize power and connect present authority to ancestral precedent. Through elaborate verbal formulas, rhythmic patterns, and musical accompaniment, griots crafted narratives that were simultaneously historical accounts and artistic performances. The form itself—the way knowledge was shaped and presented—was as important as the factual content, since the memorability of the narrative ensured its preservation and transmission across generations.

When European colonizers arrived in West Africa, the griot tradition faced unprecedented pressures. The introduction of written colonial records and missionary-sponsored literacy campaigns positioned oral tradition as backward and unreliable, a judgment that persisted long after colonial rule ended. Yet griots did not simply fade away; instead, they adapted their practices to changing circumstances, incorporating new themes and audiences while maintaining their fundamental commitment to preserving and transmitting cultural knowledge. Today, the griot tradition endures in modified forms, recognized increasingly as an invaluable repository of cultural wisdom and historical understanding that written archives alone cannot fully capture.

choices.label: D

choices.label: E

explanations.correct: The passage explains griots' important roles as historians and advisors (paragraph 2), describes the challenges they faced under colonialism (paragraph 3), and emphasizes their adaptation and endurance. B captures the passage's thesis about both function and resilience.
explanations.A: The passage explicitly states that griots 'did not simply fade away' and the tradition 'endures.'
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage emphasizes the griot's role as a 'keeper of communal memory' and advisor, not mere entertainment.

rc.passage: The Japanese haiku tradition has long been celebrated in the West as a model of poetic economy and precision. Yet most readers encounter haiku through translations that fundamentally misrepresent the form. A traditional haiku consists of seventeen syllables arranged in a 5-7-5 pattern, but this structure emerges from the phonetic properties of Japanese, where syllable counts convey rhythmic information unavailable in English. When English translators insist on maintaining the 5-7-5 syllable count, they must often distort word choice or syntax to fit the constraint, sacrificing the clarity and naturalness that define authentic haiku. The fundamental challenge lies in recognizing that haiku is not primarily a syllable-counting exercise, but rather an art form grounded in presenting a single moment of perception with absolute clarity. A haiku captures a fleeting instant—a frog leaping into a pond, a crow landing on a winter branch—and uses language so precise and unadorned that the reader experiences the moment directly, without mediation. The best English-language haiku, therefore, do not simply replicate the 5-7-5 pattern but instead focus on the haiku's true essence: economy of language and the presentation of a vivid, unmediated sensory image. This demands that translators and English poets working in the form prioritize fidelity to the image and the clarity of perception over mechanical adherence to syllable counts.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.text: Japanese haiku relies on syllable counting in ways that English haiku cannot replicate.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Translators of haiku must choose between maintaining syllable count and preserving the clarity of the original poem.

explanations.correct: Choice B captures the main thesis: the passage argues that English haiku should prioritize the presentation of vivid, unmediated sensory images over mechanical syllable-counting, thereby preserving haiku's true essence.
explanations.A: Too broad and makes a claim about global celebration not supported by the passage.
explanations.C: Correct observation but incomplete; the passage does not stop at acknowledging the syllable pattern's limits but prescribes a solution.
explanations.D: A supporting point but not the main point; the passage's concern is how English haiku should be translated, not merely how it differs from Japanese.
explanations.E: Presents the problem without the passage's solution and emphasis on prioritization.
explanations.B: Correct.

rc.passage: The medieval manuscript tradition developed a distinctive visual language to guide readers through complex theological texts. Marginalia—notes, drawings, and annotations written in the margins of pages—served not as mere decorative elements but as functional guides to interpretation. In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, as universities expanded and scholarly debate intensified, margins became increasingly crowded with interpretive apparatus. A scholar might encounter a biblical passage in the center column, surrounded on all sides by glosses—brief explanatory notes—from multiple authorities, each offering a different interpretive angle. This density of textual layers reflected the medieval understanding that meaning was not fixed in the original text alone but emerged through the accumulated wisdom of learned tradition. The practice of glossing assumed that understanding required engaging with multiple voices, and the physical layout of the glossed manuscript embodied this assumption. Rather than presenting readers with a single authoritative reading, glossed manuscripts invited—even demanded—active intellectual engagement. Readers had to navigate among competing interpretations, weigh different authorities, and construct their own synthesis of meaning. This collaborative approach to reading and interpretation anticipated modern scholarly practice, where knowledge is understood as the product of ongoing dialogue among many minds rather than the pronouncement of a single expert. The medieval manuscript thus functioned as an early model of what we might call 'distributed knowledge'—the insight that understanding emerges not from solitary contemplation but from the interaction of multiple perspectives.

rc.passage: West African griot traditions represent one of the world's oldest systems of oral history and artistic performance. Griots—professional historians, musicians, and storytellers—served as living archives of communal knowledge, preserving genealogies, historical events, and moral teachings through performance rather than written documentation. Unlike the European literary tradition, which privileges the written word as the primary repository of cultural memory, griot practice assumes that performance, memory, and social transmission constitute equally valid modes of preserving and transmitting knowledge. This assumption shaped not only how griots transmitted information but also how they conceptualized the relationship between a story and its meaning. A griot did not view a story as a fixed text to be reproduced identically each time; instead, each performance was understood as an adaptation tailored to the specific audience, occasion, and social context. The same historical narrative might be embellished differently for a child, a warrior, a merchant, or a community gathering, reflecting the griot's judgment about what aspect of the tradition was most relevant and meaningful for that particular audience. Rather than undermining the authority of the transmitted knowledge, this flexibility in performance strengthened it. By connecting the story to the immediate needs and understanding of the listener, the griot ensured that historical knowledge remained vital and applicable to contemporary life. The griot tradition thus presents an alternative model of how cultural memory can be organized and transmitted—one that emphasizes responsiveness to audience and context over fixed textuality. This model offers important lessons for modern societies increasingly concerned with how to preserve and transmit cultural heritage in ways that remain meaningful and accessible to diverse audiences.

choices.label: D

explanations.B: Correct.

explanations.D: The passage argues the opposite: flexibility strengthened, not undermined, authority.
explanations.E: The passage presents griot practice as a model; it does not recommend abandoning written records.

rc.passage:
The medieval illuminated manuscript represents one of the most remarkable achievements of Western art, yet its significance is often misunderstood. Scholars have traditionally celebrated these works primarily for their technical virtuosity—the jewel-like colors, the intricate gold leaf, the microscopic detail that required extraordinary patience and skill. However, the true importance of illuminated manuscripts lies not merely in their visual splendor, but in their role as instruments of spiritual transformation. The monks who created these works understood that beauty itself could be a path to divine contemplation.

The word "illuminate" comes from the Latin "illuminare," meaning to light up or make bright. In the medieval Christian tradition, this term carried profound metaphorical weight. Just as Christ was understood as the light of the world, illuminated manuscripts were meant to embody and transmit spiritual illumination to the reader. When a monk spent months or years laboriously decorating the margins of a Gospel or Psalter, he was not simply producing a beautiful object; he was participating in a sacred act. The decorated initials, the marginalia, and the intricate borders surrounding the text all functioned as visual prayers, drawing the reader's eye toward contemplation of the divine.

Moreover, the act of creating an illuminated manuscript was itself a form of devotion. The monastic tradition emphasized that every task performed with genuine intention and care constituted a form of worship. A monk copying and illuminating a religious text was engaging in what medieval theology called "lectio divina," a meditative reading practice that transformed both the manuscript and its creator. The repetitive, meticulous work of decoration demanded total focus and presence—a state of mind remarkably similar to modern meditation. In this sense, the illuminated manuscript was as much a spiritual practice as a finished artistic product.

rc.passage:
Among twentieth-century movements in literary study, none exerted a more durable influence on classroom practice than the school known as the New Criticism. Its proponents, writing principally in the 1940s and 1950s, urged that a poem be treated as a self-sufficient verbal object, to be interpreted without appeal to the author's biography, the reader's reactions, or the historical moment of composition. The standard account presents the movement as an austere formalism, devoted to keeping the poem in a kind of quarantine, and it is easy to see why: Cleanth Brooks famously warned against the "heresy of paraphrase," and W. K. Wimsatt's essays on the intentional and affective fallacies seemed to seal the poem off from both its maker and its audience.

This portrait, while not inaccurate in outline, obscures a subtler commitment. For the New Critics did not actually claim that biography and history were irrelevant to a poem's meaning; they claimed, rather, that such information could not substitute for the close reading of the text itself. A critic who had exhausted the poem's internal tensions — its ironies, paradoxes, and shifts of tone — was free to consult historical context, and indeed often had to, in order to gloss an archaic word or identify an allusion that the text itself signaled. What the movement rejected was the practice, common in earlier scholarship, of treating the poem as a transparent window onto the poet's intentions or the period's concerns, with little attention paid to the pressures of the language on the page.

Seen in this light, the New Criticism was less an act of quarantine than a redistribution of interpretive labor. Its leading figures wrote extensively on Donne, Keats, and Yeats, and their readings regularly draw upon biographical and historical matter; but they insisted that such matter be earned by the text — introduced only when the text's own evidence demanded it, rather than imposed on the text from without. Later critics, working under the banners of reader-response theory and cultural studies, would charge the New Critics with naïveté about the ideological freight carried by any act of reading, and about the social forces that shape what a given community is prepared to notice in a poem. That charge has force. It is worth remembering, however, that the New Critics' close-reading discipline survived their doctrines, and continues to shape how literature is taught even in departments that officially repudiate formalism.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The New Criticism rejected biography and history as sources of poetic meaning, a position that later critics correctly repudiated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The standard view of the New Criticism as a strict formalism is oversimplified; the movement's real commitment was that extratextual information be subordinated to close reading of the text.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reader-response theory and cultural studies have exposed the ideological blindness of the New Criticism and displaced its methods from the contemporary classroom.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cleanth Brooks and W. K. Wimsatt were less doctrinaire about biography than their most famous pronouncements suggest, and their readings of Donne and Keats prove it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The enduring influence of the New Criticism on the teaching of literature owes more to its pedagogical techniques than to the philosophical doctrines that originally motivated them.

explanations.correct: The passage presents the 'austere formalism' picture as the standard account, then argues that the New Critics' real position was that extratextual material had to be earned by the text, not excluded from it. B captures both halves — the received view and the author's corrective.
explanations.A: Reverses the author's corrective: the passage denies that the New Critics rejected biography and history outright.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Paragraph-level restatement of a single point in paragraph 3; the author acknowledges the force of the charge but does not make the displacement of New Criticism his thesis.
explanations.D: Too narrow — fixates on particular critics' practice rather than the broader claim about what the movement actually held.
explanations.E: Picks up the passage's closing observation and promotes it to the thesis; the pedagogical-survival point is a coda, not the main argument.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the New Criticism can most accurately be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: unreserved admiration for its rigor and its rejection of historical method

choices.label: B
choices.text: qualified respect, tempered by acknowledgment of its theoretical limitations

choices.label: C
choices.text: sharp disapproval of its formalist doctrine but appreciation for the careers of its leading figures

choices.label: D
choices.text: detached neutrality toward a movement whose influence has largely ended

choices.label: E
choices.text: enthusiasm for its pedagogical legacy and indifference toward its interpretive principles

explanations.correct: The author defends the New Criticism against a simplifying portrait and credits its lasting pedagogical influence, while conceding that the charge of ideological naïveté 'has force.' That combination is qualified respect.
explanations.A: Overstated positivity; the author concedes the later critics' charge has force and never endorses rejection of historical method.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author does not disapprove of the doctrine — he reinterprets it more sympathetically.
explanations.D: The passage is evaluative, not neutral, and explicitly says New Critical practices 'continue to shape' teaching.
explanations.E: Mixes two attitudes in the wrong combination; the author respects both the interpretive commitment and the pedagogical legacy.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the New Critics permitted a critic to consult historical or biographical information in which of the following circumstances?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When the critic wished to recover the poet's intentions in composing the poem

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only after every trace of irony and paradox in the poem had been fully resolved

choices.label: C
choices.text: When the text's own evidence demanded it, for instance to gloss an archaic word or identify an allusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whenever such information had been authenticated by scholars in the period concerned

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only when writing for students, who could not be expected to read closely on their own

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that such material was admitted when needed 'to gloss an archaic word or identify an allusion,' and paragraph 3 generalizes this: extratextual matter was to be 'earned by the text.' C matches both formulations.
explanations.A: Reverses the New Critics' explicit position; Wimsatt's 'intentional fallacy' essay, referenced in the passage, rejects recovery of intentions as the aim.
explanations.B: Altered qualifier: the passage says a critic who had 'exhausted the poem's internal tensions' could consult such material, not that every trace had to be resolved first; 'exhausted' means 'worked through,' and no absolute threshold is described.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Plausible-world detail the passage never states.
explanations.E: Out of scope; the passage does not discuss writing for students.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to Brooks's warning against the "heresy of paraphrase" and to Wimsatt's essays on the intentional and affective fallacies (paragraph 1) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate why the standard view of the New Criticism as an austere formalism has seemed well-founded

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide textual evidence that the New Critics did in fact exclude biography and history from interpretation

choices.label: C
choices.text: contrast the positions of two leading New Critics with one another

choices.label: D
choices.text: signal the author's disagreement with Brooks and Wimsatt and prepare the reader for a refutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: demonstrate that even the movement's defenders concede its philosophical naïveté

explanations.correct: These citations appear immediately after the sentence 'it is easy to see why' the standard account of the New Criticism as austere formalism arose. They are offered to motivate the received view, which the author will then complicate.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The author's whole point is that these pronouncements do not actually mean what the standard view takes them to mean.
explanations.C: No contrast between Brooks and Wimsatt is drawn; they are adduced together.
explanations.D: Too strong: the author does not refute Brooks and Wimsatt but reinterprets them sympathetically.
explanations.E: The concession of naïveté appears in paragraph 3 and is attributed to later critics, not to Brooks or Wimsatt.

questions.questionStem: The passage suggests that a scholar who treats a poem as a "transparent window onto the poet's intentions" would most likely be criticized by the author on the grounds that such a scholar

choices.label: A
choices.text: cannot explain why the New Criticism has persisted as a pedagogical influence

choices.label: B
choices.text: underestimates the ideological freight carried by any act of reading

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to give sufficient weight to the pressures that the poem's own language exerts on its meaning

choices.label: D
choices.text: relies on biographical evidence that is often unavailable or unreliable

choices.label: E
choices.text: has confused the intentional fallacy with the affective fallacy

explanations.correct: The passage says the New Critics rejected the prior practice of reading 'with little attention paid to the pressures of the language on the page,' and the author treats that rejection sympathetically. A scholar who treats the poem as a transparent window commits exactly that error.
explanations.A: Out of scope; pedagogical persistence is not the objection raised against window-style reading.
explanations.B: That criticism is the one made of the New Critics themselves, not of their opponents.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Plausible-sounding but unsupported; the passage does not raise availability or reliability of biographical evidence.
explanations.E: The passage mentions both fallacies but does not use confusion between them as a basis for any criticism.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A movement is described; two objections to it are raised; each objection is refuted in turn.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A received view of a movement is presented; that view is qualified rather than rejected; a later criticism of the movement is acknowledged and partly conceded.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two rival schools of literary criticism are contrasted; one is shown to have survived while the other has not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A critical doctrine is endorsed; its principal advocates are named; the doctrine is applied to a representative poem.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A historical controversy is sketched; competing interpretations are evaluated; a new interpretation is proposed.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 gives the standard 'austere formalism' portrait. Paragraph 2 qualifies it ('not inaccurate in outline, obscures a subtler commitment'). Paragraph 3 acknowledges the later reader-response and cultural-studies charge and concedes it has force. B matches this three-move structure.
explanations.A: The passage does not refute the later objection; it partly concedes it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No sustained contrast of two schools is developed; reader-response and cultural studies appear only briefly in paragraph 3.
explanations.D: No specific poem is analyzed.
explanations.E: No new interpretation is proposed by the author; he defends a less extreme reading of the received movement.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following interpretive practices most closely conforms to the principle the passage attributes to the New Critics?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A critic writing on a Renaissance sonnet begins by surveying the poet's letters and diaries, and uses the sonnet primarily to illustrate conclusions drawn from that archive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A critic writing on a modernist novel examines its sentence-by-sentence patterns of imagery, then consults period newspapers only to clarify a specific reference that the imagery demands.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A critic writing on a contemporary play devotes equal space to the playwright's biography, the audience's reception, and the text itself, declining to privilege any of the three.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A critic writing on an oral epic argues that its meaning is determined chiefly by the social function it served in its originating community.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A critic writing on a political poem contends that the poem's language is irrelevant to its meaning, which is fully fixed by the poet's known intentions.

explanations.correct: The passage says the New Critics required that extratextual material be 'earned by the text — introduced only when the text's own evidence demanded it.' Option B instantiates exactly that sequence: close reading first, then period research summoned only to gloss what the imagery itself requires.
explanations.A: Inverts the New Critical ordering: archive first, text second.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Treats the three sources as equal; the New Critics subordinated biography and reception to the text.
explanations.D: Treats extratextual social function as the primary determinant of meaning.
explanations.E: Endorses the very 'window' view the New Critics rejected, and in its extreme form goes further than any position described in the passage.

rc.passage:
Medieval illuminated manuscripts have long been discussed in one of two registers. Art historians of an earlier generation treated them chiefly as repositories of iconography — pictorial programs encoding theological doctrine — while bibliographers treated them as physical artifacts to be described by their bindings, quires, parchment preparation, and scripts. Both approaches produced valuable catalogues, but each tended to overlook the quality that most sharply distinguishes the illuminated page from other medieval images: its function within a reading practice.

A recent generation of scholars, led by specialists in what is sometimes called the archaeology of the book, has argued that the marginal decorations, historiated initials, and full-page miniatures of a prayerbook or psalter were not merely illustrations of the text but guides to its use. In a Book of Hours intended for private devotion, for instance, the gilded initial that opens each of the canonical hours served as a visual bookmark, allowing a reader to locate a psalm rapidly without consulting a table. The grotesques that cavort in the lower margins — hybrid beasts, acrobats, hunting scenes — have sometimes been dismissed as idle fancy, but they often mark thematic or liturgical turning points in the text and may have cued the reader to shifts in tone or intention.

This reading-centered account does not displace the older iconographic and bibliographic approaches so much as integrate them. The images still carry doctrinal meaning, and the physical features of the codex still matter; what has changed is the presumption that these dimensions can be studied in isolation from one another. The gold leaf of a historiated initial is at once theological (it figures divine radiance), material (it was beaten to a leaf one ten-thousandth of a millimeter thick and burnished with a dog's tooth), and functional (its shine catches the eye of a reader turning the page in candlelight). To pursue only one dimension is to miss how the others reinforce it. If there is a limitation to the new approach, it lies in the scarcity of direct evidence about how medieval owners actually handled their books; the reading practices reconstructed are often inferred from the books themselves rather than from external testimony such as inventories, wills, or devotional guidebooks. Still, the reconstructions are disciplined by what the page will and will not allow, and they have renewed scholarly interest in volumes that earlier generations of researchers had treated as merely decorative.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Recent scholarship has shown that earlier iconographic and bibliographic studies of illuminated manuscripts were fundamentally mistaken and should be discarded.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A reading-centered approach to illuminated manuscripts, which treats their decoration as a guide to the use of the text, supplements rather than supplants earlier iconographic and bibliographic methods.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The marginal grotesques of medieval prayerbooks, long dismissed as idle fancy, in fact mark turning points in the liturgical text and shape how readers moved through it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because external testimony about medieval reading practice is scarce, reconstructions of how illuminated manuscripts were used must remain largely conjectural.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Art historians and bibliographers produced valuable catalogues of illuminated manuscripts, but neither group appreciated the theological meaning of the pictorial programs they described.

explanations.correct: The thesis is set out at the start of paragraph 3: 'This reading-centered account does not displace the older iconographic and bibliographic approaches so much as integrate them.' B is a precise paraphrase.
explanations.A: Too strong and reverses the author: the passage explicitly says the older approaches are not displaced.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too narrow — fixates on a single illustrative case (grotesques) rather than the passage's broader claim.
explanations.D: Picks up a qualification from the final paragraph and promotes it to the thesis.
explanations.E: Misrepresents the older scholars; the passage says iconographers studied theological doctrine, the very thing this choice denies them.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the gilded initial that opens each of the canonical hours in a Book of Hours served which one of the following functions in addition to its decorative role?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It allowed the reader to locate a particular psalm quickly without consulting a table.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It identified the manuscript's owner for purposes of later cataloguing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It reproduced in miniature the theological program of the full-page miniatures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It signaled to the scribe where a new quire of the codex should begin.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It corrected errors that the reader might otherwise make in pronunciation.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states plainly: 'the gilded initial that opens each of the canonical hours served as a visual bookmark, allowing a reader to locate a psalm rapidly without consulting a table.'
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Plausible-world detail the passage never states.
explanations.C: The passage does not describe the initials as reproducing the program of the full-page miniatures.
explanations.D: Conflates scribal features (quires) with reader-oriented features (initials); the passage discusses quires only in summarizing earlier bibliographic work.
explanations.E: Out of scope; no pronunciation function is described.

questions.questionStem: The author's detailed description of gold leaf (in the third paragraph) — theological, material, and functional — most likely serves to

choices.label: A
choices.text: demonstrate that the theological meaning of illumination has been overstated by earlier iconographers

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate the author's claim that the new approach integrates rather than replaces the older ones

choices.label: C
choices.text: introduce a technical digression on medieval metallurgy

choices.label: D
choices.text: offer a counterexample to the claim that marginal decoration serves a reading-oriented function

choices.label: E
choices.text: prove that the physical features of the codex cannot be studied in isolation from its reception

explanations.correct: The sentence immediately before the gold-leaf example states the integration thesis; the three-dimension description is then given as its instance. Its function is to illustrate that thesis.
explanations.A: The description does not criticize iconographers; it credits the theological reading alongside the others.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Wrong grain: the metallurgical detail is part of a larger point, not a digression.
explanations.D: The example is not a counterexample; it supports the author's position.
explanations.E: Accurate content but wrong function: the example illustrates integration generally, not the specific sub-claim about physical features.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the reading-centered approach to illuminated manuscripts is best described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: wholehearted endorsement of an approach that has solved the difficulties facing earlier scholarship

choices.label: B
choices.text: approval qualified by awareness of the limitations of its evidentiary base

choices.label: C
choices.text: skepticism rooted in doubts about whether marginal decoration can be said to have any function at all

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutral description of a new method, with no evaluative stance of his own

choices.label: E
choices.text: reluctant acceptance forced by the collapse of the iconographic and bibliographic traditions

explanations.correct: The author endorses the new approach ('the reconstructions are disciplined... they have renewed interest') but flags a genuine limit ('scarcity of evidence about how medieval owners actually handled their books'). That is approval with qualification.
explanations.A: Overstates: the passage explicitly notes a limitation.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Opposite tone: the author treats marginal decoration as functionally meaningful.
explanations.D: The passage is evaluative, not neutral.
explanations.E: Nothing suggests the earlier traditions have collapsed; the author says they are integrated.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests which one of the following about marginal grotesques in medieval prayerbooks?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They were included chiefly to amuse wealthy patrons and had no relation to the text they accompanied.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In at least some cases, their placement correlates meaningfully with liturgical or thematic features of the text.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They were painted by a separate workshop and inserted after the main pictorial program had been completed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Earlier scholars refused to acknowledge them because they offended contemporary religious sensibilities.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Their iconography can be fully decoded once the reader identifies the associated canonical hour.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 notes that grotesques 'often mark thematic or liturgical turning points in the text' — a hedged, positive claim about correlation that B paraphrases faithfully.
explanations.A: Reverses the author's qualification: the passage denies that grotesques are 'idle fancy.'
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Plausible-world detail the passage never supplies.
explanations.D: No such motive for earlier neglect is mentioned; the passage merely says they were 'dismissed.'
explanations.E: Overreach: the author nowhere claims their iconography can be fully decoded by canonical hour.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the reading-centered approach as the author describes it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medieval scribes used different pigments for marginal decoration than for historiated initials.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several surviving Books of Hours contain no marginal grotesques at all, only full-page miniatures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Detailed diaries from medieval owners show that readers regularly skipped the illuminated pages and ignored the decorations while reciting the text.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gold leaf was also applied to liturgical objects such as chalices and altar frontals, not only to manuscript pages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some historiated initials depict scenes that do not correspond to the canonical hour they introduce.

explanations.correct: The reading-centered approach holds that illumination guided readers through the text. External testimony showing readers systematically ignored the decoration would directly undermine that functional claim — and the passage identifies scarcity of external testimony as the approach's weakest point, so this choice also targets the documented soft spot.
explanations.A: Irrelevant to whether decoration guides reading.
explanations.B: Does not undermine: a book may use initials rather than grotesques and still exhibit reading-guiding illumination.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Compatible with the passage; gold leaf's broader use does not affect its manuscript function.
explanations.E: Mild tension at most; the passage does not require a one-to-one correspondence between initial imagery and canonical hour.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Two earlier approaches are surveyed; a newer approach is presented as integrating them; the newer approach is endorsed with an acknowledged limitation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A scholarly controversy is outlined; the author sides decisively with one party; the defeated party's remaining contributions are catalogued.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A pictorial tradition is described; a chronological evolution is traced; a prediction about its future is offered.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Three methods of studying manuscripts are introduced; each is illustrated with a separate case study; the methods are ranked by explanatory power.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An approach is criticized; the criticism is answered by a new defense; the defense is shown to rest on a hidden assumption.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 surveys iconographic and bibliographic approaches. Paragraph 2 introduces the reading-centered approach. Paragraph 3 explicitly frames it as integrating the older work and endorses it while flagging a scarcity-of-evidence limit. A captures all three moves in order.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Misdescribes the author's stance: he does not treat any party as defeated.
explanations.C: No chronological evolution or future prediction is traced.
explanations.D: No separate case studies or ranking is offered.
explanations.E: The passage does not uncover a hidden assumption in the new approach.

rc.passage:
The emergence of bebop in the mid-1940s is often recounted as a revolt: a small group of musicians, chief among them Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie, turned against the polished dance arrangements of the swing era and forged a harmonically dense, rhythmically unpredictable idiom playable only by virtuosos. In this telling, bebop broke with its predecessors to become the first jazz style not primarily meant for dancing, and its difficulty was understood as a badge of independence from the demands of the commercial ballroom and the bandleaders who served it. The story has the clarity of a generational break: old music for dancers, new music for listeners.

There is something to the revolt narrative, but it flattens a more interesting continuity. Many of the harmonic substitutions that became bebop's signature — tritone replacements, chromatic ii–V interpolations, the extension of chords to include the ninth, eleventh, and thirteenth — had been quietly explored by pianists and arrangers within the big bands of the late 1930s, especially in the written introductions and brief instrumental passages that sat between vocal choruses. What the beboppers did was not so much invent these devices as expose them. By thinning the ensemble to a quintet and foregrounding the soloist, they made audible the harmonic machinery that swing arrangements had kept buried under sectional voicings and dancing tempos. The rhythmic innovations, too, grew out of practices that drummers such as Jo Jones had developed while still working within the dance-band framework.

The point is not to deny bebop's distinctiveness. Its tempos were faster, its melodic lines more jagged, its expectations of the listener more demanding, and the social setting of the after-hours club did foster a kind of musicianly freedom unavailable at the Savoy Ballroom or any comparable public ballroom. But the continuities matter, because they correct a misleading picture of the swing era itself. That era is too often remembered as an age of bland commerce whose best features bebop had to rescue. In fact, the big bands were laboratories in which the material of the new music was being assembled, and the most enterprising beboppers knew it. Parker's first professional experiences were in territory bands; Gillespie arranged for Cab Calloway; the very harmonic vocabulary they are credited with inventing had been in the room, waiting to be unpacked, while they learned their craft. What looks like revolt from a distance is, up close, a studied act of foregrounding.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bebop was an entirely unprecedented musical idiom whose harmonic vocabulary bore no meaningful relation to that of the swing era it replaced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: While bebop differed from swing in important ways, its harmonic and rhythmic innovations were extensions of devices already developed within the big bands, and the revolt narrative obscures this continuity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie deserve more credit than they have traditionally received for their early apprenticeships in territory and touring dance bands.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The rhythmic contributions of drummers such as Jo Jones have been undervalued by historians who treat bebop's rhythmic innovations as the work of its soloists.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The after-hours club provided a social setting for musical experimentation that the commercial ballroom could not have supported.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 opens the corrective ('flattens a more interesting continuity'), paragraph 3 concedes bebop's distinctiveness and then reasserts the continuity thesis and its implication for understanding swing. B captures both the concession and the main thesis.
explanations.A: Reverses the author: the passage affirms continuity, not unprecedentedness.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too narrow — fixates on the careers of two musicians.
explanations.D: Too narrow — Jo Jones is mentioned only as one example.
explanations.E: Paragraph-level restatement from paragraph 3; a concession, not the thesis.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following harmonic devices had been explored within big bands of the late 1930s before becoming a bebop signature?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Modal improvisation over static harmonies sustained for many measures

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tritone substitutions and the extension of chords to include the ninth, eleventh, and thirteenth

choices.label: C
choices.text: Twelve-tone rows distributed across the soloist and rhythm section

choices.label: D
choices.text: Atonal passages in which no underlying key could be identified

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spontaneous collective improvisation in the manner of early New Orleans jazz

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 lists 'tritone replacements, chromatic ii–V interpolations, the extension of chords to include the ninth, eleventh, and thirteenth' as devices 'quietly explored by pianists and arrangers within the big bands of the late 1930s.'
explanations.A: Modal improvisation is not mentioned; it belongs to a later jazz development.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Twelve-tone writing is not mentioned.
explanations.D: The passage never describes bebop as atonal.
explanations.E: The passage does not address New Orleans collective improvisation.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the standard "revolt" narrative of bebop's origins is best described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: total rejection of a story with no basis in the historical record

choices.label: B
choices.text: admiration for its dramatic framing of a mid-century cultural break

choices.label: C
choices.text: partial acceptance combined with the judgment that the narrative oversimplifies bebop's relationship to swing

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference, since the revolt narrative concerns matters outside the author's subject

choices.label: E
choices.text: wholehearted endorsement, provided the narrative is supplemented with attention to the after-hours club

explanations.correct: The author writes 'there is something to the revolt narrative, but it flattens a more interesting continuity.' That is partial acceptance plus the complaint of oversimplification — exactly C.
explanations.A: Overstated negativity: the author says the narrative has 'something to' it.
explanations.B: Wrong feature: the author does not praise its dramatic framing.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Opposite tone: the author is plainly engaged with the narrative.
explanations.E: Overstated positivity: the author qualifies, not endorses.

questions.questionStem: The author mentions that "Parker's first professional experiences were in territory bands" and that "Gillespie arranged for Cab Calloway" primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: establish the personal credentials of the two musicians within the professional jazz world

choices.label: B
choices.text: support the claim that the harmonic vocabulary of bebop had been accessible inside the big bands in which its leading figures trained

choices.label: C
choices.text: contrast Parker's and Gillespie's career paths with those of later bebop musicians

choices.label: D
choices.text: explain why bebop ultimately appealed more to listeners than to dancers

choices.label: E
choices.text: concede that the revolt narrative has more empirical support than the author acknowledges elsewhere

explanations.correct: The biographical items appear in the final paragraph after the claim that 'the big bands were laboratories in which the material of the new music was being assembled.' They are offered as evidence that the beboppers' own training placed them in those laboratories.
explanations.A: Accurate content, wrong function: the citations are made to support a thesis about musical continuity, not to vouch for credentials.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No contrast with later bebop musicians is drawn.
explanations.D: The listener/dancer distinction appears in paragraph 1, not here.
explanations.E: The items are offered as evidence against the revolt narrative's sufficiency, not for it.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following statements about the swing era as commonly remembered?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It has been unfairly treated as bland commerce whose best features had to be rescued by bebop.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Its surviving recordings display the same tempos and melodic contours as early bebop.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is universally regarded by historians as the true origin of modern jazz harmony.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its arrangements were largely written by the soloists who would later become beboppers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its commercial success has obscured the contribution of individual big-band leaders.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 says the era 'is too often remembered as an age of bland commerce whose best features bebop had to rescue,' and the author treats this memory as misleading. That warrants the inference in A: the treatment has been unfair.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Contradicts paragraph 3's explicit contrast of swing and bebop tempos and melodic contours.
explanations.C: Overreach: the passage does not claim universal scholarly regard.
explanations.D: The passage mentions Gillespie arranging for Calloway but does not generalize.
explanations.E: Out of scope: the passage does not discuss the memory of individual band leaders.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations is most closely analogous to the relationship between bebop and the big bands as the passage describes it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A translator renders a foreign novel into English for the first time, giving its themes a readership they previously lacked.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A chamber ensemble performs a nineteenth-century symphony using period instruments, exposing timbres that modern orchestras tend to smooth over.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A rival political party emerges that rejects the policies of the governing party and proposes new ones built on unrelated principles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A novelist invents a new genre by abandoning the conventions of every preceding literary tradition.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A company replaces its previous product line with goods manufactured in another country using different materials.

explanations.correct: The passage says bebop did not invent its devices but 'exposed' them — 'made audible the harmonic machinery that swing arrangements had kept buried under sectional voicings.' A chamber ensemble exposing timbres that modern orchestras smooth over instantiates the same mechanism: not invention, but foregrounding something already present.
explanations.A: Surface similarity (arts context) but wrong mechanism: translation makes material newly available, not audibly re-foregrounded from within the same tradition.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Matches the revolt narrative the author rejects: 'unrelated principles' is the wrong relation.
explanations.D: Same error as C in its extreme form: invention from nothing, the very view the passage opposes.
explanations.E: Substitution of different materials, not foregrounding of material already present.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No musical style can ever be called genuinely innovative, since each merely foregrounds what preceded it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bebop's reduction of ensemble size played a role in making the music's harmonic content more perceptible than it had been in swing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The commercial demands of the ballroom prevented any harmonic experimentation within the big bands of the late 1930s.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Historians who describe bebop as difficult have generally exaggerated the technical demands it placed on performers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The rhythmic innovations of bebop owed nothing to drummers who had worked in dance-band settings.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 says that 'by thinning the ensemble to a quintet and foregrounding the soloist,' the beboppers 'made audible the harmonic machinery that swing arrangements had kept buried.' B is a hedged paraphrase of this causal link.
explanations.A: Too strong: the passage allows that bebop was genuinely distinctive in tempo, melodic line, and social setting.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Reverses the passage's claim: the big bands were the laboratories where the experimentation took place.
explanations.D: Out of scope and contrary to the passage's own characterization of bebop as 'playable only by virtuosos.'
explanations.E: Contradicts the passage's explicit credit to Jo Jones and the dance-band drumming tradition.

rc.passage:
The composer Morton Feldman occupies an unusual position in twentieth-century music history: celebrated by a small but devoted critical following, yet persistently relegated to the margins of concert programming and popular musicological accounts. Standard histories of postwar American music tend to cast the 1950s as a contest between serialist rigor—exemplified by Milton Babbitt's densely calculated pitch rows—and the theatrical indeterminacy of John Cage, whose chance procedures and conceptual provocations dominated the avant-garde conversation. Feldman, despite his long personal friendship with Cage, fits neither category comfortably, and this categorical awkwardness has too often been mistaken for aesthetic lesser importance.

The truth is that Feldman's music, particularly the series of works he titled Projections and Intersections from the early 1950s, represents a third path that illuminates the limits of both prevailing models. The serialists prized precision: every note generated from a master numerical system, every parameter controlled. Cage prized release: the composer's ego dissolved into accident and environmental noise. Feldman wanted neither control nor its deliberate abdication. His scores notated duration and dynamics with unusual care while leaving specific pitches to the performer's discretion—a balance that contemporaries found difficult to classify and critics have since struggled to name. The term most often applied, "indeterminate," is technically accurate but misleading, implying a kinship with Cage that flattens the critical difference: where Cage welcomed noise and disruption as music's raw material, Feldman regarded sound itself with a hushed, almost reverential attention. His characteristic dynamic was pianissimo; his characteristic gesture, a soft chord appearing briefly and then retreating into silence.

This attention to the quality of individual sounds—what Feldman called "sounds as sounds" rather than sounds as symbols or structural arguments—aligns him more productively with the visual artists of his New York circle than with his fellow composers. He counted the painters Philip Guston and Mark Rothko among his closest interlocutors, and the influence ran both ways. Rothko's late canvases, with their hovering rectangular forms that seem to materialize and then dissolve at the canvas's edges, pursue a visual analogue to what Feldman was achieving acoustically: presence without insistence, form without argument. To call Feldman's music abstract expressionist in a strictly programmatic sense would be imprecise; but to ignore how deeply his aesthetic was shaped by painters who believed that a work of art could create an immediate, almost physical encounter with feeling, without narrative or explanation, is to miss the animating impulse of everything he wrote.

Feldman's relative obscurity, then, reflects not a poverty of achievement but the poverty of the categories through which postwar music has been filtered. A criticism adequate to his work would need to set aside the serialist-versus-indeterminacy axis entirely and attend instead to the phenomenology of listening—to what it feels like when a sound appears, persists briefly, and vanishes—and to the ethics of restraint that Feldman practiced with a consistency no other composer of his generation matched.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Morton Feldman's friendship with John Cage led him to develop a form of musical indeterminacy that surpassed Cage's own experiments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Postwar American music is best understood as a contest between serialist precision and Cagean indeterminacy, within which Feldman found a compromise position.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Feldman's marginalization in music history reflects the inadequacy of standard critical categories rather than any deficiency in his work, and a better criticism would attend to the phenomenology of his sound.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The visual artists of the New York school exerted a decisive and underappreciated influence on all major postwar American composers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Feldman's scores are technically indeterminate because they leave specific pitches to the performer's discretion, placing him firmly within the Cagean tradition.

explanations.correct: The passage argues throughout that Feldman's obscurity stems from categorical inadequacy (serialist vs. indeterminate axis) rather than aesthetic weakness, and closes by calling for a criticism grounded in phenomenology and restraint. C captures both strands of this integrated thesis.
explanations.A: The passage explicitly distinguishes Feldman from Cage; there is no claim that Feldman surpassed Cage. This answer misrepresents the relationship.
explanations.B: The passage directly contradicts this framing: Feldman 'fits neither category comfortably,' and the passage's thesis rejects the serialist-versus-indeterminacy axis as an adequate lens.
explanations.C: Correct. This integrates the diagnosis (marginalization due to bad categories) with the prescription (phenomenological criticism), matching the full arc of the passage.
explanations.D: Too broad — the passage discusses Feldman's relationship with painters, not all major postwar composers. This answer overgeneralizes from a specific claim.
explanations.E: The passage calls 'indeterminate' technically accurate but misleading and explicitly argues against grouping Feldman with Cage. This answer restates a claim the author disputes.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward standard histories of postwar American music can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: qualified admiration for their rigorous documentation of serialism and indeterminacy

choices.label: B
choices.text: critical skepticism about the adequacy of the frameworks they impose

choices.label: C
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement of their account of the Feldman–Cage relationship

choices.label: D
choices.text: mild curiosity about how they came to overlook Feldman's connections to visual art

choices.label: E
choices.text: outright rejection of every claim they make about postwar American composers

explanations.correct: The author repeatedly challenges the standard historical framework: it 'too often' mistakes categorical awkwardness for lesser importance, the 'indeterminate' label is misleading, and the 'serialist-versus-indeterminacy axis' must be 'set aside entirely.' This constitutes sustained critical skepticism about the frameworks — not outright rejection of all content, but skepticism about the organizing categories.
explanations.A: The passage offers no admiration for these histories; it argues they have distorted the understanding of Feldman. 'Admiration' is the wrong valence.
explanations.B: Correct. The author's repeated challenge to the standard two-camp framework — calling it inadequate and misleading — is best characterized as critical skepticism.
explanations.C: The author does not endorse the standard account of Feldman and Cage; on the contrary, the passage argues the kinship implied by that account is misleading.
explanations.D: 'Mild curiosity' is far too weak; the author makes a sustained argument, not a passing inquiry. This understates the author's critical engagement.
explanations.E: The author accepts that the serialist–Cage contrast is a real historical phenomenon; the critique is of the framework's inadequacy, not the factual claims within it. 'Outright rejection' overstates the author's position.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A composer is introduced; his works are chronologically surveyed; a comparison with visual artists is proposed; his place in music history is evaluated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A prevailing critical framework is described; a composer who escapes it is introduced and examined on his own terms; cross-disciplinary affinities are identified; a call for better critical tools is issued.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing aesthetic movements are described; a composer who synthesizes them is celebrated; his debt to painting is explained; a historical revisionism is proposed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A composer's obscurity is lamented; the musicians who influenced him are identified; the visual artists he influenced are discussed; a new biography is recommended.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A contrast between Feldman and Cage is developed across three paragraphs and then resolved by showing that both belong to the same tradition.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 describes the prevailing serialist-vs.-Cage framework. Paragraph 2 introduces Feldman as escaping that framework and examines his scores. Paragraph 3 identifies his affinities with New York painters. Paragraph 4 calls for a phenomenological critical approach. B tracks these four moves accurately.
explanations.A: The passage does not offer a chronological survey of Feldman's works; only the early Projections and Intersections are named. The sequence of moves described in A does not match.
explanations.B: Correct. This accurately captures the four-paragraph arc: framework, third-path composer, cross-disciplinary affinities, call for new criticism.
explanations.C: The passage argues Feldman does not synthesize the two movements but transcends their axis altogether. 'Synthesizes' misrepresents the author's claim.
explanations.D: The passage does not identify musicians who influenced Feldman, nor does it recommend a biography. This answer introduces moves the passage never makes.
explanations.E: The passage argues the opposite: Feldman and Cage belong to different traditions despite their personal friendship. The contrast is sustained, not resolved into unity.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Feldman's scores for the Projections and Intersections series differed from serialist scores in that Feldman's scores

choices.label: A
choices.text: specified dynamics and duration precisely but left specific pitches to the performer

choices.label: B
choices.text: dissolved compositional ego entirely through the use of chance procedures

choices.label: C
choices.text: generated every parameter, including pitch, from a master numerical system

choices.label: D
choices.text: welcomed environmental noise as the primary raw material for composition

choices.label: E
choices.text: left both pitch and duration to the performer's discretion in order to achieve indeterminacy

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that Feldman's scores 'notated duration and dynamics with unusual care while leaving specific pitches to the performer's discretion.' A paraphrases this precisely.
explanations.A: Correct. This is a direct paraphrase of the passage's description of Feldman's scoring practice.
explanations.B: This describes Cage's approach, not Feldman's. The passage distinguishes Feldman from Cage on exactly this point.
explanations.C: This describes the serialist method (Babbitt's 'densely calculated pitch rows'), which the passage explicitly contrasts with Feldman's practice.
explanations.D: Welcoming environmental noise is attributed to Cage, not Feldman. The passage says Feldman 'regarded sound itself with a hushed, almost reverential attention' — the opposite of welcoming noise.
explanations.E: The passage specifies that duration was notated with care; only pitch was left to the performer. Leaving both indeterminate contradicts the passage's description.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that which one of the following is true of Mark Rothko's late paintings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They were directly inspired by Feldman's musical scores for the Projections series.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They achieve their effect through the suggestion of form that emerges and recedes rather than through fixed, assertive structure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They exemplify the serialist principle that every visual parameter should be systematically controlled.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They were widely celebrated in postwar American music criticism as a model for composers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: They prioritize narrative and explanation over immediate sensory encounter.

explanations.correct: The passage describes Rothko's late canvases as having 'hovering rectangular forms that seem to materialize and then dissolve at the canvas's edges,' pursuing 'presence without insistence, form without argument.' B captures this inference — form that emerges and recedes rather than asserting itself — without overstating.
explanations.A: The passage says the influence between Feldman and the painters 'ran both ways,' but it does not assert that Rothko's paintings were directly inspired by the Projections scores specifically. This overreaches the passage's claim.
explanations.B: Correct. 'Materialize and then dissolve,' 'presence without insistence, form without argument' — all support the inference that Rothko's forms suggest rather than assert, emerge and recede.
explanations.C: Serialism is associated with Babbitt and the composers, not with Rothko. Applying a serialist description to Rothko contradicts the passage's framing of the two as analogous, not identical.
explanations.D: The passage says Rothko was among Feldman's interlocutors; it makes no claim about music criticism celebrating Rothko as a model for composers.
explanations.E: The passage explicitly states Rothko and Feldman shared a belief that art could create 'an immediate, almost physical encounter with feeling, without narrative or explanation.' E directly contradicts this.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of Cage's use of chance procedures and environmental noise (second paragraph) serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: celebrate Cage's contribution to the avant-garde as a necessary precondition for Feldman's own innovations

choices.label: B
choices.text: establish a contrast that clarifies what was distinctive and irreducible about Feldman's relationship to sound

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that Cage's approach was more radical than serialism and therefore more historically significant

choices.label: D
choices.text: support the claim that Feldman belongs squarely within the indeterminate tradition that Cage established

choices.label: E
choices.text: introduce a counterexample that the author subsequently concedes undermines the case for Feldman's originality

explanations.correct: The passage invokes Cage's 'welcome of noise and disruption' precisely to sharpen the contrast with Feldman's 'hushed, almost reverential attention' to sound. The function is contrastive: the Cage description clarifies what Feldman was not doing and why the 'indeterminate' label misleads.
explanations.A: The passage does not frame Cage's work as a precondition for Feldman's; on the contrary, it argues Feldman's path was independent of and distinct from Cage's, despite their friendship.
explanations.B: Correct. The discussion of Cage immediately precedes and motivates the sentence about Feldman regarding 'sound itself with a hushed, almost reverential attention' — a contrastive function.
explanations.C: The passage makes no comparative judgment about historical significance between Cage and the serialists. This answer introduces a claim the passage does not make.
explanations.D: The passage argues the opposite: the discussion of Cage is designed to show that calling Feldman 'indeterminate' implies a misleading kinship with Cage.
explanations.E: The author never concedes that Cage's work undermines Feldman's originality; the entire passage argues for Feldman's distinctiveness. This inverts the author's argument.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle the author invokes in arguing that the label 'indeterminate' is misleading when applied to Feldman's music?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A novelist is categorized as a realist because her books describe everyday domestic life, even though her prose style is highly experimental and her thematic concerns are closer to those of the symbolists.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A filmmaker is praised as an auteur because she writes, directs, and edits her own films, a practice she shares with several other celebrated directors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A sculptor is grouped with minimalists because he uses industrial materials, despite the fact that minimalism itself is a diverse movement with no single defining criterion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A jazz pianist is called a traditionalist because he plays standard repertoire, and this label accurately captures his approach to improvisation, harmony, and rhythm.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A poet is described as a romanticist because she uses rhyme and meter, features she shares with romantic poets, even though her subject matter is exclusively political satire.

explanations.correct: The passage's principle is: a technically accurate label ('indeterminate') is applied to Feldman because of a surface feature he shares with Cage (performer discretion over pitch), but that label obscures a critical difference in underlying aesthetic orientation (reverence vs. welcome of noise). A mirrors this exactly: 'realist' is applied because of a surface feature (domestic subject matter), but the label obscures a critical difference in aesthetic orientation (symbolist, experimental style).
explanations.A: Correct. The shared surface feature (domestic settings / pitch discretion) justifies the label technically, but the deeper aesthetic orientation diverges sharply — exactly the structure the passage describes.
explanations.B: This describes a case where a label is applied because of shared practice, and the label seems accurate; there is no misleading suppression of a critical difference. The auteur label is not shown to flatten any important distinction.
explanations.C: This describes label imprecision due to the category's own internal diversity, not because the label suppresses a critical difference between the labeled artist and the category's paradigm case. The mechanism differs.
explanations.D: Here the label accurately captures the artist's approach across multiple dimensions. This is the opposite of the passage's principle, which concerns technically-accurate-but-misleading labels.
explanations.E: Close, but in E the divergence (political satire) is primarily one of subject matter rather than underlying aesthetic orientation and the way the work engages its medium — the passage's principle concerns orientation toward the artistic medium itself (sound as reverence vs. sound as accident), not merely thematic content.

rc.passage:
The history of jazz piano is often narrated as a succession of revolutionary departures — stride giving way to bebop, bebop yielding to cool, cool dissolving into fusion — yet this chronology, however convenient for textbooks, obscures the degree to which individual artists have always negotiated between innovation and inheritance. Nowhere is this tension more productively sustained than in the work of Thelonious Monk, whose compositions and improvisations occupied a singular position in mid-twentieth-century American music: genuinely novel in harmonic conception yet deeply rooted in the stride tradition from which most jazz pianists of his generation were anxious to distance themselves.

Standard critical accounts have emphasized Monk's role as an architect of bebop, pointing to his years at Minton's Playhouse in Harlem during the early 1940s, where he joined Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker in after-hours sessions that effectively reinvented jazz improvisation. The argument runs that Monk, like the others, was rebelling against the smooth, crowd-pleasing conventions of the swing era. But this picture, while not wrong, is incomplete. Monk never fully abandoned the percussive attack, the stride-derived left-hand patterns, or the rhythmic displacement characteristic of older Harlem piano styles; where Parker and Gillespie aspired to a fleet, linear virtuosity, Monk cultivated deliberate hesitation, angular melodic leaps, and unexpected silences — qualities that bewildered critics trained to hear jazz in terms of forward momentum. His dissonances were not accidental byproducts of hurried improvisation but calculated aesthetic choices informed by a sophisticated, if unconventional, grasp of harmonic function.

What ultimately distinguishes Monk's achievement, however, is not his harmonic daring alone but the manner in which his compositions impose a kind of productive constraint on improvisers who play them. A standard jazz tune provides a harmonic scaffolding that players can decorate at will; a Monk composition, by contrast, has so distinctive a melodic and rhythmic identity that it resists neutral treatment. Musicians who perform "'Round Midnight" or "Straight, No Chaser" cannot simply overlay conventional bebop formulas without sounding incongruous; the tunes demand a responsiveness to their particular idiosyncrasies. In this sense Monk's work functions less like a backdrop and more like a collaborator — one that insists on a certain kind of attention. This quality has made his compositions perennial vehicles for subsequent generations of jazz musicians, not because his tunes are easy but precisely because they are not: they offer resistance, and resistance, in Monk's musical universe, is the condition of genuine creative encounter.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Thelonious Monk's participation in the bebop sessions at Minton's Playhouse established him as the central figure in mid-twentieth-century jazz innovation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The standard chronology of jazz piano history fails to account for the way individual artists blend tradition and innovation in their work.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Thelonious Monk's work is distinguished by its simultaneous debt to older Harlem piano traditions and its imposition of creative demands on performers, achievements that standard bebop narratives understate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monk's harmonic dissonances, unlike those of his contemporaries, were the product of calculated aesthetic choices rather than improvisational accident.

choices.label: E
