explanations.E: The passage does not weigh the merits of serialism and minimalism as equals, and no synthesis is advanced; the structure is argumentative rather than comparative.
explanations.D: Correct.

rc.passage:
The history of jazz piano has long been narrated as a story of progressive liberation: from the metronomic regularity of ragtime, through the loping stride style of Harlem's ballroom masters, and finally toward the harmonically daring improvisation that came to define bebop in the 1940s. Within this familiar arc, Thelonious Monk occupies a peculiar position — praised almost universally, yet rarely placed with confidence within any of its phases. Standard accounts tend to celebrate Monk as a visionary whose angular melodies and deliberately dissonant chord voicings anticipated the harmonic freedoms that later pianists exploited. The truth, however, is more complicated: Monk was not so much a prophet of what came after him as a renovator of what had come before.

The case for Monk as a forward-looking modernist rests largely on the surface strangeness of his playing. His use of clustered, unresolved chord voicings, his habit of striking notes and then withdrawing into silence while the rhythm section continued, and his willfully awkward phrasing struck many contemporary listeners as wilfully eccentric. Yet these very qualities, on closer inspection, reveal a deep engagement with the older vocabulary of stride piano. Monk's left hand, often dismissed as merely erratic, in fact traces the fundamental stride pattern — the alternating bass note and mid-register chord — at irregular, syncopated intervals, a deliberate deformation of the tradition rather than a departure from it. His silences, too, are not absences of ideas but rather spaces that make the stride architecture beneath them audible by contrast. Where later bebop pianists crowded their lines with chromatic runs, Monk subtracted.

What makes this interpretive tension productive is that Monk's renovation of stride was never merely nostalgic. He subjected the conventions of the tradition to an ironic pressure — elongating phrases just past the point of comfortable resolution, voicing chords in ways that simultaneously honored their functional harmonic role and exposed its arbitrariness. The effect, to borrow a phrase from one mid-century critic, was of "familiar furniture rearranged in a dark room": the listener sensed the known shapes but could not quite settle into them. This quality gave Monk's music a dual audience — it was legible to dancers and listeners trained on the Harlem stride tradition, and it was simultaneously fascinating to younger musicians searching for ways to press beyond conventional harmony. But Monk himself, by all biographical evidence, was indifferent to which audience claimed him. His primary loyalty was to the internal logic of each composition, to the feeling he described, in his characteristically laconic manner, as "making the music sound the way it is."

The tendency to read Monk's work primarily through the lens of what came after — to treat him as a way station on the road to free jazz — impoverishes our understanding of his achievement. His greatness lay not in anticipation but in compression: in the ability to hold within a single performance the stride tradition's rhythmic authority, the bebop era's harmonic restlessness, and a quality of structural irony that belonged to neither movement and to both.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Thelonious Monk's piano technique was primarily derived from the bebop movement's emphasis on chromatic improvisation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Standard accounts of jazz history have underestimated the influence of the Harlem stride tradition on the development of bebop.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monk's achievement is best understood not as a harbinger of later jazz developments but as an ironic renovation of the stride tradition he inherited.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monk's music appealed to two distinct audiences because he deliberately balanced accessibility with harmonic experimentation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The silences in Monk's playing constitute his most original contribution to jazz piano, distinguishing him from both stride and bebop practitioners.

explanations.correct: The passage argues across all four paragraphs that Monk is better understood as a renovator of stride than as a prophet of what came after — this is the thesis introduced at the end of paragraph 1 and substantiated throughout.
explanations.A: The passage explicitly argues against treating Monk as a bebop figure; bebop pianists are contrasted with Monk's subtractive approach.
explanations.B: This is a related point, but the passage's argument centers on Monk specifically, not on the broader underestimation of stride's influence on bebop generally.
explanations.C: Correct. This integrates the thesis from paragraph 1 ('renovator of what had come before') with the irony argument of paragraphs 3 and 4.
explanations.D: The dual-audience point appears in paragraph 3 but is a supporting detail, not the main thesis; the passage also notes Monk was indifferent to which audience claimed him.
explanations.E: The silence observation appears in paragraph 2 as one piece of evidence for the broader claim; treating it as Monk's 'most original contribution' overstates its role and misrepresents the thesis.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the standard account of Monk as a visionary who anticipated later harmonic freedoms can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: complete rejection, on the grounds that it misidentifies Monk's primary musical influences

choices.label: B
choices.text: partial acceptance, since the account captures Monk's surface strangeness while missing the deeper sources of his originality

choices.label: C
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement, because Monk's dissonant voicings did in fact shape the bebop pianists who followed him

choices.label: D
choices.text: measured skepticism, since the account applies to some of Monk's recordings but not to his most representative work

choices.label: E
choices.text: indifference, because the author considers questions of historical influence less important than questions of compositional logic

explanations.correct: The author does not deny that Monk sounded strange or unconventional — those surface qualities are acknowledged — but argues that the standard account mistakes the origin and character of that strangeness, attributing it to forward-looking modernism when it actually derives from a renovated stride tradition.
explanations.A: Too strong; the author does not fully reject the standard account but complicates it by pointing to what it misses. The phrase 'the truth is more complicated' signals partial, not total, disagreement.
explanations.B: Correct. The passage concedes the 'surface strangeness' reading has some basis ('the case for Monk as a forward-looking modernist rests largely on the surface strangeness of his playing') but argues it fails to reach the deeper stride-renovation story.
explanations.C: The opposite of the author's stance; the author specifically resists reading Monk through the lens of what came after.
explanations.D: The author makes no distinction among different recordings or phases of Monk's career; the argument applies to his work generally.
explanations.E: The author clearly cares about historical placement — the entire passage is an argument about where in jazz history Monk belongs — making indifference implausible.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A biographical sketch of a musician is offered, followed by an account of his stylistic evolution, and then a defense of his place in the jazz canon.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A standard interpretive view is introduced, evidence for a rival view is presented, the rival view is enriched by a further qualification, and the standard view's inadequacy is restated as a conclusion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing critical frameworks for evaluating a musician's work are described, a third framework is proposed, and the three are reconciled in the final paragraph.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A claim about a musician's historical influence is made, qualified by biographical evidence, and then extended to cover the broader development of jazz as a genre.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A widely-held view is endorsed, its strongest counterargument is presented, and the original view is ultimately reaffirmed with minor concessions.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces the standard 'forward-looking visionary' account; paragraph 2 marshals evidence that Monk was actually renovating stride; paragraph 3 qualifies that renovation as ironic rather than nostalgic; paragraph 4 restates the inadequacy of reading Monk through what came after. This matches choice B exactly.
explanations.A: The passage is not biographical and does not trace a stylistic evolution across Monk's career; it makes an interpretive argument about the nature of his achievement.
explanations.B: Correct. Each paragraph corresponds precisely: standard view (¶1), rival evidence (¶2), qualification (¶3), restatement of the standard view's inadequacy (¶4).
explanations.C: Only two interpretive frames are explicitly in tension (the modernist/bebop reading and the stride-renovation reading); no third framework is proposed.
explanations.D: Biographical evidence plays a minor role (Monk's own comment in ¶3) and is not the main vehicle of the argument; the passage does not broaden to cover jazz development generally.
explanations.E: The passage does not ultimately reaffirm the standard view; it replaces it with the author's rival reading.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following characterizes the stride piano technique that Monk employed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A continuous chromatic run in the left hand that anchored the melody played by the right hand

choices.label: B
choices.text: An alternating pattern of bass notes and mid-register chords in the left hand

choices.label: C
choices.text: A metronomic, highly regular pulse maintained throughout each performance

choices.label: D
choices.text: A preference for unresolved dissonances that exposed the arbitrariness of conventional harmonic function

choices.label: E
choices.text: A series of silences that made the structural logic of each composition audible by contrast

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 explicitly states that the stride pattern involves 'the alternating bass note and mid-register chord' in the left hand. Monk traces this pattern, though at irregular intervals.
explanations.A: Chromatic runs are attributed to bebop pianists ('later bebop pianists crowded their lines with chromatic runs'), not to the stride tradition.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the verbatim description of stride in paragraph 2.
explanations.C: Metronomic regularity is attributed to ragtime in paragraph 1, not to stride.
explanations.D: The exposure of harmonic arbitrariness is attributed to Monk's ironic renovation of stride in paragraph 3, not to stride itself.
explanations.E: The strategic use of silences is described as Monk's own practice — his deformation of stride — not as a feature of the stride tradition per se.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that which one of the following is true of bebop pianists of the 1940s?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They were directly influenced by Monk's use of stride architecture and strategic silence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Their approach to harmonic improvisation differed from Monk's in that they favored adding rather than subtracting musical material.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They regarded the stride tradition as an inferior predecessor that had to be entirely rejected before genuine innovation was possible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They were more concerned with compositional structure than with the emotional effect of individual performances.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Their work appealed primarily to younger musicians rather than to audiences trained in the stride tradition.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that 'later bebop pianists crowded their lines with chromatic runs,' while Monk 'subtracted.' The contrast implies bebop pianists added material where Monk removed it — a difference of additive versus subtractive approaches to harmonic elaboration.
explanations.A: The passage makes no claim that bebop pianists were influenced by Monk's specific techniques; the causal relationship runs the other way in the standard account (Monk anticipated them), and the author disputes even that framing.
explanations.B: Correct. The explicit contrast between bebop pianists who 'crowded their lines' and Monk who 'subtracted' supports this inference directly.
explanations.C: The passage does not characterize bebop pianists' attitude toward stride; this inference goes beyond what the passage supports.
explanations.D: No claim about bebop pianists' priorities regarding structure versus emotional effect appears in the passage.
explanations.E: The dual-audience observation in paragraph 3 applies to Monk's music, not to bebop pianists generally.

questions.questionStem: The author most likely quotes the mid-century critic's phrase "familiar furniture rearranged in a dark room" (third paragraph) primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: provide documentary evidence that Monk's contemporaries recognized his debt to the stride tradition

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate the quality of disoriented familiarity produced by Monk's ironic treatment of conventional harmonic structures

choices.label: C
choices.text: contrast Monk's reception among critics with his reception among dancers and younger musicians

choices.label: D
choices.text: suggest that Monk's music was ultimately more accessible than it appeared to first-time listeners

choices.label: E
choices.text: introduce the biographical evidence that Monk was indifferent to audience expectations

explanations.correct: The critic's phrase is cited immediately after the author describes Monk's practice of 'simultaneously honoring' harmonic convention and 'exposing its arbitrariness.' The furniture metaphor captures exactly that double quality — the listener recognizes familiar shapes but cannot settle into them — and thus illustrates the ironic pressure Monk applied to stride conventions.
explanations.A: The critic's phrase does not address Monk's stride debt; it addresses the listener's experience of his harmonic practice. Using it as documentary evidence of the stride connection would be a misapplication.
explanations.B: Correct. The phrase functions to make the abstract claim about 'ironic pressure' and 'familiar yet disorienting' harmony concrete and vivid.
explanations.C: The dual-audience contrast appears later in the same paragraph and is not the purpose of the critic's phrase.
explanations.D: The passage does not argue that Monk was more accessible than he seemed; the furniture metaphor suggests lingering disorientation, not resolved accessibility.
explanations.E: Monk's biographical indifference is introduced in the following sentence, after the critic's phrase; the phrase does not introduce it.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle the author describes as characteristic of Monk's relationship to the stride tradition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A novelist abandons the epistolary format of eighteenth-century fiction entirely and invents a radically new narrative structure with no debt to its predecessors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A choreographer employs the vocabulary of classical ballet — its positions, its vocabulary of steps — but introduces irregular rhythms and unexpected pauses that make the underlying structure visible as structure rather than as invisible convention.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A filmmaker borrows the visual iconography of the Western genre in order to satirize the political assumptions that genre has historically reinforced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A poet translates a medieval text into contemporary idiom, preserving the original's imagery while substituting modern syntax and diction throughout.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A jazz saxophonist studies the recordings of earlier masters in order to reproduce their style as faithfully as possible in live performance.

explanations.correct: The author characterizes Monk's relationship to stride as a 'deliberate deformation' rather than departure — retaining the tradition's architecture while subjecting it to ironic pressure that makes its conventions visible and strange. The choreographer in B retains classical ballet's vocabulary but deforms it through irregular rhythms and unexpected pauses, making the underlying structure 'visible as structure rather than as invisible convention.' This matches the mechanism precisely.
explanations.A: This describes wholesale rejection of a prior tradition, the opposite of what the author attributes to Monk, who retained stride's architecture rather than abandoning it.
explanations.B: Correct. Retaining the inherited vocabulary while deforming its rhythmic regularity to expose the underlying structure mirrors Monk's stride renovation exactly.
explanations.C: Satire involves using a form to critique its own assumptions, which is closer to parody — and the passage explicitly distinguishes Monk's project from parody in paragraphs 1 and 3.
explanations.D: Faithful translation of imagery while changing syntax describes adaptation, not the ironic pressure that makes familiar conventions feel both recognized and disorienting.
explanations.E: Faithful reproduction of an earlier style describes imitation without deformation, which is the opposite of Monk's approach as the author describes it.

rc.passage:
The history of jazz piano has long been narrated as a sequence of heroic solo innovators — Jelly Roll Morton, Earl Hines, Art Tatum — each superseding the last in technical virtuosity. Standard accounts treat the instrument's role in jazz as essentially soloistic: the piano stands apart from the rhythm section when it steps forward, and the pianist's task is to dazzle. The truth is that this received narrative, however seductive, obscures what may be the more consequential development in the tradition: the gradual transformation of jazz piano from a vehicle for individual display into a medium of collective conversation.

That transformation is most audible in the work of the bebop pianists of the 1940s. Thelonious Monk and Bud Powell are often cited as the period's towering figures, and for good reason — their harmonic innovations alone would secure their legacies. But the standard account tends to frame those innovations in soloist's terms: Monk's dissonant, angular voicings are praised as idiosyncratic personal signatures, and Powell's fleet single-note lines are measured against the virtuoso pianists who preceded him. What such framings miss is the degree to which both pianists were reconceiving the piano's relationship to the ensemble. Monk, notoriously, would stop comping entirely when a horn soloist took a chorus, allowing silence to function as a form of harmonic suggestion. Powell, meanwhile, developed a left-hand sparseness that opened the piano's interior register to the bass and drums, effectively inviting the rhythm section into a space the stride pianists had monopolized. These were not merely technical refinements; they were gestures of relinquishment, a willingness to let the collective voice supersede the individual one.

This shift carries implications that reach beyond bebop. The modal jazz of Miles Davis's late 1950s recordings relocated harmonic responsibility away from the piano entirely, distributing it across the ensemble; and the free jazz of the 1960s pushed further still, dissolving the very hierarchy that had placed the piano at the center of jazz harmony. Yet each of these subsequent developments was prefigured — and made imaginable — by the bebop pianists' earlier willingness to create productive vacancies in the musical texture. The solo tradition, in other words, generated the conditions of its own partial eclipse.

To read jazz piano history as a story of escalating individual achievement, then, is to mistake the surface of the music for its deeper logic. The pianists who matter most to the tradition's evolution were those who understood that to cede ground — harmonically, rhythmically, spatially within the ensemble — was not a retreat from artistry but its highest expression: a faith in the conversation that only restraint makes possible.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Thelonious Monk and Bud Powell were more technically accomplished pianists than the stride pianists who preceded them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The received narrative of jazz piano as a succession of virtuoso soloists misrepresents the tradition's deeper development toward collective musical conversation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Modal jazz and free jazz represent the most significant departures from the soloist tradition in jazz piano history.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jazz piano underwent a series of technical refinements in the 1940s that improved the instrument's integration with the rhythm section.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The history of jazz should be understood primarily in terms of how ensembles, rather than individual musicians, shaped the music's evolution.

explanations.correct: The passage opens by identifying the 'received narrative' of heroic soloists as misleading, then argues across four paragraphs that the tradition's deeper logic is one of collective conversation enabled by deliberate restraint. B integrates both the critique of the standard account and the positive claim.
explanations.A: Too narrow — the comparison to stride pianists is a supporting detail, not the main point.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Modal and free jazz are mentioned as later developments prefigured by bebop, not as the passage's central thesis.
explanations.D: 'Technical refinements' is a phrase the passage explicitly rejects as a sufficient description of what bebop pianists did.
explanations.E: The passage focuses on jazz piano specifically, not jazz history writ large, and frames the argument around individual pianists' choices rather than ensembles as such.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the standard account of jazz piano history can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: unqualified rejection of its characterization of bebop pianists

choices.label: B
choices.text: appreciative of its identification of key figures while skeptical of its interpretive framework

choices.label: C
choices.text: indifferent to its claims about virtuosity but accepting of its chronological ordering

choices.label: D
choices.text: admiration for the richness of its historical detail

choices.label: E
choices.text: hostility toward the scholars who have promoted it

explanations.correct: The author concedes that Monk and Powell are 'cited as the period's towering figures, and for good reason' before arguing that the standard account 'misses' their collective contributions. This is classic qualified acceptance of names/facts with skepticism toward interpretation. B captures both moves.
explanations.A: Too strong — the author does not reject the standard account wholesale; it grants the pianists' importance.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author is far from indifferent; skepticism toward the interpretive framework is a sustained concern.
explanations.D: The passage never praises the standard account's historical detail; it questions its interpretive logic.
explanations.E: No hostility toward scholars is expressed; the critique is aimed at the narrative framework, not its proponents.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A historical claim is introduced, challenged by a series of counterexamples, and ultimately conceded to be partly correct.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A received interpretive framework is identified, a richer alternative is developed through specific cases, later historical evidence is marshaled in support, and a broader conclusion is drawn.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing theories about jazz piano are presented in equal depth, and the passage ends without adjudicating between them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A biography of Thelonious Monk and Bud Powell is given, followed by a discussion of their influence on later jazz.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A narrow claim about bebop piano technique is stated and then generalized to all forms of twentieth-century American music.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 identifies the received soloist narrative; paragraph 2 develops the alternative (collective conversation) through Monk and Powell; paragraph 3 marshals modal and free jazz as corroborating subsequent developments; paragraph 4 draws the broader conclusion about restraint as artistry. B tracks this four-paragraph sequence accurately.
explanations.A: The passage never concedes that the received account is 'partly correct' in its interpretive logic; it only concedes the importance of individual figures.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage clearly adjudicates — it argues that the collective-conversation reading is superior.
explanations.D: The passage discusses Monk and Powell analytically, not biographically, and does not end with 'influence' as the main concern.
explanations.E: The claim is about jazz piano specifically, not all twentieth-century American music.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Monk's practice of stopping comping when a horn soloist took a chorus was significant because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: demonstrated a technical inability to accompany horn players effectively

choices.label: B
choices.text: allowed silence to operate as a mode of harmonic suggestion within the ensemble

choices.label: C
choices.text: reflected the influence of the stride piano tradition he was seeking to revive

choices.label: D
choices.text: was adopted directly from the modal jazz approach Miles Davis later popularized

choices.label: E
choices.text: shifted the harmonic burden entirely to the bass and drums

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that Monk 'would stop comping entirely when a horn soloist took a chorus, allowing silence to function as a form of harmonic suggestion.' B is a close paraphrase.
explanations.A: The passage nowhere suggests Monk lacked technical ability; the gesture is interpreted as a deliberate artistic choice.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Stride pianists are the tradition being departed from, not revived.
explanations.D: The causal direction is reversed — bebop pianists prefigured modal jazz, not the other way around.
explanations.E: The passage says Powell's left-hand sparseness opened space for bass and drums; Monk's silence is described as harmonic suggestion, not a transfer of harmonic burden.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about artistic restraint in jazz piano?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Restraint is valuable in jazz piano only when it is accompanied by exceptional technical virtuosity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The willingness to cede harmonic and rhythmic space within an ensemble can itself constitute a form of artistic mastery.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pianists who practiced restraint were generally less respected by their contemporaries than those who favored individual display.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restraint in jazz piano was primarily a response to commercial pressures rather than an aesthetic choice.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tradition of collective musical conversation ultimately proved less influential than the soloist tradition it partially displaced.

explanations.correct: The passage's final paragraph directly states that ceding ground 'was not a retreat from artistry but its highest expression.' B is a precise inference from this claim.
explanations.A: The passage does not condition restraint's value on virtuosity; the two are treated as separable concerns.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage says nothing about how contemporaries regarded these pianists; this introduces an evaluative frame absent from the text.
explanations.D: Commercial pressures are never mentioned; the passage frames restraint as purely an aesthetic-ethical choice.
explanations.E: The passage argues the opposite — that the solo tradition generated the conditions for a collective one, implying significant influence of the latter.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to Powell's left-hand sparseness (second paragraph) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate how a bebop pianist's individual innovation helped open ensemble space for other instruments

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that Powell was technically inferior to stride pianists who preceded him

choices.label: C
choices.text: contrast Powell's approach with Monk's in order to show that they pursued incompatible goals

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that bebop piano was primarily a reaction against the limitations of the rhythm section

choices.label: E
choices.text: support the claim that bebop pianists were more interested in the bass than in harmonic innovation

explanations.correct: The passage introduces Powell's left-hand sparseness as evidence that bebop pianists were reconceiving the piano's relationship to the ensemble — specifically that it 'invited the rhythm section into a space the stride pianists had monopolized.' A captures this rhetorical function: the detail illustrates the broader claim about collective musical conversation.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The passage never implies inferiority; the sparseness is framed as an advance in collective thinking.
explanations.C: The passage treats Monk and Powell as parallel examples of the same impulse, not as opposing figures.
explanations.D: The passage does not frame bebop as a reaction against the rhythm section's limitations; if anything, bebop opened space for the rhythm section.
explanations.E: No claim about the bass being more important than harmonic innovation is made or implied.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's central claim about the significance of bebop pianists to jazz history?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several modal jazz composers have stated in interviews that the harmonic models they inherited came primarily from bebop horn players, not pianists.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recordings from the late 1950s and 1960s document that bassists and drummers played more melodically active parts when performing alongside bebop pianists who practiced restraint than when accompanying more harmonically dense pianists.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bud Powell's early recordings show that he began his career imitating stride pianists before developing his signature left-hand sparseness.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Free jazz musicians of the 1960s have consistently denied any meaningful connection to bebop as a stylistic precursor.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thelonious Monk composed many of his most celebrated pieces as solo piano works intended for performance without an ensemble.

explanations.correct: The author's central claim is that bebop pianists' restraint enabled collective musical conversation within the ensemble. B directly supports this by providing evidence that other instrumentalists' roles expanded in response to that restraint — confirming the causal and collective mechanism the author argues for.
explanations.A: This would weaken the author's claim by suggesting bebop pianists were not the primary channel through which collective harmonic thinking reached later jazz.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: This is a biographical detail about Powell's development that neither strengthens nor weakens the claim about restraint's significance; it is neutral at best.
explanations.D: This would weaken the author's argument in paragraph 3 that bebop prefigured free jazz.
explanations.E: This would actually complicate the author's framing of Monk as an ensemble-oriented thinker, potentially weakening the claim.

rc.passage:
The emergence of jazz in the early twentieth century has long been narrated as a story of spontaneous communal creation — a music born of collective improvisation, resistant by its very nature to individual authorship. Standard accounts emphasize New Orleans as the crucible, the marching band and the brothel as the twin incubators, and the anonymity of the early players as evidence that jazz belonged, in some irreducibly democratic sense, to everyone and no one. The truth is that this appealing myth, however useful as a founding narrative, obscures the degree to which jazz was also shaped by deliberate compositional intelligence and the fierce, often solitary ambitions of individual artists.

The career of Duke Ellington is the most powerful refutation of the communal-origins story. Ellington did not merely perform jazz; he transformed it into a vehicle for sustained orchestral argument, producing works of structural complexity that rivaled the compositions of his European contemporaries. Yet critics wedded to the spontaneity myth have persistently underread Ellington's compositional achievement, treating his arrangements as elaborated improvisations rather than as the rigorously crafted structures they were. His practice of tailoring specific harmonic vocabularies and melodic shapes to individual soloists — a technique he called 'concerto grosso for the jazz band' — was not an accommodation to improvisation but a sophisticated compositional strategy, one that converted the unpredictable energies of his players into determinate musical arguments. To frame this as mere arrangement is to miss the point entirely.

The communal myth has also distorted how critics evaluate authenticity in jazz. Because spontaneity is coded as genuine and composition as calculating, Ellington's careful craftsmanship has sometimes been characterized as a betrayal of the music's origins — as though the only authentic jazz were jazz that refused to know itself too well. This is a category error of considerable consequence: it smuggles into aesthetic judgment a sociological assumption about who jazz is for and what kind of knowledge its creators are permitted to possess. In contrast to some who romanticize early jazz's rougher textures, Ellington found in the music's own resources — its blues tonality, its call-and-response architecture, its rhythmic elasticity — the material for an aesthetic vision that was at once deeply rooted and formally ambitious. His work demonstrates not a departure from jazz's essential character but its fullest elaboration.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Duke Ellington's compositional innovations placed him in direct conflict with other jazz musicians of his era.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The widespread myth that jazz emerged as purely communal and improvisatory fails to account for the deliberate compositional artistry exemplified by Ellington's career.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jazz historians have generally ignored the European influences that shaped Ellington's harmonic vocabulary.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The most authentic jazz is that which balances spontaneous improvisation with formal compositional structure.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Early New Orleans jazz was less sophisticated than the orchestral jazz that Ellington later developed.

explanations.correct: The passage introduces the communal-origins myth in paragraph 1, refutes it using Ellington's career in paragraph 2, and traces its distorting consequences in paragraph 3. B integrates both strands — the myth and Ellington as its refutation — across the full passage.
explanations.A: The passage does not describe a conflict between Ellington and other jazz musicians; the tension is between Ellington's practice and a critical myth.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: European influences are mentioned only comparatively ('rivaled his European contemporaries'), not as a sustained subject; the passage never claims historians have ignored this.
explanations.D: The author does not endorse a 'balance' thesis; the argument is that composition is itself authentic, not that it must be balanced with improvisation.
explanations.E: The passage does not rank early New Orleans jazz as less sophisticated; it critiques a myth about origins, not the music itself.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the 'communal-origins story' of jazz can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement of its democratic ideals

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured appreciation of its cultural utility combined with firm rejection of its historical accuracy

choices.label: C
choices.text: complete dismissal of it as a fabrication with no basis in fact

choices.label: D
choices.text: ambivalence, since the author ultimately concedes that improvisation is the heart of jazz

choices.label: E
choices.text: mild curiosity about its origins among early twentieth-century critics

explanations.correct: The author calls the communal myth 'appealing' and 'useful as a founding narrative' before pivoting to argue it 'obscures' essential truths. This two-part stance — partial acknowledgment plus substantive critique — matches B exactly.
explanations.A: The author acknowledges the myth's appeal but does not endorse it; enthusiasm is overstated.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong; the author grants that the myth is 'useful,' implying it is not a pure fabrication.
explanations.D: The author does not concede that improvisation is the heart of jazz; the entire argument contests this framing.
explanations.E: The author's stance is critical and substantive, not mild curiosity; and the myth's origins among critics are not the topic.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A theory is introduced, illustrated with a single case study, and then the limitations of the case study are acknowledged.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A widespread narrative is described and endorsed, and two examples from Ellington's career are then provided to support it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A prevailing myth is introduced, its historical inaccuracy is demonstrated through one artist's career, and its distorting effect on critical evaluation is then identified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An aesthetic debate is summarized, a compromise position is proposed, and the compromise is evaluated against existing evidence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two competing critical traditions are presented in the first paragraph, and the remainder of the passage argues for the superiority of one.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces the communal-origins myth; paragraph 2 uses Ellington's career to demonstrate its inaccuracy; paragraph 3 traces the myth's distorting consequences for critical evaluation of authenticity. C captures all three moves in sequence.
explanations.A: The author does not acknowledge limitations of the Ellington case study; on the contrary, Ellington is presented as a decisive refutation.
explanations.B: The narrative is not endorsed — it is challenged. This choice inverts the author's stance.
explanations.D: No compromise position is proposed; the author argues that composition is fully authentic, not that it must be balanced with improvisation.
explanations.E: Paragraph 1 does not present two competing traditions; it describes one dominant myth that the rest of the passage critiques.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Ellington's technique of tailoring harmonic vocabularies and melodic shapes to individual soloists was

choices.label: A
choices.text: an accommodation to the improvisatory demands of his performers

choices.label: B
choices.text: borrowed from the compositional practices of his European contemporaries

choices.label: C
choices.text: a sophisticated compositional strategy that transformed improvisation into determinate musical arguments

choices.label: D
choices.text: primarily intended to distinguish jazz from earlier New Orleans styles

choices.label: E
choices.text: criticized by Ellington himself as insufficiently rigorous

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that this technique 'was not an accommodation to improvisation but a sophisticated compositional strategy, one that converted the unpredictable energies of his players into determinate musical arguments.' C paraphrases this directly.
explanations.A: The passage explicitly denies this interpretation, calling it 'not an accommodation to improvisation.'
explanations.B: The passage compares Ellington's complexity to European contemporaries but does not say he borrowed from them.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No such contrast with New Orleans styles is attributed to this technique.
explanations.E: Ellington never criticizes his own technique in the passage; this is invented.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that critics who treat Ellington's arrangements as 'elaborated improvisations' are

choices.label: A
choices.text: applying a standard appropriate for evaluating early New Orleans jazz but not orchestral jazz

choices.label: B
choices.text: allowing a preconceived narrative about jazz's origins to distort their assessment of his compositional achievement

choices.label: C
choices.text: correctly noting that Ellington's primary artistic contribution was his skill as a performer rather than as a composer

choices.label: D
choices.text: more interested in jazz's sociological origins than in its aesthetic qualities

choices.label: E
choices.text: reacting against the overly formal European influence on Ellington's work

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that critics 'wedded to the spontaneity myth' persistently underread Ellington precisely because the myth leads them to frame his structures as improvisation. This implies their critical lens — the communal-origins story — is distorting their judgment. B captures this inference.
explanations.A: The passage does not suggest there is a separate appropriate standard for New Orleans jazz; it critiques the myth as globally misapplied.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage argues the opposite — that Ellington's compositional achievement is primary and undervalued.
explanations.D: Paragraph 3 raises sociological assumptions, but this is the author's diagnosis of the myth's error, not a characterization of what those critics are 'more interested in.'
explanations.E: No European influence reaction is described; this is outside the passage's scope.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to 'a category error of considerable consequence' (third paragraph) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: introduce a new definition of authenticity that the author will defend for the remainder of the passage

choices.label: B
choices.text: characterize the logical mistake involved in treating spontaneity as the only marker of authentic jazz

choices.label: C
choices.text: acknowledge that critics who favor improvisation have a legitimate aesthetic basis for their preference

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast the critical reception of Ellington's work in the United States with its reception in Europe

choices.label: E
choices.text: suggest that jazz critics lack the technical training required to evaluate orchestral composition

explanations.correct: The phrase 'category error' is used to label the mistake of coding spontaneity as genuine and composition as calculating — a logical confusion that smuggles sociological assumptions into aesthetic judgment. The reference diagnoses the flaw in the critics' reasoning, which is precisely what B states.
explanations.A: The author does not proceed to define a new concept of authenticity; the passage argues that Ellington's work is already authentic by existing standards, properly understood.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author does not acknowledge a legitimate basis for preferring improvisation; the 'category error' language is dismissive, not concessive.
explanations.D: No transatlantic critical contrast appears in paragraph 3.
explanations.E: The passage's critique is about conceptual assumptions, not technical training.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that Ellington's compositional technique was a deliberate artistic strategy rather than an accommodation to improvisation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several of Ellington's contemporaries in European classical music praised his orchestrations as comparable in rigor to their own.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ellington's surviving manuscript scores show detailed notation specifying the harmonic and melodic content assigned to each soloist, with little room for deviation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jazz critics of the 1950s generally preferred artists who emphasized spontaneous improvisation over those who relied on written arrangements.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ellington gave interviews in which he described his admiration for the improvisatory freedom of earlier New Orleans musicians.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Audiences at Ellington's live performances often reported being unaware that his musicians were following written parts.

explanations.correct: The author's claim is that Ellington's technique was a rigorous compositional strategy, not improvisation in disguise. Manuscript scores with detailed notation leaving little room for deviation would directly confirm that his process was predetermined and deliberate — directly supporting the claim.
explanations.A: Praise from European contemporaries supports the claim that Ellington was compositionally serious, but does not directly address whether his soloist-tailoring technique was deliberate strategy vs. accommodation.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: This describes critical preference but does not bear on whether Ellington's own technique was deliberate or accommodating.
explanations.D: Ellington's admiration for improvisatory freedom would, if anything, slightly complicate the author's claim by suggesting some openness to improvisation.
explanations.E: Audience unawareness of written parts speaks to performance texture, not to the deliberateness of the compositional process.

rc.passage:
Translation has traditionally been understood as a secondary activity — derivative, servile, and ultimately subordinate to the original text. The translator, on this account, is a craftsperson whose highest achievement is invisibility: the reader who does not notice the translation has encountered a translator working at the peak of skill. But this understanding, though it persists in popular usage and in many publishing conventions, increasingly fails to account for what translators actually do and for the interpretive choices that literary translation necessarily involves.

To translate a literary work is not to transfer a fixed meaning from one vessel to another but to reconstruct, within the resources of a different language, something of the experience the original produced in its first readers. The challenge is compounded by the fact that no two languages carve the world at exactly the same joints. Spanish distinguishes ser from estar in ways that English cannot replicate with a single verb; classical Japanese layers grammatical markers of social position into verb endings that English can only approximate through word choice and tone. Every decision a translator makes — which connotation to preserve, which to sacrifice, which grammatical structure to exploit — is an act of interpretation. The translator who renders Flaubert's imparfait as the simple past has made a claim about which temporal texture matters most; the translator who opts for a progressive construction has made a different and equally defensible claim.

What follows from this is not, as some have concluded, that translation is arbitrary or that all versions of a text are equally valid. Rather, it suggests that the translator occupies a position analogous to that of the performer in relation to a musical score: constrained by the text's possibilities but active in realizing one among many legitimate readings. Just as the pianist who chooses a slow tempo for a Beethoven sonata is not falsifying the score but inhabiting one of its genuine potentials, the translator who renders a novel's idiomatic speech with contemporary slang rather than archaic diction is not betraying the original but honoring a different dimension of its life. This does not collapse the distinction between good and bad translation; some realizations are simply more faithful, more resonant, more alive to the full range of the original's effects than others. But it does require that we grant the translator something we have long withheld: recognition as an interpretive artist whose choices constitute, and do not merely convey, meaning.

questions.questionStem: The primary purpose of the passage is most likely to

choices.label: A
choices.text: survey the history of translation theory from classical antiquity to the present

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that because translation is inherently interpretive, the translator should be recognized as an interpretive artist rather than a mere craftsperson

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that all translations of a given literary work are equally valid expressions of its meaning

choices.label: D
choices.text: compare the relative merits of literal and free translation as competing methodologies

choices.label: E
choices.text: explain why certain languages, such as Spanish and Japanese, are particularly difficult to translate into English

explanations.correct: The passage moves from the traditional 'invisible craftsperson' model (paragraph 1), through a demonstration that translation requires active interpretive choices (paragraph 2), to the conclusion that translators deserve recognition as interpretive artists (paragraph 3). B captures this arc across all three paragraphs.
explanations.A: No historical survey is offered; the passage makes a conceptual argument, not a historical one.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage explicitly rejects this conclusion in paragraph 3, stating that 'not all versions of a text are equally valid.'
explanations.D: The passage does not compare literal vs. free translation as methodologies; it argues that all translation involves interpretation.
explanations.E: Spanish and Japanese examples are illustrative details in paragraph 2, not the passage's primary subject.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the traditional understanding of translation holds that a translator's highest achievement is

choices.label: A
choices.text: producing a version so seamless that readers do not perceive it as a translation

choices.label: B
choices.text: preserving as many grammatical structures of the original language as possible

choices.label: C
choices.text: faithfully reproducing the ideological content of the source text

choices.label: D
choices.text: making the translator's interpretive choices transparent to the reader

choices.label: E
choices.text: achieving recognition as a co-author of the translated work

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 states explicitly that on the traditional account 'the reader who does not notice the translation has encountered a translator working at the peak of skill' — i.e., invisibility is the highest achievement. A paraphrases this directly.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No mention is made of grammatical preservation as the traditional ideal; this is a plausible world detail not stated in the passage.
explanations.C: Ideological content is never mentioned as the traditional criterion.
explanations.D: The traditional ideal is the opposite — invisibility, not transparency of interpretive choices.
explanations.E: Co-authorship recognition is the opposite of the traditional model; it is closer to what the author argues should be granted.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A translation that departs significantly from the grammar of the original is necessarily inferior to one that adheres closely to it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The difference between a skilled and an unskilled translator lies primarily in the number of interpretive choices the translator makes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two translations of the same novel may differ substantially yet both be legitimate realizations of the original's possibilities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Since translation always involves interpretation, original authors should be involved in approving translated versions of their work.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The conventions of literary translation are more constraining than those governing musical performance.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 uses the performer-score analogy to argue that multiple legitimate realizations exist — a slow tempo and a fast tempo are both genuine potentials of the score. Applied to translation, this means two versions can differ substantially while both being legitimate. C captures this inference directly.
explanations.A: The passage explicitly rejects grammatical fidelity as the sole criterion; the Flaubert example shows that different grammatical choices can be 'equally defensible.'
explanations.B: The passage says skilled translation is more 'faithful, resonant, alive' — a quality argument, not a quantity-of-choices argument.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Author involvement in approval is never discussed; the passage's argument is about the translator's interpretive role, not about approval processes.
explanations.E: The passage treats translation and musical performance as analogous, not as differing in degree of constraint; no such ranking is made.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the Spanish distinction between 'ser' and 'estar' and the Japanese grammatical markers of social position serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: suggest that Spanish and Japanese literature is inherently untranslatable into English

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate that linguistic differences between languages force translators to make interpretive choices rather than straightforward transfers of meaning

choices.label: C
choices.text: argue that translators should have a background in linguistics before attempting literary translation

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast European and Asian translation traditions with the Anglo-American tradition

choices.label: E
choices.text: demonstrate that English is a less nuanced language than Spanish or classical Japanese

explanations.correct: These examples appear immediately after the claim that 'no two languages carve the world at exactly the same joints,' and are followed by the conclusion that 'every decision a translator makes is an act of interpretation.' The examples thus illustrate why linguistic difference necessitates interpretation rather than transfer — precisely what B states.
explanations.A: The passage does not claim untranslatability; it argues for active interpretation as a response to linguistic difference.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No prescription about translator training is made or implied.
explanations.D: No contrast between European, Asian, and Anglo-American translation traditions is drawn.
explanations.E: The passage does not rank languages by nuance; it uses the examples to show structural divergence, not hierarchy.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the view that 'all versions of a text are equally valid' can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: full endorsement, since the passage argues that translation is always a matter of interpretive choice

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejection, on the grounds that it does not follow from the premise that translation is interpretive

choices.label: C
choices.text: cautious sympathy, since the passage acknowledges that multiple valid translations can coexist

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference, since the passage is focused on the translator's role rather than on evaluating specific translations

choices.label: E
choices.text: hostility, because the view undermines the possibility of recognizing translators as artists

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 explicitly states: 'What follows from this is not, as some have concluded, that translation is arbitrary or that all versions of a text are equally valid.' The author rejects this conclusion as a non-sequitur from the interpretive premise — which is exactly what B captures.
explanations.A: The passage explicitly denies this follows from the interpretive argument; endorsement is directly contradicted.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: While the passage allows multiple legitimate translations, it rejects the claim that all are equally valid — so 'cautious sympathy' misstates the author's position on this specific claim.
explanations.D: The author takes a clear position against this view in paragraph 3; indifference is inaccurate.
explanations.E: While the author does want translators recognized as artists, the rejection of 'all versions equally valid' is framed as a logical point, not as motivated by protecting artistic recognition — hostility overstates the tone.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle the author describes using the analogy of a pianist performing a Beethoven sonata?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A stage director who cuts several scenes from a Shakespeare play to shorten its running time, eliminating portions of the original text entirely.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A translator who renders the informal register of a nineteenth-century Russian novel's dialogue with colloquial contemporary English, thereby preserving the social texture of the speech rather than its period flavor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A biographer who selects which episodes of a subject's life to include, inevitably omitting events that other biographers would emphasize.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A film editor who rearranges the chronological sequence of scenes to create a different narrative effect than the director originally intended.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A poet who translates a foreign poem word-for-word, producing an English version that is grammatically awkward but maximally literal.

explanations.correct: The pianist analogy describes an interpreter who is 'constrained by the text's possibilities but active in realizing one among many legitimate readings' — choosing a tempo that honors a genuine potential of the score without falsifying it. The translator in B makes an active choice (contemporary slang for informal register) that honors one dimension of the original (social texture) rather than another (period flavor), precisely the structure of the analogy. This mirrors the passage's own example of using contemporary slang vs. archaic diction.
explanations.A: Cutting scenes eliminates portions of the original text rather than realizing one of its potentials; this is closer to alteration than interpretation within constraints.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Biographical selection involves omission from a life, not interpretation within a fixed textual artifact — the analogy's constraint of the 'score' is absent.
explanations.D: Rearranging scenes alters the structure against the director's intent, which is closer to falsification than to realizing a genuine potential.
explanations.E: A word-for-word literal translation exemplifies the 'invisible craftsperson' model the author critiques, not the active interpretive realization the analogy describes.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A traditional model is described and then immediately refuted; two case studies are examined; a new model is proposed and defended against a potential objection.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A traditional model is introduced and its inadequacy noted; the nature of translation is analyzed to show why interpretation is unavoidable; a revised conception of the translator's role is proposed while a misreading of that conception is preemptively rejected.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing theories of translation are presented; evidence is marshaled for each; and the author concludes that neither theory is fully satisfactory.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A historical account of translation practice is provided; a contemporary challenge to that practice is described; and the author recommends a return to earlier standards.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A philosophical puzzle about meaning is introduced; specific languages are examined to show the puzzle is unsolvable; and the author concludes that translation should be abandoned in favor of learning original languages.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces the traditional invisible-craftsperson model and notes it 'fails to account for what translators actually do.' Paragraph 2 analyzes the nature of translation — linguistic difference, connotative choice, grammatical decisions — to show interpretation is unavoidable. Paragraph 3 proposes recognizing the translator as interpretive artist, preemptively rejecting the misreading that this entails all translations are equally valid. B matches all three moves.
explanations.A: Close but inaccurate: the traditional model is not 'immediately refuted' — paragraph 1 notes its persistence and inadequacy, with the actual demonstration coming in paragraph 2; and there are not 'two case studies' but a general analysis.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No two competing theories are presented; the passage critiques one dominant model and proposes an alternative.
explanations.D: No historical account of translation practice is provided, and the author does not recommend returning to earlier standards.
explanations.E: The author never suggests translation should be abandoned; the conclusion is the opposite — translators deserve greater recognition.

rc.passage:
The history of jazz piano is often told as a story of individual virtuosos—Jelly Roll Morton, Art Tatum, Thelonious Monk—each a singular genius who remade the instrument in his own image. But this narrative, compelling as it is, obscures a quieter and perhaps more consequential development: the gradual transformation of jazz piano from a primarily melodic instrument into one capable of sustaining entire harmonic worlds on its own. That transformation reached its most eloquent expression not in the explosive improvisations of the bebop era but in the modal experiments of the late 1950s, when pianists began to treat the keyboard less as a vehicle for running chords and more as a medium for constructing atmosphere.

Standard accounts of this shift credit the influence of Miles Davis's 1959 recording Kind of Blue, which abandoned the rapid chord changes of bebop in favor of slower-moving modal scales. The truth is more textured. Pianists such as Bill Evans, who performed on that recording, had already been moving in this direction independently, drawing on classical influences—particularly the French impressionists Debussy and Ravel—to dissolve the hard edges of the bebop chord. Evans's voicings, which clustered notes in ways that blurred their individual identities into a single resonant color, owed as much to Debussy's parallel harmonies as to any jazz predecessor. The result was a piano sound that hovered between definition and ambiguity, between a clearly stated harmony and its shadow.

What made this development more than a stylistic novelty was its philosophical dimension. Evans understood the modal approach not merely as a technical reconfiguration of the instrument's resources but as an ethical stance toward musical collaboration. His liner notes for the Waltz for Debby album articulate a conviction that musical conversation—like meaningful human conversation—requires each participant to listen as attentively as they speak. His trio recordings, in which the bass and drums were granted an unprecedented melodic freedom to respond to, rather than merely accompany, the piano, gave institutional form to this conviction. Critics who have praised Evans primarily for the lyrical beauty of his right-hand melodies have, in effect, missed the argument: the beauty is inseparable from the relational structure that produces it.

It would be a mistake, however, to treat Evans as the sole architect of modal jazz piano. Contemporaries such as Herbie Hancock and Chick Corea extended the vocabulary Evans helped to establish, often in directions Evans himself resisted—toward fusion, toward electronic textures, toward a more overt engagement with popular idioms. These extensions were not betrayals of Evans's project but evidence that the modal approach was generative rather than finished, a set of questions rather than a fixed set of answers. The enduring significance of the late 1950s modal turn, then, lies not in any single recording or performer but in the opening it created: a space within jazz piano for meditative introspection, for harmonic ambiguity, and for a conception of ensemble music as genuine dialogue.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bill Evans's trio recordings represent the pinnacle of jazz piano performance in the twentieth century.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The modal turn in jazz piano during the late 1950s was a multidimensional development with lasting aesthetic and philosophical significance, not reducible to any single artist or recording.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Miles Davis's Kind of Blue was the decisive catalyst that redirected jazz piano from bebop chord changes toward modal experimentation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Critics of jazz piano have consistently underestimated the role of French impressionist composers in shaping the modal jazz aesthetic.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The development of jazz piano as a harmonic instrument was primarily the result of technical innovations introduced during the bebop era.

explanations.correct: The passage traces the modal turn across multiple paragraphs, attributes it to several pianists and influences, assigns it both aesthetic and philosophical dimensions, and closes by arguing that its significance lies in the 'opening it created' rather than in any single figure. B integrates all of these strands.
explanations.A: Too narrow — Evans is one figure among several, and the passage does not rank him as the century's pinnacle.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage explicitly complicates this account, noting that Evans had already been moving in this direction independently of Davis.
explanations.D: French impressionism is one supporting detail; the passage's main point is broader than this critical oversight.
explanations.E: The passage argues that the defining development came not from bebop but in reaction to it, through the modal experiments of the late 1950s.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward Bill Evans's contributions to jazz piano can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: unqualified admiration for his technical mastery of the keyboard

choices.label: B
choices.text: respectful appreciation for his aesthetic and philosophical innovations, tempered by recognition that he was one contributor among several

choices.label: C
choices.text: mild skepticism about whether his classical influences genuinely improved upon his jazz predecessors

choices.label: D
choices.text: enthusiasm for his right-hand melodic virtuosity above all other aspects of his work

choices.label: E
choices.text: disappointment that he resisted the fusion and electronic extensions his contemporaries pursued

explanations.correct: The author praises Evans's harmonic voicings, his philosophical stance on collaboration, and his liner-note articulations, but explicitly warns against treating him as 'the sole architect' of modal jazz piano and credits contemporaries with extending his vocabulary. B captures both the admiration and the qualification.
explanations.A: Overstated — 'unqualified' ignores the author's insistence that Evans was one figure among several, and the praise is for more than technical mastery.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No skepticism about the classical influences appears; the author treats them as genuine sources of innovation.
explanations.D: The author explicitly criticizes critics who focus on Evans's right-hand melodies, calling it a failure to grasp his argument — the author's own admiration is for the relational structure, not the melody alone.
explanations.E: The author does not express disappointment; the passage treats Evans's resistance as simply a feature of his aesthetic, not a failing.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A biographical sketch of Bill Evans is offered, followed by an analysis of his recordings, and concluded with a comparison to his contemporaries.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A conventional historical narrative is introduced, its inadequacy is identified, an alternative account is developed with aesthetic and philosophical dimensions, and the account is then broadened to encompass multiple contributors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing theories about the origin of modal jazz are presented, evidence for each is evaluated, and a synthesis is proposed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A critical problem in jazz history is posed, several failed solutions are examined, and the author's own solution is advanced in the final paragraph.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A series of jazz pianists are profiled in chronological order to illustrate the evolution of piano technique across the twentieth century.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 sets up the conventional narrative (individual virtuoso story) and signals its inadequacy. Paragraph 2 complicates the standard Davis-centric account and introduces Evans's independent development. Paragraph 3 adds the philosophical dimension of Evans's collaborative ethic. Paragraph 4 broadens the account to include contemporaries and reframes the modal turn as a generative opening rather than a finished achievement. B tracks these moves accurately.
explanations.A: The passage is not a biographical sketch of Evans; it uses him to argue a broader point about modal jazz.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage does not present two equal competing theories and evaluate evidence for each; it subordinates the Davis-centric account and develops an alternative.
explanations.D: No 'failed solutions' are examined; the passage introduces qualifications and nuances, not a sequence of refuted solutions.
explanations.E: The passage does not proceed chronologically through multiple pianists; it focuses on a specific historical moment and its significance.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Evans's piano voicings were distinctive primarily because they

choices.label: A
choices.text: reproduced the rapid chord changes that characterized bebop

choices.label: B
choices.text: clustered notes so that their individual identities merged into a single resonant color

choices.label: C
choices.text: emphasized the right-hand melodic line above all other elements of piano texture

choices.label: D
choices.text: drew exclusively on jazz predecessors rather than any classical sources

choices.label: E
choices.text: adopted the parallel harmonies of Ravel more completely than those of Debussy

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that Evans's voicings 'clustered notes in ways that blurred their individual identities into a single resonant color.' B is a close paraphrase of this statement.
explanations.A: The opposite — Evans moved away from rapid chord changes.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage criticizes critics who focus on Evans's right-hand melodies and argues that the real significance lies in the relational structure, not the melody alone.
explanations.D: The passage says Evans drew on classical influences, particularly Debussy and Ravel, in addition to jazz predecessors.
explanations.E: The passage does not distinguish between the degrees to which Evans drew on Debussy versus Ravel; it treats them together as 'the French impressionists.'

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A jazz musician's aesthetic choices are most fully understood when considered in isolation from any philosophical commitments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The significance of a musical innovation is best measured by the number of commercially successful recordings it produces.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Extensions of an artistic approach that depart from its originator's preferences can nonetheless be authentic expressions of that approach's generative potential.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Modal jazz represents the culmination of jazz piano's development and left little room for further innovation after the 1960s.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The ethical dimension of Evans's musical practice was less important to his legacy than the purely technical aspects of his piano style.

explanations.correct: In the final paragraph, the author explicitly states that the extensions pursued by Hancock and Corea—in directions Evans himself resisted—'were not betrayals of Evans's project but evidence that the modal approach was generative rather than finished.' C is a careful inference from this claim.
explanations.A: The passage argues the opposite: Evans's aesthetic choices are inseparable from his philosophical commitment to collaborative listening.
explanations.B: The passage never invokes commercial success as a measure of significance; its evaluative criteria are aesthetic and philosophical.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The passage explicitly describes the modal turn as 'a set of questions rather than a fixed set of answers,' implying ongoing openness, not culmination.
explanations.E: The author devotes an entire paragraph to Evans's philosophical-ethical stance and argues that critics who ignore it 'miss the argument,' suggesting the ethical dimension is central, not peripheral.

questions.questionStem: The author most likely discusses Evans's liner notes for the Waltz for Debby album primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate that Evans was a talented writer as well as a gifted musician

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide documentary evidence that Evans understood his modal approach as an expression of an ethical stance toward musical collaboration

choices.label: C
choices.text: contrast Evans's views on musical conversation with those held by bebop pianists

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that Evans's most important contributions were verbal rather than musical

choices.label: E
choices.text: support the claim that Evans's right-hand melodies were the primary source of his aesthetic achievement

explanations.correct: The liner notes are cited immediately after the passage introduces the 'philosophical dimension' of Evans's modal approach — specifically his conviction that musical conversation requires attentive listening. The notes serve as evidence for that philosophical claim. B captures this function accurately.
explanations.A: The literary quality of the liner notes is not the point; they are cited as evidence for a philosophical conviction, not as proof of Evans's writing talent.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage does not use the liner notes to contrast Evans with bebop pianists; the comparison to bebop occurs in paragraphs 1 and 2, not here.
explanations.D: The passage does not suggest Evans's verbal output surpassed his musical contributions; the liner notes illuminate his music, not replace it.
explanations.E: The passage explicitly criticizes critics who focus on Evans's right-hand melodies, so citing the liner notes to support that claim would contradict the author's own argument.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that Evans's modal approach drew significantly on French impressionist composers?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several jazz critics in the 1960s praised Evans's recordings for their similarity to the work of Debussy and Ravel.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Evans stated in interviews that he had never studied the scores of Debussy or Ravel and considered their music irrelevant to jazz.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Herbie Hancock and Chick Corea both acknowledged the influence of French impressionism on their own extensions of modal jazz.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The parallel harmonies characteristic of Debussy's piano writing were already present in some bebop recordings made before Evans began recording.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Evans's trio recordings received greater critical acclaim in Europe than in the United States.

explanations.correct: The author's claim that Evans drew on Debussy and Ravel rests on an inferred stylistic connection. If Evans himself disavowed any familiarity with or interest in their music, that would directly challenge the premise that his work was shaped by their influence, undermining the author's interpretive claim.
explanations.A: This strengthens rather than weakens the claim by providing corroborating critical testimony.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: This is irrelevant to whether Evans himself drew on French impressionism; it concerns his successors.
explanations.D: This might suggest the parallel harmonies had other jazz-internal sources, but the passage's claim is about Evans specifically, not about the origin of the harmonic technique in general; moreover, Evans could still have absorbed Debussy's influence directly.
