explanations.E: Geographic reception patterns have no bearing on the question of Evans's compositional influences.

rc.passage:
The history of jazz piano is in many respects a history of productive misreadings. Each generation of pianists has inherited the innovations of its predecessors and then, through selective emphasis and willful distortion, transformed them into something new. Nowhere is this process more visible than in the transition from the stride tradition of the 1920s to the bebop revolution of the 1940s — a transition that standard jazz historiography tends to describe as an abrupt rupture, but that on closer examination reveals itself as a deeply ambivalent inheritance.

Stride piano, as practiced by James P. Johnson, Fats Waller, and their contemporaries, was built on a particular tension: the left hand alternated between bass notes on the beat and midrange chords on the offbeat, producing a rocking momentum that anchored dancers to the floor, while the right hand was free to pursue melodic flights of considerable sophistication. Critics have often treated stride primarily as entertainment music — crowd-pleasing, physically engaging, and technically demanding but ultimately decorative. This reading is not false, but it is incomplete. Stride pianists were simultaneously theorizing about rhythm: the alternating left hand was not merely a groove machine but an argument about the relationship between pulse and accent, between the predictable and the surprising. What appeared on the surface as a formula for crowd satisfaction was, beneath that surface, a rigorous investigation of rhythmic counterpoint.

The bebop pianists who came of age in the 1940s — Bud Powell foremost among them — are typically seen as breaking decisively with this tradition. And in one sense they did: Powell stripped away the striding left hand almost entirely, replacing it with sparse, unpredictable chord clusters that refused to anchor the listener in any comfortable groove. But the received narrative of rupture obscures a deeper continuity. Powell's liberation of the left hand was not an abandonment of stride's rhythmic investigation; it was, rather, its logical extension. Where stride pianists had staged a dialogue between regularity and surprise within a metrically stable framework, Powell collapsed that framework itself, pushing the implicit tension in stride piano toward a limit the stride masters had approached but never crossed. The bebop left hand does not ignore the questions that stride posed; it answers them by dissolving the terms of the question entirely.

To acknowledge this continuity is not to flatten the real differences between the two traditions. Stride was communal and kinetic, designed for bodies in motion; bebop was cerebral and confrontational, designed, in Thelonious Monk's famous formulation, for listeners who would sit down and listen. Yet even this contrast conceals a shared ambition: both traditions sought to make explicit the latent complexity of rhythm that popular dance music had always exploited but never theorized. What separates stride and bebop is less a matter of musical philosophy than of audience and occasion — a shift in social context that transformed the same underlying inquiry into two apparently opposite artistic programs.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Stride piano was a more intellectually sophisticated tradition than jazz critics have generally acknowledged.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bud Powell's bebop innovations represented a complete and deliberate rejection of the stride piano tradition.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Although stride and bebop piano appear sharply opposed, they share a deeper continuity rooted in a common rhythmic inquiry, and their differences are better explained by social context than by musical philosophy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jazz historiography has systematically underestimated the influence of James P. Johnson and Fats Waller on subsequent generations of pianists.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The transition from stride to bebop illustrates the general principle that artistic movements always build on the traditions they appear to overthrow.

explanations.correct: The passage argues two interlocking claims: that the stride-to-bebop transition conceals a deep continuity (the same rhythmic inquiry extended to its limit), and that the real differences between the traditions are matters of social context rather than musical philosophy. C integrates both strands across all four paragraphs.
explanations.A: Too narrow — this captures only part of paragraph 2's argument and ignores the continuity claim that is the passage's central thesis.
explanations.B: This is the 'received narrative of rupture' that the passage explicitly contests; it is the view the author argues against, not the main point.
explanations.D: The passage mentions these pianists but does not make a claim about historiography's treatment of their influence specifically; this is a plausible-world detail that overstates a subordinate point.
explanations.E: Too broad — the passage argues for a specific mechanism of continuity in jazz, not a universal principle about all artistic movements. Generalizing beyond the passage's scope is a classic over-broad trap.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the standard jazz historiography's account of the stride-to-bebop transition can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: dismissive, because it fails to recognize any connection between the two traditions

choices.label: B
choices.text: cautiously approving, because it correctly identifies the technical demands of both traditions

choices.label: C
choices.text: partially accepting but ultimately critical, because it captures a surface truth while missing the deeper continuity

choices.label: D
choices.text: deeply skeptical of its descriptions of stride piano but fully accepting of its characterization of bebop

choices.label: E
choices.text: sympathetic, because the social differences between the two traditions do justify treating them as a rupture

explanations.correct: The author does not dismiss the standard account outright — the passage concedes that 'in one sense' the beboppers did break with stride — but argues that the rupture narrative obscures a deeper continuity. C captures this nuanced, partially-accepting-but-ultimately-critical stance precisely.
explanations.A: Too strong — the author does not dismiss the standard account as entirely wrong, only as incomplete, mirroring the same move made about stride critics in paragraph 2.
explanations.B: The author is not approving of the standard account; the passage frames the historiographical consensus as the target of correction.
explanations.D: The author does not split admiration/skepticism this way; the critique of the standard account applies to its overall narrative of rupture, not differentially to each tradition.
explanations.E: The author explicitly states that the social contrast 'conceals a shared ambition' — so social differences do not, in the author's view, justify the rupture narrative.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A general claim about jazz history is introduced; the stride tradition is described and its standard interpretation corrected; the bebop tradition is described and its standard interpretation corrected; a synthesis reconciles the two traditions while acknowledging their real differences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two competing theories of jazz history are introduced; evidence for each is presented in turn; the author concludes that neither theory is adequate and proposes a third.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A biographical account of Bud Powell's innovations is presented; these innovations are contrasted with stride piano; the contrast is then used to argue for a new theory of musical influence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The stride tradition is described in technical detail; bebop is then described as its direct descendant; the passage concludes by urging a revision of jazz curricula.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A claim about artistic misreading is introduced; two case studies illustrating the claim are examined; the passage ends by noting exceptions to the general principle.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces the general claim about productive misreadings and the stride-to-bebop transition. Paragraph 2 describes stride and corrects the entertainment-only reading. Paragraph 3 describes bebop and corrects the rupture narrative. Paragraph 4 synthesizes: real differences acknowledged, shared ambition identified, social context as the true separator. A maps onto all four paragraphs accurately.
explanations.B: The passage does not present two competing theories and then reject both in favor of a third; it presents one standard narrative and corrects it.
explanations.C: The passage is not biographical and does not focus on Powell alone; Powell is introduced as an example in paragraph 3, not as the primary subject.
explanations.D: The passage does not describe bebop as stride's 'direct descendant' in a simple lineage sense, and it makes no argument about jazz curricula — a plausible-but-unused move trap.
explanations.E: The passage does not present two distinct case studies, nor does it note exceptions to its principle at the end.
explanations.A: Correct.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, stride piano's left hand technique was characterized by which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: sparse, unpredictable chord clusters that refused to establish a groove

choices.label: B
choices.text: a continuous melodic line that competed with the right hand for rhythmic primacy

choices.label: C
choices.text: an alternation between bass notes on the beat and midrange chords on the offbeat

choices.label: D
choices.text: a metrically free accompaniment designed to liberate the right hand from rhythmic constraint

choices.label: E
choices.text: a rocking pattern derived directly from West African drumming traditions

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 explicitly states that 'the left hand alternated between bass notes on the beat and midrange chords on the offbeat.' C is a direct paraphrase of this detail.
explanations.A: This describes Powell's bebop left hand technique (paragraph 3), not stride — a wrong-sentence trap.
explanations.B: The passage describes the right hand as pursuing melodic flights, not the left; attributing a continuous melodic line to the left hand inverts the passage's description.
explanations.D: Stride's left hand was metrically stable, not free; 'metrically free' is a description that applies to bebop's departure from stride.
explanations.E: The passage makes no mention of West African drumming traditions; this is a plausible world-fact that the passage does not state.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about Bud Powell's bebop style?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It was motivated primarily by a desire to make jazz inaccessible to general audiences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It extended the rhythmic investigation implicit in stride piano by pushing that investigation past the boundaries stride had maintained.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It represented a complete departure from all prior jazz piano traditions, including stride.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It answered the questions posed by stride piano by restoring a more stable metric framework.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It was primarily significant for having introduced chord clusters as a substitute for single-note melody lines.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that Powell's liberation of the left hand 'was not an abandonment of stride's rhythmic investigation; it was, rather, its logical extension,' and that Powell pushed 'the implicit tension in stride piano toward a limit the stride masters had approached but never crossed.' B closely paraphrases this inference.
explanations.A: The passage does not attribute Powell's motivations to a desire for inaccessibility; it situates bebop's cerebral quality within a social context shift, not intentional exclusion.
explanations.C: This is precisely the 'received narrative of rupture' the author contests; attributing it to the author inverts the passage's argument.
explanations.D: The passage states the opposite: Powell 'collapsed' the stable metric framework rather than restoring one.
explanations.E: The passage mentions chord clusters as a feature of Powell's style but does not present this as his primary significance; this is a too-narrow plausible detail.
explanations.B: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The author most likely refers to Thelonious Monk's formulation that bebop was designed 'for listeners who would sit down and listen' primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate that bebop pianists were contemptuous of audiences who preferred stride piano

choices.label: B
choices.text: support the claim that bebop's cerebral quality represented a philosophical break from jazz's dance origins

choices.label: C
choices.text: provide a concrete example of the social and contextual differences between stride and bebop, while framing those differences as surface-level rather than philosophical

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that Monk, not Powell, was the central theorist of the bebop piano tradition

choices.label: E
choices.text: suggest that bebop audiences were more musically educated than the dancers who attended stride performances

explanations.correct: The Monk quotation appears in paragraph 4 to characterize bebop as 'cerebral and confrontational, designed for listeners who would sit down and listen,' in direct contrast to stride's kinetic, communal quality. But the surrounding argument immediately qualifies this contrast as concealing a 'shared ambition.' The quotation thus illustrates the real (but surface-level) social difference while the passage frames it as secondary to the underlying philosophical continuity. C captures both the illustrative and the qualifying functions.
explanations.A: The passage does not attribute contempt for stride audiences to bebop pianists; this overstates the contrast and attributes an attitude not present in the text.
explanations.B: This partially captures the quotation's role but misses the passage's point that the contrast is a matter of audience and occasion, not musical philosophy — the passage explicitly says 'less a matter of musical philosophy.'
explanations.D: The passage does not argue for Monk's centrality over Powell's; the quotation is used for its content, not to establish a hierarchy of theorists.
explanations.E: The passage makes no comparative claim about the musical education of audiences in either tradition; this is a plausible-world inference not licensed by the text.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's central claim about the relationship between stride and bebop piano?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Archival recordings show that Bud Powell attended live stride performances throughout the late 1930s and frequently discussed rhythmic counterpoint with stride musicians.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Musicological analysis reveals that bebop's tempos were, on average, significantly faster than those of stride performances.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several prominent stride pianists publicly criticized bebop as unnecessarily complex and incomprehensible to general audiences.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jazz scholars have documented that the dance halls where stride was performed had declined sharply in number by the early 1940s.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transcriptions of Powell's compositions show that his left-hand chord voicings frequently implied the metric positions that stride's alternating bass pattern had made explicit.

explanations.correct: The author's central claim is that bebop was not a rupture but an extension of stride's rhythmic investigation — specifically that Powell's left hand answered, rather than abandoned, stride's questions about pulse and accent. If Powell's chord voicings implicitly retained the metric positions that stride had made explicit, this directly supports the continuity thesis by showing that bebop preserved stride's rhythmic framework in a transformed, implicit form.
explanations.A: Powell's biographical exposure to stride would support a general influence claim, but not the specific musical-structural claim about rhythmic investigation; this is relevant but does not directly address the passage's argument about how the left hand functions.
explanations.B: Tempo differences would highlight a difference between the traditions, not the underlying continuity — this is more consistent with the rupture narrative the author contests.
explanations.C: Stride pianists criticizing bebop would support the narrative of rupture and conflict, not the author's continuity thesis; this choice slightly weakens rather than strengthens the central claim.
explanations.D: The decline of dance halls supports the social-context explanation for the shift in bebop's audience (paragraph 4), but this is a secondary point about occasion, not the primary claim about shared rhythmic philosophy.
explanations.E: Correct.

rc.passage:
The standard narrative of jazz history assigns to bebop—the fiercely complex style that emerged in Harlem clubs during the early 1940s—a primarily negative identity: bebop was, in this telling, what jazz became when it turned its back on entertainment. Dizzy Gillespie, Charlie Parker, and their collaborators are credited with wresting the music from the dance halls and depositing it, trembling with intellectual ambition, in the concert hall. The movement's virtues, on this reading, are essentially adversarial. What this narrative misses, however, is the degree to which bebop was as much an act of cultural affirmation as of aesthetic revolt.

The case for rereading bebop begins with its relationship to the African American vernacular. Far from abandoning popular forms, bebop musicians drew deeply on blues structures, on the rhythmic vocabularies of church music, and on the call-and-response patterns that had organized black communal music for generations. Parker's most dazzling improvisations were scaffolded on twelve-bar blues progressions that any churchgoer of his era would have recognized; the apparent difficulty of his melodic lines disguised, rather than replaced, their vernacular foundations. To hear bebop as a rupture with the popular is to mistake the outer garment for the body beneath. The musicians were doing something far more deliberate: they were encoding cultural memory in a syntax that demanded active listening, insisting that their audience meet them rather than simply receive them.

This demand for reciprocal engagement had a social dimension that the adversarial narrative also tends to obscure. The Harlem clubs where bebop crystallized were spaces of deliberate in-group address—not performances for a general, racially mixed audience in the manner of the swing bands that preceded them, but conversations among musicians and an initiates' community of listeners. In this respect bebop resembled less a lecture than a seminar: a form organized around shared difficulty rather than spectacle. The musicians' notorious resistance to commercial packaging—their refusal of matching suits, synchronized choreography, and the other apparatus of the swing-era entertainment industry—was not simply arrogance or aesthetic purism. It was a claim about who counted as a legitimate audience, and it enacted, in the domain of music, a broader assertion of intellectual self-determination.

None of this is to suggest that bebop's adversarial dimension was illusory; the revolt against swing's accommodations was real and consequential. But the adversarial reading, taken alone, yields a diminished account—one that reduces a multivalent cultural practice to a single polemical gesture. Bebop's deeper achievement was to hold vernacular depth and intellectual density in productive tension, refusing the choice between accessibility and rigor that the entertainment industry perpetually pressed upon African American musicians. Its legacy is not merely an argument won against the dance hall but a model of how artistic difficulty can be, at the same time, an act of communal self-possession.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bebop's primary historical importance lies in its successful rejection of the commercial entertainment industry that had dominated jazz during the swing era.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although bebop did challenge prevailing aesthetic norms, its deeper significance is as an act of cultural affirmation rooted in vernacular tradition and communal self-determination.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie transformed jazz by disguising blues progressions within melodic lines of unprecedented technical difficulty.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Harlem clubs in which bebop developed functioned as exclusive communities of listeners who deliberately excluded mainstream audiences.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bebop musicians encoded cultural memory in a complex musical syntax primarily in order to resist commercial packaging by the swing-era entertainment industry.

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly argues in paragraph 1 that the standard adversarial narrative misses bebop's role as cultural affirmation, and the final paragraph integrates both strands—adversarial revolt and vernacular depth—while insisting that the affirmative dimension is what gives bebop its deeper significance. B captures this integrated thesis.
explanations.A: This restates only the adversarial dimension the author explicitly calls insufficient; it is the view the passage complicates, not its conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too narrow—this describes only one supporting detail from paragraph 2, not the passage's overall argument.
explanations.D: This paraphrases one point from paragraph 3 without capturing the positive cultural-affirmation claim that frames the whole passage.
explanations.E: This conflates cause and effect; the passage presents the encoding of cultural memory and the resistance to commercial packaging as parallel expressions of the same impulse, not as a means-end relationship.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the standard narrative of bebop's history can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: outright rejection of a view that contains no defensible element

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured skepticism tempered by acknowledgment of the narrative's partial validity

choices.label: C
choices.text: reluctant acceptance of a narrative the author finds personally distasteful

choices.label: D
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement of the adversarial reading as the most historically accurate account

choices.label: E
choices.text: indifference to the debate, given the author's greater interest in bebop's technical innovations

explanations.correct: The author explicitly states in paragraph 4 that 'the revolt against swing's accommodations was real and consequential,' conceding the adversarial narrative's validity, while insisting throughout that the narrative taken alone yields 'a diminished account.' This is precisely measured skepticism combined with partial acknowledgment.
explanations.A: Too strong—the author does not reject the adversarial narrative entirely but calls it incomplete.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: There is no indication of reluctance or personal distaste; the author's correction is intellectual, not emotional.
explanations.D: Directly contradicted by the passage's sustained argument that the adversarial reading is insufficient on its own.
explanations.E: The passage shows deep engagement with the historical debate; technical innovations are not the author's primary interest.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A prevailing interpretation is stated, evidence against it is marshaled across two paragraphs, and a final paragraph fully replaces the interpretation with a new one.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A prevailing interpretation is introduced and found to be partially inadequate; two paragraphs develop the missing dimension; and a concluding paragraph integrates the original interpretation with the revised account.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A biographical account of key musicians is offered, followed by an analysis of their technical innovations, and concluded with a reflection on their cultural legacy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two competing interpretations are presented as equally valid, and the passage concludes by proposing a third interpretation that supersedes both.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A historical question is raised, answered by citing archival evidence, and then complicated by reference to a dissenting school of criticism.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces the standard adversarial narrative and notes what it misses. Paragraphs 2 and 3 develop bebop's vernacular roots and communal self-determination. Paragraph 4 concedes the adversarial dimension while insisting the fuller picture requires both strands—an integration, not a replacement.
explanations.A: The passage does not fully replace the standard interpretation; paragraph 4 explicitly preserves the adversarial dimension as real and consequential.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No sustained biographical account appears, and the passage is not organized chronologically around individual musicians.
explanations.D: The passage does not present two equally valid competing interpretations; it supplements one with a missing dimension.
explanations.E: The passage cites no archival evidence and does not end by introducing a dissenting school.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, bebop musicians' refusal of matching suits and synchronized choreography was primarily

choices.label: A
choices.text: an expression of indifference toward the practical demands of live performance

choices.label: B
choices.text: a claim about who constituted a legitimate audience and an assertion of intellectual self-determination

choices.label: C
choices.text: a deliberate strategy for attracting the racially mixed audiences that swing bands had cultivated

choices.label: D
choices.text: evidence that bebop musicians prioritized aesthetic purism above all other considerations

choices.label: E
choices.text: a rejection of African American vernacular traditions in favor of European concert-hall conventions

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states explicitly that the musicians' resistance to commercial packaging 'was not simply arrogance or aesthetic purism. It was a claim about who counted as a legitimate audience, and it enacted, in the domain of music, a broader assertion of intellectual self-determination.' B paraphrases this directly.
explanations.A: The passage assigns specific social and intellectual meaning to the refusal; indifference is not mentioned.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage states the opposite—bebop was addressed to an in-group, not to general mixed audiences.
explanations.D: The passage explicitly says it was 'not simply arrogance or aesthetic purism,' ruling this out as the primary characterization.
explanations.E: The passage argues bebop retained vernacular roots; this choice inverts the passage's claim.

questions.questionStem: The author's comparison of bebop clubs to a seminar rather than a lecture (paragraph 3) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate that bebop was organized around shared difficulty and reciprocal engagement rather than one-way spectacle

choices.label: B
choices.text: suggest that bebop musicians regarded their audiences as intellectually inferior to themselves

choices.label: C
choices.text: contrast the collaborative nature of bebop with the competitive individualism of the swing era

choices.label: D
choices.text: concede that bebop was ultimately as inaccessible as the abstract concert music it sought to displace

choices.label: E
choices.text: support the claim that bebop constituted a wholesale rejection of African American musical traditions

explanations.correct: The passage uses the seminar/lecture contrast immediately after describing bebop as demanding that audiences meet musicians halfway, characterizing the clubs as 'organized around shared difficulty rather than spectacle.' The comparison illustrates reciprocal engagement—a seminar requires active participants, while a lecture does not.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The passage makes no suggestion of contempt for audiences; the seminar metaphor implies a community of equals sharing difficulty.
explanations.C: Competition between swing and bebop musicians is not the point of the comparison; the contrast is between modes of audience address.
explanations.D: The passage never characterizes bebop as inaccessible in the sense of being displacing concert music; it argues for productive tension between rigor and vernacular depth.
explanations.E: The passage consistently argues against the idea that bebop rejected African American traditions.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about Charlie Parker's improvisations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Their surface complexity was designed to conceal an essentially simple musical content from uninitiated listeners.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Their technical difficulty made them largely inaccessible even to listeners familiar with blues and church music.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Their melodic elaboration, however demanding, rested on vernacular structures that a culturally informed listener could recognize.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They represented a decisive break from the twelve-bar blues progressions that had defined earlier African American music.

choices.label: E
choices.text: They were appreciated primarily by European concert-hall audiences who were receptive to their formal complexity.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that Parker's improvisations 'were scaffolded on twelve-bar blues progressions that any churchgoer of his era would have recognized' and that melodic difficulty 'disguised, rather than replaced, their vernacular foundations.' C accurately synthesizes these two claims.
explanations.A: The passage says the difficulty disguised vernacular foundations, not that it concealed simple content; 'essentially simple' misrepresents the passage's point.
explanations.B: The passage implies that culturally familiar listeners would recognize the underlying structures, so the improvisations were not inaccessible to them.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Directly contradicted—the passage states that blues progressions remained the scaffold, not that they were abandoned.
explanations.E: The passage never mentions European concert-hall audiences; its discussion of audience centers on the African American in-group community.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most support the author's claim that bebop's complexity was a form of communal self-possession rather than mere aesthetic elitism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several leading bebop musicians later recorded commercially successful albums aimed at broad popular audiences, suggesting their earlier complexity was a temporary stylistic phase.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ethnomusicological research shows that call-and-response structures analogous to those in bebop were central organizing features of West African communal music brought to the Americas.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Contemporary accounts from Harlem club regulars describe the music as immediately intelligible to listeners steeped in blues and gospel, even when the melodic lines were elaborate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some swing-era bandleaders privately admitted that their choreographed presentations were designed to maximize ticket revenues rather than to serve artistic goals.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Music critics of the 1940s were largely hostile to bebop, dismissing it as willfully obscure and disconnected from the traditions of American popular music.

explanations.correct: The author's claim is that bebop's difficulty was accessible to a culturally initiated community rather than designed to exclude. Contemporary testimony that listeners immersed in blues and gospel found the music immediately intelligible—despite its complexity—directly supports this claim by confirming the community-based accessibility the author posits.
explanations.A: Later commercial recordings undermine the idea that the complexity was a permanent artistic commitment, but they do not address whether the complexity was communal or elitist in nature.
explanations.B: This supports the vernacular-roots claim made in paragraph 2, but not specifically the communal self-possession argument about the nature of the complexity.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: This supports the passage's implicit criticism of swing's commercialism but does not directly bear on whether bebop's complexity constituted communal self-possession.
explanations.E: Critical hostility would, if anything, reinforce the adversarial reading the author is complicating, not the communal-affirmation claim.

rc.passage:
The history of jazz piano is often told as a succession of innovations—stride giving way to bebop, bebop yielding to cool, cool dissolving into fusion—but this narrative of rupture, however convenient, obscures what is perhaps the more instructive story: the degree to which each generation of jazz pianists metabolized the techniques of its predecessors while insisting on the originality of its own voice. Nowhere is this double movement more legible than in the career of Thelonious Monk, whose music has been variously described as deliberately primitive, eccentrically dissonant, and willfully obscure. Each of these characterizations, while not without a grain of truth, mistakes the surface for the substance.

The received view holds that Monk's clusters of dissonance, his habit of striking notes just beside the expected pitch, and his eccentric rhythmic hesitations represent a kind of cultivated awkwardness—a refusal of competence in the service of originality. This reading is superficially plausible: Monk did possess a piano technique that was, by conservatory standards, unorthodox. But those who studied with him or observed his practice habits report something altogether different: a musician of ferocious discipline who had internalized the entire vocabulary of stride piano, the left-hand orchestral patterns pioneered by Fats Waller and James P. Johnson, and who chose—with considerable deliberation—to stretch, delay, and deform those patterns in the service of a harmonic language no less rigorous for being unfamiliar. His dissonance was not an accident of limited technique but a hard-won argument about the emotional and expressive range of the chromatic scale.

More than merely a technical matter, Monk's harmonic idiom encoded a philosophical position about jazz and, by extension, about African American cultural expression in the postwar era. Where bebop's velocity and complexity served in part as a rebuke to the commercialized swing of the 1930s—asserting that jazz was art demanding active listening, not merely background entertainment—Monk's approach went further. His silences were as compositionally deliberate as his notes; his angular melodies refused the listener the comfort of easy resolution. In this way, his music asked its audience to sit with unresolved tension, to resist the cultural reflex toward premature closure. Critics who heard only willful difficulty missed the democratic ambition beneath it: Monk trusted his listeners enough to withhold easy satisfaction, much as the best literary modernists trusted their readers to complete meaning rather than merely receive it.

To characterize Monk's achievement as mere rebellion, then, is to repeat at a higher level of sophistication the same error as the dismissal of his work as technically deficient. Both readings fail to account for the sustained and systematic nature of his compositional vision—a vision in which stride tradition, bebop harmonic grammar, and a distinctly African American vernacular sensibility were not competing claims but mutually reinforcing strands of a single, coherent artistic argument.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Thelonious Monk's unorthodox piano technique was the product of limited formal training rather than deliberate artistic choice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The history of jazz is best understood as a series of sharp ruptures in which each generation rejects the innovations of its predecessors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monk's musical practice, though widely misread as technical deficiency or mere rebellion, constituted a rigorous and philosophically coherent artistic vision rooted in tradition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monk's primary contribution to jazz was his introduction of African American vernacular sensibility into an otherwise European musical framework.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Jazz pianists of the bebop era shared a common commitment to using dissonance as a form of social protest against racial inequality.

explanations.correct: The passage argues throughout that Monk has been mischaracterized—either as technically limited or as a mere rebel—and that the fuller truth is a disciplined, philosophically coherent vision integrating multiple traditions. C captures both strands of this argument.
explanations.A: This is precisely the received view the passage refutes; the author argues the opposite.
explanations.B: The passage explicitly challenges this 'narrative of rupture' in the opening sentence.
explanations.D: While African American vernacular is mentioned, it is one strand among several, not the primary contribution the passage identifies.
explanations.E: The passage focuses on Monk, not jazz pianists generally; it also does not frame his dissonance as social protest in the narrow racial-inequality sense.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward critics who describe Monk's work as 'deliberately primitive' or 'willfully obscure' can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: measured sympathy, since those critics correctly identified the surface features of Monk's style even if they misjudged its source

choices.label: B
choices.text: outright contempt, because such critics failed to appreciate any aspect of Monk's musical achievement

choices.label: C
choices.text: guarded approval, since their characterizations helped establish Monk's reputation for originality

choices.label: D
choices.text: complete indifference, as the author regards critical reception as irrelevant to an assessment of Monk's technique

choices.label: E
choices.text: respectful but firm disagreement, since those readings capture a surface truth while fundamentally misidentifying the substance

explanations.correct: The author grants that such characterizations are 'not without a grain of truth' but insists they 'mistake the surface for the substance'—a stance of respectful but firm disagreement. E captures both the concession and the correction.
explanations.A: The author concedes a surface truth, but 'measured sympathy' overstates the author's approval; the author is ultimately critical of these readings.
explanations.B: Too strong; the author explicitly concedes that the characterizations have 'a grain of truth,' which precludes outright contempt.
explanations.C: The author does not suggest these critics helped establish Monk's reputation; this is unsupported.
explanations.D: The author engages directly with critical reception throughout the passage, so indifference is plainly wrong.
explanations.E: Correct.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A general thesis about jazz history is stated; a particular musician's career is introduced as an exception to that thesis; evidence for the exception is presented; a broader claim about African American culture is asserted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A dominant critical narrative is challenged; the received view of a specific musician is introduced and then refuted through evidence of his discipline; the deeper philosophical significance of his work is elaborated; a concluding synthesis rejects two inadequate readings.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A biographical sketch of a jazz musician is offered; his technical innovations are catalogued; his influence on later generations is traced; a final paragraph evaluates his legacy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two opposing theories about jazz are introduced; a case study is used to adjudicate between them; the winning theory is endorsed without qualification.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A single critical misreading of a musician is identified; multiple historical examples are marshaled to correct it; a final comparison with literary modernism is used to endorse the corrected reading.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 challenges the rupture narrative and introduces Monk. Paragraph 2 presents and refutes the 'cultivated awkwardness' reading via evidence of his discipline. Paragraph 3 elaborates the philosophical dimension of his work. Paragraph 4 synthesizes by rejecting both the deficiency and the mere-rebellion readings. B tracks all four moves accurately.
explanations.A: The passage does not present Monk as an exception to a thesis; it uses him as the central illustration of a corrected understanding.
explanations.C: No biographical sketch or chronological catalogue of innovations is offered, and influence on later generations is not traced.
explanations.D: The passage does not adjudicate between two equally presented theories; it corrects a received view rather than choosing between two symmetrical alternatives.
explanations.E: The literary modernism comparison appears in paragraph 3 as an analogy, not as an endorsement mechanism; moreover, the passage addresses more than a single misreading.
explanations.B: Correct.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is true of Monk's relationship to the stride piano tradition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Monk rejected stride piano outright as an overly commercialized form unsuited to his harmonic vision.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Monk had thoroughly absorbed the vocabulary of stride piano and chose deliberately to transform its patterns for his own expressive purposes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monk incorporated stride piano techniques unchanged into his compositions as a form of nostalgic tribute.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monk considered the left-hand patterns of stride piano to be technically inferior to the orchestral voicings of bebop.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Monk learned stride piano late in his career, after he had already developed his signature dissonant style.

explanations.correct: The passage states that Monk had 'internalized the entire vocabulary of stride piano' and 'chose—with considerable deliberation—to stretch, delay, and deform those patterns.' B paraphrases this directly.
explanations.A: The passage says Monk internalized stride piano; there is no mention of rejection.
explanations.C: The passage specifies that Monk transformed and deformed stride patterns, not that he incorporated them unchanged.
explanations.D: No such comparative judgment about stride versus bebop voicings is made in the passage.
explanations.E: The passage provides no chronological account of when Monk learned stride piano.
explanations.B: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that Monk's use of silence and unresolved harmonic tension reflected which of the following assumptions about his audience?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jazz audiences were incapable of appreciating conventional harmonic resolution and required unfamiliar musical structures.

choices.label: B
choices.text: His listeners possessed sufficient musical sophistication to engage actively with unresolved tension rather than requiring easy satisfaction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The most important quality in a jazz audience was its willingness to accept dissonance as a replacement for melody.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Postwar audiences were predominantly interested in jazz as a form of social commentary rather than as an aesthetic experience.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Monk believed that audiences trained on bebop would find his music immediately accessible without prior adjustment.

explanations.correct: The passage states that Monk 'trusted his listeners enough to withhold easy satisfaction' and drew an analogy to literary modernists who 'trusted their readers to complete meaning rather than merely receive it.' B reflects this inference accurately.
explanations.A: The passage attributes Monk's choices to trust in his audience's capacity, not to a belief that they were incapable of appreciating conventional resolution.
explanations.C: The passage does not suggest Monk saw dissonance as a replacement for melody; it characterizes his 'angular melodies' as compositionally deliberate.
explanations.D: The passage does not claim Monk's audiences were primarily interested in social commentary; the social dimension is the author's interpretive framing, not attributed to the audience.
explanations.E: The passage implies Monk's music required active engagement, suggesting it was not immediately accessible—the opposite of E.
explanations.B: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to bebop's 'velocity and complexity' as a rebuke to 'commercialized swing' (third paragraph) serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: establish that bebop musicians, like Monk, were indifferent to their audiences' preferences

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide context for distinguishing Monk's philosophical ambition from that of his bebop contemporaries

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that jazz in general has always been primarily a form of social protest rather than aesthetic expression

choices.label: D
choices.text: explain why stride piano's left-hand patterns were inadequate to Monk's harmonic purposes

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that the bebop movement was commercially unsuccessful because of its complexity

explanations.correct: The reference to bebop's rebuttal of commercial swing sets up a contrast: bebop asserted art status, but 'Monk's approach went further'—his silences and refusal of easy resolution exceeded bebop's ambition. The passage uses bebop as a foil to elevate and distinguish Monk's philosophical position. B captures this rhetorical function.
explanations.A: The passage does not characterize bebop musicians as indifferent to their audiences; it characterizes their work as demanding active listening.
explanations.C: The author frames jazz's complexity as an artistic assertion, not as primarily social protest; moreover, this broad generalization is not the passage's point.
explanations.D: Stride piano's left-hand patterns are discussed in paragraph 2, not in connection with this reference.
explanations.E: No claim about commercial success or failure is made regarding bebop.
explanations.B: Correct.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most directly undermine the author's central claim about Monk's dissonance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Monk frequently expressed admiration for the harmonic language of European classical composers such as Bartók and Stravinsky.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several musicians who worked closely with Monk reported that he could not reliably reproduce his own compositions in successive performances.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Archival recordings and the accounts of Monk's students confirm that he drilled specific chromatic voicings with precise, systematic repetition over many years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bebop pianists of Monk's era were almost uniformly trained at conservatories and regarded his technique as inferior to their own.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Monk's commercial recordings were edited by producers who occasionally corrected what they perceived as wrong notes before release.

explanations.correct: The author's central claim is that Monk's dissonance was the product of 'ferocious discipline' and deliberate compositional choice, not accident or limited technique. Evidence that Monk could not reliably reproduce his own compositions would suggest his idiosyncrasies were inconsistent and unrepeatable rather than systematic—directly undermining the claim that his chromatic language was a 'hard-won argument' of disciplined rigor.
explanations.A: Admiration for Bartók and Stravinsky is consistent with—and might even support—the claim that Monk's dissonance was intellectually deliberate.
explanations.C: This would strengthen, not weaken, the author's claim about Monk's discipline.
explanations.D: Conservatory-trained peers viewing Monk's technique as inferior reflects the surface-level misreading the author critiques; it does not provide evidence against the author's deeper claim about intentionality.
explanations.E: Producer corrections affect the commercial record, not Monk's compositional intentions or live practice—the domain the author's claim concerns.
explanations.B: Correct.

rc.passage:
The eighteenth-century career of the sublime is often narrated as a tidy succession in which Edmund Burke's physiological account of terror yielded, after half a century, to Immanuel Kant's austerely cognitive one; Friedrich Schiller is then sometimes appended as a postscript who domesticated Kant's doctrine for a more recognizably moral audience. The narrative has the virtue of simplicity, but its simplicity flatters our habit of reading aesthetic history as a progression from body to mind. A closer look at the arguments themselves suggests that the three thinkers differ less over whether the sublime is bodily or cognitive than over what, in the moment of sublime apprehension, a subject has actually done.

For Burke, what the subject has done is to register, at some remove from genuine peril, the approach of an object too vast or too threatening to be possessed in perception; the tension of nerve and sinew that ensues is not incidental but constitutive, and any account that strips it away mistakes a sign for its cause. Kant's celebrated rewriting of this view appears, on first reading, to dismiss Burke's physiology outright. Yet Kant's own account turns on a parallel insufficiency, this time within the faculties themselves: imagination fails to render an overwhelming magnitude or force as a single intuition, and reason, registering that failure, seizes on it as evidence of its own supersensible vocation. The feeling of the sublime is the feeling of this two-step — defeat followed by discovery — and while it is not the tremor of a body in the presence of a threat, it is no less a report on a process the subject has undergone.

Schiller's contribution, often read as a watering-down, is in fact the most radical of the three. For Schiller the sublime is not primarily a response to an object at all but a rehearsal the subject undertakes against the conditions of its own finitude. The soul that has contemplated the storm at sea or the ruin of empires has practiced, in miniature, standing free of what would otherwise coerce it; the aesthetic feeling is prospective rather than retrospective, a preparation rather than a report. What looks like Kantian moralization is in fact a relocation of the sublime's center of gravity from event to exercise.

It would be a mistake, then, to read these three as successive refinements of a single doctrine. Each identifies a different site — the sentient body, the cognitive faculties, the ethical will in training — at which the sublime is said to occur. The question each is answering is not the same, even when the examples adduced (the storm, the mountain, the conflagration) happen to coincide. That the tradition has remembered them as a series owes more, perhaps, to the tidiness of textbooks than to the actual shape of their disagreement.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Although commonly arranged as successive refinements of one doctrine, Burke, Kant, and Schiller in fact locate the sublime in three different aspects of the subject's activity, and reading them as a sequence obscures this disagreement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kant's cognitive rewriting of Burke's physiological account of the sublime has been overstated; the two thinkers agree that the sublime is fundamentally a report on a process the subject has undergone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Schiller's treatment of the sublime, far from being a watering-down of Kant's, is the most philosophically adventurous of the three eighteenth-century treatments and ought to displace the standard narrative.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The standard textbook narrative, in which Burke's physiological sublime yields to Kant's cognitive sublime and then to Schiller's moralized version, captures the shape of an intellectual progression from body to mind.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Because Burke, Kant, and Schiller draw on the same illustrative examples — storms, mountains, and conflagrations — their theories of the sublime cannot in the end be sharply distinguished from one another.

explanations.correct: The passage opens by criticizing the 'tidy succession' narrative and closes by saying the three thinkers identify different sites (sentient body, cognitive faculties, ethical will) and are not answering the same question. A captures both halves.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Picks up a nuance (the author does say Kant's account is not straightforwardly anti-Burkean) and inflates it into the thesis; the author does not claim the two agree on a shared process.
explanations.C: Paragraph-level restatement of the passage's remark about Schiller; the main point is about all three, not the elevation of one.
explanations.D: Endorses the narrative the passage explicitly criticizes as a flattery of our reading habits.
explanations.E: Reverses the author's position: shared examples are precisely what the passage says has misled readers into treating the three as answering the same question.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the received account of the eighteenth-century sublime can most accurately be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: outright repudiation of its central claims as historically false

choices.label: B
choices.text: skeptical of its tidiness but prepared to grant that it captures something genuine in the thinkers' examples

choices.label: C
choices.text: indifferent, since the author is concerned with the doctrines themselves rather than with how they have been narrated

choices.label: D
choices.text: enthusiasm for its treatment of Kant offset by reservations about its treatment of Schiller

choices.label: E
choices.text: admiration for its pedagogical economy but rejection of the progressivist metaphysics it implies

explanations.correct: The author calls the narrative tidy and traces its appeal to textbook convenience, yet concedes that the thinkers' illustrative examples 'happen to coincide' and never denies that the account captures a pattern; this is skepticism that stops short of repudiation.
explanations.A: Too strong — the author says the received account has the virtue of simplicity and criticizes only what that simplicity obscures.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage is explicitly evaluative of the received narrative, not indifferent.
explanations.D: The author criticizes the received treatment of both Kant (dismissing Burke outright) and Schiller (as a mere postscript); splitting the critique by figure misreads it.
explanations.E: Overstates the author's endorsement — 'admiration for its pedagogical economy' is not in the passage, and the critique is not merely of metaphysics.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A standard narrative is described; its appeal is acknowledged; three positions are examined in turn to show where they actually differ; the narrative's persistence is explained by a consideration other than fidelity to the arguments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A dispute among three thinkers is introduced; each thinker's position is summarized in neutral terms; a fourth position is offered as a synthesis; objections to the synthesis are canvassed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A claim is defended chronologically from its earliest statement to its most recent; objections raised at each stage are rebutted before the narrative advances.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Three aesthetic positions are contrasted with a fourth, unnamed position held by the author; the author's position is then shown to reconcile the earlier three.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A historical puzzle is posed; two candidate solutions are weighed against each other; the second is endorsed; its implications for a related tradition are drawn out.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 presents the standard narrative and its appeal; paragraphs 2-3 walk through Burke, Kant, and Schiller to relocate each; paragraph 4 explains the narrative's persistence by appeal to textbook tidiness. A tracks this exactly.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No fourth synthesizing position appears; the author's move is to separate the three, not to synthesize them.
explanations.C: The passage is anti-progressivist; it does not defend a single claim across stages or canvass stage-by-stage rebuttals.
explanations.D: No unnamed fourth position is introduced, and the author does not reconcile the three.
explanations.E: There is no contest between two candidate solutions; the author rejects one narrative without offering a rival historical solution of that form.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would be likely to assent to which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A theorist who sought to combine Burke's physiological account with Schiller's ethical account would be attempting to reconcile positions that answer different questions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because imagination plays a central role in Kant's account, Kant should be read as having accepted, at a deeper level, Burke's claim that the sublime is fundamentally a bodily phenomenon.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Schiller's treatment of the sublime loses plausibility to the extent that the subject's preparatory exercise takes place in the absence of any actual storm or ruin.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A satisfactory theory of the sublime must identify, within the subject, a single faculty whose activity is common to all cases in which the sublime is felt.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Burke's insistence on the constitutive role of tension of nerve and sinew is the weakest element of his theory and is better dropped.

explanations.correct: The author insists each of the three locates the sublime in a different 'site' and that they are not answering the same question. A theorist attempting to combine two such accounts would therefore be trying to reconcile answers to distinct questions — exactly what the author says has long been obscured.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reverses the author's point: Kant's imagination-failure is a 'parallel insufficiency' within the faculties, not a concealed endorsement of Burke's bodily view.
explanations.C: Schiller's whole point, as the author presents it, is that the sublime for Schiller is not primarily a response to an object; the author would not treat the absence of the object as diminishing its plausibility.
explanations.D: The passage's organizing claim is that the three theorists locate the sublime at different sites; the author gives no sign of demanding a single faculty across cases.
explanations.E: The author is explicitly sympathetic to Burke's point that the physiological element is constitutive rather than incidental.

questions.questionStem: The author's remark that Schiller's contribution is 'often read as a watering-down' (third paragraph) functions in the passage primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: concede a point to readers who would deny that Schiller belongs in a discussion of the sublime at all

choices.label: B
choices.text: introduce a received impression of Schiller that the author then overturns in order to show how radically Schiller relocates the sublime

choices.label: C
choices.text: identify the chief weakness of Schiller's account and explain why Kant's treatment is to be preferred

choices.label: D
choices.text: illustrate the 'progression from body to mind' that the author endorses as the best way of organizing the tradition

choices.label: E
choices.text: contrast Schiller's approach with Burke's in order to argue that Schiller recovers what Kant had abandoned

explanations.correct: The clause is set up in order to be reversed: the author says Schiller is 'in fact the most radical of the three,' and the sentence then explains why. Its function is to introduce a received view the author rebuts.
explanations.A: No such denial is at issue; the author treats Schiller's membership in the tradition as given.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author does not prefer Kant to Schiller; he argues that the two are not even answering the same question.
explanations.D: The 'progression from body to mind' is described as the flattering habit the author criticizes, not as his own organizing principle.
explanations.E: The sentence makes no contrast with Burke and advances no recovery claim; the contrast in the sentence is between the received reading of Schiller and the author's.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following scenarios most closely illustrates the account of the sublime that the passage attributes to Schiller?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A hiker trembles at the sight of an approaching thunderstorm and afterward records the physiological sensations that the storm produced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A philosopher, confronted with the night sky, notes that imagination fails to represent its extent and infers from this failure the supersensible scope of reason.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A novice climber deliberately contemplates the ruin of an ancient fortress in order to strengthen, against future adversity, her capacity to remain unshaken by loss.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A historian catalogues the conflagrations of several cities and argues that their similarity shows a single underlying aesthetic principle at work.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A painter selects a mountain scene for its visual drama and paints it in a way designed to produce in the viewer a nervous apprehension of scale.

explanations.correct: Schiller's sublime, on the passage's reading, is a prospective rehearsal against finitude — the subject practices standing free of what would otherwise coerce her. The climber contemplating the ruin in order to strengthen herself against future adversity matches that mechanism exactly.
explanations.A: Reports a physiological response after the fact — this is Burke's account, not Schiller's.
explanations.B: Tracks Kant's two-step of imagination-failure and reason's self-discovery, not Schiller's prospective exercise.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Describes a historian's empirical comparison rather than an exercise undertaken by the subject against her own finitude.
explanations.E: Focuses on producing an apprehension in a viewer — again closer to Burke's physiological framing than to Schiller's preparatory exercise.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that Burke, Kant, and Schiller are not answering the same question?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Schiller's lectures, now lost, reportedly acknowledged Burke's physiological description as a special case of a more general account that Schiller himself developed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kant's correspondence with colleagues shows that he was aware of Burke's treatise in its German translation and approved of its examples.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A close comparison of the three theorists' definitions reveals that each, despite differences in vocabulary, defines the sublime as a specific modification of a single faculty of the subject and addresses the identical question of what that modification is.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Eighteenth-century readers typically encountered the three texts in the order in which they were written, and commentators of the period already treated them as a developmental sequence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The examples of storms, mountains, and conflagrations that appear in all three accounts were drawn from a shared stock of illustrations circulated in contemporary rhetorical handbooks.

explanations.correct: The author's claim is that each theorist locates the sublime at a distinct site and that the question each is answering is not the same. A demonstration that all three in fact define the sublime as a modification of a single faculty and are addressing the identical question would undermine that claim directly.
explanations.A: A concession by Schiller that Burke's account is a special case of his own would support, not undermine, the author's picture of divergent questions subsuming Burke under Schiller.
explanations.B: Kant's awareness of and approval of Burke's examples is consistent with the author's view that the shared examples have misled readers about the shape of the disagreement.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The author already acknowledges that the tradition has remembered the three as a series; contemporary commentators doing the same is not new evidence against his diagnosis.
explanations.E: Provides a further explanation of why the examples overlap — consistent with, not a threat to, the author's position that shared examples mask differing questions.

rc.passage:
To speak of the structuralist revolution in literary study is already to concede a framing that the movement's most careful practitioners would have resisted. Roland Barthes, in his earlier phase, is sometimes enrolled as the movement's great popularizer; Tzvetan Todorov, as its taxonomist of narrative forms; Gérard Genette, as its most austere theorist of narrative discourse. Each was, at one time or another, willing to describe his project as the extension to literature of the method Ferdinand de Saussure had proposed for language. Yet to arrange these three in a single column under the heading "structuralism" is to understate the differences in what each thought such an extension would require, and in what each believed it could deliver.

Todorov's early grammars of narrative sought what he called the "poetics" of the literary text — not a reading of any particular work but a specification of the underlying system of possibilities from which particular works are drawn. He pursued this with a confidence, later muted, that the system could in principle be fully described, and that any sufficiently careful reader could recover it from the works themselves. Genette's undertaking was more guarded. His categories of order, duration, and frequency were designed to register what a narrative does, but he treated his own apparatus as a descriptive instrument rather than as a discovery about narrative in general, and he repeatedly warned against confusing the map he was drawing with a territory that could exist independently of it. Barthes, by contrast, had by the late 1960s grown suspicious of the very project of a general poetics; his celebrated argument that the text is a "tissue of quotations" rather than the expression of a single intending author pushed against the structuralist confidence that literary works could be referred to an underlying system at all.

It is tempting to read Barthes's later turn as simply anti-structuralist and therefore as a repudiation of Todorov and Genette alike. The temptation should be resisted. Barthes continued to hold — and this is easy to miss — that literary works participate in codes, conventions, and shared stocks of meaning; his quarrel was not with the thought that such codes are at work, but with the thought that a critic's listing of them exhausts what criticism can say. Todorov's and Genette's projects, on his mature view, were not wrong so much as terminal: they described one layer of the text and then stopped where the harder work begins.

Seen this way, the standard narrative — structuralism rises with Todorov, is refined by Genette, and is dismantled by Barthes — captures the chronology but misrepresents the disagreement. All three accepted that literature operates through codes; they parted over whether recovering the codes constitutes the critic's work, supplements it, or ends only where the critic's work properly begins.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The standard narrative that structuralism rose with Todorov, was refined by Genette, and was dismantled by Barthes is chronologically accurate, and its account of the theoretical relations among the three is broadly correct as well.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Barthes's later work, properly understood, marks a full repudiation of the structuralist projects of Todorov and Genette, whose methods Barthes's argument for the text as a tissue of quotations makes obsolete.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Although Todorov, Genette, and Barthes are often grouped together as structuralists who broke in stages from a common project, their disagreement is better understood as concerning the status of the critic's work with respect to the codes that organize literary texts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Genette's cautious treatment of his descriptive apparatus as a map rather than a territory represents the most defensible version of the structuralist program and ought to displace the more ambitious account pursued by Todorov.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The extension of Saussure's linguistic method to literature, undertaken in different ways by Todorov, Genette, and Barthes, ultimately failed because the structuralist assumption of an underlying system of literary possibilities cannot be sustained.

explanations.correct: The passage opens by resisting a uniform 'structuralism' label, contrasts the three thinkers' positions on whether the critic's work is constituted by, supplements, or only begins after the recovery of codes, and closes by saying the standard narrative misrepresents the disagreement. C integrates all three strands.
explanations.A: The passage explicitly says the standard narrative misrepresents the disagreement, even while granting the chronology.
explanations.B: The passage warns explicitly against reading Barthes's later turn as a simple repudiation of Todorov and Genette.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Paragraph-level restatement: the passage treats Genette's caution sympathetically but does not argue he should displace Todorov.
explanations.E: Too strong — the author never claims structuralism 'failed,' and all three thinkers are credited with identifying something real about codes in literary texts.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the mature Barthes would object to which one of the following descriptions of a critic's work?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A critic who, having identified the generic conventions that a poem draws upon, proceeds to examine what the poem achieves by drawing upon them in just the way it does.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A critic who catalogues the narrative codes operative in a short story and, having catalogued them, presents the catalogue as a complete account of the story.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A critic who, while acknowledging that literary codes are at work in a novel, focuses her essay on the tensions and silences that the codes alone cannot explain.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A critic who denies that literary works can be referred to any underlying code or convention whatsoever, treating each work as wholly sui generis.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A critic who treats a descriptive apparatus as a map drawn for particular analytic purposes rather than as a territory existing independently of the critic's concerns.

explanations.correct: Barthes's mature view, according to the passage, accepts that codes are at work but denies that listing them exhausts what criticism can say. A critic who presents the catalogue of codes as a complete account does exactly what Barthes says one should not do.
explanations.A: Describes precisely the further work Barthes thinks begins where code-listing ends; he would endorse it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Describes the kind of critical attention Barthes on the passage's account would endorse — not object to.
explanations.D: The passage explicitly says Barthes continued to hold that codes and conventions are at work; he would also reject this description.
explanations.E: Matches Genette's stance, which Barthes treats as 'not wrong' but incomplete; the object of Barthes's objection is completing with such a description, not adopting one.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward Todorov's early work can most accurately be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: unreserved admiration for the ambition of its systematizing project

choices.label: B
choices.text: respect for the project, accompanied by recognition that the confidence that animated it was later tempered even by Todorov himself

choices.label: C
choices.text: sharp disapproval of its commitment to a general poetics and endorsement of Genette's more guarded alternative in its place

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference, since the author's primary interest lies in Barthes's later repudiation of structuralist method

choices.label: E
choices.text: enthusiasm for its descriptive economy, offset by reservations about its dependence on Saussure

explanations.correct: The passage describes Todorov's project in substantive terms without pejorative language and notes explicitly that his confidence was 'later muted.' The author neither dismisses the project nor endorses it without qualification.
explanations.A: Overstated positivity; 'later muted' signals that the author recognizes the confidence was not sustained.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author does not express disapproval of Todorov's general-poetics commitment and does not elevate Genette above him.
explanations.D: The passage devotes a substantial portion of paragraph 2 to Todorov and treats his project as central to the disagreement; it is not indifferent.
explanations.E: 'Reservations about its dependence on Saussure' is not in the passage; the author does not critique the Saussurean lineage as such.

questions.questionStem: The author's description of Genette's apparatus as a 'map' rather than a 'territory' (second paragraph) serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: contrast Genette's methodological caution with Todorov's more confident assumption that a system of narrative possibilities awaits discovery in the works themselves

choices.label: B
choices.text: align Genette's position with Barthes's later skepticism about any attempt to refer literary works to an underlying system

choices.label: C
choices.text: illustrate the extension of Saussurean method to literature by invoking a cartographic metaphor drawn from linguistics

choices.label: D
choices.text: argue that Genette's categories of order, duration, and frequency are too provisional to count as a contribution to narrative theory

choices.label: E
choices.text: anticipate Barthes's argument that the text is a tissue of quotations and that no author's intention underlies it

explanations.correct: Immediately before the map/territory remark, the passage says Todorov thought the system could in principle be fully described and recovered from the works; the map/territory distinction is deployed to mark the contrast with Genette's more guarded, instrument-not-discovery stance.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The passage treats Genette and Barthes as distinct — Barthes's objection runs deeper than methodological caution about an apparatus. The map/territory language belongs to Genette, not to a shared skepticism.
explanations.C: The cartographic metaphor is not invoked as an illustration of Saussurean method; it is invoked to distinguish two attitudes toward one's own theoretical apparatus.
explanations.D: The author presents Genette's caution as principled, not as evidence that his categories are too provisional to be a contribution.
explanations.E: Barthes's later argument is about quotation and authorship, not about the status of a descriptive apparatus as map versus territory.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, each of the following is true of the mature Barthes EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: He grew suspicious of the project of a general poetics of the literary text.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He continued to hold that literary works participate in codes, conventions, and shared stocks of meaning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He regarded Todorov's and Genette's projects as terminal rather than as simply mistaken.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He argued that the text is a tissue of quotations rather than the expression of a single intending author.

choices.label: E
choices.text: He maintained that recovering the codes at work in a literary text is, by itself, the central task of literary criticism.

explanations.correct: The passage specifically says Barthes's quarrel was with the thought that a critic's listing of codes 'exhausts what criticism can say' — the opposite of maintaining that recovering them is the critic's central task. All other choices are directly stated.
explanations.A: Stated in paragraph 2 ('grown suspicious of the very project of a general poetics').
explanations.B: Stated in paragraph 3 ('Barthes continued to hold ... that literary works participate in codes, conventions, and shared stocks of meaning').
