choices.text: The promise must have been made in the course of a commercial transaction.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The promisee must have attempted, unsuccessfully, to bargain for the promise.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that most jurisdictions require 'that the reliance be of a substantial and definite character,' along with foreseeability and the unavoidability of injustice absent enforcement.
explanations.A: Contradicts the passage: the whole point of estoppel is that it operates where consideration is lacking.
explanations.B: No writing requirement is mentioned in the passage.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The passage gives a familial illustration and does not limit the doctrine to commercial settings.
explanations.E: A failed attempt to bargain is not among the conditions listed.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to a father's pledge to pay his daughter's tuition (paragraph 1) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the kind of promise that, under the traditional consideration rule, would not be enforceable

choices.label: B
choices.text: identify a category of promises to which promissory estoppel cannot properly be extended

choices.label: C
choices.text: present an example of a promise that courts have enforced under the doctrine of promissory estoppel

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast gratuitous family promises with the commercial promises discussed later in the passage

choices.label: E
choices.text: introduce a factual dispute that the remainder of the passage will undertake to resolve

explanations.correct: The example appears immediately after the statement of the consideration rule and serves to make that rule concrete: because the daughter has given nothing in exchange, the pledge is 'a mere gratuitous undertaking, no more binding than a resolution to be generous.'
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Wrong direction: the passage does not exclude such promises from estoppel; it treats them as a setting where reliance might justify enforcement.
explanations.C: Wrong function: the example illustrates traditional non-enforceability, not a case in which enforcement has occurred.
explanations.D: No commercial/family contrast is actually drawn in the passage.
explanations.E: The example states a legal characterization, not a factual dispute.

questions.questionStem: The passage provides the most support for inferring which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A promise that induces no foreseeable change of position in the promisee is unlikely to be enforceable under promissory estoppel.

choices.label: B
choices.text: American courts have, on the whole, abandoned the requirement of consideration in ordinary contract cases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 1932 New Hampshire opinion has been formally overruled in most jurisdictions that once followed it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A promisee who has suffered no material harm may still recover full expectation damages where the promisor's conduct is egregious.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promissory estoppel is best understood as a specialized extension of the law of fraud.

explanations.correct: The author emphasizes that the reliance must be substantial, foreseeable, and detrimental. A promise that induces no foreseeable change of position fails both the foreseeability and the detriment conditions, so enforcement under estoppel would be unlikely.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too-strong: the passage says only that estoppel is an exception, not that consideration has been abandoned generally.
explanations.C: Outside scope: the status of the 1932 opinion as 'leading' suggests the opposite.
explanations.D: Contradicts the author's endorsement of reliance-measured remedies.
explanations.E: Outside scope: the passage characterizes estoppel as a response to induced harm, not as an extension of fraud law.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's position that promissory-estoppel remedies ought to be limited to the amount necessary to restore the promisee's pre-promise position?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Historical surveys of the doctrine show that early American courts granted full expectation damages only where a bargained-for exchange was present.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several state legislatures have recently codified the consideration requirement without mentioning promissory estoppel.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Commentators have praised the 1932 New Hampshire opinion for its clarity of language.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Juries tend to calculate expectation damages more easily than reliance damages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many gratuitous promises are made informally and not reduced to writing.

explanations.correct: The author's position is that expectation damages are reserved for promises supported by consideration, while estoppel should remedy only loss from reliance. A historical finding that early courts granted expectation damages only where a bargain was present directly supports that allocation of remedies.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Neutral: legislative silence on estoppel does not bear on the measure of its remedies.
explanations.C: Off-target: praise for the opinion's clarity says nothing about the proper measure of damages.
explanations.D: Actually cuts the other way: ease of calculation would be a reason to award expectation damages, not to confine recovery to reliance.
explanations.E: Outside scope: writings and formality are not the issue; the measure of recovery is.

rc.passage:
When a federal agency issues a regulation interpreting the statute it is charged with administering, the courts must decide how much weight to give that interpretation in subsequent litigation. For several decades, American reviewing courts followed a two-step approach articulated by the United States Supreme Court in a 1984 case involving the Environmental Protection Agency. Under that approach, a court first asks whether the statute is clear on the precise question at issue; if it is, the court enforces the plain meaning and the agency's view is beside the point. If instead the statute is genuinely ambiguous, the court proceeds to the second step and defers to the agency's interpretation so long as the interpretation is reasonable — even if the court, writing on a blank slate, would have read the statute differently.

The justification most commonly offered for this deference is that Congress, in leaving a statute ambiguous, has implicitly entrusted the gap-filling task to the expert agency rather than to the generalist judiciary. Agencies, after all, possess technical knowledge and continuing engagement with the regulated community that courts cannot readily match. A second justification rests on political accountability: because the agency is ultimately answerable to the elected executive, interpretive choices with policy consequences are thought to be better left with an accountable actor than with appointed judges.

These justifications have, however, invited objection. Critics note that a court asked whether a statute is 'clear' is exercising precisely the interpretive judgment the doctrine later disclaims; the result is a framework in which difficult questions of statutory meaning are partly resolved by a prior determination that the question itself is hard. Moreover, expertise and accountability explain why an agency might be a good source of policy, but they do not obviously explain why a court should depart from its ordinary duty to say what the law is.

The force of these criticisms varies with the type of statute at issue. Where a provision is highly technical — a tariff schedule, an emissions standard, an actuarial formula — the expertise rationale retains most of its persuasive power, and judicial deference can be justified on grounds that are genuinely institutional rather than merely traditional. Where, however, the disputed provision concerns the scope of the agency's own authority, deference is harder to defend: one does not ordinarily permit a party to interpret the document that defines its own powers. Reviewing courts would do well, in this author's view, to preserve deference in the first setting while withholding it in the second. Such a division respects the expertise that originally justified the doctrine without extending it to the very questions on which a disinterested judgment is most needed.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Judicial deference to agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes is justified when the disputed question is technical but not when it concerns the scope of the agency's own authority.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The two-step framework announced in 1984 should be abandoned because its first step already requires the interpretive judgment the second step disclaims.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Federal agencies, being politically accountable through the executive, are better positioned than courts to resolve all genuinely ambiguous statutory questions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The expertise and accountability rationales for judicial deference have proved insufficient and should be replaced by a new rationale grounded in constitutional structure.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts reviewing agency interpretations tend to overestimate the degree of ambiguity in the statutes they are asked to apply.

explanations.correct: The passage presents the two-step deference framework, summarizes the expertise and accountability justifications, reports criticisms of those justifications, and culminates in the author's recommended division: defer on technical provisions, withhold deference on questions about the agency's own authority.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too-strong: the author records the critical point but does not call for abandoning the framework; he proposes a principled division instead.
explanations.C: Contradicts the closing paragraph, which denies deference in a key category of cases.
explanations.D: The passage does not propose a new constitutional rationale; it argues for domain-sensitive application of the existing ones.
explanations.E: Outside scope: overestimation of ambiguity is not discussed.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A doctrine is described, the common justifications for it are presented, objections are reported, and a qualified prescription is offered.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A historical controversy is surveyed and resolved in favor of one of two long-standing positions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A judicial opinion is praised, its critics are rebutted, and the opinion is reaffirmed without qualification.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several competing doctrines are set out, and their relative merits are ranked according to a single criterion.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A statutory scheme is described, and the author argues that Congress should amend it.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 sets out the two-step doctrine; paragraph 2 gives the expertise and accountability justifications; paragraph 3 records objections; paragraph 4 offers the author's division-based prescription.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Wrong move: no historical controversy between two parties is set up and resolved.
explanations.C: Wrong move: the opinion's framework is critiqued, not reaffirmed without qualification.
explanations.D: Wrong move: only one doctrine is in view; there is no ranking.
explanations.E: Wrong target: the author addresses courts, not Congress, and proposes no statutory amendment.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is a justification commonly offered for deferring to an agency's interpretation of an ambiguous statute?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Agencies, having been created by the legislature, speak with its delegated authority on all statutory questions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The agency is answerable to the elected executive and is therefore politically accountable for interpretive choices with policy consequences.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Judicial review of agency action is constitutionally disfavored in the administrative context.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reviewing courts lack the authority to declare any federal statute ambiguous.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Agencies tend to adopt interpretations that favor regulated parties, which courts are then free to accept.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states the accountability rationale almost verbatim: 'the agency is ultimately answerable to the elected executive,' so interpretive choices with policy consequences 'are thought to be better left with an accountable actor than with appointed judges.'
explanations.A: Overstated: the passage does not claim agencies speak with delegated authority on all questions.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Contradicts the passage, which describes active judicial review.
explanations.D: Contradicts step one of the framework, which authorizes courts to determine whether a statute is clear.
explanations.E: Outside scope: agency bias toward regulated parties is not discussed.

questions.questionStem: It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Institutional competence is a more defensible basis for deference in cases involving technical regulatory details than in cases about the boundaries of agency power.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A statute should be treated as unambiguous whenever the reviewing court finds the agency's interpretation unpersuasive.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deference to agency interpretations is inappropriate whenever the statute at issue has significant policy consequences.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The expertise rationale for deference is generally stronger than the accountability rationale.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Federal courts should defer to agency interpretations only when both parties to the litigation request such deference.

explanations.correct: The closing paragraph distinguishes two settings and endorses deference in the technical one while withdrawing it where the agency is, in effect, interpreting the scope of its own power. That is precisely the institutional-competence distinction captured in A.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Overreach: the author nowhere suggests that persuasiveness of the interpretation determines ambiguity.
explanations.C: Too-strong and not supported: the author distinguishes types of ambiguity, not the presence of policy consequences.
explanations.D: Not claimed: the passage does not rank the two rationales generally.
explanations.E: Outside scope: party preferences are not mentioned.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to 'a tariff schedule, an emissions standard, an actuarial formula' (paragraph 4) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: identify kinds of statutory provisions for which the expertise rationale retains substantial force

choices.label: B
choices.text: show that most federal regulatory provisions are too technical for any court to evaluate

choices.label: C
choices.text: catalogue examples of provisions that have been found to be clear at step one of the framework

choices.label: D
choices.text: illustrate the kinds of statutes most likely to exceed the agency's granted authority

choices.label: E
choices.text: contrast modern regulatory statutes with earlier, less specialized forms of legislation

explanations.correct: Immediately before the list the author writes that 'where a provision is highly technical,' the expertise rationale retains most of its persuasive power. The enumeration provides concrete illustrations of 'highly technical' provisions for which deference is appropriate.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Overstated: the author does not claim courts cannot evaluate such provisions, only that deference there is justified.
explanations.C: Wrong target: step one concerns clarity, not technicality; the provisions listed are not being characterized as clear.
explanations.D: Opposite of the function: these examples illustrate deference-appropriate cases, not authority-exceeding ones.
explanations.E: No historical contrast with earlier legislation is drawn in the passage.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the critics described in paragraph 3 is most accurately characterized as

choices.label: A
choices.text: partial agreement, treating their objections as sound in some settings but not others

choices.label: B
choices.text: unqualified endorsement, accepting every point they raise

choices.label: C
choices.text: dismissive rejection on the ground that the critics misunderstand the doctrine

choices.label: D
choices.text: detached neutrality, refusing to take any position on the critics' arguments

choices.label: E
choices.text: mild exasperation at critics who have offered the same objections for decades

explanations.correct: In the final paragraph the author writes that 'the force of these criticisms varies with the type of statute at issue,' then accepts the critics' point for scope-of-authority questions while rejecting it for technical ones. That is partial agreement.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too-strong: the author retains deference for technical cases, contrary to the critics' broader challenge.
explanations.C: Opposite-valence: the critics' objections are treated as at least partly correct.
explanations.D: Contradicted by the author's explicit prescription.
explanations.E: No exasperation or historical frustration is expressed.

questions.questionStem: The author's proposed division is most clearly exemplified by which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A reviewing court defers to an agency's technical calculation of permissible pollutant concentrations under an ambiguous emissions statute, but declines to defer to the agency's determination that the statute authorizes it to regulate a new category of pollutant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A reviewing court defers to an agency's interpretation of a statute regardless of whether the statute is ambiguous, reasoning that agencies are politically accountable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A reviewing court rejects an agency's interpretation of an ambiguous statute because the court believes its own reading is superior on the merits.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A reviewing court refuses to decide a statutory question, remanding the entire case to the agency for further factfinding.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A reviewing court defers to an agency's claim to have acquired authority to regulate a new industry, while reviewing the agency's technical rules de novo.

explanations.correct: The author's proposal is to preserve deference where the provision is technical and withhold it where the dispute concerns the scope of the agency's own authority. A instantiates precisely that division: deference on pollutant concentrations (technical), no deference on whether the statute authorizes regulation of a new category (scope of authority).
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Ignores step one of the framework and the author's selective approach; deference is unconditional here.
explanations.C: Does not track the author's distinction; it rejects deference on the merits rather than on the technical/scope division.
explanations.D: A procedural remand is unrelated to the deference question the author addresses.
explanations.E: Inverts the author's division, deferring on scope while reviewing technical matters de novo.

rc.passage:
Contract law has long recognized the principle of unconscionability, which permits courts to refuse enforcement of a contract or particular clause when the bargain is so one-sided that it shocks the conscience. This principle emerged in the common law tradition as a safeguard against exploitation in transactions where one party holds vastly superior bargaining power. The doctrine of unconscionability operates on the premise that contracts, while generally enforceable according to their terms, must reflect a minimum degree of fairness between the parties.

Unconscionability is typically divided into two categories: procedural and substantive. Procedural unconscionability focuses on the manner in which a contract was formed—whether one party was deceived, had limited opportunity to read or understand the agreement, or lacked meaningful choice. Substantive unconscionability, by contrast, examines the actual terms of the contract itself, asking whether the obligations imposed on one party are unreasonably favorable to the other. Courts have found substantive unconscionability in cases involving exorbitant prices, unlimited liability clauses, or terms that deprive a party of essential remedies.

Applying unconscionability doctrine has proven challenging, however. Courts must balance the principle against the fundamental freedom of contract—the notion that parties should be free to agree to whatever terms they choose, no matter how disadvantageous to one side. A court that too readily invokes unconscionability risks substituting its judgment for that of the parties themselves. Yet a court that seldom applies the doctrine may permit unscrupulous merchants to exploit desperate consumers. This tension remains unresolved in jurisprudence, and different jurisdictions have adopted varying approaches to determining when unconscionability is truly present.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Procedural unconscionability is more important than substantive unconscionability in contract law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The doctrine of unconscionability exists to protect parties from unfair contracts, but courts face difficulty in applying it consistently with the principle of freedom of contract.

choices.label: C

rc.passage:
Administrative law governs the powers and procedures of government agencies and sets boundaries on how those agencies may exercise their authority. A central principle in administrative law is the requirement that agencies act within the scope of their statutory mandate—that is, the authority granted to them by the legislature. This principle is known as the doctrine of ultra vires, which prohibits agencies from exceeding the powers conferred upon them by statute.

When an agency action is challenged as ultra vires, a court must determine whether the agency had legal authority to take that action. This determination requires courts to interpret the relevant statute and assess whether the challenged action falls within the scope of the agency's authority. Courts have developed a framework for such review, examining factors including the plain language of the statute, the legislative history and intent, and the practical consequences of the agency's interpretation. If a court concludes that an agency exceeded its statutory authority, the court may invalidate the agency's action and order it to conform to the law.

However, courts generally recognize that agencies possess expertise in their respective fields, and therefore courts often defer to reasonable agency interpretations of ambiguous statutory language. This deference, known as Chevron deference in the United States, allows agencies considerable latitude in interpreting and implementing the statutes they administer. The balance between enforcing the limits of agency authority and respecting agency expertise creates a tension that courts must navigate. When statutes are clear and unambiguous, courts apply the law strictly; but when statutes contain ambiguities, courts typically uphold agency interpretations that are reasonable and consistent with the statute's purpose.

rc.passage:
Intellectual property law protects the rights of creators and inventors to control the use of their original works. Patent law, which is one branch of intellectual property protection, grants inventors exclusive rights to make, use, and sell their inventions for a limited period. This exclusivity provides inventors with economic incentives to develop and disclose new technologies. However, patent protection also creates a tension between the private interests of inventors and the public interest in accessing and building upon existing innovations.

A key limitation on patent rights is the doctrine of fair use, which permits others to use patented materials in certain contexts without obtaining permission from the patent holder. Fair use in patent law typically applies to research, education, and criticism. For example, a researcher may conduct experiments using a patented technology to understand how it works or to develop improvements, and this use would generally not constitute patent infringement. Similarly, educational institutions may use patented materials for teaching purposes within reasonable bounds. Courts have recognized that permitting such uses serves the broader public interest by advancing knowledge and fostering innovation.

However, determining the boundaries of fair use is frequently problematic. Patent holders argue that broad fair use exemptions undermine the economic incentives that patents are designed to provide, while fair use advocates contend that overly restrictive patent enforcement stifles follow-on innovation. Courts must therefore balance these competing interests when adjudicating disputes. Different jurisdictions have approached this balance differently, and the law continues to evolve as courts grapple with new factual scenarios involving patented technologies. What constitutes fair use in one context may not qualify as fair use in another, making predictability difficult for both patent holders and potential users.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patent protection provides incentives for innovation, but fair use doctrine creates tension between inventor rights and public access, and courts struggle to balance these competing interests.

choices.label: D

choices.label: E

explanations.A: The passage does not advocate eliminating fair use; it describes the balance courts must strike.
explanations.B: Fair use is described as limited to specific contexts (research, education, criticism), not unlimited.
explanations.C: Correct.

rc.passage: The law of trespass protects property owners' right to exclude others from their land. Traditionally, a person commits trespass when they intentionally or negligently enter another's land without permission. However, courts have had to address whether trespass applies when someone enters land briefly and without causing damage. In a 2001 case in Massachusetts, a homeowner sued a surveyor who had entered the homeowner's property for approximately fifteen minutes to measure boundary lines, with the homeowner's express refusal. Despite the lack of any physical damage or disruption, the court held that the surveyor had committed trespass. The court reasoned that the law of trespass protects not just against harm to the land itself, but against the property owner's right to control who accesses the land at all. This decision established an important principle: that trespass liability does not depend on the degree of harm caused, but rather on the simple fact of unauthorized entry. As a result, property owners now have a clear legal basis for excluding individuals from their property, even when those individuals pose no threat to the land's condition or value. This principle has since been consistently applied in Massachusetts courts, making the protection of property rights more certain and more accessible to ordinary property owners.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.text: Massachusetts courts have consistently rejected the idea that trespass requires damage to the land itself.

choices.label: E

explanations.correct: This choice captures the core thesis: trespass liability rests on unauthorized entry, not on harm. The passage's full arc—from definition, through the case, to the principle and its application—supports this reading.
explanations.A: Too narrow and inverts the liability mechanism: the passage notes trespass doesn't require harm, but doesn't address damages.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too specific to surveyors; the principle applies broadly to any unauthorized entry.
explanations.D: Accurate but partial—it's one aspect of the point, not the main thesis about what trespass protects.
explanations.E: Reiterates the case detail, not the broader principle the passage emphasizes.

rc.passage: Contract law recognizes the doctrine of unconscionability, which allows courts to refuse to enforce agreements that are both procedurally and substantively unfair. Procedural unconscionability refers to the bargaining process itself—whether one party lacked meaningful choice or did not have a fair opportunity to understand the terms. Substantive unconscionability refers to whether the terms themselves are unreasonably favorable to one party. Courts rarely invalidate a contract on procedural unconscionability alone; both elements must typically be present. In a 2003 case in New York, a consumer signed a credit-card agreement that she admitted she did not read. The agreement contained a clause requiring all disputes to be resolved through mandatory arbitration, which significantly limited the consumer's right to sue in court. The credit-card company had offered no negotiation and had not highlighted the arbitration clause, making the consumer's assent to that term essentially uninformed. At the same time, the arbitration requirement was exceptionally one-sided, favoring the credit-card company's dispute-resolution interests over the consumer's. The court found both procedural and substantive unconscionability, and refused to enforce the arbitration clause. This case clarified that where a consumer lacks a real opportunity to understand material contract terms and those terms are substantively unfair, courts have a duty to protect the consumer's interests. The decision has been widely followed by courts in subsequent cases, and it has made consumer protections through unconscionability doctrine more robust and more reliably available.

explanations.E: The passage focuses on fairness of the bargaining process and terms, not party intent.

rc.passage:
Few doctrines in the common law of torts have proved more resilient, or more troubling, than the rule that a landowner owes only a minimal duty of care to persons who enter her land without permission. Under the traditional formulation, still recited in many jurisdictions, the occupier must merely refrain from willfully injuring the trespasser; the elaborate apparatus of reasonable foreseeability that governs other negligence cases has no application. The rule is often defended on the ground that it protects the autonomy of the landowner and discourages wrongful entry. Yet in a series of decisions beginning in the late 1970s, the High Court of the fictitious jurisdiction of Alderney began to qualify the rule in ways that have not been fully appreciated.

The turning point was the 1981 decision in a case involving a child who had wandered onto an unfenced construction site and been injured by exposed machinery. Rather than disturb the traditional rule outright, the court carved out what it termed a "known-peril exception," under which an occupier who is aware that trespassers regularly frequent a particular portion of her land may be required to take reasonable steps to abate latent dangers there. The exception was initially confined to cases involving children, on the theory that minors cannot reliably appreciate the significance of a no-trespassing sign. In subsequent decisions, however, the court extended the doctrine to adult trespassers whose presence was, as a factual matter, anticipated by the occupier — hikers crossing a pasture to reach a beach, for instance, or commuters using an unmarked path across a rail yard.

Critics have argued that this expansion has hollowed out the traditional rule while leaving its language intact, producing a doctrine that is nominally strict but functionally indistinguishable from ordinary negligence. The charge has some force; the distinction between a peril that is "known" to the occupier and one that is merely foreseeable to a reasonable occupier is finer than the court's opinions have acknowledged, and in practice the two inquiries tend to collapse into each other. Yet the criticism overstates the case. The Alderney court has consistently declined to extend the exception to trespassers whose presence was not actually anticipated, and it has refused to require affirmative inspection of the premises for hidden dangers. The occupier is still entitled, in most cases, to assume that her land is hers to use as she wishes.

What the Alderney decisions illustrate, then, is not the abandonment of the traditional rule but its gradual domestication. The court has been unwilling to say, as courts in some neighboring jurisdictions have said, that the status of the entrant is simply one factor among many in an undifferentiated negligence calculus. Whether that reticence will survive the next generation of cases is, regrettably, uncertain.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Alderney High Court's known-peril exception has effectively abolished the traditional rule governing a landowner's duty to trespassers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although critics have charged that recent Alderney decisions have hollowed out the traditional rule on duty to trespassers, the court has in fact modified the rule only in limited ways while preserving its core.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The traditional common-law rule that a landowner owes trespassers only a duty to avoid willful injury is difficult to reconcile with ordinary principles of negligence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Courts should extend the known-peril exception developed in Alderney to cases involving adult trespassers whose presence is not actually anticipated by the occupier.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Alderney High Court's 1981 decision concerning a child injured on a construction site marked a decisive break with the traditional rule governing trespassers.

explanations.correct: The passage sets up the traditional rule, describes the Alderney court's qualifications, acknowledges the critics' charge that the rule has been gutted, and then responds that the criticism overstates the case — the court has modified but preserved the traditional rule. B integrates both strands.
explanations.A: Reverses the author's corrective: the author explicitly argues the court has not abandoned the traditional rule.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage does not argue that the traditional rule is irreconcilable with ordinary negligence; it describes how the Alderney court has navigated between the two.
explanations.D: The author reports that the court has declined to extend the exception to unanticipated trespassers, without endorsing further extension.
explanations.E: Paragraph-level restatement — the 1981 case is an illustrative turning point, not the thesis.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the critics described in the third paragraph can most accurately be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: dismissive of their characterization and confident that it rests on a simple misreading of the Alderney decisions

choices.label: B
choices.text: sympathetic to their concerns and persuaded that the traditional rule has been effectively abandoned

choices.label: C
choices.text: partially receptive but ultimately unconvinced, holding that the criticism captures a real difficulty yet overstates its consequences

choices.label: D
choices.text: uncertain whether the criticism is well founded and unwilling to reach a judgment on the question

choices.label: E
choices.text: openly hostile to the critics' methods while conceding the accuracy of their conclusions

explanations.correct: The author says the charge 'has some force' — the distinction between 'known' and 'foreseeable' peril is finer than the court has admitted — but then insists 'the criticism overstates the case.' That is exactly the 'partially receptive but ultimately unconvinced' posture.
explanations.A: Too strong — the author concedes the criticism has some force; he does not dismiss it as a misreading.
explanations.B: Mischaracterizes the author's conclusion, which is that the rule has been modified but not abandoned.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The author reaches a definite judgment; he is not simply undecided.
explanations.E: Out of register — there is nothing hostile in the author's treatment, and he does not concede the critics' conclusions.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A longstanding doctrine is described; a series of judicial modifications is traced; a critical view of those modifications is presented and partly rebutted; the author offers a concluding characterization.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two rival doctrines are introduced; evidence for each is surveyed; the author endorses the more recent and rejects the older.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A doctrine is described; its origins are traced to an early illustrative case; an opposing doctrine in a neighboring jurisdiction is compared; the two are shown to be equivalent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A legal rule is defended on policy grounds; objections to the policy defense are presented; the author concedes the objections and endorses a replacement.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A series of cases is summarized in chronological order; a general principle is derived from the series; the principle is shown to resolve a longstanding doctrinal controversy.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 sets out the traditional rule and its rationale; paragraph 2 traces the Alderney court's known-peril exception and its extension; paragraph 3 states the critics' charge and partially rebuts it; paragraph 4 offers the concluding characterization of 'gradual domestication.'
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The passage does not present two rival doctrines and endorse one; it describes modifications to a single doctrine.
explanations.C: The neighboring-jurisdiction comparison is a brief contrast in the final paragraph, not an equivalence demonstration.
explanations.D: The author does not concede the objections or endorse a replacement.
explanations.E: No general principle is derived from the cases; the passage traces qualifications to an existing rule.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the known-peril exception as developed by the Alderney High Court currently applies to which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: any trespasser whose presence a reasonable occupier would have foreseen

choices.label: B
choices.text: only children who wander onto unfenced land and cannot appreciate warning signs

choices.label: C
choices.text: adult trespassers whose presence the occupier has, as a factual matter, anticipated

choices.label: D
choices.text: trespassers injured by dangers that the occupier could have discovered through reasonable inspection

choices.label: E
choices.text: licensees and invitees who enter the land with the occupier's implied consent

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 reports that the exception was extended from children to 'adult trespassers whose presence was, as a factual matter, anticipated by the occupier.' That is the scope the doctrine has reached.
explanations.A: Altered qualifier: the author emphasizes that the court has refused to equate the 'known' peril standard with what a reasonable occupier would have foreseen.
explanations.B: Wrong sentence — the exception was originally limited to children, but the passage reports it has since been extended.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The third paragraph expressly states that the court has refused to require affirmative inspection for hidden dangers.
explanations.E: Outside scope — the passage does not address the occupier's duty to licensees or invitees.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A doctrine can be significantly modified by courts without being formally abandoned.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The distinction between a known peril and a foreseeable one is of no practical consequence in landowner-liability cases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The traditional rule concerning trespassers ought to be replaced with an undifferentiated negligence standard.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Courts in neighboring jurisdictions have reached results more defensible than those of the Alderney High Court.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The future of the known-peril exception is secure against further doctrinal pressure.

explanations.correct: The author's concluding image of 'gradual domestication' — the traditional rule qualified but not abandoned — commits him to the general proposition that significant modification need not amount to formal abandonment.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reverses the author: he says the distinction collapses in practice, but denies that it is of no consequence — the court has used it to refuse extension to unanticipated trespassers.
explanations.C: The author is describing, not endorsing, that alternative approach, and his tone suggests a preference for the Alderney court's reticence.
explanations.D: Outside scope — the author contrasts the approaches without ranking them.
explanations.E: The closing 'regrettably, uncertain' implies the author is skeptical that the reticence will survive.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference in the second paragraph to commuters using an unmarked path across a rail yard functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the expansion of the known-peril exception beyond its original application to children

choices.label: B
choices.text: suggest that the Alderney High Court has applied the doctrine in ways that are difficult to defend on policy grounds

choices.label: C
choices.text: contrast the Alderney doctrine with the approach of neighboring jurisdictions

choices.label: D
choices.text: introduce a counterexample that the author believes the court should not have accepted

choices.label: E
choices.text: explain why the traditional rule on trespassers has survived despite repeated judicial modification

explanations.correct: The commuter reference appears in the sentence that extends the exception 'to adult trespassers whose presence was, as a factual matter, anticipated' — paired with hikers as examples of that extension. Its rhetorical job is to illustrate the expansion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Accurate-content, wrong-function: the author does not treat the commuter example as a policy failure.
explanations.C: The contrast with neighboring jurisdictions appears in the closing paragraph, not here.
explanations.D: The author reports the extension without suggesting the court erred in accepting it.
explanations.E: Wrong grain — the reference illustrates an expansion, not a survival.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that the criticism discussed in the third paragraph overstates the case?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A recent empirical study of Alderney trial courts has found that judges applying the known-peril exception almost invariably find the occupier to have anticipated the trespasser's presence whenever a reasonable occupier would have foreseen it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several neighboring jurisdictions have expressly adopted the Alderney approach and applied it without reported difficulty.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Landowners in Alderney report that they now take greater precautions against trespasser injuries than they did before the 1981 decision.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In cases involving child trespassers, Alderney courts continue to apply the known-peril exception more readily than in cases involving adults.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Alderney legislature has considered, but declined to enact, a statute replacing the traditional trespasser rule with an undifferentiated negligence standard.

explanations.correct: The author's defense of the court rests on the claim that 'known' and 'foreseeable' peril are treated as distinct inquiries in practice. An empirical showing that trial courts collapse the two in application directly undercuts that defense and strengthens the critics' charge that the doctrine is functionally indistinguishable from ordinary negligence.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Wrong direction — adoption elsewhere says nothing about whether the distinction holds up in Alderney.
explanations.C: Greater landowner precaution is consistent with either side of the debate; it does not speak to the doctrinal distinction.
explanations.D: Off-target — this supports the author's picture of a differentiated doctrine, if anything.
explanations.E: Legislative inaction affects neither the court's application of the exception nor the critics' descriptive claim about its practical scope.

rc.passage:
When constitutional courts are asked to interpret open-textured provisions — clauses guaranteeing "due process," "equal treatment," or "the liberty of the person" — two broad methodological camps tend to form. The first, often labeled originalist, insists that such provisions must be given the meaning they bore at the time of their enactment; to permit the language to shift with evolving social conditions, on this view, is to license judges to amend the constitution under cover of interpretation. The second, the living-document camp, treats the constitution as a text whose general terms are designed precisely to accommodate changing circumstances, and which must be read anew in each generation if it is to continue to govern a society its drafters could not have foreseen.

The debate, as it is usually staged, presents the two positions as exhaustive rivals. The Supreme Court of the fictitious Republic of Verrania, in a notable 2004 decision interpreting that country's 1867 guarantee of "liberty," offered what it called a third way. Writing for a narrow majority, Chief Justice Harmon argued that the historical meaning of a constitutional term fixes what she termed its outer limits — the scope beyond which no interpretation may go — while leaving room for the court to select, from among the readings that remain within those limits, the one best suited to contemporary conditions. A constitutional guarantee, on this view, is neither a photograph of the drafters' intentions nor a blank check to be filled in by each generation of judges.

The position has obvious appeal. It preserves the discipline of historical inquiry without committing the court to the anachronism of imagining itself in the drafters' shoes on every question. Yet the Harmon formulation is more difficult to apply than its economy of phrase suggests. The question of how the "outer limits" of a term's historical meaning are to be fixed is itself deeply contested, and the court's opinions have been less than forthcoming about the methodology. In some cases, those limits have been drawn with reference to ordinary eighteenth-century usage; in others, with reference to specialist legal dictionaries; in still others, with reference to the purposes the drafters are thought to have been pursuing. These sources do not always converge, and the Verranian court has not told us how to choose among them when they diverge.

For this reason, some commentators have charged that the Harmon formulation is not so much a middle position as a rhetorical concession to originalism, one that permits the court to reach living-document results while invoking the vocabulary of historical fidelity. That charge is probably unfair. The court has, in several decisions since 2004, refused to adopt interpretations that commentators on the living-document side had urged, precisely on the ground that the proposed readings exceeded the outer limits of the 1867 language. What is true is that the methodology remains undertheorized. Until the court addresses that deficiency, the promise of a third way will not be fully redeemed.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Verranian Supreme Court's 2004 decision demonstrated that originalism and the living-document approach are not, as usually supposed, exhaustive alternatives for interpreting open-textured constitutional provisions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chief Justice Harmon's attempt to articulate a third way between originalism and the living-document approach is promising but remains methodologically incomplete.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Commentators who charge that the Harmon formulation is merely a rhetorical concession to originalism have correctly identified the central weakness of the Verranian court's post-2004 jurisprudence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Constitutional courts ought to reject both originalism and the living-document approach in favor of a formulation that draws the outer limits of constitutional terms by reference to the purposes of the drafters.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Verranian court's 2004 decision interpreting the 1867 guarantee of liberty has been applied so inconsistently that it should be reconsidered by the full court.

explanations.correct: The passage introduces the two-camp debate, presents Harmon's third way, notes its appeal, identifies the unspecified methodology for drawing outer limits as its central weakness, and closes by saying the promise will not be redeemed until that deficiency is addressed. B captures both the promise and the incompleteness.
explanations.A: Paragraph-level restatement of paragraph 2; the passage's overall argument goes beyond merely showing the two camps are not exhaustive.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author expressly says this charge 'is probably unfair.'
explanations.D: The author does not endorse any particular source for outer limits; the purposes-of-the-drafters source is mentioned as one among several.
explanations.E: Too strong — the author does not call for reconsideration by the full court.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward Chief Justice Harmon's formulation can most accurately be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement of its conceptual elegance and confidence in its practical application

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured approval of its theoretical aspiration tempered by concern about an unresolved methodological issue

choices.label: C
choices.text: pointed skepticism that treats the formulation as a rhetorical cover for results-driven decision making

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutral curiosity about a novel approach whose merits he is unwilling to evaluate

choices.label: E
choices.text: disappointment with a promising beginning that the court has since abandoned in practice

explanations.correct: The author grants that the position has 'obvious appeal' and defends the court against the harsher critics, but insists the methodology for fixing outer limits is 'undertheorized' and that the promise will not be redeemed until that is addressed. That is measured approval plus a specific reservation.
explanations.A: Overstated positivity: the author raises a serious methodological concern.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author expressly says the pointed-skeptic charge is 'probably unfair.'
explanations.D: The author does take a position, both in defending the court against commentators and in identifying a deficiency.
explanations.E: Wrong feature: the author does not say the court has abandoned the formulation; he says the court has applied it, if imperfectly.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the Harmon formulation treats the historical meaning of a constitutional term as

choices.label: A
choices.text: a source of guidance that judges may consult or disregard in light of contemporary conditions

choices.label: B
choices.text: the single correct reading from which no departure is permissible

choices.label: C
choices.text: a boundary that no interpretation may cross, within which the court selects the reading best suited to present conditions

choices.label: D
choices.text: a photograph of the drafters' intentions that controls interpretation in every case

choices.label: E
choices.text: a starting point that is ordinarily dispositive but may be overridden when social circumstances have changed dramatically

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 reports that Harmon treats historical meaning as fixing the term's 'outer limits — the scope beyond which no interpretation may go — while leaving room for the court to select, from among the readings that remain within those limits, the one best suited to contemporary conditions.'
explanations.A: Altered qualifier: Harmon treats historical meaning as a binding outer limit, not as optional guidance.
explanations.B: Reverses the formulation: multiple readings remain permissible within the outer limits.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The passage uses the 'photograph of the drafters' intentions' language as something Harmon rejects.
explanations.E: Nothing in the formulation permits the outer limits themselves to be overridden.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A court adopting the Harmon formulation should ordinarily give controlling weight to eighteenth-century ordinary usage over the drafters' apparent purposes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The living-document approach is, on reflection, incompatible with any meaningful discipline of historical inquiry.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The persuasiveness of the Harmon formulation would be increased if the court articulated how to adjudicate between conflicting sources of historical meaning.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Originalism is preferable to the living-document approach because it provides a more determinate methodology.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Commentators on the living-document side have been essentially correct in the specific interpretations they have urged since 2004.

explanations.correct: The author identifies the unresolved question of how to choose among divergent sources of historical meaning as the reason the formulation 'remains undertheorized,' and says the third way's promise will not be redeemed until that deficiency is addressed. He thus commits to the proposition that addressing that question would increase the formulation's persuasiveness.
explanations.A: The author describes ordinary usage as one source among several and does not rank it above the drafters' purposes.
explanations.B: Outside scope — the author does not claim the living-document approach cannot accommodate historical discipline.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The author does not endorse originalism; he describes a third way that seeks to combine historical discipline with interpretive latitude.
explanations.E: The passage reports that the court has rejected several living-document readings on historical grounds without indicating the author's view on the merits of those readings.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion in the third paragraph of the varying sources used to draw outer limits in different Verranian cases serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: establish that the Harmon formulation has been applied inconsistently across different subject-matter areas

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide support for the charge that the court has used the formulation as a rhetorical cover for results-driven decisions

choices.label: C
choices.text: identify the particular methodological question the author believes the court has left unanswered

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that historical inquiry is more difficult in constitutional law than in other areas of law

choices.label: E
choices.text: contrast the court's post-2004 practice with the methodology Chief Justice Harmon described in her 2004 opinion

explanations.correct: The paragraph catalogs ordinary usage, specialist dictionaries, and drafters' purposes precisely to pose the question the court has not answered: how to choose among them when they diverge. That is the unresolved methodological question the author flags.
explanations.A: Accurate-content, wrong-function: the author uses the variation to identify a gap in methodology, not to catalog subject-matter inconsistency.
explanations.B: The author expressly rejects the rhetorical-cover charge as 'probably unfair.'
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Outside scope — the passage does not compare constitutional law with other areas.
explanations.E: The author does not claim the post-2004 practice departs from Harmon's stated methodology; he claims the stated methodology was never sufficiently specified.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's defense of the Harmon formulation against the charge made by the commentators in the final paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In every post-2004 case in which the Verranian court has adopted a reading urged by living-document commentators, the reading was also consistent with ordinary eighteenth-century usage of the relevant term.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The commentators who have made the rhetorical-cover charge are themselves committed to the living-document approach.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A recent comparative study has found that courts in other jurisdictions invoking Harmon's formulation have disagreed about how to draw outer limits.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chief Justice Harmon has retired, and the current Verranian court contains no justice who participated in the 2004 decision.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several constitutional scholars have praised the 2004 opinion as a significant contribution to interpretive theory.

explanations.correct: The author's defense turns on the court's having refused interpretations that exceeded the outer limits of historical meaning. If every living-document reading the court accepted was also within ordinary historical usage, then the court's post-2004 record coheres with the stated methodology rather than just reaching desired outcomes under historical vocabulary — directly strengthening the defense.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The commentators' own commitments do not bear on whether the charge is accurate.
explanations.C: Wrong direction — confusion about outer limits in other jurisdictions, if anything, weakens confidence in the formulation.
explanations.D: Personnel changes say nothing about whether the formulation was methodologically cover for results-driven decisions.
explanations.E: General scholarly praise is too diffuse to speak to the specific charge.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following hypothetical judicial rulings most closely conforms to the Harmon formulation as described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A court interpreting a constitutional guarantee of "freedom of assembly" holds that the guarantee must be read to reflect contemporary social conditions, without reference to the meaning the term bore at enactment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A court interpreting a constitutional guarantee of "unreasonable search" determines that the eighteenth-century meaning of "unreasonable" forecloses any reading protective of electronic communications and declines on that basis to extend the guarantee.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A court interpreting a constitutional guarantee of "cruel punishment" surveys the range of practices the eighteenth-century drafters would have regarded as cruel, concludes that prolonged solitary confinement falls within that range, and so holds the practice unconstitutional.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A court interpreting a constitutional guarantee of "due process" establishes that the term's historical meaning permits several readings, rejects a proposed reading as falling outside that permissible range, and adopts among the remaining readings the one best adapted to present circumstances.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A court interpreting a constitutional guarantee of "equal protection" defers to the legislature's determination of what equal protection requires, citing the need to avoid judicial amendment of the constitution under cover of interpretation.

explanations.correct: The Harmon formulation has two operative features: (1) historical meaning fixes outer limits beyond which no reading may go, and (2) within those limits, the court selects the reading best suited to present conditions. D instantiates both features — rejection of an outside-the-limits reading, plus contemporary selection among the remaining readings.
explanations.A: Matches the living-document approach, which the Harmon formulation rejects as a blank check.
explanations.B: Applies only the outer-limits half of the formulation and stops there; it does not show the court selecting among permissible readings for present adaptation.
explanations.C: Does not exhibit the second operative feature: the court treats the eighteenth-century meaning as directly dispositive rather than as a limit within which a contemporary selection is made.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Describes judicial deference rather than the Harmon formulation, which concerns the court's own interpretive method.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uneasy position within the common law of contracts, for it operates as an equitable corrective to the rigors of the consideration requirement rather than as an independent principle of contractual obligation. Under classical contract doctrine, a promise is legally enforceable only when the promisee provides consideration — that is, something of legal value bargained for and given in exchange for the promise. Yet this rule, however coherent in theory, produces harsh results when a promisor makes a clear, unambiguous promise, the promisee reasonably relies upon it to their detriment, and the promisor subsequently seeks to withdraw. It was largely in response to such situations that Anglo-American courts began, in the latter half of the nineteenth century, to develop what would eventually be codified in Section 90 of the American Restatement (Second) of Contracts: the principle that a promise that the promisor should reasonably expect to induce reliance, and that does induce such reliance, is enforceable to the extent necessary to avoid injustice.

The difficulty, however, lies not in articulating the doctrine but in applying it consistently. Two elements of Section 90's formulation have generated persistent disagreement among courts. The first is the requirement that reliance be "reasonable" — a criterion that courts have interpreted both narrowly, demanding objective evidence that any person in the promisee's position would have acted similarly, and broadly, asking only whether this particular promisee's reliance was not irrational given the circumstances. The second, and more contentious, element is the phrase "to the extent necessary to avoid injustice," which courts have taken to license two distinct and often incompatible remedial approaches: some courts award expectation damages, placing the promisee in the position they would have occupied had the promise been performed; others award only reliance damages, compensating merely for out-of-pocket losses incurred in reliance on the promise. The choice between these measures is not merely technical — expectation damages can be vastly larger — and the absence of a uniform rule has left plaintiffs uncertain of what remedy to seek and courts uncertain of what to award.

This doctrinal inconsistency is particularly regrettable because it undermines the equitable rationale that prompted the doctrine's development in the first place. A promisee who reasonably reorganizes her affairs upon a firm assurance and then receives only partial compensation has not been made whole; the injustice the doctrine was designed to remedy persists. Some commentators have argued that courts should abandon the remedial ambiguity entirely and adopt a uniform expectation-damages rule whenever reliance is established, on the ground that anything less fails to honor the promisee's legitimate expectations. Others maintain that reliance damages are the more principled measure because promissory estoppel is, after all, a substitute for a true contract, and to award expectation damages would be to grant the promisee more than the equitable circumstances warrant. Whether the courts will resolve this tension through legislative intervention or through the gradual consolidation of case law remains to be seen; one hopes, however, that the resolution will be guided by a clear commitment to the doctrine's foundational purpose of preventing detrimental reliance from going uncompensated.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The doctrine of promissory estoppel was developed as an equitable response to the harsh results of the consideration requirement, and courts should uniformly award expectation damages when it applies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although promissory estoppel arose to address injustices produced by the consideration requirement, inconsistent judicial interpretation of two key elements of the doctrine has prevented it from reliably achieving its remedial purpose.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Section 90 of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts represents the most satisfactory codification of promissory estoppel, but courts have applied its remedial provisions incorrectly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The distinction between expectation damages and reliance damages is the central unresolved question in American contract law, and legislative intervention is the only viable solution.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promissory estoppel has replaced classical contract doctrine in Anglo-American courts because the consideration requirement has proven unworkable in most commercial disputes.

explanations.correct: The passage traces the doctrine's equitable origins (paragraph 1), identifies two specific sources of interpretive inconsistency (paragraph 2), and argues that this inconsistency undermines the doctrine's purpose (paragraph 3). B integrates all three strands.
explanations.A: Too narrow — the passage does not endorse the expectation-damages rule; it presents it as one contested position among two.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage does not claim the Restatement is the most satisfactory codification, nor does it say courts apply it 'incorrectly' — rather, courts interpret it inconsistently.
explanations.D: Too strong and too broad — this describes one element of the problem but excludes the 'reasonableness of reliance' element and misstates the author's view of legislative intervention (presented as one possibility, not the only solution).
explanations.E: The passage does not claim promissory estoppel has replaced classical doctrine; it is described as a corrective supplement, and the consideration requirement is not called unworkable.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, under classical contract doctrine a promise is legally enforceable only when

choices.label: A
choices.text: the promisee has relied on the promise to their detriment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the promisor had a reasonable expectation that the promisee would rely on the promise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the promisee provides something of legal value bargained for and given in exchange for the promise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: a court determines that enforcing the promise is necessary to avoid injustice.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the promise is clear and unambiguous and is made by a party with the capacity to contract.

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly: 'a promise is legally enforceable only when the promisee provides consideration — that is, something of legal value bargained for and given in exchange for the promise.' C is a close paraphrase.
explanations.A: This describes a condition for promissory estoppel, not classical doctrine.
explanations.B: This describes an element of Section 90's formulation, not the classical consideration requirement.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: This paraphrases the 'to the extent necessary to avoid injustice' standard from Section 90, not classical doctrine.
explanations.E: Capacity is not mentioned in the passage; the passage focuses on consideration as the enforcement requirement.

questions.questionStem: The passage identifies which of the following as the two elements of Section 90's formulation that have generated the most persistent disagreement among courts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The requirement that the promise be unambiguous and the requirement that the promisor have bargained for reliance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The reasonableness of the promisee's reliance and the phrase 'to the extent necessary to avoid injustice.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: The definition of consideration and the appropriate measure of damages in contract disputes generally.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The requirement that reliance be detrimental and the requirement that the promisor intend to induce that reliance.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The distinction between equitable and legal remedies and the appropriate jurisdiction for promissory estoppel claims.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 explicitly identifies 'the requirement that reliance be reasonable' and 'the phrase to the extent necessary to avoid injustice' as the two elements generating persistent disagreement.
explanations.A: Neither 'unambiguous promise' nor 'bargained-for reliance' is identified as a contested element of Section 90 — these relate to classical doctrine.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage is not about the definition of consideration in general; that belongs to classical doctrine, not Section 90.
explanations.D: Detrimental reliance and intent to induce are touched on but not identified as the two contested elements generating persistent judicial disagreement.
explanations.E: Jurisdictional questions and the equitable/legal remedy distinction as such are not the two contested elements the passage names.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Courts that award expectation damages in promissory estoppel cases are acting contrary to the equitable rationale that gave rise to the doctrine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A promisee who incurs substantial out-of-pocket losses in reasonable reliance on a promise has suffered an injustice if those losses are not fully compensated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Promissory estoppel should be abolished and replaced with a statutory scheme that precisely defines when promises are enforceable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The consideration requirement should be eliminated from classical contract doctrine because it produces uniformly unjust outcomes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts that award only reliance damages in promissory estoppel cases are always acting consistently with the doctrine's foundational purpose.

explanations.correct: The passage states that 'a promisee who reasonably reorganizes her affairs upon a firm assurance and then receives only partial compensation has not been made whole; the injustice the doctrine was designed to remedy persists.' This directly supports B.
explanations.A: The passage does not condemn expectation damages as contrary to the equitable rationale — it presents expectation damages as one of two contested approaches, and the commentators who favor it are not dismissed.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author expresses hope that the doctrine's foundational purpose will guide resolution; abolishing the doctrine entirely is not suggested.
explanations.D: The author describes the consideration requirement as producing 'harsh results' in some situations, not uniformly unjust outcomes; this overreaches the passage.
explanations.E: The passage presents reliance damages as one contested view; the author does not endorse it as 'always' consistent with the doctrine's purpose.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the current state of promissory estoppel doctrine can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: confident that legislative reform will soon resolve the competing remedial approaches adopted by different courts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: skeptical that promissory estoppel can ever be applied consistently given the inherently vague language of equitable doctrine.

choices.label: C
choices.text: critical of the doctrinal inconsistency that has emerged and hopeful that courts will orient any resolution around the doctrine's foundational purpose.

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutral as between the expectation-damages and reliance-damages approaches, viewing each as an equally valid expression of the doctrine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: dismissive of the commentators who advocate for a uniform expectation-damages rule, on the ground that such a rule exceeds the equitable scope of the doctrine.

explanations.correct: The author calls the inconsistency 'particularly regrettable' and closes with 'one hopes... that the resolution will be guided by a clear commitment to the doctrine's foundational purpose.' This combines criticism of the current state with a qualified hope for principled resolution — precisely what C captures.
explanations.A: The author says legislative intervention is one possibility, not that it will 'soon' occur; 'confident' overstates the author's tone.
explanations.B: The author does not suggest the doctrine is inherently incapable of consistent application; the problem is identified as judicial inconsistency, not structural vagueness beyond remedy.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The author is not neutral — the passage's closing sentence and the description of the inconsistency as 'regrettable' signal clear evaluative investment.
explanations.E: The author presents commentators favoring expectation damages as a coherent position; 'dismissive' mischaracterizes the author's even-handed treatment of both camps.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of expectation damages and reliance damages in the second paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate how the phrase 'to the extent necessary to avoid injustice' has produced inconsistent remedial outcomes, thereby supporting the broader claim that the doctrine is applied inconsistently.

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that expectation damages are the more equitable remedy and should be uniformly adopted by courts applying promissory estoppel.

choices.label: C
choices.text: explain how the consideration requirement in classical contract doctrine was gradually replaced by reliance-based principles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that the Restatement (Second) of Contracts deliberately left the remedial question open to allow courts flexibility in achieving equitable outcomes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: provide a historical account of how promissory estoppel was codified in Section 90, tracing its development from nineteenth-century equity courts.

explanations.correct: The second paragraph identifies two contested elements of Section 90; the discussion of expectation vs. reliance damages exemplifies how the second contested element — the 'injustice' phrase — produces divergent outcomes. This supports the paragraph's overarching claim about doctrinal inconsistency, which in turn supports the passage's main argument.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The author presents both approaches even-handedly; the discussion does not argue for expectation damages.
explanations.C: The passage describes promissory estoppel as a corrective supplement to, not a replacement for, classical doctrine.
explanations.D: The passage does not claim the Restatement deliberately left the question open; the ambiguity is treated as a problem, not a designed feature.
explanations.E: The historical account of Section 90's development appears in paragraph 1, not paragraph 2; paragraph 2 is about interpretive disagreement, not codification history.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its historical origins are described; two specific interpretive problems with the doctrine are identified and illustrated; the author argues that these problems undermine the doctrine's purpose and expresses hope for a principled resolution.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced; a single authoritative interpretation of the doctrine is endorsed; counterarguments to that interpretation are surveyed and dismissed; the author concludes that legislative intervention is required.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing contract-law doctrines are introduced and compared; their respective historical origins are traced; the author argues that one doctrine is superior to the other and should replace it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A legal problem is identified; a court case illustrating the problem is analyzed in detail; the author uses the case to derive a general principle applicable to all future promissory estoppel claims.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A legal doctrine and the traditional requirement it supplements are described; the doctrine's codification is praised as satisfactory; a single disputed element is analyzed and a resolution is proposed.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces promissory estoppel, its equitable rationale, and Section 90. Paragraph 2 identifies two contested elements and illustrates their inconsistent judicial application. Paragraph 3 evaluates this inconsistency as undermining the doctrine's purpose and closes with a hope for principled resolution. A follows this sequence accurately.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The passage does not endorse a single interpretation, nor does it dismiss counterarguments; legislative intervention is one possibility, not the author's conclusion.
