explanations.C: Only one doctrine (promissory estoppel) is at the center of the passage; classical doctrine is context, not an equal subject. The passage does not argue for replacement.
explanations.D: No specific court case is analyzed in detail; the passage is doctrinal and analytical rather than case-focused.
explanations.E: The Restatement codification is not praised as satisfactory — it is described as generating disagreement. The passage identifies two disputed elements, not one, and does not propose a specific resolution.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel represents one of the more consequential departures from the classical common-law requirement that a binding contract must rest upon consideration — that is, a bargained-for exchange in which each party gives something of legal value. Under classical doctrine, a promise made without consideration is ordinarily unenforceable, however much the promisee may have relied upon it to his or her detriment. Promissory estoppel modifies this rule by holding that a promisor may be bound if the promisee reasonably relied on the promise and suffered a demonstrable loss as a result. The doctrine thus functions as an equitable corrective, designed to prevent the unjust enrichment of parties who make promises they intend others to act upon and then seek the shelter of the consideration requirement to escape responsibility.

Yet the expansion of promissory estoppel has not been uniform across common-law jurisdictions, and the inconsistency in its application has generated considerable scholarly criticism. Courts in the United States have generally construed the doctrine broadly, treating it as an independent basis for recovery rather than merely a defensive shield against the enforcement of contracts that would otherwise fail for want of consideration. A 1965 decision from a New York appellate court, for instance, allowed a plaintiff to recover damages — measured not simply by the expenditures made in reliance but by the full expectation interest, the amount the plaintiff would have received had the promise been kept — on the strength of a gratuitous promise of continued employment. English courts, by contrast, have taken a far more restricted view, permitting the doctrine to operate only as a defense and declining to award expectation damages in reliance-only cases. This divergence creates a practical asymmetry: a promisee who would receive full contractual remedies in a United States court may obtain nothing of substance in an English court on materially identical facts.

The source of this divergence lies partly in differing views about the doctrine's theoretical foundation. American courts tend to frame promissory estoppel as resting on a theory of reasonable reliance that carries its own independent moral weight, sufficient to ground a cause of action. English courts, conversely, have been reluctant to permit reliance alone to substitute for the discipline imposed by the consideration requirement, fearing that an expansive promissory estoppel would destabilize commercial certainty by rendering a wide range of informal assurances legally actionable. There is something to be said for this concern: commercial parties frequently make statements of intent — expressions of hope, aspiration, or preliminary negotiation — that they do not intend to be legally binding. An overly permissive doctrine risks converting such statements into enforceable obligations.

Nevertheless, the English restriction appears unduly narrow. Where a party has made an unambiguous promise, with knowledge that the promisee would rely on it, and the promisee has in fact restructured significant affairs in reliance, the equitable argument for enforcement is strong. The consideration requirement in such circumstances functions not as a principled limitation on liability but as a technicality that licenses a deliberate breach. Courts on both sides of the Atlantic would do well to adopt a middle position — one that preserves the consideration requirement as the baseline rule but extends promissory estoppel as an independent cause of action in cases of clear, detrimental, and foreseeable reliance.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The doctrine of promissory estoppel was developed to correct the harshness of the consideration requirement in classical contract law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: American courts have interpreted promissory estoppel more broadly than English courts, and this divergence reflects a deeper disagreement about the doctrine's proper theoretical basis.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The inconsistent application of promissory estoppel across common-law jurisdictions stems from conflicting views about reliance and consideration, and the author argues for a balanced middle position.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The expansion of promissory estoppel threatens commercial certainty by rendering informal assurances legally actionable, and courts should therefore apply it only as a defense.

choices.label: E
choices.text: English courts have been correct to restrict promissory estoppel to a defensive role, because an expansive doctrine would undermine the principled foundation of the consideration requirement.

explanations.correct: The passage traces the jurisdictional divergence between U.S. and English courts, locates its theoretical source, acknowledges the concern for commercial certainty, and ultimately advocates a middle position that extends promissory estoppel as an independent cause of action in clear reliance cases. C integrates all of these strands.
explanations.A: This describes only the content of paragraph 1 — the origin of the doctrine — not the passage as a whole. It is too narrow and omits the comparative analysis and normative argument.
explanations.B: This is closer but incomplete: it captures the comparative observation of paragraphs 2–3 but omits the author's normative conclusion in paragraph 4, which is an essential part of the passage's thesis.
explanations.D: This misrepresents the author's position. The author acknowledges the commercial-certainty concern but ultimately rejects the restrictive English approach; the passage does not advocate limiting the doctrine to a defense.
explanations.E: This is the opposite of the author's conclusion. The author explicitly criticizes the English restriction as 'unduly narrow' and calls for promissory estoppel to operate as an independent cause of action in appropriate cases.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the English courts' restriction of promissory estoppel can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: complete rejection of a position that has no merit whatsoever

choices.label: B
choices.text: grudging acknowledgment of a concern that is ultimately outweighed by equitable considerations

choices.label: C
choices.text: full endorsement of a rule that appropriately preserves commercial certainty

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference to a doctrinal dispute that is of limited practical consequence

choices.label: E
choices.text: enthusiasm for a position that the author regards as superior to the American approach

explanations.correct: The author writes 'There is something to be said for this concern' regarding commercial certainty, conceding the English position has merit, but then calls the English restriction 'unduly narrow' and argues for broader enforcement in clear reliance cases. This is precisely the posture of B — a grudging acknowledgment that is nonetheless outweighed.
explanations.A: Too strong. The author explicitly grants that the English concern about commercial certainty has some validity ('There is something to be said for this concern'), so the rejection is not total.
explanations.C: This is the opposite of the author's conclusion. The author criticizes the English restriction and proposes an expansion of the doctrine.
explanations.D: The author plainly cares about this dispute and argues for a specific resolution; indifference is not consistent with the passage's tone.
explanations.E: The author does not endorse the English approach; the passage argues against it while acknowledging its partial merit.
explanations.B: Correct.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its historical origins traced; a jurisdictional divergence in its application is identified; the theoretical source of that divergence is examined; and the author proposes a synthesis.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two competing legal doctrines are compared; their relative merits are assessed; one is found superior; and the passage recommends its adoption across all jurisdictions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined; a single illustrative case is analyzed in detail; the case's outcome is criticized; and a reform is proposed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A legal problem is introduced; a solution proposed by American courts is endorsed without qualification; the English solution is dismissed; and a conclusion is reached.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A common-law principle is described; scholarly criticism of the principle is surveyed; the author sides with the majority of critics; and a legislative remedy is recommended.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces promissory estoppel and its doctrinal function. Paragraph 2 identifies the divergence between U.S. and English courts. Paragraph 3 locates the theoretical source of that divergence. Paragraph 4 concedes a concern but argues for a middle-position synthesis. A captures this four-part movement accurately.
explanations.B: The passage does not compare two separate doctrines — it examines two applications of the same doctrine. Nor does it find one application fully superior; the author proposes a middle position rather than endorsing either side.
explanations.C: Only one case is mentioned (the 1965 New York case), but it is cited briefly to illustrate a point about expectation damages, not analyzed in detail. The passage's structure is much broader than case analysis.
explanations.D: The author does not endorse the American approach without qualification; the passage explicitly calls for a middle position, not a wholesale adoption of U.S. doctrine.
explanations.E: The passage does mention scholarly criticism in paragraph 2, but the author does not side with a majority of critics or recommend a legislative remedy; the proposal is directed at courts.
explanations.A: Correct.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the 1965 New York appellate court decision was notable primarily because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: held that promissory estoppel could operate only as a defense against a breach-of-contract claim

choices.label: B
choices.text: awarded damages measured by the plaintiff's expectation interest rather than merely by reliance expenditures

choices.label: C
choices.text: rejected the doctrine of promissory estoppel on the grounds that no consideration had been exchanged

choices.label: D
choices.text: established that a promise of continued employment could never serve as the basis for a promissory estoppel claim

choices.label: E
choices.text: required the plaintiff to demonstrate that the promisor had been unjustly enriched before recovery could be awarded

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that the New York court 'allowed a plaintiff to recover damages — measured not simply by the expenditures made in reliance but by the full expectation interest, the amount the plaintiff would have received had the promise been kept.' B accurately paraphrases this.
explanations.A: This describes the English approach, not the New York decision. The passage presents the New York case as an example of the broader American approach, which treats promissory estoppel as an independent basis for recovery.
explanations.C: The opposite is true. The case applied promissory estoppel to enforce a gratuitous promise — one made without consideration — rather than rejecting it.
explanations.D: The passage states the promise was for 'continued employment' and the court enforced it; the decision therefore shows such promises can ground a claim, not that they cannot.
explanations.E: The passage does not state that unjust enrichment was a precondition for recovery in the New York decision; unjust enrichment is mentioned in paragraph 1 as the general rationale for the doctrine, not as a requirement of the 1965 case.
explanations.B: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that, under current English law, a promisee who has restructured significant affairs in reasonable reliance on a gratuitous promise would most likely

choices.label: A
choices.text: recover the full expectation interest from the promisor, measured as if the promise had been kept

choices.label: B
choices.text: be unable to recover any damages, because English courts do not recognize promissory estoppel in any form

choices.label: C
choices.text: receive, at most, a remedy that prevents the promisor from asserting the lack of consideration as a defense, but would not obtain expectation damages

choices.label: D
choices.text: obtain a remedy identical to that available in a United States court under the same facts

choices.label: E
choices.text: succeed automatically, because English courts treat clear and foreseeable reliance as a substitute for consideration

explanations.correct: The passage states that English courts permit promissory estoppel 'to operate only as a defense' and decline to award expectation damages in reliance-only cases. This means the doctrine can shield the promisee from a promisor's consideration defense, but no positive expectation-interest recovery is available. C captures this precisely.
explanations.A: Full expectation damages are the American approach; the passage explicitly contrasts this with the English position, which declines to award such damages.
explanations.B: Too strong. The passage does not say English courts reject the doctrine entirely — only that they confine it to a defensive role. Some remedy may be available.
explanations.D: The passage identifies a 'practical asymmetry' — the promisee who would receive full remedies in a U.S. court 'may obtain nothing of substance in an English court on materially identical facts.' The outcomes are expressly different.
explanations.E: The passage attributes this view to American courts, not English courts, and explicitly notes that English courts have resisted treating reliance alone as a substitute for consideration.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to 'expressions of hope, aspiration, or preliminary negotiation' (paragraph 3) serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the type of informal commercial statement that an expansive promissory estoppel doctrine might improperly convert into an enforceable obligation

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide examples of promises that have historically been enforced under the doctrine of promissory estoppel in the United States

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that the consideration requirement has always distinguished between binding promises and mere expressions of intent

choices.label: D
choices.text: introduce a category of commercial statements that the author believes should be subject to full expectation damages

choices.label: E
choices.text: contrast the English approach to preliminary negotiations with the American approach to the same phenomenon

explanations.correct: The reference appears in the paragraph that presents the English concern about commercial certainty: 'commercial parties frequently make statements of intent — expressions of hope, aspiration, or preliminary negotiation — that they do not intend to be legally binding.' The function is to give concrete content to the risk that a permissive doctrine might sweep in informal, non-binding statements, thereby lending some credibility to the English restriction. A captures this rhetorical function.
explanations.B: The passage does not suggest these types of statements have been enforced under U.S. promissory estoppel; the New York case involved a promise of continued employment, a much more concrete promise.
explanations.C: The passage does not make this historical claim about the consideration requirement in this passage; paragraph 1 introduces the consideration doctrine without this level of specificity.
explanations.D: The author explicitly does not advocate for enforcing these kinds of statements; the middle position proposed in paragraph 4 is limited to 'unambiguous' promises with foreseeable reliance — the opposite of the vague statements listed here.
explanations.E: The passage does not compare English and American treatment of preliminary negotiations at this point; the reference is part of a general observation about commercial risk, not a comparative legal analysis.
explanations.A: Correct.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's argument in paragraph 4 that the consideration requirement in cases of clear, detrimental reliance functions as 'a technicality that licenses a deliberate breach'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Empirical studies of commercial contract negotiations indicate that informal statements of intent are frequently misunderstood by both parties as binding commitments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Survey data show that promisors who make gratuitous promises to induce reliance often anticipate that the promisee will incur significant costs before any formal contract is signed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Legal historians have documented that the consideration requirement was introduced primarily to protect promisors from fraudulent claims, not to shield intentional non-performers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Courts in some jurisdictions have expanded promissory estoppel so broadly that the consideration requirement has become largely irrelevant in commercial cases.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Academic commentators have criticized the doctrine of promissory estoppel for failing to provide adequate guidance to commercial parties on the scope of their obligations.

explanations.correct: The author's claim is that when a promisor makes an unambiguous promise knowing the promisee will rely on it, hiding behind the consideration requirement is not a principled limitation but a deliberate exploitation of a technicality. Survey evidence that promisors typically foresee the reliance costs supports this claim by showing that the promisor's invocation of the consideration requirement is indeed a knowing choice to escape foreseeable consequences — exactly the behavior the author labels a 'deliberate breach.' B directly strengthens this characterization.
explanations.A: This actually supports the English concern that informal statements are ambiguous and that an expansive doctrine risks converting misunderstood statements into obligations — which cuts against the author's argument, not for it.
explanations.C: This information might suggest the consideration requirement is being misapplied, but it is a historical point about legislative intent rather than evidence that promisors deliberately exploit the rule. It strengthens a different, narrower historical argument.
explanations.D: This describes an existing trend in some jurisdictions but does not specifically support the moral claim that invoking the consideration requirement in the specific circumstances described is a deliberate breach; it is neutral on the question of intent.
explanations.E: This criticism of promissory estoppel's vagueness actually supports concerns about expanding the doctrine, which is the opposing view; it weakens, rather than strengthens, the author's argument.
explanations.B: Correct.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uneasy position within the common law of contracts, for it allows courts to enforce promises that would otherwise be unenforceable for want of consideration. The classical theory of contract, rooted in the exchange model inherited from nineteenth-century English jurisprudence, holds that a promise is legally binding only when it is supported by consideration — that is, when the promisee gives something of value in return for the promisor's commitment. Promissory estoppel disrupts this scheme by protecting a promisee who, receiving no formal exchange, nonetheless relies on a promise to his or her substantial detriment. The doctrine therefore raises a persistent theoretical question: whether the enforcement of such promises reflects a genuine departure from the consideration requirement or merely a subsidiary equitable remedy that leaves the classical model largely intact.

American courts in the twentieth century generally treated promissory estoppel as a narrow exception, confined to cases in which the reliance was both foreseeable and substantial. The Restatement (Second) of Contracts, published by the American Law Institute in 1981, codified this approach in Section 90, which conditions enforcement on a showing that the promisor should reasonably have expected the promisee's reliance, that the reliance in fact occurred, and that injustice can be avoided only by enforcement. Courts applying Section 90 have, however, reached strikingly inconsistent results. In some jurisdictions, the remedy awarded is full expectation damages — placing the promisee in the position she would have occupied had the promise been performed. In others, courts limit recovery to reliance damages — reimbursing only the out-of-pocket losses attributable to the promisee's detrimental reliance. This divergence is not merely technical; it reflects a deeper disagreement about whether promissory estoppel is a substitute for contract or a tort-like remedy for harm caused by broken undertakings.

The inconsistency in remedial outcomes is, regrettably, traceable in part to the ambiguity of Section 90 itself, which states only that the remedy granted "may be limited as justice requires" without specifying the circumstances that warrant limitation. Some commentators have argued that this language was deliberately flexible, designed to allow courts to calibrate relief to the equities of each case. But this defense of open-ended discretion comes at the cost of predictability, and predictability is a value that commercial actors, who must assess the enforceability of their undertakings in advance, depend on heavily. One hopes that appellate courts will eventually provide clearer guidance on the conditions under which expectation damages, rather than the more limited reliance measure, are appropriate — not merely as a matter of doctrinal tidiness, but because the practical stakes for those who reorganize their affairs in reliance on another's assurance are often considerable.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Restatement (Second) of Contracts, Section 90, introduced promissory estoppel into American contract law by replacing the consideration requirement with a reliance-based standard.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Promissory estoppel has generated inconsistent judicial outcomes because courts disagree about whether it is a true contract substitute or a tort-like remedy, a problem worsened by the ambiguity of its codified formulation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Appellate courts should adopt a uniform rule awarding expectation damages in all promissory estoppel cases to promote predictability in commercial transactions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The classical consideration requirement in contract law has been effectively abolished in American jurisdictions that follow the Restatement (Second) of Contracts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promissory estoppel is best understood as a narrow equitable exception that preserves the integrity of the classical exchange model in all but the most extreme cases of detrimental reliance.

explanations.correct: The passage traces the theoretical tension over promissory estoppel's status (contract substitute vs. tort remedy), documents the inconsistent remedial outcomes this produces, and locates the root cause in Section 90's ambiguity — all of which B captures across the full passage.
explanations.A: Too narrow and inaccurate: the passage does not say Section 90 introduced promissory estoppel or that it 'replaced' the consideration requirement; it describes Section 90 as a codification of an approach already in use.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: This states only the author's closing suggestion, which is a recommendation appearing at the end — not the main point integrating all three paragraphs.
explanations.D: Overstates: the passage says the consideration requirement is disrupted or complicated, not abolished.
explanations.E: This describes one view mentioned in the passage (the 'narrow exception' view of American courts) but not the passage's overall argument, which challenges the adequacy of that view.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the open-ended discretion afforded to courts by Section 90's remedial language can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic approval, because flexibility allows courts to respond equitably to the unique facts of each case.

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured skepticism, because while the flexibility may serve equitable goals, it undermines the predictability that commercial actors require.

choices.label: C
choices.text: strong condemnation, because deliberate ambiguity in statutory language is an abdication of legislative responsibility.

choices.label: D
choices.text: cautious approval, because predictability is less important in contract law than fairness to individual parties.

choices.label: E
choices.text: studied neutrality, because the author presents both the advantages and disadvantages of open-ended discretion without endorsing either view.

explanations.correct: The author acknowledges the commentators' defense of flexibility ('deliberately flexible, designed to allow courts to calibrate relief') but immediately counters that 'this defense of open-ended discretion comes at the cost of predictability' — signaling qualified skepticism rather than outright condemnation or approval.
explanations.A: Overstates positivity: the author acknowledges but does not endorse the flexibility argument.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong: 'regrettably' signals concern, but the author never accuses the drafters of abdication or condemns the ambiguity in such harsh terms.
explanations.D: Inverts the author's position: the author treats predictability as a weighty value, not a lesser one.
explanations.E: Wrong valence: the author does take a side — the final sentence ('one hopes') and the criticism of unpredictability reveal a clear, if measured, evaluative stance.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its theoretical tension identified; the doctrine's codification and resulting judicial inconsistency are described; the source of that inconsistency is diagnosed and a remedy suggested.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A historical overview of contract law is provided; two competing schools of judicial thought are described and evaluated; the author endorses one school over the other.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A doctrinal exception is criticized; a legislative solution is proposed; possible objections to that solution are considered and rejected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A classical legal model is explained; a court case is used to illustrate its application; the author proposes a reform of the classical model.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two opposing definitions of promissory estoppel are stated; their practical consequences are compared; the author concludes that both definitions are inadequate.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces promissory estoppel and its theoretical tension (contract substitute vs. equitable exception); paragraph 2 describes Section 90's codification and the inconsistent remedial outcomes it has produced; paragraph 3 diagnoses the ambiguity in Section 90 as the cause and closes with the author's suggestion for clearer appellate guidance.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Mis-sequencing and inaccuracy: the passage does not provide a general historical overview as its opening move, nor does it endorse one school of judicial thought over another as a final move.
explanations.C: Wrong: the passage does not propose a legislative solution, nor does it consider and reject objections to such a proposal.
explanations.D: Wrong grain: the passage's main analytical work is about the doctrine's inconsistent application, not about illustrating the classical model with a specific court case.
explanations.E: Wrong: the passage does not conclude that both definitions of promissory estoppel are inadequate; its concern is with remedial inconsistency and doctrinal ambiguity, not the definitions themselves.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is a condition imposed by Section 90 of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts for enforcement of a promise under promissory estoppel?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The promisee must demonstrate that she offered something of value in exchange for the promisor's commitment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The promisor must have had actual knowledge that the promisee would rely on the promise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The promisor should reasonably have expected that the promisee would rely on the promise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The remedy awarded must be limited to the promisee's out-of-pocket losses rather than full expectation damages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The promise must have been made in a commercial context in which predictability of enforcement is especially important.

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that Section 90 conditions enforcement on 'a showing that the promisor should reasonably have expected the promisee's reliance' — a reasonable foreseeability standard, not an actual-knowledge standard.
explanations.A: This describes the classical consideration requirement, which Section 90 displaces — the opposite of what the question asks.
explanations.B: Alters a qualifier: the passage says 'reasonably have expected' (an objective standard), not 'actual knowledge' (a subjective one) — a classic altered-qualifier trap.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Confuses the remedial question (which the passage says is left open by 'as justice requires') with an affirmative condition for enforcement.
explanations.E: A plausible world claim the passage never makes; Section 90's conditions do not include a commercial-context requirement.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that a court awarding full expectation damages in a promissory estoppel case would most likely be committed to which of the following views?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel should be treated as functionally equivalent to a fully enforceable contract rather than as a tort-like remedy for detrimental reliance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The classical consideration requirement is an outdated formalism that should be abandoned entirely in favor of a reliance-based theory of contract obligation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Predictability in commercial transactions is the paramount value in contract law and must override equitable concerns in every case.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Section 90 of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts was poorly drafted and should be replaced with a more precise statutory formulation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reliance damages are in all cases a more appropriate remedy than expectation damages because they avoid conferring a windfall on the promisee.

explanations.correct: The passage states that the divergence between expectation and reliance damages 'reflects a deeper disagreement about whether promissory estoppel is a substitute for contract or a tort-like remedy.' Awarding full expectation damages — placing the promisee where she would have been had the promise been performed — logically reflects the view that the doctrine operates as a contract substitute.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Overreaches: endorsing expectation damages in promissory estoppel cases does not commit a court to abandoning the consideration requirement altogether; the two questions are distinct.
explanations.C: Inverts: the passage associates the predictability concern with the author's critique of Section 90's ambiguity, not with the choice of expectation over reliance damages.
explanations.D: Outside scope: a court's remedial choice does not necessarily imply a view about Section 90's drafting quality.
explanations.E: Reverses: this describes the rationale for reliance damages, not expectation damages — the opposite of what the question asks.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to 'commercial actors, who must assess the enforceability of their undertakings in advance' (third paragraph) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the kind of sophisticated party for whom promissory estoppel was originally designed as a protective doctrine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: identify a concrete class of actors whose interests are specifically harmed by the doctrinal inconsistency the author has described, thereby reinforcing the practical stakes of that inconsistency.

choices.label: C
choices.text: concede that commercial parties are better equipped than individual promisees to absorb the costs of broken promises without judicial relief.

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast commercial actors with non-commercial parties to suggest that promissory estoppel should apply differently depending on the context.

choices.label: E
choices.text: support the argument that predictability is a value unique to commercial law and therefore irrelevant to the equitable concerns that Section 90 was designed to address.

explanations.correct: Immediately before this reference, the author argues that open-ended discretion 'comes at the cost of predictability.' The reference to commercial actors who need to assess enforceability in advance concretizes and reinforces this cost, showing who specifically is harmed by unpredictability — thus amplifying the critique of Section 90's ambiguity.
explanations.A: Accurate content, wrong function: the passage does not describe commercial actors as promissory estoppel's target beneficiaries; rather, they exemplify why predictability matters.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Reverses the point: the author treats commercial actors as a reason to demand more predictability, not as parties capable of absorbing broken promises.
explanations.D: The passage draws no contrast between commercial and non-commercial parties regarding differential application of the doctrine.
explanations.E: Inverts the function: the author uses commercial actors to show predictability is important broadly, not to suggest it is irrelevant to equitable concerns.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that the ambiguity of Section 90's remedial language is a significant source of the inconsistency in promissory estoppel outcomes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several jurisdictions that apply Section 90 have adopted supplementary common-law rules that specify when expectation damages rather than reliance damages are appropriate, yet those jurisdictions continue to produce divergent outcomes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Legal scholars who participated in drafting Section 90 have stated in published writings that the 'as justice requires' language was intended to provide flexibility rather than to impose any particular remedial measure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Courts in jurisdictions that have replaced Section 90 with more precisely worded statutes have shown no greater consistency in remedial outcomes than courts applying Section 90.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The divergence between expectation and reliance damages in promissory estoppel cases was well documented in case law published before the American Law Institute began drafting the Restatement (Second) of Contracts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promissory estoppel cases constitute only a small fraction of all contract disputes litigated in American courts each year.

explanations.correct: The author's claim is that Section 90's ambiguous remedial language is a significant cause of inconsistency. If courts operating under more precisely worded statutes show no greater consistency, that suggests the ambiguity of Section 90's language is not the operative cause of divergent outcomes — the inconsistency arises from something else, undermining the author's causal diagnosis.
explanations.A: This might seem to weaken the claim, but if supplementary rules exist yet inconsistency persists, that actually reinforces the idea that clarity is hard to achieve — it does not specifically exonerate Section 90's language as the source of the problem.
explanations.B: This supports rather than undermines the author's characterization of Section 90's language as deliberately flexible; it does not challenge the claim that this flexibility causes inconsistency.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: This shows the inconsistency predates Section 90, which might suggest the doctrine itself (not the codification's language) is the source of divergence — a partial weakener. However, it does not as directly target the causal role of Section 90's specific remedial language as C does.
explanations.E: Irrelevant to the author's causal claim; the frequency of such cases does not bear on whether Section 90's ambiguity causes inconsistency when those cases do arise.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uneasy position within contract law, for it operates as a means of enforcing promises that would otherwise fail for want of consideration — the traditional requirement that each party to a contract provide something of value in exchange for the other's promise. A promise unaccompanied by consideration is, under classical contract theory, a mere gift-promise and therefore unenforceable. Promissory estoppel carves an exception to this rule: where a promisee has reasonably relied upon a promisor's assurance and suffered a detriment as a consequence of that reliance, courts may enforce the promise to the extent necessary to prevent injustice. The doctrine was formally articulated in section 90 of the American Restatement of Contracts in 1932, though courts in the United States had applied its underlying rationale for several decades prior to that codification.

Difficulties arise, however, when courts must determine how far the doctrine extends. Two questions have proved particularly vexing. First, courts have divided over whether reliance-based recovery should be measured by the promisee's out-of-pocket loss — the so-called reliance interest — or by the full value of the promised performance, known as the expectation interest. Under the classical contract regime, expectation damages restore the promisee to the position she would have occupied had the promise been kept; reliance damages merely restore her to the position she occupied before the promise was made. In cases where the expected gain far exceeds the detrimental reliance, courts applying only reliance damages will award considerably less than full contract damages, a result that some commentators regard as appropriate precisely because the promisor never received consideration. Other courts, however, have rejected this reasoning and awarded expectation damages even in promissory-estoppel cases, arguing that a lesser award fails to vindicate the promisee's legitimate expectations and may create perverse incentives for promisors to make casual assurances.

The second contested question concerns the doctrine's application in commercial settings. Promissory estoppel was developed principally in the context of family arrangements and charitable subscriptions, settings where the absence of a formal bargain is unsurprising. When sophisticated commercial parties omit consideration from an agreement, a more skeptical posture seems warranted, since experienced negotiators can be presumed to understand that unbargained-for promises lack legal force. In a 1991 decision by a federal appellate court in the Second Circuit, the court held that promissory estoppel claims by commercial parties would be examined with heightened scrutiny, requiring a showing that the reliance was not merely foreseeable but was in fact induced by the promisor's conduct. Critics of this ruling have argued that it effectively reinstates consideration as a requirement in commercial contexts, thereby negating the very purpose of the doctrine. Regrettably, that tension has never been resolved at the Supreme Court level, and lower courts continue to apply varying and sometimes irreconcilable standards across jurisdictions.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The doctrine of promissory estoppel, though formally codified in the 1932 Restatement of Contracts, has been applied inconsistently by courts because its underlying rationale conflicts with classical contract theory.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Courts should award expectation damages rather than reliance damages in promissory-estoppel cases in order to adequately protect promisees' legitimate expectations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Although promissory estoppel provides an important exception to the consideration requirement of classical contract law, courts have struggled to apply it consistently, particularly regarding the measure of damages and its scope in commercial disputes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 1991 Second Circuit decision requiring heightened scrutiny for commercial promissory-estoppel claims effectively reinstates the consideration requirement and should be overturned.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promissory estoppel was originally designed for family and charitable contexts and should not be extended to sophisticated commercial parties who are presumed to understand the legal significance of consideration.

explanations.correct: The passage presents promissory estoppel's role as an exception to consideration, then develops two unresolved tensions — the damages measure and the commercial-context question — arriving at the conclusion that courts apply irreconcilable standards. C captures this full arc.
explanations.A: Too narrow: this identifies only the historical-inconsistency point from paragraph 1, ignoring the two specific contested questions developed in paragraphs 2 and 3.
explanations.B: This is one side of a debate the author describes but does not endorse; it also covers only one of the passage's two main contested questions.
explanations.D: This is a critic's position reported in paragraph 3, not the author's overall thesis. It also ignores the entire damages discussion in paragraph 2.
explanations.E: This is the reasoning used to justify heightened commercial scrutiny — a view the author implicitly questions — not the passage's overall argument.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, under classical contract theory, a promise unsupported by consideration is best characterized as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A voidable obligation that the promisor may choose to honor or rescind

choices.label: B
choices.text: An unenforceable gift-promise

choices.label: C
choices.text: A valid contract subject to reduced damages

choices.label: D
choices.text: An agreement enforceable only in family or charitable contexts

choices.label: E
choices.text: A promise that may be enforced if the promisee demonstrates reasonable reliance

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that under classical contract theory, a promise unaccompanied by consideration 'is a mere gift-promise and therefore unenforceable.' B is a direct paraphrase.
explanations.A: The passage makes no mention of 'voidable' obligations; this introduces a category not used in the passage.
explanations.C: Classical theory does not treat such promises as valid contracts at reduced damages — they are simply unenforceable.
explanations.D: The passage says promissory estoppel was developed in family and charitable contexts; it does not say classical theory enforces promises there.
explanations.E: This describes promissory estoppel's exception, not classical contract theory's baseline rule — it conflates the exception with the rule.
explanations.B: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The passage states that the difference between the reliance interest and the expectation interest is that

choices.label: A
choices.text: reliance damages place the promisee in the position she would have occupied had the promise been performed, while expectation damages restore only her pre-promise position.

choices.label: B
choices.text: expectation damages are always larger than reliance damages and are therefore inappropriate in promissory-estoppel cases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: reliance damages restore the promisee to her pre-promise position, while expectation damages restore her to the position she would have occupied had the promise been kept.

choices.label: D
choices.text: reliance damages are calculated by reference to what the promisor received, while expectation damages are calculated by reference to what the promisee lost.

choices.label: E
choices.text: expectation damages are reserved for cases in which consideration was exchanged, while reliance damages apply only where consideration was absent.

explanations.correct: The passage defines these terms precisely: 'expectation damages restore the promisee to the position she would have occupied had the promise been kept; reliance damages merely restore her to the position she occupied before the promise was made.' C reproduces this accurately.
explanations.A: This reverses the definitions — it attributes the expectation-damages description to reliance, and vice versa.
explanations.B: The passage notes expectation damages may far exceed reliance damages 'in cases where the expected gain far exceeds the detrimental reliance,' not that they are always larger. Additionally, the passage does not say expectation damages are 'therefore inappropriate.'
explanations.D: The passage nowhere ties either measure to what the promisor received; this misrepresents the basis of calculation.
explanations.E: The passage addresses whether courts award expectation or reliance damages in promissory-estoppel cases, but does not restrict expectation damages categorically to cases with consideration.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about the 1991 Second Circuit decision?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It correctly identified the need to protect sophisticated commercial parties from unexpectedly binding oral assurances.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It represents a principled and overdue clarification of an area of law that had previously been applied without adequate rigor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its requirement of heightened scrutiny for commercial parties risks undermining the fundamental purpose of the promissory-estoppel doctrine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It should be adopted uniformly by all lower courts as a means of harmonizing divergent jurisdictional standards.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It appropriately reinstated consideration as a prerequisite for enforcement in commercial contract disputes.

explanations.correct: The author reports critics' argument that the decision 'effectively reinstates consideration as a requirement in commercial contexts, thereby negating the very purpose of the doctrine,' and then laments — using 'regrettably' — that the tension remains unresolved. This editorial posture aligns the author with the critics, supporting C.
explanations.A: The passage identifies this as the reasoning behind the decision, but the author's 'regrettably' signals disapproval, not endorsement.
explanations.B: The author's tone is critical of the unresolved state of affairs; there is no indication that he views the Second Circuit ruling as principled clarification.
explanations.D: The passage states standards remain 'irreconcilable across jurisdictions,' suggesting dissatisfaction with the current fragmented situation — not an endorsement of the Second Circuit approach.
explanations.E: This describes the critics' characterization of the ruling's effect, which the author implicitly endorses as a concern, not as a desirable outcome.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of family arrangements and charitable subscriptions in the third paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the kinds of transactions in which courts have historically been most willing to waive the consideration requirement, thereby providing context for why the doctrine's extension to commercial settings raises new difficulties.

choices.label: B
choices.text: demonstrate that promissory estoppel is an outmoded doctrine whose original domain has been superseded by modern commercial litigation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: provide examples of settings in which expectation damages rather than reliance damages have typically been awarded.

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast the informality of personal relationships with the rigidity of commercial contracts in order to argue that different bodies of law should govern each.

choices.label: E
choices.text: suggest that charitable and familial promisees are less sophisticated than commercial parties and therefore deserve greater judicial protection.

explanations.correct: The author introduces family arrangements and charitable subscriptions as the doctrine's original context in order to explain the reasoning behind applying heightened scrutiny when the doctrine moves into commercial settings — where sophisticated parties can be presumed to know the legal significance of consideration. A correctly identifies this framing function.
explanations.B: The passage does not argue that the doctrine is outmoded; it presents ongoing contested application as a problem to be resolved.
explanations.C: The damages discussion is confined to paragraph 2 and is not connected to the family/charitable context in paragraph 3.
explanations.D: The passage does not argue for two separate bodies of law; it is concerned with how one doctrine — promissory estoppel — should be applied across different contexts.
explanations.E: The passage does not compare the sophistication of charitable/familial promisees with commercial parties in a way that suggests differential protection based on vulnerability.
explanations.A: Correct.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A doctrine is introduced and its historical origins described; two unresolved interpretive disputes about the doctrine are then examined; and the passage concludes with a lament that no authoritative resolution has been achieved.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined; a single illustrative case is analyzed in detail; and the author proposes a reform of the doctrine.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing legal theories are introduced; their historical development is traced; and the author argues that one theory is superior to the other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A legal exception to a general rule is described; critics of the exception are presented; and the passage concludes that the exception should be abolished.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The historical background of a doctrine is provided; the doctrine's application in a single jurisdiction is analyzed; and the passage endorses that jurisdiction's approach as a model for others.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces promissory estoppel and its origins; paragraphs 2 and 3 each develop a contested question (damages measure; commercial application); and the final sentence expresses the author's dissatisfaction that no resolution has been reached. A maps precisely onto this three-part structure.
explanations.B: The passage examines two disputes, not a single case, and does not propose a specific reform — it laments unresolved tension.
explanations.C: The passage is not structured around two competing theories being compared; one doctrine is analyzed across two problem areas.
explanations.D: The author does not argue the exception should be abolished; rather, the author wants better and more consistent application of promissory estoppel.
explanations.E: The 1991 Second Circuit decision is treated as one source of the ongoing controversy, not as a model the author endorses.
explanations.A: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The passage describes the argument that courts awarding only reliance damages in promissory-estoppel cases may create "perverse incentives for promisors to make casual assurances." Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen this argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In jurisdictions that award only reliance damages in promissory-estoppel cases, the rate of promissory-estoppel litigation is lower than in jurisdictions that award expectation damages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Empirical studies have found that in jurisdictions awarding only reliance damages, promisors more frequently make oral assurances without intending to follow through, knowing their liability is capped at the promisee's out-of-pocket loss rather than the value of the promised performance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Courts in family and charitable-subscription cases have historically awarded expectation rather than reliance damages, producing outcomes that family members and charitable organizations regard as equitable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Restatement of Contracts was amended after 1932 to specify that courts have discretion to award either reliance or expectation damages in promissory-estoppel cases.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Commercial parties routinely include consideration in written contracts precisely because they understand that oral promises lacking consideration are unenforceable under classical contract theory.

explanations.correct: The argument to be strengthened is that capping recovery at reliance damages incentivizes promisors to make casual, uncommitted assurances. B provides direct empirical support: it confirms that in reliance-only jurisdictions, promisors do in fact make more casual assurances knowing their exposure is limited. This directly supports the causal mechanism asserted.
explanations.A: Lower litigation rates would suggest promisors are less reckless, not more — this would weaken rather than strengthen the argument about perverse incentives.
explanations.C: This concerns a separate context (family/charitable) and does not bear on whether reliance-damages-only regimes encourage casual commercial assurances.
explanations.D: This is a procedural fact about the Restatement's amendment; it neither confirms nor denies that reliance-only damages encourage casual promises.
explanations.E: This concerns the behavior of commercial parties drafting written contracts, not promisors making informal oral assurances — it does not address the incentive created by a reliance-damages cap.
explanations.B: Correct.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uneasy position within the common law of contracts. Classical contract doctrine holds that a promise is legally enforceable only when it is supported by consideration — that is, when the promisee has given something of value in exchange. Promissory estoppel departs from this requirement by rendering certain promises enforceable even in the absence of consideration, provided that the promisee has reasonably relied upon the promise to his or her detriment. The doctrine was first articulated in systematic form by American courts in the early twentieth century and was later codified in the Restatement (Second) of Contracts, adopted in the United States in 1979, which states that a promise is binding if it is one that the promisor should reasonably have expected to induce action or forbearance on the part of the promisee and which does in fact induce such action or forbearance.

Despite this codification, courts have applied promissory estoppel inconsistently, producing outcomes that are difficult to reconcile. Two strands of doctrine have emerged. Under the first — sometimes called the "reliance" strand — courts treat detrimental reliance as fully substituting for consideration, so that a plaintiff who establishes reasonable reliance may recover expectation damages equivalent to those available under a fully bargained contract. Under the second — the "equitable" strand — courts treat the doctrine as a limited remedy of conscience, awarding only reliance damages designed to restore the plaintiff to the position occupied before the promise was made, not the position that performance would have secured. A 1991 decision of the New Jersey Supreme Court illustrates the tension: the court awarded full expectation damages to an employee who had relocated across the country in reasonable reliance on a promise of long-term employment, while a contemporaneous decision of a California intermediate appellate court, presented with nearly identical facts, confined recovery to moving expenses alone. The New Jersey court grounded its holding in the principle that promissory estoppel should, wherever possible, approximate the remedies available in classical contract; the California court reasoned that the absence of a bargained exchange warranted a correspondingly restrained remedy.

The inconsistency in remedial outcomes reflects a deeper theoretical disagreement about the purpose of promissory estoppel. Those who favor the reliance strand argue that the doctrine exists to protect reasonable expectations generated by promises, and that restricting recovery to reliance damages systematically undercompensates plaintiffs and undermines the policy of holding promisors to their word. Those who favor the equitable strand counter that granting expectation damages in the absence of consideration blurs the distinction between contract and promissory estoppel and may deter socially useful promises by exposing promisors to liability disproportionate to any benefit received. Neither position is without force, and the case for a unified remedial rule has not yet been made convincingly. Regrettably, it seems unlikely that courts will converge on a single approach until a legislature or a supreme court of a major jurisdiction issues authoritative guidance — guidance that, one hopes, will take seriously both the reliance interests of promisees and the reasonable expectations of promisors who make informal promises in good faith.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel was first codified in the 1979 Restatement (Second) of Contracts, which defines the conditions under which a promise lacking consideration may be enforceable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The doctrine of promissory estoppel has been applied inconsistently by courts, reflecting a deeper theoretical dispute about whether the doctrine's purpose is to protect reliance or to serve as a limited equitable remedy, and this inconsistency remains unresolved.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Courts should adopt a unified rule requiring that promissory estoppel plaintiffs receive full expectation damages whenever reasonable reliance on a promise is established.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 1991 decisions of the New Jersey Supreme Court and the California Court of Appeal illustrate why promissory estoppel should be abolished in favor of classical contract doctrine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promissory estoppel is theoretically incompatible with classical contract law because it dispenses with the consideration requirement on which all enforceable promises depend.

explanations.correct: The passage traces the doctrine's codification, then devotes two paragraphs to explaining that courts apply it inconsistently (reliance vs. equitable strand) because of an unresolved theoretical disagreement about its purpose. B captures this full arc.
explanations.A: Too narrow — this describes only the first paragraph's historical background, not the passage's overall argument about inconsistency and its causes.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Overstates the author's position. The author says 'the case for a unified remedial rule has not yet been made convincingly' and does not advocate for expectation damages across the board.
explanations.D: Inverts the passage — the author does not argue for abolishing promissory estoppel; the cases illustrate tension within the doctrine.
explanations.E: The passage treats this as background, not the thesis. The author is focused on remedial inconsistency, not theoretical incompatibility per se.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the current state of promissory estoppel doctrine can best be described as which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enthusiastic endorsement of the equitable strand, whose cautious approach to damages preserves the distinction between contract and promissory estoppel

choices.label: B
choices.text: Strong approval of the reliance strand, since courts should wherever possible approximate classical contract remedies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Resigned acceptance that no single approach will ever be adopted and that the inconsistency is a permanent feature of the common law

choices.label: D
choices.text: Critical concern about persisting inconsistency combined with measured hope that authoritative guidance will eventually produce a balanced resolution

choices.label: E
choices.text: Confident satisfaction that the Restatement (Second) has already provided sufficient guidance to resolve the tension between the two strands

explanations.correct: The author says 'neither position is without force,' notes that the case for a unified rule 'has not yet been made convincingly,' expresses regret at the lack of convergence, and ends with 'one hopes' — signaling critical concern plus cautious optimism. D captures both the negative appraisal and the guarded hope.
explanations.A: Overstates the author's sympathy for one side. The author explicitly says 'neither position is without force.'
explanations.B: Same trap as A but in the other direction — the author does not endorse the reliance strand, only reports that its proponents favor expectation damages.
explanations.C: Too pessimistic. 'Resigned acceptance' contradicts the closing 'one hopes' and the call for authoritative guidance.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Directly contradicted by the passage, which says inconsistency persists despite codification.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and contrasted with an alternative doctrine; the two alternatives are illustrated by a historical case; and the passage concludes by endorsing one alternative.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is situated within classical contract theory; the doctrine's inconsistent judicial application is illustrated by contrasting decisions; and the underlying theoretical disagreement is identified and evaluated, with a call for authoritative resolution.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A problem in contract law is identified; a legislative solution is proposed and assessed; and the passage concludes that the solution is inadequate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined; a single illustrative case is analyzed in depth; and the author concludes that the case was wrongly decided.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Competing theoretical positions on contract law are surveyed; the passage then traces their historical development in American courts; and a preferred theoretical framework is adopted.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 situates promissory estoppel within classical contract doctrine and notes its codification. Paragraph 2 presents the two judicial strands and illustrates them with contrasting 1991 decisions. Paragraph 3 identifies the theoretical disagreement driving the inconsistency and calls, with cautious hope, for authoritative guidance. B tracks this sequence accurately.
explanations.A: Mis-states the conclusion — the author does not endorse either alternative; also, the contrast is within promissory estoppel, not between it and an alternative doctrine.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No legislative solution is proposed; the passage instead calls for one and notes its absence.
explanations.D: Two cases are discussed, not one; the author does not conclude either was wrongly decided, though the New Jersey approach receives implicit approval.
explanations.E: The passage does not trace historical development in this order, and no preferred theoretical framework is adopted.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is true of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It was drafted by the United States Congress and signed into law in 1979.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It requires courts to award expectation damages whenever promissory estoppel is established.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It defines a promise as binding when the promisor could reasonably have foreseen that it would induce action or forbearance by the promisee and when it does in fact induce such action or forbearance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It abolished the consideration requirement in all contracts governed by American common law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It resolved the tension between the reliance and equitable strands of promissory estoppel by specifying the remedies available to successful plaintiffs.

explanations.correct: The passage states that the Restatement defines a promise as binding 'if it is one that the promisor should reasonably have expected to induce action or forbearance on the part of the promisee and which does in fact induce such action or forbearance.' C is a close paraphrase of this.
explanations.A: The Restatement is not a congressional statute; it was 'adopted' — a choice that omits the fact that Restatements are products of the American Law Institute, not Congress. The passage does not say Congress drafted it.
explanations.B: The passage says nothing about the Restatement specifying remedies; the remedial inconsistency arose despite the codification.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The passage says promissory estoppel 'departs from' the consideration requirement in specific circumstances; it does not abolish consideration generally.
explanations.E: Directly contradicted — the passage notes that inconsistency in remedial outcomes persists after codification.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that a court applying the equitable strand of promissory estoppel would hold which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A plaintiff who established reasonable reliance on an unfulfilled promise would be entitled to the full benefit of the bargain as though a contract had been formed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The absence of consideration in a promissory estoppel claim justifies limiting any recovery to the costs the plaintiff actually incurred in relying on the promise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Promissory estoppel claims should be resolved by applying classical contract doctrine whenever the parties had equal bargaining power.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A court applying promissory estoppel should treat the doctrine identically to a fully bargained contract in order to deter promisors from breaking informal promises.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reliance damages are appropriate only when the plaintiff can also demonstrate that consideration was given at some earlier stage of the parties' relationship.

explanations.correct: The passage describes the equitable strand as one that 'treat[s] the doctrine as a limited remedy of conscience, awarding only reliance damages designed to restore the plaintiff to the position occupied before the promise was made.' This supports B — recovery is limited to actual costs incurred, because the absence of consideration warrants a restrained remedy.
explanations.A: This describes the reliance strand, not the equitable strand.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage makes no mention of bargaining power as a criterion under either strand.
explanations.D: This mirrors the reliance strand's aspiration to approximate classical contract remedies — the opposite of the equitable strand.
explanations.E: The passage does not connect the equitable strand to any requirement of prior consideration; indeed, promissory estoppel by definition operates without consideration.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the 1991 New Jersey and California decisions serves primarily to:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Demonstrate that state courts in the United States are more willing than federal courts to award expectation damages in promissory estoppel cases.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Illustrate the concrete remedial divergence that results when courts apply competing strands of promissory estoppel doctrine to similar facts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Argue that the California court reached the correct result by limiting recovery to relocation expenses alone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Provide historical evidence that promissory estoppel doctrine was first developed in New Jersey rather than in California.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suggest that employment disputes are the most common context in which promissory estoppel claims arise.

explanations.correct: The two decisions appear immediately after the passage introduces the reliance and equitable strands, and they instantiate those strands in nearly identical factual circumstances — one awarding full expectation damages, the other confining recovery to moving expenses. Their function is to make the abstract doctrinal divergence concrete and visible. B captures this illustrative purpose.
explanations.A: The cases both involve state courts; no comparison to federal courts is made.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author does not endorse the California outcome; the passage implies sympathy for the New Jersey approach by contextualizing it within the broader reliance-protection rationale.
explanations.D: The passage says promissory estoppel was first articulated systematically by 'American courts in the early twentieth century,' not in New Jersey specifically, and the cases are from 1991.
explanations.E: The passage does not generalize about which contexts produce the most promissory estoppel claims.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the argument made by proponents of the equitable strand of promissory estoppel?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Empirical studies show that restricting promissory estoppel recovery to reliance damages causes promisors to make fewer informal promises that later induce significant reliance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many jurisdictions that award full expectation damages in promissory estoppel cases also report high rates of commercial litigation involving formal contracts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Legal scholars have argued that the consideration requirement was not part of the original common law of England.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Courts in jurisdictions that award only reliance damages in promissory estoppel cases frequently encounter difficulty calculating the precise amount of those damages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A survey of promissory estoppel plaintiffs found that a majority had sustained losses far exceeding the costs they incurred in reliance, because they had foregone other opportunities in reasonable expectation of the promised performance.

explanations.correct: The equitable strand restricts recovery to reliance damages on the grounds that this restores the plaintiff to the pre-promise position and avoids exposing promisors to disproportionate liability. If plaintiffs' actual losses routinely exceed reliance costs because of foregone opportunities — losses that only expectation damages would cover — then restricting recovery to reliance damages systematically undercompensates promisees, directly undermining the equitable strand's claim to be an adequate and fair remedy.
explanations.A: This would actually support the equitable strand's concern about deterring informal promises — it suggests that limiting liability does affect promisor behavior, but in a way that reduces beneficial promises, which cuts against both strands. The effect on the equitable strand's core argument (that reliance damages are the right measure) is unclear, making A weaker than E.
explanations.B: Irrelevant to the equitable strand's rationale. High litigation rates in expectation-damages jurisdictions might weakly support concerns about overexposure, but the connection is too attenuated.
explanations.C: This concerns the historical origins of the consideration requirement, not the merits of the equitable vs. reliance remedial debate.
explanations.D: This is a practical difficulty for courts applying the equitable strand, but it does not undermine the substantive argument that reliance damages are the appropriate measure; it is at most a procedural complication.
explanations.E: Correct.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies a contested position within contract law, functioning as an equitable corrective to the rigid requirements of classical contract formation. Under orthodox contract doctrine, a binding agreement requires offer, acceptance, and consideration — the last being the exchange of something of legal value that distinguishes an enforceable promise from a mere gift. Yet courts have long recognized that this requirement, applied without qualification, can produce injustice when one party relies to its detriment on a promise that lacks formal consideration. Promissory estoppel addresses precisely this gap: it allows a court to enforce a promise, despite the absence of consideration, where the promisor should reasonably have expected the promisee to rely on the promise, and where that reliance was both actual and detrimental.

The doctrine has, however, been applied with notable inconsistency across common-law jurisdictions. Consider two representative scenarios. In a 1971 decision by a New South Wales appellate court, a property developer promised a subcontractor that a longstanding discount on materials would continue for the duration of a major project. No formal contract was executed. When the developer later revoked the discount and demanded the full contract price, the court held that promissory estoppel operated as a complete defense, effectively extinguishing the developer's right to the higher price. But in a 1989 Ontario case involving an employer's informal promise to maintain a pension benefit, the court declined to apply promissory estoppel as a sword — that is, as an independent cause of action — and limited it to a defensive role, preventing the employer from denying the promise but awarding no affirmative relief to the employee. The divergence in outcomes illustrates that courts have not agreed upon whether promissory estoppel can generate new rights or merely prevent the unconscionable retraction of existing ones.

This asymmetry traces to a deeper doctrinal tension. Anglo-Australian courts, influenced by the broader equitable tradition, have tended to treat reliance-based estoppel as a substantive right, capable of founding an independent cause of action. North American courts, by contrast, have more frequently confined it to a defensive posture, treating it as a shield against bad faith rather than a sword of affirmative relief. The difficulty is that neither approach is fully coherent. A purely defensive doctrine leaves promisees exposed whenever they have acted on a promise not in response to a threatened lawsuit but simply in anticipation of a benefit — the more common commercial situation. Yet an unconstrained offensive doctrine risks collapsing consideration doctrine altogether, since nearly any promissory statement made in a commercial context might generate reliance. The most defensible resolution, though one courts have been reluctant to embrace uniformly, would calibrate the availability of offensive promissory estoppel to the degree of reasonable reliance and the magnitude of the promisee's detrimental act, rather than categorically barring its use as a sword.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel was developed by Anglo-Australian courts as a substantive right and has since been adopted, in modified form, by North American jurisdictions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The inconsistent application of promissory estoppel across common-law jurisdictions reflects a deeper unresolved tension over whether the doctrine generates affirmative rights or merely prevents unconscionable retractions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Courts should abandon the consideration requirement in contract law and replace it with a unified standard based on detrimental reliance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 1971 New South Wales decision and the 1989 Ontario case demonstrate that promissory estoppel is routinely misapplied by lower courts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promissory estoppel is an equitable doctrine that fills the gap left by the consideration requirement and should be applied only as a defensive shield.

explanations.correct: The passage traces an inconsistency between the Anglo-Australian and North American treatments of promissory estoppel, locates the cause in a fundamental doctrinal dispute about whether the doctrine creates rights or only blocks retractions, and concludes with the author's proposed resolution. B captures this full arc.
explanations.A: Too narrow and historically inaccurate relative to the passage — the passage does not describe North America as adopting a modified Anglo-Australian view; it describes divergence, not adoption.
explanations.B: Correct.
