explanations.C: Too strong and not the author's claim; the author proposes calibrated offensive use, not wholesale abandonment of consideration.
explanations.D: The two cases are illustrations, not evidence of routine misapplication; this is the too-narrow trap fixating on the illustrative examples.
explanations.E: This restates the North American position, which the author actually critiques as incomplete — making it a paragraph-level restatement that omits the author's evaluative conclusion.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and defined; two cases illustrating conflicting applications are presented; the conflict is traced to a deeper tension and a preferred resolution is offered.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal problem is identified; a historical account of how courts resolved the problem is provided; the author concludes that the resolution was satisfactory.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing doctrines are compared; their historical origins are traced; and the author recommends that courts adopt the older of the two.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A doctrine is defined; a single illustrative case is analyzed in depth; and the author argues that the case was wrongly decided.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An equitable principle is introduced; its abandonment by modern courts is documented; and the author proposes that it be revived through legislation.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces and defines promissory estoppel. Paragraph 2 presents two cases (New South Wales 1971 and Ontario 1989) with conflicting outcomes. Paragraph 3 traces the conflict to a deeper doctrinal tension and offers the author's preferred calibrated resolution. A maps this three-step structure exactly.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The author does not conclude that the resolution has been satisfactory — the author finds neither approach fully coherent, which is the opposite of a satisfied conclusion.
explanations.C: The passage does not compare two competing doctrines against each other; it analyzes one doctrine (promissory estoppel) with two different applications, and does not recommend the older approach.
explanations.D: There are two cases, not one, and the author does not argue that either was simply wrongly decided — the author diagnoses a systemic tension, not a single error.
explanations.E: The doctrine is not described as abandoned, and no legislative remedy is proposed — this introduces a move the passage never makes.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the 1989 Ontario case differed from the 1971 New South Wales case in that the Ontario court

choices.label: A
choices.text: rejected the principle of promissory estoppel entirely and refused to grant any relief to the promisee.

choices.label: B
choices.text: limited promissory estoppel to a defensive role and declined to award affirmative relief to the employee.

choices.label: C
choices.text: found that the employer's promise had been unsupported by any form of consideration and therefore unenforceable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: held that promissory estoppel could be used offensively but only where the detrimental reliance was substantial.

choices.label: E
choices.text: required the employee to demonstrate that reliance on the promise had been formally documented before granting any relief.

explanations.correct: The passage states that the Ontario court 'declined to apply promissory estoppel as a sword' and 'limited it to a defensive role, preventing the employer from denying the promise but awarding no affirmative relief to the employee.' B is a close paraphrase of this.
explanations.A: The Ontario court did not reject promissory estoppel entirely — it recognized the doctrine but confined it to a defensive posture. This is an altered-scope trap.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage does not say the Ontario court found the promise unenforceable for lack of consideration — the court used estoppel defensively, which is a different holding.
explanations.D: The passage says the opposite — the Ontario court rejected offensive use entirely; it did not calibrate offensive use to the degree of reliance.
explanations.E: The passage does not mention any formal documentation requirement imposed by the Ontario court; this introduces a detail from paragraph 2's discussion of aboriginal rights documentation (from the genre context), not from this passage.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The consideration requirement should be entirely eliminated from common-law contract doctrine in all jurisdictions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A court that categorically refuses to allow promissory estoppel as an offensive claim fails to protect promisees who acted in anticipation of a benefit rather than in defense against a lawsuit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Anglo-Australian approach to promissory estoppel is superior to the North American approach in every material respect.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because consideration doctrine is foundational to contract law, any doctrine that threatens it should be rejected regardless of its equitable appeal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts should treat oral promises in commercial settings as fully equivalent to written contracts for purposes of enforcement.

explanations.correct: The author states that 'a purely defensive doctrine leaves promisees exposed whenever they have acted on a promise not in response to a threatened lawsuit but simply in anticipation of a benefit — the more common commercial situation.' B restates this inferential claim accurately.
explanations.A: The author proposes calibrating offensive estoppel, not abolishing consideration — this overreaches the author's stated position.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author criticizes both approaches — noting that neither is 'fully coherent' — so endorsing Anglo-Australian superiority in every respect overstates the author's view.
explanations.D: This is essentially the position the author rejects — the purely defensive doctrine is what the author finds inadequate, so the author would not endorse this claim.
explanations.E: The passage does not address the oral vs. written distinction as a basis for enforcement; this is outside the scope of the author's argument.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the purely defensive application of promissory estoppel can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: strong approval, because it prevents the collapse of the consideration requirement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured endorsement, tempered by concern that it may occasionally disadvantage commercially sophisticated promisees.

choices.label: C
choices.text: critical acknowledgment of its partial validity, combined with the view that it is insufficient to address the most common commercial situations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: outright rejection, on the grounds that it represents a fundamental misreading of equity doctrine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: cautious neutrality, since the author refrains from assessing either the defensive or offensive approaches on the merits.

explanations.correct: The author acknowledges the concern behind the defensive approach — that an unconstrained offensive doctrine risks collapsing consideration — but then states that the defensive doctrine 'leaves promisees exposed' in 'the more common commercial situation.' This is a critical but not dismissive stance that recognizes partial validity while finding it insufficient. C captures both the acknowledgment and the criticism.
explanations.A: The author does not approve of the purely defensive doctrine; the author finds it inadequate, which is the opposite of strong approval.
explanations.B: The word 'endorsement' is too positive — the author explicitly criticizes the defensive-only approach as leaving promisees exposed, which is more than a tempered concern.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: 'Outright rejection' overstates the author's tone; the author acknowledges the logic behind the defensive approach before criticizing it, and the criticism is grounded in practical inadequacy, not a charge of fundamental misreading.
explanations.E: The author is not neutral — the final paragraph contains explicit evaluative language ('A purely defensive doctrine leaves promisees exposed'; 'neither approach is fully coherent'; 'the most defensible resolution'), making neutrality clearly wrong.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the 1971 New South Wales case and the 1989 Ontario case serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: establish that the doctrine of promissory estoppel originated in Anglo-Australian courts and was later imported into North American jurisprudence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide concrete illustrations of the cross-jurisdictional inconsistency in the application of promissory estoppel introduced in paragraph one.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that courts in both jurisdictions have reached erroneous results by misapplying the equitable principles underlying promissory estoppel.

choices.label: D
choices.text: argue that the 1971 case was correctly decided whereas the 1989 case reflects an unduly restrictive interpretation of equitable doctrine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: show that differences in outcomes between the two cases can be entirely explained by the different facts presented to each court.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 opens by stating that the doctrine has been applied 'with notable inconsistency across common-law jurisdictions' and then uses the two cases as illustrations of that inconsistency. B accurately identifies this illustrative function in relation to the paragraph's opening claim.
explanations.A: The passage does not argue for a direction of influence or importation; this is accurate content about the cases' jurisdictions but wrong about their function in the argument.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author does not characterize either court as simply erroneous — the author presents them as reflecting different doctrinal approaches, then critiques both approaches in paragraph 3. 'Erroneous results' imposes a judgment the author does not make about the individual decisions.
explanations.D: The author does not endorse the New South Wales result over the Ontario result; the author treats both as instantiating imperfect approaches and reserves judgment until paragraph 3.
explanations.E: The author attributes the divergence to doctrinal orientation, not to factual differences between the cases — in fact, the cases both involve informal promises upon which the promisee relied, suggesting the facts are structurally similar.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the resolution the author advocates for applying promissory estoppel offensively?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A court grants affirmative relief to a tenant who, relying on a landlord's assurance that a lease would be renewed, spent substantial funds renovating the property, even though no formal lease renewal was executed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A court refuses to enforce an oral promise in a commercial transaction on the grounds that the promisee could have protected itself by insisting on a written contract.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A court applies promissory estoppel as a complete bar to any claim by the promisor, regardless of the degree to which the promisee relied on the promise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A court holds that consideration doctrine is so fundamental that promissory estoppel may never be used, whether defensively or offensively, to overcome its requirements.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A court allows a promisee to sue on an informal promise solely because the promise was made in writing, without inquiring into whether the promisee actually changed its position in reliance on the promise.

explanations.correct: The author advocates calibrating offensive promissory estoppel to 'the degree of reasonable reliance and the magnitude of the promisee's detrimental act.' Situation A presents precisely this: the promisee (tenant) acted in reasonable anticipation of a benefit (lease renewal), incurred substantial detrimental reliance (renovation costs), and a court grants affirmative relief accordingly. This matches the author's proposed calibrated offensive use.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: This reflects a court declining to apply promissory estoppel altogether — the opposite of the author's recommended approach for cases of substantial detrimental reliance.
explanations.C: This describes an unconstrained offensive doctrine that the author explicitly warns would 'risk collapsing consideration doctrine altogether' — it is the very excess the author seeks to avoid.
explanations.D: This reflects the position that promissory estoppel should never be applied, which the author clearly rejects given the author's endorsement of a calibrated offensive use.
explanations.E: The author's resolution is grounded in the degree of actual reliance, not in the form of the promise — enforcing based on the written form alone without inquiring into reliance inverts the author's reasoning.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uneasy position within the common law of contracts, for it operates precisely where the formal requirements of a binding contract have not been met, yet courts have long recognized that permitting a promisor to revoke a promise upon which another party has relied to their detriment would produce a manifest injustice. The doctrine, as it has developed through Anglo-American jurisprudence over the better part of the twentieth century, holds that where a party makes a clear and unambiguous promise, where that promise is reasonably relied upon by the promisee, and where the promisee suffers a concrete detriment as a consequence of that reliance, the promisor may be held to the promise notwithstanding the absence of consideration. Yet the precise scope of this remedy remains deeply contested, particularly with respect to the measure of relief a court ought to award and the degree to which proof of reliance should suffice in the place of a fully negotiated bargain.

The tension is perhaps most visible in the divergence between two lines of judicial authority that emerged in North American courts during the latter half of the twentieth century. One line, traceable to a series of appellate decisions in the northeastern United States during the 1960s and 1970s, holds that the appropriate remedy in a promissory estoppel case is the full expectation interest — that is, the benefit the promisee would have received had the promise been performed. Proponents of this approach argue that awarding anything less than the expectation interest degrades the promisee's reasonable anticipation and effectively penalizes prudent reliance. The competing line of authority, exemplified by a 1978 appellate ruling in a Canadian commercial dispute, awards only the reliance interest — the out-of-pocket losses actually incurred in relying on the promise — on the theory that promissory estoppel is a shield against unconscionable conduct rather than a sword by which the promisee may extract a full contractual windfall.

Furthermore, courts have struggled to articulate a principled boundary between cases in which reliance is sufficiently definite to warrant enforcement and cases in which it is merely incidental or speculative. A business that, in anticipation of a promised long-term supply contract, terminates a pre-existing supplier arrangement and retains new warehouse space presents the clearest case for relief; the reliance is both tangible and specific. But consider a party that, on the strength of a preliminary letter of intent from a prospective employer, declines to pursue several other employment opportunities. Here, the lost opportunities are genuine yet difficult to quantify, and courts have split over whether the indefinite nature of the foregone alternatives precludes a finding of actionable reliance. Regrettably, the lack of a consistent doctrinal standard has left commercial actors without reliable guidance, and legal practitioners in jurisdictions that straddle both lines of authority must counsel clients against a background of persistent uncertainty. One might reasonably hope that a systematic restatement of the reliance-interest principle would bring greater coherence to this area of the law.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel was developed by courts specifically to replace the consideration requirement in all contract disputes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The divergence between the expectation-interest and reliance-interest remedies in promissory estoppel cases has produced a clear injustice to commercial parties.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Although promissory estoppel addresses genuine injustice arising from detrimental reliance, the doctrine remains incoherent in its application because courts have failed to agree on the appropriate remedy and the standard for actionable reliance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reliance-interest remedy is superior to the expectation-interest remedy because it correctly characterizes promissory estoppel as a defensive rather than an offensive doctrine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: North American courts should abandon promissory estoppel altogether and require parties to formalize preliminary agreements through fully negotiated contracts.

explanations.correct: The passage as a whole argues that promissory estoppel addresses a real injustice but is plagued by two unresolved controversies: the measure of remedy and the definition of actionable reliance. C captures both strands and the author's overall evaluative stance.
explanations.A: Too broad and inaccurate — the passage explicitly states that promissory estoppel applies where formal contract requirements are not met, but it does not claim the doctrine was meant to replace consideration in all disputes.
explanations.B: Partly accurate but overstates the author's conclusion; the passage identifies uncertainty and lack of guidance, not a demonstrated clear injustice resulting from the split.
explanations.C: Correct — integrates the doctrinal purpose (addressing detrimental reliance) with both contested issues (remedy measure and reliance standard) and matches the author's closing call for coherence.
explanations.D: Presents one side of the judicial split as the author's own conclusion; the author presents both lines of authority without endorsing either.
explanations.E: A position nowhere advanced in the passage; the author seeks better doctrinal coherence, not abolition of the doctrine.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its historical origins traced; two competing lines of judicial authority are contrasted; one line is endorsed as superior; a recommendation is offered.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine and the problem it addresses are introduced; two contested aspects of the doctrine are examined in turn; the author concludes by noting the practical consequences of the unresolved controversy and calling for greater consistency.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A legal controversy is introduced; a landmark case is analyzed; the analysis is extended to related doctrines; an analogy to tort law is drawn.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two competing doctrines are introduced simultaneously; their historical development is compared; a synthesis of the two is proposed and defended.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A doctrinal tension is described; a single authoritative case resolves the tension; the implications of the resolution are explored in subsequent paragraphs.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces promissory estoppel and its foundational tension; paragraph 2 examines the remedy-measure dispute (expectation vs. reliance interest); paragraph 3 examines the actionable-reliance standard, concludes with practical consequences of the split, and calls for systematic restatement. B tracks this sequence accurately.
explanations.A: Inaccurate at the end — the author does not endorse one line of authority as superior; both are presented without a declared winner.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No single landmark case is analyzed as central to the passage's argument, and no analogy to tort law is drawn.
explanations.D: The passage does not introduce two doctrines simultaneously, nor does it propose a synthesis of the competing remedial approaches.
explanations.E: No case resolves the tension; the passage emphasizes that the tension remains unresolved across the three paragraphs.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is a condition that courts applying promissory estoppel require before holding a promisor to an unkept promise?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The promisor must have received some benefit from the promisee's reliance, even if no formal consideration was exchanged.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The promisee must demonstrate that the promise was relied upon and that the reliance resulted in concrete detriment to the promisee.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The promise must have been made in the context of a formally negotiated commercial transaction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The promisee must prove that the promisor acted with the specific intent to deceive.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The promisee must show that all other available legal remedies have been exhausted before invoking promissory estoppel.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 explicitly states three conditions: a clear and unambiguous promise, reasonable reliance by the promisee, and concrete detriment as a result of that reliance. B accurately paraphrases two of these explicitly stated elements.
explanations.A: The passage says consideration is absent, not that some benefit to the promisor is required; this inverts the doctrine's premise.
explanations.B: Correct — directly paraphrases the reliance-and-detriment elements stated in paragraph 1.
explanations.C: The passage does not limit the doctrine to formally negotiated commercial transactions; it applies precisely where formal contract requirements have not been met.
explanations.D: Deceptive intent is not mentioned as a condition; the doctrine concerns detrimental reliance, not fraud.
explanations.E: No exhaustion requirement is mentioned anywhere in the passage.

questions.questionStem: The passage states that the line of judicial authority traceable to northeastern United States appellate decisions from the 1960s and 1970s holds that promissory estoppel plaintiffs should receive which of the following as a remedy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Compensation limited to the actual out-of-pocket costs incurred in reliance on the promise

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nominal damages intended to acknowledge the promisor's breach without compensating for losses

choices.label: C
choices.text: The full expectation interest — the benefit the promisee would have received had the promise been performed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Equitable relief in the form of specific performance compelling the promisor to fulfill the original promise

choices.label: E
choices.text: A court-determined sum calculated by averaging the expectation interest and the reliance interest

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states explicitly that this line of authority 'holds that the appropriate remedy in a promissory estoppel case is the full expectation interest — that is, the benefit the promisee would have received had the promise been performed.' C is a direct paraphrase.
explanations.A: This describes the competing Canadian line of authority that awards only the reliance interest, not the northeastern U.S. line.
explanations.B: Nominal damages are not mentioned in the passage at all.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Specific performance is not mentioned in the passage as a remedy in either line of authority.
explanations.E: No averaging formula appears in the passage; this is a fabricated remedy.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would be likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Commercial parties would benefit from a uniform doctrinal standard clarifying when reliance is actionable and what remedy follows.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Courts should eliminate the reliance-interest remedy entirely because it fails to deter unconscionable conduct by promisors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The requirement of consideration should be abolished in all contract disputes so that promissory estoppel becomes the default theory of enforcement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 1978 Canadian appellate ruling correctly resolved the dispute between the expectation-interest and reliance-interest approaches.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Employers who issue letters of intent should be held to the full expectation interest because preliminary employment promises are among the clearest cases for promissory estoppel relief.

explanations.correct: The closing sentence of the passage states that 'one might reasonably hope that a systematic restatement of the reliance-interest principle would bring greater coherence,' and the penultimate sentence notes that the lack of consistent doctrine leaves commercial actors without reliable guidance. A captures the inference that flows directly from both observations.
explanations.A: Correct — the author explicitly laments the lack of consistent doctrinal standards and calls for restatement to provide coherence, which entails agreement that commercial parties would benefit from such uniformity.
explanations.B: The author does not argue for eliminating the reliance-interest remedy; rather, the author seems to view it as the principle around which a restatement might be organized.
explanations.C: The passage never proposes abolishing consideration or making promissory estoppel the default enforcement theory; this overreaches the author's position.
explanations.D: The author does not endorse the 1978 Canadian ruling; it is cited as one example of a line of authority without editorial approval.
explanations.E: The author treats the employment letter-of-intent scenario as a harder case where courts have split, not a clear case for full expectation relief.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the business that terminates a pre-existing supplier arrangement and retains new warehouse space serves primarily to:

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate a scenario in which reliance is sufficiently tangible and specific to present a strong case for promissory estoppel relief

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that the expectation-interest remedy is more appropriate than the reliance-interest remedy in commercial supply disputes

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that courts consistently award relief in commercial supply cases while denying it in employment cases

choices.label: D
choices.text: concede that some forms of reliance are too speculative to warrant any judicial remedy under promissory estoppel

choices.label: E
choices.text: provide a historical example of a case in which a Canadian appellate court first applied the reliance-interest standard

explanations.correct: The author introduces the warehouse example immediately after raising the question of how courts distinguish definite reliance from incidental or speculative reliance, and describes it as 'the clearest case for relief' because 'the reliance is both tangible and specific.' Its function is to anchor one end of the spectrum before presenting the harder employment case.
explanations.A: Correct — the example is explicitly offered as the clearest case, functioning to illustrate what sufficiently definite reliance looks like.
explanations.B: The example is about the definiteness of reliance, not about which remedy measure is preferable; no comparison of expectation vs. reliance interest is made here.
explanations.C: The author says courts have 'split' on the employment scenario; no consistent pattern is demonstrated.
explanations.D: The warehouse example illustrates strong, non-speculative reliance — the opposite of what this choice states.
explanations.E: The warehouse example is a hypothetical, not a historical case, and no connection to the Canadian appellate ruling is drawn.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the current state of promissory estoppel doctrine can best be described as:

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic approval of the doctrine's flexibility and its capacity to do justice in cases where formal contract law falls short

choices.label: B
choices.text: unqualified skepticism about whether promissory estoppel can ever provide adequate relief to parties who have relied on unkept promises

choices.label: C
choices.text: measured concern about the doctrine's lack of coherence, tempered by an underlying endorsement of its purpose and a desire for systematic reform

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutral exposition of competing judicial approaches without any indication of the author's own evaluative stance

choices.label: E
choices.text: strong condemnation of North American courts for failing to adopt a uniform remedial standard despite decades of litigation

explanations.correct: The author opens by acknowledging that the doctrine addresses 'manifest injustice,' endorses its purpose, and then spends two paragraphs identifying serious doctrinal inconsistencies. The closing word 'regrettably' and the hope for 'greater coherence' signal measured concern paired with a desire for reform rather than either enthusiasm or hostility.
explanations.A: Overstates the positive valence; the author does not express enthusiasm and devotes most of the passage to cataloguing the doctrine's deficiencies.
explanations.B: Too negative — the author accepts the doctrine's validity and purpose, criticizing only its inconsistent application.
explanations.C: Correct — captures both the critical concern (incoherence, practical uncertainty) and the endorsement of the doctrine's underlying purpose.
explanations.D: Inaccurate — the author clearly editorializes with 'manifest injustice,' 'regrettably,' and the hope for systematic restatement.
explanations.E: Overstates the negative; 'strong condemnation' is too intense for an author who merely notes the lack of guidance with the word 'regrettably' and expresses hope for reform.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel has long occupied an uneasy position within contract law, and even in jurisdictions where it is firmly established, courts have struggled to determine with any consistency when detrimental reliance on a promise ought to give rise to legal relief. At its core, promissory estoppel permits a party who has reasonably relied to their detriment on an unenforceable promise to recover some measure of relief—even in the absence of the consideration that would ordinarily be required to bind a contract. The tension between this doctrine and classical contract theory is substantial, for traditional doctrine insists that only bargained-for exchanges are legally cognizable, whereas promissory estoppel appears to create obligations from the mere making of promises.

The difficulty is compounded when courts must decide the appropriate scope of the remedy. Courts in the United States have generally recognized two competing positions. Under the "expectation" approach, a promisee who has relied on a promise is entitled to damages sufficient to place her in the position she would have occupied had the promise been performed. Under the narrower "reliance" approach, the promisee recovers only the losses actually suffered as a result of relying on the promise—a measure that is almost always smaller. In a 1979 case decided by a federal circuit court, a commercial tenant had renovated premises in reliance on an oral promise by the landlord to renew the lease at a below-market rent. The court granted only reliance damages rather than expectation damages, reasoning that the absence of consideration counseled restraint and that full expectation recovery would effectively convert every gratuitous promise into an enforceable contract. The logic was that promissory estoppel should function as a safety valve for compelling cases of injustice, not as an alternative route to full contractual enforcement.

This conservative position has real merit, but its application has produced troubling inconsistencies. Courts applying the reliance measure often reach arbitrary stopping points when calculating what the promisee actually lost. Moreover, withholding expectation damages can itself produce injustice where the promisee has, in reasonable reliance, foregone other opportunities of equal or greater value than the expected benefit—yet recovery under the reliance measure does not compensate for those forgone opportunities. Commentators have noted that the purpose of the doctrine, which is to prevent injustice arising from disappointed reasonable expectations, is poorly served when the remedy is systematically smaller than the harm. One thoughtful resolution would be to permit courts to calibrate the remedy to the degree of injustice in each case, awarding expectation damages where the promisor's conduct was egregious or deliberate and confining relief to reliance damages where the promise was merely careless. Whether courts will adopt such a flexible approach remains to be seen, but the current regime—one of ad hoc determinations masked by doctrinal consistency—warrants critical reexamination.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel is fundamentally incompatible with classical contract doctrine and should be abolished in favor of strict consideration requirements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The conservative approach to promissory estoppel remedies, while coherent in theory, has produced arbitrary results in practice and merits a more flexible, case-sensitive framework.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Federal circuit courts in the United States have consistently awarded reliance damages rather than expectation damages in promissory estoppel cases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The doctrine of promissory estoppel was created specifically to compensate commercial tenants who relied on oral promises by landlords.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts should always award expectation damages in promissory estoppel cases because doing otherwise perpetuates the injustice the doctrine was designed to prevent.

explanations.correct: The passage introduces promissory estoppel's tension with classical contract theory, traces the two remedial approaches and the courts' conservative preference, and closes by arguing that the conservative approach produces troubling inconsistencies that warrant a more flexible remedy calibrated to each case. B captures this full arc.
explanations.A: The passage explicitly acknowledges that promissory estoppel is 'firmly established' in many jurisdictions and does not argue for its abolition—this choice contradicts the passage's position.
explanations.B: Correct. This integrates the acknowledgment of the conservative position's merit with the author's critique of its inconsistent application and the call for a flexible alternative.
explanations.C: Too narrow—the 1979 circuit court case is a single illustrative example, and the passage does not claim that all federal courts have been consistent in this way.
explanations.D: A distortion of the illustrative example; the doctrine's core purpose (stated in paragraph 1) is general and not limited to landlord-tenant relationships.
explanations.E: Too strong—the author stops short of recommending expectation damages in all cases; the proposed solution is a calibrated, case-by-case approach, not a universal rule.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the conservative reliance-damages approach to promissory estoppel remedies can best be described as which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enthusiastic endorsement tempered only by the difficulty of calculating reliance losses

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complete rejection on the ground that it is incompatible with the doctrine's foundational purpose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Qualified acknowledgment of its theoretical merit coupled with concern about its inconsistent and sometimes unjust application

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutral description of a majority judicial approach without any evaluative assessment

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mild approval based on the view that expectation damages would render promissory estoppel indistinguishable from contract law

explanations.correct: The author opens paragraph 3 with 'This conservative position has real merit'—a clear concession—before cataloguing the troubling inconsistencies and the injustice it can produce. C accurately captures both the partial approval and the critical concern.
explanations.A: Overstates approval; the author's critique of the approach occupies most of paragraph 3 and is far more prominent than mere acknowledgment of a computational difficulty.
explanations.B: Too strong in the negative direction; the author explicitly grants that the conservative position 'has real merit' and does not call for abandoning it entirely.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The passage is clearly evaluative—the author calls the current regime one that 'warrants critical reexamination'—so a neutral-description characterization is inaccurate.
explanations.E: While the 1979 court's reasoning includes this concern, the author's own attitude is more critical of the conservative approach, not mildly approving of it on this ground.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced, its incompatibility with traditional theory is established, two competing judicial remedies are described and one is illustrated by a case, and the author argues that the prevailing remedial approach is inconsistent and proposes a flexible alternative.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A historical overview of promissory estoppel is provided, followed by a comparison of American and British approaches to the doctrine, and a conclusion is reached that American courts are more consistent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A doctrinal tension is identified, three competing remedial approaches are compared in detail, a landmark case is analyzed at length, and the author endorses the expectation-damages rule without qualification.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An introduction presents a legal principle, a single case study illustrates the principle in full, and the final paragraph argues that the case was wrongly decided and should be reversed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The passage describes the origins of promissory estoppel in Roman law, traces its migration to common law jurisdictions, and evaluates recent legislative reforms.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces promissory estoppel and its tension with classical contract doctrine; paragraph 2 describes the expectation vs. reliance remedial divide and illustrates with the 1979 case; paragraph 3 concedes merit to the conservative approach but critiques its inconsistency and proposes a calibrated alternative. A tracks this structure accurately.
explanations.B: The passage does not compare American and British approaches, nor does it conclude that American courts are more consistent—it criticizes American courts' inconsistency.
explanations.C: Only two remedial approaches (not three) are compared; the 1979 case is an illustration, not an extended analysis; and the author does not endorse expectation damages without qualification.
explanations.D: The passage does not confine itself to a single case study, and it does not argue that the 1979 case should be reversed—it criticizes the broader pattern of the conservative approach.
explanations.E: The passage contains no discussion of Roman law origins or legislative reforms; it is concerned with judicial doctrine as currently applied.
explanations.A: Correct.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, under the "expectation" approach to promissory estoppel damages, a promisee is entitled to which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only those losses that were actually incurred as a direct result of relying on the promise

choices.label: B
choices.text: Damages calibrated to the degree of egregious conduct on the part of the promisor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Damages sufficient to place the promisee in the position she would have occupied had the promise been performed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Compensation for all opportunities the promisee foregone, regardless of whether reliance was reasonable

choices.label: E
choices.text: The full market value of any contract that the promisee entered into with a third party in reliance on the original promise

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states explicitly that under the expectation approach, a promisee 'is entitled to damages sufficient to place her in the position she would have occupied had the promise been performed.' C paraphrases this directly.
explanations.A: This is the definition of the reliance approach, not the expectation approach—a deliberate qualifier-swap trap.
explanations.B: This describes the author's proposed flexible remedy in paragraph 3, not the expectation approach as defined.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The passage limits expectation recovery to the benefit promised; it does not speak of compensating for all forgone opportunities regardless of reasonableness.
explanations.E: The passage does not discuss the value of third-party contracts; this is a plausible-sounding detail the passage never states.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel should be eliminated from American contract law because it undermines the consideration requirement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A promisee who has reasonably foregone valuable opportunities in reliance on a promise may suffer harm that the reliance measure of damages fails to redress.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All courts that have adopted the reliance measure of damages have done so in order to deliberately disadvantage commercial tenants.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The expectation measure of damages is always preferable to the reliance measure in promissory estoppel cases.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promissory estoppel doctrine is so well settled in American courts that no further doctrinal development is necessary.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that 'withholding expectation damages can itself produce injustice where the promisee has, in reasonable reliance, foregone other opportunities of equal or greater value than the expected benefit—yet recovery under the reliance measure does not compensate for those forgone opportunities.' B closely tracks this claim.
explanations.A: The author never argues for eliminating promissory estoppel; the passage treats it as an established and important safety valve.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No such intent is attributed to courts; the passage explains the courts' reasoning as a principled restraint rooted in the absence of consideration, not as a deliberate effort to disadvantage tenants.
explanations.D: Too strong—the author's proposed solution is a flexible, case-by-case calibration, not a categorical preference for expectation damages.
explanations.E: The opposite is true; the author calls the current regime one that 'warrants critical reexamination,' suggesting further doctrinal development is needed.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the 1979 federal circuit court case in paragraph 2 serves primarily to which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Provide a concrete illustration of how the reliance-damages approach operates and the reasoning courts offer for preferring it over the expectation approach

choices.label: B
choices.text: Demonstrate that federal circuit courts have uniformly adopted the expectation approach in commercial tenant disputes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Argue that the outcome of the case was correct and that the landlord's oral promise should not have been given any legal effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Introduce the doctrinal conflict between promissory estoppel and classical consideration theory for the first time

choices.label: E
choices.text: Show that reliance damages are always insufficient to prevent injustice in cases involving commercial real property

explanations.correct: The case is introduced immediately after defining the two competing approaches and is used to show how the reliance approach plays out in a concrete scenario, including the court's stated rationale (absence of consideration counsels restraint; full expectation recovery would convert gratuitous promises into contracts). A captures this illustrative and explanatory function.
explanations.B: The passage makes no claim about uniformity among federal circuit courts; presenting one case does not establish a universal rule, and the author's overall critique of inconsistency belies this claim.
explanations.C: The author's own attitude is critical of the conservative outcome; moreover, the passage notes that the tenant received some relief—the oral promise was given legal effect through the reliance award.
explanations.D: The doctrinal conflict between promissory estoppel and consideration theory is introduced in paragraph 1, not through the 1979 case.
explanations.E: Too sweeping—the passage does not argue that reliance damages are always insufficient; it argues that they can produce injustice in cases where forgone opportunities are not compensated.
explanations.A: Correct.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the flexible remedial approach the author proposes in the final paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A court awards a promisee expectation damages after finding that the promisor knowingly and deliberately made a false promise in order to induce the promisee to abandon a lucrative competing opportunity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A court refuses to grant any relief to a promisee because the promise was never reduced to writing, regardless of how substantially the promisee relied on it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A legislature enacts a statute requiring that all promissory estoppel claims be resolved exclusively through arbitration rather than through the court system.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A court awards expectation damages in every promissory estoppel case on the theory that the promisee's reliance is always reasonable whenever a promise is made.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A court awards reliance damages in every promissory estoppel case on the ground that uniformity in the law is more valuable than individual justice.

explanations.correct: The author proposes 'awarding expectation damages where the promisor's conduct was egregious or deliberate.' A describes precisely this scenario: a court awarding expectation damages upon finding that the promisor deliberately made a false promise to induce detrimental reliance—an egregious and deliberate act.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: This describes a categorical refusal of relief based on a writing requirement, which is the opposite of the author's flexible, injustice-sensitive approach.
explanations.C: The proposal concerns a legislative procedural mechanism, not a remedial calibration of the kind the author envisions; it is entirely outside the scope of the proposed approach.
explanations.D: The author's approach is calibrated to the degree of injustice in each case; awarding expectation damages in every case regardless of the promisor's conduct is the uniform rule the author criticizes, not the flexible alternative proposed.
explanations.E: This describes the uniform reliance-damages approach the author critiques throughout paragraph 3; awarding reliance damages in every case prioritizing uniformity is antithetical to the author's call for flexible, case-sensitive calibration.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uneasy position in the common law of contracts, serving as both a corrective instrument and a source of considerable doctrinal confusion. At its core, the doctrine holds that a party who makes a clear and unambiguous promise, upon which another party reasonably relies to their detriment, may be prevented from denying the enforceability of that promise even in the absence of formal consideration. The doctrine thus operates as an exception to the classical requirement that a binding contract must be supported by bargained-for consideration — an exchange of value between the parties. Courts in England and the United States have invoked promissory estoppel with some regularity since the mid-twentieth century, yet the precise contours of the doctrine remain contested, and its application has produced outcomes that are difficult to reconcile.

The difficulty stems in part from ambiguity in the doctrine's foundational requirement: that the promisee's reliance must be "reasonable." Courts have interpreted reasonableness inconsistently, particularly in commercial contexts. In a 1967 case in New York, a supplier who had orally promised to maintain a fixed price for a period of one year was held bound by that promise when the buyer demonstrably restructured its operations in anticipation of stable input costs. The court reasoned that any commercially sophisticated party would foresee such reliance. Yet in a 1971 English case involving nearly identical facts, the court declined to apply estoppel on the ground that, without a written memorandum, the alleged promise was insufficiently certain to justify the plaintiff's reliance. The divergence illustrates a deeper tension: courts have never fully agreed on whether promissory estoppel is an independent cause of action or merely a defensive shield, a distinction that bears directly on the scope and remedy available to a claimant.

Furthermore, even where courts agree that the doctrine applies, the question of remedy has proven vexing. Classical contract doctrine generally aims to place the injured party in the position they would have occupied had the contract been performed — the so-called "expectation interest." Promissory estoppel, by contrast, is typically said to protect only the "reliance interest": the expenditures or opportunities foregone by the promisee in consequence of the promise. In practice, however, courts have sometimes awarded expectation damages in estoppel cases, blurring the doctrinal boundary and generating uncertainty about whether promissory estoppel has quietly evolved into a full substitute for formal contract. Such an evolution would not be without practical merit — it would extend contractual protection to parties who, for reasons of sophistication or resources, are unable to insist on written agreements. Regrettably, however, the case law has developed haphazardly, leaving commercial parties without reliable guidance on when reliance will be protected and to what extent.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel should be formally codified as an independent cause of action so that commercial parties can rely on it with confidence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although promissory estoppel was designed to correct injustices arising from broken promises, courts in England and the United States have applied it in incompatible ways.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The doctrine of promissory estoppel remains doctrinally unsettled, with inconsistent judicial interpretations of its key requirements and remedies leaving commercial parties without adequate guidance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The distinction between the expectation interest and the reliance interest is the primary source of confusion in the law of promissory estoppel.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts have quietly transformed promissory estoppel into a full substitute for formal contract, a development that, while practically beneficial, has eroded the consideration doctrine.

explanations.correct: The passage surveys the doctrine's ambiguous foundational requirement (reasonableness), its contested status as cause of action versus defense, and the remedial confusion between reliance and expectation damages — all pointing to doctrinal unsettlement that leaves parties without guidance. C integrates all three strands.
explanations.A: A prescriptive recommendation that the author hints at but never makes the central claim; this is a proposed solution, not the thesis.
explanations.B: Partially accurate but too narrow — the passage is about more than a U.S./England divergence; it addresses structural doctrinal problems throughout.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Too narrow — the passage identifies multiple sources of confusion, not just the expectation/reliance distinction.
explanations.E: Overstates the author's position; the author says courts 'sometimes' award expectation damages and asks whether this 'has quietly evolved,' not that the transformation is complete.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the current state of promissory estoppel doctrine can best be described as one of

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement of the doctrine's flexibility and case-by-case adaptability.

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured criticism of the doctrine's haphazard development and the uncertainty it produces for commercial parties.

choices.label: C
choices.text: outright hostility toward the doctrine's deviation from the classical consideration requirement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: cautious optimism that recent decisions reconciling expectation and reliance damages will soon resolve the doctrinal confusion.

choices.label: E
choices.text: neutral description of competing judicial approaches without expressing any evaluative stance.

explanations.correct: The author uses phrases such as 'uneasy position,' 'difficult to reconcile,' 'vexing,' and 'Regrettably, however, the case law has developed haphazardly' — all signaling critical but measured dissatisfaction, not outright hostility. B captures both the valence and the restrained register.
explanations.A: The opposite of what the author signals; the passage describes the flexibility as a source of confusion, not a virtue to endorse.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — the author acknowledges the doctrine has 'practical merit' and does not call for its abolition.
explanations.D: Unsupported — the passage identifies no recent reconciling decisions and expresses no optimism about resolution.
explanations.E: The author clearly editorializes ('Regrettably,' 'haphazardly'), ruling out a neutral stance.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The passage introduces a legal doctrine, traces its historical development from the nineteenth century to the present, and concludes by endorsing a proposed reform.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The passage identifies a doctrinal tension, illustrates it with two contrasting judicial decisions, broadens to a second area of uncertainty, and closes with a critical assessment of the doctrine's overall state.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The passage presents a legal debate between two schools of thought, recounts the arguments of each in turn, and then proposes a synthesis.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The passage defines a doctrine, gives a single illustrative case, and then argues that the case was wrongly decided.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The passage compares the doctrine of promissory estoppel to the doctrine of consideration and argues that the former has supplanted the latter in modern courts.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces the doctrine and its doctrinal tension (exception to consideration). Paragraph 2 illustrates with the 1967 New York and 1971 English cases to show inconsistent application of the 'reasonableness' requirement. Paragraph 3 turns to the second area of uncertainty — reliance versus expectation remedy — and closes with a critical assessment. B matches this four-move structure precisely.
explanations.A: The passage does not trace a historical development from the nineteenth century, nor does it endorse a specific reform.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage does not frame two 'schools of thought' or propose a synthesis; it surveys judicial inconsistency.
explanations.D: Two contrasting cases are cited, not one, and the author does not argue either was wrongly decided outright.
explanations.E: The passage raises the possibility that estoppel is evolving into a contract substitute but does not argue it has supplanted consideration.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the classical doctrine of contract law requires which one of the following for a promise to be legally binding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A written memorandum signed by both parties.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Proof that the promisee suffered a financial loss as a result of relying on the promise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bargained-for consideration constituting an exchange of value between the parties.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Evidence that the promisor was commercially sophisticated and aware of the consequences of the promise.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A court ruling confirming that the promisee's reliance was reasonable under the circumstances.

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly states that 'a binding contract must be supported by bargained-for consideration — an exchange of value between the parties.' C is a direct paraphrase.
explanations.A: The written-memorandum requirement is mentioned in connection with the 1971 English case, not as a general requirement of classical contract law.
explanations.B: Financial loss from reliance is associated with promissory estoppel, not the classical consideration requirement.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Commercial sophistication is mentioned as a factor in the 1967 New York court's reasoning, not as a classical contract requirement.
explanations.E: Reasonable reliance is a requirement of promissory estoppel, not of classical contract formation.

questions.questionStem: The passage indicates that the 1967 New York court's conclusion that the supplier was bound by its oral price promise was based primarily on which one of the following considerations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The buyer had submitted a signed written document confirming its reliance on the promised price.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The supplier's promise was part of a formally negotiated commercial agreement supported by consideration.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A commercially sophisticated party in the supplier's position would have anticipated that the buyer would restructure its operations in response to the promise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The buyer had no alternative suppliers available and therefore had no choice but to rely on the promise.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Binding oral promises are presumed enforceable under New York commercial law regardless of reliance.

explanations.correct: The passage states that 'the court reasoned that any commercially sophisticated party would foresee such reliance,' referring to the buyer's restructuring of operations. C accurately paraphrases this reasoning.
explanations.A: No written document is mentioned in connection with the New York case; it was an oral promise.
explanations.B: The passage describes the promise as oral and lacking formal consideration — that is precisely why estoppel was required.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No mention is made of the buyer's access to alternative suppliers.
explanations.E: The passage does not state any presumption of enforceability for oral promises under New York law.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would most likely agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Courts should uniformly abandon promissory estoppel and return to the classical consideration requirement in all commercial disputes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The extension of promissory estoppel to award expectation damages would be of particular benefit to parties who lack the resources or sophistication to secure written agreements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 1971 English court's refusal to apply estoppel was correct because certainty of promise is the most important prerequisite for the doctrine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The distinction between promissory estoppel as a cause of action and as a defensive shield has no practical consequence for the relief a claimant may seek.

choices.label: E
choices.text: All oral commercial promises should be legally enforceable without any showing of reliance, because the certainty requirement imposes too heavy a burden on unsophisticated parties.

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly states that extending estoppel into a full contract substitute 'would not be without practical merit — it would extend contractual protection to parties who, for reasons of sophistication or resources, are unable to insist on written agreements.' The author presents this as a point in favor of the evolution, supporting inference B.
explanations.A: The author does not call for abandonment of estoppel; on the contrary, the doctrine's 'practical merit' is acknowledged.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author presents the 1971 English case as an example of divergence, not as the correct outcome; calling it correct would contradict the passage's critical tone.
explanations.D: The passage says the cause-of-action/defense distinction 'bears directly on the scope and remedy available,' implying practical consequence — the opposite of D.
explanations.E: The author never argues that reliance should be eliminated as a requirement; the concern is with inconsistent application of the reasonableness standard.

questions.questionStem: The author most likely discusses the contrast between the "expectation interest" and the "reliance interest" in the third paragraph primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: argue that promissory estoppel should be limited to protecting only reliance expenditures and should never yield expectation damages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate a second dimension of doctrinal uncertainty in promissory estoppel, namely that courts have not consistently adhered to the remedy the doctrine is said to provide.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that classical contract law is superior to promissory estoppel because expectation damages more fully compensate injured parties.

choices.label: D
choices.text: explain why the 1967 New York court awarded expectation damages rather than reliance damages to the buyer.

choices.label: E
choices.text: introduce the concept of consideration as the foundational principle distinguishing contract from estoppel claims.

explanations.correct: The third paragraph opens by noting that courts have 'proven vexed' by the remedy question, then shows that courts 'sometimes' award expectation damages in estoppel cases despite the doctrine's orthodox reliance-interest limitation. The function is to introduce a second, distinct area of doctrinal confusion beyond the reasonableness-of-reliance problem in paragraph 2. B captures this rhetorical purpose.
explanations.A: The author does not advocate limiting estoppel to reliance damages; the passage is descriptive and critical, not prescriptive on this point.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author does not argue classical contract law is superior; the passage notes expectation damages 'blur the doctrinal boundary,' not that their availability is objectionable.
explanations.D: The 1967 New York case is discussed in paragraph 2; paragraph 3 does not revisit that case's remedy.
explanations.E: Consideration is introduced in paragraph 1; the third paragraph's function is to address remedial uncertainty, not foundational doctrine.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uncomfortable position within Anglo-American contract law, for it permits courts to enforce promises that would otherwise fail for want of consideration — the traditional prerequisite for a legally binding agreement. Under classical contract doctrine, a promise is enforceable only if the promisee has provided something of value in exchange; without that exchange, a gratuitous promise, however sincerely made and however much the promisee has relied upon it, is ordinarily not cognizable in law. Promissory estoppel challenges this orthodoxy by holding that, where a promisor ought reasonably to have foreseen that his promise would induce the promisee to act in substantial and definite ways, and where such reliance has in fact occurred, justice may require enforcement even in the absence of consideration.

American courts have applied this doctrine with notably inconsistent results, and the source of that inconsistency can be located in a single ambiguity: whether the remedy awarded upon a successful promissory-estoppel claim should be measured by the promisee's expectation interest — placing the promisee in the position he would have occupied had the promise been performed — or only by the promisee's reliance interest — restoring the promisee to the position he occupied before the promise was made. In a 1987 case decided by a federal appellate court in the Seventh Circuit, a supplier who had prepared extensive tooling and inventory in reliance on a manufacturer's oral assurance of a long-term supply contract was awarded expectation damages, on the ground that anything less would inadequately vindicate the supplier's reasonable reliance. Yet in a 1993 decision by a state appellate court in the same region, a contractor who had restructured his workforce on the strength of an analogous assurance received only reliance damages, the court reasoning that promissory estoppel should not be permitted to collapse into ordinary contract liability. These two rulings rest on incompatible premises about the doctrine's purpose.

The deeper difficulty is that courts have never settled whether promissory estoppel is a freestanding cause of action or merely an equitable doctrine invoked to prevent unjust enrichment. If the former, it arguably demands full expectation damages; if the latter, restoration of the status quo ante may suffice. This ambiguity has allowed courts to reach pragmatically convenient outcomes without committing to any principled account of the doctrine's foundations. The consequence is a body of case law that affords contracting parties inadequate guidance and that threatens to make every informal commercial assurance a source of potential liability of indeterminate magnitude. Courts would do well to resolve this foundational question explicitly rather than continuing to finesse it on a case-by-case basis — a practice that, however understandable as a judicial management strategy, ultimately disserves both commercial certainty and the interests of relying parties.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel should be abolished because it undermines the classical requirement of consideration in contract law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: American courts have applied the doctrine of promissory estoppel inconsistently because they have not resolved whether the doctrine is an independent cause of action or merely an equitable remedy, and this unresolved ambiguity harms contracting parties.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 1987 and 1993 appellate decisions illustrate that federal and state courts apply different standards of damages in contract disputes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Promissory estoppel should always award expectation damages rather than reliance damages in order to fully vindicate the promisee's reasonable reliance.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The doctrine of promissory estoppel provides contracting parties with adequate guidance about the circumstances under which an informal assurance becomes legally binding.

explanations.correct: The passage traces inconsistent application (paragraphs 2–3) to a foundational ambiguity about promissory estoppel's nature (paragraph 3) and closes by arguing this ambiguity disserves contracting parties. B integrates both strands.
explanations.A: The author does not advocate abolition; the closing prescription is for courts to resolve the foundational question, not to eliminate the doctrine.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too narrow — the two cases are illustrative examples of the broader inconsistency problem, not the passage's main point. The passage is not primarily about federal-versus-state court differences.
explanations.D: The author withholds judgment on which damages measure is correct; the prescription is only that courts should resolve the question explicitly, not that one answer is right.
explanations.E: This directly contradicts the passage's claim that the case law leaves contracting parties without adequate guidance.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, under classical contract doctrine a promise is enforceable only if

choices.label: A
choices.text: the promisee has acted in substantial reliance upon it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the promisor could reasonably have foreseen the promisee's reliance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the promisee has provided something of value in exchange.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the promise is made in writing and witnessed by a third party.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the agreement has been reviewed by a court of equity.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 states explicitly: 'a promise is enforceable only if the promisee has provided something of value in exchange.' C is a direct paraphrase.
explanations.A: This describes the promissory-estoppel standard, not the classical consideration requirement.
explanations.B: Reasonable foreseeability of reliance is the promissory-estoppel standard articulated later in paragraph 1, not the classical rule.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The passage never mentions written form or witnessing as requirements of classical contract doctrine.
explanations.E: The passage does not state that equity court review is a prerequisite under classical doctrine.

questions.questionStem: The passage states that in the 1993 state appellate decision, the contractor received only reliance damages because the court

choices.label: A
choices.text: found that the contractor had not incurred substantial costs in reliance on the manufacturer's assurance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: concluded that promissory estoppel should not be allowed to collapse into ordinary contract liability.

choices.label: C
choices.text: determined that the oral assurance did not satisfy the requirements for promissory estoppel.

choices.label: D
choices.text: held that expectation damages were unavailable because the parties had never agreed on a contract price.

choices.label: E
choices.text: reasoned that the contractor's reliance was not foreseeable to the manufacturer at the time the assurance was made.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states: 'the court reasoning that promissory estoppel should not be permitted to collapse into ordinary contract liability.' B is a close paraphrase.
explanations.A: The passage does not indicate that the contractor's reliance was found insubstantial; the contractor did restructure his workforce.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The court awarded reliance damages, implying the promissory-estoppel claim succeeded; the dispute was about the remedy, not the doctrine's applicability.
explanations.D: The passage does not mention any disagreement about contract price as the reason for the damages limitation.
explanations.E: Foreseeability of reliance is not given as the 1993 court's rationale; the issue was the appropriate remedy.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Courts that award expectation damages in promissory-estoppel cases are more faithful to the doctrine's equitable origins than courts that award only reliance damages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A contracting party who gives an informal oral assurance should, under current doctrine, be able to predict with confidence the financial consequences of that assurance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Until courts articulate a coherent account of promissory estoppel's foundational purpose, the doctrine will continue to produce unpredictable outcomes for commercial parties.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Promissory estoppel is best understood as an equitable doctrine designed solely to prevent unjust enrichment, and expectation damages are therefore never appropriate.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The inconsistency in promissory-estoppel decisions stems primarily from the different procedural rules governing federal and state appellate courts.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 argues that courts have avoided committing to a principled account, producing indeterminate liability and inadequate guidance. C is a well-hedged inference combining those two points.
explanations.A: The author does not endorse either damages measure as more faithful; the author calls for a resolution, not for one particular answer.
explanations.B: This contradicts the passage's explicit claim that the body of case law 'affords contracting parties inadequate guidance.'
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The author presents this as one possible view but does not endorse it; the passage explicitly frames this as an unresolved question.
explanations.E: The passage locates the inconsistency in a doctrinal ambiguity, not in procedural differences between federal and state courts.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the practice of courts resolving promissory-estoppel cases on a case-by-case basis without committing to a foundational principle can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: unqualified admiration, because it allows judges to reach equitable outcomes in individual disputes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: cautious approval tempered by concern that the approach may occasionally produce anomalous results.

choices.label: C
choices.text: critical acceptance, acknowledging that it is understandable as a judicial strategy while maintaining that it ultimately disserves important interests.

choices.label: D
choices.text: outright condemnation, with the author urging that all promissory-estoppel claims be transferred to a specialized commercial court.

choices.label: E
choices.text: neutral description, with no evaluative stance expressed.

explanations.correct: The closing sentence explicitly concedes that case-by-case finessing is 'understandable as a judicial management strategy' while immediately qualifying it as one that 'ultimately disserves both commercial certainty and the interests of relying parties.' C captures both the concession and the criticism.
explanations.A: The author does not admire this practice; the passage ends with a prescription to abandon it.
explanations.B: 'Cautious approval' misreads the author's stance, which is predominantly critical despite the concession.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: 'Outright condemnation' overstates the tone, and no specialized court is mentioned; the author calls for explicit resolution, not institutional transfer.
explanations.E: The author clearly evaluates the practice negatively, so the characterization as neutral is inaccurate.

questions.questionStem: The author most likely discusses the 1987 Seventh Circuit decision and the 1993 state appellate decision in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: demonstrate that federal appellate courts consistently award more generous damages than state appellate courts in contract disputes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate, through two contrasting outcomes, that the ambiguity about the proper remedy in promissory-estoppel cases has produced incompatible rulings.

choices.label: C
choices.text: argue that the Seventh Circuit's reasoning in 1987 was legally superior to the state court's reasoning in 1993.

choices.label: D
choices.text: provide a historical account of how promissory estoppel evolved from an equitable doctrine into a freestanding cause of action.

choices.label: E
choices.text: show that oral assurances made by manufacturers are more legally risky than those made by contractors.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 explicitly says 'These two rulings rest on incompatible premises about the doctrine's purpose.' The cases are introduced to illustrate the inconsistency that the passage has already identified as the central problem. B captures this rhetorical function.
explanations.A: The passage does not advance a general claim about federal versus state generosity in damages; the two cases involve different parties and factual settings, and the author does not endorse this generalization.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author explicitly refrains from endorsing either result; the point is that the two rulings are incompatible, not that one is superior.
explanations.D: The cases are not presented as historical waypoints in the doctrine's evolution; the passage is concerned with their incompatible premises about remedies.
explanations.E: The passage draws no such comparison about the legal risk of assurances by manufacturers versus contractors.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its classical antecedents traced; two conflicting applications of the doctrine are presented; the deeper ambiguity underlying those conflicts is identified and a resolution is prescribed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and defined; a single paradigm case illustrating its correct application is analyzed in detail; a recommendation for legislative reform is advanced.
