choices.label: C
choices.text: A doctrinal controversy is described; two scholarly positions on the controversy are summarized and compared; the author endorses one position as clearly superior.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The history of a common-law rule is traced from its origins to the present day; recent judicial departures from the rule are criticized; a return to the original formulation is urged.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A doctrine's definition is provided; its inconsistent application across jurisdictions is attributed to poor judicial draftsmanship; several specific drafting improvements are proposed.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces promissory estoppel and contrasts it with classical consideration doctrine. Paragraph 2 presents the two conflicting cases. Paragraph 3 locates the deeper foundational ambiguity and closes with a prescription for courts to resolve it. A tracks all three moves accurately.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The passage discusses two cases, not one paradigm case; and the closing prescription is directed at courts, not the legislature.
explanations.C: The passage does not summarize two scholarly positions; the conflicting approaches are judicial, and the author does not endorse either damages measure as clearly superior.
explanations.D: The passage does not trace a historical evolution of the rule, and does not urge return to an original formulation; it urges a principled resolution of an existing ambiguity.
explanations.E: The passage attributes inconsistency to a foundational doctrinal ambiguity, not to poor draftsmanship, and proposes no specific drafting fixes.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uneasy position within the common law of contracts, for it grants legal relief in circumstances that classical contract theory would regard as unenforceable. Under classical doctrine, a promise is enforceable only when it is supported by consideration — that is, when the promisee has given something of value in exchange for the promisor's commitment. Promissory estoppel departs from this requirement by protecting a promisee who has reasonably relied upon a promise to their detriment, even if no formal exchange of value occurred. Courts in the United States first articulated this principle in the early twentieth century, and it was later codified in the Restatement (Second) of Contracts, which provides that a promise is binding if the promisor should reasonably have expected it to induce reliance, and if injustice can be avoided only by enforcement of the promise.

The doctrine's expansion has not proceeded without difficulty. Courts applying promissory estoppel must resolve at least two recurring tensions. First, they must determine how substantial the promisee's reliance must be before estoppel is warranted. Some jurisdictions require that the promisee demonstrate a significant and irreversible change in position — quitting stable employment, for instance, or relocating a household — while others are prepared to extend relief for more modest acts of reliance. This divergence reflects a genuine disagreement about whether the doctrine should primarily restore the promisee to the position they occupied before the promise was made, or whether it should, on occasion, enforce the expectation interest fully, placing the promisee in the position they would have occupied had the promise been kept. The former measure yields reliance damages; the latter yields expectation damages. Courts have not resolved this question uniformly.

A second tension concerns the role of promissory estoppel in commercial settings. In a 2001 case in Illinois, a supplier argued that it had acted in reasonable reliance on a buyer's assurance that a long-term contract would be formalized, and sought expectation damages when the buyer withdrew. The court declined to award full expectation damages, reasoning that sophisticated commercial parties are presumed to appreciate that preliminary assurances do not bind, and that extending estoppel broadly in such contexts would undermine the careful risk allocations that commercial contracts are designed to achieve. This ruling, while defensible on its own terms, risks leaving meritorious claims without remedy when the promisee genuinely lacked the bargaining power to insist on a formal agreement. One hopes that future courts will calibrate the doctrine more sensitively to the relative sophistication of the parties involved, rather than applying a categorical exclusion that treats all commercial actors as equally capable of self-protection.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel was first articulated in early twentieth-century American courts and later codified in the Restatement (Second) of Contracts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The doctrine of promissory estoppel, while a legitimate departure from classical contract theory, has generated unresolved tensions in its application that courts have addressed inconsistently.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Courts should abandon the consideration requirement entirely and rely on promissory estoppel to enforce all promises that induce reasonable reliance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Commercial parties should not be permitted to invoke promissory estoppel because they are presumed to understand that preliminary assurances are not binding.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The primary distinction between reliance damages and expectation damages is the central problem that courts face when applying promissory estoppel.

explanations.correct: The passage introduces promissory estoppel as a doctrinal departure from classical contract theory, then traces two recurring tensions in its application — the measure of damages and its use in commercial settings — and closes with the author's assessment that courts have handled these tensions inconsistently. B integrates all three strands.
explanations.A: Too narrow — this captures only the historical background in paragraph one, not the passage's evaluative argument.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong and unsupported — the author never advocates abandoning the consideration requirement altogether.
explanations.D: Restates the Illinois court's holding as if it were the author's thesis; the author actually criticizes this categorical approach.
explanations.E: Too narrow — the damages distinction is one of two tensions discussed and is not identified as the central problem.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the Restatement (Second) of Contracts provides that a promise is binding when which one of the following conditions is met?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The promisee has given consideration of equal or greater value than the promise itself.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The promisee has quit stable employment or relocated a household in reliance on the promise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The promisor could reasonably have anticipated that the promise would induce reliance, and injustice can be avoided only by enforcement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both parties are of unequal sophistication and the weaker party lacks bargaining power.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The promise was made in a commercial setting and was subsequently memorialized in writing.

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly states that the Restatement provides that a promise is binding if the promisor should reasonably have expected it to induce reliance, and if injustice can be avoided only by enforcement. C is a close paraphrase.
explanations.A: This restates the classical consideration requirement, which promissory estoppel explicitly displaces.
explanations.B: These are examples of substantial reliance discussed in paragraph two as a jurisdictional standard, not the Restatement's definition.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The relative sophistication of parties is discussed as a factor the author recommends, not as a Restatement condition.
explanations.E: No such requirement appears in the passage; this introduces details not stated anywhere in the text.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A promisee who relocates a household in reliance on a promise should always receive full expectation damages rather than mere reliance damages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A commercial party that lacked meaningful bargaining power may have a meritorious promissory estoppel claim even if it is a business entity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Courts should eliminate promissory estoppel in commercial settings and restrict the doctrine to purely personal transactions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The consideration requirement of classical contract law is on the whole a just and adequate mechanism for distributing contractual risk.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Preliminary assurances in commerce should be treated as fully binding promises whenever they are made in written form.

explanations.correct: The author criticizes the Illinois court's categorical exclusion for leaving meritorious claims without remedy when the promisee genuinely lacked bargaining power, and calls for calibration based on relative sophistication. This implies that a commercial party lacking bargaining power may still deserve relief — regardless of its status as a business entity.
explanations.A: Too strong — the author does not claim relocation always warrants expectation damages; the passage merely lists relocation as an example of substantial reliance in some jurisdictions.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The opposite of the author's position — the author wants more sensitive calibration, not categorical exclusion.
explanations.D: The passage treats the consideration requirement as a baseline that promissory estoppel appropriately departs from in some cases; it does not endorse the requirement as fully adequate.
explanations.E: Nothing in the passage suggests that written form transforms a preliminary assurance into a binding promise.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the Illinois court's 2001 ruling can best be described as which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Unqualified disapproval, because the ruling disregarded well-established precedent on promissory estoppel.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cautious approval tempered by concern that the ruling may be extended beyond the circumstances that justified it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Qualified acceptance of the ruling's underlying reasoning combined with concern that its categorical application may produce unjust outcomes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Strong endorsement, because the ruling correctly recognizes that commercial parties should never be permitted to invoke promissory estoppel.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Indifference, because the ruling applies only to a narrow category of commercial transactions that are unlikely to recur.

explanations.correct: The author writes that the ruling is 'defensible on its own terms' — an acknowledgment of its rationale — but then criticizes the risk of leaving meritorious claims without remedy, calling for calibration rather than categorical exclusion. C captures this dual stance precisely.
explanations.A: Too strong in both valence and rationale — the author does not call it a violation of precedent, and offers partial acceptance.
explanations.B: Partially accurate in tone but misdescribes the concern: the author worries about categorical application to all commercial parties, not extension beyond original circumstances.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: This echoes the court's apparent position, not the author's, who explicitly criticizes a categorical commercial exclusion.
explanations.E: The author's closing call for future courts to calibrate the doctrine shows engagement, not indifference.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its historical origin is traced; two applications of the doctrine are compared; the author concludes that the doctrine should be abolished.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined and distinguished from classical contract theory; two tensions arising in its application are identified and illustrated; the author offers a prescriptive assessment of one tension.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A legal controversy is introduced; competing judicial opinions are presented in full; the author synthesizes the opinions and proposes a new rule.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined; a single case study is analyzed in depth; the author generalizes from that case to propose a universal standard.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The inadequacies of classical contract law are catalogued; promissory estoppel is proposed as a complete remedy; objections to the doctrine are raised and then dismissed.

explanations.correct: Paragraph one defines promissory estoppel and contrasts it with the classical consideration requirement. Paragraph two identifies the first tension (measure of reliance and damages) and illustrates it with examples from divergent jurisdictions. Paragraph three identifies the second tension (commercial context), illustrates it with the 2001 Illinois case, and closes with the author's evaluative prescription about calibrating the doctrine. B accurately captures this three-part structure.
explanations.A: The author does not call for abolition of the doctrine — this misidentifies the concluding move.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage does not present competing judicial opinions 'in full'; nor does it propose a new formal rule.
explanations.D: The Illinois case is one illustration among others, not an extended case study from which a universal standard is derived.
explanations.E: The passage does not catalogue inadequacies of classical contract law broadly, and promissory estoppel is not presented as a complete remedy.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the 2001 Illinois case serves primarily to illustrate which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The general principle that commercial parties are always better positioned than non-commercial parties to protect their legal interests.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The tension between the doctrine's potential to protect parties who lack bargaining power and courts' reluctance to extend it in commercial settings.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The historical development of promissory estoppel from its early twentieth-century origins to its modern commercial applications.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The proposition that expectation damages are always preferable to reliance damages in cases involving preliminary assurances.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The conflict between state and federal courts over the proper scope of promissory estoppel in commercial transactions.

explanations.correct: The Illinois case is introduced to illustrate the second tension identified in paragraph three: courts' reluctance to apply promissory estoppel broadly in commercial settings, which risks leaving meritorious claimants — particularly those lacking bargaining power — without remedy. B captures both sides of the tension.
explanations.A: This overstates what the case illustrates; the author specifically questions whether all commercial parties are equally capable of self-protection.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The historical development is traced in paragraph one; the Illinois case functions to illustrate the commercial-setting tension, not history.
explanations.D: The case does not establish a preference for expectation over reliance damages; the court in fact declined to award expectation damages.
explanations.E: No state-federal conflict is discussed in the passage; both paragraphs address court practices without invoking federalism.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the Illinois court's reasoning as described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Expectation damages in promissory estoppel cases have been awarded by courts in other jurisdictions without any measurable disruption to commercial contracting practices.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The supplier in the Illinois case had retained legal counsel throughout the negotiations and was aware that no formal contract had been signed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Classical contract theory was developed primarily to protect individual consumers rather than sophisticated commercial entities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many commercial disputes involving preliminary assurances are resolved through arbitration rather than litigation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some jurisdictions require parties to commercial contracts to include written disclaimers stating that preliminary negotiations are not binding.

explanations.correct: The Illinois court's reasoning rests on the premise that broadly extending promissory estoppel in commercial settings would undermine the careful risk allocations that commercial contracts achieve. If expectation damages have been awarded in other commercial jurisdictions without disrupting contracting practices, this directly undercuts the court's central concern about destabilizing commercial arrangements.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: This strengthens the court's reasoning by suggesting the supplier was sophisticated enough to understand the risk — it supports, not undermines, the court's position.
explanations.C: The historical purpose of classical contract theory is irrelevant to whether promissory estoppel disrupts commercial risk allocations.
explanations.D: The prevalence of arbitration does not speak to whether courts should award expectation damages when disputes do reach litigation.
explanations.E: The existence of disclaimer requirements in some jurisdictions is consistent with the court's view that commercial parties should protect themselves through formal mechanisms; this neither undermines nor clearly supports the court's reasoning.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uneasy position within contract law, for it operates as a mechanism of equitable relief in circumstances where the formal requirements of a binding contract have not been met. Under orthodox common-law doctrine, a promise is enforceable only if it is supported by consideration — that is, by some return promise or act of value given by the promisee in exchange. Promissory estoppel departs from this requirement by permitting a court to enforce a promise when the promisee has reasonably relied upon it to his or her detriment, even in the absence of consideration. The doctrine thus introduces a tension at the heart of contract law: it acknowledges that formal requirements may in some cases produce unjust outcomes, yet it simultaneously risks undermining the predictability and certainty upon which commercial parties depend.

The tension becomes most apparent when courts are asked to determine the scope of the remedy available under promissory estoppel. Two competing approaches have emerged in the case law of common-law jurisdictions. The first, associated primarily with English courts, treats the doctrine as a shield rather than a sword: a defendant may invoke promissory estoppel to defend against a claim, but a claimant may not use it as an independent cause of action to recover expectation damages — that is, the full value of the promised performance. The second approach, more widely adopted in American jurisdictions following the influential Restatement (Second) of Contracts, allows promissory estoppel to operate as an affirmative cause of action, permitting courts to award whatever remedy justice requires, which in practice has sometimes included full expectation damages. The divergence between these approaches is not merely procedural; it reflects fundamentally different assumptions about whether the doctrine is corrective in nature, aimed at preventing harm to a relying party, or substitutive, aimed at placing the promisee in the position she would have occupied had the promise been performed.

Courts in neither jurisdiction have resolved this underlying tension with full consistency. English courts have at times extended the doctrine beyond its defensive posture by recognizing proprietary estoppel — a related but distinct doctrine that can ground an affirmative claim over land — while American courts have frequently limited recovery to reliance damages rather than expectation damages, notwithstanding the broader theoretical scope the Restatement affords them. The practical convergence is partial and imperfect. One might reasonably conclude that the persistence of this inconsistency reflects not a failure of judicial reasoning so much as an unresolved normative disagreement about the proper function of contract law: whether contract law should enforce the reasonable expectations of parties or only protect them from harm caused by their reliance. Until that foundational question receives a more satisfying answer in either jurisdiction, the courts will continue to apply promissory estoppel in ways that appear doctrinally ad hoc and that leave commercial parties uncertain about the extent of their obligations.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel arose in English courts as a defensive doctrine and has since been expanded by American courts into a fully affirmative cause of action.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The divergence between English and American approaches to promissory estoppel can be resolved by adopting the remedy-based framework of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Promissory estoppel reflects an unresolved tension in contract law between enforcing reasonable expectations and limiting recovery to reliance harm, producing inconsistent judicial application in both English and American courts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because promissory estoppel lacks the formal requirement of consideration, commercial parties in common-law jurisdictions cannot reliably predict the extent of their contractual obligations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The root cause of inconsistency in promissory estoppel doctrine is the failure of appellate courts in both England and the United States to articulate a clear standard for awarding expectation damages.

explanations.correct: C captures the passage's full thesis: the tension between two normative visions of contract law produces inconsistent outcomes in both jurisdictions, which is the through-line from paragraph 1 through the conclusion.
explanations.A: This is a partial historical description drawn from paragraph 2 only; it omits the normative tension that is the passage's central concern.
explanations.B: The passage explicitly rejects this: it notes that American courts frequently limit recovery despite the Restatement's broader scope, and no resolution is endorsed by the author.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The unpredictability for commercial parties is mentioned as a consequence, not the main point; the passage's argument focuses on the normative disagreement underlying the doctrine.
explanations.E: The passage locates the inconsistency in a normative disagreement about the function of contract law, not in appellate courts' failure to articulate a damages standard specifically.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the English approach to promissory estoppel differs from the American approach primarily in that the English approach

choices.label: A
choices.text: permits courts to award expectation damages whenever a promisee has reasonably relied on a promise to her detriment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: allows promissory estoppel to serve only as a defense against a claim rather than as a basis for recovering the value of the promised performance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: requires that a promisee demonstrate proprietary interests in land before invoking the doctrine in any proceeding.

choices.label: D
choices.text: limits the doctrine to commercial transactions between parties of substantially equal bargaining power.

choices.label: E
choices.text: refuses to recognize reliance damages as a permissible form of relief under any circumstances.

explanations.correct: The passage states that English courts treat promissory estoppel as 'a shield rather than a sword,' meaning a defendant may invoke it defensively but a claimant may not use it to recover expectation damages as an affirmative cause of action.
explanations.A: This describes the broader American approach, not the English one.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage mentions proprietary estoppel as a related but distinct doctrine that English courts have recognized; it does not say proprietary interests are required to invoke promissory estoppel generally.
explanations.D: No such limitation based on bargaining power is mentioned anywhere in the passage.
explanations.E: The passage does not say English courts refuse reliance damages; it focuses on the bar against using promissory estoppel as an affirmative cause of action for expectation damages.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel should be abolished in favor of a stricter application of the consideration requirement in order to restore predictability to contract law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The inconsistency in how courts apply promissory estoppel is ultimately a symptom of a deeper disagreement about the normative goals of contract law rather than a product of judicial error.

choices.label: C
choices.text: American courts have resolved the tension between corrective and substitutive conceptions of contract law more satisfactorily than English courts have.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Restatement (Second) of Contracts provides the most coherent theoretical foundation for promissory estoppel doctrine and should be adopted by English courts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Commercial parties can adequately protect themselves from the uncertainty created by promissory estoppel by drafting sufficiently detailed written contracts.

explanations.correct: The passage's closing argument explicitly states that the inconsistency 'reflects not a failure of judicial reasoning so much as an unresolved normative disagreement about the proper function of contract law,' directly supporting B.
explanations.A: The author never endorses abolishing the doctrine; the passage treats its existence as a given and focuses on the normative disagreement shaping its application.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage notes that American courts frequently limit recovery to reliance damages despite the Restatement's broader scope, suggesting neither jurisdiction has resolved the tension satisfactorily.
explanations.D: The author describes the Restatement as influential but does not endorse it as the most coherent approach or recommend its adoption by English courts.
explanations.E: The passage does not address whether careful drafting could insulate commercial parties; this is outside the passage's scope.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to proprietary estoppel in the third paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate that even the English courts, which nominally restrict promissory estoppel to a defensive role, have at times extended related doctrines to permit affirmative claims.

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that proprietary estoppel is a more doctrinally sound mechanism than promissory estoppel for protecting relying parties.

choices.label: C
choices.text: explain why English courts are more likely than American courts to award full expectation damages in promissory estoppel cases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: introduce the reader to a distinct area of land law that developed independently of promissory estoppel doctrine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: demonstrate that the English approach has been fully adopted by courts in other common-law jurisdictions outside the United States.

explanations.correct: The reference to proprietary estoppel supports the passage's claim that English courts have not applied their defensive-only posture with full consistency; by recognizing proprietary estoppel as a route to affirmative land claims, they have, in practice, moved beyond pure defensiveness.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The passage explicitly calls proprietary estoppel 'related but distinct' and draws no comparative evaluative judgment about its soundness relative to promissory estoppel.
explanations.C: The passage does not suggest English courts are more likely to award expectation damages; the reference to proprietary estoppel shows inconsistency, not a greater willingness to award expectation damages.
explanations.D: This describes content accurately but misidentifies the rhetorical function; the reference is made to illustrate a pattern of inconsistency, not to introduce a new area of law for its own sake.
explanations.E: The passage says nothing about other common-law jurisdictions adopting the English approach; this choice invents a claim the passage does not make.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined and its internal tension identified; two jurisdictionally distinct approaches to the doctrine are contrasted; the persistence of inconsistency across both jurisdictions is attributed to an unresolved foundational disagreement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined; its historical origins in English equity courts are traced; a recent American reformulation of the doctrine is described and endorsed as the superior approach.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A tension between two bodies of law is introduced; several illustrative cases are examined in detail; the author concludes that one jurisdiction has resolved the tension more satisfactorily than the other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A doctrine's departure from a formal legal requirement is explained; the doctrine's application is shown to be uniform across jurisdictions; the author recommends a legislative solution to resolve the resulting uncertainty.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two competing doctrines within contract law are introduced and compared; their respective strengths and weaknesses are evaluated; the author proposes a hybrid approach drawing on elements of each.

explanations.correct: A accurately maps paragraph 1 (definition and tension), paragraph 2 (English vs. American approaches), and paragraph 3 (inconsistency in both, attributed to normative disagreement) in the correct sequence.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The passage does not trace historical origins in equity courts at length, and it does not endorse the American approach as superior.
explanations.C: The passage mentions no specific cases examined in detail, and the author does not conclude that one jurisdiction has resolved the tension more satisfactorily.
explanations.D: The passage explicitly notes that the two approaches are divergent, not uniform; and the author proposes no legislative solution.
explanations.E: The passage compares two approaches to one doctrine, not two competing doctrines; and it proposes no hybrid framework.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the current state of promissory estoppel doctrine can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: vigorous condemnation of the courts' failure to apply established legal principles consistently.

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured concern that unresolved normative disagreement has produced doctrinal inconsistency that disserves commercial parties.

choices.label: C
choices.text: cautious optimism that recent convergence between English and American courts will soon resolve the underlying tension.

choices.label: D
choices.text: strong endorsement of the American approach on the ground that it best protects the reasonable expectations of promisees.

choices.label: E
choices.text: detached indifference, presenting the competing approaches without expressing any evaluative stance of the author's own.

explanations.correct: The author describes the inconsistency as 'ad hoc,' expresses concern that commercial parties face uncertainty, and locates the problem in an 'unresolved normative disagreement' — a tone that is critically concerned but measured rather than condemnatory or optimistic.
explanations.A: The author explicitly says the inconsistency reflects 'not a failure of judicial reasoning' but a normative disagreement, so vigorous condemnation of the courts is inaccurate.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage describes the convergence as 'partial and imperfect' and offers no suggestion that a resolution is forthcoming; cautious optimism is not supported.
explanations.D: The author does not endorse the American approach; in fact, it notes that American courts themselves frequently limit recovery despite the Restatement's broader scope.
explanations.E: The author clearly evaluates the current state as producing 'ad hoc' results that leave parties 'uncertain' — this is not detached indifference.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that the inconsistency in promissory estoppel doctrine reflects an unresolved normative disagreement about the proper function of contract law?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several American jurisdictions have recently enacted statutes codifying the Restatement (Second) approach, thereby reducing variation among American courts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Surveys of common-law judges reveal near-unanimous agreement that contract law should protect parties from harm caused by reliance rather than enforce their bargained-for expectations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Promissory estoppel claims succeed at roughly equal rates in English and American courts when reliance damages, rather than expectation damages, are sought.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Legal scholars have proposed numerous theoretical frameworks for resolving the tension between corrective and substitutive conceptions of contract law, none of which has been adopted by any court.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The divergence between English and American courts on promissory estoppel has been widening rather than narrowing over the past two decades.

explanations.correct: The author's claim is that inconsistency persists because of an unresolved normative disagreement. If judges in fact share a clear consensus on the normative goal of contract law, the disagreement is not unresolved, which would undermine the explanation the author offers for the inconsistency.
explanations.A: Greater uniformity among American courts would reduce variation within one jurisdiction but would not address the normative disagreement between the corrective and substitutive conceptions that the author identifies as the root cause.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Comparable success rates for reliance-damages claims would show procedural overlap but would not address whether judges share a normative view of contract law's purpose; it does not undermine the author's normative-disagreement thesis.
explanations.D: The existence of unadopted scholarly frameworks would, if anything, reinforce the author's point that the normative disagreement remains unresolved at the level of actual legal practice.
explanations.E: A widening divergence would be consistent with, and might even strengthen, the author's claim that the normative disagreement is unresolved.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uneasy position within the common law of contracts, for it introduces equitable principles into a body of law that has historically demanded the strict satisfaction of formal requirements. At common law, a promise is enforceable only when supported by consideration — that is, when something of legal value is exchanged between the parties. Promissory estoppel, however, allows a court to enforce a promise even in the absence of consideration, provided that the promisee has relied on the promise to her detriment and that it would be inequitable to allow the promisor to resile from what was said. The tension between these two approaches has generated considerable doctrinal instability, and courts applying promissory estoppel have not consistently identified either the conditions under which the doctrine operates or the remedy it is meant to afford.

The difficulty begins with the threshold requirement of reliance. Most courts agree that the promisee's reliance must be reasonable and foreseeable — that is, the promisor must have known, or should have known, that the promisee would act upon the promise. But courts have diverged sharply on the question of how substantial that reliance must be. Some jurisdictions require that the promisee demonstrate a significant change in position, such as the abandonment of a business opportunity or the expenditure of a large sum. Others have found detrimental reliance satisfied by comparatively modest acts, such as declining to seek an alternative arrangement. This divergence produces markedly different outcomes in cases that are otherwise substantially similar. Consider, for example, two decisions issued in the early 1990s in different American states involving employers who made oral assurances of long-term employment to candidates who had already resigned from existing positions. In one state, the court held that resignation alone was insufficient reliance; in the other, identical facts supported a successful estoppel claim. This inconsistency is difficult to justify and reflects not a principled distinction but rather the varying tolerance of different courts for departures from the consideration requirement.

Equally contested is the matter of remedy. At common law, a successful plaintiff recovers expectation damages — the benefit of the bargain — whereas promissory estoppel, rooted in equity, would seem to call for reliance damages, which restore the plaintiff to the position she held before acting on the promise. Yet courts have not uniformly confined promissory estoppel to reliance recovery. Several influential decisions in the latter half of the twentieth century awarded the plaintiff the full expectation measure, effectively treating the equitable doctrine as functionally equivalent to contract enforcement. Whether this extension is faithful to the doctrine's equitable foundations is doubtful, and it seems to conflate what are properly distinct remedial regimes. Courts that award expectation damages through the vehicle of promissory estoppel do little more than relabel contract enforcement in the language of equity, obscuring the doctrinal rationale for the remedy they grant. One may hope that a clearer articulation of when reliance recovery, rather than expectation recovery, is appropriate will eventually emerge from appellate courts willing to examine the doctrine with greater conceptual rigor.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel should be eliminated from common law jurisdictions because it undermines the consideration requirement that gives contracts their binding force.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The doctrine of promissory estoppel has been applied inconsistently by courts with respect to both the threshold reliance requirement and the appropriate remedy, reflecting deeper doctrinal instability.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Courts in the early 1990s issued contradictory rulings on employment estoppel claims, demonstrating that oral assurances of employment are unreliable bases for legal action.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Promissory estoppel and contract law are best understood as two versions of the same doctrine, since both ultimately protect the expectation interests of promisees.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Appellate courts should award reliance damages rather than expectation damages in all promissory estoppel cases in order to restore the doctrine's equitable foundations.

explanations.correct: The passage's thesis — stated in paragraph 1 and developed in paragraphs 2 and 3 — is that promissory estoppel is applied inconsistently on two fronts: the reliance threshold and the remedy. B captures this dual instability across the full passage.
explanations.A: Too strong and unsupported — the author critiques inconsistency but never advocates eliminating the doctrine.
explanations.B: Correct. This integrates both strands of the argument (reliance threshold and remedy) that span paragraphs 2 and 3.
explanations.C: Too narrow — the employment cases are an illustrative example in paragraph 2, not the main point of the passage.
explanations.D: This inverts the author's concern; the author explicitly rejects conflating estoppel with contract enforcement.
explanations.E: This is the author's closing suggestion, not the main point — a classic 'restates the closing recommendation as the thesis' trap.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward courts that award expectation damages through the vehicle of promissory estoppel can best be described as one of

choices.label: A
choices.text: cautious approval, because such awards produce outcomes that are fair to promisees who have genuinely relied on promises to their detriment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured indifference, because the choice between reliance and expectation damages has no practical effect on the plaintiff's recovery.

choices.label: C
choices.text: critical skepticism, because such courts obscure the doctrinal rationale for the remedy they grant by conflating distinct remedial regimes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: strong condemnation, because awarding expectation damages through estoppel constitutes a fundamental violation of equitable principles.

choices.label: E
choices.text: tentative acceptance, because although the practice departs from equity, it may help courts resolve the inconsistency surrounding the reliance threshold.

explanations.correct: The author states that awarding expectation damages through promissory estoppel is 'doubtful,' 'conflates what are properly distinct remedial regimes,' and 'does little more than relabel contract enforcement' — language that signals critical skepticism without rising to outright condemnation.
explanations.A: The author does not approve of this practice; the passage characterizes it as doctrinal confusion.
explanations.B: The author clearly does not view this as a matter of indifference — the passage expresses concern about the doctrinal obscuration it produces.
explanations.C: Correct. 'Doubtful,' 'conflates,' and 'obscuring' signal critical skepticism at the right intensity.
explanations.D: Overstated — the author uses measured language ('doubtful,' 'seems to conflate'), not the strong condemnation that 'fundamental violation' implies.
explanations.E: The author never suggests the practice helps resolve the reliance threshold inconsistency; this is an unsupported rationalization.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and situated within a broader tension; the inconsistency in its application is then examined on two distinct dimensions; and the passage closes with a critical assessment and an expression of hope for future clarification.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two competing theories of contract law are described; a series of court decisions is analyzed to determine which theory is superior; and the passage concludes by endorsing one theory over the other.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A problematic court decision is introduced; its historical precedents are traced across several jurisdictions; and a statutory remedy is proposed as a solution to the inconsistency it generated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A doctrine is defined; its origins in Roman law are described; its subsequent transformation in Anglo-American courts is traced; and the passage ends by noting its current obsolescence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The requirements of a legal doctrine are set out in detail; a single landmark case is analyzed at length; and the passage argues that the case was wrongly decided and should be overturned.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces promissory estoppel and its tension with consideration doctrine. Paragraph 2 examines inconsistency in the reliance threshold. Paragraph 3 examines inconsistency in remedies and closes with the author's critique and hope for appellate clarification. A captures all three moves accurately.
explanations.A: Correct. This accurately describes all three paragraphs' functions.
explanations.B: The passage does not pit two theories against each other to select a winner; it critiques internal inconsistency within one doctrine.
explanations.C: No single problematic decision is the focus; no statutory remedy is proposed.
explanations.D: No Roman law origins are discussed, and the doctrine is not described as obsolete.
explanations.E: The passage discusses multiple cases, not a single landmark; it does not argue any case should be overturned.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is a condition that most courts agree must be satisfied for the doctrine of promissory estoppel to apply?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The promisee must have suffered a financial loss that exceeds the value of the original promise.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The promisor must have reduced the promise to writing and signed it before a witness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The promisee's reliance on the promise must have been reasonable and foreseeable by the promisor.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The promise must have been made in a commercial rather than a personal or social context.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The promisee must have provided something of legal value in exchange for the promisor's assurance.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states explicitly: 'Most courts agree that the promisee's reliance must be reasonable and foreseeable — that is, the promisor must have known, or should have known, that the promisee would act upon the promise.' C paraphrases this directly.
explanations.A: The passage does not state any financial-loss-exceeds-promise-value threshold; this is not mentioned.
explanations.B: The passage explicitly notes that promissory estoppel can apply to oral assurances; a writing requirement is not stated.
explanations.C: Correct. This is stated in paragraph 2 as a point of consensus.
explanations.D: The passage discusses employment contexts but never restricts the doctrine to commercial settings.
explanations.E: This describes the consideration requirement, which the passage notes promissory estoppel operates without — directly the opposite of what is asked.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A plaintiff who prevails on a promissory estoppel claim should generally recover only enough to restore her to the position she occupied before relying on the promise.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The consideration requirement should be abolished in common law jurisdictions, since promissory estoppel demonstrates that enforceable promises need not be supported by an exchange of value.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Courts that have awarded expectation damages in promissory estoppel cases have done so because they carefully weighed the equitable foundations of the doctrine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral assurances of long-term employment should never form the basis of a promissory estoppel claim, since employment relationships require written documentation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promissory estoppel is best understood as a variant of contract law that has gradually absorbed all of contract law's remedial principles.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that promissory estoppel, 'rooted in equity, would seem to call for reliance damages, which restore the plaintiff to the position she held before acting on the promise.' The author then criticizes courts that award expectation damages instead, strongly implying endorsement of reliance recovery as the proper default. A mirrors this inference.
explanations.A: Correct. The author's characterization of reliance damages as the equity-consistent remedy, combined with criticism of expectation awards, supports this inference.
explanations.B: The author critiques inconsistency in promissory estoppel but never advocates abolishing consideration; this overreaches.
explanations.C: The author states the opposite — that such courts obscure the doctrinal rationale rather than carefully weighing equitable foundations.
explanations.D: The employment cases are used as illustrations of inconsistency; the author never says oral assurances categorically cannot support an estoppel claim.
explanations.E: The author explicitly rejects this conflation, arguing that extending expectation damages through estoppel 'conflates what are properly distinct remedial regimes.'

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the two early-1990s employment cases (paragraph 2) serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate that the reliance threshold in promissory estoppel is applied inconsistently across jurisdictions, producing different outcomes from materially identical facts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: demonstrate that oral assurances of employment are never a reliable basis for a promissory estoppel claim in any American jurisdiction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: introduce the broader historical development of promissory estoppel within the American common law tradition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: provide evidence that expectation damages, rather than reliance damages, are the appropriate remedy in employment estoppel cases.

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that the doctrine of promissory estoppel should be codified in statutory form to resolve jurisdictional inconsistency.

explanations.correct: The cases are introduced with 'Consider, for example' and directly follow the author's claim that divergence in the reliance threshold 'produces markedly different outcomes in cases that are otherwise substantially similar.' They function to concretely illustrate that general claim. A accurately captures this rhetorical function.
explanations.A: Correct. The cases are a specific illustration of the inconsistency already asserted in the paragraph.
explanations.B: The cases show inconsistency, not a universal rule against oral assurances; one state's court actually upheld the estoppel claim.
explanations.C: The cases are not introduced to provide historical background but to exemplify a specific doctrinal problem.
explanations.D: Remedies are not discussed in paragraph 2; the cases concern the reliance threshold, not the damages question.
explanations.E: No statutory codification is proposed anywhere in the passage; this is a plausible-but-unused rhetorical move.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that courts awarding expectation damages through promissory estoppel are conflating two distinct remedial regimes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several legal historians have argued that the distinction between law and equity was largely abolished in most common law jurisdictions during the nineteenth century.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In practice, promisees who have detrimentally relied on a promise frequently suffer losses that are equal in value to the benefit of the bargain they expected to receive.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some jurisdictions that recognize promissory estoppel have enacted statutes requiring courts to apply the doctrine only to written promises.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A series of appellate decisions in the late twentieth century expressly analyzed the equitable foundations of promissory estoppel before awarding expectation damages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Legal scholars have proposed that promissory estoppel be replaced by a statutory cause of action modeled on the civilian doctrine of culpa in contrahendo.

explanations.correct: The author's claim rests on the premise that law and equity operate as distinct regimes with distinct remedial logics. If the law/equity distinction was substantively abolished — making contract law and equitable doctrines part of the same unified regime — then awarding expectation damages through estoppel would not constitute a conflation of two distinct systems, thereby undermining the author's critique. A directly attacks this foundational premise.
explanations.A: Correct. If law and equity are no longer distinct regimes, the author's charge of 'conflation' loses its doctrinal foundation.
explanations.B: Even if reliance losses happened to equal expectation losses in practice, this would not justify the legal rationale for awarding expectation damages through an equitable doctrine; it addresses magnitude, not the doctrinal basis the author criticizes.
explanations.C: This concerns a writing requirement, which is unrelated to the remedy debate the author raises; it does not bear on the conflation claim.
explanations.D: Courts that analyzed equitable foundations before awarding expectation damages might show thoughtfulness, but would not demonstrate that expectation and reliance damages are part of the same regime — they would still be awarding a measure the author argues is doctrinal misfit.
explanations.E: A proposal to replace the doctrine with a civilian analogue is irrelevant to whether current courts are conflating two regimes in existing common law.

rc.passage:
Few categories in public international law have provoked as much enthusiasm, and as little analytical rigor, as the category of jus cogens — the small class of peremptory norms from which, it is said, no derogation is permitted. Since the International Law Commission's draft articles of 1966, commentators have treated jus cogens as the constitutional bedrock of the international legal order, a fixed point by reference to which lesser norms are to be tested. Yet a closer reading of the tribunals that have actually applied the concept suggests that this confidence is premature; the bedrock, if it exists, has been charted almost entirely from above.

Consider the 2011 advisory opinion of the Federation of Isuria's regional human-rights court, widely cited for the proposition that the prohibition of enforced disappearance has acquired peremptory status. The court purported to identify this status by surveying the practice of states, the pronouncements of treaty bodies, and the writings of publicists. On inspection, however, the state practice catalogued was thin, the treaty-body pronouncements largely circular (each citing the others), and the publicists predominantly the court's own former members. The court did not so much discover a peremptory norm as ratify one; and the ratification was, in the opinion's own words, "the culmination of a juridical conscience whose outlines the tribunal has already traced." Whether that culmination reflects opinio juris in the traditional sense — a belief among states that they are legally bound — or merely the opinio juris of the judges, is a question the opinion conspicuously declines to press.

A defender of the tribunal might reply that peremptory norms, precisely because they express values that transcend state consent, need not be established by the ordinary inductive methods of customary international law. This reply has the merit of candor, but it concedes the point. Once it is conceded that jus cogens is not a subset of customary norms distinguished by their gravity, but an independent category established by judicial declaration, the notion that such norms furnish an external check on state conduct becomes difficult to sustain. The check is internal to the juridical order that identifies it.

This is not to deny that certain prohibitions — of genocide, of slavery, of aggressive war — command a degree of assent that ordinary treaty norms do not. What is denied is that the current doctrine has given a stable account of how such prohibitions are to be identified, or of what work the peremptory label does beyond signaling the tribunal's own sense of moral urgency. Until that account is supplied, the category will continue to be invoked, regrettably, as a rhetorical resource rather than as a rule of recognition.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The doctrine of jus cogens lacks a principled method of identification and therefore functions less as an external constraint on state conduct than as a vehicle for judicial moral commitments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: International tribunals that have attempted to identify peremptory norms have consistently misapplied the inductive techniques of customary international law.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The prohibitions of genocide, slavery, and aggressive war, whatever their standing in positive law, are not properly characterized as peremptory norms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Commentators since the International Law Commission's 1966 draft articles have correctly identified jus cogens as the constitutional bedrock of the international legal order.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Federation of Isuria's regional human-rights court erred in its 2011 advisory opinion by relying on the writings of its own former members.

explanations.correct: The author sets up the enthusiasm for jus cogens, uses the Isuria opinion to expose the circularity of its identification, concedes that certain prohibitions command wide assent, and closes by insisting that until a stable account of identification is supplied the category operates as rhetoric rather than as a rule of recognition. A captures that integrated thesis.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too narrow — the author's deeper claim is that peremptory norms may not be a subset of customary norms at all; the critique is not merely of inductive technique.
explanations.C: Reverses the author, who explicitly concedes these prohibitions command unusual assent and denies only that the current doctrine explains how such norms are identified.
explanations.D: Restates the view the author is criticizing.
explanations.E: Paragraph-level restatement fixating on one illustrative case rather than the broader doctrinal point.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the defense of the tribunal offered at the beginning of the third paragraph can most accurately be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: initial sympathy that gives way to outright rejection on the ground that the defense misreads the tribunal's own reasoning

choices.label: B
choices.text: qualified acknowledgment of its candor combined with the judgment that it concedes the very point at issue

choices.label: C
choices.text: unqualified endorsement, since the defense rightly insists that peremptory norms transcend state consent

choices.label: D
choices.text: polite dismissal, on the ground that the defense is inconsistent with the inductive methods of customary international law

choices.label: E
choices.text: puzzled agnosticism, since the defense rests on philosophical premises the author has not evaluated

explanations.correct: The author says the reply 'has the merit of candor, but it concedes the point.' That is the exact structure: acknowledgment of candor plus the judgment that the defense gives away what it was meant to save.
explanations.A: Overstates: the author does not reject the defense as a misreading; he accepts its candor and turns its concession against it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author does not endorse the defense; he uses it to derive an unwelcome conclusion.
explanations.D: The author does not accuse the defense of inconsistency with inductive method; that is the trouble with the tribunal's practice, not with the defense.
explanations.E: Out of register — the author reaches a definite judgment.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about the relationship between jus cogens and customary international law?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jus cogens is best understood as a subset of customary norms distinguished from other such norms by the gravity of the interests they protect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The inductive techniques used to identify customary norms are inadequate to the task of identifying peremptory norms and should be abandoned in favor of judicial declaration.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Were peremptory norms established by the same inductive survey of state practice and opinio juris used for customary norms, they could plausibly serve as an external check on state conduct.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There is no meaningful difference between the authority of ordinary customary norms and the authority of putatively peremptory norms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The category of jus cogens is coherent in principle but has been badly applied by tribunals; with better-trained judges, the difficulties would dissolve.

explanations.correct: The author's critique is that once jus cogens is detached from inductive identification through state practice, it ceases to be external to the juridical order. The converse — the inference the author has not stated but would accept — is that inductive grounding would restore the external-check function. C articulates that converse precisely and in hedged terms.
explanations.A: The author's defender offers this formulation in order to reject it; the author declines to endorse it, since the tribunals have not in fact identified peremptory norms through the ordinary inductive methods.
explanations.B: Reverses the author: he criticizes judicial declaration and treats inductive methods as the alternative whose abandonment is the problem.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author concedes that certain prohibitions command unusual assent and does not deny a difference in degree.
explanations.E: The author's critique is structural, not a matter of better training; he says the doctrine has not supplied a stable account.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the 2011 Isuria advisory opinion in the second paragraph functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: offer an illustrative case in which the standard inductive method for identifying customary norms was properly applied

choices.label: B
choices.text: demonstrate that the tribunal's methodology collapsed into self-reference, thereby supporting the author's broader claim that peremptory norms have been charted from within the juridical order rather than discovered outside it

choices.label: C
choices.text: concede that even a flawed identification of a peremptory norm is preferable to no identification at all

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast the Isuria court's approach with the more rigorous approach of the International Law Commission's 1966 draft articles

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that the prohibition of enforced disappearance has not in fact achieved the degree of assent that genocide and slavery command

explanations.correct: The second paragraph is doing work for the metaphor introduced at the end of paragraph 1: the 'bedrock charted from above.' The thin state practice, the circular treaty-body citations, and the court's own former members as publicists together show self-reference, which is what the thesis needs to be demonstrated.
explanations.A: Reverses the function: the example is offered as a failure of inductive method, not a success.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author does not concede this; he denies the identification does the work claimed.
explanations.D: The ILC draft is mentioned only as the origin of the enthusiasm the author is criticizing; no rigor contrast is developed.
explanations.E: The author is silent on whether the specific prohibition has wide assent; his critique is about the method of identification, not the substantive standing of this norm.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following features of the 2011 Isuria advisory opinion's reasoning did the author identify as problematic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It relied on the writings of publicists who were not themselves former members of the tribunal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It refused to consult the pronouncements of treaty bodies on the question of enforced disappearance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It treated the opinio juris of judges as evidence of the opinio juris of states without pressing the distinction between the two.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It departed from the International Law Commission's 1966 draft articles in its definition of peremptory status.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It identified a peremptory norm without also surveying the practice of states.

explanations.correct: The author writes that 'whether that culmination reflects opinio juris in the traditional sense — a belief among states that they are legally bound — or merely the opinio juris of the judges, is a question the opinion conspicuously declines to press.' C paraphrases exactly that complaint.
explanations.A: Inverts the detail: the author complains that the publicists were predominantly the court's former members.
explanations.B: Wrong sentence: the author notes that treaty-body pronouncements were consulted but were largely circular.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The author does not contrast the opinion with the 1966 draft articles on the definition of peremptory status.
explanations.E: The author says state practice was catalogued but thin, not that no survey was conducted.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the structural problem the author identifies with the current doctrine of jus cogens?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A scientific academy declares a novel result to be an established fact by surveying journal articles, most of which were authored by members of the academy and which chiefly cite one another.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A national supreme court strikes down a statute as unconstitutional by applying a long-settled textual canon of interpretation to the statute's language.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A professional association adopts a new ethical rule after a public comment period in which a majority of practitioners endorsed the rule in writing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A regulatory agency issues a guidance document interpreting a statute the agency itself administers, basing the interpretation on the statute's legislative history.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A historian concludes that a disputed battle occurred on a particular date by triangulating among three independent archival sources maintained by different polities.

explanations.correct: The load-bearing structure the author identifies is self-reference masquerading as external discovery: the bedrock 'charted almost entirely from above,' with the court's own former members as publicists and treaty bodies citing one another. A reproduces that exact structure — a body declaring a truth by surveying sources that derive from itself and cite one another.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: A shares the surface feature of authoritative pronouncement but instantiates a different mechanism: application of an established canon to text, not self-referential identification of a novel norm.
explanations.C: The public-comment mechanism introduces an external constituency rather than instantiating self-reference.
explanations.D: Administrative interpretation grounded in legislative history is not self-reference in the relevant sense; the agency is interpreting an externally given text.
explanations.E: Triangulation among three independent polities is precisely the external, inductive method the author says jus cogens doctrine lacks.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's argument that the current doctrine of jus cogens fails to furnish an external check on state conduct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A comprehensive empirical study demonstrates that, in the decade following the Isuria opinion, states whose practice the tribunal had not surveyed nevertheless altered their conduct to conform with the tribunal's identification of the peremptory norm, citing the tribunal's reasoning in their own official pronouncements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several commentators have objected to the Isuria opinion on the ground that its list of publicists included members who had served on the tribunal in earlier decades.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Other regional human-rights courts have issued advisory opinions identifying peremptory norms using methodologies similar to that of the Isuria tribunal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The prohibitions of genocide and aggressive war were recognized as peremptory norms before the International Law Commission's 1966 draft articles.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A minority of states have rejected the Isuria opinion outright and have denied that the prohibition of enforced disappearance has peremptory status.

explanations.correct: The author's argument is that jus cogens lacks an external check because its identification is internal to the juridical order. If states not surveyed by the tribunal nevertheless conform their conduct to the tribunal's identification and cite the tribunal's reasoning as authority, then the identification does in practice operate on state conduct externally — which is the very function the author denies it performs. That most directly undermines the author's claim.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Echoes the author's own observation about the publicists rather than contradicting his structural critique.
explanations.C: Extends the pattern the author criticizes to other tribunals; it reinforces rather than undermines his diagnosis.
explanations.D: Says nothing about the method of identification or the external-check function.
explanations.E: Consistent with the author's picture: if a minority of states reject the norm outright, the supposed peremptory character does not constrain them, which cuts with rather than against the author.

rc.passage:
For nearly four decades, the administrative courts of the Republic of Caltrana have been governed by what practitioners call the Two-Step: when an agency's interpretation of a statute it administers is challenged, the court asks first whether the statute is ambiguous, and, if it is, defers to any reasonable agency reading. The doctrine was announced in a 1987 case concerning a rulemaking on flue-gas emissions and has since become a fixture of the country's public law. What has gone insufficiently noticed, however, is that the Two-Step has quietly accreted a third step — one the court has never acknowledged — that now does much of the actual work.

The accretion began, on the better reading of the cases, with a 2002 dispute over pharmaceutical labeling. The reviewing chamber purported to apply the Two-Step but prefaced its analysis with the observation that the agency's interpretation must be consistent with the statute's "animating purpose." Later opinions have elaborated this preface into a threshold inquiry: before asking whether the statute is ambiguous, the court now asks whether the agency's reading sits comfortably within what the chamber calls the statute's "ordered scheme." Only interpretations that pass this unstated step proceed to the conventional ambiguity analysis. In effect, the court has reserved to itself a prior power to pronounce on statutory coherence — a power that the original doctrine deliberately withheld from reviewing courts, precisely because coherence judgments are sensitive to the same policy considerations that the doctrine wished to leave to the agency.

Defenders of the new approach describe it as an obvious refinement: no one, they say, would wish courts to defer to readings that are in tension with the statute's evident design. The point is not without force. Yet the defense misstates what the original doctrine required. Under the 1987 formulation, a reading in tension with statutory design would ordinarily fail at step two as unreasonable; the court had no occasion to reach that question until ambiguity had been established. The effect of inserting a coherence inquiry at the threshold is not to catch interpretations the old doctrine would have missed but to permit the court to reject interpretations without undertaking the ambiguity analysis that, by its own logic, should precede any such rejection.

Whether this development represents a welcome correction or a doctrinal drift will depend, one supposes, on how much faith one has in the reviewing courts' ability to distinguish coherence from policy preference. The present author is not sanguine. The doctrine's chief virtue, when first announced, was its discipline; the accreted third step, by inviting courts to identify statutory design without the constraint of ambiguity analysis, has begun to dissolve that discipline while continuing to invoke its name.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Caltranan administrative courts have grafted an unacknowledged coherence inquiry onto the Two-Step, and the inquiry has undermined the discipline that the original doctrine was designed to supply.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Defenders of the Caltranan courts' recent approach are correct that no agency interpretation in tension with statutory design should receive deference.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 1987 Two-Step doctrine has been overtaken by more recent decisions that explicitly repudiate its premises.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reviewing courts are institutionally incapable of distinguishing judgments of statutory coherence from judgments of policy preference.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The 2002 dispute over pharmaceutical labeling should be regarded as the moment when the Two-Step doctrine ceased to be good law in Caltrana.

explanations.correct: The passage identifies a quiet accretion of a third step, traces it to the 2002 pharmaceutical case, argues that its defenders misstate the original doctrine, and closes by judging that the accretion has begun to dissolve the discipline the original doctrine was designed to supply. A captures both the descriptive and evaluative strands.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Restates the defenders' view, which the author treats as partly forceful but ultimately mistaken.
explanations.C: Too strong — the courts continue to invoke the Two-Step; the author's complaint is precisely that they do so while modifying it in substance.
explanations.D: A proposition the author's concluding skepticism is consistent with but does not establish as the main claim; the main claim is doctrinal, not epistemic-general.
explanations.E: Paragraph-level restatement fixating on the 2002 case.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An established doctrine is described; an unacknowledged modification is identified and traced to a specific case; a defense of the modification is presented and rebutted; the author offers a skeptical concluding assessment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two rival interpretations of a statute are presented; the arguments for each are surveyed; the author concludes that the second is more faithful to the statute's design.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A doctrine is described; its historical origins are traced; an analogous doctrine in a foreign jurisdiction is introduced as a superior model; the two are compared.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A judicial decision is summarized; its reasoning is criticized as internally inconsistent; a proposed correction is offered; the correction is shown to resolve the doctrinal difficulty.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A practice is defended against a familiar objection; the objection is shown to rest on a misunderstanding; the defense is extended to a range of adjacent practices.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 describes the Two-Step and flags the accreted third step; paragraph 2 traces the accretion to the 2002 pharmaceutical case and elaborates the unstated coherence inquiry; paragraph 3 presents the defenders' view and rebuts it; paragraph 4 offers the author's skeptical concluding assessment. A maps this sequence correctly.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The passage is about a doctrine's evolution, not a choice between two statutory interpretations.
explanations.C: No foreign-jurisdiction analogue is introduced.
explanations.D: The author does not propose a correction that resolves the difficulty; he diagnoses a drift.
explanations.E: Reverses the posture: a defense is presented and rebutted, not extended.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would accept which one of the following claims about the 1987 Two-Step as originally formulated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It permitted reviewing courts to reject an agency interpretation on the ground of statutory incoherence only after a finding that the statute was ambiguous.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It required agencies to adopt interpretations consistent with a statute's animating purpose as determined by the reviewing court in advance of any deference.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It made no provision for reviewing courts to reject unreasonable agency interpretations at any stage of the analysis.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It was formulated with an implicit understanding that future courts would supplement it with a threshold coherence inquiry.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It applied only to rulemakings concerning environmental emissions and did not govern agency interpretations in other areas.

explanations.correct: The author says that under the 1987 formulation, a reading in tension with statutory design would ordinarily fail at step two as unreasonable, and that the court had no occasion to reach that question until ambiguity had been established. A restates that commitment: rejection on coherence grounds occurred only after a finding of ambiguity.
explanations.A: Correct.
