explanations.B: Describes the accreted third step, which the author treats as a departure from, not a feature of, the 1987 doctrine.
explanations.C: Reverses the author, who explicitly says unreasonable interpretations could be rejected at step two.
explanations.D: The author characterizes the third step as unacknowledged and as 'doctrinal drift,' not as an anticipated supplement.
explanations.E: Outside scope — the author calls the doctrine 'a fixture of the country's public law,' not confined to emissions.

questions.questionStem: The author's observation in the third paragraph that the defenders' point is "not without force" functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: concede the plausibility of the defense before arguing that it rests on a mischaracterization of what the original doctrine required

choices.label: B
choices.text: introduce a counterexample that the author will ultimately treat as decisive against the original doctrine

choices.label: C
choices.text: signal the author's agreement with the defenders and preface the rejection of his earlier critique of the accreted third step

choices.label: D
choices.text: suggest that the coherence inquiry, although unacknowledged, has been applied in a manner consistent with the 1987 formulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: indicate that the author considers the defenders' position more persuasive than his own and is preparing to abandon his earlier diagnosis

explanations.correct: The phrase is the hinge of a classic concede-then-rebut move. The author grants that no one would wish courts to defer to readings in tension with statutory design, then uses the next two sentences to argue that the original doctrine already handled such readings at step two, so the refinement is not what the defenders claim it is.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The author does not treat the defenders' point as decisive against the original doctrine; he treats it as a concession he will absorb and then turn.
explanations.C: Reverses the passage: the author does not reject his earlier critique; he reinforces it.
explanations.D: The author's rebuttal denies that the third step is consistent with the original formulation.
explanations.E: Out of register — the author's closing 'not sanguine' shows he does not abandon his diagnosis.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the reviewing courts' ability to distinguish judgments of statutory coherence from judgments of policy preference can most accurately be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: confident that the courts possess the requisite capacity and exercise it reliably

choices.label: B
choices.text: guardedly doubtful, implying that the courts are not well positioned to maintain the distinction in the absence of the constraint that ambiguity analysis formerly provided

choices.label: C
choices.text: entirely agnostic, regarding the question as unanswerable on the evidence the passage supplies

choices.label: D
choices.text: dismissive, denying that the distinction itself is coherent

choices.label: E
choices.text: openly contemptuous of the courts' institutional competence in administrative matters generally

explanations.correct: The author writes 'the present author is not sanguine,' and explains that the accreted third step has begun to 'dissolve' the doctrine's discipline by inviting courts to identify statutory design 'without the constraint of ambiguity analysis.' That is guarded doubt tied to a specific structural cause — exactly B.
explanations.A: Reverses the closing sentence.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author reaches a judgment; he is not agnostic.
explanations.D: He does not deny that the distinction is coherent; he doubts that the courts will maintain it in practice.
explanations.E: Out of register — 'not sanguine' is measured, not contemptuous; the author addresses a specific doctrinal context, not the courts' general competence.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following judicial practices, if adopted in another area of law, would most closely conform to the structural development the author identifies in the Caltranan administrative courts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A court reviewing a contract dispute begins to ask, before the conventional inquiry into whether the contract language is ambiguous, whether the proposed construction is consistent with the contract's general commercial design, and rejects constructions that fail that threshold without reaching the ambiguity inquiry.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A court reviewing a criminal sentence applies a deferential standard to the trial court's findings of fact but reviews legal conclusions de novo.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A court hearing a constitutional challenge subjects the challenged statute to a higher standard of review when it implicates a fundamental right than when it does not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A court presiding over a jury trial instructs the jury to disregard evidence that the court has ruled inadmissible under established rules.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A court in a tort action declines to reach the question of damages until it has determined that the defendant is liable.

explanations.correct: The load-bearing structure is the insertion of an unacknowledged threshold inquiry into 'design' or 'scheme' before the conventional ambiguity analysis, which permits the court to reject interpretations without reaching the analysis that by its own logic should precede such rejection. A reproduces that exact structure in the contract-law setting.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Different standards for different issues is orthogonal to the threshold-inquiry mechanism the author is describing.
explanations.C: Tiered scrutiny of statutes is not a hidden threshold; it is an openly applied doctrine selecting the level of review.
explanations.D: Evidentiary rulings are not threshold interpretive inquiries of the kind at issue.
explanations.E: Surface similarity — issue-ordering — but the liability-before-damages order is the conventional sequence that has always been required, not an accreted threshold that displaces an earlier analytic step.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would regard which one of the following hypothetical judicial practices as consistent with the original 1987 doctrine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A chamber finds that the statute at issue is ambiguous, considers the agency's reading, and rejects that reading as unreasonable because it cannot be squared with the statute's design.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A chamber rejects the agency's reading at the threshold on the ground that the reading does not sit comfortably within the statute's ordered scheme.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A chamber defers to the agency's reading without considering whether the statute is ambiguous, on the ground that agencies generally possess greater expertise than courts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A chamber refuses to apply the Two-Step to interpretations of statutes that were enacted before the 1987 decision.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A chamber treats its own prior characterizations of a statute's animating purpose as binding in all future cases interpreting that statute.

explanations.correct: The author writes that under the 1987 formulation, a reading in tension with statutory design would ordinarily fail at step two as unreasonable — precisely what the chamber in A does, by first finding ambiguity and then rejecting the agency's reading as unreasonable on design grounds.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Describes the accreted third step the author is criticizing, not the original doctrine.
explanations.C: Skips the ambiguity analysis altogether and so is not the original doctrine either.
explanations.D: The passage gives no indication that the 1987 doctrine was limited to post-1987 statutes.
explanations.E: The passage says nothing to support binding-precedent status for a chamber's purpose-characterizations across future cases.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of jus cogens — peremptory norms of general international law from which no derogation is permitted — occupies a peculiar and contested position within the architecture of the international legal order. Unlike ordinary treaty obligations, which bind only consenting states and may be modified by subsequent agreement among the parties, jus cogens norms are held to supersede inconsistent treaty provisions and, in the view of many theorists, to invalidate customary international law that conflicts with them. The 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties codified this hierarchy, providing in its Articles 53 and 64 that any treaty conflicting with a peremptory norm is void ab initio, or, in the case of a subsequently emerging norm, void from the moment of that norm's crystallization. Yet the Convention offers no catalogue of which norms qualify as peremptory, and the International Law Commission's efforts over subsequent decades to enumerate them have yielded only a short and contested list — the prohibitions on genocide, slavery, torture, and aggression among states being the least controversial entries.

The conceptual difficulty runs deeper than the absence of an authoritative catalogue. For a norm to achieve peremptory status under the Convention's own criteria, it must be "accepted and recognized by the international community of states as a whole" — a formulation that imports a kind of tacit consent that sits uneasily with the claim that jus cogens norms bind states regardless of their assent. Scholars advancing a natural-law reading argue that the norms' peremptory character derives from their moral content, not from any act of state recognition; on this view, recognition is merely declaratory rather than constitutive. Legal positivists, by contrast, insist that a rule cannot simultaneously depend on state consent for its validity and purport to override that same consent when inconvenient. This tension has never been satisfactorily resolved, and it generates concrete doctrinal instability: domestic courts confronting claims of immunity for heads of state accused of torture must decide whether the jus cogens prohibition on torture has displaced the customary rule of sovereign immunity without any reliable mechanism for determining whether both norms operate at the same hierarchical tier.

Furthermore, the principle of lex specialis — the rule that a more specific legal norm prevails over a more general one in cases of conflict — complicates any straightforward application of jus cogens supremacy. In a series of provisional measures orders issued between 1999 and 2007, an international tribunal declined to treat jus cogens arguments as automatically displacing lex specialis regimes established by regional treaty frameworks, reasoning that the parties had crafted a self-contained regime intended to govern disputes exhaustively within its own terms. Critics of these orders argued that permitting lex specialis to trump jus cogens in procedural contexts effectively circumvents the hierarchy the Vienna Convention was designed to entrench. The tribunal's position was, in this respect, regrettably formalistic: where a peremptory norm is at stake, one ought not to permit the procedural architecture of a specialized regime to insulate state conduct from scrutiny under the broadest obligations the international community has chosen to recognize.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Vienna Convention's codification of jus cogens norms has rendered the international legal order more hierarchical than it was before 1969.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The doctrine of jus cogens, though codified in international treaty law, remains conceptually unstable and practically difficult to apply because of unresolved tensions involving consent, hierarchy, and competing legal principles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Legal positivists have identified a fatal internal contradiction in the Vienna Convention's account of jus cogens that renders the entire doctrine invalid.

choices.label: D
choices.text: International tribunals have consistently refused to apply jus cogens norms whenever lex specialis regimes are operative, thereby undermining the Vienna Convention.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The absence of an authoritative catalogue of peremptory norms is the primary obstacle to effective enforcement of jus cogens in domestic courts.

explanations.correct: The passage identifies three converging difficulties — the lack of a catalogue, the consent paradox debated by naturalists and positivists, and the lex specialis complication — and culminates in an editorial critique of the tribunal's formalism. B integrates all three strands into a thesis about conceptual instability and practical difficulty.
explanations.A: Too narrow and overstated: the passage does not claim the Convention succeeded in creating a cleaner hierarchy; indeed, it documents the hierarchy's fragility.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Overstates the positivist position: the passage says positivists have identified a tension they regard as unresolved, not that they have declared the doctrine invalid.
explanations.D: Misrepresents scope: the passage describes a specific series of tribunal orders, not a consistent pattern of refusal across all tribunals.
explanations.E: Too narrow: the absence of a catalogue is identified in paragraph one as one problem among several; the passage's larger concern is the deeper conceptual contradiction and the lex specialis conflict.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the international tribunal's provisional measures orders discussed in the third paragraph can best be described as which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Measured approval, on the ground that regional treaty frameworks deserve deference when their drafters intended them to be self-contained.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Principled neutrality, since the author presents the tribunal's reasoning and its critics' objections without endorsing either.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Qualified disapproval, tempered by acknowledgment that the tribunal's position has some procedural merit in ordinary non-peremptory contexts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Outright condemnation, on the ground that the tribunal acted in deliberate bad faith toward the international community's established legal hierarchy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Critical disapproval expressed through editorial language, on the ground that procedural formalism should not insulate state conduct from scrutiny under peremptory norms.

explanations.correct: The author uses the editorial adverb 'regrettably' and issues a normative prescription ('one ought not to permit') in the final sentence of paragraph three, signaling clear disapproval grounded in the argument that procedural architecture should not trump peremptory norms.
explanations.A: Reverses the author's position: the author sides with the critics, not the tribunal.
explanations.B: Incorrect: the closing sentence is openly prescriptive — 'one ought not to permit' — so the author does take a side.
explanations.C: Partially plausible but wrong: the passage offers no qualification that the tribunal's approach might be acceptable in other contexts; the disapproval is unqualified within its stated scope.
explanations.D: Overstates intensity: 'regrettably formalistic' implies error, not bad faith; 'condemnation' and 'deliberate bad faith' exceed the author's register.
explanations.E: Correct.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its codification described; the absence of a definitive enumeration of the doctrine's content is identified as its central weakness; and a solution proposed by international tribunals is evaluated and endorsed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its codified form described; an underlying conceptual tension in the doctrine is identified and two competing theoretical accounts of it are presented; and a further complication arising from a competing legal principle is described and critically assessed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A dispute between natural-law theorists and legal positivists is introduced; the historical origins of the dispute are traced through treaty law; and a series of tribunal rulings is cited as having resolved the dispute in favor of the positivist position.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Vienna Convention's provisions are summarized; the author argues that these provisions are fundamentally incoherent; and an alternative framework grounded in natural law is proposed and defended.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined; its practical application in domestic courts is illustrated with a series of cases; and the passage concludes by calling for legislative reform to address identified inconsistencies.

explanations.correct: Paragraph one introduces jus cogens, describes its codification in the Vienna Convention, and notes the absence of an authoritative catalogue. Paragraph two identifies the deeper conceptual tension between consent-based validity and peremptory override, presenting the natural-law and positivist accounts. Paragraph three introduces the lex specialis complication via the tribunal orders and closes with the author's critical assessment. B tracks these three moves accurately.
explanations.A: Incorrect at the third step: the tribunal's position is criticized, not endorsed.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Misrepresents the passage's opening: paragraph one does not begin with the naturalist-positivist dispute; that appears in paragraph two. The tribunal orders do not resolve that dispute.
explanations.D: The author does not propose an alternative natural-law framework; the natural-law reading is mentioned as one theoretical account among two.
explanations.E: The passage includes one domestic-court example (sovereign immunity), but this is not 'a series of cases'; the passage does not call for legislative reform.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Articles 53 and 64 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties provide that a treaty conflicting with a jus cogens norm that arose after the treaty's conclusion is:

choices.label: A
choices.text: void ab initio, as though it had never been entered into.

choices.label: B
choices.text: void only if the parties to the treaty have expressly consented to subordination of their obligations to any subsequently emerging peremptory norm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: void from the moment the peremptory norm in question crystallized, rather than from the treaty's original conclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: suspended but not voided, pending a determination by the International Law Commission as to whether the norm qualifies as peremptory.

choices.label: E
choices.text: subject to modification by the treaty parties so as to bring it into conformity with the emerging peremptory norm.

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that a treaty conflicting with a subsequently emerging jus cogens norm is 'void from the moment of that norm's crystallization,' distinguishing this from the void ab initio rule that applies to treaties conflicting with pre-existing peremptory norms.
explanations.A: This describes the rule for treaties that conflicted with a jus cogens norm already in existence at the time of conclusion — not for subsequently emerging norms. The altered-qualifier trap.
explanations.B: The passage never mentions a consent-based exception for subsequent norms; this is invented.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No such suspension mechanism is mentioned in the passage; this is a plausible-world-fact trap.
explanations.E: The passage describes the consequence as voidness, not modification; this alters the key legal effect.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that a legal positivist would regard which one of the following as a fundamental defect in the Vienna Convention's formulation of jus cogens?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Convention fails to enumerate a comprehensive list of peremptory norms, leaving states uncertain about the content of their obligations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Convention's requirement of state recognition simultaneously grounds the validity of jus cogens norms in consent and claims that those norms override consent, producing an internal contradiction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Convention inadequately addresses the relationship between jus cogens norms and lex specialis regimes established by regional treaties.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Convention adopts a natural-law methodology that is incompatible with the positivist foundations on which modern treaty law rests.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Convention's provisions on jus cogens were drafted without the participation of a sufficient number of states to constitute acceptance by the international community as a whole.

explanations.correct: The passage states that positivists 'insist that a rule cannot simultaneously depend on state consent for its validity and purport to override that same consent when inconvenient.' B is a precise paraphrase of this objection, which the passage attributes specifically to the positivist camp.
explanations.A: The passage identifies the lack of an authoritative catalogue as a problem, but does not attribute this concern specifically to positivists — it is a more general institutional observation.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The lex specialis complication is introduced in paragraph three as a separate doctrinal problem, not as the positivist objection. The passage does not attribute this concern to positivists.
explanations.D: This inverts the positivist critique: positivists are not objecting that the Convention is too positivist; they are objecting that the Convention's consent requirement is inconsistent with its peremptory-override claim.
explanations.E: No such drafting-participation claim appears in the passage; this is an outside-scope trap.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to domestic courts confronting immunity claims by heads of state accused of torture (second paragraph) serves primarily to:

choices.label: A
choices.text: introduce a separate legal problem concerning the scope of sovereign immunity that the remainder of the passage addresses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate that natural-law theorists are more successful than legal positivists in resolving actual cases involving peremptory norms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate the concrete doctrinal instability that results from the unresolved theoretical tension between consent-based validity and peremptory override.

choices.label: D
choices.text: provide a counterexample to the claim that jus cogens norms have any practical effect in domestic legal systems.

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that torture should be recognized as a jus cogens norm by all domestic courts, regardless of their national legal traditions.

explanations.correct: The reference appears immediately after the author states that the theoretical tension between consent and peremptory override 'generates concrete doctrinal instability.' The immunity example is introduced as an illustration of that instability — specifically, the problem of determining whether two norms operate at the same hierarchical tier. C captures this rhetorical function.
explanations.A: Sovereign immunity is not addressed again in the remainder of the passage; it is a brief illustrative reference, not an introduction to a new topic.
explanations.B: The passage does not say which theoretical account is more successful in actual cases; it says the tension 'has never been satisfactorily resolved.'
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The reference does not serve as a counterexample to jus cogens' practical effect; it illustrates the difficulty of applying it, not its ineffectiveness.
explanations.E: The passage makes no such prescriptive argument about domestic courts and torture; this overstates and misdirects the reference's purpose.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the critics' objection — described in the third paragraph — that the tribunal's reliance on lex specialis effectively circumvents the hierarchy established by the Vienna Convention?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The regional treaty frameworks at issue were drafted with explicit provisions acknowledging that obligations under the Vienna Convention's jus cogens articles would remain operative and could not be displaced by the regional regime.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several of the states party to the regional treaty frameworks had also ratified the Vienna Convention and were subject to both instruments simultaneously.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The International Law Commission's list of recognized peremptory norms was not expanded during the period covered by the tribunal's provisional measures orders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The procedural rulings issued under the lex specialis regime had no bearing on whether the underlying substantive conduct at issue violated the prohibition on genocide.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tribunals operating under different regional frameworks had reached the opposite conclusion and applied jus cogens norms over lex specialis objections during the same period.

explanations.correct: The critics' objection is that using lex specialis in procedural contexts 'effectively circumvents' jus cogens — that is, procedural formalism insulates state conduct from scrutiny under peremptory norms. If the procedural rulings had no bearing on the underlying substantive jus cogens question (genocide), then no circumvention actually occurred: the hierarchy was not compromised because the substantive peremptory norm remained fully available for scrutiny on the merits. This directly undermines the critics' claim.
explanations.A: This would strengthen the critics' objection, not undermine it: if the regional regime expressly preserved jus cogens obligations yet the tribunal still applied lex specialis to displace scrutiny, the circumvention would be more, not less, egregious.
explanations.B: Dual ratification is consistent with the critics' complaint; it does not address whether the lex specialis ruling actually insulated conduct from jus cogens scrutiny.
explanations.C: The ILC's enumeration activity is irrelevant to whether the tribunal's procedural approach circumvented the Convention's hierarchy; this is an off-target claim.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Contrary practice by other tribunals would weaken the precedential force of the orders described but would not address whether those specific orders actually circumvented jus cogens — it is an outside-scope claim that bears on consistency, not on the logical force of the critics' circumvention argument.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of jus cogens — those peremptory norms of international law from which no derogation is permitted, even by treaty — has long occupied an uneasy position at the intersection of customary international law and the voluntary consent-based framework that underlies the international legal order. Unlike ordinary customary norms, which may be displaced by subsequent treaty arrangements between consenting states, jus cogens norms are held to be hierarchically superior: a treaty provision that conflicts with such a norm is void ab initio, regardless of the parties' expressed intentions. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, concluded in 1969, gave formal textual recognition to this hierarchy, yet it conspicuously declined to enumerate which norms had attained peremptory status, leaving that determination to state practice, opinio juris, and — increasingly — the pronouncements of international tribunals.

The indeterminacy inherent in this arrangement has generated persistent doctrinal controversy. Proponents of a robust jus cogens catalogue argue that the norms against genocide, torture, and slavery have so thoroughly permeated domestic and international legal systems that their peremptory character is beyond serious dispute; on this view, the very universality of their prohibition is itself the marker of their elevated status. Critics, however, contend that treating any norm as non-derogable risks calcifying international law at a particular historical moment, preventing the adaptive evolution that gives the international legal order its resilience. This tension is further complicated by the emergence of lex specialis principles: where a specialized treaty regime purports to displace a general norm within a defined domain — as when certain humanitarian law conventions specify permissible conduct in armed conflict that might otherwise appear to violate general prohibitions — courts must determine whether the specialized norm merely elaborates, or actually displaces, the background peremptory standard. Regrettably, international tribunals have not applied a consistent methodology in making this determination.

A further difficulty arises from the interaction of jus cogens with the domestic law of sovereign states. Where a state's constitutional order grants international treaty obligations the force of domestic law, a finding that a given treaty is void under jus cogens creates a legal lacuna: the treaty obligation cannot be enforced domestically, yet the constitutional provision that would have incorporated it remains operative. National courts in several civil-law jurisdictions — confronting precisely this predicament following the invalidation of certain bilateral investment agreements in 2017 — responded by applying residual common-law analogues to fill the gap, a solution that raises its own concerns about the legitimacy of judicial gap-filling in a domain traditionally reserved for state negotiation. One hopes that the International Law Commission's ongoing codification project will supply the clearer hierarchical rules that tribunals and domestic courts alike have long required, though the Commission's past practice of cataloguing rather than adjudicating contested norms suggests that definitive resolution may remain elusive.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Vienna Convention's failure to enumerate peremptory norms has rendered jus cogens an unworkable concept that international tribunals should abandon in favor of ordinary customary law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The doctrine of jus cogens, though formally recognized in international law, is beset by unresolved difficulties of identification, application, and interaction with domestic legal orders, leaving courts without reliable guidance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The conflict between jus cogens norms and lex specialis principles represents the central crisis in contemporary international law and demands an urgent legislative response.

choices.label: D
choices.text: National courts have generally handled jus cogens conflicts more satisfactorily than international tribunals because domestic constitutional frameworks supply clearer hierarchical rules.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The International Law Commission's codification project offers the most promising avenue for resolving the longstanding controversies surrounding peremptory norms in international law.

explanations.correct: The passage traces three distinct layers of difficulty with jus cogens — its indeterminate identification (paragraph 1–2), its conflict with lex specialis (paragraph 2), and its disruptive interaction with domestic constitutional orders (paragraph 3) — and closes by doubting whether any resolution is imminent. B integrates all three strands without overstating or narrowing.
explanations.A: Too strong and wrong in direction — the author does not recommend abandoning jus cogens, only notes the difficulties it generates.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too narrow — the lex specialis tension is one of several difficulties; the passage does not identify it as 'the central crisis' or call urgently for legislation.
explanations.D: Contradicted by the passage, which criticizes domestic courts' gap-filling as raising 'its own concerns about legitimacy.'
explanations.E: This restates only the closing suggestion, which the author immediately qualifies with skepticism — a classic 'restates a suggestion as the main point' trap.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined and its formal recognition described; two opposing theoretical positions on the doctrine's scope are presented; the doctrine's disruptive effect on domestic legal orders is examined; and a tentative remedy is proposed and immediately qualified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined; a historical controversy over its origins is traced; the doctrine's recent rejection by international tribunals is documented; and alternative frameworks are evaluated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An international legal principle is introduced; its consistent application across multiple jurisdictions is surveyed; a single anomalous case is examined; and the principle's overall effectiveness is affirmed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A doctrinal tension is identified; the positions of proponents and critics are compared; an illustrative case study from domestic courts is introduced; and the doctrine is ultimately endorsed as coherent despite its difficulties.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A definition of a legal norm is offered; the norm's interaction with domestic constitutional law is traced historically; international tribunals' responses are catalogued; and a legislative reform is recommended.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 defines jus cogens and notes its formal recognition via the Vienna Convention. Paragraph 2 presents the proponent/critic debate and introduces the lex specialis complication. Paragraph 3 examines disruption to domestic legal orders via the 2017 investment agreement example. The final sentence proposes the ILC remedy while qualifying its likely efficacy. A tracks all four moves accurately.
explanations.B: Mis-describes the second paragraph as tracing 'origins controversy' and the third as 'rejection by tribunals' — neither is accurate.
explanations.C: Claims 'consistent application' and 'effectiveness affirmed,' both contradicted by the passage's critical thrust.
explanations.D: Claims the doctrine is 'ultimately endorsed as coherent' — the author reaches no such conclusion; the closing is skeptical.
explanations.E: Describes a historical trace and a legislative recommendation, neither of which the passage performs; the ILC project is mentioned as an uncertain hope, not a recommendation.
explanations.A: Correct.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, what feature distinguishes jus cogens norms from ordinary norms of customary international law?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jus cogens norms are codified in a comprehensive enumerated list maintained by the International Law Commission.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jus cogens norms may be displaced by subsequent treaties concluded between consenting states, while ordinary customary norms may not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jus cogens norms are hierarchically superior and cannot be derogated from even by treaty, whereas ordinary customary norms may be displaced by such agreements.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jus cogens norms derive their authority exclusively from the consent of sovereign states, unlike ordinary customary norms, which arise from state practice alone.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Jus cogens norms are enforced directly by domestic courts, while ordinary customary norms are enforceable only through international tribunals.

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly: 'Unlike ordinary customary norms, which may be displaced by subsequent treaty arrangements between consenting states, jus cogens norms are held to be hierarchically superior.' C paraphrases this distinction accurately.
explanations.A: Contradicted by the passage, which notes the Vienna Convention 'conspicuously declined to enumerate' such norms.
explanations.B: This inverts the distinction described in the passage.
explanations.D: Reverses the consent-based logic — the passage describes ordinary customary law as operating within the 'voluntary consent-based framework,' not jus cogens.
explanations.E: The passage makes no such jurisdictional claim about enforcement mechanisms.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about international tribunals' treatment of lex specialis questions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: International tribunals have uniformly held that specialized treaty regimes may never displace a background peremptory norm, regardless of the parties' intentions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The absence of a consistent methodology for resolving lex specialis conflicts against jus cogens norms represents a significant deficiency in international legal practice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: International tribunals are well positioned to resolve lex specialis conflicts because they can draw on a rich body of consistent domestic court precedent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lex specialis principles were developed primarily to expand the reach of jus cogens norms into specialized treaty domains.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The conflict between lex specialis and jus cogens arises only in domestic courts and is beyond the jurisdictional competence of international tribunals.

explanations.correct: The author states 'Regrettably, international tribunals have not applied a consistent methodology' for determining whether lex specialis displaces or merely elaborates peremptory norms. The adverb 'regrettably' signals authorial disapproval, supporting the inference that this inconsistency is a deficiency in the author's view.
explanations.A: Contradicted by the passage, which notes courts must determine whether specialized norms 'merely elaborate, or actually displace' the peremptory standard — implying displacement is at least possible.
explanations.C: The passage criticizes domestic courts' gap-filling as raising legitimacy concerns, providing no basis for this optimistic inference.
explanations.D: Inverts the passage's account; lex specialis is presented as potentially limiting, not expanding, peremptory norms.
explanations.E: The passage describes both international tribunals and domestic courts as confronting this conflict — this claim is not supported.
explanations.B: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to national courts applying 'residual common-law analogues' following the 2017 invalidation of bilateral investment agreements serves primarily to:

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate that domestic courts possess superior interpretive tools for resolving jus cogens conflicts compared to international tribunals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide a concrete example of the legal lacuna that arises when a jus cogens finding voids a treaty, and to introduce the additional legitimacy concern generated by judicial gap-filling in that context.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that civil-law jurisdictions have historically been more receptive to jus cogens doctrine than common-law jurisdictions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: argue that common-law analogues should be formally adopted as a standard remedy whenever a treaty is voided under international peremptory norms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: rebut the critics' concern that treating norms as non-derogable calcifies international law, by showing that domestic courts can adapt the law flexibly.

explanations.correct: The reference to common-law gap-filling appears immediately after the passage introduces the 'legal lacuna' problem, and the author's next clause — 'a solution that raises its own concerns about the legitimacy of judicial gap-filling' — signals that the example serves both to instantiate the lacuna and to introduce a further difficulty. B captures this dual function.
explanations.A: The passage does not praise domestic courts; it identifies the legitimacy concerns their solution generates — this is an 'accurate content, wrong function' trap.
explanations.C: The passage describes civil-law courts using common-law analogues, but the point is about legitimacy of gap-filling, not a historical comparison of legal traditions' receptiveness to jus cogens.
explanations.D: The author does not endorse common-law analogues as a standard remedy; the passage treats their use as a concern.
explanations.E: The example introduces a new problem, not a rebuttal of the critics' position about calcification.
explanations.B: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the International Law Commission's ongoing codification project can best be described as:

choices.label: A
choices.text: confident endorsement, on the grounds that the Commission's historical practice demonstrates its capacity to resolve contested legal norms definitively.

choices.label: B
choices.text: emphatic rejection, because the Commission has no legitimate authority to pronounce upon the content of peremptory norms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: cautious optimism tempered by skepticism, given the Commission's past tendency to catalogue rather than adjudicate contested norms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutral acknowledgment, treating the Commission's project as merely one of several equally viable institutional responses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: muted enthusiasm, based on the Commission's successful enumeration of jus cogens norms in prior codification exercises.

explanations.correct: The author expresses hope for the ILC project ('one hopes') while immediately noting that 'the Commission's past practice of cataloguing rather than adjudicating contested norms suggests that definitive resolution may remain elusive.' This combination of hope and qualified skepticism matches C precisely.
explanations.A: The phrase 'confident endorsement' overstates the author's hedged expression of hope; moreover, the author notes the Commission's past practice as a reason for doubt, not confidence.
explanations.B: The author never questions the Commission's authority — this is an 'overstated negativity' trap.
explanations.D: The passage does not compare the Commission to 'several equally viable' alternatives; characterizing the author's attitude as merely 'neutral' misses the hopeful-but-skeptical tone.
explanations.E: The author does not mention prior successful enumeration — in fact, the passage notes the Vienna Convention declined to enumerate norms, which is one source of the difficulty.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the critics' position as described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several states have recently concluded treaties that explicitly derogate from customary norms previously thought to be universally accepted, producing no adverse diplomatic consequences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Historical analysis of international legal practice reveals that those norms classified as peremptory have not remained static but have gradually expanded in response to evolving global consensus, without preventing the development of new treaty regimes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: International tribunals have increasingly cited the absence of an enumerated jus cogens list as a justification for declining jurisdiction over treaty-conflict cases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Domestic courts in common-law jurisdictions have consistently refused to apply jus cogens doctrine, preferring to resolve treaty conflicts through ordinary constitutional interpretation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Vienna Convention's drafting history reveals that its framers anticipated that the list of peremptory norms would remain permanently fixed at the norms recognized in 1969.

explanations.correct: The critics argue that treating norms as non-derogable 'risks calcifying international law at a particular historical moment, preventing the adaptive evolution that gives the international legal order its resilience.' B directly undercuts this by showing that jus cogens norms have in fact evolved over time and have not prevented new treaty development — i.e., the feared calcification has not materialized.
explanations.A: This would support the critics' concern about the fragility of non-derogable norms, not undermine it.
explanations.C: This is an additional problem with the indeterminacy of jus cogens but does not bear on the critics' specific calcification argument.
explanations.D: This concerns domestic courts' behavior and does not address whether peremptory norms calcify international law.
explanations.E: This would support the critics' concern about calcification by suggesting the framers intended exactly the historical freezing the critics fear — it would strengthen, not undermine, their position.
explanations.B: Correct.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of jus cogens — those peremptory norms of international law from which no derogation is permitted — occupies an uneasy position within the architecture of the international legal order. Unlike ordinary treaty obligations, which bind only the states that have consented to them, jus cogens norms are understood to bind all states regardless of consent, a proposition that sits in evident tension with the sovereignty-based foundations upon which the modern state system has rested since the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. For this reason, international tribunals and legal theorists have long debated not merely which norms qualify as peremptory but whether the category is coherent at all, given that the voluntarist tradition insists that international law can derive its force only from the free agreement of sovereign states.

The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, concluded in 1969, gave jus cogens its first formal textual recognition, declaring that any treaty conflicting with a peremptory norm is void ab initio. The Convention, however, did not enumerate which norms rise to this status; it left that determination to the international community, by which it meant, in practice, the jurisprudence of international courts and the writings of publicists. This legislative restraint was deliberate: the drafters feared that any fixed list would calcify prematurely, excluding emerging norms whose claim to peremptory status might be compelling. Yet the very openness of the criteria has generated its own difficulties. States and tribunals have asserted peremptory status for an ever-expanding catalog of norms — ranging from the prohibition of torture and the prohibition of aggression to certain rules of humanitarian law and even, in some scholarly arguments, the principle of permanent sovereignty over natural resources — without offering a principled account of the threshold separating jus cogens from merely ius dispositivum, the ordinary, derogable rules of international law.

The problem is compounded by the relationship between jus cogens and customary international law. Both arise outside the treaty framework; both claim universality. Yet customary international law is, in the traditional account, formed by the convergent practice of states accompanied by opinio juris — the belief that the practice is legally required — and it can be modified by subsequent contrary practice. Jus cogens, by contrast, cannot be modified except by a later norm of the same character. This asymmetry creates a difficult interpretive question: when a state's conduct appears to challenge what one tribunal has treated as a peremptory norm, is that conduct evidence of persistent objection that might erode the norm (as would be possible under ordinary custom) or evidence of a violation of a higher-order rule that no amount of state practice can dislodge? The International Court of Justice has, in several advisory opinions issued since 1970, acknowledged this tension without fully resolving it, preferring cautious formulations that neither entrench a comprehensive catalogue nor foreclose future development.

This judicial reticence is defensible as a matter of institutional prudence, but it exacts a cost. Litigants invoking jus cogens before domestic courts — as occurs with increasing frequency under universal jurisdiction statutes — encounter sovereign immunity defenses that many domestic tribunals are reluctant to pierce, even where the alleged conduct would constitute a clear violation of a candidate peremptory norm. A more forthright judicial elaboration of the criteria for peremptory status, even at the risk of some doctrinal rigidity, would likely produce more consistent outcomes for claimants and would reinforce, rather than undermine, the legitimacy of the norms themselves. One hopes that the International Court of Justice, in adjudicating the wave of cases implicating state responsibility for mass atrocities that has reached its docket in recent years, will supply the conceptual structure that the Vienna Convention's drafters were unwilling to provide.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties failed to define jus cogens with sufficient precision, and this failure has allowed states to invoke the doctrine to invalidate inconvenient treaty obligations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The doctrine of jus cogens is theoretically incoherent because it cannot be reconciled with the voluntarist foundations of international law and should therefore be abandoned.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The undefined boundaries of jus cogens, combined with courts' reluctance to elaborate the doctrine, produce inconsistent legal outcomes, and a more rigorous judicial articulation of peremptory norms is needed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: International courts have consistently expanded the catalogue of jus cogens norms in ways that undermine state sovereignty and destabilize customary international law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The distinction between jus cogens and customary international law is illusory, since both categories claim universality and neither can be modified by ordinary state practice.

explanations.correct: The passage traces the theoretical tension around jus cogens (¶1), the indeterminacy left by the Vienna Convention (¶2), the unresolved relationship with customary law (¶3), and culminates in the author's prescription that courts should more forthrightly elaborate peremptory criteria (¶4). C captures this arc — indeterminate doctrine + judicial reticence → inconsistent outcomes → call for clearer articulation.
explanations.A: Too narrow; the passage's concern is not that states exploit the doctrine to void treaties but rather that the lack of criteria creates systemic inconsistency across tribunals and domestic courts.
explanations.B: The author does not call for abandoning jus cogens; this choice overstates the voluntarist critique as the author's own view rather than a theoretical challenge the author acknowledges.
explanations.D: The passage says courts have been cautious and reticent, not that they have systematically expanded the catalogue; this choice inverts the passage's characterization of judicial behavior.
explanations.E: The author distinguishes the two doctrines (modifiability is the key asymmetry) rather than collapsing them; this choice misrepresents the argument of ¶3.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the International Court of Justice's handling of jus cogens doctrine can best be described as which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Unqualified admiration for the Court's restraint in avoiding premature doctrinal commitments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sympathetic understanding of the Court's caution, tempered by regret that its reticence imposes practical costs on litigants.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Outright condemnation of the Court for its deliberate evasion of a difficult but tractable legal question.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Skepticism that the Court possesses the institutional competence necessary to elaborate a coherent doctrine of peremptory norms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Approval of the Court's advisory opinions as models of careful jurisprudential reasoning under conditions of doctrinal uncertainty.

explanations.correct: The author concedes that 'judicial reticence is defensible as a matter of institutional prudence' (acknowledging the Court's position) but immediately notes it 'exacts a cost' (practical harm to litigants), and closes with 'one hopes' that the Court will supply the needed structure — a tone of measured disappointment rather than wholesale condemnation or admiration.
explanations.A: The author explicitly qualifies approval with a 'but it exacts a cost' — unqualified admiration is contradicted by the passage's fourth paragraph.
explanations.C: 'Outright condemnation' overstates the author's tone; the author accepts that caution is institutionally defensible and uses guarded hope rather than accusatory language.
explanations.D: The author expresses no doubt about the Court's competence; the prescription 'one hopes' implies the author believes the Court is capable of the task.
explanations.E: The author describes the ICJ's formulations as 'cautious' and says they neither 'entrench a comprehensive catalogue nor foreclose future development,' which is a neutral-to-critical observation, not approval of the opinions as models.
explanations.B: Correct.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A foundational theoretical tension is introduced; a landmark legal instrument that addressed but did not resolve the tension is examined; an additional complication arising from the relationship between two legal doctrines is analyzed; and a prescription for resolving the resulting practical problem is offered.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined; its historical origins are traced from antiquity to the present; a series of failed attempts by international courts to apply it are described; and an alternative approach drawn from domestic law is proposed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A controversial scholarly argument is introduced; evidence for and against it is presented from treaty law and customary law; the argument is ultimately rejected; and a less controversial replacement principle is endorsed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two competing conceptions of international legal obligation are contrasted; their respective advantages and disadvantages are weighed; one is endorsed as theoretically superior; and the other is identified as the source of a contemporary legal problem.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A legal doctrine's practical applications are surveyed; a problem of inconsistent judicial interpretation is identified; the historical causes of that inconsistency are traced; and a procedural reform to correct the inconsistency is recommended.

explanations.correct: ¶1 presents the foundational tension (jus cogens vs. voluntarist sovereignty); ¶2 examines the Vienna Convention's contribution and residual indeterminacy; ¶3 analyzes the complication arising from the relationship between jus cogens and customary law; ¶4 argues that judicial reticence has practical costs and prescribes more forthright elaboration.
explanations.B: The passage does not trace historical origins from antiquity, and no 'alternative approach drawn from domestic law' is proposed — the prescription calls for the ICJ to act, not for importing a domestic-law solution.
explanations.C: No single 'controversial scholarly argument' is introduced and then rejected; the passage is a structural analysis of doctrinal difficulties, not a rebuttal of a specific scholarly thesis.
explanations.D: The passage does not weigh two conceptions and endorse one; both jus cogens and customary law are presented as coexisting but imperfectly reconciled elements of the same system.
explanations.E: The historical causes traced in the passage are doctrinal, not 'causes of inconsistent interpretation' in the procedural sense; furthermore, no 'procedural reform' is recommended — the prescription concerns substantive doctrinal elaboration.
explanations.A: Correct.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the drafters of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties deliberately refrained from enumerating specific jus cogens norms primarily because they

choices.label: A
choices.text: could not reach consensus on which norms had achieved sufficient state practice to qualify as customary international law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: wished to preserve state sovereignty by ensuring that individual states retained the right to object to proposed peremptory norms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: feared that enumerating norms would freeze the category too early and might exclude later norms with a strong claim to peremptory status.

choices.label: D
choices.text: believed that the International Court of Justice was better positioned to compile such a list through its advisory jurisdiction.

choices.label: E
choices.text: anticipated that state practice would eventually generate a widely accepted catalogue of norms without any formal legal specification.

explanations.correct: The passage states directly: 'the drafters feared that any fixed list would calcify prematurely, excluding emerging norms whose claim to peremptory status might be compelling.' C is a close paraphrase of this.
explanations.A: The passage does not mention a failure to reach consensus on customary-law thresholds; the concern was about premature calcification, not drafting disagreement.
explanations.B: The passage nowhere attributes the drafters' restraint to a desire to protect state sovereignty; the voluntarist objection is the author's framing of the theoretical tension, not the drafters' motivation.
explanations.D: The passage says the determination was left to 'the jurisprudence of international courts and the writings of publicists,' but it does not specifically say the drafters believed the ICJ's advisory jurisdiction was better suited — this is an inference the passage does not support.
explanations.E: The passage does not suggest the drafters expected state practice alone to produce a catalogue; the open criteria were a deliberate choice to allow organic development, but no such specific expectation is attributed to the drafters.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that which one of the following is true of customary international law, as the author understands it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cannot bind states that have persistently objected to a given norm during the period of its formation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is inferior to treaty law in normative rank because it lacks the explicit consent of the states it purports to bind.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It may be altered over time by subsequent contrary state practice, whereas jus cogens norms may not be so altered.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It arises exclusively from the decisions of international courts and the scholarly writings of publicists.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is rendered obsolete wherever a treaty norm addressing the same subject matter has entered into force.

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly states that customary international law 'can be modified by subsequent contrary practice,' whereas jus cogens 'cannot be modified except by a later norm of the same character.' C directly follows from this contrast.
explanations.A: The passage mentions 'persistent objection' as a possibility that could erode ordinary custom, but it does not affirmatively state the rule that persistent objectors are not bound — this is an inference beyond what the passage directly supports.
explanations.B: The passage does not establish any normative hierarchy between customary law and treaty law; the hierarchy discussed is between jus cogens and ius dispositivum (ordinary rules, which include both treaties and custom).
explanations.D: The passage says customary international law is 'formed by the convergent practice of states accompanied by opinio juris' — state practice and belief, not court decisions or scholarly writings, which are instead cited as the source for identifying jus cogens norms.
explanations.E: The passage makes no claim that treaty law displaces customary law on the same subject; the lex specialis principle is not discussed.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to universal jurisdiction statutes in the fourth paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate a specific domestic-law mechanism through which the practical consequences of judicial reticence about jus cogens most acutely affect individual litigants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that domestic courts, rather than international tribunals, are better suited to resolve disputes implicating peremptory norms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that the expansion of universal jurisdiction has itself caused the indeterminacy in the jus cogens catalogue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast the robust enforcement mechanisms available in domestic law with the weaker remedial capacity of international courts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: provide a historical example of how state practice under universal jurisdiction statutes has contributed to the formation of customary international law.

explanations.correct: The reference to universal jurisdiction statutes appears immediately after the author states that judicial reticence 'exacts a cost,' and it specifies the setting where that cost is most visible: litigants in domestic courts invoking jus cogens face sovereign immunity defenses. The reference concretizes the abstract harm described in the preceding sentence.
explanations.B: The author does not argue domestic courts are better suited than international tribunals; if anything, the prescription is for the ICJ to supply the conceptual structure that would help domestic courts apply the doctrine consistently.
explanations.C: The passage does not suggest that universal jurisdiction statutes caused the indeterminacy; the indeterminacy stems from the Vienna Convention's drafting choice and the absence of judicial elaboration.
explanations.D: No contrast between domestic and international remedial capacity is drawn; the point is that domestic courts face a specific obstacle (sovereign immunity) that results from the lack of clear doctrinal elaboration.
explanations.E: No historical narrative about universal jurisdiction and customary law formation is offered; the reference is functional, not historical.
explanations.A: Correct.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that a more forthright judicial articulation of jus cogens criteria would produce more consistent outcomes for claimants invoking peremptory norms before domestic courts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several states that are parties to the Vienna Convention have enacted domestic legislation explicitly incorporating the jus cogens provisions of that treaty into their national legal systems.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sovereign immunity defenses that domestic courts apply in jus cogens cases are grounded in statutes that domestic courts lack authority to override regardless of how clearly a peremptory norm has been judicially defined.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The International Court of Justice has in recent years accepted jurisdiction over a significant number of cases involving alleged state responsibility for mass atrocities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Legal scholars disagree substantially about whether any norm beyond the prohibition of genocide has achieved the threshold of universal acceptance necessary for peremptory status.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Domestic courts in states with monist legal systems have been more willing than those in dualist systems to apply jus cogens norms directly without requiring domestic implementing legislation.

explanations.correct: The author argues that clearer judicial articulation of jus cogens would help litigants in domestic courts by enabling those courts to pierce sovereign immunity defenses more readily. If, however, sovereign immunity is grounded in statutory law that domestic courts cannot override regardless of doctrinal clarity, then clearer ICJ articulation would not produce the consistent outcomes the author envisions. B directly cuts the causal link between the proposed remedy and the claimed benefit.
explanations.A: Domestic legislation incorporating Vienna Convention provisions would tend to support, not undermine, the author's prescription; it suggests domestic implementation of international law norms is feasible.
explanations.C: The ICJ's acceptance of more cases is consistent with the author's hope and neither strengthens nor weakens the specific causal claim about domestic-court outcomes.
explanations.D: Scholarly disagreement about the threshold for peremptory status is evidence of the doctrinal uncertainty the author already acknowledges, but it does not directly address whether clearer judicial articulation would improve domestic-court outcomes — it bears on whether such articulation is possible, not whether it would be effective.
explanations.E: The difference between monist and dualist systems is an additional variable but does not undermine the author's causal claim; the author's prescription would still improve outcomes in monist systems even if dualist systems remained resistant.
explanations.B: Correct.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of jus cogens — peremptory norms from which no derogation is permitted under international law — occupies an unresolved position at the intersection of customary international law and treaty regimes. Unlike ordinary customary norms, which may be displaced by subsequent treaty obligations between consenting states, a jus cogens norm is, in the language of the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, one "accepted and recognized by the international community of states as a whole as a norm from which no derogation is permitted." The Convention further provides that any treaty conflicting with such a norm is void ab initio. Yet the Convention does not identify which specific norms qualify for this status, leaving that determination to a process whose doctrinal foundations remain deeply contested.

The principal difficulty is one of circular validation. A jus cogens norm is said to derive its peremptory character from the acceptance of the international community as a whole, but the machinery for registering that acceptance — decisions of international tribunals, state practice, opinio juris — is the same machinery used to establish ordinary customary norms. Critics, drawing on legal-positivist premises, have argued that this circularity renders jus cogens analytically indistinguishable from elevated custom: if a norm achieves peremptory status through the same evidentiary process as ordinary custom, no meaningful hierarchy exists between them. Defenders of the doctrine respond that the threshold is qualitatively, not merely quantitatively, different — that peremptory norms reflect a near-universal moral consensus so fundamental that no bilateral agreement ought to be capable of abrogating them. The International Court of Justice, in its 1998 advisory opinion on reservations to the Convention Against Torture, appeared to endorse the defenders' position, characterizing jus cogens norms as obligations erga omnes whose binding force is independent of reciprocity. However, the Court offered no satisfactory account of why the same consensual validation process should yield two categorically distinct classes of norm.

A related complication arises when jus cogens intersects with the principle of lex specialis — the rule that a more specific legal regime governs over a more general one where the two conflict. States have, on occasion, argued before international arbitral panels that a bilateral investment treaty constitutes lex specialis capable of displacing the more general prohibition against expropriation without compensation, itself sometimes asserted to be a jus cogens norm. Arbitral tribunals have been divided in their treatment of this argument; some have accepted that lex specialis can modulate the application of jus cogens in narrow commercial contexts, while others have treated such arguments as categorically impermissible on the ground that peremptory norms admit of no displacement whatsoever, including by specific treaty regime. The latter position is logically more consistent with the Vienna Convention's text, but it leaves arbitral panels ill-equipped to manage the significant volume of investment disputes in which compensation standards are genuinely contested.

Regrettably, neither the Court's advisory opinions nor the work of the International Law Commission's 2019 draft conclusions on jus cogens has resolved these tensions in a way that international tribunals can reliably apply. One might hope that a future multilateral treaty would enumerate specific peremptory norms and establish a standing adjudicative body to determine their interaction with lex specialis claims; in the absence of such an instrument, the doctrine will remain conceptually powerful but practically unstable.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties established jus cogens as the highest class of international legal norm, but failed to identify which norms qualify for that status, thereby provoking unnecessary litigation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although jus cogens norms occupy a theoretically superior position in the hierarchy of international law, foundational ambiguities in their validation and interaction with competing principles render the doctrine practically unreliable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Legal positivists have convincingly demonstrated that jus cogens norms are analytically indistinguishable from elevated customary international law norms and therefore serve no useful doctrinal function.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The International Court of Justice's 1998 advisory opinion on reservations to the Convention Against Torture provided the most authoritative resolution of the tension between jus cogens and lex specialis.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The proliferation of bilateral investment treaties has undermined the coherence of jus cogens by inviting arbitral tribunals to treat peremptory norms as merely presumptive rather than absolute.

explanations.correct: The passage traces two interlocking problems — the circularity in validating jus cogens norms (paragraph 2) and their contested interaction with lex specialis (paragraph 3) — and concludes that the doctrine, despite its theoretical force, remains 'practically unstable.' B integrates both strands and accurately captures the author's overall evaluative thesis.
explanations.A: Too narrow: the passage's concern is not merely that the Vienna Convention omitted a list, but that deeper validation and interaction problems persist. 'Provoking unnecessary litigation' is also not the author's characterization.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Overstates the positivist critique. The author presents it as one contested position, not a 'convincing demonstration,' and does not endorse it.
explanations.D: A paragraph-level detail masquerading as the main point; the author explicitly says the Court 'offered no satisfactory account,' making D doubly inaccurate.
explanations.E: Too narrow: bilateral investment treaties are one illustration in paragraph 3; the passage's broader concern is the foundational validation problem addressed throughout.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the International Court of Justice's 1998 advisory opinion can best be described as which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Unqualified approval, because the opinion resolved the principal controversy surrounding jus cogens validation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cautious endorsement tempered by acknowledgment that the opinion's practical impact has been limited.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Partial approval for endorsing the defenders' position on jus cogens, coupled with criticism that the opinion left the underlying theoretical problem unaddressed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutral reportage, since the author presents the opinion without evaluating its adequacy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sharp disapproval, because the opinion aligned the Court with a philosophically untenable natural-law position.

explanations.correct: The author notes the Court 'appeared to endorse the defenders' position' — a tentative approval — but then states the Court 'offered no satisfactory account' of the theoretical problem that motivated the dispute. C captures both the partial approval and the pointed criticism accurately.
explanations.A: Contradicted by the author's explicit statement that the Court provided no satisfactory theoretical account.
explanations.B: Mischaracterizes the criticism: the author's objection is theoretical, not merely about limited practical impact.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The phrase 'offered no satisfactory account' is evaluative, not neutral reportage.
explanations.E: Overstated in both valence and content; the author does not characterize the Court's position as 'philosophically untenable' or invoke natural law as the objection.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and defined; one theoretical objection to the doctrine is presented and then refuted; an unresolved practical dispute involving the doctrine is described; and a proposal for resolving the dispute is offered.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its foundational ambiguity identified; the principal theoretical controversy surrounding the doctrine is examined; a complicating interaction with a competing legal principle is analyzed; and the author concludes that neither judicial nor legislative efforts have resolved the underlying tensions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing international legal principles are introduced; each is analyzed separately on its own terms; the conditions under which one supersedes the other are delineated; and a preferred resolution is endorsed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A treaty provision is described; a series of cases applying that provision are examined in chronological order; the cases are found to be mutually inconsistent; and a reform of the treaty is recommended.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A theoretical dispute is introduced; the author endorses one side of the dispute; an illustrative case study is provided; and the endorsed position is shown to be confirmed by the case study.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces jus cogens and identifies the foundational ambiguity (no enumeration of qualifying norms). Paragraph 2 examines the circular-validation controversy between positivists and defenders. Paragraph 3 analyzes the lex specialis complication. Paragraph 4 concludes that neither the ICJ nor the ILC has resolved the tensions. B matches this four-paragraph progression precisely.
explanations.A: Inaccurate: the author does not refute the positivist objection — it is left as a live controversy — and 'a proposal for resolving the dispute' overstates the closing paragraph's tentative hope.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Misrepresents the structure: the passage does not analyze jus cogens and lex specialis 'separately on their own terms' or endorse a preferred resolution.
explanations.D: Fabricates a chronological case-law analysis; the passage does not examine cases in chronological order, and the closing is not a treaty-reform recommendation.
explanations.E: The author does not endorse either side of the positivist/defender dispute, and the lex specialis section does not confirm any endorsed position.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is a consequence specified by the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties when a treaty conflicts with a jus cogens norm?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The treaty is suspended pending review by a standing international adjudicative body.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The treaty is void from its inception.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The states party to the treaty are required to renegotiate its terms within a prescribed period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The offending provisions of the treaty are severed, leaving the remainder in force.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The treaty is voidable at the election of the state whose rights under the jus cogens norm have been infringed.

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that the Vienna Convention 'provides that any treaty conflicting with such a norm is void ab initio' — void from its inception. B is a direct paraphrase of that statement.
explanations.A: No such suspension mechanism is mentioned in the passage; this is a plausible-world fabrication.
explanations.B: Correct: 'void ab initio' means void from the beginning, precisely what B states.
explanations.C: No renegotiation requirement appears in the passage.
explanations.D: Severability of offending provisions is not discussed; the passage says the entire treaty is void.
explanations.E: The passage specifies voidness, not voidability at election — a critical legal distinction the passage does not make.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Legal positivism provides a fully adequate framework for understanding why jus cogens norms occupy a superior position in international law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A state that entered into a bilateral investment treaty prior to the establishment of a relevant jus cogens norm may have a legitimate basis for invoking lex specialis before an arbitral tribunal.

choices.label: C
