choices.text: The inability of the International Law Commission's 2019 draft conclusions to resolve the foundational tensions of jus cogens doctrine suggests that a treaty-based solution may be preferable to continued reliance on advisory opinions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because the same evidentiary machinery validates both ordinary custom and jus cogens norms, states may freely derogate from peremptory norms by concluding bilateral treaties that supersede them.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The concept of obligations erga omnes is entirely distinct from jus cogens and should not be invoked in the same analytical framework.

explanations.correct: The author states in paragraph 4 that neither the ICJ nor the ILC's 2019 draft conclusions have resolved the tensions, and closes by expressing hope for 'a future multilateral treaty' with an enumeration and a standing adjudicative body. This directly supports C's inference that the author regards a treaty-based solution as preferable to continued reliance on advisory opinions.
explanations.A: The author presents the positivist critique as a challenge, not as a complete and adequate framework; the author does not endorse it.
explanations.B: The passage notes arbitral panels are divided and does not suggest any temporal priority argument for bilateral investment treaties; this goes beyond what the passage supports.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: This restates the positivist critique in its most extreme form; the author does not endorse the conclusion that derogation is therefore permissible.
explanations.E: The passage treats erga omnes as the characterization the ICJ applied to jus cogens, implying they are related, not distinct.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of arbitral tribunals' divided treatment of lex specialis arguments (third paragraph) serves primarily to:

choices.label: A
choices.text: refute the legal-positivist claim that jus cogens norms are analytically indistinguishable from ordinary customary norms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate that the theoretical ambiguities identified in the second paragraph have concrete, unresolved consequences in institutional legal practice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that bilateral investment treaties are generally incompatible with international human rights obligations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: provide an example of a case in which the International Court of Justice's advisory opinion was directly applied by arbitral tribunals.

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that the lex specialis principle should be eliminated from international law because it consistently undermines peremptory norms.

explanations.correct: The third paragraph moves from the theoretical controversy of paragraph 2 to its real-world manifestation: arbitral panels are actually divided because the underlying doctrine is unsettled. The function is to show that the abstract circularity problem has tangible institutional consequences — that it is not merely a philosophical puzzle but a source of inconsistent adjudication.
explanations.A: The third paragraph does not address the positivist critique at all; it concerns a different doctrinal complication.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage does not generalize about human rights obligations; it uses one class of bilateral investment treaty disputes as an illustration.
explanations.D: The passage does not state that the ICJ's 1998 opinion was applied by the arbitral tribunals discussed; in fact, the author implies the tribunals' inconsistency reflects the opinion's inadequacy.
explanations.E: The author does not call for the elimination of lex specialis; the passage treats it as a legitimate competing principle that is difficult to reconcile with jus cogens.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the defenders' response to the positivist critique as that response is described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several states whose national legal systems are rooted in civil-law traditions have formally incorporated jus cogens norms into their domestic constitutions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: International tribunals have, on multiple occasions, applied jus cogens norms to invalidate bilateral treaties even over the objection of both parties to those treaties.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Empirical surveys of state practice reveal that the norms most frequently asserted as jus cogens candidates are accepted by significantly fewer than all states, with several economically powerful states explicitly registering dissent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The prohibition on torture has been recognized as a jus cogens norm by every regional human rights tribunal that has considered the question.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Scholars working in the natural-law tradition have long argued that certain moral norms are so fundamental as to bind states regardless of their consent.

explanations.correct: The defenders respond that peremptory norms reflect a 'near-universal moral consensus so fundamental that no bilateral agreement ought to be capable of abrogating them.' The defenders' response thus depends on the claim of near-universality. If, in fact, the norms asserted as jus cogens candidates are accepted by significantly fewer than all states — with powerful states dissenting — the near-universality premise collapses, and the qualitative distinction from ordinary custom becomes very difficult to sustain.
explanations.A: Strengthens rather than weakens the defenders' position by showing institutional embrace of jus cogens norms.
explanations.B: Also strengthens, demonstrating that the norms operate with the peremptory force defenders claim.
explanations.C: Correct: directly attacks the near-universality premise that anchors the defenders' qualitative distinction.
explanations.D: Strengthens the defenders' view by showing near-universal recognition of at least one specific norm.
explanations.E: Supports the defenders' philosophical underpinnings rather than undermining them, even if it does not directly resolve the positivist's evidentiary challenge.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of jus cogens — those peremptory norms of general international law from which no derogation is permitted — occupies an uneasy position in the architecture of the international legal order. Unlike ordinary treaty obligations, which bind only consenting states and may be modified or superseded by subsequent agreement, jus cogens norms purport to bind all states absolutely, rendering any treaty in conflict with them void ab initio. The 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties gave formal expression to this concept, yet the Convention conspicuously declined to enumerate which norms hold peremptory status, leaving that determination to the evolving consensus of the international community. The result has been persistent uncertainty: scholarly opinion and state practice diverge sharply over the content of the category, and international tribunals have shown considerable reluctance to declare a given norm peremptory in the absence of near-universal acceptance.

The difficulty is compounded when jus cogens intersects with the principle of lex specialis — the rule that a more specific legal regime governs over a more general one within a given field. Consider the contested question of whether a peremptory norm prohibiting torture may override a bilateral extradition treaty that, read in isolation, would require the transfer of a suspect to a state where torture is likely. Some jurists argue that the lex specialis principle dictates that the extradition treaty, as the more specific instrument, should control the bilateral relationship; others contend that no treaty can derogate from a jus cogens norm, rendering the extradition obligation unenforceable to the extent of the conflict. A 2003 advisory opinion by a regional human rights tribunal attempted to reconcile these positions by holding that the peremptory prohibition on torture functions as a kind of meta-norm — hierarchically superior to ordinary lex specialis reasoning — so that the extradition obligation is not merely suspended but extinguished with respect to the conflicting transfer. This resolution, though elegant, has attracted criticism from international legal scholars who view it as conflating the hierarchy of sources with the hierarchy of rules, a distinction they regard as analytically indispensable.

The problem is further complicated by the interaction of jus cogens with state immunity doctrine. In a series of domestic cases decided between 1999 and 2007, courts in Germany, Italy, and the United Kingdom each confronted the question of whether jus cogens violations — specifically allegations of war crimes committed by foreign state agents — could be invoked to pierce the shield of customary state immunity before domestic forums. The majority position, ultimately reaffirmed by the International Court of Justice in proceedings concluded in 2012, held that state immunity operates on a different jurisdictional plane than substantive jus cogens obligations, and that the violation of a peremptory norm does not, of itself, extinguish a respondent state's immunity from domestic judicial process. Critics of this position argue that it renders the peremptory character of such norms hollow: a norm truly incapable of derogation ought, they urge, to generate some avenue of judicial enforcement even against sovereigns. This objection has considerable intuitive force, and it is regrettable that the current framework provides no such avenue — but the appropriate remedy, if any exists, is almost certainly one of institutional design rather than doctrinal improvisation by individual domestic courts.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Vienna Convention's failure to enumerate peremptory norms has rendered jus cogens legally unenforceable in virtually all international contexts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The concept of jus cogens, while formally recognized in international law, generates persistent doctrinal tensions when it intersects with lex specialis reasoning and state immunity, tensions that current frameworks have not satisfactorily resolved.

choices.label: C
choices.text: International tribunals should adopt a consistent definition of jus cogens norms so that domestic courts can effectively enforce peremptory prohibitions against sovereign states.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The conflict between jus cogens and bilateral extradition treaties illustrates why the lex specialis principle is inadequate as a tool for resolving disputes in international law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Domestic courts in Germany, Italy, and the United Kingdom were correct to invoke jus cogens norms to pierce state immunity, but the International Court of Justice reversed these decisions improperly.

explanations.correct: The passage traces jus cogens across three distinct problem areas — definitional uncertainty, conflict with lex specialis, and friction with state immunity — and in each case concludes that existing doctrine is problematic but that the solutions proposed so far are inadequate. B captures this integrative thesis.
explanations.A: Too strong and too narrow: the passage does not say jus cogens is 'unenforceable in virtually all contexts'; it describes specific areas of tension, not total breakdown.
explanations.B: Correct. This integrates the passage's three paragraphs and accurately characterizes the author's evaluative posture — formal recognition coexists with unresolved doctrinal friction.
explanations.C: A prescriptive recommendation the passage explicitly rejects as 'doctrinal improvisation'; the author favors institutional design, not judicial activism.
explanations.D: Paragraph-level restatement: the extradition example appears in paragraph 2 only and is not the overall thesis.
explanations.E: The passage does not say domestic courts were 'correct' — it reports the majority position and the objection to it without endorsing the domestic-court view.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its historical origins are traced; a landmark treaty codifying the doctrine is then analyzed in detail; two subsequent court decisions are evaluated and compared.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined and its foundational uncertainty is identified; two specific contexts in which that uncertainty generates doctrinal conflict are then examined in turn, with the author's assessment offered at the close of each.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A legal doctrine is described; a scholarly debate over its scope is presented and resolved by reference to a regional tribunal's advisory opinion; a further difficulty is then introduced and left open.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two competing principles of international law are introduced; their historical development is traced across three jurisdictions; and a synthesis reconciling the principles is proposed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A paradox in international law is stated; several domestic court cases are analyzed to illustrate the paradox; and it is concluded that domestic courts rather than international bodies are best positioned to resolve it.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces jus cogens and its foundational indeterminacy. Paragraph 2 examines the conflict with lex specialis in the extradition context and closes with the author's criticism of the 2003 advisory opinion. Paragraph 3 examines the conflict with state immunity and closes with the author's assessment. B matches this structure precisely.
explanations.A: Mis-sequences the moves: the passage does not trace historical origins in paragraph 1, and paragraph 2 is not a detailed treaty analysis.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Inaccurate because the regional tribunal's opinion is not presented as resolving the debate — it is immediately subjected to scholarly criticism — and the final paragraph's difficulty is not 'left open' but assessed.
explanations.D: The passage does not propose a synthesis; it evaluates existing attempts at resolution and finds them wanting.
explanations.E: The passage explicitly rejects domestic-court improvisation as the solution, so this inverts the author's conclusion.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties did which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It provided a comprehensive list of norms possessing peremptory status under international law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It declared that any bilateral extradition treaty conflicting with a jus cogens norm is automatically suspended pending renegotiation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It gave formal recognition to the concept of jus cogens while leaving the identification of specific peremptory norms to the evolving consensus of the international community.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It established a hierarchy among international legal sources in which jus cogens supersedes both treaty law and customary international law in all circumstances.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It resolved longstanding disputes over the relationship between the lex specialis principle and peremptory norms by affirming the primacy of the latter.

explanations.correct: The passage states that the Vienna Convention 'gave formal expression to this concept, yet the Convention conspicuously declined to enumerate which norms hold peremptory status, leaving that determination to the evolving consensus of the international community.' C is a precise paraphrase.
explanations.A: Directly contradicted: the passage says the Convention 'declined to enumerate' peremptory norms.
explanations.B: Not stated; suspension pending renegotiation is not mentioned anywhere in the passage.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: An overstatement; the passage does not attribute such a comprehensive hierarchical declaration to the Convention.
explanations.E: Not stated; the lex specialis tension arises in paragraph 2 and is not attributed to the Vienna Convention.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The peremptory prohibition on torture should be treated as merely one factor to be weighed against competing treaty obligations in extradition proceedings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The practical enforceability of jus cogens norms against sovereign states is a problem that individual domestic courts are poorly suited to remedy through doctrinal innovation alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The International Court of Justice's 2012 ruling on state immunity correctly resolved the tension between jus cogens and sovereign immunity for all future cases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lex specialis principle should be abandoned as an organizing concept in international law because it invariably produces results incompatible with peremptory norms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regional human rights tribunals are more competent than the International Court of Justice to adjudicate conflicts between jus cogens norms and bilateral treaties.

explanations.correct: The author closes by stating that the 'appropriate remedy, if any exists, is almost certainly one of institutional design rather than doctrinal improvisation by individual domestic courts.' This directly implies that domestic courts are poorly suited to remedy the enforcement gap on their own. B captures this inference.
explanations.A: The author's treatment of the extradition scenario strongly implies that a jus cogens norm cannot simply be 'weighed' against a treaty; the 2003 advisory opinion's characterization of jus cogens as a 'meta-norm' is criticized for conflation, not for elevating jus cogens too highly.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author notes the 2012 ruling 'reaffirmed' the majority position and then characterizes it as leaving peremptory norms 'hollow' — a critical judgment inconsistent with 'correctly resolved for all future cases.'
explanations.D: Too strong; the author describes a tension between lex specialis and jus cogens but never calls for abandoning lex specialis entirely.
explanations.E: Not supported; the passage criticizes the 2003 regional advisory opinion and does not endorse regional tribunals as superior forums.

questions.questionStem: The author most likely discusses the 2003 advisory opinion of the regional human rights tribunal in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: provide an example of how international tribunals have successfully harmonized the conflict between jus cogens and lex specialis through principled reasoning.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate that even a seemingly coherent judicial resolution of the jus cogens–lex specialis tension is vulnerable to significant scholarly criticism, thereby reinforcing the passage's theme of unresolved doctrinal difficulty.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that regional human rights tribunals possess superior competence to resolve conflicts between peremptory norms and bilateral treaty obligations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: show that the distinction between the hierarchy of sources and the hierarchy of rules, while analytically indispensable, has been accepted by international tribunals as irrelevant to extradition proceedings.

choices.label: E
choices.text: introduce the state immunity doctrine as a further complication in the relationship between jus cogens and domestic legal systems.

explanations.correct: The passage presents the 2003 opinion as 'elegant' but immediately subjects it to scholarly criticism for conflating two distinctions — revealing that even an attempt at resolution has generated new controversy. This functions to reinforce the passage's central theme that current frameworks remain inadequate.
explanations.A: This misidentifies the function: the opinion is not endorsed as 'successful' — it is presented and then criticized.
explanations.B: Correct. The advisory opinion is an example of attempted resolution that nevertheless attracts authoritative criticism, thereby sustaining the passage's broader argument.
explanations.C: The passage does not endorse this conclusion; it presents the opinion and the criticisms it drew without recommending regional forums as superior.
explanations.D: The passage says scholars regard the hierarchy distinction as 'analytically indispensable' precisely because the opinion failed to respect it — not that tribunals have accepted the distinction as irrelevant.
explanations.E: State immunity is introduced in paragraph 3, not through the 2003 opinion; this choice attributes the wrong transitional function to the opinion.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the majority position on jus cogens and state immunity — as reaffirmed by the International Court of Justice in 2012 — can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: unqualified endorsement, because it upholds the principle of sovereign equality that is foundational to the international legal order.

choices.label: B
choices.text: cautious approval, because while imperfect it represents the most practically workable resolution available to international courts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: critical resignation, acknowledging that the position renders peremptory norms practically hollow but regarding individual domestic courts as the wrong instrument for correction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: strong disapproval, urging that domestic courts should have pierced state immunity wherever jus cogens violations were alleged.

choices.label: E
choices.text: detached neutrality, presenting the position and its critics without offering any evaluative judgment of either.

explanations.correct: The author calls it 'regrettable' that the framework provides no avenue of enforcement against sovereigns and concedes that the critics' objection has 'considerable intuitive force' — expressing criticism of the outcome. Yet the author explicitly rejects domestic-court improvisation as the remedy, accepting the ICJ's institutional position as practically unavoidable while lamenting its substantive consequences. C captures both dimensions.
explanations.A: The passage expresses regret about the current framework, not endorsement; sovereign equality is not mentioned as a justification.
explanations.B: 'Cautious approval' misstates the valence; the author finds the result 'regrettable' and does not describe it as 'workable.'
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Too strong; the author does not urge domestic courts to pierce immunity — that is precisely what the author says is inappropriate.
explanations.E: The author's use of 'regrettable' and the acknowledgment that critics' objections have 'considerable intuitive force' are clear evaluative commitments, not neutrality.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that the enforcement gap in jus cogens doctrine should be addressed through institutional design rather than through domestic-court improvisation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several international legal scholars have argued that the distinction between the hierarchy of sources and the hierarchy of rules is merely terminological and carries no practical significance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The International Court of Justice has indicated in dicta that it regards the current state immunity framework as normatively satisfactory and sees no need for reform.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A comprehensive study of international institutions has found that multilateral treaty bodies and intergovernmental organizations have consistently failed to create effective enforcement mechanisms for peremptory norms over a period of several decades, and that no reform proposals are currently under serious negotiation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Domestic courts in some civil-law jurisdictions have historically exercised broader jurisdiction over foreign state officials than courts in common-law jurisdictions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The 2003 regional advisory opinion on the extradition conflict was subsequently endorsed by a majority of states party to the regional human rights convention.

explanations.correct: The author's prescription rests on the premise that institutional design is a viable alternative to domestic-court action. If international institutions have consistently failed for decades to create jus cogens enforcement mechanisms and no reform is in prospect, then the 'institutional design' remedy is illusory — which would undermine the author's basis for rejecting domestic-court solutions.
explanations.A: This would affect the scholarly criticism of the 2003 advisory opinion, not the author's prescription about institutional design vs. domestic courts.
explanations.B: This would if anything support the author's concern that the current framework is inadequate, not undermine the prescription for institutional remedies.
explanations.C: Correct. It attacks the premise that institutional design can actually produce a remedy, thereby weakening the author's reason for preferring it over domestic-court action.
explanations.D: A comparative jurisdictional fact that does not bear on whether institutional design is the appropriate remedy for the enforcement gap.
explanations.E: This might add some legitimacy to the 2003 advisory opinion's reasoning but does not address the author's claim about institutional design as the preferred remedy for the state immunity problem.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of jus cogens — peremptory norms of general international law from which no derogation is permitted — occupies an anomalous position within the architecture of public international law. Unlike ordinary treaty obligations, which bind only consenting states, jus cogens norms are said to bind all states absolutely, to override conflicting treaty provisions, and to render void any agreement concluded in violation of them. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, finalized in 1969, gave formal textual expression to this concept, yet the Convention conspicuously declined to enumerate which norms qualify as peremptory, leaving that determination to the evolving practice of states and the pronouncements of international tribunals.

The indeterminacy of jus cogens has generated sustained controversy among legal scholars and practitioners alike. Positivist theorists have objected that a norm can only be binding if it derives from a recognized source of law — treaty, custom, or general principle — and that jus cogens, insofar as it is said to trump even validly formed custom, appears to float free of any such foundation. On this account, the doctrine smuggles natural-law assumptions into a legal framework that formally repudiates them. Proponents of the doctrine counter that the positivist objection misconceives the nature of international obligation: states have consistently recognized, in their diplomatic protests and judicial submissions, that certain prohibitions — against genocide, slavery, and torture — are categorically different from default treaty rules, and that consistent state recognition is itself sufficient pedigree for a peremptory norm. The debate, far from settled, is sharpened by the practical consequences that follow from a norm's classification as jus cogens: states that have withdrawn from a treaty permitting detention practices later condemned as torture cannot retrospectively cure the violation by pointing to their treaty obligations, and domestic courts have increasingly declined to extend sovereign immunity to state officials accused of acts the international community has classified as jus cogens violations.

The relationship between jus cogens and the principle of lex specialis — the rule that a more specific legal provision overrides a general one — further complicates the doctrinal landscape. Traditionally, lex specialis has operated as an ordinary conflict-of-laws mechanism: where a specialized treaty regime governs a particular subject matter in detail, it displaces the more general rules of customary international law. The International Court of Justice, in a series of advisory opinions issued during the 1990s and early 2000s, applied this principle to conclude that the lex specialis of the law of armed conflict governs the legality of state conduct during hostilities, rather than the more general provisions of international human rights treaties. Critics argued, however, that this application illegitimately subordinated non-derogable human rights protections to the permissive rules of armed-conflict law, and that jus cogens norms, precisely because they are non-derogable, should resist displacement by lex specialis reasoning. The Court's treatment of the question was, regrettably, never fully explicit on this tension, leaving subsequent tribunals to work out the relationship without authoritative guidance.

What emerges from this survey is a doctrine that is structurally essential to the aspiration of a rule-governed international order — one that can condemn the gravest violations of human dignity regardless of state consent — but that remains textually underdetermined and theoretically contested. One hopes that future multilateral negotiations will supplement the Vienna Convention's silence with an agreed catalogue of peremptory norms, thereby reducing the scope for inconsistent application without foreclosing the doctrine's capacity to evolve alongside the moral convictions of the international community.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Vienna Convention's failure to enumerate jus cogens norms has rendered the entire doctrine of peremptory norms unenforceable in domestic courts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jus cogens is a doctrinally indispensable but textually underdetermined concept whose theoretical foundations remain disputed and whose application is complicated by competing conflict-of-laws principles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Positivist theorists have convincingly demonstrated that jus cogens norms lack the legal pedigree necessary to override treaty obligations formed by consenting states.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The International Court of Justice erred in applying lex specialis reasoning to armed-conflict cases, and future tribunals should decline to follow that precedent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: International law would benefit from replacing jus cogens with a codified catalogue of non-derogable norms, thereby eliminating the need for judicial interpretation.

explanations.correct: The passage traces jus cogens from its formal recognition in the Vienna Convention through the positivist/proponent debate, the lex specialis complication, and the author's closing assessment that the doctrine is essential yet underdetermined and contested. B integrates all three strands into a single thesis.
explanations.A: Too strong and too narrow — the passage never claims the doctrine is unenforceable; it says it is inconsistently applied.
explanations.B: Correct — captures the passage's full arc: essential doctrine, textual indeterminacy, theoretical contest, lex specialis complication.
explanations.C: Inverts the author's stance; the author does not endorse the positivist objection and explicitly notes the debate is 'far from settled.'
explanations.D: This is a concern raised by critics in paragraph 3, not the author's main conclusion.
explanations.E: Overstates the author's closing suggestion; the author calls for a supplementary catalogue, not the elimination of judicial interpretation.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the doctrine of jus cogens can best be described as which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Unconditional endorsement of jus cogens as the most important development in twentieth-century international law

choices.label: B
choices.text: Skepticism that jus cogens can ever achieve consistent application given the absence of an enumerating authority

choices.label: C
choices.text: Qualified support for the doctrine's aims combined with concern about its theoretical instability and practical indeterminacy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reluctant agreement with the positivist critique that jus cogens illicitly imports natural-law reasoning into positive international law

choices.label: E
choices.text: Impartial neutrality, presenting the competing views without expressing any evaluative judgment of the doctrine's merits

explanations.correct: The author calls jus cogens 'structurally essential to the aspiration of a rule-governed international order' (support for its aims) but describes it as 'textually underdetermined and theoretically contested' (concern about instability), and uses 'regrettably' and 'one hopes' as editorial adverbs. C captures both dimensions.
explanations.A: Overstates the author's approval; the author identifies serious theoretical and practical problems.
explanations.B: Too pessimistic — the author expresses hope for improvement, not resignation to perpetual inconsistency.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The author presents the positivist critique as a live controversy, not as something the author personally endorses.
explanations.E: Incorrect — the author is explicitly evaluative, using 'regrettably,' 'one hopes,' and direct assessments of the Court's reasoning.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined; the main theoretical objection to it is introduced and decisively refuted; an illustrative case confirms the refutation; the author draws a policy conclusion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its formal source identified; two competing theoretical positions regarding its validity are examined; a conflict-of-laws complication is described; the author offers a balanced assessment and a tentative prescription.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A treaty provision is summarized; its practical consequences in domestic courts are catalogued; an international tribunal's misapplication is criticized; the author recommends abolishing the relevant doctrine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A jurisprudential dispute is introduced; one side is shown to be correct on historical grounds; the opposing side is dismissed; the author calls for statutory reform.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced; several successful applications of it are described; one problematic application is noted; the author concludes that the doctrine should be applied more broadly.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces jus cogens and locates it in the Vienna Convention; paragraph 2 presents the positivist objection and the proponent response; paragraph 3 introduces lex specialis as a complication; paragraph 4 offers the author's assessment and tentative prescription. B maps onto this structure precisely.
explanations.A: Incorrectly states the theoretical objection is 'decisively refuted' — the passage says the debate is 'far from settled.'
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage does not catalogue domestic-court consequences as the main move of paragraph 2; and the author does not recommend abolishing the doctrine.
explanations.D: Neither side is shown to be correct, and the author does not call for statutory reform (the recommendation is for multilateral negotiation, not domestic statute).
explanations.E: The passage describes no successful applications; the topic is theoretical controversy and doctrinal complication.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is a practical consequence that follows from a norm's classification as a jus cogens violation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: States that have ratified the Vienna Convention are automatically bound to renegotiate any treaty provision inconsistent with that norm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Domestic courts have increasingly declined to extend sovereign immunity to state officials accused of committing acts classified as such violations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The International Court of Justice is required to issue an advisory opinion cataloguing the norm in question for future reference.

choices.label: D
choices.text: International tribunals must apply lex specialis reasoning to resolve any conflict between the norm and the law of armed conflict.

choices.label: E
choices.text: States that consent to a treaty permitting the relevant conduct may rely on that treaty as a complete defense to any subsequent accusation of violation.

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly states in paragraph 2 that 'domestic courts have increasingly declined to extend sovereign immunity to state officials accused of acts the international community has classified as jus cogens violations.' B is a close paraphrase.
explanations.A: The passage never states that Vienna Convention parties are automatically required to renegotiate inconsistent provisions; it says conflicting agreements are rendered void.
explanations.B: Correct — directly stated in paragraph 2.
explanations.C: No such automatic advisory-opinion requirement is mentioned anywhere in the passage.
explanations.D: The passage presents lex specialis as a competing principle that the Court applied in some contexts, not as a mandatory mechanism triggered by jus cogens classification.
explanations.E: This is the opposite of what the passage states: treaty consent cannot retrospectively cure a jus cogens violation.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about the relationship between jus cogens and lex specialis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lex specialis reasoning should always override jus cogens norms whenever a specialized treaty regime exists, because specificity is a reliable proxy for the more carefully considered rule.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The International Court of Justice resolved the tension between jus cogens and lex specialis definitively in its advisory opinions of the 1990s and early 2000s.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The application of lex specialis reasoning to subordinate non-derogable human rights protections to armed-conflict law raises a legitimate concern that the Court's treatment of the tension was insufficiently explicit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jus cogens norms and lex specialis operate in entirely separate domains of international law and therefore do not come into conflict in practice.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Because lex specialis reflects the will of treaty parties in a specific subject area, it should be treated as itself a form of jus cogens, binding all states regardless of consent.

explanations.correct: The passage notes that critics argued the ICJ's lex specialis application 'illegitimately subordinated non-derogable human rights protections,' and the author adds that 'the Court's treatment of the question was, regrettably, never fully explicit on this tension.' These two moves together support C.
explanations.A: The author does not endorse this position; the critics' objection (which the author treats sympathetically by using 'regrettably') implies the opposite.
explanations.B: The passage explicitly states the Court's treatment 'left subsequent tribunals to work out the relationship without authoritative guidance' — the opposite of definitive resolution.
explanations.C: Correct — the author's use of 'regrettably' and the phrase 'never fully explicit' indicate the author shares the critics' concern.
explanations.D: The passage demonstrates that they do conflict in practice, as in the Court's armed-conflict advisory opinions.
explanations.E: This conflates two distinct doctrines in a way the passage never suggests and that would undermine the distinction the passage carefully draws.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of states that 'have withdrawn from a treaty permitting detention practices later condemned as torture' (paragraph 2) serves primarily to:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Illustrate the practical stakes of jus cogens classification by showing that prior treaty consent provides no retrospective shield against a finding of violation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Support the positivist objection by demonstrating that jus cogens norms lack a recognized source in treaty or custom

choices.label: C
choices.text: Explain why the International Court of Justice declined to apply lex specialis reasoning to detention cases involving torture

choices.label: D
choices.text: Provide a historical example of a state successfully invoking sovereign immunity as a defense to a jus cogens accusation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Introduce the doctrinal distinction between non-derogable and derogable treaty obligations for the first time in the passage

explanations.correct: The detention/torture example appears immediately after the statement that 'the practical consequences that follow from a norm's classification as jus cogens' matter significantly. Its function is to instantiate one such consequence — that treaty consent is no defense — thereby concretizing the doctrine's real-world weight.
explanations.A: Correct — the example illustrates the no-retrospective-cure consequence described just before it.
explanations.B: The example actually cuts against the positivist objection by showing jus cogens operating effectively; it does not support the objection.
explanations.C: The passage does not link this example to the ICJ or to lex specialis reasoning; those topics appear in paragraph 3.
explanations.D: The passage says no such successful invocation; treaty consent 'cannot retrospectively cure' the violation.
explanations.E: The non-derogable/derogable distinction is implicit throughout, not first introduced by this example.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the claim made by proponents of jus cogens as described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several international human rights treaties negotiated after 1969 expressly incorporate the concept of peremptory norms by reference to the Vienna Convention.

choices.label: B
choices.text: State practice in diplomatic protests and judicial submissions reveals that governments frequently contest whether particular norms qualify as peremptory, and that no consistent pattern of recognition has emerged for norms beyond the prohibitions of genocide and slavery.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Domestic courts in a majority of states have applied sovereign-immunity exceptions in cases involving alleged torture, citing jus cogens as authority.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The drafters of the Vienna Convention privately debated whether to include an enumerated list of peremptory norms before opting for a general formulation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Legal scholars working in the natural-law tradition have argued that jus cogens most closely resembles Roman-law concepts of ius gentium, suggesting ancient historical roots for the doctrine.

explanations.correct: The proponent argument rests on the claim that 'consistent state recognition is itself sufficient pedigree for a peremptory norm' and that states have 'consistently recognized' prohibitions against genocide, slavery, and torture as categorically different. B directly attacks this by showing that state practice is not, in fact, consistent — outside of two norms, no stable pattern of recognition exists — thereby removing the foundation the proponents identified.
explanations.A: This would actually strengthen the proponents' position by providing additional treaty-based recognition of jus cogens norms.
explanations.B: Correct — removes the 'consistent state recognition' pedigree the proponents rely on.
explanations.C: This would strengthen the proponents' case by showing real-world application of jus cogens principles in domestic courts.
explanations.D: The drafters' internal deliberations bear on the Vienna Convention's text but do not address the proponents' claim about state practice as pedigree.
explanations.E: Historical roots in Roman law would lend support to the doctrine's legitimacy, not undermine it; this choice slightly strengthens rather than weakens the proponents' position.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of jus cogens — peremptory norms of general international law from which no derogation is permitted — has long occupied an uneasy position in the hierarchy of international legal obligations. Unlike ordinary treaty obligations, which bind only consenting states and may be modified by subsequent agreement, jus cogens norms purport to bind all states regardless of consent, rendering void any treaty or custom inconsistent with them. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties codified this principle in 1969, but the Convention conspicuously declined to enumerate which norms qualify as peremptory, leaving the determination to evolving state practice and the judgments of international tribunals. The result has been a doctrine whose procedural architecture is more assured than its substantive content.

The difficulties that attend any effort to identify peremptory norms are considerable. Proponents of a positivist methodology insist that jus cogens must be derived from near-universal state practice accompanied by opinio juris — the conviction that the practice is legally obligatory — a standard that, rigorously applied, admits very few candidates. The prohibition on torture, the prohibition on genocide, and the rule against slavery command near-universal acceptance and are routinely cited as paradigm cases. Yet even these paradigms are contested at the margins: the permissibility of "enhanced interrogation" by states invoking national-security exceptions illustrates how a norm nominally accepted in the abstract may be systematically evaded in practice without triggering the formal machinery of derogation. Natural-law theorists respond that the positivist criterion is circular: a norm cannot derive its peremptory character from the practice of the very states it is meant to constrain. For this reason, natural-law accounts tend to ground jus cogens in considerations of human dignity that transcend positive law, though critics rightly observe that this approach offers no principled method for distinguishing genuine peremptory norms from the moral preferences of particular legal cultures.

The practical consequences of recognizing a norm as jus cogens extend well beyond the invalidation of conflicting treaties. Under the lex specialis principle, a more specific international rule ordinarily displaces a general one in cases of conflict; jus cogens, however, operates as a lex superior that displaces even lex specialis arrangements. A bilateral investment treaty that would insulate a state's expropriation of indigenous land from international review, for example, might be voided insofar as it conflicts with a peremptory norm prohibiting cultural genocide. Whether such voidance operates automatically or requires a declaratory judgment by a competent tribunal remains contested; the International Court of Justice has thus far avoided a definitive ruling on the point. Furthermore, jus cogens has been invoked to override state immunity in domestic tort proceedings brought by victims of foreign state-sponsored torture, with some national courts accepting the argument and others rejecting it on the ground that customary immunity rules are themselves of longstanding standing and cannot be displaced without clearer international consensus.

The normative incoherence of jus cogens — simultaneously the most authoritative tier of international law and the least precisely defined — has prompted some scholars to recommend confining the doctrine to a narrow, enumerated list subject to formal amendment procedures analogous to those governing constitutional revision. This proposal has considerable appeal: it would restore the rule-of-law values of predictability and equal treatment that jus cogens, in its current open-textured form, conspicuously lacks. Yet the recommendation risks calcifying norms at a particular historical moment and foreclosing the incremental evolution through which international law has historically accommodated moral progress. One hopes that international tribunals, rather than national courts acting in isolation, will assume the principal responsibility for articulating jus cogens with the rigor and consistency that its foundational ambitions demand.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The doctrine of jus cogens is fundamentally incompatible with the positivist methodology that underlies most international treaty law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although jus cogens occupies the highest tier of international legal obligation, its practical effectiveness is undermined by states that invoke national-security exceptions to evade compliance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jus cogens is a doctrine whose procedural status in international law is well established but whose substantive content and practical application remain deeply uncertain, a problem that international tribunals are best positioned to address.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Vienna Convention's failure to enumerate peremptory norms has rendered jus cogens largely unenforceable as a matter of positive international law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Proposals to codify jus cogens through formal amendment procedures would best reconcile the doctrine's foundational ambitions with the rule-of-law values of predictability and equal treatment.

explanations.correct: The passage consistently argues that jus cogens has a secure formal status (codified in the Vienna Convention, acknowledged as lex superior) but that its substantive content is poorly defined and its application inconsistent — and closes by urging international tribunals to take the lead in resolving this. C integrates both strands and captures the author's closing prescription.
explanations.A: Too narrow and misstates the argument. The passage does not claim jus cogens is incompatible with positivism; it describes a methodological debate between positivists and natural-law theorists without endorsing either.
explanations.B: Paragraph-level restatement of one portion of paragraph two. It omits the structural tension between procedural clarity and substantive uncertainty that organizes the entire passage.
explanations.D: Overstates the consequence. The author says the lack of enumeration leaves determination to evolving practice, not that the doctrine is unenforceable.
explanations.E: Restates a suggestion discussed at the end of paragraph four as the main point. The author presents this proposal but immediately qualifies it, making it one consideration rather than the thesis.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its formal codification described; two competing methodologies for identifying its content are assessed; its practical legal consequences are examined; and a reform proposal is evaluated with a qualified endorsement of a preferred institutional solution.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal controversy is introduced; historical evidence for one side is marshaled; the opposing side's evidence is dismissed as insufficient; and the author's preferred position is defended.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A doctrine is defined; its origins in natural law are traced; its positivist critique is refuted; and a proposal for replacing it with a more workable framework is advanced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced; its historical development across three eras is surveyed; its contemporary application is illustrated with two cases; and scholars' reactions to those cases are summarized.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A doctrine's formal status is contrasted with a rival doctrine; the practical advantages of each are compared; a synthesis of the two is proposed; and the synthesis is tested against a hypothetical case.

explanations.correct: Paragraph one introduces jus cogens and notes the gap between its procedural architecture and substantive content. Paragraph two examines positivist and natural-law methodologies for identifying the norms. Paragraph three surveys practical legal consequences (lex specialis displacement, state immunity). Paragraph four assesses the codification proposal and ends with a qualified prescription favoring international tribunals. A tracks these four moves accurately.
explanations.B: Mis-characterizes the structure. The passage does not marshal evidence for one side and dismiss the other; both positivist and natural-law accounts are found wanting, and the author's closing preference is institutional (tribunals), not doctrinal.
explanations.C: Wrong in two respects: the passage does not trace jus cogens to natural law as a matter of origin, and the positivist critique is not refuted — it is described as facing its own objections.
explanations.D: The passage does not survey three historical eras; its structure is analytical rather than chronological.
explanations.E: There is no rival doctrine being contrasted as a whole, and no synthesis is proposed. This description misidentifies the genre of the passage.
explanations.A: Correct.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties did which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It enumerated an authoritative list of norms qualifying as jus cogens and assigned to the International Court of Justice the task of enforcing them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It codified the principle that peremptory norms bind all states regardless of consent while leaving the identification of specific norms to state practice and tribunal judgments.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It established a formal amendment procedure by which states could collectively modify or derogate from peremptory norms over time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It recognized jus cogens as binding only on states that had ratified the Convention, thereby preserving the consent-based architecture of treaty law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It superseded earlier customary international law on state immunity by declaring torture and genocide to be automatically void under the lex specialis principle.

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that the Vienna Convention 'codified this principle in 1969, but the Convention conspicuously declined to enumerate which norms qualify as peremptory, leaving the determination to evolving state practice and the judgments of international tribunals.' B paraphrases this precisely.
explanations.A: Contradicts the passage directly. The Convention declined to enumerate norms and did not assign enforcement to the ICJ.
explanations.C: The passage mentions an amendment-procedure analogy only as a scholar's proposal; the Convention itself is not described as establishing such a procedure.
explanations.D: Inverts the passage's claim. Jus cogens binds all states regardless of consent, which is what distinguishes it from ordinary treaty obligations.
explanations.E: The passage distinguishes jus cogens from lex specialis, explaining that jus cogens operates as lex superior over lex specialis. It does not describe the Vienna Convention as superseding immunity norms via lex specialis.
explanations.B: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about the positivist methodology for identifying jus cogens norms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It should be abandoned entirely in favor of a natural-law approach grounded in universal human dignity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When applied rigorously, it would recognize a far smaller number of peremptory norms than most international lawyers currently accept.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is superior to natural-law approaches because it provides a principled method for distinguishing peremptory norms from culturally contingent moral preferences.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its requirement of near-universal state practice is rendered wholly unworkable by states that systematically evade their treaty obligations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the methodology tacitly endorsed by the Vienna Convention, which grounded jus cogens in the consent of the international community.

explanations.correct: The passage states that the positivist standard, 'rigorously applied, admits very few candidates,' implying that a strict positivist analysis would recognize far fewer peremptory norms than is conventional. B is a careful paraphrase of this claim.
explanations.A: The author does not endorse natural law as a replacement. The passage explicitly notes that natural-law accounts 'offer no principled method for distinguishing genuine peremptory norms from the moral preferences of particular legal cultures,' a criticism the author presents without rebuttal.
explanations.C: The passage identifies circularity as a problem with positivism and does not characterize it as superior to natural law. Both approaches are presented as flawed.
explanations.D: Overstates the passage. The author says states evade norms by invoking exceptions 'without triggering the formal machinery of derogation,' but does not conclude that the positivist criterion is wholly unworkable because of this.
explanations.E: The passage does not characterize the Vienna Convention as endorsing positivism. The Convention's silence on enumeration is a procedural feature, not a methodological commitment.
explanations.B: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of a bilateral investment treaty that insulates a state's expropriation of indigenous land from international review (paragraph 3) serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the practical consequence that jus cogens, as a lex superior, can void specific treaty arrangements that conflict with peremptory norms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: establish that investment treaties are the category of international agreement most frequently invalidated by peremptory norms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that the prohibition on cultural genocide is among the best-established and least-contested peremptory norms in international law.

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast the approach of international tribunals with that of domestic courts in resolving disputes over indigenous land rights.

choices.label: E
choices.text: provide evidence that the lex specialis principle has been effectively displaced by jus cogens in all areas of international economic law.

explanations.correct: The example is introduced immediately after the claim that jus cogens operates as a lex superior displacing even lex specialis arrangements. The bilateral investment treaty example concretizes exactly this legal consequence — how a specific treaty could be voided by a conflicting peremptory norm. A correctly identifies the illustrative function.
explanations.B: The passage does not claim investment treaties are the most frequently invalidated category; the example is illustrative, not taxonomic.
explanations.C: The passage frames the example hypothetically ('might be voided'), which suggests the prohibition's application here is contested, not well-established. The function is not to certify the norm's status.
explanations.D: The contrast between international tribunals and domestic courts is addressed separately in the same paragraph regarding state immunity; it is not the function of the investment-treaty example.
explanations.E: The passage says jus cogens displaces lex specialis in cases of conflict, not that it has displaced it 'in all areas of international economic law.' This answer overgeneralizes.
explanations.A: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the proposal to confine jus cogens to a narrow, enumerated list subject to formal amendment procedures can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement, because it would restore predictability and equal treatment to an area of law currently lacking both.

choices.label: B
choices.text: unconditional rejection, because it would calcify norms and prevent international law from accommodating moral progress.

choices.label: C
choices.text: qualified appreciation tempered by concern that codification risks foreclosing the incremental evolution through which international law has historically developed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutrally descriptive presentation of a scholarly debate without any evaluative stance by the author.

choices.label: E
choices.text: cautious skepticism rooted primarily in the view that the amendment procedures proposed are modeled too closely on constitutional revision to be workable in an international context.

explanations.correct: The author grants the proposal 'considerable appeal' and acknowledges it would restore rule-of-law values, but immediately qualifies this: it 'risks calcifying norms at a particular historical moment and foreclosing the incremental evolution' through which international law develops. This is a paradigm case of qualified appreciation — recognizing merit while identifying a significant risk.
explanations.A: Overstates the positivity. The author describes the appeal but does not endorse the proposal; the qualification is substantive, not perfunctory.
explanations.B: Overstates the negativity. The author does not reject the proposal unconditionally; the passage opens with praise ('considerable appeal') before entering the qualification.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The author explicitly editorializes — 'considerable appeal,' the risk of 'calcifying,' and the closing prescription to favor international tribunals all reflect an evaluative stance.
explanations.E: The author does not raise workability concerns about the amendment-procedure analogy. The concern is about foreclosing moral evolution, not about the mechanics of the proposed procedure.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the natural-law theorists' response to the positivist methodology as described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The states that most consistently comply with jus cogens prohibitions are also those with the strongest domestic constitutional traditions of human-dignity protection.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several international tribunals have relied on the positivist criterion of state practice and opinio juris to confirm that the prohibition on torture qualifies as a peremptory norm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A comparative survey of major legal systems reveals that the concept of human dignity is understood in substantially different ways across cultures, with no consensus on its minimum content.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Vienna Convention's drafters included a provision stating that jus cogens derives its authority from the consent of states, not from any pre-legal moral order.

choices.label: E
choices.text: States that invoke national-security exceptions to torture prohibitions frequently face diplomatic sanctions from other states, indicating that such evasions are not widely accepted.

explanations.correct: The natural-law theorists' response is that jus cogens should be grounded in considerations of human dignity that transcend positive law. The objection the author already notes is that this approach 'offers no principled method for distinguishing genuine peremptory norms from the moral preferences of particular legal cultures.' If human dignity is understood in substantially different ways across cultures with no consensus on its minimum content, this directly undermines the claim that human dignity can serve as a trans-positive foundation for jus cogens — it would show that the natural-law anchor is itself culturally contingent.
explanations.A: This would, if anything, lend support to natural-law theorists by suggesting a link between domestic human-dignity traditions and international compliance; it does not undermine their position.
explanations.B: This addresses the positivist methodology, not the natural-law response to it. It may support positivism but does not undermine natural law's claim about the limitations of positivism.
explanations.D: This would undermine jus cogens generally or support a positivist reading of the Convention, but the natural-law theorists' specific argument is about the normative foundation for peremptory norms — not about what the Convention's drafters intended. The natural-law claim is a philosophical one about what ought to ground jus cogens, not an empirical claim about the Convention's history.
explanations.E: This actually strengthens the positivist account by showing that state practice condemns evasion, and it is irrelevant to the natural-law theorists' separate claim about grounding norms in human dignity.
explanations.C: Correct.

rc.passage:
The doctrine of jus cogens — the body of peremptory norms from which no derogation is permitted under international law — occupies an uneasy position within the broader architecture of customary international law. Unlike ordinary customary norms, which bind states through the accumulated weight of consistent state practice and opinio juris, peremptory norms carry a categorical, hierarchically superior force: no bilateral treaty, however freely negotiated, can lawfully override a jus cogens prohibition. The 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties codified this hierarchy in Article 53, providing that any treaty conflicting with a peremptory norm is void ab initio. Yet the Convention declined to enumerate which norms qualify as peremptory, leaving that task — and the controversies attendant upon it — to international courts, arbitral tribunals, and the scholarly community.

The indeterminacy of the jus cogens catalogue has generated two distinct lines of criticism. The first, advanced by positivist theorists, holds that because the doctrine lacks a reliable procedure for identifying peremptory norms, it introduces an unacceptable degree of judicial discretion into a system premised on state consent. On this view, a tribunal that elevates a norm to jus cogens status without clear evidentiary support for near-universal acceptance does not discover existing law but rather creates new obligations retroactively — a function structurally incompatible with the sovereignty of states that never consented to those obligations. The second line of criticism, advanced by scholars sympathetic to natural-law and critical legal traditions alike, reaches nearly the opposite conclusion: the existing catalogue is too cautiously circumscribed. Prohibitions of genocide, slavery, and torture are widely acknowledged, but systematic economic coercion, severe environmental destruction, and the denial of self-determination to peoples under colonial administration arguably satisfy the evidentiary threshold for peremptory status and yet have not been authoritatively recognized. The asymmetry, these critics suggest, reflects the historical dominance of wealthy states in shaping customary international law rather than any principled distinction in the moral gravity of the harms.

The lex specialis principle further complicates the jus cogens framework in practice. Where a specialized treaty regime — such as the law of armed conflict or the World Trade Organization's dispute-resolution procedures — governs a specific relationship between states, that regime may displace the general rules of customary international law that would otherwise apply. Courts have generally held that lex specialis does not displace jus cogens prohibitions, since peremptory norms by definition cannot be contracted around. However, the boundary between a treaty clause that legitimately modifies a customary background rule and one that impermissibly derogates from a peremptory norm is rarely self-evident. In a 2003 dispute before an international arbitral panel, a respondent state argued that an investment treaty's stabilization clause — freezing regulatory obligations at the time of contract formation — effectively insulated it from the application of subsequently crystallizing environmental norms. The panel declined to rule on whether any environmental norm had attained jus cogens status, instead holding that the stabilization clause could not be read to authorize environmental harm of sufficient gravity, a resolution that carefully avoided the harder doctrinal question while leaving the underlying tension unresolved.

Regrettably, the reluctance of international courts to engage directly with the criteria for jus cogens identification has allowed the doctrine's indeterminacy to persist. One might hope that systematic engagement by a body such as the International Law Commission — whose 2019 draft conclusions on peremptory norms represent the most comprehensive multilateral effort to date — will ultimately provide the doctrinal clarity that courts have deferred. Until such clarity is achieved, however, the doctrine risks functioning less as a genuine constraint on unlawful state behavior than as a rhetorical resource, invoked selectively and resolved inconsistently.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Vienna Convention's failure to enumerate peremptory norms has rendered all jus cogens prohibitions legally unenforceable in international courts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Positivist and natural-law critics of jus cogens reach opposing conclusions, but both critiques ultimately rest on the same concern about state sovereignty.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The indeterminate scope of jus cogens, compounded by courts' reluctance to articulate clear identification criteria, undermines the doctrine's capacity to serve as a reliable constraint on unlawful state conduct.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lex specialis principle has effectively displaced jus cogens in most specialized treaty regimes, producing inconsistent outcomes in international arbitration.

choices.label: E
choices.text: International courts should adopt the International Law Commission's 2019 draft conclusions as the definitive catalogue of peremptory norms in order to resolve longstanding doctrinal disputes.

explanations.correct: The passage traces the jus cogens doctrine's hierarchically superior status, catalogues two lines of criticism rooted in its indeterminacy, illustrates how lex specialis compounds the problem through the 2003 arbitral example, and concludes that without clearer identification criteria the doctrine risks being merely rhetorical. C integrates all four paragraphs.
explanations.A: Overstates the consequence — the passage does not claim jus cogens prohibitions are unenforceable, only that their scope is uncertain.
explanations.B: Mischaracterizes the positivist critique, which is about judicial discretion and consent, not state sovereignty in the same sense as the natural-law critique; also paragraph-level rather than whole-passage.
explanations.D: Reverses the passage's claim: courts have held that lex specialis does not displace jus cogens; the difficulty is identifying the boundary, not displacement.
explanations.E: Restates a closing suggestion as the main point, a classic trap; the passage expresses cautious hope, not a recommendation.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward international courts' handling of the jus cogens identification question can best be described as which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neutral and empirical, presenting the courts' reasoning without editorial commentary.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mildly approving, on the ground that judicial caution preserves state sovereignty.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Critically disappointed, holding that courts' deference on identification criteria has perpetuated a damaging doctrinal uncertainty.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sharply contemptuous, arguing that courts have deliberately obscured peremptory norms to serve the interests of powerful states.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cautiously optimistic that recent judicial decisions have begun to resolve the indeterminacy problem.

explanations.correct: The word 'Regrettably' opens the final paragraph, and the passage closes by warning that the doctrine risks becoming 'a rhetorical resource, invoked selectively and resolved inconsistently' — a measured but clearly critical editorial stance toward courts' deferral.
explanations.A: Wrong — the passage is explicitly evaluative; 'regrettably' and the closing warning are unmistakably critical.
explanations.B: Wrong — the author nowhere endorses judicial caution as sovereignty-preserving; the positivist argument is described, not endorsed.
explanations.D: Overstates intensity and imputes deliberate bad faith, which the passage never alleges.
explanations.E: Wrong — the author's cautious hope rests on the ILC's 2019 draft conclusions, not on recent judicial decisions.
explanations.C: Correct.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its historical origins traced; two opposing schools of thought about the doctrine's validity are compared; a procedural rule that supersedes the doctrine is analyzed; and the author argues that the doctrine should be abandoned.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine and its foundational ambiguity are introduced; two lines of scholarly criticism arising from that ambiguity are described; a complicating principle and an illustrative case are examined; and the author evaluates the overall situation and expresses a qualified hope for reform.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A legal controversy is introduced; a single authoritative critique is elaborated across two paragraphs; a proposed resolution is tested against a specific arbitral case; and the author endorses that resolution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The history of a treaty provision is recounted; its application to state practice is criticized on positivist grounds; natural-law alternatives are proposed and accepted; and the author calls for ratification of those alternatives.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A hierarchical norm is defined; its relationship to state consent is explored through case law; an international commission's draft conclusions are analyzed in detail; and the author recommends adopting those conclusions.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces jus cogens and the foundational ambiguity left by the Vienna Convention. Paragraph 2 presents two distinct scholarly criticisms (positivist and natural-law/critical). Paragraph 3 introduces lex specialis and the 2003 arbitral case. Paragraph 4 evaluates and expresses guarded hope in the ILC. B matches this sequence.
explanations.A: Mischaracterizes the fourth paragraph — the author does not argue the doctrine should be abandoned, only that it needs clearer criteria; also misreads the lex specialis principle as superseding jus cogens.
explanations.C: Describes a single critique elaborated across two paragraphs, when in fact two distinct lines of criticism appear in paragraph 2; also misrepresents the author as endorsing the arbitral resolution.
explanations.D: The passage does not accept natural-law alternatives or call for ratification; it describes those arguments without endorsing them.
explanations.E: The ILC draft conclusions are mentioned only briefly in the final paragraph; the passage does not analyze them in detail.
explanations.B: Correct.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties did which one of the following with respect to jus cogens?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It enumerated the specific norms that qualify as peremptory and declared all other claimed peremptory norms non-binding.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It established the hierarchical superiority of peremptory norms over bilateral treaties but left the identification of which norms are peremptory to courts and scholars.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It provided that lex specialis regimes could override peremptory norms in specialized treaty contexts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It granted the International Law Commission sole authority to determine which norms attain jus cogens status.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It required all signatories to submit disputes involving peremptory norms to mandatory international arbitration.

explanations.correct: The passage states that Article 53 of the Vienna Convention codified the hierarchy (any conflicting treaty is void ab initio) but that the Convention 'declined to enumerate which norms qualify as peremptory, leaving that task to international courts, arbitral tribunals, and the scholarly community.'
explanations.A: Directly contradicts the passage — the Convention declined to enumerate qualifying norms.
explanations.C: The passage says courts have held lex specialis does not displace jus cogens; this choice inverts that relationship.
explanations.D: The ILC is mentioned as having produced 2019 draft conclusions; the passage does not say the Convention granted it sole authority.
explanations.E: No such requirement is mentioned anywhere in the passage; this is a plausible-world fabrication.
explanations.B: Correct.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would be likely to agree with which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The positivist critique of jus cogens is ultimately more persuasive than the natural-law critique because it rests on the foundational principle of state consent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The historical dominance of powerful states in shaping customary international law is a morally neutral phenomenon that reflects the practical realities of interstate relations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If international courts were to articulate clear and consistently applied criteria for identifying peremptory norms, the jus cogens doctrine would more effectively constrain unlawful state behavior.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The International Law Commission's 2019 draft conclusions should be adopted wholesale as binding international law without further deliberation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The prohibition of genocide and slavery satisfies the evidentiary threshold for peremptory status, but the prohibition of torture does not.
